soil-agri-013.title: Irrigation: bringing water to the crop
soil-agri-013.text: In Khuzistan, in south-west Iran, farmers were steering water onto their fields in the 6th millennium BCE. Irrigation is the application of controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, landscape plants and lawns. Many cultures have practised it for over 5,000 years. The water comes from groundwater, rivers, lakes and reservoirs, or from treated wastewater, desalinated water, drainage water and even fog collection. Usually it tops up rainfall. Only in arid lands, or outside the rainy season in semi-arid areas, does it supply nearly all of a crop's water. It does other jobs too: it revegetates disturbed soils in dry areas, protects crops from frost, suppresses weeds in grain fields and prevents soil consolidation. The main methods are {{ref:soil-agri-049}}, the oldest; {{ref:soil-agri-016}}; micro-irrigation such as {{ref:soil-agri-015}}; and {{ref:soil-agri-017}}, which raises the water table. The scale is vast. Land equipped for irrigation reached 355 million ha in 2023, more than twice the 1960s area. That is 23% of croplands, and irrigated yields average 76% above rainfed ones. Getting the amount right matters. Over-irrigation raises water tables and causes irrigation salinity, which then needs subsurface drainage. Under-irrigation controls salinity poorly, so toxic salts build up at the surface. That is why drainage is so often studied with irrigation, and why the two are often needed together to sustain high crop production.

soil-agri-004.title: Crop rotation: a different crop each season
soil-agri-004.text: Between the 9th and 11th centuries, European farmers changed how they divided their fields, moving from two-field to three-field schemes. Crop rotation is growing a series of different crops on the same land over successive growing seasons. A later four-field sequence of wheat, turnips, barley and clover was key to the British Agricultural Revolution. Rotation works on several fronts. It lessens a crop's reliance on one set of nutrients, cuts pest and weed pressure, and lowers the chance that resistant pests and weeds develop. Plants of one family share pests and pathogens, so a rotation pays attention to plant family. Changing crops then breaks pest life cycles and habitats. Legumes such as alfalfa and clover hold nitrogen in root nodules. After harvest their leftover roots decay and release it to the next, nitrogen-demanding crop. A well-designed rotation can reduce the need for synthetic fertilizers and for weed killers, and it improves soil structure and organic matter, which reduces erosion. Rotations greatly increase the carbon held in soil organic matter, and long, highly diverse rotations do so most. Disturbing the soil by {{ref:soil-agri-095}} pulls the other way, driving an exponential decline. In Brazil, conversion to {{ref:soil-agri-117}} with intensive rotations stored carbon in the soil at 0.41 tonnes per hectare per year. Mistakes are slow to surface. A faulty rotation can unbalance soil nutrients or build up pathogens, and the damage may take years to show and as long to correct.

soil-agri-021.title: Leaching: when water carries nutrients away
soil-agri-021.text: Rain that soaks through a field does not leave empty-handed. In farming, leaching is the loss of water-soluble plant nutrients from soil, carried away by rain and irrigation water. It is the same downward washing described in {{ref:soil-form-050}}, seen from the farmer's side. Growers weigh soil structure, crop planting and the type and rate of fertilizer to avoid losing too much. The word has a second, deliberate meaning. Farmers sometimes apply a small excess of salty {{ref:soil-agri-013}} water so that salts do not build up, and this usually needs drainage to remove the extra water. Leaching becomes an environmental concern when seeping water carries dissolved chemicals into groundwater. On farms the main sources are excess fertilizer, poorly stored manure and biocides, the chemicals used to kill pests. The losses can cascade. Leaching of nitrate from acidic sources can increase losses of calcium and other soil nutrients, lowering an ecosystem's productivity. Areas with high rainfall become acidic through leaching. Among the measures used to reduce nutrient leaching are {{ref:soil-fert-050}}, a charcoal added to soil, and {{ref:soil-agri-068}}, sown to take up what is left behind.

soil-agri-040.title: Land reclamation: making new ground from water
soil-agri-040.text: Almost a sixth of the Netherlands, about 7,000 km2, was once sea, lake, marsh or swamp. Land reclamation is the creation of new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds, and the result is called reclaimed land or land fill. Builders infill with heavy rock or cement topped with clay and dirt, drain submerged wetlands for farming, or dredge. The practice is old: Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty (c. 2000–1800 BC) made farmland around Lake Moeris by diverting its water with levees and canals. China has reclaimed more than 13,500 km2. New ground is fragile ground. It is highly susceptible to soil liquefaction in earthquakes, and consolidation of soft ground is a common technical risk. Fill compaction and drained {{ref:soil-water-144}} both cause subsidence, and drained marshes eventually sink below the surrounding water. Draining wetlands for ploughing also destroys habitat. Nearly 65% of the Yellow Sea's tidal flats have been reclaimed, and some countries now restrict new projects.

soil-agri-046.title: Herbicides, the chemistry of weed control
soil-agri-046.text: Between 1900 and 2000, yields of major crops per acre rose three to six times. Herbicides, substances commonly called weed killers and used to control unwanted plants, were part of that rise, together with nitrogen fertilizer and better cultivars. Selective herbicides control particular weeds and leave the crop largely unharmed. Non-selective ones kill plants indiscriminately. Before herbicides, farmers controlled weeds culturally, for example by changing soil pH, salinity or fertility. Major breakthroughs came during the Second World War. Glyphosate, marketed as Roundup from 1971, is now used very widely on crops bred to resist it. The costs are real. Herbicide use generally harms the environment, seriously damaging insects, non-target plants, animals and aquatic systems. Weeds can also evolve resistance, and switching between herbicides with different modes of action slows that selection. A well-designed {{ref:soil-agri-004}} can reduce herbicide needs, while {{ref:soil-agri-117}} may increase them.

soil-agri-001.title: Agricultural soil science: soil in the service of food
soil-agri-001.text: For most of its history, soil science was farm science. Agricultural soil science is the branch that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre. Until pedology arose in the 19th century, it was the only branch, then known as {{ref:soil-found-097}}. It belongs to agronomy, so it is also called soil agronomy, and some regions know it as agrology. The field studies the chemical, physical, biological and mineralogical makeup of soils as they relate to farming, and it develops methods that raise food and fibre production. Its favourite variables read like a soil checklist: texture, aeration and porosity, drainage, water content and water potential, horizonation, fertility, soil biota, and pH with cation-exchange capacity. Its research covers irrigation and drainage, {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, soil classification, plant nutrition and soil fertility, and newer areas such as greenhouse effect mitigation. Soil husbandry, the careful keeping of soil, is a strong tradition within it. Old problems remain. Erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination are still serious concerns, and the field puts growing emphasis on keeping soils productive in the long term. Pushing for maximum yield can carry high costs, such as massive crop diseases in monocultures or groundwater contaminated by fertilizers and pesticides.

soil-agri-028.title: Potting soil, which usually holds no soil
soil-agri-028.text: The bag says potting soil, but the contents are usually something else. Potting soil, also called growing medium or potting mix, is a substrate used to grow plants in containers. It holds little or no real soil, because soil compacts and loses pore space with repeated watering and is too heavy for pots. Instead come peat, vermiculite, {{ref:soil-agri-139}}, bark chips, perlite, sand, rice hulls and similar materials, usually mixing organic and inorganic ones. A typical recipe combines something to hold moisture, something for aeration and drainage, and fertilizer. A good medium holds water and nutrients, drains the excess, leaves pore space for root oxygen and decomposes slowly. Peat is usually limed to cut its acidity, typically 8.5 pounds of limestone per cubic yard (5.0 kg/m3). Peat is also controversial. Harvesting it degrades peatlands. They accumulate as little as 1 mm a year, yet they store up to 30% of the carbon held in soils on 3% of the world's surface. Commercial mixes are usually sterilized, and outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease have been traced to potting mix in several countries.

soil-agri-135.title: Organic farming: growing without synthetic inputs
soil-agri-135.text: By 2022, about 96 million hectares in 188 countries were farmed organically by 4.5 million farmers, about 2 percent of world farmland. Organic farming relies on natural inputs such as {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, manure and green manure, with techniques such as {{ref:soil-agri-004}} and mixed cropping. It aims at sustainability, soil fertility and biodiversity, and with rare exceptions it prohibits synthetic pesticides, synthetic fertilizers and genetically modified organisms. The movement arose in the early 20th century, partly because chemical farming brought soil compaction, erosion and declining fertility. Albert Howard, called the father of organic farming, adopted Northbourne's term in An Agricultural Testament in 1940. The trade-off is yield. A 2012 meta-analysis put organic productivity on average 25% below conventional, and a 2011 analysis found organic yields averaged 80% of conventional. That gap reshapes the environmental sums. Nitrogen leaching and nitrous oxide emissions are lower per area but higher per amount of food. Lower yields can also push more land into farming, which may cause biodiversity loss and negative climate effects.

soil-agri-049.title: Surface irrigation: letting gravity spread the water
soil-agri-049.text: In many places, farmers water their fields almost exactly as their ancestors did thousands of years ago. Surface irrigation spreads water over the soil surface by gravity, and it is by far the most common form of irrigation worldwide. It is often called flood irrigation, a name implying uncontrolled, inefficient distribution. Some forms, such as surge irrigation, are in fact closely managed. Each irrigation runs in four phases: advance, storage, depletion and recession. The depth soaking in at any point depends on the opportunity time, the time water stands on the surface there. Border strip irrigation, a hybrid of basin and furrow methods, runs water down long, narrow bays between earth banks, often for dairy pasture. Too much water causes waterlogging and deep drainage, and rising water tables can lift salt from saline layers into the root zone. Yet surface irrigation's relatively high leaching fraction makes salinization less of a problem than with other methods, unless poor subsurface drainage blocks the salt from leaching. Long use leaves its own soil, a recognisable irragric {{ref:soil-class-120}}.

soil-agri-053.title: Monocropping: the same crop, year after year
soil-agri-053.text: Between 1845 and 1849, one opportunistic species destroyed Ireland's potatoes and brought the Great Famine. A single cultivar with one resistance strategy is that exposed. Monocropping, also called continuous cropping, is growing a single crop year after year on the same land. Maize, soybeans and wheat are often grown this way, because a farmer can then use the same seed, pest control and machinery across the farm. The soil pays. Repeating one crop depletes certain nutrients and breeds pests and weeds adapted to it, so the system leans harder on pesticides and artificial fertilizers. Those chemicals seeping into soil and groundwater are a well-known concern. Monocropping also aids soil erosion, which mixed cropping and {{ref:soil-agri-004}} significantly reduce. Whether it is worth it remains disputed. Advocates say growing many crops together would be costly and could not feed everyone. Critics reject this, citing monocropping's damage to societies and the environment.

soil-agri-014.title: Irrigation efficiency: how much water the crop really uses
soil-agri-014.text: On many farms, 40% to 60% of irrigation water is lost before a crop can use it. Irrigation efficiency is the share of applied water the crop actually uses: the water it transpires divided by the water applied, times 100. The excess seeps away or runs off, carrying nutrients or pesticides with it. Sprinkler, drip or well-managed surface systems can reach 70% or more. Better design and better scheduling raise efficiency, and with it the crop grown per unit of water.

soil-agri-016.title: Sprinkler irrigation: rain on demand
soil-agri-016.text: Sprinkler irrigation pipes water to points in the field and sprays it overhead from high-pressure sprinklers or guns. In centre pivot systems the sprinklers ride on wheeled towers that circle around a central water feed, and they can irrigate all types of terrain. Newer pivots hang drop heads just above the crop, or drag hoses that wet the ground directly, to limit evaporation. This is Low Energy Precision Application, or LEPA. Using sprinkler and micro-irrigation lowers the risk of waterlogging and erosion. One hazard is the water itself: salty sprinkler water can burn leaves even where the soil is not saline.

soil-agri-017.title: Subirrigation: watering plants from below
soil-agri-017.text: Some crops are watered without a drop falling on the surface. Subirrigation artificially raises the water table so that the soil is moistened from below the plants' root zone. Farmers have long used it for field crops where water tables are high, often on lowland or river-valley grassland, setting ditch levels with pumps, canals, weirs and gates. In greenhouses a nutrient solution floods potted plants from below for 10–20 minutes and is then pumped back for reuse, saving water and nutrients. Self-watering containers and wicking beds work the same way on a small scale, drawing water up from a reservoir by capillary action.

soil-agri-018.title: Wastewater irrigation: watering crops with city sewage
soil-agri-018.text: Wastewater irrigation waters crops with recycled or untreated municipal wastewater. Its nitrogen and phosphorus act as fertilizer. The supply is cheaper than some sources, and it keeps flowing whatever the season or water restrictions. Developing countries increasingly use untreated wastewater, often unsafely. The hazards include bacteria, heavy metals, pharmaceuticals and pesticides, and their effects depend on both the wastewater and the soil. WHO's 2006 guidelines advise a multiple-barrier approach, such as stopping irrigation a few days before harvest so that pathogens die off.

soil-agri-044.title: Fallow: giving a field a season off
soil-agri-044.text: Under a two-field rotation, half the land lay idle each year. Leaving cropland unsown for one or more growing cycles is called fallow. A fallow field recovers and stores organic matter while keeping its moisture. Removing the crop also removes the hosts of pests and soil-borne pathogens, breaking their cycles. Intensive farming has shrunk fallow land, along with field margins and hedges, often by sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} instead. Rest carries a risk. A field can be most vulnerable to erosion while fallow, so keeping stubble cover, for example by {{ref:soil-agri-117}}, is key to reducing soil loss. Covered ground also holds more life: those crops raised microbial biomass carbon by about 20% and particulate organic carbon by nearly 50% compared with bare or fallow ground. An improved fallow enhances the rest period, for example by sowing yellow sweetclover, under which weeds made up only 1–12% of standing biomass.

soil-agri-042.title: Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild topsoil
soil-agri-042.text: Since farmers began turning the soil, an estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost. Regenerative agriculture is a conservation and rehabilitation approach to farming that aims to regenerate {{ref:soil-form-021}}, raise biodiversity and strengthen the health of farm soil. It is not one practice but a mix: little or no turning of the soil, {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, crop rotations, compost and grazing. The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s. Pinning it down is hard. A 2020 review of 229 articles found no legal or widely accepted definition. The evidence is mixed too. A 2023 review found that several of its practices can improve the soil's carbon, its health or yields under some climates and soils. Results vary between farming systems. Its climate claims are disputed. Scientists have criticized claims that it can mitigate climate change by locking carbon in soil as exaggerated and unsupported by evidence.

soil-agri-007.title: Choosing the crops in a rotation
soil-agri-007.text: Every crop in a rotation either gives the field something or takes something away. Choosing them means weighing organic matter, nutrients, pest control and protection from erosion. Row crops such as vegetables often pay best but tax the soil: low biomass and shallow roots leave little residue. Grasses and cereals, with dense, far-reaching roots, build structure and organic matter and compete with weeds. Two rules follow. A nitrogen-fixing legume should precede a nitrogen-depleting crop, and a low-residue crop should be offset by a high-biomass {{ref:soil-agri-066}}.

soil-agri-006.title: Rotations that hold soil in place
soil-agri-006.text: In a decade-long study, fall rye sown after the potato harvest cut soil run-off by as much as 43%. Rotations can be built to fight erosion through crop sequences and the management of residue and fallow, often alongside {{ref:soil-agri-117}}. Protection is greatest when the most crop stubble stays on the surface, slowing overland flow and its power to carry sediment. Decomposing forage crops glue particles into aggregates that resist raindrops, running water and wind. Where rain is unpredictable, sowing only when soil water is adequate gives better cover than a rigid rotation.

soil-agri-008.title: Mixed farming: crops and livestock on one farm
soil-agri-008.text: On a mixed farm, crops and animals feed each other. Mixed farming combines growing crops with keeping livestock, which helps manage rotations and cycle nutrients. The animals eat what is left of the crops after harvest, and their manure replenishes crop nutrients. Nutrients thus cycle within the farm, and less synthetic fertilizer is needed. Livestock make efficient use of sod and of crops sown to cover the ground, spreading their nutrients as manure instead of exporting them as sold hay. Regenerative grazing of ruminants on such farms has improved nutrient cycling by speeding the decomposition of crop leftovers.

soil-agri-009.title: Polyculture: several crops in one place
soil-agri-009.text: The Three Sisters plant corn with pole beans and squash. The beans supply nitrogen, and the squash spreads a canopy that suppresses weeds. Polyculture is growing two or more crops in the same place at the same time, the opposite of {{ref:soil-agri-053}}. {{ref:soil-agri-133}} and companion planting add diversity within one season. Double-cropping grows two crops in sequence in one season, or a crop alongside a ground-covering crop. This suits small farms that cannot rest land for long. Rotations work for both single crops and mixtures, so farmers can raise biodiversity in space and in time.

soil-agri-133.title: Intercropping: sharing a field to harvest more
soil-agri-133.text: Two crops in one field can yield more than either would alone. Intercropping, a form of polyculture, grows two or more crops at the same time in the same field. The goal is usually a greater yield, by using resources or ecological processes a single crop would leave unused. Crops are chosen so they do not compete for space, nutrients, water or light, for example a deep-rooted crop with a shallow-rooted one. In mixed intercropping the crops are freely mixed. Temporal intercropping pairs a fast-growing crop with a slow-growing one. Relay cropping sows the second crop while the first is still growing. Rotation does not count, because its crops grow in separate seasons. In low-input or subsistence farming, intercropping can give higher yields for the same input. Pest control by trap crops has had mixed success: of 100 examples reviewed in 2006, only 10 succeeded commercially.

soil-agri-022.title: Nitrate leaching: fertilizer that slips past the roots
soil-agri-022.text: Human activity now adds 50% more nitrogen to the land than natural sources do, and leached fertilizers and manures make up 75% of that human share. Nitrate leaching is the loss of nitrate from soil as drainage water carries the excess ions down to groundwater, streams and the sea. Soils do not hold them. Farmers place nitrate and ammonium fertilizers in the root zone because plants absorb them easily, but whatever nitrate the crop leaves behind is free to move. How much leaches depends on three things: the soil's type and structure, how much water the crop uses, and how much nitrate is already present. Sandy soils hold little water, so it drains through quickly, while clays hold much. The stakes reach the kitchen tap. Nitrate in drinking water is linked to methemoglobinemia, or blue baby syndrome, so regulators cap it at 45 to 50 mg per litre. One defence is a {{ref:soil-agri-068}}, sown to take up the nitrogen left over from fertilizing the previous crop before it can leach.

soil-agri-034.title: Soil solarization: cooking pests under plastic
soil-agri-034.text: In one study, eight days under plastic killed every Verticillium dahliae fungus 25 cm down. Soil solarization is a non-chemical pest control method that traps the sun's heat in soil until many soil-borne plant pathogens are killed or badly weakened. Moist soil is covered with a tarp, usually clear polyethylene. It must reach 35–60 °C, which kills pathogens in the top 30 cm, and temperatures fall with depth. Fungi, bacteria, nematodes, insect and mite pests, and weeds all suffer. It does not sterilize. It kills up to 90% of pathogens, while heat-tolerant beneficial microbes such as Bacillus survive and recolonize, leaving the soil more resistant to disease. Ordinary plastic covers protect crops in the coldest months; solarization covers soil in the hottest. Katan first described it in detail in 1976, and within thirty years it was applied in more than 60 countries. Concerns include the fate of the plastic, the weaker weed control of biodegradable covers, and reduced microbial richness.

soil-agri-015.title: Drip irrigation: water delivered drop by drop
soil-agri-015.text: Buried clay pots for watering were described in China in the first century BCE, but the modern drip system was invented in Israel. Drip irrigation is micro-irrigation that lets water drip slowly to plant roots, from above or below the surface, placing it in the root zone to minimize evaporation. Properly managed, it can be the most water-efficient method, with field water efficiency typically 80 to 90%. Liquid fertilizer is often mixed into the water, a practice described in {{ref:soil-fert-208}}, with reported fertilizer savings of up to 95%. Localized watering cuts fertilizer loss by leaching, keeps the root zone at field capacity, and keeps foliage dry against disease. Precision has a catch. So little water leaches that salts build up at the edge of the wetted zone, and regular slight over-watering flushes them below the roots. In 2023, 3% of the world's farmers used drip.

soil-agri-054.title: Integrated pest management: control, not eradication
soil-agri-054.text: Integrated pest management aims to keep pests in check, not to wipe them out. It combines non-chemical and chemical methods to hold pests at tolerable, economic levels while relying less on chemicals. The FAO describes it as integrating biological, chemical, physical and cultural strategies to grow healthy crops while minimizing pesticide use and its risks. Prevention comes first, through resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping. Pesticides are used only when needed, often timed to a stage of the pest's life cycle, which also helps protect water quality.

soil-agri-058.title: Crop yield: the harvest per hectare
soil-agri-058.text: A medieval cereal field in the UK gave about 500 kg/ha. The Industrial Revolution raised that to 2000 kg/ha, and the {{ref:soil-agri-138}} to 8000 kg/ha. Crop yield is the amount of a crop, or of a product such as milk or wool, produced per unit area of land. It is usually measured in kilograms per hectare or bushels per acre. Fertilizer, better tools and farming methods, and improved crop varieties drove the rise. Degraded land drags the other way. In 2025 about 1.7 billion people lived in areas with sizeable yield losses from degradation, and in rich countries intensive inputs sustain yields but mask the damage.

soil-agri-010.title: Precision agriculture: farming field by square metre
soil-agri-010.text: In 1985, researchers at the University of Minnesota varied the lime they spread across fields instead of applying one rate. Precision agriculture is a farm management strategy built on data about time, place and individual plants or animals. It fits decisions to variation across fields, for better efficiency, yield and sustainability. The concept emerged in the United States in the early 1980s, and grid sampling at one sample per hectare appeared then too. GPS lets farmers map how yield, topography, organic matter, moisture, nitrogen, pH, electrical conductivity and other soil variables change across a field. A first wave of tools brought satellite and aerial imagery, weather prediction and variable rate fertilizer; a second added precise planting, topographic mapping and soil data. The payoff is the right input in the right place at the right time. That can cut nutrient use while raising yields, which limits nitrogen leaching and protects soils and groundwater. Following GPS guidance lines also reduces soil compaction.

soil-agri-138.title: The Green Revolution and its bill for the soil
soil-agri-138.text: Norman Borlaug, called the father of the Green Revolution, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. The Green Revolution was a period in which technology transfer initiatives produced a large increase in crop yields. It combined high-yielding cereal varieties, expanded irrigation, modern management, hybrid seeds, synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. The new varieties take up more nitrogen and carry semi-dwarfing genes against lodging, the falling over of tall stems. They outperform traditional varieties only with enough irrigation, pesticides and fertilizer. Cereal production in developing nations more than doubled from 1961 to 1985, and a 2021 estimate credits a 44% rise in yields between 1965 and 2010. Wheat bred to tolerate acid, aluminium-rich soils opened the Cerrado savanna to farming. The soil paid. Over-farming caused contamination, erosion and degradation, and nutrient depletion pushed farmers to clear forest. Nitrogen applied beyond crop needs, such as broadcast urea, emits nitrous oxide and pollutes water.

soil-agri-005.title: The rotation effect: why rotated crops yield more
soil-agri-005.text: Crops grown in rotation gain a yield benefit that agronomists simply call the rotation effect. It comes broadly from relieving the drawbacks of monocropping. Better nutrition, less pest, pathogen and weed stress, and better soil structure have been linked to it in some cases. More organic matter improves water infiltration and retention, raising drought tolerance and reducing erosion. Less intensive working of the soil lets microbes thrive, and soil with low microbial activity supplies far fewer nutrients from the same biomass. Over time, rotated crops can meet production goals with fewer purchased inputs.

soil-agri-041.title: Reclaiming sea and swamp for farmland
soil-agri-041.text: Before industrialisation, farming was the main reason people reclaimed land. Agricultural land reclamation turns sea or wetland into farmland. In South China, farmers walled off shore areas near river mouths to make fish ponds, or paddy fields of more salt-tolerant rice. Draining swampy or seasonally flooded wetlands makes productive farmland and also controls mosquitoes. Salt marshes, once dismissed as coastal wastelands, were widely lost to reclamation for agriculture, urban development and salt production.

soil-agri-023.title: Phosphorus leaching: when sorption sites fill up
soil-agri-023.text: Phosphorus leaching is the loss of phosphorus from fields by downward movement through soil. It is an important pathway on flat, sandy land or on soils prone to preferential flow. Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus clings to soil particles, especially iron and aluminium oxides and hydroxides such as gibbsite and ferrihydrite. Soils given more than crops need, often for decades, have these sorption sites filled by 'legacy phosphorus', so new additions leach. Long waterlogging can also release phosphorus by dissolving ferric iron minerals, a concern when restoring drained wetlands. Phosphorus drives {{ref:soil-env-020}} in surface waters, so its loss threatens water quality.

soil-agri-139.title: Coir: the coconut husk that stands in for peat
soil-agri-139.text: One kilogram of dry coco peat swells to 15 litres of moist growing medium. Coir is coconut husk fibre, and its processed form, coco peat, goes into potting mixes as a substitute for peat. Concern over the sustainability of extracting peat has increased its use. It holds water like a sponge and has a pH of 5.5 to 6.5. It is low in nutrients, though, and incompletely decomposed coco peat ties up nitrogen as it breaks down. It is also high in sodium and potassium, so it is buffered with a calcium solution; its potassium can otherwise cause magnesium and calcium deficiencies.

soil-agri-055.title: Land restoration: returning land to an earlier state
soil-agri-055.text: Not every land project aims to make new farmland. Land restoration returns land to a different or earlier state for an intended purpose, which may include renaturalisation or rewilding. It counters human-caused damage such as pollution, deforestation and salination. That sets it apart from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems for cultivation or construction. Each project chooses a reference ecosystem to judge success and adjusts as the ecosystem responds. Against {{ref:soil-env-072}}, soil is first fixed with grasses and planted rows of trees and shrubs to stop dunes moving, then enriched with nitrogen-fixing plants and rotated crops.

soil-agri-048.title: Herbicide persistence: how long a weed killer lasts
soil-agri-048.text: Some herbicides can leave the ground almost permanently barren. Herbicide persistence is how long a herbicide stays active in soil. Residual activity is low if rain or soil reactions neutralize it within weeks or months, and high if it stays potent for the long term. Each compound's chemistry decides. Atrazine belongs to the triazine family, the herbicides most feared for groundwater contamination. It breaks down slowly in soils above neutral pH, and soil water can carry it to the water table, a 'carryover' effect. Many modern herbicides are formulated to degrade soon after application.

soil-agri-047.title: Soil-applied herbicides that work below ground
soil-agri-047.text: Some herbicides strike before a weed reaches the surface. Soil-applied herbicides are spread before planting or crop emergence, and the roots or shoots of emerging seedlings take them up. Many are absorbed by shoots still underground. EPTC and trifluralin work this way, whereas glyphosate, 2,4-D and dicamba are sprayed on foliage. Placement matters. The chemical must sit in the right soil layer, worked in mechanically or by rainfall. Left on the surface, it is lost to volatilization and photolysis, breakdown by light. Adsorption to soil colloids or organic matter often reduces the amount weeds can absorb.

soil-agri-032.title: Steaming soil clean of weeds and disease
soil-agri-032.text: Modern soil steaming was developed in Germany in 1888 and first used commercially in the United States in 1893. Soil steam sterilization fully or partly sterilizes soil with steam, in open fields or greenhouses. Steam kills weeds, bacteria, fungi and viruses by heating soil enough to inactivate enzymes and coagulate vital cell proteins. In the field it only partly disinfects, because heat-resistant spore-forming bacteria survive and revitalize the soil. True sterilization needs a laboratory autoclave. Today superheated steam at 180–200 °C is often used. It is now considered the best way to disinfect sick soil, potting soil and compost, and an alternative to bromomethane, which the Montreal Protocol curtailed. Steaming also relieves soil fatigue, the decline in fertility under poor management, and frees nutrients locked in the soil. In integrated steaming, an injected compost-based activator recolonizes the soil with beneficial microbes such as Bacillus subtilis.

soil-agri-030.title: Testing a potting mix with a water extract
soil-agri-030.text: A potting mix is not made of soil, yet it can still take a soil test. The saturated media extract is the main test of a mix's chemistry: it analyses a water extract of the mix. Reference levels are clear. Soluble salts are best at 2.0–3.5 mS/cm, with 0.75–5.0 acceptable; nitrate-N should be 100–200 ppm and phosphorus 6–9 ppm. Missing nutrients come from fertilizer: slow-release synthetics in conventional mixes, or compost in organic ones, at most 1 part compost to 1 part bulking material.

soil-agri-029.title: Specialty potting mixes for picky plants
soil-agri-029.text: A cactus and a carnivorous plant want very different pots. Specialty potting mixes are growing media adapted to the needs of a plant, or of a growth stage, for aeration, drainage, nutrition and pH. Cacti and succulents need sharp drainage from a much larger share of perlite or sand. Carnivorous plants prefer the nutrient-poor, acidic soils of bogs and fens. Small seeds start well in light germination mixes, and larger ones in seed-starting mixes. Cuttings root better in soilless mixes such as perlite, vermiculite, sand and sphagnum moss than in water.

soil-agri-024.title: How much salt a crop can take
soil-agri-024.text: Saline land covers 3,230,000 km2 worldwide. A crop's salt tolerance is the highest salt level it can withstand without losing productivity; beyond that it is harmed. The salt level is usually taken as the soil salinity or the salinity of the irrigation water. Tolerance matters most on irrigated land in arid and semi-arid regions, where salinization concerns hundreds of millions of hectares. Salty sprinkler water burns leaves. On one Australian scale, sensitive crops such as almond, apricot and citrus suffer below 178 mg/L chloride. Tolerant ones such as cotton, sorghum and sunflower only above 710 mg/L. Key studies include USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 60 in 1954, Maas and Hoffman's extensive study over 20 years later, and an FAO worldwide survey in 2002. Most data come from pots, drums or lysimeters under controlled conditions, and field data are rarer. Much research now aims to breed crops with higher salt tolerance for salinity-stricken regions.

soil-agri-038.title: Agrominerals, the rocks that feed plants
soil-agri-038.text: Rock that feeds plants has a nickname: stone bread. Agrominerals are minerals that matter to farming and horticulture because they can supply essential plant nutrients. Natural or processed, they serve as alternative fertilizers or soil amendments, and the term dates from the 19th century. Their use began with small fixes: perlite for aeration, pumice to curb evaporation, and vermiculite and zeolite to store moisture. Potash, a major source of potassium, was one of the original agrominerals. Its finite supply drives prices up, so research now seeks alternatives.

soil-agri-036.title: Agrogeology: geology put to work for farmers
soil-agri-036.text: In 1989, the Tanzania-Canada project helped farmers in southern Tanzania find and test local raw materials for their fields. It was the first agrogeology project with major funding. Agrogeology is the study of agrominerals, their origins and uses; more broadly, it is geology applied to farm soil productivity and health. It combines geology, soil science, agronomy and chemistry, using geological resources to improve the chemical and physical properties of soil. Agrogeologists work to replenish fertility where unsustainable farming has depleted agrominerals. The idea is not new: raw materials have been used as fertilizer since the 1800s. The toolkit is varied. Apatite releases phosphate slowly in acid soils, carbonates lime the soil, malachite cures copper deficiency, scoria serves as a water-saving mulch and zeolite conserves nitrogen.

soil-agri-012.title: Within-field variability: no field is uniform
soil-agri-012.text: No field is the same from one end to the other. Within-field variability is the difference in growing conditions within and between fields, which {{ref:soil-agri-010}} measures and manages. It arises from climate (hail, drought, rain), from soils (texture, depth, nitrogen levels), from cropping practices, and from weeds and disease. Permanent indicators, chiefly soil properties, describe a field's constants. Point indicators track crop status such as disease, water stress or nitrogen stress. Weather stations, sensors measuring soil electrical resistivity, and satellite imagery supply much of this information.

soil-agri-039.title: Soil remineralization: feeding fields with rock dust
soil-agri-039.text: A dressing of crushed rock can feed a field for up to 5 years. Soil remineralization replenishes a soil's mineral nutrients by working rock powder into it. Multi-nutrient rock fertilizers release potassium, calcium, magnesium and some phosphorus slowly, mimicking the natural weathering of parent material. Plants take what they need and the rest stays crystallized, whereas unabsorbed soluble fertilizer salts run off to groundwater. Combined with organic fertilizer, rock powder has matched chemical fertilizer at much lower cost. It also raises soil pH and can use local mining waste. The limits are real. It needs heavy application rates and releases nutrients slowly, so it cannot replace industrial fertilizers. Dissolution depends on organic matter, pH and the formation of secondary clays, and lab rates can be 2–5 orders of magnitude higher than field rates. Some volcanic and phosphate rocks contain toxic, heavy or radioactive elements. One prospect draws wider interest. Cations released from some powders react with carbon dioxide to form carbonate minerals, which could help mitigate global warming.

soil-agri-137.title: Do organic fields end up with better soil?
soil-agri-137.text: Whether organic farming leaves a soil better off is still disputed. Supporters say organic soil has higher quality and holds more water, which may help yields in drought years. A 2007 USDA study found that manure in tilled organic systems built soil better than {{ref:soil-agri-117}}. Yet an 18-year study on nutrient-depleted, cold-temperate soils found conventional methods better for fertility and yield, crediting organic gains to imported materials. Gunsmoke Farms, a 137 square kilometre organic project in South Dakota, suffered massive erosion from turning the soil after converting.

soil-agri-136.title: How organic farms keep their soil fertile
soil-agri-136.text: Without synthetic fertilizer, an organic farm has to grow and recycle its own nutrients. Organic soil fertility management replaces what crops remove through the natural breakdown of organic matter, using green manure and composting. Soil organisms such as mycorrhiza and earthworms release the nutrients to plants through the growing season. Supplying nitrogen when crops need it most is the hard part; legumes in rotations and green manures fix it with rhizobia. Farmers also use animal manure, seed meal and mineral powders such as greensand and phosphate rock. Farms without livestock struggle more and rely on imported manure, which is bulky and costly to haul far.

soil-agri-051.title: Basin irrigation: flooding a level plot
soil-agri-051.text: Some fields are watered by filling them like a shallow pool. Basin irrigation quickly floods a level area enclosed by earth banks and leaves the water to soak in. It is favoured on soils with relatively low infiltration rates, and traditional basins are not drained afterwards. Laser levelling and land grading now allow large rectangular basins suited to mechanised broadacre cropping. In drainback level basins, water passes from each bay to a lower one in turn, a layout common in Australian rice and wheat rotations.

soil-agri-050.title: Furrow irrigation: water down the rows
soil-agri-050.text: Furrow irrigation sends water by gravity from the top of a field down small parallel channels that follow its main slope. Furrows run from under 100 to 2,000 m long and suit row crops such as cotton, maize and sugar cane. The water's speed depends above all on the inflow rate and the soil's infiltration rate. A slow advance soaks the top end more than the bottom; a faster one improves uniformity and cuts the water needed. Surge irrigation pulses the flow on and off, sealing the surface so the water advances faster.

soil-agri-052.title: Spate irrigation: catching the desert flood
soil-agri-052.text: In dry lands, river beds that sit empty most of the year sometimes carry floods for hours or days. Spate irrigation diverts these seasonal floods onto fields or into storage basins. It is an ancient method of arid and semi-arid lands in the Middle East, North Africa, West Asia, East Africa and parts of Latin America. Intakes, spurs or bunds send the water through channel networks to command areas from a few hectares to over 25,000 ha. Fast floodwater moves large amounts of sediment, so river banks and beds can change rapidly.

soil-agri-045.title: Fallow syndrome: the hungry crop after a rest
soil-agri-045.text: Resting a field can leave the next crop hungry. Fallow syndrome is poor nutrient uptake by a crop after a fallow period. The soil lacks arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, root partners that help plants take up nutrients. Any plant roots, even those of weeds, reduce its occurrence. Susceptible crops such as corn should therefore follow a crop that hosts the fungi, such as oats or another small grain, rather than a fallow. Fields are now routinely sown with {{ref:soil-agri-066}} to prevent erosion, suppress weeds, supply green manure and lower the risk of fallow syndrome.

soil-agri-043.title: Holistic planned grazing and the carbon dispute
soil-agri-043.text: Holistic planned grazing keeps livestock herds rotating between fields to mimic how natural herds graze. Trampling is reported to aid soil restoration, plant regrowth, carbon storage and water infiltration. How much carbon it stores is disputed. A meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass. A 2016 Swedish study put the realistic rate of carbon storage seven times lower than Allan Savory's claims. Adaptive multi-paddock grazing, by contrast, has done less damage to soil than continuous grazing.

soil-agri-134.title: Alley cropping: crops in the lanes between trees
soil-agri-134.text: Alley cropping grows strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges. The trees are pruned before the crop is planted, and the cut leaves are spread over the crop area to supply nutrients. The hedges also shelter the crop from wind and reduce erosion. Leguminous Inga trees suit the method well. They fix nitrogen, grow on acid tropical soils, and drop a thick mulch that protects the soil and shades out weeds. Inga alley cropping lets land be cultivated repeatedly, an alternative to slash-and-burn farming. In the temperate strip-cropping variant, trees grow in wide strips rather than single rows.

soil-agri-037.title: Rock phosphate: phosphorus straight from the quarry
soil-agri-037.text: Much conventional fertilizer added to phosphorus-deficient soils turns into insoluble complexes, so it has to be reapplied constantly. Rock phosphate fertilizer uses phosphorite, a phosphorus-bearing sedimentary rock, as a sustainable, low-cost source of phosphorus. Its phosphorus must be processed before plants and soil can take it up. Fungi can do this by producing organic acids. Industry grinds the rock, adds water and sulfuric acid, removes impurities as gypsum, then treats the acidic liquid with ammonia vapour to make granules. A study in Zimbabwe found that mining dust mixed with processed fertilizer raised plant growth, phosphorus levels and organic carbon.

soil-agri-057.title: Zaï: planting pits that revive dry land
soil-agri-057.text: A shallow pit can multiply a harvest. Zaï is a farming technique of digging pits in poorly permeable soil to catch water and concentrate compost. The pits are 15 to 50 cm across and 5 to 15 cm deep, spaced about 80 cm apart. Farmers in the western Sahel have traditionally used it to restore degraded dry land and raise fertility, and it has spread to semi-arid East Africa. From the 1980s, filling the pits with manure and compost was reintroduced. This attracts termites, whose tunnels break up the soil, and yields of trees, sorghum and millet can rise by up to 500 percent.

soil-agri-035.title: Biosolarization: compost speeds the sun's work
soil-agri-035.text: Biosolarization adds compost or other organic amendments to soil before solarizing it, so that microbial activity shortens the treatment. It is an alternative to soil fumigation, closely related to soil solarization and to {{ref:soil-agri-056}}. All of them use solar heat or plant chemistry against nematodes, bacteria, fungi and other pests. Spanish research on strawberry production found it sustainable and cost-effective, and small farms in California use it. It can double as organic waste management, and food-industry residues can make it more efficient.

soil-agri-132.title: Deficit irrigation: watering less on purpose
soil-agri-132.text: Deficit irrigation deliberately gives a crop less than its full water needs. It waters during the drought-sensitive growth stages and limits water at other times. The aim is the highest crop water productivity, the marketable product per cubic meter of water, rather than the highest yield. Cotton irrigation in Turkey and India could be cut to up to 60 percent of the crop's water requirement with limited yield loss. Maize, sensitive all season, suffers. Less nutrient leaches, but the risk of salinization is higher than under full irrigation.

soil-agri-056.title: Biofumigation: plants that gas soil pests
soil-agri-056.text: Mustard can do a fumigant's job. Biofumigation is pest control in which a fumigant gas comes from fresh plant material chopped and buried in the soil to decompose. Brassicas such as mustard, cauliflower and broccoli release isothiocyanates from their glucosinolates. These are toxic to soil bacteria, fungi and nematodes but less persistent than synthetic fumigants. Sorghum releases hydrogen cyanide instead. The plants are chopped at flowering and worked into soil irrigated to field capacity, then covered with film for three or four weeks. The method can also replenish nutrients, but it is slow and hard to standardize, because cultivars differ in active content.

soil-agri-031.title: Soilless substrates that hold roots in hydroponics
soil-agri-031.text: In hydroponics, plants grow without soil, but their roots still need something to grip. Soilless growing substrates are inert or organic materials such as perlite or gravel that support the roots mechanically. Rock wool, spun from molten basalt or slag, is the most widely used, though its naturally high pH needs conditioning. Expanded clay pellets, fired at 1,200 °C until they swell and turn porous, are inert, pH-neutral and light. Coir swells three to four times when wet but must first be washed of salts, tannins and phenolics. Perlite holds more air and less water than vermiculite.

soil-agri-131.title: Center-pivot irrigation: watering in circles
soil-agri-131.text: A standard 400-meter center-pivot machine waters about 50 hectares in one circle. Center-pivot irrigation sprinkles a circular area of crop from a line of pipe on wheeled towers that rotates around a central pivot. Drops hang the sprinklers a few feet above the crop to limit evaporation and wind drift. The system needs less working of the soil than ground irrigation, reducing runoff, erosion and compaction. But decades of pumping have emptied parts of the Ogallala Aquifer, where the water table has dropped more than 1.5 m per year in places.

soil-agri-011.title: Variable rate application: changing the dose as you go
soil-agri-011.text: A GPS-guided spreader can raise or lower its fertilizer rate as it crosses a field, because nutrient needs differ with soil properties and sunlight. Variable rate application applies a material such as fertilizer at a rate that changes with the location or qualities of each part of a field. It is either map based, following prescription maps an advisor prepares in advance, or sensor based, calculated in real time on the applicator. Electromagnetic induction, considered cost-effective and non-destructive, can make the maps. Varying the rates of nutrients or pesticides can cut their use, saving costs and reducing harmful runoff into waterways.

soil-agri-033.title: Sheets, vacuums and sandwiches: ways to steam soil
soil-agri-033.text: Steam can be pushed into soil from above, drawn down from below, or both. Soil steaming methods fall into substrate, surface and deep soil steaming, chosen by soil structure, crop and area to treat. Sheet steaming treats 15 to 400 m2 at once, reaching 25–30 cm depth and 90 °C in 4–5 hours. Vacuum depth steaming draws steam down through pipes and penetrates best, reaching up to 80 cm with fixed drainage pipes. Sandwich steaming pushes steam in from the surface and from depth at once. Stack steaming treats compost and substrates piled up to 70 cm high.

soil-agri-025.title: Salinity classes: matching salty soils to crops
soil-agri-025.text: Bernstein graded soils by how salty they are and what will still grow in them. His classes use ECe, the electrical conductivity of a saturated soil-paste extract, in decisiemens per metre. ECe 0–2 is non-saline. From 2–4 the soil is slightly saline, and sensitive crops lose yield. From 4–8 it is moderately saline. From 8–16 it is saline, and only tolerant crops yield normally. Above 16, only very tolerant crops do. Soil salinity control draws different bounds, calling soil saline only above ECe 4. Schleiff ranks crop tolerance in narrower 2 dS/m steps than the 4 dS/m steps in Richards' 1954 USDA handbook.

soil-agri-027.title: Crops that tolerate seawater
soil-agri-027.text: Certain varieties of potato, carrot, red onion, white cabbage and broccoli thrive when watered with salt water, Dutch trials found. Crop tolerance to seawater is a crop's ability to withstand irrigation with seawater or a mix of fresh water and seawater. Salt Farm Texel tests crops on 56 plots of 160 m2 at seven salt levels, from EC 2 to 35 dS/m. The levels are made by mixing fresh water with seawater of about 50 dS/m. Thresholds varied widely even within one crop: potato ranged from 1.9 dS/m for the variety Met to 4.1 dS/m for Mignonne.

soil-agri-003.title: Agroecosystems: the ecosystems people farm
soil-agri-003.text: A farm is an ecosystem with a manager. An agroecosystem is an ecological system that people manage and shape in order to farm. Researchers study its system properties: productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability. Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s, is considered the foundation of modern {{ref:soil-agri-002}}. Some losses are permanent. Erosion can irreparably reduce an agroecosystem's productive capacity, and {{ref:soil-agri-066}} are often grown for that reason alone.

soil-agri-002.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to farming
soil-agri-002.text: Basil Bensin used the word agroecology in 1928, according to Wezel and colleagues; another account credits the German zoologist Friederichs. Agroecology is an academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems. Tischler's 1965 book Agrarökologie may be the first with the word in its title. Today the term can mean a science, a movement or a farming practice, and it is not tied to any single method, whether organic, regenerative, integrated or industrial. It draws on the sciences to study soil properties and plant-insect interactions, and on the social sciences to study farming's effects on rural communities. Ecosystem agroecology treats farms as integrated ecological systems, analysing their energy flows and nutrient cycles. As practice, it harnesses biodiversity, nutrient recycling, {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, intercropping and composting. Its certified forms are biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food. Its politics are unsettled. Researchers debate heatedly which model of agriculture policy should support, and the UN is perhaps agroecology's most prominent backer.

soil-agri-095.title: Tillage: why farmers dig, and why digging less won
soil-agri-095.text: In 1731 Jethro Tull argued that land could never be tilled too much. Tillage is the preparation of soil for farming by mechanically agitating it: digging, stirring or overturning it. By hand it means shovelling, picking, mattock work, hoeing and raking. With animals or machines it means ploughing, rototilling, rolling, harrowing and cultivating. Deeper, more thorough work is called primary tillage, and shallower, more selective work secondary. Harrowing and rototilling often do both in one pass. In farming, cultivation overlaps with tillage, but it can also mean shallow, selective tillage of row crops that kills weeds while sparing the crop. Weed control is a clear payoff. Tillage uproots weeds or buries their leaves, so they cannot compete with the crop or set seed. Tull believed soil had to be pulverized into a fine powder before plants could feed on it. Scientific observation has shown the opposite. Tillage robs soil of the structure that lets roots, water and nutrients in, speeds erosion and compacts the soil. Tilling the prairie topsoil of the American Midwest helped cause the Dust Bowl. In 2019 erosion in the United States still took an estimated 3 trillion pounds of soil. Modern agricultural science has since cut tillage sharply. With herbicides, crops tolerant of packed soil and direct-seeding equipment, crops can be grown for years without it.

soil-agri-106.title: The plough, from human muscle to the tractor
soil-agri-106.text: A Sumerian poem from the 3rd millennium BC stages a debate between the hoe and the plough over which is better. The plough, spelled plow in the United States, is a farm tool for loosening or turning over soil before sowing seed or planting. Its main work is turning over the uppermost soil, which brings fresh nutrients to the surface and buries weeds and crop remains to decay. The trenches it cuts are furrows. Ploughing and cultivating even out the upper 12 to 25 centimeters (5 to 10 in) of soil, where most plant feeder roots grow. The earliest ploughs had no wheels, a type the Romans called an aratrum. People pulled the first ploughs, then oxen, horses and mules, then steam engines, and from the early 20th century tractors. In 1837 John Deere began making polished steel ploughs strong enough for tough Midwest prairie, once thought unsuitable. A ploughed field is normally left to dry and then harrowed before planting. Where erosion threatens, shallower ploughing or other forms of {{ref:soil-agri-099}} have replaced the traditional plough.

soil-agri-126.title: Arable land, the share of farmland that can take a plough
soil-agri-126.text: In 2013 the world used 4.924 billion hectares for agriculture, but only 1.407 billion of them were arable. Arable land is land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops. FAO statistics count land under temporary crops, temporary meadows, market and kitchen gardens, and land fallow for less than five years. Land abandoned by shifting cultivation is left out. The figures record actual, not potential, use, and Eurostat defines arable land as land ploughed or tilled regularly, generally under crop rotation. Meadows, pastures and permanent crops such as orchards, vineyards and coffee plantations are farmland but not arable. Land can be unfit for cultivation through lack of freshwater, stoniness, steepness, a harsh climate, wetness that cannot be drained, or excess salts. Clay content is a major factor. Such land can still pay: about 59 percent of US non-federal pasture and unforested rangeland cannot be cultivated but is valuable for grazing. Every year {{ref:soil-env-072}} and human-induced erosion take arable land, and poor irrigation concentrates salts in the root zone. Climate change may add some back by thawing frozen ground.

soil-agri-100.title: What tillage gives a soil, and what it takes away
soil-agri-100.text: Tillage gives with one hand and takes with the other. Its effects are its consequences for a soil. On the credit side, it loosens and aerates the A horizon and mixes residue, humus and nutrients evenly through it. It destroys weeds mechanically. Autumn tillage lets frost crumble the exposed soil over winter, leaving a smooth surface for spring planting. It also cuts slugs, cutworms, armyworms and crop diseases that shelter in old surface residues. Drying the soil before seeding counts as a benefit in wetter climates, but also as a drawback. The debits run longer. Tillage breaks the cohesion between particles and destroys aggregates, the basis of soil structure. It reduces organic matter and soil life such as microbes, earthworms and ants. It tears the hyphal network of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, so the soil can infect fewer new roots. Tilled soil loses nutrients and water-storing ability, and its infiltration rate falls, so more water runs off and erodes it. Compaction into a dense layer, {{ref:soil-agri-101}}, chemical runoff and the over-enrichment of waters fed by nutrient runoff complete the list.

soil-agri-096.title: Primary and secondary tillage: rough first, fine second
soil-agri-096.text: Most tilled fields are worked twice, first roughly and then finely. Tillage divides into deeper, more thorough primary operations and shallower, often more selective secondary ones. Primary tillage, such as ploughing, loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, leaving a rough surface. It usually follows the last harvest, when the soil is wet enough to plough but still gives traction. The goals are soft soil to a reasonable depth, buried residues, killed weeds and aeration. Secondary tillage is any later operation. It works in fertilizer, reduces soil to a finer tilth, levels the surface, shapes rows and controls weeds. Its smoother finish is what many crops need for a good {{ref:soil-agri-116}}. The tool kit is long, from {{ref:soil-agri-114}} and {{ref:soil-agri-115}} to dibbles, hoes, shovels, rotary tillers, subsoilers, ridge- or bed-forming tillers and rollers. When the target is weeds, tools such as hoes usually disturb only the top few centimeters of soil around the crop plants.

soil-agri-114.title: The harrow, which smooths what the plough leaves rough
soil-agri-114.text: After the plough comes the harrow, a farm implement for surface tillage that breaks up and smooths the soil. A plough cuts the upper 12 to 25 centimeters and leaves furrows. The weeding tools in {{ref:soil-agri-115}} disturb only narrow tracks between rows. A harrow disturbs the whole surface, breaking clods into a tilth fit for planting seeds. Coarser harrowing can also remove weeds and cover seed after sowing. The four general types are disc, tine, chain and chain-disk harrows, and tine harrows include spring-tooth, drag and spike models. Harrows with angled discs, covered in {{ref:soil-agri-172}}, do heavy work, such as breaking up sod after ploughing, while chain harrows level the tilth or cover seed. Farmers commonly run a disk harrow first to slice the large clods left by the {{ref:soil-agri-109}}, then a spring-tooth harrow. The result is a smooth field with powdery surface soil. Where the tilth is very fine, or the soil light enough to blow away, a roller often goes last. The tool is old: in China the rake had developed into the harrow by the end of the Han dynasty.

soil-agri-123.title: Contour plowing: furrows that run across the slope
soil-agri-123.text: By 1938, ploughing along the contour and similar techniques had cut US soil loss by 65 percent, despite continuing drought. Contour plowing, also called contour farming, is ploughing or planting across a slope along its elevation contour lines. The level furrows run across the slope rather than down it. They form water breaks that reduce rills and gullies in heavy rain and give water time to soak in. The method also helps prevent tillage erosion, the movement of soil by tilling itself. It reduces fertilizer loss, power use, time and machine wear while raising yields. Demonstrations showed row-crop gains of up to 50% under ideal conditions, with 5 to 10% common. The Phoenicians developed contour farming and spread it around the Mediterranean, but the Romans preferred straight furrows, which became standard. The US government's soil-protection agency, set up in 1935 during the Dust Bowl, promoted it. It works only on slopes of 2% to 10% and below a certain rainfall. Steeper or wetter land adds strip cropping, and {{ref:soil-agri-073}} and {{ref:soil-agri-066}} make it more effective. In the similar practice of contour bunding, stones are placed along the contours of slopes.

soil-agri-103.title: Readying a cleared forest for new trees
soil-agri-103.text: Forests get their ground prepared too. Forest site preparation is any treatment applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting. It eases regeneration by improving access, reducing or rearranging slash, the debris logging leaves, and improving poor forest floor, soil or vegetation conditions. In Ontario around 1970 the most widely used technique was mechanical scarification, using bulldozer-mounted blades, rakes, V-ploughs or teeth, or tractor-drawn scarifiers. In a British Columbia disk-trenching trial, trees on south-, east- and west-facing microsites had larger tenth-year stem volumes than north-facing or untreated ones. Overall, choosing the planting spot mattered more than the trench's orientation.

soil-agri-105.title: Mounds that give seedlings a warm, bright start
soil-agri-105.text: Five days after planting, the soil in mounds had reached a mean of 10 °C at 10 cm depth. Untreated control ground took 58 days. Mounding is a forest site-preparation treatment that builds raised planting spots, and on cold, wet sites these have improved seedling performance. Mounds warmed fastest, averaging 10 and 7 °C warmer than the control at soil depths of 0.5 cm and 10 cm. In the first growing season they had 3 times as many days with mean soil temperature above 10 °C. They also received over 4 times the daily light energy reaching control microsites.

soil-agri-104.title: Burning logging slash, and what the fire does to the soil
soil-agri-104.text: One fire can make a soil a hundred times less acidic. Slash burning for site preparation is the broadcast or prescribed burning of logging slash, the debris left on cleared forest sites, to ready them for planting or seeding. It raises soil pH by as much as 2 units, a 100-fold change, and in central British Columbia the increase persisted more than a year. The higher pH may explain copper and iron deficiencies in white spruce foliage on burned clearcuts. Phosphorus availability rose after one burn and was still higher 21 months later, but in another study it fell below pre-burn levels within 9 months. Nitrogen is lost. Burns are patchy: in one 140-ha slash burn only 4% burned severely, 47% lightly and 49% not at all.

soil-agri-102.title: How tillage wears away ancient burial mounds
soil-agri-102.text: Powerful modern tractors did as much damage in six decades as traditional farming did in the previous six centuries. English Heritage reported that finding in 2003. Tillage and archaeology meet in the damage tilling does to buried ancient remains, such as long barrows. In the UK, half of the long barrows in Gloucestershire have been damaged, and almost all the burial mounds in Essex.

soil-agri-129.title: Crop residue, the leftovers that guard the soil
soil-agri-129.text: Farmers once treated it as trash. Crop residue is the stalks, stubble, leaves and other plant material left in a field after harvest. Keeping more than 50% of it on the surface benefits soil health, nutrient cycling, erosion control and microbial activity. Surface residue softens the impact of raindrops that break up soil particles, reducing splash and sheet erosion. It cuts evaporation, lowers surface soil temperature and reduces wind effects. As it decays, it opens routes for water to soak in quickly, reducing the need for supplemental irrigation. Residue cover even defines tillage systems: under 15% for {{ref:soil-agri-097}}, 15 to 30% for {{ref:soil-agri-098}}, and at least 30% for {{ref:soil-agri-099}}. Its nutrients return slowly. Leaving residues to decay returns their stored potassium. By the next year, though, cereal straw releases only about 10 to 15 percent of its nutrients, and pea residue about 35 percent. Nitrogen depends on the residue. Above 1.5 percent nitrogen it releases nitrogen quickly; below 1.2 percent, the microbes decomposing it immobilize soil nitrogen.

soil-agri-099.title: Conservation tillage: leave the residue, keep the soil
soil-agri-099.text: Conservation tillage is used on over 370 million acres, mostly in South America, Oceania and North America. It is a group of practices that reduce tillage and leave crop residue on the surface during the critical erosion period. The threshold is at least 30% residue cover, or at least 1,000 lb/ac (1,100 kg/ha) of small grain residue. The residue slows water movement and softens raindrop impact on soil particles, so less soil erodes. Researchers found a nearly 60 percent reduction in runoff losses, and the cover also guards the surface against crusting. Fewer passes over the field save fuel and labor and reduce soil compaction. Predatory arthropods that can help control pests benefit too. Its forms include {{ref:soil-agri-117}}, {{ref:soil-agri-120}}, mulch-till, ridge-till and rotational tillage, in which soil is tilled every two years or less often. In most years since 1997 it has covered more US cropland than the more intensive systems. By 2014 more than 75% of cropland on the Canadian Prairies had adopted it. Less exposed dark soil warms more slowly in spring, which delays planting of the next corn crop. Equipment designed to cut water erosion may not reduce tillage erosion.

soil-agri-117.title: No-till farming: growing crops without turning the soil
soil-agri-117.text: Between 1999 and 2009 the land farmed without tillage grew from about 45 million hectares to 111 million. No-till farming, also called zero tillage or direct drilling, grows crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage. Crops are sown into a plant cover killed with herbicide (sod seeding), through the previous crop's residue (direct seeding), or onto the bare surface (surface seeding). No-till means never tilling a field. It is one form of conservation tillage, as is {{ref:soil-agri-120}}, but the two terms are not equivalent. Organized opposition to ploughing began in the 1940s with Edward H. Faulkner's Plowman's Folly. Trials spread only after post-war herbicides such as paraquat. The area reached 72 million ha by 2003, and in 2014 South America held 47% of it. No-till cuts tillage-caused erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils. The top inch of no-till soil holds more aggregates and is two to seven times less vulnerable than ploughed soil. Surface residue helps rain and irrigation water infiltrate and limits evaporation, while each tillage pass loses around 0.85 to 1.9 cm of water to evaporation. Light-colored residue absorbs less solar energy than bare soil, so no-till soil warms and dries more slowly in spring, which may delay planting. Nitrogen immobilized in decomposing residue often reduces yields and calls for more fertilizer. After a transition, 4–5 years in Kansas, soil organic matter may build up.

soil-agri-097.title: Intensive tillage, the old conventional way
soil-agri-097.text: Speed buries residue. Faster travel with disks and deep-working ploughs, and steeper disk angles, bury more residue and so make tillage more intensive. Intensive tillage leaves less than 15% crop residue cover, or less than 500 pounds per acre (560 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the soil. It often takes several passes with a mouldboard, disk or deep-working plough of the kind in {{ref:soil-agri-111}}. A finisher with a harrow, rolling basket and cutter then readies the ground for seed. It is often called conventional tillage, meaning the operations standard for a place and crop, which tend to bury residues. In the United States, though, conservation tillage is now more widely used, so the label is often inappropriate.

soil-agri-098.title: Reduced tillage, the middle ground for residue
soil-agri-098.text: Between the bare field and the well-covered one lies reduced tillage. It leaves 15 to 30% crop residue cover, or 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (560 to 1100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, during the critical erosion period. It may use implements such as those in {{ref:soil-agri-111}} and {{ref:soil-agri-115}}. Tillage systems are compared by percentage residue for a simple reason: the amount of crop residue left on the surface affects soil loss by erosion.

soil-agri-118.title: Does no-till really store carbon in the soil?
soil-agri-118.text: No-till cuts nitrous oxide emissions by 40–70%, depending on rotation, and that gas is 300 times stronger than CO2 and lasts 120 years. Whether no-till also raises the organic carbon stored in soil is far less certain, and the sources disagree. Many studies report more {{ref:soil-env-108}} under no-till. Others find the effect absent in some systems, depending on factors such as climate and topsoil carbon content. Some question whether measured gains are real at all, or artifacts of flawed testing methods or other factors. A 2014 study found that the no-till subsurface layer often loses more organic carbon over time than the surface gains. It called for a uniform definition of sequestration, the locking away of carbon in soil. A 2020 study found no-till combined with cover cropping stores more carbon than either practice alone. Critics add that no-till may increase herbicide use, diminishing or eliminating its carbon benefits. One cooling effect does not depend on carbon in the soil. No-till croplands have a higher albedo, reflecting more sunlight, and that cooling is similar in magnitude to other biogeochemical processes that lock carbon away.

soil-agri-109.title: The mouldboard plough, which turns the soil upside down
soil-agri-109.text: A strip of sod rolls over and lands upside down. That is the work of the mouldboard plough. Its coulter cuts down into the soil and its share cuts horizontally, freeing the strip. The curved mould board then lifts the slice and turns it over into the previous furrow. General-purpose mould boards turn the slice gently for ploughing up to 200 mm deep. Digger boards shatter it at 300 mm or more, and semi-digger boards work at about 250 mm. The heavy iron mouldboard plough was invented in Han China in the 1st and 2nd centuries and later spread to the Netherlands. It greatly cut the time needed to prepare a field, and its ridges and furrows form channels that drain the soil. Ploughing to 20 cm aerates the soil and works in residues, manure, lime and fertilizer, speeding mineralization and cutting nitrogen loss by denitrification. It raises numbers of soil-eating endogeic earthworms but deters vertical-burrowing anecic ones. It leaves little surface residue against wind and water erosion, and over-ploughing can form a hardpan. Because it was hard to turn, it changed fields from mostly square plots into long rectangular strips, hence the furlong.

soil-agri-128.title: The three-field system: crops two years in three
soil-agri-128.text: An estate's arable land was split into three fields. In this crop rotation, a field grows one set of crops in the first year, a different set in the second, and lies fallow in the third. One field was sown in autumn with winter wheat or rye, one with peas, lentils or beans, and one was left fallow. The legumes fixed nitrogen that the cereals depleted, and livestock grazing the weedy fallow fertilized it with their excrement. Each field was cropped two years in three, whereas the older two-field system left half the land fallow. First used in China in the Eastern Zhou period, it spread in Europe from the 9th to the 11th century alongside the mouldboard plough. Summer-dry Mediterranean lands suited it less.

soil-agri-119.title: Controlling weeds when the plough stays out
soil-agri-119.text: Without tillage, something else has to kill the weeds. Weed management in no-till uses herbicides, cover plantings, mowing or crimping in place of cultivation. Herbicides such as glyphosate replace tillage for preparing the ground for seed, so no-till uses more herbicide than conventional tillage. Residue left on the surface can also bring different, greater or more frequent disease and weed problems than tilled fields have. Weed-suppressing cover plantings, described in {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, add organic residue but must be killed, typically by crimping at flowering, and the crop is planted through the remaining mulch. Herbicides are not strictly necessary, as natural farming and {{ref:soil-env-218}} show. Winter cover plantings, soil solarization and burning are alternatives.

soil-agri-127.title: Making unfarmable land grow crops
soil-agri-127.text: On the rocky Aran Islands off Ireland, people spread a shallow layer of seaweed and sand to grow crops. The islands still count as non-arable. Conversion to arable land means making land that cannot grow crops capable of cultivation. It may require irrigation canals, wells, desalination, fertilizer, pesticides, {{ref:soil-agri-061}} or heated greenhouses, and it is often prohibitively expensive. Slash-and-burn farming draws on nutrients in wood ash, but these are used up within a few years. Terra preta soils were made fertile by adding charcoal.

soil-agri-124.title: Keyline design: steering runoff so it soaks in
soil-agri-124.text: Even ordinary contour ploughing drifts off the contour, sending runoff off ridges and into valleys. Keyline design is P. A. Yeomans' system of planning farm landscapes around the natural flow of water, to make the best use of their water resources. The keyline is the contour through the keypoint, where a valley floor suddenly steepens. Cultivating parallel to it drifts runoff away from the valley center, delaying runoff concentration and giving water more time to infiltrate. Its Keyline Scale of Permanence orders farm elements from landshape and water supply through roads and structures to fences. Philipp Gerhardt's Seepage Line System replaces fixed keylines with custom contour ditches, and trials in Germany show it reduces surface runoff.

soil-agri-107.title: The ard, an ox-drawn scratch plough
soil-agri-107.text: Oxen domesticated in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BC, supplied the draft power that made the ard possible. The ard is the early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share, a cutting blade, through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow. A ploughed field from about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan, India. The ard left undisturbed strips between furrows, so fields were cross-ploughed both ways, which tended to form the squarish plots described in {{ref:soil-hist-099}}. It suits loamy or sandy soils renewed by floods, as in the Nile Delta and Fertile Crescent, and it struggled in northern Europe's heavy soils.

soil-agri-111.title: The chisel plough, which loosens deep and leaves the cover
soil-agri-111.text: Most ploughs turn the soil over; the chisel plough does not. It is a plough for deep tillage that loosens and aerates soil while leaving crop residue on the surface. That suits no-till and low-till farming, and some consider it more sustainable than the mouldboard plough. It can reduce the effects of compaction and help break up hardpans, including {{ref:soil-agri-101}}. In essence it is a heavy-duty version of the tool in {{ref:soil-agri-115}}, working 15 cm to 46 cm deep. Each shank needs 10 to 20 horsepower (7.5 to 14.9 kW). The lighter tool's teeth work near the surface, mainly against weeds, so they need far less power per shank.

soil-agri-110.title: The heavy plough that made farming communal
soil-agri-110.text: Pulling a heavy plough took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had. So farming became communal, and the manorial system rose. The heavy plough was a wheeled plough heavy enough to carry a large metal-faced mould board, and so to work the heavy soils of northern Europe. By the Han period Chinese ploughshares were wholly cast iron, the earliest known heavy iron mould-board ploughs. In Europe, adoption of the carruca heavy plough accompanied the three-field system in the later 8th and early 9th centuries, raising yields per unit of land. Heavy ploughs raised food production, coinciding with a marked rise in world population in the second millennium AD.

soil-agri-108.title: Hoe cultivation, where farming began
soil-agri-108.text: Agriculture began with the digging stick and the hoe. Hoe cultivation is turning soil with these hand-held tools. In very fertile areas such as the Nile banks, renewed by the annual flood, hoes cut furrows for seeds. Digging sticks, hoes and mattocks arose in many places, and hoe cultivation must have been common wherever farming was practiced. It is the traditional tillage of tropical and subtropical regions with stony soils, steep slopes, root crops and widely spaced coarse grains.

soil-agri-113.title: The mole plough, which drains a field from below
soil-agri-113.text: A mole plough builds a drain without digging a trench. This deep plough has a torpedo-shaped tip that leaves a drainage channel underground, or breaks up deep impermeable layers.
