Its bullet-shaped share forms a tunnel about 75 mm (3.0 in) across, and an expander presses the soil outward into a long-lasting channel. Mole drains lie up to 950 mm (37 in) deep at an angle to pipe drains, into which their water seeps and runs to a ditch. Heavy land needs such draining to bring its water content down to a level efficient for plant growth. A simple field test tells whether a subsoil suits moling. If a pencil pushed through a hand-compacted, tennis-ball-sized sample from moling depth leaves the ball unsplit, it does.

soil-agri-115.title: The cultivator, which stirs the soil around the crop
soil-agri-115.text: A harrow disturbs the whole soil surface, while a cultivator works in careful patterns that spare the crop plants. This farm implement for secondary tillage takes two forms. One is a frame with teeth dragged through the soil; the other is a machine with rotating disks or teeth, such as a rotary tiller. Before planting, it stirs and pulverizes soil to aerate it and prepare a smooth, loose bed for seeds. After the crop emerges, it kills weeds. Toothed cultivators resemble chisel ploughs, but their teeth work near the surface, while chisel shanks work deep to break hardened layers. Field cultivators also bury residue to help warm the soil, and mix the soil so the crop has enough water and nutrients.

soil-agri-122.title: Vertical tillage, a method without a settled definition
soil-agri-122.text: What counts as vertical tillage varies considerably, even among its proponents. Broadly, it is a set of tillage principles that, like {{ref:soil-agri-065}}, aims to improve soil health, raise infiltration and reduce erosion and compaction. It avoids inverting the soil and keeps residue on the surface. Small forward-facing discs slice the residue so it decomposes faster. It often adds a deep ripping tool to break hard pans and compaction left by traditional implements and heavy machinery such as combine harvesters. Its place is disputed. Proponents class it with no-till and with that wider approach, while detractors say its vigorous soil movement excludes it. The quarrel matters because US payments promote no-till.

soil-agri-125.title: The moisture at which soil crumbles best
soil-agri-125.text: Till a soil too wet or too dry and it comes up in large clods. The optimum water content for tillage is the soil moisture at which tillage breaks the soil into the largest number of small aggregates. Missing it damages structure and raises the readily dispersible clay content. The optimum can be related to the water content at the lower plastic limit; for several soils it equals 0.9 times the plastic limit. That link has limits. The plastic limit is measured on molded rather than undisturbed soil, and many sandy soils have no plastic limit. Friability, the tendency to crumble, peaks at the plastic limit. Yet many clay soils drain so slowly that they stay wetter than it unless plant roots draw the water out.

soil-agri-116.title: The seedbed, a seed's first home in the soil
soil-agri-116.text: The smaller the seed, the finer the soil it needs. A seedbed is the local soil environment into which seeds are planted. It should be loose and smooth, without large lumps, so seeds go in easily at the depth that germinates them best. Preparation breaks up compacted soil so air and water can enter and seedlings can push through. On farms, secondary tillage with harrows and cultivators usually does the work, perhaps after primary tillage with mouldboard or chisel ploughs. No-till skips this step. Organic matter such as compost or peat may be added to improve the seedbed's soil structure.

soil-agri-121.title: Minimum tillage: only as much as the crop needs
soil-agri-121.text: Minimum tillage avoids primary tillage entirely. This system for conserving soil keeps manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over. Secondary tillage is practiced only to a small extent. The system also includes minimum furrowing, organic fertilizer, biological pest control and minimal use of chemicals. Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or {{ref:soil-agri-120}}.

soil-agri-120.title: Strip-till: tilling only where the seed will go
soil-agri-120.text: Each tilled row is usually only about eight to ten inches wide. Strip-till is a minimum-tillage conservation system that tills just the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled. It combines the soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till. Also called zone tillage, it breaks up compacted layers under the row, prepares a seedbed and improves internal drainage. Breaking the crust lets air in and speeds organic matter decay, yet a two-year study found no change in organic carbon or extractable phosphorus. Fertilizer can be placed directly in the seed row during strip-tilling, so less is needed and it sits closer to the roots. Combined implements can cut field trips to two or even one, saving time and fuel and reducing compaction. Strip-till conserves more moisture than intensive tillage, though sometimes less than no-till, and its erosion is light by comparison with intensive tillage. At one low-phosphorus site it yielded 43.5 bushels/acre (2,925.5 kg/ha) against 41.5 bu/a (2,791 kg/ha) under no-till. Its yields match intensive tillage without the cost.

soil-agri-130.title: Controlled traffic farming: wheels stay in their lanes
soil-agri-130.text: Random traffic compacts about 75% of a field in one season and all of it by the second. Controlled traffic farming confines all machinery loads to the smallest possible area of permanent traffic lanes. A proper system cuts tracking to 15%, always in the same place. It needs matched implement and wheel track widths, with machines kept in the same lanes every year. That is easiest with RTK satellite guidance and auto-steer accurate to about ± 2 cm. Untracked soil gains porosity, infiltration and drainage, with less erosion and waterlogging and better rooting. Most adopters till little or not at all, because the structure no longer needs repair. The drawbacks are a high initial investment and the need for GPS guidance and adapted machines, but compacted soils can take more than 5 years to recover.

soil-agri-101.title: The plough pan, a hard floor made by tillage
soil-agri-101.text: Tillage that loosens the surface can harden the soil beneath it. A plough pan, also called a tillage pan, is a compacted layer of soil created by tillage. Continued cultivation and traffic create compacted, impermeable layers within the soil profile. Over-ploughing can form a hardpan, which farmers usually break with a subsoiler that slices through the hardened layer deep below the surface. Chisel ploughs and zone tillage are also used to break up plough pans.

soil-agri-112.title: Subsoiling: breaking hard layers below the plough's reach
soil-agri-112.text: Most tillage tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in) of soil. A subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more. Subsoiling is deep tillage with this implement, whose heavy shanks break up soil below the depth reached by ploughs, harrows or rototillers. Angled wings on the shanks lift and shatter the hardpan that compaction builds, improving crop growth wherever compaction is a problem. Afterward, roots reach deeper moisture and nutrients in hot, dry seasons. In wet weather, water drains through the shattered zones, so crops are less likely to drown. The work is slow and power-hungry: pulling one point through hard soil takes 60 to 100 horsepower (45 to 75 kW). The shanks should reach 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in) below the deepest compacted layer. A subsoiler is not a mole plough, which cuts underground drainage channels. In-row subsoiling counts among the conservation tillage practices. On poorly drained land, deep tillage may substitute for costlier tile drainage. It may also be needed where a clay-enriched lower horizon becomes too compacted.

soil-agri-059.title: Keeping topsoil in place and fertile
soil-agri-059.text: Farmers have practiced soil conservation for millennia. The ancient Phoenicians already plowed along the contour on slopes of two to ten percent. Soil conservation means preventing two kinds of loss. One is topsoil carried away by erosion. The other is fertility worn down by overuse, {{ref:soil-chem-001}}, salinization or chemical contamination. The stakes can be total. Deforestation typically brings large-scale erosion and lost nutrients, and sometimes complete {{ref:soil-env-072}}. Salinity alone is estimated to affect about one third of the earth's arable land. It is left behind when irrigation water evaporates, or when it rises from shallow saline water tables. The techniques include crop rotation, {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, conservation tillage and rows of trees planted against the wind, and each works on erosion and fertility together. Organic matter pays off in water: each one percent increase in soil organic matter helps soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre. Governments joined in on a large scale after the Dust Bowl, starting in Franklin D. Roosevelt's first 100 days in 1933. In Europe, the Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, crops kept over winter to cover the soil, plant residues and grass margins. Yet erosion is not only a farming problem. How land is valued is a governance hurdle, so solving erosion also takes political and economic action, and cultural change can shift it.

soil-agri-066.title: Cover crops: plants grown to protect, not to sell
soil-agri-066.text: Some crops are never meant for market. A cover crop is planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested. Farmers often sow it off-season, after the cash crop comes in, and let it grow over winter. Often its only job is to fight erosion. Its leaves shield the surface and scatter the energy of falling raindrops. It slows water flowing over the ground and lets more of it soak in, while its roots anchor the soil and open new pores. Below ground it stirs up microbial activity, which makes more nitrogen available to the next crop and can lift yields. A meta-analysis of 102 field studies measured these effects against bare or fallow ground. Saturated hydraulic conductivity, the ease with which water flows through soaked soil, rose about 106%. Topsoil organic carbon rose about 10% and nitrogen about 20%. Microbial biomass carbon climbed about 20%, and particulate organic carbon nearly 50%. The benefits come with trade-offs. A cover crop may use water the next crop needs, or leave yields unchanged, especially in semi-arid regions or when it is killed at the wrong time. Before the cash crop goes in, farmers end it by mowing, tilling, discing, rolling or spraying herbicide. In all, cover crops touch erosion, fertility, soil quality, water, weeds, pests, diseases, biodiversity and wildlife. They also act as nurse crops that help the main crop survive.

soil-agri-063.title: Soil management: keeping fields productive for decades
soil-agri-063.text: Conventional and organic farms alike need soil management to stay productive over decades. It means applying operations, practices and treatments that protect soil and improve how it performs, from its fertility to its mechanical behavior. It takes in soil conservation, soil amendment and the pursuit of optimal soil health. Organic farming leans on it hardest, since soil health supplies almost all of its fertility and pest control. Controlling traffic on the surface limits compaction, which can cut aeration and water infiltration. Cover crops keep soil anchored and covered off-season. Rotations alternate high- and low-residue crops to keep plant material on the surface against erosion. Conventional tillage disturbs soil most deeply, while reduced tillage and no-till keep residues in place. Fertilizers add nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and potassium, but they often acidify soils; potassium fertilizer is the exception. Organic matter added to the surface can raise the carbon stored in soil and the abundance and diversity of soil microbes. Project Drawdown counts improved nutrient management, {{ref:soil-agri-065}} and regenerative agriculture among the soil steps for slowing climate change.

soil-agri-073.title: Terraces: staircases carved into hillsides
soil-agri-073.text: On steep ground, farmers have long cut the slope into a staircase. Each step is a terrace, a flat surface carved into a hill or mountainside for growing crops. Terraced fields reduce both erosion and surface runoff, and they can hold irrigated crops such as rice. Terracing is more common on small farms. Terraced paddies carry rice, wheat and barley across much of Asia, the Mediterranean Basin, Africa and South America. Terrace farming in the Levant goes back as early as the 4th millennium BCE. Terraces in the Yemen Highlands date from the start of the Bronze Age, in the 3rd millennium BC. In the Andes, the Wari and others built terraces called andenes before 1000 AD, to use shallow soil efficiently and irrigate crops; the Inca later adopted them. Dates from the method covered in {{ref:soil-hist-124}} show a major burst of Mediterranean terrace building in the later Middle Ages, around AD 1100–1600. Some dates remain unsettled. Scholars disagree on when the terraces of the Jerusalem Mountains were built, from the Bronze Age to the Roman and Byzantine periods. Such dates there may reflect later modification. Long-term moisture management by terracing can even create anthraquic Anthrosols.

soil-agri-140.title: Agroforestry: farming with the forest as a model
soil-agri-140.text: The forester John Bene coined the word agroforestry in 1973, but the practices it names are millennia old. Agroforestry is a land use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture. It is managed to optimize the interactions among plants and animals, with the forest as its model, which makes it applied agroecology. Groundcover protects depleted soil from erosion, and trees slow runoff and evaporation so more water soaks in. Nitrogen-fixing plants such as legumes can restore soil nitrogen fertility. Carbon can build up in both soil and woody biomass. The USDA lists five temperate practices: alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture and {{ref:soil-agri-061}}. In Honduras, the Quesungual system replaced slash-and-burn hillside farming, whose exposed soil washed away. It keeps nitrogen-fixing trees that cut erosion and hold moisture. In 2025, 91 countries and areas reported 55.4 million hectares under agroforestry, most of it in Asia.

soil-agri-061.title: Windbreaks: rows of trees that hold the soil down
soil-agri-061.text: A few rows of trees can change the climate of a whole field. A windbreak, also called a shelterbelt, is one or more rows of trees or shrubs planted to shelter land from the wind and protect soil from erosion. Shelterbelts run perpendicular to the prevailing wind, while woodlots are more extensive areas of woodland. Behind a windbreak, the wind is slowest at about 3 to 5 times the windbreak's height downwind, then recovers. Evergreens protect all year, but deciduous trees may be enough if they are in leaf while the soil is bare. Farmers plant windbreaks to cut wind erosion of loess, and very light soils need them in dry weather. Besides sharply reducing erosion, they reduce evapotranspiration, improve the microclimate for crops, shelter beneficial birds, sequester carbon and improve the landscape. They separate fields and shield them from pesticide spray drift. They hold snow on fields, where it supplies water as it melts in spring. With woodlots, they help fix the soil against {{ref:soil-env-072}}.

soil-agri-072.title: Strip farming: alternating bands that act as dams
soil-agri-072.text: Where a slope is too steep, or no other method can prevent erosion, farmers turn to strips. Strip farming, also called strip cropping, divides a field into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation. Strips of close-sown hay, wheat or forage, serving mainly as cover crops, alternate with row crops such as corn, soybeans, cotton or sugar beets. Laid out along the approximate contour, the sod strips act as natural dams. They slow water and hold back soil washing from the cultivated strips. Strips are usually 25 feet (7.6 m) to 75 feet (23 m) wide, and 50 feet (15 m) suits most machinery. On the dry-farmed Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, strips run at right angles to the wind. Contour strip cropping, used mainly on gentle slopes, makes the protective strips wider so they intercept runoff. In strip intercropping, narrower contiguous strips suit machinery and let neighboring crops benefit from each other. In the Midwestern United States, strips of native plants, described in {{ref:soil-agri-142}}, serve as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters that build soil health and curb erosion.

soil-agri-067.title: Green manures: cover crops that feed the soil
soil-agri-067.text: Some cover crops are grown not to guard the soil but to feed it. Fertility-building cover crops are called green manures, and they are often plowed under before they mature. Legumes do this best. Their roots are nodulated by bacteria such as Bradyrhizobium, which fix nitrogen from the air into ammonium. A leguminous cover crop can often supply all the nitrogen a crop needs. This ability to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer is called fertilizer replacement value. It matters beyond the farm. Nitrogen fertilizer lost to waterways causes {{ref:soil-env-020}}, as in the Gulf of Mexico's summer dead zone of over 22,000 square kilometers. Some scientists see biological nitrogen fixation, mainly through cover crops, as the only alternative to fossil-fuel-dependent industrial nitrogen fixation for future food production. Other nutrients can benefit too. In Nigeria, a velvet bean cover crop increased soil phosphorus availability after rock phosphate was applied.

soil-agri-065.title: Conservation agriculture: disturb little, cover always
soil-agri-065.text: Tillage was once thought to raise fertility. It is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting. Conservation agriculture is one response. The FAO defines it as a farming system that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land. It rests on minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species. Plowing is eliminated or greatly reduced, as in no-till farming, and mulch or cover crops keep the ground covered. The mulch slows runoff, softens raindrop impact, and keeps soil moister and warmer than yearly tillage would. With less plowing, earthworms thrive and a mull-like agricultural humus form called agri-mull develops. Mineral fertilizer is cut to the crop's strict requirements and is sometimes unnecessary. No-till can save producers 30% to 40% of their time and labor. The drawbacks are real. Benefits can take many years, new planters or drills cost money, and in developing countries the residues it needs are traditionally fed to livestock. With regenerative and organic agriculture, it counts as sustainable agriculture.

soil-agri-076.title: Soil stabilization: engineering weak ground for roads
soil-agri-076.text: A road is only as strong as the ground beneath it. Soil stabilization is any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose. It raises the bearing capacity, tensile strength and overall performance of unstable subsoils, sands and waste materials, chiefly to strengthen roads. Traditional binders for a road base are bitumen, tar emulsions, asphalt, cement and lime, along with fly ash, cement kiln dust and tree resins. Each has drawbacks. Bitumen is not environmentally friendly and turns brittle when dry, and Portland cement is often expensive. Newer stabilizers include enzymes, surfactants, synthetic and bio-polymers, fiber reinforcement and chloride salts. Some form water-repelling layers that keep out water and frost. Many so-called green products work like soap powder, only lubricating and realigning the soil without binding it. Many new approaches rely instead on clay's own binding properties. The Deep Mixing Method injects through a small probe to strengthen weak or loose soil strata and repair sinkholes. Adding stabilizing materials can also limit a soil's ability to shrink and swell.

soil-agri-062.title: Fewer pesticides, healthier soil
soil-agri-062.text: Pesticides do not vanish after spraying. They can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time, and they affect soil structure and its living and nonliving makeup. Cutting their use is one way to protect soil. Alternatives include irradiation, cultivation methods, biological controls such as pheromones and microbial pesticides, genetic engineering and disrupting insect breeding. Composted yard waste has also controlled pests. Researchers have studied policy tools too, among them differentiated taxation schemes.

soil-agri-060.title: Soil-conservation farming and its critics
soil-agri-060.text: Repeated plowing degrades soil and kills its beneficial fungi and earthworms. Soil-conservation farming avoids that harm by combining no-till, green manures and other soil-enhancing practices. No-till and cover crops hold nitrogen and other nutrients, raising soil organic matter. Advocates say it can revive damaged soil and minimize erosion at lower labor and cost. They add that it can remove the need for nitrogen fertilizer or fungicide and protect crops in drought or flood. Critics disagree. They call no-till and related methods impractical and costly, cite advantages of conventional tillage in some settings, and say no-till complicates pest control and residue management.

soil-agri-064.title: How farm soils can warm or cool the climate
soil-agri-064.text: Farm soil can work on either side of the climate ledger. Management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide in the soil, described in {{ref:soil-env-108}}. Fertilizer use, irrigation and tillage all contribute to nitrous oxide emissions, and soil management accounts for over half of the agriculture sector's emissions. Using biochar may cut nitrous oxide emissions from soils by an average of 54%. Converting natural land to farmland releases carbon. How much carbon a soil can store depends on climate, land-use history and management. Cropland could sequester 0.5–1.2 Pg C/year, and grazing and pasture land 0.3–0.7 Pg C/year. Storage rises with more biomass inputs, smaller losses of that stored carbon and a longer mean residence time for that carbon. No-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation significantly enhance carbon storage in soil. All four are more common in organic than in conventional farming.

soil-agri-069.title: How cover crops steer rain into the ground
soil-agri-069.text: Cover crops change the path rain takes through a field. Their biomass shields the surface from rain, and their roots open pores that let water filter down instead of running off. Greater infiltration can improve soil water storage and aquifer recharge. Because they curb erosion, cover crops also reduce the rate and amount of water draining off fields, a risk to waterways downstream. Where water is scarce, cover crops used as mulch shade and cool the surface, reducing evaporation.

soil-agri-071.title: Cover crops that trap pests and fight disease
soil-agri-071.text: White mustard and radish set a trap. Nematodes enter the roots of these resistant plants but cannot reproduce there, and their populations fall by 70–99%. Cover crops can break pest and disease cycles, lure pests away as trap crops and attract the pests' natural enemies. Mustards and other Brassicaceae suppress fungal diseases with toxic chemicals, released as compounds in the plants called glucosinolates break down. Grasses, legumes and brassicas also raise soil organic matter and microbial activity, making cash crops more resilient to insect pests and pathogens. Findings on predators and pests are mixed, though, so effects depend on the cover crop and its management.

soil-agri-070.title: Smothering weeds with a cover crop
soil-agri-070.text: A cover crop fights weeds twice: by competing with them while it grows, and by smothering or poisoning them after it dies. Flattened on the surface, it forms a nearly impenetrable mat that blocks light and cuts weed germination. This is the smother effect. Some cover crops also release compounds that inhibit other plants, the process called allelopathy. Rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards all do this. After termination, yellow sweetclover residues held weeds 75–97% below their levels in fallow systems. Rye residues used as mulch gave 80% to 95% control of early-season broadleaf weeds.

soil-agri-075.title: Contour trenches that catch the rain
soil-agri-075.text: On a dry hillside, rain that runs straight off is rain lost. Contour trenching digs continuous trenches along a slope's contour to conserve water and soil and raise crop yields. Each trench catches water flowing downhill so it soaks into the soil. Crops between the trenches draw on this subsoil reserve during the drier growing season, so they suffer less from later water shortage. Fertile particles are no longer lost to water and wind erosion. Each trench must hold all the water, with its upslope side protected by grass, shrubs or fabric. It is one of the techniques used to reverse {{ref:soil-env-072}}.

soil-agri-079.title: The 1936 law that paid farmers to save soil
soil-agri-079.text: The Supreme Court declared the Agricultural Adjustment Act unconstitutional, and Congress passed the Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936 in its wake. This US federal law let the government pay farmers to cut production in order to conserve soil and prevent erosion. It amended and renamed the Soil Conservation Act of 1935, to preserve soil fertility and reduce the exploitation and unprofitable use of national soil resources. Landlords now had to share the payments with the sharecroppers and tenants who worked their land. On the Dust Bowl's high plains, the act directed conservation work: educating farmers and planting trees and native grass.

soil-agri-081.title: Lynchets: the stepped hillsides of ancient Britain
soil-agri-081.text: A lynchet is an earth terrace on a hillside, typical of the ancient field systems of the British Isles. The word is the diminutive of lynch, an old term for an agricultural terrace. Lynchets often run in vertical rows, called strip lynchets, mostly in southern Britain near Iron Age forts and older earthworks. The traditional theory credits long plowing, which makes soil slip downslope. That builds a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops. Yet the size, spacing and number of rows show that many were man-made, most likely dug to make the most of land for farming.

soil-agri-074.title: Terracettes: the catsteps of steep pastures
soil-agri-074.text: Steep pastures are often ribbed with small, irregular steps. These terracettes, also called catsteps or cattle terracing, are roughly parallel, step-like ridges on a steep hillside. How they form is disputed. Darwin (1904) thought grazing animals made them, and trampling sheep or cattle do worsen soil creep and surface erosion. But some end abruptly at rock faces or soil changes, and livestock trails cut across others. Geomorphologists doubt animals alone could form such regular steps. Soil processes offer another explanation. Saturated soil swells, then shrinks as it dries, so particles creep slowly downhill; freeze–thaw and heating–cooling cycles can do the same.

soil-agri-080.title: The Great Plains Shelterbelt: 220 million trees against dust
soil-agri-080.text: In 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt answered the Dust Bowl's dust storms with trees. The Great Plains Shelterbelt was a US project to plant windbreaks across the Great Plains states. Trees around farms were meant to cut wind speed and soil moisture loss. The first tree, an Austrian pine, went into an Oklahoma farm in 1935. Farmers were paid to plant and tend native trees such as red cedar and green ash along fence rows. By 1942, 30,233 shelterbelts held 220 million trees over 18,600 square miles (48,000 km2). They filled a 100-mile wide zone from North Dakota's Canadian border to the Brazos River in Texas. By 2010 many were old and declining, and federal grants funded their renovation in Kansas, North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska.

soil-agri-141.title: Check dams: small barriers that slow the flow
soil-agri-141.text: A low wall of rocks across a ditch can slow it down. A check dam is a small, sometimes temporary dam built across a swale, ditch or waterway to counter erosion by slowing the water. Builders use rocks, gravel, logs, hay bales or sandbags, and the dam is usually less than 2 to 3 feet high. It flattens the channel gradient, so the flow slows, more water soaks in and erosion drops. Coarse and medium sediment settles behind it while finer grains pass through, but it is not mainly a sediment trap. In arid areas, check dams are built to increase groundwater recharge.

soil-agri-068.title: Catch crops: grabbing leftover nitrogen between harvests
soil-agri-068.text: After a harvest, surplus nitrogen from the last crop often lingers in the soil. A catch crop is a fast-growing crop, a type of cover crop, grown between two successive main crops. Usually a fast-growing cereal, it takes up that leftover nitrogen before leaching, denitrification or volatilization can carry it off. The nitrogen returns to the soil when the crop is worked in as green manure or decomposes. Its residue roughens the surface against splash and runoff, and its decaying roots leave biopores, channels that increase infiltration. Sowing date, harvest date and tillage decide its benefit, and sowing later than recommended reduces its nitrogen uptake.

soil-agri-078.title: Magnesium chloride: a salty answer to road dust
soil-agri-078.text: Magnesium chloride pulls water out of the air at a relative humidity of just 32%. Spread on unpaved roads and dusty sites, it keeps the surface damp and binds gravel and clay particles to the road, so fine particles stay grounded. It works better in humid than in arid climates, and its chief benefit is lower maintenance costs for gravel roads. Its use is controversial. Advocates cite cleaner air and safer roads. Yet the dissolved salts reach groundwater and surface water, where chloride above 250 mg/L is regulated. Salts building up in roadside soils harm plants, partly by raising the osmotic pressure of the soil solution.

soil-agri-077.title: Geogrids and geocells: holding soil grains in place
soil-agri-077.text: A soil layer grows stronger when its particles cannot move. Mechanical soil stabilization confines them, for example with geogrids or three-dimensional geocells. Geogrids confine aggregate by interlocking with it. Geocells hold it by the hoop stress of their cell walls, the tension running around each cell. On Swedish forest roads, geocell-reinforced sections markedly raised bearing capacity and reduced permanent deformation under repeated traffic. Locally sourced infill may perform as well as or better than imported crushed aggregate. Better drainage, for instance with stone mattresses, also stabilizes roads by removing excess pore water and spreading loads.

soil-agri-142.title: Prairie strips: a tenth of a field that guards the rest
soil-agri-142.text: Giving 10% of a corn field to native plants can reduce sediment movement by 95%. Prairie strips are strips of native perennial vegetation placed within row-crop fields to protect soil and water and support biodiversity. The same set-aside cuts runoff losses of phosphorus by 90% and of nitrogen by 85%. Native prairie plants stabilize soil and concentrate more organic carbon in it than corn and soybean do. Farmers place the strips as contour buffers and edge-of-field filters, often on hard-to-farm areas. They also supported twice as many aphid-eating insects as soybean fields.

soil-agri-082.title: Soil survey: putting an area's soils on the map
soil-agri-082.text: For decades, a US county's soil survey arrived as a printed book, and it could take years to publish. A soil survey, also called soil mapping, classifies the soil types and other soil properties of an area and records where each one lies. It applies soil science and draws heavily on geomorphology, physical geography, patterns of vegetation and land use, and theories of {{ref:soil-form-042}}. Its primary data come from field sampling and from remote sensing, mainly aerial photography. LiDAR and other digital techniques are steadily gaining ground. In the second half of the 20th century, soil mapping meant field survey and drawing soil-type boundaries by hand. Map scales varied by country and purpose. Surveyors carried paper air photos, topographic maps and mapping keys. Many now carry a rugged tablet with GPS, digital imagery, LiDAR and soil geodatabases. In the United States, the program described in {{ref:soil-hist-051}} once published a book for each county. A typical county survey held a general map of soils and a detailed map of indexed soil series. It added a section on soil use and management, and tables of land-use suitability. Today surveys appear on the web, the story of {{ref:soil-agri-170}}, through a service run by the federal agency known as the NRCS, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. There users build custom surveys, and changes go live in moments. The agency has maps and data online for more than 95 percent of US counties.

soil-agri-084.title: The soil map, from hand-drawn polygons to predicted grids
soil-agri-084.text: Farmers who practice precision agriculture read soil maps to adjust what they put on each field. A soil map shows where soil types lie across an area, or how properties such as pH, texture, organic matter or horizon depth vary. It is usually the product of a soil survey. Traditional maps show only the general distribution of soils and accompany the survey report. Some maps are hand-drawn polygons of soil types. Others predict or simulate soil properties in two or three dimensions, or predict soil classes. Maps of primary attributes show what was described or measured in the field. Maps of secondary, inferred attributes show properties for a use, such as production capacity or degradation. Most maps serve land evaluation, spatial planning, agricultural extension and environmental protection. Many new ones come from {{ref:soil-agri-089}}. They show more detail but are not necessarily more accurate, though statistical maps can include an estimate of their own uncertainty.

soil-agri-088.title: Prime farmland: the best soils, and the cities on them
soil-agri-088.text: Many cities grew up in rich farming country, so the best land for crops is often well suited to houses too. The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) calls the best of it prime farmland. This land has the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fiber and oilseed crops, and it is still available for those uses. Its soil quality, growing season and moisture supply give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management. It generally has a dependable water supply and a favorable temperature and growing season. Its acidity or alkalinity is acceptable, as is its salt and sodium content, and it has few or no rocks. It is not excessively erodible or long saturated with water. It either rarely floods or is protected from flooding. The designation helps growth management keep such land farmed, through zoning, conservation easements and green belts. Three USDA designations complement it: farmland of statewide importance, farmland of local importance and unique farmland. Unique farmland is used for specific high-value crops such as nuts, olives, cranberries and citrus. State and local agencies set the criteria for the statewide and local categories in cooperation with the USDA. Preserving prime soils is hard where they cover less than 60% of an area. A universal way to mark them out, joining science and policy, is still needed.

soil-agri-087.title: Germany's soil value, scored from 0 to 100
soil-agri-087.text: Germany's soil value, or Bodenwertzahl, rates soil quality from 0, very low, to 100, very high. For arable land it combines field assessments of soil type, soil development and parent material. It expresses the soil's relative net income under proper management. Heavy to clayey loams score 31–50, partly loess-covered loams 51–70 and loess-covered loams 71–90. Adjusting for terrain, climate and location gives the field value, or Ackerzahl. It began with the Reich Soil Assessment under the 1934 Soil Assessment Act, which set a Magdeburg Börde farm at 100 for farm tax ratings. A record 102.8 was later measured near Hildesheim.

soil-agri-089.title: Digital soil mapping hands the pen to computers
soil-agri-089.text: ISRIC's world maps, described in {{ref:soil-meth-017}}, cover the whole globe at 250 m resolution, and machine learning drew them. They are a product of digital soil mapping, also called predictive soil mapping: the computer-assisted production of maps of soil types and soil properties. The Working Group on Digital Soil Mapping defines it as building geographically referenced soil databases at a set resolution. Field and laboratory observations are linked to environmental data by quantitative relationships. In traditional mapping, field soil scientists draw boundaries by hand, though those maps can also be digitized. Digital mapping relies on GPS, field scanners and remote sensing, plus geostatistical interpolation, GIS, grids of ground-surface heights ({{ref:soil-agri-164}}) and data mining. It tries to overcome old maps that often only outline soil classes, offer no basis for modeling changing soil, and resist quantitative study of soil function. Semi-automated methods lower costs. The products are routinely checked for accuracy and uncertainty, and they are easier to update as new data arrive. EU maps of texture and bulk density, for example, rest on about 20,000 LUCAS topsoil samples.

soil-agri-083.title: Reading a soil survey for farms, buildings and gardens
soil-agri-083.text: Survey data are of little use to a planner until someone interprets them. Soil survey interpretation uses survey information to predict the potentials and limitations of soils for particular uses, such as crops, building or gardens. Farmers and ranchers learn whether a soil suits crops or livestock and what management it needs. Architects and engineers use soil engineering properties to judge construction sites. The predictions guide land use and management on areas from small tracts to several million acres. They must still be weighed with economic, social and environmental considerations before becoming valid land-use recommendations. Published US surveys include land-use suitability tables based on NRCS standards.

soil-found-069.title: The European Soil Database, one grid for a continent
soil-found-069.text: Europe has only one harmonized soil database, and many other soil data, information and services draw on it. The European Soil Database is based on experts' knowledge. The European Commission's LUCAS topsoil survey adds sampled soil data across the European Union. Its v2 Raster Library holds public-domain grids of 1 km x 1 km cells, aligned with the INSPIRE reference grid. They cover texture, parent material, WRB soil type, soil depth, mineralogy, cation exchange capacity and available water capacity. Combined with land cover, climate and topography data, it gives the most homogeneous data on the organic carbon content of European soils.

soil-agri-086.title: SSURGO, the database behind US soil surveys
soil-agri-086.text: The soil surveys that once filled county books now sit in a database. SSURGO, the Soil Survey Geographic database, is digital soil data produced and distributed by the NRCS. It is the dataset in which the NRCS maintains its soil information. It records soil types and where they occur, their characteristics and properties, and their limits, risks and suitability for various uses. Its data reach users through the online service described in {{ref:soil-agri-170}}, which the NRCS runs as the single authoritative source of US soil survey information.

soil-agri-092.title: Pedometrics: measuring soil with mathematics
soil-agri-092.text: The name says it plainly: the Greek pedos, 'soil', joined to metron, 'measurement'. Pedometrics applies mathematical and statistical methods to the distribution and genesis of soils. It is a sub-discipline of pedology focused on quantitative techniques, especially for mapping soil properties. It tackles soil problems clouded by deterministic or random variation, vagueness and lack of knowledge. Its simulation models build on chaos theory, statistical distributions or fuzzy logic. Its advance is tied to better remote and close-range sensing, and to wavelets, fuzzy sets and data mining.

soil-agri-091.title: Pedometric mapping turns soil into continuous grids
soil-agri-091.text: A traditional surveyor infers soil bodies from a mental model and draws them by hand. The result is subjective and hard to test for accuracy without extra sampling. Pedometric mapping, also called statistical soil mapping, produces soil property and soil class maps from data by statistical methods. It works largely through the statistics of data spread across space, the subject of {{ref:soil-meth-001}}. It predicts soil variables at unsampled places and estimates the uncertainty of each prediction. Its outputs come from rigorous statistical computing, so they are reproducible. Traditional mapping shows soil types as discrete bodies on polygon maps. Pedometric mapping shows measured properties as continuous grids, with maps of prediction error. Unlike {{ref:soil-agri-089}} as a whole, it relies strictly on these statistics and draws no discrete soil types. It leans on detailed covariate layers, maps of other variables such as elevation-model derivatives, remote sensing imagery, climate, land cover and geology. The aim is practical: predicting how a soil-plant ecosystem will respond to management.

soil-agri-093.title: Matheron's three-part model of soil variation
soil-agri-093.text: Every soil measurement hides three parts. The universal model of soil variation writes a soil variable as Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″. The three parts are a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise. Spatially autocorrelated means nearby values are related. French mathematician Georges Matheron introduced the model, and it has proven the best unbiased linear predictor for spatial data. The method of {{ref:soil-meth-004}} uses it to predict or simulate soils; this variant of {{ref:soil-meth-003}} is also called its universal form. The trend is often modeled from the classic soil-forming factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the CLORPT model.

soil-agri-094.title: The Storie index, where one zero sinks the score
soil-agri-094.text: Multiply a string of ratings together, and a single zero wipes out all the rest. That is the logic of the Storie index, a soil rating method based on the soil characteristics that govern a land's potential use and productive capacity. R. Earl Storie developed it at the University of California, Berkeley, in the 1930s for land valuation, independent of other physical or economic factors. It rates soil depth and texture, permeability, chemical characteristics, drainage and runoff, and climate where climate is not uniform. Its ratings are subjective, and O'Geen and colleagues updated the method in 2008 to reduce this.

soil-agri-090.title: The scorpan model: clorpt made digital
soil-agri-090.text: In 2003, McBratney and colleagues extended Jenny's clorpt model so that soil-environment relationships could be applied digitally. The result is the scorpan model. It keeps climate, organisms, relief, parent material and age, the {{ref:soil-form-043}} behind {{ref:soil-form-049}}, and adds two factors. The s stands for intrinsic soil properties captured by remote and proximal sensors, and n for spatial coordinates or position relative to a geographic phenomenon. A quantitative function f links individual scorpan factors, or a combination, to the soil property or class being predicted. Its strength is flexibility. It combines existing soil surveys with remote sensing, elevation, climate, land use and geology data, all as raster layers re-projected to one projection and resolution. Relief, usually from a digital elevation model, is the most used factor in {{ref:soil-agri-089}}, soil is second, and climate is one of the least used, partly because topography proxies for local climate. Age is rarely used because soil age is hard to put into a GIS-friendly form. The position factor can use sample coordinates or distance to a feature. Pedometrics applies mathematical and statistical methods to the distribution and genesis of soils. Its digital techniques date from the 1970s, and technology made them practical products since the 2000s. A map needs three ingredients: environmental layers representing scorpan factors, geo-referenced soil data, and a model relating soil to environment to predict at unsampled locations. It is usually supervised learning. Sample locations are intersected with the environmental layers to build a training set, and a fitted classification or regression function is then applied to all cells, linking back to {{ref:soil-form-042}}.

soil-agri-085.title: Soil information systems hold the whole inventory
soil-agri-085.text: Behind every digital soil map sits a larger store of data. A soil information system is a systematic, consistent collection of gridded or vector maps of soil properties and classes. It covers a whole area of interest and comes with a report, manual or metadata. Digital soil maps are visualizations of the soil inventories it stores, and its major part is a soil geographical database. Most systems combine polygon and point maps linked to attribute tables for profile observations, soil mapping units and soil classes. ISRIC works to strengthen national, regional and continental systems, and a new global one is being developed under the initiative described in {{ref:soil-env-190}}.

soil-agri-151.title: Farming that keeps the soil it farms
soil-agri-151.text: Under conventional {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, farm fields lose soil more than 100 times faster than new soil forms. Even without it, erosion runs 10 to 20 times the formation rate. Sustainable agriculture is farming that reduces environmental harm, sustains and expands natural resources and uses non-renewable ones productively. The USDA defined it in 1977 as an integrated, site-specific system that meets food needs over the long term while enhancing the environment and the resource base. Its tools include {{ref:soil-env-218}}, {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, mixed farming, {{ref:soil-agri-147}} and {{ref:soil-agri-004}}. The stakes are concrete. Over a billion tonnes of southern Africa's soil erode each year, enough to halve harvests within thirty to fifty years. Intensive farming drains carbon from the soil, yet changed practices can make soil a net store of it. One sustainably managed wheat farm held more organic matter, microbes and nutrients than its conventional neighbor. Its yields were slightly lower, but its net returns were 22.4% higher. Microbes help here too: phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms and mycorrhizae free phosphorus locked up by aluminium, calcium and iron.

soil-agri-149.title: Crop a plot, then let the forest take it back
soil-agri-149.text: Weeds, more often than tired soil, end the harvest. In shifting cultivation a farmer crops a plot for a while, then abandons it to regrow as {{ref:soil-agri-044}} and moves on to another. Cropping stops when the soil shows exhaustion or, more usually, when weeds overrun the field. The cropping period is usually shorter than the fallow, during which the land regenerates. Land is often cleared by slash-and-burn, and the ashes add potash to the soil. It is one of the first forms of agriculture, and its survival suggests a flexible, highly adaptive way to grow food. That balance is fragile. Population growth, cash crops and chainsaws have shortened fallows and lengthened cropping. Fragile tropical soils farmed permanently after a single burn, with little nutrient replacement, can degrade fast. Its role in forest loss is contested. The FAO named it a cause of {{ref:soil-env-269}} while leaving logging out, and environmental groups and later observers have disputed that view.

soil-agri-150.title: Fire, ash and a few good harvests
soil-agri-150.text: Somewhere between 200 and 300 million people farm by fire. In slash-and-burn agriculture, a form of {{ref:soil-agri-149}}, forest or woodland plants are cut, left to dry and burned to make a field called a swidden. The burn leaves a layer of nutrient-rich ash that raises fertility and briefly clears weeds and pests. After about three to five years, depleted nutrients and returning weeds cut yields, and the plot is abandoned. Recovery takes from five to more than twenty years. On leached tropical soils such as the Amazon's, which are extremely poor, it is one of the few kinds of farming possible. But it needs much land or few people. As populations grow and plots are burned too often, the forest is eventually destroyed. One proposed fix is slash-and-char: charring the slash rather than fully burning it, then ploughing the charcoal in to boost yields.

soil-agri-146.title: One crop, one field, mounting trouble
soil-agri-146.text: A field of one crop is easy to plant and easy to harvest. That is monoculture: growing a single crop species in a field at one time. It describes diversity in space, as polyculture does, whereas monocropping and {{ref:soil-agri-004}} describe diversity over time. The short-term ease fades. Lost biodiversity and depleted nutrients leave the crop more open to pests and disease. Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soil and favor soil-borne diseases. As soil health falls, farmers add more synthetic fertilizer, and the excess nitrogen can leach into ground and surface waters.

soil-agri-144.title: Growing grain on last winter's rain
soil-agri-144.text: Crops can grow where only 230 millimetres of precipitation fall in a year. Dryland farming grows crops without {{ref:soil-agri-013}}, usually where a cool wet season charges the soil with water for the dry season that follows. In places marked by {{ref:soil-class-148}}, grain grows on that bank of stored {{ref:soil-water-155}}, not on rain during the growing season. Farmers space plants widely, control traffic, disturb the soil little and weed strictly, so weeds do not drink the stored water. Summer {{ref:soil-agri-044}} grows one crop on two seasons' precipitation, leaving stubble and residue to trap snow. An old idea held that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} sealed in moisture under a dust mulch. One account calls this controversial; another says testing showed working the soil actually increases evaporation. The method is prone to wind erosion, since fallow years leave fields bare. Frequent cultivation may save water but costs topsoil, usually the more important long-term asset. {{ref:soil-agri-061}}, no-till, mulch and {{ref:soil-agri-072}} help.

soil-fert-208.title: Feeding crops through the irrigation line
soil-fert-208.text: Fertigation injects fertilizers and other water-soluble products into an irrigation system, so the water carries the food. Growers use it to add nutrients or fix deficiencies that plant tissue analysis reveals, mostly on high-value crops: vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals. Nitrogen is the commonest nutrient, supplied as anhydrous ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea. Phosphorus comes as ammonium phosphates and potassium as muriate of potash. Dosing with the water allows tiny amounts at a precise time and rate, and it reduces leaching. Drip systems, especially buried ones, can raise fruit and flower yield and quality. Most need a backflow preventer to protect drinking water.

soil-agri-148.title: Fukuoka's farm of five refusals
soil-agri-148.text: Masanobu Fukuoka built a farming method out of things not to do. Natural farming, also called the Fukuoka method or do-nothing farming, rests on five principles: no {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, no fertilizer, no pest or weed killers, no weeding and no pruning. Weeds, clover and legumes keep the ground covered and are cut and left to return their nutrients. The last crop's straw mulches the topsoil. Fukuoka meant it as a closed system needing no human inputs. After 25 years his farm matched the yields of Japan's most advanced farms. On slopes he grew trees and shrubs instead of building {{ref:soil-agri-073}} to stop erosion.

soil-agri-145.title: Clay baked into bubbles
soil-agri-145.text: Heat clay to about 1,200 °C in a rotary kiln and the gases trapped inside swell into thousands of tiny bubbles. The result is expanded clay aggregate, or LECA: light, porous pellets from 0.1 to 25 millimetres across, weighing 250 to 510 kg/m3. It extends the {{ref:soil-agri-031}} and starts from ordinary {{ref:soil-found-040}}. Mixed into heavy soil, it improves aeration and drainage. Blended with soil and peat, it resists compaction and holds water through drought. In hydroponics the round pellets air the roots while the clay soaks up water and nutrients. In semi-hydroponics a pot of LECA stands in a nutrient reservoir and wicks moisture up to the roots.

soil-agri-147.title: Two harvests or twelve from one plot
soil-agri-147.text: In the Garhwal Himalaya, farmers practicing barahnaja sow 12 or more crops on a single plot and harvest them at different times. That is multiple cropping at its fullest: growing two or more crops on the same land within one year. Crops grown together count as {{ref:soil-agri-133}}. Double-cropping plants a second crop once the first is harvested, a close cousin of {{ref:soil-agri-004}}. Relationships between crops can cut input costs and lower the risk of weeds, pests and disease. Water decides where it happens. Only 5% of global rainfed cropland is multiple cropped, against 40% of irrigated cropland.

soil-agri-143.title: The soil fumigant that ate the ozone
soil-agri-143.text: One small molecule of carbon, hydrogen and bromine long kept seed fields clean. Methyl bromide, CH3Br, was widely used as a fumigant and soil sterilant, mainly in seed production but also for strawberries and almonds. It was safer and more effective than some other sterilants. Its flaw lay in the sky: it releases bromine radicals that destroy ozone. The Montreal Protocol phased it out, and developed countries reached 100% reduction by 2005. Seed growers turned to {{ref:soil-agri-032}}, mechanical roguing and fallow seasons. Chemical substitutes include chloropicrin, 1,3-dichloropropene and methyl isothiocyanate, which spreads poorly through soil and needs far more irrigation to activate.

soil-agri-152.title: When a field grows tired of its crop
soil-agri-152.text: Plant the same crop year after year and the soil itself can seem to turn against it. Soil sickness is a decline in fertility and yield, often after long {{ref:soil-agri-053}}. It is marked by a shift in the balance of harmful and beneficial microbes around the roots, in the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. The idea is old. In 1832 the Swiss botanist De Candolle suggested that substances exuded by crop plants caused it. Aged tea plantations show one mechanism: polyphenols build up in the soil, shift its microbial communities and erode {{ref:soil-fert-149}}.

soil-agri-174.title: Setting the stubble alight
soil-agri-174.text: After the rice or wheat harvest, a match is the cheapest plough. Stubble burning deliberately sets fire to the straw stubble left in the field, a quick way to dispose of {{ref:soil-agri-129}}. It clears land fast, helps fight pests and weeds and can reduce nitrogen tie-up. The costs come later. Burning wastes nutrients, and years of it kill beneficial soil microflora and fauna, cutting organic matter and upsetting the carbon–nitrogen balance. The smoke spreads particulate pollution, linked to lung cancer, respiratory infections and harm to people with chronic lung disease. The practice is illegal in India and Pakistan, though weakly enforced, and has effectively been banned in the United Kingdom since 1993. Alternatives exist. Spraying an enzyme that decomposes stubble into fertiliser improves the soil and spares the air. Residues can also become particle board or biofuel, though hauling them away can still cause erosion and nutrient loss.

soil-agri-172.title: Angled discs that slice and lift
soil-agri-172.text: A disc harrow is a {{ref:soil-agri-114}} whose cutting edges are rows of concave metal discs set at an angle. Each cupped disc runs offset from the direction of travel, so it slices the ground repeatedly and lifts what it cuts. Heavy primary models, at 120 to 454 kg per disc, break virgin land and work residue into the topsoil to speed its decay. Lighter ones break clods into a fine bed for seed. It is the preferred tool for mixing lime and gypsum into soil, reaching a 50/50 blend that lowers topsoil acid saturation. Since lime does not move in soil, zero-till farming faces a critical challenge.

soil-agri-171.title: Ploughing below half a metre
soil-agri-171.text: An ordinary {{ref:soil-agri-106}} rarely cuts below 20 cm. Deep ploughing goes deeper than 50 cm, aiming to change how the soil holds water for the long term. In a 35-year test, deep-ploughed plots averaged 3,138 kg of grain per hectare a year, 10% more than the 2,858 kg from unploughed ones. In soils such as Podzols it can shatter a {{ref:soil-form-025}} and help release nutrients, and it is sometimes advised before planting vineyards. Still, farming is moving away from ploughing, deep ploughing most of all, to save topsoil and organic matter. That same long study found that skipping the plough does not conserve ground moisture.

soil-agri-175.title: Leaving the stubble standing
soil-agri-175.text: The simplest cover for a resting field is the last crop's leftovers. Stubble mulching leaves stubble or {{ref:soil-agri-129}} in place on the surface during a {{ref:soil-agri-044}} period, a kind of {{ref:soil-fert-066}} the field grows for itself. That cover can keep wind and water from carrying soil away, and it conserves soil moisture until the next crop goes in.

soil-agri-173.title: Tilling everything, burying only part
soil-agri-173.text: Mulch tillage is a compromise between turning the soil and protecting it. The whole surface is tilled and {{ref:soil-agri-129}} is mixed in, but some residue stays on top as a {{ref:soil-fert-066}}. Farmers do it with a wide variety of cultivators. In the United States it counts as {{ref:soil-agri-099}}.

soil-agri-176.title: Ridge tillage: seedbeds on raised ridges
soil-agri-176.text: Ridge tillage builds ridges or beds for the seed zone and keeps fixed traffic lanes. It is one of the conservation tillage practices ({{ref:soil-agri-099}}) that aim to keep 30% or more of the surface under crop residue, alongside no-till, in-row subsoiling and strip-till. Ridges let the seed zone dry and warm faster, give some weed control and reduce saturation after heavy rain. Fixed travel lanes reduce overall compaction. Poorly drained fields, where the {{ref:soil-water-247}} sits near the surface, benefit greatly, because the sensitive seedling root zone stays aerobic when wet (see {{ref:soil-phys-150}}).

soil-agri-158.title: A green border between field and stream
soil-agri-158.text: A strip of grass at a field's edge can stop much of the field from reaching the river. A buffer strip is land kept under permanent vegetation, mostly on farms, to protect soil, water and air, a staple of {{ref:soil-agri-059}}. It slows {{ref:soil-water-019}}, so sediment settles and nutrients and {{ref:soil-env-237}} are filtered out before they reach surface waters. Roots bind soil particles, cutting wind erosion and holding stream banks against {{ref:soil-water-001}} and landslides. Plantings range from grass alone to mixes of grass, trees and shrubs, and more diverse strips protect better. Governments often pay for them because they cut nitrogen losses to water and soil lost to wind. Siting starts with drainage. Poorly drained ground ponds, very well drained ground turns droughty, and medium drainage suits grasses best. On slopes, the NRCS finds contour strip cropping most effective at 4 to 8%.

soil-agri-157.title: Rain gardens that clean the runoff
soil-agri-157.text: Bioretention cleans stormwater by passing it through planted soil, where plants and microbes hold and break down pollutants. A typical cell has a sand bed, a layered filter soil and plants on top; stored water seeps away over days. Filtration, chemical change, biological breakdown and {{ref:soil-chem-068}} do the work, with clay gripping hydrocarbons, heavy metals and nutrients. Lab cells removed 94% of zinc, 88% of copper, 95% of lead and over 95% of cadmium. Capacity is finite, so the media eventually needs replacing. Loamy sand suits best; clay above 25 percent or slopes above 20 percent may rule it out.

soil-agri-159.title: Grass bands across the hillside
soil-agri-159.text: Contour buffer strips alternate bands of perennial vegetation with wider strips of crops across a slope, following the logic of {{ref:soil-agri-123}}. They work best when runoff arrives evenly as a sheet, and they excel at trapping pest-killing chemicals and curbing the small channels water cuts into fields. Each band must be at least 15 feet (4.6 m) wide, and the strips often stand in cheaply for terraces. Vegetative barriers are a narrower version: rows of hardy native perennial grasses or shrubs that slow wind and water and trap sediment.

soil-agri-160.title: The last line before the water
soil-agri-160.text: A filter strip is a band of grass or other permanent vegetation at a field's edge. It shields the {{ref:soil-water-263}} from {{ref:soil-water-046}}, pest-killing chemicals, pathogens and nutrients carried in runoff. It protects stream banks and water quality, and works best when other practices steer water toward it. Once mainly agricultural, filter strips are now common in towns, where water quality is a growing concern. Field borders, perennial strips along cropland edges, also reduce wind and water erosion. They help only with runoff that actually flows across them.

soil-agri-161.title: A grass hedge that builds its own terrace
soil-agri-161.text: Plant one grass in a line across a slope and, given time, it builds a terrace by itself. The Vetiver System conserves soil and water with hedgerows of vetiver grass. The dense hedge slows and spreads runoff, and sediment piling up behind it gradually forms a lasting {{ref:soil-agri-073}}. Its roots can reach 3–4 m deep in the first year. It tolerates roughly pH 3 to pH 11 and most heavy metals. A good hedge can cut runoff by as much as 70% and sediment by as much as 90%. It is used in more than 100 countries for {{ref:soil-water-051}}, slope stabilization and cleaning polluted soil.

soil-agri-163.title: Reading the land from orbit
soil-agri-163.text: A satellite can gauge the moisture in a field it will never touch. Remote sensing gathers information about an object or area from a distance, usually with sensors on satellites or aircraft, instead of measuring on site. It is active when the sensor sends out a signal and catches the reflection, passive when it detects reflected sunlight. Soil moisture, surface water storage, precipitation and evapotranspiration can all be measured this way, at various resolutions and accuracies. Land cover and land use maps reveal {{ref:soil-env-269}} and track the health of crops and native plants. Interferometric synthetic aperture radar, a radar technique, builds precise elevation models of large terrains. The view from above still needs the ground. Agricultural and environmental statistics usually combine classified satellite images with field samples, the same ground truth a {{ref:soil-agri-082}} depends on.

soil-agri-165.title: Maps that answer questions
soil-agri-165.text: Location is the thread that ties unrelated facts together. A geographic information system, or GIS, is computer hardware and software that store, manage, analyze, edit and display geographic data, using location as the key index. The first was the Canada Geographic Information System. It handled the Canada Land Inventory, which mapped soils, agriculture, forestry and land use at 1:50,000 to judge rural land capability. GIS data usually show features such as roads, land use, elevation and waterways. Masses such as an area's soil types, the stuff of a {{ref:soil-agri-084}}, are represented less directly. Data from digital survey instruments can flow straight into a GIS by coordinate geometry.

soil-agri-164.title: The ground surface as a grid of heights
soil-agri-164.text: A digital elevation model, or DEM, is a computer representation of elevation that depicts terrain or the objects on it. A terrain model shows bare ground; a surface model may include tree canopy and buildings, though the terms are used loosely. DEMs usually come from {{ref:soil-agri-163}} such as photogrammetry, lidar or radar interferometry, but land surveys work too. They are widely used in a {{ref:soil-agri-165}}. They feed drainage modelling and land-use studies, supply terrain measures for {{ref:soil-water-295}} and help model soil wetness through depth-to-water indexes.

soil-agri-162.title: Erosion seen from the air
soil-agri-162.text: One of Fairchild's first government contracts was an aerial survey of New Mexico to study soil erosion. Aerial photography takes pictures of landscapes from aircraft and other airborne platforms, an early form of {{ref:soil-agri-163}}. Vertical photographs underpin photogrammetry, mapping from aerial photographs, which was pioneered commercially in the 1930s. It is the usual basis of topographic maps and serves land-use planning. Terrain analysts have often viewed overlapping pairs in stereo to draw those maps.

soil-agri-166.title: Is this land fit for that use
soil-agri-166.text: Cultivating a steep slope may be possible, yet still a bad idea. Land suitability classification is the FAO method of land evaluation for answering that question. It appraises and groups land by its fitness for one defined use, drawing on {{ref:soil-agri-083}}. Land can be judged as it is now or after improvements. The scheme has four levels of decreasing generality. Orders give the kind of suitability, classes the degree, subclasses the kind of limitation, and units the minor differences in management. There are just two orders. S marks land whose sustained use yields benefits that justify the inputs without unacceptable damage. N marks land whose qualities seem to rule that use out. Land falls into N for three reasons. The use may be impracticable, or it may cause severe degradation, as cultivating steep slopes would. Most often, it simply would not repay its costs. The answers are not fixed. Climate change shifts suitability for many crops, usually toward higher latitudes and altitudes.

soil-agri-168.title: What land could do, not what it does
soil-agri-168.text: A land use capability map shows the potential uses of each unit of land, usually for farming. That sets it apart from a land use map, which shows how land is used now. It typically rests on five physical factors: rock type, soil type, slope, the degree and type of erosion, and vegetation. Each draws on a {{ref:soil-agri-084}} and {{ref:soil-agri-083}}. In the United States the Soil Conservation Service developed the Land Capability System in 1951, and soil survey standards keep data consistent with it.

soil-agri-177.title: Judging a forest site by its tallest trees
soil-agri-177.text: A 50-year-old red oak standing 70 feet (21 m) tall gives its site a site index of 70. Site index is the forester's measure of a site's potential for tree growth: the height of dominant and co-dominant trees at a base age. Base ages of 25, 50 and 100 years are used, and each index belongs to one tree species. Foresters can find it from tree height, from understory indicator plants or from a {{ref:soil-agri-084}}. In the United States the NRCS measured site index on surveyed soils and tabulated soils against indexes for important species. Indirect estimates use the dominant species, lesser vegetation, and topographic, climatic and soil factors. It has shortcomings, yet it has been the most widely used way to estimate site productivity in North America.

soil-agri-167.title: From highly suitable to never suitable
soil-agri-167.text: Within each FAO order of {{ref:soil-agri-166}}, numbered classes rank land in decreasing suitability. The number of Suitable classes is not fixed, but should stay small, probably never more than five. With three, S1 is highly suitable, S2 moderately suitable and S3 marginally suitable, barely justifying the inputs. Not Suitable land normally has two classes. N1 has limitations that might be overcome in time, but not at acceptable cost now. N2 has limitations that rule out any sustained use.

soil-agri-170.title: Web Soil Survey: soil maps on demand
soil-agri-170.text: New surveys of the same county once took 30 to 60 years to appear. Web Soil Survey, run by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, ended that wait. US surveys are no longer printed as books. They are published online, holding everything in the old county reports plus extra tools, and can be updated as needed. It gives access to data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey, building on the {{ref:soil-agri-082}} and the {{ref:soil-agri-084}}. A user picks an area of interest anywhere in the United States where survey data exist. The Soil Map tab then shows the component soil map units, and a report can be saved as a PDF. The Soil Data Explorer gives properties for each map unit, such as depth to water table, surface texture, bulk density, pH and depth to a restrictive layer. It also gives suitability ratings, with reasons, for uses such as dwellings with basements, local roads and streets, vegetative productivity and wastewater disposal by irrigation. It is one recognized basis, alongside measured infiltration rates, for choosing the hydrologic soil group of a site.

soil-agri-178.title: Turning height and age into a site index
soil-agri-178.text: Site index curves and equations turn a stand's dominant height and age into its {{ref:soil-agri-177}}. Height is measured on a dominant or co-dominant tree with a clinometer, laser hypsometer or releskop; age comes from an increment borer or planting records. A 60-foot (18 m) tree in a 50-year-old stand is read where age 50 meets 60 feet, and the nearest curve gives the index. One equation is lnS = lnHd − b1(A⁻¹ − Ai⁻¹), with S site index, Hd dominant height, A stand age and Ai index age. Planted white spruce curves fail below about 15 years, since early growth is hard to predict.

soil-bio-001.title: The crowded underworld that keeps soil alive
soil-bio-001.text: Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity. Soil biology is the study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live there. Its subject is soil life, also called soil biota or edaphon. That covers every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface. The cast runs from bacteria, fungi, protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} to earthworms and arthropods. It even includes some snakes and burrowing mammals such as gophers, moles and prairie dogs. These organisms break down {{ref:soil-found-045}}, releasing nutrients for plants. In doing so they strongly shape the soil's fertility, plant growth, soil structure and carbon storage. Soil life powers the nutrient cycles. Without it, organic material would pile up as undecayed litter, with no dark, stable residue formed and no nutrients available to plants. Soil life also guards what it gathers: nitrogen and phosphorus held in its bodies are kept from leaching away. Microbial exudates help hold soil structure together, and earthworms mix the soil as they burrow. For all that, soil biology is a relatively new science with much still unknown. The discovery of {{ref:soil-bio-121}} in 1996 showed that basic questions about how elements cycle through soil remained open.

soil-bio-011.title: Soil microbiology and the 33,000 species on a beet root
soil-bio-011.text: In 2011, researchers detected more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species on the roots of sugar beet. Soil microbiology studies such microorganisms: what they do and how they affect soil properties. Its subjects are grouped as bacteria, including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes, archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and protozoa. Their history is long. The first cyanobacteria arose two to four billion years ago. They fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil. How diverse a soil's microbes are depends on its pH, texture, soil organic matter content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals. That diversity pays off. Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses. A more diverse soil microbiome, the whole community of soil microbes, generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields. The microbes also signal to one another through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular polysaccharides. They trade metabolites that support each other's growth. Farmers can encourage them: sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} raises microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

soil-bio-063.title: Biomineralization: life that builds with stone
soil-bio-063.text: Every major lineage of living things has members that make minerals. Biomineralization is the process by which organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often to harden or stiffen their tissues. Over 60 different minerals have been identified in organisms. Most are silicates, carbonates or phosphates. Algae, diatoms and sponges build with silica, invertebrates with carbonates, and vertebrates with calcium phosphates and carbonates. Calcium phosphate and carbonate salts are the most common. Paired with organic polymers such as collagen and chitin, they give bones and shells their structural support. Microbes work on a geological scale. Bacteria take part in forming copper, iron and gold deposits, and microorganisms can both precipitate metals from solution and catalyze the dissolution of minerals. Soil sits inside a planetary loop. Bicarbonate released by weathering travels through soil to the sea, where it is turned into carbonate minerals for shells and skeletons. That makes biomineralization a store that locks carbon away, and a force in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. It can even clean up pollution. Microbes that release phosphate precipitate uranium phosphate minerals in contaminated groundwater, so the uranium moves less. The first evidence of biomineralization dates to some 750 million years ago, and organisms have made mineralized skeletons for the past 550 million years.

soil-bio-008.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch
soil-bio-008.text: The organisms living beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the relationship between soil and that variety of life, including the aspects of soil that can be managed with it in mind. Soil is chiefly a habitat for microbes such as bacteria and fungi. It also houses tiny animals such as protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, small ones such as potworms and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and larger ones such as earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their primary role is to recycle dead organic material from the plant-based food web above ground. In turn, their activity is a primary factor in how soil forms, physically and chemically. The link shows on maps: natural and farm vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales. Microbial exudates are now accepted as the main force that binds soil particles into clumps and shields carbon from further breakdown. Soil health depends on this diversity. Living covers on the soil and carbon-containing amendments improve it. {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, crop diversification, legume intercrops and organic inputs all correlate with more diverse soil life.

soil-bio-078.title: Burning a sample to measure its organic carbon
soil-bio-078.text: To count the organic carbon in a sample, a lab burns it. Total organic carbon is that analytical measure: the concentration of organic carbon present. The carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, for example by combustion at 1000 to 1200 °C or on a catalyst at 680 to 950 °C. Most modern analyzers read the gas by non-dispersive infrared. They measure only total carbon, which adds inorganic carbon, such as that in carbonate minerals, to the organic part. So the inorganic share is subtracted, or driven off first with acid. Soil organic matter content can be calculated from the result, and in the UK, guideline values for pollutants such as phenol and toluene depend on it. The measure also serves as a general indicator of water quality and as the first chemical test on potential petroleum source rock.

soil-bio-005.title: Why ecologists treat soil as an ecosystem
soil-bio-005.text: Soil organisms live under constant threat of drying out. Soil ecology studies how they interact with one another and with their environment. It is especially concerned with nutrient cycling, the formation of soil aggregates and soil biodiversity. Because soil is so complex and internally connected, soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. It is an uneven mix of minerals and soil organic matter, and its variations in structure, nutrients, moisture, temperature and pH support different organisms. Moisture is a major limit, and microbial communities shift through cycles of drying and rewetting. Temperature swings less with depth and governs microbial and enzyme activity, the release of nutrients and the pace of decay. Most soil organisms need oxygen. Microbes grow in air-filled micropores, while larger animals need macropores or water films to move. Patchy soils across a landscape, and changes between horizons, make communities patchy and layered with depth. Yet soil organisms remain underrepresented in studies and models, partly from an assumption that much below-ground diversity is ecologically redundant.

soil-bio-060.title: Oligotrophs, the slow specialists of scarcity
soil-bio-060.text: Some life thrives on almost nothing. An oligotroph is an organism able to live where nutrients are available only at very low levels. The word joins the Greek oligos, 'few', and trophikos, 'feeding'. Oligotrophs are contrasted with {{ref:soil-bio-088}}, organisms that prefer nutrient-rich settings. They grow slowly, run low metabolic rates and generally live at low population densities.
