Their homes have very low concentrations of nitrates, iron, phosphates and carbon sources: deep ocean sediments, caves, polar ice, aquifers, deep subsurface soil and leached soils. They cope with scarcity by switching on genes during lean periods. A feast is a problem: excess nutrients overwhelm their metabolism, and their enzymes struggle in rich conditions. Lichens, with their extremely low metabolic rate, and the cave-dwelling olm are examples. Rising carbon dioxide could favor them. It would speed plant and microbial growth but slow the cycling of carbon in soil, rewarding slower, more resource-efficient oligotrophs.

soil-bio-020.title: Why so many animals choose life underground
soil-bio-020.text: About 30% of all arthropods live in soil. Soil animals are those that spend their whole life there, or at least their larval stage. The soil shelters them from swings in temperature and moisture and from predators. It supplies food all year and a safe place to lay eggs. By body size they fall into four classes: 20 μm to 200 μm, 200 μm to 2 mm, 2 mm to 2 cm, and more than 2 cm. Size sets an animal's place in the {{ref:soil-bio-025}}, since bigger species eat smaller ones or reshape their surroundings. Many bear the marks of underground life. They tend to be smaller, blind, unpigmented, legless or short-legged, and often reproduce asexually. They are tightly bound to microbes, which feed them and help digest tough compounds. In return, the animals' guts, feces and cavities house microbes, spread them and regulate their numbers. Soil may even have been a crucible for the evolution of land invertebrates, a step between life in water and life in air. Studying them is slow. Each animal must be extracted, expelled, trapped or hand-sorted, then named by a specialist. DNA barcoding now yields full species lists, cryptic species included. One question stays open: researchers still debate whether and how fertilizers affect soil animals. In the sources, {{ref:soil-fert-010}} raised soil animal numbers while mineral fertilizers did not.

soil-bio-040.title: The earthworm, which Darwin ranked among history's great movers
soil-bio-040.text: In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world. He meant the earthworm, a soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida. The name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta. Earthworms live mostly in moist, compost-rich soil. They eat the remains of dead plants and animals, along with protozoa, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important eaters of dead matter. Adults range from 10 mm to 3 m long, though the typical common earthworm grows to about 360 mm. A worm moves by waves of muscle contraction, anchored by bristles called setae. It has no special respiratory organs and breathes through its moist skin. Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture. Most favor neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them. As they feed and burrow they aerate and mix the soil, help release nutrients for plants to take up, and bind soil organic matter to soil minerals. That makes them indicators of soil health. Healthy soil holds more of them, and their gut microbes reveal its condition. They are also vulnerable. {{ref:soil-fert-007}} create acidity fatal to worms, and pesticides kill them. At least three species are listed as extinct and many more as endangered.

soil-bio-052.title: Detritivores, the shredders that keep litter from piling up
soil-bio-052.text: Dead leaves and stems do not pile up in nature, and detritivores are the reason. A detritivore is a heterotroph, an organism that must eat to get its carbon, that feeds on {{ref:soil-bio-112}}: decomposing plant and animal parts and feces. It swallows discrete lumps of matter. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi instead absorb their food at a molecular scale, and the two terms are often confused. Typical soil detritivores include millipedes, {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, woodlice, slugs and many worms. They do the first stage of returning dead matter to mineral form, fragmenting plant remains so decomposers can complete the second. Together the two groups return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil for plants. They keep litter moving even though cellulose, xylan and other woody compounds decay much more slowly than other organic molecules. Oddly, these feeders mainly digest the protein-rich microbes growing on dead matter and excrete the dead matter itself little changed. Moist soil increases their feeding. In deserts they shelter in burrows and are the main clearers of fallen plant matter. The past shows a world without full decay. In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria could not yet digest {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, so dead plant tissue piled up and later became fossil fuels.

soil-bio-025.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land
soil-bio-025.text: All soil organic matter passes through a living gut of sorts. The soil food web is the community of organisms living all or part of their lives in soil. It is seen as a network of feeding links that passes energy among them. A food chain follows one linear energy pathway; a food web shows all the potential pathways. Plants are the producers. Using sunlight, they make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals, and their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground. Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and protozoa to {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients. In this way the web processes dead material much as a digestive system processes food. The work reaches beyond the soil. The web keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and helps water soak in. Its members prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground. Once thought simple, soil food webs turned out to have common omnivory and long, complex chains. Those chains still resist drying, freezing and fumigation. Some influence escapes the diagram, though. Litter transformers, mutualists and {{ref:soil-bio-004}} strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

soil-bio-033.title: Soil respiration: the ground breathes out carbon
soil-bio-033.text: Each year the world's soils release an estimated 77 Pg of carbon, more than human sources such as fossil fuel burning. That flow is soil respiration: the carbon dioxide produced by respiring roots, the microbes around them and soil animals below ground. It is a key ecosystem process. Carbon fixed by photosynthesis returns to the air as CO2, respired either by roots or by the heterotrophs that consume plant material. Rates vary enormously with temperature, moisture, nutrient content and oxygen. Inside soil aggregates, oxygen gradients create anoxic microsites, tiny oxygen-free pockets where anaerobic metabolism dominates. Decaying litter is a major part of the total. It releases CO2 while locking up or freeing nutrients, so respiration rates track microbial turnover and the release of mineral nitrogen. Turning the soil with {{ref:soil-agri-095}} usually increases soil respiration, depleting soil organic matter. The stakes are global. Soils hold up to 3150 Pg of carbon, more than four times the atmosphere, so a small change in soil respiration can upset the balance of atmospheric CO2. Between 1989 and 2008 soil respiration rose by about 0.1% per year. Respiration also forms a positive feedback with climate: warming raises it, and so raises CO2. A 2 °C rise is estimated to add 10 Pg of carbon a year from soils.

soil-bio-041.title: Litter dwellers, soil eaters and deep diggers
soil-bio-041.text: Not all earthworms live the same life. Ecologists group them by where they live and feed into three categories: epigeic, endogeic and anecic. Epigeic worms live in leaf litter or compost where litter meets soil. They do not burrow, and they eat decaying plant and animal matter; Eisenia fetida is one. Because they eat fresh waste without burrowing and tolerate the heat of compost heaps, epigeic Eisenia species suit {{ref:soil-bio-044}}. Endogeic worms live in topsoil or subsoil. They eat soil itself and dig horizontal burrows in the upper 10–30 cm. Anecic worms, whose name means 'reaching up', include the common earthworm. They build permanent, deep vertical burrows and come up to gather leaves. In doing so they mix surface plant matter into the mineral soil below. The categories help in judging land. Healthy soil holds a larger number and biomass of earthworms, especially endogeic and anecic species.

soil-bio-042.title: How earthworms turn leaf fall into fertile soil
soil-bio-042.text: Darwin estimated up to 53,000 worms per acre of cropland. Newer figures run from 250,000 per acre on poor soil to 1,750,000 per acre on rich farmland. Richly organic topsoil averages 500 earthworms per square meter, weighing up to 400 g/m2. All those worms improve soil for plants by fragmenting, mixing, grinding and digesting plant debris. Anecic worms pull leaf fall and manure into their burrows, shred it and mix it with soil, turning it into {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Their casts can hold 40 percent more of it than the top 230 mm of soil. Grit in the gizzard grinds swallowed particles, sand grains up to 1.3 mm included, into a paste whose large surface favors microbes and enzymes. Casts are richer in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus than the surrounding soil, with nutrients in forms plants can use. On rich ground, one worm may produce over 4.5 kilograms of casts a year. Burrows keep soil structured, aerated and drained, and worms speed the formation of water-stable macroaggregates, large crumbs that hold together when wet. Their effect on carbon was long debated: do worms hasten its loss as CO2, or preserve it? A consensus now credits them with storing carbon, since most is stabilized deep in the soil with clay. Their greenhouse gas emissions, direct or through soil microbes, are not yet fully quantified but likely add to global warming.

soil-bio-074.title: Petrichor, the smell of rain on dry ground
soil-bio-074.text: Pliny the Elder noticed the pleasant smell of earth when rain follows drought, and took it as a sign of fertile soil. That earthy scent now has a name: petrichor. Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Grenfell Thomas introduced the term in a 1964 Nature paper, replacing the older 'argillaceous odour'. They built it from the Greek petra, rock, and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods. The smell is a mixture of volatiles. In dry spells, oils from plant matter build up on mineral surfaces. Moisture pushes them out of rock and soil pores, joined by the microbial compounds {{ref:soil-bio-075}} and 2-methylisoborneol. The scent offers a glimpse of the soil atmosphere, because infiltrating rain flushes out the soil air after a drought. Pinning it down took time. In 1891 Marcellin Berthelot and G. André steam-distilled an odorous substance from soil but could not identify it. In 1965 Bear and Thomas reported that small amounts of the oily extracts delay seed germination and early plant growth. High-speed filming at MIT in 2015 showed raindrops on porous surfaces trapping air bubbles that burst as aerosols. Light or moderate rain made more aerosols than heavy rain. A 2026 study in dryland soils reaching into the Negev Desert found 58 volatile organic compounds released on rewetting, which may feed atmospheric ozone and secondary aerosol formation.

soil-bio-039.title: Soil enzymes, the chemical tools of decay
soil-bio-039.text: Microbes face a problem of scale: much of their food comes as large molecules left by dead plants and animals. Soil enzymes solve it. Released mainly by microbes, they break down soil organic matter and free nutrients for plants. Fungi, bacteria and archaea excrete them, and plant roots produce some. They speed the breakdown of compounds such as cellulose, starch and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, which makes them prominent agents in the cycling of carbon and nitrogen. Some work inside cells, some stay attached to cells, and some float free. Enzymes bound to clay and humic particles are protected from rapid breakdown but are less active, a trade-off between protection and activity. Their spread is highly patchy, varying at the millimeter scale with nutrients, microbes and roots, and from single trees to whole catchments. Farming steers them. Some fertilizers include {{ref:soil-fert-085}}, which hold back the enzyme that breaks down that compound so nutrients are released over a longer period. Enzyme activity was higher with manure than with inorganic fertilizer, though other studies found a mix of mineral and organic inputs better still. Enzymes both stabilize and degrade soil structure, and they play a decisive role in keeping soil healthy.

soil-bio-002.title: Billions in a teaspoon: the bacteria of the soil
soil-bio-002.text: A teaspoon of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria. In and around plant roots, up to 10 billion culturable cells live in each gram. Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes, cells without a nucleus, and they are the soil's most numerous inhabitants. They live in soil water, including the moisture film around particles, where some swim with whip-like flagella. When conditions suit, they multiply fast by splitting in two. Most beneficial soil bacteria need oxygen and are most active in moist but unsaturated soil of neutral pH with plenty of food. Those that live without oxygen tend to putrefy dead plant and animal matter. Away from roots, most rest as drought-resistant colonies in a polysaccharide matrix coated with clay platelets. They wait until {{ref:soil-bio-142}} or earthworm mucus reach them. Hostile conditions send them dormant: Gram-positive Bacillus and Clostridium form spores, and Gram-negative bacteria enter a resting stage in which they cannot be cultured. Bacteria run key steps of the {{ref:soil-fert-099}}. Some capture nitrogen from the air, some turn ammonia toward nitrate, and others return nitrate to gas where oxygen is absent. Pseudomonas can metabolize a wide range of chemicals, while {{ref:soil-fert-147}} gets its energy only by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate. Soil archaea, also prokaryotes, are still poorly known but may matter in that ammonia-to-nitrate step and in methanogenesis. Some bacteria colonize minerals and speed their weathering.

soil-bio-075.title: Geosmin, the earthy molecule noses catch in traces
soil-bio-075.text: People can smell geosmin at just 0.006 to 0.01 micrograms per liter of water. Geosmin is a chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water. Its name joins the Greek geō-, 'earth', and osmē, 'smell'. Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier coined it in 1965 after isolating it from actinomycete cultures, and Gerber worked out its structure in 1968. It is a secondary metabolite, a by-product rather than a necessity of life, of cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Phormidium and Planktothrix and of actinomycetes, mainly {{ref:soil-bio-225}}. It gives beetroot its earthy taste and contributes to petrichor. The natural (−) form is about eight times more potent than the other, with a mean threshold of 9.5 ng/L against 78 ng/L. With 2-methylisoborneol it is the main biological cause of muddy tastes in drinking water and farmed fish worldwide. It is nontoxic to humans and breaks down in acid, yet standard water treatment cannot remove it, so suppliers need combined methods such as advanced oxidation. In the soil it carries signals. It attracts {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, which feed on these bacteria and spread their spores, and it repels the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.

soil-bio-003.title: Seven hundred kilometers of fungal thread in a gram of soil
soil-bio-003.text: A gram of garden soil can hold around one million fungi and around 700 km of fungal threads, called hyphae. Soil fungi are the yeasts, molds and other fungi of the soil. They lack chlorophyll, spread through the soil as a web of threads described in {{ref:soil-bio-217}}, and feed on dead plant and animal matter. Bacteria may outnumber them in cell counts, but fungi can contribute more biomass and respiration in some soils. As chemo-heterotrophs, they need organic substrates for their carbon. These threads break fresh remains down into {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and carbon dioxide. In that work the key fungi are {{ref:soil-bio-125}}, which turn dead matter into mineral forms such as nitrate, ammonium and phosphate that plants can use. Dead matter is colonized by a succession of species: sugar and starch users first, then those able to break down cellulose and tougher woody compounds. Many fungi are parasites that cause plant disease. Others are beneficial partners, such as {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and fungi also help bind soil into crumbs and feed larger soil organisms. Compared with bacteria, fungi fare relatively well in acidic soils and in dry soils, which hold more of the oxygen they need. Fruiting bodies such as mushrooms release spores that spread by wind, water and fungus-eating animals and can lie dormant for years.

soil-bio-079.title: Lumbricus terrestris, the nightcrawler that remakes forest soils
soil-bio-079.text: The common earthworm, lob worm or nightcrawler is Lumbricus terrestris, a large, reddish worm thought to be native to Western Europe and now spread around the world. It is generally 110–200 millimeters long and 7–10 millimeters across, with around 120–170 segments. Through much of Europe it is the largest naturally occurring earthworm. A deep-burrowing anecic worm, it digs vertical burrows, pulls surface litter down into the mineral soil and leaves casts of mixed organic and mineral material on the surface. Where it has invaded {{ref:soil-class-138}}, it has erased their banded profile of litter, pale E and colored B horizons. Thin litter and a dark, worm-mixed Ap horizon over the B are left behind. In the north central United States it is invasive. It thrives in fence rows and woodlots and reduces the regrowth of native plants and trees, though it fares poorly in tilled fields.

soil-bio-012.title: Actinomycetes: the branching bacteria behind earthy smell
soil-bio-012.text: The sweet, earthy smell of healthy soil comes from volatile metabolites of actinomycetes. These are soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota (formerly Actinobacteria), Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, many of which grow fungus-like branching mycelia. The order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi. Fungi play a similar role, but these bacteria are much smaller and likely fill a different niche. The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups, and among {{ref:soil-bio-002}} it includes Streptomyces, one of the largest bacterial genera. Streptomyces and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils. They decompose the organic matter of dead organisms so plants can take it up anew. They build humus by breaking down cellulose, lignin and arthropod chitin. Lignin is hard for most organisms to break down and often shields cellulose from decomposition, so splitting large lignin molecules into smaller pieces matters. Some, such as Frankia, live symbiotically with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars. They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi. They also yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, and agricultural compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.

soil-bio-043.title: How a few earthworm species hitched rides around the world
soil-bio-043.text: Of around 7,000 earthworm species, only about 150 are widely distributed. These are the peregrine or cosmopolitan earthworms, carried by people into regions where they are not native. In the United States and Canada, 70 of the 308 earthworm taxa, or 23%, are introduced species. Humans have spread surface-dwelling earthworms into many new regions, where they speed up carbon cycling. The effects reach deep into the soil profile. In {{ref:soil-class-138}}, invading worms can erase the banded layers, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.

soil-bio-044.title: Vermicomposting: putting worms to work on waste
soil-bio-044.text: Vermicomposting feeds organic waste to earthworms and collects what comes out the other end. It usually relies on the brandling worms Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil. In the tropics, the African nightcrawler and the Indian blue are used. The end product is {{ref:soil-fert-039}}, also called worm castings. Worms fed partly composted material excrete castings that make nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium available to plants. Added to soil, ideally spread on the surface, this humified material improves moisture and nutrient availability and benefits soil microbes.

soil-bio-004.title: Ecosystem engineers, the builders of soil habitat
soil-bio-004.text: Some species matter less for who eats them than for what they build. Ecosystem engineers are species that create, significantly modify, maintain or destroy a habitat. In soil they are chiefly burrowing animals such as earthworms, ants and termites, along with fungi. Engineers are defined by how they modify resources for other organisms, not by being eaten, which sets them apart from keystone species. Allogenic engineers change materials mechanically, as burrowers do. Autogenic engineers create habitat with their own bodies, as Sphagnum moss builds {{ref:soil-water-136}}. Earthworms, ants and termites mix the soil as they burrow. They strongly affect soil formation and the fate of soil organic matter while building crumbly, granular structure. Ant and termite nests enrich soil in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and mix particles from different depths. Moles, gophers and prairie dogs turn soil, spread fungi that partner with roots, and open corridors used by arthropods, birds, small mammals and reptiles. Fungi are engineers too. By linking distant patches and moving nutrients between them, even shifting carbon between trees, they control nutrient cycles. Where earthworms do little, potworms take on the role, digging galleries in which they leave their feces. Earthworms are particularly sensitive to many contaminants, and losing such engineers dramatically changes the organic layers at the soil surface. Not everyone likes the term. Some ecologists call it a buzzword, arguing that it implies intent or that every species would qualify.

soil-bio-047.title: Bioturbation: how burrowers stir the earth
soil-bio-047.text: In the 1800s Darwin watched a field slowly swallow a layer of chalk. Spread on the surface, the chalk lay 18 centimeters deep after 30 years, a burial rate of 6 millimeters per year that he credited to earthworms. That began the formal study of bioturbation: the reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains. Walruses, salmon and pocket gophers are conspicuous bioturbators, but small invertebrates such as earthworms, polychaete worms, shrimps and midge larvae dominate. Bioturbation differs from bioirrigation, the mixing of water and dissolved substances in sediments, which is one of its effects. Burrowers carry oxygen into oxygen-poor layers, changing how microbes live and speeding the breakdown of soil organic matter. Their burrows shelter other species. The process profoundly affects the environment and is thought to be a primary driver of biodiversity. Nathaniel Shaler added ants and trees to the story in 1891. Rudolf Richter coined the term in 1952, and it has been widely used in soil science and the study of landforms since the 1980s. The process itself is far older. Since it began around 539 million years ago it has changed ocean chemistry, and it is thought to have been a co-factor of the Cambrian Explosion. Pollution can run it backward. When pollution harms earthworms, termites and ants, bioturbation falls and the {{ref:soil-bio-095}} shifts toward mor.

soil-bio-018.title: Farming with microbes: promise and pitfalls
soil-bio-018.text: Healthy soil life can supply crops with nutrients such as nitrogen and protect them against pests and diseases, while reducing the need for water and other inputs. Using and managing soil microorganisms toward those ends is the agricultural use of soil microbes. The partnership is fragile. Fertilizer and pesticide used without offsetting their effects can destroy the rhizobiome, the microbial ecosystem around roots. Excess fertilizer, phosphorus above a threshold in particular, can suppress the fungi that partner with roots and turn symbiotic bacteria into competitors. Almost all registered microbial products are biopesticides, now about 10% of the global pesticide market. Long-marketed examples include Trichoderma fungi, which suppress disease-causing fungi, and the caterpillar killer Bacillus thuringiensis. The field is hard going. Many strains that look promising in the lab fail outdoors because of soil, climate and ecosystem effects. Introduced populations can fade, as Bacillus subtilis does when it lacks a niche it can defend. Using several collaborating strains helps. Rules demanding safety evidence have even led many products to call themselves by the label discussed in {{ref:soil-fert-205}} rather than 'biopesticides'.

soil-bio-070.title: Microbial inoculants: bottled helpers for crops
soil-bio-070.text: An estimated 836 million USD is spent on microbial inoculants each year. These farm amendments, also called soil inoculants or bioinoculants, use beneficial microbes that live around or inside roots to promote plant health. Many of the microbes form mutually beneficial partnerships with the crop. Besides improving nutrition, they can promote growth by stimulating the plant's hormone production. Bacterial inoculants, called plant growth promoting {{ref:soil-bio-154}}, include nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers. The most commonly applied is {{ref:soil-bio-239}}, which fixes nitrogen inside legume roots, in the growths covered in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are used to supply phosphorus. In one greenhouse with reduced fertilization, these fungi plus root bacteria gave tomato yields at 70% fertility that matched those at 100%. Inoculants can also induce systemic acquired resistance, a whole-plant defense, shown so far against powdery mildew, take-all, leaf spot and root rot. Mixing strains raises nutrient uptake from soil and fertilizer. Several strains together even raise the activity of the nitrogen-fixing enzyme when only one of them fixes nitrogen. Inoculants often change the soil's existing microbial community. Results so far are mixed. Research in 2024 suggests as few as one in nine commercial products are beneficial, and with commercial products root colonization by these fungi was under 10%. Large-scale application is not yet economically viable, so inoculants are not widely used in industrial agriculture.

soil-bio-048.title: Gophers, worms and fallen trees: how soil gets stirred
soil-bio-048.text: Pocket gophers may produce soil on a scale equal to non-living processes. Bioturbation in soils is the mixing and moving of soil by burrowing animals and plant roots. It matters for soil production, burial, soil organic matter content and the movement of soil downslope. Plants and animals disturb the upper soil and bring weathered rock, saprolite, up from depth to the surface. Gopher mounds carry little-weathered rock up, speeding soil formation, and are easily eroded downslope. The mounds also bury plants, which decay into nutrient hotspots. Burrows, even when backfilled, lower soil density. Burrows of earthworms and small mammals carry air and water. They change porosity, nutrient content and how particle sizes are spread with depth. Trees play their part. Roots add soil organic matter and leave voids when they rot, and uprooted trees throw up mounds and can turn sections of soil upside down. Burrowers that eat dead matter build the organic-rich topsoil called the soil biomantle, and so help form soil horizons.

soil-bio-077.title: Sorting bacteria by how they eat and breathe
soil-bio-077.text: Bacteria can be sorted by three questions: where their energy comes from, which electron donors they use and where they get their carbon. Electrons are the currency of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Phototrophs get their energy from light by photosynthesis, while the organisms of {{ref:soil-bio-205}} get it by oxidizing chemical compounds. Bacteria that take electrons from inorganic compounds such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide or ammonia are covered in {{ref:soil-bio-056}}; those that use organic compounds are the subject of {{ref:soil-bio-206}}. Heterotrophs take their carbon from organic compounds, while autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and some purple bacteria fix carbon dioxide. Aerobes use oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and anaerobes use nitrate, sulfate or carbon dioxide. Facultative anaerobes switch between fermentation and different acceptors as conditions change.

soil-bio-056.title: Lithotrophs, the microbes that eat rock
soil-bio-056.text: Life's last universal common ancestor is thought to have been a chemolithotroph, a microbe living on the chemical energy of inorganic substances. A lithotroph is any organism that takes the electrons it needs from an inorganic substance, usually of mineral origin, rather than from organic compounds. It uses them to build cells or make energy. The name joins the Greek lithos, rock, and troph, consumer: lithotrophs are 'eaters of rock'. Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946. The opposite strategy, covered in {{ref:soil-bio-206}}, gets electrons by breaking down organic compounds. In the broad sense, lithotrophs include light-using photolithotrophs such as plants. Chemolithotrophs, though, are exclusively microorganisms, all in the domains Bacteria and Archaea. Lithoautotrophs take their carbon from carbon dioxide in the air, as plants do. Lithoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon dioxide and must consume organic compounds; only a few bacteria are fully lithoheterotrophic. Many lithotrophs are mixotrophs, topping up the carbon they fix with organic material. They live in the deep subsurface, soils, mines and endolith communities inside rock. There they take part in soil formation and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other elements. In the cycling of iron they can use it both ways: as an electron donor, turning Fe(II) into Fe(III), or as an electron acceptor, turning Fe(III) into Fe(II).

soil-bio-057.title: Chemolithotrophy: making a living from minerals in the dark
soil-bio-057.text: Some microbes build living matter in total darkness, from nothing but minerals and gases. {{ref:soil-hist-013}} first characterized their metabolism, chemolithotrophy. In 1887, working with the bacterium Beggiatoa, he discovered the first known form of lithotrophy. In chemolithotrophy a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen. The oxidation is coupled to making ATP, the cell's energy carrier. Electrons taken from the inorganic donor pass into respiratory chains that make ATP. Most chemolithotrophs also fix carbon dioxide, usually through the Calvin cycle, an energetically expensive pathway. The group includes sulfur oxidizers, iron oxidizers, hydrogen oxidizers and the bacteria that turn ammonia into nitrite and nitrite into nitrate. Oxygen is the usual electron acceptor in the best-documented forms. Nitrate and other acceptors are also used, and the list of chemolithotrophs that live without oxygen is growing. Energy yields depend on the fuel. Oxidizing hydrogen sulfide to sulfur gives 50 kcal/mol (210 kJ/mol), while oxidizing sulfur to sulfate gives 150 kcal/mol (627 kJ/mol). On low-energy fuels such as ferrous iron, cells must process large amounts of material for a little energy, which keeps them from thriving in many places. Because this kind of chemosynthesis needs no sunlight, chemolithotrophs can build living material in the dark. Some thrive above 110 degrees Celsius or below pH 2.

soil-bio-009.title: What acid, salt and the plow do to soil life
soil-bio-009.text: In Dutch soils below pH 5, biodiversity fell as pH fell, in grasslands and heathlands alike. Threats to soil biodiversity are soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinization, sodicity, structure decline and erosion. Many are driven by how soil is managed. Acidification cuts the numbers of most large soil animals, earthworms included. It harms the survival of the bacteria covered in {{ref:soil-bio-239}} and may slow decay and the capture of nitrogen from the air. Salt works differently. At low salinity microbes are active and soil respiration is high; as salinity rises, microbes have less available water and respire less. Prolonged high sodium leaves soil cement-like, holding and passing less water and breaking down soil organic matter more slowly. Erosion strips topsoil, soil organic matter and nutrients and breaks down structure, making it a major threat. Constant {{ref:soil-agri-095}} redistributes soil organic matter, degrading structure and altering populations of earthworms and other organisms. Even a common fertilizer can harm. Chloride from potassium chloride raises salinity and is biocidal, harming the growth, survival and reproduction of soil organisms, including the bacteria that make nitrate.

soil-bio-084.title: Thatch, the spongy mat that builds up under lawns
soil-bio-084.text: In lawn care, thatch is a layer of plant material that builds up around the base of the grass plants. It mixes living and dead crowns, stolons, rhizomes and roots. About 25% of it is {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, which resists decay. Grass clippings add little, because soil microbes break them down easily. Thatch builds up when acid soils cannot support enough decomposers, or when insecticides cut earthworm activity and so bioturbation. Excess nitrogen fertilizer adds to it by spurring growth and acidifying the soil. A thin layer insulates against swings in temperature and moisture. Too much causes root problems and mowing difficulties, and is removed with a dethatcher.

soil-bio-023.title: Macrofauna, the soil animals big enough to see
soil-bio-023.text: Earthworms, termites, ants, millipedes, woodlice, beetles, slugs and snails all belong to the soil macrofauna: soil and litter invertebrates between 2 mm and 2 cm long. Earthworms, termites, ants, some millipedes and some insect larvae make pore spaces and so change soil structure. Diets differ widely. Millipedes, woodlice and some earthworms eat leaf litter. Lower termites eat wood, while endogeic earthworms and higher termites eat dark, decayed soil organic matter. Centipedes and spiders hunt prey. Shredding plant remains speeds decay, and so does waking dormant bacteria in the soil the animals swallow. Researchers call this the 'Sleeping Beauty' paradigm, with the earthworm as 'Prince Charming'. Animals that eat dead matter need enzymes from gut microbes to digest wood or soil organic matter. In lower termites, partner flagellates help digest the tough fibers of wood. Food ground in earthworm gizzards or chewed by termites leaves pasty feces that harden into stable earthworm casts and termite mounds. Macrofauna are abundant in fertile soils and typical of the mull type of {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, with many feeding niches and more complex food webs. They need much calcium and nitrogen, so they depend on plants with fast-decaying litter. By speeding nutrient cycling, they favor such plants in return: a positive feedback between life above and below ground.

soil-bio-022.title: Mesofauna, the mites and jumpers of the pore spaces
soil-bio-022.text: Between 0.2 mm and 2 mm long, the soil mesofauna are mostly the tiny jointed-legged animals of {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, such as mites and {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, plus potworms ({{ref:soil-bio-087}}). The springing kind breed fast and live in large populations. They are prey for predatory mites, pseudoscorpions and macrofauna, which makes them pivotal in soil food webs. Mesofauna feed on plant remains, microbes, lichens, spores, pollen and other animals. Their heavy consumption of litter and microbes gives them an important part in the cycling of carbon. They also eat and break down the feces of larger animals, such as earthworm casts. These small animals cannot reshape soil and must use the existing macropores, which makes them very sensitive to compaction. Potworms instead dig galleries. By eating fungal threads and spores, mesofauna help regulate fungal communities, including fungi that partner with roots, both spreading and severing them. Their community make-up reflects environmental differences, so mesofauna are good bioindicators of soil quality. Being sensitive to environmental hazards, they are likely to be harmed by climate change, land use change and farming intensification.

soil-bio-085.title: Springtails, the tiny jumpers that graze on fungi
soil-bio-085.text: Estimates reach 100,000 springtails in a single square meter of ground. Springtails, class Collembola, are tiny six-legged arthropods, no longer counted as insects, that live in moist soil and leaf litter almost everywhere on Earth. More than 9,000 species are known. They are omnivorous and free-living, and prefer moist conditions. Temperate deciduous woodland litter typically holds 30 to 40 species, and the tropics may exceed 100. Springtails do not break down dead matter directly. They speed its decay by fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbes. They mostly eat fungal threads and spores, but also plant material, pollen, animal remains and bacteria. Geosmin from the bacteria of {{ref:soil-bio-225}} attracts some species, which eat and spread its spores. Mesostigmatan mites and soil centipedes hunt them. Springtails escape by jumping with a spring-like organ, the furcula, though that is hard to do inside soil. Their communities change with depth, from canopy to litter to deeper horizons, and across landscapes with acidity, moisture and light. As a group they are highly sensitive to drying out. Unlike earthworms, they are very sensitive to herbicides. Folsomia candida is used in standardized toxicity and avoidance tests for soil pollution, and springtails serve as bioindicators of soil quality. On lawns they act as 'thatch busters', helping break down the thatch between the grass and the soil surface.

soil-bio-087.title: Potworms, the earthworms' small white cousins
soil-bio-087.text: Over 700 species of enchytraeids are described. They form a family of small, earthworm-like oligochaete worms, and the land-dwelling species, called potworms, live in highly organic soils. Most are whitish or transparent and a few millimeters long. They eat decaying plant and animal matter and its microbes, aiding decay and nutrient cycling. Like earthworms, they are ecosystem engineers, shaping soil structure by building aggregates of various sizes. They feed on earthworm casts and turn them into fluffy masses of their own feces. Those masses make up the bulk of the OH horizon in the moder type of {{ref:soil-bio-095}}. They are less sensitive than earthworms to farming intensification. So they replace earthworms in soils with heavy pesticide use and serve in standard ecotoxicity tests (ISO 16387).

soil-bio-017.title: Slime molds and myxobacteria, single cells that act as one
soil-bio-017.text: A slime mold makes complex decisions about food with no coordinating center at all. Slime molds and myxobacteria are soil microorganisms whose single cells band together. Slime molds, which are eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, merge into syncytia: one vast cell with many nuclei. Myxobacteria, which are prokaryotes, gather into swarms. Both glide in a coordinated way while foraging, a behavior still largely unexplored. Both also form spores in fruiting bodies, which are often iridescent and conspicuous.

soil-bio-013.title: Soil algae, sunlight harvesters at the surface
soil-bio-013.text: Soil algae are photosynthetic microorganisms that live at or near the soil surface and make their own carbon compounds from light. Needing light, they spread wherever sunlight and moderate moisture reach, but not far below the surface. Deeper down, some live on given steady temperature and moisture, taking in ready-made carbon such as glucose. Soil algae divide into green Chlorophyceae and golden-brown diatoms, which owe their color to the carotenoid pigment fucoxanthin. One alga, Chlorella vulgaris, has been shown to promote plant growth together with bacteria around roots.

soil-bio-016.title: Phages, the viruses that prey on soil bacteria
soil-bio-016.text: Viruses that infect soil bacteria, called bacteriophages or phages, are among the most abundant yet least studied members of soil microbial communities. Their richness varies with season, soil moisture, location and plant growth, and rises with the number of bacteria. Soil phages follow three strategies. Lytic phages kill the host to release new virus particles. Lysogenic phages join the host's genome. Chronic phages release particles without killing it. By killing hosts, lytic phages affect how bacteria cycle carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Phages are also a major route by which genes move between bacteria. They can even open plants to disease: phage ΦGP100 kills Pseudomonas fluorescens, a bacterium that produces antifungal compounds.

soil-bio-014.title: Protozoa, the soil's single-celled grazers
soil-bio-014.text: Heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million in a gram of soil. They are the smallest of the soil protozoa, single-celled eukaryotes grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates. Most protozoa eat bacteria. Others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of decayed plant and animal matter. Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films. {{ref:soil-bio-195}} shelter in shells against drying out, and they serve as indicators of past climates. Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

soil-bio-015.title: The microbial loop: how predators free nutrients for roots
soil-bio-015.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles. It names the pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web. 'Microbial food web' is now often used instead. In soil, the loop concerns carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} eat bacteria fed by roots. It runs like this. Roots pushing into new soil prime resting bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat. That frees mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb. Predation by amoebae and free-living roundworms raises the rate at which nutrients are released, which in turn stimulates root growth. This loop is Clarholm's hypothesis, and it is hard to verify by experiment. Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial bodies in a form plants can use. A related idea, the model in {{ref:soil-bio-266}}, has plants add carbon through {{ref:soil-bio-142}} and litter. Microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in a stable pool as dead microbial matter, called necromass. They transform plant carbon outside the cell with enzymes and inside it as their populations grow and die. The balance between pathways that release CO2 and those that build carbon sets how much carbon the soil keeps. Fresh plant carbon can also prime microbes to break down carbon already stored in soil organic matter faster than models expect. Much remains unknown. Most of the soil microbiome has never been cultivated, which leaves its part in carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

soil-bio-049.title: When burrowers scramble the archaeologist's layers
soil-bio-049.text: Archaeologists date finds relatively by stratigraphy: in a stack of deposits, the topmost layer is the youngest. Burrowing organisms break that rule. By moving material up, down and sideways, bioturbation blurs the order in which deposits were laid down, confusing the archaeological record and making relative dating harder. Archaeologists study it alongside geologists and biologists.

soil-bio-081.title: Dwarf forests, where poor soil grows miniature trees
soil-bio-081.text: On Mount Hamiguitan in the Philippines, 6,834 hectares of forest grow in miniature. It is the largest known pygmy forest in the country and possibly the world. A dwarf forest, also called an elfin or pygmy forest, is an uncommon ecosystem of small trees, home to small animals such as rodents and lizards. Most grow at high elevations, where the air is humid but the soil is poor. The two main types are coastal temperate and montane tropical. In tropical mountains the trees reach only 5–8 m, with shallow roots and abundant epiphytes, plants that grow perched on other plants. High winds largely set their height.

soil-bio-069.title: Soil-borne pathogens, the enemies waiting below the crop
soil-bio-069.text: Some of a plant's worst enemies wait in the ground beneath it. A soil-borne pathogen is a disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host, and it tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil. Common examples are Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, Verticillium, Rhizopus, Thielaviopsis and roundworms such as Meloidogyne. Many are fungi, even though other soil fungi are helpful partners of plants. Their propagules are the spores and fragments that spread them. Chemicals released by plants can stir them to germinate in the soil around a seedling's lower stem. They then start the stem rots that cause damping-off, the collapse of young seedlings. Monoculture and chemical fertilization often bring these diseases, along with acidification and degradation that lower productivity. Growers have several defenses. Fallowing disrupts pathogens by removing their hosts for a while. Heating the soil with sunlight, {{ref:soil-agri-034}}, kills or badly weakens many. Disease-suppressive soils inhibit them, and teas brewed from {{ref:soil-fert-028}} suppress them too. Growing roots in substrates instead of soil, as {{ref:soil-fert-167}} does, eliminates soil-borne diseases and pests altogether.

soil-bio-045.title: Worm casts, the soil that has passed through a worm
soil-bio-045.text: A small coil of soil on a lawn is the end of a digestive journey. A worm cast is a pile, coil or pellet of soil or sand that burrowing worms push out at the surface. A {{ref:soil-bio-040}} swallows soil along with its microbes and {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Digestion breaks up mineral particles and partly breaks down that dead material, and the rest leaves through the burrow. Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the soil around them, and they build stable aggregates, the crumbs that give soil its structure. On lawns and grasslands they are read as a sign of active, healthy soil. On beaches and tidal flats, burrowing polychaete worms leave coiled casts like spaghetti.

soil-bio-035.title: Heat, water and nitrogen set the pace of soil breathing
soil-bio-035.text: Warm soil breathes faster, but only up to a point. Three non-living factors chiefly set how fast carbon in soil is respired to CO2. They are temperature, moisture and nitrogen. {{ref:soil-bio-033}} rises exponentially with temperature to a maximum, then falls to zero as enzymes fail. Roots start to shut down above 35 °C. Microbes divide the range among them. Cryophiles work best below 20 °C, mesophiles between 20 and 40 °C, and thermophiles above 40 °C, so mixed communities respire over a broad span. Moisture traces a hill: respiration is low when dry, peaks at intermediate moisture and falls when water shuts out oxygen. Nitrogen costs roots energy. Taking in nitrate costs 0.4 units of CO2, and reducing it costs 2. Nitrogen-rich litter also decomposes faster.

soil-bio-036.title: Putting a lid on the soil to measure its breath
soil-bio-036.text: To measure how fast soil breathes, researchers put a lid on it. A closed chamber is sealed over the soil, and the flux comes from how fast CO2 builds up over a few minutes, using F=bV/A. Longer runs underestimate it, because some CO2 is stored in the soil instead. Open systems pump fresh air through the chamber and read the flux at equilibrium. Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars. Stable carbon isotopes reveal where the CO2 comes from. Swapping C3 and C4 crops, plants with two different kinds of photosynthesis, or spraying C4 cane sugar, tells old carbon from new and microbial respiration from root respiration.

soil-bio-037.title: How a changing planet is changing soil's breath
soil-bio-037.text: Soil breathing shifts with every change people make to air and land. Free air CO2 enrichment (FACE) studies raise CO2 over open plots. Elevated CO2 boosted soil respiration through more roots and microbial activity, by up to 40.6% in sweetgum and poplar forests. Warming may hit hardest in the Arctic. There, thawing permafrost turns aerobic, and its large carbon stores are respired much faster. Rainfall matters too. Dry soils burst into respiration after rain and slow as they dry, so more frequent, intense rain should raise respiration sharply in arid lands. Nitrogen fertilization since the era covered in {{ref:soil-agri-138}} has boosted plant growth, root respiration and root biomass, and soil respiration along with them.

soil-bio-034.title: Roots, microbes and animals: who breathes out soil CO2
soil-bio-034.text: Roughly half the CO2 rising from soil comes from roots. Root respiration accounts for approximately half of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}, though values range from 10 to 90% with plant type and conditions. The rest comes from the organisms around them. Up to 20% of the carbon a plant captures in photosynthesis leaks into the soil from roots, and bacteria decompose most of it. Fungi partnered with roots also respire sugars the plant gives them. Most of the CO2 comes from the TCA cycle of cellular respiration. Fermentation, which works without oxygen, adds more in the oxygen-poor soil right around roots. Soil animals contribute by grazing bacteria and fungi and by fragmenting litter, which exposes more surface to microbes.

soil-bio-067.title: Bacteria that turn loose soil into stone
soil-bio-067.text: Bacteria can glue sand grains together with crystals of their own making. Microbiologically induced calcite precipitation is a biogeochemical process in which microbes cause calcium carbonate to precipitate within the soil. It is a form of {{ref:soil-bio-063}}. The main microbes able to induce it are photosynthetic cyanobacteria and microalgae, sulfate-reducing bacteria and some species that cycle nitrogen. Bacteria can trigger it by breaking down {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, by {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, by sulfate production or by iron reduction. Autotrophic pathways use up carbon dioxide, while heterotrophic ones run through the cycling of nitrogen and sulfur. The first route, ureolysis, shows the chemistry step by step. A microbial enzyme, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-224}}, splits this nitrogen compound into ammonium and carbonate. Hydroxide ions formed along the way raise the pH and shift bicarbonate to carbonate. That carbonate meets calcium and drops out as calcium carbonate crystals. The process feeds itself. A first layer of calcite makes bacteria cling more strongly to the soil surface, so further layers build up. The carbonate can form as calcite, aragonite or vaterite, in that order of usual stability. Such biological precipitation goes back to the Precambrian. Proposed uses include repairing cracks in concrete, preventing its corrosion and making biogrout. The process can also lock away radionuclides and heavy metals. They are trapped by co-precipitation into the calcite lattice, and binding to the precipitate makes lead in soil less available. Its use to strengthen sand is {{ref:soil-bio-068}}.

soil-bio-019.title: Soil zoology, the science of animals underfoot
soil-bio-019.text: In Russia in the 1940s, Mercury Ghilarov built a science around the animals underfoot. Soil zoology, or pedozoology, studies animals that live wholly or partly in the soil. Ghilarov noticed that the smaller soil organisms are, the more numerous they are. He also suggested that soil may have been the transitional environment between life in water and life on land. The English term was apparently first used at a 1955 conference of soil zoologists at the University of Nottingham. The field has practical value. Studying how {{ref:soil-bio-020}} interact can help farmers cut chemical use through {{ref:soil-agri-054}}.

soil-bio-066.title: When a living thing makes a crystal, is it a mineral?
soil-bio-066.text: Is a crystal grown by a living thing a mineral? The geological definition of a mineral normally excludes compounds found only in living beings. Yet calcite is often biogenic, and organisms make hydroxylapatite, which also occurs in rocks. As of December 2020, the International Mineralogical Association, the recognized standard body, had accepted 5,650 official mineral species out of 5,862 proposed or traditional ones. Its decision to exclude biogenic crystalline substances divides geologists and mineralogists, and the dispute remains open. Lowenstam noted in 1981 that organisms form some minerals that cannot form inorganically. Skinner, in 2005, counted any element or compound formed through biogeochemical processes as a mineral, amorphous or crystalline. Mineral-forming microbes live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface, down to at least 1,600 meters below the sea floor.

soil-bio-065.title: Geomycology: fungi that build and break minerals
soil-bio-065.text: Fungi quietly do geology. Geomycology is the study of the part fungi play in geological processes, including forming, transforming and dissolving minerals. Fungi deposit minerals on an organic matrix, such as a protein, that gives crystals a place to start. Proteins they secrete control the size and shape of the carbonate minerals they precipitate. Using organic phosphorus, fungi can even precipitate uranium-bearing phosphate minerals and gather them in their mycelium. Aspergillus niger and Paecilomyces javanicus tolerate uranium. Fungi also break minerals down, joining in {{ref:soil-found-052}}. The main culprits are strains that produce oxalic acid: Aspergillus niger, Serpula himantioides and Trametes versicolor corrode apatite and galena.

soil-bio-064.title: Three degrees of control in living mineral-making
soil-bio-064.text: Living things build minerals with very different degrees of control. One scheme, following a 2009 framework by Dupraz and colleagues, sorts {{ref:soil-bio-063}} into three kinds. In the biologically controlled kind, the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location. Mollusc and brachiopod shells are built this way. In the biologically induced kind, the metabolic activity of microbes, covered in {{ref:soil-bio-208}}, creates chemical conditions that favor mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete. Stromatolites and other microbial mats form like this. In the biologically influenced kind, abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals. The terms have no standardized definitions, and their use varies widely.

soil-bio-071.title: Ammonia fungi, which fruit where nitrogen floods the soil
soil-bio-071.text: Where an animal dies or leaves its dung in a forest, a particular set of fungi follows. Ammonia fungi fruit quickly and germinate readily when ammonia or other nitrogen-rich material makes the soil alkaline. Heavy additions of ammonia or {{ref:soil-fert-021}} do the same, raising the pH of soil litter to 8–10 and interrupting the recycling of nutrients. The fungi thrive until the soil reverts, which takes up to 2 years for soil ammonia, helped by late-phase fungi. Most live in temperate forests on well-rotted wood, plant debris or dung. They are most active in the O horizon, then the A and B horizons. They help maintain the cycling of nitrogen, and some are predators: Laccaria bicolor catches and kills springtails.

soil-bio-059.title: Acid mine drainage, sulfuric acid brewed by microbes
soil-bio-059.text: Streams below some mines run at pH 2–3. Acid mine drainage is the acid runoff made when lithotrophic microbes in mining areas oxidize pyrite and other reduced sulfur minerals to sulfate. The acid-loving bacterium Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, for example, uses iron sulfide to generate sulfuric acid, which drains from the mine with runoff. It changes the chemistry of groundwater and streams and may endanger plant and animal populations downstream. This is {{ref:soil-bio-057}} on an industrial scale. The same activity runs far more modestly in nature: in soil and talus, on glacier beds, on stone buildings and monuments, and in the deep subsurface.

soil-bio-058.title: How microbes living on bare rock start a soil
soil-bio-058.text: On bare rock, soil formation begins with microbes that can live on stone. Rock-colonizing lithotrophs, cyanobacteria above all, take that first step. Cyanobacteria are nitrogen-fixing photolithotrophs. They take energy from sunlight and use inorganic nutrients from rock as reductants, the electron donors their chemistry needs. That lets them grow on native, nutrient-poor rock and leave behind organic material that other organisms can then colonize. Colonization can start the breakdown of organic compounds, a primary factor in soil genesis. The mechanism is thought to have helped shape the early biological Earth, and it makes cyanobacteria classic {{ref:soil-found-085}}.

soil-bio-086.title: Oribatid mites, the slow-living shredders of forest litter
soil-bio-086.text: About 12,000 species of oribatid mites have been described, and the true total may run from 60,000 to 120,000. Also called moss or beetle mites, these slow-living mites are the most prevalent arthropods in forest soils. They measure 0.2 to 1.4 millimeters. They eat living and dead plant and fungal material, lichens and carrion, and none is parasitic. That diet makes them essential for breaking down organic debris and distributing fungi. Like earthworms, they speed decay. Unlike many earthworms, they do not mix it with mineral matter. Some mine conifer needles from the inside. They develop slowly and have few offspring, taking months to two years to mature in temperate forest soils. They are densest in forests with thick organic layers.

soil-bio-010.title: Counting soil life by reading its DNA
soil-bio-010.text: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed, so measuring the diversity of soil life is hard. The answer, increasingly, is to read DNA instead of growing cells. Next-generation sequencing of DNA extracted directly from the soil is opening {{ref:soil-bio-008}} to study. Omics approaches for microbes are advancing fast. One method, described in {{ref:soil-bio-221}}, reads the genes of a whole community, metatranscriptomics its active genes and proteomics its proteins. Metaphenomics has been proposed to add environmental constraints. Much remains unknown. A 2020 FAO report found major gaps in knowledge about biodiversity in soils.

soil-bio-028.title: Bottom-up control: feed the base and the web swells
soil-bio-028.text: Feed the base of a food web and the whole web grows. In bottom-up control, the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels. The evidence is correlation: consumers rise and fall with their resources. On land, the biomass of herbivores and detritivores rises with primary productivity, the rate at which plants make new growth. In the {{ref:soil-bio-025}} the chain is easy to follow. More productivity means more leaf litter, then more bacteria and fungi, more {{ref:soil-bio-193}} that eat them, and more mites and predatory roundworms. The whole web swells.

soil-bio-032.title: The external rumen: animals that let microbes cook their food
soil-bio-032.text: An isopod kept from eating its own feces can die. That odd fact reveals an external rumen: a partnership in which litter-eating animals let microbes enrich their fecal pellets outside the body, then eat the pellets again. Isopods and other litter transformers excrete pellets that are moister and richer in nutrients than the soil around them. Bacteria and fungi colonize those pellets. On nutrient-poor litter, the microbes turn them into better food. Fungi do the same for wood-eaters. They enrich nutritionally scarce dead wood, so xylophages, the animals that eat wood, can develop and speed its decay. Standard food webs miss such partnerships, because they emphasize competition and predation.

soil-bio-031.title: Funnels, cores and lamps: getting animals out of soil
soil-bio-031.text: Counting soil animals starts with getting them out of the soil. Samples are often taken with a metal core. Large animals such as earthworms can be picked out by hand, but that is impossible for {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and small arthropods. A dry Berlese funnel drives the animals of {{ref:soil-bio-209}} downward, away from light and heat, into a collecting vial. A wet Baermann funnel collects these worms, which sink because they cannot swim. Microbes need other tricks. They are characterized by their respiration, by genetic profiling of extracted cell components, or by biomass estimated before and after fumigation.

soil-bio-029.title: Do soil predators rule the web from the top?
soil-bio-029.text: Do the hunters in soil control the hunted? In top-down control, consumers higher in a food web set the abundance, diversity or biomass of the levels below. Its signature is the trophic cascade, in which predators affect organisms at least two links down. Whether cascades matter on land is actively debated. In soil they occur in the bacterial and fungal channels, but they may be infrequent. Omnivory, dormancy and the spatial separation of predator and prey all damp top-down effects. Soil webs are also donor controlled: decomposers cannot change how fast litter falls. Added predators or parasites can still matter. A roundworm that kills insects, {{ref:soil-bio-083}}, killed root-eating ghost moth caterpillars and so protected bush lupine. That is the principle behind biological control.

soil-bio-030.title: Why tangled soil food webs hold together
soil-bio-030.text: Theory once said that complexity makes food webs unstable. May's models, built on randomly linked community matrices, predicted exactly that, and soil webs were long thought simple. The random matrices drew much criticism. Soil food webs did not fit the predictions. Their long, complex, omnivorous chains resisted drying, freezing and fumigation. Several features promote that stability: many weak interactions, donor control, the buffering of soil structure, and dormancy in organisms such as bacteria. Donor control is the same limit that weakens {{ref:soil-bio-029}}. One practice works against stability. Nitrogen-containing fertilizers reduce it because they acidify soil.

soil-bio-026.title: Three ways to draw who eats whom in soil
soil-bio-026.text: In 1912, a food web traced the predators and parasites of the cotton boll weevil. It was the first topological web, the earliest of three ways to draw a food web. Topological webs map which organisms eat which, without numbers. Flow webs add numbers to the links, as {{ref:soil-bio-027}} shows. Interaction webs show how one group influences another. Each link has a positive effect on the consumer and a negative one on the resource, and these links can cause indirect effects. Community matrix models describe every link with differential equations. They use Lotka–Volterra equations and data on biomass and feeding rate to calculate interaction strengths. Comparisons stay difficult, because authors lump different numbers of species into functional groups.

soil-bio-027.title: Flow webs put numbers on soil's feeding links
soil-bio-027.text: In 1987, Hunt and colleagues put numbers on a soil food web for the first time. Their flow web covered the shortgrass prairie of Colorado. It estimated how much nitrogen passed between soil organisms and how fast each released it in mineral form. A flow web traces how much carbon or other nutrients move from producers to consumers. Building one starts from a topological web. Each functional group's biomass is then calculated, usually in kg carbon/hectare. Assuming populations are at equilibrium lets researchers derive feeding rates. Flow webs revealed three main energy channels. The bacterial and fungal channels carry the largest flow, the root-herbivory channel much less. Bacteria and fungi are now widely recognized as critical to decomposing carbon and nitrogen.

soil-bio-007.title: Does life underground follow the map of life above?
soil-bio-007.text: Does life underground follow the same map as life above it? Studies disagree, and the question is open. A survey of 17,516 18S rRNA gene sequences from 20 phyla of soil animals hinted that below-ground animal diversity may run opposite to above-ground diversity. Soil biodiversity lacks the clear latitudinal gradients, the shifts with distance from the equator, seen in plants. In 2007, salinity, not temperature or pH, was found to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity. A 2014 global study found fungal richness unrelated to plant diversity and better explained by climate, then soil and spatial factors. The stakes are disputed too. Some studies find that losing soil organisms reduces many ecosystem functions; others find plant diversity a better predictor.

soil-bio-006.title: Microbial hotspots, the crowded corners of soil
soil-bio-006.text: Soil microbes do not spread evenly. They crowd into hotspots, small sites rich in resources such as moisture or nutrients. One is the soil around roots. Another is the detritusphere, where dead organic material accumulates. In both, decaying root litter and compounds released by roots regulate the supply of carbon and nitrogen and so steer microbial processes. Root tips are hotspots of cellulase and chitinase, enzymes that break down plant and fungal materials. Between hotspots, microbes are separated in space. That separation, shaped by easily used carbon, temperature and moisture, affects how they interact and how the soil ecosystem works.

soil-bio-061.title: Living on almost nothing in deep and frozen soils
soil-bio-061.text: In farmed and frozen soils, microbes live on very little. These oligotrophic soil environments are home to the specialists described in {{ref:soil-bio-060}}. Nutrients thin out with depth. Surface microbes quickly consume what decomposes from plant and animal debris, and their wastes build up toxic chemicals lower down. Water and oxygen also diffuse less easily as depth increases. Aggregates, pores and extracellular enzymes help water, oxygen and nutrients move into the soil. Frozen polar soils are dominated by Actinomycetota, Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Cyanobacteria. Actinomycetota keep their enzymes working across a wide range of low temperatures. The bacterium Collimonas survives by digesting chitin from fungi and by weathering rocks and minerals for electron sources.

soil-bio-062.title: How plants thrive on the poorest soils
soil-bio-062.text: Plants on nutrient-poor soils get by in three ways: they take up nutrients more efficiently, use less of them and store them. Root adaptations improve uptake, among them nitrogen-fixing {{ref:soil-bio-179}}, fungal partners and {{ref:soil-bio-191}}. These plants grow very slowly. They use abundant ions to keep their cells firm and save scarce nutrients for building tissue. Many store nutrients, in trunk tissue for example, and remobilize them when demand rises. On the ancient sandplains of southern Western Australia, most plants rely on these roots for phosphorus and sulfur. Yet the vegetation is highly diverse. The white-sand soils of the Rio Negro basin in northern Amazonia, with pH below 5.0, tell another story. They carry low-diversity, extremely fragile forests and savannahs.

soil-bio-046.title: The drilosphere, soil remade by earthworms
soil-bio-046.text: Every earthworm burrow is wrapped in a lining of altered soil. The drilosphere is the part of the soil shaped by earthworm secretions, burrowing and casts: soil that has passed through their gut or lines their burrows. The lining averages 2 mm thick but can reach about 8 mm around the burrows of litter-feeding earthworms. It is generally richer in nitrogen, phosphorus and well-decayed organic material than the soil around it, probably because earthworms prefer to eat leaf and root litter. Microbes gather there too. In one soil it held 40 percent of the aerobic and 13 percent of the anaerobic nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and 16 percent of the denitrifiers. Through it, earthworms steer soil microbes and, with them, the fate of nutrients.

soil-bio-024.title: Moles, gophers and badgers: the giants that dig soil
soil-bio-024.text: Moles, pocket gophers, voles and badgers are the giants of soil life. Soil megafauna are soil animals over 2 cm long, mostly burrowing vertebrates that dig nests and galleries and throw earth up into mounds. Besides these digging mammals, they include burrowing birds, reptiles, amphibians, large earthworms and big arthropods. They are most common in arid areas. Most dig without eating soil. Still, stirring the horizons improves nutrient availability, infiltration, aeration, seed germination and the spread of fungi that partner with roots. Burrows create nutrient-rich patches and raise porosity and infiltration, reducing runoff on slopes. These animals are often treated as pests. Yet their loss from whole landscapes has been called an ecological catastrophe, especially in dry lands, where they are keystone species for healthy soil.

soil-bio-021.title: Soil microfauna, the animals that live in water films
soil-bio-021.text: A tardigrade dried out in soil can wait as a shrunken tun and revive within a few hours. Tardigrades belong to the soil microfauna, the smallest soil animals at 20 μm to 200 μm. The group includes protozoa, {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and rotifers. They move through mesopores (30–75 μm) and macropores (>75 μm) and mostly live in the water films around aggregates and roots. There they eat microbes or one another. Their grazing rejuvenates microbial colonies, and they excrete nutrients such as ammonium in a form plants can use. Tied to pore water, they are sensitive to drying. Cysts, dauer larvae and tuns are their survival stages. Unlike most soil invertebrates, they may not suffer critically from climate warming, but they are highly sensitive to acid rain.

soil-bio-083.title: Entomopathogenic nematodes, worms that hunt insects
soil-bio-083.text: Within 24–48 hours of a tiny worm getting inside, an insect is dead. Entomopathogenic nematodes are thread worms that infect and kill only insects, living as parasites inside them. Their targets live in the soil, from the larvae of moths, flies and beetles to adult grasshoppers and crickets. An infective juvenile enters an insect and releases gut bacteria, Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus, that kill it. After about a week, hundreds of thousands of new juveniles leave the cadaver. Hunting styles differ. Ambushers such as Steinernema carpocapsae wait at the surface for surface insects. Cruisers such as Heterorhabditis bacteriophora hunt deeper, so {{ref:soil-agri-095}} cut the first's numbers but left the second's unchanged. Both groups are used in biological pest control. Together they cut plum curculio populations by as much as 70–90% in northeastern American orchards. They fail against foliage pests, because UV light and drying harm them.

soil-bio-088.title: Copiotrophs, the microbes that live for the feast
soil-bio-088.text: Some bacteria live for the feast. A copiotroph is an organism of nutrient-rich environments, especially rich in carbon, and the opposite of an oligotroph. Copiotrophs grow at organic substrate levels up to 100 times higher. They live a feast-and-famine life. Motile and chemotactic, they move toward chemical cues, rush to nutrients and use them fast. Once supplies run out they survive poorly, and oligotrophs outcompete them. Their genes are built for speed: they carry up to fifteen ribosomal RNA operons, against one in oligotrophs, but use carbon less efficiently. Soil bacterial phyla can be sorted into the two groups. Soils rich in organic carbon favor copiotrophs, key players in carbon cycling when plants exude simple compounds such as sugars.

soil-found-076.title: The fungal loop that links desert plants and crusts
soil-found-076.text: In dry lands, life wakes in pulses after rain, and fungi may keep the pulses connected. The fungal loop hypothesis proposes that soil fungi in arid ecosystems link plants with a {{ref:soil-phys-032}}, which responds to a different amount of moisture. Crusts wake after small rains. Fungi hold their nutrients until larger rains activate plants, which then pass carbon back to their fungal partners. Carbon and nutrients thus stay cycling in living pools instead of washing away or escaping to the air between rains. Fungi suit the job. They work at higher temperatures and in drier soil than bacteria, so they likely drive nutrient cycling in hot, dry ecosystems. Direct tests remain rare. One isotope study found nitrogen moving up to 100 cm per day in both directions between plants and crust.

soil-bio-053.title: Saprotrophic bacteria, which digest the dead from outside
soil-bio-053.text: Many soil bacteria digest their food before they eat it. Saprotrophic bacteria, mostly soil-dwelling, feed on dead organic material. They release enzymes that digest it outside the cell, then absorb the products. Alongside saprotrophic fungi and water molds, they drive the breakdown of dead matter and the cycling of nutrients, and they feed higher trophic levels. Bacteria outcompete fungi for easily available food. In forest soils, though, their higher nitrogen demand and inability to move nutrients make them less efficient at breaking litter down. Their community make-up and growth rates signal the soil's condition, since growth responds quickly to change. Some are pathogens spread through contact with excrement, such as Escherichia coli. Others ferment cellulose in the rumen of cows.

soil-bio-082.title: The Mendocino staircase, where old soil grows pygmy pines
soil-bio-082.text: On the northern California coast, a pine with 80 or more growth rings may stand barely three or four feet high. It grows on the Mendocino ecological staircase, a flight of uplifted marine terraces. Each terrace is about 100,000 years older than the one below and carries its own soils, microbes, plants and animals. Plant succession repeated on each terrace eventually forms a very acid, nutrient-poor soil, the Blacklock series, with a clay or iron hardpan beneath. These pygmy forest soils are low in macro- and micronutrients and high in exchangeable aluminum. The iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage. On younger soils nearby, the same pine species grows many dozens of feet high. {{ref:soil-hist-010}} studied the pygmy forest on a 500,000-year-old terrace. The staircase shows one soil passing through several successive steady states. In 1974 the site became the Pygmy Forest National Natural Landmark.

soil-bio-072.title: The order in which fungi follow a flood of ammonia
soil-bio-072.text: When ammonia or {{ref:soil-fert-021}} reaches forest soil, {{ref:soil-bio-071}} fruit in a set order as the pH falls. Anamorphic fungi come first, tolerating pH above 8. Once they bring the pH to 7, cup fungi (Ascomycota) develop, and at pH 6 small basidiomycetes follow. These early-phase fungi fruit 20 to 200 days after application, in alkaline to neutral soils rich in ammonium-nitrogen. They usually run only one cycle. Late-phase agarics, with larger fruiting bodies, develop once the pH is 3.5–6.0, typically 2–3 years after application. They gradually turn soil ammonium into nitrate-nitrogen. Late-phase fungi are larger and more numerous and can recur over several cycles. Most are biotrophic, living off living partners, and few feed on dead matter.

soil-bio-068.title: Biocementation: bacteria that keep sand from liquefying
soil-bio-068.text: In triaxial tests, bio-cemented Ottawa sand grew 1.8 times stronger in shear. Biocementation uses {{ref:soil-bio-067}} as a cementing technique to strengthen sand that might otherwise liquefy. Treated sand gains shear strength, compressive strength, stiffness and resistance to liquefaction, because grains are bonded and the soil becomes denser. Strength comes mostly from point-to-point contacts between carbonate crystals and sand grains. Trickling solution from the surface forms crystals at the bridges between grains, so it gives more strength per amount of calcite. The method could be a cheap, green alternative to chemical grouting, whose synthetic additives are costly and, except for sodium silicate, toxic. It has limits. Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm, so it suits soils with few fines (USCS GW, GP, SW, SP, ML and organic soils). Enriching native urea-splitting bacteria in place can help.

soil-bio-055.title: The enzymatic latch that holds decay in check
soil-bio-055.text: In {{ref:soil-class-070}}, one family of enzymes holds the key to decay. The enzymatic latch is the control of breakdown in this waterlogged material by phenol oxidases. Phenolic compounds inhibit the hydrolase enzymes that digest dead material. Phenol oxidases destroy those phenolics and so release decay, which means limits on the microbes limit breakdown. Saprotrophic bacteria release microbial extracellular enzymes (MEEs) when their energy and nutrient needs are unmet, so MEEs signal nutrient availability. Several tell a story. One, {{ref:soil-bio-257}}, releases sugars that give microbes energy and easily used carbon. Acid and alkaline phosphatases show the potential to free phosphorus from organic forms. Phenol oxidases can also degrade or detoxify aromatic pollutants into carbon sources.

soil-bio-054.title: How fast soil bacteria grow and replace themselves
soil-bio-054.text: Next to young roots, a soil bacterial population can turn over in well under a day. Soil bacterial growth rate measures how fast bacteria produce new biomass and replace their populations. Under normal conditions production stays fairly steady, as growth is balanced by predation and other deaths. Estimates of turnover vary widely. Leucine or thymidine incorporation suggests days to weeks at around 20 °C. Other studies estimate 107–160 days at 25 °C, a gap put down to methods and temperature. The soil around roots is a special case. Compounds released by roots cut turnover there to 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots. Growth rises with soil moisture. Added glucose boosts it at low concentrations but inhibits it at very high ones.
