soil-bio-038.title: The Birch effect: a burst of breath when rain hits dry soil
soil-bio-038.text: When rain falls on dry soil, its respiration usually bursts to a very high level, then declines as the soil dries. This is the Birch effect, the influence of soil moisture on the cycling of carbon in soil. Sudden wetting can burst bacterial cells. Their released contents feed other bacteria and briefly boost {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. Through repeated drying and rewetting, microbial communities shift in diversity and composition.

soil-bio-050.title: Biofilms, the slime cities where soil bacteria live
soil-bio-050.text: In soil and on plant surfaces, most bacteria live bound in biofilms, nicknamed cities for microbes. A biofilm is a community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime described in {{ref:soil-bio-080}}. The slime mixes polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA, and can hold many times its dry weight in water. It shelters residents, lets them share nutrients and keeps enzymes close as an external digestion system. Soils with more clay minerals hold more bacteria as biofilms on clay surfaces. On roots, biofilms of growth-promoting bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas and the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-237}} can prime a plant's resistance to pathogens. Biofilms help cycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and oxygen. Their internal gradients let nitrate-making microbes work near the surface, while oxygen-free microbes deeper inside run {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. In soil, biofilms can clog pores. In sewage works and slow sand filters they are put to work stripping pollutants from water.

soil-bio-080.title: Extracellular polymeric substances, the glue of microbial life
soil-bio-080.text: Between 50% and 90% of the organic material in a biofilm is the slime its microbes secrete. Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) are high-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms release into their surroundings. They are mostly polysaccharides and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic compounds. They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials. Exopolysaccharides help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, so the bacteria can colonize roots and the soil around them. EPS also shape the soil itself. Together with microbial cells they can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity. They make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates. They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps clean up heavy metals. EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger even remove {{ref:soil-env-199}} from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

soil-bio-051.title: Five stages from a lone cell to a biofilm
soil-bio-051.text: A {{ref:soil-bio-050}} grows up in five major stages. It starts with reversible attachment. Free-floating cells settle on a surface, held at first by weak van der Waals forces and hydrophobic effects. In stage two, attachment becomes irreversible as cells anchor with structures such as pili and more cells gather. Stages three and four are maturation, as cell clusters embedded in the matrix grow into micro-colonies. The fifth stage, dispersal, releases cells that go on to colonize new surfaces.

soil-bio-133.title: Roots, the hidden half that anchors and feeds a plant
soil-bio-133.text: Roots left their mark in rock long before any animal walked on land. Fossil roots go back to the late Silurian, about 430 million years ago. Most are voids that filled in after the roots rotted, and they are easily confused with animal burrows. A root is the plant organ, usually below the soil surface, that anchors the plant and takes in water and dissolved nutrients. Its skin cells, the epidermis, and their fine outgrowths, described in {{ref:soil-bio-140}}, take up soil water and dissolved ions. These then travel to the shoot through the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue. Roots also store reserves and make growth regulators. A cap of cells guards each growing tip and helps the new root push through soil. As the root deepens, the cap sheds cells and leaves a slimy, lubricating surface. The depth and spread of a root system decide which soil horizons the plant can draw water and nutrients from. Roots rarely work alone. Most vascular plants partner with certain fungi, described in {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and bacteria and many other organisms live close to roots too. On rangeland, grass roots hold soil together and reduce erosion. When the old roots of perennial grasses decay, they add organic matter and release nutrients.

soil-bio-182.title: The legume family and its nitrogen-making guests
soil-bio-182.text: About 19,000 species of flowering plants share one underground talent. The legume or pea family, Fabaceae, includes soybean, beans, pea, chickpea and alfalfa. Many legumes host bacteria, described in {{ref:soil-bio-178}}, in small swellings on their roots. These guests take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form the plant can use. The swellings are common across the family, though rarer in the Caesalpinioideae, and some species in every subfamily lack them. One plant can host several kinds: those of Acacia senegal can hold seven bacterial species from three genera. That talent is why farmers rotate crops with legumes and why green-manure crops are commonly legumes.

soil-bio-139.title: Taproots, the single deep anchor
soil-bio-139.text: Snap a dandelion off at ground level and it simply grows back. Its taproot survives below: a large, central, dominant root, usually straight, thick and tapering, with smaller roots branching sideways. Unless that root is cut several centimeters down, the weed resprouts. Dicots, plants with two seed leaves, start life with a taproot grown from the seed's first root, the radicle. It may last the plant's life but is more often replaced by {{ref:soil-bio-138}}. Soil shapes it. Deep, rich soils favor vertical taproots in many oaks, while clay soils promote several. Carrot, radish and turnip are taproots built for storage.

soil-bio-138.title: Fibrous roots, the dense mat near the surface
soil-bio-138.text: A mature tree 30–50 m tall spreads its roots as far as its height or more, yet well over 95% of them lie in the top 50 cm. Within a few years, most trees switch from a taproot to this wide, shallow kind of network. A fibrous root system is a dense mat of many thin, similar-sized roots growing from the stem base, the opposite of a taproot system. It forms when the embryonic root dies back while the plant is young, leaving thin roots and no distinct taproot. In many species most of the mat is adventitious roots, roots that sprout from the stem base. Monocots, the flowering plants with one seed leaf, all have one, as do ferns; wheat and rice are typical. Fibrous roots bind soil, take up surface nutrients quickly and control erosion. Forage crops cover a whole field and anchor its top layer of soil. The root mats of meadow grasses may even help hold radioactive materials in place.

soil-bio-136.title: How roots feel their way through the soil
soil-bio-136.text: Roots are not blind diggers. They sense gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and they steer their growth in response. Gravitropism, growth guided by gravity and worked through auxin, one of the {{ref:soil-bio-245}}, sends roots downward from germination. Each root type holds its own set angle. Air, nutrients and water pull roots toward them, and roots turn away from dry or otherwise poor soil. Roots hunting for nutrients can sense compacted soil through the diffusion of ethylene gas, and avoid it. They can even tell their own roots from other plants' roots in the same soil. Given years, roots crack foundations, snap water lines and lift sidewalks.

soil-bio-134.title: Root system architecture, the shape of the hidden half
soil-bio-134.text: Two plants in one field can lay out their roots in entirely different shapes. Root system architecture is that layout: how a plant's whole root system branches, spreads and angles through the soil. It is described by branching pattern (herringbone, dichotomous or radial) and by link length between branches, link radius and root angle. The species, the soil's composition and the nutrients on offer all shape it. So do gravity, light, water and oxygen, and the supply or lack of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, aluminum and sodium chloride. A system built in dry soil may work less well when the soil floods.

soil-bio-135.title: How deep roots go, and what stops them
soil-bio-135.text: The deepest living root ever observed turned up in an open-pit mine in Arizona, at least 60 meters (200 ft) down. Rooting depth describes how a plant's roots spread down through the soil. It depends on the plant's form, on where and when water and nutrients are available, and on the {{ref:soil-phys-040}}. Most roots of most plants still lie fairly close to the surface, where nutrients are more available and aeration is better. Rock, compacted soil just below the surface or a lack of oxygen can physically stop them. Deserts and temperate coniferous forests generally have the deepest roots; tundra, boreal forest and temperate grasslands the shallowest. In continuous permafrost, roots cannot pass below the thin top layer that thaws each summer. Plants there must be shallow-rooted, and trees are limited to specialists such as larch. Some roots grow as deep as their tree is tall.

soil-bio-137.title: Roots that breathe, pull, prop and store
soil-bio-137.text: Not every root just anchors and drinks. Specialized roots take on other tasks; they include aerial, prop, buttress, storage and contractile roots, and the tufts described in {{ref:soil-bio-191}}. Those tufts of short rootlets form when phosphate or iron runs low, notably in the Proteaceae. Mangroves raise aerating roots, or {{ref:soil-bio-199}}, above ground or water to exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited. Contractile roots expand sideways and shorten lengthwise, pulling bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper. Swellings in virtually all legumes, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}, house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Coralloid roots near the surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

soil-bio-140.title: Root hairs, where most of the water comes in
soil-bio-140.text: Most of the water a root takes in passes through hairs finer than a pencil line. A root hair is a thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell near the root tip. Each is 15–17 micrometers across and 80–1,500 micrometers long, long enough to reach in between soil particles. Together they raise the root's surface area relative to its volume. They grow only in the zone of maturation, perhaps because older hairs are sheared off as the root pushes on. Root hair cells secrete malic and citric acids, which change the oxidation state of minerals so their ions are easier to absorb. The hairs are also the main meeting point with fungal partners, described in {{ref:soil-bio-157}}. In legumes they curl around bacteria so that an infection thread can grow inward and start a nodule. Transplanting or repotting can strip many hairs off and make the plant wilt.

soil-bio-187.title: Roots that move water from wet soil to dry
soil-bio-187.text: During a drought, a deep-rooted plant can draw up groundwater and release it into parched topsoil. Hydraulic redistribution is this passive movement of water by roots from moist soil to dry soil. It happens in plants rooted in both wet and dry soil. It is strongest in those with taproots reaching the water table and side roots near the surface. In drought, water rises up the taproot and seeps from the laterals into the dry surface soil. Under flooding, roots move water the other way. The xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue, links taproot to laterals. Wet or dry soil around the laterals then sets up a pressure gradient, much like transpirational pull, the tug of water evaporating from leaves. It was once described as hydraulic lift: roots releasing water and nutrients into soil, mostly at night. Researchers now see two-way movement, helped by fungal networks described in {{ref:soil-bio-164}}. Hydraulic lift is regulated by the root endodermis, an inner sheath of root cells, and by stomata, the pores in leaves. Cavitation, air breaking the water column in the xylem, can stop it. By smoothing out differences in soil moisture, the process affects crop irrigation and helps seedlings establish. Scientists trace it with deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, and with sap flow and soil moisture measurements. Efforts are under way to add it to land-surface models.

soil-bio-142.title: Root exudates, the food roots give away
soil-bio-142.text: Roots leak food into the soil on purpose. Root exudates are the organic compounds, such as sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA, that roots release into the surrounding soil. They help protect roots against bacterial and fungal infection and help them push through the soil. They can also create a microclimate that benefits the plant. Exudates feed microbial activity and add carbon to the soil. Organic acids among them change the chemistry and the living communities right next to the root, compared with soil farther away. Each plant species releases its own mix and so recruits its own microbes from the surrounding soil. Root and microbial exudates can even extract phosphorus from apatite, the most common mineral source of soil phosphorus. One group, described in {{ref:soil-bio-172}}, works with soil phosphorus to steer how fungal threads grow through the soil.

soil-bio-143.title: The rhizosphere, the crowded zone around every root
soil-bio-143.text: Each gram of soil in and around roots can hold up to 10 billion bacterial cells that grow in culture. In 1904 a German plant physiologist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-075}}, named this crowded zone the rhizosphere. He meant soil around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release. Today it is defined as the narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms living with the roots. The roots pay generously for their company. They may exude 20–40% of the carbon they fix by photosynthesis as sugars and organic acids. Microbes in the zone's pores feed on these root exudates and on sloughed-off root cells, a process described in {{ref:soil-bio-148}}. The result is a hotspot of microbial diversity. Much of the nutrient cycling plants need happens right beside roots, and so does disease suppression by microbial antibiotics. Organic acids and sugars affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available. Root respiration and exudation can create pockets without oxygen next to roots. In acid soils, the pH rises close to roots. At the very center lies the rhizoplane: the root surface itself, with the soil particles closely bound to it.

soil-bio-157.title: Mycorrhiza, the ancient pact between root and fungus
soil-bio-157.text: In some ecosystems up to 80% of plant nitrogen and 90% of plant phosphorus reaches the plant through fungi. A mycorrhiza is the partnership behind those numbers. It is a symbiosis in which fungal hyphae, the fungus's fine threads, interconnect with plant roots and meet them at the level of single cells. The plant pays the fungus in sugars or lipids made by photosynthesis, perhaps 20–40% of its carbon. The fungus returns water and soil nutrients such as phosphorus, nitrogen and zinc. Some fungi colonize root tissue inside the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. Others grow between the cells, as in {{ref:soil-bio-173}}. The partnership occurs in 92% of plant families studied, covering 80% of species. Some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot form it at all. A plant short of phosphorus is quick to recruit fungi, and nitrogen starvation also plays a part. The deal is normally mutualistic, good for both sides, but in some species or circumstances it turns parasitic. It is also ancient. Mycorrhizae emerged as early as 450–500 million years ago, and early fungal partners may have been key to plants colonizing land.

soil-bio-149.title: Bulk soil, the quiet ground beyond the roots
soil-bio-149.text: Step away from a root and the soil goes quiet. Bulk soil is the soil outside the rhizosphere, not penetrated by plant roots. Natural organic compounds are much scarcer there. Its microbes are more varied but less abundant than those near roots, and bulk-soil organisms are generally smaller than the same species beside roots. Most bacteria here are quiescent. They rest in slimy colonies glued together with clay particles, which protect them from drying out and from grazing protozoa and nematodes. Bulk soil tends to have smaller pores and to hold more moisture at a given matric potential than the rhizosphere, which affects which microbes survive. Its chemistry is described by organic matter, organic carbon, nutrient content, cation-exchange capacity, free ions, pH and base saturation. Its respiration responds to temperature swings. Added nutrients or warming can strongly change its microbes, especially in sandy soils.

soil-bio-158.title: Sugar for minerals: how the mycorrhizal trade works
soil-bio-158.text: Most mycorrhizal hyphae are far finer than the smallest root or root hair. That fineness is the fungus's whole advantage. Mycorrhizal nutrient exchange is the trade in which the fungus gets carbohydrates from its host and in return improves the plant's uptake of water and minerals. Sugars such as glucose and sucrose travel from their source, usually the leaves, down to the roots and on to the fungus. In exchange, the hyphae explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface. They may secrete organic acids that dissolve or chelate ions, or free ions from minerals by ion exchange. They reach phosphate and iron that roots alone cannot, including nutrients immobilized in clay-rich or strongly basic soils. Some mycorrhizal fungi decay organic matter directly. In some nutrient-poor forests their hyphae take phosphate straight from leaf litter, bypassing the soil. Farmers can lean on the trade. {{ref:soil-agri-134}} with Inga, proposed as an alternative to slash-and-burn, relies on the fungi in Inga roots to stop rain washing phosphorus out of the soil. The trade helps most in nutrient-poor soils. Yet in boreal forests the fungi have been found hoarding nitrogen in times of scarcity, so the deal may be more than simply mutualistic.

soil-bio-161.title: Fungal partners as bodyguards against stress
soil-bio-161.text: A fungal partner is also a bodyguard. Mycorrhizal fungi protect plants against soil-borne disease, drought, salt and toxic metals. Mycorrhizal plants often resist soil-borne pathogens better, and the fungi secrete enzymes toxic to soil organisms such as nematodes. Forming the partnership primes the plant's immune system, so its defense responses are stronger. In one study the fungi tracked soil water level rather than aggregate stability, and they can make plants more resistant to drought. Salt can harm the fungi, yet many reports show mycorrhizal plants growing better under salt stress. The fungi also shield plants rooted in acidic, contaminated or metal-rich soils. Pines inoculated with Pisolithus tinctorius tolerated contaminated sites well. Zinc-tolerant Suillus bovinus protected Scots pine, probably by binding the metal in its external mycelium without blocking useful exchange.

soil-bio-159.title: Inside the cell or around it: the kinds of mycorrhiza
soil-bio-159.text: The first question about any mycorrhiza is how far the fungus gets into the root. Mycorrhizal types group these partnerships by how the fungus colonizes the root. The main split runs between {{ref:soil-bio-173}} and endomycorrhizas. In the first kind, the hyphae never enter individual root cells. In endomycorrhizas they pass through the cell wall, up to the cell membrane. The endomycorrhizas include the types described in {{ref:soil-bio-166}}, {{ref:soil-bio-176}} and {{ref:soil-bio-186}}, along with arbutoid and monotropoid forms. The lifestyle evolved independently many times. The fungi of the first of those endomycorrhizal types form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life. Not every fungus inside a root is a partner of this kind. Fungal {{ref:soil-bio-202}} live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside. Mucoromycotina fungi of this kind, living in the roots described in {{ref:soil-bio-242}}, were long mistaken for partners of the first type. They seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils. In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the flow runs backward. The plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

soil-bio-166.title: Arbuscular mycorrhiza, the most widespread plant partnership
soil-bio-166.text: Earth's topsoils hold an estimated 110 quadrillion kilometers of one kind of fungal thread. It belongs to the arbuscular mycorrhiza, the most widespread plant symbiosis known. In this type the fungus enters the cortical cells of a root, the cells of its outer tissue layer, and builds tree-like arbuscules inside them. Arbuscules are where nutrients and carbon change hands; balloon-like vesicles often store reserves. The fungi, from the Glomeromycotina and some Mucoromycotina, help plants capture phosphorus, sulfur, nitrogen and micronutrients. They partner 80% of vascular plant families and about 80% of plant species, on every continent except Antarctica. The fungi are obligate symbionts with little ability to live on dead matter, and up to 20% of the host's carbon may pass to them. About 40% of their hyphae lie in wild grasslands, and the total holds about 300 megatons of carbon. They are vital on poor volcanic soils and sand dunes. Their hyphae and a soil protein described in {{ref:soil-bio-121}} improve soil aggregate stability.

soil-bio-173.title: Ectomycorrhiza, the fungal sheath of forest trees
soil-bio-173.text: Only about 2% of plant species form ectomycorrhizas, yet they include trees that dominate whole ecosystems. In this kind of mycorrhiza the fungus sheathes the root tip and grows between the root's outer cells without entering them. The fungi, mostly Basidiomycota and Ascomycota, build a mantle up to 40 μm thick and a net between epidermal and cortical cells, described in {{ref:soil-bio-185}}. Their hyphae reach several centimeters into the soil. Hosts are mostly woody plants such as birch, beech, willow and pine. Nitrogen is scarce in most ecosystems and locked in hard-to-break-down organic matter. The fungi reach further than roots and extract it from the organic layer. They receive an estimated 15% of the host's food and supply up to 86% of its nitrogen needs. Heavy fertilizer nitrogen breaks the deal: in one study, fungal species fell from over 30 at low-nitrogen sites to 9 at high-nitrogen sites. Laccaria bicolor even lures and kills springtails; eastern white pine inoculated with it got up to 25% of its nitrogen from them.

soil-bio-177.title: Glomeromycota, the fungi behind most root partnerships
soil-bio-177.text: About 230 described species of fungi partner the roots of most of the world's plants. They make up the Glomeromycota, the group whose members form arbuscular mycorrhizas. They live in soils worldwide, partnering over 80% of plant species, even in salt marshes. Most evidence shows they depend on land plants for carbon and energy, which long made them hard to grow in the laboratory. They reproduce asexually by spores 80–500 μm across, and new colonization tracks the density of spores in the soil. A survey of arid land found 5.4% of fungal rRNA reads were Glomeromycota, suggesting earlier PCR-based studies had underestimated them.

soil-bio-164.title: The common mycorrhizal network and its disputed powers
soil-bio-164.text: Trees in a forest may be linked underground, though how much passes along the links is disputed. A common mycorrhizal network forms where the hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi join the roots of two or more plants, of the same or different species. Suzanne Simard described these networks in 1997, and their apparent roles in woodland earned them the nickname 'Wood Wide Web'. The two main types follow their fungi: arbuscular hyphae enter root cells, while ectomycorrhizal hyphae thread between them. Studies report carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus moving between plants, with nitrogen flowing from nitrogen-fixing to non-fixing plants. Carbon labelling showed carbon passing both ways between paper birch and Douglas fir, and the fir ended with a 2% to 3% net gain. An insect-damaged Douglas fir appeared to warn a nearby ponderosa pine, which then made defense enzymes. Critics call these claims weakly supported. Connections are hard to verify in the field, and the birch-to-fir carbon was not shown to travel through a network rather than through the soil.

soil-bio-183.title: Glomus, a large genus of root fungi
soil-bio-183.text: With about 85 described species, Glomus is the largest genus of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and every species in it forms mycorrhizae with plant roots. It is not a natural group, though: its members do not all descend from one shared ancestor. The species are thought to be obligate symbionts that cannot be cultured without a host. They live in nearly all land habitats, from farmland and deserts to tundra. Several, such as G. aggregatum, are cultured and sold as mycorrhizal inoculant for farm soils. Not every member helps: G. macrocarpum causes tobacco stunt disease.

soil-bio-151.title: The root microbiome, the company a root keeps
soil-bio-151.text: Before the 1970s, most scientists thought microbes blanketed the whole root surface. In fact they cover about 10% of three-week-old root segments and about 37% of three-month-old roots. The root microbiome is the changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots. The communities inside the root, in the rhizosphere and in bulk soil differ, though some species overlap. Helpful members include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, growth-promoting microbes, mycorrhizal fungi, protozoa and organisms that fight disease. Some bacteria, fungi and nematodes do harm. Root partners live on carbon-rich products of the host's photosynthesis. Mycorrhizal fungi stretch far into the bulk soil, widening the root system's reach. Archaea that make methane or oxidize ammonia are common, especially in wetlands and other soils without oxygen. Plants also pick their company: in finger millet, only about 8% of the core microbiota was consistently shared between soil and plant.

soil-bio-154.title: Rhizobacteria, the bacteria that live on roots
soil-bio-154.text: Not every bacterium on a root is a friend. Rhizobacteria are bacteria that live with plant roots and can harm plant growth, leave it alone or help it. In practice the word usually means the helpful ones, described in {{ref:soil-bio-155}}; they make up about 2–5% of rhizosphere bacteria. Some colonize the root surface or the spaces between outer root cells, often forming nodules. Others live inside the plant, in the apoplast, the spaces outside its cells, the subject of {{ref:soil-bio-202}}. One of their most useful acts is turning N2 gas, which plants cannot use, into ammonia the host can take up. That service is costly. Building and keeping nodules can take 12–25% of a plant's total photosynthetic output. Rhizobacteria also release organic acids and phosphatases that turn insoluble soil phosphorus into usable forms such as H2PO4−. Free-living nitrogen fixers live just outside the roots of many grasses. In rice they supply more fixed nitrogen when the plant's demand is high. Organic amendments such as sugarcane straw, goat manure and filter mud boost these free-living helpers, even without nodules.

soil-bio-178.title: Rhizobia, the bacteria that feed legumes nitrogen
soil-bio-178.text: Every year 12–20 million hectares of soybeans are inoculated with live bacteria. Those bacteria are rhizobia: soil bacteria that fix nitrogen once they have settled inside swellings on legume roots, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}. The first known species, of the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-239}}, was identified in 1889. Rhizobia are a mixed group of alpha- and betaproteobacteria, mostly in the order Hyphomicrobiales. They live freely in the soil but need a plant host to fix nitrogen. Inside the nodule they turn atmospheric N2 into ammonia, which is exported to fuel the legume's growth. In return the plant feeds them organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source. It is a classic mutualism. When the legume dies, its nodules break down and release the bacteria back into the soil. Much fixed nitrogen leaves the field in harvested grain or hay. Enough stays behind, as higher soil nitrate, to feed the next crop, which matters most where no fertilizer is used. Inoculation tends to raise yields, and inoculants have been used in North America for over 100 years. The partnership has its cheats. Some strains hoard plant resources while fixing little nitrogen. Legumes answer by sanctioning poorly fixing nodules, cutting their growth or their supply of carbon or oxygen. Conditions matter too. Nutrient deposition has favored less productive strains, and extra nitrogen lets other plants outcompete legumes for light.

soil-bio-184.title: Rhizophagus irregularis, a fungus sold by the bag
soil-bio-184.text: One fungus turns up in many commercial mycorrhizal fertilizers. Rhizophagus irregularis, formerly called Glomus intraradices, is an arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus used as a soil inoculant in agriculture and horticulture. It occurs in almost all soils, especially in forests and grasslands, and most crops benefit from inoculation with it. Studies show it raises phosphorus uptake in many plants, and its hyphae improve soil aggregation. It colonizes new plants from spores, hyphae or colonized root fragments. Researchers use it widely to study how arbuscular fungi improve plants and soil.

soil-bio-167.title: Sugar for phosphorus: the arbuscular bargain
soil-bio-167.text: Phosphorus can flow into mycorrhizae up to six times faster than into root hairs. That speed explains why so many plants buy their phosphorus from fungi. Arbuscular mycorrhizal nutrient exchange is the trade in which these fungi take sugars from their host and supply it above all with phosphorus. Phosphorus reaches roots mainly by diffusion, a slow creep through soil water, and fungal hyphae shorten the distance. In some cases the hyphal network takes over uptake entirely, and all of a plant's phosphorus comes through the fungus. The fungi take the host's photosynthetic products as hexoses, simple sugars. They store carbon as trehalose, glycogen and lipids, and about 25% of the carbon they receive is stored in their hyphae outside the root. The bargain is reciprocal. More carbon to the fungus means more phosphorus back to the plant, and less means less. Some fungi are poor partners that take much carbon for little phosphorus. The fungi also change the root zone. By taking up ammonium selectively and releasing H+ ions, they lower the pH, which makes phosphorus precipitates more soluble. Their ammonium uptake also raises the flow of nitrogen to the plant. As the hyphal network grows and dies back, it adds a substantial amount of carbon to the rhizosphere and to the organic carbon stored below ground.

soil-bio-168.title: Farming with arbuscular fungi instead of against them
soil-bio-168.text: Plowing a field tears up more than soil. It breaks the soil's larger structure and the fungal hyphal network, leaving the fungus unable to infect new roots and cutting the plant's phosphorus supply. Managing arbuscular mycorrhizae in agriculture means arranging {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, fertilizer and cropping so that crops can keep working partnerships with these fungi. Heavy fertilizer and fungicide use, poor rotations and breeding for such conditions all hinder the partnership. Heavy phosphorus fertilizer inhibits colonization: as plant phosphorus rises, the fungus's carbon drain stops paying. Losing the fungi can then cause shortages of micronutrients such as copper. Systems that till less may need less phosphorus fertilizer. Cover crops extend fungal growth through autumn, winter and spring, and the fungus survives winter to colonize the next crop early. Crops poor at finding nutrients, such as flax, depend heavily on the fungi at low and intermediate soil phosphorus. The payoff is greatest in organic and low-input systems, where soil phosphorus is generally low.

soil-bio-141.title: Root mucilage, the slime that greases every root tip
soil-bio-141.text: Plants use up to 40% of the energy they make by photosynthesis secreting one product: slime. Root mucilage is a gelatinous secretion of plant-specific polysaccharides, long chains of sugars, that coats the protective tip described in {{ref:soil-bio-198}} as part of the root exudate. How it is secreted is still debated. Growing evidence points to root-cap cells that are continually shed and burst as roots push through soil, releasing polysaccharides made in their Golgi apparatus and cell walls. Maize mucilage is rich in galactose, xylose, arabinose, rhamnose and glucose, the building blocks of pectin and other plant polysaccharides. Mucilage glues soil to the root, keeping the contact needed to regulate water uptake. It cuts friction as roots penetrate and maintains a microclimate. It can also reduce evaporation and store water, which helps plants cope with water deficit. Soil fungi feed on broken-down mucilage and in return raise the plant's uptake of water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus.

soil-bio-176.title: Ericoid mycorrhiza, the heath plants' nitrogen miners
soil-bio-176.text: On bogs and heathlands, mineral nitrogen is very scarce, yet heath plants thrive there. Ericoid mycorrhiza is part of the reason: a mutualism between plants of the heath family, Ericaceae, and several lineages of mycorrhizal fungi. The fungi form coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots. Each coil, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars, works for only a few weeks before degrading. Their enzymes break down complex organic molecules, taking nitrogen even from cellulose, pectin, chitin and the woody compound described in {{ref:soil-bio-116}}. In acidic, slowly decaying litter layers they pass that nitrogen straight to their hosts.

soil-bio-192.title: Siderophores, the iron hooks of soil microbes
soil-bio-192.text: Soil is full of iron, yet plants and microbes can still starve for it. In aerobic soils iron is mostly ferric (Fe3+), which forms insoluble, rust-like solids. Siderophores solve the problem. They are small iron-binding compounds secreted by bacteria, fungi and some plants, and they are among the strongest known Fe3+ binders. They pull iron into soluble complexes that cells take up by active transport. Microbes switch on production when iron runs short. Plants on calcareous soils, 30% of the world's farmland, often lack iron; grasses, cereals and rice answer by secreting phytosiderophores such as deoxymugineic acid. Siderophores from rhizosphere microbes raise iron availability to plants, and oats can take up iron through them. Fluorescent pseudomonads make pyoverdine siderophores that starve pathogens of iron. Siderophores can also chelate other metals, from aluminum and copper to lead, cadmium and uranium.

soil-bio-179.title: Root nodules, the pink factories of fixed nitrogen
soil-bio-179.text: Cut open a working nodule and its fixing zone is pink, colored by an iron-containing protein that manages oxygen, {{ref:soil-fert-219}}. A root nodule is a growth on the roots of some plants, chiefly legumes, that houses nitrogen-fixing bacteria: rhizobia in legumes, or {{ref:soil-bio-200}} in other plants. Fixation is very sensitive to oxygen. Nodules form when soil nitrogen is scarce; plenty of it blocks them. Legume roots release flavonoids that attract rhizobia and switch on {{ref:soil-bio-201}}. These make root hairs curl, and an infection thread carries the bacteria into the cortex. Leaf sugars pay for splitting N2. Determinate nodules, as on soybean, stop dividing early and are round. Indeterminate ones, as on pea, alfalfa and clover, keep a growing tip and are cylindrical. Heat, acidic soils, drought and nitrate limit it. When the plant dies, its fixed nitrogen fertilizes the soil, which is why traditional rotations include a legume such as clover.

soil-bio-150.title: The spermosphere, a seed's first neighborhood
soil-bio-150.text: Within hours of planting, a seed can be under attack. Pathogens such as Fusarium and Pythium ultimum may colonize it, though helpful microbes the seed attracts can keep them out. The contest plays out in the spermosphere, the zone around a germinating seed where soil, microbes and seed interact. It typically reaches 1–10 mm from the seed, varying with seed type, soil microbes and moisture. Seed exudates inhibit or stimulate microbes, but the soil's organic matter matters more. Once the radicle emerges, it grows into the rhizosphere below, and above into the zone around the stem described in {{ref:soil-bio-073}} and onto the leaf surfaces.

soil-bio-146.title: Allelopathy, chemical warfare from the roots
soil-bio-146.text: Some plants fight their neighbors with chemistry. Allelopathy is the release by some plants, often from their roots, of chemicals that hold back the growth of other organisms. Invasive garlic mustard is believed to stop trees forming mycorrhizae in North American forests. Its chemical weapon, benzyl isothiocyanate, inhibited three ectomycorrhizal fungi on white pine seedlings. Farmers turn the effect on weeds: cover crops such as rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards suppress them this way. Rotating crops relieves allelopathy and also raises yields through better nutrient availability.

soil-bio-147.title: Reading the root zone through its genes and chemistry
soil-bio-147.text: Most life around a root is invisible, so researchers read it through genes and chemistry. Rhizosphere research methods range from pH measurements to DNA sequencing of its microbes. Marker genes, 16S rRNA for bacteria and the ITS region for fungi, are amplified and sequenced to reveal a community's makeup and diversity. Metagenomics and metatranscriptomics sequence all the DNA or RNA present, showing what a community could do and which genes are active. Microelectrodes, agar techniques and microsampling follow pH and water movement near roots. Pyrolysis–field ionization mass spectrometry detects the dark organic acids and residues of decayed matter in field soils.

soil-bio-145.title: The chemical conversation around roots
soil-bio-145.text: Roots send chemical messages, and the soil around them is full of listeners. Rhizosphere signalling is the exchange of chemical signals among roots, microbes, fungi and insects, which decides who colonizes the root zone. Hundreds of root metabolites recruit microbes, letting plants favor helpful bacteria. Rhizobia detect flavonoids from legume roots and reply with {{ref:soil-bio-201}} that lead to root nodules, and each signal pair is strictly specific. Root signals described in {{ref:soil-bio-172}} make mycorrhizal spores germinate and colonize the root. There are eavesdroppers. The parasitic plant Striga germinates when it detects the same signals.

soil-bio-160.title: Dual mycorrhiza, plants with two kinds of partner
soil-bio-160.text: A few plant species refuse to choose between fungal partners. Dual mycorrhiza is their ability to host both arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi in the same root system at once. Its costs and benefits seem to depend on the plant's life stage and on nonliving conditions, and switching between fungal types has also been reported. Dual-mycorrhizal plants often have broader ranges, spreading into habitats where one fungal type is missing. They aid succession and recovery on nutrient-poor soils and are valued in restoration where trees lack fungal inoculum. Ectomycorrhizal woodland trees have been seen establishing around dual-mycorrhizal willows amid vegetation dominated by arbuscular partnerships.

soil-bio-165.title: From a pale forest plant to a fungal genome
soil-bio-165.text: The study of root-fungus partnerships began with a puzzling plant. In 1881 Franciszek Kamieński showed that Monotropa hypopitys depends on fungi from neighboring trees for nutrition. In 1885 A.B. Frank formally described and named mycorrhizal fungi. In 1899 Noël Bernard established that orchids such as Neottia nidus-avis need a specific fungus to germinate. Paleobotanists working on the Rhynie chert later showed that mycorrhiza-like associations existed in early land plants 407 million years ago. In 2008 Laccaria bicolor became the first ectomycorrhizal fungus to have its genome sequenced, opening the molecular era of the field.

soil-bio-163.title: Mycorrhizae in a warming, polluted world
soil-bio-163.text: Extra carbon dioxide in the air sounds like a gift to plants and their fungi. If nothing else is limiting, more carbon dioxide should directly benefit both. Yet climate change may also damage mycorrhizae. They tend to do better in cool conditions, so warming could harm them. That matters most in the Arctic, where nitrogen and water are hard to get and the fungi are crucial to plant growth. Pollution adds pressure. SO2, NOx and ozone from human activity may reduce fungal propagules, root colonization, links between trees and ectomycorrhizal enzyme activity. The breakdown of excess atmospheric ammonia can damage fine mycorrhizal structures.

soil-bio-162.title: Why plants struggle on barren soil without fungi
soil-bio-162.text: Plant a seedling in sterile soil and it often does poorly, unless someone adds spores or hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi to colonize its roots. Without these fungi, plant growth can lag in early succession and on degraded land. The fungi can also tilt competition. Introducing alien mycorrhizal plants into nutrient-poor ecosystems puts native non-mycorrhizal plants at a disadvantage. Some partnerships bring extra help. Knobbly ectomycorrhizae of Suillus tomentosus on lodgepole pine host nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which let the pines colonize nutrient-poor sites.

soil-bio-185.title: The Hartig net, a fungal trading floor inside the root
soil-bio-185.text: In 1842 the German forest biologist Theodor Hartig reported a hidden root-fungus interface. The Hartig net, named after him, is the network of fungal hyphae that grows between the epidermal and cortical cells of a root in an ectomycorrhiza. It is where fungus and plant trade. The outer mycelium releases nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, micronutrients and water into the spaces between root cells. Plant sugars pass back to feed the fungus. With pine-family hosts the net reaches deep into the root cortex; with many flowering plants it may stop at the epidermis.

soil-bio-181.title: Fungal endophytes, a plant's hired guards
soil-bio-181.text: Some plants hire fungi to guard them against grazers. In fungal endophyte defense, fungi living inside a plant's tissues protect it indirectly from herbivores. In exchange for carbohydrates, the fungi can raise the plant's water or nutrient uptake and protect it from insects, birds or mammals. Once settled, they change the plant's nutrient content and start or boost production of defensive compounds. Infection even reduces below-ground attackers such as nematodes and root-feeding insects. The defense has a price. Fungal toxins in forage harm livestock, causing fescue toxicosis and more than 600 million dollars in livestock deaths each year.

soil-bio-186.title: Orchid mycorrhiza, the fungus that raises orchid seedlings
soil-bio-186.text: An orchid seed, 0.35–1.50 mm long, carries virtually no energy reserve. Its seedling must get carbon from a fungus, and nearly all orchids depend on one at some stage. Orchid mycorrhiza is the symbiosis between orchids and the endomycorrhizal fungi that colonize their roots and seeds. Inside root cortex cells the fungus forms coils called pelotons, the defining structure, which the plant can later digest for carbon and nitrogen. The fungi are typically basidiomycetes such as Ceratobasidium (Rhizoctonia), Sebacina, Tulasnella and Russula. Phosphorus shortage often decides whether the partnership forms.

soil-bio-170.title: How arbuscular fungi reshape life around the root
soil-bio-170.text: An arbuscular fungus changes far more than its host. By altering the amount and makeup of root and fungal exudates, colonization decides the diversity and abundance of rhizosphere bacteria. The effect runs both ways with rhizobia. Rhizobia in the soil raise fungal colonization, and good colonization in turn increases nodulation and the nitrogen legumes fix. Greater fungal diversity increases plant diversity, and dominant arbuscular fungi can keep non-mycorrhizal plants from invading. At higher soil nutrient and moisture levels the fungi become less common and less diverse, because plants give them less carbon.

soil-bio-171.title: Finding hidden arbuscular fungi by their molecules
soil-bio-171.text: Arbuscular fungi hide inside roots and among soil grains, so researchers track them by their molecules. DNA methods target markers in the 18S rRNA region, and quantitative PCR measures targeted fungal DNA in roots or soil. The phospholipid fatty acid 16:1ω5 is the most used marker of fungal mycelium in soil; with 18:1ω7 it makes up about 58% of their phospholipid fatty acids. Stable isotope probing feeds substrates enriched in 13C, 15N or heavy-oxygen water, then traces labelled DNA or RNA to find which fungi are active.

soil-bio-169.title: Putting fungi back to heal degraded land
soil-bio-169.text: Replanting degraded land works better when the right fungi go in with the plants. Where native plant cover is disturbed in areas threatened by {{ref:soil-env-072}}, soil structure, nutrient availability and organic matter often decline. Mycorrhizal inoculation adds arbuscular fungi during replanting to rebuild the soil's biological and physical properties. A mixture of native fungi improved soil quality over the long term more than a single exotic species or no inoculum. Benefits included more plant growth, phosphorus uptake, soil nitrogen and organic matter, and better aggregation, infiltration and aeration, helped by more legume nodulation. Native strains also help extract heavy metals from polluted soils.

soil-bio-175.title: Ectomycorrhizal fungi in forestry and restoration
soil-bio-175.text: A eucalyptus planted far from home often needs more than water to prosper. Trees transplanted far from their range, or with specific partners, such as Eucalyptus and Pinus in plantations, often need native ectomycorrhizal inoculum. Foresters use these fungi when planting trees and restoring disturbed ecosystems. Losing a habitat's mycorrhizal fungi is a major soil disturbance, so adding them back is an important part of restoring vegetation. One use is controversial. Pine and eucalyptus plantations are promoted as carbon sinks, but their fungi tend to deplete the carbon stored in the soil. In farming these fungi matter little, since most mycorrhizal crops partner with arbuscular fungi.

soil-bio-174.title: Fungi that let trees endure poisoned ground
soil-bio-174.text: Some fungi thrive where metals poison most life. Ectomycorrhizal fungi can survive, and help their hosts survive, soils high in heavy metals, salts, radionuclides and organic pollutants. They limit heavy-metal uptake by binding metals at the cell wall and locking them inside cells in complexes, metallothioneins or vacuoles. They can also concentrate metals in their fruiting bodies. Suillus luteus and S. bovinus have forms adapted to zinc, cadmium and copper. Tolerance seems widespread, yet contaminated sites have less diverse fungal communities, while naturally metal-rich soils such as those covered in {{ref:soil-class-060}} do not. Some species help hosts survive salty soil, some break down persistent pollutants such as PCBs, and many hyperaccumulate radionuclides.

soil-bio-073.title: The laimosphere, the busy zone around buried stems
soil-bio-073.text: Its name comes from the Greek laimos, 'throat', for a connecting neck. The laimosphere is the microbe-rich zone of soil around the underground parts of plant stems, the stem's counterpart of the rhizosphere and spermosphere. It surrounds any buried organ other than roots, such as hypocotyls, the seedling stem below the first leaves, and stems, stolons, corms, bulbs and leaves. Sugars and amino acids exuded there stimulate microbes. As a seedling grows, the spermosphere extends downward into the rhizosphere and upward into the laimosphere. Those exudates can also wake pathogens such as Fusarium, Phytophthora, Pythium and Rhizoctonia, which start the stem rots of damping-off.

soil-bio-155.title: Growth-promoting bacteria, from seed coat to root
soil-bio-155.text: Joseph W. Kloepper first used the term plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, or PGPR, in the late 1970s. They are soil bacteria that colonize plant roots after being inoculated onto seed, and they enhance plant growth. Directly, they fix nitrogen, make siderophores that chelate iron for the root, solubilize minerals such as phosphorus and make plant hormones. Indirectly, they limit the damage pathogens do to yield, through induced systemic resistance and antifungal compounds. To work they must survive on the seed, multiply in the spermosphere, attach to the root and colonize the root system. Failure to colonize often explains poor field results. Inoculants usually go on the seed coat so that enough bacteria establish, and those at the root tip were found most active. Most are Pseudomonadota and Bacillota, such as Pseudomonas putida and the lipoferum species of the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-237}}. As {{ref:soil-fert-048}} and biopesticides, they could raise yields and cut disease while reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

soil-bio-188.title: Disease suppressive soils, where pathogens fail
soil-bio-188.text: In some soils, pathogens arrive and fail to establish. These disease suppressive soils hold microbes that keep pathogens out of the rhizosphere. They develop as growth-promoting rhizobacteria settle around roots and outcompete pathogens by releasing suppressive metabolites. Pathogenic fungi that reach the rhizosphere release enzymes that break down root cell walls. Beneficial Pseudomonas and Bacillus answer with metabolites that break up the fungal hyphae. Plants under attack recruit these bacteria from the bulk soil through their exudates, but only microbes already in the soil can be recruited. Greater plant diversity brings greater microbial diversity near roots and can mean stronger suppression. Informed rotation of crops and the practice described in {{ref:soil-agri-034}} can create such soils. They can even make plants more resistant to leaf-feeding insects, by promoting helpful bacteria and priming plant defenses.

soil-bio-180.title: Actinorhizal plants, the nitrogen fixers that are not legumes
soil-bio-180.text: Some alders fix as much as 300 kg of N2 per hectare per year, close to the highest legume rates. They do it with {{ref:soil-bio-200}}, a nitrogen-fixing actinomycete living in nodules on their roots, and plants with this partnership are called actinorhizal. Apart from the herbaceous Datisca, they are trees or shrubs, in three orders, eight families and twenty-six genera, such as alder, sea-buckthorn and Casuarina. Their nodules let them pioneer nitrogen-poor ground such as moraines, volcanic flows and sand dunes, enriching the soil for later species. Altogether these plants fix roughly as much nitrogen as rhizobial partnerships.

soil-bio-189.title: Do arbuscular fungi feed plants nitrogen too?
soil-bio-189.text: Phosphorus is the famous gift of arbuscular fungi; nitrogen is the disputed one. Their outer mycelium takes up nitrogen as ammonium, nitrate or organic compounds and hands it over inside the root. In laboratory cultures, 29% to 50% of root nitrogen has come via the fungus. Nitrogen can also pass between plants through common mycorrhizal networks: about 25% of labelled nitrogen given to a grass reached a grapevine. Yet a soybean–corn field study found negligible transfer. No growth benefit has been shown conclusively, and some researchers doubt the fungi matter much for plant nitrogen in nature.

soil-bio-152.title: Friend or parasite: a sliding scale for root microbes
soil-bio-152.text: A root microbe is not simply friend or foe. The mutualist–parasite continuum holds that the same microbe can behave anywhere between the two, depending on its host, the environment and the host's health. A parasite takes carbon from the plant while giving no benefit, or too little for what it takes, and so lowers the host's fitness. The host's immune response keeps symbionts in check; if it fails, the relationship slides toward the parasitic end. High nutrient levels can push some microbes into parasitism just when the plant no longer needs their help. Symbionts may be biotrophic, living off living tissue, or necrotrophic, living off dead tissue.

soil-bio-153.title: Chosen or chance: how root microbe communities form
soil-bio-153.text: How does a crowd of microbes sort itself onto a root? Two explanations compete, and the debate is open. One holds that 'everything is everywhere, but the environment selects'. The other says that when microbes are equally fit, neutral processes such as distance and dispersal barriers decide who arrives. Most likely both act, with some microbes more limited by one than the other. Selection clearly matters. Root tips, fine roots, the root surface and the rhizosphere each host different communities, because exudates favor microbes with matching metabolism. Nutrient levels, pH, moisture, temperature, soil structure and disturbance also shape assembly.

soil-bio-156.title: Deleterious rhizobacteria, the root bacteria that harm crops
soil-bio-156.text: In one sugar beet trial, root bacteria cost the crop 48% of its yield. Deleterious rhizobacteria are root-colonizing bacteria that harm plant growth, first described from sugar beet. Seeds inoculated with them germinated less and grew short, distorted roots with lesions, more fungal infection and poorer growth. Six strains have been identified, in the genera Enterobacter, Klebsiella, Citrobacter, Flavobacterium, Achromobacter and Arthrobacter. Growth-promoting rhizobacteria hold them back. Plots given both kinds rose 39% in production, while plots given only the harmful strains fell 30%.

soil-bio-191.title: Cluster roots, phosphorus miners of poor soils
soil-bio-191.text: Some plants grow a special tool for the phosphorus-poor native soils of Australia. Cluster roots, also called proteoid roots, are clusters of closely spaced short side rootlets. They may form a mat 2 to 5 cm thick beneath the leaf litter. They appear when phosphate or iron is scarce and boost nutrient uptake, possibly by chemically changing the soil to dissolve nutrients. Adolf Engler first described them in 1894 on the Proteaceae. They are now known in 27 Proteaceae genera, about 30 species of other families, and crops such as lupins and macadamia. Such crops need slow-release, low-phosphorus fertilizers; more phosphorus causes toxicity and sometimes iron deficiency.

soil-bio-190.title: One ancient signal chain for fungi and bacteria
soil-bio-190.text: Plants let two very different guests in through the same door. The common symbiosis signaling pathway is a highly conserved chain of signals in root cells that admits symbiotic microbes such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and rhizobia. Receptor kinases at the cell membrane perceive the guests' Myc or Nod factors. The signal reaches the nucleus as pulses of calcium, decoded by a protein called CCaMK, which activates CYCLOPS to switch on arbuscule or nodule genes. Its origins predate plants' move onto land: plants and arbuscular fungi have co-evolved for over 500 million years. Rhizobia probably co-opted it later, since both processes share genes such as the receptor SYMRK.

soil-bio-148.title: Rhizodeposition, what living roots leave behind
soil-bio-148.text: A living root sheds itself as it grows. Rhizodeposition is the addition of organic matter to soil by living roots, which exude compounds and slough off cells, especially at their tips. These rhizodeposits supply many forms of organic carbon and nitrogen. They feed the communities around roots and strongly change the chemistry next to them. They also stimulate bacterial activity in the rhizosphere, whereas most bacteria in the bulk soil stay quiescent. Together with fungal hyphae and the sticky polymers microbes make, rhizodeposition enmeshes soil and improves aggregate stability.

soil-bio-144.title: Trade, theft and hunting in the root zone
soil-bio-144.text: Around every root runs a small economy of trade, theft and hunting. Rhizosphere ecology is the web of mutualism, predation and competition among the microbes and soil animals that rhizodeposition supports. Its food web has three channels and two energy sources. Fungal and bacterial channels run on dead organic debris, while nematodes, symbionts and some arthropods run on root energy. The bacterial channel turns over faster, because bacteria use more accessible resources and regenerate faster. Nematodes grazing on bacteria have been shown to affect nitrogen availability and plant growth. Plants and microbes compete indirectly by locking scarce carbon and nitrogen into their biomass, and microbes take up amino acids better than plants do. Teams of microbes, such as growth-promoting bacteria with mycorrhizal fungi or Trichoderma, can give plants combined benefits. The web can also go wrong. Growing one crop for many years can cause the decline described in {{ref:soil-agri-152}}, a shift in pathogens and helpers that lowers fertility and yield. In aged tea plantations, built-up soil polyphenols have been linked to such a shift.

soil-bio-172.title: Strigolactones, the root signals fungi and parasites heed
soil-bio-172.text: Fungal hyphae bathed in exudates from phosphorus-starved roots grew more and branched further than those in exudates from well-supplied plants. The signals behind that difference are strigolactones, carotenoid-derived molecules that roots secrete into the rhizosphere. They make fungal spores germinate and boost the fungi's metabolism, growth and branching. They also prompt the fungi to send back signals the plant can detect. Together with soil phosphorus, they control how hyphae grow through soil: low phosphorus raises both hyphal branching and the plant's output of branching signals. The parasitic plant Striga eavesdrops, germinating when it detects strigolactones and then feeding on the root.

soil-bio-106.title: Plant litter, the fallen cover on the soil
soil-bio-106.text: Leaves make up about 70 percent of what a forest drops each year. Plant litter is all the dead plant material, such as leaves, bark, needles and twigs, that falls onto the soil surface. It forms the litter layer, the {{ref:soil-form-006}} at the top of many soils. Fresh litterfall is undecomposed, and its species and type are easy to recognize. Pieces over 2 cm in diameter count as coarse litter, smaller ones as fine litter. Soil scientists split the layer by decay: L for little decomposed, F for partly decomposed and H for fully decomposed and mostly unrecognizable. Grasslands, with little perennial tissue above ground, shed little litter. Litterfall also declines with latitude. Fast decay keeps tropical rainforest litter thin, while slow decay builds thick litter in boreal forests. The loose cover does real work. It shields aggregates from raindrop impact, so clay and silt do not plug the pores, and it helps rain soak in. It keeps soil moist, reduces erosion and shelters small animals. As it rots, litter becomes {{ref:soil-bio-112}} and releases nutrients. Most of the plant growth made on land, its net primary production, ends up eaten by herbivores or as litterfall. Litter therefore indicates how productive an ecosystem is and helps predict nutrient cycling and how fertile a soil will be. Fire can remove it completely, and regions with frequent wildfires have sparser vegetation and less litter.

soil-bio-114.title: Organic matter, the carbon left by living things
soil-bio-114.text: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made {{ref:soil-fert-021}} in a laboratory, and an old idea began to crack. That idea, vitalism, equated organic with living. Organic matter is the large pool of carbon-based compounds derived from the feces and remains of plants, animals and other organisms. Its basic structures come from cellulose, tannin and {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, plus the leaf coating in {{ref:soil-bio-233}}, with proteins, lipids and carbohydrates. After an organism dies, microbes and fungi break it down. The small products can recombine into larger, complex molecules. Its molecules range from 200 to 20,000 amu, and up to one-third of its carbon sits in stable rings that are hard to break. In soil, litter decayed beyond recognition counts as {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Organic matter carries nutrients, holds water and buffers solutions towards neutral pH. Most measurements capture only organic carbon, so they only approximate the amount of once-living matter.

soil-bio-115.title: Decomposition, the breakdown that recycles the living world
soil-bio-115.text: Rotting plants release over 90 percent of the carbon dioxide given off each year. That rotting is decomposition: the breakdown of dead organic substances into simpler matter such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts. It recycles the finite matter of the biosphere. Chemical or physical forces drive abiotic decomposition. Living organisms, mostly microbes, drive biotic decomposition, the process traced in {{ref:soil-env-231}}. Plant matter decays in stages. Water first leaches out the soluble carbon compounds. Soil invertebrates then fragment the litter, and microbes chemically alter what remains. In soil the reactions fall into three groups. Enzymes oxidize compounds to carbon dioxide, water and heat; nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur are released; and resistant compounds form that make up {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. The rate depends on temperature, moisture, soil properties, the amount and quality of dead material, and the microbes themselves. Decay is slow in very wet or very dry soil and fastest in damp soil with enough oxygen. When dry soil is rewetted, many bacterial cells burst and release a pulse of nutrients. Materials differ too. Sugars and amino acids are labile, quick to break down. Cellulose and {{ref:soil-bio-232}} are moderately labile. In a temperate climate their half-life is 12–18 days. {{ref:soil-bio-116}} and {{ref:soil-bio-233}} resist, so resistant material builds up as soil organic matter ages. Acid and clay-rich soils decompose organic matter more slowly, because clay binds it out of microbes' reach. Turning the soil speeds decay by adding oxygen and exposing fresh organic matter.

soil-bio-089.title: Humus, the dark and stable end of decay
soil-bio-089.text: Humus usually makes up five percent or less of a soil's volume, yet soils lean on it heavily. Humus is the stable, well-decomposed form of soil organic matter, derived from the breakdown of plant and animal remains. The word is Latin for ground or earth. It is brown to black and made largely of carbon, with high amounts of nitrogen and smaller amounts of phosphorus and sulfur. Its {{ref:soil-fert-184}} commonly runs between 8:1 and 15:1, with a median of about 12:1. Only fully decomposed matter counts as humus. Material still decomposing is {{ref:soil-bio-112}}, and since the change is gradual, no sharp line divides them. Neither is truly dead, for bacteria, fungi and other microorganisms permeate both. Humus is amorphous, lacking the cellular structure of the organisms it came from. It occurs mostly in the upper soil. A humic layer of finely divided organic matter, with a large surface area, lies above the topsoil and below the leaf litter. Humus is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture qualities. In sands and other coarse soils it holds moisture, and it lowers bulk density. Farmers also use the word for mature woodland {{ref:soil-fert-028}} spread to improve soil.

soil-bio-112.title: Detritus, where most of the land's food ends up
soil-bio-112.text: On land, far more material is broken down as dead matter than is ever eaten alive. That dead matter is detritus: the decomposing remains of organisms and plants, together with feces. On land it occurs as plant litter and as organic matter mixed into the soil, such as the humic soil beneath a layer of fallen leaves. In forests, leaf, twig and bacterial litter dominate it by biomass. It shelters seedlings, arthropods, reptiles and amphibians. Dead remains and feces gradually lose their form, worn down by physical processes and by grazers, bacteria and fungi. Communities of microorganisms usually colonize detritus and remineralise it, returning it to simple mineral forms. The organisms at work may be rot organisms, detritivores or coprophages, which eat dung. Late in decomposition, mesophilic microorganisms, which favor moderate temperatures, break down the residue and release heat. The same effect warms a heap of {{ref:soil-fert-028}}. As detritus decomposes on the ground, it feeds plants with inorganic salts. Water has its detritus too. In fresh water most of it is leaf litter from nearby land, the main carbon source of small streams. At sea it settles as marine snow of dead plankton and fecal pellets.

soil-bio-120.title: Mineralization, turning dead tissue back into plant food
soil-bio-120.text: Soil microbes face a nitrogen shortage. Most organic matter reaching soil holds too little nitrogen for the microbes that consume it. Mineralization is the decomposition, or oxidation, of organic compounds that releases their nutrients in soluble inorganic forms plants can take up. It raises the availability chiefly of nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. Its opposite is {{ref:soil-fert-121}}, in which microbes lock nutrients into their own cells. Which process wins depends on a nutrient's concentration relative to the carbon in the organic matter. Above a carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of about 30:1, microbes absorb mineral nitrogen from the soil and keep it away from plants. As they work, they release carbon dioxide, and the ratio falls. Below about 25:1, further decomposition releases inorganic nitrogen as ammonium. Nitrogen can end as ammonium, nitrite, nitrate or nitrogen gases. Carbon becomes carbon dioxide, carbonates and methane, and phosphorus becomes phosphate ions. When decomposition is complete, the freed nitrogen adds to the soil's total mineral nitrogen. The fraction that escapes mineralization goes the other way, into {{ref:soil-bio-090}}.

soil-bio-118.title: Particulate organic matter, the fast fuel of soil life
soil-bio-118.text: Pass soil through a fine sieve, and some organic matter stays behind. Particulate organic matter, or POM, is the fraction that does not pass a filter or sieve with openings usually between 0.053 millimeters (53 μm) and 2 millimeters. It still shows its original cellular structure: partly decomposed plant litter, animal feces, microbial detritus and pollen. Its carbon is particulate organic carbon, or POC, and there is typically about twice as much POM as POC. Most POM turns over in less than 10 years, though less active parts may take 15 to 100 years. Its decay supplies much of the energy of soil organisms and a steady release of nutrients. Fungal threads colonizing it bind particles with sticky polysaccharides into aggregates, improving infiltration, aeration and resistance to erosion. Manure and crop residues raise POM, while repeated working of the soil and turning native grassland into farmland deplete it. Because it responds quickly to management, it is often used as an indicator of soil quality.

soil-bio-090.title: Humification, how part of the litter becomes humus
soil-bio-090.text: Not all decaying matter vanishes into carbon dioxide. In humification, soil organisms feeding on litter turn part of it into humus instead of mineralizing it completely. The raw materials are plant detritus, dead animals and microbes, called necromass, the excreta of all soil organisms and black carbon from past fires. Fungi and bacteria that feed on dead matter do the work, along with earthworms, nematodes, protozoa and arthropods. Earthworms are major contributors. The ingredients disappear in order. Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids go first and fast. Cellulose and {{ref:soil-bio-116}} follow more slowly, and fats, waxes and resins persist longest. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} transform that tough polymer quickly, making it a main precursor of humus. Resistant leftovers, such as modified {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, oils, fats and waxes, join newly made compounds like polysaccharides to form the basis of humus. Reactions with proteins lock nitrogen and other nutrients inside, protecting them from mineralization. Early work pictured humification as building polymers that microbes could not attack. Recent research shows microbes can digest humic substances in redox reactions. Humification happens naturally in soil and artificially in {{ref:soil-fert-029}}, and it can darken soils, a change called melanization. For storing carbon long term, stimulating it beats slowing litter decay. Not everyone accepts the idea, though. Some authors reject humification as a distinct process, arguing that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds.

soil-bio-094.title: Why farmers prize humus
soil-bio-094.text: Weight for weight, humus holds nutrients many times better than clay. Its main gifts to farm soils are better structure and a large surface that holds nutrients until plants need them. Humus is a negatively charged colloid, and it raises a soil's cation-exchange capacity. Nutrient cations cling to it where roots can reach them instead of leaching away. On a dry-weight basis its cation and anion exchange capacity is many times that of clay colloids. Humus can hold the equivalent of 80–90% of its weight in moisture, helping soil withstand drought. It increases microporosity, and microbial mucilages secreted during humification glue particles into a crumbly, well-aerated tilth. It buffers soils against excess acidity or alkalinity. It also chelates, or chemically grips, heavy metals and excess nutrients, keeping them from leaching. Its dark color helps cold soils warm in spring. Whether roots absorb humic substances was long debated. The consensus now is that humus acts on plants hormonally, not simply as food.

soil-bio-093.title: Why some humus lasts centuries and some a decade
soil-bio-093.text: Much of the humus in soil today has persisted for more than 100 years. It survives because it hides inside small soil aggregates or binds tightly to clays, out of reach of microbes and their enzymes. Humus without that protection mostly decomposes within 10 years and is called labile. The two kinds do different jobs. Labile, or effective, humus is a ready nutrient supply for microbes. Stable humus offers plants few nutrients but helps maintain soil structure as a long-term reservoir. Its most stable forms, often called {{ref:soil-bio-105}}, may persist for centuries if not millennia. Earthworms, termites and some millipedes build mineral-organic complexes in their guts. Surface layers shaped by such animals therefore store more carbon than those where litter simply piles up. Charcoal powder mixed into topsoil slowly oxidizes into a very stable humus, probably important in creating the fertile Amazonian {{ref:soil-class-053}}. Only humus with multi-century permanence matters for drawing down excess carbon dioxide from the air. In subtropical and tropical climates, heat and heavy leaching oxidize litter and humus rapidly. Without new organic inputs, humus content declines.

soil-bio-125.title: Saprotrophs, the organisms that digest outside their bodies
soil-bio-125.text: A saprotroph never swallows its food. It feeds on dead organic matter or waste by secreting chemicals that digest it outside its body, unlike detritivores, which eat it. Fungi such as Mucor and soil bacteria do most of this work, and microscopic saprotrophs are also called saprobes. Their enzymes split proteins into amino acids, lipids into fatty acids and glycerol, starch into disaccharides and cellulose into glucose. Fungi take the products back into their hyphae and pass them through the mycelium for growth and repair. Saprotrophs need water, and fungi are 80–90% water. They also need oxygen, a neutral to mildly acidic pH below 7 and temperatures of 1 to 35 °C, growing best at 25 °C. Fungi decompose efficiently, which makes them among the main saprotrophs. Mycorrhizal fungi evolved from saprobic ancestors. Because saprotrophs recycle nutrients, the Royal Horticultural Society advises leaving them in gardens where possible.

soil-bio-107.title: How fallen leaves return nutrients to the soil
soil-bio-107.text: Before a leaf falls, the plant takes some of its nutrients back. Plants reabsorb part of their nutrients from aging leaves, and plants on poor sites reabsorb more, so their litter is nutrient-poor. What falls still feeds the soil. Litterfall nutrient cycling is the return of nutrients from plants to soil through fallen litter and its decomposition. It is the main pathway for recycling nitrogen and phosphorus. Organisms of decay turn the litter's simple carbon compounds into carbon dioxide and water. They release ions such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which plants take up again. Fungi play a large role. Rain and throughfall, the water dripping through the canopy, leach breakdown products into the soil. They add to its cation exchange capacity, especially in highly weathered tropical soils. Litter can also reshape a soil. Leaching of iron, aluminum and organic matter from litter drives podzolization. It is intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolics and fulvic acid. Nutrient-rich litter decomposes faster. Nutrient levels measured by remote sensing therefore serve as an index of potential decomposition rate. An ecosystem's uptake equals the nutrients stored each year in plant tissues plus those replacing losses from litterfall and leaching.

soil-bio-126.title: The forest floor, between living trees and mineral soil
soil-bio-126.text: In tropical rainforests, termites and millipedes process litter so fast that the forest floor may vanish seasonally. Elsewhere it piles up. The forest floor, also called duff, is the layer of decaying litter and other dead plant matter between a forest's living vegetation and its mineral, humus-rich soil. In Canada and some other countries the term means the L, F and H layers: litter, visibly decomposing material and well-decomposed matter of unrecognizable origin. Specialists disagree on whether it equals the O horizon or leaves out the litter. Its mass reflects the balance of litter inputs and decay, set by site, vegetation and disturbance history. It is heaviest and deepest in boreal and mountain forests, where decay is slow. Its decomposition supplies a large share of a forest's nutrient needs. It is also an important fuel in forest fires. In one study of Douglas-fir seedlings, removing forest floor debris and compacting soil cut ectomycorrhizal fungal diversity and abundance by 60%.

soil-bio-095.title: Humus forms, the signature of how litter rots
soil-bio-095.text: Charles Darwin, a year before his death, published a detailed study of the crumbly surface soil he called mould. Today it is known as {{ref:soil-bio-096}}, one of several humus forms. A humus form is the group of organic and mineral-organic horizons at or near the surface that shows how litter becomes humus in a given place. It may include L, F, H and Ah horizons, but never B or C. Danish forester {{ref:soil-hist-012}} first described mull and its opposite, {{ref:soil-bio-104}}, linking them to the high and low fertility of beechwoods. Franz Hartmann later added {{ref:soil-bio-103}} between them. Five humus systems are now described on land: those three plus {{ref:soil-bio-097}} and {{ref:soil-bio-098}}. They occur from forests and grasslands to tundras and deserts. Soil organisms drive them, so humus profiles change within a few years, while whole soil profiles take decades to centuries. Foresters care because the humus form influences whether seedlings and saplings can establish and the forest can regenerate. Most humus classifications are national, such as the French, Belgian, German, Canadian and Russian ones, and focus on temperate forest soils. Bogs and marshes are classified differently. Their humus forms are sorted by the depth and seasonal swings of the water table and by dominant vegetation, such as sphagnum or herbs.

soil-bio-109.title: Raking the forest floor for animal bedding
soil-bio-109.text: In 1853 Europeans raked an estimated 50 Tg of dry leaf litter from their forests. That year was the peak of forest litter raking, an old practice widespread in Europe since the seventeenth century. Farmers gathered the litter to bed livestock in place of straw. Combined with other degradation, the raking could promote podzolization. Managed well, for example by burying the used litter, repeated removal may not harm soil formation. Primary forests hold more abundant, deeper and moister litter than secondary forests.

soil-bio-108.title: Litterbags, a simple tool for measuring decay
soil-bio-108.text: A mesh bag on the ground can measure a forest's metabolism. A litterbag is a container or mesh bag set out for a fixed time, either to collect falling litter or to measure how fast confined litter decays. Researchers place the bags at random, mark them by GPS or local coordinates and check them at set intervals. Weighing the dry contents gives the litterfall flux: total litter mass in kilograms divided by bag area in square meters, per year. Under a mass-balance approach, decomposition over a period should equal litterfall input over the same period. Different mesh sizes let researchers study different groups of soil animals.

soil-bio-111.title: Mangrove litter, where crabs do the cleanup
soil-bio-111.text: In some mangrove forests, crabs carry off 80% of the fallen leaves. Mangrove litterfall is litter that falls in mangrove forests or reaches coasts from rivers, and it follows a very different path from litter on land. Tides, crabs and microbes remove it, and which matters most depends on the tides. Where crabs dominate, they forage at low tide. Their droppings pass the leaves' tough woody compounds, undigested, into sediments and water. Each plant species' carbon can be traced from plant through crab to sediment.

soil-bio-132.title: Decomposers, the role that frees nutrients from the dead
