soil-bio-132.text: A tree cannot hunt for its food. Plants and other sessile autotrophs, organisms that stay put and make their own food, cannot seek out nutrients or digest other organisms. They rely on decomposers, organisms that break down the dead and release the nutrients locked in dead matter. The word names a role, not a kind of organism. Fungi and bacteria fill it by digesting food outside their bodies. Earthworms and woodlice digest internally and release nutrients in their feces, so one organism can be both detritivore and decomposer. On land the work happens mainly in or on soil, and it makes soil more fertile. Earthworms and roots first grind and churn the material, a mixing called bioturbation. Enzymes do the rest. Enzymes for fats, proteins and starch are widespread, so these go first. Cellulases occur in far fewer organisms, and enzymes that digest {{ref:soil-bio-116}} in fewer still. Fungi are the primary litter decomposers in many ecosystems. Their hyphae penetrate large pieces that bacteria can only feed on from the surface, and only wood-decay fungi can modify that tough polymer.

soil-bio-110.title: Leaf litter as a home and a pantry
soil-bio-110.text: A layer of fallen leaves feeds and shelters a crowd. Its decomposer community includes fungi, bacteria, amoebae, nematodes, rotifers, tardigrades, springtails, potworms, insect larvae, mollusks, mites, woodlice and millipedes. Some plants are adapted to it. Bluebell shoots pierce the layer in spring, and rhizomatous wood sorrel thrives there. Salamanders and caecilians live in its damp microclimate, and the ovenbird needs it for foraging and nest material. In boreal forests, fallen lichens feed wintering deer and elk. In British Columbia they sustain mountain caribou through a 'manna effect'.

soil-bio-116.title: Lignin, the plant polymer that resists rot
soil-bio-116.text: Wood owes much of its strength to lignin. These complex polymers build the support tissues of plants, especially wood and bark. In cell walls it fills the spaces between cellulose, pectin and another polymer ({{ref:soil-bio-232}}) and cross-links them, so the plant stands firm and its vascular tissue can conduct water. Lignin resists decay and acid or base hydrolysis, and it shields cellulose from microbial enzymes. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} break it down with secreted peroxidases, and actinomycetes also decompose it. Under temperate conditions its half-life is about six months. Bound to proteins and microbial by-products, it becomes one of the main precursors of humus.

soil-bio-091.title: What humus is made of, and why it is hard to say
soil-bio-091.text: Chemists in the 1940s and 1960s tried to take humus apart, and they failed. Their extractants reacted with the organic matter and created artifacts. Humus remains a very complex substance that is still not fully understood. Its core is very large molecules, built partly from lignin and other plant polyphenols and partly from similar molecules made by microbes. Proteins, amino acids and {{ref:soil-bio-260}} attach to this base, giving humus a moderate nitrogen and sulfur content. The method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}} shows the base, mostly lignin and black carbon, can be very old, while the attachments are much younger. Microbes strip the protein more readily than they break the base, and younger protein may take its place. In the classical view of {{ref:soil-hist-018}}, fully humified humus is amorphous, uniformly dark, spongy and jelly-like. Yet under a light microscope it may still show tiny plant, animal and microbial remains, broken up mechanically but not chemically.

soil-bio-113.title: The detritus food chain, eaten again and again
soil-bio-113.text: Detritivores eat dead matter, but they mostly digest the microbes living on it. In the detritus food chain, or detritus cycle, microbes multiply on detritus and detritivores feed on both. The microbes quickly take up small proteins, lipids and sugars and slowly decompose complex carbohydrates. They take carbon from the detritus but nitrogen and phosphorus from their surroundings. Detritivores digest mainly these protein-rich microbes and excrete the detritus barely changed. Microbes regrow on that dung over several days, and it is eaten again. Each passage thins and fragments it until its complex carbohydrates disappear. Bacteria and fungi recycle the rest.

soil-bio-117.title: The priming effect: feeding soil can speed its decay
soil-bio-117.text: Add fresh organic matter to soil, and the old organic matter may start to disappear faster. This is the priming effect: a change, positive or negative, in how fast soil organic matter decomposes after something is added to soil or {{ref:soil-fert-028}}. Löhnis discovered it in 1926 while studying how {{ref:soil-fert-026}} decomposed. Bingeman named it in 1953, but it was widely disregarded until the 1980s–1990s. Pulsed or continuous inputs of fresh organic matter usually trigger it, and usually it accelerates mineralization. The common explanation is that microbes, fueled by energy and nutrients from the fresh material, become more active. Positive priming speeds mineralization. Negative priming causes the opposite, leaving nitrogen locked up and unavailable. Many things can prime decomposition: fertilizers, plant litter, detritus, root exudates, plowing, and drying and rewetting. Where priming occurs, soil organic matter turns over at least one order of magnitude faster than in the bulk soil. It appears within days or weeks. It is larger in carbon- and nitrogen-rich soils and with larger additions, and it has not been seen in sterile environments. Its mechanisms are more complex than first thought and remain poorly understood. Similar mechanisms may operate in water.

soil-bio-105.title: Humin, the most stubborn part of soil organic matter
soil-bio-105.text: About half of soil organic matter will not dissolve in anything. Soil organic components split into a soluble fraction, largely humic acids, and an insoluble fraction, the humins, which make up about 50%. Humin is that insoluble, carbon-based fraction of giant molecules, the most resistant of the humic substances. It has the greatest molecular weight and darkest color of them. It is insoluble in acids, alkalis and water at any pH, and it resists microbes most. As the most stable form of humus, it may persist for centuries if not millennia. Biorefineries also make humins as by-products of sugar dehydration.

soil-bio-130.title: The hydrogen cycle and the soil that soaks it up
soil-bio-130.text: Soil is where most hydrogen gas leaves the air: biological uptake by soil is the dominant sink of atmospheric H2. The hydrogen cycle is the exchange of hydrogen compounds between living and non-living sources and sinks, centered on molecular hydrogen. Microbes make H2 with hydrogenase and {{ref:soil-fert-101}} enzymes and by fermenting organic matter without oxygen. Over 30% of microbial taxa carry hydrogenase genes. Other organisms use that H2 to reduce CO2 to methane or acetate, sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, or Fe3+ to Fe2+. H2 is an indirect greenhouse gas, because it can hinder the removal of methane from the air.

soil-bio-096.title: Mull, where animals mix the litter into the soil
soil-bio-096.text: Under mull, fallen leaves disappear fast. Mull is a humus form in which burrowing animals mix organic matter thoroughly into the mineral soil. The result is a well-developed, granular A horizon of humus bound to mineral particles, with no thick organic layers and no OH horizon. Earthworms are its most widespread makers. Polydesmida millipedes in Appalachian old-growth forests, darkling beetles in dry regions and burrowing mammals also form mull. It occurs in deciduous forests and grasslands under mild climates with moderate rainfall, on parent materials rich in weatherable minerals. Its plants drop easily decomposed litter with a low ratio of carbon to nitrogen, which releases nutrients instead of locking them up. Fuller decomposition oxidizes organic acids, raising soil pH and base saturation. A positive feedback follows: better litter speeds decomposition and nutrient cycling, which speeds plant growth. Because its litter is quickly buried and bound to minerals, mull ultimately stores more carbon than {{ref:soil-bio-103}} or {{ref:soil-bio-104}}.

soil-bio-104.title: Mor, where litter piles up and fungi rule
soil-bio-104.text: Mor and thick moder were long confused under one name, raw humus. Mor is the humus form of coniferous forests and heaths in which litter decomposes very slowly and piles up on the soil, barely mixing into the mineral soil. Evergreen needles, heath twigs and woody debris rot slowly because of low pH, few nutrients, much lignin, tannin or terpenes, and cool, wet conditions. Bacteria are inactive at low pH and earthworms are absent, so fungi do most of the work. A thick OL horizon lies on an OF horizon matted with roots and fungal hyphae, then a variable OH horizon. The change to mineral soil is sharp, with no A horizon. Organic matter instead leaches in solution through the E horizon to the B horizon, as in podzolization. High C:N and C:P ratios lock up nitrogen and starve plants, which then drop nutrient-poor litter, closing a loop. Ectomycorrhizal and ericoid fungi pass nitrogen straight from the slowly rotting remains to plants. Mor goes with very cold climates, high altitude or latitude, pines and heath, or heavy pollution.

soil-bio-121.title: Glomalin, a soil glue no one has isolated
soil-bio-121.text: In 1996 USDA scientist Sara F. Wright proposed glomalin, a sugar-bearing protein said to coat arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. The name comes from Glomerales, an order of fungi. It is usually assumed to glue soil into stable aggregates and reduce erosion. A related measure, glomalin-related soil protein (GRSP), correlates strongly with aggregate water stability. GRSP declines when the fungi are removed, hinting at a fungal origin. It takes 7–42 years to biodegrade and is thought to supply up to 30 percent of the carbon in soils where the fungi live. Yet the protein has never been isolated, and its origin and role in storing carbon are disputed.

soil-bio-103.title: Moder, the busy middle ground between mull and mor
soil-bio-103.text: Franz Hartmann placed moder midway between mull and mor. Like mor, it piles partly to fully humified material on top of the mineral soil. Unlike mor, it teems with animal life. Moder is the humus form in which litter decomposes slowly and builds up mainly as the fecal pellets of litter-dwelling invertebrates. Its makers do not burrow: springtails, oribatid mites, millipedes, woodlice, insect larvae, snails, slugs, surface-dwelling earthworms and enchytraeid worms. It forms under conifers, and in deciduous forests where acidity and poor litter keep earthworms and bacteria scarce. Moder is highly acidic and rich in carbon, with a high C:N ratio and low cation exchange capacity, nitrogen and base saturation. Still, more nutrients are available than in mor. Its hallmark is a loose OF horizon full of droppings and animal activity. Its thin A horizon is built of sub-millimeter feces, mostly from enchytraeids. Fine tree roots and their ectomycorrhizal hyphae penetrate these feces to capture nutrients.

soil-bio-131.title: Kerogen, organic matter locked in rock
soil-bio-131.text: Most of Earth's organic compounds are not in living things but in rock. Kerogen, the solid, insoluble organic matter of sedimentary rocks, exceeds the organic content of living matter 10,000-fold. It forms from dead plants, algae and microorganisms compressed and heated over geological time. Labile kerogen yields mainly oil, refractory kerogen mainly gas, and inert kerogen no hydrocarbons, only graphite. Humic kerogen comes from land plants, from precursors such as cellulose, lignin, terpenes and phenols. With coal, kerogen is one source of natural organic matter in groundwater.

soil-bio-119.title: Four fractions of soil organic matter
soil-bio-119.text: About 15% of soil organic matter is alive, including roots. The other 85% falls into four groups, in order of decreasing ease of decomposition. First come simple compounds dissolved in soil water, such as organic acids, sugars, amino acids and root mucilages; they turn over in less than 12 months. Particulate organic matter comes next. Humus, amorphous colloidal particles under 53 microns, is usually the largest share, 45 to 75%, and persists for decades. Resistant organic matter, such as charcoal, graphite and coal, lasts hundreds of years and improves structure, water holding and cation exchange.

soil-bio-128.title: Dissolved organic matter, soil's most mobile carbon
soil-bio-128.text: Some of the carbon in soil travels with the water. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is the fraction that passes a filter with pores of about 0.22 to 0.7 micrometers; its carbon is dissolved organic carbon (DOC). In soil it comes from rain, litter, crop residues, manure, root exudates and decaying organic matter. It is one of the most active and mobile stores of carbon, affecting soil charge, acid-base reactions, nutrient retention and the trapping of heavy metals. Clays and iron and aluminum oxides hold it. Leached DOC can reach the water table in well-drained soils, and under mor it moves from the E to the B horizon.

soil-bio-102.title: How humus forms shift with forests, farms and climate
soil-bio-102.text: A site's humus form is not fixed. It shifts with vegetation, land use, pollution and climate. During forest succession organic horizons thicken, from mull in early stages towards moder under mature stands; in old natural forests the two alternate. Converting conifer forest to broadleaf turns moder into mull, and conifer plantations on deciduous land do the reverse. Farming that encourages earthworms can create a mull-like form called agri-mull. Pollution that harms earthworms slows decomposition and pushes the form towards mor, so humus forms offer a cheap early warning of contamination. Warmth favors mull, yet it also speeds microbial decomposition, depleting humus and leaving many soils with a negative carbon balance. A 3 °C rise in alpine grasslands reduced soil humus content. Earthworms disperse slowly, so change can lag, and adding them to turn moder into mull has given mixed results.

soil-bio-100.title: Reading the layers of a humus form
soil-bio-100.text: A hand lens and a knife are enough to read a humus form. Along a knife-cut profile, or by hand from a small block of soil, its horizons follow the stages of litter decay and its mixing into mineral matter. On top is the OL horizon, called Oi in the American system: recognizable leaves or needles that animals have not yet fragmented. Only in the most active mull does it vanish for part of the year. Below lies the OF horizon (Oe), litter chewed by feeding animals and mixed with their fecal pellets. Those pellets range from 30-50 micrometers, from enchytraeids, mites and springtails, to 1-2 millimeters, from earthworms and millipedes. Next is the OH horizon (Oa). It is humus formed once plant remains are no longer visible but not yet mixed with mineral matter, often piled-up fecal pellets. Fine roots and ericoid mycorrhizal fungi there can decompose resistant organic matter and pass its nitrogen to the host plant. In the A horizon, burrowing animals mix organic and mineral matter. Larger animals build aggregates over 250 μm, smaller ones aggregates under 250 μm. The E horizon is a white or ashy, carbon-poor layer through which water, solutes, clay and humus are leached.

soil-bio-097.title: Amphi humus, mull and moder stacked together
soil-bio-097.text: Amphi humus, also called twin mull or amphimull, combines moder-like OF and OH horizons with a mull-like granular A horizon. It occurs where seasons contrast sharply. Summer drought in Mediterranean areas and winter frost in mountains drive earthworms deeper, so activity at different depths peaks at different times of year. Amphi shows that litter thickness alone cannot identify a humus form: the mineral horizon below must be examined too. With two carbon sinks side by side, it may store carbon better than any other humus form.

soil-bio-099.title: HUMUSICA, a worldwide key to humus forms
soil-bio-099.text: National humus classifications mostly describe temperate forests. HUMUSICA, created in the 2010s, covers terrestrial, semi-aquatic, cultivated and man-made environments worldwide. It sorts humus forms by both their structure and their function. Mull, moder and mor become humus systems, or humus interaction systems. Each holds several humus forms that differ in the thickness of their organic and mineral-organic horizons. Mull splits into Eumull, Mesomull, Oligomull and Dysmull, while Amphimull is a system of its own. It has also been suggested that the pedon be split into humipedon, copedon and lithopedon, in decreasing order of biological influence and speed of change.

soil-bio-098.title: Tangel, the deep organic mat on mountain limestone
soil-bio-098.text: On hard limestone and dolomite in cold, humid mountains, organic matter can pile up as a layer up to 1 m thick. Kubiëna named it the tangel layer. Tangel humus rests this mat on rock, with little or no A horizon. Tangel and mor are two pathways of organic matter in such mountains: tangel on alkaline substrates, mor on acidic ones. Its biology is little studied. One northern Alps study found microbial activity, fungi and bacteria falling with depth while archaea increased.

soil-bio-122.title: Is glomalin real? The extraction behind the debate
soil-bio-122.text: No one has ever isolated glomalin itself. What exists is a heat-and-citrate extraction yielding material reactive to the antibody Mab32B11, first detected by ELISA in 1987. Labs without ELISA measure a crude extract with the Bradford assay, so three different things share one name. The extraction heats citrate to 121 °C for at least an hour. Analysis in 2010 showed it also pulls out humic substances, so the glue effect may not be glomalin. Proteomics finds most extracted proteins are not of mycorrhizal origin. The fungi can even cause net losses of carbon from soil. Sources still disagree on whether glomalin exists and how much carbon it holds.

soil-bio-123.title: Canopy soils, gardens in the treetops
soil-bio-123.text: Soil can form high above the ground. Where branches and crevices in a forest canopy trap leaves and fine branches, the matter weathers into canopy, or arboreal, soil. In some temperate rainforests it reaches 30 cm deep. Epiphytes, plants rooted on trees, grow in it, add organic material and speed its development. Older canopies and lower positions gather more. Soils high up face extreme swings of sun, wind and moisture. They abound in southern-hemisphere temperate rainforests that stayed largely ice-free during the Last Glacial Maximum. Logging and climate change destroy them faster than they can be studied.

soil-bio-101.title: The Humus Index, a number for humus forms
soil-bio-101.text: The Humus Index turns humus forms into a ranked number. It covers all lowland terrestrial humus forms, ordered by the growing share of organic layers in the profile. It runs along gradients such as Eumull to Dysmull and Hemimoder to Dysmoder. Because it can be rank-correlated with soil or vegetation measurements, it serves as an indicator of soil condition or forest stand development. It covaries with fertility, forest management, tree age, pollution level and plant species richness.

soil-bio-127.title: Litter quality: why some leaves rot faster
soil-bio-127.text: Not all leaves rot at the same pace. Litter quality is the chemical make-up of fallen plant material, such as its nutrient, lignin and tannin content. It governs how fast litter decomposes and which humus form develops. Nutrient-rich litter decomposes faster, slowing as those nutrients fall. Deciduous 'improving' litter goes with mull. It decomposes easily, has a low C:N ratio, releases nutrients and encourages bioturbation. Coniferous 'acidifying' or 'recalcitrant' litter goes with moder or even mor. Its low pH, low nutrients and high lignin, tannin or terpene contents slow decay. Tannins protect plants from insects and infection, but they also lower soil pH and can lock nitrogen into resistant tannin-protein complexes. A positive feedback ties it together: better litter speeds decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth.

soil-bio-092.title: The soil continuum model and the case against humus
soil-bio-092.text: Some soil scientists doubt that humus, as textbooks describe it, exists at all. The soil continuum model holds that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds, not a set of distinct, persistent humic substances. Its starting point is a blurry line. The boundary between humus and other soil organic matter is ambiguous, so some authors contest the terms humus, humic substances and humification. Supporters say the evidence does not show large, persistent humic molecules forming in soils. Critics of the humic-substance concept add that the alkali extracts used to isolate it misrepresent soil organic matter. Others push back. They hold that humus has distinct properties, mostly from its richness in functional groups, the reactive clusters of atoms on its molecules. Those properties, they argue, justify keeping the term. The humification theory persists in the field and in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced many conflicting definitions. The question stays open: soil scientists still disagree on whether humus and humic substances are distinct materials or artifacts of extraction.

soil-bio-124.title: Nitrogen cycling high in the canopy
soil-bio-124.text: Canopy soils release nitrogen faster than the forest floor does. That makes them a main nitrogen source for epiphytes at different heights. Their gross production of nitrate is about the same as or lower than on the forest floor, possibly because canopy soils are more acidic. Nitrogen capture there depends on environmental variation, especially seasonal changes in tropical rainforests. Storing nutrients in the canopy cycles them tightly and keeps them from washing out of the ecosystem. That cycling also affects the fertility of the forest floor below.

soil-bio-129.title: White-rot fungi, the lignin breakers
soil-bio-129.text: Leaves or needles bleached pale in the litter layer may be the work of white-rot fungi. These wood- and litter-decaying fungi break down lignin, one of the main precursors of humus. Lignin decays very slowly, mainly through white-rot fungi and actinomycetes. Brown-rot fungi, by contrast, decompose cellulose and hemicellulose and leave lignin behind. By cutting the lignin and tannin in residues, white-rot fungi and bacteria make them more palatable to earthworms, which helps form mull.

soil-bio-193.title: Nematodes, the most numerous animals on Earth
soil-bio-193.text: Earth's topsoil holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes, roughly 60 billion for every person. Nematodes are roundworms, or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda. Most live freely and feed on microbes, but many are parasites. They often exceed a million individuals per square meter, and they make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth. Densities peak in tundra and boreal forests. About 90% of soil nematodes live in the top 15 cm. They do not break down dead material. They eat living things instead, up to 5,000 bacteria per minute, and so regulate bacterial numbers and the mix of bacterial kinds. By releasing nitrogen in mineral form, they can play an important part in the movement of nitrogen through soil. They are prey too: the fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-215}} trap them with lassos or sticky structures, or release toxins on contact. Species are hard to tell apart, so estimates of their number run from over 25,000 to close to one million. The soil-dwelling Caenorhabditis elegans is a major model organism. In 2023 a Panagrolaimus kolymaensis was revived after 46,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

soil-bio-194.title: Plant-parasitic nematodes, the hidden thieves of crops
soil-bio-194.text: Each year about 10% of the world's crops are lost to worms too small to see. Plant-parasitic nematodes attack crop plants, chiefly their roots, or spread plant viruses between them. Major kinds include root-knot Meloidogyne, cyst-forming Globodera and Heterodera, and lesion-causing Pratylenchus. Root-knot species leave visible galls on roots, a field clue for diagnosis. Others, such as Xiphinema index, carry viruses. Farmers fight back with rotations of resistant crops, marigolds grown between crops and antagonistic fungi and bacteria. In CSIRO plots, Brassica juncea worked into the soil while green cut densities 13- to 14-fold. Soil steaming kills them before planting, but it also kills the beneficial soil fauna.

soil-bio-195.title: Testate amoebae, single cells that carry a shell
soil-bio-195.text: Some single cells build their own houses. Testate amoebae are amoeboid protists partly enclosed in a shell, or test, with an opening for their pseudopodia, flowing arm-like extensions. The cell either makes the test itself, from organic, siliceous or calcareous material, or glues it together from mineral grains. They live in most fresh waters, soils and {{ref:soil-water-137}}. In soil the shell guards against drying, and they may stay encysted until conditions improve. Tests outlast their makers. Some species respond to temperature, pH and conductivity, so their shells serve as bioindicators and records of past climate, and of land-use change during soil formation.

soil-bio-198.title: The root cap, a helmet that steers the root
soil-bio-198.text: Every growing root pushes through soil behind a small shield. The root cap, or calyptra, covers the tip of each growing root. It protects the apical meristem, the zone of dividing cells, and eases the root's passage. It also steers. Statoliths, dense grains, settle in its gravity-sensing statocytes and drive gravitropism, growth in response to gravity. Remove the cap and the root grows at random. It secretes a mucilage layer that cuts friction and may foster signaling with soil microbes. The cap renews itself as its oldest outer layers slough off, in cereals and many legumes as long-lived border cells.

soil-bio-202.title: Endophytes, the microbes living quietly inside plants
soil-bio-202.text: Every plant species studied so far carries hidden tenants. An endophyte is a microbe, often a bacterium or fungus, that lives inside a plant for at least part of its life without causing apparent disease. Most of these relationships are still poorly understood. Some pass from parent to offspring through seeds, called vertical transmission. Others spread between plants by spores, called horizontal transmission. Many are mutualists. They help hosts cope with pathogens, drought, heat, poor soils, salinity and grazing animals, and they receive carbon in return. They can raise uptake of scarce soil elements such as phosphorus and make rock phosphate and atmospheric nitrogen available to the plant. Systemic endophytes stay harmless for the plant's whole life. Non-systemic ones vary with conditions and can turn pathogenic when the host is stressed. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are one group of fungal endophytes, while bacterial endophytes come from many unrelated groups. Fungicides harm endophytic fungi, and fertilizers lessen a plant's reliance on them. Epichloë endophytes are used commercially in turf grasses.

soil-bio-200.title: Frankia, the nitrogen fixer once mistaken for a fungus
soil-bio-200.text: In 1886 Brunchorst named the genus Frankia, taking it for a fungus. In 1970 Becking redefined it as a prokaryotic actinomycete. These filamentous bacteria fix nitrogen in the root nodules of actinorhizal plants, much as {{ref:soil-bio-178}} do in legumes. With a special enzyme they turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, often meeting most or all of the host's needs, so hosts thrive in poor soils. Most strains are host-specific. Hosts include all alders, some Casuarina species, sea-buckthorn, Myrica and Ceanothus. Infection runs through deformed root hairs or between root cells, and a nodule primordium forms.

soil-bio-201.title: Nod factors, the signal that tells a legume to build a nodule
soil-bio-201.text: A legume and its bacteria agree to build a nodule by trading chemical messages. Plant flavonoids activate the bacterial regulator NodD, which switches on the nod genes. These make Nod factors, the signals that trigger root nodule formation. They are lipochitooligosaccharides: chains of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine carrying a fatty acid, with strain-specific additions. Receptors called NFR1 and NFR5, first isolated in Lotus japonicus in 2003, perceive them. Calcium floods in and early nodulin genes start. The root hair curls round the bacteria, and an infection thread carries them inward to where they fix nitrogen as bacteroids.

soil-bio-199.title: Pneumatophores, roots that rise to breathe
soil-bio-199.text: Oxygen diffuses four orders of magnitude faster in air than in water. In waterlogged soil, roots starve for it. Pneumatophores are specialized aerial roots that let plants breathe there. They grow down from the stem or up from ordinary roots. Porous lenticels lead into air-filled aerenchyma, spongy tissue that helps gases spread through the plant. Black and grey mangroves bear them, and mangrove aerial roots serve aeration rather than water uptake. Cypress knees were once thought to be pneumatophores. But they lack aerenchyma and exchange little gas, and their function remains unclear.

soil-bio-196.title: Leaf mold, the slow fungal compost of autumn
soil-bio-196.text: A heap of autumn leaves can take one to three years to rot. Leaf mold is the compost that forms as fallen leaves decompose, mainly through slow, cool fungal breakdown rather than bacterial decay. The leaves are low in nitrogen and rich in cellulose and lignin, which resist decay. A succession of fungi, isopods, millipedes and earthworms turns them into fine, dark brown humic matter. In temperate deciduous woodland it slowly returns nutrients to plants. Poor in nutrients itself, it still improves soil, with a structure and moisture retention that suit seedling roots.

soil-bio-197.title: Coarse woody debris, the fallen trees that feed a forest
soil-bio-197.text: A fallen tree keeps working for centuries. Coarse woody debris means fallen dead trees and the remains of large branches lying in forests, rivers and wetlands. Authors set the minimum diameter anywhere from 2.5 to 20 cm. Saprotrophic fungi and detritivores consume it, recycling carbon, nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus. The wood is poor in nitrogen yet hosts free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Fungi and other saprotrophs move its carbon into the soil, and in old-growth forests this storage can continue for hundreds of years. On slopes it slows the creep of organic matter and mineral soil, traps leaves, improves infiltration and slows evaporation.

soil-bio-226.title: Symbiosis, the long partnership of unlike organisms
soil-bio-226.text: In 1879 Heinrich Anton de Bary called it "the living together of unlike organisms." Symbiosis is any close, long-term interaction between two organisms of different species. Some writers keep the word for {{ref:soil-bio-251}}, where both partners benefit. A partnership can be obligate, meaning required, or facultative, meaning optional. An ectosymbiont lives on its partner, while an endosymbiont lives inside its tissues. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} in the roots of legumes are one example; nitrogen-fixing {{ref:soil-bio-200}} in alder roots is another. Not every link is friendly. Black walnut secretes juglone, which destroys many herbaceous plants within its root zone.

soil-bio-216.title: Hyphae, the threads that fungi grow by
soil-bio-216.text: The hyphae of the fungi in {{ref:soil-bio-166}} alone are estimated to stretch about 110 quadrillion kilometers through Earth's topsoils. A hypha is a long, branching filament of a fungus, an oomycete or an actinobacterium, like those in {{ref:soil-bio-012}}. It is one or more cells inside a tubular wall, usually of chitin. In most fungi, perforated cross-walls called septa divide it. Hyphae average 4–6 μm across and grow at their tips. In most {{ref:soil-bio-003}} they are the main mode of growth, and together they form a {{ref:soil-bio-217}}. Specialized forms include arbuscules, which trade nutrients with plant cells, and cords that move nutrients over long distances.

soil-bio-217.title: Mycelium, the hidden body of a fungus
soil-bio-217.text: A single Armillaria colony spans thousands of acres, while others are too small to see. Each is a mycelium, the root-like body of a fungus: a mass of branching, thread-like hyphae, described in {{ref:soil-bio-216}}. It feeds in two stages. Hyphae secrete enzymes that break polymers into small units such as monomers, then absorb them. Growing mycelia decompose plant material, add to the soil's organic fraction and release carbon dioxide. Their networks make up 20-30% of soil biomass, though traditional biomass measures fail to detect them. The mycelium of {{ref:soil-bio-157}} fungi helps most plants take up water and nutrients. By some estimates it receives well over 10% of the host's photosynthetic output. Many soil invertebrates eat mycelium. In compost, fungi break down the woody compound {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, which many other microbes cannot. They also degrade petroleum products and some farm chemicals, a cleanup described in {{ref:soil-env-033}}. Spread on logging roads, mycelium binds disturbed soil.

soil-bio-212.title: Termites, the engineers of tropical soils
soil-bio-212.text: The northern part of Kruger National Park alone holds about 1.1 million active termite nests rising as mounds. Termites are eusocial insects, living in cooperative colonies, that eat decaying plant material: mostly wood, leaf litter and soil humus. Primarily detritivores, they eat dead plants at any stage of decay. Higher termites also eat feces, humus, grass, leaves and roots. In subtropical and tropical regions they are important decomposers, and their recycling of wood and plant matter is of considerable ecological importance. Most species build underground colonies, using soil for their nests and mounds. Other nests are epigeal, built as mounds, or arboreal, in trees. Many species are ecosystem engineers. They change soil hydrology, decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth, and so the biodiversity around their large mounds. Of 3,014 classified species, 754 live in Africa, where mounds are fertile islands in savannas. Around 330 species of the Macrotermitinae farm Termitomyces fungi on their fecal pellets. Disturbance hits termites hard: loss of trees and soil cover, and trampling by cattle and goats, cut their diversity and abundance.

soil-bio-211.title: Millipedes, slow shredders of the forest floor
soil-bio-211.text: A single millipede species is estimated to eat between 1 and 11 percent of all leaf litter, depending on species and region. Millipedes are arthropods of the class Diplopoda, with two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments. Most are slow-moving detritivores of forest leaf litter that eat decaying leaves and dead wood. Some eat fungi or suck plant fluids. Their gut fragments litter and excretes it as pellets of leaf fragments, algae, fungi and bacteria, which helps microbes decompose it further. Their burrowing mixes organic with mineral matter. That makes them soil ecosystem engineers, especially where earthworms are scarce, as in some tropical forests.

soil-bio-229.title: How invading earthworms are eating North America's forest floor
soil-bio-229.text: Most northern forests of North America have had no native earthworms since the last ice age. The Wisconsin glaciation wiped them out, so a deep layer of dead leaves and litter became typical, and many native plants rely on it. From the 18th century, European worms arrived in soil with settlers, likely in the root balls of imported plants. Recreation, bait and construction now spread them, one case of {{ref:soil-bio-043}}. The invaders burrow, eat litter and leave casts, mixing nutrients beyond the reach of shallow roots, where they may be leached. The organic layer thins, nutrient release and decomposition speed up, and bulk density rises. Banded soils, {{ref:soil-class-138}}, lose their E horizons. Plant diversity, seedlings and mycorrhizal associations decline, while invasive plants such as buckthorn and garlic mustard increase. Asian jumping worms of Amynthas and Metaphire breed faster and live denser than European species, stripping the ground of organic matter. Worms cannot be removed from soil, so control aims to slow their spread: fewer bait releases, regulated soil movement and heat-treated compost or mulch.

soil-bio-207.title: Light or chemicals, rock or food: how life gets fed
soil-bio-207.text: Every living thing must answer three questions: where do its energy, its electrons and its carbon come from? The answers sort life into primary nutritional groups. Energy comes from light, for phototrophs, or from chemical compounds, for {{ref:soil-bio-205}}. Electrons come from organic donors, as in {{ref:soil-bio-206}}, or from inorganic ones, for lithotrophs. Carbon comes from organic compounds, for heterotrophs, or from carbon dioxide, for autotrophs. A name combines one term from each pair. A chemoorganoheterotroph, for example, takes its carbon from organic substrates and its energy from breaking down an organic compound. The pairs often travel together. Organisms that draw electrons from organic matter are often heterotrophs too, and lithotrophs are often autotrophs that use carbon dioxide. Plants count as lithotrophs because water is the electron donor of their photosynthesis. Cyanobacteria, algae and land plants are therefore photolithoautotrophs. Decomposers are chemoorganoheterotrophs, taking carbon and electrons from dead organic matter. All animals, fungi and protozoa, and some bacteria, are chemoheterotrophs. The labels are not always fixed: plants and some bacteria can switch between phototrophy and chemotrophy depending on the light. One distinction is easy to confuse. Aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation describe the electron acceptor used, the substance that finally takes the electrons, and do not define a nutritional group.

soil-bio-205.title: Chemotrophs, life powered by chemistry instead of light
soil-bio-205.text: Hydrogen sulfide, ferrous iron and ammonia can all power life without sunlight. A chemotroph gets its energy by oxidizing electron donors from its surroundings, unlike phototrophs, which use light. The donors may be organic, for chemoorganotrophs, or inorganic, for chemolithotrophs. Chemoautotrophs build all their organic compounds from carbon dioxide; nitrifiers, methanogens and sulfur oxidizers are among them. Chemoheterotrophs, including most animals and fungi, cannot fix carbon themselves. Methanogens finish organic matter breakdown only once richer electron acceptors, oxygen, nitrate and sulfate, are used up. Thawing frozen soils is expected to raise their methane output.

soil-bio-219.title: Microbial ecology: studying microbes beyond medicine
soil-bio-219.text: {{ref:soil-hist-013}} studied microbes outside medicine. He discovered chemosynthesis, life powered by chemical energy. {{ref:soil-hist-016}} invented a way to grow chosen microbes, described in {{ref:soil-hist-017}}. {{ref:soil-hist-075}} recognized the bacteria behind three nitrogen processes: {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, {{ref:soil-fert-112}} and {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Their field is microbial ecology, also called environmental microbiology: the study of how microorganisms interact with their environment. Microbes drive the cycles of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and carbon, making nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium available in soil. Their relationships include {{ref:soil-bio-251}}, commensalism, amensalism and parasitism, all forms of living together first met in {{ref:soil-bio-226}}.

soil-bio-227.title: The microbiome, a community with an address
soil-bio-227.text: Up to 40% of the DNA sequenced from soil can be relic DNA, left behind by cells that are no longer alive. A microbiome is the community of microorganisms usually found living together in a given habitat. Whipps and colleagues first defined the term in 1988 while studying microorganisms of the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. They described a characteristic community in a well-defined habitat with distinct physico-chemical properties. TerraGenome, a project to build a reference set of soil DNA, began in 2008. Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer may barely change which microbes make up a soil microbiome, yet it drastically reduces how connected their network is.

soil-bio-221.title: Metagenomics: reading the DNA of a whole soil
soil-bio-221.text: A single gram of soil holds about 10^9 to 10^10 microbial cells, and roughly one gigabase of sequence. Metagenomics studies all the genetic material from every organism in such a sample, revealing composition, diversity and functional potential. It profiles communities without culturing species, and early environmental gene studies showed that cultivation had missed most microbial diversity. Norman Pace proposed cloning DNA directly from environmental samples in 1985, and his group first reported doing so in 1991. It differs from amplicon sequencing, or metabarcoding. That method reads marker genes and shows which taxa are present. The 16S rRNA gene identifies bacteria and archaea, and 18S rRNA or ITS identifies fungi; more similar sequences are taken to mean closer evolutionary relatedness. Metagenomics sequences all the DNA, so it also recovers enzymes and pathways. Functional metagenomics explores plant-microbe interactions and the roles of uncultivated or rare members in nutrient cycling and plant growth. There is a catch. Sampling is uncontrolled, so the most abundant organisms dominate shotgun sequence data. Long-read sequencing of soils in industrial zones showed that chronic heavy metal contamination restructures the soil microbial community. Soil communities are among the most complex known, which makes {{ref:soil-bio-011}}, {{ref:soil-bio-008}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-227}} natural targets.

soil-bio-218.title: Geomicrobiology: microbes that make and break minerals
soil-bio-218.text: Some bacteria gain energy by reducing dissolved metal ions, and as a side effect they concentrate those metals into what can become ore deposits. This is the territory of geomicrobiology, the field between geology and microbiology. It studies the role of microbes in geological and geochemical processes, and the effects of minerals and metals on microbes. Its interactions run through rocks, minerals, soils, sediments, the atmosphere and the hydrosphere. There microbes drive the cycling of elements, precipitate and dissolve minerals and concentrate metals. In soil they change the speciation, or chemical form, of minerals and metals, along with their toxicity and mobility. They immobilize and detoxify metals, radionuclides, sulfur and phosphorus. Chromium shows the payoff. Cr(VI) is mobile and toxic, while Cr(III) is less toxic and precipitates in soils above pH 6. Microbial reduction of Cr(VI) is therefore a low-cost way to clean up soil, a form of {{ref:soil-env-023}}. Sulfate-reducing bacteria precipitate metals as sulfides and add bicarbonate alkalinity that neutralizes acid mine drainage. Applications include pollution cleanup, mining, slowing climate change and drinking water supply.

soil-bio-225.title: Streptomyces, the bacteria that make soil smell like soil
soil-bio-225.text: The earthy odor of soil comes from geosmin, a volatile compound released by Streptomyces. This is the largest genus of actinomycete bacteria, found mainly in soil and decaying vegetation. They are filamentous, Gram-positive bacteria with branched hyphae 0.5–2.0 μm across. Their substrate mycelium scavenges organic compounds, and most produce spores. Streptomycetes make over two-thirds of the clinically useful natural antibiotics; streptomycin is named after the genus. Several species are plant pathogens, causing scab of potatoes and soft rot of sweet potatoes.

soil-bio-224.title: Azotobacter, the nitrogen fixer that works alone
soil-bio-224.text: Azotobacter survives in dry soil as cysts for up to 24 years. This genus of aerobic, free-living soil bacteria fixes atmospheric nitrogen and release it into the soil as ammonium. Unlike {{ref:soil-bio-239}}, it needs no plant partner, and fixation stops when ammonium or nitrate is available. It favors neutral and weakly basic soils, not acid ones. It shields its oxygen-sensitive nitrogen-fixing enzyme, {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, by speeding up its metabolism. Besides the molybdenum-iron enzyme, it has a vanadium one that works down to 5 °C. {{ref:soil-hist-016}} described the genus in 1901. It makes auxins, a kind of {{ref:soil-bio-245}}, and goes into azotobacterin, a {{ref:soil-fert-048}}.

soil-bio-203.title: Bacterivores, the grazers of the microbial world
soil-bio-203.text: Some bacteria are never eaten: the spores of Clostridium perfringens are one example. A bacterivore gets its energy and nutrients mainly or entirely by eating bacteria. The term mostly covers free-living microscopic heterotrophs such as nematodes, amoebae and other protozoa. Some larger invertebrates, certain arthropods among them, eat bacteria too, and springtails are listed among bacterivores. Many are generalist predators of any bacteria, though not all bacteria are easily digested. In the lab, bacterivores contaminating samples hinder the growing of bacteria for study. Cycloheximide can suppress them but also inhibits some anaerobic prokaryotes.

soil-bio-204.title: Fungivory: the many creatures that eat fungi
soil-bio-204.text: Beetles, ants and termites each took up fungus farming 40 to 60 million years ago. Today about 330 termite species cultivate Termitomyces fungi in their nests. Fungivory, or mycophagy, is the eating of fungi, and organisms that eat nothing else are fungivores. Fungus eaters include birds, mammals, insects, plants, amoebae, snails, slugs, nematodes, bacteria and other fungi. Trichoderma fungi detect other fungi, bind to their hyphae and digest their cell walls with enzymes such as chitinases. They have protected crops from pathogens such as Rhizoctonia solani. Bacterial mycophagy, a term coined in 2005, means bacteria growing at the expense of living fungal hyphae.

soil-bio-214.title: Fossorial animals, the diggers that remake soil
soil-bio-214.text: Ants, termites and earthworms move so much soil that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift. Such burrowers are fossorial animals: adapted to digging and living mainly, though not only, underground. Moles, badgers, naked mole-rats, armadillos and wombats are examples, as are many clams, beetles, wasps, bees and spiders. Their digging, a form of {{ref:soil-bio-047}}, changes soil composition, structure and vegetation, usually shifting plant species and raising plant diversity. Mounds and bare burrowed soils hold more ammonium and nitrate than vegetated soils. They also have a greater potential to turn ammonium into nitrate, mainly because the grass cover is gone.

soil-bio-213.title: Termite mounds, earthen towers built by insects
soil-bio-213.text: The largest termite mound on record measured 12.8 meters. Termite mounds are nests that protrude above the soil surface, built of earth and mud and stronger than underground nests. Macrotermes builds some of the largest, 8 to 9 meters high, with chimneys, pinnacles and ridges. Compass termites build wedge-shaped mounds aligned north–south, which warm quickly in the morning but avoid overheating at midday. Mounds are rich in clay, so where rain is torrential and continuous they risk erosion. They shelter birds, lizards, snakes and scorpions, and 54 ant species are known to live in Nasutitermes mounds.

soil-bio-228.title: The detrital food web, where most food ends up
soil-bio-228.text: Most of what an ecosystem's plants produce is never eaten. Instead it is recycled through {{ref:soil-bio-112}}, the dead remains of living things, into useful nutrients. That means any non-living organic matter: leaf litter, dead wood, carrion, dead microbes and feces among others. In a detrital food web, decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break it down, and it passes to detritivores and then to carnivores. Raymond Lindeman emphasized the soil's decomposer community among the basal species of food webs. This web links to the grazing web. Mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat earthworms that consume decaying leaves.

soil-bio-206.title: Organotrophs, which take their electrons from food
soil-bio-206.text: Animals and many bacteria share a habit: they pull their electrons from organic matter. An organotroph obtains hydrogen or electrons from organic substrates. Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946 to classify microorganisms by how they obtain electrons for respiration. Many organotrophs, animals and many bacteria among them, are also heterotrophs, and they can be aerobic or anaerobic. The counterpart is the lithotroph, which takes its electrons from inorganic substrates. Both terms belong to the scheme of {{ref:soil-bio-207}}.

soil-bio-208.title: How microbes make a living, from fermenting to eating methane
soil-bio-208.text: A microbe's metabolism largely decides its ecological niche, and it can make the microbe responsible for whole cycles of elements through soil and air. Microbial metabolism is the means by which a microbe obtains the energy and nutrients, such as carbon, that it needs to live and reproduce. Following {{ref:soil-bio-207}}, metabolisms are sorted three ways. By carbon source they are autotrophic, heterotrophic or mixotrophic. By source of reducing equivalents, the electrons they use, they are lithotrophic or organotrophic. By energy source they are phototrophic or chemotrophic. Nitrifying, sulfur-oxidizing and iron-oxidizing bacteria are chemolithoautotrophs. Most bacteria, Bacillus and the Actinomycetota among them, are chemoorganoheterotrophs. Oxygen is not always on hand. Fermenters use organic carbon instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor. Facultative anaerobes respire with oxygen when it is present and switch to fermentation when it is not. Many of them also denitrify, because nitrate, like oxygen, has a high reduction potential, a strong pull on electrons. They reduce nitrate step by step through nitrite, nitric oxide and nitrous oxide to dinitrogen, a form of {{ref:soil-chem-128}}. {{ref:soil-env-280}} oxidize methane step by step to carbon dioxide. The process needs oxygen, so all conventional ones are obligate aerobes. Ammonia and nitrite oxidation yield so little energy that nitrifiers grow very slowly. In 2015 one genus, {{ref:soil-fert-221}}, was shown to carry out both oxidation steps on its own, a process called {{ref:soil-fert-110}}.

soil-bio-209.title: Microarthropods, tiny animals that travel by pore
soil-bio-209.text: A microarthropod can move only through pores that already exist in the soil. These small arthropods, usually one to several millimeters long, live mostly in soil. They include springtails, mites such as Oribatida and Mesostigmata, small centipedes, small insects and their larvae, and small crustaceans. They are most common in fallen leaves, litter and the upper soil layers. There they speed the decomposition of organic matter and help form soil structure. They are very sensitive to changes in ecosystems, so their communities serve as bioindicators for environmental assessment.

soil-bio-210.title: Soil mites, eight-legged recyclers of leaf litter
soil-bio-210.text: Leaf litter teems with mites, small eight-legged arachnids, and many species live in soil as decomposers. They inhabit organic debris of all kinds. Soil mites span a range of taxa. Oribatida and Prostigmata are more numerous in soil than Mesostigmata and have more soil-dwelling species. After a disturbance such as agriculture, most mites recolonize soil within a few months, but Oribatida take several years. Most are beneficial, helping decompose organic material as part of the cycling of carbon. Some Laelapidae are even used to control fungus gnats and soil pests.

soil-bio-215.title: Nematophagous fungi, the soil's worm hunters
soil-bio-215.text: More than 700 species of fungi hunt nematodes. These nematophagous fungi are carnivores specialized in trapping and digesting the worms. Some catch prey with adhesive hyphae, knobs or nets, others with hyphal loops that tighten on contact. Still others stun nematodes with toxins or infect them or their eggs as parasites. Trappers concentrate in the upper soil, pastures and leaf litter, mostly in nitrogen-deficient habitats. Arthrobotrys oligospora builds its costly snares only when it detects nematode pheromones such as ascarosides. Purpureocillium lilacinum, which attacks the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita, is studied for biological control, though field results have been mixed.

soil-bio-222.title: Counting the living with membrane fats
soil-bio-222.text: Phospholipids, the fats of cell membranes, break down rapidly when an organism dies. So the phospholipid in a soil sample is taken to come from living cells. Phospholipid fatty acid analysis, or PLFA, uses their fatty acids as chemical markers to estimate the living mass and make-up of microbial communities in soil and water. A 1965 article proposed using molecules made by organisms as biomarkers, and D.C. White pioneered the method in the early to mid 1980s. Lipids are extracted from dried soil with a chloroform–methanol–phosphate buffer. Saponifying the phospholipids releases their fatty acids. These are analyzed as methyl esters by {{ref:soil-meth-029}} and compared with those of known organisms. The method spread because it measures the dominant microbes sensitively and reproducibly, without cultivation, which is costly and biased. It has limits. The same fatty acids occur in plant roots, fungi and bacteria, so assigning them to microbial groups needs care. Archaeal lipids are ether-linked rather than ester-linked, so routine preparation misses archaea. Extraction is cumbersome, though a 96-well plate procedure raised throughput 4-to-5 fold.

soil-bio-223.title: Fatty-acid fingerprints of bacteria and fungi
soil-bio-223.text: In a flooded rice paddy, fatty acids showed archaea rising from 24% to 37% of the microbes. Such readings rest on signature fatty acids in a PLFA profile that point to particular groups. Iso- and anteiso-branched acids such as 15:0 iso estimate Gram-positive bacteria, and a methyl branch at the 10th carbon marks actinomycetes. Monounsaturated plus cyclopropane acids estimate Gram-negative bacteria; a high cyclopropane-to-monounsaturated ratio signals stress. Linoleic acid, 18:2 ω6c, indicates fungi, and 16:1 ω5c is recommended for the fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. In that paddy, aerobic bacteria fell from about 44% to 27% under longer flooding, while facultative anaerobes rose from 32% to 36%.

soil-bio-220.title: Is every microbe everywhere? Mapping microbial life
soil-bio-220.text: In 1934 Lourens Baas Becking concluded that "everything is everywhere, but the environment selects." Microbial biogeography puts that idea to the test. It studies where microorganisms live, at what abundance and why, across space and time. The field grew as cheaper, higher-throughput DNA sequencing allowed global analyses. Clear geographic patterns in microbial life now dispute Baas Becking's view. Unlike most larger organisms, global topsoil microbiomes are more diverse in temperate zones than in the tropics. Soil bacterial patterns usually track soil pH, which may stand in for the climatic water balance that controls carbon inputs and how well water-filled habitats connect.

soil-bio-245.title: Plant hormones, the tiny signals that steer roots
soil-bio-245.text: When a growing root hits an obstacle underground, its ethylene production surges and cell elongation halts. Ethylene is one of the plant hormones, signal molecules made within plants in extremely low concentrations that control growth and development. Every plant cell can make them. They are not nutrients but chemicals that, in small amounts, steer how cells grow and differentiate. Auxins promote root initiation and the growth of side roots and adventitious roots. Synthetic auxins such as IBA and NAA are sold as rooting powders for cuttings. When roots run short of water, a signal triggers the formation of ABA. Roots release it to the leaves, where it closes the stomata. {{ref:soil-bio-172}}, exuded into soil, promote the growth of the symbiotic fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. Fungi and bacteria make very similar chemicals that also affect plant growth, though in microbes they act as secondary metabolites. Went and Thimann coined the term phytohormone in their 1937 book.

soil-bio-251.title: Mutualism, the partnerships where both sides win
soil-bio-251.text: About 80% of land plant species rely on fungi for inorganic compounds and trace elements, through {{ref:soil-bio-157}}. The plants pay in carbohydrates, a "biological barter." This is mutualism, an interaction between two or more species in which each gains a net benefit. Partnerships with these fungi are linked to the colonization of land by plants. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates. In Three Sisters farming, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn they climb. Mutualism can also unravel. Plant lineages in nutrient-rich places have abandoned their fungal partners many times, and those fungi can turn parasitic on weak or dying plants.

soil-bio-239.title: Rhizobium, the nitrogen fixer inside legume roots
soil-bio-239.text: In 1888 {{ref:soil-hist-016}} isolated a microbe from legume nodules and named it Bacillus radicicola; it is now placed in Rhizobium. This genus of aerobic, rod-shaped, nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria lives in root nodules, mainly of legumes. Inside, the bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia with an enzyme, {{ref:soil-fert-101}}. They pass it to the plant as glutamine or ureides and receive photosynthate, the products of photosynthesis, in return. Rhizobium can also solubilize phosphate. Not every member helps: Rhizobium rhizogenes causes hairy root disease by injecting root-inducing T-DNA into plants.

soil-bio-250.title: Plant–soil feedback: how plants shape the soil that judges their offspring
soil-bio-250.text: A plant leaves its mark on the soil, and the next plant to grow there feels it. In plant–soil feedback, plants change the biological and physical qualities of their soil, which then changes how well plants can grow in it later. Feedback is negative when a species grows worse in soil previously occupied by its own kind, and positive when it grows better. On average it tends to be negative, with many exceptions, such as many invasive species. Negative feedback was once blamed on the soil running out of nutrients. Recent work points mainly to a build-up of soil-borne pathogens, with mutualists and allelopathy also involved. That build-up helps species coexist. Abundant plants accumulate their pathogens, while rare plants escape them. Negative plant–soil feedback has been called a particular case of the Janzen–Connell hypothesis. It is best measured with Bever's interaction coefficient. Two species are grown in soil conditioned by their own kind, called home, and by the other, called away. With G for growth, Is = Gx(home) + Gy(home) − Gx(away) − Gy(away). A negative Is favors coexistence.

soil-bio-240.title: The fungal web that reaches out from ectomycorrhizas
soil-bio-240.text: Starve a host plant of phosphorus, and the fungal threads around its roots can grow tenfold. These threads are the extramatrical, or extraradical, mycelium: the mass of hyphae growing out into the soil from ectomycorrhizas, described in {{ref:soil-bio-173}}. It is the fungus's main body: it gathers phosphorus and other minerals, makes enzymes, colonizes new root tips and feeds invertebrates. Some hyphae branch finely to explore the soil. Others aggregate into rhizomorphs, durable water-repellent cords that carry materials like xylem. Ectomycorrhizas are small, so these hyphae greatly enlarge the surface touching soil, reaching water and nutrients that roots cannot. Lab studies predict about 23% of plant carbon goes to this mycelium, with 15-30% of that lost to respiration. In some forest soils it may hold a third of the mass of soil microbes and half the dissolved organic carbon. Its lifespan, from a few months to several years, is estimated with ergosterol or PLFA analysis, 14C dating or sand-filled ingrowth bags.

soil-bio-247.title: The mycorrhizosphere, where roots, fungi and microbes meet
soil-bio-247.text: Fungal hyphae are thinner than roots, so they reach moisture and nutrients that roots cannot. The mycorrhizosphere is the zone they help build: roots, the hyphae of their {{ref:soil-bio-157}} fungi, associated microorganisms and the soil under their direct influence. Here roots release nutrients, and the fungus raises microbial numbers and activity. Its bacteria affect nutrient uptake, protect against pathogens and help capture nitrogen from the air and weather minerals. The fungi guard against pathogens too. Glomus intraradices reduces germination of Fusarium oxysporum but stimulates the harmless Trichoderma harzianum. The fungal partner even sets protozoan numbers. A Paxillus involutus mycorrhiza lowers protozoan density, whereas Lactarius rufus and Suillus bovinus raise it. Nematodes, mites and earthworms forage on its roots, hyphae and microbes.

soil-bio-246.title: Mycorrhiza helper bacteria, the third partner underground
soil-bio-246.text: A partnership between a root and a fungus often has a third member. Mycorrhiza helper bacteria associate with ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and improve the symbiosis. They come from many phyla. Pseudomonas and Streptomyces are the most commonly reported, and Bacillus is another. They enhance fungal growth and function and nutrient uptake by fungus and plant. Some weather minerals, releasing protons and iron that lower soil pH and recycle nutrients. Phosphate-solubilizing {{ref:soil-bio-154}} build a phosphate pool that mycorrhizas draw on, helping them establish where phosphorus is limiting. Some fix nitrogen in the soil around mycorrhizas, without the root changes legumes make. In soils rich in toxic metals they help block plant uptake of lead, zinc and cadmium, which makes them candidates for cleaning up polluted soils. Most studies show them fighting pathogens with acids and antifungal metabolites and promoting plant defenses. In a few cases, though, they aided pathogenic fungi. How these interactions work is not well understood.

soil-bio-242.title: Fine roots, the working ends of a root system
soil-bio-242.text: The birth, death and decay of fine roots can account for 20-80% of net primary production in the cycling of carbon and nutrients through forests. Fine roots are usually defined as two millimeters or less in diameter. They take up and move water and nutrients, making them the root-system counterpart of leaves and twigs. They make up most of a root system's length. When they meet a nutrient patch, they lengthen, branch more and start more side roots. Their biomass and nitrogen concentration decrease with depth. They release labile carbon in exudates, feeding the soil's organic carbon directly and by stimulating microbes. Root tensile strength rises as diameter falls, so fine roots are stronger than coarse roots and help reinforce slopes against erosion. In trees, fine roots are usually colonized by a single mycorrhizal type, arbuscular or ecto.

soil-bio-244.title: Lateral roots, the branches that spread a root system
soil-bio-244.text: Two lateral roots never form directly opposite each other. A lateral root grows sideways from the primary root. It arises in the pericycle, a layer inside the root, and builds up the branching pattern of a root system. Their number matches the number of xylem bundles. Lateral roots anchor the plant, increase water uptake and nutrient extraction, and enlarge the root system's surface area. Some form symbioses with rhizobia and mycorrhizal fungi that raise nutrient uptake further. The hormone auxin, or IAA, is required at several stages of their development.

soil-bio-238.title: Bradyrhizobium, the slow grower that feeds soybeans
soil-bio-238.text: Grain legumes grown on about 1.5 million km2 a year fix about 44–66 million tons of nitrogen, almost half of the nitrogen used in agriculture. Bradyrhizobium is a genus of Gram-negative soil bacteria, many of which fix nitrogen in legume root nodules. They are slow-growing rhizobia, taking 3–5 days to cloud a liquid medium, unlike the fast-growing {{ref:soil-bio-239}}. Bradyrhizobium japonicum nodulates soybeans, cowpeas and mung beans, and commercial inoculants are available. The genus is also a major member of forest soil microbial communities, where its strains usually cannot fix nitrogen or form nodules.

soil-bio-252.title: Rhizotrons, laboratories built underground
soil-bio-252.text: Some laboratories are built below ground. A rhizotron is an underground laboratory for studying soil and its interactions with plants and animals. A central corridor usually has viewing windows into the soil profiles on either side. Separate outside bays allow experiments that vary the soil composition and the plants and animals in it. Rhizotrons operate at Kew Gardens, at a USDA research station in Houghton, Michigan, at Treborth Botanic Garden in Wales and at Charles Sturt University in Australia.

soil-bio-237.title: Azospirillum, a root partner sold by the million
soil-bio-237.text: Over 113 plant species in 35 families have benefited from Azospirillum. These Gram-negative bacteria prefer low oxygen, fix nitrogen and can promote plant growth. They live in soil and fresh water, especially close to roots. Many excrete plant hormones that make roots grow more branches and fine root hairs, and they make nitrogen and phosphorus more available. They curb disease by competing with pathogens for space and iron. How much nitrogen they supply by fixation is still debated. In the 1970s Johanna Döbereiner's group in Brazil found root-associated strains that fix nitrogen. Commercial inoculants appeared in 2009 and exceeded 3 million doses a year by 2018.

soil-bio-241.title: Exploration types: sorting fungi by how far they reach
soil-bio-241.text: In 2001 Agerer proposed sorting ectomycorrhizal fungi into exploration types. The scheme classes them by the growth pattern and biomass of their extramatrical mycelium and whether they form rhizomorphs. Four types are commonly recognized: contact, short-distance, medium-distance and long-distance. Long-distance types form rhizomorphs with hollow, vessel-like tubes, take up more organic nitrogen and are thought less competitive in disturbed systems. In pine systems they dominate where roots are sparse. Short-distance types, cheaper in carbon, dominate where roots are dense. Many fungi fall along a gradient rather than into one type. The DEEMY database compiles exploration types for over 550 species.

soil-bio-248.title: How farming feeds or starves the mycorrhizosphere
soil-bio-248.text: Fungal hyphae secrete {{ref:soil-bio-121}}, an adhesive that builds stable soil aggregates and resists erosion. It accounts for about 5% of global organic carbon and nitrogen storage. How a farm is run decides whether the mycorrhizosphere that crops rely on for nutrients and pathogen resistance thrives. Growing crops side by side, as in {{ref:soil-agri-133}}, raises arbuscular mycorrhizal colonization. So do {{ref:soil-agri-098}} and less herbicide and fertilizer. Growing one crop alone, {{ref:soil-agri-053}}, weakens the symbiosis. So does frequent plowing, which severs hyphal networks, and so do fertilizers that make plants less reliant on the fungi. Mesoamerican milpa farming limits plowing and fertilizer, and maize grown with beans yields more through their shared mycorrhizosphere.

soil-bio-243.title: Sorting fine roots by size, rank and job
soil-bio-243.text: The traditional two-millimeter cutoff for a fine root is arbitrary. Roots under 0.5 mm are called very fine roots. Other schemes divide fine roots by position in the branching hierarchy or by function. Order-based classes follow the Horton–Strahler scheme. Unbranched distal tips are first-order, and two roots of the same order join to form the next order. As order rises, diameter, life span and secondary growth increase, while nitrogen content, mycorrhizal colonization and turnover decrease. Function-based classes separate absorptive fine roots, the low-order distal segments, from transport fine roots formed where they merge.

soil-bio-249.title: Plant-growth promoting fungi, helpers that are not mycorrhizas
soil-bio-249.text: Most of the fungi that help roots without forming mycorrhizas belong to the Ascomycota. Plant-growth promoting fungi are non-pathogenic, filamentous soil fungi that colonize roots, chiefly in the rhizosphere, and benefit plant health and development. They are the fungal counterpart of {{ref:soil-bio-155}}, and mycorrhizal fungi are not counted among them. Directly, they make auxins such as IAA that shape root architecture, solubilize phosphorus with organic acids and capture iron with siderophores. Indirectly, they suppress harmful soil microbes through antibiotics, mycoparasitism and competition, and trigger induced systemic resistance. Some Trichoderma species can remediate heavy metals, organometallic compounds and agrochemicals.

soil-bio-232.title: Hemicellulose, the mixed-sugar glue of plant walls
soil-bio-232.text: About a fifth of all land-plant biomass is hemicellulose. It is a group of branched polysaccharides, long sugar chains such as arabinoxylans, that sit with cellulose in almost every plant cell wall. Cellulose is built only from glucose. Hemicellulose mixes xylose, arabinose, glucose, mannose and galactose, in chains of 500 to 3000 units. In {{ref:soil-bio-115}}, it counts as moderately labile, slower to go than simple sugars. Brown-rot fungi attack it first. Modern {{ref:soil-class-070}} is mostly lignin, with 5% to 40% cellulose and hemicellulose.

soil-bio-236.title: Photodegradation: sunlight as a quiet decomposer
soil-bio-236.text: Gardeners are told to spread the iron chelate Iron EDDHA in the evening. Daylight would break it down. That breakdown is photodegradation, the alteration of materials by light, often used loosely for sunlight and air acting together. It helps remineralize biomass. With {{ref:soil-env-231}} and flocculation, it is one of three main processes that remove {{ref:soil-bio-128}} from water, often turning tough molecules into easily used ones. Makers of {{ref:soil-env-237}} products pick compounds that resist it, so they last long enough to work.

soil-bio-233.title: Cutin, the waterproof skin of leaves and stems
soil-bio-233.text: Every leaf and stem above ground wears a waxy coat called the cuticle. Its main builders are two polymers, cutin and cutan. Cutin is an insoluble, waterproof polyester: omega hydroxy acids joined by ester bonds. Its building blocks fall into two main families, the C16 and C18 families. Cutan survives far better in the fossil record. In soil, cutin turns up in {{ref:soil-bio-106}}, and chemists must handle it with care. Extracting humic substances alters the ester bonds in such plant polyesters.

soil-bio-234.title: Suberin, the cork that guards roots and bark
soil-bio-234.text: Cork takes its name from the cork oak, Quercus suber, and so does suberin, its major constituent. Suberin is a fatty, water-repelling polyester of plants, built from long-chain fatty acids and glycerol. Interlinked with {{ref:soil-bio-233}} and lignin, it forms a barrier in cell walls that blocks water and dissolved substances. In roots it lines the endodermis as the Casparian strip. Water must then pass through living cells, so the plant chooses which solutes go on. In bark it may hold off microbial decay.

soil-bio-230.title: Microbial necromass, the dead that build soil carbon
soil-bio-230.text: Much of the carbon in soil was once inside a microbe. Microbes cycle the carbon in soil so thoroughly that their necromass, the dead biomass left as cells die, can make up 30 to 80% of it. The remains join {{ref:soil-found-045}} as the cells break apart. One model, the {{ref:soil-bio-266}}, gives carbon taken up by microbes two fates. It is either respired to the atmosphere or locked into a stable store as necromass. Necromass is one of the primary raw materials of humification, the slow making of humus. It joins plant detritus, the excreta of soil organisms and black carbon from past fires. Pollutants follow the same route. Once metabolized or immobilized in living or dead biomass, they become part of stable humus.

soil-bio-235.title: Saprophagy: the animals that eat the dead
soil-bio-235.text: Fallen leaves are taken apart largely by small animals of the soil. They are saprophages, organisms that feed on decomposing dead plants or animals, and their habit is saprophagy. Specialists have their own names: necrophages eat dead animals, thanatophages dead plants, and sapro-xylophagous animals dead wood alone. Larger saprophages that digest wood or soil organic matter rely on enzymes from microbes living in their guts. As these animals and microbes digest litter, carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. The remaining material's C/N therefore falls, feeding {{ref:soil-bio-115}} onward.

soil-bio-253.title: Exoenzymes: digesting food before eating it
soil-bio-253.text: A bacterium cannot swallow a log, so it digests the log from outside. Exoenzymes are enzymes a cell secretes to work beyond its walls, most often breaking large molecules apart. The small pieces can pass through the cell membrane and be used inside. There, endoenzymes, which work within the cell, finish the processing. Bacteria and fungi feed this way. In soil, cellulases target carbohydrates, oxidases lignin, phosphatases organic phosphates, chitinases chains of {{ref:soil-bio-260}} and proteases proteins. Grouped as hydrolases, lyases, oxidoreductases and transferases, they set the pace of {{ref:soil-bio-039}} activity by degrading biopolymers. Fungi used to clean polluted ground secrete oxidative exoenzymes, such as laccases, from their growing hyphal tips. Cell-free exoenzymes can also clean up pollution, but they are often fragile and hard to get into soil. The word entered English in 1908; pepsin and trypsin were probably the first known.

soil-bio-254.title: How fungi spend energy to dismantle litter
soil-bio-254.text: Most of the enzymes working outside cells in leaf litter and soil come from fungi. Fungal extracellular enzyme activity is this secretion of {{ref:soil-bio-253}} to break down complex organic matter. The work is costly. Making and exporting enzymes takes a lot of energy, so evolution favors restraint. Some enzymes are made steadily at low levels and boosted when their target is plentiful. Glucose, a ready meal, represses cellulase production. The setting matters too. Soil pH, temperature and moisture alter which enzymes are made and how well they work. So do litter type and quality. {{ref:soil-fert-001}} and plowing, {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, shift that activity through the profile. Decay follows a sequence. Cellulose and other easy substrates go first, cut by endoglucanases, cellobiohydrolase and {{ref:soil-bio-257}}. {{ref:soil-bio-116}} is broken down later, as oxidative enzymes such as phenol oxidases, peroxidases and laccases rise. Two of these, {{ref:soil-bio-258}} and {{ref:soil-bio-259}}, are hallmarks of basidiomycetes and are used to gauge their activity. Enzyme activity also serves as an indicator of soil quality.

soil-bio-261.title: Amplicons, copied DNA that names the microbes
soil-bio-261.text: Most soil microbes are identified not by sight but by copied DNA. An amplicon is a piece of DNA that is the source or product of amplification or replication. It is usually made by the polymerase or ligase chain reaction, so the term is used interchangeably with PCR product. Bacteria and archaea are classified by comparing amplicons of the highly conserved 16S rRNA gene with known sequences. Fungi are classified from the 18S rRNA gene and the ITS1 region. Counting identical taxa gives their relative abundance.

soil-bio-262.title: Metabarcoding: a census of a whole sample
soil-bio-262.text: Barcoding identifies one organism. Metabarcoding identifies many taxa in one sample at once, from their DNA or RNA, to learn the sample's species composition. It runs through DNA extraction, {{ref:soil-bio-261}} production by PCR, sequencing and data analysis. Soil can be a bulk sample of collected organisms or a source of {{ref:soil-hist-090}}, taken without separating the organisms. Soil holds inhibitors, so its DNA needs special isolation techniques. Researchers still lack consensus on the best experimental design and bioinformatics criteria.

soil-bio-258.title: Lignin peroxidase, a fungal tool for tough wood
soil-bio-258.text: Lignin resists decay so well that only higher fungi and some bacteria can break it down, by oxidation. Lignin peroxidase is one of their tools. It is a heme-containing enzyme, one of the ligninases, that uses hydrogen peroxide to cleave lignin-like compounds. Fungi such as Phanerochaete chrysosporium secrete it as an {{ref:soil-bio-253}}. It works with veratryl alcohol, a white-rot fungal metabolite that acts as its cofactor. After twenty years of study, its mechanism is still not fully worked out.

soil-bio-265.title: Michaelis–Menten: how fast an enzyme can work
soil-bio-265.text: Add more food and an enzyme speeds up, but only to a limit. Michaelis–Menten kinetics, the simplest model of enzyme speed, captures this for one substrate turning into one product. Its equation is v = Va/(Km + a), where a is substrate concentration. V, or Vmax, is the limiting rate when substrate saturates the enzyme. Km, the Michaelis constant, is the concentration giving half that rate. Michaelis and Menten published it in 1913, building on Victor Henri's 1902 equation. Copiotrophic microbes have a higher Km than oligotrophs.

soil-bio-259.title: Manganese peroxidase, a metal messenger against lignin
soil-bio-259.text: This enzyme attacks lignin through a go-between. Manganese peroxidase is a heme peroxidase that uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize manganese(II) to manganese(III), raising its {{ref:soil-chem-178}}. White-rot fungi secrete it; found in Phanerochaete chrysosporium in 1985, it seems unique to Basidiomycota. The unstable Mn(III) leaves bound to a carboxylic acid, most often oxalate. It then oxidizes phenolic parts of lignin and can cleave alkyl–aryl bonds. More Mn(II), hydrogen peroxide or lignin around the cell boosts its production.

soil-bio-260.title: Amino sugars, the nitrogen-carrying sugars of chitin
soil-bio-260.text: Swap one hydroxyl group on a sugar for an amine group and the result is an amino sugar. More than 60 are known. One of the most abundant, N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, is the main component of chitin. Soil microbes break chains of amino sugars apart with chitinases. In {{ref:soil-bio-115}}, plant material yields simpler forms, including sugars and amino sugars. These become the bodies of microbes or join humic assemblages.
