soil-bio-256.title: Acid phosphatase, the key to locked-up phosphorus
soil-bio-256.text: Much soil phosphorus is bound inside organic molecules, out of reach. Acid phosphatase frees it. This enzyme strips attached phosphate groups from other molecules, working best at an acidic {{ref:soil-found-014}} below 7. It uses water to split a phosphate monoester into an alcohol and phosphate. Soil microorganisms rely on phosphatases to reach organically bound phosphate. Some roots, especially cluster roots, exude carboxylates with this activity to mobilize phosphorus in poor soils. Measuring phosphatase activity reveals how much a soil's life is demanding phosphate.

soil-bio-269.title: Microbial biomass, the living fraction of soil
soil-bio-269.text: A hectare of temperate grassland has held 1–2 t of bacteria and 2–5 t of fungi. That living mass, with its metabolites, is microbial biomass. It is only a few percent of {{ref:soil-found-045}}, and it turns over quickly. One way to estimate it is to weigh soil before and after fumigation. Small as it is, it matters. Microbes compete with plants for inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium and tie them up in their cells, a process called {{ref:soil-fert-121}}. The biomass also stores carbon, one way microbes sequester it. Worldwide it averages a C:N:P ratio of 60:7:1. Farming moves it quickly. Plowing can cut microbial biomass carbon and nitrogen at once, while sowing a {{ref:soil-agri-066}} raised the carbon by roughly 20% in one meta-analysis. Microbial biomass and activity are standard measures of soil health.

soil-bio-264.title: Ecological stoichiometry: life as a balance of elements
soil-bio-264.text: A termite's body holds about five parts carbon to one of nitrogen. Its wood holds 300–1000. Ecological stoichiometry studies such gaps: how the balance of energy and elements shapes living things, and how they reshape it. Like chemical stoichiometry, it rests on mass balance, an idea traced to Liebig, Lotka and Redfield. A mismatch between need and food is an elemental imbalance. Plants vary widely in composition, while animals hold close to a fixed recipe. The approach has been applied to the recycling of elements, competition for resources, animal growth and the scarce elements that limit whole ecosystems. A 2007 study found global average C:N:P ratios of 186:13:1 in soil and 60:7:1 in soil {{ref:soil-bio-269}}. The growth rate hypothesis adds a twist. It holds that phosphorus demand rises during active growth, to build phosphorus-rich nucleic acids.

soil-bio-257.title: β-Glucosidase, the last cut in cellulose breakdown
soil-bio-257.text: Cellulose is a chain of β-1,4-linked glucose, and three enzymes take it apart. Cellulases cut it, cellobiosidases trim it, and β-glucosidase finishes the job. This enzyme removes terminal glucose units, splitting cellobiose into glucose. Clearing cellobiose also lifts its brake on the other cellulose enzymes. White- and brown-rot fungi both secrete it, and it can also cleave xylose, mannose and galactose. Soil and litter assays track cellulose breakdown through cellobiohydrolase and β-glucosidase activity on pNP or MUF substrates.

soil-bio-255.title: Soil enzyme assays: measuring invisible work
soil-bio-255.text: Enzymes cannot be counted by eye, so their work is measured. Soil enzyme assays mix soil or litter with buffers and a substrate. Hydrolytic enzymes are read by color with p-nitrophenol substrates or by fluorescence with 4-methylumbelliferone ones. Phenol oxidase oxidizes L-DOPA, pyrogallol or ABTS; peroxidase is the extra activity when hydrogen peroxide is added. Transport, storage, pH, substrate concentration, temperature and preparation all sway results. Assays mostly catch enzymes cutting from chain ends, so molecular methods now count enzyme genes to link enzymes to their makers.

soil-bio-270.title: Carbon use efficiency: growth versus upkeep
soil-bio-270.text: A microbe can spend carbon on growing or on staying alive. Microbial carbon use efficiency measures how much of its carbon intake goes into biomass rather than maintenance energy. Copiotrophs tend to score lower than oligotrophs, making less protein per gram of oxygen consumed. In soil, two flows decide the result. Catabolism releases carbon as CO2, as in {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. Anabolism builds stable carbon compounds. Their balance controls how much carbon the soil keeps.

soil-bio-266.title: The microbial carbon pump: making carbon hard to eat
soil-bio-266.text: Microbes can lock carbon away by making it unappetizing. The microbial carbon pump turns {{ref:soil-bio-128}} into refractory forms that resist further microbial attack. In the ocean it can store carbon for centuries to millennia, unlike the biological pump, which relies on sinking particles. Warming there sends extra carbon to CO2 rather than new biomass. A soil model of the same name describes how microbes transform and stabilize organic matter. Carbon is either respired or enters the stable pool as {{ref:soil-bio-230}}.

soil-bio-263.title: Stable-isotope probing: following labeled food
soil-bio-263.text: Feed microbes a heavier version of their food, and the eaters reveal themselves. Stable-isotope probing traces uptake with substrate enriched in a heavy stable isotope. Isopycnic centrifugation then sorts labeled biomarkers from unlabeled ones by density. With 13CO2, heavy DNA is spun out and sequenced to show who uses fresh photosynthate. 18O-water shows who is actively growing. 13C is used most; 15N shifts DNA density less, because DNA holds fewer nitrogen atoms. Quantitative SIP, or qSIP, uses the predictable shift to estimate how much isotope went in.

soil-bio-267.title: Q10: how much warmth speeds up life
soil-bio-267.text: Warm most living systems by 10 °C and their chemistry runs two to three times faster. That factor is Q10, the temperature coefficient: a unitless measure of how much a rate changes with a 10 °C rise. It assumes rates rise exponentially with temperature, following Q10 = (R2/R1)^(10 °C/(T2−T1)). It applies to processes such as respiration, including {{ref:soil-bio-033}}, and photosynthesis. Environmental scientists often use 0 °C or 10 °C as the reference. The idea is thought to come from van 't Hoff's work in the late 19th century.

soil-bio-268.title: The resistome: soil's ancient store of drug resistance
soil-bio-268.text: Antibiotic resistance is older than antibiotics. Sequences from ancient permafrost show it existed millennia before people made the drugs. The resistome is the full set of antibiotic resistance genes in bacterial communities, harmful or not. Soil samples from cities, farms and forests held spore-forming {{ref:soil-bio-002}} resistant to most major antibiotics. Their resistance genes sit on mobile genetic elements, so soil and water communities act as reservoirs for pathogens. Sequencing has found genes shared between soil bacteria and clinical pathogens, some matching exactly across five antibiotic classes.

soil-chem-076.title: The chemistry hidden in a handful of soil
soil-chem-076.text: Nine-tenths of a soil's weight is rock-born. Minerals, derived from the parent rock or regolith, make up about 90% of the total weight of soil. Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil, and those characteristics depend on three things: mineral composition, soil organic matter and environmental factors. Plants take part too. They trade the elements they feed on with microorganisms, and they absorb them. That creates concentration gradients of cations and anions, the positively and negatively charged ions. Each of these elements follows its own cycle through rock, air, water and life. Nitrogen passes from a gas into nitrate and nitrite, while phosphorus moves in mineral form held in rock. The field has a founder. In the early 1870s J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. Until the late 1960s the questions stayed close to the farm: the reactions behind soil formation and plant growth. On farms today the chemistry still serves plant feeding, the fertility of soil and the ingredients farmers spread to feed crops. Concern over pollution then shifted the field toward the environment, the turn traced in {{ref:soil-chem-077}}.

soil-chem-079.title: Clay minerals, the sheet silicates born of water
soil-chem-079.text: For a long time clay looked like ordinary rock ground very fine. Only with X-ray diffraction in the 1930s did it prove to be mainly sheet silicates formed as secondary minerals, not tiny grains of quartz, feldspar or mica. A clay mineral is a hydrous aluminium phyllosilicate: a silicate built in sheets that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations. Its structure rests on flat hexagonal sheets like those of the mica minerals. Water is essential. Clay minerals form in its presence, as common products of {{ref:soil-found-052}}, including the weathering of feldspar, and of low-temperature hydrothermal alteration. That need for water makes them rare in the Solar System, though they have been detected on Mars, Ceres and other bodies. On Earth they are very common in soils and in fine-grained rocks such as shale, mudstone, siltstone, slate and phyllite. In a soil they never stop forming. For as long as the soil exists, new clay arises by inheritance, by neoformation or by transformation of earlier minerals. Most soil clays are crystalline, but some are amorphous. A soil's clay is a mixture of types, often with one dominating according to the kind of soil. The charges on clay minerals matter for crops. With soil organic matter, they supply most of a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, its power to hold cations that plants feed on, such as potassium and ammonium.

soil-chem-107.title: Diatomaceous earth, a powder of fossil shells
soil-chem-107.text: Diatomaceous earth is a rock made of fossils. Also called diatomite or kieselgur, this soft sedimentary rock crumbles into a fine white powder. It is the silica shells of diatoms, piled up in lake or marine sediments over millions of years, and is usually 80–90% silica. Its particles are typically 10 to 200 μm, and high porosity makes the powder light. FAO soil description lists it among the materials of limnic L layers. Gardeners use it as a bonsai medium and conditioner: like {{ref:soil-fert-072}}, it holds water yet drains freely.

soil-chem-104.title: Goethite, the iron mineral in rust and yellow soils
soil-chem-104.text: Every patch of rust holds a soil mineral. Goethite is the α form of the iron(III) oxide-hydroxide FeO(OH). It is the main component of rust and of bog iron ore, which forms in swampy ground at the head of springs. In soil it often forms by weathering of other iron-rich minerals. As iron-bearing minerals reach the soil's oxidation zone, ferrous iron(II) becomes ferric iron(III). The parent mineral's shape is kept, so goethite often forms pseudomorphs, crystals in another mineral's outline. Some bacteria make it too. It is concentrated in {{ref:soil-form-065}}, alongside quartz and other iron and clay minerals. Goethite is yellowish to reddish to dark brown or black, and it helps tint soils yellow to red. Its grip on nutrients is fierce: clays rich in goethite hold phosphorus so tightly that plants cannot absorb it. Heating converts it to {{ref:soil-chem-166}}, which raises soil magnetism. Long used as the pigment brown ochre, it was first described in 1806 and named after Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

soil-chem-080.title: Two kinds of sheet that build every clay
soil-chem-080.text: Every clay mineral, however varied, is assembled from just two kinds of sheet. The tetrahedral sheet is made of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron shares three oxygens with its neighbors in a hexagonal array. The fourth, apical oxygen points the same way on every tetrahedron. The octahedral sheet holds small cations such as aluminium or magnesium, each surrounded by six oxygens. The apical oxygens also form one face of the octahedral sheet, which locks the two together. An extra oxygen above each hexagonal gap bonds to hydrogen as a hydroxyl group. Fitting them together corrugates the tetrahedral sheet and flattens the octahedral one. The clay in {{ref:soil-chem-088}} shows the shorthand: its T sheet holds silicon among four oxygens, its O sheet aluminium among six oxygens or hydroxyls. Depending on composition, a finished layer is neutral or carries a net negative charge. Interlayer cations such as Na+ or K+ balance that charge, or a lone octahedral sheet does. A clay crystal is a stack of these layers separated by interlayers.

soil-chem-081.title: One-to-one or two-to-one: how clay sheets stack
soil-chem-081.text: Clay mineralogists sort their subjects with two numbers. A 1:1 clay builds each layer from one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet. A 2:1 clay places an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets. That difference decides how the layers hold together. 1:1 layers carry no charge and cling to each other by hydrogen bonds. 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge, so something positive must bind them. In some groups that is a scatter of cations; in others, a whole octahedral sheet. Four main groups result. The kaolin group, typified by {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, also holds dickite, {{ref:soil-chem-090}} and nacrite, all 1:1 clays like serpentine. The 2:1 groups are three. {{ref:soil-chem-091}} includes {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, nontronite, saponite and the clay of {{ref:soil-chem-152}}, and its layers are bound by cations. So are those of {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. {{ref:soil-chem-087}} is bound by octahedral sheets instead. Talc and {{ref:soil-chem-095}} are 2:1 clays too. Soil scientists usually give the same four groups for soils. Some clays break the pattern. {{ref:soil-chem-110}} and the clay of {{ref:soil-chem-167}} are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure. Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, either randomly, coded R0, or in order. Perfectly ordered R1 mixes have their own names, such as rectorite and corrensite.

soil-chem-095.title: Vermiculite, the clay named for breeding worms
soil-chem-095.text: Heat vermiculite and it exfoliates, splitting and swelling apart. That habit gave the mineral its name, from the Latin vermiculare, 'to breed worms', when it was first described in 1824 at Millbury, Massachusetts. Vermiculite is a hydrous 2:1 clay mineral. It forms by weathering or hydrothermal alteration of two micas, biotite and phlogopite. These lose the potassium between their sheets, and magnesium and iron take its place. Hydrated magnesium holds the crystals loosely, so vermiculite swells, though less than {{ref:soil-chem-093}}. That makes it a limited-expansion clay with a medium shrink–swell capacity. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} of 100–150 meq/100 g, milliequivalents per 100 grams, is high, above that of the clays in {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. It occurs interlayered with biotite, phlogopite and {{ref:soil-chem-087}}, typically where felsic rocks meet mafic or ultramafic ones. Pure vermiculite contains no asbestos. Ore from some deposits, notably the Libby mine in Montana, was contaminated, and some products contained asbestos until the early 1990s.

soil-chem-088.title: Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics
soil-chem-088.text: Paper, porcelain and hot, wet soils share one clay. Kaolinite, also called kaolin, is a common 1:1 clay mineral, Al2Si2O5(OH)4. Soft, earthy and usually white, it forms by chemical weathering of aluminium silicates such as feldspar. Each layer bonds a silica tetrahedral sheet to an aluminium octahedral sheet. Tight hydrogen bonds hold successive layers together, so water cannot get between them, so kaolinite does not swell and has a low shrink–swell capacity. The layers carry no net charge, so no large cations sit between them, hence its low {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, just 1–15 meq/100 g. Its surfaces often carry positive charges instead. Moist, it is plastic: a film of water binds its plate-like crystals yet lets them slip. Dried, it is rigid but fragile. Kaolinite abounds in soils formed by chemical weathering in hot, moist climates. The INERA classification calls soils whose clay is mostly kaolinite kaolisols. Rock rich in it is kaolin or china clay, an industrial raw material used above all for paper and ceramics.

soil-chem-094.title: Illite, the potassium clay that will not swell
soil-chem-094.text: Illite is the only clay mineral that contains potassium, and that potassium shapes its character. Also called hydromica, it is a group of closely related, non-expanding 2:1 clay minerals, structurally close to the mica muscovite. Poorly hydrated potassium ions fill the space between its layers and bind them strongly, so illite does not swell. Those bonds also shrink its active surface. What little swelling it shows depends on how far potassium feldspar has weathered. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, typically 20–30 meq/100 g, is higher than kaolinite's but lower than that of {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Illite forms by alteration of muscovite and feldspar in weathering and hydrothermal settings, and from swelling clays exposed to potassium-rich groundwater. It is common in sediments, soils and argillaceous rocks, and its share of soil clay rises relative to kaolinite toward cooler climates. It was first described in 1937 from the Maquoketa shale of Calhoun County, Illinois, and named after the state.

soil-chem-105.title: Gibbsite, what remains when silica is gone
soil-chem-105.text: Strip a clay of its silica and gibbsite is what remains. Gibbsite is a mineral form of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3. It is built of stacked sheets of linked octahedra, each an aluminium ion bonded to six hydroxide groups, with a third of the octahedral sites left empty. Each sheet is electrically neutral, so no ions glue the sheets together. Only weak residual bonds hold them, which makes gibbsite very soft and easily cleaved. Identical aluminium hydroxide 'gibbsite layers' sit sandwiched between silicate sheets in the illite, kaolinite and {{ref:soil-chem-091}} clay groups. Gibbsite forms by intense weathering of other clay minerals, and {{ref:soil-chem-097}} alters to it where silica is removed. Where heavy rainfall leaches most silica from alumino-silica clays, it is among the less soluble oxides left behind, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils. As one of the three main phases of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, it is an important aluminium ore. It is named after the American mineral collector George Gibbs (1776–1833).

soil-chem-108.title: Bauxite, the rock behind the world's aluminium
soil-chem-108.text: The world's aluminium comes mainly from one weathered rock. Bauxite is a sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content. It consists mostly of gibbsite, boehmite and diaspore, mixed with goethite, {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, kaolinite and a little anatase. Lateritic bauxites, found mostly in the tropics, form by lateritization of silicate rocks such as granite, gneiss, basalt and shale. Karst bauxites lie over limestone and dolomite. Bauxite needs even more intense weathering and better drainage than iron-rich laterites. Those conditions dissolve kaolinite and precipitate gibbsite. Most deposits lie within 1 to 20 metres of the surface, so bauxite is usually strip mined.

soil-chem-077.title: What becomes of a pollutant once it reaches soil
soil-chem-077.text: A chemical spilled on soil does not simply sit there. Environmental soil chemistry studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them. Processes such as {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, {{ref:soil-chem-147}}, precipitation, polymerization, dissolution, hydrolysis, hydration, complexation and oxidation–reduction can each raise or lower a chemical's toxicity. Knowing these reactions helps predict a contaminant's fate and design sound, cost-effective clean-up, though clean-up engineers often disregard them. The field grew from worry, since the late 1960s, about pollution and its ecological and health risks.

soil-chem-078.title: How soil chemists test a sample without spoiling it
soil-chem-078.text: Drying a soil sample changes the very chemistry under study. Air-drying at about 25 °C and sieving to 2 mm markedly disrupt structure, microbial life and properties tied to pH. Many chemists now keep samples, taken from undisturbed horizons, field-moist at 4 °C. In batch equilibration, a solution of known ion content is shaken with soil, say 25 mL with 5 g. The liquid is then analyzed for mg of ion per g of soil. Column studies leach a solution through soil at a controlled rate, mimicking rain and snowmelt. Surface spectroscopy, such as infrared or X-ray methods, shows how ions bind to particles without disturbing the soil.

soil-chem-084.title: Soil colloids, the tiny particles that do the chemistry
soil-chem-084.text: Most of a soil's chemistry happens on particles too small to see. Soil colloids, chiefly clay and the dark decayed material called {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, have at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 1 μm. Their charged surfaces hold ions and trade them with the soil water. Clay, a colloidal and usually crystalline phyllosilicate, is the most active mineral part of soil. It owes that to its high specific surface area and its unbalanced negative charges. Negative charges on colloids hold cations, and positive charges hold anions. Together they give soil its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and {{ref:soil-chem-053}}. This exchange does quiet, constant work. It buffers soil pH, alters structure and purifies percolating water by adsorbing cations, both useful and harmful. Soil clays fall into four kinds: layered alumino-silica clays, crystalline chain carbonates and sulfates, young {{ref:soil-chem-099}}, and old, highly leached {{ref:soil-chem-106}}. The organic colloids are richer still: on a dry-weight basis their exchange capacity is many times that of clay. Climate can strip colloids away. In tropical rainforests, heat and heavy rain largely destroy clay and organic colloids, leaving only oxide clays that hold few cations.

soil-chem-112.title: Hematite, the blood-red oxide of old soils
soil-chem-112.text: Hematite takes its name from the Greek for blood. It is a common iron oxide mineral, Fe2O3, widely found in rocks and soils. Clay-sized hematite forms as a secondary mineral during soil weathering. With goethite and the other minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, it gives many tropical, ancient or highly weathered soils their red color. It grows from {{ref:soil-chem-111}}, a metastable precursor of both hematite and goethite. Red ochre is clay colored by 20% to 70% unhydrated hematite. Older ironstone crusts in {{ref:soil-class-137}} contain more hematite and boehmite than plinthite does.

soil-chem-083.title: Did life begin on the surface of clay?
soil-chem-083.text: The first living things may have had help from clay. In 1985 Graham Cairns-Smith proposed that complex organic molecules arose on non-organic, replicating silicate crystal surfaces in water. Clay minerals form only where water is present, and many theories of how life began involve them. Laboratory work lends weight to the idea: {{ref:soil-chem-093}} has been shown to catalyze the joining of nucleotides into RNA in water, and the formation of membranes from lipids. In 1998 Hyman Hartman went further. He proposed that the first organisms were self-replicating iron-rich clays that fixed carbon dioxide into oxalic and other dicarboxylic acids.

soil-chem-082.title: Telling one clay from another in the laboratory
soil-chem-082.text: Clay minerals are usually too fine for ordinary optical study. X-ray diffraction is the main tool for identifying them, aided by electron diffraction, spectroscopy and SEM-EDS. To put numbers on a soil's clays, analysts first measure its soil organic matter, carbonates, free oxides and non-clay minerals. They then estimate clay percentages from how much glycol a sample takes up, {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, K2O and thermal data. This glycol test, a case of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, measures how much ethylene glycol enters a clay's interlayer sites over eight hours of exposure to the vapor at 60 °C. Illite is estimated from its potassium oxide content, since it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.

soil-chem-087.title: Chlorite, a green clay with no chlorine in it
soil-chem-087.text: Chlorite contains no chlorine; its name is Greek for green. It is a chemically varied group of 2:1 clay minerals. Aluminium replacing silicon gives their layers a negative charge. A positively charged hydroxide sheet of hydrated magnesium, called a brucite sheet, binds the layers, not the scattered cations of vermiculite or mica. With two silicon planes, one aluminium and one magnesium plane, chlorite is described as a 2:2 clay. Water is not adsorbed between its layers, so it does not swell, and its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low. A common weathering product found widely in clay, it also forms in low-grade metamorphic rocks.

soil-chem-097.title: Allophane, the shapeless clay of volcanic ash
soil-chem-097.text: Allophane never quite becomes a crystal. This hydrous aluminium silicate has only short-range order, so it counts as a mineraloid. It forms from weathering or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and feldspars, typically at pH 5–7, with an Al:Si ratio usually of 2. Electron micrographs show hollow spherules about 3–5 nm across. Its structure has been debated; one account describes curved alumina and silica layers like those of clays. It alters to {{ref:soil-chem-090}} where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed. It is among the amorphous materials that define the volcanic-ash soils of {{ref:soil-class-092}}.

soil-chem-098.title: Imogolite, a clay built of nanotubes
soil-chem-098.text: Some clay comes as tubes about 2 nm across. Imogolite, Al2SiO3(OH)4, is an aluminium silicate clay mineral made of a network of these nanotubes. Each tube is 1 nm wide inside, with walls of gibbsite sheets and orthosilicate groups. It was first described in 1962 in Kumamoto prefecture, Japan, and named from imogo, a brownish-yellow soil derived from volcanic ash. It occurs in such soils with allophane, quartz, cristobalite, gibbsite, vermiculite and the iron mixture of {{ref:soil-chem-165}}. Where tephra is basic or the climate dry, allophane and imogolite develop, and {{ref:soil-class-119}} receive the Silandic qualifier.

soil-chem-096.title: Expanded vermiculite in the potting bench
soil-chem-096.text: Once heated and expanded, vermiculite becomes a gardener's material. Mixed with {{ref:soil-class-070}} or composted pine bark, exfoliated vermiculite makes soilless growing media. These speed rooting and hold air, plant food and moisture for release as plants need them. Alone or mixed with soil, it germinates seeds with very little watering. In heavy, sticky soils, mixing in vermiculite up to half the soil's volume creates air channels. In sandy soils it helps the soil hold water and air. Agromineral practice uses vermiculites and zeolites to store moisture in soil, alongside {{ref:soil-fert-072}} for aeration.

soil-chem-111.title: Ferrihydrite, iron oxide as a nanoparticle sponge
soil-chem-111.text: A single gram of ferrihydrite offers several hundred square metres of surface. This widespread, poorly crystalline hydrous iron(III) oxyhydroxide exists only as fine-grained nanoparticles. It forms in soils, waters, aquifers and mining areas, precipitating from oxygenated iron-rich water or through bacterial activity. Its nanoporous particles adsorb arsenic, lead, phosphate and the organic acids met in {{ref:soil-chem-059}} and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Ferrihydrite is metastable, a precursor of hematite and goethite, though adsorbed impurities such as silica usually block that change in nature. Under reducing conditions, as in gley soils and often with microbial help, it can turn into {{ref:soil-chem-170}}, here in the form covered in {{ref:soil-chem-109}}. Brief contact with air oxidizes it back to ferrihydrite.

soil-chem-109.title: Fougèrite, the green rust of waterlogged soils
soil-chem-109.text: Fougèrite does not last long in air. This naturally occurring mineral, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-170}}, is a layered double hydroxide of ferrous and ferric iron, described only relatively recently. It was first found in forest soils near Fougères, Brittany. The International Mineralogical Association accepted it as a mineral species in 2002. Its brucite-like layers hold Fe2+ and Fe3+, with loosely bound carbonate and water between them. It forms clay-like hexagonal platelets under a micron across. It occurs as fougèrite in {{ref:soil-class-127}}. Exposed to air, it oxidizes, dehydrates and loses carbonate, turning to ferrihydrite and finally to goethite or the rust described in {{ref:soil-chem-164}}.

soil-chem-110.title: Palygorskite, a clay of bristles instead of plates
soil-chem-110.text: Palygorskite grows as bristles rather than plates. Also called attapulgite, it is a fibrous magnesium aluminium clay mineral, (Mg,Al)2Si4O10(OH)·4(H2O). Unlike the layered clays of {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, it has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains linked to magnesium–aluminium octahedral sheets. It forms in shallow lakes, rivers, waterlogged ground and soils, favored by semi-arid conditions and alkaline water rich in magnesium and silica. Its bristle-like crystals do not swell and have a high specific surface area of about 75 to 400 m²/g. It is one type of {{ref:soil-chem-102}}. Farmers use it to carry plant food and to improve water retention and aeration.

soil-chem-089.title: Growing kaolinite from dissolved silica and aluminium
soil-chem-089.text: Kaolinite can crystallize in soil at ordinary temperature and pressure, but only if its ingredients arrive the right way. Silica must come as single molecules in very dilute solution. Aluminium must be six-coordinated with oxygen, as in gibbsite. The reaction is 2Al(OH)3 + 2H4SiO4 → Si2O5·Al2(OH)4 + 5H2O, so five water molecules must be removed for each unit of kaolinite formed. Seasons matter. On basalt in Kivu, kaolinite formed only where wet and dry seasons alternate, not in perennially swampy ground. Wetting–drying cycles also help allophane turn into kaolinite. In soils, disordered amorphous material seems to become ordered kaolinite fairly quickly, without major environmental change.

soil-chem-099.title: Amorphous clays, young minerals not yet in order
soil-chem-099.text: Not every clay has had time to crystallize. Amorphous clays are young mixtures of silica and alumina that have not yet formed regular crystals. They are common in recent volcanic ash deposits such as tephra. Most of their charge comes from hydroxyl groups that gain or lose a hydrogen ion as soil pH changes. That lets them buffer soil pH and attract either cations or anions. High proportions of glass and amorphous colloids, including allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite, define {{ref:soil-class-092}}. Clays without plate-shaped minerals, such as allophanic clays, tend not to show a residual shear strength.

soil-chem-090.title: Halloysite, the kaolinite-group clay that grows as tubes
soil-chem-090.text: Halloysite shares kaolinite's formula, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, but grows as nanotubes. Their walls are 10–15 sheets thick, their outer diameters 50–60 nm and their lengths 0.5–10 μm. This clay of the kaolinite group occurs mainly in recently exposed volcanic soils. It also forms from primary minerals in tropical soils, and glassy basaltic rocks alter to it most readily. Water changes it. Hydrated halloysite has a layer spacing of 1 nm, dehydrated meta-halloysite 0.7 nm. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} rises with hydration, from 5–10 to 40–50 meq/100 g. Allophane alters to halloysite under resilicating conditions. In acidic cave settings at pH 5 or lower, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} alters to its hydrated form, endellite.

soil-chem-085.title: Isomorphous substitution: how clays gain a fixed charge
soil-chem-085.text: A clay's charge is set as the clay forms. While its crystals grow, some cations in the structure are replaced by others of lower valence, carrying less positive charge. This is isomorphous substitution, and it leaves the clay a lasting negative charge. The arithmetic is simple. In the silica sheet, Al3+ may replace Si4+. A site that balanced +4 against −4 now holds +3 against −4, a charge of −1. In the alumina sheet, up to a quarter of the Al3+ may give way to Zn2+, Mg2+ or Fe2+. Mg2+ in place of Al3+ gives +2/−3, again −1. Where the swap happens matters. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} carries its charge mostly in the octahedral sheet, from magnesium replacing aluminium. The clay of {{ref:soil-chem-152}} carries it mostly in the tetrahedral sheet, from aluminium replacing silicon. Substitutions in outer layers count for more than inner ones, since charge strength falls off with the square of the distance. Cations in the interlayer must balance the excess negative charge. It attracts water and positively charged ions, some of them useful to plants. Kaolinite has undergone almost no substitution, which is why its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low. This charge does not change with time. That sets it apart from the charge described in {{ref:soil-chem-049}}, which rises as pH rises.

soil-chem-091.title: Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior
soil-chem-091.text: Smectite clays swell because their layers are not rigidly joined. Smectite is a group of swelling 2:1 clay minerals, chiefly {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, that take water and cations between their layers. The name depends on place: smectite is the usual term in Europe, while North America uses the name of its chief member, and industry calls these clays {{ref:soil-chem-100}}. Each layer is two silica tetrahedral sheets cross-linked through an octahedral sheet of alumina or iron oxide. Isomorphous substitution in both kinds of sheet gives the layers their negative charge. The interlayer between them holds hydrated cations and water. These enter reversibly, so the clay swells as they come in. That open interlayer also gives smectites the highest {{ref:soil-chem-046}} of the clays common in soils; only vermiculite and some zeolites exceed it. Smectites form by weathering of basalt, gabbro and silica-rich volcanic glass, and where hot water or seawater dissolves much of the silica from volcanic ash. Soils with smectite clay expand when wet. Clay soils containing smectite also suffer more problems from {{ref:soil-chem-142}} than illite or kaolinite clay soils.

soil-chem-093.title: Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold
soil-chem-093.text: Montmorillonite can swell up to ten times its dry volume. Named after Montmorillon in France, where it was first described in 1847, it is a soft 2:1 clay of the smectite group. An alumina sheet sits between two silica sheets, and its water content varies. Its plate-shaped particles average about 1 μm across and 0.96 nm thick. Resolving one takes about 25,000-fold electron-microscope magnification. Magnesium replacing aluminium in the central sheet leaves nearby oxygens negatively charged and able to attract cations. Its crystals are loosely bound, not bonded face to face. Water enters between them, and the whole surface is open to reactions, which gives it a high {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. It is a characteristic component of swelling soils. It occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions, often mixed with chlorite, muscovite, illite and kaolinite. It is added to drought-prone soils to hold water, and its swelling suits it to drilling mud, earthen dams and levees.

soil-chem-100.title: Bentonite, the swelling clay that seals landfills
soil-chem-100.text: Bentonite can absorb enough water to grow up to eight times in volume. This absorbent swelling clay is made mostly of montmorillonite, in either its sodium or its calcium form. Geologists use the name for a clay rock formed from volcanic ash, usually in seawater, as up to 40–50 wt.% of its silica dissolves away. Sodium bentonite swells far more than calcium bentonite. Adding 5–10% of a soluble sodium salt converts the calcium form to the sodium form. Swelling makes sodium bentonite a self-sealing, low-permeability barrier. It lines landfills, and nearly sodium-saturated clay forms impermeable curtains in soil below dams.

soil-chem-102.title: Fuller's earth, the clay that cleaned wool
soil-chem-102.text: Fuller's earth is named for a trade. Fullers kneaded it with water into woolen cloth to absorb lanolin, oils and other greasy impurities. Today the name covers various clays used as an absorbent, filter or bleaching agent. Products sold as fuller's earth are usually palygorskite, also called attapulgite, or bentonite. Its clays commonly include montmorillonite and kaolinite. In some places the name means calcium bentonite, altered volcanic ash made mostly of montmorillonite. It has a dangerous side. Saturated by heavy rain, it can become thixotropic, so hills, cliffs and slopes that contain it can be unstable.

soil-chem-092.title: Swellers and collapsers: the cations between clay layers
soil-chem-092.text: Whether a clay swells depends on what sits between its layers. In 2:1 clays, the interlayer cations govern how much the clay swells or shrinks as it gains or loses water. Two traits of each cation explain it: how strongly it hydrates, and its hydrated radius. Highly hydrated magnesium ions act as swellers, fully opening vermiculite's interlayer. Poorly hydrated potassium ions act as collapsers, fully closing illite's. In smectites the main interlayer cations are Na+ and Ca2+. Sodium gives the most swelling. With sodium as its main exchangeable cation, montmorillonite can swell to several times its original volume. Calcium smectite swells much less but also shrinks less when dried. Potassium replacing sodium collapses the interlayer, so smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater turns into non-swelling illite. Ammonium is caught the same way. It is fixed mainly between the layers of illite, vermiculite or montmorillonite, with potassium and other ions of similar size and low hydration energy. These cations help set a clay soil's {{ref:soil-phys-028}}.

soil-chem-101.title: Clay that brought worn-out Thai fields back
soil-chem-101.text: In northeast Thailand, farmers restored degraded fields with clay. Bentonite applied to those soils dramatically reversed the degradation and brought higher yields, better crop prices and greater returns. Field trials by the International Water Management Institute and partners in 2002–2003 found that locally sourced bentonite raised yields of rain-fed forage sorghum. Clay-using farmers had higher costs. Their larger, better harvests still let them invest and grow more than farmers who did not use clay. Clays such as calcium bentonite also help water-repellent soils, giving them more surface area per unit volume and supporting aggregation.

soil-chem-086.title: From swelling clays to oxides: the weathering sequence
soil-chem-086.text: A soil's clay records how hard it has been weathered. As weathering and leaching intensify, the dominant clay minerals change: from 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite, through kaolinite, to oxides of iron and aluminium. The starting point depends on the parent material and on the minerals in solution, so source rock and climate both matter. Montmorillonite occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions. Depending on its origin, it may also occur in humid climates. Where rainfall is high, acid soils lose more silica than alumina from their clays, leaving kaolinite. Heavier weathering still produces {{ref:soil-chem-106}}. Rock and chemistry steer the result as well. Acid weathering of feldspar-rich rock in warm climates yields kaolin, alkaline weathering yields illite, and intense weathering of other clay minerals yields gibbsite. Climate gradients show the same pattern. Kaolinite abounds in soils of hot, moist climates. Toward cooler climates illite increases, and toward drier ones smectite. Because clay content tracks climate, the clays of buried ancient soils are used to infer past climates.

soil-chem-106.title: Sesquioxide clays, the last residue of deep weathering
soil-chem-106.text: A sesquioxide clay takes hundreds of thousands of years of leaching to form. These old, highly leached clays are oxides and hydroxides of iron, aluminium and titanium. They remain after heavy rainfall removes most of the silica from alumino-silica clays. They include hematite, iron hydroxide, gibbsite and the manganese mineral birnessite, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils. The name comes from the Latin sesqui, 'one and one-half', for three parts oxygen to two of metal. Not all of them fit that ratio. They are not sticky and do not swell. Soils rich in them, such as lateritic soils, behave much like sand and pass water rapidly. Their {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low, but because their charge varies, they can hold anions as well as cations. They hold large amounts of phosphate, a hold that humified soil organic matter partly blocks. The more goethite they contain, the more phosphorus is locked away from plants. Their dominant iron oxides color these soils from yellow to red.

soil-chem-103.title: Five stages of clay meeting water
soil-chem-103.text: Dry clay packets sit in face-to-face stacks like a deck of playing cards. Clay–water interaction names what happens next, in five stages. First, hydration: the clay absorbs water and swells. In dispersion, water pushes the platelets so far apart that they lose their attraction and spread through the water. Once shearing stops, surface charges draw them back together in flocculation. Deflocculation, or peptization, reverses flocculation. A chemical deflocculant covers the platelets' positive edge charges and greatly weakens their attraction. Finally, in aggregation, ionic or thermal conditions alter the platelets' water layer, strip off the deflocculant and let them stack again.

soil-chem-058.title: Humic substances, the dark core of soil organic matter
soil-chem-058.text: Most soil organic matter is not fresh leaves or roots but something darker and older. Humic substances are dark, relatively decay-resistant organic compounds that form as biomass residues break down and change over long periods. They make up most of the organic material in soil, {{ref:soil-class-070}}, coal and sediments, and much of the organic material dissolved in lakes, rivers and sea water. Their color runs from bright yellow through brown to black, and the name comes from the Latin word for 'soil, earth'. Microbes make them from dead material such as {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, cellulose and charred wood. Yet how they form is among the least understood parts of the chemistry of soil organic matter. Maillard proposed a sugar-amine condensation theory in 1911, and Waksman, in 1932, a theory built on that woody compound. Those formed in soil over hundreds to thousands of years carry more oxygen and nitrogen than those from coal, formed over millions. Chemists split them by solubility into three fractions. They also supply 50 to 90% of a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-069.title: Chelation: how molecules grip metals like a claw
soil-chem-069.text: A crab holds its prey with two pincers, and some molecules hold metal atoms the same way. Chelation is the bonding of a metal atom by a molecule that grips it at two or more points, closing a ring. The name comes from the Greek chēlē, 'claw', and Morgan and Drew first used the word 'chelate' in 1920. The gripping molecule, or ligand, is called a chelant, chelator, chelating agent or sequestering agent. It is usually organic, though it need not be. Most metal complexes in nature sit in some kind of chelate ring, held by a humic substance or a protein. In soil, these chelates govern how metals move. They also control how plants and microorganisms take up and store metals. As a negatively charged colloid, {{ref:soil-bio-089}} raises a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and so its ability to store nutrients by chelation. People use the same grip in nutritional supplements, chelation therapy for toxic metals, MRI contrast agents, catalysts, water treatment and fertilizers. The process can also run backward. In dechelation, acidifying the solution with a mineral acid forms a precipitate and recovers the chelating agent.

soil-chem-068.title: Sorption: the many ways one substance sticks to another
soil-chem-068.text: Some soil organic matter is more than a century old, and part of the reason is that it is stuck. Sorption is any physical and chemical process by which one substance becomes attached to another. It covers absorption into a substance of a different state, adsorption of ions and molecules onto the surface of another phase, and the swapping of ions. For a dilute solute, the rates of adsorption and absorption can be calculated with Fick's laws of diffusion. Much soil {{ref:soil-bio-089}} persists for over 100 years partly because it is tightly sorbed or bound to clays, out of reach of microbes and their enzymes. Sorption also steers nutrients. Molybdenum is sorbed most strongly in acid soils, so adding lime often relieves a shortage of molybdenum by loosening that hold. Aluminum sorbed onto exposed hydroxyl groups gives the edges of clay plates a slight positive charge. Those edges stick to the negative faces of other particles, and the clay flocculates. In {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, ammonium from {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, a strongly sorbing cation, trades places with weakly sorbing sodium and releases it into the water.

soil-chem-049.title: Variable charge: soil surfaces that shift with pH
soil-chem-049.text: Part of a soil's grip on nutrients turns up and down with acidity. Variable charge is surface charge on clay edges and soil organic matter that changes with the pH of the soil water. It comes from hydroxyl groups, pairs of oxygen and hydrogen atoms, that give up their hydrogen ions. The broken edges of clay sheets expose many acidic hydroxyl groups. At the pH of many soils these lose their hydrogen and leave negative charges behind. Soil organic matter does the same: hydrogens on its hydroxyl groups ionize into solution, leaving an oxygen with a negative charge. Its many charged groups give it a large share of a soil's power to hold cations, positively charged ions, and that share depends heavily on pH. Raising the pH means fewer hydrogen ions in solution. More groups then lose their hydrogen, the variable charge grows, and so does the {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-073.title: Leonardite, the oxidized coal rich in humic acid
soil-chem-073.text: Lignite left near the surface slowly oxidizes into something else. Leonardite is a soft, waxy, black or brown mineraloid formed by the oxidation of lignite, and it dissolves easily in alkaline solutions. First described from North Dakota, it is named after A. G. Leonard, first director of the North Dakota Geological Survey. Up to 90% of it can be {{ref:soil-chem-059}}. It conditions soil when applied directly, or as a source of that acid or of {{ref:soil-chem-074}}. It also serves in water treatment, as a drilling additive and in the cleanup of polluted ground. Added to contaminated soil, especially with {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, it reduces the metals plants take up.

soil-chem-065.title: Making humic substances in hours instead of years
soil-chem-065.text: Nature needs years to make humic substances, and chemists can do it in hours. Artificial humic substances are humic-like materials made by people: by composting {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, adding {{ref:soil-fert-050}} or synthesizing them from organic feedstocks. Hydrothermal processing turns biomass in an alkaline solution at 180 °C–250 °C into all three humic fractions within minutes to hours. Oxidizing lignite does it too, reversing coal formation; China widely uses this 'mineral-derived' {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Such products have eased drought's effects on soil microbes and helped save a 160-year-old beech tree in Park Sanssouci, Potsdam.

soil-chem-062.title: Inside humic substances: thousands of molecules, no settled shape
soil-chem-062.text: Mass spectroscopy finds thousands of distinct components in humic material. Humic substances mix many molecules built from aromatic, aliphatic and carbohydrate units, carrying mainly carboxylic and phenolic groups. These groups supply most of the charge and reactivity, giving up hydrogen around pK 4 and pK 8, as in {{ref:soil-chem-049}}. They also bind Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, often as chelates, regulating how available those metals are. Molecular weights are lower than once thought. Researchers still disagree whether the molecules are large poly-condensates tied to clay or loose supramolecular associations of small ones.

soil-chem-064.title: Does organic matter feed plants? A dispute since the 18th century
soil-chem-064.text: People once believed plants fed directly on {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Then Liebig showed that plants grow on inorganic compounds, and soil organic matter came to be valued only for the nutrients it released as it broke down. Soil scientists now at least agree that it affects fertility by helping soil hold water. Its other effects on plants have been disputed since the 18th century. Plants may absorb soluble humic material, perhaps to take up iron, but this is not settled. Studies found humic products boosted growth even at low rates.

soil-chem-070.title: Why two grips beat one: the chelate effect
soil-chem-070.text: A molecule that holds a metal at two points beats two molecules holding it at one point each. That is the chelate effect: a chelating ligand's greater affinity for a metal ion than similar ligands that bind it only once. Bidentate, or two-pronged, ligands close a chelate ring around the metal, and as in organic chemistry, 5- and 6-membered rings predominate. Cadmium holds ethylenediamine, which forms a five-membered ring, far more strongly than two methylamine ligands of about the same donor power. The enthalpy changes, the heat given off, of the two reactions are about equal. So the advantage comes mainly from entropy, the measure of disorder.

soil-chem-072.title: Chelated fertilizers keep micronutrient metals in solution
soil-chem-072.text: The phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn trace metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants. Chelated fertilizers avoid that trap by supplying manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelates. EDTA is the typical chelating agent, and iron is often given as EDTA or EDDHA chelates. Sprayed on leaves, a chelated nutrient is absorbed and moved better, and less is lost to soil and groundwater. Use of EDTA and NTA is falling 6% a year over toxicity concerns, as greener EDDS and citrate gain ground.

soil-chem-071.title: Living chelators: how microbes and roots fetch metals
soil-chem-071.text: Living things make their own claws for metal. Natural chelating agents are molecules made by organisms that bind metal ions as chelates: proteins, polysaccharides, organic acids and microbial pigments. Malate, glutamic acid, histidine and the peptide phytochelatin are typical. Pseudomonas bacteria secrete the water-soluble pigments pyochelin and pyoverdine, which bind iron, and some root-dwelling bacteria use such pigments to hand iron to plants. Organic chelators such as peptides and sugars are even credited with chemical weathering, pulling metal ions out of rocks.

soil-chem-075.title: Point of zero charge, where a surface's sign flips
soil-chem-075.text: At one pH, a charged soil surface carries no net charge at all. That pH is its point of zero charge. Below it the surface turns positive and adsorbs anions, negatively charged ions; above it, the surface turns negative and adsorbs cations. The idea came from studies of colloid flocculation, since particles at this point flocculate fastest. Chemists find it by titrating a colloid suspension with acid and base. It governs how readily a surface adsorbs harmful ions, and even shifts soil emissions of nitrous acid.

soil-chem-060.title: Fulvic acid, the humic fraction that always dissolves
soil-chem-060.text: One fraction of humic substances dissolves in water at any pH, acid or alkaline. That fraction is fulvic acid. Compared with {{ref:soil-chem-059}}, it has more carboxylic groups, a lower average molecular weight and stronger acidity. Measured number-average molecular weights of fulvic acid from water are below 900. Fulvic acids hold more exchangeable cations, interact more strongly with fertilizers and form soluble chelates of trace metals. Those metal chelates are strongly leached and redeposited, an important part of cheluviation.

soil-chem-059.title: Humic acid, the fraction that strong acid leaves behind
soil-chem-059.text: Humic acid stays dissolved in neutral or alkaline water but not in strong acid. It is the fraction of humic substances that dissolves at neutral and alkaline pH but not below pH 2. It is a complex mixture of acids with carboxyl and phenolate groups that behaves as a dibasic acid, giving up two hydrogen ions, or occasionally three. Its number-average molecular weight is below 6000. {{ref:soil-fert-026}} lowers the pH of {{ref:soil-chem-019}} by generating humic acid. Its potassium salt, {{ref:soil-chem-074}}, comes from leonardite.

soil-chem-066.title: Humate, the humic rock that is mined
soil-chem-066.text: In New Mexico, soil amendment has been dug from the ground since the 1970s. The material is humate, which in economic geology means rock rich in humic acids. Weathered coal beds such as leonardite count, as do mudrock and the material filling pores in sandstone. The Fruitland Formation had produced nearly 60,000 metric tons of humate by 2016. Humate deposits may also play an important part in forming uranium ore bodies.

soil-chem-067.title: When humic acid meets chlorine in drinking water
soil-chem-067.text: Water from peaty uplands brings a chemistry problem to the treatment plant. Humic and fulvic acids react with chlorination chemicals to form disinfection byproducts such as dihaloacetonitriles, which are toxic to humans. So humic acid in water meant for drinking or industry affects how well that water can be treated and disinfected. Measuring it matters most for supplies drawn from upland peaty catchments in temperate climates. Exact measurement is cumbersome, so its concentration is usually estimated from total or dissolved organic carbon.

soil-chem-061.title: Splitting organic matter three ways with alkali and acid
soil-chem-061.text: In 1786 Franz Karl Achard treated {{ref:soil-class-070}} with potassium hydroxide, a strong alkali. Chemists still split natural organic material much the same way. Soil is extracted with 0.1 M NaOH under nitrogen to prevent oxidation, and the fraction left behind is {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. From natural waters, the acids are caught on a resin column at pH 2, and humic acid is then precipitated at pH 1. Commercial humic acid is made by these procedures. So humic substances are largely defined by the method used to extract them.

soil-chem-063.title: Do humic substances exist, or does the lab make them?
soil-chem-063.text: Since the 18th century, soil chemists have pulled organic material out of soil with alkali. That alkaline extraction led to a theory: a process called {{ref:soil-bio-090}} creates distinct humic acid, fulvic acid and {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. Critics now ask whether these substances exist in soil at all, or are made by the extraction itself. Modern analysis of unprocessed mineral soil has not directly observed large humic molecules. That suggests extraction alters the material it is meant to reveal. Because humic and fulvic acids are defined by the separation, it is unclear whether the categories reflect the natural state of soil organic matter. Some researchers argue that the method misrepresents humic substances because it uses highly alkaline extracts rather than water. Yet that theory persists, even in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced conflicting definitions, which hamper communication across the field. The question stays open: the old fractions may describe real soil, or they may be products of the flask.

soil-chem-074.title: Potassium humate, humic acid in granules
soil-chem-074.text: The best potassium humate starts as well-oxidized lignite. Potassium humate is the potassium salt of humic acid, made by alkaline extraction of leonardite and used mainly to condition soil. Makers extract it in hot water with potassium hydroxide and other agents, then dry it into granules that can be mixed into fertilizer. There it makes nitrogen and phosphorus inputs more efficient. Less oxidized coal yields less potassium humate, and low-ash sources give the best quality.

soil-chem-048.title: Permanent charge, locked into the clay crystal
soil-chem-048.text: Some of a clay's charge is fixed the moment the clay forms. Permanent charge is negative charge built into a clay's crystal where atoms of lower charge replace atoms of higher charge. In layered clays of aluminum and silicon oxides, Mg2+ taking the place of Al3+ leaves a net negative charge. This isomorphous substitution never changes with time, and it releases no hydrogen ions, so the charge ignores pH. Kaolinite has almost no substitution and a low cation-holding power, while montmorillonite owes its power to magnesium replacing aluminum.

soil-chem-047.title: Cation exchange: how soil trades nutrients with its water
soil-chem-047.text: Calcium, potassium and ammonium do not simply wash through a good soil. They cling to it, loosely, and trade places with other ions in the soil water. That trading is cation exchange: negatively charged sites on soil colloids attract positively charged ions and swap them with ions in solution. It is one case of ion exchange, a reversible swap of like-charged ions between an insoluble solid and the surrounding solution. Natural exchangers include zeolites, montmorillonite, clay and soil organic matter. The hold is weak. Held cations keep a shell of water and form no direct chemical bond with the surface, so other cations displace them easily. Some cations win more often than others: at equal amounts Al3+ replaces H+, which replaces Ca2+, then Mg2+, then K+ and NH4+, then Na+. Sheer numbers can also win. A cation added in large amounts, as in potash or lime, crowds out the rest, an effect called the law of mass action. As soil water turns more acidic, hydrogen ions take over exchange sites and push weakly held cations into solution. Plants can then use them, but they can also be leached away. Roots exploit this, making organic acids that release H+ and free cations next to the root. Exchange also buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by holding both useful and harmful cations. Because held cations resist washing downward, they preserve fertility where rainfall is moderate and temperatures are low.

soil-chem-046.title: Cation-exchange capacity, the measure of a soil's nutrient store
soil-chem-046.text: A soil's store of calcium, potassium and ammonium has a ceiling, and electric charge sets it. Cation-exchange capacity, or CEC, measures how many positively charged ions a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles. Negative charges on those surfaces bind the cations but let them swap with others in the surrounding soil water. CEC is the exchangeable positive charge per mass of soil, usually given in centimoles of charge per kilogram, cmolc/kg. Older texts use the equivalent me/100g or meq/100g. Because it counts charge, a CEC of 10 cmolc/kg could hold 10 cmol of singly charged Na+ per kilogram. It could hold only 5 cmol of doubly charged Ca2+. Most of the charge sits on clay minerals and soil organic matter. So CEC is usually highest near the surface, where soil organic matter is richest, and falls with depth. Soils differ enormously. Measured at pH 7, average CEC in US soils runs from 3.5 cmolc/kg in {{ref:soil-class-104}} through 18.7 in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and 35.6 in {{ref:soil-class-106}} to 128 in {{ref:soil-class-098}}. Parent material and the conditions of formation set a soil's CEC. The same factors set its pH, which has a major influence on CEC in turn. Hot, wet climates leach and decompose fast, leaving little clay or soil organic matter, which explains the apparent infertility of tropical soils. CEC therefore serves as a measure of fertility. It shows how well a soil keeps nutrients such as K+, NH4+ and Ca2+ within reach of plants. It also shows how much of a pollutant cation such as Pb2+ the soil can hold.

soil-chem-053.title: Anion-exchange capacity, the smaller store for nitrate and phosphate
soil-chem-053.text: In most soils, cation-exchange capacity far exceeds its mirror image. Anion-exchange capacity, or AEC, is a soil's ability to hold negatively charged ions, such as nitrate and phosphate, on positively charged surfaces and release them later by exchange. Kaolinite, allophane and iron and aluminum oxides often carry positive surface charges. Amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the highest AEC, followed by iron oxides, and colloids with low CEC tend to have some AEC. Iron and aluminum hydroxide clays can swap their own hydroxide anions for other anions. Anions are held with decreasing strength from phosphate (H2PO4−) to sulfate, nitrate and chloride, so phosphates tend to stay on exchange sites. Exchangeable anions amount to tenths to a few milliequivalents per 100 g of dry soil. In highly weathered soils such as ferralsols, or {{ref:soil-class-103}}, AEC can exceed CEC. AEC falls as pH rises, because the extra hydroxyls push anions off colloids into solution.

soil-chem-052.title: Base saturation: how much of the exchange holds nutrients
soil-chem-052.text: Take a soil with a CEC of 20 meq, 5 meq of it held by aluminum and hydronium. Its base saturation is 15 ÷ 20 × 100% = 75%. Base saturation is the percentage of the CEC occupied by the base cations Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+. They are called base cations because they are non-acidic, not because they are bases in the usual chemical sense. Hydronium, the hydrogen ion in water, together with aluminum and iron, makes up the acid-forming cations. Base saturation rises almost in direct proportion to pH. It indexes how weathered a soil is and how available its exchangeable cation nutrients are to plants. It also helps work out how much lime a soil needs. That sum must count the acid cations held on colloids, called exchangeable acidity, not only those in the soil water. Soil classes turn on it. {{ref:soil-class-090}} have at least 35% base saturation, the more leached {{ref:soil-class-104}} less than 35%, and {{ref:soil-class-101}} more than 50%.

soil-chem-055.title: The base-cation saturation ratio and its 'ideal' soil
soil-chem-055.text: From the late 1930s, William Albrecht in Missouri set out an ideal balance for the cations on a soil's exchange sites. The base-cation saturation ratio, or BCSR, interprets soil tests by adjusting cations to such 'ideal' ratios. Albrecht's ideal was H 10%, Ca 60 to 75%, Mg 10 to 20%, K 2 to 5%, Na 0.5 to 5.0% and other cations 5%. F.E. Bear's 1945 bulletin with Prince and Malcolm proposed 65% Ca, 10% Mg, 5% K and 20% H. Most university laboratories instead simply keep each nutrient between deficiency and excess. Supporters say balanced ratios improve crops, livestock and soil life, but controlled studies disagree. Trials saw no yield difference across ratios so long as calcium dominated. Albrecht did not control pH, and much of his evidence is explained by it. A 3-year SARE trial found BCSR fertilizer cost $9.27 per acre more each year with no higher yield.

soil-chem-051.title: Measuring CEC by flooding the soil with one cation
soil-chem-051.text: To count the cations a soil holds, chemists evict them all. A concentrated solution of one cation displaces every bound cation, and the lab measures either the displaced cations or the added cation retained. Barium (Ba2+) and ammonium (NH4+) are frequent choices, though many other methods exist. Because CEC depends on pH, it is often measured in a buffer at a set pH. This potential CEC misstates the real value when the buffer's pH differs from the soil's. Effective CEC, measured at the soil's own pH, is closer to the real value but makes soils harder to compare. Applications of CaCO3 and CaSO4 can lead to an overestimate.

soil-chem-050.title: The diffuse double layer, a cloud of ions around every clay
soil-chem-050.text: Clay platelets are never bare in soil water. Each is wrapped in a diffuse double layer: two parallel layers of charge, the surface charge itself and a loosely held layer of attracted ions that screens it. Exchangeable cations sit in that outer layer, held by electric attraction but kept moving by thermal motion rather than bonded to the surface. Double layers matter most where surface area is large relative to volume, as in colloids. Adding salt thins the layer and destabilizes the colloid. In {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, abundant Na+ crowds into the double layer of clay particles and displaces Ca2+, raising the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}.

soil-chem-054.title: Base-rich and base-poor ground
soil-chem-054.text: Ground over limestone is base-rich, and ground over granite is base-poor. Base-richness is the level of chemical bases, such as calcium, potassium or magnesium ions, in soil or water. Bases neutralize acids, so base-rich places are neutral or alkaline, with pH above 7. Maritime settings are base-rich, while sandstone and ground fed only by rainfall are base-poor. A higher CEC lets a soil hold more base cations. Yet base-richness shows no correlation with available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

soil-chem-057.title: Thomas Way and the discovery of cation exchange
soil-chem-057.text: The finding that soils swap cations came from Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 19th century. There, Thomas Way and the man profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-074}} showed that soils exchange cations. Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society in England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. William Albrecht is sometimes credited with the discovery. He may only have been the first to link cation exchange with colloidal clay particles.

soil-chem-113.title: Redox: the electron trade behind rust and breath
soil-chem-113.text: A rusting nail and a breathing animal run the same kind of chemistry. Redox, short for reduction–oxidation, is any reaction in which the reactants' electron bookkeeping, set out in {{ref:soil-chem-178}}, changes. Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in that bookkeeping number. Reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in it. The two always happen together. Neither can occur on its own. When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide, while oxygen is reduced by taking up the electrons the iron releases. The same trade powers respiration, photosynthesis, combustion and the corrosion of metals. The words are older than the idea of the electron. Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen. Reduction meant the weight lost when ore is heated to extract its metal. Both were later widened to mean electron transfer. The word redox itself first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner. In soils, sediments and water, redox differs from place to place. Those differences drive the cycling of elements through living things and their surroundings, as {{ref:soil-chem-121}} shows.

soil-chem-118.title: Electrons and protons, the two currencies of soil chemistry
soil-chem-118.text: Every chemical reaction in soil trades protons, electrons or some mix of the two. Redox in soils is the set of electron-transfer reactions beneath many soil processes and properties. Soil scientists track it as a voltage, Eh, explained in {{ref:soil-chem-123}}, or as pe, the negative log of electron activity, read much like pH. With pH, it is a master variable that both controls and reflects soil reactions. Early theory grew out of flooded soils and rice growing. It shaped later work on redox thermodynamics and the growth of plant roots, then spread to heavy metals, soil formation, organic compounds, mapping wet ground and cleanup. Microbes organize along electron transport chains, even building electrically conductive films and networks of bacterial nanowires. Redox also marks the soil itself, and its color features are critical clues for interpreting soils. Understanding how redox changes through a soil matters for carbon storage, cleanup by microbes, marking the edges of wet land and soil-based microbial fuel cells.

soil-chem-120.title: Redoximorphic features: colors that record wet and dry
soil-chem-120.text: Soil keeps a diary of its wetness in color. Redoximorphic features are color patterns from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix color. They form by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix color is set by ferrous iron. A pattern counts as redoximorphic only once the processes that formed it are known or inferred. Reducing conditions give disrupted color with complex mottled patterns and points of color concentration, whereas aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes. As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles. Fluctuating water levels give red and yellow blotches mixed with gray. Continuous strong reduction from long-term waterlogging gives gleyed conditions in dark gray to blue to black. Eh, the voltage measured in a soil, expresses the potential for these reactions. Classification uses the features: Vertisols with aquic conditions and redoximorphic features are Aquerts, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them. They provide critical information for soil interpretation. See also {{ref:soil-chem-118}}, {{ref:soil-found-025}} and {{ref:soil-found-028}}.

soil-chem-119.title: Breathing and photosynthesis as electron transfers
soil-chem-119.text: Every breath is a redox reaction. Aerobic respiration oxidizes fuels such as glucose and reduces oxygen to water. Photosynthesis does roughly the opposite: it reduces carbon dioxide to sugars and oxidizes water to oxygen. It complements respiration, yet it is not simply its reverse. Living things often store and release energy through such reactions, relying on the steady cycling of the carriers NAD+ and NADH.

soil-chem-114.title: Oxidizing agents, the electron takers
soil-chem-114.text: Of all the electron takers covered in {{ref:soil-chem-176}}, oxygen pulls hardest. An oxidizing agent oxidizes another substance by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced in the process. It is also called an oxidant, or an electron taker. Oxidants usually hold elements in a highly oxidized form ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}), as permanganate does, or are highly electronegative elements such as oxygen and chlorine. In oxidizing soils, oxygen accepts electrons and is reduced to water.

soil-chem-115.title: Reducing agents, the electron givers
soil-chem-115.text: In soil, the main giver of electrons is soil organic matter. A reducing agent reduces another substance by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized. It is also called a reductant, the role taken up in {{ref:soil-chem-177}}. Electropositive metals such as lithium, sodium, magnesium, iron, zinc and aluminium give up electrons readily, which makes them good reducing agents. Underground, donors include that same material, hydrogen, methane, reduced sulfur and iron compounds, and ammonium. Biochemists speak of a reducing equivalent: whatever transfers the equivalent of one electron, whether an electron or a hydrogen atom.

soil-chem-116.title: Redox couples: splitting a reaction into halves
soil-chem-116.text: The naming trips up many students. In any redox reaction the reductant passes electrons to the oxidant, so the reductant is oxidized and the oxidant reduced. That is why the reagent that gets oxidized is called the reducing agent. The two agents in a given reaction form a redox pair. A redox couple is a reducing species and its oxidized form, such as Fe2+ and Fe3+. The oxidation and the reduction, taken alone, are each a half-reaction. In electrochemical reactions the two halves happen at the same time but in different places.

soil-chem-117.title: Standard electrode potential: ranking the electron takers
soil-chem-117.text: Fluorine scores +2.866 V, zinc ions −0.763 V, and hydrogen ions exactly zero. These are standard electrode potentials: the equilibrium voltage of a half-reaction under standard conditions, measured against the reference of {{ref:soil-chem-179}}. Also called a reduction potential, the value measures how strongly an oxidizing agent tends to be reduced. Hydrogen sits at zero by definition. Stronger oxidants score positive, weaker ones negative. The value is given in volts or millivolts. A cell's potential is the cathode potential minus the anode potential.

soil-chem-130.title: Biofilters: letting microbes eat the pollution
soil-chem-130.text: Engineers have hired microbes to clean water since 1893, when England introduced the trickling filter for wastewater. A biofilter is a bioreactor holding living material that captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically. Microorganisms attach to a bed of sand, crushed rock or gravel and grow into a thin living film that degrades the pollutants. Biofilters treat wastewater, catch harmful chemicals or silt washed off the land, and oxidize air pollutants. {{ref:soil-water-092}}, wetlands and {{ref:soil-water-263}} work the same way. One drawback: buildup of biomass can clog the bed.

soil-chem-123.title: Eh, the voltage that tells oxidizing soil from reducing soil
soil-chem-123.text: A cultivated field typically reads between +300 and +500 mV. Redox potential, written Eh, is the tendency of electrons to pass from a giver of electrons ({{ref:soil-chem-177}}) to a taker ({{ref:soil-chem-176}}), measured in volts. It is zero for the couple of {{ref:soil-chem-179}}, the reference from {{ref:soil-chem-117}}. Positive values mean an oxidizing setting that accepts electrons; negative values, a reducing one that donates them. It can be calculated from half-reactions with the Nernst equation. Three things set it: how oxidized the species present are ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}), pH and the amount of oxygen. Higher potentials occur at lower pH. Soil Eh generally spans −300 to +900 mV. Plants are generally held to tolerate +300 to +700 mV, and in the soils of wet land 300 mV divides aerobic from anaerobic conditions. Aerated waters usually read positive, while submerged soils, swamps and marine sediments normally read negative. Microbes sort by it. Strict aerobes are generally active at positive Eh and strict anaerobes at negative Eh. Facultative anaerobes also work at negative Eh when nitrate or sulfate is present.

soil-chem-131.title: Destroying pollution underground with strong oxidizers
soil-chem-131.text: In situ chemical oxidation injects strong oxidizers into contaminated soil or groundwater to destroy contaminants where they lie. Hydrogen peroxide was first used this way in 1985, on a formaldehyde spill in Springfield, Massachusetts. It treats many organic compounds, even some that resist natural breakdown, and suits chlorinated solvents and gasoline compounds such as benzene and toluene. Oxidants go in through rods or injection wells, or by soil mixing and hydraulic fracturing in tight ground. Success depends on the site's rocks, the dose, and real contact with the contaminant. Rising carbon dioxide signals that oxidation is working. Every main oxidant is hazardous to handle.

soil-chem-121.title: Redox gradients: oxidizing above, reducing below
soil-chem-121.text: The Earth as a whole is oxidizing at its surface and increasingly reducing below it. A redox gradient is a series of redox reactions sorted by redox potential. Such gradients form in space and in time, from differences in microbial processes, chemical makeup and oxidative potential. Oxygen supply, soil hydrology, the chemical species present and microbial activity drive them. They are typical of waterlogged soils, wetlands, lakes, coastal marshes, contaminant plumes and marine sediments. At large scale they are well understood. Redox at the micro-scale, in patchy, mixed settings, still needs more research and better ways to measure it.

soil-chem-122.title: The redox ladder: which electron acceptor goes first
soil-chem-122.text: Microbes spend their electron acceptors in a set order, best first. The redox ladder is that order, fixed by the free energy each redox pair yields. The most favorable reaction sits at the top, the least favorable at the bottom. From oxidizing to reducing, the usual sequence runs aerobic respiration, then nitrate reduction to nitrogen gas, then manganese, iron and sulfate reduction. For respiration without oxygen, the nitrate–nitrogen couple ranks just below oxygen, above manganese, iron, sulfate and, last of all, carbon dioxide to methane. In sediments, oxygen dwindles with depth, so these pathways stack in vertical layers. Yet thermodynamics alone does not decide where microbes live. Ecology and physiology matter too.

soil-chem-128.title: Breathing without oxygen: anaerobic respiration
soil-chem-128.text: A few millimetres of standing water are enough to smother a soil. Under that thin layer, bacteria that feed on soil organic matter use up the oxygen, forcing a switch to anaerobic respiration. This is respiration that ends its electron transport chain with an inorganic acceptor other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate or sulfur. These acceptors have lower reduction potentials than oxygen, so less energy is released and the process is less efficient. It differs from fermentation, which passes electrons to organic compounds. Even well-aired soil holds oxygen-free pockets, because oxygen gas diffuses slowly. The products leave their mark. Nitrate respiration is the main route returning fixed nitrogen to the air as N2. Sulfate respiration makes hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg smell of coastal marshes. Aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide, while anaerobic pathways such as {{ref:soil-chem-129}} release methane. Others change the oxidation state of iron and manganese. Bacterial sulfate reduction was discovered by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-016}}. Because decay in waterlogged soils runs without oxygen, those soils store large amounts of organic carbon.

soil-chem-125.title: How a flooded soil runs out of oxygen
soil-chem-125.text: Flood a soil warmer than about 5 °C, and its microbes strip out the oxygen within a few days. Reduction in waterlogged soils is that shift from oxidizing to reducing conditions as oxygen runs out and anaerobic microbes take over. The fuel is soil organic matter, the main source of electrons in soil. Decomposers consume oxygen as they break it down, and Eh falls. Next, nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced. Iron tells the story. At high redox potential it is deposited as ferric hematite, the oxidized form. Under low redox conditions ferrous iron builds up, and decay slows. Prolonged saturation can dissolve ferric iron minerals that hold phosphorus, releasing it to leaching. Hydrology rules the process. Flooding turns soil from oxic to anoxic, and draining and drying restore its starting Eh. Even soil that is not saturated can hold small anoxic hotspots inside its pores.
