soil-chem-129.title: Methanogenesis: the last step of decay without air
soil-chem-129.text: Methane has 25 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide, averaged over 100 years, and wet soils make a lot of it. Methanogenesis is the making of methane by the microbes in {{ref:soil-chem-174}}, all of them archaea, as the final step in breaking down dead plant and animal material without oxygen. It sits at the bottom of {{ref:soil-chem-122}}. Once every electron acceptor except carbon dioxide is spent, only methanogenesis and fermentation can proceed. Without it, much carbon would pile up as fermentation products. In most freshwater wetlands sulfate is scarce, and methanogenesis takes over only once sulfate is used up. In sediments, sulfate reducers take most of the hydrogen in upper layers, while the methane makers dominate lower down. In the oxygen-free layers of {{ref:soil-class-070}}, they combine carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas into methane and water. Production runs high in flooded rice fields, wetlands, and anoxic floodplain, lake and reservoir sediments. Other microbes, {{ref:soil-env-280}}, oxidize methane back to carbon dioxide. Aerating such soils raises sulfate and nitrate, which cut methane output. In upland soils, methanogenesis is often confined to anoxic microsites inside otherwise aerobic soil.

soil-chem-133.title: Paddy fields: rice, flooding and methane
soil-chem-133.text: Rice paddies release an estimated 50 to 100 million tonnes of methane a year, about 10% of global methane emissions. A paddy field is a flooded crop field used to grow semiaquatic crops, above all rice and taro. Paddy farming began in the Neolithic rice cultures of the Yangtze River basin and remains the dominant way to grow rice. Draining paddies so the soil aerates interrupts methane production and can boost yield. Ammonium-based fertilizers raise emissions. Early soil redox theory grew out of flooded paddy soils, and long wet-field cultivation can turn them into the human-made soils described in {{ref:soil-class-120}}.

soil-chem-132.title: Permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone
soil-chem-132.text: Four strong oxidizers are the usual choices in {{ref:soil-chem-131}}: permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone. Fenton's reagent, hydrogen peroxide catalysed by iron, and permanganate have the longest record. Permanganate needs double bonds in its targets and is used up by other carbon-based material in soil. Persulfate, introduced in the late 1990s, avoids both problems. Fenton's reagent makes hydroxyl radicals but needs lowered pH to keep iron dissolved. Whether field use at near-neutral pH is truly a Fenton reaction remains disputed. Ozone, about 12 times more soluble than oxygen, is injected from below so its bubbles rise through the contamination.

soil-chem-124.title: Measuring Eh with a platinum electrode
soil-chem-124.text: Soil Eh is read with a platinum electrode, referenced to the standard hydrogen electrode. Measuring redox potential means either sampling in the field for lab analysis or placing an electrode in soil or water for readings on the spot. Each choice has a cost. Many samples give fine detail across space but little over time. Fixed electrodes give continuous readings but cover little ground. Waters, soils and sediments can be highly patchy, which complicates both. Induced-polarization imaging can track redox finely in space and time, though its signal is not yet fully understood.

soil-chem-126.title: Microbes that sharpen the gradients they live on
soil-chem-126.text: Microbes do more than live along redox gradients: they sharpen them. By switching how they respire, to sulfate reduction or methanogenesis for instance, they suit local conditions and amplify the gradient. Organic pollutants break down fastest where oxygenated and oxygen-free zones meet, such as the groundwater capillary fringe, because electron donors and acceptors abound there. Cable bacteria, which oxidize sulfide, link zones short of electrons with zones holding a surplus. Thin films of metal- or sulfate-reducing bacteria create gradients on the micrometre scale.

soil-chem-127.title: Redox layers in lakes, seas and their sediments
soil-chem-127.text: Water columns and the mud beneath them carry redox gradients of their own. Oxic, suboxic and hypoxic water layers, from well oxygenated to poorly oxygenated, each allow different redox reactions. Oxygen minimum zones add to the layering. In bottom sediments, gradients arise from differences in minerals, dead organic material, structure and sorption. Slow electron transport and varied pore sizes make these sediments highly patchy.

soil-chem-008.title: Salt in the soil, and how it gathers
soil-chem-008.text: Egypt's Aswan High Dam was built in 1970. Afterward, a persistently high water table salinized farmland. Soil salinity is the salt content of a soil, and salinization is the process that raises it. A handful of ions do the work: sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+) and chloride (Cl−). Salts arrive through {{ref:soil-found-052}}, in dust and in precipitation. With enough rain they are leached away. Under intense evaporation they rise instead by capillarity and gather near the surface. That is why salts accumulate naturally in dry regions, as across large parts of Australia. People add to the load with irrigation, road salt and disrupted drainage. Growing dryness from human-induced global warming also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils. Salinity seriously degrades land. It harms plant growth and yield, damages roads, bricks, pipes and cables, and degrades water quality. The usual cure is to leach salts out with extra good-quality irrigation water, combined with water-table control and drainage from below. Calcium helps as well, easing effects such as plants' reduced water uptake.

soil-chem-001.title: How soils turn sour over time
soil-chem-001.text: Acid soils begin with lichens and algae. As they break down bare rock surfaces, acidification starts, and with time and weathering soils in natural ecosystems grow more acidic. Soil acidification is the build-up of hydrogen cations in a soil, which lowers its pH. It follows two routes. One adds a proton donor: an acid such as nitric, sulfuric or carbonic acid, or a compound such as aluminium sulfate that releases protons in the soil. The other removes base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium by leaching. Soils on parent materials low in basic cations start out acid and stay that way. {{ref:soil-chem-002}}, agriculture and pollution speed the process up. The costs are real: fewer available nutrients, more toxic elements and weaker biological functions such as {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Acidification is not always harmful, since it helps alkaline soils. It degrades land when it cuts crop productivity and biological activity and leaves soil more open to contamination and erosion. It is most common in Southeast Asia, the Amazon Rainforest, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Eastern United States, each with its own causes. Spreading lime on the surface, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-055}}, can prevent it, as can less fertilizer and irrigation.

soil-chem-010.title: How watering a field can salt it
soil-chem-010.text: Even good water brings salt. Water holding just 0.3 g/L, applied at a modest 10,000 m3/ha a year, delivers 3,000 kg of salt to every hectare each year. Most irrigation water is saltier and applied more heavily, so irrigated areas often receive more than 3,000 kg/ha a year, some as much as 10,000 kg/ha. This is irrigation salinity, the irrigated form of {{ref:soil-chem-008}}. Nearly all water carries dissolved salts, and when plants use the water, the salts stay behind in the root zone. Salinization occurs where evaporation concentrates them faster than drainage flushes them away. Poor drainage and saline irrigation water greatly increase it. In cities it often stems from watering gardens and recreation areas with salt-laden reclaimed water, combined with groundwater processes. Waterlogging is the secondary cause. Irrigation is at most about 70% efficient, so 30% or more of the water goes underground. The water table rises and blocks leaching. Good management prevents the problem by supplying enough drainage water to leach the added salts. Water applied beyond the plants' needs to carry salts away is called the leaching fraction.

soil-chem-011.title: Flushing salt out to keep irrigated fields alive
soil-chem-011.text: About 62 million hectares, 20% of the world's irrigated land, is salt-affected, up from 45 million in the early 1990s. Irrigation is the main human cause, since river water and groundwater carry salts that stay in the soil after the water evaporates. Soil salinity control means preventing that build-up and reclaiming soils already saline. The main method lets 10–20% of the irrigation water leach the soil and leave through a drainage system. Where salinity is stable, drainage water is normally 5 to 10 times saltier than the irrigation water, so salt export matches salt import. During reclamation it may at first be 50 times saltier. After one or two years a new, favorable equilibrium is reached. The stakes are high. In the Indo-Gangetic Plain, yield losses on salt-affected land could be 40% for wheat, 45% for rice, 48% for sugarcane and 63% for cotton. Salinization normally affects 20% to 30% of the land in irrigation projects, and depressions in undulating land degrade most. Salty drainage water can harm areas downstream, so drainage is best limited to wet seasons where possible.

soil-chem-009.title: Sodic soils, where sodium rules the clay
soil-chem-009.text: A soil can be acidic, neutral or alkaline and still be crippled by one element. A sodic soil is one in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations, the ions traded through {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. Sodic soils tend to have very poor structure, which limits or prevents water infiltration and drainage. Where clays are saturated with sodium, the soil breaks down easily into fine particles that wash away. Near the surface these soils tend to form columnar peds. They can also accumulate boron and molybdenum in the root zone at levels toxic to plants. Gypsum is the most common compound for reclaiming them. Salt-tolerant plants, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-045}}, and salt-loving bacteria of the root zone may help. The term is used loosely, often interchangeably with {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, defined as pH above 8.2, exchangeable sodium above 15% of the cation-exchange capacity, or both.

soil-chem-002.title: Acid rain and the soils it soaks through
soil-chem-002.text: Even clean rain is sour. Atmospheric carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, leaving natural rain at around pH 5.0–5.5. Acid rain and snow are more acidic still, and they acidify soil rapidly, mainly through sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollutants. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides come from lightning, volcanoes or human emissions, and react with water in the air to form those stronger acids. Fossil fuels are the largest human source of sulfuric gases, and motor exhaust the largest of nitrogen oxides. As acid rain flows through soil, it leaches calcium and other base cations, and aluminium and proton levels rise. This is {{ref:soil-chem-001}} on a fast clock. Snow brings its own hazard. It holds more nitric than sulfuric acid, so a spring meltwater pulse, up to 50% of annual precipitation, can sharply but briefly lower the pH of drainage water. That drop can release Al3+, which is toxic to fish, especially newly hatched fry. Soils buffer part of the acid. Adsorbing sulfate releases OH−, and organic-rich surface layers in forests cut the H+ load reaching the mineral horizons below. Prevention works. Cutting sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions reduces acid rain and soil acidification, as improving water pH in Ontario lakes showed.

soil-chem-005.title: How fertilizers make soil more acidic
soil-chem-005.text: Feeding a crop can sour the soil beneath it. Fertilizer-induced acidification is the lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers. It is one cause behind {{ref:soil-chem-001}}. Most nitrogen fertilizers acidify, ammonium-based ones most of all: ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate, and ammonium nitrate. Urea and compost acidify less. Nitrification of ammonium releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, which keep acidifying the soil. Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify and can slightly raise pH. Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH. Most commercial nitrogen fertilizers are acid forming, but many manures are not. Generally 4-7 pounds of lime neutralize the acid from each pound of nitrogen applied. Monoculture with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation. Sugarcane monoculture raised acidity, lowered fertility and shifted soil microbes.

soil-chem-039.title: Duricrust, the hard shell some dry soils wear
soil-chem-039.text: Some soils grow a stone lid. A duricrust is a hard layer on or near the soil surface where soluble minerals have precipitated and hardened. It can be a few millimeters thick or several meters. The general term is not to be confused with duripan. Duricrusts form as mineral-bearing waters move up, down or sideways by capillary action and deposit soluble minerals, often helped by evaporation in arid settings. In the per ascensum model, evaporation draws solutions up from a shallow water table to form thin crusts. In the per descensum model, downward-percolating solutions build thick ones. Each type is named for its dominant mineral. Ferricrete is rich in iron sesquioxides, alcrete in aluminium sesquioxides, silcrete in silica, calcrete in calcium carbonate and gypcrete in gypsum. The same layers go by other names, among them laterite, bauxite, {{ref:soil-chem-036}} and {{ref:soil-chem-038}}. Duricrust found at the Viking 2 and Phoenix landing sites on Mars, the latter confirmed water-based, may help show the planet once had more water.

soil-chem-024.title: Dryland salinity: clear the trees, raise the salt
soil-chem-024.text: Salt can ruin land that has never seen an irrigation ditch. Dryland salinity is salinity in unirrigated landscapes: a rise in the salt of soil, water or the wider environment beyond normal levels. It is natural, but human activity greatly worsens it. It results from groundwater recharge, movement and discharge. Native vegetation forms a 'soil sponge' of roots and soil up to 6 metres deep that keeps the water table low. Shallow-rooted crops such as wheat thin that sponge to 1 metre or less. Once deep-rooted plants are cleared, excess water seeps past the root zone and the water table rises. Capillary action then brings salt to the surface. This happens when the water table is two to three metres down in clayey soils, but less than a metre in sandy ones. Clearing as little as 25% of a catchment can cause salinity. In many Australian landscapes, aquifer capacity is orders of magnitude below the altered recharge. Salts accumulate wherever evaporation outpaces rainfall's replenishment of groundwater, as in arid environments. Saline groundwater discharge cuts farm production, degrades natural environments and surface water, damages roads and leads to soil erosion. Restoring the balance needs deep-rooted vegetation such as mallee eucalyptus or perennial grasses, or farming adapted to shallow saline groundwater.

soil-chem-028.title: Australia's ancient salt, set loose by clearing
soil-chem-028.text: Australian soils have been gathering salt for thousands of years, from ocean winds, evaporated inland seas and weathered parent rocks. Before British settlement in 1788, groundwater levels were in equilibrium, because deep-rooted native vegetation used groundwater year-round. Land clearing replaced that vegetation with crops and pasture. Groundwater rose and brought the stored salt up, and evaporation left it in the soil. By 1999 about 2.5 million hectares had become salinized since European farming began. Some 5.7 million hectares now have high potential, a figure expected to reach 17 million by 2050. Most states are affected, above all south-west Western Australia, with around 70% of the country's salt-affected land. The causes differ by place: irrigation in the Murray River valley, land clearing near Werrimull in Victoria. Salt cuts plants' water uptake by osmosis, burns leaves through sodium and chloride and upsets nutrient balance. It also damages roads, buildings, pipes and cables. Predictions for climate change are mixed. Lower rainfall may reduce salinity, but heavier downpours may add excess water to aquifers.

soil-chem-017.title: Sodium adsorption ratio: a number for clay's stability
soil-chem-017.text: Sodium and calcium pull clay in opposite directions. Sodium and potassium disperse clay particles, while calcium and magnesium flocculate them into clumps. The sodium adsorption ratio, or SAR, weighs one side against the other. It is an irrigation water quality index calculated from sodium, calcium and magnesium concentrations: SAR = [Na+]/√([Ca2+]/2 + [Mg2+]/2), in milliequivalents per liter. Measured on pore water extracted from the soil, it is also the standard diagnostic of a soil's sodicity hazard. Below an SAR of 3 there is no problem. Above 9, fine-textured soils have severe problems, while sandy soils suffer less. For irrigation, SAR should not be much above 20, and preferably below 10. The damage builds slowly. Years of high-SAR water let sodium displace soil calcium and magnesium, ruining aggregate stability, structure and tilth and reducing infiltration and permeability. After long exposure, a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-018}} comes to roughly equal the water's SAR. SAR addresses sodium only. The potassium adsorption ratio (PAR) and the cation ratio of structural stability (CROSS) extend it to other cations.

soil-chem-030.title: Acid sulfate soils, harmless until they meet air
soil-chem-030.text: Left undisturbed below the water table, acid sulfate soils are benign. Drain them, dig them up or expose them to air, and their sulfides react with oxygen to form sulfuric acid. These are soils, sediments or organic substrates such as {{ref:soil-class-070}}, formed under waterlogged conditions, that contain iron sulfide minerals, mainly {{ref:soil-chem-134}}, or their oxidation products. Drained, they can turn extremely acidic, below pH 4. The acid releases iron, aluminium and other metals and metalloids, particularly arsenic. Together these kill vegetation and fish, acidify groundwater and surface water, and degrade concrete and steel structures to the point of failure. The most prone formed within the last 10,000 years. Then the last major sea level rise mixed seawater sulfate with land sediments rich in iron oxides and organic matter. They are widespread around coasts. In Australia, coastal acid sulfate soils cover an estimated 58,000 km2 beneath estuaries and floodplains. Canal, housing and marina works often disturb them, and droughts can expose them too. Some drained 100 years ago still release acid. Potential acid sulfate soils, or cat-clays, are often left uncultivated or planted with rice to keep them wet. The term was coined for the first International Symposium on Acid Sulfate Soils, held in 1972 at Wageningen.

soil-chem-012.title: Measuring salt by the current soil water carries
soil-chem-012.text: Seawater may hold 30 g/L of salt, or 3%, and has an electric conductivity of 50 dS/m. Soil salinity is measured on the same two scales: the salt concentration of the soil solution in g/L, or its electric conductivity (EC) in dS/m. The units relate by about 5/3, so y g/L corresponds to 5y/3 dS/m. The standard is the EC of an extract of a saturated soil paste, obtained by centrifugation and written ECe. A 2:1 or 5:1 water:soil mixture is easier to measure, and ECe is about 4 times the EC of a 2:1 mixture. Soils are saline when ECe exceeds 4. They are slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, and severely saline above 16. Sensitive crops already lose vigor in slightly saline soils. Most crops suffer in moderately saline ones, and only salt-resistant crops thrive in severely saline soils.

soil-chem-004.title: Rocks that leave acid soils behind
soil-chem-004.text: Some soils are acid from the start because of the rock beneath them. Acidic parent materials are rocks and sediments whose weathering acidifies the soils formed on them. Granites and allied igneous rocks are called 'acidic' because their abundant free quartz yields silicic acid on weathering. They are also low in calcium and magnesium. Sulfide-rich shale and coal, when hydrated and oxidized, produce sulfuric acid, much stronger than silicic acid. Many coal soils are too acidic for vigorous plant growth. Marine clays are often sulfide-rich and become very acidic if drained to an oxidizing state.

soil-chem-003.title: How roots and fallen needles acidify soil
soil-chem-003.text: Plant roots release protons and organic acids to chemically weather soil minerals. That is one face of biological acidification, the acidifying of soil by living things. Decaying plant remains add to it. Litter acidifies the O horizon more under conifers such as pine, spruce and fir, which return fewer base cations than deciduous trees. Cause and effect are tangled, though, since such pH differences often existed before the vegetation. Calcium held in living biomass also strongly affects soil pH, by an amount that varies between species.

soil-chem-006.title: What acid soil does to roots and life
soil-chem-006.text: In acid soil, roots come up short. Plants develop smaller, less durable roots with damaged tips, along with reduced height, poorer germination and stunted growth overall. Much of the harm traces to {{ref:soil-found-019}}. Leaching of base cations raises the availability of toxic ions such as aluminium, which inhibits root growth. Acidification also reduces the diversity of microbes and of larger creatures living in soil, and it is directly linked to declines in endangered plant species. Leaves yellowing between the veins can signal it, though alkaline or nutrient-poor soils cause the same symptom. At large scale, it cuts agricultural productivity.

soil-chem-007.title: Lime and careful habits against acid soil
soil-chem-007.text: {{ref:soil-fert-055}} of acidic soils under sugarcane, soybean and corn restored nutrients, raised pH, increased root biomass and improved plant health. Lime is the chief way to prevent or reverse soil acidification, alongside organic amendments, {{ref:soil-fert-050}} and careful fertilizer and irrigation management. Working lime in deeper works better than spreading it on the surface, but it is costlier and harder. Prevention starts with less acidifying fertilizers, timed so less nitrate washes out of the soil. Irrigating with acid-neutralizing water helps, as does weighing basic nutrients against the nitrogen removed in crops. Sulfur fertilizers belong only on responsive crops with a high rate of crop recovery.

soil-chem-041.title: The hidden costs of watering dry land
soil-chem-041.text: Irrigated land covers about 16% of the world's agricultural area but grows roughly 40% of its total harvest. That harvest has a price. The environmental impact of irrigation covers the changes it makes to the quantity and quality of soil and water. It also covers their effects on nature and society in river basins and downstream. Direct effects include reduced river flow downstream, more evaporation in the irrigated area and a rising water table from increased groundwater recharge. Slower but longer-lasting effects follow: waterlogging, salination, ecological damage and socioeconomic impacts. Deep percolation losses are commonly 40% to 60%, raising water tables. Where tables are shallow, less water is applied, the soil is no longer leached and salinity develops. Over-irrigation causes {{ref:soil-chem-010}} through rising water tables, while under-irrigation fails to flush salts out. About one-third of irrigated land in the major irrigation countries is or soon will be badly salt-affected. Estimates run 13% in Israel, 15% in China, 20% in Australia, 30% in Egypt and 50% in Iraq. Pumping wells beyond recharge mines groundwater and can make the land sink and, on coasts, draw in the sea ({{ref:soil-chem-141}}). Stagnant water tables at the surface also raise the incidence of water-borne diseases such as malaria and schistosomiasis.

soil-chem-035.title: Calcareous soils, built on chalk and limestone
soil-chem-035.text: Soils formed on limestone or chalk lean alkaline, and the reason is simple chemistry. A calcareous soil is one formed from or containing a high proportion of calcium carbonate, as calcite or aragonite. The carbonate ion is a base, so soils whose parent material contains it are relatively alkaline. They may have a calcic horizon, a layer of secondary carbonates. It holds above 15% {{ref:soil-fert-060}} and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below. {{ref:soil-class-086}} grows on soils rich in calcium carbonate from underlying chalk or limestone. {{ref:soil-class-121}} are common on calcareous parent materials in arid and semi-arid environments, and loess is often calcareous. In such low-acidity soils, earthworms mix decomposed organic matter into the mineral soil below, forming {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-chem-036.title: Caliche, the rock that grows inside dry soils
soil-chem-036.text: Where rain is scarce, soil can make its own rock. Caliche is an accumulation of calcium carbonate at depth, where it precipitates and binds other materials such as gravel, sand, clay and silt. Also called calcrete or kankar, it forms layers from a few inches to feet thick, sometimes called a K horizon. Root carbon dioxide in the A horizon, up to 15 times atmospheric levels, dissolves calcium carbonate as bicarbonate. In the less active B horizon below, it reverts to carbonate. Caliche forms where annual precipitation is under 65 centimeters and mean annual temperature exceeds 5 °C. Wetter climates leach the calcium away. Its depth follows rainfall: about 25 centimeters down at 35 centimeters of rain a year, about 125 centimeters at 75, and gone above 100. It occurs worldwide in dry-region soils, from central and western Australia to the Kalahari and the High Plains of the western United States. Deposition takes several thousand years, and the calcium can arrive as windblown dust even over calcium-poor bedrock. Impermeable caliche blocks drainage and roots, and the basic soil it creates can cause iron deficiency that yellows the youngest leaves. Caliches store significant carbon, and calcretes in the geologic record preserve past climates.

soil-chem-038.title: Gypcrust, the gypsum armor of the driest lands
soil-chem-038.text: Where it is too dry even for calcrete, gypsum takes over. A gypcrust is a hardened soil layer made of around 95% gypsum, calcium sulfate. It is the arid-climate counterpart of calcrete, which cannot form in very arid climates. Gypcrust horizons can be up to 5 m thick with 75–97% gypsum. They form mostly where annual rainfall averages under 250 mm, since gypsum is moderately soluble and leaches under higher rainfall. Formation runs in three stages: crystallization from surface brines or groundwater, transport and redeposition by wind or water, and alteration above or below the capillary fringe. Gypsum cements are rarely as strong as calcretes or silcretes, though gypcrete has been used for road construction in the Sahara.

soil-chem-014.title: Drains that pull salt and water away
soil-chem-014.text: In many cases, a water table 0.6 to 0.8 m down, as a seasonal average, is deep enough. Drainage for salinity control carries salty water away and lowers the water table, usually with horizontal systems but also with vertical ones. A fluctuating water table helps the soil breathe, expelling root carbon dioxide and drawing in oxygen. A water table that is not too deep also discourages over-irrigation, since crop yields would fall as it rose. Where wet and dry seasons are marked, running drains only in the wet season saves irrigation water. This is called controlled drainage.

soil-chem-013.title: Leaching requirement: the water it takes to hold salt down
soil-chem-013.text: The leaching requirement is the amount that must percolate through the root zone to hold soil salinity at a desired level, worked out from the salt balance. That desired level depends on the crop's tolerance to salt. The calculation rests on the water balance of the zone above the water table. It sets infiltration of rain and irrigation against evaporation, percolation to groundwater and capillary rise. Leaching efficiency is often 0.7 to 0.8 but can be lower in poorly structured heavy clays. In Portugal's Leziria Grande it was only 0.15. From the requirement, the irrigation and drainage needed for salinity control can be computed.

soil-chem-016.title: Computer models that forecast salt in fields
soil-chem-016.text: Soil salinity models are computer models of water and salt movement in soil, used to predict salinity under irrigation and drainage. Most, such as SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, pair two equations. Richards' equation handles unsaturated water flow, and Fick's convection–diffusion equation handles the salts. These models need hard-to-measure soil properties, short time steps and daily or hourly data. They are also hard to calibrate, because field salinity varies greatly. Simpler models such as SaltMod use monthly or seasonal water and salt balances for long-term predictions, and {{ref:soil-chem-040}} adds spatial variation with groundwater.

soil-chem-015.title: Sacrificing strips of land to save the rest
soil-chem-015.text: One way to beat salt is to surrender some land to it. In strip cropping for salinity control, alternate strips are irrigated and those between are never planted. The irrigated strips have a higher water table, which pushes groundwater toward the unirrigated ones. That flow acts as subsurface drainage and lets the cropped strips leach. In the dry, sacrificial strips, groundwater rises by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts behind, so these strips salinize. They need not be wasted. They can carry livestock, salt-resistant grasses or deep-rooted salt-tolerant trees such as Casuarina, Eucalyptus or Atriplex, or be used for salt harvesting.

soil-chem-037.title: Chile's nitrate-rich caliche of the Atacama
soil-chem-037.text: Chile's Atacama Desert holds vast deposits also called caliche, though they are not the carbonate layers of {{ref:soil-chem-036}}. They mix gypsum, sodium chloride, other salts and sand with nitrate minerals called salitre, which is sodium and potassium nitrate. The deposits average 7.5% sodium nitrate, with sodium sulfate, sodium chloride, borate, iodine and perchlorate. Salitre earned Chile important export revenue until the early 1930s, when Europe began making nitrates industrially in large quantities. Caliche is also Chile's main iodine ore, and the country hosts over half the world's iodine reserves. Its origin is unclear. An evaporated prehistoric inland sea and weathering of the Andes have both been proposed.

soil-chem-040.title: SahysMod, a salt forecaster for field engineers
soil-chem-040.text: SahysMod was designed for field technicians, engineers and planners rather than specialized geohydrologists. Developed by the land-improvement institute ILRI, the program predicts the salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water in irrigated land. It also predicts water table depth and drain discharge. It maps spatial variation with a network of polygons, up to 240 internal and 120 external. Groundwater levels and flows between polygons come from numerically solving the Boussinesq equation. The program runs on seasonal inputs and outputs, with one to four seasons a year. Salt balances are computed for each soil reservoir separately, and farmers' responses to waterlogging and salinity can be built in.

soil-chem-045.title: Halophytes, the plants that thrive on salt
soil-chem-045.text: Beans and rice tolerate irrigation water with about 1–3 g/L of dissolved solids, and barley and date palm about 5 g/L. Salicornia bigelovii grows well at 70 g/L. It is a halophyte, a salt-tolerant plant that grows in soils or waters of high salinity, such as salt marshes, mangroves and saline semi-deserts. Perhaps only 2% of plant species are halophytes. Most are glycophytes, which high salinity damages fairly easily. In 1936 Iversen grouped halophytes by soil NaCl: oligo-halophytes at 0.01 to 0.1%, meso-halophytes at 0.1 to 1%, and euhalophytes above 1%. Some, such as Suaeda salsa, store salt ions taken from soil. They can lower soil salinity enough for glycophytes to grow again.

soil-chem-042.title: Framboids, the microscopic raspberries of pyrite
soil-chem-042.text: Under a microscope, some pyrite looks like a raspberry. A framboid is a roughly spherical cluster of tiny crystals, common in some sedimentary minerals, especially pyrite. Clusters average 5–20 μm across and are built of regular microcrystals around 0.5 μm in diameter. Rust first used the name in 1935, from the French framboise, raspberry. In {{ref:soil-chem-030}}, bacteria such as Desulfovibrio desulfuricans reduce sulfate to hydrogen sulfide. It reacts with ferrous iron to form fine, highly reactive framboidal pyrite. This pyrite is common in coastal sediments of marshes, estuaries and beaches, and greigite is considered an essential precursor. Framboids were once thought to be fossil bacterial colonies. They have since been made in the laboratory and found in places hostile to microbial life.

soil-chem-026.title: Keeping water out of salty groundwater
soil-chem-026.text: The drier a soil enters winter, the more water it can store instead of leaking it to groundwater. Soils take up water according to their field capacity and starting dryness. Managing dryland salinity builds on that. It means cutting groundwater recharge through soils and vegetation, and coping with salt where groundwater discharges. Returning recharge to pre-clearing levels is usually infeasible, because too few profitable perennials can replace crops. The aim is to minimize it instead, with alley farming, perennials and leaf cover through winter and spring. In discharge areas, salinity is managed with salt-tolerant plants or with engineering such as deep open drains, pumps and siphons. There is a trade-off, since recharge is also the source of fresh groundwater.

soil-chem-025.title: Natural salt and the salt people make
soil-chem-025.text: Not all salty land is a human failure. Salinity divides into primary salinity, which is natural, and secondary salinity, which human activity induces. Primary salinity occurs naturally in arid and saline settings such as salt lakes, marshes, pans and salt flats. Past cycles of drainage, desiccation and sea winds left it there. Secondary salinity results directly from development, agriculture and irrigation, and it harms biodiversity and land productivity. Secondary salinization can also make soils dispersive, so excess salt needs managing at landscape scale.

soil-chem-027.title: Saline seeps, where salty groundwater surfaces
soil-chem-027.text: Crusts of alkali salt crystals mark a saline seep, a place where salty water reaches the surface and evaporates. Seeps form by capillary rise from a water table below the surface, or where a water table flows out at the surface. Saline discharge areas are called seeps where groundwater meets the soil surface, and scalds where water is lost by evaporation only. They harm agriculture by reducing yields and restricting growth. Yet they also host salt-adapted and often endemic organisms.

soil-chem-031.title: How drained pyrite turns into sulfuric acid
soil-chem-031.text: Let air reach pyrite in a drained soil, and the mineral becomes acid. The overall reaction is 4FeS2 + 15O2 + 14H2O → 16H+ + 8SO42− + 4Fe(OH)3. It yields sulfuric acid and iron(III) hydroxide, and it can make the soil extremely acidic. The orange iron(III) hydroxide precipitates and locks up the alkalinity, while the acidity stays active as sulfuric acid. That acidity frees large amounts of Al3+ from clay minerals, harmful to vegetation. It leaves behind hydrogen clay, which is stable but poor in nutrients. Other products include hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, hematite, goethite and iron sulfates such as jarosite. So these soils range in color from black and blue-gray to red, orange and yellow.

soil-chem-033.title: Acid base accounting: balancing a soil's acid books
soil-chem-033.text: How much lime does a load of dug-up or dredged sulfidic material need to neutralize it? Acid base accounting answers questions like that. It quantifies the sources of acidity and alkalinity in acid sulfate soils so they can be managed. Net acidity is potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralizing capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil. Potential sulfidic acidity measures oxidizable reduced inorganic sulfur such as iron sulfides. The chromium reducible sulfur test measures it without interference from sulfate minerals or organic matter. Samples oxidize rapidly in air, so they should be cooled below 4°C at once, and monosulfidic samples frozen.

soil-chem-034.title: Keeping acid sulfate soils wet and safe
soil-chem-034.text: On a Malaysian oil palm estate, drainage was deepened in 1962. Yields fell from 17 tons of fresh fruit per ha in 1960 to 2 in 1965, recovering after the water table was raised in 1966. Managing acid sulfate soils means keeping them wet, restoring their water table or neutralizing their acid, and the estate shows why. Aggressive drainage of potentially acid sulfate soils in the second half of the 20th century had disastrous results: barren land and clear, lifeless water. Where soils cannot be kept wet, surface drainage in rainy periods removes acids formed in dry spells and can reclaim the soil in the long run. When Australia's millennium drought exposed them, a bund, pumping and aerial limestone dosing were used to stop acidification of the Lower Lakes.

soil-chem-032.title: Sulfidic and sulfuric: naming the danger in the mud
soil-chem-032.text: Two words mark the stages of an acid sulfate soil. Sulfidic material holds detectable inorganic sulfides, at least 0.01% sulfidic sulfur in layers at least 30 mm thick. Sulfuric material has a pH below 4 from their oxidation. Sulfidic material splits into hyposulfidic, hypersulfidic and monosulfidic classes. Hypersulfidic material would fall below pH 4 if exposed to oxidizing conditions. Hyposulfidic material would not, though its weathering still yields saline solutions with hazardous metals. Coined mainly by Fanning, Rabenhorst and Fitzpatrick, the terms are diagnostic features in two classification systems, the Australian and the international one. The label 'self-neutralizing' acid sulfate soil is discouraged, because it suggests the soil is not hazardous.

soil-chem-043.title: Maas–Hoffman: the yield line that bends under salt
soil-chem-043.text: Up to a point, salt costs a crop nothing. The Maas–Hoffman model draws crop response to soil salinity as a horizontal line that breaks into a downward slope. The breakpoint, or tolerance, is the salinity up to which yield is unaffected. Beyond it, yield falls. In symbols, yield Y equals the maximum C below the breakpoint Pb, and AX + B above it. Here X is soil salinity, A the slope and B the regression constant. Pb is found by regression and optimization for the best fit. A flat tail in the data, though, can give a misleadingly low breakpoint. An inverted form serves factors such as water table depth, which cut yields only at low values.

soil-chem-018.title: Exchangeable sodium percentage and the swelling of clay
soil-chem-018.text: Clays almost fully saturated with sodium are called bentonite, and they are used to make impermeable curtains below dams. Their exchangeable sodium percentage, or ESP, is near 100%. ESP is the share of a soil's exchangeable cations, and so of its {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, that is sodium. It is calculated as sodium divided by total cations, times 100, and it is a key indicator of dispersive soils. High sodium makes wet particles repel one another. Soils with a high ESP therefore lose structure as their aggregates disperse. Clay with an ESP above 16, in contact with non-saline water, has an expanded double layer, so the soil swells and disperses. Applying gypsum lowers ESP by displacing sodium with calcium.

soil-chem-019.title: Alkali soils, clay ruined by sodium carbonate
soil-chem-019.text: Sodium carbonate is about 78000 times more soluble than calcium carbonate. That gap explains alkali soils: clay soils with a high pH, generally above 8.5, often with poor structure and low infiltration capacity. Na2CO3 can push pH above 8.5, the most that calcium carbonate in equilibrium with dissolved carbon dioxide allows. The sodium carbonate and bicarbonate come from weathering minerals or arrive in irrigation and flood water. As Ca2+ precipitates, clays take up Na+ and their ESP rises. Above an ESP of 16 they swell and disperse, crusting and compacting the topsoil and cutting infiltration. Such soils, also called alkaline sodic soils, often have a hard calcareous layer 0.5 to 1 metre down. Alkalinity is worse in swelling montmorillonite or smectite clays. In principle alkaline soils are not saline, since alkalinity worsens as salinity falls. Rainwater stagnates and evaporates on the surface, so farming is mostly limited to crops tolerant of waterlogging, such as rice. Irrigating with softened water, its calcium and magnesium replaced by sodium, dissolves organic matter and disperses clay, giving the structure typical of alkali soils.

soil-chem-020.title: How people make soils alkaline
soil-chem-020.text: Global sodium chloride consumption reached 280 million tons in 2020. Sodium from industrial and household salts enters surface water and groundwater. Man-made soil alkalinity is alkalinity caused by people, mainly through sodium salts and lime that reach soil in irrigation water, effluent and industrial emissions. Fly ash from coal-fired boilers contains calcium oxide, which dissolves to slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, and water washing off the land carries it into rivers and irrigation systems. Lime softening precipitates Ca2+ and Mg2+ from water and converts its sodium bicarbonate into sodium carbonate. Sodium salt loads are worst downstream in intensively cultivated river basins. There, salts concentrate in the water left after transpiration and evaporation.

soil-chem-022.title: Farming fish on land too salty for crops
soil-chem-022.text: Shrimps, crabs, shellfish and fish such as sea bass and grouper can all be raised in inland saline-alkali water. Saline-alkali aquaculture uses such fish and seafood farming on salty, alkaline land to leach salts, add organic matter and put land unfit for crops to use. Since the 1990s, research and experiments in China and elsewhere have combined agriculture and aquaculture on alkali land with considerable success. China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs recommends it as an economically viable and environmentally beneficial way to use saline-alkali land.

soil-chem-023.title: Residual sodium carbonate: rating water's alkali threat
soil-chem-023.text: Water need not be salty to ruin a clay field. The residual sodium carbonate index, or RSC, rates the alkalinity hazard that irrigation water or soil water poses to soil. RSC = (HCO3− + CO32−) − (Ca2+ + Mg2+), in meq/L. For irrigation it should not be much above 1, and preferably below 0.5. It judges water for clay soils with a high cation-exchange capacity. There, sodium high relative to calcium and magnesium makes clay swell or disperse and infiltration collapse. Unlike saline water, high-RSC water does not raise osmotic pressure against root uptake. Yet irrigating clay soils with it creates alkali soils that are left unfarmed. Soda ash from weathered basalt, lime from burnt calcareous coal and industrial soda ash raise river water RSC, often making lower reaches unfit for irrigation.

soil-chem-044.title: Gypsum, the calcium cure for sodium-sick soils
soil-chem-044.text: In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, Nova Scotia gypsum, called plaster, was a sought-after fertilizer for US wheat fields. Agricultural gypsum is calcium sulfate applied to soil as a fertilizer and amendment. It supplies calcium and sulfur without generally changing soil pH. It is used to reclaim saline and sodic soils regardless of pH, lowering the exchangeable sodium percentage. In sodic and acidic soils it turns soluble sodium metaborate into less soluble calcium metaborate, and it reduces aluminium and boron toxicity. It also improves soil structure, water absorption and aeration.

soil-chem-021.title: Reclaiming alkali soils with calcium, acid and drains
soil-chem-021.text: Gypsum does two jobs in an alkali soil. It supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex, and it turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulfate. Reclaiming alkali soils means supplying calcium or acidifying material to replace or neutralize the excess sodium, then leaching the sodium away. That needs enough natural or artificial subsurface drainage for rain or irrigation water to carry it off. Acidifying minerals such as pyrite, alum or aluminium sulfate, calcium chloride, calcium nitrate and spent acids can also be used. Soils with solid CaCO3 can be reclaimed with grass, compost and other organic waste, which add acidifying material and release CO2 to dissolve calcium. Efforts usually target the top 10 cm, and treatments need repeating in about 5 years as amendments leach or decompose. Halophytes such as glasswort, saltwort or barilla absorb sodium carbonate into their tissues, a form of plant-based cleanup, and their ash yields soda. Saline soils are a different case. They are mostly also sodic but keep good structure, so leaching does not usually turn them into alkali soils, and they mostly need no gypsum.

soil-chem-135.title: Mica, the mineral that peels into thin elastic sheets
soil-chem-135.text: Mica comes apart in thin plates that bend and spring back. That property, perfect basal cleavage, defines the group: sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily along flat planes. They belong to the {{ref:soil-found-033}}, and the group holds 37 of them. Muscovite and the biotite series are common examples. Each layer is a sandwich, a pattern called TOT-c. Two tetrahedral sheets are bonded to one octahedral sheet between them. Only interlayer cations, positively charged ions, hold the layers together, and weakly, hence the cleavage. In most micas aluminium replaces one in four silicon ions. That swap leaves each layer with a negative charge, which interlayer sodium, potassium or calcium ions neutralize. Dioctahedral micas have a gibbsite-like aluminium sheet. Trioctahedral ones have a brucite-like sheet of magnesium or ferrous iron. Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rocks and appears as small flakes in some sedimentary rocks. Very fine-grained, variable 'clay micas' include {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, which is short of potassium between its layers. Weathering turns muscovite into this clay and, together with feldspars, into kaolin minerals such as dickite.

soil-chem-134.title: Pyrite, the fool's gold that turns to acid
soil-chem-134.text: Fool's gold has a sour side. Pyrite is iron sulfide, FeS2, the most common sulfide mineral. It occurs in igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks. It is common in coal beds and in shale, where it precipitates from seawater that lacks oxygen. Exposed to oxygen and water, it breaks down into iron oxyhydroxides and sulfuric acid, a {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reaction that Acidithiobacillus bacteria speed up. Fine framboidal pyrite, made by sulfate-reducing bacteria in clayey muds, oxidizes faster still. That oxidation causes {{ref:soil-bio-059}}. In coal mines, spreading limestone dust neutralizes the acid and slows the reaction.

soil-chem-199.title: Zeolites, the mineral sponges that swap ions
soil-chem-199.text: Some minerals behave like sponges built by a chemist. Zeolites are a group of crystalline aluminosilicates, a family of {{ref:soil-found-031}} riddled with microscopic pores. They are widely used to catch other substances on their surfaces and to speed up reactions as catalysts. Their frameworks carry negatively charged aluminium centres. Positive ions must sit beside them, and these can be swapped for others, so zeolites exchange ions. Over 40 natural frameworks are known among 253 identified by December 2018. Altered {{ref:soil-chem-200}} has formed zeolite deposits. Yet much material sold as zeolite is ground volcanic tuff holding little of it, used for building stone, aggregate, cement and products that improve soil.

soil-chem-186.title: Bowen's reaction series: the order in which magma freezes
soil-chem-186.text: Cool a basaltic magma slowly, and its minerals appear in a fixed order. The petrologist Norman L. Bowen worked out that order in the early 1900s. He melted powdered rock and noted which minerals formed as the temperature fell. Olivine and calcium plagioclase crystallize first. Pyroxene, amphibole and biotite follow, then sodium plagioclase, orthoclase, muscovite and finally quartz. This sequence of {{ref:soil-found-031}} is Bowen's reaction series. It has two branches. In the continuous branch, feldspars grow steadily richer in sodium as the melt cools. In the discontinuous branch, one mafic mineral, rich in iron and magnesium, gives way to the next. The order explains why some minerals tend to occur together in {{ref:soil-form-135}} and others almost never do. It also matters for soil. Minerals are most stable near the conditions where they formed, so the series ranks resistance to weathering at Earth's surface. Quartz, the last to form, lasts longest.

soil-chem-187.title: Goldich's ladder: which minerals weather first
soil-chem-187.text: Apatite and quartz can weather millions of years apart. S. S. Goldich ranked why in 1938, after studying soil profiles beside the rocks beneath them. His dissolution series orders common minerals of {{ref:soil-form-135}} by how fast they weather at Earth's surface. Minerals formed at higher temperatures and pressures are less stable, so the order echoes {{ref:soil-chem-186}}. Mafic minerals, rich in iron and magnesium, go faster than felsic, silica-rich ones. Apatite weathers quickest and quartz slowest. That is why quartz is so common as a leftover mineral in residual soils. Mafic rocks weather to serpentine, magnesium- and calcium-rich clays and oxides of iron; felsic rocks to clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. The series covers only a mineral's own properties. Climate also controls the rate, through the water-to-rock ratio, pH and {{ref:soil-chem-142}}. And White and Brantley (2003) found K-feldspar and plagioclase weathering at similar rates, so the series may not hold for every process.

soil-chem-200.title: Volcanic glass, rock that froze before it could crystallize
soil-chem-200.text: When magma cools too fast for crystals to grow, it freezes as glass. Volcanic glass is this amorphous product, with no crystal structure at all. That disorder makes it reactive. Water attacks it easily, and over time it breaks down into new minerals. Its weathering, with that of feldspars, forms {{ref:soil-chem-097}}. Glass in ash beds that turns crystalline becomes {{ref:soil-chem-100}}. Some young volcanic soils, with limited soil formation, still contain much glass. Soils with {{ref:soil-form-027}} layers are often found in volcanic areas and show traces of ash or glass.

soil-chem-196.title: Glauconite, the green mineral of slow seafloors
soil-chem-196.text: A green, crumbly mineral in a field can mark an ancient seabed. Glauconite is an iron potassium mineral among the {{ref:soil-found-033}}, a member of the {{ref:soil-chem-135}} group. It forms in place in the sea, commonly where oxygen is scarce, and indicates continental shelf deposits laid down slowly. It is very friable and has very low resistance to weathering. As the main component of greensand, it is a common potassium source in fertilizers and is used to adjust soil pH. Greensand is low in potassium, though, so it pays to haul it only short distances. In 1896, the master's thesis of {{ref:soil-hist-008}} dealt with its origin, composition and weathering.

soil-chem-197.title: Jarosite, a store of slow-release acid
soil-chem-197.text: Rovers have found jarosite on Mars, a sign of strongly oxidizing surface conditions. On Earth it is a basic hydrous sulfate of potassium and ferric iron, KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, one of the {{ref:soil-found-036}}. It forms when iron sulfides oxidize. It is common in drainage from mines and in strongly acid soils that form where sulfides oxidize. When iron sulfide in clay oxidizes, jarosite's potassium comes mainly from {{ref:soil-chem-094}} or K-feldspar. Together with {{ref:soil-chem-198}}, it holds retained acidity, releasing it slowly as Fe3+ and Al3+ hydrolyze. The horizon suffix j marks their accumulation.

soil-chem-195.title: Birnessite, the manganese mineral microbes make
soil-chem-195.text: Microbes probably built most of the manganese mineral at Earth's surface. Birnessite, a hydrous manganese dioxide, nominally MnO2·nH2O, is the main one. It occurs as fine, poorly crystalline aggregates in soils, sediments, marine nodules and rock coatings such as desert varnish. Biological oxidation of Mn(II) is faster than the abiotic kind, which is why microorganisms are thought to make most of it. Its layers contain vacancies, balanced by interlayer cations such as calcium, copper, zinc, lead and cadmium. Manganese oxides like it, among the {{ref:soil-found-035}}, can oxidize trivalent chromium in soils to {{ref:soil-env-255}}.

soil-chem-198.title: Schwertmannite, the orange crust of acid waters
soil-chem-198.text: Streams and lakes fouled by mine drainage are often coated with an orange precipitate. That coating is commonly schwertmannite, an iron oxyhydroxysulfate, ideally Fe8O8(OH)6(SO4)·nH2O, usually seen as brownish-yellow crusts. It forms in iron-rich, acidic sulfate waters with a pH of 2 to 4. Like other {{ref:soil-found-036}}, it belongs to a wider chemistry. It is central to iron-sulfur geochemistry in the strongly acid, sulfur-rich soils of coastal lowlands. First described in 1994, it is named for the soil scientist Udo Schwertmann of the Technical University of Munich.

soil-chem-185.title: Pedogenic carbonate, made in the soil itself
soil-chem-185.text: Not all the carbonate in a soil came from its rock. Pedogenic carbonate forms in place within the soil, unlike carbonate inherited from bedrock or {{ref:soil-form-087}}. One route is carbonation, acid hydrolysis by dissolved carbon dioxide, described in {{ref:soil-found-060}}. It can weather primary minerals into secondary {{ref:soil-found-034}}. Carbonate can also form as a soil wets and dries, which underlies proposed clues to past seasonality. Horizon descriptions mark accumulated secondary carbonates with the suffix k. These carbonates also sort soils in the international classification: some soil groups are defined by accumulating them, others by lacking them within one meter. Ancient soils keep a record too. Carbon isotopes in carbonate nodules of {{ref:soil-form-072}} help reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide.

soil-chem-184.title: Soil mineralogy: where plant nutrients begin
soil-chem-184.text: Most of the elements a plant needs come from the chemical breakdown of minerals. Soil mineralogy is the study of the minerals in soil. With soil physics, chemistry and biology, it is one of the branches through which soil processes are studied quantitatively. As roots remove nutrients from the soil solution, weathering of minerals helps replenish them, along with ion exchange and decaying organic matter. Minerals hold phosphorus too. In acid soils it binds to iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides; in neutral soils and in {{ref:soil-chem-035}} it precipitates onto calcite. Organic matter clings to minerals and stays longer in soil. Weathering also releases salts, which drainage flushes out or evaporation concentrates near the surface. Mineralogy mainly influences soil color. Size can mislead: gypsum, calcite, feldspar or quartz grains can be clay-sized without behaving like a true {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. Advances here have added new tools to the study of soil formation.

soil-chem-188.title: Powder diffraction, a fingerprint for every crystal
soil-chem-188.text: Every crystalline solid leaves its own fingerprint when struck by radiation. Powder diffraction reads it. The method aims X-rays, neutrons or electrons at powdered or microcrystalline samples. Diffraction happens when radiation of a wavelength comparable to atomic spacings reflects off planes of atoms and the reflections reinforce one another. Bragg's law, nλ = 2d sin θ, links the wavelength λ, the lattice spacing d and the glancing angle θ. The Braggs proposed it in 1913. Line positions, set by lattice spacings, and their intensities identify the solid. A soil sample is a mixture, so its patterns lie on top of one another, and from them the relative amount of each phase can be found. Preparation is simple and measurement fast. The method mainly identifies known phases rather than solving unknown structures, and the 2021 Powder Diffraction File held over 1,047,661 reference materials.

soil-chem-189.title: X-ray fluorescence: making minerals glow with their elements
soil-chem-189.text: Hit a mineral with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays, and it answers with X-rays of its own. Their energies reveal which elements are present, and their intensities how much. This is X-ray fluorescence, a non-destructive method used in geochemistry, archaeology and forensic science. Minerals may be ground and pressed into a tablet or, for accurate work, dissolved in borate glass and cast into a bead. Pressed powders have pitfalls: finer minerals gather at the surface, and mixtures absorb in ways that depart from theory. XRF tools increasingly ride cone penetration test probes to measure soil in place.

soil-chem-191.title: Electron probe microanalysis: chemistry from a speck
soil-chem-191.text: A single mineral grain can record its own history from core to rim. Electron probe microanalysis reads that record. It bombards small volumes of a solid with an electron beam and measures the emitted X-rays, much as {{ref:soil-chem-189}} does, without destroying the sample. Scanning electron microscopes share the principle, but the probe holds its beam fixed and aims at analysis rather than images. Mineralogists and petrologists use it to trace chemical zoning in grains. {{ref:soil-hist-135}}, which dates layers of volcanic ash, usually fingerprints ash with the probe. Light elements such as hydrogen, lithium and beryllium are hard to measure this way.

soil-chem-190.title: Infrared spectra that reveal water in minerals
soil-chem-190.text: Some minerals have no long-range order, yet still announce themselves. {{ref:soil-chem-097}} is one, identified by its distinctive infrared spectrum and its X-ray diffraction pattern. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy records how a solid, liquid or gas absorbs or emits infrared light over a wide range of wavelengths at once. A mathematical Fourier transform converts the raw data into the spectrum, which gives the method its name. Geologists use it to quantify water and carbon dioxide in minerals and glasses. With X-ray and electron diffraction, infrared spectroscopy is a standard way to study clays.

soil-chem-194.title: Dissolving one iron mineral and sparing the rest
soil-chem-194.text: A soil chemist can dissolve one kind of iron mineral and leave another largely alone. Selective extractions target particular iron- and aluminium-bearing phases, mostly {{ref:soil-found-035}}, so they can be measured. Acid ammonium oxalate at pH 3 pulls iron and aluminium from poorly crystalline minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-111}}, from iron(II) minerals such as magnetite, and from organic matter. Dithionite works differently. It is a {{ref:soil-chem-115}}, with a reduction potential of −0.66 V at pH 7. Paired with a complexing agent such as citric acid, it turns iron(III) oxyhydroxides into soluble iron(II) and removes amorphous iron(III) phases.

soil-chem-193.title: Heavy minerals, the dense grains that betray a sand's origin
soil-chem-193.text: A pinch of dense grains can reveal where a sediment came from. A heavy mineral is one denser than 2.9 g/cm3, usually a minor part of siliciclastic sediments, those built of silicate rock fragments that may harden into {{ref:soil-form-136}}. Zircon, tourmaline, rutile, garnet and magnetite are common examples, dense and resistant to weathering. Because they resist, deep weathering concentrates them in residual accumulations. Their relative proportions, a heavy mineral suite, help trace the provenance of sediments. Being scarce, they are separated for study in a dense liquid such as bromoform, in a funnel or centrifuge.

soil-chem-192.title: Environmental magnetism: climate and fire written in iron
soil-chem-192.text: Magnetic minerals in soil keep a diary of climate, moving sediment, pollution and fire. Environmental magnetism reads it, using their magnetic properties as proxies. The main magnetic minerals are oxides of iron, among the {{ref:soil-found-035}}, such as magnetite, and iron sulfides such as greigite and pyrrhotite. Magnetic susceptibility and remanence estimate mineral size and composition, and the measurements are quick and non-invasive. Susceptibility profiles through alternating loess and {{ref:soil-form-072}} in north-central China mapped Quaternary monsoon variations. Heat leaves a mark too. It converts {{ref:soil-chem-104}} and {{ref:soil-chem-111}} into {{ref:soil-chem-166}}, raising soil magnetism.

soil-chem-154.title: Colloids, particles too small to settle quietly
soil-chem-154.text: The most active particles in soil are less than 1 μm across. Mixed into water, particles this small form a colloid: a mixture in which microscopically small insoluble particles are dispersed through another substance. The suspended particles are the dispersed phase; the medium around them is the continuous phase. IUPAC puts colloidal particles roughly between 1 nanometer and 1 micrometer in at least one dimension, and says those limits are not rigid. Some colloids look translucent because their particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect. The particles push and pull through several forces, from electrostatic attraction or repulsion to always-present, short-range van der Waals attraction. In soil, the colloidal fraction is tiny particles of {{ref:soil-found-040}} and {{ref:soil-bio-089}} whose positive or negative charges vary with soil pH. Francesco Selmi began the study of colloids in 1845, and Thomas Graham coined the word in 1861.

soil-chem-160.title: Zeta potential, the voltage that keeps particles apart
soil-chem-160.text: A colloid's fate can hang on a few tens of millivolts. As a particle moves through liquid, a thin film of fluid travels with it. The boundary where that film ends and the still fluid begins is the slipping plane. The electrical potential there is the zeta potential, written ζ and usually given in millivolts. It is not the same as the potential at the particle's surface, but it is often the only way to characterize the charged layers around a {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. It is also a handy gauge of stability. Magnitudes of 0 to 5 mV give rapid coagulation, 30 to 40 mV moderate stability, 40 to 60 mV good stability and over 61 mV excellent stability. To measure it, an electric field is applied. Particles drift toward the opposite electrode at a velocity proportional to their zeta potential, tracked by laser Doppler anemometry. Where pH–zeta potential curves cross titration curves lies the {{ref:soil-chem-075}}.

soil-chem-155.title: Colloidal stability: why some suspensions never clear
soil-chem-155.text: Whether a cloudy suspension stays cloudy comes down to a contest of forces. Colloidal stability is the ability of particles to stay suspended instead of clumping. A {{ref:soil-chem-154}} stays stable while the attraction between particles is below kT, the energy of thermal motion. Above that, they begin to clump: aggregation, flocculation or coagulation. Coagulation may mean permanent clumping, flocculation a reversible kind that forms a floc. The clumps settle out or cream to the top, ending the suspension. Particles are held apart electrostatically, by the like charges of their surrounding layers of counterions, or sterically, by adsorbed polymer or surfactant layers. Adding salt shrinks the charged layer, and shifting pH neutralizes surface charge. Either removes the repulsion and lets van der Waals forces win. When {{ref:soil-chem-160}} falls below about ±5 mV, rapid coagulation tends to follow. Charged polymers can also bridge particles: negatively charged clay flocculates when a positively charged polymer is added.

soil-chem-158.title: Particle aggregation: how suspended grains clump and fall
soil-chem-158.text: A stable suspension can be undone by a pinch of the right salt. Particle aggregation is the sticking together of dispersed particles into irregular flocs or agglomerates, which destabilizes a {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. It also goes by coagulation or flocculation. Salts or chemicals called coagulants or flocculants trigger it, and it can be reversible or irreversible. Growing agglomerates settle out as sediment. In concentrated suspensions they link instead into a colloidal gel. The reverse, {{ref:soil-chem-161}}, hardly happens on its own, though stirring or shear can drive it. Salt works by screening the repulsion of the charged layers around each particle, so van der Waals attraction dominates. Chemists track this with the stability ratio W. It is near one in fast aggregation and very large in a stable suspension. Each counter-ion charge has a critical coagulation concentration. Because particles are often negative, multivalent metal cations are highly effective coagulants. Polymers cut both ways. They can protect particles by steric repulsion, or, when loosely adsorbed, bridge two particles in bridging flocculation. The way particles meet matters too. Aggregation driven only by diffusion is perikinetic; aggregation sped up by shear, such as stirring, is orthokinetic. The clusters are mass fractals, shapes whose density changes with size. Fast, diffusion-limited aggregation builds loose clusters (d ≈ 1.8), and slow, reaction-limited aggregation compact ones (d ≈ 2.1). These outcomes follow from the balance described in {{ref:soil-chem-155}}.

soil-chem-157.title: DLVO theory: attraction, repulsion and the barrier between
soil-chem-157.text: Two charged particles in a liquid feel a pull and a push at once. DLVO theory adds them up. It sums van der Waals attraction and electrical double-layer repulsion to give a quantitative account of {{ref:soil-chem-155}}. Both forces grow as particles approach, and their sum traces a curve. A deep primary minimum lies at very close range, an energy barrier further out, and a shallow secondary minimum beyond it. The barrier's height shows how stable the dispersion is; if it does not exceed the thermal energy, particles aggregate. Particles trapped in the primary minimum coagulate for good, while those in the secondary minimum are held weakly and easily redispersed. Derjaguin and Landau proposed the theory in 1941, and Verwey and Overbeek reached it independently in 1948. Unlike the earlier Levine–Dube theory, it explained how stability depends on the {{ref:soil-chem-202}} of the electrolyte. Yet other forces matter too, and it cannot describe colloidal crystals forming in dilute, low-salt dispersions.

soil-chem-161.title: Peptization: turning a precipitate back into a colloid
soil-chem-161.text: A settled precipitate can be coaxed back into suspension. Peptization does this by shaking the solid with a suitable electrolyte, a peptizing agent, until its particles form a {{ref:soil-chem-154}} again. It is the reverse of flocculation, also called deflocculation. Concentrated salt compresses the charged layer around each particle, which collapses in very salty solutions, so particles coalesce into an easily filtered precipitate. Wash it with too much deionized water and that layer re-expands, repulsion returns, and the precipitate peptizes. Freshly precipitated aluminium or iron hydroxide is very hard to filter, because its fine particles pass through paper.

soil-chem-167.title: Sepiolite, the fibrous clay of dry lands
soil-chem-167.text: Sepiolite is a soft, white, fibrous magnesium silicate clay, Mg4Si6O15(OH)2·6H2O, also known as meerschaum. It is one of the {{ref:soil-found-033}}. The fibrous clays form a continuous series from sepiolite, the richest in magnesium, to {{ref:soil-chem-110}}; sepiolite has the wider structural channels. It occurs as a secondary mineral with serpentine and can precipitate in arid environments. Soils of South Africa's arid west hold much of it, grading inland to palygorskite. It raises the water plants can use in sandy soils, but its cemented layers hamper mining. That cemented material is called sepiocrete.

soil-chem-150.title: Reading clay layers with X-rays
soil-chem-150.text: Clay minerals look nearly alike side to side. What sets them apart is height: the thickness of each stacked layer. Clay mineral X-ray diffraction measures that spacing. Ordered atoms diffract an X-ray beam at particular angles and intensities, from which the structure is calculated. Randomly oriented powders help little, because clays share similar X and Y dimensions. The diagnostic Z dimension is the height of the T-O or T-O-T layer described in {{ref:soil-chem-081}}, so samples are laid flat to strengthen basal (00l) reflections. The Z spacing shifts with cation substitution in the sheets and with the presence and size of the interlayer cation. Bragg's law, written l λ = 2d sin θ, gives the spacings, so successive 00l peaks are evenly spaced. Clays give broad peaks. Patterns are matched against known samples, such as the Clay Mineral Society's reference collection, because calculated patterns rarely fit. Harder nonclays such as quartz and feldspars are removed first by light crushing and sieving.

soil-chem-162.title: Hydrous oxides, porous metal compounds that grab other substances
soil-chem-162.text: Hydrous oxides are inorganic compounds of a metal, hydroxide and weakly bound water. Examples include hydrous ferric oxide (HFO), hydrous aluminium oxide (HAO), hydrous cupric oxide and hydrous titanium oxide. HFO and HAO precipitate in highly porous, poorly crystalline or amorphous forms. That open structure makes them good adsorbents, used for example in water treatment. They also form in nature. Oxidative {{ref:soil-found-058}} of rocks can produce HFO and HAO, giving clay soils rich in iron and aluminium hydrous oxides.

soil-chem-163.title: Iron oxides, the minerals that color and feed soils
soil-chem-163.text: Rust is the most familiar of a large family. Iron oxides are compounds of iron and oxygen, together with related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust. They hold ferrous iron, ferric iron or both, and are often non-stoichiometric, with no fixed ratio of elements. Only a few matter at Earth's surface, chiefly wüstite, magnetite and {{ref:soil-chem-112}}. Among the oxyhydroxides, {{ref:soil-chem-104}} and {{ref:soil-chem-164}} are the commonest and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils. Others include akaganéite, feroxyhyte, {{ref:soil-chem-111}} and {{ref:soil-chem-170}}. Iron(III) oxyhydroxide ranges from yellow through dark brown to black, depending on hydration, particle size and shape, and crystal structure. It precipitates from iron(III) solutions at pH 6.5 to 8 and forms readily when iron(II) hydroxide meets air. Some bacteria, such as Shewanella oneidensis and Geobacter species, even breathe on these minerals, handing them the electrons left over from their metabolism.

soil-chem-164.title: Lepidocrocite, the scaly red rust of wet places
soil-chem-164.text: Iron that rusts underwater forms lepidocrocite, an iron oxide-hydroxide, γ-FeO(OH), also called esmeraldite or hydrohematite. Red to reddish brown, it is common where primary iron minerals weather. Its layers of iron(III) oxide octahedra are held by hydrogen bonds through hydroxide layers, as in boehmite. These weak bonds give the mineral its scaly habit. In oxidizing conditions {{ref:soil-chem-170}} generally turns into lepidocrocite and {{ref:soil-chem-104}}. First described in 1813 from Moravia, it takes its name from the Greek for scale and fibre.

soil-chem-166.title: Maghemite, the magnetic mark of fire
soil-chem-166.text: A bushfire can leave its signature in the soil's magnetism. Maghemite, γ-Fe2O3, is a ferrimagnetic iron oxide with the formula of {{ref:soil-chem-112}} but the spinel structure of magnetite. It forms by weathering or low-temperature oxidation of iron(II) spinels such as magnetite, or as lepidocrocite and ferrihydrite lose water. It is a widespread brown or yellow pigment in sediments and soils. Heat converts goethite and ferrihydrite to maghemite and raises soil magnetism. Maghemite enrichment across a landscape therefore points to fire. A soil's magnetic susceptibility reflects magnetic iron oxides such as maghemite, and geoarchaeologists measure it.

soil-chem-165.title: Limonite, the iron ore that is really a mixture
soil-chem-165.text: Limonite was once thought to be a single mineral. It is now a field term for an iron ore made of a variable mixture of hydrated iron(III) oxide-hydroxides, including {{ref:soil-chem-104}}, lepidocrocite, akaganeite and jarosite. Only X-ray diffraction can settle its exact makeup. It forms by hydration of hematite and magnetite, oxidation of iron sulfides and weathering of iron-rich minerals, and is often the main iron component of lateritic soils. Its name comes from Greek words for a damp meadow or marshy lake, after its occurrence as bog iron ore. Its yellowish-brown streak tells it from hematite, with a red streak, and magnetite, with a black one.

soil-chem-168.title: Measuring surface area: the answer depends on the ruler
soil-chem-168.text: The surface area of a powder has no single true value. Measuring {{ref:soil-phys-043}}, the area per unit mass, is most often done by gas {{ref:soil-chem-145}} with the BET method. Results depend on the probe molecule's size, the exposed crystal faces and the temperature. The BET method captures fine structure and deep texture, but values can differ markedly with the gas used. Calculating area from particle sizes needs an assumed shape and misses surface texture. Gas permeability through a powder bed is quick and simple but misses much deep texture. Standards such as ISO 9277 govern the measurement.

soil-chem-153.title: Layer charge, the negative pull of clay sheets
soil-chem-153.text: Swap a silicon ion for an aluminium ion, and a clay layer gains a negative charge. Layer charge is the net negative charge created when ions of lower charge, such as Al3+, replace Si4+ through {{ref:soil-chem-085}}. Interlayer cations balance it. Where the charge sits defines minerals. In nontronite usually more than 60% lies in the tetrahedral sheet, generally balanced by Ca2+ or Mg2+, and {{ref:soil-chem-152}} is defined by more than 50% there. In the manganese oxide {{ref:soil-chem-195}}, cations and water between layers offset the charge, letting it exchange cations. The size of the balancing cation changes the layer spacing seen by X-ray diffraction.

soil-chem-152.title: Beidellite, a smectite charged in its silica sheet
soil-chem-152.text: Beidellite is a {{ref:soil-chem-091}} clay in which more than half the {{ref:soil-chem-153}} comes from aluminium replacing silicon in the tetrahedral sheet. It is a dioctahedral smectite, grouped with montmorillonite and nontronite, whereas saponite is trioctahedral. Beidellite is also one of the clays that make soils shrink and swell, along with smectite, montmorillonite, illite and vermiculite.

soil-chem-159.title: The Schulze–Hardy rule: why aluminium salts clump clay best
soil-chem-159.text: Doubling an ion's charge does far more than double its power to clump colloids. The Schulze–Hardy rule says the critical coagulation concentration of an electrolyte varies as the inverse sixth power of its counter-ion's charge. For trivalent counter-ions it falls to 0.03 to 0.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L. So multivalent cations flocculate colloids far better than monovalent ones: AlCl3 beats CaCl2, which beats NaCl. The rule can be derived from {{ref:soil-chem-157}}. Ions of the same charge still differ somewhat, reflecting particle properties or how strongly ions favor the surface.

soil-chem-149.title: Clay chemistry, from fertile fields to Mars
soil-chem-149.text: In 2009, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted clay minerals on Mars, strong evidence that the planet once had water. Clay chemistry is the applied branch of chemistry that studies the structures, properties and reactions of clays and clay minerals. These minerals are built of nanometer-scale layers. They carry fixed and exchangeable charges, take molecules onto their surfaces and between their layers, and form stable colloidal dispersions. Their capacity to hold cations balances the commonest soil cations and controls pH, directly affecting how fertile a soil is. Their interactions with organic substances help fix nutrients and decide whether {{ref:soil-env-237}} and other contaminants are held or leached.

soil-chem-145.title: Adsorption, the art of sticking to a surface
soil-chem-145.text: Every surface is a little unfinished. Atoms inside a solid are surrounded by neighbors, but those at the surface are not, and that leftover surface energy lets them attract other substances. The result is adsorption: the adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or solution to a surface. It builds a film of adsorbate on the adsorbent. Unlike absorption, it does not penetrate into the bulk of the material. {{ref:soil-chem-068}} covers both, and {{ref:soil-chem-147}} is the reverse. The bonds vary in strength. Physisorption works through weak van der Waals forces; chemisorption through covalent bonds. Electrostatic attraction can also hold adsorbates. The difference shows with water. Physically adsorbed water on a solid is removed by drying, while chemically adsorbed water may split into surface -H and -OH groups. Adsorption, ion exchange and chromatography are all sorption processes. Each selectively moves substances from a fluid onto insoluble particles. In soil, the fluid is often the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. The German physicist Heinrich Kayser coined the word in 1881.

soil-chem-146.title: Adsorption isotherms: counting what a surface holds
soil-chem-146.text: How much will a surface hold if the supply keeps rising? An adsorption isotherm answers. It describes how much substance is adsorbed as a function of its pressure, or its concentration in solution, at constant temperature.
