The amount is nearly always divided by the adsorbent's mass, so materials can be compared. Freundlich and Kuster published the first isotherm, a purely empirical fit. Langmuir derived the first scientifically based one. His model assumes equivalent sites holding one molecule each, a uniform surface and at most a single layer, assumptions seldom all true. The 1938 BET isotherm allows multiple layers. Langmuir usually suits chemisorption, BET physisorption on surfaces without tiny pores. Choosing between Langmuir and Freundlich should rest on adsorption enthalpies, not best fit: constant in Langmuir's model, falling with coverage in Freundlich's. A Langmuir fit also yields the monolayer capacity, from which surface area can be calculated.

soil-chem-147.title: Desorption, letting go of a surface
soil-chem-147.text: Desorption is {{ref:soil-chem-145}} run backward: the release of adsorbed atoms or molecules from a surface into the surrounding fluid or vacuum. It happens when a molecule gains enough energy to overcome the barrier and binding energy holding it. Heat, light, energetic particle beams or reactions such as oxidation or reduction can supply it. The Polanyi–Wigner equation describes desorption driven by heat, linking surface coverage to desorption rate. The same idea cleans soil. As a cleanup method, {{ref:soil-env-230}} heats contaminated material to 90–560 °C, driving off water and organic contaminants for a gas treatment system to collect or destroy.

soil-chem-148.title: Chemical equivalents: counting charge, not just atoms
soil-chem-148.text: A millimole of calcium does twice the work of a millimole of sodium. The chemical equivalent captures this. It is the amount of a substance that reacts with, or supplies, one mole of hydrogen ions in an acid–base reaction. In a {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reaction, it is one mole of electrons. The number of equivalents of an ion equals its moles times its valence. So 1 mmol of Na+ is 1 milliequivalent, but 1 mmol of Ca2+ is 2 milliequivalents. The quantity is archaic, yet small amounts are still given in milliequivalents (meq), thousandths of an equivalent.

soil-chem-202.title: Ionic strength: why a doubly charged ion counts fourfold
soil-chem-202.text: Dissolve magnesium sulfate in water and it counts for four times as much as the same concentration of table salt. The yardstick is ionic strength, a measure of the ions in a solution weighted by their charge. In molar form it is I = ½ Σ ci zi², summed over every ion, where c is molar concentration and z the ion's charge number. Squaring the charge makes multivalent ions weigh heavily: for NaCl the ionic strength equals the concentration, while MgSO4 gives four times as much. It can be molar or molal, so units should be stated, and molality is preferred for non-ideal solutions. In {{ref:soil-found-079}}, total electrolyte concentration shifts dissociation constants and the solubility of salts. It also sets the Debye length, the thickness scale of the charged double layer around a surface. That length is inversely proportional to the square root of ionic strength, so more or higher-valence counterions compress the layer. Lewis and Randall introduced the concept in 1921, while describing how strong electrolytes depart from ideal behavior.

soil-chem-201.title: Activity coefficients: correcting for crowded ions
soil-chem-201.text: Soil water is crowded. Small volumes of it hold high concentrations of electrolytes, which is why activity coefficients matter so much in soil chemistry. An activity coefficient is a factor that corrects a substance's concentration for how far a mixture departs from ideal behavior. Activity equals the coefficient times concentration. In an ideal electrolyte solution every coefficient equals one, a state only very dilute solutions approach. As concentration rises, ions interact more and the coefficients change. Cation and anion values cannot be measured separately, so chemists use a mean activity coefficient, γ±. Even pH rests on this limit: it is defined from hydrogen ion activity, a definition IUPAC calls only notional. Coefficients come from the Debye–Hückel equation or its extensions, the Davies and Pitzer equations, or from specific ion interaction theory. Uncharged species such as dissolved CO2 follow a salting-out model, log10 γ = bI, with b for CO2 0.11 at 10 °C.

soil-chem-203.title: Debye and Hückel explain why salt water misbehaves
soil-chem-203.text: Unlike charges attract and like charges repel, and in a salt solution that simple rule spoils the arithmetic. Ions are not scattered at random, so the solution departs from ideal behavior. Debye–Hückel theory, published by Peter Debye and Erich Hückel in 1923 in Physikalische Zeitschrift, explains why. It pictures each ion surrounded by a statistically averaged cloud of net opposite charge. It assumes complete dissociation, spherical unpolarized ions and a solvent that acts only as a medium of constant permittivity. The result, a linearized Poisson–Boltzmann model, predicts mean ionic activity coefficients accurately in dilute solution. Its limiting law makes the logarithm of the mean activity coefficient proportional to the square root of {{ref:soil-chem-202}}. That law fits measurements below about 10⁻³ mol/L but drifts at higher concentrations and with more highly charged ions. The extended equation holds up to ionic strength 0.1; beyond that, the Pitzer equations should be used. The theory still underlies modern treatments.

soil-chem-208.title: Inner sphere complexes: ions that bond straight to minerals
soil-chem-208.text: Some ions hover near a mineral surface; others grab it. In an inner sphere complex, an ion binds directly to the surface with no water molecules between them. In an outer sphere complex, water keeps the two apart. Only ions with a high affinity for surface sites form the inner kind, including specifically adsorbed ions that bond covalently. Surface hydroxyl groups act as electron-donating ligands. On oxide surfaces the metal ion is a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor, and the ligand a Lewis base, an electron-pair donor. Sorption of protonated ligands therefore depends on pH. These complexes govern how trace elements move or stay put in soil, where natural sorbents are often metal oxides. Sulfate held this way can slow or prevent the dissolution of iron and manganese oxides. Alkaline earth metals sorb less as their ions get larger, so they grow more mobile during weathering. Through such bonds, soil properties decide whether nutrients and pollutants are retained or lost.

soil-chem-206.title: Langmuir's model: one molecule per parking space
soil-chem-206.text: Irving Langmuir won the 1932 Nobel Prize for his surface chemistry, and one idea from it still opens most adsorption studies. The Langmuir adsorption model pictures a surface of identical sites, each holding at most one molecule, with adsorption and its reverse, {{ref:soil-chem-147}}, both possible. Each binding is a reaction between a molecule and an empty site, with an equilibrium constant K. The fraction of occupied sites is θ = K p / (1 + K p). At low pressure θ is about Kp; at high pressure θ approaches 1 as the single layer fills. The model assumes a flat, uniform surface, immobile molecules, equal energy at every site and no interaction between neighbors. Real surfaces are rough, with several site types, and adsorbed molecules do interact, so it often deviates. A competitive form lets two species vie for the same sites. Langmuir presented it in 1916, and it remains the first choice for most adsorption models.

soil-chem-209.title: Partition coefficients: how a compound splits between liquids
soil-chem-209.text: Shake a compound with water and octanol, and it divides itself between the two layers. The partition coefficient is the ratio of its concentrations in two immiscible phases at equilibrium. With water and octanol, it measures how water-loving or water-shunning a substance is. Hydrogeologists use this octanol–water coefficient, Kow, to predict how dissolved hydrophobic organic compounds migrate in soil and groundwater. Strictly it covers only the un-ionized form, while the distribution coefficient covers all forms. One or both phases can even be solid.

soil-chem-204.title: Coprecipitation: solids that drag dissolved metals down
soil-chem-204.text: A forming precipitate can carry down substances that would otherwise stay dissolved. That is coprecipitation. The captured material may sit inside the crystal lattice, be sealed in as the crystal grows, or cling to the precipitate's surface. Trace elements too dilute to precipitate alone ride down with a carrier of similar crystal structure. The process matters in {{ref:soil-bio-059}}, in heavy metal transport, wastewater treatment and radionuclide migration around waste repositories. Wetlands built for treatment, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-260}}, remove phosphorus by coprecipitation with iron, aluminum and calcium compounds, and iron coagulants strip arsenic from water the same way.

soil-chem-205.title: The Freundlich equation, a rule fitted to rough surfaces
soil-chem-205.text: Freundlich fitted his equation to organic acids adsorbing on coal from water, and it outlived that modest start. The Freundlich equation, dating from 1909, is an empirical adsorption isotherm. It links the amount adsorbed on a solid to the gas pressure or solute concentration. It reads x/m = K c^(1/n), where x/m is adsorbate mass per adsorbent mass and K and n are constants for a given pair at a given temperature. In log form, log x/m = log K + (1/n) log c, it becomes a straight line. It can also be derived from an uneven surface: high-energy sites fill first, then weaker ones, so the heat of adsorption falls as coverage grows. A good fit makes such a surface likely, not proved; calorimetry can confirm it. The equation fails at high pressure, where adsorption saturates. Being empirical, it should give way to theory-based isotherms such as Langmuir's or BET when those fit.

soil-chem-210.title: X-ray absorption fine structure reveals an atom's neighbors
soil-chem-210.text: An X-ray absorption spectrum carries fine detail that maps the surroundings of a single kind of atom. This X-ray absorption fine structure divides into the edge, the XANES region spanning 50–100 eV around the threshold, and the EXAFS region; XAFS means the two together. EXAFS arises as the ejected photoelectron scatters once off neighboring atoms, giving local structure. Multiple-scattering peaks in XANES give its geometry. Surface EXAFS reveals the coordination and chemical state of adsorbed ions. With X-ray diffraction, both methods show how microbes sorb and mineralize radionuclides when they are used to clean up contamination, as in {{ref:soil-env-023}}.

soil-chem-211.title: Chemical speciation: naming every form an element takes
soil-chem-211.text: Knowing how much of a metal a solution holds says little about what form it takes. Chemical speciation is the calculation of the concentrations of all the chemical species present. Geochemical equilibrium models predict them from measurements of bulk solution composition, for plant nutrients in soil and for regulated metals in stored wastes. Trace metals form complexes with hydroxide, carbonate and chloride, and their speciation changes between oxidized and reduced conditions. An element's toxicity also depends on how oxidized it is, so food regulations require speciation of some elements.

soil-chem-207.title: Geochemical models, from hand sums to reactive transport
soil-chem-207.text: In 1962 Garrels and Thompson built a geochemical model by hand. From a solution's bulk composition, they predicted its species, its saturation with each mineral and the fugacities of its gases. Geochemical modeling now does this mostly by computer, using thermodynamics, kinetics or both to analyze reactions in geological systems, including low-temperature waters near Earth's surface. A model starts from a basis of aqueous species, minerals and gases, as many as the system has components. It then solves mass action and mass balance equations for equilibrium. A mineral's saturation index, log Q/K, is zero at equilibrium, positive when the mineral is likely to precipitate and negative when it tends to dissolve. Helgeson's 1968 program added mass transfer, creating reaction path models of processes such as weathering. Linking to water-flow models gives reactive transport along a flowpath. Uses run from {{ref:soil-chem-211}} of plant nutrients to contaminant mobility in groundwater. One weakness is seldom considered: thermodynamic databases differ, causing large uncertainties.

soil-chem-176.title: Electron acceptors, the last stop for every electron
soil-chem-176.text: All organisms get energy by moving electrons from a donor to an acceptor. An electron acceptor is a chemical species that takes up electrons transferred from another compound, so it is an oxidizing agent, described in {{ref:soil-chem-114}}. Its pull is measured by its redox potential. In biology, the terminal electron acceptor receives the last electron in a transport chain, such as oxygen in aerobic respiration, though organisms use many kinds. The weedkiller paraquat is a potent acceptor: it takes electrons from photosynthesis and passes them to oxygen, forming toxic reactive oxygen species.

soil-chem-178.title: Oxidation states: bookkeeping for electrons
soil-chem-178.text: Iron in magnetite, Fe3O4, has an oxidation state of 8/3, an average rather than a whole number. An oxidation state is the hypothetical charge an atom would carry if all its bonds were fully ionic. It records how far the atom has been oxidized. A rise is oxidation and a fall is reduction, and in redox reactions the two always occur in pairs. Pure elements sit at zero, and the oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule sum to zero. Stock nomenclature writes the state as a Roman numeral after the element, as in iron(III) oxide.

soil-chem-177.title: Electron donors: the fuel behind natural cleanup
soil-chem-177.text: Soil organic matter, petroleum hydrocarbons and even vinyl chloride can all hand electrons to microbes. An electron donor is a chemical species that transfers electrons to another compound, acting as a reducing agent, the role described in {{ref:soil-chem-115}}, and being oxidized itself. In respiration, donors release electrons and energy. Microbes capture that energy as the electrons pass along a transport chain to an electron acceptor. Less chlorinated solvents and reduced inorganic compounds serve as donors too. These reactions drive the natural breakdown of organic contaminants by microbes, a major part of the monitored cleanup described in {{ref:soil-env-026}}.

soil-chem-169.title: Microbes that breathe iron instead of oxygen
soil-chem-169.text: Where oxygen runs out in soils and sediments, some microbes breathe metal instead. Dissimilatory metal reduction is a form of {{ref:soil-chem-128}} in which bacteria and archaea use a metal, rather than oxygen, as the terminal electron acceptor. Iron and manganese are the metals most used. Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II) and Mn(IV) to Mn(II), and most Fe(III) reducers can also reduce Mn(IV). Vanadium, chromium(VI), molybdenum, cobalt, palladium, gold and mercury can serve as well. The process runs without oxygen, but the organisms include both strict anaerobes such as the Geobacteraceae and facultative ones such as Shewanella. Their challenge is reach. In near-neutral soils and sediments, iron is held in solid oxidized minerals. So these microbes reduce metals outside the cell, passing electrons out through cytochromes c in their membranes. Some reduce minerals at a distance using electron shuttles, and humic acids common in soils and sediments can act as such shuttles. Many Fe(III) minerals can be reduced, including magnetite, hematite, goethite, lepidocrocite, ferrihydrite, smectite, illite and jarosite. New minerals such as magnetite, siderite, vivianite and the iron hydroxide in {{ref:soil-chem-170}} can form as by-products.

soil-chem-179.title: The hydrogen electrode that defines zero volts
soil-chem-179.text: Every redox potential is measured against one agreed zero. The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference electrode that sets that zero on the thermodynamic scale of oxidation–reduction potentials. Its {{ref:soil-chem-117}} is declared to be zero volts at any temperature, though its absolute potential is estimated at 4.44 ± 0.02 V at 25 °C. The potentials of all other electrodes are compared with it at the same temperature. Soil Eh, for example, is the potential of a platinum electrode measured against it. It is a theoretical ideal-solution standard. It replaced the older normal hydrogen electrode, platinum in 1 N acid with bubbling hydrogen.

soil-chem-175.title: Obligate anaerobes, microbes poisoned by air
soil-chem-175.text: For some microbes, ordinary air is lethal. Obligate anaerobes are microorganisms killed by normal atmospheric concentrations of oxygen. Tolerance varies: some survive up to 8% oxygen, while others lose viability above 0.5%. Oxygen harms them through reactive oxygen species, which aerobes detoxify with enzymes these microbes barely make. They respire sulfate, nitrate, iron or manganese, or ferment, both yielding less ATP than aerobic respiration. Facultative anaerobes, by contrast, use oxygen but survive without it. Obligate anaerobes inhabit deep soil sediments, landfills and still waters; some Mycobacterium and Rhodococcus species, and some of the bacteria in {{ref:soil-bio-225}}, live in soil.

soil-chem-174.title: Methanogens, the methane makers of paddies and bogs
soil-chem-174.text: Wetlands, rice paddies, landfills and animal guts share a population of methane makers. Methanogens are anaerobic archaea that produce methane as a by-product of their energy metabolism. Methanogenesis is their only biochemical pathway for making ATP, and all known methanogens belong to the domain Archaea. They live in oxygen-free settings, including sediments and wastewater plants, and grow at a redox potential below −0.3 V. Their oxygen sensitivity varies, though. Methanogenesis is often detected in temporarily oxygenated soil of the kind described in {{ref:soil-class-160}}, and one wetland and soil species works in anoxic microsites within aerobic soil.

soil-chem-171.title: Iron-oxidizing bacteria and their reddish-brown slime
soil-chem-171.text: Bog iron ore deposits formed where oxygen-free groundwater emerged and met the air. That boundary is home to iron-oxidizing bacteria, chemotrophic bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing dissolved iron. They live where oxygen-free water meets an oxygenated setting, turning dissolved iron into an insoluble reddish-brown slime. They need at least 0.3 ppm dissolved oxygen. Other soil microbes create their habitat: feeding on organic matter dissolved in liquid seeping from landfills or septic fields, they can strip oxygen from groundwater. Some species oxidize Fe(II) without oxygen by coupling it to nitrate reduction, a light-independent metabolism found in sediments including flooded rice soils.

soil-chem-170.title: Green rust, the iron mineral that fades in air
soil-chem-170.text: Some bluish-green soils turn ochre once exposed to air, and green rust is the suspected reason. Green rust is a family of green layered iron(II)–iron(III) hydroxides that hold another anion, such as carbonate, chloride or sulfate, between their layers. In nature it occurs as the mineral fougerite, suspected in soils formed under alternating redox conditions. In oxidizing conditions it generally converts to goethite and lepidocrocite. Iron-reducing bacteria such as Shewanella putrefaciens produce it while oxidizing organic matter, a process thought to occur in soil solutions and aquifers. Sulfate green rust can also reduce nitrate and nitrite to ammonium.

soil-chem-172.title: The manganese cycle, from bedrock to seafloor
soil-chem-172.text: Manganese makes up only about 0.1% of the Earth's crust, yet it never sits still. The manganese cycle is the natural circuit, biological and geological, that moves it through the atmosphere, water, living things, rocks and soils. It is cycled much like iron, but by distinct redox pathways. Bacteria push it both ways. Some oxidize manganese to insoluble oxides, while others reduce it to soluble Mn2+ in order to use it. Weathering of regolith and dissolution of bedrock carry manganese into rivers. From there it travels to the ocean, where it can form minerals and be buried. People now tilt the cycle. Mining, mineral processing and the burning of fossil fuels are altering it globally. Near iron and steel plants in North America and Europe, over half the manganese in ridge soils came from industrial waste and settled airborne particles.

soil-chem-181.title: Solubility equilibrium: dissolving and precipitating in balance
soil-chem-181.text: A crystal resting in its saturated solution looks still, but it is busy. In a solubility equilibrium, a solid compound and its solution exchange material, with dissolution and precipitation going on at equal rates. Each such equilibrium has a temperature-dependent solubility product, which works like an equilibrium constant. Strictly it is a quotient of activities, but it is usually converted to one of concentrations. A solution at equilibrium with undissolved solid is saturated; one holding more solute than its solubility is supersaturated and can precipitate. Acid rain leaching aluminum from soil is dissolution with reaction: aluminosilicates react with the acid to give soluble Al3+.

soil-chem-183.title: Electron activity: redox measured like pH
soil-chem-183.text: Chemists borrowed the logic of pH and applied it to electrons. Electron activity, written pe, is the negative logarithm of electron activity, a dimensionless measure of redox potential. Environmental chemists often prefer it to Eh because it works directly on a logarithmic scale. At 25 °C, pe = Eh/0.05916 = 16.903 × Eh. Environmental values run from −12 to +25, because beyond them water itself is reduced or oxidized. Along with pH, Eh or pe is a master variable in soils, both controlling and governed by chemical and biological reactions. Together, redox potential and pH constrain how soluble manganese is.

soil-chem-180.title: Pourbaix diagrams: maps of what is stable in water
soil-chem-180.text: A Pourbaix diagram plots the thermodynamically stable phases of an aqueous system against Eh or pe and pH. Lines mark the 50/50 boundaries between predominant dissolved species or solids. Water is stable only between two parallel lines, EH = −0.05916 pH and EH = 1.229 V − 0.05916 pH. Outside them it is reduced to hydrogen or oxidized to oxygen. Like a phase diagram, it assumes equilibrium and says nothing about reaction rates. Used in corrosion, geochemistry and environmental science, the diagrams are named after the Belgian engineer Marcel Pourbaix (1904–1998).

soil-chem-173.title: Manganese in soil, a nutrient steered by pH and pe
soil-chem-173.text: In photosynthesis, manganese acts as a catalyst in the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II. That makes it a key soil micronutrient, one whose solubility is set by redox potential and pH. Fungi in soil oxidize soluble Mn2+ and may reprecipitate it as manganese oxides. Much of the soil cycle is biological, though inorganic reactions also oxidize manganese. As pH rises, manganese speciation becomes less sensitive to pe. In acidic soils, at pH 5 with pe above 8, manganese is mostly in reducible forms. There, exchangeable and soluble manganese fall sharply as pe rises.

soil-chem-182.title: Hydromorphic soils, shaped by standing water
soil-chem-182.text: Leave a soil waterlogged long enough and the water starts to shape it. A hydromorphic soil is one formed under such wetland conditions. The 1938 USDA taxonomy listed hydromorphic soils as an intrazonal group. One sub-type was the gley soils, saturated and airless, so that their iron is reduced. The soils described in {{ref:soil-class-137}} form by the accumulation of iron under hydromorphic conditions, and gypcretes can form in these soils, among other settings. Strong zinc sorption can leave hydromorphic soils with little plant-available zinc.

soil-chem-142.title: Alkalinity, a stream's defense against acid
soil-chem-142.text: Some streams can absorb acid inputs; others cannot. Alkalinity is the capacity of water to resist acidification, set by its buffer of weak acids and their conjugate bases. It is not the same as basicity, which is an absolute position on the pH scale. It is measured by titrating with an acid such as HCl to an endpoint, and expressed in meq/L or mg/L as CaCO3. Fresh water on non-limestone terrain is low in alkalinity, which is one of the best measures of a stream's sensitivity to acid. Acid rain from SOx and NOx emissions can change it over the long term.

soil-chem-143.title: Electrolytic conductivity, a quick read on salt
soil-chem-143.text: Sea water conducts electricity far better than drinking water: about 50 mS/cm against a typical 200–800 μS/cm. Electrolytic conductivity measures how well a solution of ions conducts electricity, and so gauges how much dissolved salt it holds. Its SI unit is the siemens per meter (S/m). Measuring it is a fast, cheap and reliable way to find a solution's ionic content. It is often linked directly to total dissolved solids.

soil-chem-141.title: Saltwater intrusion: the sea creeping into aquifers
soil-chem-141.text: Along coasts, the sea presses inland underground. Saltwater intrusion is the movement of saline water into freshwater aquifers, degrading groundwater quality. It happens naturally, because denser saline water pushes inland beneath the fresh water. Pumping from coastal freshwater wells lowers the fresh groundwater's pressure and lets saltwater flow further inland. Agricultural and drainage channels, sea level rise and storm surges drive it too. Seawater moving into rivers can harm agriculture in upstream areas.

soil-chem-137.title: Halotolerance: living with more salt than needed
soil-chem-137.text: Salt pulls water out of living cells. Halotolerance is the ability of an organism to live in salt concentrations above those it needs for growth. Halotolerant bacteria, archaea and fungi live in saline waters and soils; unlike halophiles, they do not need high salinity. High salt upsets ionic balance, impairing respiration and photosynthesis and slowing growth or killing sensitive plants. Because salinity brings both osmotic and ionic stress, tolerant organisms retain water and sequester salt. Halotolerant bacteria can even remediate saline soil, lowering its sodium content and sodium adsorption ratio and degrading toxic compounds.

soil-chem-140.title: Road salt: winter safety that lingers in the soil
soil-chem-140.text: Millions of tons of salt are spread on roads each year, making it one of the most widely used chemicals in urban infrastructure. Sodium chloride is the most common form; calcium and magnesium chlorides are used too, especially in colder weather. The salt does not leave with the ice. Its chloride persists in soils, surface waters and groundwater, harming aquatic life, roadside vegetation and drinking water. In roadside soils the build-up raises salinity, hindering plant growth, killing sensitive species and adding to erosion.

soil-chem-139.title: The Van Genuchten–Gupta curve of yield against salt
soil-chem-139.text: As soil grows saltier, the yield of a crop traces an inverted S. The Van Genuchten–Gupta model describes that curve. It is named after Martinus Theodore van Genuchten and Satyandra K. Gupta, from their work in the 1990s. Yield is Y = Ym / (1 + (C/C50)^P). Ym is maximum yield, C the soil salt concentration, C50 the concentration giving 50% yield and P a fitted exponent. A logistic S-function or a cubic regression of yield on soil salt concentration can be used instead.

soil-chem-138.title: Critical loads: how much acid rain a landscape can bear
soil-chem-138.text: How much acid can a landscape take before it is harmed? A critical load answers with a number. It is the pollutant exposure below which, as far as is known, significant harm to specified sensitive parts of the environment does not occur. Most work has centered on sulfur deposition and on {{ref:soil-fert-124}}, which can acidify soils and surface waters. They strip calcium from soil and release toxic aluminum, harming plants and animals. Deposition above the critical load is an exceedance, putting the biota at greater risk. In Europe, a sensitive element is tied to a chemical criterion, such as a soil base cation to aluminum ratio of Bc/Al = 1. A mass balance model then gives the deposition that reaches it. Today a two-dimensional function is often calculated, with nitrogen on one axis and sulfur on the other. Empirical critical loads come from observed ecosystem responses; steady-state ones come from models that can include soil chemistry and mineral weathering rates. The concept says nothing about how long effects take to appear, so target load functions add a time dimension.

soil-chem-136.title: Biosaline agriculture: farming land too salty for crops
soil-chem-136.text: Soil salinization from poor irrigation helped bring down the civilizations of Mesopotamia, from 2400 BC to 1700 BC. The problem has only spread. Salinization affects an estimated one billion hectares worldwide, with another one million hectares added each year. Salinity affects one quarter of the world's arable cropland, and that share is projected to double by 2050. Biosaline agriculture turns salt into a growing condition rather than a dead end. It grows plants with saline groundwater or on saline soil, using salt-tolerant plants to farm land too salty for ordinary crops. Halophytes are its cornerstone, used for food, forage, medicine, biofuel and restoring salty land. Irrigating with high-salinity water eases pressure on scarce fresh water, especially in arid and semi-arid regions. Repeated cycles of halophyte growth can restore degraded soil and water, and the plants accumulate heavy metals too. The field was formalized in the late 1990s, with the International Center for Biosaline Agriculture founded in 1996.

soil-chem-144.title: Manganese toxicity, when acid soil poisons plants
soil-chem-144.text: Acid soil can turn a micronutrient into a poison. Manganese toxicity is the poisoning of plants by manganese that becomes soluble at low soil pH. Together with aluminum toxicity, it is a serious problem in the soils described in {{ref:soil-class-118}}, whose low pH makes normally insoluble metals soluble enough to harm intolerant plants. It may occur in strongly acidic horizons, especially when they are waterlogged. Spreading finely ground limestone or dolomite, the practice in {{ref:soil-fert-055}}, brings acid soil near neutral and reduces both aluminum and manganese toxicity.

soil-class-001.title: Putting the world's soils in order
soil-class-001.text: Long before modern science, priests in Egypt were sorting soils. Inscriptions at the temple of Horus at Edfu record a soil classification used to choose temple sites, and ancient Greek scholars devised several more. Soil classification is the systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used. Modern systems group soils by measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed. Soil science, engineering and environmental management all classify soils, to judge their properties and decide on suitable land use. Soil can be treated as a material, as geotechnical engineers do when judging foundations and building material, or as a resource. The major modern systems include {{ref:soil-class-006}}, the {{ref:soil-class-016}} and engineering systems that judge stability and performance, met in {{ref:soil-class-002}}. Standard systems matter because they let soils be compared across regions and uses. Knowledge of where soils occur has also grown dramatically. The project of {{ref:soil-meth-017}} now maps soils worldwide at 1.00–0.25 km resolution, built from soil profiles and environmental data. Still, the subject keeps moving. The structure of systems, the definitions of classes and their use in the field all continue to change.

soil-class-016.title: World Reference Base: one name for a soil everywhere
soil-class-016.text: A soil can carry the same name all over the world, in English and with capital letters. That is the promise of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources, or WRB, an international system for naming soils and building soil-map legends. A working group of the {{ref:soil-hist-047}} edits it. It grew out of the {{ref:soil-class-021}} and the union's International Reference Base project. Its first edition appeared in 1998, at the world congress of soil scientists in Montpellier. That year the ISSS endorsed it as its correlation system, and it replaced the FAO scheme as the international standard. The U.S. system, {{ref:soil-class-006}}, became a correlation system too in 2014. Further editions followed in 2006, 2014, updated in 2015, and 2022; the current fourth edition is open access under a Creative Commons license. The system has just two levels. At the top sit 32 {{ref:soil-class-020}}, each refined by adding qualifiers, of which there are 202. Classes rest mainly on soil morphology, from field and laboratory data, read as an expression of how the soil formed. The climate of the soil counts only as a soil-forming factor, never as a soil characteristic. The two-level design resembles the French {{ref:soil-class-035}}, whereas the U.S. system is strongly hierarchical with six levels. The WRB is not meant to replace national systems, which may be more detailed for their own areas. The European Union uses it.

soil-class-005.title: Soil type, the word many systems avoid
soil-class-005.text: Few terms in soil science are so common, or so slippery. A soil type is a taxonomic unit: all the soils that share a defined set of properties. In hierarchical systems it usually sits at a higher or intermediate level, split into subtypes and combined into higher categories. The first U.S. classification, by Whitney in 1909, did the reverse: there the soil type was the lowest level and the mapping unit. Systems also disagree on what defines a type. German soil systematics uses mainly features made by soil formation. The WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}} add traits inherited from the parent material, and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} ignores origin. Horizons make a convenient basis, but some young soils lack clear ones, so types may rest on whole-profile properties. The WRB, for instance, defines one group by sand content alone. Many systems also define types that reflect human activity. Because the word is so general, many systems avoid it. In early U.S. mapping, 'soil type' was the original name of the soil phase, which records surface texture, slope, stoniness, saltiness and erosion.

soil-class-006.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series
soil-class-006.text: The United States sorts its soils into 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series. USDA soil taxonomy is the classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the National Cooperative Soil Survey. It sorts soils by their properties into six levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series. The lab manual describes it as a quantitative hierarchy running from 12 broad orders to more than 23,000 series, and says it helps carry management research between similar soils worldwide. Sources differ on the series count: the more than 14,000 above is the United States figure. It uses properties that can be measured: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content. It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and soil management, and it supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units. Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed. It builds on {{ref:soil-class-001}}, {{ref:soil-class-005}}, {{ref:soil-found-001}} and {{ref:soil-form-017}}. Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system. Work began by 1945. A series of approximations followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.

soil-class-021.title: The FAO map legend that became a world system
soil-class-021.text: The first truly international soil classification began life as the key to a map. The FAO soil classification, developed by the Food and Agriculture Organization, is a supra-national system that generalizes how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors. It started as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO map of the world's soils, published from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend. It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with soil phases, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock were called {{ref:soil-class-040}}. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-023.title: Canada's system, built for cool-climate soils
soil-class-023.text: Canada classifies its soils with a system closer to the U.S. one than any other, yet built to cover only Canadian soils. Introduced in 1955, it was designed to separate soils formed by soil-forming processes in cool climates. Earlier Canadian work had used U.S.-like systems. It has five levels: order, great group, subgroup, family and series. It drops the suborder, and it separates sodium-affected and waterlogged soils at the order level, as the {{ref:soil-class-029}} and the {{ref:soil-class-028}}. Ten orders sit at the top. Below them, 31 great groups reflect differences in how the soils formed. The unit classified is the pedon, a 3-dimensional body of soil commonly 1 meter across and 1 to 2 meters deep. A key sorts it using horizon thickness, Munsell color and pH. Subgroups follow the sequence of horizons and often intergrade toward other orders. Families add parent material and the climate of the soil. A series name such as Breton implies all the properties of its order, great group, subgroup and family, which supports many judgments of land suitability. Class limits are arbitrary, since nature has few sharp breaks in the soil continuum. The system changes as mapping and research add knowledge, and recent research proposes a new order for soils that are shallow or over bedrock.

soil-class-022.title: Australia's fifteen orders for an old, weathered land
soil-class-022.text: Australia's soils needed names of their own, many of them shaped by an arid, strongly weathered continent. The Australian Soil Classification is the general-purpose, hierarchical system now used to describe and classify them. It has five levels: order, suborder, great group, subgroup and family. Ray Isbell, a retired CSIRO soil scientist, developed it and first published it in 1996. Later editions came in 2002, 2010 and March 2021. It superseded the Factual Key of 1960 and the {{ref:soil-class-046}} of 1968. Since Isbell's death in 2001, the National Committee on Soil and Terrain has led its updates. Its fifteen orders run from {{ref:soil-class-044}} and Calcarosols to Sodosols, Tenosols and Vertosols. In seven orders, suborders name the dominant color of the upper B2 horizon: Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey or Black. One of those orders is {{ref:soil-found-070}}, so a soil there takes a color and an order as its name. Other orders have their own suborders. Hydrosols, for instance, split into Intertidal, Supratidal, Salic, Redoxic and other Hydrosols. The system defines soil types without asking whether their properties result from soil formation. Some names translate directly: soils called {{ref:soil-class-098}} elsewhere are Organosols here, and the {{ref:soil-class-138}} becomes the Podosol.

soil-class-002.title: How engineers classify soil to build on it
soil-class-002.text: To an engineer, soil is a material to build on or to build with. Engineering soil classification groups soils by the properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material. Modern systems are designed to move easily from field observations to basic predictions of how a soil will behave. In North America the most common is the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS. It and the fuller engineering description are standardized in ASTM D 2487. Europe's standard, {{ref:soil-class-152}}, closely resembles the USCS but codes soils differently. It also adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays. In the United States, the {{ref:soil-class-036}} rates soils and aggregates for pavement construction. The Modified Burmister system works like the USCS but codes more properties. Moderately organic soils count as subdivisions of silts and clays. They are told apart by how their plasticity and Atterberg limits change on drying. A full geotechnical description goes further than any code. It adds color, moisture and strength in place, and more detail about the material than the USCS code carries.

soil-class-003.title: Natural classes and technical classes
soil-class-003.text: A soil can be classified for what it is, or for what it is good for. Natural systems group soils by their intrinsic properties, behavior or genesis. Technical systems group them by fitness for a particular use. Experience shows that natural classes can be interpreted for many different uses. Some natural systems, such as the French {{ref:soil-class-035}}, rest on presumed soil genesis. USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB use morphology and laboratory tests as the criteria for their hierarchical classes. Each system's approach reflects its own ideas of how soils form and of which features matter for land use. In U.S. soil mapping the two kinds meet. Map units classed by soil taxonomy are also sorted into technical classes such as Land Capability Classes, {{ref:soil-water-119}} and {{ref:soil-agri-088}}. A third route is numerical classification, or ordination. It groups soil individuals by multivariate statistics such as cluster analysis, producing natural groups without any inference about genesis.

soil-class-011.title: Moisture regimes: how wet a soil stays all year
soil-class-011.text: A desert soil may stay moist for less than 90 consecutive days; a waterlogged soil may sit saturated and almost airless. A soil moisture regime is a class describing how wet a soil stays through the year, defined by the groundwater table and the water available to plants. It often reflects climate, and it is a major control on the productivity of land ecosystems, farms included. In USDA soil taxonomy, regime names modify soil names at the suborder level. Aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling; they are common in {{ref:soil-water-124}} areas. At the other end, aridic soils are dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days, as in deserts. Soils of the {{ref:soil-found-101}} stay moist enough for plants year-round in most years and are common in humid regions. Between that regime and aridic soils lies the {{ref:soil-class-041}} regime. There moisture is usually available in the growing season, but severe droughts occur; such soils are common in semi-arid regions. Xeric soils belong to Mediterranean-type climates, with cool, moist winters and long summer droughts.

soil-class-012.title: The 1938 U.S. system and its three orders
soil-class-012.text: Before modern soil taxonomy, the United States sorted soils by what had made them. The 1938 system divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors. It grew from Curtis Marbut's scheme, begun in 1920, which became the 1935 system. Modified, it was published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture, Soils and Men. Its {{ref:soil-class-015}} order reflected climate and vegetation. Its {{ref:soil-class-013}} order reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them. At the top level, soils were split into carbonate-rich pedocals of drier climates and the {{ref:soil-class-042}} group, rich in aluminum and iron. Its root 'alfer' later became part of a modern order name, {{ref:soil-class-090}}. The 1938 scheme was a strictly natural system, and after 1938 classifying individual series under it met with mixed success. Work on a replacement began by 1945.

soil-class-004.title: OSHA soil types: keeping trench walls standing
soil-class-004.text: On a U.S. building site, three letters decide how a trench wall is held back. The OSHA soil classification is a U.S. workplace-safety scheme that sorts soils by strength, so that excavations and trenches can be protected against collapse. It uses three soil types plus stable rock. Type A soils are cohesive and plastic, with unconfined compressive strength above 1.5 tsf (144 kPa). Type B lies between 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) and 1.5 tsf. Type C falls below 0.5 tsf, or is granular or seeping. The lateral earth pressure each type induces rises from 25 psf per foot of depth for Type A to 45 for Type B and 80 for Type C. Each type dictates sloping, shoring or shielding, for safety rather than for the study of soil formation.

soil-class-017.title: The diagnostic toolkit behind every WRB name
soil-class-017.text: Every soil name in the WRB rests on a checklist of named features. These are its diagnostics: diagnostic horizons, diagnostic properties and diagnostic materials. Diagnostic horizons are typical products of soil formation with a minimum thickness, so they form a recognizable layer. Diagnostic properties are typical results of soil-forming processes, or they reflect particular conditions of soil formation. Diagnostic materials influence or indicate soil formation, and they may be inherited from the parent material or produced by soil formation. Each has a name, such as argic horizon, stagnic properties or fluvic material. Organic carbon draws one boundary. Mineral material has less than 20% organic carbon; organic material has 20% or more. Diagnostic horizons entered the international system from the 1960 '7th approximation' of USDA soil taxonomy, by way of the FAO legend. Only the diagnostic criteria decide whether a diagnostic is present in a soil.

soil-class-020.title: The 32 Reference Soil Groups, in the order of the key
soil-class-020.text: The WRB sorts the world's soils into just 32 top-level classes, and it always lists them in the same order. These are the Reference Soil Groups, each with a two-letter code, arranged as the key runs. The key opens with {{ref:soil-class-098}}, soils with thick organic layers. Then come soils under strong human influence: the long and intensively farmed {{ref:soil-class-120}} and the artefact-rich {{ref:soil-class-145}}. Next are groups that limit root growth, with permafrost, thin or stony ground, a sodium-rich clayey subsoil, shrink–swell clays or soluble salts. Eight groups are set apart by iron and aluminum chemistry, among them the {{ref:soil-class-127}} and the {{ref:soil-class-138}}. Four have organic-rich mineral topsoils, led by the {{ref:soil-class-123}}. Three more accumulate secondary silica, gypsum or carbonates. Clay-enriched subsoils mark five groups, split by clay activity and by whether exchangeable aluminum exceeds base cations. The key ends with little-differentiated soils: moderately developed, built of stratified sediments, very sandy, or with no significant development at all. Group names are plural in map legends and singular everywhere else.

soil-class-010.title: Temperature regimes, measured 50 cm down
soil-class-010.text: A soil temperature regime is a class set by mean annual and seasonal temperatures 50 cm below the surface, used to classify soils in USDA soil taxonomy. Mean annual soil temperature is normally taken as mean annual air temperature plus 2 °C. Classes run from pergelic, about −8 to −4 °C, through subgelic to frigid, about 0 to 8 °C. Mesic covers 8 to 15 °C, thermic 15 to 22 °C, and hyperthermic 22 °C or higher. Where summer and winter means differ by less than 6 °C, 'iso' is added to the name. Frigid, mesic and thermic classify soils at lower levels; the cryic regime separates some higher-level groups.

soil-class-007.title: Suborders and great groups: the second and third rungs
soil-class-007.text: Xeralfs, Durixeralfs, Abruptic Durixeralfs: each added piece of the name moves a soil one level down. Suborders, the second level of USDA soil taxonomy, split each order by properties tied to soil moisture and temperature. Moisture regime names act as modifiers at this level. Great groups, the third level, split suborders by the kind and sequence of horizons. Horizons marked by clay, iron, humus or hardpans tell them apart, as do self-mixing shrink–swell clays, temperature and large amounts of salts. In the United States, forty-seven suborders and about 185 great groups are recognized. The great group Durixeralfs, for instance, holds the subgroup Abruptic Durixeralfs, which includes the San Joaquin series.

soil-class-008.title: Typic, intergrade, extragrade: the subgroup level
soil-class-008.text: Every great group has its textbook soils, its borderline soils and its misfits. The fourth level of USDA soil taxonomy, the subgroup, names each kind. A typic subgroup carries the basic, typical concept of its great group. An intergrade subgroup has properties grading toward another great group, suborder or order, but not strongly enough to place it there. Extragrade subgroups have aberrant properties that keep them out of any other class. About 1,000 subgroups are defined in the United States.

soil-class-009.title: Soil families: grouping soils by how they behave
soil-class-009.text: 'Fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, calcareous, Typic Torrifluvents' is not a list. It is the name of one soil family. The family is the fifth level of USDA soil taxonomy: soils within a subgroup that share the physical and chemical properties governing their response to farming and engineering. Families are told apart by texture, mineralogy, pH, permeability, structure, consistency, precipitation pattern and soil temperature. Sometimes the percentages of silt, sand and coarse fragments count too. About 4,500 families are recognized in the United States, and each may contain several series. The family above belongs to the suborder Fluvents and includes the Jocity series.

soil-class-037.title: Soil series: named for a town, mapped across states
soil-class-037.text: Haugan, Montana, gave its name to a soil. A soil series is named after a town or landmark near where it was first recognized, yet a series such as Hagerstown can range across several states. The series is the lowest level of USDA soil taxonomy. It groups pedons with similar pedogenesis, soil chemistry and physical properties. Their horizons match in color, texture, structure, pH, consistency, composition and arrangement in the profile, so the soils perform alike for land use. The concept dates from 1903. Series were then meant as soils alike in origin, from the same kind of rock or sediment, but differing in texture. More than 14,000 series are recognized in the United States, the most homogeneous classes in the taxonomy; another source counts even more. A series can mean two things. As a taxonomic unit it is the conceptual core of a class. As a mapping unit it outlines similar soils on the land, and the two need not fully coincide. Map units carry the name of their dominant series. In Greenbrier County, West Virginia, unit LhE is 80% Lily series, and the rest is Dekalb, Berks and less stony soils.

soil-class-038.title: State soils, official emblems like flowers and birds
soil-class-038.text: North Carolina's state soil, the Cecil, runs from Virginia to Alabama. A state soil is one that a U.S. state has chosen as having special significance to it. Every state has selected one, and twenty have been established by law, giving them the same standing as official state flowers and birds. Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands have chosen representative soils too. California picked San Joaquin in 1997, Oklahoma named Port Silt Loam in 1987, and Illinois chose Drummer in 2001.

soil-class-039.title: What a vineyard asks of its soil
soil-class-039.text: The best vineyard soil is thin. Vineyard soils are the soils in which grapevines grow, and their make-up is one of the most important considerations in planting a vineyard. Soil anchors the vine's roots and governs drainage and the minerals and nutrients the vine receives. The ideal is thin topsoil and subsoil that hold enough water yet drain well, so roots are not waterlogged. Soil that stores or reflects heat also affects ripening. Growers name soils by rock or texture. Limestone-based Kimmeridgian soil is the principal type of the Loire Valley, Champagne and Burgundy. Sandy soils drain well but hold water poorly, and the phylloxera louse does not thrive in them.

soil-found-101.title: Udic soils: moist enough, most years
soil-found-101.text: In humid climates, water moves down through the soil at some time in most years. The udic moisture regime belongs to such climates, where stored moisture plus rainfall roughly equals or exceeds evapotranspiration, the water lost from soil and plants to the air. In USDA soil taxonomy, udic soils are moist enough year-round in most years to meet plant needs. Drier soils fall into the {{ref:soil-class-041}} regime, between udic and aridic. Suborders with a udic regime include udalfs, part of {{ref:soil-class-090}}; udepts, part of {{ref:soil-class-100}}; and udolls, part of {{ref:soil-class-101}}.

soil-class-036.title: AASHTO groups: rating the soil beneath a road
soil-class-036.text: One sieve, with openings of 0.075 mm, splits road soils into two camps. The AASHTO Soil Classification System is an American highway-engineering system for soils and soil–aggregate mixtures used in road construction. Hogentogler and Terzaghi first developed it in 1929, and it has been revised several times since. Soils with 35% or less passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve are granular materials; those with more are silt–clay materials. Groups run from A-1 to A-7. They are set by sieve results and by the liquid limit and plasticity index of the fraction passing 0.425 mm (No. 40). As road subgrade, granular materials rate excellent to good, and silt–clay materials fair to poor.

soil-class-018.title: Naming a soil the WRB way, one qualifier at a time
soil-class-018.text: A WRB soil name can read like a short description. The WRB builds it in two steps: key the soil out to a Reference Soil Group, then add every qualifier that applies. The key asks, in a fixed sequence, whether given diagnostics occur in given depth ranges, plus traits such as clay content. The soil goes to the first group whose criteria it meets. Principal qualifiers precede the group name, the highest-ranked closest to it, and Haplic is used if none applies. Supplementary qualifiers follow in brackets. Specifiers such as Epi-, for 0 to 50 cm, and Endo-, for below 50 cm, turn qualifiers into depth-related subqualifiers such as Epiarenic. In the worked example, a loess soil with clay migration becomes an Amphialbic Endostagnic soil of the {{ref:soil-class-133}} group, with supplementary qualifiers such as Anosiltic, Endoloamic and Aric.

soil-class-019.title: How map scale sets the length of a WRB name
soil-class-019.text: A map of soils has room for only so many words. The WRB's rules for naming map units make the number of qualifiers depend on the map's scale. Three scale levels use the Reference Soil Group alone, the group plus its first applying principal qualifier, or the group plus the first two. Matching these levels to actual map scales is difficult, because the choice depends on how uniform the landscape is. Each map unit names an association of soils. Dominant soils cover at least 50%, codominant soils 25 to 50% and associated soils 5 to 25%; smaller shares are ignored. Only the third and later editions can build map legends; the second edition could only name soils.

soil-class-045.title: The argillic horizon, where washed-down clay collects
soil-class-045.text: In 44% of U.S. soil series, a 2014 study by James Bockheim found a clay-enriched layer below the surface. That layer is the argillic horizon, the USDA soil taxonomy term for a subsurface horizon enriched in clay. Clay builds up mainly by illuviation, the downward washing of existing clay, while some forms in place. To qualify, the horizon needs at least 1.2 times the clay of any overlying eluvial horizon. It usually shows clay films or bridges visible by eye or hand lens. It is a diagnostic horizon used to define higher categories. The orders in {{ref:soil-class-090}} and {{ref:soil-class-104}} require it, those in {{ref:soil-class-098}} and {{ref:soil-class-094}} never have it, and other orders vary. It is the starting point for kandic horizons, dominated by low-CEC 1:1 clays, and for natric horizons, rich in exchangeable sodium. Fragipans commonly form within it. The WRB equivalent is the argic horizon, from the same Latin root argilla; it needs at least 8% clay and a texture class other than sand. Buried paleo-argillic horizons, as in the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon, show that the climate was once hot and wet enough to form them.

soil-class-040.title: Rankers: a thin topsoil straight on rock
soil-class-040.text: Some soils are little more than a topsoil laid directly on unaltered rock. A ranker is a soil developed over non-calcareous material, usually rock. It is often called an A/C soil, because its topsoil, the A horizon, sits directly on unaltered parent material, the C horizon. Some classifications group it as lithomorphic, together with the {{ref:soil-class-050}}, the similar soil over calcareous material. In the 1974 FAO legend, thin soils on acid rock were called Rankers. The {{ref:soil-class-034}} keeps rankers as a type of weakly developed soil, matched to the WRB's {{ref:soil-class-139}} group and to USDA Udorthents and Udifolists.

soil-class-041.title: Ustic soils: water, but not always enough
soil-class-041.text: In Brazil's Cerrado, a long dry season gives farmers a wide harvest window, and they harvest grain at a leisurely pace. That dry season marks the ustic regime, in which water is present but limited at times when conditions suit plant growth. It lies between aridic and udic. The name comes from Latin ustus, 'burnt', and the regime is common in semi-arid and sub-humid climates. Averaged over the year, stored moisture plus rainfall is less than the water lost by evapotranspiration. Ustic soils suit drought-tolerant crops. Maize there generally needs supplemental watering, which udic soils do not require.

soil-class-034.title: Poland's soil system and its three-part description
soil-class-034.text: Poland describes every soil three ways at once. The Polish Soil Classification is the system used to describe, classify and organize knowledge about the country's soils. Each soil gets a type, from its genesis and diagnostic horizons; a kind, the geological origin of the bedrock; and a texture class. The type is the basic unit, and types are grouped into orders by the presence or absence of diagnostic horizons and properties. The {{ref:soil-hist-057}} published editions in 1956, 1959, 1974, 1989, 2011 and 2019. Early ones followed Dokuchaev's natural criteria; the 2011 edition defined diagnostic horizons, materials and properties quantitatively. It borrows much from USDA soil taxonomy (1999) and the WRB (2006) and gives equivalents. Its rusty soils, sandy soils with rusty horizons, match WRB Arenosols and the U.S. {{ref:soil-class-108}} soils.

soil-class-043.title: Miami, Indiana's state soil on glacial till
soil-class-043.text: Some 794,994 acres (3,217 km2) of Indiana are mapped as one soil series, the Miami. It belongs to the Wisconsin Till Plains and is Indiana's state soil. It formed under native hardwood forest, in up to 18 inches (46 cm) of loess or silty material over calcareous loamy till. The fertile, gently sloping soils grow corn, soybeans and winter wheat, and they help rank the state in farm output. USDA soil taxonomy classifies it as fine-loamy, mixed, active, mesic Oxyaquic Hapludalfs, a member of the order in {{ref:soil-class-090}}. It is an old series: by 1906 it already held 16 soil types from glaciated regions.

soil-class-042.title: Pedalfers, the iron-and-aluminum soils of 1938
soil-class-042.text: At the top of Marbut's classification stood two camps: carbonate-rich pedocals and pedalfers. In the 1938 U.S. system, pedalfers were a major group of soils rich in aluminum and iron. In them, sesquioxides increase relative to silica as the soil forms. Pedalfers were a subdivision of the zonal order. They began at about the udic border, and lateritic soils were one of their three subdivisions. The term is no longer used in U.S. soil classification, but it survives in college geology texts. Its 'alf' lives on in the name of the order in {{ref:soil-class-090}}.

soil-class-032.title: Brunisolic soils, Canada's in-between order
soil-class-032.text: Almost 790,000 square kilometers of Canada, 8.6% of the country, is covered by soils that fit no other order. These are Brunisolic soils: soils with developed B horizons that meet the requirements of none of the other orders. They occur in all regions south of the permafrost zone. Many have brownish B horizons, without the clay build-up of {{ref:soil-class-031}} soils or the amorphous material of {{ref:soil-class-027}} soils. Some evolve into one or the other. Four great groups follow the A horizon and acidity. Melanic Brunisols have an Ah at least 10 cm thick and pH above 5.5, and Sombric Brunisols a thick Ah below pH 5.5. Eutric and Dystric Brunisols lack a thick Ah.

soil-class-025.title: Canadian Organic soils: the peatland order
soil-class-025.text: Organic soils cover almost 374,000 km2 (4.1%) of Canada, with large areas in Manitoba, Ontario and northern Alberta. They are the Canadian order of soils made mostly of organic matter, over 30% by weight in the upper half metre, without permafrost near the surface. They are the main soils of peatlands such as swamps, bogs and fens, mostly built from plants of waterlogged ground. Some come from lake deposits or forest litter on rainy, rocky slopes. Four great groups follow decomposition. Little-decomposed soils with over 40% fibre, mostly from Sphagnum, are Fibrisols. Others have 10-40% or up to 10% fibre, and a fourth group is thick forest-litter soils over rock. Wetland soils with an O horizon at least 40 cm thick are Organic. With less than 40 cm or none they are Gleysolic. See {{ref:soil-class-023}}, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and {{ref:soil-bio-114}}.

soil-class-030.title: Chernozemic soils of Canada's southern grasslands
soil-class-030.text: Decaying grass roots darken the topsoil across the grassy southern Interior Plains of Canada. These are Chernozemic soils, the Canadian order of grassland soils whose A horizon is darkened by organic matter. The A horizon is neutral to slightly acid and rich in bases such as calcium. The C horizon usually holds lime and may hold gypsum. With mean annual soil temperatures above 0 °C, these soils cover more than 4% of Canada. Four great groups follow surface color and dryness: Brown soils in the driest areas, Dark Brown soils, thick-topped Black soils under tall grass, and transitional Dark Gray soils.

soil-class-024.title: Cryosolic soils, frozen beneath 40% of Canada
soil-class-024.text: About 40% of Canada sits on soils with permafrost close below the surface. The Cryosolic order holds soils with permafrost within 1 meter of the surface, or 2 meters if strongly churned by frost. They cover about 3,672,000 square kilometers and dominate much of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. Because permafrost blocks roots and water, the seasonally thawed {{ref:soil-env-146}} above it can turn saturated and semifluid in spring. Disturbing the boreal forest or tundra cover melts ground ice. The thawing soil can then slide and settle, disrupting roads, pipelines and buildings. The order was defined in 1973 after surveys in the Mackenzie Valley. Its three great groups are Turbic Cryosols, mixed by cryoturbation; Static Cryosols, on sandy or gravelly material; and Organic Cryosols, rich in plant remains.

soil-class-028.title: Gleysolic soils: gray ground where water lingers
soil-class-028.text: Flood a soil warmer than about 5 °C, and microbes use up its oxygen within days. Nitrate and ferric oxide are then reduced, and losing ferric oxide turns the soil gray. When it dries, reoxidized iron forms yellow-brown mottles. Poor drainage and a drab gray color therefore identify the Gleysolic order: Canadian soils periodically or permanently saturated with water and depleted of oxygen. They cover about 117,000 square kilometers, 1.3% of Canada, in depressions and level areas of subhumid and humid climates. Three great groups are defined: the Humic group, with a dark organic A horizon; a plain group, without one; and the Luvic group, with a clay-enriched B horizon.

soil-class-031.title: Luvisolic soils, where clay moves down under forest
soil-class-031.text: Under forest, clay can leave one layer of a soil and settle in the next. The Luvisolic order holds Canadian soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon, where the washed-down clay has been deposited. They typically form under forest, in subhumid to humid climates where the parent material holds appreciable clay. In saline or calcareous material, salts and carbonates leach out before the clay moves. Luvisolic soils cover about 809,000 square kilometers, 8.8% of Canada, largely in the central to northern Interior Plains. Two great groups split by soil temperature. The Gray Brown group, at 8 °C or more, lies in the Great Lakes–St Lawrence Lowlands; the Gray group belongs to the boreal Interior Plains.

soil-class-027.title: Podzolic soils under Canada's conifers
soil-class-027.text: Organic acids from forest litter can free iron and aluminum and carry them down through a soil. The result is the Podzolic order: acid soils whose B horizon accumulates amorphous humified organic matter bound to aluminum and iron. These soils form mostly in sandy materials under forest or shrubs in cold, humid climates. Percolating water leaches bases. The metal–organic complexes become insoluble and settle in the B horizon once the metals reach a critical proportion. Podzolic soils occupy 14.3% of Canada, in the Appalachian Uplands, the Canadian Shield and British Columbia, usually under coniferous forest. Great groups follow the B horizon. The Humic group is low in iron, the Ferro-Humic group holds at least 5% organic carbon, and the Humo-Ferric group, the commonest, holds less than 5%.

soil-class-033.title: Regosolic soils, too young for layers
soil-class-033.text: Some soils still look much like the material they came from. The Regosolic order holds Canada's weakly developed soils, whose properties are essentially those of their parent material. They support plants but have not been stable long enough to develop well-differentiated horizons. The name joins Greek rhēgos, 'blanket', with Latin solum, 'soil'. These soils cover about 0.8% of Canada. Two great groups are defined: one made essentially of C horizons, and a humic one with an Ah horizon at least 10 cm thick.

soil-class-029.title: Solonetzic soils, rock-hard when dry, sticky when wet
soil-class-029.text: Some Canadian subsoils are very hard when dry and swell into a sticky, compact mass when wet. Sodium is the reason. Its ions make the clay disperse and swell on wetting, closing large pores and stopping water flow. Soils with such a B horizon form the Solonetzic order, which usually develops in saline parent materials of semiarid and subhumid regions. It covers almost 73,000 square kilometers, 0.7% of Canada, mostly in southern Alberta. As leaching moves salts and sodium downward, the soil develops from saline parent material through two sodium-rich stages to a final, leached stage called Solod. Resalinization can reverse the sequence.

soil-class-026.title: Vertisolic soils, churned by their own clay
soil-class-026.text: Some clay soils turn themselves over. In the Vertisolic order, clay-rich soils shrink and swell markedly as they dry and wet. The movement cuts shiny slickensides in the subsoil, mixes former surface material downward, and prevents or scrambles subsurface horizons. These soils form mainly in clayey materials of the semiarid to subhumid Interior Plains and cover less than 1% of Canada. The order was recognized in the 1990s, after studies of Great Plains pedons. Its two great groups are told apart by the darkness of the A horizon, the darker one being humic.

soil-class-044.title: Anthroposols, soils that people built or remade
soil-class-044.text: An Anthroposol is a soil profoundly modified or constructed by people, with one or more natural horizons altered, removed or replaced. Such soils occur on industrial, commercial, urban and resource-extraction sites, and along transport, fuel and power corridors. Classification systems long left them out, because criteria built for natural soils often do not apply. A proposed Canadian order requires a disturbed D horizon at least 10 cm thick, or removed natural horizons. Its great groups would be set by artefacts or organic carbon, and ordinary plowing does not qualify. The WRB splits such soils into two groups: long-cultivated {{ref:soil-class-120}} soils and {{ref:soil-class-145}} soils holding industrial products and artefacts. Australia's system also has an Anthroposol order.

soil-found-070.title: Kurosols: a light topsoil over acid clay
soil-found-070.text: In eastern and southern Australia, many soils change abruptly a short way down. Kurosols are one of the fifteen orders of the Australian Soil Classification: soils with a sharp texture contrast between a lighter surface and a strongly acidic, clay-rich subsoil. The upper B horizon sets them apart from other texture-contrast orders. It is strongly acidic in kurosols, sodic in sodosols, and neither in chromosols. That acidic subsoil generally has a pH below 5.5 measured in water. Kurosols are widespread in higher-rainfall, strongly leached and weathered landscapes. The dense clay and the acidity can restrict roots and water and cause aluminum and manganese toxicity. Lime corrects surface acidity, but deep acidity is hard to fix.

soil-class-035.title: France's Référentiel pédologique
soil-class-035.text: France names its soils with words like Colluviosol, Fluviosol and Reductisol. These belong to the Référentiel pédologique, the French soil reference system, a natural classification based on presumed soil genesis. Like the WRB, it has two hierarchical levels. Versions appeared in 1992, 1995 and 2008. Its reference soil types, relevant to European soils, include Brunisol, Calcarisol, Colluviosol, Fluviosol, Podzosol and Reductisol, refined by terms such as humic or typic.

soil-class-047.title: Greyzem, the grey earth of the FAO system
soil-class-047.text: A Greyzem's name is half English, half Russian: 'grey' plus zemlja, 'earth'. This soil group of the FAO soil classification is named for the uncoated silt and quartz grains in its organic-rich layers. It forms in decalcified loose deposits such as wind-blown, river and lake sediments and glacial till. With {{ref:soil-class-123}}, {{ref:soil-class-130}} and {{ref:soil-class-135}} soils, it forms a set of steppe and prairie soils with a mollic horizon, where organic matter accumulates faster than leaching removes it. One of the original 26 FAO groups, it remained among the 28 of the 1988 revision, with two units: gleyic and haplic greyzems. It correlates most closely with the Dark Gray great group of Canada's Chernozemic order, and with Albolls and Boralfic Boroll subgroups in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-046.title: The Handbook of Australian Soils
soil-class-046.text: Before today's system, Australians classified their soils with a handbook. The Handbook of Australian Soils, first published in 1968, was an earlier system developed for the continent's soils. It built on the great soil group classification that J. A. Prescott published in 1931. The Australian Soil Classification has since superseded it, as it did the 1960 Factual Key.

soil-class-015.title: Zonal soils, shaped by regional climate
soil-class-015.text: In the 1938 U.S. system, a zonal soil was one whose character reflects the regional climate and vegetation. Both pedocals and pedalfers were subdivisions of this order. The idea long shaped how soils were explained. Fertile, carbon-rich dark soils of North America and Eurasia were long read as zonal soils of dry continental climates under steppe or prairie. Only later was past human activity recognized as a driver of them.

soil-class-014.title: Azonal soils, never given time to mature
soil-class-014.text: On Himalayan slopes, fine weathered material slides downhill so constantly that soil has no time to form. Such places hold azonal soils: immature soils that never develop because their material keeps sliding downslope or is buried by fresh deposits. River flood plains are the other classic case. New alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile. The label is also given to the {{ref:soil-class-127}} group, found in nearly all climates. Canada's system calls Anthroposols azonal soils, highly modified or built by people.

soil-class-013.title: Intrazonal soils, ruled by local conditions
soil-class-013.text: Limestone or waterlogged ground can outweigh the regional climate in shaping a soil. Intrazonal soils are those whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation. Calcimorphic soils develop from limestone. They include the thin {{ref:soil-class-050}}, with limited available water, and the deep red {{ref:soil-class-051}} of wetter climates. Hydromorphic soils form in waterlogged ground. In gley soils, waterlogged, airless pores reduce iron and turn the soil grey-blue with red flecks. In soils of {{ref:soil-class-070}}, plant remains never fully break down. Halomorphic soils form through salinization.

soil-class-089.title: Twelve names ending in -sol: the USDA soil orders
soil-class-089.text: Twelve names, each ending in -sol, sort the world's soils at the top of {{ref:soil-class-006}}. These are the USDA soil orders, and their criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed. Each order reflects distinct soil-forming processes and traits, shaped by climate, vegetation and mineral makeup. Many hinge on a diagnostic horizon, such as an argillic horizon of washed-in clay or a mollic epipedon, a deep, dark topsoil. Ranked by increasing development, they run {{ref:soil-class-094}}, {{ref:soil-class-100}}, {{ref:soil-class-093}}, {{ref:soil-class-101}}, {{ref:soil-class-090}}, {{ref:soil-class-099}}, {{ref:soil-class-104}} and {{ref:soil-class-103}}. {{ref:soil-class-098}} and {{ref:soil-class-106}} can appear at any stage. {{ref:soil-class-092}} and {{ref:soil-class-096}} complete the twelve. The least-developed order also covers the most ground: 16.3% of the world's ice-free land. Next come the desert order at 12.7%, the young-soil order at 9.9% and the clay-subsoil order at 9.6%. The volcanic-ash order is smallest, at 0.7%. Mountain soils, a mixture of orders or soil-free 'Rugged Mountains', make up the remaining 11.6%. The United States looks different. The dark-topsoil order leads there with 22.4% of ice-free land, and the clay-subsoil order follows with 14.5%. The tropical oxide-rich order covers less than 0.01%. The list has grown over time. The 1975 taxonomy recognized 10 orders; the 1999 second edition recognized 12.

soil-class-101.title: Mollisols, the deep dark soils of the grasslands
soil-class-101.text: No soil order grows more food than this one. Mollisols are the world's most agriculturally productive order, and among the most economically important. Their mark is a deep, dark surface horizon rich in organic matter and nutrients, called the mollic epipedon. It is typically 60 to 80 cm deep and usually has a soft, granular structure. It builds up slowly, from long-term additions of organic matter by roots. Mollisols must also have base saturation above 50%. They are common in grasslands, and they form in savannas and mountain valleys, as in Central Asia and the North American Great Plains. Fire long shaped those landscapes, while ants and earthworms churned the soil. The order covers about 7% of the world's ice-free land but 22.4% of the United States, more than any other order there. Little of its native grassland survives: a 2003 estimate found only 14 to 26 percent still relatively natural. A dark topsoil alone does not settle the name. Where shrink–swell clays rule, the soil keys out as a {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Where volcanic-ash traits take precedence, it becomes an {{ref:soil-class-092}}. In the WRB, Mollisols split into three groups, among them {{ref:soil-class-123}}. Their rise is tied to the cooling and drying of global climate in the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene. Fossil Mollisols are confidently known from the Eocene.

soil-class-090.title: Alfisols, fertile soils with a clay-rich subsoil
soil-class-090.text: Calcium, magnesium and potassium: an Alfisol keeps enough of all three to feed crops well. An Alfisol is a moderately leached soil with a clay-enriched subsoil and relatively high native fertility. It forms in semi-arid to humid areas, typically under hardwood forest, and must have an argillic, natric or kandic horizon. The name comes from 'alf', for aluminum (Al) and iron (Fe), a root inherited from the old pedalfer group. By definition an Alfisol has at least 35% base saturation. That threshold is the line against {{ref:soil-class-104}}, which are more leached and fall below 35%. Productive and abundant, Alfisols are among the most important orders for food and fiber. Yet Australian and African Alfisols lack nitrogen and phosphorus, and monsoonal ones acidify under heavy cultivation. They cover about one-tenth of the ice-free land, 9.6% globally and 14.5% of the U.S. They dominate areas such as the Ohio River basin, the Baltic region and Sudan. In eastern North America, Alfisols occur in glaciated areas, while their more leached neighbors lie south of the limit of maximum glaciation. Suborders follow wetness and climate: oxygen-depleted Aqualfs, cold Cryalfs, humid Udalfs, semiarid Ustalfs and Mediterranean Xeralfs.
