In the WRB most Alfisols fall in the {{ref:soil-class-133}} or {{ref:soil-class-132}} groups.

soil-class-106.title: Vertisols, the clay soils that plow themselves
soil-class-106.text: Some soils turn themselves over without a plow. A Vertisol is rich in expansive clays that crack deeply when dry and swell when wet. It is both a USDA order and a Reference Soil Group of the {{ref:soil-class-016}}. It needs more than 30% clay to 50 cm and usually has a mollic epipedon, the dark topsoil of a Mollisol. Vertisols form in clay-rich material, often from basic rocks such as basalt, in seasonally humid or erratic climates. Alternate shrinking and swelling mixes the soil, a process called argillipedoturbation. Some end up with a very deep A horizon and no B horizon, and the subsoil heaves up as gilgai. Colors range from gray or red to deep black. Australians speak of 'black earths', East Texans of 'black gumbo' and East Africans of 'black cotton' soils. Found between 50°N and 45°S, Vertisols dominate eastern Australia, India's Deccan Plateau, parts of Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya and the lower Paraná. They cover 2.4% of the world's ice-free land. The heavy, unstable soil makes it hard for trees to grow, so the natural cover is grassland, savanna or grassy woodland. Very hard when dry and sticky when wet, Vertisols are hard to farm without irrigation, and most are grazed by cattle or sheep. Their near-impermeability when saturated suits rice. Shrink–swell damages buildings and roads, but it lets the soil recover quickly from compaction. Australians, who call them Vertosols, prize them as among the few soils not acutely short of phosphorus.

soil-class-092.title: Andisols, the young, fertile soils of volcanic ash
soil-class-092.text: Wet rice on Java feeds some of the world's densest populations, and it grows on volcanic ash. An Andisol is a soil formed in such ash, rich in glass and in amorphous colloids such as allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite. To qualify it must have andic properties: abundant poorly crystalline iron and aluminum minerals, high phosphorus, low bulk density and high organic matter. Being generally young, Andisols are usually very fertile. The exception comes where phosphorus is easily fixed, as sometimes happens in the tropics. That fertility supports intensive use. Besides Java's rice, Andisols grow fruit, maize, tea, coffee or tobacco, and those of the Pacific Northwest carry very productive forests. They cover about 1% of the world's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire. The belt runs from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand's North Island. Suborders are wet Aquands, very cold Gelands, very dry Torrands, semiarid Ustands, dry-summer Xerands and young, glassy, coarse Vitrands. The WRB calls these soils {{ref:soil-class-119}}, though the two systems do not match exactly. Fossil Andisols occur far from present-day volcanoes. Some are dated to the Mesoproterozoic, 1.5 billion years ago.

soil-class-098.title: Histosols, soils built from organic matter
soil-class-098.text: Leave a waterlogged soil alone long enough and it can turn into coal. A Histosol is a soil made primarily of organic materials, recognized by both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy. It has 40 cm or more of organic soil material starting within 40 cm of the surface. Organic material means at least 12% organic carbon in Soil Taxonomy, or 20% in the WRB. Histosols form wherever organic matter accumulates faster than it is destroyed. Usually poor drainage is the cause, because it prevents aerobic decay. Their materials grade from muck to {{ref:soil-class-070}}. Soil Taxonomy's suborders Saprists, Hemists and Fibrists follow those materials, alongside drier Folists and submerged Wassists. With {{ref:soil-class-096}}, Histosols store large quantities of organic carbon, which makes them ecologically very important. They have very low bulk density, and many are acidic and short of major nutrients. Rain-fed {{ref:soil-water-122}}, cut off from groundwater, are especially poor. Histosols are hard to cultivate. Drained ones on young glacial land can make good dairy or beef pasture. But dried organic matter can blow away as powder, and heavy structures subside. Most lie in Canada, Scandinavia, the West Siberian Plain, Sumatra, Borneo and New Guinea, and they cover 1.2% of the world's ice-free land. Australia calls them Organosols. As fossils they appear with the first extensive land vegetation, in the Devonian.

soil-class-093.title: Aridisols, the slow-forming soils of the deserts
soil-class-093.text: Deserts and dry shrublands make up about one-third of Earth's land surface, and Aridisols dominate them. Named from the Latin aridus, 'dry', they are the soils of arid and semi-arid climates, also called desert soils. Water shortage defines them. They have an aridic {{ref:soil-class-011}}, with fewer than 90 consecutive moist days in the growing season, and they are not leached. They also need enough age to show weathering in the subsoil, including some diagnostic subsurface horizon. An ochric epipedon is common. Sparse vegetation leaves them very low in organic matter, and soil formation is slow. Because little water passes through, the subsoil keeps what it gathers. Subsurface horizons collect deposited clay, sodium, calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts, sometimes cemented, as in caliche or duripans. Many have well-developed Bt horizons, built from clay moved down in past wetter periods. Salt building up at the surface can cause salinization. Aridisols cover 12.7% of the world's ice-free land. In the WRB most fall into four groups, including {{ref:soil-class-121}} and {{ref:soil-class-142}}.

soil-class-104.title: Ultisols, the red clay soils at the end of weathering
soil-class-104.text: The red clay of the Southern United States sits at the end of a very long road. Ultisols are strongly weathered, acid mineral soils, commonly known as red clay soils. The name comes from 'ultimate'. They were seen as the end product of continuous weathering in a humid climate, never renewed by glaciation. Taking hundreds of thousands of years to form, they stop sharply at the limit of maximum Pleistocene glaciation in North America. They hold no calcareous material, under 10% weatherable minerals in the top layer and under 35% base saturation throughout. They must also have an argillic or kandic horizon. Iron oxide colors them from purplish-red to pale yellowish-orange. They are typically quite acidic, often below pH 5, and kaolinite is often the main clay. Short of calcium and potassium, Ultisols need lime and fertilizer for settled farming. They are more easily exhausted than Alfisols or Mollisols, though organic-rich Humults are relatively fertile. Kaolinite has an upside: it gives good bearing capacity and no shrink–swell. Well-drained Ultisols such as the Cecil series therefore suit urban development. They dominate the Southern United States, southeastern China and Southeast Asia, and cover 8.5% of the world's ice-free land. In the WRB most are {{ref:soil-class-117}} or {{ref:soil-class-118}} soils.

soil-class-094.title: Entisols, soils that have barely begun
soil-class-094.text: The most common soil order on Earth is the one that has done the least. Entisols show no profile development beyond an A horizon and have no diagnostic horizons, so they are little changed from their parent material. They cover about 16% of the world's ice-free land, and 12.2% of the U.S. Many things can hold development back. The parent material may not weather, or erosion may strip the surface away. Floods, wind or slope processes may keep burying it under fresh deposits. Bedrock may lie shallow, or the material may be toxic, such as serpentine or mine spoil. So Entisols are common on river and beach sediments and on volcanic ash. Some are just an A horizon on bedrock. The suborders show the range. Aquents are saturated soils of riverbanks and mudflats, and Fluvents are alluvium renewed by floods. Shallow {{ref:soil-class-095}}, sandy {{ref:soil-class-108}} and Wassents, under water over 21 hours a day, complete the list. Entisols are so varied that their suborders match different WRB groups; Fluvents, for instance, correspond to {{ref:soil-class-126}}. In Australia most Entisols are called Rudosols or Tenosols. Most fossil soils from before land plants spread in the Silurian are Entisols. Unlike other orders, though, they reveal little about past climate.

soil-class-100.title: Inceptisols, young soils just starting a subsoil
soil-class-100.text: Between bare beginnings and maturity sits a large and varied order. Inceptisols are young soils with little to moderate development and weathering, more developed than Entisols. A B horizon has begun to form, but there is no diagnostic subsurface horizon of another order. Soils that fit no other order may default to Inceptisols. Profiles vary widely, but most have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Some have histic or plaggen epipedons, calcic horizons, duripans or fragipans. Inceptisols occur everywhere except extremes such as deserts and permafrost. They lie on mountains, sand dunes, fresh coastal and river deposits and late Pleistocene glacial drift. They also develop on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have supported more developed Alfisols. Suborders follow temperature, moisture, saturation and epipedon: wet Aquepts, human-made {{ref:soil-found-110}}, cold Gelepts and Cryepts, humid Udepts, semiarid Ustepts and dry-summer Xerepts. Many crops grow on Inceptisols. Ustepts and Xerepts may need irrigation, and Aquepts need drainage. Aquepts with a sulfuric horizon are the exception, because draining them can produce sulfuric acid. Inceptisols cover 9.9% of global and 9.1% of U.S. ice-free land.

soil-class-103.title: Oxisols, the most weathered soils on Earth
soil-class-103.text: The oldest fossil Oxisols date from the first free oxygen in the atmosphere, about 2,200 million years ago. Oxisols are very highly weathered soils rich in iron and aluminum oxides, best known from tropical rainforest within 25 degrees of the Equator. They show the most profile development of any order. They must have an oxic horizon within 150 cm, and at all depths they hold no more than 10% weatherable minerals. Iron(III) and aluminum oxides and hydroxides make them always red or yellowish, alongside quartz and kaolin. The name comes from 'oxide'. Weathering, humification and mixing by animals form them. Rain, acidified by forest litter, leaches the minerals away, so plants depend on nutrients from decaying litter. Oxisols have a low cation exchange capacity, and their iron and aluminum oxides fix phosphorus strongly. Permanent cropping is therefore hard. Regions able to afford lime and fertilizer farm them intensively, as with Brazilian soybeans. Today Oxisols occur almost only in tropical South America and Africa, mostly on stable cratons. They cover 7.6% of global ice-free land but under 0.01% of the U.S. Suborders are wet Aquox, continuously humid Perox, humid Udox, semiarid Ustox and arid Torrox. Torrox are always paleosols from wetter times, mainly in Southern Africa. In the WRB Oxisols are mainly Ferralsols, and some were once classed as laterite soils. In warm periods such as the Mesozoic, they reached North America and Europe.

soil-class-096.title: Gelisols, soils over permanently frozen ground
soil-class-096.text: When frozen ground thaws, large structures subside. That makes permafrost a heavy limit on building, and it defines Gelisols, the soil order of very cold climates. Sources word the depth limit slightly differently. The order table requires permafrost within 100 cm, or cryoturbation within 100 cm plus permafrost within 200 cm. The name comes from the Latin gelare, 'to freeze', after the cryoturbation caused by alternate freezing and thawing. Organic matter builds up on top, so most Gelisols are black or dark brown over a shallow mineral layer. Calcium and potassium leach easily above the permafrost, which limits fertility. Slow decomposition makes these soils an important sink for carbon dioxide. Gelisols lie chiefly in Siberia, Alaska and Canada. Smaller areas lie in the Andes, Tibet, northern Scandinavia and ice-free Greenland and Antarctica. Together they cover 8.6% of the world's ice-free land. Gelisols key out before Histosols in soil taxonomy. Organic permafrost soils are therefore Histels there, but Cryic Histosols in the WRB, where most Gelisols are Cryosols. Fossil Gelisols are known from Precambrian ice ages 900 million years ago.

soil-class-108.title: Psamments, sandy soils that hold almost nothing
soil-class-108.text: The species-rich Fynbos of South Africa's Cape grows on sand that is extremely poor in nutrients. Such soils are Psamments, a suborder of Entisols made of unconsolidated sand. They occur in shifting dunes, or in very coarse parent material weathered for millions of years. A Psamment has no distinct horizons and must be loamy sand or coarser all the way through. The sand is poorly graded and constantly mixed, so it holds very little water. Being highly siliceous, it is extremely low in nutrients, especially phosphorus. It is also highly acidic, except in very arid climates. Young glacial Psamments of northern Europe are somewhat more fertile. Plants on them are often remarkably well adapted, as in the Fynbos and the Kwongan of Western Australia. Few Psamments are farmed. Fertilizing is costly, yields stay below other soils of the region, and the sand erodes very easily. Psamments cover 3.4% of the global land mass. They are abundant in the deserts of Africa and Australia, on old landforms of eastern South America and in Florida and Nebraska's Sand Hills. USDA soil taxonomy divides them by temperature and moisture regime into Cryopsamments, Torripsamments, Ustipsamments and Xeropsamments. Quartzipsamments, with over 90 percent resistant minerals, form a fifth group. In the WRB most are Arenosols, but those of river, lake or marine origin belong with {{ref:soil-class-126}}.

soil-class-111.title: Paleopedology, reading the soils of lost worlds
soil-class-111.text: Around 1795, observers in Scotland saw cliff soils that seemed to be remains of a former land surface. Paleopedology, the study of soils of past geological eras, began there. Its methods combine soil science and paleontology. Hilgard related soils to climate in the United States in 1892, and by the 1920s Glinka had found Russian soils that were relics of warmer climates. Fossil soils lie under sediment or volcanic ash, or where younger soil has eroded away, as in South Dakota, home of the ground in {{ref:soil-water-269}}. Buried soils lose their vegetation and organic matter. Yet the shape and size of root traces still reveal what grew on them. X-ray diffraction, developed since the 1960s, now lets paleosols be placed in the 12 soil orders. Many Precambrian soils fit no modern order. These 'green clays' are colored by unoxidized minerals that formed before free oxygen.

soil-class-095.title: Orthents, skeletal soils of steep slopes
soil-class-095.text: On very steep mountain slopes, erosion strips material too fast for deep soil to form. What remains is often an Orthent, a suborder of Entisols that lacks horizon development. Typically exceedingly shallow, Orthents are also called skeletal soils, or lithosols in the FAO classification. Any former soil has been removed or truncated. In Australia and parts of Africa they also occur on flat land whose rock has no weatherable minerals. They are unfit for arable farming and carry only low stocking rates, but they are important wildlife habitat. Many belong to the WRB's {{ref:soil-class-139}} or {{ref:soil-class-131}} groups.

soil-class-115.title: What fossil soils reveal about the history of land
soil-class-115.text: Very few fossil soils are of extinct types, unlike fossil plants and animals. That makes them useful for reading past ecosystems. The paleopedological record is chiefly paleosols buried by flood sediments or volcanic deposits, or preserved at geological unconformities. Burial changes them. Organic matter decays, iron oxidizes from Fe2+ to Fe3+ and hydrous ferric oxides dry out, so fossil soils grow harder to recognize. Telltale signs remain: downward-branching root traces, gradual alteration below a sharp former land surface, and crack patterns like peds and cutans. Most fit the twelve USDA orders, usually identified by X-ray diffraction. With little or no ozone layer, Precambrian soils eroded fast, and most are undeveloped Entisols or Inceptisols. Outside ice ages Oxisols have dominated the record, because new soil formation needs the glaciation and mountain building of cooler times. Land plants brought new orders: Histosols in the Devonian, then Alfisols and Ultisols. Mollisols spread only from the Miocene, as grasslands evolved.

soil-class-109.title: Sapric material, organic matter rotted past recognition
soil-class-109.text: In sapric material, decay has gone so far that plant parts and even fecal matter can no longer be identified. It is organic soil material of the kind found in a Histosol. The WRB defines it as having less than one-sixth of its volume as recognizable plant tissue within 100 cm. USDA soil taxonomy uses a fiber content below one-sixth. Muck is sapric soil that is naturally waterlogged or artificially drained. Canada places muck soils in its Organic order, with at least 30% organic matter and a depth of at least 40 cm. Sapric soils are deep, dark and friable, often underlain by {{ref:soil-fert-079}} or marly clay.

soil-class-102.title: Seven Mollisol suborders, sorted by water and warmth
soil-class-102.text: Water and warmth split Mollisols into seven suborders, set mainly by soil moisture and temperature regimes. Albolls and Aquolls are wet soils with an aquic moisture regime, and Albolls also have an eluvial horizon. Cryolls have a frigid or cryic temperature regime, and Gelolls a mean annual soil temperature below 0 °C. Udolls, Ustolls and Xerolls carry the udic, ustic and xeric moisture regimes of humid, subhumid and Mediterranean climates. Mollisol-like permafrost soils of Tibet and the Andean altiplano, called Molliturbels or Mollorthels, are not acidic. They make the best grazing land in those cold climates.

soil-class-091.title: Alfisols, the oldest forest soils
soil-class-091.text: The oldest forest soils on Earth are Alfisols, probably because of their fertility. Their fossil record reaches back to woodland and early forest soils of the Late Devonian. The oldest lie in the Aztec Siltstone of Victoria Land, Antarctica, with fossil wood and spores of Archaeopteris-Callixylon trees. Large woody roots pipe water and clay downward and leave material in the subsoil as they decay. That is the likely reason argillic horizons, Alfisols and forests go together. All tetrapod bones and tracks from Late Devonian and Mississippian paleosols of New York and Pennsylvania occur in Aridisols and Alfisols.

soil-class-107.title: Six Vertisol suborders, timed by their cracks
soil-class-107.text: Six USDA suborders sort Vertisols by wetness, temperature and how long their cracks stay open. Aquerts have aquic conditions and redoximorphic features. Slow permeability brings ponding. Cryerts, with a cryic regime, are most extensive in the Canadian Prairies. Xererts, with cracks open in summer and closed in winter, mark the eastern Mediterranean and California. Usterts, with cracks open at least 90 cumulative days a year, are the most extensive worldwide, though Torrerts lead in Australia. Uderts, with cracks open less than 90 days a year, are rare, mostly in Uruguay and eastern Argentina.

soil-class-105.title: Turning red clay Ultisols into garden soil
soil-class-105.text: A North Carolina Ultisol is roughly 82% mineral, 2% organic matter and 16% pore space. Gardeners aim for about 45% mineral, 5% organic matter and 50% pore space. Amendments are generally needed every year, guided by soil tests, and lime raises the pH. Mulch makes the soil more porous. Mixing 2 to 3 inches of compost and manure to a shovel's depth adds organic matter. Fall is best, so microbes release nutrients in time. Some gardeners skip amending with raised beds or {{ref:soil-fert-088}}, or grow native plants adapted to damp, poorly drained soils.

soil-class-116.title: More than 20,000 kinds of soil in one country
soil-class-116.text: The United States has identified over 20,000 soil series, each a unique kind of soil, classified in USDA soil taxonomy. Soil maps cover more than 95 percent of U.S. counties. Counting territories, Mollisols lead with an estimated 21.5% of the land. Alfisols follow at 14%, then Entisols at 12.3%, Inceptisols at 9.7% and Ultisols at 9.2%. Oxisols cover just 0.02%. Gelisols occur only in Alaska, and {{ref:soil-class-099}} lie under cool conifer forest and in Florida. Federal authority for mapping U.S. soils dates from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896. Today the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}, led by the NRCS, carries it out.

soil-class-097.title: Histels, Turbels and Orthels: the three Gelisol suborders
soil-class-097.text: Gelisols split three ways, by how much frost has churned them. Histels resemble Histosols but have permafrost within two meters and 80% or more organic material in the top 50 cm. They dominate subarctic and low-arctic permafrost regions. Turbels show cryoturbation through more than a third of the {{ref:soil-env-146}}, with broken horizons, involutions, patterned ground and ice or sand wedges. They lie mainly in continuous permafrost. Orthels show little cryoturbation, affecting less than a third of that layer. They occur mainly in discontinuous permafrost and alpine areas. Churning is much stronger on exposed sites, where Turbels dominate, than in sheltered valleys.

soil-found-110.title: Anthrepts, Inceptisols marked by people
soil-found-110.text: Some soils carry the marks of long human use. Anthrepts are a suborder of Inceptisols in USDA soil taxonomy for soils showing evidence of human habitation and farming. They have a plaggen or anthropic epipedon, a surface horizon that signals intense and prolonged human activity.

soil-class-114.title: Finding the starting material of a fossil soil
soil-class-114.text: A soil starts out much like its parent material and loses its features over time. To judge how far formation went in a fossil soil, researchers need that starting point. They estimate the vanished parent material from nearby materials. Estimates rest on four assumptions. The proxy is fresh, it was uniform through the profile, at least one constituent survived weathering, and volume change tracks thickness and density. No constituent is fully immune to weathering. Quartz is fairly stable above pH 9, alumina between pH 4.5 and 8, and lead and zirconium over wider ranges.

soil-class-112.title: Soil climate, the weather inside the pores
soil-class-112.text: Every soil has a climate of its own, hidden in its pores. Soil climate is the moisture, temperature and other climatic conditions there, a special kind of microclimate. In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate. In waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere. Classifying soils by climate data has been challenged by classifying them on observable features. The WRB counts soil climate only as a soil-forming factor. Climate-sensitive features let paleosols give a broad reading of past climate, though soils record it less precisely than instruments.

soil-class-113.title: Burrows, dung and roots: trace fossils in old soils
soil-class-113.text: A burrow, unlike a bone, usually stays where its maker lived. Trace fossils in paleosols are footprints, burrows, coprolites, or fossil dung, and root traces, all evidence of past organisms at work. They rarely identify a species, but their fixed position records behavior, as with the shallow burrows of solitary bees. Root-trace patterns and horizon sequences reveal the plant formation, such as forest, woodland or grassland, even when the species cannot be named. A paleosol can itself be seen as a trace fossil of a whole ancient ecosystem.

soil-class-110.title: Muck farming, vegetables from drained swamps
soil-class-110.text: Onions, carrots, celery and potatoes grow well on drained swamp. Muck farming works such soils of sapric organic matter, mostly for vegetables. It matters to farming in New York, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Wisconsin and Florida. Torrey Farms' muckland at Elba, New York, is thought to be the world's largest continuous section. The 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) of the {{ref:soil-class-150}} are the largest U.S. concentration outside the Everglades. The light soil needs windbreaks and can burn underground for months. It also oxidizes away each year, growing shallower and releasing carbon dioxide. Because draining wetlands destroys habitat, muck farming is controversial. U.S. environmental regulations make new muckland unlikely.

soil-class-099.title: Spodosols, acid soils of the cool conifer forests
soil-class-099.text: Florida's most prominent soil order also lines the cool forests of southeastern Alaska. Spodosols are acid soils with a spodic horizon, where organic matter complexed with iron and aluminum has accumulated after leaching from the layer above. That horizon must lie within 2 m of the surface, and the soil must lack andic properties. Most Spodosols also have a bleached albic horizon. Their B horizon holds illuviated aluminum with organic matter, and often iron. They are typical of coniferous and boreal forests in cool, moist climates, such as southeastern Alaska and the Great Lakes. They cover 2.6% of global and 3.3% of U.S. ice-free land. They correspond to the {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils of Russia and northern and central Europe, and to Canada's Podzolic soils. Australia calls them Podosols. Spodosols are known only from the Carboniferous onward. Less acidic look-alikes from the Mesozoic and Tertiary may be an extinct suborder.

soil-class-138.title: Podzol, the ash-grey soil beneath northern forests
soil-class-138.text: Peasants breaking such soils for the first time ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash. Dokuchaev named the soil for it in 1875: podzol is Russian for 'under-ash'. A Podzol is an acid soil with an organic topsoil over a bleached, ash-grey leached layer and a subsoil enriched in iron, aluminum or humus. It is the typical soil of boreal and coniferous forests, and of the eucalypt forests and heathlands of southern Australia too. Under 5 to 10 cm of decomposing litter lies an E horizon, usually 4 to 8 cm thick and poor in iron and aluminum oxides and humus. Below it sits a red or red-brown podzolic B horizon. {{ref:soil-form-061}} builds this profile. Dissolved organic matter binds iron and aluminum into chelates, and percolating water carries them from the E to the B horizon. Sometimes they cement a hardpan called ortstein. Podzols form mostly on quartz-rich sands, sandstone or debris of magmatic rock under high rainfall. In cool humid climates decay is slow, so acid layers of litter called mor build up. Most Podzols make poor farmland: sandy, short of water and nutrients, acidic, low in phosphate and toxic with aluminum. Grazing suits them best, though limed and fertilized loamy types can crop well. They cover about 4,850,000 square kilometers, mostly in the temperate and boreal Northern Hemisphere. Other systems give them other names. USDA and Chinese taxonomy say Spodosols, Canada has its Podzolic order, Australia uses Podosols and Brazil Espodossolos.

soil-class-123.title: Chernozem, the black earth of the steppes
soil-class-123.text: Some of the richest farmland on Earth goes by a plain name: black earth. Chernozem joins the Russian words for 'black' and 'earth', and the soil is also called regur. It holds 4% to 16% humus, with plenty of phosphorus and ammonia compounds. In the WRB key a Chernozem has a very dark, well-structured topsoil and secondary carbonates, lime deposited within the soil itself. That dark layer runs from a few centimeters to 1.5 meters (60 inches) thick in Ukraine and the Red River Valley. Chernozem covers about 230 million hectares in two belts. One is the Eurasian Steppe. The other runs from the Canadian Prairies south through the Great Plains to Kansas. Dokuchaev studied the steppe soils of Poltava in 1883. That year he published {{ref:soil-hist-002}}, the first description of the soil in European Russia. The soil is very fertile and holds much moisture. Long cropping still needs fertilizer, because its humus, and the nutrients that come with it, steadily declines. Its value has even fed a black market. Ukraine banned farmland sales from 1992 to 2020, but soil trucked away could be sold. In 2011 that trade was put at about US$900 million a year. In the WRB the USDA Mollisols split three ways: Chernozems, {{ref:soil-class-130}} and {{ref:soil-class-135}}. Together they match Canada's Chernozemic order.

soil-class-142.title: Solonchak, where salt builds up in the soil
soil-class-142.text: Solonchak is Russian for 'salt marsh', from sol, 'salt'. In the WRB it names a group of pale or grey, poorly drained soils of arid to subhumid lands that hold high concentrations of soluble salts. Its neighbors say a lot about it. Many lime-rich soils, the {{ref:soil-class-121}}, lie next to Solonchaks that are really salt-affected members of that same group. Solonchaks also turn up beside {{ref:soil-class-143}} soils, along with {{ref:soil-class-127}} and {{ref:soil-class-130}}. Crossing to the U.S. system shows the same family resemblance. Most USDA Aridisols fall into just four WRB groups: Solonchaks, the lime-rich soils above, and the soils rich in gypsum or silica described in {{ref:soil-class-129}} and {{ref:soil-class-125}}. People can make Solonchaks too. Irrigation with saline groundwater has caused catastrophic salinization and Solonchak formation, as in Central Asia. Water meant to grow crops left salt behind instead.

soil-class-143.title: Solonetz, the soil with a sodium-laden subsoil
soil-class-143.text: Many Ukrainian villages carry the folk word solontsi, meaning salty soil. The WRB name Solonetz comes from the same Russian root, sol, 'salt'. A Solonetz has a clay-enriched subsoil high in exchangeable sodium within the upper 100 cm. That layer is the natric horizon, named from Latin natrium, 'sodium'. It holds more clay than the layer above, and over 15% of its exchange sites carry sodium, a share measured as the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}. Solonetz zones go with Solonchaks, {{ref:soil-class-127}} and {{ref:soil-class-130}}. In USDA soil taxonomy Solonetz are sodium-rich Alfisols, and any Alfisol or Mollisol with a natric horizon keys out as Solonetz. Canada's soils show how such a soil ages. Starting from saline parent material, it develops into Solonetz, then Solodized Solonetz, then Solod, as leaching removes the salts. In the end the sodic B horizon may disintegrate. The name has deep roots in the science. Solonetz is one of the Russian soil terms, with chernozem, podzol and gley, that Dokuchaev's work brought into international use.

soil-class-120.title: Anthrosols, soils remade by centuries of farming
soil-class-120.text: Some soils carry a human signature. Anthrosols are soils formed or heavily changed by long-term human use, such as irrigation, added organic waste or paddy-field cultivation. They can form from any parent soil and are common where people have farmed for centuries. The clues are distinctive: high phosphate from bones, tissue or excrement, dark color, high pH from added wood ash, and buried tools or waste. A qualifier in the name records the cause. Plaggic means long manuring, irragric flooding or watering over the surface, hortic deep cultivation and kitchen waste, and anthraquic man-made water management such as terracing. In north-western Europe they commonly have plaggic or terric horizons built up with manure, together covering some 500,000 hectares. Rich in minerals and decayed organic matter, Anthrosols are good for farming, and well-managed ones store carbon. Archaeologists use them too. Spotted by eye or even from satellite images, they mark sites of long-term habitation. Similar soils carry many national names, among them {{ref:soil-class-149}}, paddy soils, the Amazon's {{ref:soil-class-053}}, Agrozems in Russia and Anthroposols in Australia and Canada. That variety raises a real question. Because Anthrosols differ so widely in composition and structure, soil scientists debate whether they should be an independent soil group at all.

soil-class-148.title: Aridity, the drying of the land
soil-class-148.text: Arid areas make up about 43% of the world's land. Aridity is the condition of regions with low annual precipitation, high temperatures and little available water, and such regions tend to have degraded soils. Where it falls depends mainly on the general circulation of the atmosphere, which shifts with climate change. Land-use change can also raise the demand on soil water. A December 2024 UNCCD report found that over three-quarters of Earth's land has become permanently drier in recent decades. A quarter of people live in dry regions that keep expanding. Warming-driven aridity also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils.

soil-class-127.title: Gleysols, soils stained by groundwater
soil-class-127.text: Break open a clod from a Gleysol and its inside is grey or blue, while its outer faces are rusty. These gleyic colors mark a soil saturated by groundwater long enough, unless drained, to change its iron. Gleysols are also called meadow soils, groundwater soils or Gleyzems. The WRB draws a sharp line by the source of the water. Redox features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol; those from stagnant surface water make a {{ref:soil-class-144}} or a {{ref:soil-class-136}}. Gleysols form in many unconsolidated sediments, mostly river, marine and lake deposits, in depressions and low positions with shallow groundwater. They cover an estimated 720 million hectares and occur in nearly all climates. They are most extensive in northern Russia, Siberia, Canada, Alaska, China and Bangladesh. About 200 million hectares lie in the tropics, mainly in the Amazon, equatorial Africa and the coastal swamps of Southeast Asia. Drained, they carry arable crops, dairy farming and horticulture, and in the tropics and subtropics they are widely planted with rice. They also hold an unusual mineral. Green rust, a layered iron(II)-iron(III) hydroxide, occurs in them as fougerite. In USDA soil taxonomy they match the Aqu- suborders of Entisols, Inceptisols and Mollisols.

soil-class-126.title: Fluvisols, the young layered soils of floodplains
soil-class-126.text: In prehistoric times people already prized these soils, for their natural fertility and for dry living sites on river levees. Fluvisols are genetically young, stratified soils in river, lake or marine sediments. They show clear layering and weak horizons, and under natural conditions they flood from time to time. They occur on alluvial plains, river fans, valleys and tidal marshes on every continent and in every climate zone. Large areas lie along the Amazon, the Ganges plain and Lake Chad, and in deltas such as the Mekong, Mississippi and Nile. With water control, many dryland crops grow on them. Paddy rice is widespread on irrigated and drained tropical Fluvisols. The coast is harder ground. Coastal Fluvisols with sulfidic material are acid sulfate soils, limited by low pH, toxic aluminum and salt. Strongly saline tidal land is best left under mangroves. In USDA soil taxonomy Fluvisols correspond to the fluvents and fluvaquents.

soil-class-117.title: Acrisols, weathered tropical soils ruled by aluminum
soil-class-117.text: Around the Amazon's fertile patches of {{ref:soil-class-053}} lies a 'common soil', and most of it is infertile Acrisol. Acrisols are strongly weathered soils with low-activity clays, clays with a low cation exchange capacity. In them exchangeable aluminum exceeds the exchangeable base cations. They go with humid tropical and subtropical climates, such as Brazil's, and often carry forest. Low fertility and toxic aluminum limit farming. Many Acrisols therefore serve for forestry, low-intensity pasture or protected areas. Where climate allows, tea, rubber, oil palm, coffee and sugar cane can be grown on them. In USDA soil taxonomy they match the Humult, Udult and Ustult suborders of the Ultisols, plus Oxisols with a kandic horizon and some Alfisols. Going the other way, most Ultisols are classed in the WRB as either Acrisols or {{ref:soil-class-118}}.

soil-class-131.title: Leptosols, thin soils from the tropics to the peaks
soil-class-131.text: Leptosols cover about 1.7 billion hectares, from the tropics to polar regions and from sea level to the highest peaks. They are very shallow soils over continuous rock, or deeper soils packed with gravel and stones. Mountains hold many of them, notably in Asia, South America, northern Canada and Alaska, and so do the Saharan and Arabian deserts. Elsewhere they occur on hard rock, or where erosion has kept pace with soil formation or stripped the topsoil. The most extensive Leptosols on Earth are Lithic Leptosols in mountain regions, less than 10 cm deep. They hold little water, so they are poor for rainfed farming, though some suit tree crops or extensive grazing. Older names linger. The 1974 FAO legend called Leptosols on limestone {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock Rankers. In the WRB such a limestone soil may key out as a Leptosol, Chernozem, {{ref:soil-class-130}} or {{ref:soil-class-135}}. In USDA terms many orthents, and shallow or gravelly Mollisols, belong to the Leptosols.

soil-class-122.title: Cambisols, soils just beginning to change
soil-class-122.text: Some of the most productive soils on earth are barely formed. Cambisols are moderately developed soils at the beginning of soil formation, shown by weak brownish color or structure in the profile. Temperate Cambisols rank among the most productive soils on earth, and most Cambisols make good, intensively used farmland. They form in medium- and fine-textured material from many rock types, mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits. Worldwide they cover an estimated 15 million square kilometers. They are widespread in temperate and boreal lands glaciated in the Pleistocene. There the parent material is young and soil formation is slow. In the tropics they are less common, appearing mainly where active erosion keeps soils young. Europe's weakly leached soils known as {{ref:soil-class-048}} are Cambisols in the WRB. Poland's brown forest soils correspond to Cambisols and to USDA Udepts.

soil-class-133.title: Luvisols, fertile soils with clay washed downward
soil-class-133.text: Over time, water seeping down through a Luvisol moves clay from the upper soil into the layer beneath. The result defines the group: an argic horizon, a subsurface layer with more clay than the material above, formed as water washes clay downward. Where uneroded, a paler, clay-depleted eluvial horizon lies above it. The clays are little weathered, high-activity 2:1 types. They give a high cation exchange capacity and high base saturation, with base cations equal to or greater than exchangeable aluminum. Luvisols cover 500–600 million hectares, mainly in temperate zones. They form on many parent materials and are generally fertile and widely farmed. In Mediterranean regions hematite colors them red as Chromic Luvisols. Such soils with strong wet-dry seasons, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-class-063}}, are called calcic and chromic luvisols. In USDA soil taxonomy most Luvisols are Alfisols. Canada's system also has Luvisols, whose clay-enriched Bt horizon forms mainly by {{ref:soil-form-060}}.

soil-class-145.title: Technosols, the soils of cities, mines and dumps
soil-class-145.text: A landfill, a heap of mine spoil and a city pavement can all count as soil. Technosols are soils whose properties and formation are dominated by their technical, human-made origin. A Technosol holds a significant amount of artifacts, objects made by people, or has a geotechnical liner, or is sealed by technic hard material unlike natural rock. The group covers soils of landfills, sludge, cinders, mine spoil and ash, pavements with their underlying material, and the engineered soils covered in {{ref:soil-class-157}}. Natural soil that has merely been transported does not count. Often called urban or mine soils, Technosols occur near cities, roads, mines, dumps, oil spills and fly-ash deposits, usually in small patches. They can change fast: a Technosol can differentiate A and O horizons at more than one centimeter per year. They are more likely than other soils to be contaminated, and many must be handled with care because of toxic industrial substances. Some are made on purpose to cover wastes such as mine tailings, as at Andacollo in Chile. Their closest relatives are {{ref:soil-class-120}}, soils created by long-term measures to raise fertility for farming.

soil-class-139.title: Regosols, the leftover group for barely formed soils
soil-class-139.text: Regosols are what remains when a soil fits no other group. They are very weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated material, with no significant profile development. Weak soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols are excluded. Their profiles stay minimal because they are young or form slowly. They cover about 260 million hectares, mainly in arid areas of the mid-western United States, northern Africa, the Near East and Australia. They are also extensive in eroding mountains. They match USDA Entisols and Australian Rudosols. Most are lightly grazed, some are irrigated intensively, and mountain Regosols are best left under forest.

soil-class-121.title: Calcisols, dryland soils rich in lime
soil-class-121.text: Some 10 million square kilometers may be Calcisols, almost all in the arid and semi-arid subtropics. These soils hold a substantial secondary accumulation of lime, calcium carbonate deposited within the soil. They are common on calcareous parent materials and widespread in arid and semi-arid lands, and older systems called them Desert soils and Takyrs. They develop mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits of base-rich weathering material, on level to hilly land. Natural vegetation is sparse: drought-adapted shrubs and trees and short-lived grasses. Dryness, stoniness or a shallow petrocalcic horizon, a layer cemented by lime, limit farming. Yet irrigated, drained and fertilized Calcisols can be highly productive. Many occur alongside Solonchaks that are in fact salt-affected Calcisols. In the other direction, most USDA Aridisols fall into four WRB groups: Calcisols, Solonchaks, {{ref:soil-class-129}} and {{ref:soil-class-125}}.

soil-class-118.title: Alisols, acid soils with active clays
soil-class-118.text: Alisols pair lively clays with acid conditions. In these soils the clays are high-activity, yet exchangeable aluminum exceeds the exchangeable base cations. Their clay-enriched argic horizon has a high cation exchange capacity but low base saturation in the subsoil. Their clays are far more active than those of {{ref:soil-class-132}}, Acrisols and Ferralsols, and they tend to lie on younger or more geologically active terrain. They occur in tropical and humid subtropical climates and also in temperate regions. Farming them needs lime and fertilizer, and they erode easily. At their low pH, aluminum and manganese dissolve and can poison intolerant plants.

soil-class-119.title: Andosols, the dark soils of volcanic ash
soil-class-119.text: Wet rice grown on the Andosols of Java feeds some of the world's densest populations. Andosols are soils formed in volcanic ash and other tephra, rich in allophane or in complexes of aluminum and organic matter. The name comes from Japanese an, 'dark', and do, 'soil', and it is a synonym of kuroboku. They develop in glass-rich parent material. While much volcanic glass remains they are called Vitric, and as the glass weathers they gain andic properties. The path depends on the ash and the climate. Acidic tephra in humid climates yields aluminum-organic complexes, giving Aluandic Andosols. Basic tephra or dry climates yield allophane and imogolite, giving Silandic Andosols. Both kinds hold much ferrihydrite and have a bulk density of 0.9 kg/dm3 or less. Silandic Andosols are very fertile unless phosphorus is fixed, bound so tightly that plants cannot use it. Andosols cover about 1–2% of Earth's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand. In USDA soil taxonomy many are Andisols, though some fall in the Inceptisols. The type is also very old. Fossil Andosols far from today's volcanoes have been dated as far back as the Precambrian, 1.5 billion years ago.

soil-class-144.title: Stagnosols, soils waterlogged from above
soil-class-144.text: Stagnosols get wet from the top down. Surface water stagnates in them, and the redox processes it drives leave strong mottling, without a marked change in texture. Periodically wet, they are mottled in topsoil and subsoil, sometimes with concretions or a fully bleached albic topsoil. Many national systems call them pseudogley. They cover 150–200 million hectares, mostly on flat to gently sloping land in humid temperate West and Central Europe, North America, south-east Australia and Argentina. Water stagnating above a dense subsoil starves roots of oxygen. Unlike Gleysols they often need deep loosening or ploughing, not just drains, and once drained they can be fertile. Many are Aqualfs, Aquults, Aquents, Aquepts or Aquolls in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-136.title: Planosols, sandy topsoil on a clay floor
soil-class-136.text: A Planosol changes abruptly from one layer to the next. A pale, coarse-textured topsoil sits directly on a dense, slowly permeable, much more clayey subsoil. The sharp break comes from layered deposits, or from clay being destroyed and removed. Water perches above it, creating temporary reducing conditions and a stagnic color pattern. Planosols cover about 130 million hectares of seasonally waterlogged flats in subtropical and temperate regions with marked wet and dry seasons. Oxygen shortage when wet, the dense subsoil and sometimes toxic aluminum hamper roots. Most are grazed and yields stay modest, though Southeast Asia grows paddy rice on them. The 1938 US classification already used the name; USDA soil taxonomy now puts most in the Albaqualfs, Albaquults and Argialbolls.

soil-class-135.title: Phaeozems, dark prairie soils without lime
soil-class-135.text: Phaeozems are dark soils with a high base status, much like Chernozems, but with no secondary carbonates within one meter of the surface. They form on loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe. Extensive areas lie in the United States, Argentina and China. They typically hold about 5% organic matter and have a pH of 5–7. Farmers use them intensively for wheat, soybean and cotton and as improved cattle pasture. Most Phaeozems match the Udolls, a suborder of the Mollisols in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-130.title: Kastanozems, the chestnut soils of dry grasslands
soil-class-130.text: Kastanozems are named for the chestnut, from the Russian and Latin words for it, after the color of its husk. Also called chestnut soils, they have a dark, humus-rich topsoil and secondary carbonates, yet they are paler than Chernozems. Native grassland gave them a brown surface layer within the first meter. They hold a high level of exchangeable calcium, and their secondary carbonates start within 70 cm of the mineral surface. They occupy relatively dry zones receiving 200 to 450 mm of rain a year. In USDA soil taxonomy they relate to the Mollisols.

soil-class-132.title: Lixisols, weathered tropical soils that keep their bases
soil-class-132.text: Lixisols are hard-weathered tropical soils that still keep their bases. They develop under intense tropical weathering in subhumid to semi-arid climates. Low-activity clays build up below the surface, and base saturation stays high: base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminum. With Acrisols they are the FAO groups of tropical climates with clay-enriched layers. In Amazonia they are among the natural soils too poor in minerals to resupply nutrients. Most USDA Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols in the WRB.

soil-class-149.title: Plaggen soils, built one sod at a time
soil-class-149.text: Farmers in north-west Europe built their own soil, one sod at a time, from the Middle Ages on. They cut sods of heath or grass with roots and humus, and used them as bedding for cattle or sheep. In spring they spread the slurry-soaked bedding on their fields as manure. Centuries of this turned poor Podzols into plaggen soil, a deep, humus-rich plaggic Anthrosol 40 cm to over 1.50 m deep. Modern arable soils reach about 30 cm. The fields rose with sharp edges, called Plaggenesche in Germany or Es in Dutch. The practice ended around 1900 with the arrival of fertilizers. Orkney had such soils by the 12th to 13th centuries, and parts of Shetland kept the method until the 1960s. Far away, Maori farmers in New Zealand used plaggen-like practices to improve drainage for kumara.

soil-class-134.title: Nitisols, deep red soils with shiny clods
soil-class-134.text: Break a Nitisol and its blocky clods show shiny pressure faces, shaped by iron oxides and high water content. Nitisols are deep, red, well-drained tropical soils with at least 30% clay and a strong polyhedral or blocky structure. The clay-rich layer extends as deep as 150 cm. They form from fine material weathered from intermediate to basic rock. Kaolinite, halloysite and iron oxides dominate, and they fix phosphorus. They occur in the tropics and subtropics, extensively in the highlands of Ethiopia, Kenya, the DR Congo and Cameroon. They correlate with kandic Alfisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols of USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-146.title: Umbrisols, dark topsoils poor in bases
soil-class-146.text: An Umbrisol has a dark, organic-rich mineral topsoil, yet its base saturation is low. That makes it the low-base counterpart of Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems. It develops in weathered siliceous rock. Umbrisols cover about 100 million hectares. They lie above the tree line in the Andes, Himalaya and Central Asia, and lower down in cleared northern and western Europe and on North America's Pacific seaboard. Slopes and a wet, cool climate restrict most to extensive grazing, improved by better grasses and lime, and many erode easily. In New Zealand they became productive sheep and dairy land. USDA soil taxonomy places such soils in great groups of Entisols and Inceptisols. The British soils described in {{ref:soil-class-049}} are Umbrisols in the WRB.

soil-class-140.title: Retisols, where pale soil reaches down in a net
soil-class-140.text: In a Retisol, pale soil reaches down into the darker layer below in a net-like pattern. The pale part is a clay-poor eluvial horizon; the dark part is the clay-rich argic horizon. The interfingering is called retic properties, from Latin rete, 'net'. Retisols entered the WRB in its third edition in 2014, absorbing the more narrowly defined {{ref:soil-class-147}} of 1998 and 2006. They resemble the FAO's Podzoluvisols. They occur mainly in former periglacial areas of the last glaciation in Europe and North America, along a belt from Belgium to Russia, though rarely over large areas. Water drains through the clay-poor tongues. The dense, nutrient-richer clay parts are often too dry and hard for roots, and earthworms avoid them. Most Retisols are forest or pasture.

soil-class-150.title: The Black Dirt Region, onion country on drained muck
soil-class-150.text: By the late 20th century, onions on this ground averaged 30,000 lb/acre (3.4 kg/m2). The Black Dirt Region is a drained former marsh in Orange County, New York, and Sussex County, New Jersey. It is named for its dark, extremely fertile {{ref:soil-class-109}} muck. The muck formed on an ancient glacial lake bed, enriched by decades of Wallkill River floods. Its 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) are the largest such tract in the US outside the Everglades. Early settlers avoided the flood-prone land. A drainage canal was dug in 1835, and Polish and Volga German immigrants used to similar soils began farming it. Farmers now also grow vegetables, sod, hemp and cannabis. The muck is poor ground for building, so development of the farmland is considered unlikely.

soil-class-137.title: Plinthosols, soils that can harden into ironstone
soil-class-137.text: Some tropical soils can turn to stone. Plinthite, a red, clay-rich material rich in iron oxides, sometimes over 80%, hardens irreversibly into ironstone with repeated wetting and drying. Plinthosols are defined by plinthite, petroplinthite or pisoliths, iron-oxide concretions, in a plinthic horizon starting within 50 cm of the surface. They form in wet-dry tropics where water tables rise and fall. Saturated soil reduces and mobilizes iron, which precipitates as ferric oxides in mottled patterns when the soil dries. Fertility is low. Bottomlands waterlog, shallow areas suffer drought, and shallow petroplinthite often leaves only grazing, though cocoa and cashew are grown in places. Soils with plinthite cover about 60 million hectares. Soft plinthite dominates the humid Amazon and Congo basins, while hardened caps cover drier Sudano-Sahelian landforms.

soil-class-129.title: Gypsisols, gypsum soils of the driest lands
soil-class-129.text: Water can make a Gypsisol sink. These soils hold a substantial secondary accumulation of gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) and are confined to the driest arid lands. Probably about 100 million hectares in all, they lie around Mesopotamia, central Asia, the Libyan and Namib deserts, Australia and the south-western United States. Calcium sulfate, with or without carbonates, collects in and below the B horizon of soils formed in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits. Deep Gypsisols near water can grow many crops, but a shallow petrogypsic horizon cuts yields. Gypsum dissolving in irrigation water makes the land subside unevenly, so canals must be lined. They are Gypsids in USDA soil taxonomy and Desert soils in the Russian classification.

soil-class-125.title: Durisols, dryland soils cemented by silica
soil-class-125.text: Durisol comes from Latin durus, 'hard', and the name fits. In these free-draining dryland soils, secondary silica cements the grains in the upper meter, as nodules or as a continuous hardpan. The cemented layer is called a duripan, hardpan in Australia or dorbank in South Africa. Durisols form mainly in alluvial and colluvial deposits on plains, terraces and gentle piedmont slopes in arid, semi-arid and Mediterranean regions. Erosion often exposes the hard layer. Most are fit only for extensive grazing; crops need irrigation. Large areas occur in Australia, South Africa, Namibia and the south-western United States. As a new group, though, they are rarely mapped, and their extent is unknown.

soil-class-124.title: Why chernozem is black: an open question
soil-class-124.text: How chernozem got its thick black topsoil has been argued since 1763. That year Lomonosov pointed to decaying plants and animals. Murchison proposed weathered Jurassic marine shales in 1840, others marine sediments in 1851, and Ruprecht decomposed steppe grasses in 1866. The puzzle is still open. No single reconstruction of past climate explains the geochemical variation of central European chernozems. Evidence of human-made pyrogenic carbon, carbon formed by burning, led to a burning theory from Schmidt in 1999. Chernozem has the highest magnetic susceptibility of the major soil types. Heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, which points to fire, likely set by early humans. Yet humification alone can darken soils. So 'chernozem' may cover black soils that look alike but formed in different ways, and no single explanation yet fits them all.

soil-class-141.title: Five groups with clay-rich subsoils, and how to tell them apart
soil-class-141.text: Five WRB groups must have an argic horizon, a clay-enriched subsoil: Retisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols. The key sorts them with a few measurements. Retisols stand apart first, as the only group with retic properties. The other four are separated by the cation exchange capacity per kg of clay in the argic horizon, and by the effective base saturation of the subsoil. Low-activity clays with more exchangeable aluminum than base cations make an Acrisol. Low-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminum make a Lixisol. High-activity clays dominated by aluminum make an Alisol. High-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminum make a Luvisol. One exception guards the edge. A soil with an argic horizon and retic properties dominated by stagnant water is classed instead as a Retic Stagnosol. The groups also map onto the U.S. system. Most USDA Alfisols become Luvisols or Lixisols, and most Ultisols become Acrisols or Alisols.

soil-class-147.title: Albeluvisols, a soil group retired in 2014
soil-class-147.text: Albeluvisols lasted just two editions of the WRB, in 1998 and 2006. The group held soils with a thin dark topsoil over a bleached albic horizon that tongues into a clay-enriched Bt horizon. The third edition, in 2014, replaced them with the more broadly defined Retisols. They formed in glacial till, lake and river deposits or loess on plains under coniferous or mixed forest. They cover an estimated 320 million hectares, mostly on former Pleistocene permafrost. Acidity, few nutrients and problems with ploughing and drainage limit farming, so those of the northern taiga are almost all forest. They correlate with the Glossaqualfs, Glossocryalfs and Glossudalfs of USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-070.title: Peat, the half-rotted store of the world's soil carbon
soil-class-070.text: Peat covers just 3% of the land surface, yet it stores up to 550 Gt of carbon. That is 42% of all the carbon held in soils, more than all other vegetation on Earth, forests included. Peat is an accumulation of partly decayed vegetation and organic matter, found in bogs, moors and other waterlogged ground. Sphagnum, or peat moss, is one of its commonest parts, though many other plants contribute. It forms in wet places where flooding or stagnant water cuts off oxygen and slows decomposition. Soils made mainly of peat are {{ref:soil-class-098}}. The world holds about 4 trillion cubic meters of it. Estimates of its share differ: Joosten and Clarke say peat-covered land holds one third of the carbon in the world's soils. In principle peat is renewable. In practice it regrows only about 1 mm a year, and only in 30–40% of peat areas, far slower than industrial extraction. Over geological time it is often the first step toward coal, especially low-grade lignite. Centuries of burning and draining peat have released much CO2, adding to human-caused climate change. Engineers see a different problem. Highly organic peat consolidates poorly, so it makes an unstable foundation for roads and buildings.

soil-class-074.title: Draining peat lets ancient carbon escape
soil-class-074.text: Under water, peat gathers organic carbon for thousands of years. Drainage opens that store to the air. Peat drainage is the draining of peat soils, often through canals, for agriculture, forestry and peat extraction. Once exposed, the carbon decomposes to CO2. About 12% of the world's peat areas have been drained and damaged. As of 2022 they emitted an estimated 4% of human-made greenhouse gases, before counting fires. England's peat stores 584 million tonnes of carbon, but they release around 11 million tonnes of CO2 a year through damage and draining. The Netherlands shows the long-term result. About 2,500 years ago the country was largely peat. Compaction, oxidation and digging, all driven by drainage, have left about 2,733 km², 10% of its land. Draining peat also destroys the habitat of many species.

soil-class-075.title: Peat fires that smoulder underground for years
soil-class-075.text: A fire in peat can outlast the season, the year, even the century. Peat fires burn in peat deposits and smoulder underground for long periods, and light rain does not put them out. Peat's high carbon content lets it burn once dry. A wildfire reaching below the surface can ignite it. Then it smoulders, creeping undetected through the ground for months, years or even centuries. Fire is not wholly foreign to peat bogs. Bogs burn naturally and depend on wildfires to stop woody plants from lowering the water table and shading out bog plants. The damage comes at scale. In 1997 peat and forest fires in Indonesia released between 0.81 and 2.57 gigatonnes of carbon, equal to 13–40% of the carbon from global fossil fuel burning. A 2010 heat wave of up to 40 °C ignited peat in Central Russia. In June 2019 Arctic peat fires emitted 50 megatonnes of CO2. Climate change now makes such fires much more likely than before.

soil-class-071.title: How stalled decay builds a bog
soil-class-071.text: Peat is what happens when rot stalls. Peat formation is the build-up of plant material that fails to decay fully under acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions, the setting described in {{ref:soil-chem-125}}. Most of the material comes from bog plants such as mosses, sedges and shrubs. The process feeds itself. Accumulating peat holds water, so conditions slowly grow wetter and the bog spreads. Sphagnum is especially good at this. It secretes tannins that preserve organic material, and its water-holding hyaline cells keep the bog constantly wet. Most modern peat bogs formed 12,000 years ago at high latitudes, after the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age. Growth is slow, usually about a millimeter a year. Boreal peat bogs therefore take thousands of years to reach their average depth of 1.5 to 2.3 m. The result is a vast store of carbon: an estimated 415 gigatonnes in the north, 50 Gt in the tropics and 15 Gt in South America.

soil-class-060.title: Serpentine soil, where heavy metals rule
soil-class-060.text: Some soils are poisoned by their own bedrock. Serpentine soil is an uncommon soil formed from weathered ultramafic rock, such as peridotite and serpentinite, rock in which iron or magnesium minerals make up more than 70%. Its minerals belong to the serpentine group: antigorite, lizardite and chrysotile, or white asbestos. Serpentinite forms when olivine-rich peridotite reacts with water, mostly in oceanic crust near mid-ocean ridges. The terrain is steep, rocky and prone to erosion, so the soils stay shallow, and sparse plant cover leaves them hot and dry. They hold little organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium, and too little calcium for their magnesium. High chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel make them poor for farming. Adding gypsum or other soluble calcium fixes the ratio enough for crops and pasture. These soils occur from the Balkans, Cyprus and the Alps to Cuba and New Caledonia, and most North American ones are in California. Dust from the crushed rock carries asbestos, a health hazard.

soil-class-048.title: Brown earth, the easy farmland of temperate lands
soil-class-048.text: Brown earths cover 45% of England and Wales. These well-drained, fertile soils of humid temperate climates lie mostly between 35° and 55° north. The largest expanses lie in western and central Europe, Russia, eastern North America and eastern Asia. They form where rainfall is moderate, usually below 76 cm a year, and their pH runs from 5.0 to 6.5. Soil organisms and roots mix mull humus into the mineral matter, building a brownish A horizon over 20 cm deep with a blurred lower edge. Below lies a lighter B horizon of weathered parent material. Limited leaching moves only the more soluble bases down. Rust-like iron oxides give the rich color, and the B horizon lacks the gray colors and mottles of gley soils. Permeable and easy to work most of the year, brown earths are prized for farming, and much of their deciduous woodland has been cleared. The WRB calls them Cambisols, and German taxonomy calls them Braunerde.

soil-class-083.title: Charcoal, wood baked without air
soil-class-083.text: Charcoal is what remains when wood or other plant and animal material is strongly heated with little oxygen. Water and volatile compounds are driven off, leaving a lightweight black carbon residue. Traditional burners built a kiln or conical pile that burned part of its own wood to char the rest. Modern retorts do the job more efficiently. Large-scale production has long driven deforestation, particularly in Central Europe. Research on {{ref:soil-class-053}}, an Amazonian dark soil, revived charcoal in horticulture. Growers use it to improve soils and to lock away carbon. {{ref:soil-fert-050}} is a form of charcoal, sometimes modified, meant for uses such as adding to soil.

soil-class-053.title: Terra preta, the black soil people made in the Amazon
soil-class-053.text: Clear a patch of Amazon forest and rain or flooding soon strips the soil of its nutrients. Yet scattered through the basin lie patches of soil that stay dark and fertile. This is terra preta, a human-made {{ref:soil-class-120}}. Pre-Columbian farming communities created it between 450 BCE and 950 CE. They added charcoal, bones, broken pottery, {{ref:soil-fert-028}} and {{ref:soil-fert-023}} to poor Amazonian soil. Weathered charcoal gives the black color. Charcoal from {{ref:soil-fert-087}} stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients, so terra preta resists leaching. It holds on average three times the organic matter of the soils around it, up to 150 g/kg, and phosphorus reaches 200–400 mg/kg. Its A horizon holds more than 13–14% organic matter, and the soil can reach 2 m deep. It is reported to regenerate at 1 cm a year. The WRB calls it Pretic Anthrosol, and most began as Ferralsol. Around it lies infertile terra comum, mainly Acrisols, Ferralsols and Arenosols. Lighter, brownish terra mulata, the farmed land around settlements, falls in between for fertility. Its extent is uncertain. Estimates run from 0.1–0.3% of low forested Amazonia, or 6,300 to 18,900 square kilometers, to 10% or more, and model-based predictions put it at 3.2% of the forest. Plots average 20 hectares.

soil-class-050.title: Rendzina, the thin dark soil on limestone
soil-class-050.text: On limestone slopes the soil can be little more than a dark skin over broken rock. Rendzina is a shallow, humus-rich soil formed on carbonate-rich, or occasionally sulfate-rich, parent rock, recognized in British, German and some older classifications. Limestone is by far the commonest base, but rendzinas also form on dolomite, gypsum, marble, chalk and {{ref:soil-fert-079}}, typically on slopes in karst and mountain landscapes. Water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves the carbonate and carries it away. Insoluble clay minerals stay behind in the upper soil. There, organisms build humus, and the clay protects it from further decay; together they give dark colors and crumb structure. In Wales the profile is simply dark calcareous topsoil straight onto shattered limestone. Calcium and magnesium are plentiful, but potassium is often low. Rendzinas are a passing stage. Once they lose their carbonate they become another soil, unless erosion keeps stripping soil away. Shallow and sloping, they store little water, so they often keep semi-natural vegetation.

soil-class-073.title: Peat archives, a diary kept in layers
soil-class-073.text: Peat keeps a diary. Because it builds up over thousands of years, its layers preserve pollen, spores, plants, animals and archaeological remains, letting scientists reconstruct past vegetation, climate and land use. Harry Godwin, a scientist of peat bogs, coined the phrase peat archives in 1981. Researchers compare peat records with modern bogs to gauge how people have changed the movement of mercury. They date the layers by methods such as the vertical spread of lead-210. Acidic, tanning water and an antibiotic called sphagnan preserve bog bodies almost perfectly, such as Denmark's Tollund Man, who lived in the 4th century BC.

soil-class-077.title: Burning peat for heat, power and whisky
soil-class-077.text: For centuries people warmed their homes with the ground itself. Peat fuel is dried peat burned for heat and power, traditionally cut by hand and left to dry in the sun. In Ireland and Scotland stacked peat fed cooking fires and home heating, a tradition traced to the Roman period. Ireland's state-owned Bord na Móna milled peat for power stations and sold peat briquettes for homes. In 1929 peat supplied over 40% of the Soviet Union's electricity, falling to 1% by 1980. Some Scotch whisky distilleries, such as those on Islay, dry malted barley over peat fires.

soil-class-076.title: Peat hags, the overhanging banks of eroding bogs
soil-class-076.text: In damaged peat the ground can break into steep banks capped by an overhanging lip of plants. These are peat hags, a form of erosion at the sides of gullies cut into peat. They form when flowing water cuts down into the peat, or when fire or heavy grazing exposes its surface. Exposed peat then wears away further under wind, water and livestock. The banks are too steep and unstable for plants to take hold, so they keep eroding unless restored.

soil-class-078.title: Gardening without peat
soil-class-078.text: Peat has long filled garden pots, but that is changing. Peat in horticulture means its use as a raw material for gardening, now restricted in some places. In 1999 the UK set its horticulture industry a target of 90% peat-free by 2010. Kew Gardens has discouraged peat as a soil additive since 2003, and the Royal Horticultural Society promotes peat-free gardening. Peat-free mixes based on bark and {{ref:soil-agri-139}} are rising in the UK, while other European countries, Canada and parts of the US still use peat. Chile has forbidden peat extraction since April 2024. Peat grow cups have about 4.5 times the carbon footprint of single-use plastic cups.

soil-class-072.title: Fibric, hemic, sapric: grading peat by decay
soil-class-072.text: Not all peat has rotted equally. Soil scientists divide peat material into three kinds by how far it has decomposed. Fibric peat is the least decomposed and consists of intact fiber. Hemic peat is partly decomposed. Sapric peat is the most decomposed of all. The source plants matter too. Phragmites peat, made of reed grass and other grasses, is denser than many other kinds.

soil-class-080.title: Frozen peat and the carbon it guards
soil-class-080.text: Around half the area of northern peat bogs is frozen year-round. This peatland permafrost covers about a tenth of all permafrost area and holds about a tenth of permafrost carbon, 185 ± 66 Gt. Dry peat insulates well, with a thermal conductivity of around 0.25 W m−1 K−1. It shields the frozen ground from thaw, forming raised features called {{ref:soil-water-266}} and peat plateaus. Thaw tends to raise methane emissions while only slightly increasing CO2 uptake, so it adds to the warming feedback from thawing permafrost carbon. Under 2 °C of global warming, 0.7 million km² of peatland permafrost could thaw.

soil-class-079.title: Rewetting a peatland back to life
soil-class-079.text: A drained bog can often be healed by blocking its ditches. Peatland restoration repairs damaged peat bogs, usually by blocking drainage channels so they rewet and native vegetation recovers. Rewetting limits carbon release in the short term. Later, the new vegetation supplies the litter that restarts peat formation. Actively reintroducing bog plants re-establishes typical communities within 5 years, helping animals, insects and birds return. Pools add microhabitats and raise the variety of life. The Convention on Biological Diversity names peat areas as key ecosystems to protect, and wet habitats in general are also protected under the 1971 treaty covered in {{ref:soil-water-262}}.

soil-class-051.title: Terra rossa, the red soil of Mediterranean karst
soil-class-051.text: Across the Mediterranean, a rust-colored soil lies in patches over limestone. Terra rossa is a well-drained, reddish, clayey to silty soil of neutral pH. It covers limestone and dolomite bedrock in karst regions as a discontinuous layer from a few centimeters to several meters thick. Its red comes from hematite forming in preference to goethite. For a clay-rich soil it drains surprisingly well, because the karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage and a neutral pH. That drainage makes it popular for wine, in La Mancha in Spain and in Coonawarra and the Barossa Valley in Australia. Soils of this red Mediterranean kind developed fastest from the Miocene to the Late Pleistocene, during large climate swings. The 1938 USDA taxonomy described terra rossa as deep, red and formed under higher rainfall than rendzina. Systems such as the FAO's formally replaced the class, but it is still in common use, and as of 1997 it remained in Israel's and Italy's national classifications. Its equivalents are chromic Luvisols on the UNESCO/FAO world map and rhodustalfs in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-057.title: Dark earth, the soil left by centuries of settlement
soil-class-057.text: Dark earth is an organic-rich layer up to 1 m thick that, in geology and archaeology, marks long-lasting human settlement. Charcoal gives its color, and it may hold fragments of pottery, tile, animal bone and other artifacts. It is read as soil enriched with sooty remains of thatch from chimneyless houses and other waste. In England it covers many areas built up in the Roman period, especially Londinium, between deposits dated to the 2nd–5th centuries and the 9th century. Archaeologists first called London's layer 'black earth', then renamed it to avoid confusion with chernozem, whose color is traditionally put down to humus rather than soot. They still disagree whether it records Roman refuse or gardening, a population decline, or deposits formed after the city was abandoned. For at least 700 years West African farmers have built their own dark earth around their towns with rotted kitchen, animal, farm and fire waste.

soil-class-054.title: Why Amazonian charcoal still feeds the soil
soil-class-054.text: The charcoal in terra preta was not just any charcoal. Indigenous farmers added low-temperature charcoal, a form of pyrogenic or black carbon, to poor soils. Some terra preta holds up to 9% black carbon against 0.5% in the soils around it, and other measurements found carbon 70 times higher than in nearby Ferralsols. Poly-condensed aromatic groups, tightly bonded ring structures of carbon, keep it stable against microbes for thousands of years. Slow oxidation creates carboxylic groups that raise the soil's cation exchange capacity. Its pores hold organic matter, water and dissolved nutrients, and pollutants such as pesticides too. Low-temperature charcoal carries an inner layer of condensates that bacteria consume; charring at high temperature burns it off and adds little fertility. Fresh charcoal must first be charged with nutrients, for example by soaking two to four weeks in a liquid nutrient, or it briefly depletes available nutrients. The earthworm Pontoscolex corethrurus eats charcoal and mixes it, finely ground, into the mineral soil.

soil-class-084.title: Fill dirt, the earth used to raise the ground
soil-class-084.text: Kansai International Airport stands on a new island of fill about five square kilometers in area. Fill dirt is earthy material used to fill a hole or depression, build mounds or otherwise change the level of land. It is usually subsoil and the parent material beneath, with little organic matter or life. Rotting organic matter leaves voids that let fill settle and damage structures on top. Most is mined from sand and gravel pits to an engineer's grading specifications. Common uses include building up highway shoulders and raising low construction sites against flooding.

soil-class-081.title: Tropical peat, built from fallen trees
soil-class-081.text: Tropical peat covers about 380,000 km², roughly 0.25% of Earth's land, yet it holds 50,000–70,000 million tonnes of carbon, about 3% of the carbon in the world's soils. It is a Histosol of tropical latitudes, found in South East Asia, Africa and Central and South America. Temperate peat is typically built of sphagnum, but tropical peat forms mostly from dead trees. Its organic matter content usually exceeds 75%, and its dry bulk density is low. About 46% of its area is in South America, though the world's largest tropical peat deposit lies in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The forests growing on this peat yield timber, bark, resins and latex, and they shelter endangered species such as the orangutan. Clear the forest and drain the peat, and the surface peat oxidizes, losing carbon rapidly as CO2. The sinking ground then floods. Plantations, logging and fire are shrinking the store, and Indonesia's burning peat bogs contain more than 50 billion tonnes of carbon. Leaving these emissions out underestimates the rise in greenhouse gases and human-induced climate change.

soil-class-055.title: Who made terra preta, and how
soil-class-055.text: Early theories traced them to ashfall from Andean volcanoes, or to sediment settling in ancient lakes or ponds. Sources still differ. Some terra preta was clearly made on purpose. Much may have built up by accident, since soil rich in charcoal and pottery gathers near dwellings. Many patches probably formed under kitchen refuse heaps, the kind described in {{ref:soil-hist-102}}. Recent research suggests terra preta may even be natural, with pre-Columbian people using and improving scattered patches of existing fertility. The soils vary so much that it remains unclear whether all were made deliberately, or whether the lightest are by-products of daily life.

soil-class-056.title: Recreating Amazonian dark soil
soil-class-056.text: Synthetic terra preta is a {{ref:soil-fert-001}} made from materials meant to copy those of the original: crushed clay, blood and ground bone, animal dung and charcoal made for soil. Because it is particulate, it can move down the soil profile and add fertility and carbon to existing peds and aggregates. Poor tropical soils can also be enriched to terra preta nova by adding charcoal and condensed smoke. It might lock away carbon while reversing declining fertility and the spread of desert, but whether this works at large scale is unproven. A related idea, terra preta sanitation, pairs lactic-acid treatment in urine-diverting dry toilets with worms that break down the waste.

soil-class-058.title: Red soil, the iron-stained clay of warm lands
soil-class-058.text: About 13% of Earth's soil is red. Red soil is a reddish, clay-rich soil that typically develops in warm, temperate and humid climates, usually from weathered ancient crystalline and metamorphic rock. Thin, heavily leached organic layers rest on a red layer of river-laid sediment. High iron gives colors from reddish brown to reddish yellow, and Ultisols, Alfisols and Oxisols count as red soil once they take on this color. No single composition defines the group: one type may be infertile in one region but rich in nutrients in another.
