Heavy leaching leaves them acidic and low in water-holding capacity, nutrients and humus. Nitrogen is often deficient, and phosphorus and potassium run short after repeated harvests. Adding lime raises their pH for acid-intolerant crops, though it can stimulate microbes that deplete organic matter and harm structure. Organic matter added as dung, suitable cultivation and changing crops from year to year raise fertility and water retention. Red soils cover about 102 million hectares in China and about 350,000 km², 10.6% of the country, in India.

soil-class-085.title: Bay mud, the soft floor of estuaries
soil-class-085.text: Bay mud is thick deposits of soft, water-saturated, loose silty clay on the floors of certain estuaries, mostly in temperate regions shaped by glacial cycles. Tributary streams wash in its clay, silt and sand. It has low shear strength, high compressibility and low permeability, with a typical bulk density of about 1.3 g/cm³. That makes it hazardous to build on in earthquake zones such as San Francisco Bay. Heavy buildings need deep foundations on stiffer layers below, and even then the ground around them settles, damaging utility connections. At low tide it forms mudflats that feed shorebirds and root eelgrass, cordgrass and pickleweed.

soil-class-049.title: Brown podzolic soils, halfway between two kinds
soil-class-049.text: Brown podzolic soils are a class of the British soil classification, grouped with the podzolic soils but halfway between a Podzol and a brown earth. They form on hilly land in western Europe. There, more than about 900 mm of precipitation outstrips evaporation for much of the year, so the profile is leached. Unlike true podzols, they lack a continuous E horizon. Soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminum oxides, which build up as a distinctive orange-brown B horizon. The WRB calls them Umbrisols. They are common in Ireland, Scotland, western England and Wales, where they cover about 20% of the country.

soil-class-065.title: Brickearth, the wind-blown silt of southern England
soil-class-065.text: Brickearth is a superficial deposit of uniform loam or silt, first named in southern England, and it is wind-blown loess. In the cold, dry periods of the Pleistocene, wind picked up fine sediment from glacial outwash and dropped it where the wind slackened. It lies in patchy spreads up to a meter deep across southern England and South Wales. With little or no added material it makes stock bricks, which harden at lower temperatures than clay bricks. It gives rich farmland, but it collapses rapidly when saturated and makes a poor foundation.

soil-class-064.title: Stagnogley, the waterlogged soil over a dense layer
soil-class-064.text: Stagnogley is a loamy or clayey soil with a dense, impervious horizon beneath the surface, classed among the gleyic soils. Continual waterlogging bleaches its topsoil, and it often forms on sandy material over dense subsoil in cool, moist climates. Nutrient-poor, often highly acidic and poorly aerated, it suits woodland such as English oak better than crops. Where it stays saturated all year it becomes bog stagnogley and eventually bog, as in the missen of the Black Forest. Related to the pseudogleys, stagnogleys occur in very humid climates and on steep slopes, in Germany's Central Uplands and on the Midvale Ridge in the UK.

soil-class-068.title: Subaqueous soil, soil beneath the water
soil-class-068.text: Soil does not stop at the shoreline. Subaqueous soil forms in the sediment of shallow, permanently flooded places, or anywhere under water too deep for rooted plants. These sediments undergo soil-forming processes and can support rooted plants such as eelgrass. They also meet the definition of soil in {{ref:soil-class-006}}, opening a new frontier for {{ref:soil-agri-082}}. They differ from submerged soils, which formed on land and were later flooded by rising water tables, beaver dams or sea level rise. Subaqueous soils formed under a continuous water column, as in an estuary. The US concept arose only in the early 1990s. George Demas pioneered it in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay. He saw that these areas supported rooted plants and had formed horizons. Survey inventories use an arbitrary water depth limit of 2.5 m, which some states have extended to 5 m. Treating them as soils lets scientists trace linked horizons across the underwater landscape, aiding seagrass restoration.

soil-class-086.title: Calcareous grassland, the grazed turf of chalk downs
soil-class-086.text: Calcareous grassland, also called alkaline grassland, grows on thin, basic soils such as those of chalk and limestone downland, where shallow soils like {{ref:soil-class-050}} are common. Large areas occur in northwestern Europe, especially on Salisbury Plain and the North and South Downs of England. One variant on calcium-rich shell sand is {{ref:soil-class-158}}. Short, hardy grasses and herbs such as clover dominate, held at a plagioclimax, a stage fixed by sheep or cattle grazing. It is an important habitat for insects, particularly butterflies and ants. Its lichens, favored by stable flints and nutrient-poor soil, have declined since the mid-20th century through reduced grazing, nitrogen settling from the air and habitat loss.

soil-class-067.title: Takir, the bare clay flats of Central Asia
soil-class-067.text: In the deserts of Central Asia, seasonal rain floods shallow hollows of heavy clay soil. When the water evaporates, it leaves a takir: a smooth, bare clay flat, similar to a salt flat. The Turkic name means 'smooth, even, or bare'. A dried, fissured crust forms on the surface, often colonized by threadlike cyanobacteria. Similar flats are called playas or salt flats in the southwestern United States and sabkha in Arab countries. Calcisols were formerly known internationally as Desert soils and Takyrs.

soil-class-062.title: Serpentine barrens, grassland where forest should be
soil-class-062.text: Where the climate should grow forest, serpentine rock can hold open grassland instead. Serpentine barrens are grassland or savanna on serpentine outcrops, an ecoregion in parts of the United States. They are likeliest where the ultramafic rock never received richer sediment carried by water, glaciers or wind, such as loess, sand or volcanic ash. They occur in small patches of the Appalachians and the Pacific Coast Ranges. Grazing them is risky: one study found toxic nickel in the kidneys of 20% of grazing animals and toxic copper in the livers of 32%. Fire suppression turned Pennsylvania's Rock Springs barren into forest, while controlled burns since 1995 have restored sparse species at Buck Creek, North Carolina.

soil-class-061.title: The tough, rare plants of serpentine soils
soil-class-061.text: In California, 10% of the state's plants are serpentine endemics, found only on these soils. Serpentine plant communities are marked by poor productivity, many such endemics, and tolerance of drought, heavy metals and scarce nutrients. Low calcium-to-magnesium ratios limit root growth and nutrient uptake, while heavy metals stunt growth and yellow the leaves. Plants respond with deep roots, by excluding or storing metals, or by tolerating them. Many are stunted, with dull, waxy gray-green leaves that hold water and reflect sunlight. Tolerance has evolved many times, and patchy, isolated habitats limit gene flow and promote new species. In California 45% of serpentine-associated taxa are rare or endangered.

soil-class-087.title: Blue goo, the clay that slides off California hills
soil-class-087.text: Blue goo is a sticky, plastic, bluish-gray clay soil formed from highly weathered serpentinite mélange, a jumble of sheared rocks. Its source is the Franciscan Complex: greenstones, cherts, basalts, shales, sandstones, schists and serpentinites sheared between the Pacific and North American plates. Gleying without oxygen gives the color, and a grayer variant is called grey goo. The clay holds much water and drains poorly. Saturated, it slips, especially in shallow soils under heavy rain, feeding {{ref:soil-water-057}} on the Northern California coast. It has been found only in the Trinidad and Orick regions of Humboldt County, California.

soil-class-063.title: Duplex soils, sand over clay in Australia
soil-class-063.text: Duplex soil is an Australian term for a soil with a sharp contrast in texture between its horizons. In Northcote's Factual Key, the B horizon is at least one and a half texture classes finer than the A horizon. The change is clear to sharp, within 0.1 m. Topsoils range from coarse sand to clay loam, subsoils from light to heavy clay, and some have a bleached A2 horizon. Northcote used color to separate brown, red and yellow duplex soils. The Australian Soil Classification spreads them among Podosols, Sodosols, Chromosols and Kurosols. Similar soils in strongly seasonal climates such as the Mediterranean are called calcic and chromic Luvisols.

soil-class-052.title: Where terra rossa came from: three rival answers
soil-class-052.text: What is terra rossa made of? Geologists, geomorphologists and soil scientists have long argued over its origin and its link to the carbonate rock beneath, and they still disagree. One group holds that it is insoluble residue: sediment and chert left concentrated as the underlying carbonate rocks dissolved. Another says residue alone cannot explain it. In this view the soil is polygenetic, formed by more than one process, with parent material that includes volcanic ash and non-carbonate or wind-blown sediment, depending on location. A third group proposes metasomatic replacement, the chemical swapping of one rock's minerals for others.

soil-class-059.title: Latosol, the deep red soil of the rainforest
soil-class-059.text: Latosols can reach 20–30 m deep, against 1–2 m for podzols. A latosol, also called tropical red earth, is a rainforest soil with a relatively high content of iron and aluminum oxides. It is usually classed as an Oxisol in USDA soil taxonomy or a Ferralsol in the WRB. Iron oxides color it red or yellowish-red throughout. A thin but very fertile humus layer from the forest above lies over an infertile layer stripped by rapid leaching under heavy rain. Fertility depends wholly on the rainforest. Once it is felled and the humus is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

soil-class-066.title: Gumbo, the clay that turns to sticky mud
soil-class-066.text: Gumbo soil is dominated by very fine clay particles, often with small amounts of sand or organic material. It holds water exceptionally well. Rain, though, turns it into a sticky mud that is hard to work with large farm machinery. Skipping the plow seems to pay: farming gumbo without plowing appears strongly linked to higher yields than traditional methods.

soil-class-082.title: Mesotrophic soil, the middle rank of fertility
soil-class-082.text: Soils can be ranked by their inherent fertility. A mesotrophic soil sits in the middle, between rich eutrophic soils and poor oligotrophic ones. One measure for placing it is base status, an indicator of fertility. Base status relates the major nutrient cations, calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium, to the soil's clay percentage. It is commonly expressed in hundredths of a mole of cations per kilogram of clay, written cmol(+) kg−1 clay.

soil-class-069.title: Mapping soils from the water
soil-class-069.text: Subaqueous soil mapping surveys underwater soils much as land soils are mapped, except that the mapper works from the water. Bathymetric maps, which chart the depth of the bottom, take the place of topographic maps and aerial photographs for identifying underwater landforms. Augers with extendable shafts, peat corers and vibracores replace shovels for sampling. Several US states have begun the work, each NRCS state office setting its priority by local conservation concerns. Interpretations for different uses are still being developed and should grow as more areas are surveyed.

soil-class-155.title: Aquic conditions: soil that runs out of oxygen
soil-class-155.text: A few days of saturation each year is enough to change a soil's label. Aquic conditions describe a {{ref:soil-class-011}} in which the soil stays saturated long enough to become virtually free of dissolved oxygen. In plain terms, every pore fills with water, the measure tracked by {{ref:soil-water-166}}. The telltale marks are {{ref:soil-chem-120}}. Clay-rich {{ref:soil-class-106}} soils often show them for some time in most years, because heavy clay slows the passage of water. Many {{ref:soil-class-098}} soils show aquic conditions too, unless they have been artificially drained.

soil-class-154.title: The aridic regime, where soil stays dry
soil-class-154.text: In arid and semi-arid climates, soil is dry for at least half the growing season. That defines the aridic moisture regime, also called torric. The soil is moist for less than 90 consecutive days. Its control section sits at 50 cm depth, and dry and moist days count only when the soil is warmer than 5 °C and 8 °C. The ustic regime is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic. The desert soil order, {{ref:soil-class-093}}, must have an aridic regime. The torric name reappears in groups such as Torripsamments, members of {{ref:soil-class-108}} with an aridic regime.

soil-class-152.title: ISO 14688, the engineer's international soil yardstick
soil-class-152.text: An engineer in one country needs to call a soil by the same name as an engineer in another. ISO 14688 is the international standard that sets basic principles for identifying and classifying soils for {{ref:soil-class-002}}. Part 1 covers natural soils in place, similar man-made materials and soils redeposited by people. It grades clay as particles smaller than 2 μm. Sand splits into fine, medium and coarse at 0.063, 0.2, 0.63 and 2.0 mm. Gravel follows at 2, 6.3, 20 and 63 mm. The system closely resembles the Unified Soil Classification System, but it codes soils differently and adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

soil-class-153.title: The xeric regime of Mediterranean soils
soil-class-153.text: Cool, moist winters and warm, dry summers mark the Mediterranean climate, and its soils carry the xeric moisture regime. Like the ustic regime, it brings long summer droughts. The regime lends its name to whole groups of soils in USDA taxonomy. Xerolls are Mediterranean examples of {{ref:soil-class-101}}, and Xeralfs belong to {{ref:soil-class-090}}. Greek examples of {{ref:soil-class-058}} fall partly in Rhodoxeralfs, Palexeralfs and Xerochrepts, xeric members of those orders and of {{ref:soil-class-100}}.

soil-class-162.title: Five ways to be an Ultisol
soil-class-162.text: Not all {{ref:soil-class-104}} soils behave alike. {{ref:soil-class-006}} splits them into five suborders by wetness, organic matter and climate. Aquults have a water table at or near the surface for much of the year. Udults belong to humid climates and Ustults to semiarid and subhumid ones. Xerults are temperate, with arid summers and moist winters. Humults stand apart: well drained and rich in organic matter, they are relatively fertile, as in the Olympic series. Each suborder seeds longer names below it. The Cecil series is a Typic Kanhapludult, the Bama series a Typic Paleudult.

soil-class-161.title: Calcids, desert soils cemented with carbonate
soil-class-161.text: Too little rain falls on a Calcid to wash its lime away. This suborder of {{ref:soil-class-093}} has piled up high levels of calcium carbonate, either left from carbonate-rich parent material or delivered as dust. Rainfall has been too low to remove it or carry it deep. The result is a {{ref:soil-form-121}}, a hypercalcic horizon or a {{ref:soil-form-029}} whose top lies within 1.0 m of the surface. Most Calcids serve as rangeland or wildlife habitat. Where they are irrigated for crops, micronutrient deficiency is normal. Great groups include Salicalcids, Gypsicalcids, Petrocalcids, Hypercalcids and Haplocalcids.

soil-class-157.title: Constructed soil, built to bring dead ground back
soil-class-157.text: A spent mine or a capped landfill has no usable topsoil left. Constructed soil fills that gap: a designed mixture of organic and mineral materials, often including repurposed organic waste, made to approximate natural soil and grow plants. Such soils are classed as {{ref:soil-class-145}}. They beat imported {{ref:soil-form-021}}, because harvesting topsoil degrades a second site and usually costs more. A mineral fraction sets texture, an organic fraction supplies nutrients, and a slowly decomposing carbon source, such as wood chips or {{ref:soil-fert-050}}, lasts longer. Organic matter in the top layer should not exceed 15% by weight, or the soil settles and waterlogs. A {{ref:soil-fert-184}} near 20:1 releases nutrients steadily. Layers thicker than about 45 cm can mimic natural {{ref:soil-found-001}} layers, with a sand or gravel drainage layer. Abrupt changes between layers decide whether water flows sideways or down, and where it perches. Living organisms and stable structure come later, as plants return. Every batch must meet legal limits for pathogens, harmful trace elements, salinity and pH.

soil-class-156.title: The acrotelm, a bog's living upper skin
soil-class-156.text: An undisturbed {{ref:soil-class-070}} bog, a {{ref:soil-water-121}}, has two layers, and only the upper one is alive. The acrotelm holds the living plants and overlies the deeper catotelm. The water table rises and falls within it, so conditions swing between airy and airless. Its lower edge usually matches the water table's lowest level. Water moves through it more easily than through the layer below, and it is less dense. Ditching before peat harvest thickens and dries it. A fully developed acrotelm, found only in bogs fed by rain alone, lets researchers study what falls from the atmosphere.

soil-class-158.title: Machair, grassland built from broken seashells
soil-class-158.text: On the Outer Hebrides, waves roll shell fragments ashore, break them up and the wind blows them inland. William MacGillivray first proposed this origin in 1830 for machair, a fertile, low-lying dune grassland on north-western coasts of Ireland and Scotland. The beaches hold 20% to 80% calcium carbonate, making machair a strongly {{ref:soil-chem-035}}, with pH typically above 7. Yet the sand holds nutrients poorly and lacks copper, cobalt and manganese. Cattle need supplements, and only some oats, rye and bere barley thrive. Early farmers spread seaweed, and buried kelp composted into fertile beds.

soil-class-159.title: Black cotton soil of the Deccan Plateau
soil-class-159.text: Lava flows of the Deccan traps gave India about 300,000 square kilometres of black, clayey soil. Called black cotton soil, or regur, it covers the north-western Deccan Plateau and takes its name from its suitability for cotton. It is rich in {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, so it retains water well, and it holds calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. In hot, dry spells it cracks, which lets air in. Dry, it is very hard; wet, it turns to mud, so it needs deep {{ref:soil-agri-095}} to drain. Engineers find it highly compressible, with low bearing capacity and low shear strength.

soil-class-160.title: Paddy soil, where flooded rice breeds methane
soil-class-160.text: Flooding a rice field changes the soil beneath it. Paddy soil, the soil of flooded {{ref:soil-chem-133}} plots, counts among the soils shaped by people, alongside the {{ref:soil-class-120}} group. Organic matter decomposes there without oxygen, and methane-making microbes thrive, through {{ref:soil-chem-129}}. They keep working even though the soil is temporarily oxygenated. One analysis of its fatty-acid markers found the bacteria and archaea about 44% aerobic bacteria, 32% facultative anaerobes and 24% archaea. Paddy soils can also be superbly productive. The smectite-rich ones of Thailand's Central Plains rank among the most productive in the world.

soil-env-102.title: The carbon cycle: one element circling through soil, sea and sky
soil-env-102.text: Limestone cliffs and living cells are built partly of the same element. Carbon is the main component of biological compounds and a major part of many rocks. The carbon cycle is the part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles, described in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}, in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere. Scientists divide it into reservoirs: the atmosphere, the land's living things and soils, the ocean, sediments and Earth's interior. Chemical, physical, geological and biological processes shift carbon between them. Near Earth's surface, the ocean holds the largest active store. Photosynthesis is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the air and enters land and ocean life. Left alone, the flows between air, ocean, land and sediments are fairly balanced, so carbon levels would stay roughly stable. Humans have upset that balance for centuries. They changed land use, and they mined and burned coal, petroleum and gas. By 2020 atmospheric carbon dioxide stood nearly 52% above pre-industrial levels, driving global warming. Today the land and the ocean each absorb about one-quarter of human carbon emissions every year.

soil-env-106.title: Soil carbon, a store three times the atmosphere's
soil-env-106.text: Soils hold about 2,700 gigatons (Gt) of carbon, roughly three times as much as the atmosphere. Soil carbon is the solid carbon stored in soils, and it comes in two forms. About 1550 GtC is organic, from plants, animals and microbes, the material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Another 950 GtC is inorganic, held in the carbonate minerals met in {{ref:soil-found-034}}. Peat and wetlands hold a further 150 GtC, and surface plant litter 50 GtC. This store is far from idle. About 60 GtC a year accumulates in soil, and an equal 60 GtC a year is respired back to the air. Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition set how much carbon stays on land. Soil carbon underpins water holding capacity, nutrient retention and soil structure. It matters for climate too, since soil takes up carbon in the global cycle, and data on it feed global climate models. Those data are inconsistent, with some regions far better covered than others. Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil carbon, yet people could also deliberately return carbon to the soil.

soil-env-116.title: Carbon sinks: places that take in more than they give
soil-env-116.text: During the growing season, land plants pull more carbon from the air than they release. That makes them a carbon sink. A sink is a natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere. It takes up more carbon than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally the two most important are vegetation and the ocean, which absorbs carbon through its solubility and biological pumps. Soil is both an important carbon store and an active sink. Artificial sinks lock carbon in building materials or deep underground. No major artificial system yet removes carbon from the atmosphere at large scale. For gases other than CO2, a sink need not store anything. Nitrous oxide, for example, can be reduced to harmless nitrogen gas, N2. Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change. Keeping and enhancing natural sinks, mainly soils and forests, is therefore important for slowing it.

soil-env-167.title: Climate change mitigation: cutting the gases that warm the planet
soil-env-167.text: Almost 20% of greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture and forestry. Climate change mitigation, also called decarbonisation, is action to limit the greenhouse gases that cause climate change. It includes conserving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy. Another key measure is managing carbon sinks so they remove more CO2 and store it durably. The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based AFOLU options and puts their economic potential at 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq a year. Cutting nitrogen fertilizer use could avoid nitrous oxide equal to 2.77 - 11.48 gigatons of CO2 from 2020 to 2050.

soil-env-212.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away
soil-env-212.text: Turn natural or semi-natural land into cropland, and its soil loses about 30-40% of its organic carbon. Carbon sequestration works in the opposite direction. It is the storing of carbon in a reservoir of the carbon cycle, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. It comes in two main types, biological and geological. Biological sequestration, or biosequestration, captures CO2 through living processes such as photosynthesis. Land-use and farming changes that speed it up are called carbon farming. Sequestration is sometimes confused with carbon capture and storage, which separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed. Biological stores can be temporary, because wildfire, disease, economic pressure and politics can release their carbon again. Mineral sequestration is far more durable, locking carbon in insoluble carbonate salts for thousands to millions of years. In soil, carbon keeps changing after land is cleared until a new equilibrium is reached. Leaving residues, using manure and adding perennial crops, with their larger below-ground biomass, all raise carbon input. Outside permafrost, about 70% of the organic carbon in the upper metre lies deeper down, stabilized by its association with minerals.

soil-env-110.title: Soil carbon and climate: a two-way street
soil-env-110.text: Climate shapes soils, and soils answer back. Changing temperature and moisture alter soil formation. Climate change is therefore likely to affect fertility, salinity, moisture, temperature, organic carbon and aggregation. In return, soil carbon losses or gains alter the climate. Plants fix carbon dioxide into soil, building a pool of around 1500 petagrams (Pg) in the first few metres. Some 20-40% of it lasts more than 100 years. Forest soils are a large part of that pool, and deforestation releases carbon that may markedly raise greenhouse gases in the air. Soil microbes break soil carbon down, and changes in their activity as temperatures rise could add to climate change. Regions respond differently. In polar regions, melting permafrost can open land to more plant growth and carbon uptake. In the tropics, warmer soils lose aggregation and quality. Researchers are looking for ways farming and other human interventions can restore carbon to soils.

soil-env-162.title: How a warming climate makes farming harder
soil-env-162.text: One study linked 1°C of warming to a 3 to 7% fall in global yields of major staple crops. Climate change alters farming in many ways, and most of them make it harder for agriculture to provide global food security. Drought, heat waves and flooding lower crop yields. Climate change is also likely to worsen farming's environmental impacts, by lowering productivity, weakening agrochemicals and increasing soil erosion and pests. The land itself shifts. Sea level rise takes coastal farmland, while thawing frozen ground opens new arable land. Soil fertility and growing seasons change. CO2 fertilization, the extra growth that more carbon dioxide can bring, offsets a small part of the harm. Yet it lowers essential micronutrients in crops and does little for C4 crops like maize. The future extent of soil erosion and groundwater depletion are among the main uncertainties. Farmers can adapt through management practices, agricultural innovation, institutional change and climate-smart agriculture.

soil-env-107.title: Carbon locked in minerals: soil's carbonate store
soil-env-107.text: In arid and semi-arid lands, most soil carbon is not organic at all. It is soil inorganic carbon: carbon held as minerals, mainly carbonates such as calcite and dolomite. Some carbonate comes ready-made from bedrock or parent material. Some forms in place in the soil and is called pedogenic carbonate. It arises from the weathering of parent material, or from soil minerals reacting with CO2 from the air. Worldwide, inorganic carbon makes up about 950 GtC, roughly a third of all soil carbon. The store can be undone. The reactions are reversible: when carbonate meets hydrogen ions from acids, as it does in soils, it forms water and releases CO2 back to the air.

soil-env-108.title: Soil organic carbon, built from roots, leaves and dead microbes
soil-env-108.text: The remains of dead microbes, called microbial necromass, can make up 30 to 80% of soil carbon. Microbes cycle it that thoroughly. This is soil organic carbon: the carbon held in soil organic matter, which is about 50% carbon by dry weight. In humid environments most soil carbon takes this form. Its main source is dead plant material arriving as roots, fallen leaves and crop residue, with animal bodies and excreta adding more. Living plants pass 5–20% of the carbon they fix to the soil as root exudates, feeding rhizosphere organisms such as mycorrhizal fungi. Cellulose, starches, proteins and lipids break down fast. Lignin, humus, aggregate-bound organic matter and charcoal persist. Most upland topsoils hold 0.5% to 3.0% organic carbon. Below 0.5% is mostly limited to deserts, and above 12–18% soils are classed as organic soils. Carbon builds up where waterlogging slows decomposition, as in swamps, bogs and marshes. Charcoal and other fire-derived carbon typically supply 5–50% of it, and more than 50% in mollisols, chernozems and terra preta.

soil-env-111.title: Managing soil carbon: stop the losses, build the stock
soil-env-111.text: Exchange of carbon between soils and the atmosphere is a significant part of the global carbon cycle, and humans and farming now affect it most. Managing soil carbon means choosing land and farm practices to avoid losses of soil organic carbon, covered in {{ref:soil-env-108}}, and to build it up. Losses come from several directions. Land-use change such as deforestation has caused substantial soil carbon losses, though exact amounts are hard to measure. Fire strips soil cover and causes immediate and continuing losses. Tillage, described in {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, and drainage expose organic matter to oxygen, and peatlands in the Netherlands, East Anglia, Florida and the California Delta have subsided severely as a result. Grazing that leaves soil bare, through too long or too short recovery periods, also loses carbon. Building carbon is not simple, because soil organisms consume and release carbon and become more active when nitrogen fertilizer is added. Still, past losses mean farmed soils can store more. Reducing tillage intensity and summer fallow cuts losses, while manure, biochar, cover crops, residue retention, perennials and good fertilization raise inputs. Farmers are discouraged from stubble burning and over-cultivation and encouraged to work in organic material such as manure.

soil-env-154.title: Carbon in the deep freeze: the permafrost carbon cycle
soil-env-154.text: Permafrost-affected soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of its soil organic carbon. The permafrost carbon cycle is the Arctic part of the global carbon cycle. Carbon moves from frozen soils to plants, microbes and the air. It returns to permafrost through burial and sedimentation driven by freezing, or cryogenic, processes, while some passes to the ocean and the wider cycle. The cycle includes exchanges of carbon dioxide and methane with the air. It also includes transfers to water as dissolved and particulate carbon, both organic and inorganic. Because permafrost responds slowly to climate, it keeps carbon out of the air for long periods. The method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}} shows much of it is thousands of years old. Early carbon estimates and climate models often neglected this reservoir, but research on it has grown enormously since the 2000s. Microbial respiration is the main route by which old permafrost carbon re-enters the air. Soil temperature, moisture, nutrients and oxygen set its rate. Minerals can slow the escape. Iron oxides can hold back respiration, and iron and aluminum can adsorb freed carbon, especially in the sandy layers often found over permafrost. Despite the huge stores, the whole pool is unlikely to mobilize, because much permafrost will stay frozen even as thaw deepens.

soil-env-146.title: The active layer, the ground that thaws each summer
soil-env-146.text: In northeastern Siberia, Alaska and Greenland, summer thaws the ground to less than 50 centimetres. In southern Norway and Mongolia it thaws past 600 centimetres. That seasonal skin is the active layer: the top layer of soil in permafrost regions that thaws each summer and freezes again in autumn. In 2018 it averaged about 145 centimetres across the Northern Hemisphere. Soil temperature is steadier at depth than at the surface, so seasonal heating and cooling fade downward. In winter a frost front forms in the soil. In spring and summer the soil thaws from the top down. Where summer heat cannot thaw it completely, permafrost forms. The year-round frozen soil below is the inactive layer, and the boundary is sometimes called the permafrost table. Water cannot drain below the active layer, so permafrost lands tend to be very poorly drained and boggy. Roots cannot grow below it either, which restricts trees over continuous permafrost to shallow-rooted species such as larch.

soil-env-118.title: Why soils hold more carbon than plants and air combined
soil-env-118.text: A tropical field cleared by slash-and-burn stays fertile for only two to three years. Heat and rain are the reason: in tropical and subtropical climates, litter and humus oxidize fast and rain leaches them away. Taken as a whole, though, soils are a short- to long-term carbon store, holding more carbon than all land vegetation and the atmosphere combined. Plant litter and other biomass, charcoal included, build up as soil organic matter. Tougher compounds such as lignin, waxes and terpenoids are retained together as humus. Organic matter accumulates in cold regions such as the boreal forests of North America and the Russian taiga. Grasslands store it mainly in fibrous root mats, and natural grass fires leave stable biochar. Since the 1850s much of the world's grassland has been tilled into cropland, rapidly oxidizing large amounts of soil organic carbon. Methods that markedly raise carbon storage, such as no-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation, are called carbon farming.

soil-env-168.title: Soil carbon sequestration: drawing carbon down into the ground
soil-env-168.text: In 2004 Science published a paper on soil carbon sequestration by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-026}}. It was the first to report that restoring soil organic matter does two jobs at once. It improves soil health, and it reduces atmospheric CO2. Soil carbon sequestration is that process: drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon. It is both a major soil property and an ecosystem service. Farming can deplete soil carbon, but conservation farming can protect it and repair the damage over time. Methods include cover crops, no-till farming, residue mulching and crop rotation. For European soils the best practices are converting arable land to grassland, straw incorporation, reduced tillage, ley cropping and cover crops. Trees exude more carbon below ground than they capture above it, helping build a carbon-rich soil described in {{ref:soil-env-119}}. Biochar retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years. The potential is large. Protecting healthy soils and restoring that sponge could remove 7.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, more than annual US emissions. The many measures make soil carbon hard to measure and account for. Yet they carry fewer trade-offs than afforestation or BECCS, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage.

soil-env-170.title: Pingos, hills with a heart of ice
soil-env-170.text: John Franklin first described a pingo in 1825. In 1938 Alf Erling Porsild borrowed the Inuvialuit word, meaning conical hill, for scientific use. A pingo is an ice-cored hill, 3–70 m high and 30–1,000 m across, that grows only in permafrost. More than 11,000 exist, the most, 1,350, on the Tuktoyaktuk peninsula. Closed-system pingos form as an infilled lake freezes and squeezes trapped water upward. Open-system pingos are fed by artesian groundwater. Pingos grow a couple of centimetres a year. When the ice core melts, they collapse into depressions that show permafrost once existed.

soil-env-139.title: Permafrost thaw: the frozen ground is shrinking
soil-env-139.text: In parts of Northern Alaska, permafrost warmed by up to 3 °C between the early 1980s and the mid-2000s. Permafrost thaw is the warming and thawing of permafrost under climate change, seen as a thickening active layer and shrinking frozen ground. Globally, permafrost warmed by about 0.3 °C between 2007 and 2016, more where it is continuous than where it is patchy. In the Russian European North it warmed by up to 2 °C from 1970 to 2020. The active layer has thickened too. Its average rose from about 127 centimetres to about 145 centimetres between 2000 and 2018, roughly 0.65 centimetres a year. Frozen ground is retreating. In Yukon the zone of continuous permafrost may have moved 100 kilometres poleward since 1899, though accurate records span only 30 years. Model projections, process understanding and evidence from past climates make it virtually certain that permafrost will keep shrinking as climate warms. The volume of permafrost in the upper 3 m is expected to fall by about 25% per 1 °C of global warming.

soil-env-130.title: Continuous to isolated: grading permafrost by coverage
soil-env-130.text: About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's ice-free land sits directly on permafrost, yet 22% lies within a permafrost zone. The difference comes from how the zones work. Permafrost zones divide frozen regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost. In the continuous zone 90%–100% is, in the discontinuous zone 50%–90%, and in the sporadic zone 10%–50%. Isolated patches cover 10% or less. Soil scientists abbreviate the continuous zone CPZ, the extensive discontinuous zone DPZ and the sporadic zone SPZ. Temperature sets the pattern. Permafrost usually forms wherever mean annual air temperature is below freezing. Humid boreal forests are the exception, because snow insulates the ground there. Where the mean annual soil surface temperature lies between −5 and 0 °C, permafrost usually stays discontinuous, forming only in sheltered spots. Below −5 °C, not even a slope's aspect, the direction it faces, can thaw it, and a continuous zone forms.

soil-env-112.title: What extra soil carbon does for a whole catchment
soil-env-112.text: Raising soil carbon does more than store carbon. Carbon catchment health names those wider benefits, for the soil and for its catchment, the land that drains to a waterway. More stable aggregates resist erosion and sedimentation, and soils that keep their strength when wet are less prone to mass movement. Nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways. Greater water holding capacity cuts overland flow and keeps water available to plants. The benefits are hard to quantify, because natural resource systems are complex and soil health is open to interpretation.

soil-env-113.title: Counting the carbon: how countries track soil stocks
soil-env-113.text: One model puts the organic carbon in the topsoil of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt. Figures like that come from soil carbon monitoring: estimating organic carbon stocks and their changes by field survey and modelling. Climate reporting requires it. Under the UN climate convention, countries report changes in five carbon stores, soil carbon among them, following IPCC good practice guidance. Tanzania, with the FAO, runs a forest soil carbon programme that combines survey and modelling. For Europe, the European Soil Database gives the most consistent data. Australian farm soils, typically 1.6–4.6% carbon today, may once have held twice as much.

soil-env-109.title: How organic carbon keeps a soil working
soil-env-109.text: In one study of sandy soils, organic carbon accounted for up to 76% of the variation in cation exchange capacity, the soil's power to hold nutrient ions. That is one of many services organic carbon sustains. Together they add up to soil health, a soil's capacity to provide services. Carbon benchmarks used to judge it include CO2 release, humus levels and microbial metabolic activity. In sandy soils, bulk density falls as organic carbon rises, and bulk density is needed to calculate carbon stocks. Organic carbon also rises with silt and clay content and is highest in the clay fraction, where fine particles bind decomposing matter into protective aggregates.

soil-env-103.title: Two speeds of the carbon cycle
soil-env-103.text: Some carbon turns over in years; some takes millions. The carbon cycle splits into a fast biological cycle and a slow geological one. The fast cycle runs through living things, moving carbon between the atmosphere, land and marine ecosystems, soils and seafloor sediments. It includes annual cycles driven by photosynthesis and decadal cycles of vegetation growth and decomposition. The slow cycle runs through rocks. Weathering returns carbon to the atmosphere by degassing and to the ocean by rivers, over spans of millions of years. Between 10 and 100 million tonnes of carbon move around it in a given year.

soil-env-114.title: When warming soils breathe out more carbon
soil-env-114.text: A warming experiment at Harvard, run since 1991, suggests the top metre of soils could release about 190 petagrams of carbon by 2100. That release is the soil carbon feedback: carbon leaving soils in response to global warming, which in turn adds to the warming. Soils hold roughly two to three times as much carbon as the atmosphere, so the feedback is crucial for future climate. Faster soil respiration is the main cause. Measurements imply that 4 °C of warming raises annual soil respiration by up to 37%. Between 1989 and 2008, global soil respiration rose by about 0.1% a year, most likely because warming sped up the decomposition of soil organic matter. A 2018 study found climate-driven soil carbon losses already occurring across many ecosystems, with a detectable global trend. Observations of thawing permafrost suggest a linear, chronic release of greenhouse gases as warming continues. Gaps remain. Global decomposition models poorly represent soil animals such as insects and worms, and their interactions with microbes.

soil-env-117.title: Carbon pools, the Earth's carbon reservoirs
soil-env-117.text: The atmosphere, the oceans, soil, plants and fossil fuels share one label: each is a carbon pool. A carbon pool is any reservoir in the Earth system where carbon resides in some chemical form for a period of time. It is the overarching term, and a carbon sink is one type of pool. The two words mean slightly different things, and both matter for understanding the carbon cycle. Related terms are reservoir, sequestration, source and uptake.

soil-env-104.title: Carbon on land, above and below ground
soil-env-104.text: About 500 gigatons of carbon sit above ground in plants and other organisms, while soil holds approximately 1,500 gigatons. Together they make up the terrestrial carbon pool: the carbon held in all living and dead land organisms and in soils. Most land carbon is organic, but about a third of soil carbon is inorganic, in forms such as calcium carbonate. Because land uptake depends on living things, it follows daily and seasonal cycles. Those rhythms show up in the Keeling curve of CO2 measurements. Carbon leaves the land pool by burning or respiration, or by export to the ocean in rivers. Some stays sequestered in soils as inert carbon, for up to thousands of years, until erosion washes it into rivers or soil respiration releases it. How long soil holds carbon depends on local climate, so it changes as the climate changes.

soil-env-105.title: Clearing forests, releasing carbon
soil-env-105.text: Replace a forest with cropland or a town, and carbon once stored on land ends up in the atmosphere. Cropland and urban land store comparatively little carbon. That release, chiefly from turning forest into farmland or towns, is the carbon cost of land-use change. Since the invention of agriculture, people have shifted the carbon cycle over centuries by changing the mix of vegetation on land. The change has also cut biodiversity, lowering ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air. Reforestation, deliberate or natural, can reverse the effect.

soil-env-213.title: Feedbacks that speed up or slow down warming
soil-env-213.text: The IPCC estimates that permafrost could release the equivalent of 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2 per 1 °C of warming. Releases like that are climate change feedbacks: natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions. Positive feedbacks amplify warming, and negative ones damp it. The labels do not mean good or bad. Physical feedbacks include less reflective snow and ice and more water vapour. Biological ones mostly involve how fast plants take up CO2. The carbon cycle absorbs more than half of yearly CO2 emissions into plants and the ocean. That share will fall as sinks saturate and drought and wildfire increase. Methane from land, especially wetlands, and nitrous oxide from land and oceans are a known positive feedback. The sum of all feedbacks is negative but becoming less so, so warming will accelerate if emissions continue at current levels. The carbon side remains uncertain, and permafrost thaw releases CO2 and methane in ways that are hard to model.

soil-env-131.title: Frozen ground on the high mountains
soil-env-131.text: In 2009 permafrost was found on Mount Kilimanjaro. Alpine permafrost is permafrost at high elevations, in mountains cold enough to keep the ground frozen year after year. Extensive alpine permafrost generally needs a mean annual air temperature of −3 °C, though some mountains hold it at −1 °C. It is hard to study, and systematic research began only in the 1970s. Regional estimates collected in 2014 put its global extent at 3,560,000 km2. The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau holds the largest area, 1,300,000 km2. The frozen layer can even lie beneath warmer soil that supports vegetation.

soil-env-138.title: Building on frozen ground without thawing it
soil-env-138.text: Norilsk and Yakutsk, both in Russia, are the only two large cities built on continuous permafrost. Their engineers face one central danger. Heat from a building or pipeline can thaw the soil, and as ice turns to water the ground loses its ability to support the structure. Construction on permafrost therefore keeps the ground frozen. Wood pile foundations, pioneered by Mikhail Kim in Norilsk, should reach 15 metres, where the temperature stays at about −5 °C all year. Other methods are gravel pads 1–2 m thick and ammonia heat pipes, as in the supports of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

soil-env-145.title: From a blocked well in Yakutsk to a world science
soil-env-145.text: In 1684 frozen ground stopped well digging in Yakutsk, one of the earliest reports of permafrost. Until the mid-20th century most of the literature on it was in Russian. Karl Ernst von Baer, often called the founder of scientific permafrost research, published from 1838 and wrote the first permafrost textbook in 1843. The English word arrived in 1943. Siemon William Muller coined it from permanently frozen ground, translating the Russian vechnaia merzlota. The First International Conference on Permafrost met at Purdue University in November 1963, and the International Permafrost Association was created in 1983.

soil-env-135.title: Massive ground ice, frozen soil that is mostly ice
soil-env-135.text: In massive ground ice, the ice exceeds 250 percent of the dry soil by mass. Its beds are at least 2 m thick and 10 m across, ranging from icy mud to pure ice. Of the four kinds of ground ice, only buried surface ice and intrasedimental ice, which grows within the sediment, get large enough to count as massive. Pore ice and ice wedges do not. Segregational ice, the main intrasedimental type, forms as water migrates to the freezing front, mostly in silts of low salinity. In the top 2.5 m, forming it takes 1–1000 years in clay, 10–10,000 years in peat and 1,000–1,000,000 years in silt.

soil-env-152.title: Yedoma, Ice Age permafrost packed with carbon
soil-env-152.text: Yedoma covers more than one million square kilometers from northeast Siberia to Alaska and Canada, in many places tens of meters thick. It is ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass and 50–90% ice by volume. It forms in poorly drained, severely cold lowlands with ice wedge polygons, sparse vegetation, intense periglacial weathering and nearby sources of sediment. Yedoma may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, a multiple of yearly fossil fuel emissions. As it thaws it becomes a significant methane source, about 4 Tg of CH4 a year. It has done this before. At the end of the last ice age, thawing yedoma and its thaw lakes may have caused 33 to 87% of the high-latitude rise in atmospheric methane.

soil-env-133.title: When permafrost reached Hungary
soil-env-133.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, continuous permafrost covered all of ice-free Europe south to about Szeged in Hungary. In East Asia it reached as far south as present-day Changchun. North America had only a narrow belt south of the ice sheet, but in the drier west it stretched to the southern borders of Idaho and Oregon. The Southern Hemisphere also shows evidence of former, probably discontinuous permafrost, in central Otago and Argentine Patagonia.

soil-env-134.title: How deep permafrost goes, and how slowly
soil-env-134.text: In the northern Lena and Yana River basins of Siberia, permafrost runs 1,493 m deep. Its bottom, the permafrost base, lies where Earth's geothermal heat balances the mean surface temperature at 0 °C. Base depth ranges from less than a meter to that Siberian extreme. Growth slows sharply after the first few metres. At Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, permafrost reaches 4.44 m after 1 year but 687.7 m only after 775,000 years. That deep layer took over half a million years to form, spanning several Pleistocene glacial cycles. Permafrost in soil conducts heat less well than permafrost in bedrock, so the geothermal gradient affects it less.

soil-env-137.title: Life above and within permanently frozen ground
soil-env-137.text: Even frozen, permafrost soil typically holds from 1 to 1000 million microorganisms per gram. Permafrost ecology is how permanently frozen ground shapes the plants, animals and microbes that live with it. Only shallow-rooted plants survive over permafrost. Black spruce tolerates limited rooting zones and dominates where permafrost is extensive. Most permafrost bacteria and fungi cannot be cultured in the lab, so scientists identify them by DNA-based techniques. The living ones show adaptations to sub-zero conditions, including reduced metabolism and anaerobic metabolism, which runs without oxygen.

soil-env-136.title: Polygons, slumps and mounds: the shapes of frozen ground
soil-env-136.text: Frozen ground sculpts its own surface. Permafrost landforms are the features built as that ground freezes, cracks and thaws. Thermal contraction cracks that become ice wedges, together with solifluction downslope, create polygons, rings, steps and other patterned ground. Melting ground ice in ice-rich permafrost starts the collapse features described in {{ref:soil-env-153}}: lakes, thaw slumps, thermal-erosion gullies and active layer detachments. In Arctic bogs, meltwater trapped over deep permafrost freezes into ice lenses that push the ground up into mounds. These grow into palsas, peat mounds 15–150 m long but under 6 m tall, and larger pingos, 3–70 m high and up to 1,000 m across.

soil-env-142.title: Thawing ground under Arctic towns and roads
soil-env-142.text: As of 2021, 1162 settlements with about 5 million people sit on Arctic permafrost. Beneath 42% of them, the permafrost is expected to thaw by 2050. That threat reaches settlements, roads, pipelines and buildings alike. By 2050 nearly 70% of infrastructure in permafrost areas could be at high risk, including 30–50% of critical infrastructure, at costs of tens of billions of dollars. In Alaska alone, damages by 2100 would reach $4.6 billion under the high-emission RCP8.5 scenario. The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau is warming at twice the global rate. Already 40% of its permafrost is warm, and around 30% of its roads are damaged.

soil-env-143.title: Toxic waste and mercury waiting in the ice
soil-env-143.text: An estimated 800,000 tons of mercury lie frozen in permafrost soil. For much of the 20th century, permafrost was thought to preserve buried material indefinitely, so it became a popular site for hazardous waste disposal. About 4500 industrial facilities handle hazardous chemicals in Arctic permafrost areas. Some 13,000 to 20,000 heavily contaminated sites, 70% of them in Russia, are trapped in the frozen ground. Thaw could release them. After thaw, around 70% of the mercury is taken up by vegetation. Under the high-emission RCP8.5 scenario, enough would reach the Yukon River basin by 2050 to make its fish unsafe to eat under EPA guidelines.

soil-env-144.title: Ice Age life waiting in the frozen ground
soil-env-144.text: In 2012 Russian researchers brought a plant back to life from tissue 30,000 years old. They found it in an Ice Age squirrel burrow sealed in frozen ground and grew Silene stenophylla, the oldest plant tissue ever revived. Permafrost also holds dormant bacteria and inactive viruses. Some scientists worry that thaw could free unknown pathogens of humans, livestock or crops. Others note that pathogens such as influenza and smallpox seem unable to survive thawing, and a scientific review rates the risk as generally low. The question is still argued.

soil-env-132.title: Subsea permafrost, the Ice Age land the sea drowned
soil-env-132.text: Some permafrost lies under the sea. Subsea permafrost sits beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves. It froze on dry land during the last Ice Age, when sea levels were low, and the rising sea later flooded it. Warmer, saltier conditions have slowly shrunk it ever since. Today it covers an estimated 2 million km2, about a fifth of the land permafrost domain and 30–50% less than at the Last Glacial Maximum. It holds around 560 GtC in organic matter and 45 GtC as methane, and releases 18 and 38 MtC a year as it still responds to post-glacial warming. Under the RCP 8.5 scenario it could release 43 GtC by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300. Yet the effects of human-driven warming will show there only after hundreds or thousands of years.

soil-env-141.title: Drunken trees and sliding slopes on thawing ground
soil-env-141.text: Trees tilting at random, so-called drunken trees, are a sure sign that the ground beneath them is thawing. As permafrost ice melts and the water drains or evaporates, soil structure weakens and can turn viscous. Warming has increased slope disturbances on permafrost, sharply raising the sediment that rivers carry, and thaw can also drain and dry northern wetlands. In high mountains, thaw builds pore-water pressure and lowers slope stability, leading to slope failures and rockfalls such as the 1987 Val Pola landslide. Thaw also forms frozen debris lobes, slow landslides of soil, rock, trees and ice. By December 2021, 43 had been identified in Alaska's southern Brooks Range.

soil-env-120.title: The root fungi that hold much of the soil's carbon
soil-env-120.text: On forested islands in Sweden, fungi living on tree roots hold 50 to 70 percent of the carbon stored in leaf litter and soil. These are the mycorrhizal fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, partners of the roots of almost all plants. Alongside plants, decomposers and minerals, they are emerging as important keepers of soil carbon. Plants send them an estimated 5 to 20% of the carbon they take up. In some ecosystems the fungal biomass rivals that of fine roots. It also turns over quickly, and in some places it is the main route by which living carbon enters the soil carbon pool. The two main groups, arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi, belong to separate evolutionary lines and often act in very different ways. Researchers therefore weigh the evidence for each separately. Their effect on dead roots is mixed. Ectomycorrhizal fungi speed fine root decay in some ecosystems but slow it in the roots of Pinus edulis.

soil-env-169.title: Rewetting wetlands to keep their carbon locked away
soil-env-169.text: Peatland covers just 3% of the land surface, yet it stores up to 550 gigatonnes of carbon, 42% of all soil carbon. Wetland restoration aims to keep such places sequestering carbon and storing water. It offers moderate to great mitigation potential on limited land, with low trade-offs and costs, and wetlands store about 45 million tonnes of carbon a year. Peatlands are threatened by drainage for farming, by logging and by peat sales for compost. Blocking the drainage channels lets natural vegetation recover. The gain has a catch: some wetlands are significant sources of methane, and some also emit nitrous oxide.

soil-env-157.title: How thaw lets ancient Arctic carbon escape
soil-env-157.text: Some Arctic carbon has sat frozen for decades, some for millennia. Warming is setting it loose. As the Arctic heats up, the active layer, the soil that thaws each summer, grows deeper. That exposes long-stored carbon to microbes, whose decomposition releases it into the air. Warming also intensifies the Arctic water cycle, and more warm rain deepens the thaw further. The amount that escapes depends on four things. They are how deep the thaw goes, the carbon content of the thawed soil, physical changes to the ground, and the activity of microbes and plants. The change lasts. Once thawed, ground will not return to permafrost for centuries, even if warming reverses. Whether the region already gives off more than it takes in is contested. A 1993 study found the tundra had been a carbon sink until the late 1970s and a net carbon source since. The 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated a net release of 0.3 to 0.6 Pg C a year. Winter emissions, it found, exceeded what vegetation takes up in the growing season. But a 2022 study of atmospheric records from 1980 to 2017 found permafrost regions had been gaining carbon on net. The form of the carbon matters too. Methane lasts under 12 years in the air but warms around 80 times more than CO2 over 20 years. So which gas escapes matters as much as how much carbon.

soil-env-140.title: The permafrost carbon feedback: thaw that feeds itself
soil-env-140.text: Northern circumpolar permafrost holds organic matter equal to 1400–1650 billion tons of carbon, about twice the carbon in the atmosphere. Most of it, ~1,035 billion tons, lies in near-surface permafrost no deeper than 3 metres. When thaw releases that carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, the extra warming drives more thaw. This loop is the permafrost carbon feedback, a northern case of {{ref:soil-env-114}}. Where thawed soil has air, microbes respire the carbon as CO2; where it lacks air, they make methane. Methane will be a small share of the carbon, yet it is expected to cause 40–70% of this century's warming from thaw. Only a fraction of the store will escape. Even under the RCP8.5 scenario of over 4 °C warming, about 5% to 15% of permafrost carbon is expected to be lost over decades and centuries. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases equal to 14–175 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide per 1 °C of warming. Arctic greening will offset some emissions, but very unlikely all of them, and more Arctic wildfires can speed the release. There is widespread agreement that permafrost emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small to cause runaway warming. Gradual thaw would add around 0.09 °C by 2100 if warming is held to 2 °C. Abrupt collapse near 4 °C of warming could add 0.2–0.4 °C. Whether thaw is a global tipping point is debated. Locally it perpetuates itself, but taken together it proceeds gradually with warming.

soil-env-156.title: Counting the carbon locked in frozen soils
soil-env-156.text: In 2003 Tarnocai and colleagues tallied the carbon in cryosols, soils with permafrost within two meters of the surface, using the Northern and Mid Latitudes Soil Database. Later estimates more than doubled the carbon previously known in permafrost soils. Soil organic carbon in the northern circumpolar permafrost region now stands at around 1,460–1,600 Pg, more than twice the carbon in the atmosphere. Much of it sits within reach of thaw. The top 0–30 cm holds about 200 Pg, the top 0–100 cm about 500 Pg and the top 0–300 cm about 1024 Pg. Yedoma, with 400 Pg, and Arctic deltaic deposits, with 240 Pg, add more, generally deeper than the 3 m of traditional studies. Include the Tibetan Plateau, and Northern Hemisphere permafrost holds around 1832 Gt.

soil-env-150.title: Taliks, the ground that never freezes in permafrost country
soil-env-150.text: Even in permafrost country, some ground stays soft all winter. A talik is a zone that remains unfrozen all year within a permafrost area. In continuous permafrost, taliks often lie under shallow lakes in thaw hollows, described in {{ref:soil-env-153}}, and under rivers whose deep water does not freeze in winter. Taliks come in three kinds. A closed talik is surrounded by permafrost. An open talik opens at the top. A through talik also connects to unfrozen ground below the permafrost. One study suggests open taliks are more widespread in fault zones and near large rivers.

soil-env-166.title: The greenhouse gases that rise from farms and fields
soil-env-166.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Some of that comes directly from rice and livestock farming. Some comes indirectly, when forests and other land are converted to farmland. Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of direct agricultural emissions. What farm soils give off depends on soil type, climate and management. Conservation tillage, precision agriculture, better water use and biochar can cut these emissions and store soil carbon at the same time.

soil-env-163.title: How a warming climate wears down soil fertility
soil-env-163.text: Erosion can strip up to 22% of soil carbon in 50 years, and a warmer world gives it more chances. A more vigorous water cycle brings extreme rainfall, making erosion, compaction and a general decline of the soil more likely. Warmth works below ground too. Warmer soils decompose organic matter faster, lowering soil organic carbon and with it the soil's hold on nutrients and water. Soil microbe populations could rise 40–150%, and warmth would favor certain bacteria, shifting the community's makeup. Extra carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth and slow the soil carbon cycle. It would favor slow-growing, efficient microbes called oligotrophs over copiotrophs, which thrive where food is plentiful.

soil-env-165.title: Rising seas and the rice fields at the shoreline
soil-env-165.text: A one-metre rise in the sea would cover several square kilometres of Vietnam's rice paddies. Rising seas threaten farming mainly by flooding low-lying land, especially in South East Asia, through erosion, submerged shorelines and a saltier water table. Bangladesh, India and Vietnam face major rice losses. The sea also pushes saltwater into freshwater wells, which become unusable once saltwater exceeds 2–3%.

soil-env-164.title: New farmland in the thawing far north
soil-env-164.text: Siberia has warmed by three degrees Celsius on average since 1960, much more than the rest of the world, a 2005 study reported. A 2025 study of Arctic Western Siberia projects more permafrost thaw by 2100 and a northward shift of the permafrost zone's southern boundary. Thawing ground could open new farmland. Reports on Russian agriculture expect fields to extend northward, but they warn of possible productivity losses and greater drought risk. Across the Arctic, farming and forestry are expected to gain new opportunities.

soil-env-153.title: Thermokarst, the hollow land left by melting ground ice
soil-env-153.text: When ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground sags into a jumble of marshy hollows and small hummocks. This terrain is called thermokarst, a name that comes from its resemblance to karst, the pitted landscape of dissolving limestone. It occurs across Arctic areas and, on a smaller scale, in mountains such as the Himalayas and the Swiss Alps. Where permafrost holds over 30% ice by volume, thaw depressions fill with water and become thermokarst lakes. These lakes tend to form and drain in a cycle. Each one warms the ground beneath it, so the permafrost below is shallower, and unfrozen ground ({{ref:soil-env-150}}) lies under lakes that are deep enough. The lakes also feed the warming. As permafrost thaws around them it releases methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide, a positive feedback that drives more thaw.

soil-env-147.title: Thaw depth, how far summer reaches into frozen soil
soil-env-147.text: On Ellesmere Island summer thaws the ground only 10 cm deep. At Yakutsk it reaches about 2.5 m, and at Yellowknife 5 meters. Thaw depth is the level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, with frozen soil below. Its maximum over two years is the active layer thickness. Maximum air temperature is the main control, but the ground matters too. Coarse sandy or gravelly parent material conducts heat better, giving active layers up to five times deeper than in loam- or clay-rich material. Vegetation and soil organic matter change bulk density and so thermal conductivity, how well soil carries heat. Thaw depth matters for both ecology and construction.

soil-env-119.title: The soil carbon sponge that drinks the rain
soil-env-119.text: Healthy topsoil weighs about 1 gram/cc. The parent mineral soil beneath it weighs 2.6–3.5 grams/cc. The light, porous, well-aggregated layer is what the Australian scientist Walter Jehne called a soil carbon sponge: soil that soaks up water and holds it well. In his 2017 paper Regenerate Earth he linked soil carbon to a restored water cycle that could cool the planet. Bare soil, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation speed the oxidation of its carbon and shrink the sponge. Fire and flooding harm it too. Afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build it back, and the growing sponge also serves as a carbon sink.

soil-env-171.title: Permafrost that grows upward as the ground builds up
soil-env-171.text: Frozen ground does not only thaw. It can also grow upward. When new material piles onto a site under freezing conditions, the frozen ground rises to take it in. This syngenetic growth is efficient compared with heterogenetic growth, in which cold works down into unfrozen ground of uniform composition. The new layers come from river sediment, debris fallen from hillsides, wind-blown material and lake-bottom deposits. As the surface rises it buries organic and mineral soil, making this one of the two main ways permafrost stores carbon. Ice wedges growing upward into permafrost cracks can count as syngenetic too. Studies draw on the permafrost tunnel near Fairbanks, Alaska.

soil-env-158.title: Carbon dioxide, the main gas from thawing permafrost
soil-env-158.text: Most permafrost soils hold oxygen, so their microbes breathe out carbon dioxide. That gas makes up the overwhelming majority of permafrost and Arctic emissions. Studies from the early 2020s add a twist. In the growing season soil microbes respire mostly modern carbon, but in winter they live on ancient carbon. Researchers debate whether rising emissions come mainly from that old frozen carbon or from faster respiration of fresh plant litter in warmer soils. Plants push back. On thawed ground they root deeper, grow larger and take up more carbon, generally the main counteracting feedback. Wildfires push the other way, burning off the insulating organic mat, warming the soil and deepening the active layer.

soil-env-155.title: Two ways plant carbon ends up frozen underground
soil-env-155.text: Permafrost makes no carbon of its own. Carbon from plants must first enter the soil and then be built into the frozen ground. Two processes do this. In syngenetic growth, wind or river sediment or peat raises the surface, by up to 0.5mm/yr for peat and 0.7mm/yr for sediment, burying carbon into permafrost. In cryoturbation, freeze–thaw cycles mix the soil, most often by frost heaving, and carry surface carbon down until the permafrost takes it in. Storage runs faster when cryoturbation and sediment deposition act together.

soil-env-159.title: Methane from waterlogged thaw and Arctic lakes
soil-env-159.text: Methanogenesis, the making of methane by microbes, needs ground with no oxygen at all. So permafrost methane centres on Arctic lakes, where 2022 observations show at least half of the methane made reaches the air. How much thaw will yield is still a matter of debate. A 2015 review found sites without oxygen emitted 75–85% less than sites with it. Yet a 2018 incubation study found methane matched CO2 once methane-making microbes were established. Most of the carbon is young. A 2017 paper found less than 10% of methane from thawing peatlands came from old, thawed carbon, the rest from decay of modern carbon. Peatland methane after thaw starts high, at 82 milligrams per square meter per day, then falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

soil-env-215.title: Arctic methane and a feedback still taking shape
soil-env-215.text: Arctic-Boreal lands release about 48.7 Tg of methane a year, a 2024 assessment found, and marine sources add about 4.9 Tg. The gas comes mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, the breakdown of clathrates and the melting Greenland ice sheet. Clathrates are icy solids that trap gas inside, and they hold about 20 Gt of permafrost-associated methane. Permafrost itself holds almost twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. The emissions form a positive climate feedback. Thaw exposes organic material to methanogenesis, and methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Thermokarst lakes are frequent sources, and at least half the methane made in them reaches the atmosphere. Dating by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}} suggests 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon was released as methane and CO2 over the last 60 years. The future pace is debated, as {{ref:soil-env-159}} showed. A 2015 review found anaerobic thaw sites, those without oxygen, emitted 75-85% less in total than aerobic ones. A 2018 seven-year incubation found methane production matched CO2 once methanogenic microbes became established. For now, no evidence ties the Arctic to the methane rise since about 2018, which points instead to tropical wetlands. Its role, though, will very likely grow.

soil-env-161.title: Putting numbers on permafrost's future emissions
soil-env-161.text: Early estimates missed the fast route. Preliminary 2011 analyses put permafrost emissions at around 15% of human emissions, but they could not account for {{ref:soil-env-160}}. A 2020 study looked at northern permafrost peatlands, 3.7 of the 18 million km2. It found they would cause ~1% of human radiative forcing, the extra warming push from greenhouse gases, by 2100, and become net carbon sinks within 200 years. A 2021 estimate that included sudden collapse gave 150–200 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2100 at 1.5 °C of warming. It gave 220–300 at 2 °C and 400–500 above 4 °C. A 2022 assessment found that this fast thaw adds 50% to gradual rates, or 14 billion tons of CO2 equivalent by 2100 per degree of warming.

soil-env-149.title: Pereletok, the frost that outlasts a summer
soil-env-149.text: The Russian word pereletok means that which survives over the summer. It names a layer of frozen ground that stays frozen through several summers but eventually thaws, also called intergelisol. Some schemes split frozen ground into permafrost, pereletok and seasonally frozen ground by how long it stays frozen. Pereletok can be seen as part of the active layer that stays frozen after an unusually cool summer or cold winter. Its boundary with permafrost has no universal definition and is hard to draw in the field.

soil-env-148.title: How soils form in the thin layer that thaws
soil-env-148.text: Above permafrost, the ground churns itself. Cryoturbation, mixing by freezing and thawing, dominates soil formation in the active layer and tends to make it uniform. Yet these soils still vary markedly with their parent rock, because weathering is so slow in the very cold climate. Decay is slow too. That makes gelisols, the permafrost soils, an important sink for carbon dioxide. The same stored carbon is a hazard. Permafrost thaw may accelerate global warming, especially if the carbon predates the recent glacial maxima.

soil-env-172.title: Black carbon, the charcoal hidden in soil
soil-env-172.text: The terra preta soils of central Amazonia average three times more soil organic matter than the soils around them. They are rich in black carbon: charcoal particles and soot from vegetation fires or deposited from the air. Black carbon typically makes up 1 to 6% of the organic carbon stored in soils, and up to 60%. In tropical soils it serves as a reservoir of nutrients, and soils without much of it are significantly less fertile. Slash-and-burn farming adds black carbon to soil. Slash-and-char would add it while avoiding high emissions of CO2 and volatile black carbon.

soil-env-160.title: Abrupt thaw, when frozen hillsides collapse in days
soil-env-160.text: In 2020 a heatwave struck Siberia. Afterward, thaw slumps on the northern Taymyr Peninsula rose 17-fold, from 82 to 1404, and the soil carbon they mobilized rose 28-fold. This is abrupt permafrost thaw. Hillsides collapse in retrogressive thaw slumps, and thermokarst lakes form, exposing deep soil to microbes within days. Climate models long focused on gradual thaw, because the abrupt kind is hard to model. Some sites have not waited for the models. In 2019, three permafrost sites expected to stay frozen for 70 more years under the intermediate RCP4.5 pathway had already thawed abruptly. The stakes are large. Abrupt thaw adds between 60 and 100 gigatonnes of carbon by 2300, raising emissions by ~125–190% over gradual thaw alone. It often raises methane's share relative to carbon dioxide, a major source of uncertainty in projections of permafrost methane. In peatlands, methane after thaw starts high, 82 milligrams per square metre per day, but falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

soil-env-151.title: The unfrozen gap that warming opens above permafrost
soil-env-151.text: Sometimes ground that thaws in summer fails to refreeze in winter. An unfrozen layer then opens between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost below: a supra-permafrost talik. Ordinary taliks are usually tied to lakes and rivers, but this one results from climate warming. It forms in moderately cold regions. Colder regions simply thaw deeper in summer, and warm, shallow permafrost just disappears. As air temperature or snow depth rises, the talik thickens until the deep permafrost vanishes. This type of talik has recently been observed in Russia.

soil-env-115.title: The compost bomb, a proposed runaway in peat
soil-env-115.text: Microbes release heat as they decompose organic matter, yet climate models do not account for it. A 2011 study identified a possible consequence, the compost-bomb instability. It is a proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands. The authors noted that for any fixed atmospheric temperature, soil carbon has a unique stable equilibrium. Peatlands are predicted to shift from carbon sink to source this century. Even so, they are still left out of the main Earth system models.

soil-env-214.title: Carbon cycle feedbacks, mostly on the side of cooling
soil-env-214.text: So far, Earth's carbon cycle has mostly worked against warming. Land and ocean sinks absorb around half of current emissions. That fraction could rise to three-quarters if emissions fall, or drop to one-third by 2100 if they rise. If emissions stay very high after this century, land ecosystems would become a net carbon source. Some processes push back. Through CO2 fertilization, more carbon dioxide raises plant productivity, and plants lose less water through their stomata, the pores in their leaves. Over the geological long term, chemical weathering removes CO2, and current warming is increasing it.

soil-env-126.title: How weathering rock pulls carbon from the sky
soil-env-126.text: Rain slowly scrubs carbon dioxide from the air. Rain and groundwater carry carbonic acid, which dissolves silicate and carbonate minerals and removes CO2 from the atmosphere. In theory, silicate weathering sequesters 1 mol of CO2 for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+ released, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure. The dissolved bicarbonate travels through soil and groundwater to the ocean, where organisms build carbonate shells. Over geological time this is thought to stabilize climate. Carbonate weathering followed by carbonate precipitation sequesters no net CO2. The reactions also reverse when carbonate meets acids, as in soils. Liming acid soil neutralizes hydrogen ions but releases CO2 from the limestone.

soil-env-125.title: Enhanced weathering: crushed rock as a carbon trap
soil-env-125.text: Crushed basalt spread on a field starts pulling carbon dioxide from the air. Enhanced weathering speeds up the natural weathering of {{ref:soil-env-126}} by grinding silicate rock fine so that it reacts with water and air. Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 and stores it permanently, in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity. Methods are land-based, such as in-situ carbonation of silicates, or ocean-based. Ultramafic rock could store hundreds to thousands of years' worth of CO2 emissions. Mine tailings and alkaline industrial wastes such as steel slag or biomass ash could serve first, though more basalt mining might eventually be needed. Crushed rock mixed into soil can also benefit plant health when calcium or magnesium is present. In July 2020 a group of scientists judged that spreading finely crushed basalt on fields has potential for national carbon dioxide removal. A 2020 analysis put its cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne of CO2. That compares with US$100–200 for BECCS, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, and US$100–300 for direct air capture. Overall it could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year, with cost estimates in the US$50–200 per tonne range.

soil-env-128.title: Mineral carbonation, turning rock and CO2 into stone
soil-env-128.text: In 1990 Seifritz proposed locking carbon dioxide into rock on purpose. Mineral carbonation dissolves silicate minerals and turns them into carbonate, which holds the CO2.
