Lackner and colleagues and the Albany Research Center developed the idea. Early work reacted crushed silicates in reactors at about 180 °C and 15 MPa of CO2. In-situ methods instead inject CO2 into silicate rock formations. Research has mostly targeted CO2 from flue gas, the exhaust of furnaces and boilers. Using CO2 taken from the air instead, it could serve as geoengineering. Soil remineralization with crushed rock contributes to the same process of enhanced weathering.

soil-env-127.title: Spreading rock dust on land and the questions it raises
soil-env-127.text: Crushed silicate rock spread over the ground does not dissolve at a fixed speed. In this land version of enhanced weathering, the rate depends on the rock's reactive surface area, the pH and buffer capacity of the soil, and soil biological activity. It remains uncertain. That uncertainty drives the costs. Grinding takes energy, and how much depends on how quickly the rock dissolves. A 2012 study found a wide range of possible costs, mostly because dissolution rates are uncertain. Water is the other open question. Weathering slows as the soil solution saturates, so some researchers argue low rainfall limits it. Others say new minerals or plant uptake keep it going.

soil-env-122.title: How root fungi build crumbs that guard carbon
soil-env-122.text: Soil aggregates, crumbs of particles stuck together, shield organic carbon from soil microbes. So more aggregates can mean more stored carbon, and mycorrhizal fungi help build them. Much evidence shows that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increase aggregate formation, possibly through the protein glomalin. Even if glomalin itself decays readily, it may still store carbon by promoting aggregates that protect other organic matter. Ectomycorrhizal fungi are another story. Their only links to aggregation are anecdotal, from sand bags, with no evidence yet that they aid aggregates in field soils.

soil-env-124.title: When root fungi starve the decomposers
soil-env-124.text: In 1971, researchers in New Zealand's Pinus radiata plantations excluded roots and their fungi from the soil, and the soil lost carbon on net. It was the first report of a surprising effect. Ectomycorrhizal fungi can slow decomposition by competing with free-living decomposers for nutrients or water. Several later studies found these fungi reduce decomposer activity and so increase soil carbon storage. A theoretical model shows one route. Fungal access to organic nitrogen should slow decomposition by leaving decomposers short of nutrients. Koide and Wu argued in 2003 that competition for soil water may matter more than competition for nutrients.

soil-env-123.title: When root fungi feed the decomposers instead
soil-env-123.text: Mycorrhizal fungi can also speed up decay. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been shown to increase soil carbon decomposition in nutrient-rich patches. They are thought to lack the enzymes to do this themselves. Instead, they are believed to stimulate free-living decomposers by exuding easily used carbon compounds, a form of the priming effect. In lab experiments, soils with arbuscular fungi lose more carbon than soils without them, and the gap widens under elevated CO2. For ectomycorrhizal fungi the evidence is inconclusive. Field data suggest faster carbon loss, but lab tests show root exudation, the release of compounds from roots, falls as ectomycorrhizal colonization rises.

soil-env-121.title: Do tough fungal tissues keep carbon in the soil
soil-env-121.text: How slowly a fungus rots may decide how long its carbon stays underground. Glomalin, made only by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, accumulates in some soils and may be a substantial share of their carbon. Its importance is now disputed. Later experiments found that arbuscular fungi cause net soil carbon losses. Protein analysis showed that most proteins extracted as glomalin are not mycorrhizal at all, so its role is likely overestimated. Ectomycorrhizal tissue had its own suspect, chitin, long thought to slow decay. In 2012 Fernandez and Koide found that it does not decompose more slowly than other compounds.

soil-env-058.title: Soil degradation: when a stable soil starts to slide
soil-env-058.text: Over the last 30 years, the quality of 33% of the world's pastureland has deteriorated. So has that of 25% of its arable land and 23% of its forests, and 3.2 billion people depend on this land. Soil degradation is the name for that slide. Strictly, it is a regressive change in which a stable soil loses its equilibrium. More broadly, it is any disturbance to a soil judged harmful or undesirable. Degradation, also called pedolysis, departs from the natural course of soil formation. Secondary plant communities replace the mature vegetation, and the amount and makeup of humus change with them. Degradation is tied directly to human activity, while its companion process, {{ref:soil-env-059}}, is driven mainly by erosion. Erosion is still the main factor, acting through water erosion, wind erosion, and chemical and physical decline. Roads add impermeable surfaces that shed runoff and soil. Grazing too many animals, monoculture, row cropping, tillage, crop removal and land-use conversion all speed erosion. Age matters too. Soils naturally climb to high productivity and then decline as mineral nutrients are removed, so older soils are more vulnerable to damage people cause. On farms, erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination remain serious concerns.

soil-env-062.title: Land degradation: when land loses its power to provide
soil-env-062.text: By one 2007 estimate, up to 40% of the world's agricultural land was seriously degraded. The UN has warned that the global economy could lose $23 trillion by 2050. Land degradation is the process behind those numbers: land growing less healthy and productive through human activities or natural conditions. Definitions differ in emphasis. The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment called it the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of {{ref:soil-env-077}}. The FAO describes a persistent decline in the land's ability to sustain ecosystem functions and services, driven by deforestation, too many grazing animals and unsustainable farming. People are usually the main cause, above all through unsustainable land management. Natural hazards are excluded, though people can indirectly affect floods and wildfires. The impacts range from subtle productivity losses to the complete abandonment of farmland. Degraded land grows less food and loses species. It can also lose its natural capacity to store and filter water, leading to water scarcity, so both food security and water security suffer. Judgments differ, too. A steep, rainy slope worries scientists about erosion, but it may promise farmers high yields.

soil-env-065.title: What drives land degradation, near and far
soil-env-065.text: More than 1 660 Mha of land, over 10 percent of the world's land area, has been degraded by unsustainable land use and management. More than 60% of it is cropland and pasture. Researchers sort the causes into two tiers. Proximate drivers are biophysical factors and unsustainable land management. Underlying drivers are social, economic and institutional. Agriculture, deforestation and climate change top the list, with clearcutting and overlogging among the ways land is cleared. On farms, leaving soil bare after harvest and deep plowing deplete nutrients. Areas under conventional tillage degrade 5-10 times faster than no-till areas. Monocultures, grazing beyond the livestock carrying capacity and inappropriate irrigation add to the damage. So does pollution from littering, urbanization, mining, oil spills, pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers and animal waste. Crowding alone is not the culprit. High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

soil-env-063.title: How much of Earth's land is wearing out
soil-env-063.text: Every year about 120,000 km2 of productive land is degraded, an area roughly the size of Greece. The cause is exploitation without planning for long-term sustainability. Erosion from farm fields runs 11 to 20 times faster than soil forms under no-tillage, and more than 100 times faster under conventional tillage. Global tallies vary with who counts and when. The IPCC's 2019 Special Report on Climate Change and Land put about a quarter of Earth's ice-free land under human-induced degradation, with medium confidence. In 2014 the UN estimated that around 30% of land was degraded, with around 3.2 billion people living on it. In 2024 it claimed that 75% of soils are degraded to some extent, a share that might reach 90% by 2050 if trends continue. In 2025 around 1.7 billion people lived where degradation causes sizeable crop yield losses, nearly 1 billion of them in middle-income countries. Eastern and Southern Asia hold the largest affected populations, pairing a large accumulated degradation debt with high population densities. In 2021, two-thirds of Africa's productive land was claimed to be severely affected.

soil-env-067.title: The bill for degraded land: harvests, water and lives
soil-env-067.text: Each year the world loses 76 billion tons of soil, at a cost of about US$400 billion. Land degradation as a whole is estimated to cost US$44 billion a year. The first loss is productive capacity, temporary or permanent, seen as lost biomass, changed vegetation cover or depleted soil nutrients. Slight degradation cuts yield potential by 10% and moderate degradation by 10–50%. Severely degraded soils have lost more than 50% of their potential. Most of them are in developing countries; in Africa yields fall 2–40%, an average loss of 8.2% for the continent. Eroded soil also carries nitrogen, phosphorus, farm chemicals and heavy metals into surface water, clouding it and risking {{ref:soil-env-020}}. Degradation disturbs soil microbes, removes mature vegetation and shrinks animal habitat, so biodiversity falls. Floods degrade soil, and degraded soil causes floods. Scarce farmland breeds conflict: all except 3 internal conflicts in African states in the 1990s are linked to competition for it.

soil-env-070.title: Sustainable land management: keeping land in working order
soil-env-070.text: Reverse just 10% of human-induced cropland degradation, and an additional 154 million people a year could be fed. Restoring abandoned cropland could feed between 292 and 476 million. Sustainable land management chases such gains by managing land to prevent and reverse degradation while conserving soil and water. Its actions fall broadly into three groups: prevention, mitigation and restoration. It raises soil moisture and infiltration while cutting runoff, erosion and flood discharge, which supports water security. Regenerative agriculture pursues the same goal through continuous ground cover, minimal soil disturbance, diverse crop rotations and rotational grazing. Degradation also harms pastures and wider ecosystem services, which are public goods, so restoring land requires collective action. Public awareness, education and outreach help communities adopt such practices and act as stewards of the land.

soil-env-093.title: Soil sealing: burying living ground under asphalt
soil-env-093.text: Pave a field and its soil stops working almost for good. Soil sealing is the loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction. Topsoil is covered or replaced by asphalt and cement, and the layers below are compacted. The loss of the soil's ecosystem services is mostly irreversible. Sealing is a serious form of land take, and together they destroy the soil's biological, physical and chemical functions completely. Water suffers first. Sealed ground becomes the kind of surface described in {{ref:soil-water-231}}: it hinders infiltration and increases surface runoff. Sealing for underground construction also alters water movement and weakens the soil's ability to purify water. Heat-absorbing concrete and asphalt, with no vegetation to cool them, create urban heat islands. Fertile farmland under buildings no longer produces food, and countries with fast-growing populations and economies are losing notable areas this way. Sealing fragments habitats and causes soil biodiversity loss, made worse by falling soil carbon, nitrogen and respiration. It also removes urban green spaces that offer recreation, learning and a sense of belonging. Researchers assess sealing with raindrop impact tests in the field and laboratory, and with indices such as the NDVI and the Normalized Difference Built-up Index.

soil-env-101.title: Land consumption: open country that never comes back
soil-env-101.text: From 1990 to 2000 the United States consumed 1.4 million hectares of open space. Germany consumes more than 70 hectares every day. Land consumption is the conversion of land with healthy soil and intact habitats into industrial farmland, roads and, above all, urban settlements. The European Environment Agency names three such activities. One is expanding built-up area. Another is extending the land exploited for farming, forestry and other uses. The third is over-intensive exploitation of farm and forest land. Because these changes are virtually irreversible, the term land loss is also used. Erosion and the spread of desert land, covered in {{ref:soil-env-072}}, also cause land loss, mostly traceable to people. Land take in 21 EU countries reached about 1.2 million hectares over 1990–2006. The damage includes lost habitat, lost or contaminated topsoil, compaction that eradicates soil life, and impervious surfaces that disrupt water and biogeochemical cycles. Consumption also reaches abroad. A region's land footprint is the area at home and abroad needed for what it consumes. It can far exceed the region's own land, and Europe depends most on such imported land. Yet the land economy still lacks full-cost accounting for the long-term costs of environmental degradation.

soil-env-060.title: From bare rock to climax: a soil grows up
soil-env-060.text: On bare rock, lichens and mosses arrive first, then herbs, shrubs and finally forest. Beneath them a humus-bearing A horizon forms, then mineral B horizons. This evolution is succession, and its endpoint is a steady balance between soil and vegetation, the highest development the environment can produce. Some ecologists call it the climax, others the natural potential. The journey takes tens to thousands of years for fast soils with only an A horizon, and more than a million years for slow ones. Regional climate and biome set the general course, while parent rock and local drainage explain specialized cases such as peat bogs.

soil-env-059.title: Soil retrogression: sliding back toward bare rock
soil-env-059.text: A soil at its climax tends to stay stable. Its vegetation supplies humus, moves material upward and shields the ground from water and wind, while roots bind the particles together. Destroy that cover on a large scale, by an avalanche or by people, and erosion strips away the upper horizons. This reversion toward pioneer conditions is soil retrogression. It can be partial, or total, leaving bare rock. Clearing a sloping site exposed to violent rains can destroy its soil completely. People often drive it more slowly. Clearing, excessive cutting, forest grazing and litter raking replace the climax vegetation, as when broadleaf forest gives way to moorland or pine plantations. Many such cases stem from very old practices. Recovery is possible. After a disturbance, secondary succession usually takes over, and it runs much faster than primary succession because a soil already exists. Succession and regression can follow each other over short intervals under human action, or over long ones as the climate changes.

soil-env-061.title: Rebuilding a degraded soil with a dose of clay
soil-env-061.text: No technique can fully restore a soil, with its fauna and flora, that took more than a thousand years to build. Rebuilding still helps, chiefly by improving structure, adding organic matter and limiting runoff. On low-clay soils in northern Thailand, one application of 200 kg of bentonite clay per rai (6.26 rai = 1 hectare) helped hold water and nutrients. Yields rose by an average of 73%. A 2008 survey of 250 farmers in the northeast found output 18% higher among clay users, and some switched to vegetables, which need more fertile soil. On degraded sandy soils, bentonite also cut the risk of crop failure in drought years.

soil-env-077.title: Drylands: where evaporation spends nearly every drop
soil-env-077.text: Drylands cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface and are home to more than 2 billion people. They are zones defined by scarce water, where precipitation is balanced by evaporation and plant evapotranspiration. UNEP counts tropical and temperate areas whose score on a dryness measure, explained in {{ref:soil-env-206}}, falls below 0.65. They come in four sub-types: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid. The UN convention described in {{ref:soil-env-100}} leaves hyper-arid zones out. Drylands cover 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America, and include 45% of the world's agricultural land. Of all drylands, 72% lie in developing countries, as does almost all hyper-arid land. Arid lands make up about 10% of the world's land. Hyper-arid lands cover about 8% and get irregular rain barely above 100 mm. Unlike more humid biomes, drylands move water mostly as above-ground runoff. They are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate and land-use change. From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of them degraded because of human-caused climate change. Pressure to farm marginal drylands also brings too many grazing animals, land exhaustion and overdrafting of groundwater to many poorer countries.

soil-env-072.title: Desertification: fertile land turned to desert
soil-env-072.text: Some 6 to 12 million square kilometres of land are affected by desertification, and a billion people are threatened by its further spread. Desertification is the gradual degradation of fertile land into arid desert through natural processes and human activities combined. Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation. Drought, climatic shifts, acid rain, tillage, grazing by too many animals and cutting forests for fuel or building materials can strip it, alone or together. Plant cover matters enormously: in many environments erosion and runoff fall exponentially as cover increases. Once the cover goes, unprotected dry topsoil blows away or washes off in flash floods. The infertile layers left behind bake in the sun into an unproductive hardpan. Wind erosion, especially when people raise it far above natural rates, is a major source, and erosion can end in desertification. Some 10–20% of drylands are estimated to be degraded. The worst-hit areas are the Sahel in Africa, the Gobi Desert and Mongolia in Asia, and parts of South America. The effects include sand and dust storms, food insecurity and poverty, and desertification is recognized as a major threat to biodiversity. Remedies include improving soil quality, greening deserts, managing grazing, reforestation and afforestation.

soil-env-100.title: The UN treaty built to fight desertification
soil-env-100.text: Only one internationally legally binding framework addresses desertification: the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, or UNCCD. It is also the only convention to stem directly from Agenda 21 of the Rio Conference. Adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994, it entered into force in December 1996. It works through national action programmes backed by international cooperation, built on participation, partnership and decentralization. These National Action Programmes, drawn up with local communities, set out practical steps for specific ecosystems. The convention has 197 parties: all 193 UN member states plus the European Union. Canada withdrew in 2013 and rejoined in 2017. The Conference of the Parties is its supreme decision-making body, meeting annually from 1997 to 2001 and every two years since. A Committee on Science and Technology reviews data on the natural and human causes. The 2018–2030 Strategic Framework, adopted in 2017, aims to restore ecosystems, support {{ref:soil-env-071}}, improve living conditions and strengthen drought resilience. At COP16 in Riyadh in December 2024, more than US$12 billion was pledged. How much the 2006 International Year of Deserts and Desertification, declared to publicise the convention, achieved is still debated.

soil-env-076.title: A warming world grows its drylands
soil-env-076.text: By the end of this century, drylands could cover 50% or 56% of the continents, up from 38% in the late 20th century. Those figures come from RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5, two scenarios of future greenhouse gas concentrations. Most of the growth is expected in southwest North America, the northern fringe of Africa, southern Africa and Australia. The change is already under way. A 2020 attribution study found that 6% of the world's drylands underwent desertification between 1982 and 2015. Unsustainable land use drove it, compounded by human-caused climate change. Despite average global greening, that climate change has degraded 12.6% of drylands, or 5.43 million km2. It affects 213 million people, 93% of them in developing economies. Research is complex, because no single metric captures every aspect of desertification.

soil-env-084.title: Why halting desertification is harder than it looks
soil-env-084.text: The know-how to fight desertification exists; the incentives often do not. Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when society and the environment benefit. Lack of political will and of funding for land reclamation also holds programmes back. Still, countermeasures keep coming. Some countries have biodiversity action plans to protect endangered plants and animals from desertification. The FAO launched its Drylands Restoration Initiative in 2012, and in 2015 it published global guidelines for restoring degraded dryland forests and landscapes. UN Sustainable Development Goal 15 adds global advocacy for combating desertification and restoring affected land.

soil-env-086.title: Greening the desert, one kind of desert at a time
soil-env-086.text: In Niger, farmers have reclaimed some 30,000 square kilometers of degraded land with the method described in {{ref:soil-env-087}}. Desert greening is the reclamation of deserts and desertified land, with methods matched to each kind of desert. Ethiopia's Humbo Assisted Regeneration Project uses the same techniques. It is paid for by the World Bank's BioCarbon Fund, which backs carbon sequestration in forests and farmland. Salt flats in Saudi Arabia's Rub' al Khali are among the most promising sites for seawater agriculture, which needs no freshwater and little energy. The best-known approach is large tree-planting belts. China's version appears in {{ref:soil-env-088}}, and the African Union's belt along the Sahara in {{ref:soil-env-089}}.

soil-env-085.title: Fixing, watering and feeding desert soils
soil-env-085.text: Contour trenches 150 m long and 1 m deep, edged with stone walls, follow a slope's contour so water cannot flow downhill and cause erosion. Such techniques supply water to dryland soils, fix them in place and enrich them. Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks of trees and bushes hold the soil, reducing erosion and evapotranspiration, while sand fences control drifting sand. Short of water, clay soils can consolidate instead of staying porous; techniques such as zaï or tillage still let crops be planted. Plants restore fertility, chiefly nitrogen-fixing legumes, succulents such as Opuntia, and crops and trees such as grains, barley, beans and dates. Nitrogen-rich fertilizer works too, but its cost deters smallholders, so India, Zambia and Malawi subsidize it. Research centres are inoculating arid-zone trees with mycorrhizal fungi, which greatly enlarge the root surface that gathers nutrients. Models suggest bioengineered soil microbes, especially photosynthesizers, could strengthen the cooperative loops between microbes and dryland plants.

soil-env-066.title: Climate change and degraded land feed each other
soil-env-066.text: From 1961 to 2013, the area of drylands in drought grew by more than 1% a year. Climate change worsens land degradation, especially on low-lying coasts, river deltas, drylands and permafrost. Heavy rainfall and extreme weather make erosion, soil degradation and compaction more likely. Rising seas can flood deltas and low islands with seawater, raising salinity until farming becomes impossible. The 2022 IPCC report found degradation responding more directly to climate change, with all types of erosion and soil organic matter decline increasing. The loop runs both ways: degraded land releases greenhouse gases, which worsen climate change. People bear the cost. In 2015 about 500,000,000 people lived in areas that had undergone desertification during the 1980s–2000s. Some 74% of the world's poor are reported to be directly affected by land degradation.

soil-env-091.title: Solar panels that help desert soil recover
soil-env-091.text: The Kubuqi Desert gets around 300 mm of rain a year, yet a 2025 study found its soil recovering under solar farms. Microbial counts, soil quality and nutrients improved most under integrated agrivoltaic systems, which pair solar panels with planted vegetation. Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation. The panels also acted as windbreaks that kept sand from burying plants, and with the vegetation they created a better microclimate. A 2 GW project in Inner Mongolia plans to apply this at scale to restore vegetation, stabilize dunes and weaken dust storms.

soil-env-073.title: More than 100 ways to define desertification
soil-env-073.text: By 2005, desertification had more than 100 formal definitions, and the proper one is still considerably disputed. The UNCCD defines it as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions, resulting from factors including climatic variations and human activities. That wording ties desertification to land use and management and highlights its economic, social and environmental implications. The original idea, that it meant the physical expansion of deserts, has been rejected as the concept evolved. Sub-groupings such as 'man-made desert' and 'non-pattern desert' remain disputed too.

soil-env-078.title: Desertification raises the dust
soil-env-078.text: Global annual dust emissions rose 25% between the late nineteenth century and the present day. As desertification leaves more loose material for the wind, storms of sand and dust grow more frequent. In the Middle East, long-term rainfall decline has lowered soil moisture and plant cover, and dust storms are becoming more frequent and intense. They contribute to pneumonia and asthma, pollute open water and can halt most transport. Airborne dust also scatters sunlight and warms the atmosphere, shortening cloud lifetimes and reducing rainfall, which can worsen desertification in turn.

soil-env-079.title: Drylands feed the world, and they are shrinking
soil-env-079.text: Drylands hold 44% of agricultural land, and that land supplies 60% of the world's food production. Desertification threatens this supply by shrinking the land that can be farmed sustainably. Food demand keeps growing with population while the farmland shrinks, so demand may soon exceed supply. The squeeze has already turned violent. Climate change, land degradation and population growth have worsened herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria, Sudan, Mali and other Sahel countries.

soil-env-080.title: Desertification and the road from farm to slum
soil-env-080.text: In sub-Saharan Africa, environmental refugees are projected to rise from 14 million in 2010 to nearly 200 million by 2050. Desertification deepens poverty by lowering what dryland farms and pastures produce. Investors avoid low-potential arid zones, and without infrastructure, markets and suitable techniques most such zones are left out of development. When rural land can no longer support its people, they migrate to cities, particularly in Africa, creating unemployment and slums. In Mongolia, where 90% of the land is fragile dryland, many herders move to the city for work.

soil-env-082.title: The Gobi, Earth's fastest-growing desert
soil-env-082.text: Each year the Gobi turns over 3,600 km2 of grassland into wasteland, and large sand dunes are forming only 70 km from Beijing. It is spreading across northern China and southern Mongolia faster than any other desert on Earth. About 13% of Mongolia's desertification is put down to natural factors. The rest comes mainly from too many grazing animals and erosion of cultivated soils, and over 70% of the country's land is degraded. From 1940 to 2015 Mongolia's mean air temperature rose by 2.24 °C while precipitation fell by 7%. Cashmere exports added pressure: herds shifted from sheep to goats, which eat roots and flowers and so degrade grazing land.

soil-env-081.title: The Sahel, where the Sahara's edge keeps moving
soil-env-081.text: Over the past 50 years the Sahel has lost approximately 650,000 km2 of productive agricultural land. This hot, dry belt gets 100–600 mm of rain a year, and there climate change and human activity combine. Since 1900 the Sahara has reportedly expanded 250 km southward along a 6,000 km west–east front. Lake Chad has shrunk by over 90% since 1987 through irrigation withdrawals and lower rainfall, displacing millions of people. The desert's edge has always moved. The Sahara has swung between wet grassland and dry desert every 20,000 years, linked to a roughly 40,000-year cycle in Earth's axial tilt between 22° and 24.5°.

soil-env-092.title: Deserts that came and went long before people
soil-env-092.text: Beyond the present edges of deserts such as the Sahara lie paleodeserts: large sand seas now held in place by vegetation. Deserts grew and shrank for ages, mostly independently of people. Centuries ago, severe land deterioration in arid regions centred on three densely populated areas: the Mediterranean, the Mesopotamian Valley and China's Loess Plateau. The earliest known discussion followed the French colonization of West Africa, when the Comité d'Etudes commissioned a study of the Sahara's prehistoric spread. The modern study of desertification grew out of research on the Sahel drought of the 1980s.

soil-env-069.title: Farmland bears most of the damage
soil-env-069.text: By 2025, unsustainable farming had degraded 996 Mha of agricultural land, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation. Farmers' local choices shape it, and so do global drivers such as trade, climate change and demographic change. In high-income countries, heavy fertilizer use masks severe per-hectare losses. It brings diminishing returns and can worsen degradation through acidification, nutrient imbalances and pollution. Sub-Saharan Africa shows low yield losses from degradation, mainly because limited access to inputs, machinery, credit and markets dominates its yield gaps. The human cost is stark. In 2025, 47 million stunted children under five lived where stunting overlaps significant yield losses from degradation. Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa combine degraded land with high poverty.

soil-env-068.title: How fragile is a landscape? Sensitivity and resilience
soil-env-068.text: A landscape that bends is not the same as one that breaks. Two measures together describe how vulnerable land is to degradation. Sensitivity is the degree to which a land system changes under natural forces, human intervention or both. Resilience is a landscape's ability to absorb change without altering the balance of species in its community, and to return to its original state afterwards. Land-use management can raise or lower resilience. Degraded land is less resilient, so a shock can drive it into further degradation.

soil-env-064.title: The many faces of land degradation
soil-env-064.text: More than 36 types of land degradation can be assessed, and people cause or worsen every one of them. Some have been known for centuries: water, wind and mechanical erosion, and physical, chemical and biological decline. Four types have emerged in the last 50 years. They are pollution, loss of arable land to construction and expansion, artificial radioactivity, and limits on land use from armed conflict. The full list includes contamination, acidification, sheet erosion, silting, aridification, salinization and urbanization.

soil-env-088.title: China's Great Green Wall against the Gobi
soil-env-088.text: Begun in 1978, China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program is planned to finish around 2050 as a barrier about 4,828 km long and up to 1,448 km wide. Its windbreak strips, called shelterbelts, were meant to hold back the Gobi Desert and supply timber. It set out to raise northern China's forest cover from 5 to 15 percent. By 2000, water use, mining, excess farming and wood cutting had desertified 29.7% of China. By 2009 China's planted forest covered more than 500,000 square kilometres, the largest artificial forest in the world. The Gobi grew by 10,000 square kilometres a year in the 1980s but was shrinking by more than 2,000 a year in 2022. In 2024 China finished a 3,000 km green belt around the Taklamakan Desert, and desert cover fell from 27.2% to 26.8% over a decade. Reports credit the program with reversing the Gobi's spread, but critics question tree survival, water use and whether it tackles the causes. A 2023 study found only a fifth of surviving forests became forest stands within 10 years, and a tenth were alive after 40. Dense exotic plantings on the Loess Plateau may worsen water shortages. Monoculture left trees open to disease: in 2000 one billion poplars in Ningxia were lost to a single disease.

soil-env-089.title: Africa's Great Green Wall, from tree line to mosaic
soil-env-089.text: In the 1950s Richard St. Barbe Baker proposed a 'Green front', a 50-kilometre-deep buffer of trees against the expanding desert. The African Union adopted its own version in 2007: a belt of trees across the Sahel from Djibouti to Dakar, 15 km wide and 7,775 km long. The wall grew into a mosaic of water harvesting, protected greenery and improved indigenous land use that helps the ground retain seasonal rainfall. By 2030 it aims to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs. Progress figures differ widely. A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered, while about 18 million hectares were restored by 2023 and about 30 million by 2024. Nigeria has restored 4.9 million hectares and Ethiopia has reclaimed 15 million. Critics question the colonial origins of the word 'desertification', the mostly European funding and top-down strategies that push sedentarization, the settling of mobile herders. Little monitoring has been done. By 2023, terrorist threats, weak political leadership and too little funding put the project at risk of collapse.

soil-env-087.title: Farmer-managed natural regeneration and the underground forest
soil-env-087.text: A field that looks bare may hide an 'underground forest' of living stumps. Each stump can send up 10 to 30 stems, and farmers keep the tallest and straightest. This is farmer-managed natural regeneration, a low-cost way to regrow trees and shrubs from living stumps, roots and seeds. Australian agricultural economist Tony Rinaudo developed it in West Africa in the 1980s, adapting the centuries-old practices of coppicing and pollarding. Trees among crops and pastures raise yields, soil fertility, organic matter and soil moisture, and reduce wind damage and erosion. Pruned residue mulches the fields, raising water retention and cutting evaporation. Faidherbia albida, the 'fertiliser tree', fixes nitrogen, and its falling leaves add nutrients and organic matter. Trials and long-running programs suggest the method can at least double crop yields on low-fertility soils. By 2004 it was practised on over five million hectares, half of Niger's farmland, after nurseries and tree planting had largely failed. One obstacle was legal. From the 1930s until 1993, Niger's forestry laws took tree ownership out of people's hands, until property-law changes eased it.

soil-env-096.title: Overgrazing: when herds eat faster than grass grows
soil-env-096.text: Overgrazing is thought to be the principal cause of grassland decline, and it is one of the farming activities that cause desertification. It happens when animals eat grass faster than it can grow back, as when pastures are stocked above their livestock carrying capacity. Rapid eating and constant trampling stop the grass regrowing. The suppressed sward, the grass cover, then invites rats and insects that hold growth back further. Overgrazing is among the improper farming practices that accelerate soil erosion and degrade land. It is also a main cause of shrubs and bushes spreading into grasslands and savannas. Shrinking farmland makes it worse. Urbanization leaves less land, so farmers pack small plots densely with animals and must still gather much grass for long alpine winters.

soil-env-074.title: How land is stripped bare and turned to desert
soil-env-074.text: Population growth can turn once-acceptable farming into unsustainable overgrazing, over-farming and deforestation. Those human pressures act alongside natural ones. Overgrazing keeps livestock on land for long periods without replanting grass, leaving it bare to harden in the sun and lose nutrients to the wind. Overcultivation and monocropping drain nutrients. The depleted soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks. Intensive farming needs more fertilizer, pesticides and machinery, and continuous use rapidly depletes soil nutrients. Nature works on its own schedule. The Sahara owes its existence to natural changes in solar insolation, the sunlight reaching the ground, caused by Earth's orbital precession. These alter the West African Monsoon and trigger vegetation and dust feedbacks. Regional studies find soil health, human activities and weather all contribute, in different balances. In Shaanxi, meteorological factors work against desertification while the soil worsens it.

soil-env-075.title: Do people make deserts? A long-running dispute
soil-env-075.text: Early studies named overgrazing, the overconsumption of vegetation by livestock, as one of the most common causes of desertification. Today the role of local overexploitation in recent desertification is controversial. The Sahel is the test case. Its drought is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures. Those temperatures are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases. Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions have since re-greened the Sahel. That has led some scholars to call vegetation loss caused by farming a minor factor. Others look further back. Overgrazing by local cattle may have partly driven the mid-Holocene change of the Sahara from savanna to desert. Meanwhile, studies of critical regions confirm that human activities and soil health join meteorological factors as main contributors. The weight of each remains disputed.

soil-env-083.title: South America's spreading dry ground
soil-env-083.text: A quarter of South America is drylands, and over 68% of the continent has suffered soil erosion from deforestation and overgrazing. Between 27 and 43% of the land in Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador and Peru is at risk of desertification. In Argentina, Mexico and Paraguay, more than half the land is degraded by desertification and cannot be farmed. Rural Mexico loses about 1,000 km2 of land a year this way. Drought in Central America has driven unemployment, food insecurity and migration.

soil-env-090.title: Managed grazing and its contested carbon promise
soil-env-090.text: In managed grazing, herds move through many small fenced paddocks every day or two, mimicking natural grazers so the grass can regrow. Restored grasslands store atmospheric CO2 as plant material, whereas confined grazing livestock keep grass growth low. Proponents claim wider use could raise soil carbon across the world's 3.5 billion hectares of agricultural grassland and offset nearly 12 years of CO2 emissions. Many researchers dispute these claims. They say the method neither reverses desertification nor offsets its emissions.

soil-env-095.title: Grassland degradation: brown patches that spread for decades
soil-env-095.text: In China's Tibetan and Inner Mongolian region, 2,460 km2 of grassland is degraded every year. Grassland degradation, also called vegetation or steppe degradation, is a biotic disturbance in which grass struggles to grow or disappears. Overgrazing, burrowing small mammals and climate change are the usual causes. Since the 1970s it has hit alpine meadows and grasslands, notably in that region and in the Philippines. It works slowly. Dead brown patches appear first and, if untreated, spread over many acres across years or decades, and restoration is just as slow. Warming speeds evaporation, and both heavy rain and drought hinder grass. Most sources link the problem to climate change, but some scientists dismiss it as an insignificant cause. Roads, herders' settlements and their animals, monocropping of converted grassland, deforestation and medicinal plant gathering add to the damage. A spiral follows. Less arable land and lower harvests push farmers onto smaller plots that are more easily overgrazed and exhausted, and livestock numbers fall. With fewer plants to anchor the soil, erosion and dust storms increase, and more carbon and nitrogen may escape to the atmosphere. On the Tibetan Plateau 15–20% of species are now endangered, and carbon and nitrogen losses cost $8,033/ha and $13,315/ha respectively. In northern China it affects 400 million people a year, with 54 billion yuan of annual economic loss.

soil-env-207.title: When native shrubs crowd out the grass
soil-env-207.text: About 500 million hectares of grassland, savanna and woodland, on every continent, are filling in with bushes. This is woody plant encroachment: the spread and thickening of native woody plants, bushes and shrubs at the expense of grasses and forbs, the non-woody flowering plants. Encroachers are native, unlike introduced invasive species. They count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species. Encroachment has run at unparalleled rates since the mid-19th century and is classed as a type of grassland degradation. Per decade, rates reach 10-20 percent in North America, 8 percent in South America, 2.4 percent in Africa, and 1 percent in Australia and the Eurasian steppes. Open grassland can become closed woodland. Many treat this as land degradation that harms biodiversity, groundwater recharge, carbon storage and grazing capacity. In North America, each 1 percent increase in woody cover cuts carrying capacity by 0.6 to 1.6 cattle per 100 hectares. Others argue it is natural succession, and its impacts depend on context. In arid lands it has been called 'green desertification', though grass can survive between the canopies, whereas desertification leaves bare soil without organic matter. Soil quality declines under encroachment in arid and semi-arid regions. In Mediterranean and very humid climates it often improves, with more topsoil carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus.

soil-env-206.title: Measuring dryness with the aridity index
soil-env-206.text: A drought ends; aridity stays. Aridity is permanent, whereas drought is temporary. The aridity index puts a number on how dry the climate is at a given place. UNEP's 1992 index compares average annual precipitation with potential evapotranspiration in the same units, so it rises as conditions get wetter. Its classes are hyperarid (below 0.05, 7.5% of land), arid (0.05-0.20, 12.1%), semi-arid (0.20-0.50, 17.7%) and dry subhumid (0.50-0.65, 9.9%). One of the first indices, by Köppen and Geiger, set an annual rainfall threshold that depends on mean annual temperature and the season the rain falls in.

soil-env-094.title: Soil unsealing: prying the pavement off
soil-env-094.text: In the Walloon Region and Germany, new urban projects are offset by removing sealed surfaces elsewhere, under a 'no net land take' principle. Soil unsealing removes asphalt, cement and other human-made covers so a sealed soil can perform its natural functions again. Because sealing losses are mostly irreversible, unsealing is very difficult, and research on it is very limited. Urban, barren or old dumping soils can become parks, green roofs and gardens, but only after thorough decontamination. In a Palermo field trial, vegetated de-sealing stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity over eighteen months. Crushed asphalt kept higher permeability but less plant cover.

soil-env-205.title: Restoring drylands, one island of plants at a time
soil-env-205.text: Rangelands cover about 25% of drylands, and restoring them counts as a climate mitigation option because of their potential to sequester carbon. Dryland restoration returns degraded drylands to their former function, or manages them so they degrade no further. It is especially hard: rain is rare and variable, temperatures are high, soils are infertile and invasive species spread. One answer is restoration islands, small well-placed plantings that spread into neighbouring ground. They suit patchy dryland vegetation and reduce soil erosion. Soil fauna improve structure, nutrient cycling and infiltration. They can be helped with endemic species, nucleation sites and mulching to keep the soil moist.

soil-env-098.title: Light, moderate, high: grading grassland decline
soil-env-098.text: At its worst, grassland becomes heitutan, 'black beach' or black-soil-land: bare, unusable black soil extending 10–15 cm below ground level. Before that, grassland degradation passes through three stages. Lightly degraded grassland has scattered patches of dead or missing grass. In moderately degraded grassland the patches grow in size and number, plant and animal diversity clearly falls, and pests such as rats and insects damage soil and plants. Highly degraded grassland is a vast expanse of dead grass, fit for neither crops nor livestock, with very low diversity and a few poisonous plants.

soil-env-099.title: Matching the cure to the damage on grassland
soil-env-099.text: Grassland restoration fits the treatment to how badly the land is degraded, and early action makes it easier. Lightly degraded land can be fenced from grazing, fertilized or weeded. Grazing may continue at a lower, monitored intensity, for example by rotating fields seasonally. Moderately degraded land needs reseeding and rodent control, and active brush control, the subject of {{ref:soil-env-211}}, can restore areas invaded by woody plants. Highly degraded land with 30% or more plant cover gets semi-artificial grassland. Worse heitutan land needs artificial grassland, with weed and rodent control, plowing, seeding and fertilizing. Success also needs recognition in policy, standard indicators of degradation, scientific innovation, knowledge transfer and data sharing.

soil-env-097.title: Burrowing small mammals: culprits or bystanders?
soil-env-097.text: Marmots, voles, pikas and zokors are blamed for damaging grassland as their populations grow. Their burrowing and gnawing encourage soil erosion and make it hard for plants to root, leaving grass patchy. Not everyone accepts the charge. Others argue that burrowing recycles soil nutrients and that the population rise simply follows increased grazing. Control, by shooting, sterilizing or low-toxicity poison such as Botulin toxin C, aims to manage these populations rather than wipe them out.

soil-env-211.title: Bush control: thinning shrubs, not erasing them
soil-env-211.text: Bush control works best early, at around 3% shrub cover, and prevention is thought cheaper than treatment. Also called brush management, it is action to manage the density and mix of bushes and shrubs in an area. Encroaching native woody plants are thinned, not eradicated, because they still provide functions such as animal habitat. Measures are preventive, such as suitable stocking rates and rotational grazing. They can also be responsive, such as bush thinning, or maintenance, keeping the thinned density. Waiting is costly: encroached grassland can become a stable state that will not recover without intervention. Method matters too, since chemical control can lose more carbon than mechanical thinning.

soil-env-208.title: Why shrubs are winning against grass
soil-env-208.text: Grasses drink from the topsoil and woody plants from the subsoil. By this two-layer theory, overgrazing the grass lets more water reach the subsoil, where bushes use it. Fire suppression and the loss of wild herbivores also favour woody plants. Global change helps them too. Woody plants with the C3 photosynthetic pathway thrive under high CO2, unlike C4 grasses. When rainfall intensity rises, deep soil water usually increases, which benefits bushes more than grasses. The ground matters as well. Coarse-textured soils promote woody growth and fine-textured soils limit it, while moisture and nutrients make downslope and cooler slopes more prone.

soil-env-209.title: More wood, but not necessarily more carbon
soil-env-209.text: Count only the trunks and branches, and invading shrubs look like a carbon sink. Add the grass and soil organic carbon they replace, and the answer turns uncertain. Several studies find above-ground carbon gains entirely offset by below-ground losses. Soil organic carbon tends to rise under encroachment in dry ecosystems and fall in mesic, moderately moist, ones. In tropical savanna soils most of it comes from grass. A meta-analysis of 142 studies found changes in soil organic carbon (0-50 cm) from -50 to 300 percent, with gains under leguminous shrubs and on sandy soils. Rooting depth increases with encroachment, on average by 38 cm and up to 65 cm.

soil-env-210.title: Thirsty bushes and the rain that never reaches the soil
soil-env-210.text: In South Africa, woody canopies catch and evaporate about 44% of rainfall, and up to 10% less rain enters the soil. Bushes use far more rainwater than grasses, so their spread reduces groundwater recharge and alters streamflow. Denser canopies raise transpiration and the evaporation of soil moisture, and enhanced soil porosity can speed soil drought. In arid and semi-arid lands, encroachment reduces stream flows, while woody plant control can improve the connectivity of water resources.

soil-env-071.title: Land degradation neutrality: a target for 2030
soil-env-071.text: By 2030, the world is meant to become land degradation-neutral. Land degradation neutrality is the policy goal behind that date, set in UN Sustainable Development Goal 15. Target 15.3 calls for combating desertification and restoring degraded land and soil, including land hit by desertification, drought and floods. It asks the world to strive for a land degradation-neutral world. Money followed. The Land Degradation Neutrality Fund, launched at UNCCD COP 13 in 2017, invests in projects with environmental, socio-economic and financial returns. It was initially capitalized at US$100 million and is expected to grow to US$300 million. The European Investment Bank agreed to invest up to $45 million. Supporting the goal is one objective of the UNCCD's 2018–2030 Strategic Framework.

soil-env-185.title: Rebuilding soil faster than it is lost
soil-env-185.text: Soil can be made, not only spent. Soil regeneration is the creation of new soil and the restoration of soil health. It means keeping topsoil loss low, holding more carbon than escapes, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working. It is a form of ecological regeneration within restoration ecology, reforming degraded soil through biological, chemical or physical processes. Healthy soil mixes living organisms, organic matter and mineral material, and air and water typically fill half its volume. Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by microbes in the rhizosphere. That bargain keeps the living biomass mostly fungal and raises soil carbon. Carbon is also the best gauge, since organic carbon content is one of the most predictable signs of a degraded soil. Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon and lets the soil recover. For optimal plant growth, the carbon to nitrogen ratio must stay at 20–30:1. A diverse soil life also crowds out disease, because competition shrinks the niche open to parasites. The rewards are carbon stored against climate change, less erosion and a sturdier soil overall.

soil-env-177.title: Testing a soil's health, not just its nutrients
soil-env-177.text: A routine {{ref:soil-fert-187}} asks which nutrients a field holds. Soil health testing asks a broader question: how well does the soil deliver its ecosystem services, judged against benchmarks? It combines physical, chemical and biological analyses. Benchmarks include carbon dioxide release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium. Woods End Laboratories has offered a soil quality package since 1985, and Cornell University a Soil Health Test since 2006. Both combine aggregate stability, mineral balance and CO2 respiration, now seen as hallmarks of the field. Other labs add a respiration test called the CO2-Burst to routine chemical tests. Testing is spreading in the United States, Australia and South Africa. Yet many labs and scientists resist the new biological tests. Fertility metrics rest on crop-response models, and none exist for soil health; critics add that novel tests may miss management changes. Others say the old models, built for maximum yield, have failed. US soils may have lost up to 75% of their carbon over the past 40 years, though that figure is debated. In practice, testing still serves mostly agronomic goals.

soil-env-173.title: Soil science beyond the farm gate
soil-env-173.text: Soil science does not stop at the edge of the field. Environmental soil science studies how people interact with the pedosphere and with the living world, rock, water and air around it. It is one of the general subfields of edaphology, alongside agricultural soil science, and looks beyond crop production. Its topics run from surface water quality, stormwater and erosion control to {{ref:soil-env-195}}, wastewater land treatment and wetland restoration. It covers polluted ground and its cleanup, soil degradation and nutrient management. It tracks viruses and bacteria moving through soil, and {{ref:soil-env-023}}, the use of microbes to break down pollutants. Land use, global warming and acid rain belong to it too, as do human-made soils such as terra preta. Much of its research relies on models. Soil chemistry itself has shifted toward this field, because its knowledge is key to predicting where contaminants in soil end up.

soil-env-176.title: Healthy for whom? The many meanings of soil health
soil-env-176.text: An ecologist and a farmer can disagree about one soil's health. Users weigh a soil's functions differently, so the term only makes sense against the user's aims and the soil's boundaries. Ecological landscape assessment and agronomic goals each claim their own criteria, and a soil may work well ecologically yet serve crops poorly. Benchmarks also shift with a soil's inherited traits and geography. Generically, a healthy soil absorbs and cycles well, sheds clean runoff, keeps carbon and productivity near climatic limits and leaks few nutrients. Unlike soil quality, soil health is never tied to a purpose such as preparing a roadbed.

soil-env-178.title: Measuring how far farmed soil falls short
soil-env-178.text: How healthy should a farmed soil be? In 2020 Maharjan and colleagues proposed an answer: compare it with native land in the same region. The soil health gap is the shortfall between managed soils and that local benchmark. The idea filled a hole. Without site- or region-specific benchmarks, research on how different farm management affects soil health had been limited. Meanwhile, soil's importance for food security, farm ecosystems, the environment and human life had pushed research strongly toward soil health.

soil-env-175.title: Soil health and soil quality: two overlapping ideas
soil-env-175.text: Soil health sounds like the newer idea, but it is the older one. The phrase grew out of European organic and biological farming movements, well before soil quality became a discipline around 1990. Swiss soil biologist Otto Buess's 1978 essay 'The Health of Soil and Plants' still largely defines the field. Soil quality means fitness for a use, such as growing maize or preparing a roadbed. Soil health takes a holistic view of soil as a self-sustaining living system. Soil health has largely replaced the older term, though the two still overlap considerably.

soil-env-218.title: Permaculture: designing farms on nature's model
soil-env-218.text: In 1978 Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined a word for land management and settlement design that copies flourishing natural ecosystems: permaculture. Its three ethics and Holmgren's twelve design principles are widely cited. Practitioners bury wood to hold soil water, a method called Hügelkultur, and use sheet mulching, no-till gardening, keyline design and vermicomposting. Its standing is contested. It has stayed largely isolated from science, and critics call it pseudo-scientific or poorly defined. Yet some 21st-century studies support claims that it improves soil quality and biodiversity. A 2024 review found that it strongly enhances carbon stocks and soil quality.

soil-env-186.title: Four ways a soil wears out
soil-env-186.text: One third of the globe's land has degraded soil, with around 500 million hectares degraded in the tropics and subtropics alone. Poor management wears soil down in four general ways. The first is erosion, in which water runoff or wind carries soil away, typically from bare fields. Excessive tillage, especially ploughing, leaves soil open to the wind. The second is physical degradation, a change in structure that keeps water and air out. Heavy farm vehicles cause it through compaction. Urban construction compacts and seals soil too, which intensifies storm runoff and erosion. The third is chemical degradation: heavy metals or hydrocarbons, acidification, salinization, nutrient leaching, and toxins from mining and waste management. Cities concentrate pollutants that leach into their soils. The fourth is biological degradation, a loss of biological activity. Chemical fertilizer is one cause. It suppresses nitrogen-fixing microbes and raises nitrous oxide emissions. As fertility falls, more fertilizer goes on, a positive feedback loop. Overgrazing strips away plant roots, and with them organic matter and the partnership between plants and soil microbes. The toll includes lost biodiversity, more greenhouse gas emissions and less carbon storage.

soil-env-188.title: Cover crops, compost and the toolkit of soil repair
soil-env-188.text: A field planted with one crop year after year slowly runs down. Monoculture depletes soil carbon and nutrients, because each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients. Regenerative soil practices, many drawn from conservation agriculture, work to reverse that. Cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced disturbance, mulch retention and integrated nutrient management store more carbon and cut fossil fuel use. Permaculture uses mixed, native and perennial crops and avoids tilling, so microbes and roots stay in longer contact. Holistic management, from Allan Savory's work, claims planned grazing can improve soil health and reverse desertification; researchers dispute the desertification claim. Amendments, chosen to suit the soil's current state, lock up toxins, balance pH, add nutrients and encourage soil life. Inorganic ones improve texture and structure and limit heavy-metal availability. Wood ash, ground limestone and red mud are alkaline amendments; gypsum and dredged materials are mineral ones. Organic amendments such as mulch, compost, biochar, manure and biosolids improve biological activity, water permeability and structure. Biosolids are nutrient-rich, so they should be used sparingly.

soil-env-184.title: How soil withstands shocks and recovers
soil-env-184.text: Soils have outlasted an atmosphere without oxygen, the arrival of land plants 420 million years ago and, since the last ice age, long wet, dry and fire periods. Soil resilience is a soil's ability to resist destabilizing influences or recover its healthy state afterward. Strictly, soil resistance is the inherent capacity to withstand disturbance, and resilience is the capacity to recover after it. Time sets the frame. Soil formation takes thousands of years, while humans have depended on and changed soil for only a short while. Parent material and topography are passive soil-forming factors; climate and living things are active ones, and shifts in them amount to environmental change or shock. Resilience is limited by how fast and how far humans change a soil, against the time it needs to recover. Australia shows the cost. Little more than 200 years of European-style farming has brought salinity, acidity, nutrient decline, erosion and structural decline. Open questions remain: should a soil stay constant or settle at a new equilibrium, and how long can it hold out?

soil-env-180.title: Judging soil quality by what can be measured
soil-env-180.text: Soil function itself is hard to measure directly, so scientists measure stand-ins. These soil quality indicators fall into three groups. Physical indicators include texture, bulk density, porosity, water content at saturation, aggregate stability and penetration resistance. Together they show infiltration and the water available to plants. Chemical indicators include soil pH and nutrient levels, and a typical soil test checks only these. Biological indicators reflect organisms such as earthworms, millipedes, centipedes, ants and spiders, which regulate structure, break down contaminants and cycle nutrients. The Soil Management Assessment Framework pulls such readings together, and Germany rates farm soil on its soil value scale, the Bodenwertzahl. Very few monitoring systems give near real-time indicator data, and almost all report only at research level.

soil-env-189.title: Who decides how soil is used
soil-env-189.text: Since December 2013, by a UN General Assembly decision, the world has marked 5 December as a day for soil, an idea soil scientists put forward in 2002. Behind it lies soil governance: the policies, strategies and decisions that nation states and local governments apply to soil use. It differs from soil management, the practices that raise and maintain a soil's fertility, structure and carbon. Governance needs governments, local authorities, industries and citizens to agree on coherent policies that regulate use, avoid conflicts between users and promote sustainable land management. Globally it has taken a farming view, because food insecurity grips the most populated regions. It focuses on how degradation hurts food production, and on conflict between land for settlements and land for farming. It usually sits within land governance, so urban and industrial soils get little attention. Concern over erosion built awareness, making science and technology the link between management and governance. FAO and UNESCO made a global soil map in 1981, and an ISRIC-led consortium is building a new one with GIS and remote sensing.

soil-found-112.title: Healing land after mines, farms and disasters
soil-found-112.text: Reclaiming abandoned US mines is estimated to cost $9.6bn, and Australian mine rehabilitation bonds total $9.49 billion. Land rehabilitation returns damaged land to some degree of its former state after industry, natural disasters or other harm. Mining, farming and forestry often degrade land. In parts of the United States, reclamation means returning disturbed land to an improved state. At mines, crews contour waste dumps against erosion and cap sulfide ore with clay to stop acid forming. Landfills and tailings get a cover of topsoil, or soil and vegetation.

soil-env-187.title: The carbon that farming has pulled from the ground
soil-env-187.text: The top two meters of soil hold an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes of carbon. That is more than the atmosphere's 879 billion and vegetation's 600 billion together. Each year some 61 billion tonnes leave soils as organic carbon decomposes and oxidizes. A similar amount returns through decomposition and plant–microbe symbiosis. Farming and fossil fuel use tip that balance. Since farming began, an estimated 133 billion tonnes of carbon has been lost from soil, mostly in the last two centuries of mechanized agriculture. Cutting soil emissions cuts overall greenhouse gas emissions, and regenerative practices can act as natural carbon dioxide removal.

soil-env-194.title: Engineering with living plants
soil-env-194.text: Some of the sturdiest slope defenses are alive. Soil bioengineering uses living plant materials, from seeds to whole plant communities, for engineering jobs such as stabilizing slopes and controlling erosion. A discipline of civil engineering, it sometimes replaces classical works but more often complements them. Used for many centuries and promoted with European examples by Schiechtl in 1980, it is now practiced worldwide on eroding slopes and embankments. Plantings shield soil from wind, rain, frost and flowing water. They slow flow along banks, bind soil, trap snow, sand and sediment, and roughen slopes against avalanches. Their roots loosen soil, and they improve the water regime, even out temperatures and enrich raw soils. They also heal scars left by landslides, wildfires, mining and construction. The method works wherever its plants grow well, from tropical to temperate zones. It is limited in arid, frost, alpine and arctic regions and in species-poor areas. It is not always cheaper to build. Over its lifetime, though, it is normally more economical, because the works become living systems that maintain themselves by succession.

soil-env-183.title: Maps that show what a soil can do
soil-env-183.text: A soil map can show more than soil types. Soil mapping identifies, describes and delineates those types from field observation or from inferences drawn from sources such as aerial photographs. Mapping soil functions goes further, turning properties into interpretations for a purpose: food production, environmental protection or civil engineering. A map may show one property, such as critical nutrient or heavy-metal levels, or a combined interpretation such as an erosion risk index. The method extends soil survey, pairing maps of soil components with pedotransfer functions and soil inference models to infer how mapping units will perform.

soil-env-182.title: Soil as the land's filter and buffer
soil-env-182.text: Water that passes through soil comes out cleaner. Soil particles capture contaminants, so what reaches aquifers and rivers carries less of them. This is one of soil's functions: regulating water, and filtering, buffering and transforming materials that move between the atmosphere, plant cover and water table. Soil also transforms and decomposes waste materials into new materials. And it can store large amounts of carbon as soil organic matter, which lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide and helps mitigate climate change.

soil-env-195.title: How a drain field lets soil microbes clean wastewater
soil-env-195.text: Sewage leaving a {{ref:soil-env-216}} still needs cleaning, and soil finishes the job. A septic drain field, or leach field, is a subsurface facility that removes contaminants from that liquid. It usually has trenches of perforated pipe and porous material, often gravel, covered with soil to keep animals and surface runoff away. The tank is sized for anaerobic organisms, which live without oxygen. The field is sized for aerobic soil microbes, which turn the tank's anaerobic effluent into aerobic water. A biofilm on the trench walls uses atmospheric oxygen to break down organic compounds. Incomplete oxidation shows as hydrogen sulfide odors or iron bacteria in nearby wells. Design is hydraulic, for wastewater volume, and catabolic, for its long-term biochemical oxygen demand. The microbes barely touch petroleum products and chlorinated solvents and cannot remove dissolved metals. Bleach or sanitizers can slow or stop them. Fields with several areas let one rest while nematodes eat built-up biofilm and fats, though percolation rarely regains its first clean-water rate. A biofilter lowers the effluent's oxygen demand, not its volume, so the field can be smaller.

soil-env-216.title: The septic tank: sewage treatment in a buried chamber
soil-env-216.text: In 2008 about 20 percent of US households relied on a septic tank. It is an underground chamber of concrete, fiberglass or plastic where household sewage gets primary treatment. Solids settle and are digested without oxygen in the first chamber. The liquid flows to a septic drain field, whose soil must pass a percolation test. Sludge outpaces decomposition, so a vacuum truck removes it every few years, or every 10-20 years in some systems. Tanks remove little nitrogen. Soils usually retain phosphorus, but sandy soils near water can saturate and pass it on, risking {{ref:soil-env-020}}. Dense development can push the contamination traced in {{ref:soil-env-242}} past acceptable limits.

soil-env-196.title: Will this soil take septic effluent?
soil-env-196.text: A drain field site must be permeable enough for effluent to percolate away, yet fine enough to hold back disease-causing bacteria and viruses. Aerobic conditions must kill those pathogens before they reach wells or surface water. Sand and gravel pass wastewater too fast; silt and clay limit flow. A percolation test times clean water dispersing from a trench. Where seasonal high water tables limit sizing, a soil scientist reads the soil's morphology instead. Texture, structure, pores and the color signatures of a fluctuating water table all count. In service, biofilm, fine particles, congealed fats, rising groundwater and frozen ground clog the trench's soil interface, and percolation falls.

soil-env-217.title: Putting a mined landscape back together
soil-env-217.text: An open-cut mine is refilled in layers. Rock backfills the pit, then stored pre-mining soil, topsoil and vegetation. This is mine reclamation: modifying mined land so it is ecologically functional or economically usable again. The original landscape cannot always return. Usually the limit is how far mine waste can be physically and chemically stabilized. The Forestry Reclamation Approach calls for a loosely graded, uncompacted rooting layer at least four feet deep, of topsoil or weathered sandstone. In the United States, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 makes operators file a reclamation plan and a bond before mining. A coal tax funds abandoned-mine reclamation.

soil-env-197.title: India's soil health cards for millions of farmers
soil-env-197.text: By 16 May 2017, India had distributed 725 lakh soil health cards. The Soil Health Card Scheme, launched on 19 February 2015, gives farmers cards with crop-wise nutrient and fertilizer advice based on soil tests. Experts flag micronutrient deficiencies, and balanced fertilizer use should raise yields at lower cost. The government allocated ₹568 crore (US$61 million), and the 2016 Union budget added ₹100 crore (US$11 million). By July 2015 only 34 lakh cards had been issued, against a 2015–16 target of 84 lakh. It followed Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006, credited with helping the state's farm growth reach three times the national rate in 2009.

soil-env-191.title: Europe's unfinished soil law
soil-env-191.text: The European Union treats soil as a non-renewable resource, yet leaves its governance largely to member states. A 2006 European Commission proposal for a soil protection framework would have unified scattered EU rules. Member states rejected it under the subsidiarity principle, arguing that their own strong soil policies sufficed. The EU still has no cohesive soil governance policy. Under the European Green Deal, the EU Soil Strategy for 2030, launched in 2021, aims at healthy soils for food security and climate mitigation. Its Soil Monitoring Law was first meant to be legally binding on soil health; the final version set no obligatory targets and covers only monitoring.

soil-env-190.title: A worldwide partnership for limited soils
soil-env-190.text: In December 2012 the FAO and its members set up the Global Soil Partnership to govern the planet's limited soils better. Its goal is food security and restored ecosystem services, by conserving, enhancing and restoring soils through productive, sustainable use. Membership is open and voluntary. FAO member countries work with universities, research centres, soil science societies, UN agencies, NGOs, companies, farmer associations and donors, through Regional Soil Partnerships. Its First Plenary Assembly, at FAO headquarters in June 2013, set up the Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils. The panel's 27 experts from all regions advise on science and advocate sustainable soil management.

soil-env-192.title: Soil policy in a nation of farmers
soil-env-192.text: In 2010 agriculture employed 58.2% of India's workforce and contributed 15.7% of its GDP. India's soil policy is shaped by that weight and by widespread farmland degradation. Excessive, miscalculated fertilizer use aimed at higher output has left nearly two-thirds of India's farmland classed as degraded or sick. Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006 tested farmers' soil and advised on fertilizer and crops. The Ministry of Agriculture later extended it nationwide. India's National Programme to Combat Desertification builds capacity in soil and water management, micro-credit for women and marginalized groups, alternative energy, and land laws for industry and mining.

soil-env-193.title: Guarding soils in cities and industrial zones
soil-env-193.text: In the developing world, industrialization and urbanization are emerging as major causes of soil degradation. Industry alters soil chemistry with heavy metals and effluents. Construction and landfills compact and excavate soil, disturbing how it purifies and stores water. Poor knowledge of soil management and disregard for the environment drive the damage. Developing countries often lack the resources to enforce policies, leaving soil and water heavily polluted. Urban soil management takes an interdisciplinary approach. It protects soil-dependent biodiversity, reduces industrial pollution and makes soil more resilient to construction compaction. In Central Europe, networks of universities and municipal authorities design soil strategies for selected cities.

soil-env-001.title: Soil contamination: when the ground holds what it should not
soil-env-001.text: In 2012 the member states of the European Union reported more than 2.5 million potentially contaminated sites. That is the scale of soil contamination, also called soil or land pollution: the presence in soil of human-made chemicals or other changes to the natural soil environment. It is one form of {{ref:soil-env-062}}. Most of it comes from industry, farm chemicals or poor waste disposal. The commonest chemicals are petroleum hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, {{ref:soil-env-018}} and the compounds described in {{ref:soil-env-199}}. The main worry is health. People meet contaminants by touching soil, eating plants grown in it, breathing its vapors, or drinking groundwater polluted from below. Yet soil is not defenseless. At low levels, contamination often falls within a soil's own capacity to treat waste. Soil organisms transform it, mainly through microbial enzymes, while organic matter and clay adsorb it. Overload that capacity, and soil life and soil function suffer. The worst cases are derelict soils, damaged so badly by industrial contamination or development that the land cannot be used safely or productively. Mapping such sites and cleaning them up is slow and costly. It calls on geology, hydrology, chemistry, computer modelling and mapping software, along with the site's pollution history. The problem is best known in North America and Europe, where many countries have legal frameworks for contaminated land; elsewhere regulation tends to be looser. Of the EU's potential sites, about 342 thousand had been identified, and mineral oil and toxic metals made up around 60% of the contamination. In China, sampling found about 100,000 square kilometers of cultivated land polluted. Add land irrigated with contaminated water or buried by solid waste, and that is one-tenth of its cultivable land.

soil-env-015.title: Nonpoint source pollution: many small leaks from a wide land
soil-env-015.text: The leading cause of water pollution in the United States has no single address. Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse pollution of water or air that does not come from one discrete source. It is often the sum of small amounts of contaminants gathered from a large area, unlike {{ref:soil-env-204}}, which comes from one source. It travels in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, precipitation, atmospheric deposition, drainage and seepage, which makes it hard to trace. Its water pollutants are sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and germs, from towns, farms, highways, forests, mines and marinas. Nitrogen leaching from fertilized fields is a typical example. Even a factory smokestack, a single source, becomes a nonpoint source where long-range transport scatters its fallout. Because this pollution stems from everyday acts such as fertilizing lawns and spraying pesticides, it is hard to regulate. Towns fight it with grass buffer strips that let soil absorb pollutants, retention ponds where contaminants settle, porous pavement and constructed wetlands. In the United States, the chief culprits are farm runoff and hydromodification, the altering of how water flows.

soil-env-019.title: Nutrient pollution: fertilizer that feeds the wrong water
soil-env-019.text: The nitrogen and phosphorus that crops fail to use do not vanish. They leave the field and degrade the air and the water downstream. Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, entering water bodies. It is a primary cause of {{ref:soil-env-020}}. In lakes, rivers and coastal waters, the excess feeds a surge of algae. Sources include farm runoff, septic tank waste, feedlots, emissions from burning fuels and raw sewage. Much of it is nonpoint source pollution, spread thin over a landscape. The two nutrients travel differently. Many forms of phosphorus cling to soil particles, so phosphorus reaches water mostly through soil erosion. Nitrate moves mainly in water passing through the soil, such as interflow and tile drainage. Excess nitrogen also drives harmful algal blooms, oxygen-starved water, acid rain, nitrogen saturation in forests and climate change. People feel the effects directly.
