Excess nitrate in drinking water causes blue baby syndrome, water treatment can create harmful disinfection by-products, and swimming in algal blooms brings rashes and breathing problems. The bill is large too: higher water treatment costs, losses to commercial fishing, shellfish and recreational fishing, and lost tourism income. Remedies include vegetated buffer zones, constructed wetlands and vegetated ditches on farms, better wastewater treatment, and permits based on the polluter pays principle.

soil-env-012.title: Soil remediation: dig it up, treat it or wall it in
soil-env-012.text: Before contaminated land is redeveloped, it may first have to be cleaned. Soil remediation is that cleanup: removing, treating or containing pollutants to restore the soil's functions and values. Planning starts with field measurements of soil chemicals and with computer models of how those chemicals move and change. Every method falls on one side of a line. Ex situ methods excavate soil or pump groundwater for treatment at the surface. In situ methods treat the contamination where it lies. The traditional approaches are digging soil out for landfill and pumping out and treating groundwater, as in {{ref:soil-env-250}}. Excavation even extends to dredging contaminated bay muds and canals. Physical options include aerating soil on site, at the risk of air pollution, or heating it so contaminants turn to vapor and can be drawn off. Living things offer another route. Microbes, plants such as willow and fungi can break contaminants down or take up toxic metals, as {{ref:soil-env-023}} explains. Other in situ tools include solidifying and stabilizing the soil, reactive barriers that treat passing groundwater, chemical oxidation, and heating in place. Sometimes the answer is to leave the pollution and contain it. Barrier walls such as slurry walls must be impermeable and resist attack by the waste for their whole lifespan. Cleanup follows regulations. Where no standards exist, or they are only advisory, it rests on assessments of health and ecological risk.

soil-env-023.title: Bioremediation: putting microbes to work on pollution
soil-env-023.text: After the 2010 Gulf of Mexico oil spill, bacteria and archaea that could live on petroleum helped restore the coast. They used the oil as a source of both carbon and energy. That is bioremediation: using organisms, living or dead, to remove pollutants from soil, water, air and other media. The usual workers are bacteria, microalgae, fungi or plants. The method exploits their natural ability to absorb, accumulate and degrade pollutants, building on the living world of {{ref:soil-bio-011}}. It aims to be more sustainable, cheaper and more scalable than physical and chemical treatment. Most bioremediation is inadvertent, done by native organisms without help. Research focuses on speeding it up by inoculating sites with organisms or supplying nutrients. Chemically, most of these processes are redox reactions. An added electron acceptor, usually oxygen, oxidizes pollutants such as hydrocarbons, making them more soluble in water and easier to degrade. In the end, the breakdown described in {{ref:soil-env-231}} turns hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water. Alternatively, an added electron donor reduces pollutants such as nitrate, perchlorate and chlorinated solvents. Toxic metals mark the hard limit. They cannot be biodegraded, only oxidized or reduced, so bioremediation offers few solutions for them. Techniques work in situ, at the site itself, or ex situ, on excavated material. They range from pumping air into soil to heaping dug soil in aerated piles, and plants can join in, as {{ref:soil-env-037}} shows. The main challenge is rate. The processes are slow.

soil-env-037.title: Phytoremediation: plants as slow, green cleanup crews
soil-env-037.text: A poplar tree can work as a pump. It draws water up through its roots and out through the plant, slowing the downward drift of soluble contaminants towards groundwater. This biological hydraulic containment is one face of phytoremediation: using living plants to clean up contaminated soil, air and water, a type of bioremediation. Plants can pull pollutants into their tissues, lock them in place, release them into the air or filter them from water. Plants and the microbes around their roots can also break pollutants down. Salt-tolerant plants called halophytes can extract salt from saline soil, and growing them reduces sodium carbonate in alkali soils. Breeding and genetic engineering can help. Tobacco given a bacterial nitroreductase gene removed the explosive TNT faster and resisted its toxicity. Bacteria in the {{ref:soil-bio-143}} speed metals into the roots of plants that hoard them, by producing chelating or dissolving agents. For all its promise, phytoremediation has never been used at large scale, and microbial bioremediation has so far done better.

soil-env-018.title: Heavy metals: the contaminants that never break down
soil-env-018.text: Within 1.1 km of the Sudbury nickel-copper smelter in Canada, soil held up to 5,104 ppm nickel and 2,892 ppm copper. Nearby plants carried nickel, copper and aluminium too. Heavy metals in soil are metals such as lead, mercury, zinc and cadmium that resist breakdown and rank among the commonest soil contaminants. They come from sewage sludge, mining, vehicle exhaust, burning fuels, industry, landfills and some fertilizers. In China, heavy metals and metalloids contaminate 19% of agricultural soils, and some 12 million tonnes of grain are contaminated each year. Unlike organic pollutants, they cannot be degraded. Microbes can at best immobilize them, as when mobile uranium U(VI) is reduced to less mobile U(IV), an approach still more conceptual than practical. Iron, cobalt, copper and zinc are essential nutrients that turn toxic in larger amounts. Arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead are highly poisonous. Even the name is disputed. Definitions cover up to 96 elements, and IUPAC calls the term meaningless and misleading, yet it remains widely used in science.

soil-env-033.title: Mycoremediation: fungi that digest what bacteria cannot
soil-env-033.text: In creosote-soaked soils rich in {{ref:soil-env-199}}, fungi have proven the most successful way to stop the pollution spreading. Mycoremediation is a form of bioremediation that uses fungi to decontaminate the environment. Their menu is long: heavy metals, organic pollutants, dyes, petroleum fuels, pharmaceuticals, pesticides and herbicides. Fungal enzymes are non-specific, so they break down substances that bacteria degrade poorly, such as the drug paracetamol and fragrances. The method needs no expensive equipment. That suits small jobs such as filtering household wastewater or industrial effluent through fungi. Cold-tolerant Antarctic fungi degrade petroleum where removing contaminated soil would be costly. Acid- and radiation-resistant species may help treat radioactive waste. In burnt forests, pellets of fungal spores coated in agarose can break down toxins and stimulate regrowth. Even the by-products have value, from enzymes such as laccase to edible and medicinal mushrooms.

soil-env-009.title: How contamination ripples from soil chemistry up the food chain
soil-env-009.text: The thickness of a forest floor can betray a poisoned soil. The ecological effects of soil contamination begin with changes to soil chemistry and to the organisms living in the soil. Many hazardous chemicals change soil chemistry radically even at low concentrations, altering the metabolism of soil microbes and animals. Wiping out part of the base of the {{ref:soil-bio-025}} can have major consequences for predators and other consumers. Earthworms and other soil ecosystem engineers are very sensitive to contaminants. As they decline, the humus form shifts from mull, with good crumb structure, to undecayed mor over compact soil. So a quick look at forest-floor thickness and the mineral horizon below has been proposed as a cheap early check for contamination. On farmland, heavy metals and metalloids alter plant metabolism and often cut yields. The weakened crops then shield the soil less from erosion. Some contaminants have long half-lives, and others decay into derivative chemicals that are contaminants themselves.

soil-env-007.title: How soil contaminants find their way into people
soil-env-007.text: Some studies estimate that 90% of human exposure to soil contaminants comes from eating contaminated food. Exposure pathways are the routes by which those contaminants reach people: swallowing soil or dust, eating food grown in it, skin contact, and breathing its vapors or dust. Most exposure is accidental. Toxic metals climb the food chain through plants growing in metal-rich soils, which tends to lead to pollution-related diseases. A potentially greater threat lies underground. Contaminants can seep into aquifers used for irrigation or drinking, sometimes far from any visible source, a pattern called long-range diffuse soil contamination. Even soil's defenses can backfire. Organic matter and clay adsorb contaminants, but as suspended colloids, tiny particles adrift in water, they can also carry them down into the subsurface.

soil-env-004.title: Pesticides: most of the spray misses its target
soil-env-004.text: More than 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides end up somewhere other than their target, including the air, water and soil. Pesticides are chemical or biological agents used to kill pests such as weeds, insects and fungi, and they are a major class of soil contaminant. Herbicides are the most common type, at about 50% of all pesticide use worldwide. Soil bacteria break down most herbicides, and they quickly turn glyphosate into a compound called AMPA. Yet glyphosate residues still turn up in drinking water, farm produce and food. The herbicides 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T can carry dioxin as an impurity, lethal even at low concentrations. Paraquat, banned in the EU, is highly toxic and lingers because clay lattices adsorb and protect it. Synthetic insecticides form three main groups. There are persistent organochlorines, described in {{ref:soil-env-005}}, organophosphates that block nerve transmission, and neonicotinoids that act on the insect central nervous system. Neonicotinoid residues have risen greatly with heavy use, and they harm pollinators as well as pests.

soil-env-002.title: Where soil contaminants come from, from tyres to coal ash
soil-env-002.text: In areas industrialized before about 1960, a common source of soil contamination was ash from coal burned for heating and ore smelting. Coal concentrates arsenic, cadmium, lead and zinc, and burning leaves all but the mercury in the ash. The ash also carries {{ref:soil-env-199}}, known human carcinogens whose acceptable soil levels typically range from 0.1 mg/kg to 10 mg/kg depending on the compound. Sources of soil contamination are the activities and materials that put contaminants into soil. They include mining and heavy industry, spills, leaking underground storage tanks and agrochemicals. Lead-based paint, nuclear waste, sewage, landfills and electronic waste add more. Road traffic adds lead from exhaust and cadmium and zinc from tyre wear, and some rocks are naturally rich in toxic elements. Treated sewage sludge, or biosolids, is a controversial fertilizer. It is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium, but generally carries more organisms, pesticides and heavy metals than other soil. In vineyards and orchards, repeated fungicide sprays build up copper, even on organic farms.

soil-env-020.title: Eutrophication: when nutrients smother a lake
soil-env-020.text: Every summer a mass of oxygen-starved bottom water forms where the Mississippi River enters the Gulf of Mexico. This dead zone is comparable in area to New Jersey. It is a product of eutrophication. That is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, boosting algae and other organisms that may then use up its oxygen. Eutrophication can be natural, a slow build-up of sediment and nutrients over geological time. Or it can be cultural, when sewage, industrial wastewater and fertilizer runoff release nutrients, the nutrient pollution of the last entries. Which nutrient matters depends on the water. Phosphorus usually limits plant growth in fresh water, and nitrogen in the sea. So excess phosphorus fuels the problem in lakes, and excess nitrogen in marine waters. The sequence is grim. Algal blooms shade out plants on the bottom. When the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up the oxygen, and fish and invertebrates die. Severe blooms called red tides release toxins as they die and can leave dead zones with no life at all. The problem grew with chemical fertilizers in the mid-1900s green revolution. Since phosphate detergents were phased out in the 1970s, sewage and agriculture dominate phosphate inputs. Prevention means cutting nutrients from sewage, farms and other sources. Shellfish and seaweed can also take up nitrogen and so curb cyanobacterial blooms.

soil-env-199.title: PAHs: soot-born rings that cling to carbon
soil-env-199.text: Across 76 sites in London's urban soils, the 16 parent PAHs ranged from 4 to 67 mg/kg of dry soil, averaging 18 mg/kg. Most were four- to six-ring forms from combustion. A polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, or PAH, is an organic compound made of several fused aromatic rings, formed mostly by incomplete burning of organic matter. Sources include engine exhaust, incinerators, forest fires, coal, petroleum, oil spills and creosote. Burning moorland vegetation adds PAHs to the peat surface. Light two- and three-ring forms spread widely, dissolved in water or as gases. Heavier ones ride on particles and settle more locally. PAHs have a strong affinity for organic carbon, so organic-rich sediments are substantial sinks. Unlike many long-lived pollutants, PAHs do not concentrate up food chains, because most vertebrates metabolize and excrete them fairly quickly. Exposure is linked to cancers. The EU and US EPA regulate PAHs in air, water and soil, with benzo[a]pyrene the usual marker compound.

soil-env-198.title: Persistent organic pollutants: the chemicals that reach the poles
soil-env-198.text: Chemicals never used in Antarctica or the Arctic turn up there anyway. Persistent organic pollutants, or POPs, are toxic organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and light-driven breakdown and persist in the environment. Most are pesticides or insecticides. Others are solvents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals, and only a few arise naturally, as from volcanoes and forest fires. They are typically halogenated, and their carbon-chlorine bonds resist being split by water or light. They dissolve poorly in water but readily in oils and fats, and solid particles capture them easily. That fat solubility lets them build up in fatty tissue. They volatilize from soils, vegetation and water, travel long distances in air and settle again. Indoors, levels in air and dust often exceed those in outdoor air and soil. The 2001 Stockholm Convention named a 'dirty dozen', including aldrin, chlordane, dieldrin, DDT, PCBs and dioxins, and newer POPs such as PFOS have been added since. Efforts focus more on banning their production and use worldwide than on removing them from the environment.

soil-env-005.title: DDT, the cheap insecticide that never quite left
soil-env-005.text: In 1970 the world used 72,000 tonnes of DDT. It was a cheap, potent and persistent organochlorine insecticide, used on a massive scale from the 1930s. DDT turned up worldwide in fish and birds and even in Antarctic snow. Barely soluble in water but very soluble in fats, it thins birds' eggshells. It is blamed for the 1950s decline of ospreys and peregrine falcons, which are now recovering. The Stockholm Convention banned it in 2001. In 2006 the World Health Organization allowed it back only for controlling vector-borne diseases in some tropical countries. In soil it lingers. Soils and sediments soak it up, then act as long-term sources of exposure. Its half-life in soil is 2 to 15 years, though depending on conditions it can range from 22 days to 30 years. Aerobic and anaerobic microbes break it down, but its products DDE and DDD are just as persistent. A 2018 study still found residues in European soils and Spanish rivers, and people carry levels 5 to 10 times lower than in the 1970s.

soil-env-016.title: Farm runoff: the diffuse pollution of the countryside
soil-env-016.text: Ploughing a large tract exposes and loosens buried soil. The next storm erodes it more easily and carries more fertilizer and pesticide into nearby water. That is agricultural nonpoint source pollution: diffuse pollution of water by nutrients, agrochemicals and sediment washed or carried off farmland. Nitrogen and phosphorus arrive as {{ref:soil-fert-001}}, manure, wastewater or sludge. They also enter runoff from crop residues, irrigation water, wildlife and atmospheric deposition. Pesticides such as DDT or atrazine travel through waterways or drift on the wind as spray. Farmers have many controls: contour ploughing, mulching, crop rotation, perennial crops, riparian buffers, conservation tillage, nutrient management plans and integrated pest management.

soil-env-026.title: Natural attenuation: letting a site clean itself, under watch
soil-env-026.text: Sometimes the best cleanup crew is already in the ground. Natural attenuation is the breakdown of contaminants by a site's own microbes, with no human intervention, though the site must still be monitored. It is one of the broad categories of bioremediation, beside feeding the native microbes and adding new ones. Time helps in other ways too. Contaminants can become less bioavailable, harder for living things to take up, while microbes and whole ecosystems adapt to them. Monitored natural attenuation is one technique for remediating derelict soils, alongside leaching, {{ref:soil-env-240}}, soil conditioners, phytoremediation and other bioremediation. Stepping in can even backfire. Where reducing conditions favor anaerobic bacteria, injecting oxygen to speed aerobic attenuation can suppress the anaerobic kind.

soil-env-011.title: Why the same pollutant harms one soil and spares another
soil-env-011.text: The same amount of a contaminant can be toxic in one soil and harmless in another. Heavy metals and other contaminants disrupt soil functions, such as the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, by altering the activity, mix and numbers of soil microorganisms. How much harm they do depends on the soil. Its pH, organic matter content and texture strongly modify how mobile, bioavailable and toxic a pollutant is. Over time, the slow self-cleaning described in {{ref:soil-env-026}} can make contaminants less available, and microbes and ecosystems can adapt. So risk assessment and remediation must be soil-specific.

soil-env-008.title: What soil contaminants do to the human body
soil-env-008.text: At high enough doses, many soil contaminants can kill through contact, inhalation or ingestion. Most harm is slower. The health effects of soil contamination vary with the pollutant, the route of exposure and how vulnerable the exposed people are. Long exposure to chromium, lead and other metals, petroleum, solvents and many pesticides can cause cancer, birth defects or other chronic disease. Benzene at sufficient concentrations is linked to leukemia, mercury and cyclodienes to kidney damage, and PCBs and cyclodienes to liver toxicity. Nitrate and ammonia from livestock manure are hazards in soil and groundwater too.

soil-env-006.title: The poisoned ground that wars leave behind
soil-env-006.text: Along the former World War I front in Belgium and France, abandoned sites where munitions were dismantled are still contaminated with arsenic and lead. War-related soil contamination is pollution left by munitions, chemical agents and other agents of war. Disposal of munitions, and careless manufacture under wartime urgency, can contaminate soil for long periods. Mustard gas stored in World War II contaminated some sites for up to 50 years. Anthrax weapon tests left Gruinard island quarantined for 48 years. Little is published on the subject, largely because governments restrict publication of material related to the war effort.

soil-env-200.title: PFAS: the 'forever chemicals' in soil and food
soil-env-200.text: A 2024 study tested 45,000 groundwater samples from areas with no obvious source of pollution and found harmful PFAS levels in 31% of them. PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are synthetic chemicals with many fluorine atoms on a carbon chain. They are so stable they are called 'forever chemicals'. Thousands have been made since Teflon in 1938, for waterproof fabrics, carpets, food packaging, firefighting foam and cosmetics. Levels peak at wastewater plants and landfills, and firefighting foam has contaminated land near airports and air bases. Soil PFAS has been found as far away as Antarctica. Contaminated soil raises PFAS in foods such as white rice, coffee and animals raised on the land. On average, concentrations double with each step up a food web, though compounds vary widely. Exposure is linked to cancers, thyroid disease, lowered immunity and fertility, and high cholesterol. Two of them, PFOS and PFOA, joined the Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants in 2009 and 2019. Treatment can trap them on activated carbon or biochar, or destroy them by oxidation, plasma or incineration.

soil-env-010.title: Biomagnification: how poisons concentrate up the food chain
soil-env-010.text: Herring carry about 0.01 ppm of mercury. Sharks carry more than 1 ppm. The difference is biomagnification: the rise in a substance's concentration in the tissues of organisms at each higher level of a food chain. It differs from bioaccumulation, the build-up within one organism from its food and surroundings. Persistent, fat-soluble compounds are the classic case. DDT and other organochlorines are stable and lipophilic, or fat-loving, so they build up in bodies and food chains. Birds that ate DDT-laden prey got weaker eggshells and more chick deaths, and some species were threatened with extinction. PCBs are easily retained in organisms, so they both accumulate over a lifetime and magnify up food webs. Mercury takes a microbial detour. Bacteria and archaea turn inorganic mercury into methylmercury, which builds up in fish such as tuna and swordfish and magnifies further up the chain. Scientists measure the effect with the biomagnification factor, the ratio of predator to prey concentration. The trophic magnification factor does the same across a whole food web. Values above 1 mean magnification. Reviews suggest the effect is rarer than once thought. Still, DDT, DDE, PCBs, toxaphene, and organic mercury and arsenic clearly do biomagnify.

soil-env-045.title: Soil vapor extraction: vacuuming pollution out of the ground
soil-env-045.text: Volatile trichloroethene in permeable sand low in carbon comes out of the ground readily. Naphthalene held in clay layers takes much longer. Both fates follow from how soil vapor extraction works. It is a physical, in situ treatment that removes volatile contaminants from unsaturated soil, the {{ref:soil-water-230}}, by drawing them out as gas. Vacuum blowers and extraction wells pull gas through the ground. Contaminants move from sorbed, dissolved and pure phases into that gas, which is treated above ground. It suits contaminants with high Henry's law constants, which escape readily from water into air, such as many chlorinated solvents and hydrocarbons. The US EPA treats it as a mature presumptive remedy. It uses standard wells and off-the-shelf equipment, disturbs the site little, and treats large soil volumes at reasonable cost. But zones of low air flow, high moisture or strong adsorption cause tailing and rebound, and extraction rates typically fall over time.

soil-env-003.title: Microplastics: the plastic specks farm soils quietly collect
soil-env-003.text: Every agricultural soil sample tested in southwestern China held plastic particles, and 92% of them were microfibers. Microplastics are insoluble synthetic plastic particles between 1 micrometer and 5 millimeters across, polluting soil as well as water and air. Primary microplastics, such as clothing microfibers and pellets, are already small when released. Secondary ones form as larger plastic items weather and break apart. The Chinese fibers probably came from string, twine and irrigation water used to wash clothes. Biosolids from sewage sludge, and compost, add more. About half the sewage sludge in Europe and North America goes onto farmland. In Europe that delivers an estimated 113 to 770 tonnes of microplastics per million inhabitants to farm soils each year. Earthworms, mites and springtails may grind swallowed plastic into still smaller pieces. A 2024 meta-analysis of 180 studies found microplastics raised soil carbon dioxide emissions by 25.7% and soil organic carbon by 25.4%, and cut aboveground plant biomass. Effects depend strongly on the type of plastic. Yet most studies report only that microplastics are present, not their origin or quantity.

soil-env-038.title: Phytoextraction: harvesting pollution in leaves and stems
soil-env-038.text: Some plants mine the soil without meaning to. Phytoextraction uses plants whose roots absorb contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in above-ground growth that can be harvested and carried away. The stars are plants that take up very high amounts, described in {{ref:soil-env-050}}. The Chinese brake fern, which accumulates arsenic, has been proposed for stripping arsenic from contaminated soil. Fast-growing ordinary plants such as poplars and willows take up little per plant. Grown in bulk, they could still remove a considerable amount. A common snag is that heavy metals are often too immobile for roots to absorb. Assisted phytoextraction adds a chelator, a compound that binds the metal and makes it more soluble. The idea even has a commercial twist. Metal-hoarding plants underpin a proposed way to collect valuable metals without excavation, described in {{ref:soil-env-051}}.

soil-env-047.title: Electrokinetic remediation: pulling metals out with electric current
soil-env-047.text: In its first test, the Lasagna Process removed 98% of the trichloroethylene from the soil. Developed at Paducah, Kentucky, in 1995, it built horizontal treatment layers through the ground. It is one form of electrokinetic remediation: passing direct current through the ground to draw organic, inorganic and heavy-metal contaminants out of soil. Anode and cathode electrodes sit in reservoir wells placed to fit the contaminant plume. An injected electrolyte conducts the current and carries contaminants away. Two motions drive it. Charged particles migrate toward the electrodes, the dominant effect, while pore fluid flows the opposite way by electro-osmosis. Contaminants must be dissolved as ions to move. Usefully, the low pH that develops keeps metals off soil particles and releases sorbed ones. Its main targets are cadmium, chromium, mercury, zinc, lead and copper. It works in situ in tight soils, removing up to 90% of heavy metals from kaolinite and clayey sands. Counterintuitively, highly permeable soils lower its efficiency. Undissolvable contaminants stay put, long runs acidify soil near the electrodes, and buried metal objects short-circuit the system.

soil-env-055.title: Biostimulation: feeding the microbes already on site
soil-env-055.text: Molasses can help clean polluted ground. Biostimulation modifies the environment to stimulate bacteria already present that can carry out bioremediation, chiefly by adding nutrients or electron acceptors or donors. Additions include phosphorus, nitrogen, oxygen and carbon sources such as molasses. For halogenated contaminants where oxygen is absent, organic electron donors let native microbes use the contaminants themselves as electron acceptors. The main advantage is the workforce. Native microbes are already suited to the subsurface and spread through it. Adding specialized cultures, described in {{ref:soil-env-032}}, can enhance the effect. Delivery is the hard part. Tight clays make additives hard to spread, and fractures channel them, so subsurface investigation and a pilot study should come before full-scale design. It is used mainly for hydrocarbon and chemical spills, with nitrogen and phosphorus key for marine oil spills, and it may also help with herbicides.

soil-env-048.title: Mapping contamination with geographic information systems
soil-env-048.text: At Idrija, Slovenia, soil absorbed mercury from a mine worked for over 500 years. A GIS model mapped how that mercury escapes from the soil, and the emissions peaked in July. GIS in environmental contamination means using geographic information system software to map and analyze contaminants in soil, water and air. Drawing on remote sensing, lidar, GeoAI and WebGIS, spatial analysis flags high-risk metal-contaminated sites for remediation. Spatial interpolation, estimating values between sample points, makes cleanup and monitoring more efficient. Urban soils gather heavy elements from transport, industry and natural weathering, and some of the most contaminated soils surround mines.

soil-env-017.title: Germs in runoff, from livestock yards to drinking water
soil-env-017.text: Runoff can carry disease. Pathogens in runoff are disease-causing bacteria and viruses carried in polluted runoff, a danger chiefly when they reach public drinking water. They include Cryptosporidium parvum, Giardia lamblia, Salmonella, norovirus and other viruses, and parasitic worms. Sources include poorly managed livestock, faulty septic systems, pet waste, over-applied sewage sludge and sewer overflows. Testers often look for coliform bacteria in runoff. These are a common indicator of water pollution but do not themselves cause disease.

soil-env-028.title: Anaerobic bioremediation: cleanup without oxygen
soil-env-028.text: Some pollutants are best broken down where there is no oxygen at all. In anaerobic bioremediation, an added electron donor drives the reduction of oxidized pollutants such as chlorinated solvents, explosives and nitrate. Added organic substrates are first fermented to hydrogen and volatile fatty acids such as acetate and lactate, which feed the bacteria. They go in through wells, by direct push, or in trenches such as biowalls. Slow-release edible oils stay in place longer. The chemistry can stall. Breakdown of the solvent TCE may stop at DCE and vinyl chloride, suspected or known carcinogens, but Dehalococcoides bacteria can carry it on to harmless ethene.

soil-env-027.title: Biopiles and windrows: composting contaminated soil
soil-env-027.text: Contaminated soil can be dug up and treated much like compost. In biopiles and windrows, excavated soil is heaped and aerated to speed microbial breakdown of pollutants. Biopiles use pumps, pushing air in under pressure or drawing it out by suction, to boost aerobic breakdown of petroleum. Windrows are turned regularly, which aerates the soil and spreads contaminants evenly. Both are ex situ methods. These usually cost more than in situ ones, because the soil must be excavated and hauled to a treatment facility.

soil-env-025.title: Biosparging: bubbling oxygen below the water table
soil-env-025.text: Oxygen can be pushed into the saturated ground below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Biosparging does exactly that, injecting oxygen, and possibly nutrients, into contaminated saturated zones so that native bacteria degrade pollutants faster. It is the counterpart of {{ref:soil-env-024}}, which aerates the unsaturated zone above. The air must go in hard. In {{ref:soil-env-240}}, it is injected below the water table at a pressure high enough to overcome the water's hydrostatic pressure and the soil's resistance to air flow.

soil-env-024.title: Bioventing: helping soil microbes breathe
soil-env-024.text: Microbes readily break down gasoline, kerosene, diesel and jet fuel when oxygen is plentiful. Bioventing supplies that oxygen, raising the flow of air into the unsaturated zone to speed the natural in situ breakdown of hydrocarbons. It is the commonest aerobic bioremediation. Oxygen serves as the electron acceptor that oxidizes petroleum, PAHs, phenols and other reduced pollutants. Heavier molecules are harder for microbes to break down, a process covered in {{ref:soil-env-231}}. The method is inexpensive, but cleaning a site can take a few years. Below the water table oxygen is scarcer, because water in equilibrium with air holds only 8 to 10 mg/L. There it comes from aerated water, pure oxygen, peroxides or bubbled air, the method of {{ref:soil-env-240}}.

soil-env-031.title: Engineering microbes to clean up pollution
soil-env-031.text: Pseudomonas strains given the lux gene can detect the pollutant naphthalene. Genetically engineered bioremediation uses genetic engineering to design organisms for cleanup, and it is still at the stage of preliminary research. Inserted genes either code proteins that break pollutants down or, like lux, report on pollution. Modified organisms have been made to treat oil spills and break down plastics such as PET. Release raises fears that the genes will pass to other organisms. So engineered organisms can be built to survive only under set conditions, and tagged with bioluminescence genes for tracking.

soil-env-030.title: Why bioremediation is so rarely used
soil-env-030.text: For all its appeal, bioremediation is rarely used. Its drawbacks are slow rates, pollutants that cannot biodegrade, and highly specific microbial needs. Heavy metals and radionuclides do not biodegrade, though they can sometimes be immobilized. Microbes may not fully break a pollutant down, and can leave a more toxic compound behind. Treatment often takes longer than landfilling or incineration, and small test results are hard to scale up to the field. It needs plenty of microbes able to degrade the pollutant in time, preferably native rather than invasive, and control of many environmental factors.

soil-env-029.title: Microbes against pesticide residues
soil-env-029.text: Many sites worldwide are contaminated with agrochemicals, which often resist biodegradation by design. Pesticide bioremediation uses microbes to break down these residues, and it is seen as more promising than other ways of dealing with them. The need is plain. Lindane, a common 20th-century insecticide still produced today, reduces beneficial soil bacteria such as nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Grouped strains of Actinobacteria degrade pesticides more efficiently. So far they have been used only in the laboratory, and their cost and scalability are unproven.

soil-env-053.title: Landfarming: tilling oily waste into the topsoil
soil-env-053.text: Ordinary farm equipment can treat refinery waste. In landfarming, contaminated soil, sediment or sludge is mixed into the surface soil and periodically tilled so that microbes degrade the contaminants. It has long handled drill cuttings, oily sludge and other petroleum refinery wastes. A clay or composite liner commonly catches leaching contaminants to protect groundwater. Not everything breaks down. PAHs with more rings, and more chlorinated or nitrated compounds, degrade slowly, and creosote, pentachlorophenol and bunker C oil resist. Inorganic contaminants are not degraded, hydrocarbon levels above 7% poison the microbes, and the microbes turn hydrocarbons into greenhouse gases.

soil-env-201.title: Brownfields: the abandoned sites cities struggle to reuse
soil-env-201.text: The word brownfield was first used in 1992, at a US congressional hearing. Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may carry pollution or a risk of it from past industrial use. Abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations are typical. So are their contaminants: hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead. Definitions vary between countries, mainly on whether pollution must actually be present. The US EPA counts land whose reuse is complicated by actual or potential contamination. Many sites sit unused for decades because cleanup would cost more than the land is then worth. Unknown buried tanks or drums can raise costs further, so developers often insist on a full site investigation first. Cleanups use heating in place, bioremediation, in situ oxidation, soil vapor extraction, binders that stop leaching, and plants that take up metals. By September 2023 the EPA's brownfields program had readied 134,414 acres for reuse.

soil-env-040.title: Phytodegradation: plants as a green liver
soil-env-040.text: Plants have been called a 'green liver', because they handle foreign compounds much as the human liver does. Phytodegradation, also called phytotransformation, is the use of plants to degrade organic pollutants. It has been proposed for herbicides, trichloroethylene and methyl tert-butyl ether. Researchers have also proposed a pathway by which plants transform the explosive TNT.

soil-env-044.title: Phytoscreening: reading groundwater pollution in tree trunks
soil-env-044.text: A tree can report on the groundwater beneath it. Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene turn up in tree trunks at concentrations related to those in groundwater. Phytoscreening uses plants this way, as biosensors that map contaminant plumes underground. Standard methods take a core from the trunk, often with an increment borer, for laboratory analysis. It could streamline site investigations and lower cleanup costs, but it has not yet been put to practical use.

soil-env-039.title: Phytostabilization: plants that hold pollution in place
soil-env-039.text: Some cleanups never remove the pollutant at all. Phytostabilization uses plants to contain pollutants for the long term by lowering their mobility, holding them near the roots rather than in plant tissue. The plants reduce erosion, runoff and leaching, and make the contaminant less bioavailable. Vegetative caps have been used to stabilize and contain mine tailings. Root mats of meadow grasses may immobilize radioactive materials. The chemistry is fickle, though: some soil amendments reduce mobility at one concentration but increase it at another.

soil-env-041.title: Phytostimulation: roots that feed pollutant-eating microbes
soil-env-041.text: Roots release carbohydrates and acids into the soil, and microbes respond. Phytostimulation, also called rhizodegradation, harnesses this to boost microbial breakdown of organic contaminants in the rhizosphere, the soil around roots. The stimulated microbes then biodegrade the contaminants. Plant litter and organic matter also help keep soil microbial diversity from being lost to contaminants. The approach has been tested with petroleum, PCBs and PAHs.

soil-env-042.title: Phytovolatilization: plants that release pollutants into the air
soil-env-042.text: Selenium can leave the soil through a plant as volatile dimethyl selenide, and mercury as the element. Phytovolatilization removes substances from soil or water through plants that turn them into more volatile, often less polluting forms and release them into the air. Poplars, with their high transpiration rates, have been promoted for removing volatile organic compounds.

soil-env-054.title: In situ thermal desorption: baking pollutants out of the ground
soil-env-054.text: Soil heated in place to as much as 900 °C gives up its pollutants by vaporization, steam distillation, oxidation or pyrolysis. This in-place form of {{ref:soil-env-230}}, also called thermal conduction heating, does exactly that, sometimes under vacuum. Arrays of electric or gas-fired thermal wells heat the soil by conduction, and vapor extraction wells collect the released contaminants. It works in tight soils such as clay, above and below the water table, at temperatures from under 100 °C to above the boiling point of water. Shell Oil developed it in the late 1980s from research on enhanced oil recovery, and commercialized it in the mid-1990s.

soil-env-022.title: Tracing a river's nutrient load back to its sources
soil-env-022.text: In Europe, agriculture is typically the main source of nitrogen in water bodies, while in many countries households and industry supply most of the phosphorus. Nutrient source apportionment estimates such shares: how much of the load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after attenuation or treatment. Load-oriented models work back from in-stream monitoring data. Source-oriented models calculate diffuse emissions from export coefficients of similar catchments. Ireland's Source Load Apportionment Model needs no in-stream data. It combines point discharges, diffuse land-use sources and catchment hydrogeology.

soil-env-021.title: Nutrient trading: a market for cleaner water
soil-env-021.text: Two polluters in the same watershed can face very different costs to control the same pollutant. Nutrient trading turns that gap into a market. It is a form of water quality trading in which polluters exchange credits for reducing nutrient pollution. Those with cheap controls sell reduction credits to those with costly ones. Its principle is 'polluter pays', usually tied to a regulatory requirement to take part. A 2013 review found three kinds of funders: beneficiaries, polluters and public good payers. Governments and NGOs initiated most payments.

soil-env-204.title: Point source pollution: one pipe, one smokestack
soil-env-204.text: A single factory outfall or smokestack is the classic point source. Point source pollution comes from one identifiable source, so small in extent that models can treat it as a mathematical point. That sets it apart from nonpoint and area sources. Water point sources include factories, power plants, municipal sewage treatment plants and some farms, such as concentrated animal feeding operations. They can contaminate natural, man-made and groundwater reservoirs, threatening human health.

soil-env-056.title: Surfactant leaching: flushing oily contaminants from soil
soil-env-056.text: Surfactants are compounds that let oil and water blend, and they can wash pollution out of the ground. Surfactant leaching mixes contaminated water or soil with surfactants, then leaches out the emulsified contaminants. In surfactant-enhanced aquifer remediation, surfactant solution is pumped from injection wells through contaminated zones to extraction wells. It removes non-aqueous phase liquids, pollutants that stay separate from water. In oil recovery the commonest surfactants are ethoxylated alcohols and nonylphenols, sulfates, sulfonates and biosurfactants.

soil-env-203.title: Radioactive contamination: fallout in the soil
soil-env-203.text: Between the 1950s and 1980s, 520 atmospheric nuclear explosions spread fallout widely. Radioactive contamination is the unintended presence of radioactive substances on surfaces or within solids, liquids or gases. It is hazardous because their decay emits ionizing radiation. Some sources are natural. Uranium, thorium and their decay products occur in rock and soil, and mining, oil and gas extraction and coal use can concentrate them. Others are man-made. A nuclear weapon blast or reactor breach contaminates nearby air, soil, people, plants and animals with fuel and fission products, as around Chernobyl and Fukushima. The hazard depends on the concentration, the energy and type of radiation, and how close the contaminants come to body organs. Large contaminated areas may be covered with concrete, soil or rock to stop spread, and cleanup itself produces radioactive waste. After Fukushima, one goal was to strip 80 to 95% of cesium-137 from soil without destroying its organic content. The aim was to bring exposure down to 1 mSv a year above background.

soil-env-034.title: Fungi that soak up metals, and even gold
soil-env-034.text: Filtering electronic waste through fungi has recovered 80% of its gold. In fungi, the process in {{ref:soil-env-219}} is the capture of metals: they bind them on their cell surfaces and concentrate them in their fruiting bodies for later removal. Pleurotus, Aspergillus and Trichoderma remove lead, cadmium, nickel, chromium, mercury, arsenic, copper and zinc, on land and in water. Metals enter the mycelium passively, and strains from long-polluted sites tolerate them best. Some mushrooms become bioindicators: the edible shaggy ink cap signals mercury well, but can then be toxic to eat. Even dead fungal cell walls can filter heavy metals and radionuclides from industrial effluents.

soil-env-035.title: Fungi that digest pollutants the way they digest wood
soil-env-035.text: Lignin and cellulose are long-chain carbon compounds, much like many organic pollutants. That resemblance explains fungal degradation of organic pollutants. Fungi, especially {{ref:soil-bio-129}}, break pollutants down with the enzymes and acids they secrete to digest lignin and cellulose. The enzymes include lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase, laccase and cytochrome P450. Fungi degrade petroleum fuels, phenols, polyurethane and PCBs in soil, though sometimes they only prepare the way for later microbial activity. White rot fungi break down the pesticides endosulfan, chlorpyrifos and atrazine in clay-loam soils, and dyes such as the carcinogenic Congo red.

soil-env-036.title: Mycorrhizal fungi as partners in plant cleanup
soil-env-036.text: Fungal threads can stretch a plant's reach beyond its roots. Mycorrhizoremediation uses mycorrhizal fungi to remove soil contaminants and so strengthen phytoremediation. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi relieve plants' pollutant stress, so the plants grow more biomass, and they supply nutrients, especially phosphorus. The fungi also make proteins that bind heavy metals, lowering their bioavailability. Their fast-spreading mycelium extends the root zone into the hyphosphere, reaching more nutrients and contaminants and boosting helpful bacteria. Pairing Rhizophagus intraradices with Robinia trees or vetiver grass has removed lead, and mycorrhizal reeds have degraded benzene and MTBE from wetland groundwater.

soil-env-202.title: Permeable reactive barriers: a treatment wall for groundwater
soil-env-202.text: A permeable reactive barrier is a treatment zone set across a contaminant plume, cleaning groundwater as it flows through. It is built by digging a trench across the groundwater flow, filling it with reactive material such as iron, carbon or limestone, and covering it with soil. Contaminants are immobilized by sorption or precipitation, which may require replacing the medium. Or they are transformed into less harmful forms, usually by redox reactions. Zerovalent iron was the first barrier material and remains the main one. Barriers most likely fail by losing reactivity rather than permeability, and estimates of their life range from 10 to 100 years.

soil-env-049.title: DRASTIC: scoring how easily an aquifer is polluted
soil-env-049.text: Seven factors spell DRASTIC: depth to water, net recharge, aquifer media, soil media, topography, impact of the vadose zone and hydraulic conductivity. Together they make an index, often mapped with GIS, that rates how prone an aquifer is to contamination. Each factor carries a weight from one to five. A lower index means a lower risk of contamination. The score shows authorities which areas are most vulnerable, so they can put protective measures in place.

soil-env-052.title: Metallophytes: plants that live on metal-rich ground
soil-env-052.text: Some plants survive only where heavy metals are present. A metallophyte is a plant able to survive in metal-rich soil. Obligate metallophytes are confined to such soils, while facultative ones tolerate metals but are not restricted to them. They fall into three classes. Metal excluders absorb metals only at their roots. Metal indicators accumulate heavy metals in shoots and leaves but eventually succumb to their toxicity. The third class is described in {{ref:soil-env-050}}.

soil-env-050.title: Hyperaccumulators: plants that store metal in their leaves
soil-env-050.text: Alpine pennycress can hold up to 380 mg/kg of cadmium in its leaves. It is a hyperaccumulator, a metallophyte that absorbs metals through its roots and stores them in its leaves. Such plants concentrate metals to levels toxic to related species not adapted to metal-rich soils, and about 85–90% of them are obligate metallophytes. One threshold is over 1000 mg/kg of dry weight for nickel, copper, cobalt, chromium or lead, and over 10,000 mg/kg for zinc or manganese. About 450 species, including Arabidopsis and other Brassicaceae, take up metals at 100–1000 times the levels in sister species. Toxic leaves may deter herbivores and pathogens, the 'elemental defense hypothesis'. These plants are widely discussed for cleanup, but commercial use remains aspirational. After the Chernobyl accident, sunflowers removed cesium-137 and strontium-90 from a pond. Introduced species can also invade. Nickel-accumulating Alyssum, brought to Oregon in the 1990s to harvest metal, spread into serpentine habitats and was declared a noxious weed in 2009.

soil-env-051.title: Phytomining: farming metal from the soil
soil-env-051.text: In 1983 Rufus Chaney, a USDA agronomist, proposed harvesting metals with plants. Phytomining, also called agromining, extracts heavy metals with hyperaccumulating plants, then collects and refines the metals from the harvested biomass. Chaney and Alan Baker first tested it in 1996. In principle it could harm the environment less than conventional mining and recover low-grade metals from mine waste. Practice has lagged. A 2021 review judged its commercial viability limited because it is slow and inefficient. By mid-2024 one nickel project had extracted less than a kilo of usable nickel. Still, in 2025 a start-up raised 45 million dollars to commercialize nickel phytomining from mine tailings.

soil-env-046.title: Cleaning the vapor that soil extraction pulls out
soil-env-046.text: The gas drawn from a soil vapor extraction well is still contaminated. SVE off-gas treatment cleans it before release, most often by thermal oxidation or adsorption on activated carbon. The choice depends on the contaminant, its concentration, throughput and cost. Granular activated carbon suits streams below 500 ppmV, oxidation those up to 4,000 ppmV, and vapor condensation those above. Thermal oxidizers run at 730 to 820 °C, while catalytic oxidizers work at 316 to 427 °C. Activated carbon must be replaced as it saturates, and it does not remove heavy metals. Incineration is controversial because it risks releasing dioxins.

soil-env-032.title: Bioaugmentation: adding specialist microbes to a polluted site
soil-env-032.text: Municipal wastewater plants commonly add microbial cultures to restart their activated-sludge bioreactors. That is bioaugmentation, a type of bioremediation that adds specialized microbes to boost the breakdown of pollutants. Elsewhere it remains more aspirational than practical at scale. For soils it has been proposed against chlorocarbons from dry cleaners and hydrocarbons from gas stations, usually with biostimulation to favor dechlorinating microbes. Failures come from the wrong organism, predation, competition with native bacteria and too-small doses. Many trials weighed only a strain's degrading ability, not its fitness among the existing microbes.

soil-env-043.title: Rhizofiltration: roots that strain metals from water
soil-env-043.text: In one study, sunflower roots cut uranium levels by nearly 95% in 24 hours. Rhizofiltration is phytoremediation that filters contaminated groundwater, surface water or wastewater through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients. Like phytoextraction, it traps contaminants, mainly heavy metals, in harvestable biomass, but it treats water rather than soil. Plants are usually raised in a greenhouse first, then planted at the site or fed contaminated water brought to them. Removing radionuclides with sunflowers was estimated at $2 to $6 per thousand gallons treated. It misses contaminants below rooting depth, can take years, and harvested plants threaten health unless non-fodder crops are used.

soil-env-013.title: Contaminated land risk assessment: how much is too much
soil-env-013.text: Nobody wants to pay for assessing or cleaning contaminated land, and findings on nearby plots may go on property titles and lower their value. That makes contaminated land risk assessment contentious. It is the staged evaluation of whether a site's contaminants pose unacceptable risk. It moves from a qualitative conceptual site model to generic and then detailed quantitative assessment. Work starts once a site is suspected of contamination, often with a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, and the site's past uses guide sampling and analysis. Generic screening values are set conservatively for standard land uses. Exceeding one shows only that harm is possible, prompting site-specific study of contaminants, pathways and receptors. Neighboring land is often contaminated too, by decades of emissions or contaminated fill. So nearby topsoil, ceiling dust and water should be tested before and after remediation. National standards include the US EPA's Regional Screening Levels, the Dutch standards, Australia's investigation levels and Canada's provincial standards. The EU is moving towards Europe-wide standards, though most industrialized European nations still set their own.

soil-env-279.title: Methane, the gas behind a third of near-term heating
soil-env-279.text: Rising methane emissions cause up to one-third of the global heating expected in the near term. Methane emissions are the release of this potent greenhouse gas to the air, from human activities and from natural sources such as wetlands. In 2019 about 60% came from people and 40% from nature. Most natural methane is made by methanogens, microbes that produce it in warm, moist soils and in animal guts, the process described in {{ref:soil-chem-129}}. Wetlands supply about three-quarters of the enduring natural sources. Farming copies them. Plant agriculture contributes about 15% of human emissions, and rice is the largest single source. Waterlogged paddies behave like wetlands: in 2022 they emitted about 30 million of 400 million tonnes. Land use shifts the balance too. Converting forests to farmland adds nitrogen to the soil, and that nitrogen inhibits methane oxidation, the microbial breakdown of methane. Moving the water table up or down can switch a soil between methane source and methane sink, a theme taken up in {{ref:soil-env-283}}.

soil-env-280.title: Methanotrophs, the microbes that eat methane
soil-env-280.text: Some microbes make their living from the very gas that methanogens release. Methanotrophs are bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of both carbon and energy. They live in wetlands, soils, marshes, rice paddies and landfills, mostly close to methane sources, though some oxidize methane straight from the atmosphere. By cutting the methane that reaches the air, they play a significant part in the global methane budget. Aerobic methanotrophs combine oxygen with methane. Enzymes called methane monooxygenases perform the first step. The products are formaldehyde, which is built into organic compounds, and carbon dioxide. Two groups divide the territory. Type I methanotrophs tend to dominate cold, oxygen-poor, methane-rich settings. Type II are more stress-tolerant and dominate methane-limited and acidic ones. In anoxic soils, rice paddies and sediments, some methanotrophs oxidize methane with nitrate, nitrite, iron, sulfate or manganese instead of oxygen.

soil-env-278.title: Counting the carbon that land use adds and removes
soil-env-278.text: Clearing a forest for farmland releases carbon that no smokestack ever emitted. Greenhouse gas inventories record it in a sector called land use, land-use change and forestry, or LULUCF. It covers the emissions and removals that result from how people use land, change its use and manage forests. These activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or take it out, through their effects on the carbon cycle, but they are hard to measure. The IPCC estimates that land-use change, such as turning forest into farmland, adds a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt of carbon a year. Fossil fuels and cement add 6.3 ± 0.6 Gt. Updated assessments put LULUCF emissions at 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt of carbon, or 4.1 ± 2.6 Gt of carbon dioxide, a year over 2014–2023. Under the Kyoto rules the activities fall into two classes. Accounting is mandatory for afforestation, reforestation and {{ref:soil-env-269}}. It is voluntary for managing forests, cropland and grazing land. Carbon is not the whole story. Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration, and a 2021 study found it had affected 17% of land between 1960 and 2019.

soil-env-272.title: How long biochar keeps its carbon locked away
soil-env-272.text: Biochar counts as carbon removal only if the carbon stays put. Its permanence is how long that carbon remains stored before returning to the atmosphere. Multi-pool models give biochar in soil a turnover of centuries to millennia, depending on feedstock, production conditions, application rate and site. Biochar made above 600 °C resembles inertinite, a stable component of coal. Under certain conditions 97% of its organic carbon is highly refractory, meaning it resists decay. The question is not settled. Some studies report turnover within a century. Re-analyses argue that the common two-pool decay model behind them is badly parameterised, so permanence is generally underestimated. Part of the trouble is what gets measured. Incubation experiments have mostly tracked the labile, easily decayed fraction, which falls from about 16% to 1% across production temperatures of 350–800 °C.

soil-env-273.title: Selling biochar's stored carbon as credits
soil-env-273.text: In 2024 biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases. Biochar carbon credits are certified credits for carbon dioxide removed by making biochar and storing it durably, traded on voluntary carbon markets. Abatement costs are high, so these credits sell at prices an order of magnitude above credits from emission reductions. Standards such as the European Biochar Certificate list the permissible feedstocks. Certified suppliers must also be carbon net-negative, removing more carbon than they emit.

soil-env-271.title: Letting rice paddies dry out to cut methane
soil-env-271.text: Rice need not stand in water all season. Alternate wetting and drying, or AWD, lets lowland rice fields dry for a few days before they are flooded again. In 'safe' AWD a perforated tube shows the water table. When it falls 15 cm below the soil surface, the field is re-flooded to 5 cm, and it stays flooded at flowering. Each dry spell ends the anaerobic conditions in which methane forms. Seasonal methane emissions fell by up to 85%, and the 2006 IPCC methodology assumes an average cut of 48%. AWD also saves about 38% of water without harming yields, and drying lowers arsenic and cadmium in the grain. The main drawback is higher nitrous oxide emissions. It suits areas where soils can be drained in 5-day intervals, mainly in the dry season.

soil-env-274.title: Three escape routes for wetland methane
soil-env-274.text: Methane made in a wetland soil still has to get out, and it has three routes. The water table marks the boundary. Below it, in soil without oxygen, methane is produced; above it, in aerated soil, methanotrophs consume it. A low water table forces rising methane past these microbes. The first route is molecular diffusion. It is slow through peat full of undecayed organic matter and matters more in drier, loosely packed soils, since methane moves faster through soil than through water. The second runs through aerenchyma, porous tissue in some plants. It shunts methane straight from the roots to the air, bypassing oxidation. The third is ebullition, or bubbling. Methane builds up in soil pockets until the pressure bursts them, releasing it too fast for methanotrophs to consume. Piezometers detect these pockets.

soil-env-275.title: What decides how much wetland methane escapes
soil-env-275.text: A wetland's methane output is a race between makers and eaters. Net flux depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens reaches the surface before methanotrophs oxidize it. Four controls set the result: water table, temperature, substrate and ecosystem production. Large fluxes have followed drought-driven drops in the water table. With water at or above the surface, bubbling and transport through plants dominate. Soil temperature sets how fast microbes produce and consume methane, and with the water table it drives seasonal cycles. Substrate matters too. Soils rich in acetate, or in hydrogen and carbon dioxide, favor production, and a steady supply of cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 are optimal.

soil-env-277.title: Draining a wetland can cut methane, or raise it
soil-env-277.text: Wetlands are drained for development, housing and farming, and the effect on methane is mixed. Lowering the water table increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs. That can turn a wetland from a methane source into a sink. The drains themselves can undo the gain. Ditches that stay saturated, especially when drains sit too close together, become warm, wet mini-wetlands that emit much methane.

soil-env-276.title: Wetland nitrous oxide, flowing both ways
soil-env-276.text: Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential 300 times that of carbon dioxide. It is also the leading ozone-depleting emission of the 21st century. Wetland soils exchange it with the air in either direction. Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, raise the outward flux through denitrification and nitrification. In mangroves of Shenzhen and Hong Kong, measured fluxes ranged from 0.14 to 23.83 micromoles of nitrous oxide per square meter per hour. Negative fluxes are common as well: the soil consumes the gas instead of releasing it.

soil-env-284.title: Computer models that put soil into the climate
soil-env-284.text: Climate forecasts need a ground floor. Land surface models represent vegetation, soil and terrain inside simulations of climate and the carbon and water cycles. Such a model combines vegetation cover, soil type and terrain with rainfall data. It then estimates how much water soaks into the ground and how much becomes streamflow. Earth system models go further, extending climate models to include the biosphere and land use change. Even under identical emission scenarios, they predict a wide range of future carbon uptake by land and ocean. One gap stands out. The main Earth system models still omit peatlands, although peatland carbon balance is expected to shift from sink to source this century.

soil-env-283.title: Soils that swallow methane
soil-env-283.text: Soil can soak up methane as well as release it. Methanotrophic microbes in soils consume methane, including methane from the atmosphere, which makes soils a natural methane sink. Land use can weaken that sink. Converting forests and natural land to farmland raises soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation by methanotrophs. Water decides the balance most directly. Changing the water table shifts a soil between methane source and sink, and lowering a wetland's water table can make it a sink. Even landfills can help: nutrient-supplemented cover soils, rich in methanotrophs, can act as small methane sinks.

soil-env-281.title: Rewetting drained peatlands by blocking the drains
soil-env-281.text: A drained peatland heals by getting wet again. Peatland rewetting returns the land to its original waterlogged state, so peat-forming vegetation recovers and peat can accumulate once more. Workers keep the soil moist and slow drainage by blocking and filling canals and digging deep wells. Peat itself makes good dams. Unoxidized peat dug from the channel bottom is stable, impermeable and resistant to erosion. Plastic dams of interlocking piling can hold deep pools, but they work only on peat, not on mineral soil.

soil-env-282.title: Paludiculture: farming a peatland that stays wet
soil-env-282.text: Rewetting a peatland need not end farming on it. Paludiculture rewets drained peatlands and keeps farming them with crops suited to wet conditions, such as berries, herbs, timber and biomass for biofuel. Raising the water table restores a peatland ecosystem that stores large amounts of carbon. The same land then serves as both carbon sink and farmland. It can also fix an old problem. Degraded farmed peatlands are often nutrient-rich, and paludiculture can remove the excess nutrients over time, a cheaper alternative to stripping the topsoil.

soil-env-269.title: Deforestation and the soil left behind
soil-env-269.text: Forests now cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread. Half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees and the conversion of the land to non-forest uses such as farms, ranches or towns. Agriculture is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 nearly 90% of global deforestation came from cropland expansion and the creation of pasture. The soil feels the change quickly. Topsoil often erodes once the trees are gone, and rivers carry more sediment. Tree roots bind soil, so cleared slopes become more prone to landslides. Clearing also alters soil microbial communities and reduces soil properties such as hydraulic conductivity, and sandier soils suffer more than clayey ones. In a simulation of the Amazon, surface and soil temperatures rose by 1 to 3 °C after clearing. The changed soil properties could even turn the soil into a carbon source. Repeated slash-and-burn with shortened fallows, the rest periods between crops, leaves less vegetation and lower soil biomass on burned land.

soil-env-313.title: Rangeland management, a lesson of the Dust Bowl
soil-env-313.text: The Dust Bowl showed what overgrazing and misuse of arid land could do, and rangeland management grew up in the United States in response. It is the science and practice of conserving rangelands and managing them sustainably, adjusting their parts to yield the best mix of goods and services over time. At first it focused on grazing and the proper use of range vegetation by livestock. Today it aims to protect and enhance soils, riparian zones, watersheds and vegetation while still producing meat, water, wood and fiber. Its scope has widened to the benefits described in {{ref:soil-env-285}}. Growing degradation, such as woody plant encroachment, makes rehabilitation part of the job. Climate adds pressure: heatwaves, droughts and floods are expected to alter rangelands' ecological states and cut forage production. The field draws on animal science, plant ecology, soil science, wildlife management, climatology and anthropology.

soil-env-270.title: When farmers give up the land
soil-env-270.text: Land farmed hard for a long time is sometimes simply given up. Land abandonment is that giving up of farmed land. In areas with a long history of intensive farming, threshold effects of land degradation may lead to it. Trees and shrubs then often re-establish on the former fields, a process called woody plant encroachment. Climate change may add to the pressure. Farmland values in parts of southern Europe are projected to fall by more than 80% by 2100, which could cause abandonment.

soil-env-308.title: Rain gardens, where city runoff sinks in and gets cleaned
soil-env-308.text: Every roof and road sends rain racing toward the drains, carrying pollutants with it. A rain garden, also called a bioretention facility, is a designed planted site that lets this runoff soak into the soil and be cleaned. Plants and natural or engineered soil hold the stormwater, delay its infiltration, and filter and remediate its pollutants. Deep roots open extra channels for water and keep the soil permeable. They also sustain the microbes that break down pollutants and remove nitrogen. The cleaning works by settling, filtration, assimilation, adsorption to roots, soil particles and organic matter, and microbial decomposition. A typical garden removes about 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals. A 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%. Rain gardens restore groundwater recharge and cut stormwater volumes. Unless remediation materials are built into the filter layers, though, they may not reduce pollution.

soil-env-306.title: Urban soil: stripped, squeezed and contaminated
soil-env-306.text: Under a city lawn or sidewalk, the soil is rarely the soil that was there before. Urban soil is soil in cities and towns, often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity. It holds more heavy metals, especially lead, copper and nickel, and has a lower pH than comparable soil in the wild. With the {{ref:soil-form-021}} typically stripped away, it has low aeration, porosity and drainage. Compaction, as in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}, and contamination limit root growth and tree health. Contamination persists in cities with a history of industry, leaded gasoline or lead-based house paint. Construction rather than farm machinery is the usual cause of urban compaction. Jobs on tight schedules ignore the risk of working wet soil, and topsoil is stripped or fill added. Disturbed urban soils are low in organic matter and biological activity, and construction debris such as concrete often raises the pH because concrete contains lime. The Polish soil classification's 'urban soils' type corresponds to Urbic, Mollic or Ecranic Technosols in the WRB. Management is interdisciplinary, aiming to protect soil biodiversity, cut industrial pollution and make soils more resilient to construction compaction. Recovery is possible: in a Palermo trial, de-sealing long-sealed urban soils and revegetating them stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity within eighteen months.

soil-env-311.title: Spoil tips and the disaster at Aberfan
soil-env-311.text: In October 1966 a spoil tip at Aberfan, Wales, collapsed onto a school and killed 144 people. It had been built over a spring and was saturated by heavy rain. A spoil tip is a pile of spoil, the waste earth removed during mining or large excavations. Spoil may be ordinary soil and rock or heavily contaminated with chemical waste. Clean spoil can be used for land reclamation. Tips trap solar heat, which hinders plants and encourages erosion and unstable slopes. They also cause acid rock drainage and leach noxious chemicals into groundwater. Regreening uses geotextiles to control erosion while the site is resoiled and seeded. Old tips may later shelter rare plants, but without nearby seed sources invasive species dominate.

soil-env-312.title: Growing trees in cramped city soil
soil-env-312.text: A street tree lives in a hard place. Urban forestry is the care and management of single trees and tree populations in towns and cities to improve the urban environment. Street trees face limited soil volume, high compaction and harsh microclimates, so they grow and survive less well than trees elsewhere. Species are chosen to tolerate alkaline and compacted soils, low soil volume, de-icing salts and drought. A healthy large tree needs about 1,000 cubic feet of soil. In return, canopies intercept rain, and roots slow and filter water and return it to the air. Urban forests also support nutrient cycling and soil formation.

soil-env-309.title: The engineered soil inside a rain garden
soil-env-309.text: The soil in a rain garden is a recipe. A bioretention soil mix is the engineered growing soil through which the garden filters its water. A typical mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil. More compost improves filtering; more sand speeds infiltration but may retain fewer nutrients. The sandy mix must not be blended with less sandy surrounding soil. Clay would settle between the sand grains into a concrete-like mass that drains poorly. Where native soil drains too slowly, as Type D soils do, it should be replaced and an underdrain installed. Yet a five-year USGS study found rain gardens in urban clay soils worked without either, if infiltration before installation was at least 0.25 inches per hour.

soil-env-307.title: Artefacts, the human objects buried in soil
soil-env-307.text: Fragments of pottery, tile and animal bone turn up in dark earth. Such objects are artefacts in soil: things recognizably made or extracted from the earth by humans. They are a defining feature of human-made soils. A significant amount of artefacts, a geotechnical liner or a seal of technic hard material qualifies a soil as a Technosol. The WRB also marks human-transported natural material, with the horizon suffix τ.

soil-env-310.title: Saving dug-up topsoil in a stockpile
soil-env-310.text: Topsoil dug out for a building need not be lost. A soil stockpile is a pile of topsoil excavated during construction of buildings or infrastructure and kept for later use. Once the construction infrastructure is removed, the soil goes into landscaping or restoration. That makes it a resource for both construction and ecology. Before it is reused, the stockpiled soil may be tested for contamination.

soil-env-285.title: Ecosystem services, the work nature does for people
soil-env-285.text: New York City faced a $6–8 billion bill for a water filtration plant. Instead it restored its Catskill watershed for $1–1.5 billion. There, soil absorption and filtration, roots and soil microbes brought the water back to standard. That work is an ecosystem service, one of the many benefits people derive from ecosystems, such as clean water, food, decomposition of wastes and flood control. The UN Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularized four categories: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services. Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, make the others possible, from food supply to flood regulation and water purification. Regulating services include decomposing and detoxifying wastes. Erosion regulation affects people indirectly, through environmental conditions. Evaluations of ecosystem services may assign them an economic value.

soil-agri-169.title: Treating household sewage in the backyard soil
soil-agri-169.text: Where no public sewer reaches, a house must handle its own wastewater. An onsite sewage facility treats and disposes of effluent on the property that produces it. Most are conventional systems: a septic tank plus a subsurface infiltration system. Such systems handle about 25% of domestic wastewater in the US. Decomposition by natural organisms remains the main disposal mechanism. Rules therefore set minimum retention times and distances to surface water and wells. Site evaluation characterizes soils, slopes and local hydrology and geology to set the design and placement of each component. Poor siting, design or maintenance makes systems fail. Septic systems are the third most common source of pollution in US groundwater.

soil-env-237.title: Pesticides: millions of tonnes that mostly miss their mark
soil-env-237.text: In 2023 the world's farms applied 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients, double the 1990 figure. That works out to 2.40 kg on every hectare of cropland. A pesticide is any chemical or biological agent used to deter, incapacitate or kill pests. The family includes herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides. Herbicides, the weed killers, are the most common, at about 50% of all use worldwide. Most of the spray never reaches a pest. Over 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides end up elsewhere, in air, water and soil. Persistence once made this worse. The Stockholm Convention banned long-lived pesticides such as {{ref:soil-env-005}}, which has a soil half-life of 2–15 years and still turns up in people. Modern pesticides must be degradable. Halogens in a molecule slow aerobic breakdown, and binding to soil slows a pesticide's movement but also hides it from the microbes that would break it down. Pests fight back too. They evolve resistance, which prompts new products or higher doses, and more pollution.

soil-env-249.title: Environmental remediation: remove it, treat it or wall it in
soil-env-249.text: Before a polluted site can be built on again, it often has to be cleaned. Environmental remediation is that cleanup: removing, treating or containing hazardous substances in soil, groundwater, sediment and other media. It is the practical answer to {{ref:soil-env-001}}. Developers may even get incentives to clean up voluntarily. Regulations govern the work. Where no standards exist, a risk assessment of harm to people and ecosystems decides instead, and Europe often uses the Dutch standards. The simplest method is excavation, which can mean hauling soil to a regulated landfill or aerating it to release volatile organic compounds, or VOCs. Sometimes the contamination stays put. Barrier walls, built by deep soil mixing, jet grouting, freezing or slurry walls, contain contaminants instead of removing them.

soil-env-242.title: Groundwater pollution: how a spill becomes a plume
soil-env-242.text: A leak at a petrol station can surface years later in a spring. Groundwater pollution is the contamination of {{ref:soil-phys-203}} by pollutants released to the ground, or by unwanted natural constituents, that reach an {{ref:soil-phys-201}}. The sources are many: on-site sanitation, landfill leachate, leaking sewers, petrol stations, fracking and over-applied fertilizer. Nature adds arsenic and fluoride. A pollutant often spreads through the aquifer as a plume and can reach wells, seeps and springs. Diffusion, adsorption, precipitation and decay govern its travel, so analysis weighs soil, geology and hydrogeology. The subsurface can be a reliable natural barrier, but only under favorable conditions. Karst limestone and faults give contaminants quick routes. Some pollutants change on the way: chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene partly decompose into dichloroethylene and vinyl chloride. Nitrate is the most common chemical contaminant of the world's groundwater, and it does not degrade where oxygen is plentiful. Prevention means monitoring, land zoning and careful siting of sanitation. Once a well is polluted, the choices are point-of-use treatment, remediation or abandonment.

soil-env-235.title: Agricultural pollution: what farms leave behind
soil-env-235.text: A 2021 FAO study estimated that farming throws away 10 million tons of plastic a year. Sheeting, mulch and storage bags carry much of it into soil. Agricultural pollution is the full set of farming byproducts, living and nonliving, that contaminate or degrade ecosystems or harm people. It ranges from discharges at a single point to diffuse pollution spread across whole landscapes, and into the air. The pollutants include sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts. They reach lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater. Poor practice drives much of it: badly run animal feeding operations, overgrazing, plowing, and too much fertilizer or pesticide applied at the wrong time. Persistent herbicides such as 2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years, and pesticides build up in animals that eat contaminated pests and soil organisms. Even manure has a hidden load.
