Manures and biosolids can carry pharmaceuticals and personal care products along with their fertilizer value.

soil-env-257.title: Metal toxicity: when a needed element turns poisonous
soil-env-257.text: In 1956 a release of methylmercury at Minamata alerted the world to bioaccumulation, the buildup of a toxin inside living things. Metal toxicity is harm to plants, animals or people from excessive concentrations of metals. Some metals are double-edged. Copper, iron, manganese and zinc are essential at low levels but toxic at high exposure. Arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and thallium have no biological role in animals at all. Only soluble metal compounds are toxic. Turning them into insoluble forms, or binding them with chelators, molecules that grip metal ions, detoxifies them. Chromium, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead bind strongly to sulfur. They latch onto enzymes through sulfur-bearing thiol groups and block their work. The usual label is shaky: IUPAC calls 'heavy metals' meaningless and misleading, since not all heavy metals are toxic and some toxic metals are not heavy. The sources differ too. Arsenic poisoning comes mainly from naturally arsenic-rich groundwater, lead poisoning from leaded gasoline and plumbing.

soil-env-231.title: Biodegradation: almost everything rots, except elements
soil-env-231.text: Given time, almost every compound breaks down. Elements do not, so heavy metal pollutants never biodegrade. Biodegradation is the breakdown of organic matter by bacteria, fungi and other microbes, the engine of {{ref:soil-bio-115}}. It runs in three stages. Biodeterioration weakens the material, biofragmentation splits its polymer bonds, and assimilation draws the products into microbial cells. Breakdown with oxygen is faster. Without oxygen it also yields methane and shrinks the mass more. Light, water, oxygen, temperature and the compound's availability set the pace, which soil respirometry tests measure through the CO2 microbes release.

soil-env-246.title: Groundwater remediation: cleaning water you cannot see
soil-env-246.text: Between 25 and 40 percent of the world's drinking water comes from boreholes and dug wells. Groundwater remediation is the treatment of that polluted water, either by removing the pollutants or by turning them into harmless products. It applies {{ref:soil-env-249}} to the hidden water described in {{ref:soil-env-242}}. Much of the damage is old. Wastes long dumped on land percolated down, and fertilizer, pesticides, spills, urban runoff and landfills still add more. The toolkit has three drawers. Biological methods include adding microbes ({{ref:soil-env-032}}), bioventing, biosparging, phytoremediation and {{ref:soil-env-247}}. Chemical methods include precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation and surfactants. Physical methods include {{ref:soil-env-250}}, {{ref:soil-env-240}} and dual-phase extraction. Most treatments combine several technologies.

soil-env-259.title: Ecotoxicology: following a poison through an ecosystem
soil-env-259.text: The animals at the top of a food web often suffer most from a pollutant they never touched. Toxicants move up through what each creature eats and accumulate along the way. Ecotoxicology studies how toxic chemicals affect organisms, populations and ecosystems, joining toxicology with ecology. It spans every level from molecules to whole ecosystems. Environmental toxicology, by contrast, centres on organisms, especially human health. Death is not the only harm. Sublethal doses can impair movement or feeding, which shifts competition and the balance between predators and prey. Diversity helps: species-rich communities recover from contamination more readily than poorer ones. The field's findings help predict and prevent damage from {{ref:soil-env-001}}, and show how to restore ecosystem services where harm is done.

soil-env-241.title: Arsenic in well water: a poisoning hidden underground
soil-env-241.text: From the 1970s, millions of tube wells were sunk in Bangladesh. They caused one of the largest mass poisonings. Arsenic contamination of groundwater is pollution, often natural, by high concentrations of arsenic in deeper aquifer water. A 2007 study found over 137 million people in more than 70 countries were probably affected. In Bangladesh the natural contamination was discovered in 1993. Chemistry explains the source. Organic matter in aquifer sediments creates anaerobic conditions, with a low {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Microbes then dissolve iron oxides and release the arsenic bound to them, so arsenic-rich water is often iron-rich. The arsenic occurs as arsenite and arsenate, both soluble; arsenite is somewhat more acutely toxic. Depth matters. In the Ganges Delta the affected wells are mostly 20 to 100 meters deep, and deeper water meets older sediments already stripped of arsenic. The WHO recommends a limit of 10 μg/L, often unattainable because arsenic is hard to remove. Irrigating with this water may add significantly to the arsenic in people's food.

soil-env-220.title: DNAPLs: heavy liquids that sink out of reach
soil-env-220.text: Some pollutants sink straight through groundwater. A dense non-aqueous phase liquid, or DNAPL, is denser than water and does not dissolve in it. Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene, PCBs, some PFAS and some pesticides are examples. Spilled in quantity, DNAPLs drop below the water table and stop only at clay or tight bedrock. That makes them hard to find and clean up. They flow down the slope of that layer, even against the groundwater's flow. A pool keeps dissolving slowly, feeding plumes for years. Where removal is impractical, containment may be the only option.

soil-env-227.title: In situ chemical reduction: iron that disarms solvents
soil-env-227.text: Plain iron metal can clean up some of the most stubborn solvents. In situ chemical reduction lowers contaminant levels by injecting chemical reductants, or placing them in a plume's path, at the site itself. It mirrors {{ref:soil-chem-131}} and treats compounds that resist natural breakdown. Zero-valent iron is the main reductant, used against trichloroethylene and {{ref:soil-env-255}}. On iron surfaces, electrons from the metal, iron released by corrosion or hydrogen strip chlorine from halocarbons. It is often built as a permeable reactive barrier, a trench of iron, though nanoscale iron can be injected directly.

soil-env-222.title: Phytotoxicity: when chemicals stunt or kill plants
soil-env-222.text: Even fertilizer can poison a crop. Phytotoxicity is any harmful effect of a chemical on plant growth, physiology or metabolism. Effects range from disrupted photosynthesis, water and nutrient uptake, cell division or germination to stunted growth and death. Over-applied fertilizer salts, urea and the ammonia it releases, and poorly humified compost can all do it. Herbicides harm non-target plants through spray drift or through contaminated straw or manure spread on soil. Metals follow two rules. Co, Cu, Fe, Ni and Zn are needed in trace amounts but turn toxic past a threshold; As, Cd and Pb are toxic at any concentration.

soil-env-240.title: Air sparging: bubbling solvents out of groundwater
soil-env-240.text: Air sparging cleans groundwater by blowing bubbles through it. Clean air or gas is pumped through wells below the water table into contaminated saturated soil. The small bubbles turn dissolved volatile organic compounds into vapor and carry them up into the unsaturated soil. There, vacuum points pull the vapors into a {{ref:soil-env-045}} system, and granulated activated carbon treats the off-gas. It suits light gasoline constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene. Heavier fuels such as kerosene and diesel do not respond.

soil-env-255.title: Hexavalent chromium: an industrial carcinogen
soil-env-255.text: Hexavalent chromium is rare in nature but made on a large scale, because virtually all chromium ore is processed through sodium dichromate. The name covers any chromium compound in the +6 {{ref:soil-chem-178}}. Inhaled, it can cause lung cancer, and in drinking water it has been found to cause cancers of the mouth and small intestine. At neutral pH, chromate slips into cells through sulfate channels. Inside, it is reduced to chromium(III), which binds DNA and damages genes. Cleanup uses the same step: water is treated by reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III), which activated sludge can also do.

soil-env-238.title: How pesticides break down, and why traces linger
soil-env-238.text: Every year an estimated 1 to 2.5 million tons of active ingredients are used, a large diffuse chemical input. Pesticide degradation is the transformation of a {{ref:soil-env-237}} into a benign substance compatible with the place where it was applied. On paper it is quick: documented soil half-lives are typically days to weeks. Yet residues turn up everywhere, at ng/liter to low μg/liter levels. Microbes do most of the work, through {{ref:soil-env-231}}. Chemical reactions and sunlight add smaller shares. Sunlight's reach is tiny, though, since photochemistry penetrates only submillimeter layers of soil. Underground, redox gradients in soils, sediments and aquifers often decide which reactions are possible. Some microbes are specialists. Bacteria able to cleave glyphosate's stable carbon–phosphorus bond are widespread, and bacterial enzymes in soil strip chlorine from atrazine to make hydroxyatrazine. In groundwater, by contrast, pesticides persist for decades. One explanation is that microbial breakdown stalls at very low concentrations in nutrient-poor settings. Isotopes offer proof that breakdown is happening. Microbes prefer the lighter carbon-12, so a rising 13C/12C ratio in the remaining parent compound is direct evidence of degradation.

soil-env-262.title: In situ bioremediation: cleaning soil where it lies
soil-env-262.text: Digging up polluted soil spreads risk and costs money. In situ bioremediation avoids both by treating the material where it lies. It is {{ref:soil-env-023}} carried out at the site, with microbes that are introduced or fed with nutrients. It treats soils and groundwater polluted by hydrocarbons, chlorinated compounds, nitrates and toxic metals. Left alone, it is one mechanism of natural attenuation. Accelerated forms add nutrients or an electron donor to grow a target microbe, or add microbes outright, which is bioaugmentation. Oxygen supply is often what limits its speed and success. Compared with treatment off site, it costs less and carries less risk of cross-contamination.

soil-env-253.title: Entomoremediation: insects that eat their way through pollution
soil-env-253.text: Insects can clean soil. Entomoremediation is a form of {{ref:soil-env-023}} that uses fly larvae, beetles, ants and {{ref:soil-bio-212}} to decontaminate it. It relies on hardy saprophytic larvae, which feed on dead matter and store toxic heavy metals in their bodies. Black soldier fly larvae have cut the dry weight of a polluted substrate by 49%. They concentrate cadmium with a bioaccumulation factor of 5.6.

soil-env-252.title: Nanoremediation: tiny particles with huge surfaces
soil-env-252.text: Nanoremediation fights pollution with particles too small to see. It uses nano-sized reactive agents to degrade or lock up contaminants in soil or groundwater. The particles are injected in situ or used in pump-and-treat systems. They break down organic pollutants through redox reactions, or adsorb metals such as lead and arsenic. Most field work has used nano zero-valent iron, the same reductant as {{ref:soil-env-227}}. Their large surface per unit mass makes them react fast. It also makes them clump or react with soil particles, limiting how far they spread.

soil-env-250.title: Pump and treat: fast at first, then stubborn
soil-env-250.text: Pump and treat is one of the most widely used ways to clean groundwater. Contaminated water is pumped to the surface and purified, usually through vessels of an adsorbent such as activated carbon. It can quickly cut high concentrations. The last traces are harder. Contaminants keep trading between soil and water by {{ref:soil-chem-145}} and release, so the low levels standards demand are hard to reach. Being slow and expensive, it works best to control the groundwater's flow and stop a release from spreading.

soil-env-251.title: Locking contaminants in place with binders
soil-env-251.text: Sometimes the cleanest answer is to stop contaminants from moving. Solidification and stabilization mix a binder into contaminated soil to stop or reduce the mobility of contaminants. Stabilization adds reagents that make constituents chemically more stable. Solidification locks contaminants in a solid product that air and rain cannot reach. Binding agents such as cement or asphalt prevent or slow release from the soil. As a form of {{ref:soil-env-012}} for {{ref:soil-env-001}}, its uptake is held back by cheap landfill disposal, doubts about durability and contaminant release, and liability for contaminants left on site. CO2 emissions from the cement used are a growing obstacle.

soil-env-254.title: Surfactant flushing: washing heavy solvents from aquifers
soil-env-254.text: Surfactant enhanced aquifer remediation washes an aquifer much as soap washes a greasy pan. A surfactant solution is pumped from injection wells through the contaminated zone to extraction wells. Surfactants make contaminants stuck to saturated soil, or pooled as a {{ref:soil-env-220}}, more mobile and soluble. Extracted water is treated above ground, and the surfactants, non-toxic and biodegradable, are reused. It is used most often on DNAPLs such as trichloroethylene, often as a first step before in situ oxidation or bioremediation.

soil-env-245.title: Mapping which aquifers pollution can reach
soil-env-245.text: Not every aquifer is equally exposed. Shallow unconfined aquifers are most at risk because fewer layers filter contaminants, while the unsaturated zone above can slow or remove pathogens. Aquifer vulnerability mapping overlays maps of such physical factors to show where pollution would reach groundwater most easily. The GOD method uses groundwater confinement, overlying strata and depth to groundwater. EPA's {{ref:soil-env-049}} uses seven factors, including soil media and the impact of the unsaturated zone. Hydrogeologists still disagree on one basic point: whether to rate vulnerability once for all contaminants or separately for each pollutant.

soil-env-243.title: Geogenic contamination: when the rocks poison the water
soil-env-243.text: Not all polluted groundwater has a human culprit. Geogenic contamination arises naturally, from geological processes such as {{ref:soil-found-052}}. Arsenic and fluoride are the most widespread offenders; salinity, iron, manganese, uranium, radon and chromium matter more locally. WHO tests found 20% of 25,000 Bangladesh boreholes above 50 μg/L arsenic. High fluoride usually reflects fluoride minerals such as fluorite and a lack of calcium in the aquifer. Above 1.5 mg/L it can cause dental fluorosis, a mottling of the teeth.

soil-env-244.title: How soil filters germs from latrine seepage
soil-env-244.text: Soil is a slow but real germ filter. Liquid leaching from pit latrines and septic tanks loses pathogens as it trickles through the unsaturated soil, as they die off or stick to grains. Travel time to the well matters most. Most, but not all, pathogens die within 50 days underground. Soil type, aquifer type and distance change the result, and long heavy rain can flush the zone and open fast pathways. The topsoil, the most biologically active layer, removes the most. A general guideline sets a pit's base at least 2 m above groundwater and 30 m from a water source.

soil-env-233.title: Neutralizing acid mine drainage
soil-env-233.text: Treating {{ref:soil-bio-059}} means neutralizing its acid and stripping out dissolved metals. Crushed limestone is the cheapest neutralizer, but its grains get armored with gypsum and an iron–aluminium film that stops them dissolving. Lime slurry instead raises the water to about pH 9, where most toxic metals settle out as sludge. Constructed wetlands are cheap. Their sediment bacteria turn sulfate into sulfide, which binds and drops heavy metals, though only limited loads. Sulfate-reducing bacteria in reactors also yield bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid.

soil-env-234.title: Yellow boy, the orange stain of mine water
soil-env-234.text: Streams below old mines often run a lurid yellow-orange. The color is yellow boy, the iron(III) hydroxide that settles out when the pH of {{ref:soil-bio-059}} rises above 3. Other iron compounds, including oxyhydroxides and sulfates such as jarosite, can form too. All of them discolor water and smother life on the streambed. Their formation releases more hydrogen ions, which lowers the pH further. Very rich deposits can even be recovered as pigment.

soil-env-230.title: Thermal desorption: baking pollutants out of soil
soil-env-230.text: Cooking pollutants out of soil leaves surprisingly little behind. Removing 500 mg/kg of organics from 20,000 tons of soil yields under 3,000 US gallons of liquid, less than one tank truck. Thermal desorption heats contaminated soil until its contaminants evaporate, then collects or destroys them. A system has a desorber and an offgas treatment system, and it is not incineration. Rotary cylinders and heated screws are common desorbers. Used at 69 US Superfund sites through FY2000, it counts as a permanent remedy at competitive cost, unlike stabilization, which leaves contaminants on site.

soil-env-221.title: LNAPLs: pollutants that float on the water table
soil-env-221.text: Some pollutants float. A light non-aqueous phase liquid, or LNAPL, is a hydrocarbon that does not dissolve in water and is lighter than it. Benzene, toluene and xylene are examples. Once an LNAPL soaks into the ground, it stops at the {{ref:soil-water-247}} and spreads there as a separate layer. That buoyancy is good news. Sitting on top, LNAPLs are easier and cheaper to find and remove than {{ref:soil-env-220}}, which sink.

soil-env-219.title: Biosorption: dead cells that grab metals
soil-env-219.text: Dead bacteria can outperform living ones at catching metal. In one test, dead Bacillus sphaericus cells took up 13–20% more chromium than live cells. Biosorption is a passive process in which certain biomass binds contaminants such as heavy metals to its cell surface. Unlike bioaccumulation, it needs no living, respiring organism and no energy. The binding is reversible, and pH, biomass concentration and competing metal ions shape it. Cheap wastes such as eggshells, peat, fungi, seaweed and crab shells work, at about a tenth the cost of ion-exchange resins.

soil-env-236.title: Pesticide leaching: the slow trip to groundwater
soil-env-236.text: A pesticide that dissolves can travel far beyond the field it was meant for. Pesticide leaching is that movement of dissolved pesticides down through the soil, a major source of groundwater pollution. Three things decide it: the soil, the pesticide, and the rainfall and irrigation. It is worst for water-soluble pesticides that cling weakly to soil, on sandy soils, and when heavy watering follows soon after spraying. Treated fields are not the only source. Mixing areas, machinery-washing sites and disposal areas leak too.

soil-env-258.title: Five ways to deal with metal-polluted soil
soil-env-258.text: Metals never break down, so cleanup must move them, trap them or change them. The remediation of metal-contaminated soil has five broad routes. Isolation quarantines the soil with caps, membranes or buried barriers. Immobilization alters the soil itself so metals cannot travel. Toxicity reduction oxidizes or reduces metal ions, chemically or biologically, into less toxic or less mobile forms. Physical separation sorts them out of the soil, and extraction pulls them out with chemicals, high-temperature volatilization or electrolysis, on or off site. The contaminant and the site decide which fits.

soil-env-256.title: Cadmium poisoning: a metal that stays for decades
soil-env-256.text: Cadmium settles into bone and stays, with a biological half-life of about 30 years. Cadmium poisoning comes from a naturally occurring toxic metal met in industry, in plant soils and in tobacco smoke. Farming can add to it: some phosphate fertilizers carry up to 100 mg/kg cadmium, which builds up in soil. Chronic exposure softens and weakens bones and permanently damages the kidneys, which can shrink by up to 30 percent. Daily intake is about 8 to 30 μg in Europe and the US. In parts of Japan, where people ate rice irrigated with contaminated water, it reached 59 to 113 μg.

soil-env-247.title: Bioslurping: sipping oil off the water table
soil-env-247.text: Bioslurping works like a straw dipped into floating fuel. It combines {{ref:soil-env-024}} with vacuum pumping of free product, the LNAPL floating on groundwater. A slurp tube reaching into the fuel layer draws up liquid and soil gas together. It lifts oil off the water table and the capillary fringe, the damp band just above it. Meanwhile air pulled into the unsaturated zone feeds microbes that break down the remaining hydrocarbons aerobically.

soil-env-248.title: Dual-phase extraction: one well for water and vapor
soil-env-248.text: The dirtiest layer at a spill is often the thin damp band just above the water table, the capillary fringe. Dual-phase vacuum extraction, also called multi-phase extraction, reaches it with a high vacuum. A single well removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor. Pumping lowers the water table and exposes the fringe. {{ref:soil-env-045}} then draws its contaminants out. Treating that layer can shorten the cleanup of a site.

soil-env-223.title: Pneumatic fracturing: cracking the ground to clean it
soil-env-223.text: Tight ground keeps its pollution. Pneumatic fracturing breaks it open by injecting gas at a pressure above that of the gases already present. The fractures spread like a spider web. Pumps can then draw contaminated water out through the cracks. The same cracks carry injected substrates that speed the cleanup of soil and groundwater.

soil-env-224.title: Total petroleum hydrocarbons: one number for crude oil
soil-env-224.text: Crude oil holds several hundred hydrocarbon compounds, far too many to measure one by one at a spill. Total petroleum hydrocarbon, or TPH, solves this by measuring them all as a single total. It adds the volatile, gasoline-range compounds, with six to ten carbon atoms (C6–C10), to the extractable ones. Diesel-range organics span C10–C28. The mix includes hexane, benzene, toluene, xylenes, naphthalene and fluorene.

soil-env-229.title: Electrical resistance heating: boiling pollutants out
soil-env-229.text: Electrical resistance heating turns the ground into a kettle. Alternating current runs between buried electrodes, and the soil's resistance heats it until water boils at depth. The steam strips out volatile contaminants, which a vapor recovery system captures and treats at the surface. It works best on volatile compounds such as perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene; diesel needs more energy. Current flows through the thin water film on grains, so it works in any soil and in sedimentary bedrock. Electrodes typically sit 15 to 20 feet apart, and runs last under a year.

soil-env-232.title: Microbial biodegradation: putting microbes to work on pollution
soil-env-232.text: For years, scientists doubted that hydrocarbons and halogenated compounds could break down without oxygen. Then bacteria that do exactly that were isolated. Microbial biodegradation harnesses microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants, from oil, PCBs and PAHs to pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals. Bioavailability, the share of a pollutant microbes can physically reach, is key. In one study, most soil clays, kaolinite excepted, slowed bacterial breakdown of 2-picoline by adsorbing it. At sea, hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria remove a considerable share of the petroleum that enters.

soil-env-260.title: Ecotoxicity tests: how hazard gets a number
soil-env-260.text: How toxic is a chemical to an earthworm? Ecotoxicity testing answers with standardized acute and chronic tests on soil and aquatic organisms, including {{ref:soil-bio-040}}. LC50 is the concentration that kills 50% of test organisms within the test, which can last up to 96 hours. EC50 is the concentration causing an adverse effect in 50% of them. NOEC is the highest dose with no statistically significant effect. Acute toxicity below 1 part per million puts a substance in Class I, 1–10 ppm in Class II and 10–100 ppm in Class III.

soil-env-239.title: Breakdown products that outlive the pesticide
soil-env-239.text: A pesticide's breakdown is not always the end of the story. Its transformation products can keep, or even exceed, the parent's harmful activity. Smaller and more polar than the parent, they reach groundwater and surface water more readily. Europe sorts these metabolites as nonrelevant, groundwater-relevant or ecotoxicologically relevant. A metabolite is groundwater-relevant when it is likely above 0.1 μg/liter and as toxic as its parent. Allowing up to 10 μg/liter of nonrelevant metabolites in groundwater is disputed. Some see no proven health risk; others see a breach of the precautionary principle.

soil-env-264.title: How soil microbes eat spilled oil
soil-env-264.text: Up to twenty percent of soil microbes can live on petroleum. Hydrocarbon biodegradation in soil is their breakdown of these compounds for energy and carbon, mostly with oxygen, ending in carbon dioxide and water. Structure decides speed. Long straight chains degrade most readily; short, branched and quaternary ones less so. Ring compounds with two or three rings break down at useful rates. Those with four or more resist, yielding only to cometabolism, breakdown alongside another food. Porous, carbon-rich biochar traps {{ref:soil-env-199}} and gives microbes good conditions to degrade them.

soil-env-263.title: The Raymond process: feeding microbes in a loop
soil-env-263.text: Richard Raymond devised a way to speed up {{ref:soil-env-262}} by feeding the microbes underground. Groundwater is pumped up downstream of the contamination, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream. The loop repeats. The oxygen serves as the {{ref:soil-chem-176}} the microbes need. It can arrive through injection wells or galleries, or as ozone, half of which turns to oxygen within twenty minutes.

soil-env-228.title: Breaking down PCBs takes two teams of microbes
soil-env-228.text: PCBs, once used as dielectric fluids and coolants, are stable, poorly soluble {{ref:soil-env-198}}. Natural degradation takes 3 to 37 years, depending on how chlorinated they are. Bioremediation of PCBs uses microbes in sequence. Anaerobic bacteria first strip off chlorine, using PCBs as electron acceptors. Aerobic microbes then break the products down. The job is hard: PCBs bind tightly to soil, especially soil rich in organic carbon and clay. They are toxic to bacteria above 1000 mg/kg, and breakdown slows sharply below 50 mg/kg.

soil-env-268.title: Geochemical background: what counts as normal
soil-env-268.text: To call soil contaminated, you first need to know what is natural there. Geochemical background is the natural level of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as {{ref:soil-found-052}}. Typical soils hold no more than about 100 mg/kg of arsenic, lead and nickel, 2 mg/kg of cadmium, 150 mg/kg of copper and 300 mg/kg of zinc. Chromium stays under 500 mg/kg and selenium under 1 mg/kg. Remediation results are compared with these local levels as well as zoning standards, and {{ref:soil-env-287}} makes setting them a priority.

soil-env-261.title: Emerging contaminants: pollutants the rules have not caught
soil-env-261.text: Monitoring keeps finding pollutants that no law yet covers. Contaminants of emerging concern may harm ecosystems or health and are usually unregulated. They include pharmaceuticals, personal care products, industrial byproducts and agricultural chemicals, which often escape detection and treatment and persist. Runoff after rain or irrigation carries pesticides and pharmaceuticals from soil into rivers, lakes and groundwater. Treatment must not just shift them into sludge, since sludge spread on land returns them. Explosives such as TNT are major contaminants of groundwater and soils.

soil-env-265.title: Living cleanup crews for radioactive soil
soil-env-265.text: Digging up radioactive soil and hauling it far away could cost the US more than a trillion dollars. Bioremediation of radioactive waste offers another route. Bacteria, plants and fungi catalyze reactions that change radionuclides' solubility, availability and mobility, speeding their stabilization. The commonest natural radionuclides in soils are radium-226, radon-222, thorium-232, uranium-238 and potassium-40. Some fungi can even use ionizing radiation as energy. Oyster mushrooms can bioremediate plutonium-239 and americium-241.

soil-env-266.title: Bioreduction: bacteria that pin uranium in place
soil-env-266.text: Bacteria can turn dissolved uranium into a solid. In bioreduction, their enzymes reduce radionuclides to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity. Anaerobes use the radioisotope as the final electron acceptor, reducing soluble uranium(VI) to insoluble uranium(IV). Sulfate-reducing and metal-reducing bacteria also act indirectly, through the metabolites they excrete. Microbes can work the other way too. Siderophores and other bacterial chelators raise radionuclide solubility and availability.

soil-env-267.title: Plants that pull radioactivity from soil
soil-env-267.text: In the Chernobyl zone, mustard greens removed up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season. Phytoextraction of radionuclides uses plants that carry them from the roots into the shoots. It works for caesium-137, strontium-90, technetium-99, plutonium-240 and americium-241, among others. It leaves soil structure and fertility largely intact and suits large areas of low-level contamination. The catch is that it needs plants that grow big, fast.

soil-env-226.title: Sustainable remediation: a cleanup should not do more harm
soil-env-226.text: A cleanup can sometimes hurt more than the pollution. Pump-and-treat and dig-and-haul have at times left lasting side effects worse than the contamination itself. Sustainable remediation weighs a remedy's environmental, economic and social effects and shrinks the footprint of the cleanup. Footprint analysis covers energy, air and atmosphere, materials and waste, land and ecosystem, and water. The stakes are large: the US alone has more than 450,000 brownfield sites needing major reinvestment. Some newer in situ methods have cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by 50 to 80 percent.

soil-env-225.title: Vapor intrusion: pollution that seeps indoors
soil-env-225.text: Contaminated groundwater can poison the air inside a house. Vapor intrusion is the migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from soil or groundwater into buildings above or nearby. The vapors diffuse up through the porous {{ref:soil-water-230}} and enter through foundation cracks, drawn in by the building's stack effect. Pipes, storm drains and elevator shafts offer easy paths. Indoors they can cause headaches, raise the risk of some cancers and even threaten explosion. Fixes include a fan that depressurizes the space under the slab, or over-pressurizing the building.

soil-env-298.title: Itai-itai disease, the poisoned rice of the Jinzū River
soil-env-298.text: For 55 years, people along Japan's Jinzū River fell ill without knowing why. Itai-itai disease was a mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, beginning around 1912 and named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused. It is the best-known case of the illness in {{ref:soil-env-256}}. Mines upstream released cadmium into the river from 1910 to 1945. The metal travels with zinc, because the zinc ore sphalerite is almost always paired with greenockite. Residents irrigated their rice with the river water. The highly soluble cadmium soaked into paddies and grain, and body burdens rose. It built up in the kidneys, and damaged kidneys upset the body's calcium balance, bringing bone pain and deformities. Cadmium was suspected only in 1955. A 1961 investigation tied it to the Kamioka mine, 55 years after the first reports. It became one of the Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan, and the mining company was successfully sued.

soil-env-293.title: Valley fever, the illness that rides on dust
soil-env-293.text: In 1977 a windstorm near Arvin, California, caused several hundred cases of a lung disease hundreds of miles from where it normally occurs. The disease was coccidioidomycosis, or valley fever: a fungal disease of mammals caught by inhaling spores of the soil fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii. Like the fungi in {{ref:soil-bio-003}}, it grows as a web of threads, in soils of the southwestern US, northern Mexico and parts of Central and South America. Rain starts its growth. In long dry spells its threads, the hyphae, break into light spores called arthroconidia. Construction, farming, dust storms or earthquakes then lift them into the air. Cases rise after wet winters that follow drought, and one model projects the endemic region could more than double in area by 2100 under high warming. Planting grass and wetting soil keep the dust down. NIOSH counts it an occupational hazard in farming, construction, archaeology and mining. Dogs, which dig and sniff at the ground, are exposed earlier than people and serve as sentinels.

soil-env-287.title: Medical geology: when the ground decides who falls ill
soil-env-287.text: Hippocrates and Aristotle were the first to link disease to the elements of the earth. Medical geology is the modern form of that idea: the interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals. The International Union of Geological Sciences established the field in 1990. It covers exposure to, or deficiency of, trace elements and {{ref:soil-found-029}}, along with mineral dusts, volcanic emissions, radionuclides, microbes and pathogens. Two priorities lead the work. One is the bioavailability of trace elements, the share the body can actually absorb. The other is the baseline background level of harmful natural materials in soil, water, air and food. People who live off the land meet both extremes. In Maputaland, impoverished soils cause diseases of mineral imbalance. In India and Bangladesh, an excess of elements causes toxicity. A shortage of iodine is among the biggest geochemical diseases, partly because humus and clay in soil trap iodine and keep it from people. Other problems are regional. Fluoride troubles Africa and India, and arsenic troubles Argentina, Chile and Taiwan. Selenium is a problem in parts of the US, Venezuela and China, and nitrate in farm areas. Paracelsus summed up the field in one dictum: the dose makes the poison. Its goal is the right balance of element intake.

soil-env-295.title: Iodine, the element missing from inland mountains
soil-env-295.text: About two billion people get too little iodine simply because of where their food grows. Iodine deficiency is a lack of this essential dietary trace element, which the thyroid hormones need. It is common in remote inland and especially mountainous areas. There, food grows in iodine-poor soil and nobody eats marine foods. The burden falls particularly on the Western Pacific, South-East Asia and Africa. The lack causes goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland, which affected 187 million people in 2010. In the womb it causes a syndrome of developmental delay, making it a preventable cause of intellectual disability. The main prevention is cheap. Adding small amounts of iodine to table salt costs only a few cents a ton. A shortage of selenium, described in {{ref:soil-env-296}}, is among its risk factors.

soil-env-296.title: Selenium: when the soil runs short, so does the body
soil-env-296.text: Finland adds selenium salts to its chemical fertilizers to raise the selenium in its soil. The reason is selenium deficiency: a shortage of this critical nutrient below the levels an organism requires. People who depend on food grown in selenium-deficient soil are at risk. Croplands and diets run low in regions of China, Europe, Russia and New Zealand. Climate change is predicted to strip selenium from croplands and make the shortage commoner. Combined with Coxsackievirus, it causes {{ref:soil-env-297}}. Together with a lack of iodine, it contributes to Kashin-Beck disease of cartilage. Livestock suffer too. In them it causes white muscle disease. Ruminants, the cud-chewing grazers, are especially prone because they absorb less selenium, particularly from forage. Recommended adult intake is 55 μg/day in the US and 70 μg/day from the European Food Safety Authority.

soil-env-294.title: Melioidosis, the soil bacterium called a time bomb
soil-env-294.text: Soldiers came home from Vietnam apparently healthy and fell ill years later. Those latent infections earned melioidosis the name 'Vietnam Time Bomb'. It is an infectious disease caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil-dwelling bacterium of the kind met in {{ref:soil-bio-002}}. People catch it by contact with contaminated soil or water. The bacterium is most abundant 10 to 90 cm deep in soil and also lives in ponds, streams and rice paddies. It is hardy. It survives more than 16 years in nutrient-poor settings such as desert soil, and tolerates pH 4.5 for 70 days. It enters the body through wounds, inhalation or ingestion. The disease is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and cases rise with heavy rain and storms. A 2016 model estimated about 165,000 infections and 89,000 deaths a year. Diabetes is a major risk factor. There is no approved vaccine, so prevention means protective gear and avoiding direct contact with soil and water.

soil-env-288.title: Geophagia, the ancient habit of eating earth
soil-env-288.text: Over 100 species of primates eat dirt on purpose. Geophagia is the deliberate eating of earth or earth-like substances such as clay, chalk or termite-mound soil, by animals and people. In primates it protects against parasites, supplies minerals and helps neutralize toxic compounds in leaves. The oldest evidence comes from Kalambo Falls, where calcium-rich white clay lay alongside the bones of Homo habilis. In people it is most often reported in children and pregnant women, and it is classed as a form of pica, the eating of things that are not food. {{ref:soil-chem-079}} may protect the stomach against toxins, parasites and pathogens, and many soils supply calcium, iron and zinc. In Cameroon markets kaolin is sold for eating, and pregnant women take it against nausea despite possibly dangerous levels of arsenic and lead. Soil has other risks. Faecally contaminated earth can pass on the eggs of parasitic worms such as Ascaris, which survive in soil for years, as well as tetanus and lead poisoning. The habit also has a commercial side. Bentonite and kaolin are sold as digestive aids, and attapulgite clay is an active ingredient in anti-diarrhoeal medicines.

soil-env-292.title: Roundworms in the soil, the commonest human parasites
soil-env-292.text: About two billion people carry worms picked up from soil, and four billion are at risk. Soil-transmitted helminthiasis is infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces. It takes three forms: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm. Together they make the most common human parasitic disease. The worms are nematodes, the animals of {{ref:soil-bio-193}}. Eggs passed in faeces mature into infective larvae in the soil, and people swallow them on unwashed produce or hands. Hookworm larvae work differently: they hatch and penetrate the skin. Open defecation, lack of hand washing and walking barefoot on contaminated soil are the main causes. So the disease is commonest in warm, moist, poorly sanitized regions. Hookworm affects an estimated 740 million people and is the leading cause of anaemia and protein deficiency in developing nations. Deworming reduces worm burdens, but reinfection follows continued exposure. Improved water, sanitation and hygiene lower the odds of infection.

soil-env-304.title: Prions, the infectious proteins that cling to clay
soil-env-304.text: A prion carries no DNA or RNA, yet it spreads disease. It is a misfolded protein that makes normal copies of the same protein misfold, causing fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative diseases. Scrapie, BSE, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and {{ref:soil-env-305}} are among them. Shed from carcasses and body fluids, prions may linger in soil by binding to clay and other minerals. Unbound prions degrade over time, but soil-bound ones stay stable or increase, so prions likely accumulate in the environment. Repeated wetting and drying may reduce their infectivity, depending on soil type. Hamsters fed grass grown where an infected deer was buried became ill, so plants can carry prions.

soil-env-297.title: Keshan disease, a heart illness written in the soil
soil-env-297.text: A belt of heart disease once ran from northeast to southwest China. Keshan disease is a congestive cardiomyopathy, a failing of the heart muscle, caused by dietary selenium deficiency together with a mutated strain of Coxsackievirus. It is named after Keshan County. Every case traced back to selenium-deficient soil, and the disease peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands. The shortage appears to let a more virulent viral strain dominate. Decades of selenium supplementation reduced it. Some patients use Astragalus, a herb that accumulates selenium from soil. Garlic, onions and broccoli are good selenium sources only if their soil contains it.

soil-env-303.title: One Health: people, animals and soil as one system
soil-env-303.text: Diseases that jump from animals to people, called zoonotic diseases, gave rise to One Health. It is an integrated approach that seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together. It grew from the awareness that human health, animal health and ecological change are interdependent. Antimicrobial resistance is treated as a One Health issue. Misuse of antimicrobials in medicine, veterinary care and farming selects resistant organisms, and wastewater, soil and runoff spread them. The FAO, WHO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and UNEP back the approach.

soil-env-291.title: Podoconiosis, red clay that swells the legs
soil-env-291.text: An estimated 4 million people have legs swollen by the soil they walk on, 1.5 million of them in Ethiopia. Podoconiosis, also called nonfilarial elephantiasis, is a disease of the lymphatic vessels of the lower legs, caused by long-term barefoot contact with irritant soils. After lymphatic filariasis, it is the second most common cause of tropical lymphoedema, a disfiguring swelling of the legs. It strikes genetically susceptible people on red clay soils formed over alkaline volcanic bedrock, in highlands with about 1500 mm of rain at 1500 m altitude. Soil particles penetrate the feet. Macrophages, immune cells that engulf foreign matter, take them up, and the particles collect in lymph nodes. Ernest Price found silicon, aluminium and other soil metals inside macrophages in patients' lymph nodes. The result is chronic inflammation, scarring and blockage. Affected areas are rich in kaolinite and gibbsite. Smectite, mica, quartz and iron oxides are also suspects, but no single culprit is proven. Wearing shoes and using floor coverings prevent it.

soil-env-305.title: Chronic wasting disease and the ground that spreads it
soil-env-305.text: For grazing deer, the ground itself may be the main danger. Chronic wasting disease is a fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy, a brain-wasting illness caused by prions, in deer, elk, moose and their relatives. Animals catch it by eating grass from soil where infected animals shed prions. The prions stay infectious there for years and bind so tightly to soil particles that the ground may be a major route of transmission. Prions mixed with clay infected deer through the nose. After a Quebec outbreak, inspectors ordered 25 cm of soil decontaminated in parts of the farm.

soil-env-302.title: Mycobacterium vaccae, the soil microbe that calmed mice
soil-env-302.text: In Uganda, locals said a muddy substance could cure ailments. There, scientists first isolated Mycobacterium vaccae, a nonpathogenic bacterium, one that causes no disease, which lives naturally in soil. It belongs to the Mycobacteriaceae, and its name comes from cow dung, where the first strain was cultured. Heat-killed cells injected into mice raised serotonin and lowered anxiety. Mice fed live cells ran a maze twice as fast, with less anxiety. Vaccines made from killed cells are being studied for asthma, depression, psoriasis, eczema and tuberculosis.

soil-env-299.title: Replacing the poisoned paddies of the Jinzū River
soil-env-299.text: Cleaning up after {{ref:soil-env-298}} took decades. The cleanup of cadmium-polluted farmland along the Jinzū River followed the lawsuit over that disease. Japan's 1970 agricultural soil contamination law stopped planting for restoration wherever soil held 1 ppm cadmium or more. By 1977, 1,500 hectares had been designated. Topsoil replacement, one of the options in {{ref:soil-env-012}}, began in 1979. By 2012 it had covered 863 hectares at a cost of ¥40.7 billion. By 1996 cadmium in the farmland had returned to a background level of 0.1 ppb.

soil-env-289.title: Why parrots flock to eat one layer of clay
soil-env-289.text: On the Manu River, parrots eat from one specific soil layer and ignore the layers a metre above or below it. Avian geophagy is the eating of clay-rich soil by birds, notably South American parrots at clay licks. The preferred soils are rich in smectite, kaolin and mica and have far higher cation-exchange capacity. That lets them bind toxins from seeds, which become positively charged in the stomach. Yet the eaten soils are also consistently higher in sodium, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean. Sodium is likely the main driver.

soil-env-290.title: Cattle and sheep that eat soil with every bite
soil-env-290.text: Grazing animals swallow soil without meaning to. Soil ingestion by livestock happens when the hooves of cattle and sheep press soil onto pasture plants, which the animals then eat. It is measured from the ash content of their faeces. Intake is greatest on weak, poorly drained soils in wet autumn and winter conditions. The soil is not all harm. It supplies iron, manganese, zinc, cobalt, copper, selenium and iodine that herbage lacks. It can, however, wear down sheep's incisors.

soil-env-300.title: Biofortification: breeding nutrients into the crop itself
soil-env-300.text: In Mozambique, sweet potatoes rich in beta-carotene cut vitamin A deficiency in children by 24%. That is biofortification: breeding crops, conventionally or by genetic engineering, so that they contain more nutrients as they grow. It targets shortages of micronutrients such as vitamin A, zinc and iron in low- and middle-income countries. It reaches the rural poor, who rarely get fortified foods. In India, iron- and zinc-rich pearl millet improved iron status. Researchers are developing bread grain biofortified with selenium to raise low selenium levels in British grains. Critics warn it may simplify diets further and urge that it be part of wider food diversification.

soil-env-301.title: The hygiene hypothesis and the microbes that may tune immunity
soil-env-301.text: Most mammalian evolution took place in mud and rotting vegetation. The hygiene hypothesis is the idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system. In 2003 Graham Rook recast it as the 'old friends' hypothesis, focused on microbes that co-evolved with humans rather than recent crowd infections. It is not about personal cleanliness: poor hygiene raises infection risk without lowering allergy risk. The question is still open. Much evidence supports the hypothesis, yet many scientists reject it, and it struggles to explain allergies in less affluent regions.

soil-fert-181.title: Nutrients, the raw materials of every living thing
soil-fert-181.text: The minerals on a dinner plate began in the soil. Plants take their minerals from the soil, so the minerals in the human diet come from plants eaten directly or from animals that ate them. A nutrient is any substance an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce. Animals, plants, fungi and protists all need nutrients, though different kinds of organism have different essential ones. Some nutrients are organic, such as proteins, fats, sugars and vitamins. Others are inorganic, such as iron, selenium and zinc. An essential nutrient is one an organism needs for normal function but cannot make itself, at all or in sufficient amounts. Plants absorb a wide range of minerals through their roots and take in carbon dioxide and oxygen through their leaves. Too little of a nutrient is a deficiency. Harm from too much is nutrient toxicity.

soil-fert-149.title: Soil fertility: what lets a field feed a crop year after year
soil-fert-149.text: A fertile soil does far more than hold a plant upright. Soil fertility is the ability of a soil to sustain agricultural plant growth, giving plants a habitat and steady, high-quality yields. Such a soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and proportions. It is also free of toxic substances, such as Fe2+, that inhibit growth. Several properties add up to fertility. A fertile soil is deep enough for roots and stored water, drains and breathes well inside, and has an organic-rich topsoil. Its nutrients are in plant-available forms, and its microorganisms support plant growth. A soil pH between 5.5 and 7.0 suits most plants, though some prefer or tolerate more acid or alkaline conditions. Beneath all this runs constant cycling. Microbes decomposing plant and animal wastes release inorganic nutrients, while microbes competing with plants tie them up again. Negatively charged clay and humus hold nutrient cations, such as potassium and many trace elements, by cation exchange, which strongly influences fertility. Growing crops does not by itself exhaust a soil, as long as mineral weathering replaces the nutrients carried off in harvests. Improper irrigation and acid rain can still deplete it. On farmed land, keeping fertility usually requires conserving the soil itself, because erosion and other degradation lower soil quality. History shows the cost of neglect. Colonial land practices, slavery, and the rise of intensive farming and forestry have all damaged soil fertility and quality.

soil-fert-156.title: Plant nutrition: what a plant feeds on, and how
soil-fert-156.text: For most of history, nobody knew what plants actually fed on. Aristotle and later investigators puzzled over what plant nutrients were and how plants absorbed and transported them. Plant nutrition is the study of the chemical elements and compounds plants need for growth, reproduction and metabolism, and of how they are supplied. An element counts as essential if a plant cannot complete a normal life cycle without it. It also counts if it is part of an essential plant constituent or metabolite. {{ref:soil-hist-004}} proved in 1840 that plants need nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus. In 1939 Arnon and Stout grew plants without soil to show that molybdenum is essential to tomatoes. Plants take carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water. Most other nutrients, nitrogen included, come from the soil. There the elements sit as salts, so plants absorb them as ions, atoms or small molecules carrying an electric charge. Amount alone is not enough. Nutrients must arrive in suitable ratios, and needs vary between species and even between individuals of one clone. Most soils can fully nourish the plants adapted to them. Cropped soil is different. It needs {{ref:soil-fert-001}} to sustain yields, because a nutrient deficiency limits growth even when water and light are ample.

soil-fert-151.title: Soil depletion: spending the soil's nutrient bank
soil-fert-151.text: Topsoil takes hundreds to thousands of years to form, and it can be spent far faster. Soil depletion is the decline of a soil's fertility when what makes it fertile is removed and not replaced. The conditions that support fertility are not maintained either. It leads to poor harvests and is becoming a global problem. On farms it stems from overly intensive cultivation and careless handling of the land. Over-tillage, salinization and overuse of nutrient inputs all contribute, the last of these mining the soil's nutrient bank. Rapid changes in land use can also severely challenge soil fertility. As of 2008, depletion was among the most widespread problems in tropical zones, where soils are low in nutrients. In the Middle East, drought, erosion and lack of irrigation hamper farming, and productivity has fallen most steeply in hilly and dryland areas. Across much of Africa fertile soil is being depleted, notably in the Sahel under high population pressure. Farmers there use artificial and natural fertilizers to restore nutrients. The stakes can be enormous. Topsoil depletion, the erosion or exhaustion of organic topsoil, has been blamed for the collapse of many past civilizations.

soil-fert-169.title: Sixteen elements every plant must have
soil-fert-169.text: A plant's whole life rests on a short list of chemical elements. The essential plant nutrients are the elements a plant must have to complete its life cycle, and sixteen are usually listed. They are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium, iron, boron, manganese, copper, zinc, molybdenum and chlorine. Some sources add nickel, for seventeen. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from carbon dioxide and water. Nitrogen comes from {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Every other element comes originally from the soil's mineral fraction. Plants can take up a nutrient only in a plant-available form, mostly as ions absorbed from the soil water. That is the catch. Most nutrients are locked in primary and secondary minerals that weather too slowly for rapid growth. Even ground feldspar or apatite seldom supplies enough potassium or phosphorus. A more accessible reservoir sits on clay colloids and organic matter, which hold nutrients exchangeably and refill the soil solution as plants draw it down. Microbial decomposition of organic matter refills it too, which matters most for nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus and boron. Gram for gram, humus holds far more nutrients and water than clay minerals, and it supplies most of a soil's cation exchange capacity. Balance counts as well. Under {{ref:soil-fert-182}}, a nutrient short in the soil solution keeps others from being taken up at the best rate, so optimal growth needs a particular nutrient ratio.

soil-fert-187.title: Soil tests: asking a field what it lacks
soil-fert-187.text: Before adding fertilizer, a grower can ask the soil what it needs. A soil test is a laboratory or in-situ analysis of a soil's chemical, physical or biological characteristics. The most widely run tests estimate plant-available nutrient concentrations to guide fertilizer recommendations. It reveals deficiencies and possible toxicities, and it is meant to mimic how roots take up minerals. Sampling matters. Labs such as Iowa State and Colorado State recommend 10–20 sample points per 40 acres, and composite sampling mixes soil from several spots. Nutrients vary with depth and time, so samples are best analyzed within about 24 hours, or else frozen or air-dried. Methods differ widely. Europe alone uses more than 10 tests for plant-available phosphorus, and their results are not directly comparable. Some labs analyze all 13 mineral nutrients plus a dozen potentially toxic elements with one 'universal soil extractant', ammonium bicarbonate DTPA. Do-it-yourself kits usually test only N, P, K and pH and are less accurate.

soil-fert-152.title: How colonial New England wore out its soil
soil-fert-152.text: Colonists in New England let their herd animals roam and did not return the animals' dung to the soil. Settlers unfamiliar with Indigenous farming also burned land intensively and turned cattle loose to save labor, ruining fertility and preventing sustainable cropping. Historian William Cronon blamed the erosion that followed on forest removal, more destructive floods, compaction and close-cropping by grazing animals, and plowing. The damage did not stay in New England. About one-half of the Great Plains' original topsoil has disappeared since farming began there in the 1880s, as {{ref:soil-water-075}} showed.

soil-fert-155.title: When irrigation water helps or harms a soil
soil-fert-155.text: About 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated today, and the water's chemistry shapes every soil it soaks. Highly alkaline water builds up sodium salts that ruin drainage, so roots cannot penetrate deeply into the resulting alkali soils. Acidic water drains away useful Ca, Mg, K, P and S, and dissolves aluminum and manganese salts that impede growth. Saline water, or poor drainage of irrigated land, turns soil saline and infertile. Saline water also hinders roots' uptake of water and nutrients. Handled well or badly, irrigation can maintain, degrade or improve a soil's fertility and tilth.

soil-fert-153.title: Worn-out land on the slave plantations of the South
soil-fert-153.text: Southern plantation owners sought to maximize the labor they extracted, not the output of each acre. Historian David Silkenat explains that they treated the landscape as disposable and enslaved Africans as expendable. After forcing enslaved people to clear forests, planters abandoned the worn land and moved on to more fertile ground. Swamps were drained, forests cleared to grow single crops and to fuel steamships, and invasive species introduced. The results were eroded hillsides, rivers clogged with sterile soil, and extinct native species.

soil-fert-154.title: Albert Howard's case: health begins in the soil
soil-fert-154.text: In 1945 Albert Howard wrote that all future studies of disease must begin with the soil. He called soil fertility the basis of the public health system of the future. His idea was that the health of crops, livestock and people starts with a fertile, well-kept soil. Howard is credited as the first Westerner to publish Native techniques of sustainable agriculture. He argued that industrial agriculture upsets the balance of nature and irrevocably robs the soil of its fertility.

soil-fert-192.title: Nutrient management: right source, rate, time and place
soil-fert-192.text: Using less nitrogen fertilizer could avoid nitrous oxide emissions equal to 2.77–11.48 gigatons of carbon dioxide from 2020 to 2050. That saving is one prize of nutrient management. It links soil, crop, weather and water conditions with farming and conservation practices. The goal is to use nutrients efficiently for yield, quality and profit while losing little to the environment. It matches the rate, source, timing and placement of nutrients to each field's soil, climate and crop, an approach known as 4R nutrient stewardship. The International Plant Nutrition Institute's 4R manual sets out the right source, rate, time and place. Managers plan applications for achievable yields and budget all nutrient sources and sinks at the site. They manage soil, water and crop to curb leaching, runoff and volatilization, the escape of nutrients as gas. The pathways interact. A practice that cuts runoff of one nutrient may increase leaching of others.

soil-fert-182.title: Liebig's law: the scarcest nutrient sets the limit
soil-fert-182.text: Farmers who added more of a plentiful nutrient saw no gain in growth, while adding the scarce one worked. Explaining that puzzle gave agriculture one of its best-known rules. Liebig's law of the minimum holds that growth is set not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one, the limiting factor. It was developed in agricultural science in 1840 by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-072}}, and the chemist Liebig later popularized it. In soil terms, when one nutrient is short in the soil solution, stoichiometry keeps the plant from taking up the others at an optimal rate. Stoichiometry means the fixed proportions in which elements are combined. The law spread well beyond the farm. It has been extended to biological populations, and ecosystem models commonly use it for factors such as sunlight, nitrate or phosphate. In the sea, phytoplankton can be limited by iron in nutrient-rich coastal upwellings and by nitrogen and phosphorus in the nutrient-poor open ocean. In natural resource management it implies that growth is restricted by the scarcest input. Phosphorus has no substitute, so it will have to be recycled. The law is not the last word, though. Diagnosing limiting factors is still a common study, but the approach has been criticized. In plant nutrition, models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced it.

soil-fert-158.title: Macronutrients and micronutrients: sorting by appetite
soil-fert-158.text: The labels describe a plant's appetite, not the soil's pantry. Macronutrients are taken up in relatively large amounts, and micronutrients are needed only in small amounts. Neither term says how abundant an element is in the soil. The soil supplies the macronutrients nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur in relatively large amounts. Four elements dominate a plant's body: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and carbon together make up over 95% of its dry biomass. The micronutrients are iron, boron, chlorine, manganese, zinc, copper, molybdenum and nickel. They occur in plant tissue at 0.1 to 200 ppm, or parts per million, under 0.02% of dry weight. Soil laboratories use a three-way split instead. Major nutrients are N, P and K. Secondary ones are S, Ca and Mg. Minor ones are Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, Mo and Cl. Beyond plants, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur are the elemental macronutrients of all organisms.

soil-fert-150.title: Fertilizing soil: topping up phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium
soil-fert-150.text: Soil fertilization adds the nutrients a soil most often lacks for crops: phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, the three elements every commercial fertilizer analysis lists. Bioavailable phosphorus is the element most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils. Inorganic fertilizers need less labor and carry more concentrated nutrients than organic ones. Plants take up N, P and K in inorganic forms, so these fertilizers act at once. Relying on them too heavily upsets the soil's nutrient balance. Soil quality and organic matter fall, erosion risk rises, and soluble nitrate pollutes water. Slow-release fertilizers can cut leaching and spread the supply over a longer period.

soil-fert-179.title: Micronutrients: tiny doses that run every enzyme
soil-fert-179.text: Every process that supports plant growth runs through a protein containing a micronutrient. Plant micronutrients are essential elements needed only in very small amounts, mostly as required parts of enzyme systems. In order of importance they include chlorine, iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper and molybdenum. Manganese builds the structure of photosystem II and helps build chloroplasts. Copper aids photosynthesis and the forming of lignin, and chlorine serves osmosis and ionic balance. Nickel activates the enzyme of {{ref:soil-fert-224}}, which processes {{ref:soil-fert-021}}; without nickel, this nitrogen compound builds up to toxic levels and causes necrotic lesions. Molybdenum is part of nitrate reductase and of {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, the enzyme bacteria use to fix nitrogen. Soil minerals generally supply enough, but heavy phosphate use can cause zinc and iron deficiency by forming insoluble phosphates. Too little uptake causes deficiencies, such as a yellowing of leaves ({{ref:soil-fert-228}}), from a lack of copper, iron, manganese or zinc. Too much causes toxicity. Some micronutrients can be applied as seed coatings, and acidifying fertilizers that supply nitrogen keep their cations soluble longer in alkaline soils.

soil-fert-162.title: Where symptoms show: nutrients that move and nutrients that stay
soil-fert-162.text: Where a leaf yellows on a plant is a clue to what the plant lacks. Nutrient mobility is how readily a nutrient can be moved within a plant from older tissues to where it is most needed. Plants send nutrients preferentially to their younger leaves. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium are mobile, so their deficiencies show first on the oldest leaves. Nitrogen moves in the xylem, the water-carrying tissue, as nitrate or organic compounds. In the phloem, the sap-carrying tissue, it moves as amides, amino acids and ureides. Calcium is immobile in the phloem and arrives only with transpiration through the xylem, so its deficiency shows in new growth. Boron and sulfur cannot be remobilized from older leaves either, so their deficiencies appear first in the youngest tissues. Where symptoms appear therefore helps diagnose which nutrient a plant lacks.

soil-fert-163.title: Reading a hungry plant: signs of nutrient deficiency
soil-fert-163.text: Crops can starve without looking starved. Nutrient deficiency covers the effects of too little of an essential nutrient, from slightly slower growth to stunting, deformity, discoloration and death. Clear-cut symptoms are rare, because most deficiencies are multiple and moderate. Nitrogen is most often the nutrient in shortest supply. Its lack brings stunted, slow growth and yellowing leaves, a sign covered in {{ref:soil-fert-228}}, sometimes with purple stems and leaf undersides from the pigment anthocyanin. A shortage of phosphorus, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-232}}, is hard to diagnose, though leaves may turn intensely green, reddish or purple. Calcium shortage, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-227}}, weakens root systems and causes blossom end rot in tomatoes, peppers and watermelons, bitter pit in apples and black heart in celery. A shortage of potassium, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-233}}, starts in older tissues, with necrosis or yellowing between the veins, wilting, more disease and greater frost and heat damage. Iron, manganese and copper deficiencies show on new growth, molybdenum on older growth, zinc on old and new leaves, and boron on terminal buds. That yellowing is not always about nutrients. Solarization looks similar, but unlike deficiency it causes no early leaf drop.

soil-fert-197.title: Molybdenum deficiency and the whiptail cauliflower
soil-fert-197.text: In cauliflower and other Brassica crops, molybdenum deficiency shows up as whiptail. It arises from soils low in molybdenum, or from strong sorption that holds it unavailable. Sorption is strongest in acid soils, so acid sandy soils suffer most. Plants need molybdenum for nitrate reductase, xanthine dehydrogenase and the nitrogen-fixing enzyme. Deficient plants therefore accumulate nitrate, and legumes fix less nitrogen. Leaves turn pale and scalded. Leaf contents of 0.2–2.0 mg/kg suffice for most crops. Adding lime often helps by reducing sorption, but molybdenum fertilizer such as sodium molybdate is often far more cost-effective.

soil-fert-172.title: Nitrogen, the nutrient plants want most
soil-fert-172.text: Plants are bathed in nitrogen yet often starve for it. Air is nearly 79% N2, but the triple bond in that molecule makes it almost inert. It must be fixed as ammonium or nitrate before plants can use it. Nitrogen is the most critical nutrient plants take from soil and often limits growth, except in tropical rainforests, where phosphorus limits instead. Its compounds make up 40% to 50% of the dry matter of protoplasm. Most soil nitrogen is bound in organic matter and must be mineralized, released as ammonium or nitrate. Mycorrhizal fungi give plants access to some organic nitrogen. Net mineralization adds about 50 kg per hectare on average, the main usable source in unfertilized fields. Bacteria in legume root nodules may add 200 to 300 kg per hectare per year, possibly enough for the crop. Cultivation lowers soil nitrogen, and no-till soils keep more than tilled ones. Plants take up most nitrogen as nitrate, but ammonium dominates in acid environments such as boreal forests, where the microbial conversion of ammonium to nitrate is less likely.

soil-fert-184.title: The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio: why some residues starve plants
soil-fert-184.text: Mix redwood sawdust into a garden and the plants may go hungry. Sawdust runs about 1020:1 in one list and 250 in another, while bacteria are only 4. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is the ratio of the mass of carbon to the mass of nitrogen in organic residues. In soil it expresses the balance between energy food for microbes, represented by carbon, and protein-building material, represented by nitrogen. See {{ref:soil-fert-172}}. Plant residues typically run from 13:1 to 100:1, from alfalfa at 13 to oat straw at 80. A second list gives microorganisms 8:1, clover hay 20:1, barnyard manure 25:1, corn stalks 73:1 and barley straw 450:1. Microbes themselves are about 10:1. A ratio around 24:1 gives high microbial activity, and 30:1 is recommended for soil materials. Above 30:1, residues leave microbes short of nitrogen, so they take up soil ammonium and nitrate and immobilize them. Below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants. Excess carbon makes microbes compete with plants for soil nitrogen until the microbes die. Excess nitrogen is left behind but may be leached. As microbes and soil fauna digest organic matter and release CO2, the ratio falls, and a lower soil ratio correlates with higher productivity. Compost, manure and mulch can modify a soil's ratio, and a soil test can measure it. Related: {{ref:soil-found-045}} and {{ref:soil-found-048}}.

soil-fert-170.title: How nutrients travel the last few millimeters to a root
soil-fert-170.text: A root quickly empties the soil it touches. Nutrients in contact with a root are used up within about 2 mm, so most ions must travel some distance through the soil solution. Three routes bring them. In mass flow, dissolved nutrients ride with the water moving toward a transpiring root, like leaves floating down a stream. In diffusion, ions move by random motion from richer soil toward the depleted zone at the root surface. Diffusion keeps going even when closed stomata, the pores of leaves, halt mass flow. Root interception, the slowest route, works as roots grow into new, undepleted soil. The routes split the work unevenly. For corn, mass flow is estimated to supply 98.8% of nitrogen and 95.0% of sulfur. Diffusion supplies 90.9% of phosphorus and 77.7% of potassium. Roots absorb these two so fast that their concentration next to the root falls almost to zero, which drives the diffusion. Decomposing organic matter holds 90–95% of soil nitrogen and sulfur and 20–75% of soil phosphorus, so it supplies much of plants' anion nutrients. Where crops are grown, this natural replenishment of the soil solution usually has to be topped up with fertilizer or organic matter.

soil-fert-157.title: Root uptake: how ions cross into a plant
soil-fert-157.text: Roots do not simply soak up nutrients; they trade for them. Root hairs pump hydrogen ions into the soil. These displace cations held on negatively charged soil particles, freeing them for uptake. Root nutrient uptake is how plants take essential elements in through their roots, above all the root hairs, and pass them to the conducting tissues. In the root apoplast, the spaces in and between cell walls, H+ is exchanged for other cations, and bicarbonate and hydroxide for nutrient anions. Ions then travel to the stele, the root's central core, to reach the xylem and phloem. On the way, the Casparian strip blocks passive flow and so regulates what enters. Uptake works three ways. Nonpolar molecules cross by simple diffusion, others by facilitated diffusion through transport proteins, and still others by active transport against a concentration gradient, using ATP-powered pumps. Because uptake is an active metabolic process, waterlogging, compaction, extreme soil temperatures and poor sugar supply to roots can all inhibit it. The root's structure and architecture can change the rate too. Partners help. Nitrogen-fixing rhizobia and mycorrhizal fungi, which enlarge the effective root surface, both enhance nutrient uptake.

soil-fert-174.title: Phosphorus: the energy element that stays put
soil-fert-174.text: The world may already have passed its peak of phosphorus. Rock phosphate reserves are limited and being depleted by fertilizer use. The peak in phosphorus output, {{ref:soil-fert-046}}, is estimated to have come in 1988 for the U.S. and 1989 for the world. After nitrogen, phosphorus is probably the element most likely to be deficient in soils. In plants it forms DNA, RNA and membrane phospholipids, and as part of ATP it underpins every energy transfer in the cell. Total soil phosphorus averages 0.06 percent by weight, mostly in organic forms that stay unavailable until mineralized or passed to plants by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Dissolved phosphate not quickly taken up forms insoluble calcium phosphates or ends up with iron and aluminum hydrous oxides. In tropical soils, leaching and weathering have depleted it, and unlike nitrogen it cannot be replenished from the air. Phosphorus is largely immobile in soil. It builds up in the surface layer if not cropped and reaches roots mainly by diffusion. It is most available at pH 6.5 in mineral soils and 5.5 in organic soils. On some soils, spruces and other conifers depend on mycorrhizae for it.

soil-fert-175.title: Potassium, the gatekeeper of a leaf's pores
soil-fert-175.text: Potassium opens and closes a leaf's stomata through an ion pump. It therefore controls water loss from leaves and raises drought tolerance. This primary nutrient is present in all plant parts and activates enzymes of photosynthesis and respiration, yet it is built into no major plant constituent. In plant tissue it is outstandingly mobile and soluble. Soils hold 3 to 100 tons of potassium per hectare in the top 20 cm, but only 2 per cent of it is available to plants. Biotite mica and potassium feldspar are common mineral sources, and rhizobacteria help dissolve it with organic acids. Once dissolved, about half is held as exchangeable cations on clay minerals and half stays in the soil solution. As soils dry, potassium can be fixed between the layers of 2:1 clays such as illite, vermiculite and montmorillonite, up to 90 percent within ten minutes. It leaches easily from low-clay soils unless dressings of animal dung or lime offset their poor cation exchange capacity. Potassium-rich soils also yield quality fruit, with better color, shape and sugar content.

soil-fert-189.title: Soil tests for engineers
soil-fert-189.text: Engineers test soil for different reasons than farmers do. In geotechnical engineering, soil tests measure physical characteristics such as water content, void ratio and bulk density. They also give information on shear strength, rate of consolidation and permeability. Grain size analysis, by sieve or hydrometer, is one example. Constant-head and falling-head permeability tests are others.

soil-fert-188.title: Grid sampling for site-specific rates
soil-fert-188.text: Grid soil sampling splits a large field into points and analyses each separately, to guide site-specific nutrient and lime rates. The general recommendation is 2.5- to 5-acre grids, especially where manure and fertilizer rates varied; some areas use one-acre grids. Unaligned grids are advised: points are shifted randomly off the regular grid so that a past applicator malfunction is not unknowingly sampled in a line. Each point still needs 10-15 cores within about 30 feet. Because grid testing is expensive, do it once per rotation, when lime may be needed, or every five to eight years. Fertility patterns often do not follow soil survey maps, which is why the grid earns its cost. It extends the basic {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-fert-190.title: Testing garden soil for lead
soil-fert-190.text: Lead is a particularly dangerous soil contaminant, and a soil test can judge how much risk a garden carries. Other common mineral contaminants include arsenic, barium, cadmium, copper, mercury and zinc. Children and pregnant women should avoid soil with an estimated total lead content above 300 ppm. Levels of 500–1000 ppm are rated medium, and 1000–3000 ppm high. Advice includes siting gardens away from old painted buildings and busy roads, adding {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, and raising the soil to pH 6.5, which minimizes lead availability.

soil-fert-160.title: Boron, the micronutrient of flowers and growing tips
soil-fert-160.text: Boron cannot travel in the phloem, so it must reach a plant's growing parts through the xylem. When it runs short, terminal growing points die and growth is stunted. This micronutrient affects flowering, fruiting, pollen germination, cell division and cell walls. Mobile in soil, it leaches readily from sandy soils but little from silt or clay. Decomposing organic matter leaves boron in the topmost layer, so deficiency appears in dry weather, when plants cannot draw on that drying layer. More than one ppm in the soil solution is toxic to most plants, but toxic soils are mostly limited to arid regions.

soil-fert-167.title: Hydroponics: growing plants without soil
soil-fert-167.text: Plants need what soil provides, not the soil itself. Hydroponics grows them in a water-nutrient solution instead of nutrient-rich soil or substrate. The most common solution, developed by D. R. Hoagland and W. C. Snyder in 1933, holds all the essential macro- and micronutrients in the proportions most plants need. Aerators prevent hypoxia, a shortage of oxygen that inhibits root respiration and so nutrient uptake. In the nutrient film technique, a thin film of solution flows past roots that are not fully submerged, keeping them aerated.

soil-fert-159.title: Iron, the metal behind green leaves
soil-fert-159.text: Iron is not part of chlorophyll, yet a plant cannot make chlorophyll without it. This micronutrient is an enzyme cofactor, a helper the enzymes need, in photosynthesis and electron transport. Deficiency yellows the tissue between the veins, a form of {{ref:soil-fert-228}}, and causes necrosis. It can stem from excess heavy metals or lime in the soil, or from a lack of copper. Iron(II) is the most useful form because it is more soluble at neutral pH. Plants can also use iron(III) through the photo-reduction of ferric citrate. In the field, iron fertilizer is supplied as a chelate, a compound that holds the metal in a form plants can take up.

soil-fert-165.title: When one nutrient gets in another's way
soil-fert-165.text: Feeding a plant one nutrient can starve it of another. Nutrient interactions are the ways the supply of one nutrient affects the uptake, movement or action of another. Calcium and magnesium inhibit uptake of trace metals, and copper and zinc reduce each other's uptake. Such effects depend on species and growing conditions.
