The amount of ammonium available can influence potassium uptake. Potash fertilizers can reduce uptake of phosphorus, magnesium and calcium, so imbalanced potassium fertilizing can markedly lower yields. Heavy nitrogen applications on sulfur-poor fields can cause sulfur deficiency by dilution, as faster growth raises the plant's sulfur demand.

soil-fert-164.title: Too much of a good thing: nutrient toxicity
soil-fert-164.text: An element a plant cannot live without can also poison it. Plant nutrient toxicity is harm from a nutrient present at too high a level. Excess soluble boron, molybdenum and chloride are toxic. Boron above 1 ppm in soil water harms most plants. Within plants, 10 to 50 ppm is toxic for small grains, while tolerant crops such as sugar beets withstand 200 ppm. A fertile soil lacks toxic substances such as Fe2+. Diagnosis is tricky. Deficiency of one element can look like toxicity from another, and an abundance of one nutrient can cause deficiency of another.

soil-fert-166.title: Plant tissue analysis: asking the crop instead of the soil
soil-fert-166.text: Sometimes the surest way to learn what a soil supplies is to analyze the plant. Plant tissue analysis describes a plant's nutrient status, also called its ionome or nutrient profile. Interpreting the results has been controversial. In recent decades, mathematical models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced the nearly two-century-old Liebig's law in this work. Tissue tests can identify nitrogen deficiencies, and sensing chlorophyll content allows variable nitrogen rates during the season. Analysis can also reveal a shortage of boron, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-226}}, early enough to correct it. Once symptoms appear, crop loss cannot be prevented.

soil-fert-161.title: Zinc, the most widely missing micronutrient
soil-fert-161.text: Zinc is the most widely deficient micronutrient in industrial crop production, followed by boron. A large number of plant enzymes need it, and it is essential to DNA transcription. A zinc-starved plant shows 'little leaf': its leaves are stunted because the growth hormone auxin breaks down by oxidation. Shortened internodes, the stem lengths between leaves, stack the leaves together. Heavy phosphate applications can cause deficiency by forming insoluble zinc phosphates, though soil pH can modify the effect. Copper and zinc reduce each other's uptake, and zinc also affects a plant's iron levels.

soil-fert-185.title: Balancing carbon and nitrogen in a rotting heap
soil-fert-185.text: A heap of rotting plant matter needs the same balance of carbon and nitrogen that soil does. In {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, the microbes prefer feedstocks with a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 30–35:1, though some carbon, especially lignin, is not fully digested. An imbalanced ratio slows the process and lowers its temperature. Below 15:1, ammonium can outgas, causing odor and nitrogen loss. The finished product has a C:N of around 10:1. Feedstock contents come from lookup tables. A mixture's ratio is the summed carbon of all its components divided by their summed nitrogen.

soil-fert-186.title: Reading old mud: the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of sediments
soil-fert-186.text: The mud on a lake bed records what once grew around it. The sediment C/N ratio uses the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of sediments as a clue to the sources of their organic matter and to past climate. Ratios of 4–10:1 usually mean marine sources, while land vascular plants tend to exceed 20. Algae lack cellulose and hold more protein. Bacteria eat the nitrogen-rich part of sinking matter first. The ratio therefore rises with depth, to about 10 at 1000 m and up to 15 below about 2500 m. In lake cores, abrupt shifts between algal and land-plant sources suggest deep-water or shallow, marshy phases.

soil-fert-201.title: Iron deficiency chlorosis: yellow leaves in iron-rich soil
soil-fert-201.text: Azaleas, camellias, raspberries and pears can turn yellow in soil full of iron. Iron deficiency chlorosis, also called lime-induced chlorosis, is a disorder in which a plant gets too little iron to make enough chlorophyll. Soil iron becomes unavailable when soil pH is above 6.5, and excess manganese can also block uptake. Iron is not mobile in the plant, so yellowing appears between the veins of new leaves. Organic matter, acidifying ammonium sulphate or slow-acting elemental sulphur can lower the pH toward 6.5–7. For quick relief, iron sulphate and Fe EDTA work only up to pH 7.1, but Fe EDDHA works up to pH 9.

soil-fert-193.title: The nutrient management plan, rewritten every year
soil-fert-193.text: A nutrient management plan is never finished: it is reviewed and updated every year. It makes a crop's nutrient sources more efficient while lowering production and environmental risk. It is generally agreed to have ten components. It begins with a field map of reference points, acreage and soil types, and a soil test to set nutrient rates. It weighs crop sequence, yield estimates from historic records, nutrient sources such as animal dung, and sensitive areas near streams or wells. It then sets rates, timing and methods, favoring injection where feasible. For animal feeding operations it may center on {{ref:soil-fert-098}}. Some U.S. agencies require one.

soil-fert-180.title: Beneficial elements: helpful, but not required
soil-fert-180.text: Some elements help a plant without being strictly required. Beneficial elements improve plant health, but their absence does not stop the life cycle. Examples include cobalt, strontium, vanadium, silicon and nickel. Silicon strengthens cell walls and improves drought and frost resistance, resistance to lodging and pest defenses. Cobalt seems unneeded by most plants but is essential for the bacteria that fix nitrogen with legumes. Sodium can partly take over potassium's control of the stomata and is essential for C4 plants. Selenium fertilizers raise crop selenium and help animals fed from selenium-deficient soils. Such elements may join the essential list as their importance is weighed.

soil-fert-176.title: Calcium, the builder of cell walls
soil-fert-176.text: Calcium helps hold a plant together as part of its cell walls. This secondary macronutrient also aids root development and acts as a messenger in the cytosol, the fluid inside cells. Soil calcium occurs as insoluble calcite and dolomite, as a divalent cation in solution, as exchangeable ions on particle surfaces, and complexed with organic matter. It is more available than potassium because calcite dissolves more readily than feldspar. Mass flow alone usually brings enough to roots. Being soluble, it leaches, so it runs low in sandy, heavily leached or strongly acidic soils, which then need {{ref:soil-fert-055}}.

soil-fert-171.title: Carbon: the nutrient plants pull from the air
soil-fert-171.text: About 45% of a plant's dry mass is carbon, and most of it comes from the air. Plants take carbon mainly as carbon dioxide, through photosynthesis. They also take dissolved carbon from the soil solution and receive it through mycorrhizal networks. At its normal 0.03% in air, CO2 can limit growth when water and nutrients are not scarce. Raising CO2 strongly promotes growth, up to levels above 300 ppm. Soil air holds 10 to 100 times the atmospheric concentration. When porosity is low or flooding blocks diffusion, it can reach toxic levels.

soil-fert-177.title: Magnesium, the metal inside chlorophyll
soil-fert-177.text: Every chlorophyll molecule contains magnesium. This secondary macronutrient also activates many enzyme reactions, working closely with energy-supplying phosphorus compounds. In most soils it is one of the dominant exchangeable cations, after calcium and potassium. Weathering of hornblende, biotite and vermiculite releases it. Highly weathered and sandy soils may become deficient as heavy rain leaches it away.

soil-fert-173.title: Three ways nitrogen escapes from soil
soil-fert-173.text: Nitrogen rarely stays where it is put. Nitrate leaches easily, unlike ammonium, and pollutes groundwater or runoff, especially under heavy fertilizer use. In poorly aerated soil, bacteria short of oxygen respire with nitrate and release N2 or N2O. This {{ref:soil-fert-108}} can remove 25 percent of the nitrogen in fertilizer and animal dung on heavy clay. On alkaline soils ammonium turns to ammonia gas, and ammonium fertilizer applied there can lose as much as 87 percent this way. These losses drive aquifer and air pollution, soil acidification and the overfeeding of lakes and rivers, causing severe biodiversity loss in natural ecosystems.

soil-fert-194.title: Nitrogen management: keeping a restless nutrient in the field
soil-fert-194.text: Careful choice of fertilizer source, rate, timing and placement can cut nitrous oxide emissions per unit of crop by up to half. Nitrogen management aims for crops to use applied nitrogen as fully as possible, with as little as possible lost. Of the 16 essential nutrients, nitrogen is usually the hardest to manage, because plant-available nitrogen changes quickly with soil water. It escapes by leaching, runoff, erosion, ammonia volatilization and loss as gas from oxygen-starved soil. Nitrate is the form most at risk. Rates should allow for nitrogen mineralized from organic matter and legume residues, and for nitrogen in animal dung, irrigation water and the atmosphere. Applying nitrogen close to crop uptake in split doses reduces losses. So do slow-release products and additives that keep nitrogen as ammonium. Working ammonium fertilizers into the soil cuts ammonia losses. Deep-rooted rotations capture leftover nitrate, while buffers and built wetlands strip nitrogen from runoff and drainage water. Models such as NLEAP and Adapt-N use daily soil, weather and crop data to predict the fate of applied nitrogen.

soil-fert-195.title: Testing soil and crops for nitrogen
soil-fert-195.text: Nitrogen needs can be checked before, during and after a season. Soil and crop nitrogen tests judge whether, and how much, nitrogen a crop needs. Preplant soil tests show the soil's nitrogen-supplying power, and late-spring or pre-side-dress tests decide whether more is needed. Amino sugar tests, grid mapping and real-time sensors can refine those needs. Plant tissue tests identify deficiencies. After harvest, tests check the season's management. Corn stalk nitrate tests taken after black layer show whether the last crop got too little, enough or too much nitrogen.

soil-fert-178.title: Sulfur, the nutrient that follows organic matter
soil-fert-178.text: Sulfur behaves much like phosphorus in the soil. Most of it becomes available as decomposing organic matter releases it, so it declines with depth along with organic matter. This secondary macronutrient is part of some amino acids and vitamins and is essential for chloroplasts. Plants need it to turn nitrate into amino acids and protein, and legumes need it to fix nitrogen. Some soils, especially sandy ones, are deficient and need sulfur added when cropped. Sulfur cannot be moved out of older leaves, so yellowing and stunting appear first in the youngest tissues.

soil-fert-196.title: Nutrient depletion: when the first link of the food chain fails
soil-fert-196.text: Overfarming can turn fertile soil into barren land within a few years. Nutrient depletion is the loss of nutrients and micronutrients from a habitat, most often the soil, and a form of resource depletion. It ends in nutrient deficiency. Its opposite is {{ref:soil-env-019}}, and both tend to reduce biodiversity. Nutrients are the first link in food chains, so their loss disturbs the flow of nutrients through ecosystems and whole food chains, reaching people as malnourishment. Growing the same crop with the same fertilizer on the same land every year yields decreasing returns.

soil-fert-199.title: Barren vegetation: sparse plants on hard ground
soil-fert-199.text: Barren vegetation marks land where plant growth is sparse or stunted and biodiversity may be limited. Toxic or infertile soil, high winds, coastal salt spray and climate are often key causes. Barren does not always mean poor in species. Serpentine barrens form on soils weathered from ultramafic bedrock, short of water, nitrogen and phosphorus. Yet they carry very diverse floras with many endemics, plants found nowhere else. The Pine Barrens grow on acidic, coarse sands and gravels whose mature soils are siliceous, highly permeable podzols.

soil-fert-191.title: The Illinois Soil Nitrogen Test: beyond guessing by the bushel
soil-fert-191.text: Since about 1975, Corn Belt farmers have often sized nitrogen doses by the bushel, applying 1.1 to 1.4 lbs per bushel of expected corn. Illinois trials found this yield-based method usually over-applies nitrogen. The excess is lost to air or water and appears to speed the decomposition of soil organic matter. The Illinois Soil Nitrogen Test, introduced in 2007, offers an alternative. It estimates amino sugar nitrogen to measure the soil nitrogen available to plants. For corn and soybeans the optimal range is around 225 to 240 mg/kg. Below it, some nitrogen fertilizer is needed. Above it, more nitrogen will not increase yield.

soil-fert-183.title: Liebig's barrel: a crop is only as full as its shortest stave
soil-fert-183.text: A barrel with staves of unequal length holds water only up to its shortest stave. Dobenecks used this picture to explain Liebig's law: a plant's growth is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply, as the barrel is by its shortest stave. The image has a twist. Adaptation acts like a cooper lengthening the shortest stave, so well-adapted systems compensate for their limiting factor as far as possible. Hence a paradox. A law of the minimum seen in artificial systems should be violated in nature, where adaptation evens out the load among factors.

soil-fert-200.title: The Law of the Maximum: growth as a product of many factors
soil-fert-200.text: Arthur Wallace built his rule around about 70 growth factors. His Law of the Maximum holds that total crop growth is proportional to them and cannot exceed their aggregate value. Each factor scores from 0, no growth, to 1, maximum, and growth is their product. Three factors at 0.5 give 12.5% of optimum; three at 0.9 give 72.9%. In a demonstration, low phosphorus alone gave 83% of optimum growth and low nitrogen 71%. Both together gave 57%, close to the predicted 59%. The factors span nutrients, soil conditions, soil biology, weather and management. Unless limiting factors are corrected, other inputs are wasted.

soil-fert-168.title: Luxury consumption: when a plant takes more than it needs
soil-fert-168.text: Give a plant more potassium than it needs and it may take it anyway. Luxury consumption is uptake of more of a nutrient than healthy growth requires. Macronutrients, normally 0.15% to 6.0% of plant dry matter, are sometimes taken up beyond need, especially when fertilizer is applied in excess. Potassium uptake rises with root temperature and depresses calcium uptake. Calcium itself was long regarded as a luxury but is now considered essential, for cell walls and membranes among other roles.

soil-fert-140.title: Biogeochemical cycles: how the same atoms keep coming back
soil-fert-140.text: Sunlight enters a forest once and leaves as heat, but the forest's atoms stay in play. Energy flows one way through ecosystems, while the matter of living things is conserved and recycled. A biogeochemical cycle is the path an element or compound takes as it moves and changes between living things, the air, water and Earth's crust. The soil sits on that path, part of the layer covered in {{ref:soil-found-084}}. Each cycle runs through the biosphere, the world of living things, and through three lifeless spheres: the atmosphere, the lithosphere of rock and the hydrosphere of water. The major cycles are those of carbon, nitrogen and water. Others move oxygen, hydrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron and sulfur. Carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur are the main elements of organic molecules, and each can persist for long periods in air, land, water or rock. Microorganisms drive much of the traffic. Without them, many of the steps would not happen at all. The cycles interlock, helping to regulate climate and to support plant growth and healthy ecosystems. People can knock them off balance. Burning fossil fuels and heavy fertilizer use disrupt the cycles, adding to climate change and pollution.

soil-fert-099.title: The nitrogen cycle: scarcity in an ocean of air
soil-fert-099.text: Every breath is mostly nitrogen, yet nitrogen is what many ecosystems run short of. Nitrogen gas makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere, the largest nitrogen store, but little of it is available to living things. The nitrogen cycle is the path nitrogen follows as it changes chemical form and moves among air, land and sea. Its main steps capture nitrogen from the air, release it from dead matter as ammonium, turn that ammonium into nitrate, and finally return it to the air as gas. Both biological and physical processes drive them. The first step is {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Along the way nitrogen takes many forms: organic nitrogen, ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, nitrous oxide, nitric oxide and nitrogen gas. Organic nitrogen sits in living organisms, in humus and in partly decomposed matter, the store described in {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Microbes run many of the steps, some to harvest energy and others to gather the nitrogen they need to grow. In most ecosystems, capture from the air is the main source of nitrogen plants can use. Where bedrock is rich in nitrogen, its breakdown supplies some too. The same cycle runs in the ocean, where cyanobacteria do most of the capturing. Ecologists watch it closely, because nitrogen supply can set the pace of plant production and of decomposition. They have reason to worry. Fossil fuel burning, synthetic fertilizers and nitrogen in wastewater have dramatically altered the global cycle, harming ecosystems and human health.

soil-fert-100.title: Nitrogen fixation: cracking the air's toughest bond
soil-fert-100.text: Two nitrogen atoms in the air cling together with a triple bond so strong that most organisms cannot break it. Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of this abundant but unreactive gas into usable compounds such as ammonia and nitrate. Life depends on it, because DNA, proteins and other vital organic compounds all contain nitrogen. It is the gateway into {{ref:soil-fert-099}}, and it happens in three ways. Lightning does it naturally, making nitrogen oxides that form nitrous and nitric acids. These seep into soil as nitrate that plants can use. Industry does it artificially. About 30% of all fixed nitrogen is now made by the method in {{ref:soil-fert-104}}. Living things do the rest. Lightning fixes 5 to 10 billion kg a year, but free-living or symbiotic bacteria do most of the work. They are the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-102}}. Their tools are enzymes, described in {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, made by microorganisms such as cyanobacteria and rhizobia. Some of these microbes live in partnership with legumes, mosses and the water fern covered in {{ref:soil-fert-204}}. Looser associations also occur, for example on rice roots.

soil-fert-127.title: The phosphorus cycle, slowest of the life cycles
soil-fert-127.text: Phosphorus never drifts through the air. Unlike many cycles, the phosphorus cycle has almost no gas phase, so it is tracked mainly as orthophosphate, a dissolved phosphate ion, moving through land and water. The cycle carries phosphorus through rocks, water and living things. Every cell needs it, for DNA, RNA, the energy carrier ATP and the phospholipids of cell membranes. Plants take it up as phosphate and build it into organic compounds, the nutrient role covered in {{ref:soil-fert-174}}. Phosphate races through plants and animals but crawls through soil and ocean, making this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles. Over geological time, tectonic uplift raises phosphate rock such as apatite, and {{ref:soil-found-052}} breaks it down. That rock is the main source of phosphorus living things can use on land. In the short term, soil phosphorus changes through chemistry and biology. Soil microbes act as both sinks and sources of available phosphorus. When it runs low, plants and soil microbes both grow slowly. Soil phosphorus also washes into rivers and lakes and on to the ocean. Of what sinks to the deep sea, only about 1% is buried in sediments. Too much causes trouble. Phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can over-enrich lakes and streams, and excess phosphorus generally causes freshwater algal blooms.

soil-fert-133.title: The sulfur cycle and its shifting electrons
soil-fert-133.text: Sulfur is a chemical shape-shifter. Its oxidation state, a count of electrons gained or lost, ranges from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides. Elemental sulfur sits between them and can either give or take electrons. The sulfur cycle moves this element between rocks, waters and living things, changing its oxidation state as it goes through the reactions of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Life needs sulfur for many proteins and cofactors, and its compounds serve as oxidants or reductants in cellular respiration. Plants, fungi and many prokaryotes take up sulfate and reduce it to build their own sulfur compounds. When they die, decomposition mineralizes their organic sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, elemental sulfur and sulfide minerals. Deamination, the stripping of nitrogen from organic compounds, releases nitrogen in much the same way. Two groups of microbes then pull in opposite directions. Sulfur oxidizers turn sulfide and elemental sulfur into sulfate, and sulfate reducers turn sulfate back into sulfide. Most sulfur is not in living things at all. It sits in seawater and sedimentary rocks, and left alone it stays in rock for millions of years. Uplift, erosion and weathering eventually set it free.

soil-fert-121.title: Immobilization: when microbes eat the crop's nitrogen
soil-fert-121.text: Plough straw into a field and the next crop can go hungry for nitrogen. The cause is immobilization: microbes or plants convert inorganic nutrients into organic compounds, putting them out of the crop's reach. It is the opposite of {{ref:soil-bio-120}}. Soil bacteria take up inorganic nitrogen and build it into amino acids and other large biological molecules. The two processes run side by side, steadily shifting decomposing nitrogen between organic and inorganic states. Which one wins depends on the balance of carbon to nitrogen in the residues, explained in {{ref:soil-fert-184}}. Above a C:N ratio of about 30:1, microbes draw on mineral nitrogen such as nitrate. Below about 25:1, decomposition releases surplus nitrogen. High-carbon materials such as sawdust or straw stimulate microbes and raise their nitrogen demand. Microbes then out-compete plants for ammonium and nitrate, so crops easily become nitrogen deficient. The hunger is temporary. As decomposition releases carbon dioxide, the ratio falls. Once decay is nearly complete, soil mineral nitrogen ends higher than at the start. Nitrogen is locked up in two places: in the microbes' own bodies, and in the by-products of their activity.

soil-fert-139.title: The calcium cycle, from seashell to leaf and back
soil-fert-139.text: Limestone began in the sea. Shell-building organisms turn dissolved calcium into calcium carbonate, the main marine sink for calcium and the origin of limestone. The calcium cycle moves calcium between dissolved and solid forms through rocks, soils, waters and living things. Rocks store it mainly as calcium carbonate or calcium silicate, in minerals such as calcite, dolomite, phosphate and gypsum. As they slowly dissolve, part of {{ref:soil-found-052}}, they release calcium ions. Calcium minerals weather more easily than magnesium minerals, so waters are richer in calcium. Calcium held as lime is useless to plants until carbonic acid, formed from carbon dioxide and water, dissolves it. Small particles dissolve faster than large rocks. Lime leached into soil raises calcium, stabilizes pH and supplies soluble Ca2+ ions that roots can absorb. Inside a plant, calcium rises with water in the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue. As calcium pectate it stiffens cell walls, and it helps enzymes signal growth. Released calcium also helps soil microbes reach phosphorus and other micronutrients. When plants and animals die, decomposers return their calcium to the soil. Fertilizers have raised soil calcium as well.

soil-fert-146.title: Nutrient cycles: an ecosystem's own recycling
soil-fert-146.text: In 1749 Linnaeus described nature recycling its own materials. A nutrient cycle, also called ecological recycling, is the movement of inorganic and organic matter back into the making of new living matter. Textbooks often treat it as a synonym of {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. Usually, though, the term means cycling within one ecosystem, linked to the larger global cycles by inputs and outputs. Energy passes through once, but mineral nutrients go round, in cycles of carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen. Much of the recycling is regulated during decomposition. Cellulose-degrading enzymes, for example, recycle plant material. Earthworms speed things up. Their bodies add mineral nutrients, their burrows carry nutrients into mineral soil, and their casts open nutrients to bacteria and other decomposers. Some ecosystems are nutrient sinks in debt, while others are sources. The differences relate to climate, topography and geological history, which leave different parent materials. Farms show the loop's limits. Organic farms rely on biodiversity to recycle nutrients instead of synthetic fertilizers, but produce sold off the farm opens the cycle, and its nutrients may need replacing. Boussingault showed from 1836 to 1876 that plants need minerals and nitrogen, and in 1872 Ferdinand Cohn described a 'cycle of life'. The term nutrient cycle appears in an 1899 pamphlet on silviculture, before Vernadsky, in 1926, coined the term for the science described in {{ref:soil-fert-218}}.

soil-fert-106.title: Ammonification: turning the dead into ammonium
soil-fert-106.text: When a plant or animal dies, or an animal excretes waste, its nitrogen is locked in organic forms such as amino acids and DNA. Ammonification unlocks it. Bacteria and fungi convert that organic nitrogen into ammonia or ammonium. The process is also called nitrogen mineralization, and it is the last step of {{ref:soil-fert-099}} that involves organic compounds. Many enzymes take part, including dehydrogenases, proteases and deaminases. Rates climb with soil organic nitrogen, microbial biomass and annual precipitation, and they respond closely to temperature. They slow under vegetation with a high carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and when sugar is added to the soil. Oxygen is not essential. In waterlogged peat, organic matter decomposing without oxygen still yields ammonium. Ammonification is half of a larger job. Together with the next step, {{ref:soil-fert-112}}, it makes up mineralization, the complete breakdown of organic material into mineral nitrogen.

soil-fert-112.title: Nitrification: two oxidations from ammonium to nitrate
soil-fert-112.text: Soil holds on to ammonium but lets nitrate slip away, and that difference makes this step matter. Nitrification is the biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrate, by way of nitrite. It takes up the ammonium released by {{ref:soil-fert-106}} and is an important step of the nitrogen cycle in soil. Small groups of bacteria and archaea carry it out, and they need oxygen. They are chemoautotrophs: they draw energy from both oxidation steps and take their carbon from carbon dioxide. In the first step, nitritation, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and archaea turn ammonia or ammonium into nitrite. This is usually the rate-limiting step. In the second, nitratation, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn nitrite into nitrate. In some bacteria, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-110}}, one organism does both. Rates depend on ammonium supply, aeration, soil moisture, temperature and a near-neutral pH. Adding lime, the practice in {{ref:soil-fert-055}}, raises soil biological activity and fertility, in particular by increasing nitrification. The process has costs. Soil's net negative charge holds ammonium tightly but not nitrate, so turning fertilizer ammonia into nitrate increases leaching to groundwater. Nitrification also releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas about 300 times more potent than carbon dioxide. It contributes 6% of greenhouse warming.

soil-fert-113.title: Nitrifying bacteria, a crew that works in two shifts
soil-fert-113.text: Nitrifying bacteria work in two shifts. They are chemolithotrophs, microbes that live by oxidizing inorganic chemicals, as {{ref:soil-bio-057}} explains; these ones oxidize ammonia or nitrite. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria make nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn it into nitrate, so the two groups grow together. In soil, the first group converts ammonia from decomposing organic matter or fertilizer, and the second uses the nitrite. Soil genera include Nitrosospira, an ammonia oxidizer, and the nitrite oxidizers {{ref:soil-fert-221}} and the genus in {{ref:soil-fert-147}}. Key enzymes sit on their internal membranes: ammonia monooxygenase, hydroxylamine oxidoreductase and nitrite oxidoreductase. They are most numerous where ammonia is plentiful, such as sites of heavy protein decomposition and sewage treatment plants. Winogradsky described the two-step process in 1890.

soil-fert-114.title: Nitrosomonas, an ammonia eater that needs air
soil-fert-114.text: Fertilized fields feed a microbe that lives on ammonia. Nitrosomonas is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria that oxidize ammonia to nitrite, one of five genera of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria. It takes its energy from ammonia and its carbon from carbon dioxide, and it needs oxygen. Two enzymes, ammonia monooxygenase and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase, do the conversion. When oxygen is low, nitrous oxide and nitric oxide form as by-products. It thrives at pH 6.0–9.0 and 20–30 °C where ammonia is abundant. On farms its work can leach away nitrogen, which the chemicals in {{ref:soil-fert-116}} limit. Wastewater plants use it to remove nitrogen.

soil-fert-122.title: Reactive nitrogen, the forms life can use
soil-fert-122.text: Breaking the triple bond of nitrogen gas takes a large amount of energy, 226 kcal per mole. So the gas must be fixed into other forms before living things can grow on it. Reactive nitrogen, also called fixed nitrogen, is every form of nitrogen in the environment except that unreactive gas. Common forms are nitrogen oxide gases, ammonia, nitrous oxide and nitrate. Ammonium salts, nitrate and the compound in {{ref:soil-fert-021}} also go into fertilizers. Soil bacteria and archaea fix nitrogen gas mainly into ammonia, some in partnership with legumes, the process of {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Just over half of all reactive nitrogen entering the biosphere now comes from human activity such as industrial fertilizer production. The microbial process in {{ref:soil-fert-108}} eventually returns it to nitrogen gas, but an excess can cause problems such as the over-enrichment of waters. Every form enters the nitrogen cycle, so a surplus spreads quickly through the environment. Its problems must be tackled together.

soil-fert-143.title: The iron cycle: plentiful metal, scarce nutrient
soil-fert-143.text: Iron is abundant in Earth's crust, yet it limits life in most regions. The iron cycle is chiefly iron's switching between the +2 ferrous and +3 ferric oxidation states. Where oxygen is present, ferric iron is stable but dissolves poorly. Iron-oxidizing bacteria turn soluble ferrous iron into insoluble ferric iron. Without oxygen, bacteria such as Shewanella and Geobacter reverse this, freeing the more usable ferrous form. Iron is an essential micronutrient, part of hemoglobin, ferredoxin and the enzymes that fix nitrogen. Ferric hydroxides also bind phosphorus, released when microbes reduce the iron, and ferrous iron can reduce nitrate.

soil-fert-105.title: How bacteria were caught pulling nitrogen from the air
soil-fert-105.text: In 1838 the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-073}} discovered biological nitrogen fixation. Explaining it took the rest of the century. Experiments in 1855 and 1887 had shown that nitrogen did not enter plants directly from the air. Between 1886 and 1888, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth found the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, opening a new era of soil science. Some sources date their discovery to 1880 or 1887. In 1901 Beijerinck showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen. It was the first known free-living fixer of its kind, the group covered in {{ref:soil-fert-102}}.

soil-fert-108.title: Denitrification: microbes that breathe nitrate
soil-fert-108.text: When soil floods and oxygen runs out, some bacteria switch to breathing nitrate. Denitrification is the microbial reduction of nitrate, through a series of gaseous nitrogen oxides, to nitrogen gas. It takes the nitrate made by {{ref:soil-fert-112}} and sends it back to the air. Facultative anaerobic bacteria, which can live with or without oxygen, use it as the kind of respiration described in {{ref:soil-chem-128}}. They oxidize an electron donor such as organic matter and hand the electrons to nitrate instead of oxygen. Nitrate becomes nitrite, then nitric oxide, then nitrous oxide, and finally nitrogen gas, completing the nitrogen cycle. The process needs very low oxygen, below 10%, plus an electron donor such as organic carbon, hydrogen gas or reduced sulfur. Waterlogged soils suit it well. A carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 2:1 can support full nitrate reduction, whatever the temperature or carbon source. Soil pH and texture moderate it, and higher pH drives it closer to nitrogen gas rather than nitrous oxide. That matters, because nitrous oxide is an ozone-depleting greenhouse gas with a considerable influence on global warming. For farmers, denitrification is a loss. Nitrogen gas is inert and unavailable to plants, so the soil loses nitrogen. Elsewhere the same loss is useful. Because it removes nitrate and cuts leaching to groundwater, it is used to treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal wastes.

soil-fert-119.title: Denitrifying bacteria, a crowd from many branches
soil-fert-119.text: Over 50 genera and 125 species can denitrify, an estimated 10–15% of the bacteria in water, soil and sediment. Denitrifying bacteria are a diverse group, drawn from many phyla, that carry out {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. They use nitrate and nitrite in place of oxygen as the final electron acceptor. Most are facultative aerobic heterotrophs, organisms that feed on organic carbon, such as species of Pseudomonas, Alcaligenes and Bacillus. They switch to nitrate when oxygen runs out. Four enzymes act in turn: nitrate reductase, nitrite reductase, nitric oxide reductase and finally the enzyme of {{ref:soil-fert-225}}, which yields nitrogen gas. Their electrons come from organic carbon, or from hydrogen, reduced iron or sulfur. In one soil, the drilosphere, the soil shaped by earthworms, held 16 per cent of them. By sending nitrogen back to the atmosphere they lower soil fertility, releasing nitric oxide and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide on the way. Wastewater plants put them to work, feeding them organic carbon in an oxygen-free basin so nitrate bubbles off as nitrogen gas.

soil-fert-116.title: Nitrification inhibitors: keeping nitrogen as ammonium
soil-fert-116.text: In Illinois, about 50% of the anhydrous ammonia applied in fall goes on with a nitrification inhibitor. This is a chemical added to fertilizers based on ammonia, ammonium or the compound in {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, to slow their conversion to nitrate, the process of {{ref:soil-fert-112}}. Also called nitrogen stabilizers, inhibitors keep nitrogen as ammonium, because nitrate, a negatively charged ion, leaches more readily. Most work by suppressing the bacteria that oxidize ammonia, typically by binding the active site of their enzyme ammonia monooxygenase. Common ones are dicyandiamide, ammonium thiosulfate and nitrapyrin. They usually raise fertilizer nitrogen recovery in row crops, though benefits depend on conditions and show most at less than optimal nitrogen rates. The environment adds to their appeal, since nitrification yields nitrate that leaches to groundwater and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide. Some, such as nitrapyrin, also suppress bacteria that oxidize methane.

soil-fert-104.title: Haber–Bosch: making fertilizer from the air
soil-fert-104.text: Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues was pulled from the air by one industrial process. The Haber–Bosch process makes ammonia by combining nitrogen from the air with hydrogen over an iron catalyst. It is the industrial route to {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. It answered a looming crisis. In the 19th century, fertilizer nitrogen came from mined niter and guano, and by 1900 those reserves were thought insufficient. Air is about 78% nitrogen, but the gas is exceptionally stable. Fritz Haber showed the reaction working in the laboratory in 1909. Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF, and the first industrial plant opened at Oppau in 1913. Breaking nitrogen's triple bond is the slowest step. The catalyst needs at least 400 °C, and pressures of 15–25 MPa raise the yield. Only about 15% converts per pass, so unused gases are recycled. Most of the hydrogen comes from natural gas. The process uses 1–2% of the world's energy and causes about 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions. In 2018 it made about 230 million tonnes of ammonia, mostly for fertilizer. It is used directly or turned into products such as {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. It now makes about 30% of all fixed nitrogen, and fertilizer production is the largest human source of fixed nitrogen on land. It enabled world population to grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018. The costs are real. Nitrogen use efficiency is typically under 50%, so losses wash nitrate into groundwater and over-enrich lakes and streams. Cheap fertilizer also discourages legume rotations.

soil-fert-123.title: How people doubled the planet's nitrogen flow
soil-fert-123.text: Until 1850, farms got their nitrogen only from natural and legume-driven fixation and from added organic matter. Today, agricultural and industrial nitrogen inputs exceed natural fixation, largely because of fertilizers and fossil fuel burning. Growing legumes, making fertilizer and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly transfer of nitrogen into usable forms. After the 1950s, the method in {{ref:soil-fert-104}} became the largest fertilizer source. From 1890 to 1990, human-made reactive nitrogen rose almost ninefold, while the human population more than tripled. In farm soils, fertilizer has boosted nitrification and denitrification, and both leak nitric oxide and nitrous oxide. As ammonium accumulates, nitrification releases hydrogen ions that acidify the soil. Mobile nitrate then leaches out, carrying calcium and magnesium with it. Human activities produce 35% of global nitrous oxide emissions, about 20% from agriculture such as fertilizer use and the handling of manure. Some sources put the human share at about 40%. Excess fertilizer nitrogen is also a significant source of nitrate pollution in groundwater and surface water.

soil-fert-107.title: Nitrogen assimilation: building nitrate into living tissue
soil-fert-107.text: Nitrate in the soil is not yet part of a plant. Nitrogen assimilation is the uptake of nitrate or ammonium by plants and microbes and its incorporation into their own organic compounds. Plants take up either form through the structures described in {{ref:soil-bio-140}}. Absorbed nitrate is reduced first to nitrite and then to ammonium. Only then is it built into amino acids, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. Plants with rhizobia receive some nitrogen straight from their nodules, partly as amino acids exchanged with the bacteria. Many bacteria and other heterotrophs can use ammonium as their only nitrogen source.

soil-found-065.title: The oxygen cycle's largest store is rock
soil-found-065.text: Most of Earth's oxygen is locked in stone. By weight, 99.5% sits in the silicate and oxide minerals of the crust and mantle, while air, water and life together hold under 0.05%. The oxygen cycle moves oxygen through the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and crust. The reactions of {{ref:soil-chem-113}} shift its atoms between oxidation states in ions, oxides and molecules. Photosynthesis is the main source of free oxygen in the air. Respiration and decay are the main losses, as animals and bacteria consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

soil-fert-141.title: Reservoirs and exchange pools: where elements wait
soil-fert-141.text: Carbon in a coal seam can sit for a very long time, while carbon in a plant soon moves on. A reservoir holds a chemical for a long time, as coal deposits store carbon. An exchange pool, such as plants and animals, holds elements only briefly before releasing them back to the air or surroundings. Reservoirs are generally lifeless, while exchange pools are generally living. Residence time, also called turnover time, is how long a chemical is held in one place. Every {{ref:soil-fert-140}} runs between these two kinds of store.

soil-found-066.title: The mercury cycle and its poisonous turn
soil-found-066.text: Over 5000 metric tons of mercury reach the atmosphere each year. The mercury cycle moves this metal between chemical forms and environments, driven by both natural and human processes. Mercury occurs in three oxidation states: 0, or elemental; I, or mercurous; and II, or mercuric. Weathering of minerals, geothermal activity and active volcanoes release it naturally, and its main ore is cinnabar, a mercury sulfide. Gold mining, coal burning and copper or lead production add more. Bacteria and archaea turn inorganic mercury into methylmercury. This form builds up in organisms and concentrates up food chains.

soil-fert-128.title: Weathering rock sets an ecosystem's phosphorus budget
soil-fert-128.text: Phosphorus can arrive on the wind. Dust from northern Africa, carrying phosphorus-bearing particles of weathered rock, is thought to help sustain the Amazon rainforest. On most land, though, phosphorus comes from slow release by weathering: the freeing of phosphate from minerals such as apatite as rocks break down. Apatite, the main primary phosphorus mineral, breaks down by carbonation, attack by carbon dioxide dissolved in water, a form of {{ref:soil-found-058}}. The rate of that release limits how much phosphorus an ecosystem has, so apatite dissolution is a key control on productivity. Little of the freed phosphorus reaches living things, because most reacts with other soil minerals. Available phosphorus cycles biologically in the upper soil, while deeper phosphorus is mostly tied up with secondary minerals. Time tightens the squeeze. As weathering and soil development advance, phosphorus precipitates into insoluble forms. Over thousands of years, land loses its available phosphorus.

soil-fert-129.title: Why soils lock up the phosphorus farmers add
soil-fert-129.text: Much of the soluble phosphate spread as fertilizer is rapidly immobilized and becomes unavailable to plants. Soil phosphorus retention is the binding of phosphate by soil minerals, by adsorption or precipitation, which keeps dissolved phosphorus low. Adsorption, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-068}}, holds ions on mineral surfaces. Precipitation turns them into new solids. Which one acts depends on the acidity described in {{ref:soil-found-014}}. In acidic soils, phosphate adsorbs onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides. In neutral to calcareous soils, it precipitates onto calcite. Retention is usually seen as the most important control on available phosphorus in mineral soil. Living things push back. Plants and microbes use special strategies to gather phosphorus from the low concentrations left in soil solution. Phosphorus-starved bacteria release iron-binding molecules and may dissolve iron minerals to reach the phosphate held on them. Water can undo the lock. Waterlogging can make a poorly drained soil chemically reducing within 7–10 days, sharply raising dissolved phosphorus and the risk of leaching.

soil-fert-102.title: Diazotrophs, the microbes that live on air
soil-fert-102.text: A small water fern in rice paddies carries its own nitrogen supply. {{ref:soil-fert-204}} harbours the cyanobacterium Anabaena, and farmers value it as a living nitrogen source for rice, the practice covered in {{ref:soil-fert-026}}. Anabaena is a diazotroph: an organism, usually a bacterium or archaeon, that can fix atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds such as ammonia. Diazotrophs are scattered across many groups of bacteria and a few archaea, including rhizobia, Frankia and Azospirillum. Symbiotic diazotrophs were long thought to matter more globally, but free-living ones are also significant fixers. Obligate anaerobes such as Clostridium live in low-oxygen soils and decaying plant matter, and methanogenic archaea fix nitrogen in oxygen-poor soils. Fixation costs so much energy that diazotrophs cut it back when other nitrogen is available and, in many species, when oxygen is high. Aerobic fixers such as Azotobacter vinelandii shield their fixing enzymes, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, with very high respiration rates and protective compounds. On land, diazotrophs supply the nitrogen that primary producers use, and that fixed nitrogen can reduce the need for fertilizer.

soil-found-067.title: The silica cycle runs through plants and stone
soil-found-067.text: Silica freed by dissolving phytoliths is estimated at double the rate of global silicate weathering. The silica cycle moves silica, including silica made by living things, between Earth's systems. On land, weathering is the main source. Plants build phytoliths, rigid silica structures that strengthen their cells and deter herbivores. Rivers carry silica to the ocean at approximately 6 Tmol Si per year, the main land sink. Over 400 years, expanding agriculture has exposed more rock and soil, raising weathering and silica leaching. Through continental weathering, the cycle also helps lock away carbon.

soil-fert-115.title: Ammonia-oxidizing archaea, the overlooked majority
soil-fert-115.text: Until 2005, bacteria were thought to be the only organisms that could oxidize ammonia. Ammonia-oxidizing archaea overturned that idea. These archaea, mainly of the group Nitrososphaerota, carry out the first step of {{ref:soil-fert-112}}, turning ammonia into nitrite. They outnumber ammonia-oxidizing bacteria in both soils and the sea, so they may do more of the work there. Crenarchaeol, a lipid thought to be made only by these archaea, has been proposed as a biomarker, a chemical fingerprint that reveals them.

soil-fert-117.title: Proving that microbes make nitrate
soil-fert-117.text: In 1862 Louis Pasteur suggested that turning ammonia into nitrate is a biological process. Proof came in 1877, when Schloesing and Müntz showed it was microbial, using sewage and sterilized sand. Robert Warington confirmed it in garden soil at the station in {{ref:soil-hist-053}} in 1878. In 1879 Warington first saw that nitrification, the process in {{ref:soil-fert-112}}, has two steps, and John Munro confirmed this in 1886. Percy and Grace Frankland probably isolated the first pure ammonia-oxidizing culture in 1890. Winogradsky succeeded in 1891.

soil-fert-147.title: Nitrobacter, living on a thin energy margin
soil-fert-147.text: Nitrobacter lives on scraps. Oxidizing nitrite to nitrate yields only −74 kJ per mole of nitrite, so its metabolism is highly specialized. This genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria performs the second step of {{ref:soil-fert-112}} in soil and the sea, and it fixes carbon dioxide through the Calvin cycle. All members are obligate aerobes with a doubling time of about 13 hours, so oxygen and phosphorus tend to limit them. Widespread in water and soil, it makes nitrate, a primary source of inorganic nitrogen for plants. It grows best at pH 7.3 to 7.5. Winogradsky named the genus in 1892.

soil-fert-145.title: Bioavailability: the share living things can absorb
soil-fert-145.text: Bioavailability is the amount of an element or compound in soil that an organism can actually take up across its cell membranes. Roots and soil organisms take up almost only dissolved substances. Sorbed or precipitated forms, described in {{ref:soil-chem-068}}, must dissolve again in the soil solution first. Soil pH, ion exchange capacity, organic matter, texture and porosity all shape it. Bioavailability also falls the longer a contaminant stays in contact with soil, an effect called ageing. In farm and environmental use, the term mostly concerns pollutants, for example when judging the risk of spreading sewage sludge.

soil-fert-135.title: Dissimilatory sulfate reduction: breathing sulfate
soil-fert-135.text: Where oxygen is gone, sulfate can stand in for it. In dissimilatory sulfate reduction, microbes use sulfate to oxidize organic compounds, chiefly organic acids, and reduce it to hydrogen sulfide. It is a form of {{ref:soil-chem-128}}. Without microbes, high temperature can do the same, a route called thermochemical reduction. Both give hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide, carbonates, sulfur and metal sulfides. Under reducing conditions these bacteria turn the sulfate of gypsum back into sulfide, and they deposit pyrite in sediments. Beijerinck isolated the first known sulfate reducer, now called Desulfovibrio desulfuricans.

soil-fert-148.title: Sulfate reducers and the smell of the mudflat
soil-fert-148.text: The rotten-egg smell of a mud flat comes from sulfate-reducing microorganisms. These bacteria and archaea respire without oxygen, using sulfate as the final electron acceptor and reducing it to hydrogen sulfide. They reduce large amounts for energy and expel the sulfide. Other organisms reduce only a little sulfate, to build cell parts. They help break down organic matter by oxidizing the organic acids and alcohols left by fermenting bacteria. Their sulfide reacts with metal ions to form insoluble black or brown sulfides such as ferrous sulfide. They are the main source of neurotoxic methylmercury in aquatic systems, and some have helped clean up contaminated soils.

soil-fert-136.title: How coal and oil reshaped the sulfur cycle
soil-fert-136.text: Mining coal and extracting petroleum mobilize 150 × 10^12 g of sulfur a year, more than double the rate of 100 years ago. Sulfur dioxide from this pollution forms sulfuric acid, which can drop rain pH to 4.3 or lower. Over the most polluted areas, sulfate deposition has risen 30-fold. Then the story turned. As pollution controls cut sulfur from the air, sulfur deficiency became widespread in many European countries. Sulfur is now increasingly added to fertilizers. Heavy nitrogen fertilizing on low-sulfur fields can also cause sulfur deficiency by dilution.

soil-fert-134.title: Microbial sulfur oxidation: living on sulfide
soil-fert-134.text: Some microbes run on rotten-egg gas. Microbial sulfur oxidation is the conversion of sulfide and elemental sulfur to sulfate by bacteria and archaea, often to gain energy. Aerobic sulfide oxidizers are usually autotrophs. They use the energy to fix carbon dioxide, the lifestyle described in {{ref:soil-bio-057}}. Intermediates include elemental sulfur and thiosulfate. At low oxygen, microbes stop at elemental sulfur and store it as globules. Photosynthetic green and purple sulfur bacteria, and some chemolithotrophs, oxidize hydrogen sulfide to elemental sulfur.

soil-fert-137.title: The potassium cycle and the fields that drain it
soil-fert-137.text: Crops take potassium from fields faster than weathering puts it back. So of the 32 Tg mined each year, about 28 Tg goes onto farmland, mostly as potassium chloride. The potassium cycle moves potassium through Earth's rocks, soils, living things, air and waters. With nitrogen and phosphorus, potassium is one of the three major nutrients plants need in large amounts, as {{ref:soil-fert-175}} described. It controls the opening of stomata, the pores in leaves. Potassium makes up 2.6% of Earth's crust, held in feldspar, biotite and muscovite. Chemical weathering supplies up to 11% of plant demand. Some plants and bacteria release organic acids that make soil potassium accessible, and plants can 'pump' it from deeper layers to the surface. It is the most abundant ion in plant cells. Because it exists only as the small, soluble K+ ion, it leaches from plants faster than nitrogen or phosphorus. It returns to the soil as plant matter decays, so leaving crop leftovers to decay on fields limits depletion. At current use, K2O reserves are expected to last 100 years. Leaching and erosion carry 1400 Tg of potassium a year to groundwater, rivers and oceans. The hydrosphere, Earth's water, is the largest potassium reservoir.

soil-fert-131.title: Mining phosphorus faster than rocks can replace it
soil-fert-131.text: From 1900 to 2022, global phosphate mining rose 72-fold. About 110 teragrams of phosphorus have been added to the environment since mining spread in the 1840s, speeding up {{ref:soil-fert-127}}. Most mined phosphorus becomes fertilizer, and at current rates the geological system cannot replace what is taken. Repeated excess applications of liquid hog manure harm the cycle, and treated sewage solids can raise available soil phosphorus. Over the last 40 years the N:P ratio has risen from 19:1 to 30:1, leaving phosphorus less available to ecosystems.

soil-fert-130.title: Enzymes that free phosphorus from dead matter
soil-fert-130.text: Plant growth depends on roots quickly taking up the phosphorus released from dead organic matter. Organic phosphorus mineralization is the breakdown of organic phosphorus compounds by enzymes into free phosphate that plants and microbes can use. Phosphatases, nucleases and phytase are among the enzymes involved, members of the group in {{ref:soil-bio-039}}. This hydrolysis, the splitting of molecules with water, is essential for plant and microbial nutrition, and it moves organic phosphorus from soil to water. Soil phosphatase activity can serve as an indicator of phosphorus mineralization potential and availability.

soil-fert-118.title: Soil nitrous oxide: a greenhouse gas from microbes
soil-fert-118.text: Most of a soil's yearly nitrous oxide can escape in a few short 'hot moments' or from small 'hotspots', which makes it hard to measure. Soil nitrous oxide emissions are the release of this gas as a by-product of {{ref:soil-fert-112}} and {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. Nitrous oxide is the third most important greenhouse gas for warming and a major ozone-depleting substance. Microbes make it by several routes: autotrophic nitrification, heterotrophic denitrification, nitrifier denitrification and fungal denitrification. A non-biological route, chemodenitrification, adds more. Output depends on the supply of mineral nitrogen and organic matter, acidity, soil type, soil temperature and water content. Soils under natural vegetation give 60% of naturally produced nitrous oxide. Farming adds more. Cultivation, fertilizer nitrogen and the handling of animal waste stimulate soil bacteria to produce the gas. Fertilized farm soils and livestock manure make up 42% of human emissions, and runoff and leaching of fertilizers another 25%. There are remedies. Modest additions of charred organic matter, the material in {{ref:soil-fert-050}}, can cut emissions by up to 80%.

soil-fert-101.title: Nitrogenase, the costly enzyme that splits the air
soil-fert-101.text: Each reaction of nitrogenase burns 16 ATP, the cell's energy currency, and wastes some as hydrogen gas. That makes fixation expensive. Nitrogenase is the enzyme complex that reduces nitrogen gas to ammonia in nitrogen-fixing microbes such as those in {{ref:soil-fert-102}}. It has two proteins: a catalytic MoFe protein and a reducing Fe protein that contains only iron. The nitrogen is converted at a metal cluster called FeMoco. Three forms carry molybdenum, iron or vanadium in the active site, and the molybdenum form is the most common. Oxygen rapidly destroys it. Many bacteria stop making it when oxygen is present, and cyanobacteria house it in special cells called heterocysts.

soil-fert-120.title: Bacteria that eat methane by breathing nitrate
soil-fert-120.text: In deep lakes such as Lake Constance, bacteria that burn methane with nitrate are a dominant methane sink. Denitrification-coupled methane oxidation is the oxygen-free oxidation of methane by denitrifying bacteria, which use the electrons to reduce nitrate. It removes methane and fixed nitrogen at once. First observed in 2008, it works in habitats from sediments to waterlogged peat and layered water columns. In Lake Constance it is the work of Methylomirabilis oxyfera-like bacteria. It can strip excess nitrate from fertilizer runoff even when oxygen is scarce.

soil-fert-126.title: The nitrogen cascade: one atom, many harms
soil-fert-126.text: The same nitrogen can cause trouble again and again. The nitrogen cascade is the passage of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next, with effects at each step. Most reactive nitrogen applied to farmland cascades through air, water and land until {{ref:soil-fert-108}} turns it back into nitrogen gas. That final microbial step matters, because the atmosphere is the ultimate sink for reactive nitrogen. Some systems store reactive nitrogen along the way, delaying the cascade and intensifying its local effects. Managed vegetated borders, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-158}}, and wet areas can remove much of the nitrate leaving farms, damping the cascade.

soil-fert-124.title: Nitrogen deposition: fertilizer falling from the sky
soil-fert-124.text: Reactive nitrogen falls from the sky. Nitrogen deposition is its arrival from the atmosphere onto land and water. It comes as nitrate, ammonium and organic nitrogen in rain and snow, as ammonia and nitric acid gases, or as fine aerosol particles of the salt in {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. More of it can acidify soils, streams and lakes and change forest and grassland productivity. Grasslands gain at first, then decline past critical thresholds. Extra nitrogen favours fast-growing plants that shade out slower ones, so species richness falls. On nitrogen-poor heathland, invading grasses replace heath. Ammonia and ammonium can also harm plants adapted to nitrate, stunting their roots and shoots.

soil-fert-125.title: Nitrogen saturation: when a forest has too much
soil-fert-125.text: At Harvard Forest, 15 years of added nitrogen brought more leaching, higher pine mortality and an end to biomass gain. Nitrogen saturation is the state in which available nitrogen exceeds what plants, soil and microbes can take up, so the excess is lost to water and air. At first, microbes often lock added nitrogen away, the process of {{ref:soil-fert-121}}. Whether extra nitrogen helps forests is still disputed: studies report both gains and losses in growth and carbon storage. Saturation can upset nutrient balance, for example as calcium leaches away with nitrate, and may lead to forest decline.

soil-fert-110.title: Comammox: one microbe doing both shifts
soil-fert-110.text: Nitrification was long thought to need two groups of microbes, one making nitrite from ammonia and another making nitrate from nitrite. A single organism doing both was predicted in 2006 and found in 2015, in the genus Nitrospira. This complete ammonia oxidation, or comammox, prompted an update to the nitrogen cycle. It pays. The full oxidation yields −349 kJ per mol of ammonia, more than ammonia oxidation at −275 kJ or nitrite oxidation at −74 kJ alone. Comammox occurs in freshwater, on land and in water-treatment systems, but its genes are not abundant in the oceans.

soil-fert-109.title: Nitrate ammonification: keeping nitrogen in the soil
soil-fert-109.text: Not every microbe that breathes nitrate sends the nitrogen away. Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium, also called nitrate ammonification, is a respiration without oxygen. Microbes oxidize organic matter and reduce nitrate to nitrite, then to ammonium. Unlike {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, which loses nitrogen as gas, it keeps nitrogen available as soluble ammonium, and the two groups of microbes compete for nitrate. It usually makes up about 15% of total nitrate reduction, favoured where organic carbon is plentiful relative to nitrate. Only organisms with the nrf gene can carry it out. Some nitrous oxide may still escape, more at higher pH.

soil-fert-111.title: Anammox: ammonium straight to nitrogen gas
soil-fert-111.text: Some bacteria turn ammonium and nitrite directly into nitrogen gas and water, with no oxygen and no organic carbon. This is anammox, short for anaerobic ammonium oxidation. Bacteria of the phylum Planctomycetota, first identified in 1999, do it inside a membrane-bound compartment called the anammoxosome. Unlike {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, it uses ammonium and nitrite directly and releases less nitrous oxide. It occurs in freshwater lakes, riverbanks and farm soils such as rice paddies. In the ocean it may account for 30–50% of the nitrogen lost.

soil-fert-138.title: Soil potassium pools: mostly locked away
soil-fert-138.text: Almost all soil potassium is out of a plant's reach. The soil holds it in three pools. Fixed potassium, locked in feldspar, mica and illite, makes up 96–99% of the total. Exchangeable potassium, held on clay particles and organic matter by {{ref:soil-chem-047}}, makes up 1–2%. Potassium dissolved in soil solution is the form plants absorb most readily, yet it is only 0.1–0.2% of the total. Soil potassium is most concentrated in the uppermost layers.

soil-fert-132.title: Phosphate solubilizing bacteria: freeing locked phosphorus
soil-fert-132.text: Coating seed with the right bacteria can replace half the phosphate fertilizer a crop needs. Seed inoculation can match 30 kg/ha P2O5, or 50 percent of the need. Phosphate solubilizing bacteria are beneficial soil bacteria that dissolve inorganic phosphate from insoluble compounds, the form described in {{ref:soil-fert-129}}. They release small organic acids whose hydroxyl and carboxyl groups grab the cations bound to phosphate, so it dissolves. Mycorrhizal fungi release oxalic acid, freeing phosphorus held by aluminium, iron and calcium. In the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}, this solubilizing is considered one of the most important traits for plant phosphate nutrition.

soil-fert-001.title: Fertilizer, the material behind up to half of every harvest
soil-fert-001.text: Conservative estimates credit fertilizers with 30 to 50% of what crops yield. A fertilizer is any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or to plant tissues to supply plant nutrients, the elements described in {{ref:soil-fert-181}}. That supply is what sets it apart from acid-correcting materials and other additions that bring no nutrients. Modern fertilization centers on three macronutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Ground rock, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-075}}, sometimes supplements them with micronutrients. Most fertilizers work by feeding the plant, but some also improve the soil's water-holding capacity and aeration. Before synthetic products, farmers kept their land fertile with decomposed organic waste, animal and human dung, mined minerals, rotating crops and by-products such as fish waste or bloodmeal. How much to apply depends on the crop and on {{ref:soil-fert-149}}, usually measured by a soil test. Legumes fix their own nitrogen and generally need no nitrogen fertilizer. The scale is vast. In 2023 agriculture used 190 million tonnes of inorganic fertilizer nutrients, and 112 million tonnes of that, 58%, was nitrogen. Excess carries a price. Nutrients washed off fields pollute water and overfeed it, the process in {{ref:soil-env-020}}, and some mined fertilizers add heavy metals to soil.

soil-fert-028.title: Compost, waste turned back into living soil
soil-fert-028.text: About a fifth of landfill waste is food and other material that could have rotted usefully elsewhere. Decaying without oxygen in a landfill, it releases methane. Compost is the alternative: a mixture of decomposed organic materials used as plant fertilizer and to improve the soil's physical, chemical and biological properties. It forms when plant and food waste, recycled organic materials and animal dung break down, the process of {{ref:soil-bio-115}}. The finished product teems with life, from bacteria and fungi to protozoa and nematodes. Worked into the ground, it feeds crops, conditions the soil and adds organic matter, raising its humus or humic acid content. Its microbes widen the soil's microbial diversity and suppress pathogens and soil-borne diseases. Gardens, horticulture, urban agriculture and {{ref:soil-agri-135}} use it to depend less on chemical fertilizers. Compost also reclaims land and streams, helps construct new marshland and covers landfills. Decomposing waste in heaps and long rows is also one way to clean polluted ground, the approach in {{ref:soil-env-023}}. Alkaline soils containing solid calcium carbonate can be reclaimed by working in compost and other acidifying organic materials. The practice is old. Cato the Elder described it in 160 BCE, in the early Roman Empire, and the first industrial compost station opened in Wels, Austria, in 1921.

soil-fert-063.title: Soil conditioners loosen, feed and rebalance the ground
soil-fert-063.text: Compacted soil can starve a plant that sits among plenty, because its roots struggle to take up water and nutrients. Loosening it is the most common job of a soil conditioner. That is a material added to soil to improve its physical qualities, usually its fertility and sometimes its mechanics. Conditioners are usually seen as a subset of soil amendments, a broader category that also takes in many fertilizers and non-organic materials. Examples range from straw, peat, vermiculite and sulfur to water-absorbing polymers, compost and {{ref:soil-fert-050}}. Many add carbon, nitrogen, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, and amendments can greatly raise cation-exchange capacity. Organic material can greatly improve water retention in sandy soils. Conditioners can also adjust pH for particular plants, or make very acid or alkaline soils usable. A soil test should come first, to show which one suits the soil. Too much harms plants through excess salts, nitrogen and metals, and surplus nutrients can run off into waterways. Builders use the same idea under another name, described in {{ref:soil-agri-076}}.

soil-fert-066.title: Mulch, a blanket laid over the soil
soil-fert-066.text: A layer just 5 centimetres (2 in) deep can change what happens beneath it. Mulch is a layer of material applied to the surface of soil, and such layers are normally that deep or deeper. It conserves {{ref:soil-water-155}}, improves fertility and soil health, suppresses weeds, regulates soil temperature and makes beds look better. Mulch is usually organic but not always. Plastic sheeting is permanent; bark chips are temporary. Early in the season, mulch keeps in heat that would otherwise escape at night, warming the soil enough for earlier sowing. Later it steadies both temperature and moisture. It cuts evaporation, but it can also catch light rain, and overly thick layers can reduce oxygen in the soil. On slopes it is laid to prevent erosion. Worms and other organisms work mulches of compost and animal dung into the soil on their own. The choice of material weighs availability, cost, appearance, effects on soil chemistry and pH, durability, decomposition rate and freedom from weed seeds and pathogens.

soil-fert-050.title: Biochar, charcoal made to be buried
soil-fert-050.text: Charcoal made for the soil can persist there for thousands of years. Biochar is a form of {{ref:soil-class-083}}, sometimes modified, made by heating biomass with little oxygen. What remains after this pyrolysis is a light, black residue of carbon and ash. It is sterile when made and comes alive only after soil organisms reach it. Farmers add it mainly to improve aeration and fertility, cut greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient leaching, and reduce acidity. It may also raise the water content of coarse soils. Too much, or a feedstock unsuited to the soil, can harm soil organisms, reduce available water, alter pH and raise salinity. The word, joining the Greek bios, life, with char, dates from the late 20th century, but the practice is older. Pre-Columbian Amazonians smoldered farm waste under soil in pits or trenches, and settlers called the result terra preta. Whether those farmers meant to improve the soil is unknown. Beyond soils, biochar goes into animal feed, concrete mixes and water treatment, where it removes heavy metals, dyes and organic pollutants.

soil-fert-014.title: The hidden bill for feeding the world's crops
soil-fert-014.text: Fertilizer washing off farmland helps create dead zones in the ocean. That is one of the direct costs of fertilizers, whose production and use harm water, soil, air and ecosystems. It also contaminates waterways, the soil microbiome degrades and toxic compounds accumulate. Indirect costs reach further: nitrogen-crop-pest cascades, fracking for the gas the Haber process needs, and the biodiversity and soil loss tied to industrial agriculture. The climate pays too. Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, with methane supplying the hydrogen for ammonia. The IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land names fertilizer production and its associated land use among the drivers of global warming. Organic sources are not blameless, since too much pig slurry can contaminate aquifers and overfeed the waters they supply. Solar energy, waste treatment and electrolysis are proposed alternatives for production. On the farm, plowing less and planting the streamside borders of {{ref:soil-agri-158}} can lessen the damage. Policy favors sustainable or regenerative farming, with less synthetic fertilizer, better care of the soil and more of the biological fertilizers in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}.

soil-fert-011.title: Feeding the crop when it is hungry
soil-fert-011.text: A crop's appetite is not constant. Its nutrient uptake peaks from early to mid-season, so fertilizer applied near seeding works well. Fertilizer timing means matching when and how much fertilizer goes on to the crop's needs, the weather and the type of farming, a core part of {{ref:soil-fert-192}}. Hitting peak demand is essential for both yield and quality. For fall-planted grains such as winter wheat, autumn nitrogen followed by a spring topdressing is likely the best combination. Weather matters too. Soluble fertilizers such as {{ref:soil-fert-071}} are not applied during heavy rain, which would carry most of it away and pollute the aquifer. Farms practicing {{ref:soil-agri-065}}, and smallholdings, cut mineral fertilizer to the crop's strict needs, sometimes to none. After harvest, a fast-growing, nitrogen-hungry crop such as white mustard can take up leftover nitrate before it reaches groundwater. Buried afterward, it forms humus.

soil-fert-002.title: From ancient dung to factory nitrogen
soil-fert-002.text: Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans all left records of using minerals or animal dung to make their farms more productive. The industry came much later. {{ref:soil-hist-004}} is often called the father of the fertilizer industry, although scientific study of plant nutrition began before him. In 1837 {{ref:soil-hist-074}} began testing fertilizing materials on potted plants. In 1842 he patented phosphates treated with sulfuric acid, founding the artificial fertilizer industry. He and Joseph Henry Gilbert then ran crop experiments together at the Institute of Arable Crops Research. Industrial nitrogen began with processes such as Birkeland–Eyde, which fixed atmospheric nitrogen into nitric acid. The Haber and Ostwald processes rose in the 1910s and 1920s. After World War II, nitrogen plants expanded for bomb making were turned to farm use. Between 1961 and 2019 nitrogen fertilizer use grew 800%, a crucial part of the farm productivity gains described in {{ref:soil-agri-138}}. Phosphate use climbed from 9 million tonnes a year in 1960 to 40 million in 2000.

soil-fert-003.title: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium: the big three of fertilizer
soil-fert-003.text: Three letters, NPK, sum up most of what fertilizers deliver: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Fertilizers supply these in varying proportions, along with micronutrients. Each has its own job. Nitrogen drives leaf and stem growth. Phosphorus builds roots, flowers, seeds and fruit. Potassium gives strong stems and aids water movement, flowering and fruiting. None is applied as a pure element; fertilizers are compounds that contain them. Nitrogen matters most, as part of proteins, DNA and chlorophyll. The air holds plenty of it, but in a form plants cannot use. Plants get it from weathering of nitrogen-bearing rocks and from bacteria that fix it, some free-living and some in legume roots. Phosphate goes into DNA, the energy carrier ATP and the phospholipids of cell membranes. Macronutrients make up 0.15% to 6.0% of plant dry matter. Overfertilized plants take up more than they need, a habit called luxury consumption. Calcium, long thought a luxury, is now considered essential for keeping cell walls and membranes intact.

soil-fert-004.title: Sorting fertilizers by nutrient count and origin
soil-fert-004.text: Every fertilizer sits on two scales at once: how many nutrients it carries, and where it came from. On the first scale, straight fertilizers supply a single nutrient such as N, P or K. Multinutrient, or complex, fertilizers supply two or more. NP fertilizers supply nitrogen and phosphorus together. Monoammonium phosphate, or MAP, holds 11% N and 48% P2O5; DAP, the fertilizer in {{ref:soil-fert-206}}, holds 18% N and 46% P2O5. NPK fertilizers supply all three main nutrients, in two styles. Compound NPKs bind the nutrients chemically, while blends are physical mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers. The second scale is origin. Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-bearing materials, except {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. They are also called synthetic, because chemical treatments are needed to make them. The other class, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}, is usually recycled plant- or animal-derived matter such as compost or animal dung. Solubility also differs between products. More than 90% of a typical {{ref:soil-fert-094}} dissolves in water, against about 85% of MAP and DAP.

soil-fert-007.title: Nitrogen fertilizer, pulled from the air by industry
soil-fert-007.text: About a third of the world's annual food production relies on ammonia from the {{ref:soil-fert-104}}, supporting nearly half the world's population. Nitrogen fertilizers are made from that ammonia. In this energy-intensive process, natural gas usually supplies the hydrogen and the air supplies the nitrogen. The ammonia is then the feedstock for other fertilizers, such as {{ref:soil-fert-071}} and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and the Ostwald process turns it into nitrates. That salt of ammonium and nitrate carries 34-35% nitrogen. Blended with limestone or dolomite, it carries 24-28%. Sodium nitrate, or Chilean saltpeter, from the Atacama Desert was one of the first nitrogen fertilizers, used from 1830 and still mined. In 2012 the world used about 110 million tons of nitrogen fertilizer a year. Only part becomes plant matter; the rest accumulates in the soil or washes away. In soil, bacteria such as Nitrosomonas oxidize ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate, which dissolves readily and is easily leached.

soil-fert-021.title: Urea, from urine and the laboratory to the field
soil-fert-021.text: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from inorganic starting materials, contradicting the doctrine of vitalism. Urea is a simple organic nitrogen compound, CO(NH2)2, found in mammal urine. More than 90% of the world's industrial urea now goes onto fields as a nitrogen-release fertilizer. At 45-46% nitrogen, it has the highest nitrogen content of the common solid nitrogen fertilizers. That makes it cheap to transport per unit of nitrogen, and it is non-explosive. In the soil, bacteria with the enzyme urease convert it to ammonium, which roots take up. In some soils, bacteria then oxidize the ammonium to nitrate. Nitrogen lost to the air or washed away is wasteful and harmful, so urea is coated in inert sealants or converted to urea-formaldehyde compounds that release nitrogen slowly. Urea washed off fertilized land may help make algal blooms toxic. Biuret, the most common impurity in synthetic urea, impairs plant growth. Where it is cheap, urea also reduces soil alkalinity: ammonium from its hydrolysis displaces sodium from the soil's exchange sites.

soil-fert-010.title: Organic fertilizers: plant food from living things
soil-fert-010.text: Seaweed, feathers and treated sewage can all feed a crop. Organic fertilizers are fertilizers of biological origin, derived from living or formerly living materials, the stuff of {{ref:soil-bio-114}}. They include animal wastes, crop wastes, seaweed, compost and treated sewage sludge, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-045}}. Slaughter adds bloodmeal, feather meal and {{ref:soil-fert-090}}. The term also covers packaged products that meet the rules of {{ref:soil-agri-135}}, which limit or avoid synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. Sewage sludge may be unacceptable there, because of residual contaminants and public perception. Most organic fertilizers hold less-concentrated nutrients that are harder to quantify, but they can build soil. Compost can raise nutrient availability by improving cation-exchange capacity or by boosting microbes that free nutrients. Peat, the most used packaged organic amendment, improves aeration and moisture but adds no nutrients, so it is an amendment rather than a fertilizer. Fresh sawdust can draw down soil nitrogen as wood-decay fungi colonize it, which can also capture excess mineral nitrogen.

soil-fert-023.title: Manure, the oldest way to feed a field
soil-fert-023.text: Long before factories made fertilizer, Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans were recorded using manure or minerals to make their farms more productive. Manure is organic matter, mostly animal feces, used as organic fertilizer in agriculture. In managing soil today it stands beside two other main classes: compost and {{ref:soil-fert-026}}. Manure builds fertility through a chain. It adds organic matter and nutrients such as nitrogen. Those feed soil bacteria and fungi, which in turn feed the rest of the soil food web. Like compost or mulch, it can also change a soil's {{ref:soil-fert-184}}. Long manuring leaves a lasting mark in the soil profile. Anthrosols of northwestern Europe often carry plaggic or terric horizons, built this way, across some 500,000 hectares. Language has shifted too. The term artificial manure, once in wide use, meant what are now called artificial fertilizers. Manure has also become a product: it is composted, bagged and sold as a soil amendment.

soil-fert-026.title: Green manure, a crop grown to be plowed under
