soil-fert-026.text: Greek farmers were plowing beans into the soil by about 300 BC, and the Romans used faba beans and lupines. Colonists later carried the practice to North America. Green manure is a crop grown specifically to be worked into the soil while still green. Its biomass is plowed or disced in, as with ordinary manure, mainly to add organic matter. Legumes such as clover and vetch are favorites, because their root-nodule bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, as described in {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre) of nitrogen is released. Usually 40-60% of the green crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop. Decay also releases phosphorus, potassium and sulfur, and deep-rooted species bring up nutrients that shallower crops cannot reach. The added organic matter, microbial mycelium and sticky substances improve aggregation, infiltration, water retention and aeration. While growing, the crop suppresses weeds, helps control erosion and feeds pollinators. In alkali soils it lowers pH by generating humic acid.

soil-fert-076.title: Carbon farming: putting the air's carbon back in the field
soil-fert-076.text: Turning forest, grassland or savanna into cropland cuts the organic carbon in its soil by about 30–40%, largely because harvests remove carbon-bearing plant material. Carbon farming tries to reverse that. It is a set of methods that aim to store carbon in soil and biomass, for a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere. Farmers change how they plow, graze and choose crops, spread compost or plant-based mulch, and work with biochar and terra preta. Leaving harvest residues, applying manure or rotating in deep-rooted perennial crops all add carbon back. The gains are reversible. Disturbance or heavy plowing turns soil into a greenhouse gas source, and after several decades soils saturate and stop absorbing carbon. The method costs US$3–130 per tonne of CO2 sequestered, depending on region. Some claims remain disputed: many researchers question the carbon benefits claimed for {{ref:soil-env-090}}, and the effect of added carbon on yields is not settled.

soil-fert-059.title: Agricultural lime, crushed rock against acid soil
soil-fert-059.text: Soils turn acid in three main ways: leaching under high rainfall, crops removing minerals, and the reactions of modern chemical fertilizers. Agricultural lime is a common answer. It is pulverized limestone or chalk whose main active component is calcium carbonate. Unlike quicklime and slaked lime, ground limestone needs no burning in a kiln, only milling. All these limes supply a base that corrects acidity. Lime raises the pH of acid soils, supplies calcium, helps water penetrate, and improves plant uptake of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Still, lime is not a fertilizer, though it can be used together with one. Dolomitic lime acts similarly but supplies magnesium as well as calcium. A soil test is the best way to tell whether a soil is acid or short of calcium or magnesium. Fields once usually received burnt lime instead, because affordable fine milling of stone only developed after the mid-19th century. Wood ash, magnesium oxide, basic slag, silicate rock dust and oyster shells also raise soil pH.

soil-fert-055.title: Liming: calcium against the aluminum in acid soil
soil-fert-055.text: Most acid soils are saturated not with hydrogen ions but with aluminum, and their acidity generally comes from aluminum hydrolysis. Liming answers that by adding calcium- and magnesium-rich materials such as chalk, limestone, burnt lime, hydrated lime or {{ref:soil-fert-079}}. In acid soils these act as a base and neutralize acidity, often improving plant growth and soil bacterial activity. Oversupply, though, can harm plants. Sandy, heavily leached or strongly acid mineral soils are low in calcium and need liming most. It can also offset the poor cation-exchange capacity that lets potassium leach away. Raising the pH frequently relieves molybdenum deficiency by decreasing molybdenum sorption. Not every effect is welcome. A German forestry study comparing stands two and twenty years after liming found it washed more nitrate out of the soil and lowered phosphorus in some leaves. Before modern liming, farmers spread raw chalk and lime debris, a practice with evidence dating to the 1200s in the British Isles.

soil-fert-073.title: Leachate, the liquid that carries a material away
soil-fert-073.text: Rain falling on a landfill does not leave it clean. Leachate is any liquid that passes through a material and carries away its dissolved or suspended components. In environmental science, the word means a liquid carrying harmful substances that can enter the environment, most often from landfills. Compost sites produce it in wet periods, as rain washes decomposed matter away. Stockpiled coal and mine wastes yield it when exposed sulfide minerals form sulfuric acid, often rich in metals. Acidic leachate flushed from acid sulfate soils can harm groundwater and surface waters, with effects that may persist or peak after dry spells.

soil-fert-072.title: Perlite, volcanic glass that swells in the heat
soil-fert-072.text: Heated to 850–900 °C, perlite swells to 7–16 times its original volume. Perlite is an amorphous volcanic glass, usually formed by hydration of obsidian. The heat vaporizes its trapped water and leaves a brilliant white material. As a soil amendment it is highly permeable, holds little water and helps prevent compaction. On its own it serves for hydroponics and for rooting cuttings. In potting mixes, perlite and vermiculite improve aeration and water retention. Cacti and succulents need a large share of perlite or sand for drainage.

soil-fert-034.title: Using finished compost on fields and in beds
soil-fert-034.text: A field needs only a thin dusting of compost, about 6 mm (0.24 in). Compost applied is finished compost used on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients (see {{ref:soil-fert-028}}). On open fields it is broadcast in that thin layer and worked in before planting. A layer of 25 mm (0.98 in) or more is used to rebuild poor soils or control erosion. Added to soil, coir or peat, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients. Tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility. Compost is rarely used alone. It is mixed with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules, and blends of 20-30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings. Seeding directly into compost is not advised: it dries fast, immature compost may hold germination-inhibiting phytotoxins, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen. Ready compost is dark brown or black with an earthy smell, and it can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests. Finished compost supplies little readily available nitrogen, since composting converts much N to stable organic forms while P and K availability is unchanged. It still releases other nutrients slowly and raises organic matter. Annual high rates set by nitrogen need overload soil with phosphorus and potassium, and salts may build up under high tunnels and greenhouses. Soil tests should guide a switch to legume cover crops.

soil-fert-029.title: Inside a compost heap: carbon, nitrogen, air and water
soil-fert-029.text: A well-run compost heap holds itself at 54–71 °C (130–160 °F) until its materials are broken down. Composting is the aerobic decomposition of organic solid wastes into compost, a humus-like material. Its organisms need four ingredients. Carbon gives energy, and its oxidation releases heat. Nitrogen lets them grow. Oxygen oxidizes the carbon. Water must be plentiful, but never waterlogging. Aerobic bacteria need oxygen above 5%, so heaps are turned to keep up both oxygen and the right moisture. Bacteria and fungi convert the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide and ammonium ions, and over months the materials become humus. The recipe hinges on the {{ref:soil-fert-184}}. Composting runs most efficiently at about 25:1. Above 30 the mix is starved of nitrogen; below 15 it tends to lose nitrogen as ammonia. Green waste such as grass, leaves and food scraps supplies nitrogen. Brown waste such as stalks, paper and wood chips supplies carbon. Fresh grass sits near 15:1, dry autumn leaves near 50:1. On farms, manure is the usual nitrogen source and bedding such as straw or sawdust the carbon source. Poultry manure needs blending with high-carbon materials, and wet pig manure with straw.

soil-fert-019.title: What heavy fertilizing does to life underground
soil-fert-019.text: Heavy fertilizer use, especially beyond plant needs, can break down the symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi. Organic and organic–mineral fertilizers increase the abundance of soil animals, while mineral fertilizers do not. Chemical fertilizers boost microbial growth without changing its diversity. Acid stress combined with high nitrogen, rare before industrial agriculture, weakens the links between the aboveground and belowground parts of farm ecosystems. Nitrogen deposition is even turning Sphagnum bogs from stores of carbon into sources of it, by stimulating decomposers. How fertilizers affect soil animals is still debated, since group-specific responses mask the overall effect.

soil-fert-020.title: The climate cost of nitrogen fertilizer
soil-fert-020.text: Around 5% of human greenhouse gas emissions come from making and using nitrogen fertilizer. The gases are carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. About one third comes from production and two thirds from use in the field. Soil bacteria convert nitrate to nitrous oxide, the third most important greenhouse gas. Per ton it is 296 times stronger than carbon dioxide, and it also contributes to ozone depletion. Human nitrous oxide emissions, mostly from fertilizer, came to an estimated 700 million tons of CO2 equivalent between 2007 and 2016. Ammonium-based fertilizers also increase methane emissions from crop fields, notably rice paddies.

soil-fert-006.title: Micronutrient fertilizers: tiny doses, outsized effects
soil-fert-006.text: Some plant nutrients occur in tissue at just 0.15 to 400 ppm, less than 0.04% of dry matter. Yet as enzyme co-factors, their impact far exceeds their concentration. Micronutrient fertilizers supply these elements, typically boron, zinc, molybdenum, iron and manganese, as water-soluble salts. Iron is often given as a chelate such as EDTA or EDDHA, because at moderate pH and phosphate it turns insoluble. Needs depend on plant and setting. Sugar beets need boron and legumes cobalt, while heat or drought makes boron less available. Zinc deficiency is common in soils worldwide, affecting plants and people alike, and zinc fertilizers are widely used against it.

soil-fert-005.title: Reading the three numbers on a fertilizer bag
soil-fert-005.text: A bag marked 10-10-10 carries three promises. The NPK rating is a label of three numbers, separated by dashes, giving a fertilizer's content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. They are percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O. Yet the fertilizer contains no actual P2O5 or K2O; the oxides are a conventional shorthand for its phosphorus and potassium. UK rules let the elemental phosphorus and potassium values follow in parentheses, so a label can read 15-30-15 (15-13-13). Australia adds a fourth number, for sulfur, and gives elemental values for all nutrients.

soil-fert-071.title: Ammonium nitrate, stable nitrogen with a dangerous edge
soil-fert-071.text: The salt that feeds a wheat field can, mixed with fuel, become an explosive. Ammonium nitrate is a salt of ammonium and nitrate ions and an important nitrogen fertilizer, with an NPK rating of 34-0-0. It is less concentrated than urea, at 46-0-0, but more stable, and it does not rapidly lose nitrogen to the atmosphere. Factories make it by reacting ammonia from the Haber process with nitric acid. Natural deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert were mined until the Haber–Bosch process made nitrate mining obsolete. Because it forms explosive mixtures with fuels, it is a greater security risk than urea, which is not an oxidizer.

soil-fert-009.title: Potash, named for ashes soaked in a pot
soil-fert-009.text: Before the industrial era, potash was made by soaking plant or wood ashes in water in a pot, which gave it its name. Potash is a mixture of potassium minerals, and potassium fertilizers are made from it. About 90% of potash goes to fertilizer. Potassium is the third major crop nutrient, after nitrogen and phosphorus. The main straight potassium fertilizer is muriate of potash, 95–99% potassium chloride. Others are potassium sulfate, carbonate or nitrate. Labels report potassium as K2O equivalent for comparison, though plants do not take up K2O and the fertilizers contain none.

soil-fert-012.title: Granules or solutions: the two forms of fertilizer
soil-fert-012.text: About 90% of fertilizers reach crops as solids: granules, powders or prills. Urea, potassium chloride and the compound in {{ref:soil-fert-206}} are the most common. Liquid fertilizers are water-based solutions of ammonia, urea or the salt in {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. Liquids act faster and cover more evenly, while granules are cheaper to ship, store and apply. Dissolving fertilizer in the water piped to crops is the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-208}}. It places nutrients where the water goes and allows small doses, reducing fertilizer use and leaching. Growers use it mostly on high-value crops such as vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals.

soil-fert-018.title: Why foods hold fewer trace minerals than they used to
soil-fert-018.text: Iron, zinc, copper and magnesium concentrations in many foods have fallen over the last 50–60 years. Why is still argued. Intensive farming with synthetic fertilizers is often blamed, and farming without them is often proposed as the remedy. The evidence points mostly elsewhere. Higher yields driven by NPK fertilizers do dilute other nutrients. But much of the decline is attributed to higher-yielding crop varieties with lower mineral concentrations. Fertilizers more often cure trace deficiencies than cause them. Zinc, copper, manganese, iron and molybdenum shortages found in Western Australia in the 1940s and 1950s are now corrected routinely.

soil-fert-048.title: Biofertilizers: living microbes as plant food
soil-fert-048.text: Some fertilizers are alive. A biofertilizer contains living microorganisms that colonize the {{ref:soil-bio-143}} or the plant's interior and promote growth by increasing the supply or availability of nutrients. They add nutrients by fixing nitrogen and dissolving phosphorus. Plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria and mycorrhizae make inorganic phosphorus soluble, raise mineral bioavailability and produce hormones such as auxins and gibberellin. The microbes also restore the soil's natural nutrient cycle and build organic matter. They suppress plant pathogens, protect against drought and other stresses, and detoxify pollutants below ground. Reported yield increases reach about 10–40%. Effects vary between and even within environments, and are most marked in drier climates. Biofertilizers can reduce synthetic fertilizer and pesticide use but cannot yet replace them. Compost-based inoculants serve too, including those made from {{ref:soil-fert-035}} and {{ref:soil-fert-039}}.

soil-fert-024.title: Animal manure, from farmyard straw to liquid slurry
soil-fert-024.text: Not all dung is equal. Animal manure comes from livestock dung and urine, handled either as farmyard manure or as liquid slurry. Farmyard manure includes straw bedding that has soaked up feces and urine. Slurry comes from intensive units that use concrete or slats instead of straw. Manures from horses, cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry, and guano from seabirds and bats, differ in quality and need different application rates. Sheep manure is high in nitrogen and potash, and pig manure relatively low in both. Cattle manure supplies nitrogen and organic carbon; chicken litter is rich in nitrogen and phosphate. Fresh poultry droppings harm plants but become valuable fertilizer after composting. Horse manure can carry grass and weed seeds, because horses do not digest seeds as cattle do. Manure improves soil aggregation, so the soil holds more water and nutrients. Strong-smelling slurries, such as those from intensive pig farms, are usually injected into the soil to limit odor.

soil-fert-075.title: Rock flour, ground stone that feeds the soil
soil-fert-075.text: Glaciers grinding over bedrock leave behind rock flour: fine, silt-sized rock particles. Artificial grinding gives a similar powder. The particles are ground quartz and feldspar, not clay minerals, and wind can carry them far to form loess. As rock dust, it serves organic growers as a soil conditioner that supplies micronutrients. Basalt and granite are richest, while limestone is often deficient. A 2022 study found basalt dust raised available phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium within months. Nutrient-poor soils may need 10 to 50 tonnes per hectare. The German miller Julius Hensel reported success with stonemeal in the 1890s.

soil-fert-079.title: Marl, the clay-and-carbonate earth of lakes and fens
soil-fert-079.text: Marl is an earthy material rich in carbonate minerals, clay and silt. It typically holds 35–65% clay and 65–35% carbonate, mostly calcite, and hardens into marlstone. It forms in marine or fresh water, often through algae. Marl lakes in recently glaciated areas, and very rich fens, deposit it from calcium-rich water. Farmers use it as a soil conditioner and to neutralize acid soil, adding calcium, improving structure and making other nutrients more available. Because its carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, crops on marl-treated land may show magnesium deficiency unless magnesium is also supplied.

soil-fert-039.title: Vermicompost, compost made by worms
soil-fert-039.text: Worm castings can hold 10 to 20 times more microbial activity than the soil and organic matter the worm eats. Vermicompost is the product of composting with worms: a mix of decomposing food or plant waste, bedding and worm castings, or vermicast. The usual workers are red wigglers, Eisenia fetida or E. andrei. Composting worms are surface-dwelling epigeic species; burrowing anecic Lumbricus species adapt poorly to shallow bins. Redworms feed fastest at 15–25 °C, survive 10 °C and may be harmed above 30 °C. Bin moisture must stay above 50%, ideally 70–80%. The method treats wastes faster than conventional composting. Castings hold fewer contaminants and more concentrated nutrients than the original materials, and the worm mucus coating them slows nutrient release so nutrients do not wash away. Vermicompost can be mixed into soil or steeped as worm tea. The leachate draining from bins is different: uncomposted, it may carry pathogens.

soil-fert-022.title: Controlled-release fertilizer feeds crops slowly on purpose
soil-fert-022.text: On average, 16% of conventional nitrogen fertilizer escapes as ammonia, nitrous oxide or nitrogen gas, or washes away. Controlled-release fertilizer aims to waste less. It is a granulated fertilizer, usually supplying nitrogen, that releases its nutrients into the soil gradually over a controlled period. Ordinary fertilizers dissolve and disperse, but these are not water-soluble. Their release rate depends on low solubility in soil moisture, the breakdown of pellet coatings, and conversion of the chemicals into ammonia or another usable nutrient. Most slow-release types are urea derivatives, such as urea-formaldehyde, first made in 1936 and sold from 1955. Coated types wrap ordinary fertilizer in sulfur or plastic. Sulfur-coated urea releases as microbes degrade the sealant and through cracks, typically over 6 to 16 weeks in turf. Slow release protects crops from damage by excess fertilizer, needs fewer applications, and in most cases improves yield by more than 10%. It can also cut nitrogen pollution and nitrous oxide emissions, which arise when microbes act on ammonia faster than plants absorb it.

soil-fert-054.title: Biochar in the field: big promise, uneven results
soil-fert-054.text: Biochar does the most for degraded tropical and nutrient-poor soils, and less in temperate regions. Farmers mix it into the soil or spread it on top to raise fertility, hold water and nutrients, and store carbon over the medium to long term. Its pores and high specific surface area make it hygroscopic, so it keeps water and dissolved nutrients in the upper soil and lowers fertilizer needs. Modest additions cut nitrous oxide emissions by up to 80% and eliminate methane emissions. It can reduce leaching of E. coli through sandy soils and remove heavy metals. Soil biologist Elaine Ingham stressed its value as habitat for beneficial microbes. The drawbacks are real. Significant yield gains appear to need 2.5–20 tonnes per hectare, a cost often prohibitive for low-input field crops. Its strong adsorption can weaken pesticides, especially with high-surface-area biochars. Results depend on the biochar, the dose, the soil, temperature and humidity, and the mechanisms are still poorly understood.

soil-fert-053.title: Biochar carbon removal: locking carbon underground
soil-fert-053.text: Making biochar releases CO2, up to 50% of the biomass. The carbon left behind, though, is stable and can stay in the ground for hundreds to thousands of years. Biochar carbon removal locks carbon away on the strength of that stability. The World Bank says biochar keeps 10–70% of the original biomass carbon, about 50% on average, and slows its decomposition by one or two orders of magnitude. Charcoal-rich black spots in Belgian arable soils, left by kilns before 1870, show lower respiration and slower carbon turnover. Biochar set into concrete and tar counts too. How much it can remove is disputed. A 2021 review put the potential at 1.6–3.2 billion tonnes of CO2 a year, with roughly 0.3–1.8 Gt economically feasible below US$100 a tonne. Actual production is a few hundred thousand tonnes a year, giving well under 1 Mt CO2 of certified removal. A 2018 study doubted enough biomass exists, and some authors warn of a boom and bust.

soil-fert-084.title: How urea's nitrogen escapes into the air
soil-fert-084.text: Spread urea on dry ground, and up to thirty percent of its available nitrogen can vanish into the air within seventy-two hours. This loss of fertilizer nitrogen as ammonia gas, when urea breaks down at the soil surface, is ammonia volatilization. It starts with an enzyme. Urease hydrolyzes urea to unstable carbamic acid, which breaks down without enzymes into ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia escapes unless it reacts with water to form ammonium, which plants can use and ammonia cannot. The reaction also makes hydroxide, raising the pH near each urea particle to around 9.0. That speeds volatilization and makes the zone toxic for several hours. Losses rise with temperature, pH and drying soil. Urea hydrolyzed completely within two days on soils of pH about 8.2 or more, but took twice as long at pH 5.2. Surface residues and organic-rich soils carry more urease, so they lose more. About 0.1 inch of rain soon after application moves urea into the soil. Incorporating or injecting it also reduces losses, because good soil contact buffers pH and slows ammonia formation. The stakes are high, since urea makes up more than fifty percent of the world's nitrogen fertilizers.

soil-fert-030.title: The crew that turns waste into compost
soil-fert-030.text: Bacteria do most of the work in a compost heap. They are the most abundant of the compost organisms, which range from chemical decomposers such as bacteria and fungi to physical ones such as worms and insects. Bacteria excrete plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium. Moderate-temperature mesophilic or heat-loving thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase. Thermophiles, inactive between −5 and 25 °C, wake once mesophiles warm the heap and thrive at 40–60 °C. Actinomycetota break down tough paper, bark, lignin and cellulose, and fungi handle woody material bacteria cannot. Earthworms eat partly composted material, and their castings free nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium.

soil-fert-035.title: Compost tea, a brew of microbes for crops
soil-fert-035.text: Compost tea is a liquid of fermented water extracts leached from composted materials and applied to crops. It is usually made by adding compost to water at 1:4–1:10 and stirring occasionally to release microbes, with or without aeration. Field studies show benefits from its organic matter, nutrients and microbial activity, and from suppressing plant pathogens and soil-borne diseases. Aerated tea brews faster with more microbes and suppresses pathogens better than unbrewed compost extracts. Non-aerated tea is cheaper, but studies conflict on its harm to plants ({{ref:soil-env-222}}) and pathogen risks. Its added nutrients can let E. coli and Salmonella regrow. Whether aeration is worth it remains debated.

soil-fert-036.title: Composting at industrial scale
soil-fert-036.text: Large-scale composting relies on three main methods. In-vessel composting confines material in tanks or bunkers where airflow and temperature are controlled, as in a bioreactor. It treats sewage sludge, food waste and municipal organics, sanitizing pathogens so the waste can be reclaimed as a soil amendment, while limiting odors, emissions and polluted water. Aerated static piles stay aerobic by forcing air through perforated pipes instead of turning, and roofs reduce leachate. Windrow composting piles manure, leftover crop material and other wastes in long rows. Such large operations can get hot enough to kill beneficial microbes while pasteurizing the waste.

soil-fert-031.title: The rise and fall of a compost heap's temperature
soil-fert-031.text: Under ideal conditions, a compost heap passes through a fixed sequence of temperature stages. In the first, mesophilic phase, microorganisms decompose the material at moderate temperatures. As the heap warms, thermophilic bacteria take over at 50 to 60 °C (122 to 140 °F). When high-energy compounds run out, the temperature falls through a cooling and a maturation phase. Mesophilic bacteria then cure the compost, making it more bioavailable to plants. Semicomposting, of volumes too small for full composting, never reaches the thermophilic stage.

soil-fert-032.title: Hot compost in weeks, cold compost in a year
soil-fert-032.text: A home heap can take up to a year to finish; a well-run hot pile, 18 days. Hot and cold composting differ in pile size and temperature, and so in how long they take. Time depends on volume, particle size, and how much the material is mixed and aerated. In hot composting, usual on municipal and farm sites, large piles reach high temperatures and stay thermophilic for days or weeks. The Berkeley method finishes in 18 days. It needs at least 1 cubic meter of material, turned every two days after the first four, with C:N at 30:1 or less. Cold composting in piles under 1 cubic meter, like most home heaps, needs no turning, but parts may go anaerobic.

soil-fert-033.title: How a compost heap's heat kills germs
soil-fert-033.text: Stabilized compost that has reached 50–70 °C poses very little risk. Those temperatures kill pathogens and weed seeds, and even make oocysts unviable. The lethal temperature depends on the organism, on how long the heat lasts, from seconds to weeks, and on pH. Finished compost also fights plant disease. Compost teas and extracts inhibit crop pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum, Rhizoctonia and Pythium, and compost supplies biocontrol agents such as Bacillus subtilis. Sterilizing compost weakens this effect. Compost that has not passed 50 °C should be turned wearing a respirator and gloves, against aspergillosis, farmer's lung, Legionnaires' disease and tetanus.

soil-fert-081.title: Seaweed, a fertilizer from the shore
soil-fert-081.text: Brown seaweeds are the most used source of seaweed fertilizer, an organic fertilizer that raises soil fertility and plant growth. Seaweed may be laid as mulch, composted, dried and powdered, or made into liquid extracts. It supplies macro- and micronutrients, humic acids and plant hormones, and can raise crop tolerance of low moisture, high salinity and freezing. As a {{ref:soil-fert-063}}, its humic acid and soluble alginates give clay soils short of organic matter better texture, aeration and water retention. There are drawbacks. Heavy metals accumulated by seaweed may pass into crops, and the spread of diseases and invasive species is another challenge.

soil-fert-082.title: Fertilizer burn: when plant food parches a plant
soil-fert-082.text: Fertilizer burn is damage caused by too much fertilizer, the wrong type, or too little water applied with it. Excess salt, nitrogen or ammonia impairs photosynthesis and respiration, causing visible burns. When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots, so the plant responds as if in drought. Early signs are white salt marks and crusts around the roots. Later the leaves brown and die, root growth stops and roots may rot. Dry, overheated plants suffer most. Heavy watering washes the salts away; otherwise the roots are cleaned and the plant repotted.

soil-fert-086.title: Raised beds: soil that nobody walks on
soil-fert-086.text: Because no one walks on a raised bed, its soil is not compacted and roots grow easily. Raised-bed gardening means growing in soil raised above ground level, usually enclosed in a frame. The soil is usually enriched with compost. Crops are planted so close that their touching leaves suppress weeds and conserve moisture. Beds also extend the season and avoid poor native soil. Built along contour lines on slopes, they help control erosion and conserve water and nutrients. Gardeners on heavy red clay Ultisols use raised beds, or {{ref:soil-fert-088}}, to avoid amending the soil.

soil-fert-088.title: Hügelkultur, a garden bed built on rotting wood
soil-fert-088.text: Hügelkultur plants a raised bed on a mound of decaying wood and other compostable plant matter. The term was first published in a 1962 German gardening booklet by Herrman Andrä. Advocates claim it improves fertility, water retention and soil warming. Wood has one of the highest carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, so its decay may tie up soil nitrogen at first, lowering fertility for perhaps one to two years. Peer-reviewed studies are few, though a student thesis found hügel mounds held almost twice as much water as flat control plots. Advocates rely largely on personal experience. Critics say the method lacks genuine scientific principles. It also runs counter to soil building by litterfall, since in nature wood decays at the surface.

soil-fert-090.title: Bone meal, the slow phosphorus of ground bones
soil-fert-090.text: Before chemistry offered a faster route, farmers on worn-out soils crushed bones gathered from battlefields such as Waterloo and Austerlitz. Bone meal is ground animal bones and slaughterhouse waste, fed to livestock and spread as a slow-release organic fertilizer. It supplies phosphorus and calcium with little nitrogen: a typical N-P-K rating is 3–15–0, with about 12% calcium. Bone does not dissolve in water. Soil acidity or microbial acids must break it down, so it releases nutrients only in acidic soils, below pH 7.0, over 1 to 4 months. Around 1840 Liebig suggested dissolving bones in sulfuric acid, a process first used in Britain in 1841.

soil-fert-025.title: What can go wrong with animal manure
soil-fert-025.text: Manure feeds the soil, but it can carry more than nutrients. Any manure may hold pathogens or food-spoilage organisms, spread by flies, rodents and other vectors, that threaten food safety. Under intensive land use it is spread less precisely than mineral fertilizer, so crops use its nitrogen poorly, and it can give off nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas. In 2007 a University of Minnesota study found corn, lettuce and potatoes taking up antibiotics from soils spread with drug-laden manure. Organic standards therefore require non-organic manure to be rotted or composted first. That breaks down drug residues and kills pathogenic bacteria.

soil-fert-065.title: Water-hoarding polymers that promised more than they gave
soil-fert-065.text: Some synthetic polymers can soak up several hundred times their own weight in water. These hydroabsorbent polymers, such as polyacrylamides and polymethacrylates, have been tested as soil conditioners. The first synthetic conditioners appeared in the 1950s, chiefly hydrolyzed polyacrylonitrile. Trials in farming, horticulture and landscaping from the 1960s stalled when the polymers proved phytotoxic, poisonous to plants, because of leftover acrylamide monomer. Even after monomer levels fell below toxic levels, few studies show them improving plant quality or survival. Such materials are judged on cost-effectiveness, on how long they keep soil moist, and on their effects on microbes, nutrients and plant survival.

soil-fert-064.title: Polyacrylamide, a synthetic binder for heavy clay
soil-fert-064.text: In 1951 a symposium on improving soil structure heard about a new kind of additive. Synthetic polyacrylamide polymers, introduced in the 1950s as linear soil conditioners, are added to soil to improve its structure and the way it handles water. Water-soluble forms increase pore space and infiltration in clay soils. The soil turns friable, crumbly and easy to work, and it dries enough to be worked sooner after rain. Cross-linked forms hold water strongly and go into horticulture, farming and some potting mixes. On construction sites they control erosion, protecting the water quality of nearby streams.

soil-fert-069.title: Living mulch, a groundcover that grows with the crop
soil-fert-069.text: A mulch does not have to be dead. Living mulch is a low groundcover grown under a main crop to slow weeds and give the other benefits of mulch. Its plants are usually fast-growing and keep growing alongside the crop, whereas {{ref:soil-agri-066}} plants are worked into the soil or killed. Some bring extras. Clovers can fix nitrogen from the air, and creeping comfrey can gather nutrients from the subsoil. The partnership has limits. A living mulch may eventually have to be killed, mechanically or chemically, to stop it competing with the crop.

soil-fert-067.title: Organic mulch and the hidden cost of straw and sawdust
soil-fert-067.text: A layer of straw looks harmless, yet it can briefly slow the plants beneath it. Organic mulch is made of plant or animal residues, such as leaves, straw, bark, wood chips or manure, and it decays over time. Straw, peat, sawdust and wood products are rich in carbon but poor in nitrogen, so the microbes decomposing them draw nitrogen from the soil. Such mulches can also mat into a barrier to water and air. Growers use fully composted material to avoid the plant damage described in {{ref:soil-env-222}} and seed-free material to keep out weeds. Peat moss lowers surface pH, which suits acid-loving plants, but once wetted and dried it can form a crust that water cannot soak into.

soil-fert-068.title: Plastic mulch, the film over millions of acres
soil-fert-068.text: Across millions of acres each year, vegetables grow through slits in plastic. Plastic mulch is thin sheeting laid over soil, with crops planted through holes in it, and it dominates large-scale vegetable growing. Black and clear films capture sunlight and warm the soil. Because the plastic lets no water through, drip tape usually runs underneath. Polyethylene mulch must come up at the end of the season. Left in place, it breaks into fragments that pollute the soil with ketones and aldehydes. Biodegradable films made from plant starches or sugars avoid that problem. Soil microorganisms break them down into water and carbon dioxide, so they can be tilled in.

soil-fert-070.title: Sour mulch, when a pile smells of vinegar
soil-fert-070.text: Mulch that smells of vinegar, ammonia, sulfur or silage has gone sour. It has turned anaerobic, decaying without oxygen. This happens when nitrogen-rich material is not turned often enough and forms pockets of intense decomposition. The anaerobic process makes small amounts of phytotoxic compounds, chemicals that harm plants. They can linger for a while even after the material is aerated again. Low-growing and newly planted plants suffer most, and some seeds may fail to germinate.

soil-fert-051.title: How biochar is made: heat without flame
soil-fert-051.text: Heat biomass without oxygen and it does not burn. It decomposes. That process, pyrolysis, is the main way biochar is made. It yields three products: a solid (biochar), a liquid (bio-oil) and a gas (syngas). Most biochar sold in the United States comes from gasifiers, which run through oxidation, drying, pyrolysis and reduction; their pyrolysis zone runs at 250–550 °C. Smallholders need no equipment: they light crop-waste piles from the top and quench the embers with soil or water. This top-down or conservation burn gives far less smoke than open burning. Hydrothermal carbonization also yields a carbon-rich solid, but because the process differs, its product is called hydrochar.

soil-fert-087.title: Slash-and-char: clearing land without losing its carbon
soil-fert-087.text: Slash-and-burn leaves only 3% of the organic carbon in the soil. Slash-and-char can keep up to 50%, in a highly stable form. The difference lies in the fire. Instead of burning cleared vegetation, farmers char it, leaving biochar for the soil. Burned plots soon lose their nutrients and are abandoned, whereas biochar-enriched soils can sustain cropping indefinitely. Mixed with crop leftovers, food waste or manure and buried, the char can form terra preta, itself a product of Amazonian slash-and-char farming. A worldwide shift to the practice could lock away an estimated 0.22–0.42 Gt of carbon a year.

soil-fert-052.title: What sets one biochar apart from another
soil-fert-052.text: A biochar's physical and chemical makeup is set by the feedstock and the production method, and it explains how each one performs. Properties are grouped by proximate and elemental composition, pH and porosity, and the International Biochar Initiative publishes standard methods for evaluating them. Two ratios, hydrogen-to-carbon and oxygen-to-carbon, track polarity and aromaticity. Both fall during carbonization as hydrogen- and oxygen-bearing groups are driven off. Temperature reshapes the carbon itself. At 450–550 °C it stays amorphous; hotter runs progressively turn it into turbostratic graphene sheets. Higher temperatures raise conductivity, aromaticity and intrinsic recalcitrance, the resistance to decay that governs how long the carbon lasts.

soil-fert-089.title: UAN, the nitrogen fertilizer that stays liquid
soil-fert-089.text: Urea and ammonium nitrate dissolve far better together than either salt does alone. UAN is that pair dissolved in water, a stable solution with 32% total nitrogen. It can only be used as a liquid. The mixture has a very low critical relative humidity, 18% at 30 °C, so as a solid it would pull water from the air. The commonest grade, UAN 32, is 45% ammonium nitrate, 35% urea and only 20% water. UAN 28, UAN 30 and UAN 18 also exist. The solutions corrode mild steel. Mixed with calcium nitrate solutions, they form a precipitate that can plug nozzles.

soil-fert-092.title: Foliar feeding: fertilizer through the leaves
soil-fert-092.text: In the 1950s H. B. Tukey and S. H. Wittwer at Michigan State sprayed radioactive phosphorus and potassium on leaves. They traced it moving through the plant at about one foot per hour. Foliar feeding applies liquid fertilizer directly to the leaves, which absorb nutrients through their stomata, the leaf pores, and their epidermis, the outer skin. Skipping the soil avoids leaching losses. It helps most with phosphorus, zinc and iron, which soils fix or hold in poorly available forms. Timing matters: early morning or late evening, below 24 °C (75 °F), since heat closes leaf pores in some species.

soil-fert-204.title: Azolla, the floating fern that feeds rice
soil-fert-204.text: Rice farmers were fertilizing their paddies with a small floating fern 1500 years ago. Azolla, the mosquito fern, is a genus of seven such aquatic ferns. Each hosts a partner, the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae, which fixes nitrogen from the air and passes directly from one generation of fern to the next. Azolla can double its biomass in 1.9 days and yield 8–10 tonnes of fresh matter per hectare in Asian paddy fields. Planted in flooded rice paddies, it covers the water and suppresses weeds, then releases nitrogen to the rice as it dies. The earliest known written record is Jia Sixie's Qimin Yaoshu of 554 CE. It is still widely used in southeast Asia.

soil-fert-098.title: Manure management: handling a useful hazard
soil-fert-098.text: Hydrogen sulfide deadens the sense of smell at about 100 to 150 ppm, and 500 to 700 ppm can kill within 30 to 60 minutes. That gas rises from stored manure, so manure management is about safety as much as fertility. It covers the capture, storage, treatment and sustainable use of manure, whether liquid, slurry or solid, bedding and urine included. Stored manure also gives off methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide, peaking when it is agitated for pumping; in confined spaces these gases can kill. About 33% of global ammonia emissions in 2018 could be attributed to manure. As part of nutrient management, the aim is to spread enough to enrich soil without polluting water. Over-application can acidify soil and build up heavy metals. Water running off and draining through manured fields carries nutrients, pathogens, antibiotics, hormones and heavy metals. In streams and lakes, those nutrients overfeed the water. Remedies include anaerobic digestion to biogas and {{ref:soil-fert-096}}, composting, separating solids from liquids, and vegetated borders between field and water, described in {{ref:soil-agri-158}}.

soil-fert-203.title: Bokashi: pickling food waste for the soil
soil-fert-203.text: Bokashi treats food waste more like silage than like compost. Waste is mixed with a specialized bran carrying yeast, photosynthetic bacteria and lactic acid bacteria. It ferments for a few weeks in an airtight vessel, preserved by lactic acid. Dug into soil, it is eaten by soil life, mainly bacteria, within weeks. Unlike aerobic compost, bokashi barely heats. It loses little carbon as carbon dioxide and almost no nitrogen as nitrous oxide or ammonia, and it lowers the risk of nutrient leaching. Begun in Korea, the method is best known through Teruo Higa's commercial 'EM' (Effective Microorganisms) method of 1982. Nobody disputes that EM starts the fermentation, but other claims, such as whether particular microbes bring the benefits, are robustly contested.

soil-fert-096.title: Digestate, what remains after biogas is made
soil-fert-096.text: Anaerobic digestion has two main products. One is biogas; the other is digestate, the material left behind. Its chemistry depends on the feedstock: sewage sludge, livestock manure, energy crops such as maize, food and municipal waste, crop leftovers or industrial wastes. Acidogenic digestate is fibrous solid matter, rich in lignin and cellulose, that holds moisture well. Methanogenic digestate is a liquid sludge high in ammonium and potassium. The liquid fraction is up to 90% of the volume, with 2–6% dry matter and most of the soluble N and K. The solid fraction keeps most of the phosphorus. Ammonia is usually 60–80% of total nitrogen, and up to 99% from kitchen food waste. Digestate serves mainly as a soil conditioner: the solid part adds organic matter and water retention, the liquid part nutrients, and it can protect soil from erosion. It is not technically compost, which forms aerobically and breaks lignin and cellulose down further, and it carries more phosphorus and potassium. In the UK, digestate meeting PAS110 ceases to be waste and can be sold as a biofertilizer.

soil-fert-091.title: IBDU, urea that dissolves slowly
soil-fert-091.text: Urea dissolves at once and acts fast. Isobutylidenediurea, or IBDU, does neither. This organic compound derived from urea is not water-soluble, and its low solubility limits how fast it hydrolyzes, splitting back into fast-acting urea. It is made by condensing isobutyraldehyde with two equivalents of urea. Once dissolved, it releases nitrogen by the reverse reaction, which makes it a controlled-release nitrogen fertilizer. Related urea-based slow-release materials include crotonylidene diurea and urea-formaldehyde products such as ureaform.

soil-fert-056.title: Lime requirement: how much lime an acid soil needs
soil-fert-056.text: The acid-forming ions held on soil colloids, the finest charged particles, must be neutralized along with those in the soil water, or they will restore the original pH. The lime requirement is the dose that does this, worked out by soil-testing laboratories from the soil's base saturation. How far a given dose raises pH depends on the soil's buffer capacity, which is generally related to its cation-exchange capacity. Low-CEC soils show a sharper pH rise but lose the added bases faster to leaching, so they turn acid sooner unless limed again. Over-liming is most likely on them, as on sands that lack organic matter and clay to buffer them.

soil-fert-058.title: Does liming add or remove soil carbon?
soil-fert-058.text: Liming changes the organic carbon stored in soil through three processes that pull in different directions. First, better growing conditions raise yields, so more organic matter returns to the soil as dying roots and crop leftovers. Second, a more favorable pH briefly stimulates soil biological activity, speeding mineralization and the turnover of organic matter, which works against storage. Third, calcium drives flocculation, building more stable aggregates, and that better structure protects organic carbon from mineralization. The net change is the balance of all three.

soil-fert-057.title: Structure liming, lime that firms up clay
soil-fert-057.text: Structure liming aims at the crumbs of a clay soil. It usually uses calcium oxide or hydroxide mixed with calcium carbonate, to improve aggregate stability. The lime brings high calcium concentrations and high ionic strength, a high total of dissolved ions, to the soil solution. Both enhance flocculation of clay minerals, which then form more stable aggregates. Firmer aggregates can reduce losses of clay and nutrients from the soil.

soil-fert-027.title: How green manure feeds the next crop
soil-fert-027.text: A green manure only helps once bacteria have eaten it. Heterotrophic bacteria, which feed on organic matter, break the worked-in plants down into nutrients the following crop can use. Warmth and moisture drive the process, as in composting. The decaying matter gives off carbon dioxide and weak acids that free nutrients from insoluble minerals. On soils rich in calcium minerals, it can raise the phosphate content. The plant's {{ref:soil-fert-184}}, which varies with species and age, must be below 30:1. Otherwise the decomposers deplete soil nitrogen and starve the crop. Working the plants in too short a time before planting can cause the same nitrogen shortfall.

soil-fert-077.title: One dose of compost that stored carbon for years
soil-fert-077.text: A 2013 study found that a single compost application raised grassland carbon storage by 25–70%, significantly and durably. The method is simple: spread compost over the soil surface without tilling, so its carbon is stored in a stable form. Forage output rose as well, by 78% at a drier valley site and 42% at a wetter coastal one. Methane and nitrous oxide emissions showed no significant rise. Two obstacles remain. Composting is not an NRCS-approved technique, and commercial compost supplies are too limited to cover large areas.

soil-fert-078.title: Can grazing cattle build soil carbon?
soil-fert-078.text: Advocates credit rotational grazing with building carbon in grassland soils. The method moves herds through small paddocks so that each paddock can rest. Rest favors deep-rooted perennials over shallow-rooted annual grasses that die once grazed. The carbon payoff is disputed. Only a small amount of carbon may be stored in grassland soils, through root exudates and manure, while the animals themselves emit methane. Many researchers argue the approach cannot deliver the benefits claimed. Some studies find that simply excluding livestock from semi-arid grasslands recovers both vegetation and the carbon in the soil. The question remains open.

soil-fert-062.title: How farm lime misleads archaeologists
soil-fert-062.text: Archaeologists read strontium in ancient remains to work out where prehistoric people lived. Agricultural lime can distort those studies. The effect is significant in areas with calcium-poor soils. In Denmark's Karup River catchment, more than half the strontium washed in from agricultural lime rather than the natural environment. Comparing remains with lime-contaminated burial sites has led researchers to wrongly conclude that some prehistoric people came from far away.

soil-fert-060.title: Calcium carbonate equivalent: rating a lime's strength
soil-fert-060.text: Some limestone outperforms pure calcium carbonate at its own job. Calcium carbonate equivalent, or CCE, compares a liming material's neutralizing power with that of pure calcium carbonate. Limestones containing dolomite can rate above 100 percent, because magnesium carbonate is lighter than calcium carbonate. Fineness matters too, since soil acids are weak. Particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and anything finer than 60 mesh fully effective. The effective calcium carbonate equivalent (ECCE) combines CCE with fineness; commercial aglime typically ranges from 45 to 110 percent. Marl, with less calcium carbonate, is spread at rates adjusted by its CCE.

soil-fert-061.title: The lime that turned Brazil's cerrado into farmland
soil-fert-061.text: Before the 1960s, Brazil's inland cerrado was considered unfit for farming. Its soil was too acidic and too poor in nutrients. Then lime arrived on a vast scale. By the late 1990s Brazil was spreading 14–16 million tonnes a year, rising to 25 million tonnes in 2003 and 2004, about five tonnes per hectare. The result helped make Brazil the world's second-biggest soybean exporter.

soil-fert-080.title: Marling, one of farming's oldest soil fixes
soil-fert-080.text: In 18th-century Lancashire, almost every field had its marl pit. Marling, spreading marl or raw chalk and lime debris on fields, is one of the oldest soil amendments in agriculture. Britain used it sporadically from prehistoric times, and Pliny the Elder mentioned it in the 1st century. Wider use from the 16th century contributed to the early modern agricultural revolution. Early in the 19th century, lime and imported mineral fertilizers gradually replaced it. Yet by the late 19th century New Jersey was mining marl industrially, grading it and publishing detailed chemical analyses.

soil-fert-041.title: Night soil, the town's waste carted to the fields
soil-fert-041.text: Ancient Athens channeled its sewage to the Cephissus valley as fertilizer. In Edo, compost merchants sold feces to farmers, and Aztec chinampas were built of mud and human waste. Night soil is the old euphemism for such waste: human excreta collected, usually at night, from cesspools, privies, pail closets and pit latrines. It came from towns without sewers or septic systems, gathered undiluted by water, and was sometimes carted out of town and sold as fertilizer. Unprocessed, it is risky. Parasitic worm infections such as ascariasis are linked to its use, because the eggs pass from person to person in feces. Composting and other proper handling of fecal sludge reduce these risks.

soil-fert-042.title: Closing the loop: human excreta as fertilizer
soil-fert-042.text: In Africa, the nutrients theoretically recoverable from human excreta match all current fertilizer use. That makes excreta a possible alternative for smallholders, who often cannot afford chemical fertilizer. Reusing treated excreta for its nutrients, organic matter and energy 'closes the loop' between sanitation and farming, and it is central to {{ref:soil-fert-207}}. The products differ: urine, dried feces, composted feces, fecal sludge, sewage and sewage sludge each fertilize in their own way. Treatments such as urine diversion and drying, composting, and sludge treatment remove pathogens to varying degrees and cut water content. The advantages are real. Fertilizers made from mined phosphate rock can carry cadmium and uranium into the food chain, but excreta-based ones generally lack these heavy metals. Their nutrients are bound in organic compounds or held on humic acids, so they release slowly and leach less readily than mineral fertilizers. Like other nitrogen fertilizers, though, they can let nitrate leach away. Pharmaceutical residues in excreta break down better in soil than in water. People have farmed with excreta for centuries, often in unregulated and unsafe ways in developing countries. Whether reuse is cost-effective is still debated.

soil-fert-037.title: Humanure, compost made from people
soil-fert-037.text: Organic farmer Joseph Jenkins coined the word humanure for human excreta used as a nutrient-rich composting input. In soil it builds organic matter and healthy microbial communities. Feces supply nitrogen, urine supplies phosphorus, and both are a good source of potassium. Feces can carry bacteria, viruses and parasitic worms, but proper fermentation kills pathogens and parasite eggs within two weeks to six months, depending on climate. Urine helps. Added to compost, it raises the temperature, helping destroy pathogens and seeds, and unlike feces it does not attract flies or carry worm eggs.

soil-fert-038.title: The composting toilet: sawdust instead of a flush
soil-fert-038.text: Most composting toilets use no flush water at all. They are dry toilets that treat human waste by composting it into a compost-like material. After each use, a carbon additive such as sawdust, {{ref:soil-agri-139}} or peat moss goes in. It makes air pockets, improves the C:N ratio and cuts odor. Most rely on mesophilic composting, at moderate temperatures. Long retention or a second composting step kills more pathogens and gives a humus-like product that can enrich soil where rules allow. Its nutrients are more available to plants than those in dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets. Using it in one's own garden is regarded as safe, though because pathogens can survive, legal restrictions may apply.

soil-fert-045.title: Biosolids: sewage sludge returned to the land
soil-fert-045.text: Farmers began spreading sewage sludge in the 1920s. Treated, that sludge is called biosolids: solid organic matter recovered from sewage treatment and used as fertilizer or soil conditioner. Research confirms biosolids hold nutrients similar to those in animal manures. They can supply nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur and micronutrients, and they are 60–65% organic matter that stimulates soil microbes. They come as cake, granules, pellets or liquid, spread and worked into the soil or injected directly. Sludge has been shown to raise soil available phosphorus, and soil salt levels too. The trouble is what else rides along. Biosolids can contain synthetic organic compounds, radionuclides and heavy metals. {{ref:soil-env-200}} from spread biosolids have contaminated farm soils, groundwater, animals and crops. Heavy metals and persistent pharmaceutical pollutants make spreading sludge controversial in the USA and parts of Europe, and some places ban biosolids on farmland. One study found that high-temperature pyrolysis of biosolids into biochar reduced those chemicals below detectable limits.

soil-fert-043.title: Urine, the nitrogen-rich share of human waste
soil-fert-043.text: Urine makes up less than 1% of the volume of sewage, yet it carries about 70% of its nitrogen and more than half its potassium. As a crop fertilizer it is rich in nitrogen, mostly as urea, and in potassium. Design values are 4 kg nitrogen, 0.36 kg phosphorus and 1.0 kg potassium per person per year, about 7:1.5:2.2 as N:P2O5:K2O. The amounts vary with diet, and nitrogen rises with the protein eaten. Its fertilizing effect is comparable to commercial nitrogen fertilizers, and it holds far less lead, mercury and cadmium than sewage sludge. Undiluted urine can burn leaves or roots, especially in dry soil. So it is diluted, 1:5 for container crops or 1:8 for general use. Too much brings excess nitrogen and salts such as sodium chloride, and can cause excess ammonia, acidity or other harm to plants. In storage its urea quickly hydrolyzes to ammonia. Delivering it through perforated hoses about 10 cm below the surface cuts odor, ammonia loss and pathogen transfer. Health risks are generally regarded as negligible, especially when urine goes into the soil rather than onto edible plant parts.

soil-fert-044.title: Feces as fertilizer: nutrients plus carbon
soil-fert-044.text: By Swedish default values, an adult excretes 0.55 kg nitrogen, 0.18 kg phosphorus and 0.36 kg potassium in feces a year. That gives wet feces an NPK% of 1.1:0.8:0.9. Urine, by comparison, can hold up to 90% of the nitrogen, 50% of the phosphorus and 70% of the potassium in human excreta. Feces also add organic carbon. Post-treated dried feces from urine-diverting dry toilets raise harvests through their nutrients and improve soil fertility through that carbon. Fecal sludge from pit latrines, septic systems and dry toilets can be made fit for farm use by dewatering, drying, composting, pelletizing or anaerobic digestion.

soil-fert-047.title: The multiple barrier approach to safe reuse
soil-fert-047.text: Reusing excreta safely depends on a series of barriers rather than any single step. World Health Organization guidelines of 2006 on safe reuse of wastewater, excreta and greywater rest on this multiple barrier approach. Treatment is one barrier. Others include the choice of crop, farming and application methods, and farmer education. How much treatment is needed depends on which other barriers are in use. Temperatures above 50 °C, as in thermophilic composting or digestion, inactivate most pathogens. So does a pH above 10, from ammonia or lime treatment. Helminth eggs, the eggs of parasitic worms, are among the hardest pathogens to destroy, so reuse schemes use them as indicator organisms.

soil-fert-083.title: The salt index: how hard a fertilizer pulls on water
soil-fert-083.text: Potassium chloride has a salt index of 116.2. Urea scores 74.4, and the fertilizer in {{ref:soil-fert-206}} scores 29.2. The fertilizer salt index measures how much a fertilizer raises the osmotic pressure of water, the pull dissolved salts exert, compared with sodium nitrate set at 100. Fertilizers with an index above 20 are not recommended for particularly sensitive crops. Using too much fertilizer, or one with too high an index, builds up salts in the soil and causes burns.

soil-fert-049.title: The microbes inside a biofertilizer
soil-fert-049.text: The longest-used biofertilizer organisms are nitrogen fixers: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum and blue-green algae. Each suits different crops. Rhizobium inoculant serves legumes. Azotobacter goes to crops such as wheat, maize, cotton and potato, and Azospirillum mainly to sorghum, millets, maize, sugarcane and wheat. Blue-green algae such as Nostoc and Anabaena inoculate paddy crops. Anabaena paired with the water fern Azolla can add up to 60 kg/ha of nitrogen a season. Other organisms used include Bacillus and Bradyrhizobium bacteria, Trichoderma fungi and Gigaspora mycorrhizal fungi. In coastal districts, seaweeds rich in potassium, phosphorus and trace elements are widely used in place of manure.

soil-fert-202.title: Coated urea: a shell that slows the nitrogen
soil-fert-202.text: Coat a urea prill, a small bead of fertilizer, in something less soluble and its nitrogen seeps out slowly. Coated urea releases urea gradually, lowering the risk of fertilizer burn and allowing less frequent applications. Sulfur-coated urea, developed by the Tennessee Valley Authority, holds 32% to 41% nitrogen. It releases once water enters cracks in the coating; a wax seal slows it further until microbes degrade it. Polymer-coated urea releases nitrogen more precisely, with release delayable for 10 months, but it costs more. Combination products coat urea with sulfur and then polymer, a cheaper route to precise release.

soil-fert-085.title: Urease inhibitors: buying time for urea
soil-fert-085.text: Urea left on the soil surface can lose its nitrogen to the air. Urease inhibitors block the urease enzyme, so urea stays in its non-volatile form for longer. That gives rain time to carry the urea into the soil, where hydrolysis happens below the surface and less nitrogen escapes. The inhibitors also shrink the zones of high pH around untreated urea. Most studies find they reduce nitrogen losses when fertilizer must be applied in poor field conditions. They help most under high-residue {{ref:soil-agri-099}}.

soil-fert-013.title: Stabilized nitrogen: slowing fertilizer down in the soil
soil-fert-013.text: Nitrogen fertilizer works better when it changes form more slowly in the soil. Two kinds of additive slow it. Nitrification inhibitors, also called nitrogen stabilizers, suppress the biological oxidation of ammonia into nitrate, an anion more prone to leaching. Urease inhibitors such as NBPT, added to urea fertilizers at 0.05 weight percent, slow urea's enzymatic hydrolysis into ammonia, which can evaporate or be turned into nitrate. A fertilizer carrying such an additive is called stabilized: its nitrogen stays in the soil longer in urea or ammonium form. Using them lets farmers limit the polluting effects of nitrogen washing off their fields.

soil-fert-074.title: Landfill leachate, the liquid that seeps from waste
soil-fert-074.text: Rain falling on a landfill does not simply vanish. It percolates through the waste and emerges as landfill leachate, a contaminated liquid that can pollute groundwater if not managed. Its makeup varies with the landfill's age and waste type. It carries dissolved and suspended matter, and decomposition adds organic acids, aldehydes, alcohols and simple sugars. Siting landfills on impermeable ground, or lining them with geomembranes or engineered clay, cuts the risk; bentonite is used to line landfill bases. In a 2012 New York survey, all double-lined landfill cells leaked less than 500 liters per hectare per day. Granular laterite in purpose-built treatment beds has removed phosphorus and heavy metals from leachate.

soil-fert-008.title: Phosphate fertilizers, from rock to soluble salt
soil-fert-008.text: Each ton of phosphoric acid made from phosphate rock leaves five tons of an impure radioactive waste, {{ref:soil-fert-213}}. The world produces 100 to 280 million tons of it a year. That waste is the shadow of phosphate fertilizers, which supply phosphorus from rock whose main minerals are fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite. Acid treatment turns those minerals into water-soluble phosphate salts, and this use is the main reason so much sulfuric acid is made. The main straight phosphate fertilizers are the acid-treated rock products of {{ref:soil-fert-094}}. The single kind has 14–18% P2O5 plus this waste; the triple kind has 44–48% P2O5 and no gypsum. A maize crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per hectare needs 31–50 kg of phosphate fertilizer, and soybeans about half, 20–25 kg. Billions of kilograms of rock are mined each year, but the remaining ore is shrinking in size and quality, making future supply a critical issue. Phosphate also pollutes. Normally a limiting nutrient in water, at high concentrations it promotes cyanobacteria and algae, and it is the main contributor to {{ref:soil-env-020}}.

soil-fert-017.title: The cadmium, fluoride and uranium in some fertilizers
soil-fert-017.text: Monoammonium phosphate can hold anywhere from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg of cadmium, and phosphate rock up to 188 mg/kg. Some fertilizers, especially phosphate and slag-based ones, add such contaminants to soils: cadmium, fluoride, uranium and other heavy metals. Continued use of high-cadmium fertilizer can contaminate soils and plants, so producers now choose phosphate rock by its cadmium content. Phosphate rock is rich in fluoride too, and phosphate fertilizers have raised soil fluoride. Plants take up little, so the greater concern is livestock that eat contaminated soil. Uranium-238 runs from 7 to 100 pCi/g in phosphate rock and 1 to 67 pCi/g in phosphate fertilizers. Heavy use can raise levels in soils and drainage water several-fold. Yet the added health risk from radionuclides in food is very small, less than 0.05 mSv/y. Steel slag, recycled as an amendment for its calcium, magnesium and trace elements, can carry arsenic, cadmium, chromium and nickel, though it helps immobilize lead. Mixed with biochar, steel slag makes a good amendment for immobilizing heavy metals in farm soils.

soil-fert-015.title: How fertilizer reaches rivers, lakes and wells
soil-fert-015.text: Coastal dead zones are increasing, and nitrogen-rich water draining off farmland is the primary cause of serious oxygen depletion in coastal zones, lakes and rivers. Rain and snowmelt carry nitrogen and phosphorus off fertilized land into surface water, and leaching carries them down into groundwater. In fresh water the main culprit is phosphate. It feeds algae and cyanobacteria whose decay uses up the oxygen, the process of {{ref:soil-env-020}}, and farm drainage is a major contributor. Much of the nitrogen that plants do not take up, becomes easily leached nitrate. Groundwater above 10 mg/L can cause blue baby syndrome. Even where this can be reversed, decades of careful land care may pass before natural denitrification clears the accumulated nitrate.

soil-fert-095.title: Phosphorite, the rock behind phosphate fertilizer
soil-fert-095.text: Average sedimentary rock holds under 0.2% phosphorus. Phosphorite, or phosphate rock, ranges from 4% to 20% P2O5. It is a non-detrital sedimentary rock, one not built from worn fragments of older rock, and it is rich in phosphate minerals. The phosphate is mostly fluorapatite in very fine masses, with hydroxyapatite often derived from bones and teeth. Phosphorites form mostly in shallow seas, most commonly where strong upwelling brings deep, phosphate-rich water to the coast. About 90% of the rock goes to fertilizer and animal feed supplements. For fertilizer it must be beneficiated, upgraded by washing, flotation and similar steps, to at least 28% P2O5; most marketed grades reach 30% or more. Mined rock becomes wet-process phosphoric acid. With more rock, that acid gives the triple form of {{ref:soil-fert-094}}; with ammonia, it gives ammonium phosphates. World economic reserves stood at 70 gigatonnes in 2018, but high-grade ore is declining. Beneficiated rock is also sold as an 'organic' phosphate source, and an FAO report finds that applying it directly can be more sustainable in certain soils and countries.

soil-fert-094.title: Superphosphate, the first chemical manure
soil-fert-094.text: The world's first chemical manure went into industrial production in 1842. Its inventor, met in {{ref:soil-hist-074}}, began making his patented 'super phosphate of lime' from fossil coprolites. Superphosphate is made by treating phosphate-rich material with acid. The first, in the 1840s, used bones and sulfuric acid; makers then turned to phosphate coprolites and later to phosphorite. Single superphosphate comes from phosphate rock and sulfuric acid, and a typical fertilizer grade holds 20% P2O5, though other sources give 14–18%. Triple superphosphate, mainly monocalcium phosphate, comes from rock and phosphoric acid and holds 45%. Double superphosphate mixes both. Much of its phosphate is soluble and immediately available, giving plants a quick boost, and it is cheap enough to be widely used in developing regions. In soil, though, phosphate readily binds to clays, aluminum and iron salts or organic ligands, and much of it becomes unavailable to plants. Continuous use can acidify soils, especially poorly buffered ones. Soluble phosphate, and phosphate bound to fine particles, also washes into rivers, where it is lost to farming and feeds the overgrowth of algae.

soil-fert-046.title: Peak phosphorus: will the rock run out?
soil-fert-046.text: Phosphorus for fertilizer comes from a limited resource, and a shortage of mined phosphorus would threaten food security worldwide. Peak phosphorus names that potential shortage of economically mineable phosphorus. The term arose from the limited occurrence of rock phosphate. One estimate puts the US peak in 1988 and the world peak in 1989; others place it within the next few hundred years. Two responses could stretch supplies. Phosphorus can be recovered from excreta, for example as {{ref:soil-fert-097}} from urine or from sludge treatment liquids. And using less fertilizer, as when mycorrhizal inoculants allow lower rates, helps prolong the finite reserves.

soil-fert-040.title: Phosphate-rich organic manure: compost that unlocks rock
soil-fert-040.text: Rock phosphate locks its phosphorus in insoluble tricalcium phosphate, and composting can free it. Phosphate-rich organic manure is made by co-composting very finely ground, high-grade rock phosphate: 80% finer than 54 microns and 32% ± 2% P2O5. Microbial organic acids slowly dissolve the phosphate, and the organic matter stops other ions locking it into insoluble forms. Phosphorus dissolves best between pH 5.5 and 7. Below 5.5, aluminum, iron and manganese block its release; above 7, magnesium and calcium do. An alternative to diammonium phosphate and single superphosphate, it may add phosphorus more efficiently than chemical fertilizers and feeds a second crop as well as the first. Acidic waste solids from biogas plants can be used to make it.

soil-fert-097.title: Struvite, the mineral that clogs pipes and feeds crops
soil-fert-097.text: Wastewater plants fight a mineral that scales their pipes and pumps. Struvite, magnesium ammonium phosphate (NH4MgPO4·6H2O), forms in alkaline conditions from equal molar amounts of magnesium, ammonium and phosphate. It builds up especially after anaerobic digesters release ammonium and phosphate. It dissolves readily in acid but only sparingly in neutral or alkaline water. That nuisance is also a resource. First described as a fertilizer in 1857, struvite supplies phosphorus, nitrogen and magnesium. It can be made from urine by raising the pH and adding magnesium, and recovering phosphorus from manure and municipal wastewater as struvite appears promising.

soil-fert-228.title: Chlorosis, when green leaves fade to yellow
soil-fert-228.text: A pale leaf belongs to a plant short of food. Chlorosis is the condition in which leaves make too little chlorophyll and turn pale, yellow or yellow-white. Such a plant makes little carbohydrate by photosynthesis and may die unless the cause is treated. Causes include soil shortages of iron, magnesium, zinc or nitrogen, a soil pH that locks up minerals, waterlogging and damaged or compacted roots. On French limestone vineyards, grafting vines onto American rootstocks after phylloxera worsened this lime chlorosis. Remedies match the cause: iron chelate or sulfate, magnesium or nitrogen feeds, lime on acid soils and sulfur on alkaline ones.

soil-fert-231.title: Nitrogen deficiency and the sawdust that robs it
soil-fert-231.text: Sawdust dug into a garden can starve the plants it was meant to help. Soil organisms feeding on such high-carbon matter use up the available nitrogen, 'robbing' it from roots. The result is nitrogen deficiency: stunted plants, poor flowering and fruiting, and chlorosis. Older leaves yellow first, because the plant moves nitrogen to younger tissue. Other stresses mimic these signs, so soil and tissue tests or chlorophyll meters confirm it, since leaf nitrogen tracks chlorophyll. Crops grown over winter and plowed under, as in {{ref:soil-fert-026}}, limit leaching, and leguminous ones fix extra nitrogen. Feeds such as ammonium phosphate correct it.

soil-fert-238.title: Mitscherlich's curve of diminishing yield
soil-fert-238.text: In 1909 Alexander Mitscherlich gave the harvest a curve. His law of physiological relations ties yield to the quantity of plant food through a logarithmic function, so each added dose brings a smaller gain. It recast the limiting-factor idea that Liebig had framed as {{ref:soil-fert-182}} and that Blackman later discussed. When the two were compared in 1942, Mitscherlich's function proved to be virtually the law of diminishing returns.

soil-fert-229.title: Manganese deficiency and the checkered young leaf
soil-fert-229.text: A four-manganese core drives the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II, the heart of photosynthesis. That is why most broad-spectrum fertilizers contain manganese. Manganese deficiency is commonest in poorly drained soils and where organic matter is high, and at high pH the metal may be unavailable. Leaves yellow between the veins in a checkered pattern. Young leaves show it first, because manganese is immobile in the plant, unlike magnesium. It is often confused with {{ref:soil-fert-201}}, and the two occur together. Ammonium sulfate lowers pH at once; sulfur works slowly through soil bacteria. The US used about 20,000 tons of manganese fertilizer compounds in 2000.

soil-fert-226.title: Boron deficiency, the world's commonest micronutrient gap
soil-fert-226.text: No micronutrient shortage is more widespread in crops than boron deficiency. Without boron, cells stop expanding, growing points die and fertility falls. Soils typically hold an adequate 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg; below 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, depending on crop and soil, deficiency is common. High-pH soils are prone, because boric acid stays undissociated there and roots cannot absorb it. So are soils under 1.5% organic matter and leached sandy soils. In calcareous fields in Pakistan, 35 to 56 percent are deficient. Boric acid, borax or Solubor at about 1.1 kg boron per hectare corrects it, but excess is toxic.

soil-fert-232.title: Phosphorus deficiency and the purple warning
soil-fert-232.text: Most of the phosphorus in a soil sits in forms plants cannot absorb. Plants take it up as phosphate ions, and soil pH sets which forms of phosphate exist; between pH 6 and 7 the least is bound up. Phosphorus deficiency slows maturity and makes plants store excess starch. Some turn dark purple from anthocyanin, a pigment, but only once the shortage is fairly severe. Soil tests such as Bray 1-P, Mehlich 3 and Olsen extract phosphorus for colorimetric measurement. Roots fight back by favoring lateral roots and secreting phosphatases and organic acids. Larger roots and mycorrhizal partners raise uptake.

soil-fert-233.title: Potassium deficiency and the scorched leaf tip
soil-fert-233.text: Potassium slips easily out of light, sandy soils. With little clay to hold it, the soluble nutrient leaches away, and potassium deficiency, also called potash deficiency, follows. Leaf tips scorch brown and curl, with yellowing between the veins. Older leaves show it first, because potassium is mobile in the plant. Deficient plants suffer more from frost and disease, though potassium above the optimum adds no extra resistance. Potassium chloride is the main remedy. Dry soil cuts uptake, while adding lime or raising organic matter can improve retention.

soil-fert-230.title: Zinc deficiency, from cereal fields to dinner plates
soil-fert-230.text: Almost half the world's cereal crops grow on zinc-deficient soils, so zinc deficiency is widespread in people too. In plants it means limited growth, because roots cannot take up enough of this essential micronutrient. Some soils hold little zinc, such as sandy soils and highly weathered soils. Others, such as calcareous and saline soils, bind it tightly to their particles. Low organic matter and compaction add risk. Phosphorus fertilizers and lime frequently induce it, lime by increasing that binding. Leaf zinc of 20 to 100 mg/kg suffices for most crops. Zinc sulfate or oxide at 5 to 100 kg/ha corrects it, though perhaps not in alkaline soils.

soil-fert-235.title: Nitrogen use efficiency: the share a crop actually uses
soil-fert-235.text: Crops worldwide generally absorb less than half the nitrogen offered to them. Nitrogen use efficiency is the proportion of the nitrogen present that a plant absorbs and uses, and for most crops it falls below 50%. Raising it cuts fertilizer runoff and production costs while increasing yield, making farming more sustainable. Better fertilizers and crop management help, as do selective breeding and genetic engineering. Efficiency can be measured for the plant, the soil, the fertilizer or the whole ecosystem.

soil-fert-227.title: Calcium deficiency, a problem of water more than soil
soil-fert-227.text: Blossom end rot in tomatoes and peppers, bitter pit in stored apples and tipburn in lettuce share one cause. Calcium deficiency comes from too little available calcium or, more often, from low transpiration of the plant or the affected tissue. Calcium does not move in the phloem, so low-transpiring tissues and new, fast-growing parts suffer first. Acidic, sandy or coarse soils often hold less calcium, and high-phosphorus soils tend to lock it into insoluble forms. Adding lime to acid soils toward pH 6.5 can help. Adding calcium at the roots seldom cures it, so steady watering is key.

soil-fert-234.title: Hoagland solution, the standard recipe for soilless plants
soil-fert-234.text: More than 21,000 citations point to one recipe for feeding plants without soil. Hoagland and Snyder devised the Hoagland solution in 1933, a standard hydroponic nutrient solution that supplies every essential plant element. It was meant to imitate a nutrient-rich soil solution, and its high nitrogen and potassium suit large plants such as tomato and bell pepper. Revisions added ferric chelates to keep iron in solution. In 1938 the trace elements were cut to the accepted essentials: B, Mn, Zn, Cu, Mo, Fe and Cl. Arnon's 1950 revision changed only molybdenum, from 0.048 to 0.011 ppm.

soil-fert-236.title: Reading a leaf's nitrogen without picking it
soil-fert-236.text: A laboratory tissue test usually takes one to two weeks, and by then the time to act may have passed. Non-destructive tissue tests answer in the field. They estimate a crop's nitrogen status from leaf chlorophyll without destroying the sample. The link is chemical: each chlorophyll molecule contains four nitrogen atoms. Absorption meters shine light through a leaf. Brands report different units, such as SPAD, which convert, and readings are linear only below 300 mg/m2. Fluorescence-ratio meters read up to 675 mg/m2 and can measure small, curved or thick samples.

soil-fert-218.title: Biogeochemistry, the science of Earth as a living whole
soil-fert-218.text: Vladimir Vernadsky saw the Earth as a living whole. His 1926 book The Biosphere made that case, and he is called the founder of modern biogeochemistry. The field studies the chemical, physical, geological and biological processes that govern the make-up of the natural environment, the pedosphere included.
