At its center are the biogeochemical cycles of elements and their passage through living things, especially carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, iron and phosphorus. Its roots reach back to eighteenth-century agricultural interest in soil chemistry, which improved the understanding of nutrients. An 1844 paper by Dumas and Boussingault counts as a milestone. A systems science close to systems ecology, it lives in many disciplines, from ecology, geology and oceanography to soil science. Research ranges from recovery after soil and water acidification to the carbon storage of {{ref:soil-env-212}}. Evolutionary biogeochemistry turns the same lens on Earth's geologic history and the evolution of life.

soil-fert-224.title: Urease, the enzyme that decides urea's fate
soil-fert-224.text: More than half of all synthetic nitrogen fertilizer is one compound, described in {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and one enzyme decides how much of it is wasted. Urease, which contains nickel, breaks that compound down into carbon dioxide and ammonia. The reaction runs in two stages through carbamic acid, and the basic ammonia raises the pH around it. A key catalyst of the nitrogen cycle, urease occurs as a {{ref:soil-bio-039}}, likely because soil microbes gain from the ammonium it frees. Rapid breakdown wastes fertilizer, so inhibiting urease with chemicals such as NBPT is an agricultural goal. Its activity also serves as an indicator of the health of microbial communities.

soil-fert-221.title: Nitrospira, the bacterium that broke a nitrification rule
soil-fert-221.text: A long-held view said nitrification needs two organisms, one for each step. Nitrospira helped overturn it. This genus of bacteria oxidizes nitrite to nitrate, the second step, yet some members, such as Nitrospira inopinata, carry out both steps alone, as {{ref:soil-fert-110}} describes. First described in 1986 from the Gulf of Maine, it lives in forest soils, rice paddies and farmland as well as water systems and wastewater plants. It is hard to culture, so most knowledge of it comes from molecular and genomic data. Some make their own urease, and the ammonia it frees lets ammonia oxidizers live alongside them.

soil-fert-219.title: Leghemoglobin, the red guardian of the root nodule
soil-fert-219.text: Legume root nodules hold a red protein that closely resembles hemoglobin. This is leghemoglobin, an oxygen-carrying plant globin made only when rhizobia colonize the roots. It solves a dilemma. {{ref:soil-fert-101}} is oxygen-sensitive, yet energy-hungry nitrogen fixation needs respiration, and respiration needs oxygen. Leghemoglobin builds up to millimolar levels, keeping free oxygen in the nanomolar range while holding enough total oxygen. Plants need it for symbiotic fixation but not for growth when fixed nitrogen is supplied. Its main job is still debated. A 1995 study pointed to oxygen delivery; 2005 knockout studies found it both buffers and delivers oxygen.

soil-fert-222.title: The selenium cycle, a loop of give and take
soil-fert-222.text: Selenium moves through living things in a loop. Bacteria, fungi and plants, especially species of Astragalus, reduce its oxidized forms, selenate and selenite, to selenide; other organisms oxidize it back. On semi-arid seleniferous soils, rich in selenium, accumulator plants return organic selenium to the soil as they decay. Yet soil selenium there stays mainly inorganic, evidence that it is re-oxidized. In sediment, selenate reduced to selenite sticks to clay and reacts with iron, locking selenium away. Some organic forms escape as vapor from water, sediment or plants. Oxidation and methylation by roots and microorganisms return selenium to food chains.

soil-fert-223.title: Sulfur assimilation, from sulfate to cysteine
soil-fert-223.text: Plants spend energy to take up sulfur. Sulfur assimilation is how living things build sulfur into their molecules. In plants it begins at the root, which takes up sulfate actively at a cost in ATP. Uptake generally reaches its maximum rate at sulfate levels of 0.1 mM and lower. The transpiration stream carries sulfate to the shoot, where chloroplasts reduce it to sulfide and build it into cysteine, an amino acid. When sulfate runs short, most sulfate transporter genes are expressed up to 100-fold more strongly. Bacteria and fungi follow a similar route, reducing sulfate through APS and sulfite to sulfide for cysteine.

soil-fert-225.title: Nitrous oxide reductase, the last brake on a greenhouse gas
soil-fert-225.text: Nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas, and one bacterial enzyme keeps much of it out of the air. Nitrous oxide reductase performs the last step of denitrification, reducing nitrous oxide to nitrogen gas. By consuming the gas inside cells, it greatly limits emissions to the atmosphere. Only denitrifying prokaryotes can make this conversion. Some communities do only this step, while some denitrifiers lack the enzyme and stop at nitrous oxide. Encoded by nos genes, it is a copper enzyme in the bacterial periplasm. Its catalytic CuZ site is a cluster of four copper atoms bound with sulfide. Acetylene is its most specific inhibitor.

soil-fert-220.title: Nitrogen-15 tracing: following one heavy atom
soil-fert-220.text: Soil ammonium can be made and used up at the same moment, so its concentration alone hides what is happening. Nitrogen-15 tracing follows the heavy stable isotope nitrogen-15 through the nitrogen cycle to measure each conversion. Natural-abundance methods need no disturbance; they express 15N as delta values relative to air. The 15N site preference within nitrous oxide helps tell nitrification from denitrification. Enrichment methods add 15N-labeled ammonium or nitrate, allowing precise rate calculations, though the added nitrogen can bias natural transformations. Rates of simultaneous processes are solved numerically, for example with the Ntrace model, based on a Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation.

soil-fert-209.title: Guano, the seabird dung that fed the world
soil-fert-209.text: Andean people may have spread seabird droppings from Peru's coastal islands on their fields for as long as 5,000 years. Guano, a word from Quechua, is the accumulated excrement of seabirds or bats, used as fertilizer. It is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium. Both kinds exceed 40% organic matter, and bat guano may hold up to 6% available P2O5. After Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1802 and Humphry Davy praised the Peruvian kind, guano became popular in Europe in the 19th century. European guano was poorer, its potency leached by high rainfall and humidity. The seabird guano trade played a pivotal role in the rise of modern input-intensive farming. Demand fell rapidly after 1910 with the Haber–Bosch process, but organic food has revived it in the 21st century. The cost is real. Unsustainable mining has destroyed habitat and killed millions of seabirds, and harvesting bat guano can drive bats from their roosts.

soil-fert-215.title: Wood ash, a liming agent from the fireplace
soil-fert-215.text: Burning wood leaves about 6–10% of it behind as ash, a powdery residue made largely of calcium compounds. As a fertilizer it supplies potassium and calcium carbonate, which acts as a liming agent to neutralize acid soils. Calcium carbonate may make up 25% or even 45% of its weight. Ash typically holds 7–33% calcium, 3–10% potassium, 1–2% magnesium and 0.3–1.4% phosphorus. Hotter fires leave less ash and drive off potassium, sulfur and boron. Ash also carries trace heavy metals, such as lead at 2–500 ppm and cadmium at 0.18–60 ppm.

soil-fert-205.title: Biostimulants, neither fertilizer nor pesticide
soil-fert-205.text: Some products help crops grow without being fertilizer or pesticide. These biostimulants are substances, microbial cultures or mixtures used to promote crop growth. A proposed standard definition says they work through emergent properties of their constituents, not merely through known nutrients, growth regulators or protective compounds. Ingredients include humic substances, amino acids, seaweed extracts and chitin derivatives. Living agents include growth-promoting rhizobacteria and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Registered endophytic strains, microbes living inside plants, have improved nutrient use efficiency and stress tolerance in the field. With no agreed definition, as of 2016 no country had a specific regulatory framework for them.

soil-fert-210.title: The Guano Age, when bird droppings ran a treasury
soil-fert-210.text: Peru once funded its state on bird droppings. From 1840 it made guano an exclusive state resource, and the royalties became the country's largest source of revenue. This Guano Age ran from Humboldt's investigations at Callao in 1802 to the War of the Pacific. By 1846, 462,057 tonnes had left Ichaboe Island off Namibia for Britain. Peru's exports peaked above 700,000 tonnes in 1870, though the Chincha Islands were nearly exhausted. The US Guano Islands Act of 1856 let citizens claim unclaimed guano islands, and nearly 100 were annexed. Afterward Chile saltpeter eclipsed guano.

soil-fert-211.title: Liquid manure, from slurry pit to vegetable field
soil-fert-211.text: Post-war tractors changed how farms handle dung. Powerful enough to haul heavy tanks, they let farmers spread liquid manure evenly near plant roots. Liquid manure is a mixture of animal waste and organic matter, sometimes thinned with water, developed in the 20th century as an alternative to fermented manure. A slurry pit can age and concentrate it. Like solid manure, it is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from the animals' feed. Concentrated animal feeding operations supply most of it spread on US vegetable fields, a route for E. coli O157:H7. Runoff from such operations contaminated wells in the fatal Walkerton outbreak.

soil-fert-216.title: Turning an NPK label into real phosphorus and potassium
soil-fert-216.text: A bag labeled 18-51-20 does not hold 51% phosphorus. Labels give phosphorus as P2O5 and potassium as K2O, so a simple calculation recovers the elements. P2O5 is 43.6% phosphorus by weight, so elemental phosphorus is 0.436 times the P value. K2O is 83% potassium, so elemental potassium is 0.83 times the K value. The N value already gives elemental nitrogen and needs no conversion. That 18-51-20 fertilizer thus holds 18% nitrogen, 22% phosphorus and 17% potassium. Pure potassium chloride, 52% potassium, would read 0-0-63; sylvite, which contains other compounds, usually reads 0-0-60.

soil-fert-207.title: Ecological sanitation: closing the loop from toilet to field
soil-fert-207.text: A toilet can be the first step in growing food. Ecological sanitation aims to reuse human excreta safely in agriculture, closing the nutrient loop between sanitation and farming. It is an approach, not a technology; urine-diverting dry toilets are its most common technology but not the only one. Trials around the world show measurable benefits from treated excreta, especially urine, as fertilizer and soil conditioner. It may also ease a possible phosphorus shortage. One review suggested phosphate collected from urine could meet 22% of total demand. Whether its treatments destroy pathogens safely is still debated, though WHO reuse guidelines with a multiple barrier concept give a common framework.

soil-fert-214.title: Polyhalite, four nutrients from deep under Yorkshire
soil-fert-214.text: The only polyhalite mined lies more than 1,000 m below North Yorkshire, in a layer 260 million years old. Boulby Mine has worked it since 2010. Polyhalite is an evaporite mineral, one left behind by evaporating water, and a hydrated sulfate of potassium, calcium and magnesium. As fertilizer it supplies four nutrients and little chloride: 48% SO3, 14% K2O, 6% MgO and 17% CaO. As a soil amendment it can improve drainage and fertility and help reduce soil acidity.

soil-fert-212.title: Nutrient budgeting, keeping the books on a farm's soil
soil-fert-212.text: A farm can keep accounts for its nutrients as well as its money. Nutrient budgeting compares all the nutrients applied to a farm's soil with all those removed. Inputs include fertilizer, rainfall, brought-in supplements and spread effluent. Outputs include sold stock, crops, milk, meat and wool, plus leaching of nitrate, volatilization and phosphate runoff. A surplus builds up nutrients and the risk of loss; a deficit drains reserves and risks deficiencies and lower yields. Budgets are less exact than financial statements, drawing on yield history, past applications and average removal coefficients. They are a best management practice in the 4R strategy.

soil-fert-217.title: Fertilizer placement: broadcast or banded with the seed
soil-fert-217.text: Where fertilizer goes can strongly affect how much of it a crop takes up. Fertilizer placement is that choice, such as broadcasting over the field or banding with the seed. Broadcast urea beyond what plants use causes nitrous oxide emissions and water pollution. Banding has its own hazard. Hydrolyzing urea creates a toxic high-ammonia zone, so urea fertilizers should not be applied or banded with seed at more than 10–20 kg/ha, depending on the crop. Feeding through irrigation, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-208}}, places nutrients wherever the water goes.

soil-fert-206.title: Diammonium phosphate and its delayed acid twist
soil-fert-206.text: Ammonia meets phosphoric acid, and the product is diammonium phosphate, (NH4)2HPO4, a water-soluble salt used as fertilizer. Its typical NPK rating is 18-46-0: 18% nitrogen, 46% P2O5 and no K2O. Its effect on soil pH reverses with time. At first it raises pH, but over the long term the ground becomes more acidic than before as its ammonium is nitrified. Its solution averages pH 7.5–8. Alkaline chemicals turn its ammonium into ammonia, so the two are incompatible. In air it slowly loses ammonia, and at around 70 °C it breaks down to ammonia and monoammonium phosphate.

soil-fert-213.title: Phosphogypsum, the radioactive leftover of fertilizer acid
soil-fert-213.text: Every ton of phosphoric acid leaves about five tons of waste. That waste is phosphogypsum, a calcium sulfate hydrate, mainly gypsum, left when phosphoric acid for fertilizer is made from phosphate rock. Output reaches an estimated 100 to 280 million tonnes a year. Uranium at 5–10 ppm, thorium and their daughter nuclides make it weakly radioactive, so most is stored indefinitely. Up to 15% is used, partly as a soil amendment. In 1990 the US EPA banned most uses above 10 picocuries of radium-226 per gram. Storage remains controversial. The EPA approved its use in roads in 2020 over environmentalists' objections, then withdrew the rule in 2021.

soil-form-134.title: Rock, the solid stuff the Earth is built from
soil-form-134.text: Almost the whole planet is rock. It makes up the Earth's crust and most of its interior, apart from the liquid outer core and pockets of magma. A rock is any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter, built from the crystals described in {{ref:soil-found-029}}. Geologists sort rocks by the minerals they contain, their chemical composition and how they formed. That last test gives three main groups: {{ref:soil-form-135}}, {{ref:soil-form-136}} and {{ref:soil-form-137}}. The second group matters most to soil, because it is made from the wreckage of other rocks. Weathering breaks existing rock down, and water, wind and ice carry and deposit the pieces as sediment. From smallest to largest, those sediments are clay, silt, sand and gravel, the same grains soil is made of.

soil-form-136.title: Sedimentary rock, a thin skin over most of the land
soil-form-136.text: Sedimentary rock covers 73% of the Earth's land surface, yet it makes up only about 8% of the crust's volume. It is a thin skin. This rock forms when mineral or organic particles deposited at the surface are cemented together. Its mineral debris comes from {{ref:soil-found-052}} and erosion of older rock, carried by water, wind, ice or mass movement. Clastic sedimentary rocks are cemented rock fragments, commonly grains of quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, the clay-forming minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-079}} or flaky {{ref:soil-chem-135}}. They are subdivided by their dominant particle size. Mudrocks, for example, contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized particles.

soil-form-147.title: Limestone, the rock that dissolves and sweetens soil
soil-form-147.text: Limestone is rock that water can slowly eat. It is a carbonate sedimentary rock made mostly of calcite and aragonite, two forms of calcium carbonate, and it is the main source of lime. About 20% to 25% of sedimentary rock is carbonate rock, most of it limestone and much of the rest dolomite. Limestone is partly soluble, especially in acid. Water and organic acid from the soil widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the {{ref:soil-found-118}}. The result is karst country of pavements, caves and gorges. Farmers turn the same chemistry to use: pulverized limestone, spread as {{ref:soil-fert-059}}, neutralizes acidic soils.

soil-form-135.title: Igneous rock, frozen from molten magma
soil-form-135.text: Every igneous rock was once liquid. It forms when magma or lava cools and solidifies, and it is one of the three main rock types. Some freezes below the surface as intrusive rock, slowly enough to grow mineral grains the eye can see. Some freezes at the surface as extrusive rock, so fast that it ends up glassy or very fine-grained. Geologists classify it chiefly by that particle size, which depends largely on cooling history, and by its {{ref:soil-found-029}} content. Born hot and deep, igneous rock is unstable near the surface. There acidic soil water and groundwater readily dissolve it and break it down.

soil-form-137.title: Metamorphic rock, remade by heat and pressure
soil-form-137.text: A metamorphic rock is a rock that has been cooked into something new. Heat and pressure transform an existing rock, a process called metamorphism. The starting rock, the protolith, may be {{ref:soil-form-135}}, {{ref:soil-form-136}} or an older metamorphic rock. It is heated above 150 to 200 °C, often under 100 megapascals of pressure or more. Its minerals then recrystallize while the rock stays mostly solid. Metamorphic rocks form 12% of the Earth's land surface. Gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite are familiar examples.

soil-form-148.title: Grus, granite crumbled into coarse grit
soil-form-148.text: Granite can fall apart grain by grain. The result is grus, an accumulation of angular, coarse sand and gravel left when crystalline rocks, especially granitoids, disintegrate through weathering. Both chemical and mechanical weathering make it, generally in arid or semiarid regions. Most Late Cenozoic {{ref:soil-form-100}} mantles in Europe are grus. Older Mesozoic and Early Cenozoic saprolites are different: they are made of kaolinitic and ferrallitic material, rotted much further. Cement grus sand together and it becomes a sandstone called arkose.

soil-form-139.title: Lithology, describing a rock at a glance
soil-form-139.text: Before naming a rock, a geologist describes what can be seen. Lithology is that description of a rock unit's physical characteristics, visible at outcrop, in hand or core samples, or under low magnification. It records colour, texture, the size of the grains and composition, building on the skills in {{ref:soil-found-038}}. The word can also mean a summary rock name, such as sandstone, slate, basalt or limestone. Lithology is the basis for dividing rock sequences into lithostratigraphic units for mapping and correlation. Site investigations describe it in standard terms, as in the European geotechnical standard Eurocode 7.

soil-form-140.title: Primary minerals, inherited unchanged from rock
soil-form-140.text: Much of a soil's grit was never made in the soil at all. Soil minerals come in two types. Primary minerals are found in soil but did not form there. They crystallized with their host igneous rock and have not been chemically altered since. Secondary minerals, by contrast, form as primary minerals weather. Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm. They make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions. {{ref:soil-form-135}} supplies them: quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-142}}, muscovite, {{ref:soil-form-144}}, amphibole, pyroxene and {{ref:soil-form-145}}. Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil, and quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates, silicates built as a three-dimensional framework. The chain runs from primary rocks, the source of primary minerals, to the parent rocks those minerals compose.

soil-form-141.title: Feldspar: the rock mineral that becomes clay
soil-form-141.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust and 41% of the continental crust by weight. They are rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium. The commonest are the sodium-calcium plagioclase feldspars and the potassium-sodium alkali feldspars. Formed at high temperature, they are unstable at the surface, especially plagioclase, so they weather easily. Hydrolysis, described in {{ref:soil-form-172}}, turns them into clay minerals including illite, smectite and kaolinite, and because feldspars are so abundant, clays are abundant too. Clay-replaced feldspar looks chalky beside glassy unweathered grains. Feldspar-rich sediment therefore points to little chemical weathering before burial.

soil-form-145.title: Olivine, the mantle mineral that fades fast at the surface
soil-form-145.text: Olivine is common underground and rare in the open. This magnesium iron silicate, (Mg,Fe)2SiO4, is the main component of the upper mantle. At the surface it weathers quickly. It ranks among the least stable common surface minerals in {{ref:soil-chem-187}}, a ranking of minerals by how fast they weather, so it is rarely found in sedimentary rock. With water it readily alters to iddingsite, a mix of clay-forming minerals, oxides of iron and {{ref:soil-chem-111}}. That eagerness to react has a proposed use. Spreading fine olivine on beaches to speed its weathering could be a cheap way to sequester CO2.

soil-form-142.title: Plagioclase, the striped feldspar that weathers first
soil-form-142.text: Plagioclase is a sliding scale rather than a single mineral. It is a continuous series of framework silicates within {{ref:soil-form-141}}, running from albite, NaAlSi3O8, to anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8, as sodium and calcium substitute for each other. It is abundant in igneous and metamorphic rock and common as a detrital grain in sedimentary rock. In hand samples, fine parallel striations called polysynthetic twinning often give it away. Plagioclase weathers relatively rapidly to clay-forming minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Sandstones therefore usually hold more of the more resistant alkali feldspar.

soil-form-144.title: Biotite, the dark mica that yellows with age
soil-form-144.text: Biotite peels apart in thin, dark flakes. It is a group of phyllosilicate minerals in the family of {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, approximately K(Mg,Fe)3AlSi3O10(OH,F)2. Its sheets of iron, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, oxygen and hydrogen are held together only weakly, by potassium ions. It occurs in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks and makes up as much as 7% of the exposed continental crust. Fresh biotite is greenish to brown or black. Weathered, it can turn even yellow.

soil-form-146.title: Mafic: dark rocks rich in magnesium and iron
soil-form-146.text: Mafic is a word made from two elements: magnesium and ferric, for iron. Coined in 1912, it describes silicate minerals, magmas and igneous rocks rich in magnesium and iron and relatively low in silica. Mafic rocks have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium. They are dark and dense. At the other end of the spectrum sit felsic rocks, light, less dense and enriched in aluminium, silicon, potassium and sodium. Common mafic minerals are {{ref:soil-form-145}}, pyroxene, amphibole and biotite. Common mafic rocks are basalt, diabase and gabbro.

soil-form-143.title: Orthoclase, the potassium feldspar of granite
soil-form-143.text: Orthoclase is the feldspar that carries potassium. Its formula is KAlSi3O8, and it is an important tectosilicate of {{ref:soil-form-135}}. It is a type of alkali feldspar, also called potassium feldspar or K-spar. It is a common constituent of most granites and other felsic igneous rocks, the light-coloured, silica-rich kind. Like other feldspars it does not last forever at the surface. It commonly alters to sericite, a fine-grained flaky mineral, or to clay.

soil-form-138.title: The rock cycle, from basalt to sediment and back
soil-form-138.text: No rock is permanent. The rock cycle describes how {{ref:soil-form-136}}, {{ref:soil-form-137}} and {{ref:soil-form-135}} turn into one another through geologic time. Each type changes when forced out of the conditions it formed in. Basalt, for example, breaks down and dissolves when exposed to the atmosphere. Weathering and erosion break exposed rock into fragments and carry away dissolved material, on the way to new sedimentary rock. Plate tectonics and {{ref:soil-water-079}} drive the whole loop. On planets with life, living things join in, so the loop is a {{ref:soil-fert-140}} as well as a geologic one.

soil-form-152.title: Volcanic ash, a fertile gift that can smother
soil-form-152.text: Wind can carry volcanic ash thousands of kilometres from the eruption that made it. Ash is fragments of rock, mineral crystals and glass chilled from lava, all under 2 mm across. Coarser explosive products fall under tephra, the fragmental material of an eruption whatever its size. Washed into the soil, ash minerals form a nutrient-rich layer that is very good for farming, the kind found in {{ref:soil-class-092}}. Too much at once does harm. Heavy ashfalls can bury pasture and sterilize the soil by cutting off its oxygen. Rehabilitation includes mixing the ash into the buried soil, adding to its {{ref:soil-form-087}}.

soil-form-153.title: Lichens, the first soil makers on bare stone
soil-form-153.text: On bare rock high in the mountains or far toward the poles, lichens often arrive first. They are symbiotic colonies of fungi with algae or cyanobacteria, and they slowly turn stone into soil. They disrupt minerals physically and degrade them chemically, a clear case of {{ref:soil-found-063}}. Their metal-binding exudates and the new minerals they form, especially metal oxalates, make them important agents of chemical weathering. In deserts, lichen crusts stabilize sand and hold water. Some plant seeds establish only there.

soil-form-154.title: Desert varnish, a dark skin painted by dust and dew
soil-form-154.text: Desert rocks often wear a coat only about one micrometre thick. Desert varnish is that orange-yellow to black coating on exposed rock in arid places. It forms only on stable surfaces, safe from frequent rain, fracturing or sandblasting by wind, and is mostly {{ref:soil-found-040}} with iron and manganese oxides. Windblown clay traps other substances, which react as the rock heats in the sun and is wetted by dew. Black varnish holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%. Microbes that oxidize manganese may explain it. Where the local pH exceeds 7.5, iron-rich orange varnish forms instead.

soil-form-149.title: Glacial drift, named for a theory that sank
soil-form-149.text: Glacial drift carries the name of a mistake. Murchison introduced the term in 1839, following Lyell's idea that the sediments were dropped by drifting sea ice. The hypothesis died; the name outlived it. Drift is now all sediment, from clay to boulders, carried by a glacier and deposited by the ice or its meltwater. It splits in two. Unstratified drift is {{ref:soil-form-090}}, which builds the ridges described in {{ref:soil-form-150}}. Stratified drift is sorted and laid down by meltwater, forming {{ref:soil-form-151}}, eskers, kames and varves. In the United Kingdom the word is broader, covering all Quaternary surface deposits mapped apart from bedrock, including loess, river deposits and colluvium.

soil-form-150.title: Moraines, the rubble ridges glaciers leave behind
soil-form-150.text: A glacier dumps what it carries along its edges and at its snout. A moraine is any such accumulation of loose glacial debris, often till, in regions that are or once were glaciated. It ranges from boulders down to gravel and sand, set in a groundmass of fine clayey glacial flour. Lateral moraines form at the side of the ice. Terminal moraines form at its foot and mark the glacier's furthest advance. Recessional moraines are small ridges left where a retreating glacier paused. Ground moraines are till-covered sheets of gently rolling relief under 10 meters, laid at the ice base as lodgment till.

soil-form-151.title: Outwash plains, where meltwater sorts the glacier's load
soil-form-151.text: Meltwater pouring off a glacier sorts its load by size. Boulders settle near the {{ref:soil-form-150}} at the ice front, and the finest silt travels furthest. The result is an outwash plain, or sandur: a plain of {{ref:soil-form-091}} built at the end of a glacier. Braided streams rework its surface. Kettle lakes form where buried blocks of ice melted. Not every sandur is active. Fossil sandar lie in formerly glaciated areas, long after the ice has gone.

soil-found-121.title: Spheroidal weathering, peeling rock like an onion
soil-found-121.text: Square blocks of rock can rot into round boulders. Spheroidal, or onion-skin, weathering is the chemical attack on jointed bedrock that leaves concentric shells of decayed rock inside {{ref:soil-form-100}}. Water enters along the joints. Each block therefore weathers inward fastest at its corners, then its edges, then its faces, leaving a rounded core. These corestones, or woolsacks, stand as freestanding boulders or tors once erosion strips away the rotten rock around them. The alteration forms secondary minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, and swells the rock's volume. It has often been wrongly blamed on physical weathering alone, yet much of it happened in past humid, even tropical, climates.

soil-form-116.title: Slickensides, polished cracks in swelling clay
soil-form-116.text: Some soil cracks shine as if polished. In pedology, slickensides are those glossy crack surfaces, formed in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays. They are a type of {{ref:soil-found-068}}, a coating or surface feature on soil aggregates. In {{ref:soil-class-022}}, slickensides together with lens-shaped aggregates mark one soil order, {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Geologists use the same name for something larger: fault surfaces smoothed by friction and striated in the direction of movement.

soil-form-121.title: The calcic horizon, where lime collects in dry soils
soil-form-121.text: In dry soils, lime washed down from above can pile up in a layer of its own. A calcic horizon is that layer of secondary carbonate accumulation, carbonate built from {{ref:soil-found-118}}. It must hold more than 15% carbonate, measured as {{ref:soil-fert-060}}, and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below. This {{ref:soil-form-017}} marks several dryland soil groups. {{ref:soil-class-161}} have a calcic, hypercalcic or petrocalcic horizon whose upper boundary lies within 1.0 m of the surface. Calciorthids are distinguished by one, and most Ustolls have one too. {{ref:soil-class-093}} have even been redefined as soils with a calcic horizon less than 1 meter deep.

soil-form-120.title: The kandic horizon, a clay layer that holds little
soil-form-120.text: Not every clay-rich subsoil is rich in nutrients. A kandic horizon is a subsoil layer of washed-in clay, a kind of {{ref:soil-class-045}}, whose clays are mainly 1:1 silicate clays. These clays carry little exchangeable charge, so the horizon stores nutrients poorly. It is a {{ref:soil-form-017}} that helps sort soils into orders. {{ref:soil-class-090}} must have a clay-enriched, natric or kandic horizon. {{ref:soil-class-104}} must have a clay-enriched or kandic one. In the world system, {{ref:soil-class-134}} correspond to kandic soils of those two orders and of {{ref:soil-class-100}}. {{ref:soil-class-117}} correspond partly to {{ref:soil-class-103}} with a kandic horizon.

soil-form-118.title: The mollic epipedon, the dark topsoil of grasslands
soil-form-118.text: The black topsoil of a grassland is built by roots, year after year. Long-term additions of organic matter from plant roots create a mollic epipedon, a fertile, dark surface horizon with typically soft, granular structure. It is a kind of {{ref:soil-form-018}}, a dark version of the {{ref:soil-form-008}}. It defines {{ref:soil-class-101}}, which must have one and a {{ref:soil-chem-052}} above 50%. These soils are common in grasslands. Other traits can override it. Where shrink–swell clays dominate, a soil with a mollic epipedon is classed with {{ref:soil-class-106}}. In {{ref:soil-class-092}} the andic properties take precedence. {{ref:soil-class-047}} combine a mollic horizon with dry-forest vegetation, where organic accumulation outweighs {{ref:soil-form-050}}.

soil-form-119.title: The natric horizon, a clay layer loaded with sodium
soil-form-119.text: Natrium is Latin for sodium, and it names a troublesome soil layer. A natric horizon is a subsoil layer of washed-in clay in which large amounts of exchangeable sodium have built up. It develops from a clay-enriched layer of the kind described in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. It is a {{ref:soil-form-017}} in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-143}} soils have a natric horizon within the upper 100 cm. Soils of two other orders, {{ref:soil-class-090}} and {{ref:soil-class-101}}, belong mainly to that group when they have one.

soil-form-122.title: Soil monoliths, whole profiles carried into museums
soil-form-122.text: A soil profile can be lifted out of the ground and hung on a wall. A soil monolith is a {{ref:soil-form-002}} dug out in one piece, without disturbing its layers, and preserved for study or display. Each one is processed for a month or longer before it is mounted. The {{ref:soil-hist-041}} shows some 80 monoliths and stores about 1000 from over 70 countries. Each comes with site data and a description of every {{ref:soil-found-001}}. The Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil holds about 330, representing the world's soil diversity.

soil-form-117.title: The spodic horizon, where iron and humus settle
soil-form-117.text: Under conifer forests, iron and aluminium travel downward and stop together. A spodic horizon is the subsurface layer of the soils in {{ref:soil-class-138}}, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with decayed organic matter, giving it an iron-rich look. It is a {{ref:soil-form-017}} in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-099}} must have one within 2 m of the surface, usually beneath a pale, bleached albic horizon. They are acidic soils of coniferous and boreal forests. The Polish classification uses the spodic horizon to define its order of soils formed mainly by {{ref:soil-form-061}}.

soil-form-126.title: Periglaciation, the shaping power of freeze and thaw
soil-form-126.text: About a quarter of Earth's land is shaped by freeze and thaw today. Periglaciation is the set of landform processes that result from seasonal freezing and thawing, very often where the ground stays frozen year-round. Walery Łoziński introduced the term in 1909. The name suggests the edges of glaciers, but periglacial environments are anywhere freeze and thaw significantly modify the landscape. Another quarter or fifth of the land had such conditions during the Pleistocene. Its hallmark processes are {{ref:soil-phys-153}}, {{ref:soil-water-056}} and the growth of ice wedges, all driven by the force described in {{ref:soil-found-054}}.

soil-form-125.title: Ecological succession, how life builds its own soil
soil-form-125.text: Bare rock, a fresh lava flow or newly exposed till starts with no life at all. Ecological succession is the change in a community's species over time, and on such surfaces it is called primary succession. Secondary succession follows a disturbance instead. Pioneers come first: microorganisms, lichens and mosses. Grasses, shrubs and trees follow. As plants grow they change the soil, adding organic matter to litter and {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and altering nutrients and pH. That is how {{ref:soil-form-046}} lets soil form. The soil in turn steers what grows next, since its properties and the cycling of its nutrients shape further succession.

soil-form-124.title: Tree throw, how falling trees plough the land
soil-form-124.text: When a big tree topples, it tears out a pit several meters across and 1–2 metres deep. Tree throw is that bowl-shaped pit in the subsoil, made by a falling tree's rootwad or by long root growth. It exposes humus-poor, mineral-rich soil and is a form of {{ref:soil-form-080}}. It drives bedrock weathering and {{ref:soil-form-042}}, fastest where soils are of intermediate thickness. Under soils deeper than the roots reach, no bedrock is upturned. Before trees appeared about 370 million years ago, bedrock weathering was too slow to keep thick soils on hilly terrain. In old-growth forest, the pits and the mounds of rotting fallen trees form pit-and-mound topography.

soil-form-123.title: Argillipedoturbation, clay that churns itself
soil-form-123.text: Some clay soils mix themselves. Argillipedoturbation is soil mixing caused by the shrinking and swelling of {{ref:soil-chem-091}} clays, sometimes called self-mulching. Wetting and drying cycles drive it, and it needs at least 30% clay. As the soil dries, vertical cracks open up to 2 centimetres wide and 50 centimetres or more deep. Surface material sloughs into them. Over time this {{ref:soil-form-080}} can blend horizons until they are hard to tell apart. It also produces {{ref:soil-phys-030}}, a hummocky surface, and the polished cracks in {{ref:soil-form-116}}. Such soils are very productive when irrigated but hard to plough and manage.

soil-form-127.title: Soil geography, the map of where soils lie
soil-form-127.text: Why is one soil here and another there? Soil geography is the branch of physical geography that answers that question, dealing with how soils are distributed across the terrain. It studies their spatial distribution in relation to topography, climate, soil life and the minerals within soils, the same {{ref:soil-form-043}} that build every {{ref:soil-found-077}}. It sits beside {{ref:soil-water-295}}, climatology, {{ref:soil-phys-207}} and biogeography among the fields that study the Earth's surface. Its key is an understanding of {{ref:soil-form-042}}. That knowledge explains soil patterns today, the business of soil geography, and in past geologic periods, the business of {{ref:soil-class-111}}. Pedodiversity was brought into pedology to analyse soil spatial patterns and to test theories of soil formation. The Russian Geographical Society awarded {{ref:soil-hist-008}} its Lütke Gold Medal for his work in the field.

soil-form-131.title: Tropical soils, lush forests on poor ground
soil-form-131.text: Rainforests look rich, yet most of the soils beneath them are poor. The soils of the humid tropics are mostly strongly leached and low in nutrients, though some areas are fertile. On younger substrates, especially volcanic ones, they can be quite fertile. The poverty comes from heat and rain. Most of a soil's nutrient-holding capacity sits on particles of clay and {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, and fast {{ref:soil-form-050}} and decomposition remove them. Phosphorus is often the scarcest nutrient, because intense weathering depletes the mineral pool and, unlike nitrogen, it cannot be replenished from the air. Leaching also strips silica and leaves iron and aluminium oxides, the source of the typical red colour. So these soils draw their fertility almost wholly from organic matter, whose decayed fraction holds nutrients and releases them to roots. Clear the forest and some harden irreversibly into a surface crust of laterite or {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Burrowing ants, termites and worms keep them churned, so they often lack the clay-enriched subsoils of midlatitude soils. Farmers add charcoal, modelled on the fertile Amazonian {{ref:soil-class-053}}, to improve them.

soil-form-132.title: Lithosequences, soils that differ only in their rock
soil-form-132.text: To see what rock alone does to a soil, compare soils where everything else is the same. A lithosequence is a set of soils formed under similar conditions on different {{ref:soil-form-087}}. The soils share similar weathering conditions. Their differences in composition therefore reflect how fast each parent's minerals weather. {{ref:soil-chem-187}}, which ranks minerals by weathering rate, can be applied to them. Lithosequence studies give the clearest picture of the role of parent material in soil formation, even in ancient buried soils.

soil-form-133.title: The soils of Australia, ancient and starved of phosphorus
soil-form-133.text: Australia's soils are among the oldest anywhere, and many are naturally short of phosphorus. Plants have adapted. Those with proteoid, or cluster, roots grow in these very nutrient-poor soils, and dense mats of fine hairs on their roots can absorb enough rain to prevent runoff. James Arthur Prescott described the continent's soils in CSIR bulletin 52. Its title was The Soils of Australia in Relation to Vegetation and Climate. {{ref:soil-class-022}} later replaced earlier systems, including the Factual Key (1960) and {{ref:soil-class-046}} (1968).

soil-form-102.title: Bedrock, the solid floor beneath the soil
soil-form-102.text: Dig deep enough almost anywhere and the spade strikes solid rock. Bedrock is that solid rock, lying beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits in the crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet. Where it breaks the surface, the exposed patch is an outcrop. Its buried top, where it meets the material above, is the rockhead. Locating rockhead by digging, drilling or geophysics matters in most civil engineering projects, and it can lie hundreds of metres down. Exposed bedrock weathers physically or chemically and then erodes. At its buried upper boundary, weathering below ground turns it into {{ref:soil-form-100}}. Fragments torn from it and found higher up, among the weathered layers and soil, are called floaters. Geological maps show bedrock as if every soil and {{ref:soil-form-103}} had been stripped away, unless the cover is too thick to map through. In mapping such cover, every deposit older than the Quaternary counts as bedrock.

soil-form-097.title: Regolith, the loose blanket over solid rock
soil-form-097.text: Few plants can grow in solid rock, and animals need loose material to burrow. Most life on land therefore rests on regolith: a blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock. George P. Merrill coined the word in 1897 from the Greek rhegos, blanket, and lithos, rock. He meant the whole mantle of loose material, whatever its origin. It includes dust, broken rock and related materials. It occurs on Earth, the Moon, Mars, some asteroids and other terrestrial planets and moons. On Earth it comes from weathering and biological processes, and it ranges from absent to hundreds of metres thick. Its age varies just as widely. Fresh ash from eruptions ({{ref:soil-form-152}}) or river sediment is instantly regolith, while parts of Australia carry Precambrian regolith hundreds of millions of years old. The blanket has several ingredients: transported cover, deeply weathered rock, interbedded volcanic deposits, hard crusts, groundwater salts and living things. Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter, is what is conventionally called soil. Regolith matters well beyond biology. Engineers build on it, mineral deposits lie in it, and it supplies sand, gravel, lime and gypsum. It is also the zone through which underground water stores recharge and discharge.

soil-form-100.title: Saprolite, the rotten rock that keeps its shape
soil-form-100.text: Saprolite means rotten rock. It is chemically weathered rock, formed in the lower zones of soil profiles as weathering eats deep into the bedrock surface. It commonly keeps the structural details of its bedrock. It also inherits that rock's texture, pH and minerals. Hydrolysis, {{ref:soil-chem-069}}, hydration and freeze–thaw turn granite and other rocks into it. Quartz resists the attack and can be left behind as sandy soil, a process called arenization. Iron compounds supply most of its color. One, {{ref:soil-chem-104}}, is yellow when fine and brown when coarse. Another, {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, is red when fine and grey to black when coarse. Upper saprolite is fully oxidized bedrock, and lower saprolite is reduced, partly weathered rock. Below lies saprock, bedrock weathered only along its fractures. Younger than its parent rock and older than any thick cover such as lava, saprolite can sometimes be dated relatively. Burrowing plants and animals bring it up to the surface. In Western Australia, poorly weathered saprolite grit forms aquifers that can yield groundwater fit for livestock.

soil-form-098.title: Asteroid regolith, soil-like dust on tiny worlds
soil-form-098.text: Asteroids wear loose blankets too. Asteroid regolith is the loose surface layer of an asteroid, produced by impacts and other processes that alter its surface. Spacecraft show it ranging from fine-grained deposits to coarse, boulder-rich debris. The Hayabusa mission's samples from Itokawa were the first asteroid regolith grains studied in a laboratory. They showed {{ref:soil-hist-079}} and particles implanted by the solar wind. Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020, and OSIRIS-REx from Bennu in 2023. Both hold organic- or carbon-rich material and water.

soil-form-099.title: Titan, where ice behaves like rock
soil-form-099.text: On Saturn's moon Titan, ice does the job of rock. The word regolith traditionally covered only loose mineral grains or rock fragments. Ice grains were left out because, like snow on Earth, they melt and fuse easily. Titan is so cold that ice behaves like rock, with its own erosion and its own wind-driven and sedimentary processes. Its loose icy material behaves mechanically like regolith elsewhere, so it earns the name. Data from an instrument the Huygens probe pushed into the ground suggest a sand of ice grains on a plain of somewhat rounded pebbles.

soil-form-101.title: Deep weathering, rock rotting for millions of years
soil-form-101.text: At 20 m per million years, weathering needs several million years to build a deep regolith, and cooler climates need longer. Deep weathering is that long-continued chemical attack. It builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history. Three conditions favor it. Relief must be gentle enough to prevent erosion and let water carry dissolved material down. The crust must stay tectonically stable for a long time. The climate must be humid, tropical to temperate, with warmth to speed the reactions. Deeply weathered profiles are widespread between latitudes 35°N and 35°S. In parts of Africa, India, South America, Australia and southeast Asia, regolith has been forming for over 100 million years. Regoliths range from a few metres to over 150 m thick, depending on surface age, tectonics, climate history and bedrock. The process sorts the elements as it goes. Sulfides and carbonates leave readily. Nickel, cobalt, copper and zinc held in iron- and magnesium-rich minerals stay higher. They reprecipitate with iron–manganese oxides in the middle and lower saprolite. The result is secondary and supergene ores, enriched near the surface by weathering: {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, iron ores, saprolitic gold, supergene copper, uranium and residual {{ref:soil-chem-193}}. Sweden shows the process across deep time. There it formed thin clay-rich saprolites 1,000 to 500 million years ago, thick ones 200 to 66 million years ago, and medium-thick immature ones 5 million years ago.

soil-form-103.title: Superficial deposits, the young loose cover
soil-form-103.text: Most of the loose ground people walk on is geologically young. Superficial deposits are recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age, less than 2.6 million years old. They include stream channel and floodplain deposits, beach sands, talus gravels, raised beaches and {{ref:soil-class-065}}. Glacier-laid material belongs too, as {{ref:soil-form-149}} and {{ref:soil-form-150}} describe. Most are gravel, sand, silt and clay. Onshore they form relatively thin, often discontinuous patches. Geological surveys keep databases of their properties. Farmers and foresters use them to judge erosion, growing conditions and the risk of nutrients washing out.

soil-form-087.title: Parent material, the stuff every soil grows from
soil-form-087.text: Every soil carries a family likeness to the material it grew from. Rock is the source of all soil minerals and of every plant nutrient except nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon. Parent material is the underlying geological material in which soil horizons form, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit. It may be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock. For a metamorphic rock, the original rock before it changed is the protolith. It may also be loose glacial, river or volcanic deposits. Typical parent minerals include quartz, calcite, feldspar and biotite, one of the minerals covered in {{ref:soil-chem-135}}. The parent leaves a clear mark. Mudstone or shale give clay-rich soils, while sandstone weathers into sandy soils. Parent material also strongly shapes how many basic ions a soil contains. Weatherable minerals in the parent rock favor one kind of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, called mull, while a shortage of them goes with another, called moder. Soil scientists sort parent materials by how they were deposited. Residual material weathered in place. Transported material was carried by water, wind, ice or gravity. Cumulose material is organic matter that accumulated where it formed. Because soils inherit so much of their structure and minerals from their parent, they are often classified by whether it is consolidated and how it was last transported.

soil-form-089.title: Transported parent material, soil from somewhere else
soil-form-089.text: Most soils form in material that wind, water, ice and gravity have carried many miles. Transported parent material is loose, uncemented material moved this way, and it is named for its last means of transport. Material a glacier carried and streams then redeposited counts as stream-transported, or glacial fluvial, parent material. The recognized carriers are wind, water, gravity, ice, lakes and oceans, and the entries ahead give each deposit its name. Water-carried material is split three ways: by rivers, in lakes or in the sea. Wind sorts its load. It moves silt and fine sand hundreds of miles to build {{ref:soil-form-106}}. It seldom moves clay, which sticks into stable clumps. Wind also piles sand-sized grains into dunes and drops {{ref:soil-form-152}} at various distances from a volcano. In the field, rock fragments that thin out with depth, especially over saprolite, suggest the soil material has moved downslope.

soil-form-106.title: Loess, the wind-blown silt that buries whole regions
soil-form-106.text: Ten percent of Earth's land lies under loess or similar deposits. Loess is a clastic sediment, built of fragments, that is mostly silt-sized and formed by the build-up of wind-blown dust. It holds 20% or less clay, with roughly equal parts sand and silt, typically 20 to 50 micrometres across. Calcium carbonate often cements it loosely. It is even-textured, porous, crumbly, pale yellow or buff and usually unlayered. Its angular grains of quartz, feldspar and {{ref:soil-chem-135}} let it stand in vertical banks. In parts of China people dig cave dwellings into them. Deposits exceed a hundred metres in north-western China, reaching 350 m on the {{ref:soil-form-110}}, and run tens of metres thick in the US Midwest. Pye in 1995 listed four requirements: a dust source, enough wind to carry it, a place to accumulate, and time. Von Leonhard described Löss along the Rhine in 1823–1824, and Lyell popularized the term in 1834. Its wind-blown origin was recognized later, notably by von Richthofen in China in 1878.

soil-form-112.title: Alluvium, the sediment that rivers leave behind
soil-form-112.text: Some of the earliest human civilizations grew on river mud. Alluvium is loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in {{ref:soil-water-293}} or similar settings. Floodplain alluvium can be highly fertile. It is usually geologically young and unconsolidated, and most of it is Quaternary. It is often called cover, because it hides the bedrock beneath. Running water sorts what it drops, so alluvium is generally fine-grained and well sorted. Seasonal floods leave it in layers on floodplains. The fans coarsen toward the uplands, and deltas at river mouths are fine-grained. Sediment laid down in seas, estuaries, lakes or ponds is not called alluvium. Beyond that, geologists still disagree over which other deposits the term should include. The word is old. Antoine Furetière's dictionary, published in 1690, defined alluvion as new land formed by sediment along rivers and seas. In the 19th century alluvium meant river sediment lying above older diluvium, which was ascribed to Noah's flood. Once that idea was rejected, diluvium became older alluvium.

soil-form-113.title: Colluvium, the jumble at the foot of the slope
soil-form-113.text: At the base of a hillslope, debris gathers. Colluvium is loose, unconsolidated sediment deposited there by rainwash, sheetwash, slow downslope creep or a mix of these. It is a varied blend of rock types and sizes, from silt to rock fragments, typically angular and loosely consolidated. It builds gently sloping aprons or fans at the foot of slopes, or fills gullies and hollows, sometimes several metres thick. Where gravity moves material, talus cones at the base of steep slopes make it obvious. Unlike alluvium, colluvium involves no running water, so it is poorly sorted where alluvium is well sorted. Where the source material is fine and uniform, though, it can be hard to tell which process laid a deposit down. Thick colluvium often holds buried soils, plant and animal remains and archaeological deposits. Together they record long-term climatic change.

soil-form-110.title: The Loess Plateau, China's yellow highland
soil-form-110.text: The Yellow River owes its name and its color to the loess in its banks. Around the river's upper and middle reaches lies the Loess Plateau, some 640,000 km2 covered by loess. It holds the thickest known loess deposit, up to 350 m. Farmed for over a thousand years, it has produced phenomenal yields. Yet its soil has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth. Wind-borne loess particles from it add to the Asian Dust pollution problem.

soil-form-109.title: Why loess soils are so fertile and so fragile
soil-form-109.text: Soils developed on loess tend to be very rich. Under suitable climates they rank among the most agriculturally productive in the world. Their fine grains weather quickly because of their large surface area. Their fertility comes mainly from {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and its many pores, not from organic matter. Soils underlain by loess also tend to drain too freely. Their weakness is erosion. Even well-managed loess farmland can lose well over 2.5 kg/m2 a year. Under autumn moldboard plowing, Iowa's Loess Hills at times lost over 10 kg/m2 a year. Their fertility rests on 10,000 years of dark prairie organic matter. Once that surface layer erodes, the loess beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

soil-form-111.title: Loess–paleosol sequences, climate diaries in silt
soil-form-111.text: Some loess cliffs read like a climate diary. Their stacked layers of loess, separated by buried soils, the {{ref:soil-form-072}}, form layered sequences studied as archives of past climate and environmental change. In China a strong north-west winter monsoon laid down the loess layers. The buried soils record a moist south-east monsoon. Without robust numerical dating, even the place of the last interglacial soil in Austrian and Hungarian loess was long debated. Since the 1980s, luminescence methods have dated when grains last saw daylight. SAR protocols give last-glacial ages accurate to between 5 and 10%. The method of {{ref:soil-hist-120}} gives reliable ages for the last 40–45 ka, or thousand years, when charcoal or snail shells lie in place.

soil-form-108.title: Non-glacial loess, dust from deserts and volcanoes
soil-form-108.text: Not all loess owes its origin to ice. Non-glacial loess comes from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or {{ref:soil-form-152}}, not from the sediment washed out of glaciers. Desert loess forms as wind-driven quartz grains abrade one another. Volcanic loess occurs in Ecuador and Argentina, and there are tropical and trade-wind kinds too. China's thick loess deposits blew in from deserts in the north of the country. Loess on the Great Plains of Nebraska, Kansas and Colorado is considered non-glacial desert loess, as is loess in Australia and Africa.

soil-form-088.title: Residuum, weathered rock that never moved
soil-form-088.text: In the United States as little as three percent of soils are residual. Residuum is weathered rock that stays in place instead of being moved by erosion, and in time it helps form soil. It is purely mineral, unlike organic parent materials, and wind, water and gravity have not moved it. Soils formed from it, residual soils, should resemble their underlying bedrock in mineralogy and general chemistry. They imply a stable landscape, which explains their rarity. Regolith covers all loose material above bedrock, transported sediment included, while residuum is strictly untransported. Saprolite keeps its bedrock's structure. Residuum has lost it, transformed further and shrunk in volume. It forms mainly by chemical weathering in every climate, as a thin blanket over bedrock in temperate regions and much thicker in the tropics. On limestone the boundary with bedrock is sharp but irregular. Pinnacles of fresh rock rise into reddish residual silts and clays, and resistant chert or sandstone remains as float.

soil-form-105.title: Eluvial deposits, the riches weathering leaves behind
soil-form-105.text: Brazil's Pitinga tin deposit, one of the largest tin mines in the world, is what weathering left behind. In geology, eluvial deposits are deposits and soils derived from weathering in place, or from weathering plus movement or accumulation by gravity. What was removed is irrelevant; the eluvial deposit is what remains. Winnowing away lighter material enriches eluvial ores such as tungsten and gold placers, concentrations of heavy grains. Diamonds in weathered kimberlite can count as eluvial too. In Ontario, supergene weathering of an apatite-rich carbonatite rock produced a significant eluvial phosphate ore.

soil-form-090.title: Glacial till, the unsorted load a glacier drops
soil-form-090.text: A boulder in a field may have come from an outcrop hundreds of kilometres away. Glacial till is unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice. No liquid water carried it, so it is unsorted and unlayered. It is mostly clay, silt and sand with scattered pebbles, cobbles and boulders, often in a bimodal size distribution with two peaks. Its stones are often faceted, scratched or polished by glacial abrasion. Basal till, laid beneath the glacier, is typically very compact and slow to take in water. Ablation till, dropped as the ice melts, is less compacted. Till builds the terminal, lateral, medial and ground forms described in {{ref:soil-form-150}}, and the ridges called drumlins and flutes. Archibald Geikie first applied the term to primary glacial deposits in 1863. The older name, boulder clay, has fallen out of favor. Melting glaciers rework till into outwash and into lake or sea deposits such as varves.

soil-form-095.title: Cumulose parent material, soil built from plants
soil-form-095.text: Not every parent material is rock. Cumulose parent material is organic, built up in place from plant residues such as sphagnum moss. Groundwater standing high keeps oxygen low, which slows decay and preserves the residues. {{ref:soil-class-070}} and muck soils both form this way. Unlike other parent materials, it is never moved; it originates from organic material deposited where it lies. The results differ sharply. The first may form sterile soils, while muck soils may be very fertile.

soil-form-091.title: Glaciofluvial deposits, ice debris sorted by meltwater
soil-form-091.text: Meltwater sorts what the ice did not. Glaciofluvial deposits are boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited. They are laid down beside, below or downstream from the ice. As retreating glaciers carry this sediment downstream, they leave {{ref:soil-form-151}}. Much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene sand and loess derived from glacial outwash.

soil-form-107.title: Periglacial loess, dust from dried-out meltwater rivers
soil-form-107.text: Each autumn and winter, the meltwater flowing from the great ice sheets dwindled. Bare floodplains of braided rivers dried, and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, dropping it downwind. The result is periglacial loess: loess blown from the floodplains of rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps. The loess along both sides of the Mississippi River alluvial valley is a classic example. The northern European loess belt, from southern England to southern Ukraine, shows strong periglacial influence. In England it has its own name, {{ref:soil-class-065}}. Loess ridges aligned with last-glacial winds are called paha ridges in America and greda ridges in Europe.

soil-form-093.title: Lacustrine parent material, the silt of old lakebeds
soil-form-093.text: Lake Bonneville and many soils around the Great Lakes share an origin in still water. Lacustrine parent material is sediment that settled in lakes. It forms a well-sorted, fine-textured parent material rich in silt and clay. Its high clay content makes the soils formed in it let water through only slowly. Beach ridges may mark where ancient lakes once washed up sand.

soil-form-092.title: Glaciolacustrine deposits and the yearly layers of varves
soil-form-092.text: Lakes at the edge of an ice sheet collect what glaciers shed. Glaciolacustrine deposits are parent material formed from glacier-derived sediment carried into lakes, typically lakes at the ice margin. Inflowing rivers drop their larger rocks and stones near the lake edge. Their suspended sediment settles across the whole lake bed. Annual deposition can leave clear layers called varves.

soil-form-094.title: Marine parent material, old sea floors turned to soil
soil-form-094.text: Parts of the US Gulf Coast were once sea bed. Marine parent material is material that rivers carried to the sea, where it sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material. Soils along the Gulf Coast and in California's Imperial Valley formed on such ancient sea beds, exposed as the land was uplifted. Glaciomarine sediments reached the ocean by glacier or iceberg. They may hold large ice-dropped boulders amid fine-grained sediment.

soil-form-096.title: Volcanic ash, a fast-weathering parent material
soil-form-096.text: Volcanic ash is made largely of glass, and it weathers fast. Ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano is called tephra, the most common volcanic parent material. Volcanic ash and lava flows interbedded with loose material are part of Earth's regolith. Soils of siliceous ash consist of glass bubbles and shards with a high internal surface area. They weather rapidly to the clays {{ref:soil-chem-098}} and {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. These soils, classed as {{ref:soil-class-092}}, are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and particularly light for their volume. Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

soil-form-115.title: River channel migration, how rivers wander
soil-form-115.text: An alluvial river never stays put. River channel migration is the sideways shift of its channel across its floodplain over time. Bank erosion drives it, combined with point bar deposition, the building of a sediment bar, on the opposite side of the channel. Around each bend, water moves in a corkscrew-like helicoidal flow. It undercuts banks into cut banks and moves sediment across the channel. Cut-bank erosion usually equals point-bar deposition, and point bars push flow into the opposite bank, so meanders become better defined over time. The typical features are point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

soil-form-114.title: Stone stripes, bands of rock sorted by frost
soil-form-114.text: Bare bands of broken basalt streak the hillsides of north central Oregon. A stone stripe, or lava stringer, is an elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff. Most lie at 900 to 1,100 m. Each runs a few metres to over 150 m long, 0.3 to 3 m wide and 20 to 65 cm deep. They probably formed in the near-glacial cold of the Quaternary, through frost action, surface erosion, the washing down of fine material and slow downhill movement under gravity. Intense freeze–thaw cycles likely sorted the rock debris. Frost reached no deeper than about 1 m, which explains their shallowness. On level ground the same processes form stone rings around soil mounds, and these grade into stripes as the slope steepens.

soil-form-021.title: Topsoil, the thin living layer that feeds plants
soil-form-021.text: One inch (2.5 cm) of topsoil can take 500 to 1,000 years to form. The United States loses almost 3 tons of it per acre every year. Topsoil is the upper layer of soil, richest in soil organic matter and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place. It is a mix of mineral particles and soil organic matter, usually 5–10 inches (13–25 cm) deep. The water and air it holds encourage that activity. Roots concentrate here, because plants draw most of their nutrients from this layer. Bacteria and fungi break down organic material, while insects aerate and turn the soil. Its depth runs from the surface to the first densely packed layer, described in {{ref:soil-form-023}}. Classification systems label it as one of two horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-006}} and {{ref:soil-form-008}}. More soil organic matter helps its particles hold together. Dried-out topsoil loses much of its volume, and the wind carries it off more easily. The optimum {{ref:soil-fert-184}} for UK topsoil is less than 20:1. Today, use and erosion strip topsoil faster than new soil forms. Cover crops, {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}} and windbreaks slow the loss and keep it fertile.

soil-form-023.title: Subsoil, where the rain drops its cargo
soil-form-023.text: Rain does more than wet the ground. It carries weathering products such as clay and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} downward, dissolved or as fine suspended particles, and most of them settle in the subsoil. Subsoil is the layer beneath {{ref:soil-form-021}}, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less soil organic matter. With so little of it, the subsoil's color comes mainly from those iron minerals. Physical, chemical and biological activity cluster its particles into a definite arrangement, and that sets it apart from the barely altered substratum below. It is not sterile, but it holds few soil organisms compared with the rich layer above. Most soil mapping systems give it the letter B, with a substratum lettered C beneath; {{ref:soil-form-010}} and {{ref:soil-form-011}} return to both. Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments. Builders have used clay-rich subsoil for millennia, as adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub.

soil-form-001.title: Soil morphology: describing a soil by eye and hand
soil-form-001.text: Dokuchaev's team noticed something striking. Profiles with similar horizons turned up hundreds of kilometers apart, wherever climate and vegetation were similar. Observing like that is soil morphology, the branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their texture, color, structure and consistence. Nineteenth-century agro-geologists, studying soils in natural settings, were the first to do it scientifically. Once soils were seen as independent natural bodies, morphology became a way to judge the combined influence of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Official guidelines first appeared in the 1930s, from Charles Kellogg and the USDA in the United States and from G.R. Clarke in the United Kingdom. Today a describer works in the field on several horizons exposed by a pit, a push tube or an auger. Many US soil scientists record site, horizons, color, texture and structure on a standard USDA-NRCS field sheet. Structure is best judged fairly dry, because moist clumps swell and press together. Together with the study of how soils form and how they are classified, morphology belongs to pedology.

soil-form-033.title: Eluviation: how percolating water empties the upper soil
soil-form-033.text: Where more rain falls than evaporates, water keeps moving down through the soil, and it takes things with it. That removal of soil material from upper layers by percolating water is eluviation. It carries mineral and organic particles fine enough to stay suspended in water, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. That sets it apart from {{ref:soil-form-050}}, a distinct soil-building mechanism. Acid conditions speed it up, because organic acids make iron and aluminum more soluble. {{ref:soil-form-061}} is the extreme case, stripping out the oxides of iron and aluminum. The layer that loses material is an eluvial horizon. It may be a light-colored zone at the base of the surface mineral horizon, labelled Ae. Where the process is most intense, it forms a separate layer beneath, lettered E and described in {{ref:soil-form-009}}. Some sources count both of these layers as the eluvial zone. What leaves must land somewhere. The material builds up lower down as an illuvial deposit, the process of {{ref:soil-form-032}}. On a slope the exchange also runs downhill: upper facets lose salts while lower facets gain them.

soil-form-017.title: Diagnostic horizons, the layers that decide a soil's name
soil-form-017.text: To name a soil, a classifier checks each of its horizons against a list of criteria. A diagnostic horizon is one defined by such a set of criteria. Its presence or absence at a given depth decides which taxonomic unit the soil belongs to. The WRB lists 40 of them. The WRB, {{ref:soil-class-006}} and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} all work this way, while the German system defines soils by whole sequences of horizons. Diagnostic horizons usually carry names rather than symbols, such as the one in {{ref:soil-form-117}} or the one in {{ref:soil-form-031}}. The USDA system separates diagnostic surface horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-018}}, from subsurface ones. Among those are the spodic and oxic horizons and the clay-rich layer in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Most systems also use other soil characteristics to define their units.

soil-form-006.title: The O horizon, a blanket of leaves and needles
soil-form-006.text: Leaves, conifer needles, twigs, mosses and lichens gather on many soils and slowly decompose in place. The result is the O horizon: a surface layer of organic material built from plant residues, not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods. The WRB counts material as organic when it holds at least 20% organic carbon by weight. The upper part is often barely decomposed litter, while the lower part may be strongly humified, broken down into dark, stable organic material. The Australian system splits it into O1 and O2 on that basis. It also keeps loose leaf litter, which has no weathered mineral particles, out of the soil altogether. Organisms in the O horizon break down the residues and release nutrients. Strong acidity, cold or pollution slow them, so undecomposed material piles up over the mineral soil. Though it forms on top, an O horizon can be buried at depth by landslides, floods or wind-blown dust.

soil-form-008.title: The A horizon, where life and minerals mix
soil-form-008.text: Earthworms, potworms, arthropods, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots in the A horizon, which is why some call it the biomantle. It is the uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified soil organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material. Often called topsoil, it holds dark, decomposed soil organic matter. Burrowing animals stir it into the mineral matter, a mixing described in {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. The original rock structure is fully or largely gone. Biological activity reaches much deeper, though, so it cannot be the chief test, and A horizons are defined mostly relative to the layers beneath. Layers changed by plowing or pasturing count as A horizons, and the suffix p marks plowed ones. The Australian system divides it into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, a transition to the layer below.

soil-form-009.title: The E horizon, a pale layer washed clean
soil-form-009.text: Old, well-developed soils often hide a band paler than the layers around it. That is the E horizon, E for eluviated. It is a mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminum, soil organic matter or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz. Where eluviation is pronounced, it appears below the A horizon and above a layer lettered B, covered in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. It differs from that lower layer by higher color value or lower chroma, coarser texture, or both. Sometimes it takes the color of its own sand and silt. The lost substances first had to form or collect in place, so an E horizon marks an advanced stage of soil development. In gravelly soils, burrowing animals commonly leave a stone layer near its base. The Australian system does not use E; it labels such washed-out layers A or B with the suffix e.

soil-form-025.title: Hardpans, the buried floors that stop roots
soil-form-025.text: Some soils have a floor that roots and water cannot get through. A hardpan is a dense, largely water-impervious layer, usually lying just below the topsoil. Some form naturally, when deposits such as dissolved silica, {{ref:soil-chem-163}} or calcium carbonate fuse and bind the soil particles. Acidic soils suffer most, because iron and calcium salts form hard complexes with soil particles under acid conditions. Other pans are man-made, compacted by repeated plowing, especially with moldboard plows, by heavy traffic or by pollution. Clay-rich soils compact easily, and sodium in wastewater can bind clay into a local pan, a common cause of septic system failure. Hardpans impede drainage and restrict roots on farms and in gardens. A broadfork, digging fork, spade or tractor-drawn chisel plow can break them. Manure, compost or peat improve drainage and encourage earthworms that slowly break pans. Lime and gypsum help with harder ones, though amendments may take years. {{ref:soil-water-242}} turns irreversibly into an ironstone hardpan when wetted and dried again and again.

soil-form-032.title: Illuviation: where washed-down material comes to rest
soil-form-032.text: Everything water carries out of an upper layer has to stop somewhere. Illuviation is that stopping: the deposition in a lower layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above. It is the matching half of eluviation. Illuvium includes soil organic matter, silicate clay and the iron and aluminum compounds of {{ref:soil-chem-162}}. These collect in subsoil horizons lettered B, the zones of illuviation, described in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. The movement is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the sideways transfer by running water. It works in two ways. In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, the pull of water into fine pores. Fine coatings are left along the channels, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-068}}. In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried down by percolating water are deposited where the chemistry of the soil changes, especially its pH and its {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough washed-in clay are the ones named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and gathers in the subsoil.

soil-form-010.title: The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone
soil-form-010.text: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, because it holds less soil organic matter than the A horizon above. It is a subsurface mineral horizon, formed below a horizon lettered A, E, H or O. Its original rock structure is largely gone, and soil-forming processes have altered or enriched its material. It is commonly called subsoil. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. Its marks include residual oxides or clay, lost carbonates or gypsum, and washed-in clay, iron, aluminum, organic material, carbonates, gypsum or silica. It generally has a structure or consistency that differs from the layers above and below. Gleying alone does not make a B horizon, nor do carbonates cut off from a genetic horizon above. The Australian system splits it into B1, transitional from A, B2, with concentrated clay or oxides, and B3, transitional to the C or D horizon.

soil-form-011.title: The C horizon, raw material soil barely touched
soil-form-011.text: Below the layers that soil-forming processes have reshaped lies material it has barely touched. The C horizon is that layer: anything above hard bedrock that those processes have little affected and that lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons. It includes sediments, saprolite and soft bedrock that a spade can dig when moist and that usually slakes, crumbling in water, within 24 hours. It forms in deposits such as loess, flood deposits and landslides, or by weathering of bedrock in place. Unless a change in parent material separates them, a break covered in {{ref:soil-form-015}}, it resembles the parent material of the soil above, though C material may differ. Plant roots can penetrate it, so it is an important growing medium. It may be enriched with carbonates and other soluble compounds washed down from above. Layers cemented by silica, carbonates or gypsum stay C unless soil-forming processes have clearly affected them; then they become B horizons.

soil-form-034.title: Cryoturbation: how frost churns the ground
soil-form-034.text: In the frozen north, the soil mixes itself.
