Cryoturbation is frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in permafrost soils. It occurs to some degree in most Gelisols, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze. Autumn freezing forms ice wedges in the most erodible parts of the parent rock. In summer the active layer lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold permafrost table, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with ice lenses. These lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface. Separation of coarse from fine material produces patterned ground. It is the dominant force in the active layer and tends to make it uniform in composition. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of the active layer, with distorted horizon boundaries, Orthels in less. In frost boils it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients. In effect, ice scrambles the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}.

soil-form-002.title: The soil profile, a record read from the top down
soil-form-002.text: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. A soil profile is a vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface. Formally, it is one face of the three-dimensional block described in {{ref:soil-form-003}}. Soil scientists expose a profile by digging a pit or extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons. Some soils, such as those of the {{ref:soil-class-094}} order, have only one horizon or none. Young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces are examples. Wind or running water can strip the upper horizons and bury them downslope, a natural process that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} aggravates. Major earthworks or regular deep plowing can leave a soil almost without distinct horizons. The horizons also hold clues to the past. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains can reveal changes in climate or land use, and large pieces of charcoal allow dating by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}.

soil-form-024.title: The solum, the part of the soil that formed together
soil-form-024.text: A 10 cm surface layer on bedrock can be a complete solum, while fresh alluvium has none at all. The solum is the upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, developed under the same soil-forming conditions. In horizon terms it covers the A, E and B horizons, the blended layers between them and some O horizons. Its base is relatively unweathered parent material. Layers where carbonate or salt accumulated belong too, if they formed at least partly in the same period. A solum has no minimum or maximum thickness. Its lower limit should relate to how deep the roots of perennial plants are expected to reach, though in some soils it can only be set arbitrarily. Hardened carbonate or gleying many meters down is hard to count, since such deep features may be relict or geological rather than products of soil development. The living part of the soil stays largely within the solum and is most prominent in the A horizon.

soil-form-007.title: The H horizon, peat that sits in water
soil-form-007.text: Not every organic layer stays dry. The H horizon is an organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained. In the WRB an H layer is saturated for more than 30 consecutive days in most years, or drained. An O horizon, by contrast, is saturated for no more than 30 days and not drained. Many H horizons consist mainly of sphagnum mosses. After drainage, O horizons may form on top of them. The Australian system calls these waterlogged layers P, for peats, with at least 12 to 18% organic carbon depending on clay content.

soil-form-012.title: The R layer, bedrock at the bottom of the pit
soil-form-012.text: At the base of the profile, the spade stops. The R layer is the hard, consolidated bedrock beneath the soil: granite, basalt, quartzite, or hard limestone or sandstone. It is too coherent to dig by hand with a spade, and air-dry chunks do not slake in water within 24 hours. Its few small cracks let few roots in. Where no change in parent material separates them, the R layer resembles the parent material of the solum above.

soil-form-004.title: Horizon designations, a soil's layers written in code
soil-form-004.text: Ah-E-Bt1-2Bt2-2BwC-3C1-3C2 looks like a serial number. It is a whole soil profile written in horizon designations, the code of letters and numbers that names each horizon. A capital letter gives the master horizon, such as O, A, E, B, C or R. Lowercase suffixes add details of how the layer formed, and several may be combined. Some master horizons, including O, B and L, must always carry one. Numbers do two jobs. A number in front marks a change in parent material, covered in {{ref:soil-form-015}}. A number behind splits one horizon into subdivisions, such as Bt1, Bt2 and Bt3. Hyphens join the horizons of a profile into one string. That short notation summarizes color, size, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules or concretions. The world has many systems of horizon symbols, and the same horizon may be labelled differently in each. No system is more correct than another. Because their symbols are defined differently, though, the systems cannot be mixed.

soil-form-014.title: Horizon suffixes, small letters with big meanings
soil-form-014.text: One lowercase letter can say what happened in a layer. Horizon suffixes are added to a master symbol to record particular features or soil-forming processes. In the USDA field book, t marks illuvial silicate clay, k pedogenic calcium carbonate, g strong gleying and p a plow layer. Others include b for a buried genetic horizon, f for permanently frozen ground, x for {{ref:soil-form-028}} features and y for gypsum. WRB letters borrow from other languages: k from German Karbonat, t from German Ton, clay, n from natrium and z from Dutch zout, salt. Suffixes combine in order of dominance, as in Btng or Btgb.

soil-form-015.title: Lithologic discontinuities, numbering a change of material
soil-form-015.text: Not every profile grew from a single material. A lithologic discontinuity is a change in parent material within a soil profile, shown by a number in front of the horizon symbol. By convention the uppermost material carries no number, and each lower stratum gets 2, 3 and so on, as in Oi-Oe-Ah-E-2Bt-2C-3R. Numbers after a symbol, by contrast, mark subdivisions within a single horizon. Where no discontinuity separates the solum from the C horizon below, that C horizon resembles the solum's parent material.

soil-form-016.title: Buried horizons, old surfaces under new ground
soil-form-016.text: Soils are often pictured as forming in place, but burial makes the process far more complicated. Wind- or water-laid sediments can cover a fully formed profile and later form a new profile on top, most commonly in coastal areas. A buried soil horizon is a genetic horizon that formed at the surface and was later covered by new mineral material; it carries the suffix b. Numerical prefixes describe such stacks, as in O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21, 2B22, 2C, where the buried profile starts at 2A2. Fossil soil horizons also occur within sedimentary rock sequences, where they record past environments.

soil-form-013.title: Transitional horizons, where one layer shades into the next
soil-form-013.text: Some layers belong to two horizons at once. A transitional horizon combines the properties of two master horizons and is written with both capital letters, the dominant one first, as in AB or BA. Where separate bodies of the two are intermingled, a slash joins the symbols, as in A/B or B/A. The WRB writes superimposed horizons without a separator, as in AhBw. It keeps the slash for separate bodies, as in Bt/E, where E material interfingers into a Bt horizon. The Australian A3, B1 and B3 are loosely defined and used at the describer's discretion. I, L and W layers never appear in transitional designations.

soil-form-028.title: Fragipans, brittle layers that still puzzle soil scientists
soil-form-028.text: A fragipan holds virtually no roots, yet its air-dry fragments fall apart in water. It is a diagnostic horizon of {{ref:soil-class-006}}: an altered, dense subsurface layer that blocks water and roots. Written Bx or Btx, it limits land use much as the layer in {{ref:soil-form-027}} does. It contains no calcium or magnesium carbonate and does not fizz in dilute HCl. Proposed origins include glacial compaction, frozen ground, physical ripening, inheritance from ancient buried soils, and hydroconsolidation, the collapse of structure under loading and wetting. Soil scientists still debate how fragipans form, how to define them and whether they exist in some landscapes.

soil-form-022.title: Topsoil by the truckload
soil-form-022.text: Topsoil is also a product. Commercial topsoil is any soil mixture sold as topsoil: natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use, or a blend manufactured from minerals, {{ref:soil-fert-045}}, compost or paper mill sludge. Buyers use it to improve gardens and lawns, fill containers and grade the ground around buildings, though it suits potting less well than {{ref:soil-agri-028}} or compost. In the UK it must be classified under British Standard BS 3882 (2015), with thresholds for nutrients, phytotoxic elements, particle size, soil organic matter, pH and contamination. The United States has no federal legal definition of it. Low-quality artificial topsoil helped rehabilitate an open-cut coal mine in Victoria, Australia.

soil-form-005.title: Horizon boundaries, sharp or gradual, smooth or wavy
soil-form-005.text: Where one horizon ends, a describer records two things. Horizon boundaries are the lower borders of horizons, described by how sharp they are, called distinctness, and how their shape varies sideways, called topography. Distinctness runs from very abrupt and abrupt through clear and gradual to diffuse. Boundaries are often not parallel to the surface and may be broken, so the topography classes are smooth, wavy, irregular and broken. Official series descriptions record them. The Cecil series, for instance, has an abrupt smooth boundary below its Ap horizon and gradual wavy boundaries further down.

soil-form-020.title: Soil micromorphology, the profile under the microscope
soil-form-020.text: Some soil features are too small to see with the unaided eye. Soil micromorphology describes, measures and interprets them. Work may begin in the field with a 10x hand lens, but thin sections under a petrographic polarizing microscope reveal far more. A recognized technique for some 50 years, it spread from studies of soil development and ancient buried soils to the soils and sediments of archaeological sites. Micromorphologists have also characterized humus-form horizons on thin soil sections.

soil-form-027.title: Duripans, subsoil set as hard as concrete
soil-form-027.text: Duripans form almost only in arid or Mediterranean climates, and they can be as hard as concrete. A duripan is a diagnostic horizon of {{ref:soil-class-006}} in which silica washed down from above has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. Silica from fast-weathering glassy lava ({{ref:soil-chem-200}}), feldspars or iron-magnesium minerals precipitates there as microaggregates that grow into a pan. Criteria include cementation of over half the volume, roots only along fractures 10 cm or more apart, and breaking down in KOH but not HCl. That test separates it from fragipans and from the carbonate-cemented layer in {{ref:soil-form-029}}. Its soils are seldom cultivated and serve mostly for grazing or wildlife.

soil-form-036.title: Ice wedges, cracks that freeze and grow each winter
soil-form-036.text: An ice wedge is a crack in the ground holding a narrow wedge of ice up to 3–4 meters long at the surface. By the widely accepted thermal contraction theory, winter cold opens cracks a few cm wide that fill with snowmelt, freeze and crack again. A mean annual air temperature of −6 to −8 °C or colder is thought necessary. Epigenetic wedges grow in existing {{ref:soil-env-129}} and widen to 3–5 m. Syngenetic ones grow upward as sediment accumulates and can reach 25 m deep. Where the frozen ground has gone, melted wedges fill with sediment. These casts help estimate climates of hundreds of thousands of years ago.

soil-form-026.title: Claypans, where water perches and topsoil washes away
soil-form-026.text: Across about 4 million ha of the central United States, in states such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Illinois, a dense layer of clay lies beneath the fields. A claypan is a compact, slowly permeable subsoil layer with much more clay than the material above, separated from it by a sharp boundary. Bare ground, the mix of grain sizes and heavy rain favor it: raindrops rearrange fine sand, silt and clay until they plug the pores. Its dense structure restricts roots and the entry of water, so water perches on top of it and saturates the soil above. Runoff rises, leaving the organic-rich topsoil highly vulnerable to erosion. Dominated by {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, it shrinks hard in the dry season and turns wet and sticky in the wet season, with poor aeration. It holds much water, but most is unavailable to plants, because the pores are tiny and the water evaporates. Acidic and clay-rich, it binds phosphorus so tightly that much P fertilizer is needed, while its potassium stays available. It also occurs in south-west Queensland.

soil-found-103.title: Silcrete, the stone early toolmakers heated
soil-found-103.text: At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, toolmakers were heat-treating silcrete between 60,000 and 80,000 years ago. Silcrete is a hard crust, a kind of {{ref:soil-chem-039}}, formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica. It forms much as its cousins do: one cemented by calcium carbonate, and one cemented by iron oxide, described in {{ref:soil-form-038}}. Microcrystalline silcretes form in arid settings as pH rises, lacustrine ones where pH falls. It often caps landforms in arid Australia and Africa. Aboriginal Australians and Middle Stone Age Africans prized it for tools, heating it so it flaked more easily, possibly the first use of pyrotechnology.

soil-form-029.title: Petrocalcic horizons, subsoil cemented by carbonate
soil-form-029.text: Carbonates typify the alkaline soils of arid and semiarid climates, and a drop of hydrochloric acid makes them fizz. In a petrocalcic horizon, secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. It is a diagnostic horizon in {{ref:soil-class-006}} and the WRB. Water carries carbonates from parent material or dust downward, and they precipitate as it evaporates. Over time they build a massive, continuous cemented layer, with or without silica. Roots get through only along vertical fractures 10 cm or more apart. The horizon marks advanced soil evolution in older soils, and most formed before the Holocene.

soil-form-030.title: Umbric horizons, dark but acid
soil-form-030.text: Shade is in the name: umbric comes from the Latin umbra. An umbric horizon is a thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases. It normally has a pH below 5.5 and a {{ref:soil-chem-052}} under 50 percent. WRB criteria include Munsell chroma and value of 3 or less when moist, and at least 0.6% organic carbon. It must be at least 100 mm thick on hard rock, otherwise 200 mm. Roots growing horizontally can indicate its acidity. Similar dark, base-poor layers made by deep cultivation, manuring or the kitchen refuse heaps in {{ref:soil-hist-102}} are told apart by artifacts, spade marks or land-use history.

soil-form-038.title: Ferricrete, the iron-cemented coffee stone
soil-form-038.text: In rural South Africa, road builders use a rock they call koffieklip, Afrikaans for coffee stone. Ferricrete is a hard, erosion-resistant layer of sedimentary rock, usually conglomerate or breccia, cemented by the iron minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} into the kind of crust described in {{ref:soil-chem-039}}. The cement comes from the oxidation of percolating iron-salt solutions, and the name joins ferruginous and concrete. It forms at or near the land surface and may hold sediments brought from elsewhere. Its other names include hardpan and ironpan. Some deposits of {{ref:soil-form-065}} contain ferricrete, and one suggestion is that it forms in their wetter, leached parts.

soil-form-040.title: Pedocals, the carbonate soils of an older scheme
soil-form-040.text: Marbut's classification split soils at its highest level into two groups: pedocals and {{ref:soil-class-042}}, the latter rich in aluminum and iron. Pedocals are soils of semiarid and arid regions, rich in calcium carbonate and low in soil organic matter. They were once a class of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-015}}. Under a thin A horizon, calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up in the B horizon. There they form a cemented layer, {{ref:soil-chem-036}}. The term is not used in the current US classification, but it often appears in college geology texts.

soil-found-068.title: Cutans, the coatings left by moving clay
soil-found-068.text: Soil surfaces keep a record of what water carried past them. Cutans are changes in soil texture or structure at the natural surfaces of particles, pores and clumps, caused by illuviation. They are oriented deposits of any soil component: clay skins, or coatings of silica, iron and aluminum oxides, manganese, organic material or carbonate. Clay skins are also called argillans, and a horizon with enough washed-in clay is the kind named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Common and visible in the field, they are focal points of chemical and biological reactions. Reading them, a core skill in soil morphology and the study of ancient soils, shows the degree and nature of soil development.

soil-found-072.title: Paralithic horizons, weathered bedrock beneath the soil
soil-found-072.text: Bedrock does not always meet the soil as solid stone. A paralithic horizon is a weathered layer of bedrock. The name comes from the Greek para, akin to, and lithic, stony. A paralithic contact is one of the depth limits used to define soil classes, as in the definitions of the {{ref:soil-class-097}}.

soil-form-031.title: Cambic horizons, the first signs of change below ground
soil-form-031.text: The cambic horizon is the diagnostic horizon of last resort. It is a subsurface horizon showing early change by soil-forming processes, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon. It lacks appreciable illuviated clay, organic carbon, iron and aluminum oxyhydroxides, carbonate, gypsum or soluble salts. Its texture must be no coarser than loamy fine sand or very fine sand. It is commonest in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and {{ref:soil-class-100}}, also occurs in {{ref:soil-class-092}} and is written Bw or Bg. Along a {{ref:soil-form-063}}, it gains clay and develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon once the soil becomes one of the {{ref:soil-class-090}} kind.

soil-form-035.title: Tepetate, Mexico's hardened volcanic layers
soil-form-035.text: In the volcanic regions of Mexico, some horizons have hardened by compaction or cementation. Mexicans call such a horizon tepetate, from the Nahuatl tepetlatl. At the surface, tepetates are hard, poorly drained and infertile, which makes them a problem for farming. Buried under soil, they bring a different danger. Water runs off sideways instead of soaking in, raising the risk of erosion and landslides.

soil-form-019.title: Albic horizons, bleached layers below the surface
soil-form-019.text: Bleached and pale, the albic horizon is what remains when soil-forming processes move clay and oxides downward. It is a light-colored subsurface diagnostic horizon in both the WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}}. {{ref:soil-class-099}}, acidic soils common in coniferous and boreal forests, usually have one. In {{ref:soil-class-147}} soils it tongues down into a clay-rich Bt horizon. In {{ref:soil-class-144}}, the topsoil can be completely bleached. {{ref:soil-class-137}} often show eluviation as an albic horizon beneath an umbric surface layer.

soil-form-018.title: Epipedons, the diagnostic surface horizons of USDA taxonomy
soil-form-018.text: {{ref:soil-class-006}} gives the top of the soil its own set of names. An epipedon is a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil. There are eight: the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons. {{ref:soil-form-118}}, fertile and built by long additions of root-derived organic material, is the defining feature of {{ref:soil-class-101}}. {{ref:soil-class-098}} must have a histic epipedon, while an ochric epipedon is common in {{ref:soil-class-094}} and {{ref:soil-class-093}}. {{ref:soil-class-100}} usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.

soil-form-003.title: The pedon, the basic block of field soil study
soil-form-003.text: The fundamental unit of field soil study is imaginary. A pedon is the three-dimensional unit of soil large enough to show the full range of properties of a particular soil. A soil profile is one face of it. Pedons generally cover 1 to 10 square meters of land. The Canadian system defines one as a body commonly 1 meter across and 1 to 2 meters deep. To classify a soil, every horizon of its pedon is checked against the criteria for diagnostic horizons. One proposal splits the pedon into a living humipedon, a copedon where most mineral weathering occurs, and a lithopedon in contact with the subsoil.

soil-form-042.title: How bare rock slowly becomes living soil
soil-form-042.text: In the Mediterranean climate of Sicily, weathering makes new soil at roughly 1/10 mm a year. That slow work is soil formation, also called pedogenesis: the development of soil as shaped by place, environment and history. It begins with the {{ref:soil-found-052}} of freshly accumulated parent material. New soils then deepen through further weathering and through deposition, including settling dust. Microbes feed on the nutrients that weathering releases. They produce organic acids and proteins that speed the breakdown of minerals, and their residues help build the dark, decayed organic matter of the topsoil. As the soil develops, pioneer species arrive first, then richer plant and animal communities through {{ref:soil-form-125}}. Topsoil deepens as remains of dead plants and microbes accumulate and mix with weathered minerals. With maturity come layers. Accumulating organic matter, mineral weathering and the washing of dissolved material downward create horizons that differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. Biogeochemical processes both build and destroy order within a soil. Differences in the conditions that shape soils produce patterns in where soil types occur. Pedogenesis is studied as a branch of pedology. It explains how soils are spread across the land today and how they were spread in past geological periods.

soil-form-050.title: Leaching: how water strips a soil from the top down
soil-form-050.text: Water soaking down through a soil does not travel empty. Leaching is the removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile. It differs from eluviation, which moves tiny mineral and organic particles, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, rather than dissolved material. Both tend to strip the topsoil and enrich the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation. Climate sets the pace directly. Leaching is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze. The red tropical soil described in {{ref:soil-form-065}} develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, and intensive leaching leaves it less fertile than other soils. Its signature shows in the profile. In one brownish leached soil, {{ref:soil-class-049}}, water washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon. Iron and aluminum oxides, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-085}}, gather in the B horizon and color it rusty orange-brown. The Canadian system for naming soils marks strongly leached layers as light gray Ae horizons. In Solonetzic soils, progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward. The process can also defeat reclamation: intensive leaching has left reclaimed {{ref:soil-chem-030}} infertile.

soil-form-043.title: Five forces behind every soil, from climate to time
soil-form-043.text: Every soil on Earth answers to the same five intertwined influences: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time. These are the soil-forming factors. Reordered as climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, they spell the acronym CLORPT. Parent material, the mineral material a soil forms from, becomes soil as it is weathered, transported, deposited and precipitated. Climate is regarded as the dominant factor, and soils show the distinctive marks of the climate zones in which they form. Topography can either hasten or slow the work of climate. Each soil also has its own mix of microbial, plant, animal and human influences. Time acts through all the others. How long a profile takes to develop depends strongly on climate, parent material, relief and living things. The factors once sorted the soils of a whole nation. An early US scheme, {{ref:soil-class-012}}, divided soils into three orders according to their dominant factors. In one of them, a local factor of relief or parent material outweighed the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

soil-form-072.title: Paleosols, soils from vanished worlds
soil-form-072.text: Some soils formed more than 2.5 billion years ago. A paleosol is an ancient soil that formed in the past. Geologists use the word for a former soil buried under sediments such as alluvium or loess, or under lava or volcanic ash. In older deposits it has hardened into rock. Soil scientists mean a soil formed long ago whose properties bear no relation to today's climate or vegetation, found on old cratons and outliers of ancient rock. Over the last 50 million years, drying climates hardened former tropical soils across much of Australia into crusts so unweatherable that only poorly developed soils form on them. These relict soils are exceedingly infertile, yet often hold exceptional biodiversity. Paleosols also keep records. Pollen, carbon isotopes and leaf waxes in them reveal past plant life, including the balance of C3 and C4 plants. Glacial loess layers separated by paleosols record glaciations, and stacked paleosols help reveal past earthquakes.

soil-form-044.title: Climate, the dominant hand in shaping soil
soil-form-044.text: Where warmth and plentiful water meet in a soil, weathering, leaching and plant growth all run at their peak. Climate works chiefly through temperature and effective precipitation: rainfall minus the water lost to evaporation and plant transpiration. Together they set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes. Water must first penetrate the regolith, and the deeper it goes, the deeper the soil weathers and develops. Percolating water carries clay and dissolved organic material from upper layers to lower ones, separating horizons. In dry regions, salts are not leached. They can build up enough to curb plant and microbial growth, while carbonates accumulate in hard layers. Colder or drier climates fix less carbon as organic matter but also decompose less of it. So profiles are more distinct in wet, cool climates than in wet, warm ones, where organic matter is quickly consumed. Climate also acts through vegetation: trees in humid climates, grasses in subhumid and semiarid regions, shrubs in arid lands.

soil-form-046.title: Snails, fungi and fire: life as a soil builder
soil-form-046.text: In the Negev desert, land snails grazing on lichens process between 0.7 and 1.1 metric tons of limestone per hectare each year, starting soil formation. Organisms, meaning plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans, form one of the soil-forming factors. Microorganisms drive key mineral transformations. Some bacteria fix nitrogen from the air, and some fungi extract deep phosphorus and add carbon to the soil. Plants hold soil against erosion and build organic matter. Working with fungi and bacteria around their roots, they release chemicals that break down minerals. Burrowing animals mix soil and open pores for water and gases. That mixing tends to undo the processes that create distinct horizons. Old burrows in lower horizons often fill with A-horizon material, leaving features called crotovinas or krotovinas. Humans belong here too, and with them fire. Clearing, tillage, irrigation, fertilizer and lime can change soil formation abruptly. Neolithic fires set by people are now accepted as helping form the soils of {{ref:soil-class-123}} and {{ref:soil-class-053}}.

soil-form-047.title: Time: from fresh flood mud to a developed profile
soil-form-047.text: A fresh layer of flood mud shows no soil development at all. The old surface lies buried beneath it, and soil formation starts anew in the deposit. Time is the span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, and it shapes how far a soil has developed. Texture and clumping alone do not make a developing soil; a distinct B horizon does. A profile takes from decades to several thousand years to form, depending strongly on climate, parent material, relief and living things. Even stable landscapes, some lasting millions of years, keep gaining, losing and altering material. The soil life cycle ultimately ends in conditions that leave the soil vulnerable to erosion, though most cycles are long. Researchers study time by comparing soils of different ages that differ little otherwise, and through paleosols, which record earlier conditions. The very idea of development toward a mature profile has critics. They argue that soil never stops changing, because the soil-forming factors themselves keep fluctuating.

soil-form-045.title: Slope, height and aspect: how relief shapes soil
soil-form-045.text: On a steep slope, soil is lost quickly to erosion, and less rain soaks in. Soils there tend to be shallower and less developed than those on nearby level sites. Topography, or relief, shapes soil through slope, elevation and aspect, the direction a slope faces. It controls runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile. Soils at the foot of a hill get more water, and slopes facing the sun's path are drier than those that do not. Gravity carries water, dissolved substances and fine particles downslope, enriching the ground at the foot of hills and mountains. In swales and hollows where runoff collects, the regolith weathers more deeply and profiles are more advanced. In the lowest spots, saturation restricts drainage and aeration. Weathering and decay slow, while iron and manganese are lost faster, and wetland soils, saline marshes or peat bogs may form. Recurring patterns of relief produce repeating sequences of soils, explored in {{ref:soil-form-054}}.

soil-form-048.title: Dokuchaev writes soil as an equation
soil-form-048.text: {{ref:soil-hist-001}}, often called the father of pedology, reached his conclusion in 1883: soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material. In 1898 he wrote it as an equation, soil = f(cl, o, p) tr. Soil is a function of climate, organisms and parent material, and tr is relative time: young, mature or old. Jenny's later version, {{ref:soil-form-049}}, differs in two ways. It treats time as a full factor, and it adds topographic relief.

soil-form-049.title: Jenny's equation and its open-ended list of factors
soil-form-049.text: In 1941 the pedologist in {{ref:soil-hist-010}} wrote soil formation as S = f(cl, o, r, p, t, ...). Soil is a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time, and whatever else may matter. The trailing dots were deliberate. Unlike Dokuchaev's equation, Jenny's treats time as a factor, adds relief, and leaves room for more state variables as understanding improves. It is often remembered by the mnemonic Clorpt. The equation can be solved by deduction or empirically. The empirical route, varying one factor while holding the others constant, is the one mostly used today. It produced a family of models: climofunctions, biofunctions, topofunctions, lithofunctions and chronofunctions. Since 1941, soil surveyors worldwide have used the equation as a qualitative checklist of the factors behind a region's soil pattern. Critics grant that the five-factor model is parsimonious and useful. They argue it leaves out biodynamic processes, such as those that produce buried layers of stones.

soil-form-051.title: Modeling how irrigation water flushes out salt
soil-form-051.text: All irrigation water contains salts, so irrigated land must be flushed. A leaching model is a hydrological model of how irrigation water washes dissolved substances, notably salt, out of soil. It describes the process over time and against the amount of water applied, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties. Leaching is used to reclaim salty soil or keep irrigated land's salt content favorable. Curves from the Chacupe pilot area in Peru show deeper-layer salt first rising as salts arrive from the topsoil, then falling as more water percolates. Models such as {{ref:soil-water-237}} help set drainage requirements.

soil-form-054.title: The catena: a chain of soils down one hillside
soil-form-054.text: On a hillside at Bukalasa in central Uganda, the chemist W.S. Martin described soils changing in sequence from top to bottom. Geoffrey Milne named the pattern catena, Latin for chain. A catena is a series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material. The slope divides into ridge, crest, midslope and toeslope. Crests drain freely. Steep middle facets erode faster and are thinner and drier. The flatter top and bottom carry thicker, deeper soils, and toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter. Upper facets lose materials such as salts by eluviation, and lower facets gain them by illuviation. A catena is an open system. Its sequence becomes predictable when climate is uniform along the slope and each facet's inputs and outputs reach equilibrium. A mature catena balances erosion and deposition. In wet western Scotland, on acid schists, one catena runs from peat bog to peaty forms of the bleached soil described in {{ref:soil-class-138}}.

soil-form-080.title: Pedoturbation: the churning that blurs soil layers
soil-form-080.text: Soil horizons are not sealed compartments. Clays churn, frost heaves and animals burrow, and material crosses from one layer to the next. Pedoturbation is this mixing of material between horizons, an important factor in soil formation. It includes the churning of clays, cryoturbation, and mixing by living things. It transforms soils through destratification, mixing and sorting. It also opens preferential paths for air and infiltrating water. Mixing by animals tends to counteract the processes that create distinct horizons. Together with weathering and the build-up of decayed organic matter, animal mixing is a main process in forming one order of deeply weathered tropical soils. Not every disturbance counts. When surface salts precipitate, they disrupt soils locally, but they do not mix horizons, so they are not pedoturbation. Pedoturbation belongs to a wider family called perturbation: the pedological and sedimentary processes that change water-borne alluvial sediments and soils in place over time.

soil-form-055.title: The biomantle, the living upper skin of soil
soil-form-055.text: In the stable humid tropics, termites, ants and worms work year-round, and the churned upper soil often reaches 5–6 m or more. In the midlatitudes it is often less than 1–2 m thick. This is the soil biomantle: the organic-rich, animal-mixed upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die. It is mainly a product of organic activity. Animals, plants and fungi mix and destratify the parent material, and often sort its particles. In a midlatitude A-E-B-C profile, the biomantle is everything above the B horizon. As originally defined, it must show at least 50% biofabric, the pelleted fabric made by invertebrates. Light and full of channels, it speeds water downward and, above dense subsoils, sideways downslope. Two-layered biomantles have a basal layer of stones and form in mixed fine and gravelly material. One-layered ones form in uniform sands, loess or gravels. In some desert, mountain and freshly eroded bedrock soils, the biomantle is the whole soil.

soil-form-063.title: Chronosequences: centuries read from months of fieldwork
soil-form-063.text: Forest development takes decades or centuries, yet a chronosequence lets researchers study it from field data gathered in a few months. A chronosequence is a set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age. In soil science, the sites have developed for different lengths of time, with only small differences in the other soil-forming factors, so they reveal time as a factor. A classic use traces plant and microbial succession on recently deglaciated ground. One 2005 study used distance from a glacier's nose as a stand-in for site age. Along a chronosequence, a cambic horizon develops into a clay-enriched Bt horizon as the soil matures. The method has a weak point. It assumes that nothing but age differs between sites, and this often cannot be tested. Its use in field studies of succession has therefore been debated.

soil-form-085.title: Sesquioxides: the iron and aluminum oxides that color soils
soil-form-085.text: A sesquioxide is an oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as Fe2O3 and Al2O3. Many contain a metal in the +3 state ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}). In soil, the ones that matter are the oxides of iron and aluminum. Their movements show up as color. One strong form of leaching, {{ref:soil-form-061}}, washes them out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer. In another process, {{ref:soil-form-081}}, silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red color. Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual accumulation.

soil-form-065.title: Laterite, the brick-red earth of the tropics
soil-form-065.text: In 1807 Francis Buchanan-Hamilton named a formation in southern India laterite, from the Latin later, brick. The compact soil cuts easily into building blocks. Laterite is a kind of soil rich in iron and aluminum that often forms in hot, wet areas, mostly in the tropics. Nearly all laterites are rusty red from their high iron oxide content. Yves Tardy calculated that they cover about one-third of Earth's continental land, including most land between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. On one plateau in Madhya Pradesh, India, the laterite cap is 30 m thick. Laterites outside today's humid tropics formed when the land lay near the equator. They are read as signs of climatic change, continental drift or both. The term itself is disputed. It has been applied to cemented sesquioxide-rich horizons, any reddish surface soil, a rock type, whole weathering profiles and even a theory of weathering. Researchers such as Paton, Williams and Ollier call the usage confused, and some urge abandoning the word.

soil-form-061.title: Podzolisation: acid litter bleaches the upper soil
soil-form-061.text: Under boreal pines, a light, ash-pale layer can form just beneath the dark surface. Podzolisation is the extreme form of leaching behind it: it eluviates iron and aluminum sesquioxides from the upper soil. It generally occurs where precipitation exceeds the water returned to the air by evaporation and plants. The chemistry starts in the litter. Decaying organic matter releases organic acids that act as chelating agents, molecules that grip metal ions. Under conifers, a thin litter layer yields an acidic decaying layer called mor, at pH 4.5, rich in these agents. They break down clay and release iron and aluminum, which become sesquioxides and move from the A horizon down to the B horizon. Bases such as calcium and potassium wash out too. Quartz and silica remain, in a light, eluviated AE horizon at the base of the A horizon. Below, the B horizon holds a dark layer of illuviated organic matter and bases over a red-orange layer of sesquioxides. If water saturates the A horizon above the B horizon, mottling or gleying follows. The process is especially intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolic compounds and the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Tropical forests show little or none.

soil-form-066.title: Laterization: rain, drought and millions of years
soil-form-066.text: Laterization was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary, 35 to 1.5 million years ago, and it has not stopped. It is the prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite. It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons. Rain leaches the rock, and in the dry season capillary action lifts the dissolved ions to the surface. Acid dissolves the host minerals. Hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminum oxides, while sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away. Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to the iron and aluminum oxides, leaving mainly those two metals behind. The first products are weathered rocks called saprolites, and quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock. Gentle crests and plateaus help by protecting the weathered cover from erosion. The parent rock shapes the result. Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, granitic iron-poor rocks yield aluminum ores, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites. The process slowed with abrupt global cooling and continues today at a reduced rate.

soil-form-083.title: Stonelayers: buried stones that trace the land surface
soil-form-083.text: A stonelayer is a subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm, and it generally mimics the shape of the ground above. One stone thick, it shows in a pit as a stone line; several stones thick, it is a stone zone. Its stones may be quartz-rich rock fragments, iron–manganese nodules, artifacts, shells or precious stones. It often acts as a subsurface drain or even holds groundwater. Stone lines in soils follow the surface and their stones do not overlap like shingles, pointing to a soil origin. Water-laid stone lines in sediments do overlap, and their origin is geological.

soil-form-059.title: Biorhexistasy: climate swings between building and stripping soil
soil-form-059.text: In 1951 the pedologist Henry Erhart proposed that climate switches the land between two phases, biostasy and rhexistasy. In biostasy, abundant regular rain under protective vegetation drives chemical alteration, eluviation and illuviation. Eluvial horizons, clay-enriched horizons and sesquioxide-rich subsoils build up. In rhexistasy, a drier climate thins the vegetation and soil formation slows. Physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt. Pleistocene glacial periods are considered times of rhexistasy, and interglacials times of biostasy.

soil-form-064.title: Pedodiversity: counting soils the way ecologists count species
soil-form-064.text: In 1995 Ibáñez and colleagues counted soils the way ecologists count living things. They first applied ecological diversity indices, richness, relative abundance and the Shannon index, treating soil classes as taxa. Pedodiversity is the variation of soil properties within an area, usually expressed through soil classes. Studies began with how the number of soil classes grows with area, in work by Beckett and Bie in 1978. McBratney developed the term in 1992 while discussing landscape preservation. A 2003 US study found the West richest in soil taxa. At the finest level, taxa increased steadily with area, a sign of considerable soil endemism. Variety can be very local. In eastern North Carolina and the Ouachita Mountains, variability within plots, tied to individual trees and local rock, outweighed differences between plots. Conventional indices ignore how similar soil classes are. The mean soil taxonomic distance, which accounts for it, has been shown to be a better measure. Knowing natural pedodiversity helps preserve the soil cover and rebuild quasi-natural soils on degraded land.

soil-form-076.title: Reading ancient air from ancient soils
soil-form-076.text: Soils form in near-constant contact with the atmosphere, so old soils hold clues to old air. Paleoatmosphere reconstruction uses paleosol chemistry to infer that past composition. How oxidized a paleosol is has served as an indicator of atmospheric oxygen, which has risen over Earth's history. Carbon dioxide has been reconstructed three ways. Researchers use gas exchange between soil and air, carbon isotopes in carbonate nodules formed in the soil, and mass balances of several gases. Researchers on the early Earth are still actively developing these methods.

soil-form-075.title: Ancient soils as rain gauges and thermometers
soil-form-075.text: Rates and styles of weathering depend on climate, so a paleosol can gauge the climate it formed in. Mean annual precipitation and mean annual air temperature are the variables most often reconstructed. Many proxies, measurable stand-ins for a past condition, track chemical changes through the profile during weathering, burial and later alteration. Not every proxy suits every paleosol. Most work only for Phanerozoic paleosols, because landscape processes changed sharply after land plants arose. Proxies for seasonality rely on carbonate formed in the soil as it wets and dries, and they are still being tested and refined.

soil-form-074.title: Naming ancient soils with a modern rulebook
soil-form-074.text: A forest soil could not exist before there were trees. That simple fact shows why paleosol classification is hard. It mostly borrows the top-level orders of the US system, {{ref:soil-class-006}}, because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly. Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the paleosol record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago. The forest soil order, {{ref:soil-class-090}}, is also defined by chemical properties that rock does not preserve. That hierarchy cannot be applied to paleosols below the order level. A naming scheme made for paleosols has been proposed but is used only sporadically.

soil-form-073.title: How to recognize a soil turned to stone
soil-form-073.text: How can anyone tell that a layer of rock was once a soil? Paleosol identification answers with criteria. Rye and Holland set out five in 1998. They apply to paleosols of any age. They include formation in place on bedrock, soft-sediment deformation at the top of the profile, and up-profile changes in chemistry, texture and mineralogy that match weathering on land. In the field, signs include horizons, bedrock corestones within finer overlying material, and traces of surface processes such as roots and burrows. Diagnostic horizons and features separate paleosol types. All have an A horizon, but those of the order described in {{ref:soil-class-098}} also have an O horizon above it.

soil-form-069.title: Laterite aquifers: groundwater held in red earth
soil-form-069.text: In rural tropical areas, the bedrock is often impermeable granite, gneiss, schist or sandstone. Water cannot pass through it, so the laterite above becomes the usable store of groundwater. Thick, porous and slightly permeable, these laterite layers hold water and yield it to wells. Sri Lanka's Southwestern Laterite, or Cabook, Aquifer recharges rapidly with the April–May rains and the monsoon, and supports shallow dug wells. In some dense suburbs, its water level can fall to 15 m below ground after more than 65 dry days.

soil-form-068.title: Laterite blocks that harden in the open air
soil-form-068.text: Laterite is mined below the groundwater level while wet and soft, and cut into blocks. As the moisture evaporates, its iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather. Khmer builders used it with sandstone in the Angkor monuments, including the foundations and inner parts of Angkor Wat behind its sandstone face. After 1000 AD, Angkorian construction shifted to rectangular temple enclosures of laterite, brick and stone. Since the mid-1970s, laterite has replaced stone as a road base course in trials. In 1984 Malawi saved US$40,000 per km this way.

soil-form-070.title: Red earth that scrubs phosphorus from wastewater
soil-form-070.text: In Northern Ireland, phosphorus from farms enriches the lakes, and local laterite offers a fix. Rich in iron and aluminum, laterite can remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater. At sewage works, this low-grade aluminum ore is used in acid solution, followed by precipitation. Laboratory tests removed 99% of phosphorus from solution, and a pilot-scale facility removed 96%. Columns of laterite with water percolating through them lowered cadmium, chromium and lead to undetectable concentrations.

soil-form-067.title: Farming laterite soils: rich in clay, poor in nutrients
soil-form-067.text: Laterite soils are rich in clay but heavily leached, an awkward mix for farmers. Their clay helps them hold water and nutrients, and makes them more plastic than sandy soils. It also slows the passage of water, so rain enters slowly. Intensive leaching leaves them less fertile than other soils. Yet they respond readily to manure and irrigation, and suit plantation crops such as oil palm, tea, coffee and cashew. If their structure degrades, a hard surface crust forms. It blocks water entry and seedling emergence and increases runoff. In Niger, 'bio-reclamation of degraded lands', using planting pits, residues and drought-tolerant crops, has rehabilitated degraded laterite soils.

soil-form-071.title: Lateritic ores: metals concentrated by tropical weathering
soil-form-071.text: About 70% of Earth's land-based nickel resources lie in laterites, which currently supply about 40% of world nickel production. Laterites concentrate many metals: aluminum, iron, manganese, nickel, copper and gold. Aluminum is found in the ore described in {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, iron and manganese in iron-rich hard crusts, nickel and copper in disintegrated rock, and gold in mottled clays. That main aluminum ore is a variety of laterite. It averages 45 to 60% Al2O3 and 20 to 30% Fe2O3 by weight. Northern Ireland's basaltic laterites, up to 30 m thick, were once a major source of iron and aluminum ore.

soil-form-086.title: How fast bedrock turns to soil under a growing blanket
soil-form-086.text: The thicker the soil, the more slowly the rock beneath it weathers. The soil production function expresses the rate at which bedrock weathers into soil as a function of soil thickness. A general model has weathering decline exponentially with thickness h: de/dt = P0 exp(−kh). P0 is the maximum weathering rate and k an empirical constant. Temperature swings and average water penetration both fall off exponentially below the surface. At northern California sites P0 ranged from 0.08 to 2.0 mm/yr, and in southeastern Australia from 0.05 to 0.14 mm/yr. Yet k varied little, from 2 to 4 m−1. G.K. Gilbert's older humped model, from 1877, puts the fastest weathering under an intermediate thickness, since bare rock sheds the water that chemical weathering needs.

soil-form-060.title: Lessivage: how clay travels down through a soil
soil-form-060.text: Rain soaking into a soil can carry clay with it. Lessivage, also called argilluviation, is the washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil. It is the main mechanism forming the clay-enriched argic, or Bt, horizon of Luvisolic soils. Clay particles carry a negative charge. Infiltrating water picks them up as a colloidal suspension and carries them down until a change in conditions makes them clump together and settle. Clay settles where water stagnates or meets positive ions deeper down. As it accumulates, pores in the illuvial horizon become finer and trap still more clay. Texture matters. Lessivage is most common in medium-textured soils under moderate to high rainfall, especially beneath deciduous and mixed forests, whose organic acids disperse clay. Very sandy soils drain too fast and lack clay. Clay-rich soils drain so slowly that clay moves only a short way. The process is widespread in central and eastern Canada, parts of Europe and temperate Asia. Its results cut both ways. The deposited clay helps the subsoil hold nutrients, but a thick clay-rich layer can make soils prone to compaction, surface ponding and restricted root growth. If the layer becomes too compacted, limiting traffic, deep loosening and buried drain pipes ({{ref:soil-phys-227}}) may be needed.

soil-form-081.title: Ferrallitisation: why so many tropical soils are red
soil-form-081.text: Many tropical soils are red, and ferrallitisation explains why. It is the process that turns rock into a soil of {{ref:soil-chem-088}} clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminum. In the humid tropics, with consistently high temperatures and rainfall, chemical weathering breaks rock down rapidly into clays. Those clays later break down further, releasing silica. The silica is leached away, while the iron and aluminum sesquioxides remain and give the soil its characteristic red. The process is the reverse of podsolisation, in which silica remains and iron and aluminum are removed. Climate decides the details. Year-round rain in tropical rainforests produces ferrallitic soils, while savannas with alternating wet and dry seasons have ferruginous soils.

soil-form-052.title: Leaching efficiency: why some salty clays resist reclamation
soil-form-052.text: Dense clay in Portugal's Tagus delta proved so hard to flush of salt that it was left as coarse pasture. Its leaching efficiency measured only 0.10 to 0.15. This parameter of the leaching model departs from one where salt is unevenly distributed or the soil's build is irregular. Clay soil in Egypt's Nile delta does much better, at 0.7 to 0.8. Hard to measure directly, it is calibrated by fitting model curves to observed salt levels, giving a value of about 0.75 at Mashtul. Tabulated values run from 0.80 for Tunisian silty clay down to between 0.11 and 0.20 for some clays in Peru, Portugal and Thailand.

soil-form-084.title: Stone lines: geology or the work of burrowers?
soil-form-084.text: Few Earth-science topics have caused more controversy than the stone line. The argument spans archaeology, geology, the study of landforms, ecology and pedology, on every continent but Antarctica. At issue is whether stonelayers formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, ones. Sharpe coined 'stone-line' in 1938 from South Carolina, reading it as abiotic mass transfer on slopes. He was unaware of earlier names and drawings, including Darwin's. Others have read it as glacial evidence, or as an eroded pavement buried under tropical loess. Morrás and colleagues argued in 2009 that it is the base of soil biomantles. The literature remains divided, and an interpreter's view often reflects background and training.

soil-form-058.title: Why most prehistoric artifacts lie in a churned layer
soil-form-058.text: Most prehistoric cultural materials lie in the soil biomantle, where animal mixing has moved them out of their original context. The exceptions are a few stratified caves and rare open-air sites buried faster than the mixing could destratify them. Artifacts wider than burrows, such as cleavers, core-stones and grinding stones, settle downward and join the basal stonelayer. Smaller flakes spread through the upper biomantle and turn up in the spoil heaps of gophers, moles and mole-rats. Since Darwin, the earthworm has been recognized as a key mixer of biomantles and the artifacts in them.

soil-form-056.title: Gophers, termites and worms: three ways animals rework soil
soil-form-056.text: A pocket gopher, a termite and a worm all rework soil, but in different ways. Animal mixing in the biomantle has three overlapping sub-processes, which together abrade and break down particles, a process called particle comminution. Biomixing is churning by burrowing vertebrates such as pocket gophers, moles, badgers, wombats, aardvarks and pigs, and tree uprooting matters too. Biotransfer moves soil to the surface or within the biomantle, mainly by 'conveyor-belt' ants, termites and worms. Termites may dig many meters for mound-building soil. In biosorting, burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle into a stonelayer at the biomantle's base. Invertebrates are the main biosorters in tropical soils. Small burrowing vertebrates dominate in many midlatitude deserts, prairies and steppes.

soil-form-057.title: Dynamic denudation: everything happening in the biomantle at once
soil-form-057.text: Plants' role in soil formation is well understood. The role of animals in making soil, horizons, the features in {{ref:soil-water-133}} and stone lines was poorly understood until recently. The dynamic form of {{ref:soil-water-272}} is the sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle. They include organic matter production, eluviation and illuviation, weathering, erosion and deposition, freeze–thaw, shrinking and swelling, and gravity movements. Normally all are subsidiary to animal mixing. Wilkinson and Humphreys offer evidence that this mixing appears to be the most active soil-forming process in many soils. It dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly the soils of {{ref:soil-class-106}} and {{ref:soil-class-024}}.

soil-form-062.title: Cheluviation: metals ride organic carriers downward
soil-form-062.text: A gray-white leached layer above a dark brown or red one is a typical signature of cheluviation. In this process, metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic molecules called ligands, forming chelates. The chelates move downward by eluviation and are then deposited. Iron, aluminum, manganese, calcium, magnesium and trace elements can all be chelated, mostly by ligands from soil organic matter. Chelates with the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}} leach and deposit strongly. Iron and aluminum move easily at low pH and under reducing conditions, but precipitate as pH rises to around 7–8 or under oxidizing conditions. Clay adsorbs chelates and weakens their leaching, while coarse-textured or water-saturated soils enhance it.

soil-form-078.title: Soil memory: a record written over and over
soil-form-078.text: Dokuchaev called soil 'a mirror of the landscape'. In 1953 Nikiforoff echoed him with a new term, soil memory: the idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity. Soils store that record like a page written over and over, with newer features overprinting older ones. This is pedomemory; layered sediments instead store lithomemory, like a book in datable order. The idea is used to study climate change, land-use history and archaeological evidence. Persistent genetic traces in cultivated soils, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-090}}, are read as a 'memory effect'. Yet most soils have developed under more than one set of conditions, so the record is partial and 'censored'. Equifinality, different paths leading to the same result, complicates reading it, and the concept serves as an exploratory tool.

soil-form-079.title: Bacteria that remember an Iron Age village
soil-form-079.text: Distinctive bacterial communities still mark an Iron Age settlement in Sicily, Iron Age cremation burials, medieval activity areas and Neolithic ditch infills. Microbial soil memory is the ability of soil microbes to change their community structure, diversity and activity, and to keep those changes over time. Many bacteria survive in dormant states for long periods, persisting through large environmental changes. PCR and next-generation sequencing characterize soil bacterial communities from their DNA, and they are well suited to detecting traces of past influences.

soil-form-077.title: Polygenetic soils: one profile, several histories
soil-form-077.text: Most soils carry more than one history. A polygenetic soil, such as a paleosol, shows evidence of continued soil development under later conditions. Most soils are polygenetic, so a younger soil-forming signal may overprint, mask or erase an older one. Examples with ancient clay-enriched horizons include the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon and the Berino Paleosol of New Mexico. The soil described in {{ref:soil-class-051}} has been proposed to be polygenetic. Its altered parent material includes volcanic ash, non-carbonate sediments and wind-blown sediments.

soil-found-079.title: Soil solution: the water that is never just water
soil-found-079.text: The water in soil is never pure. It carries hundreds of dissolved substances, so soil scientists give it a more accurate name: the soil solution. It is the water held in the pores of soil, together with everything dissolved or suspended in it. These substances, organic and inorganic, sit in the liquid as ions or molecules. The solution is also a force of change. Water dissolves {{ref:soil-found-029}}, deposits new ones and washes material down through the soil, which makes it a critical agent in how soil develops. Its makeup shifts constantly. Soils wet and dry, plants take up {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, salts wash away, and acids or alkalis arrive. Plant foods held on {{ref:soil-found-040}} and on {{ref:soil-found-045}} buffer those swings, steadying the mix. One measure tracks the solution's acidity: {{ref:soil-found-014}} gauges its hydrogen ion activity, which governs how available those plant foods are.

soil-found-119.title: Mineralogy, the science of how minerals are built
soil-found-119.text: Talc sits at one end of a scale and diamond at the other. Mineralogy is the branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical properties of {{ref:soil-found-029}}, optical ones included. It asks how minerals form, how to classify them, where they occur and how people use them. Some crystallize from molten rock deep in the crust; others grow as rock weathers at the surface or in soil. Identification starts with a hand sample. Hardness is a first clue, ranked on the Mohs scale from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. X-ray diffraction, shown in 1912, later revealed crystal structures.

soil-found-118.title: Calcite, the mineral that fizzes in acid
soil-found-118.text: A drop of acid on calcite starts a fizz, as the mineral dissolves and gives off carbon dioxide. Calcite is the most stable crystal form of calcium carbonate, CaCO3, and one of the {{ref:soil-found-034}}. It is very common, especially in {{ref:soil-form-147}}, and it marks hardness 3 on the Mohs scale. Water moving underground can either dissolve it or deposit it, depending on temperature, pH and the ions it carries. Less dissolved carbon dioxide makes calcite come out of solution. It also breaks a common rule: it grows less soluble as water warms.

soil-found-120.title: Phytoliths, the glass skeletons plants leave behind
soil-found-120.text: Plants drink stone. They take up dissolved silica from the soil as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, and it can make up 0.1% to 10% of their dry weight. Inside the tissue, the silica hardens into phytoliths: rigid, microscopic mineral deposits that often outlast the plant itself. They can survive in soils for thousands of years and are abundant in the fossil record from the Late Devonian onward. That durability makes them useful clues to past environments and changing vegetation. Carbon sealed inside them also resists decay for millennia. It builds up in soils, in stores that vary by species, biome, climate and soil.

soil-found-122.title: Weathering rinds, the stone clocks of old gravel
soil-found-122.text: A pebble's skin can tell its age. A weathering rind is a discolored, chemically altered outer layer on a rock fragment, formed as {{ref:soil-found-058}} works inward. Rinds grow on stones from pebbles to boulders, at the surface or buried in river, slope or glacial deposits, wherever air or shallow underground water reaches them. They are often enriched in iron, manganese and silica, and oxidized to yellowish or reddish hues. Thicker rinds on gravel of similar rock mean older deposits. Calibrated against radiocarbon-dated deposits, an age–thickness curve can date others, on the assumption that the relation is logarithmic.

soil-found-117.title: Core samples, columns of earth pulled out intact
soil-found-117.text: Dated cores of ocean floor, soil and ice have rewritten the history of the Pleistocene. A core sample is a cylinder of {{ref:soil-water-046}}, rock or soil, usually drilled out with a hollow tube. The material is pushed more or less intact into the tube, then removed in the laboratory for study. Hand coring with a simple tube or piston corer is cheap and quick, but in clay soils it reaches only a few decimeters. Cores are rarely perfect. Tools often crack them and lose weaker layers, which complicates reading them. Drilling that brings up only cuttings yields no undisturbed core at all.

soil-found-116.title: Trial pits: digging down before building up
soil-found-116.text: Before a building goes up, someone often digs a hole. A trial pit, also called a test pit, is an excavation dug to study or sample what lies below the surface. Most are dug for a site investigation or a soil or geological survey. A pit reveals a site's geology and how deep the water stands, and it lays bare the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}. Pits usually run 1 to 4 meters deep, dug by hand or with a mechanical digger. Regulations require any pit deeper than 1.2 meters to be secured against collapse if people will enter it.

soil-found-077.title: Soil: rock, water, air and life in one mixture
soil-found-077.text: A single gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species, most of them microbes that no one has yet explored. Soil is a natural mixture of minerals, {{ref:soil-bio-114}}, gases, water and organisms that together support the life of plants and soil creatures. All of Earth's soil, taken together, forms one layer with a name of its own, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-084}}. Soil is a three-state system. A solid framework of minerals and dead plant and animal material is laced with pores. Those pores hold gases, the soil atmosphere, and water carrying dissolved substances, {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Much of a soil is empty space. A dry sample of most soils weighs 1.1 to 1.6 grams per cubic centimeter, yet the particles themselves weigh 2.6 to 2.7. Soil is made by climate, relief, organisms and the rock or sediment beneath acting together over time, and it never stops developing. It is also young. Little of it is older than the Pleistocene and none is older than the Cenozoic, though fossilized soils survive from as far back as the Archean. Soil has four important functions. It grows plants, stores and purifies water, modifies Earth's atmosphere and houses soil organisms. It is a large reservoir of carbon, and possibly one of the most sensitive to human disturbance and climate change. Soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. Some scientific definitions keep the word dirt for soil that has been moved out of place.

soil-found-090.title: Soil science: one resource, many disciplines
soil-found-090.text: Engineers, agronomists, chemists, geologists, ecologists, microbiologists, archaeologists and planners all add to what is known about soils. Soil science gathers that knowledge into the study of soil as a natural resource. It asks how soil forms and how it is classified and mapped. It measures soil's physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and asks how they bear on its use and management. The field has two main historical branches. {{ref:soil-found-095}} studies soil in its natural setting. {{ref:soil-found-097}} studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it. Both draw on the physics, chemistry and biology of soil. Soil occupies {{ref:soil-found-084}}, one of the spheres the geosciences use to organize the Earth. Climate change, greenhouse gases and {{ref:soil-env-212}} now drive much new research, along with interest in biodiversity and in past cultures. Soil scientists also worry about preserving soil and farmland as population and food consumption grow and more land is degraded. Mapping, which classifies the soils of an area and geo-encodes them, increasingly relies on digital methods and remote sensing. In 1998 a new international system, {{ref:soil-class-016}}, replaced the older one from the FAO. Its current 4th edition dates from 2022.

soil-found-084.title: Where four spheres meet: the pedosphere
soil-found-084.text: Soil forms only where four of Earth's great systems touch. The pedosphere is the outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil, where soil forms and wears away by erosion. It lies at the meeting point of the lithosphere, the rocky shell, with the atmosphere, the hydrosphere of Earth's waters and the biosphere of living things. Soil develops only where all four interact. The pedosphere is the foundation of every ecosystem on land, and it passes chemical and biogeochemical flows into and out of the other spheres. It sits within a wider interface that runs from vegetation through aquifers and loose material down into solid rock, described in {{ref:soil-found-115}}. Soil begins to form as minerals over solid rock break down, chemically or physically. It can start without life, but biological reactions speed it up greatly. Chemical attack on silicon-bearing minerals dominates the work. Acids from {{ref:soil-found-085}} help, and so does carbonic acid from the atmosphere. The rock below sets the starting conditions, and few rock types locally enrich scarce elements such as phosphorus and nitrogen. Over time the soil's bulk chemistry drifts away from the rock's. It comes to reflect the reactions taking place in the soil itself.

soil-found-095.title: Pedology: reading how a soil came to be
soil-found-095.text: Every soil has a life story, and pedology sets out to read it. Pedology is the branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve, and builds frameworks for describing them, often where they lie in nature. Pedologists observe a soil's form, where soils occur and how they fit into wider settings of time and space. From those observations come classifications, soil maps and theories. As a soil forms, it slowly deepens and develops characteristic layers, approaching a steady state. Fallou conceived pedology in the 19th century as a fundamental science, separate from agrology, the applied forerunner of {{ref:soil-found-097}}. For a long time agronomists saw soil as a static production medium, while pedologists studied its ties to landscape history. The two approaches are now integrated. One sub-discipline characterizes and maps soils with numbers. Another, built on {{ref:soil-water-295}}, links landform processes with the way soils form.

soil-found-097.title: Edaphology: what soil does for living things
soil-found-097.text: Long before the word existed, Xenophon and Cato were practicing edaphology. Cato recommended working the soil, rotating crops and growing legumes to build soil nitrogen. He also devised the first soil capability classification for crops. Edaphology is the branch of soil science concerned with how soils influence living things, especially plants. Alongside pedology, it is one of the field's two main divisions. It covers how soil shapes people's use of land for plant growth and other purposes. Its general subfields deal with farming, called agrology in some regions, and with the environment. The environmental side ranges from septic fields, wastewater and storm runoff to controlling erosion, contamination and cleanup, restoring wetlands and managing nutrients. At first the two branches were poorly distinguished. Russian soil scientists used edaphology as a synonym for pedology, and Spanish ones preferred the term. In the 20th century edaphology was driven out of a pedology-centered science. It is now recognized as a necessary branch, complementary to pedology.

soil-found-078.title: Half solid, half empty: what a soil is made of
soil-found-078.text: Half of a typical soil is not solid at all. About 50% of its volume is solids, 45% mineral grains and 5% material from living things, alive or dead. The other 50% is pores, half filled with water and half with gas. Soil composition describes these proportions. In the short term the mineral and organic shares stay constant, while water and gas trade places. A rise in one is balanced by a fall in the other. Pore space matters because air and water must enter and move through it, and both are critical for soil life. Squeezing a soil, especially under heavy machinery, shrinks its pores and keeps air and water from roots and organisms. Mineral particles, interacting with the organic share, water and gases, clump together into crumbs. Where these crumbs can be identified, the soil is said to be developed. Most nutrients are held by the finest particles of clay and organic material. They cling to clay surfaces, sit bound inside {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, or are locked in living organisms and in long-decayed organic remains. Apart from nitrogen fixed from the atmosphere, most plant nutrients first came from the minerals of the rock or sediment the soil formed from. Living things shape a soil most strongly near the surface. With depth, geochemical influences take over.

soil-found-081.title: From food to foundations: how people use soil
soil-found-081.text: Soil resources produce 98.8% of the food humans consume. In farming, soil anchors plants and is their primary nutrient base. The kind of soil and the moisture available decide which plants can be grown. Yet soil is not strictly essential. Systems that grow plants in water or mist, with no soil at all, show as much. Soil is also the foundation for most construction and the basis of many building materials. Surface mining, road building and dam construction move massive volumes of it. Waste treatment relies on soil too. Septic systems, covered in {{ref:soil-env-195}}, and wastewater spread on land use soil processes that need oxygen, and landfills use soil as daily cover. Water percolating down to become groundwater is filtered on the way, losing pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals and excess nutrients. Organic soils are a significant fuel and horticultural resource, and drained peatlands are farmed in Nordic countries. Animals and humans even eat soil-like substances, a habit called geophagy. Some monkeys eat soil with their leaves to ease tannin toxicity.

soil-found-082.title: Soil reclamation: rebuilding ground after disturbance
soil-found-082.text: A disturbed site cannot simply be seeded and left. Soil reclamation is the part of land reclamation that rebuilds soil, usually after infrastructure removal, recontouring and contaminant cleanup and before revegetation. Land reclamation converts disturbed or damaged land to its former or another productive use, and covers soils, hydrology, flora and fauna. Soil reclamation and soil remediation are components of it. The goals depend on the end land use. Regulatory requirements are stricter for agricultural land and land people will occupy than for industrial land, and the end use may mean a different ecosystem. Stripped {{ref:soil-found-077}} is normally replaced in its natural horizon sequence. Careful placement limits horizon mixing, and compaction on replacement can be eased by tillage. Damage is reduced by working under frozen or dry conditions, and soil quality is kept if stockpiles are held only briefly. Bare reclaimed soil is exposed to wind and water erosion, as in {{ref:soil-water-001}}, so contouring, amendments, erosion control blankets, mulch and bioengineering such as live staking are used. Clay can be part of the fix. Soils rich in swelling smectite clays, a type of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, are often very fertile: the smectite-rich paddy soils of Thailand's Central Plains are among the world's most productive. On low-clay soils in Thailand, adding bentonite clay once at 200 kilograms per rai (1,300 kg/ha) raised yields by an average of 73% in field trials. Soils too high in clay or salts can be balanced with gypsum, washed river sand and organic matter. Sandy, nutrient-poor soils benefit from compost or ramial chipped wood.

soil-found-091.title: Dokuchaev's idea: soil as a natural body with a history
soil-found-091.text: As late as 1914, an encyclopedia defined soil as forms of earth made as rocks weather. That was the old view. Soil was a product of chemical changes in rock, a dead substrate from which plants draw their nutrients. Fallou and Dokuchaev are both credited among the first to treat soil as something distinct from geology and from crop production. Fallou came first, but Dokuchaev's work proved more significant. He saw soil as a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the solid rock beneath it. Rock becomes soil, he held, under the action of climate, vegetation, country, relief and age. In the 20th century the concept became one of earthy material altered by living processes. It is still being refined to take in energy moving within soil. Nikiforoff's 1959 definition fits this modern understanding: soil is the 'excited skin of the sub aerial part of the Earth's crust'.

soil-env-181.title: Everything soil does for people and ecosystems
soil-env-181.text: About 50% of people live in houses built from soil. That is one of many jobs a {{ref:soil-found-077}} does, and together they are called soil functions: the general capabilities that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses. For food and biomass, soil stores and supplies nutrients, holds water in its pores and moderates temperature. It is a habitat and gene reserve for many organisms, and it turns the remains of dead plants and animals into simpler mineral forms other life can use. Soil also governs whether rain runs off or recharges aquifers, purifies septic drain field wastes and stores atmospheric carbon in organic matter. It supplies raw materials, and it carries cultural meaning, giving a sense of place and preserving artifacts of the past. Productive soil is limited in area, so extracting it needs to be controlled.

soil-env-174.title: Soil health: treating the ground as a living system
soil-env-174.text: Some microbiologists believe that 80% of a soil's nutrient functions are essentially controlled by microbes.
