That view sits at the heart of soil health, the state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as suits its environment. The underlying principle is that soil is a living, dynamic, ever-changing environment. It is not the inert growing medium that intensive farming tends to assume. Put simply, health arises from favorable interactions among all of a soil's parts, living and non-living, from microbes to plants and animals. The term spans sustaining plant and animal productivity, enhancing biodiversity, maintaining water and air quality, and supporting human health and habitation. Soils highly fertile for crops are also biologically lively. Temperate grassland soils hold 1–2 t/ha of bacterial biomass and 2–5 t/ha of fungal biomass. By analogy with human health, a healthy soil is in biological, chemical and physical well-being. It is not degraded, it resists degradation, and it keeps cycling nutrients, carbon and water. Soil health depends on the variety of life in the soil. Keeping protective living covers on the soil and adding natural, carbon-containing amendments improve it. Inorganic fertilizers need not harm it, if they are not used in excess and the extra plant growth returns more carbon-containing residues. The idea remains debated. A soil can be healthy for its ecosystem without directly serving crop production, so scientists still disagree on how to define and measure soil health.

soil-env-179.title: Soil quality, the standard no one has fixed
soil-env-179.text: Water and air have established quality standards. Soil does not, because its quality is difficult to define or quantify. Soil quality is the condition of a soil judged by its capacity to perform ecosystem services for human and non-human life. It reflects how well a soil maintains biodiversity and productivity, partitions the flow of water and dissolved substances, filters and buffers, cycles nutrients and supports plants and structures. Management has a major impact. Planting cover crops, for example, raises soil quality by adding plant remains over time. Soil organisms contribute in countless ways, and the amount and diversity of soil life appears proportional to soil quality. Fungi that partner with plant roots help their hosts establish on degraded soil and improve its quality and health.

soil-found-096.title: The ground rules pedologists use to explain soils
soil-found-096.text: Much of the world's shale began as soil. Soils are natural clay factories, and their clay, eroded into ocean basins, later hardened into rock. Pedologists explain how soils form with a set of working principles. The first is that external factors drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns. Five major factors dominate: climate, organisms, relief, the rock or sediment beneath, and time. Complexity is more common than simplicity, and today's soils carry imprints of past processes that may be hard to observe. Those processes create and destroy order within a soil, often at once, and its layers record the balance. Uniformitarianism, the idea that present processes also ran in the past, applies too: they have worked since organisms first appeared on land. Few soils are geologically old. Most date no further back than the Pleistocene. Knowing soil genesis aids classification, mapping and management. Yet classifications cannot rest on genesis alone, since its processes are seldom observed and change over time.

soil-found-093.title: What soil scientists actually do
soil-found-093.text: Almost every area of the United States has had its soils surveyed and published, with tables on how their properties support or limit different uses. Mapping soils is the traditional work of soil scientists. Increasingly, they also take on land and environmental problems across disciplines. They protect environmentally critical areas and valuable habitats, manage land for productivity and remediate damaged land. Some applications are less obvious: dating past activity at a site, reading archaeological layers, vitrifying radioactive waste and using soil microbes to degrade contaminants. The concept of {{ref:soil-found-115}} frames research across soil, rock, air, water and living resources at Earth's surface.

soil-found-092.title: Red, hot, fat or sandy: soils by their folk names
soil-found-092.text: The earliest known scheme for sorting soils comes from China. The Yu Gong, from the 5th century BCE, sorted soil into three categories and nine classes by color, grain and water. Vernacular classifications are folk systems that give soils unique names or name them by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy. They judge soils by appearance, performance and the plants growing on them. A familiar example contrasts heavy, clayey soils with light, sandy ones. Light soils are easier to cultivate and resist compaction by trampling cattle, but they erode more easily. Despite the name, they are not lighter or more porous than heavy soils.

soil-found-086.title: What the sky drops into the soil
soil-found-086.text: After water itself, nitrogen is the most abundant ingredient of rain. The reason is that water vapor uses tiny airborne particles, called aerosols, to form droplets. Rain is one of three main inputs the pedosphere receives from the air. The others are wind-blown sediment and gases diffusing in. Wind carries aerosols, pollen and dust into soils, a process called eolian sedimentation. Gases move both ways. Carbon dioxide from roots and microbes keeps the bicarbonate in soil water far above balance with the air. Together with dissolved metals, this makes the soil more acid. Gases escape back to the air from dissolving carbonates, decay, chemical reactions and microbial photosynthesis.

soil-found-087.title: Forest soils, leached into sharp bands
soil-found-087.text: In a forest, more water falls as rain and snow than evaporates or passes back out through plants. The surplus percolates down through the soil layers. Forest soils form in these conditions and are usually well developed, with thick layers of well-decayed organic remains. Slow decay releases large amounts of a soluble organic acid, which greatly enhances the chemical breakdown of minerals. Percolating water and this breakdown carry magnesium, iron and aluminum downward, a process called podzolization. The result is marked contrasts in color and chemistry between layers. Forest soils can also build a thick sponge of stored carbon.

soil-found-089.title: Grassland and desert soils, shaped by drought
soil-found-089.text: Drought writes itself into a soil. Grassland and desert soils form where rain and snow equal or fall short of the water lost to evaporation and plants. Little water and few organic acids percolate downward. So the washing out of dissolved substances slows, along with chemical breakdown of minerals and soil development itself. Evaporation builds up calcium in the upper profile, where it clumps clay and dissolved organic acids together. Lower down, calcium settles out as a hard layer of the mineral in {{ref:soil-found-118}}. In deserts a layer of gypsum and halite may lie beneath it. Where rain and washing out increase, the clay-richest layer sits deeper.

soil-found-085.title: Lichens, microbes and the first bite into bare rock
soil-found-085.text: Bare rock starts becoming soil when living things attack it with acid. The first colonizers, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, begin the work. Lichens and other microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, green algae, fungi and bacteria, secrete oxalic acid. Lichens have long been seen as the pioneers of soil. Seed-bearing plants can colonize faster, but lichens tolerate harsher conditions and dominate in alpine regions. Organic acids from roots and decay, such as citric and phenolic acids, {{ref:soil-chem-059}} and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}, speed chemical breakdown by gripping metal atoms and pulling them from minerals. As the soil thickens, earthworms, burrowing mammals and large animals above ground go on altering its chemistry and fertility.

soil-found-088.title: Why tropical forest soils turn rusty red
soil-found-088.text: No other environment gets as much sunlight and rain over such long growing seasons as the tropical forest. Its plants produce as much as 800 grams of carbon per square meter per year, or 8 tons per hectare. Heat and abundant water speed the chemical breakdown of minerals. Decay is fast too, leaving less organic acid to wash metals downward. So unlike temperate {{ref:soil-found-087}}, tropical forest soils show little or no podzolization and lack marked contrasts between layers. Mobile magnesium, iron and aluminum instead settle out as oxides, giving the soil a rusty red color.

soil-found-099.title: How industrial farming changed soil and crop
soil-found-099.text: Heavy metals from mechanized production have built up in soils, and they have turned up in crops as well. Industrialization has changed how soils interact with plants, the core concern of {{ref:soil-found-097}}. Greater use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides has decreased the nutrients soils make available. Growing a single crop over and over lowers biodiversity. That reduces soil nutrients further and deepens dependence on chemical fertilizer. Intensive plowing and digging disturb the soil microbes that help keep soil moist and its air circulating.

soil-found-098.title: Van Helmont's willow and a pot of soil
soil-found-098.text: For five years Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil, supplying nothing but rainwater. At the end, the tree had gained more weight than the soil had lost. Van Helmont concluded that the willow was made of water. He was only partly correct, but the experiment reignited interest in edaphology, the study of how soils shape plant life.

soil-found-115.title: The critical zone, from living soil down to bedrock
soil-found-115.text: Nearly all life on land depends on a zone that ends deep in solid rock, where life and water stop significantly changing the rock's chemistry. Earth's critical zone is the near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact. Together they regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources. The zone runs through the pedosphere, the unsaturated ground below it and the saturated groundwater zone. In practice it essentially equates to the pedosphere. Its uppermost, biota-rich layer is called the biomantle. Its processes govern the exchanges of mass and energy behind biomass production, chemical cycling and water storage. Critical Zone science integrates landscape evolution, rock breakdown, hydrology, geochemistry and ecology, across scales of space and time and human influence. Tsakalotos coined the term in chemistry in 1909. Gail Ashley applied it in 1998 to the connection of vegetation to soil and weathered materials. It is studied at Critical Zone Observatories, for which the US National Science Foundation sought proposals in 2006.

soil-found-080.title: Can lifeless ground be called soil?
soil-found-080.text: Is the ground on Mars soil? Only part of the scientific community accepts the word for the surface material of the Moon and Mars. The question belongs to an unsettled debate over where soil ends and other loose surface material begins. One classic definition says soil has formed once dead plant and animal material accumulates and fine particles washed down from above build a distinct lower layer. That definition is somewhat arbitrary. Mixtures of mineral grains and decayed organic remains support biological and farming activity before such a layer forms. Twentieth-century thinking cast soil as earthy material altered by living processes. On that view, soil without a living component is simply part of Earth's outer layer of loose material, described in {{ref:soil-form-097}}. More recent definitions embrace soils with no organic content at all, such as loose layers formed on Mars and in comparable deserts on Earth. Engineers sidestep the question. For them, soil is simply part of the loose material above solid rock, found also on the Moon and other celestial bodies. The sources still disagree on whether lifeless material, such as the surface material of the Moon or Mars, should be called soil.

soil-found-045.title: Soil organic matter: the small fraction that shapes everything
soil-found-045.text: Soil organic matter is present in small amounts, typically 1 to 6% by weight in agricultural soil, yet it strongly affects almost all soil properties. It is about twice the organic carbon level. Its parts are described as the living, the dead and the very dead. They are living organisms, fresh residues, and molecules from well-decomposed residues. The living part is about 15% of soil organic matter, and soil organisms are estimated at about 25% of the world's biodiversity. Fresh residues, the active fraction, feed soil organisms and release nutrients. Easily decomposed molecules like proteins, amino acids, sugars and starches do not last long, while lignin decomposes more slowly. Waterlogged peats and mucks hold much undecomposed organic matter that does not give the benefits of fresh residues. Organic matter also builds structure. Sticky substances on earthworm skin and fungal products bind particles, and sticky root substances plus fine roots and mycorrhizae promote stable aggregates. Organic compounds produced as fresh residues decompose also bind soil particles and give good structure. Earthworms and some fungi make channels that improve infiltration, water status and aeration. The link to {{ref:soil-bio-001}} is direct, since the living part is the soil's biology.

soil-found-029.title: Minerals, the crystals that build rock and soil
soil-found-029.text: As of August 2026, the International Mineralogical Association recognized 6,228 official mineral species. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. That last condition matters. Opal and obsidian are natural solids with no definite crystal structure, so they are more properly called mineraloids. Structure can even split one compound in two. Quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide, yet they count as two species. A mineral must also form by natural geological processes. That rule excludes purely human-made products, and biological ones such as seashells. A rock is something else: a bulk solid geologic material made of one mineral or an aggregate of several. Mineralogists classify minerals by their key chemical constituents, chiefly in the Dana and Strunz systems. One family dominates. The minerals described in {{ref:soil-found-031}} make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust. In soil, minerals form the gritty bulk. The sand and silt fractions are mostly inert rock particles such as quartz, {{ref:soil-found-118}}, {{ref:soil-form-141}} and {{ref:soil-chem-135}}.

soil-found-052.title: Weathering: how solid rock starts becoming soil
soil-found-052.text: Rock of the kind described in {{ref:soil-form-136}} covers 66% of the continents, and all of it is made from rock that was broken down first. That breakdown is weathering: the decay of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things. Weathering happens in place. That sets it apart from erosion, where water, ice, wind, waves or gravity carry rock and mineral material away. It comes in two kinds. One is physical, the mechanical breakdown of rock by heat, water, ice and wind. The other is chemical, the reaction of rock with water, gases and biological chemicals. Water drives both, though oxygen and carbon dioxide from the air, and the activities of organisms, also matter. The two kinds work as a team. Cracks widened by force expose more surface to chemical attack, which speeds disintegration. The material left behind then combines with organic material, the {{ref:soil-found-045}}, to create soil. Weathering is a crucial part of the cycle described in {{ref:soil-form-138}}, and it begins with the solids described in {{ref:soil-found-029}}.

soil-found-050.title: How climate decides how much organic matter a soil holds
soil-found-050.text: Cold soils are rich in organic matter and hot ones are poor. Temperature, soil moisture and topography are the main factors in how much accumulates. In the US, warmer southern climates hold less: more vegetation grows, but faster decomposition by more active organisms for longer each year becomes the dominant influence. Heavy rain and heat in the tropics speed decomposition and nutrient leaching, so forests there depend on efficient recycling of nutrients by living biomass. Organic matter builds up where cold or waterlogging, which makes soil anaerobic, slows decomposers. Arctic and alpine soils receive little in their short growing seasons but are rich in it because cold slows decomposition. Warming and thawing now release it as CO2 and methane. Arid soils usually have little, because plant growth and decomposition are low, though rain triggers a rapid burst of decomposition. Generally it rises with annual precipitation as more plant growth returns more residue, though wet, poorly aerated soils decompose it more slowly. Steep slopes under cultivation encourage erosion of the topsoil, which holds most of the raw material that would otherwise become humus. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-found-049.title: Soil organic matter in the global carbon cycle
soil-found-049.text: The largest amount of carbon on land is stored in soil organic matter, not in living plants. It holds about four times as much as plants, and world soils hold two to three times the atmosphere's amount. Seven inches of soil with 1% organic matter holds as much carbon as the air above a field. The global soil carbon pool is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the atmospheric pool of 750 gigatons and 4.5 times the biotic pool of 560 gigatons. Organic carbon, mostly as {{ref:soil-found-045}}, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons. The rest is soil inorganic carbon, mainly carbonates and bicarbonates. Plants remove carbon dioxide from the air using sunlight and build organic molecules. Plants and animals release it again by respiration, and burning fuels adds more. As organic matter is depleted the soil becomes a carbon dioxide source. Clearing and burning forest, then rapid loss under agriculture, gives a secondary, often larger flush. Agricultural conversion of forests and grasslands is second only to fossil fuel burning as a contributor to rising atmospheric CO2. Soils managed to build organic matter can become net carbon sinks. It is no silver bullet, but on a massive scale it can slow CO2 increase for a while and also raises soil resilience to storms and dry spells.

soil-found-058.title: Chemical weathering: rock remade for life at the surface
soil-found-058.text: Most rock is born hot and squeezed. It forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface. Chemical weathering is the result. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition. It does three things at once. It turns some of the minerals the rock formed with, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, into new secondary minerals. It carries other substances off in solution. And it leaves the most stable minerals unchanged, as a resistate. Water is the main agent. Through the reactions in {{ref:soil-found-060}}, it turns many of these original minerals into fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides. Oxygen oxidizes minerals, and carbon dioxide drives carbonation. The new set of minerals sits closer to equilibrium with surface conditions. True equilibrium is rare, though, because water keeps washing the dissolved products away. Chemical weathering is usually much more important than the mechanical kind in {{ref:soil-found-053}}. Mountains show its reach. Uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

soil-found-063.title: Lichens, roots and microbes that wear down rock
soil-found-063.text: Two common minerals, albite and muscovite, weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil. Living things make the difference. Biological weathering is weathering started or sped up by soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots. Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils. Lichens are among the most effective agents. In a New Jersey study, hornblende granite under lichen weathered three to four times faster than bare rock. Most commonly, plants release carbon dioxide along with chelating compounds, chemicals that grip metal ions, such as organic acids and {{ref:soil-bio-192}}. Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases. The chelating acids strip metal ions, especially aluminum and silicon, from rock. Where they build up, they can reshape whole soils. Partnerships help too. Root-dwelling fungi free nutrients from minerals such as {{ref:soil-form-144}} or apatite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth. Life also works by force. Seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae, their thread-like filaments.

soil-found-059.title: Dissolution: when a mineral vanishes into water
soil-found-059.text: Some minerals leave nothing behind when they weather. In dissolution weathering, also called simple or congruent dissolution, a mineral dissolves completely and no new solid forms. Rainwater easily dissolves soluble minerals such as halite and gypsum. Given enough time, it dissolves even quartz, which goes into solution as silicic acid. Limestone meets a special version. Rainwater and carbon dioxide form weak carbonic acid, which turns limestone into soluble calcium bicarbonate. Cold water holds more dissolved carbon dioxide, so this carbonate dissolution is favored at low temperature. That makes it important in glacial weathering. Pollution sharpens the attack. Unpolluted rain has a pH of around 5.6, where lower numbers mean more acid. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acid rain that can lower it to 4.5 or even 3.0.

soil-found-061.title: Oxidation weathering: iron that reddens and weakens rock
soil-found-061.text: A reddish-brown crust on a rock is often a sign of iron changing inside it. Oxidation weathering is chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+. Oxygen and water drive the change. They turn Fe2+ into Fe3+ oxides and hydroxides such as {{ref:soil-chem-165}}. The new surface crumbles easily, and the rock beneath grows weaker. Sulfide minerals oxidize too. Chalcopyrite, for example, turns to copper hydroxide and {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, leaving colored deposits. The process reaches into the soil. Oxidizing {{ref:soil-form-140}}, especially sulfides and those containing Fe2+, generates soil acidity.

soil-found-053.title: Physical weathering: breaking rock without changing it
soil-found-053.text: A rock can be shattered into pieces that are chemically identical to the original. That is physical weathering, also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation: breaking rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry. Most of it comes from expansion and contraction as temperature changes, as in freeze–thaw and thermal fracturing. Unloading, the loss of weight from rock above, is the exception, since it works without any temperature change. Ice is the most important agent, as {{ref:soil-found-054}} explains. Next comes wedging by plant roots, which enter cracks and pry them apart. Burrowing worms and other animals help, and lichens pluck grains loose. Physical weathering is usually much less important than chemical weathering. In subarctic or alpine settings, though, it can be significant.

soil-found-048.title: What fallen leaves and roots are made of
soil-found-048.text: Fresh plant debris is mostly water, 60% to 90% of it. Dry it, and carbon, oxygen and hydrogen make up about 92% of the weight. The rest includes nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium and trace nutrients. Its organic compounds range from simple sugars to cellulose, along with fats, nitrogen-bearing proteins and, from older woody parts, {{ref:soil-bio-116}}. This debris is the raw material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. One leftover stands apart. Charcoal, the elemental carbon left by incomplete burning, is highly resistant to decomposition.

soil-found-046.title: Most soil carbon lies below the top 20 cm
soil-found-046.text: About 70% of the organic carbon in the world's soils lies deeper than 20 cm. The surface layer has higher carbon concentrations. Deeper soil still stores more overall, because there is far more of it by mass. Radiocarbon dates show the carbon growing older with depth, a sign that deep soil keeps it longer. The forces at work change too. Living things shape organic carbon near the surface, while minerals take over at depth, binding carbon as {{ref:soil-found-047}}.

soil-found-054.title: Frost weathering and the ice that splits rock
soil-found-054.text: Water expands 9.2% when it freezes. Inside rock, the pressure this creates has a realistic upper limit of 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals. Frost weathering is physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops. Frost wedging, the classic explanation, was long believed the main mechanism. It needs small, twisting cracks in almost saturated rock and daily freeze–thaw cycles. Those conditions are unusual, so it is unlikely to matter in the tropics, polar regions or arid climates. Growing theoretical and experimental work now favors {{ref:soil-phys-179}} instead, though the question is still open. Water drawn to the growing ice layers covered in {{ref:soil-phys-154}} can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging. It works best between −4 and −15 °C.

soil-found-062.title: Mineral hydration, water's first grip on a crystal
soil-found-062.text: Before water can take a crystal apart, it has to attach to it. In mineral hydration, water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral. The minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} turning into iron hydroxides, and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum, are examples. Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, hydrolysis and oxidation. But hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in hydrolysis. Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−. Protons then replace the positive ions at the surface, freeing them. Loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminum hydroxides. In the mineral of {{ref:soil-form-141}}, this starts at defects on the crystal surface, in a layer only a few atoms thick.

soil-found-056.title: Pressure release: rock that peels as it rises
soil-found-056.text: Granite and other intrusive rocks form deep underground, under great pressure. When erosion strips away the rock above, their outer parts expand. This is pressure release weathering, also called unloading. The expansion opens fractures parallel to the surface, and sheets of rock break away along them. Geologists call this exfoliation or sheeting. Where rock is buttressed, the stress toward the free surface can reach 35 megapascals, easily enough to shatter rock. A retreating glacier can do the same by lifting its weight off the rock beneath.

soil-found-057.title: Salt weathering: crystals that pry rock apart
soil-found-057.text: Salt can split stone. In salt weathering, also called haloclasty, salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there. Like {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, the grains draw in more dissolved salt through tiny gaps. They grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock. Sodium and magnesium salts work best. Salt weathering happens wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts. In the rocks of {{ref:soil-form-136}}, weathering of {{ref:soil-chem-134}} to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can grow salt lenses too.

soil-found-055.title: Thermal stress: rock cracked by heat and cold
soil-found-055.text: Rock swells as it warms and shrinks as it cools, and the strain adds up. Thermal stress weathering is weathering caused by these temperature changes. It takes two forms. In thermal shock, which is uncommon, rock cracks at once. In the more typical thermal fatigue, repeated cycles of stress gradually weaken it. Deserts, with their large day–night swings, are the classic setting. Yet any large temperature change can drive it, including wildfire, so it is likely as important in cold climates. It works best when heated rock is buttressed by surrounding rock and can expand in only one direction. Its reputation has swung. Geologists long discounted it after early 20th-century oven experiments. Those experiments have since been criticized as unrealistic, and geomorphologists now re-emphasize the process.

soil-found-030.title: Eight elements and the swaps that multiply minerals
soil-found-030.text: Just eight elements make up over 98% of the Earth's crust by weight. In decreasing order they are oxygen, silicon, aluminum, iron, magnesium, calcium, sodium and potassium. Oxygen alone forms 47% and silicon 28%. Mineral chemistry explains how this supply, and the swapping of one ion for another, decides which minerals exist and how varied they are. The minerals that form are those most stable at the temperature and pressure of formation, within the limits set by the rock's overall chemistry. Ions substitute for one another only when close in size and charge. Al3+ commonly replaces Si4+, since the two are similar in charge, size and crustal abundance. In the silicon–oxygen minerals of {{ref:soil-found-031}}, that swap leaves a charge to balance. This is why so many different minerals of that family exist. Change a rock's composition, by weathering or by hydrothermal alteration, and its minerals change with it.

soil-found-035.title: Oxide minerals, where oxygen holds the metals
soil-found-035.text: The world's chief aluminum ore is a product of extreme weathering. This ore, {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, is a mixture of hydroxides that forms where chemical weathering is very intense. It belongs to the oxide minerals, those in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, or negatively charged ion. They fall into three groups: simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides. Corundum (Al2O3) and the iron oxide Fe2O3, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, belong to the corundum group of simple oxides. Magnetite is strongly magnetic because it holds iron in two charge states, Fe2+ and Fe3+, as {{ref:soil-chem-178}} explains. Oxides also form during weathering. Water converts many original rock minerals, covered in {{ref:soil-form-140}}, to fine sheet minerals or hydrated oxides through the reactions described in {{ref:soil-found-060}}.

soil-found-037.title: The handful of minerals that build most rock
soil-found-037.text: Thousands of mineral species exist, but a few do most of the building. Rock-forming minerals are the species and groups far more abundant in rocks than the rest. The main ones are quartz, {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, amphiboles, pyroxenes, and the minerals described in {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-145}} and {{ref:soil-found-118}}. All but the last are silicates. A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids. Some rocks are mostly one mineral: limestone is that one non-silicate and quartzite is quartz. Others, like granite, are defined by the proportions of key minerals. Rocks need not be mineral at all. Coal is a rock of the kind in {{ref:soil-form-136}}, made mainly of organically derived carbon.

soil-found-031.title: Silicates: one building block, many ways to link it
soil-found-031.text: Approximately 90% of the Earth's crust is silicate minerals, and all of them share one building block. It is the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, a silicon atom surrounded by four oxygens. Silicon almost always sits in this four-fold, tetrahedral arrangement with oxygen. What varies is how the tetrahedra link. They polymerize, or join up, to different degrees, and mineralogists group silicates by that degree. At one end are isolated tetrahedra, the orthosilicates. Then come paired tetrahedra, rings and chains. Single-chain silicates are mostly pyroxenes, which make up about 10% of the crust. Double-chain silicates are often amphiboles. Next come two-dimensional sheets, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-033}}. At the far end are three-dimensional frameworks sharing all four corners, the tectosilicates of {{ref:soil-found-032}}. One substitution adds variety. Al3+ often replaces Si4+ in the tetrahedra, because the two ions have similar radius and charge. The swap changes how the structure's charge must be balanced, as {{ref:soil-found-030}} showed.

soil-found-032.title: Quartz and feldspar, the sturdy framework silicates
soil-found-032.text: Quartz is the most abundant mineral species, making up 12% of the crust. It belongs to the framework silicates, whose tetrahedra share all four corners. This is the most polymerized class. Strong covalent bonds make these minerals particularly stable chemically, and quartz is highly resistant. That toughness makes it a marker. A rock rich in quartz is considered mature, because quartz, one of the {{ref:soil-form-140}}, is the one that survived heavy weathering. The most abundant mineral group in the crust is the one described in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. In them, Al3+ takes the place of some Si4+, and added potassium, sodium or calcium balances the charge. These minerals matter to soil for another reason: their weathering is a common source of the fine minerals in {{ref:soil-found-040}}.

soil-found-033.title: Phyllosilicates: minerals built in stacked sheets
soil-found-033.text: Some minerals split into thin, flexible flakes. These are the phyllosilicates, or sheet silicates, made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra. The class includes {{ref:soil-chem-135}} and the minerals at the heart of {{ref:soil-found-040}}. Each tetrahedron is bound to its neighbors at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5. That leaves the tetrahedral sheet negatively charged, and a sheet of octahedra balances it. These tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers, and the stacking defines the groups. In 1:1 minerals, T-O stacks are held together by hydrogen bonds. In 2:1 minerals, T-O-T stacks are held by weaker van der Waals forces. This peeling mineral is also a T-O-T stack, with a difference. It puts aluminum in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas the 1:1 and 2:1 minerals hold Al3+ in the octahedral sites. Metal ions bond its layers together, making them harder. Because the bonds between layers are weak, phyllosilicates show a prominent basal cleavage, a tendency to split along flat planes. Octahedral sheets come in two kinds. When every site is filled they are trioctahedral. When some sites are empty, as in pyrophyllite, they are dioctahedral.

soil-found-040.title: Clay, the finest and busiest part of soil
soil-found-040.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards date to around 14,000 BCE, which makes clay the longest-known ceramic raw material. Clay is a fine-grained natural soil material containing {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, the hydrous aluminum sheet silicates described in {{ref:soil-found-033}}. In pure form these minerals are mostly white or pale. Impurities color natural clays, and small amounts of iron oxide give red or brown tones. Wet clay is plastic, and firing hardens it. In a field, clay is a mixed blessing. Clay soils drain poorly, which makes them generally less suited to crops. Yet they are more fertile, because they hold on to more positively charged nutrients. Soils rich in swelling clays, which expand as they absorb water, are a major challenge in civil engineering. Mix sand, silt and less than 40% clay, and the result is {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Clay lasts in rock as well. Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common {{ref:soil-form-136}}.

soil-found-051.title: Soil texture: the sand, silt and clay recipe
soil-found-051.text: Rub a moist pinch of soil between your fingers and you are already measuring its texture. Soil texture is the quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles. It considers only particles less than two millimetres across. Texture classes rest on the percentages of the three; the USDA and WRB systems use 12 classes and the UK-ADAS system 11. Albert Atterberg proposed the first classification, the international system, in 1905. Texture can be judged by feel or measured, for example by the hydrometer method, which rests on Stokes' law. Because it is fixed by the mineral part of a soil, it does not change with farming, unlike soil structure. Texture matters because it shapes so much else. Field capacity, the soil water content best suited to plant growth, rises as particles get finer, from sand to clay. Texture helps decide which crops suit a soil and predicts its response to drought or its lime needs. Together with structure it is called a master variable, since it directly influences many other properties. A clayey soil has more surface area, cation exchange capacity, total porosity and organic matter than a sandy one, but less macroporosity. The first of these traits comes from {{ref:soil-found-040}}, and the proportions of all the components are laid out in {{ref:soil-found-078}}.

soil-found-041.title: How rain and time turn feldspar into clay
soil-found-041.text: Granite carries the makings of clay. One of its minerals, a kind of {{ref:soil-form-141}} described in {{ref:soil-form-143}}, weathers to {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions. Clay formation is the making of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into deposits. The work is done largely by acid hydrolysis. Weak carbonic acid in rainwater, or acid released by plant roots, breaks the bonds between aluminum and oxygen. Other metal ions and silica come loose, the silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid. Source rock and climate decide the product. Feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm, acid weathering, and {{ref:soil-chem-094}} under alkaline conditions. Under alkaline conditions, the rock of {{ref:soil-form-135}} yields {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Intense weathering of other such minerals produces an aluminum hydroxide. Hydrothermal activity can also make them locally. Then the clay may travel. Primary clays stay where they formed, as residual soil deposits. Secondary clays are carried off by flowing water and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

soil-found-044.title: Clay walls, brick and the barrier under a landfill
soil-found-044.text: Between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population still live or work in buildings made with clay, often baked into brick. Clay is one of the oldest building materials on Earth. It served as mortar in brick chimneys and stone walls where protected from water. Because it is relatively impermeable, it also seals pond linings, dam cores and landfill barriers against toxic seepage. Early 21st-century studies have tested its absorption capacity for removing heavy metals from waste water and for purifying air.

soil-found-042.title: Kaolinite, smectite, illite: the main kinds of clay
soil-found-042.text: There are about 30 types of pure clay, but nature rarely serves one alone. Most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals. The main kinds of clay are grouped by their dominant {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, each with its own entry later: {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. A few others, among them talc and pyrophyllite, are sometimes also classed among them. Chemical and physical tests struggle to tell them apart. X-ray diffraction identifies them most easily. One clay keeps a calendar. Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

soil-found-043.title: From Jōmon pots to pencil lead: clay at work
soil-found-043.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards come from central Honshu in Japan. Linked to the Jōmon culture, they date to around 14,000 BCE. People have shaped and fired clay ever since. Different clays, minerals and firing conditions produce earthenware, stoneware and porcelain. Ancient Mesopotamians inscribed cuneiform on clay tablets, the first known writing medium. Industry still relies on clay, in paper making, cement production and chemical filtering, and as a filler in pencil lead.

soil-found-060.title: Hydrolysis and carbonation, the acid attack on rock
soil-found-060.text: Weathering rock helps set how much carbon dioxide stays in the air. Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate. The reactions behind it are hydrolysis and carbonation. In them, only part of a mineral dissolves, and the rest becomes a new solid, often one of the fine minerals of clay. Most is acid hydrolysis: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals. Carbonic acid, from dissolved carbon dioxide, is the main source of those protons, though organic acids also matter. The textbook case is the potassium mineral of {{ref:soil-form-143}}, one of the group in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. With carbonic acid and water, it yields {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution. The weakest bonds between metal and oxygen go first. So igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, a sequence described in {{ref:soil-chem-186}}. There are exceptions, such as silica, which is unusually unstable. Carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide. It can also turn minerals inherited from rock ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) into the secondary minerals of {{ref:soil-found-034}}, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.

soil-found-064.title: From granite and basalt to soil: weathering's ledger
soil-found-064.text: Turning rock into soil takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time. In that span, weathering turns the minerals of rock into {{ref:soil-chem-079}} and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}. Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. The dark sheet mineral of {{ref:soil-form-144}} then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay and oxides of iron. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It gains at least 50% in aluminum and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude. Basalt weathers more easily than granite. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, then to {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, {{ref:soil-form-065}}. Geologists track the progress with the chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O). It runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

soil-found-039.title: Should minerals made by living things count?
soil-found-039.text: Over 60 biominerals had been named before the International Mineralogical Association drew up its listing, yet they are not on its official list. The IMA definition excludes crystalline substances made by living things, and mineralogists still disagree about that choice. In 1981, Lowenstam argued that organisms form a diverse array of minerals, some of which cannot form inorganically. In 2005, Skinner counted biominerals, created by organisms' metabolism, as minerals, and allowed a mineral to be crystalline or amorphous. The question touches soil directly. Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface. They can precipitate metals from solution and speed up mineral dissolution.

soil-found-034.title: Carbonate minerals and the geologist's acid test
soil-found-034.text: Field geologists carry dilute hydrochloric acid for a quick test. All carbonates react with acid, so a drop tells them apart from other minerals. Carbonate minerals are those whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−. The chief ones are aragonite, dolomite and the mineral in {{ref:soil-found-118}}. That last one, CaCO3, is the most common, and the main constituent of limestone and marble. Dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO3)2. Carbonates usually form as biogenic or chemical sediments in marine settings. Weathering by dissolved carbon dioxide, sometimes called carbonation, can also produce secondary carbonate minerals.

soil-found-038.title: Scratch, streak and shine: telling minerals apart
soil-found-038.text: Color is the most obvious thing about a mineral, and often not diagnostic at all. Mineral identification tells minerals apart by physical properties: crystal habit, hardness, luster, color, streak, cleavage and specific gravity. Hardness is usually measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond. The streak is the color of the powdered mineral, and trace elements and weathering do not change it. Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or X-ray diffraction analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming. Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that X-ray diffraction can determine.

soil-found-036.title: Sulfate minerals and the gypsum left by evaporation
soil-found-036.text: As saline water evaporates, minerals precipitate out of it. Sulfate minerals, which contain the sulfate anion [SO4]2−, commonly form this way, as evaporites. Gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O, is by far the most common hydrous sulfate. It forms alongside other evaporites such as calcite and halite, and its anhydrous counterpart is anhydrite. Sulfates also occur in hydrothermal veins, or as oxidation products of sulfide minerals.

soil-found-047.title: Organic matter that minerals keep for centuries
soil-found-047.text: Some carbon in soil lasts a few years; some lasts centuries. The difference often lies in what it is stuck to. Mineral-associated organic matter is soil organic matter chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces. It is thought to consist of small plant and microbial molecules. They bond to charged mineral surfaces or are locked inside aggregates, crumbs of soil particles stuck together. Binding to minerals makes this carbon harder for decomposers to reach. So it resists microbial breakdown and stays in the soil's store of carbon. It typically persists for centuries. By contrast, {{ref:soil-bio-118}}, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

soil-found-014.title: Soil pH, the number that runs soil chemistry
soil-found-014.text: On the pH scale, 3.5 and 9.5 look like near neighbors. In hydronium ions they are a millionfold apart. Soil pH measures how acidic or basic, also called alkaline, a soil is. Strictly, pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydronium ion activity, hydronium being the acid-carrying form of the hydrogen ion. Because the scale is logarithmic, a solution at pH 3.5 holds one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5. For soils, pH is read in a slurry with water or with a salt solution such as 0.01 M CaCl2. Values normally fall between 3 and 10, with 7 neutral. Ultra-acidic soils below pH 3.5 and very strongly alkaline soils above pH 9 are rare. Soil scientists call pH a master variable. It controls the chemical forms of nutrients and the reactions they undergo, and so what plants can take up. Most plants do best between pH 5.5 and 7.5, though many have adapted to thrive outside it. Most crops prefer pH 6.5 on mineral soils and 5.5 on organic soils. Highly acidic soils tend to hold toxic amounts of aluminum and manganese. Climate pushes pH both ways. In high-rainfall soils, hydronium ions displace basic cations, positively charged ions such as calcium, and the soil acidifies. In dry areas unleached calcium pushes pH to 8.5, and sodium held on the soil can raise it to 10. Where weathering is more advanced, pH is generally lower.

soil-found-001.title: Soil horizons, the layers that record a soil's life
soil-found-001.text: Cut down through a soil and you usually cross a series of bands. Each band is a horizon: a layer roughly parallel to the surface whose physical, chemical and biological traits differ from those above and below. Horizons are made by soil-forming processes. Layers those processes have not touched are simply called layers. Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons. They differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries. Most are recognized by color and texture, described outright or relative to their neighbors, as coarser, sandier or darker. No profile has every major horizon, and some soils, such as soils described in {{ref:soil-class-094}}, have one horizon or none at all. Horizons are also fragile. Erosion can strip the upper ones and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks disturb or erase them. Going down a profile goes back in time. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows a horizon to be dated by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}. Most classification systems define soil types by horizons, either as whole sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons. A shorthand of letters and numbers labels each one, recording color, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

soil-found-024.title: Buffering: why some soils shrug off acid
soil-found-024.text: Add the same acid to two soils, and one barely budges while the other's pH plunges. The difference is buffering capacity, a soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added. It works through {{ref:soil-chem-047}} and neutralization, and carbonates also regulate pH. Different buffer systems take over at different pH, from calcium carbonate to iron. Pure sand has almost no buffering ability. Soils rich in fine mineral or organic particles, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, buffer strongly. Within one kind of soil, buffering rises with {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. So clay- and humus-rich soils need more lime for the same change in pH. The reason is stored acidity. Lime must neutralize the acid cations held on these particles, not just the free acid in solution, or the stored cations restore the original pH. The lime needed depends on how finely it is ground and on buffering capacity. Once the particles are saturated with hydronium, the buffer is spent, and further acid drives pH lower.

soil-found-025.title: Soil color, the first thing anyone notices
soil-found-025.text: Soils come brown, red, yellow, black, gray, white and even blue or green. Color is often a soil's most visually apparent property and the first impression it makes. It varies across landscapes, between horizons and even within a single clod. Color itself does not change how a soil behaves. It forms through chemical and biological weathering, especially the reactions described in {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Elements released from the original minerals combine into new colored compounds. Ordinary conditions give uniform or gradual changes in color. Reducing environments, short of oxygen, produce disrupted, mottled patterns with points of concentrated color. Mineralogy is the main influence. Because color, especially its lightness, changes with moisture, it may be described both moist and dry. Sources disagree on what color is worth. One says it has little use in predicting soil characteristics. Another says it reveals soil organic matter, mineralogy, moisture and how much has been washed out.

soil-found-019.title: Aluminum, the hidden poison of acid soils
soil-found-019.text: Every soil contains aluminum, yet in most it does no harm. Aluminum toxicity is damage to plants from dissolved aluminum, and it is the most widespread problem of acid soils. The toxic form, the dissolved ion Al3+, is most soluble at low pH. Above pH 5.0 most soils hold little soluble aluminum. Roots show the damage first. Root tips and side roots thicken, fine branching is lost and the tips may turn brown. The poison then disrupts the uptake and transport of calcium and other nutrients, cell division, cell wall formation and enzyme activity. Acid soils add other stresses: hydrogen toxicity, manganese poisoning ({{ref:soil-chem-144}}), and shortages of calcium and magnesium. Manganese symptoms appear below pH 5.6. Acid rain is the main force mobilizing aluminum from natural sources. The shift near pH 5 also marks a boundary in soil life, from acid-tolerant to acid-intolerant communities.

soil-found-018.title: What pushes a soil toward acid or alkaline
soil-found-018.text: Rain itself is slightly acidic. At an average pH of 5.6, from dissolved carbon dioxide, it washes basic cations out of soil and raises the share of aluminum and hydrogen ions. Many forces set a soil's pH, beginning with the minerals the soil formed from and the weathering they have undergone. In warm, humid climates soils acidify as weathering products wash away. In dry climates, weaker weathering and less washing leave soils neutral or alkaline. Life adds acid too. Respiration and decay release CO2, and roots release H+ ions when plants take up more cations than anions, the negatively charged ions. Ammonium fertilizers, acid rain and oxidizing sulfide minerals in mine spoil or {{ref:soil-chem-030}} acidify further. Soils turn more alkaline with minerals rich in sodium, calcium, magnesium and potassium, and with bicarbonate-rich irrigation water. Where too little water flows through, carbonates and bicarbonates build up. Soils rich in calcium carbonate range from pH 7.0 to 9.5, depending on whether calcium or sodium dominates.

soil-found-016.title: Reading pH from heather, litmus and glass electrodes
soil-found-016.text: A soil's pH can be read before any instrument comes out. The profile gives hints. A poorly mixed organic layer suggests strong acidity, a layer of {{ref:soil-chem-036}} alkaline conditions, and columnar structure sodic, or sodium-rich, conditions. Plants are clues too. Calcifuges, plants of acid soils, such as heathers, rhododendrons and gorse, mark acid ground. Calcicoles, lime-lovers such as ash, dogwoods and clematis, mark lime-rich ground. Cheap kits mix soil with an indicator solution that changes color. Litmus paper dipped in a soil–water mix turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if it is basic. Electronic meters insert an electrode into moist soil or a soil–water suspension and give a digital reading. Spectrophotometric methods, developed in the 2010s, add an indicator dye to a soil extract instead. They avoid the drift and suspension effects of glass electrodes. The USDA laboratory method mixes 20 g of soil with 20 mL of water and reads pH after standing 1 h. It then adds CaCl2 and reads pH again in 0.01 M CaCl2.

soil-found-020.title: How pH decides which nutrients plants can reach
soil-found-020.text: A soil can be full of nutrients and still starve a crop. Soil pH governs which ions are released or held, and so which nutrients plants can take up. Most minerals dissolve more readily in acid soils. Yet, trading toxicity against need, most nutrients are best available at moderate pH. Below pH 5.0, roots damaged by aluminum take up less, and deficiencies of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium are frequent. Raising pH works unevenly. Molybdenum becomes more available, while zinc, iron, copper and manganese become less so. At high pH these trace nutrients move poorly, a deficit that water-soluble chelates, compounds that hold a metal in soluble form, can correct. Phosphorus was long thought most available near neutrality, at pH 6.5–7.5. Between pH 5.5 and 6.5, though, raising pH may increase, decrease or not affect it. In soils above 2% calcium carbonate, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-035}}, supplying phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper or zinc is often more efficient than trying to acidify.

soil-found-002.title: O, A, E, B, C, R: the alphabet of a soil profile
soil-found-002.text: Six capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R, name the main layers of a soil profile. These are the master horizons. Many soils start with an organic surface layer, O. The mineral soil usually begins with an A horizon, the layer with the most organic matter and soil life. Below may lie an E horizon, a leached layer. A B horizon is a well-developed subsoil where substances moving down from the topsoil accumulate. A C horizon is loose but poorly developed material beneath. R is hard bedrock that cannot be dug by hand. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, and the A and B together normally make up the part described in {{ref:soil-form-024}}. Suffixes of lowercase letters and figures split the master horizons further. Most systems define more horizons and layers than these, and the letters may differ. The USDA field book adds L for limnic, or lake-laid, materials, W for water and M for root-limiting manufactured layers. Because the systems define their symbols differently, they cannot be mixed, and none is more correct than another.

soil-found-023.title: Turning an alkaline soil more acid
soil-found-023.text: Sometimes the goal is a more acid soil. Lowering soil pH means adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials to an alkaline soil. Elemental sulfur, 90–99% pure, is applied at 300–500 kg/ha and slowly oxidizes in the soil to sulfuric acid. Some fertilizers also work, because their ammonium oxidizes to nitric acid: ammonium sulfate, {{ref:soil-fert-071}} and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. Sphagnum moss and the material described in {{ref:soil-class-070}} are acidifying organic additions. There is a limit. In high-pH soils with more than 2% calcium carbonate, acidifying is very costly and ineffective.

soil-found-017.title: Lime lovers and lime haters among plants
soil-found-017.text: Plants take sides on pH. Each species is adapted to its own range of soil pH. Calcifuges prefer acid soils and calcicoles lime-rich ones. Calcicole species outnumber calcifuges, so plant diversity tends to rise from pH 3.5 toward pH 9. Some ranges are narrow: Monterey pine grows at pH 4.5–5.2, while vetiver grass tolerates pH 3.0–8.0. The soil matters too. Soybeans may fail at pH 5.5 where molybdenum is low, yet grow optimally at that pH where it is sufficient. Breeders use differences between varieties to develop aluminum- and manganese-tolerant cereals for strongly acidic soils.

soil-found-022.title: Soil life and pH, each shaping the other
soil-found-022.text: pH shapes soil life, and soil life shapes pH. Microbes and animals respond to pH directly and through nutrient status, {{ref:soil-env-257}} and the forms described in {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, so communities shift as pH changes. At low pH, aluminum causes oxidative stress that harms soft-bodied fauna without a hard outer skeleton: protists, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, {{ref:soil-bio-087}} and earthworms. The traffic runs both ways. Many fungi acidify soil by excreting oxalic acid, which locks calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Earthworm mucus, weakly alkaline at pH 7.5 to 8, buffers pH. Burrowing animals that mix organic and mineral matter reduce acidity, as in {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-found-021.title: When pH extremes leave plants thirsty
soil-found-021.text: A soil can hold water that plants still cannot use, and extreme pH is one reason. Strongly alkaline soils are sodic, rich in sodium, and dispersive, their particles drifting apart. Water soaks in slowly, moves through poorly and is stored badly. When wet, these soils are poorly aerated. When dry, they quickly lose plant-available water and turn hard and cloddy. Strongly acidic soils fail differently. Aluminum toxicity stunts roots so badly that plants run short of water even when the soil is relatively moist.

soil-found-015.title: From ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline: pH classes
soil-found-015.text: US soil surveyors give each stretch of the pH scale a name. The classes come from {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. On the acid side, ultra acidic is below 3.5, extremely acidic 3.5–4.4, very strongly acidic 4.5–5.0, strongly acidic 5.1–5.5, moderately acidic 5.6–6.0 and slightly acidic 6.1–6.5. Neutral is a band, not a point: pH 6.6–7.3. Above it, slightly alkaline is 7.4–7.8, moderately alkaline 7.9–8.4, strongly alkaline 8.5–9.0 and very strongly alkaline above 9.0.

soil-found-011.title: How Australia names its soil horizons
soil-found-011.text: The Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009) adds P and D horizons, drops E, and numbers sub-horizons of A and B. P horizons, named after peats, are organic layers formed in soil saturated with water, with 12 to 18% or more organic carbon depending on clay content. A splits into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, transitional to B. B splits into B1, B2 and B3. Leached layers are classed as A or B by their other properties. D marks material below the {{ref:soil-form-024}} that is unlike the layers above. As a rule of thumb, layers thinner than about 5 cm are described as pans or segregations within one horizon, and excessive subdivision is to be avoided.

soil-found-010.title: The international code for soil layers
soil-found-010.text: The manual of {{ref:soil-class-016}} sets out its horizon and layer symbols in Chapter 10 of its manual, 4th edition, published in 2022. It first separates organic layers, with at least 20% organic carbon, from organotechnic layers rich in artefacts, objects made by people, and from mineral layers. Its master symbols are H, O, A, E, B, C and R. I marks permanent layers of at least 75% ice, and W marks water. H layers are saturated for over 30 consecutive days in most years or have been drained; they are typically the material of {{ref:soil-class-070}}. O layers are not. Fine earth is the soil fraction of 2 mm or less. The soil surface is taken below any litter layer, which is over 90% recognizable dead plant tissue.

soil-found-026.title: Munsell charts: color as hue, value and chroma
soil-found-026.text: In a survey record, a Cecil soil horizon is not just red. It is red (10R 4/8) clay. That notation comes from the Munsell color system, which specifies a color by hue, value and chroma and is the standard way surveyors record soil color. Albert H. Munsell created the system early in the 20th century. The USDA adopted it for soil research in the 1930s, and the soil charts keep only the colors most relevant to soil. Hue is the dominant spectral color, in soil generally yellow or red. Charts conventionally show 40 hues in steps of 2.5, such as 10R to 2.5YR, and each page of the soil color book shows one hue. Value, lightness or darkness, increases from the bottom of the page to the top. Chroma, the intensity of color, increases from left to right, and a chroma of 0 is neutral gray, written N with a value, as in N 5/. Soil counts as moist when adding water no longer changes its color, and as dry when air-dried.

soil-found-027.title: What a soil's color says about its history
soil-found-027.text: A soil keeps its history on its surface, and color is how it shows it. Dark brown or black usually means high organic matter, which coats mineral particles and darkens them; accumulated charcoal also turns soil black. An Illinois handheld chart links nearly black soil to 3.5-7% organic matter, dark brown to 2-3% and yellowish brown to 1.5-2.5%. Red points to iron accumulation or oxidation in well-aerated soil, and yellow also reflects iron, in less oxygen-rich settings. Gray or blue marks saturated, anaerobic soil where iron has been reduced or depleted. Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as glauconite, melanterite and celadonite. White is common where salts or carbonates accumulate, often in arid places, and jarosite can color acidic soils yellow. A B horizon takes its color mainly from iron oxides, usually brownish or reddish. Sodium helps humus disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark color extends.

soil-found-028.title: Gleying: how waterlogged soil turns gray
soil-found-028.text: Waterlogged soil turns gray, and the reason is iron. Gleying is the development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colors in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed. Without oxygen, microbes convert iron from the ferric form, Fe3+, to the ferrous form, Fe2+. Less often they reduce manganese from Mn4+ to Mn2+. Reduced iron is soluble. During prolonged saturation it can be carried away, exposing the light gray of bare silicate minerals. When the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidizes locally into yellow-brown, reddish or orange mottles, often along root channels and burrows. Gleyed material can begin a few centimeters below the surface and continue almost unchanged for many meters.

soil-hist-119.title: Reading the clocks hidden inside rocks and soil
soil-hist-119.text: Rocks, fossils and sediments carry their own birth certificates, for anyone who can read them. Geochronology is the science of finding their age from signatures held in the materials themselves. Absolute ages come from radioactive isotopes. Radiometric dating measures how far an isotope of known half-life, the time it takes half of it to decay, has decayed. Slowly decaying isotopes reach further back but give less exact ages in years. So {{ref:soil-hist-120}} suits organic samples younger than about 60,000 years, and uranium–lead dating samples older than about 1 million years. Uranium–thorium dating spans a few years to about 700,000 years, on speleothems, the mineral deposits of caves, and on corals, carbonates and fossil bones. Relative ages come from paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios. Marker horizons, such as dated volcanic ash layers, are so distinctive that their age-equivalence across sites is certain. Incremental methods such as dendrochronology, tree-ring dating, and lichenometry build year-by-year chronologies. Amino acid dating is cheap, but gives no numbers without calibration from other methods at the same site. Combining several indicators, fossils among them, sharpens any age.

soil-hist-120.title: Radiocarbon dating and the clock that starts at death
soil-hist-120.text: Every living thing carries a faint radioactive clock, and death starts it ticking. High in the atmosphere, cosmic rays strike nitrogen and constantly make carbon-14. Plants take it in through photosynthesis, and animals get it from the plants they eat. Radiocarbon dating finds the age of material containing organic carbon from how much carbon-14 is left. Once an organism dies, it stops exchanging carbon and its carbon-14 decays. The half-life is about 5,730 years, so reliable dates reach back roughly 50,000 years. Willard Libby developed the method at the University of Chicago in the late 1940s. It won him the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Its impact on archaeology was so great that histories of the field call it the 'radiocarbon revolution'. Dates must be corrected for fractionation and reservoir effects. Fossil-fuel burning and the nuclear tests of the 1950s–1960s complicate them further. Small impurities matter: 1% modern carbon makes a 17,000-year-old sample look 600 years younger. Accelerator mass spectrometry counts every carbon-14 atom rather than only decays, so it can date a single seed.

soil-hist-124.title: Luminescence dating: when a grain last saw the sun
soil-hist-124.text: A quartz grain buried in a dune keeps a running tally of radiation. Luminescence dating is a group of methods that find how long ago mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight or strong heating. In buried quartz or feldspar, radiation from cosmic rays and traces of potassium, uranium, thorium and rubidium builds up trapped charge. Light or heat releases it as a glow whose intensity reflects burial time. The age is the equivalent dose, in grays, divided by the environmental dose rate, typically 0.5–5 Gy per 1000 years. The methods assume the grains were 'bleached' at burial: 1–100 s of daylight resets quartz, as usually happens in dunes, loess and some water-laid deposits. Quartz ages typically span 100 to 350,000 years before present, with uncertainties of 5–10% of the age. Feldspar may reach a million years. Needing no organic material, it avoids errors from old, carbon-14-deficient carbon. At Lake Ulaan in Mongolia, wind-blown old carbon made radiocarbon dates up to 5800 years too old. Luminescence was unaffected. {{ref:soil-hist-126}} first dated unheated sediments in 1965, and optical dating followed in 1984.

soil-hist-132.title: Palynology, the science of pollen that refuses to dissolve
soil-hist-132.text: Pollen is tough enough to survive acid baths that dissolve rock minerals. Palynology is the study of acid-resistant microscopic organic remains, such as pollen and spores, found in sediments and sedimentary rocks. These palynomorphs, 5 to 500 micrometers across, also include dinoflagellate cysts, fungi and plant tissue. Laboratories free them from soils, rocks and sediment cores by ultrasonic treatment, wet sieving and acid digestion. Potassium hydroxide removes humic substances, and hydrofluoric acid digests silicate minerals. Acetolysis dissolves the cellulose that hampers work on peat. Quantitative pollen analysis began with Lennart von Post, whose 1916 lecture in Kristiania spread the method. Analysts count each taxon's grains under the microscope and draw a pollen diagram, with depth on the y-axis and abundance on the x-axis. Records from peat or lake sediments reconstruct past vegetation and climate. They also reveal human effects such as logging and land use. Geologists, archaeologists, pedologists and physical geographers all use it, including for dating strata relative to one another.

soil-hist-127.title: Cosmogenic nuclides, atoms forged by rays from space
soil-hist-127.text: Earth's surface sits under a constant, invisible bombardment. When a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus and knocks out protons and neutrons, it can leave a rare isotope: a cosmogenic nuclide. These form within rocks and soil, in the atmosphere and in meteoroids. The useful ones are absent from the host material when it forms. Their build-up therefore records how long it has been exposed since. Beryllium-10, with a half-life of 1,387,000 years, dates the exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores. Aluminum-26 and chlorine-36 date rocks and sediment. Rock absorbs most of the cosmic-ray flux within its first meter, and that is where new nuclides form. Spallation, the chipping of nuclei by direct hits, dominates in the top 0 to 60 cm. Muon capture takes over a few meters down. Neutron capture depends on snow, soil moisture and trace elements. Altitude matters too: air pressure changes production in minerals by a factor of 30 between sea level and the top of a 5 km mountain.

soil-hist-131.title: δ13C, the carbon signature plants leave in soil
soil-hist-131.text: Plants stamp their soil with a signature of how they photosynthesize. δ13C is a normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12. It compares a sample's 13C/12C ratio with a reference standard and reports the difference in parts per thousand, or per mille (‰). The original standard, a Cretaceous belemnite fossil called PDB, ran out and was replaced by standards such as VPDB. Organisms take up light carbon-12 preferentially, so they sit near −25‰, depending on their metabolic pathway. C4 plants, one such pathway group, range from −16 to −10‰; C3 plants run from −33 to −24‰. That gap lets researchers trace the rise of C4 grasses through time. The ratio also separates carbon dioxide from ecosystem respiration from that of burned fossil fuels, the basis of the Suess effect. In a paleosol, carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide. On the Loess Plateau, the δ13C of such carbonate rose by 5% over the Late Miocene and Pliocene, a sign of drying.

soil-hist-125.title: Optically stimulated luminescence: grains that glow on cue
soil-hist-125.text: Shine light on an old buried quartz grain and it answers with a faint glow. Optically stimulated luminescence reads a mineral's absorbed radiation dose from that light, to date sediments. Radiation traps electrons at impurities and defects in quartz and feldspar. Light frees them, and they emit light as they recombine at luminescence centers. Grains, usually coarse at 100–200 μm or fine at 4–11 μm, must be extracted without exposure to light. It dates minerals, not organic material, such as the deposition of wind-blown and river sediments. David J. Huntley and colleagues developed it in 1984. Most laboratories now use single-aliquot regeneration (SAR).

soil-hist-135.title: Tephrochronology: volcanic ash as a time marker
soil-hist-135.text: An eruption spreads one moment in time across a whole landscape. Ash falls almost instantly over wide areas. Tephrochronology dates and correlates sequences by their position between layers of volcanic ash, or tephra, of known date. Each eruption leaves a tephra horizon with a unique chemical fingerprint. Once the eruption is dated, that horizon becomes a time marker. It links distant sequences into one 'age-equivalent' chronology and checks other dating methods. Fingerprinting uses the electron microprobe and laser-ablation ICP-MS on single shards, though basaltic tephra chemistry can alter over time. Since the late 1990s, invisible 'cryptotephra' layers have been extracted from peat, lake sediment and loess.

soil-hist-126.title: Thermoluminescence dating and the reset of heat
soil-hist-126.text: Heating a pot in a kiln, or melting rock into lava, sets a clock to zero. Thermoluminescence dating measures the radiation dose crystalline material has gathered since it was last heated, or since sediment last saw sunlight. Heat or sunlight empties its electron traps. Afterwards the surrounding radiation steadily refills them. Heating the sample in the laboratory measures the dose. Dividing it by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays, gives the age. The soil's own dose affects accuracy, so it is ideally measured at the find spot over a long period. Heated objects must have gone above 500 °C. The method serves where radiocarbon dating cannot, as for sediments.

soil-hist-121.title: Radiocarbon calibration: turning lab numbers into calendar dates
soil-hist-121.text: A raw radiocarbon age is not quite a calendar date. The simple decay equation assumes a constant level of atmospheric carbon-14, but that level has varied significantly. Radiocarbon calibration fixes this with a curve of past atmospheric carbon-14, converting a measurement into an estimated calendar age. Tree-ring sequences gave the first calibration data, and Hans Suess published the first curve in 1967. The IntCal curves, first published in 1998 and updated to 2020, come in northern (IntCal20), southern (SHCal20) and marine (MARINE20) versions. Uncalibrated 'conventional radiocarbon ages' still use the Libby half-life of 5568 years. That value was agreed in 1962 to stay consistent with early papers.

soil-hist-122.title: Why soil and peat are hard to radiocarbon date
soil-hist-122.text: Soil mixes young carbon into old, an awkward trait in a clock. Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter in soils and peat is hard to do reliably, because younger humic acid tends to contaminate it. Old carbon from limestone or groundwater can give apparent ages of thousands of years. Humus can do the same or, if younger, lower the apparent age. For soil it is better to sieve out fragments of organic origin and date them with methods that tolerate small samples. In peat, the humins give the most reliable date. They are insoluble in alkali and less contaminated than humic or fulvic acid. Dating soil organic carbon and lake methane showed 0.2 to 2.5 Pg, or petagrams, of permafrost carbon released over the last 60 years.

soil-hist-128.title: Surface exposure dating: how long a rock has seen the sky
soil-hist-128.text: A boulder left by a retreating glacier starts collecting cosmic-ray atoms once exposed. Surface exposure dating estimates how long a rock has been at or near Earth's surface. It dates glacial advances and retreats, erosion history, lava flows, rock slides and fault scarps. It works best for exposures of 10³ to 10⁶ years. Measured concentrations of cosmogenic nuclides, with the cosmic-ray flux and their half-lives, give exposure time, burial time or how fast a drainage basin erodes. Beryllium-10 and aluminum-26 form from the oxygen and silicon in quartz. Their ratio dates burial below the production depth, typically 2–10 meters. Rates are calibrated on samples dated by radiocarbon or luminescence; accelerator mass spectrometry measures the nuclides.

soil-hist-129.title: Beryllium-10, a rain-borne tracer of soil
soil-hist-129.text: Rain delivers a slow clock to the soil surface. Beryllium-10 is a cosmogenic isotope formed in the atmosphere, with a half-life of 1.387 million years, and it traces soil formation and erosion. Beryllium dissolves below about pH 5.5, so rain carries it down. It drops out as the water turns more alkaline, so it accumulates at the soil surface, where its long half-life does not limit how long it stays. It has been used to study soil erosion, soil formation from regolith, the development of lateritic soils and the age of ice cores. Its short-lived relative beryllium-7, with a half-life of 53.22 days, shows that sediments are fresh: less than about 3–4 months old.

soil-hist-123.title: The bomb pulse, a nuclear-age spike in carbon-14
soil-hist-123.text: Above-ground nuclear tests almost doubled the relative concentration of carbon-14 in the atmosphere. That sudden rise, from the first tests in 1945 until the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty, is the bomb pulse. Since the ban the excess has fallen by about 4% a year. That steady decline lets scientists date recent tissues and deaths. The pulse has also tested atmospheric transport models and tracked carbon moving between the atmosphere and oceanic or terrestrial sinks. If no more nuclear weapons are detonated above ground, it will die out around 2030.

soil-hist-130.title: Lead-210 dating, a century of soil movement
soil-hist-130.text: A fine, steady fallout from the sky settles on soils all over the world. It comes from the decay products of radon-222 gas. Among them is lead-210, a radioactive isotope in the uranium-238 decay chain with a half-life of 22.20 years. Excess lead-210 from this fallout builds up in surface soils. Its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century. That gives erosion and deposition rates and tests conservation practices. Its deposition is continuous and global, so it complements the medium-term record from human-made radionuclides such as caesium-137. It suits sedimentation chronologies on time scales shorter than 100 years.
