soil-hist-133.title: Rhizoliths, the fossil ghosts of roots
soil-hist-133.text: Roots rot away, but the shapes they leave in soil can outlast them. A rhizolith is an organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or paleosols. The family includes root molds, casts, tubules, petrifactions and rhizocretions. Some roots secrete bicarbonate rather than hydrogen ions, raising the surrounding pH. Calcium carbonate may then precipitate around them as rhizocretions. Rhizohaloes are gray reduced zones with reddish rims around decayed roots. Rhizolith mineralogy shows how waterlogged a paleosol was. They help identify paleosols, but only in post-Silurian beds, since plants with extensive roots did not flourish before then.

soil-hist-134.title: When roots first broke rock into soil
soil-hist-134.text: Earlier non-vascular plants lacked the deep roots needed to break solid rock into regolith and soil. The Silurian-Devonian Terrestrial Revolution was the rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago. The new roots eroded rock and built the pedosphere, a water-holding layer rich in minerals and organic matter. With their microbial partners they formed the rhizosphere, which sped weathering and released phosphates, calcium and magnesium, as pedogenic carbonates show. Enhanced silicate weathering is thought to have cut atmospheric CO2 from around 6300 to 2100 ppmv. Researchers still disagree, though. Another view holds that plants slowed weathering and lowered CO2 mainly by burying organic carbon in wetlands.

soil-hist-088.title: Taphonomy: the journey from death to fossil
soil-hist-088.text: Between death and discovery, every bone and shell goes through a long series of changes. Taphonomy is the study of how organisms decay and become fossilized or preserved. The Soviet scientist Ivan Efremov introduced the term in 1940 for the passage of remains from the biosphere to the lithosphere. Its processes fall into two stages: biostratinomy, between death and burial, and diagenesis, after burial. In archaeology it weighs burning, rodent disturbance, gnaw marks and soil pH. Archaeologists observe these processes at real sites to judge how they alter what survives.

soil-hist-092.title: Geoarchaeology: reading a site as a landscape
soil-hist-092.text: An archaeological site is also a piece of ground, shaped by sediments, soils and landforms. Geoarchaeology is a multidisciplinary field that applies the theories and techniques of the geosciences to archaeology. It draws on geomorphology, sedimentology, pedology, geochronology and the study of layered deposits. It has three aims: to place sites in time, to understand the natural processes that create them, and to reconstruct their landscapes. It also studies how natural processes affect buried sites and artifacts after deposition. Its principles of layering go back to Nicolas Steno in 1669 and James Hutton in 1788. It became a subfield of archaeology in the 1970s–1980s. In monolith sampling, workers hammer narrow metal tins into a section in overlapping sequence. That captures a site's complete profile for laboratory study. There, a sample's particle-size distribution may show the conditions under which its layer was deposited.

soil-hist-090.title: Environmental DNA, the genetic traces left in soil
soil-hist-090.text: A scoop of soil holds the genes of creatures no one has seen. Environmental DNA is DNA collected from samples such as soil, sediment, water, snow or air rather than from an individual organism. Sequencing it reveals which species are present in an ecosystem, including microscopic ones not otherwise detectable. Many microbes cannot be cultured in the laboratory, so eDNA is the only access to their genetic make-up. Extracellular DNA can reach 2 μg/L in soil and 88 μg/L in natural waters. It was first applied to terrestrial sediments. They yielded DNA of extinct and living animals and plants, known as sedimentary ancient DNA, or 'dirtDNA'.

soil-hist-098.title: Soil marks: buried features that show through as color
soil-hist-098.text: A freshly ploughed field can reveal a vanished earthwork as a change of color. A soil mark is a difference in soil color caused by archaeological features beneath it. A ploughed-out bank leaves hard, dry material, while its ditch leaves damper soil. A feature may also cut through the topsoil to expose chalk. Black or red soil can show organic or burnt deposits, and so whether fire was used. Soil marks usually show in ploughed or harrowed fields before crops grow. They can also reveal former river channels, or slightly raised dry ground on floodplains that attracted settlement.

soil-hist-102.title: Middens, the rubbish heaps that keep the past
soil-hist-102.text: Bones, shells, broken pots and even human excrement: an old rubbish heap keeps them all. A midden is an old dump for domestic waste. Besides animal bones and mollusc shells, it may hold plant material, potsherds and stone tools. Damp, anaerobic conditions inside can preserve organic remains. Shell middens are alkaline from calcium carbonate. That slows decay driven by soil acidity, so organic material survives. Wind, water and animal digging lay down sediment among the refuse. This matrix yields seasonal and climatic information.

soil-hist-096.title: The law of superposition: oldest at the bottom
soil-hist-096.text: In a stack of undisturbed layers, the bottom one came first. The law of superposition states that in undeformed layered sequences the oldest layers lie at the bottom, and newer material stacks on top. Nicolas Steno first proposed it in 1669. William 'Strata' Smith popularized it in English and used it to make the first geologic map of Britain. Nature can scramble the order: animals, vegetation and limestone crystallization disrupt the original layering. At archaeological sites, layers can form by undercutting earlier ones, so applying the law needs interpretation.

soil-hist-095.title: Stratigraphy: putting a site's events in order
soil-hist-095.text: A ditch must be dug before anyone can fill it in. That simple logic drives archaeological stratigraphy, the study of a site's sequence of superimposed units, or contexts, to learn when and how its deposits formed. Each context is a single event that leaves a discrete trace. It may be a deposit, such as a ditch's back-fill, or a structure, such as a wall. It may also be a 'cut' that removes earlier material. Two long-accepted principles guide the reading. Lower units are older than upper ones, and a layer is no older than the most recent artifact in it. E.C. Harris added original horizontality, lateral continuity and stratigraphic succession. A Harris matrix represents a site's formation in space and time. A context sealed between two dated layers must date between them. Yet older 'residual' finds and later 'intrusive' finds can enter a context, so dating rests on its latest evidence.

soil-hist-084.title: Forensic geology, from Sherlock Holmes to the courtroom
soil-hist-084.text: Sherlock Holmes could tell where someone had been from the clays on their shoes. Ray Murray traces the idea behind forensic geology to that fiction by Arthur Conan Doyle. The field studies earth materials as evidence to answer questions raised by the legal system. In 1891 Hans Gross used microscopic analysis of soil from a suspect's shoes to link him to a crime scene. Today its main use is trace evidence: soil and sediment particles can link a suspect to a crime or crime scene. That rests on Edmond Locard's exchange principle, that every contact leaves a trace. Murray and John Tedrow published the book Forensic Geology in 1975. Ground-penetrating radar is used mainly to find buried bodies. It narrows the search area and cuts excavation time.

soil-hist-085.title: Matching a muddy shoe to a crime scene
soil-hist-085.text: Soils differ over very short distances, which makes them telling evidence and tricky to sample. Forensic soil comparison sets a questioned sample of unknown origin beside control samples, such as soil from the crime scene, to find similarities or differences. Because soils vary so locally, examiners study the questioned sample first, then choose where to sample at the scene. Color is one of the most important properties. It is matched to the Munsell soil chart, though people perceive color differently. Spectrophotometry using CIELAB coordinates gives objective numerical values instead. Particle-size distribution is among the most discriminating properties, measured by microscope, laser diffraction or sieving. Soil pH can point to elements such as P, Zn, B, Cu and Fe, and to lime requirement. A lump of soil is kept whole to preserve its layers. Ground samples come from horizons differing in color, minerals and texture. Samples are dried before collection, or refrigerated if damp, so microbial activity cannot change them.

soil-hist-099.title: Celtic fields, small prehistoric plots with a misleading name
soil-hist-099.text: The Celtic fields of north-west Europe have nothing to do with Celtic culture. The name is an old one for traces of prehistoric field systems, and O. G. S. Crawford gave it. The fields date from the Early Bronze Age, around 1800 BC, to the early medieval period. They survive as earthworks or soil marks. Plots were rarely more than 2,000 m², small enough for one person or household to cultivate. Lynchets at their upper and lower ends are evidence of early ploughing.

soil-hist-100.title: Ridge and furrow, the ripples of medieval ploughing
soil-hist-100.text: Some grassland still ripples with ridges built by medieval ploughs. Ridge and furrow is the pattern of ridges and troughs left by a ploughing system used in medieval Europe, typical of the open-field system. Non-reversible ploughs turned soil toward the center of the same strip each year. Gradually a ridge rose, with a furrow between strips. The ridges drained wet soils into the furrows; only some well-drained soils were left flat. Surviving ridges stand up to 61 cm (24 inches), but in use some topped 1.8 m (6 feet). The pattern survives where land became grassland and was never ploughed again. Elsewhere, reversible ploughs erased it.

soil-hist-086.title: Forensic palynology: pollen as a witness
soil-hist-086.text: Pollen clings so well that a suspect can hardly get rid of it. Forensic palynology uses pollen, spores and other palynomorphs to prove or disprove a link between objects, people and places in criminal and civil cases. Regions, and even parts of one garden, have distinctive pollen assemblages. Pollen can also show the season it was picked up. It adheres to soil, clothing, hair and rock. In a 2023 Argentine case, soil in the suspect's car and on the suspect's shoe soles matched the palynomorph mix of the coast where the body was found. A Bolivian study built a forensic database of pollen in high-altitude, non-seasonal soils.

soil-hist-087.title: Forensic archaeology: finding graves through the soil
soil-hist-087.text: A grave gives itself away through the soil above it. Forensic archaeology, a branch of forensic anthropology, uses archaeological methods in legal cases, such as finding overlooked graves and processing mass graves. Differences in the soil guide the search. Burying a body leaves a small mound of soil from the grave fill. Grave sites typically have looser, darker, more organic soil than the area around them. Loose soil and nutrients from the decomposing body also make plants grow differently from their surroundings.

soil-hist-089.title: Geotaphonomy: how a burial changes the ground
soil-hist-089.text: A body in the ground changes the ground itself. Geotaphonomy is the study of how a decomposing body and its burial affect the surrounding environment. It examines how the soil was disturbed, how the pH around the body changed, and whether plant growth sped up or slowed. It also reads tool marks from digging the grave, and changes to land and drainage from adding an unnatural mass. It belongs to forensic taphonomy, which studies post-mortem changes to remains caused by soil, water, plants, insects and animals. William M. Bass created the first body farm to study decomposition in conditions such as partial or full burial.

soil-hist-093.title: Magnetic susceptibility: fire's lasting mark in soil
soil-hist-093.text: Fire leaves a magnetic signature in soil. Magnetic susceptibility analysis measures how readily a soil or sediment becomes magnetized in an external magnetic field. The value reflects magnetic iron oxides such as maghemite, not total iron content. Burning and microbial activity form magnetic iron, as in topsoils and some anaerobic deposits. So the method finds hearths and burning residues. It also tells reddening by fire from natural reddening, such as gleying. It can identify buried soils, too, and soil material redeposited in peat or lake sediments.

soil-hist-091.title: Geophysical survey: mapping a site without digging
soil-hist-091.text: Most archaeological sites lie within the top meter of ground, close enough to sense without a spade. Geophysical survey uses ground-based physical sensing techniques to image or map buried archaeological features. Instruments detect features whose physical properties contrast measurably with their surroundings, without digging or damage. Targets may be as faint as organic staining from decayed wooden posts. The usual instruments are magnetometers, electrical resistance meters, ground-penetrating radar and electromagnetic conductivity meters. A stone foundation resists electric current, while organic midden deposits conduct it more easily than surrounding soils. Magnetometers respond strongly to brick and burned soil. They also pick up subtle anomalies from disturbed soils or decayed organic matter. Ploughed fields add magnetic noise, but old tracks can show through differential compaction. Radar works best in uniform sandy soils. Conductive clays and silts weaken its signal, and rocky sediments scatter it. The approach was pioneered in Britain in the 1940s and 1950s.

soil-hist-094.title: Soil phosphate survey: the chemical footprint of people
soil-hist-094.text: One hundred people excrete about 62 kg of phosphate a year, and their rubbish adds about as much again. Soil phosphate survey measures and maps that phosphate, which comes from people, their animals, rubbish and bones, to find former activity areas and sites. Most of it is quickly fixed on soil clay and can persist for thousands of years. So human activity soon makes large differences. The human body holds about 650 g of phosphate, raising levels at burial sites. Detection uses the molybdate blue reaction, whose color deepens in proportion to concentration.

soil-hist-097.title: Cropmarks: buried walls drawn in growing grain
soil-hist-097.text: From the air, crops can trace buried walls. A cropmark is a pattern in growing crops, visible from the air or high ground, that reveals buried archaeological, natural or recent features. It comes from differential growth, in which soil conditions are key. A buried wall diverts water and displaces fertile soil, stunting the crop above it. An organic-rich ditch fill holds water and boosts growth. Cropmarks show only seasonally and may need very wet or dry years. Droughts make them appear even in hardy grass. Thermal imaging can show them at any growth stage, because water loss depends on the water available to roots.

soil-hist-101.title: Raised fields: farming on mounds above the water
soil-hist-101.text: Pre-Hispanic farmers in Latin America lifted their crops above wet ground. A raised field is a large cultivated mound, usually bounded by water-filled ditches, used to control moisture, frost damage and flooding. Such fields were used, for example, in the Llanos de Moxos of lowland Bolivia. The Tiwanaku culture built them near Lake Titicaca, where the technique is called Waru Waru. The Maya farmed raised fields at Pulltrouser Swamp in Belize. The Aztecs built chinampas on Lake Texcoco.

soil-hist-114.title: Farm trials that outlast the people who began them
soil-hist-114.text: Some farm experiments outlive everyone who started them. Long-term agricultural experiments are field trials run for decades, some for more than 100 years, to test the sustainability of farming practices from yield trends. Examples include the Park Grass Experiment at Rothamsted, the Morrow Plots (1876), Sanborn Field (1888), the Magruder Plots (1892) and Auburn's Old Rotation (1896). Why so long? Nitrogen released from soil organic matter can hide a legume nitrogen shortfall for a decade or more, so short trials cannot prove sustainability. Rothamsted showed that wheat and barley monocultures can sustain grain yields for almost 150 years, given organic or inorganic fertilizer every year. Even so, abundant evidence shows that crop rotation and organic inputs are often beneficial. The Old Rotation showed that legume nitrogen ploughed in as green manure can balance the nitrogen harvests remove. The Haughley Experiment ran organic farming without outside nutrients. Whether its yield decline came from soil nutrient depletion is disputed. In 2017 Rothamsted began the Large Scale Rotation Experiment, to study regenerative approaches such as no-till and crop rotation.

soil-hist-115.title: Broadbalk, a wheat field sown every year since 1843
soil-hist-115.text: One field at {{ref:soil-hist-053}} has grown winter wheat every year since 1843. This is the Broadbalk experiment. It is one of the classical field experiments begun by Lawes and Gilbert that remain in place as a resource for agricultural and environmental research. Its continuous wheat revealed a surprise about disease. Take-all built up to a peak in the 3rd to 5th crop, then declined, restoring yields to 80 to 90% of early levels.

soil-hist-118.title: Humus theory, the belief that plants eat rot
soil-hist-118.text: For decades, scientists believed plants drew their carbon from rotted plant matter. Humus theory was the once-prevalent view that humus, decayed plant matter, was plants' main source of carbon. Fertilizers were thought to work by breaking humus down so plants could absorb it more easily. The German agronomist {{ref:soil-hist-103}} supported it and dismissed Humphry Davy's idea of atmospheric carbon. His Principles of Agriculture (1809–12) set out the theory, which was still accepted between 1800 and 1860. {{ref:soil-hist-004}} argued against it.

soil-hist-117.title: The Soil Map of the World, ten volumes long
soil-hist-117.text: From 1971 to 1981, FAO and UNESCO published a map of the whole world's soils in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. This is the Soil Map of the World. The FAO soil classification was first developed as its legend, then applied by United Nations projects. A Revised Legend of the Soil Map of the World followed in 1988. The world's 3,230,000 km² of saline land has been mapped by region from it. In 1996, at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science, the World Soil Museum was created to support it.

soil-hist-116.title: The Virgin Lands campaign and the eroded steppe
soil-hist-116.text: A plan to feed the Soviet Union became an environmental disaster for the Kazakh steppe. In 1953 Nikita Khrushchev launched the Virgin Lands campaign to boost farm output by ploughing new land in southern Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan. After early success, output fell considerably. The region got only 200 to 350 mm of rain a year, mostly at harvest, and its soils had high salt content. Strong winds blew snow off the fields in winter and caused soil erosion in spring. Monoculture, with grain on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted the soil of nutrients. Severe erosion followed.

soil-hist-106.title: Edmund Ruffin and the marl that revived worn-out fields
soil-hist-106.text: More than a century of tobacco monoculture had worn the land out when a young planter began spreading marl on it. Edmund Ruffin (1794–1865) was an American planter, politician and scientist, and he started these experiments in his twenties. Marl, a calcareous earth, was his main tool. He recommended crop rotation and amendments for exhausted soils. He studied bogs and swamps to learn how to correct soil acidity, and he tried lime to raise the pH of peat soils. His book An Essay on Calcareous Manures explained how marl had cut acidity and raised corn and wheat yields. Few farmers took his advice in his own time. He has since been called the father of soil science in the United States. Yet he is best known as an early advocate of secession of the Southern slave states, and he farmed his plantations with enslaved labor.

soil-hist-105.title: Edgar Buckingham names the pull of soil on water
soil-hist-105.text: Edgar Buckingham spent only four years as a soil physicist, yet textbooks still cite him. The American physicist (1867–1940) worked at the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 to 1906. He began with aeration: how carbon dioxide leaves soil and oxygen replaces it. Gas diffusion, he found, barely depended on structure, compactness or water content. He gave the diffusion coefficient as an empirical function of air content. Soil gas exchange, he concluded, runs by diffusion and largely ignores outside barometric pressure. His water work appeared in 1907 as Bulletin 38, Studies on the movement of soil moisture. Soils can strongly inhibit evaporation, he showed, especially where capillary flow through the top layers is cut off. He named the capillary potential arising from soil–water interactions, now called matric or water potential. He was the first to tie hydraulic conductivity to that potential, applying a formula equivalent to Darcy's law to unsaturated flow.

soil-hist-108.title: Joseph Henry Gilbert, the chemist behind Rothamsted's long trials
soil-hist-108.text: Some field experiments Joseph Henry Gilbert started in 1843 are still running. Gilbert (1817–1901) was an English chemist and a former doctoral student of Justus von Liebig at Giessen. In 1843 he became director of the chemical laboratory at Rothamsted, the experiment station of John Bennet Lawes. He stayed from that June until his death, and he conducted most of the meticulous studies published under both names. That same year the two men began their long-term field experiments. The results contradicted Gilbert's old teacher. Cereal crops, they found, take up nitrogen from the soil, while Liebig had held that it came only from the air. Their work made Rothamsted a leading center of agricultural research.

soil-hist-109.title: Konstantin Gedroits and the soil that holds on
soil-hist-109.text: Konstantin Gedroits (1872–1932) wanted to know how soil holds what it holds. The Russian soil scientist, of Lithuanian origin, founded colloidal soil chemistry in Russia. He introduced the concept of the soil absorbing complex. He also split soil absorption capacity into three types: mechanical, physico-chemical and biological. He then classified soils by composition. Soils unsaturated with cations stood apart from those saturated with calcium, and from those saturated with sodium ions. The same chemistry explained how saline soils evolve. It also laid the theoretical basis for liming and for adding gypsum to soil. Gedroits led the chemistry laboratory of the Dokuchaev Soil Institute in 1915–17 and headed the institute in 1929–30. He received the Lenin Prize in 1927, and from 1927 to 1930 he was president of the {{ref:soil-hist-047}}.

soil-hist-104.title: Charles Darwin and the worms beneath the loam
soil-hist-104.text: Shown ground where cinders had vanished under loam, Charles Darwin named a culprit: earthworms. The English naturalist, geologist and biologist (1809–1882) is best known for evolutionary biology. His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, made him an eminent geologist. On 1 November 1837 he presented his theory of the earthworm's role in soil formation to the Geological Society. He came back to worms at the very end. His final book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881), counts among his works of great importance.

soil-hist-110.title: Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure finds plant carbon in the air
soil-hist-110.text: Where does a plant get its carbon? Most of Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure's immediate predecessors said from soil humus. The Swiss chemist and plant physiologist (1767–1845) showed that it comes from carbon dioxide in the air, which made him a major pioneer in the study of photosynthesis. He studied plant gas exchange and how different soils affected growth, gathering the work in Recherches chimiques sur la Végétation (1804). Unlike some before him, he based his conclusions on extensive quantitative data. He also showed that plants need mineral nutrients taken up from the soil. That disproved the idea that plant minerals arose by transmutation inside the plant. His findings were largely neglected for decades. Then Liebig revived them and used them to critique humus theories, and Boussingault's field research confirmed the importance of soil mineral nutrients.

soil-hist-103.title: Albrecht Thaer puts farming into a system
soil-hist-103.text: Albrecht Thaer trained as a physician and loved flower gardening before he turned to agriculture. The German agronomist (1752–1828) became known across Europe for applying science to farming practice. He is described as the first agricultural scientist to arrange the existing facts and theory of agriculture into a proper system. In 1802 he founded the first German agricultural training institute at Celle, where he experimented with crop rotation to raise yields. In 1804 came the first German agricultural academy, at Möglin, renamed the Royal Prussian Academy of Agriculture in 1819. The academy analyzed many soils and classified them by dominant component, such as sand, lime or red and blue clay, each marked with a colored label. This classification came into common use on large German estates. His four-volume Grundsätze der rationellen Landwirthschaft (1809–1812) covered the theory of soil, plowing, manuring and irrigation. It appeared in English in 1844 as The Principles of Agriculture. Its humus theory of plant nutrition was still accepted in the period 1800–1860.

soil-hist-107.title: Francis D. Hole, the pedologist who gave Wisconsin a state soil
soil-hist-107.text: Wisconsin has an official state soil, Antigo silt loam, because Francis D. Hole campaigned for it. The legislature named it in 1983. Hole (1913–2002) was an American pedologist, educator and musician. He created the periodical Soil Survey Horizons in 1960 and co-created the Soils of Wisconsin Map of 1968. With Stanley Buol and Ralph McCracken he wrote Soil Genesis and Classification, first published in 1973 and used worldwide. His Soils of Wisconsin (1976) followed Hans Jenny's factors of soil formation and divided the state into regions A to J.

soil-hist-111.title: Thomas Lyttleton Lyon and the Cornell field plots
soil-hist-111.text: Principles of Soil Management went through 10 editions. Its author, Thomas Lyttleton Lyon (1869–1938), was an American soil scientist who wrote on the nitrogen cycle. From 1912 he headed the department of soil technology at the Cornell University College of Agriculture. At Cornell's Caldwell Field he ran many field studies, including lysimeter and plot experiments. In 1913 he and James A. Bizzell won the Howard N. Potts Medal for a paper on how certain non-leguminous plants relate to soil nitrate content. He had been publishing soil science textbooks since 1907.

soil-hist-112.title: Milton Whitney, a chief whose views met resistance
soil-hist-112.text: Milton Whitney was the first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, the forerunner of the federal soil survey. He held firm views on soil chemistry and fertility, and the evidence did not always agree. Franklin Hiram King found that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yield, which undermined those views. Whitney's ideas also shaped what the Bureau released. George Nelson Coffey's map never became an official Bureau map, because it did not fit Whitney's prevailing soil classification concepts.

soil-hist-113.title: Nikolai Sibirtsev, Dokuchaev's partner in a new science
soil-hist-113.text: Nikolai Sibirtsev (1860–1900) led the Russian school of soil science together with Vasily Dokuchaev. From 1870 that school, under the two men, developed a new concept of soil. Sibirtsev taught soil science as a professor. When he fell ill, Konstantin Glinka took over his teaching. He is also counted among the Russian geographers who made great contributions to physical geography.

soil-hist-136.title: Geoderma, an international journal of soil science
soil-hist-136.text: Geoderma is an international soil science journal. In 1967 Roy Simonson became its editor-in-chief, and he published numerous articles in its pages.

soil-hist-137.title: The Viking landers ask Martian soil if anything lives there
soil-hist-137.text: In 1976 two landers scooped up Martian soil to test it for life, and scientists still argue over the answer. The Viking landers carried four biological experiments to the surface of Mars to look for microbes. Viking 1 worked near the equator and Viking 2 farther north, each loading soil into sealed chambers with a robotic arm. A gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer, sensitive to a few parts per billion, found no significant organic molecules. Martian soil held less carbon than lifeless Apollo lunar soil. Fed nutrients and water under helium, soil in the gas exchange experiment made oxygen disappear on contact and kept giving off carbon dioxide. The pyrolytic release experiment exposed soil to carbon-14-labeled CO and CO2, then baked it at 650 °C to detect carbon fixed as biomass. Any positive result was to be checked on a heat-sterilized duplicate: persisting activity meant chemistry, a lost response meant biology. The general view blames oxidative reactions, since constant ultraviolet light has given the soil a thin layer of very strong oxidant. Yet perchlorate, found by Phoenix in 2008, destroys organics on heating and yields chloromethane and dichloromethane, the very compounds Viking detected. A 2018 reanalysis suggested organics may in fact have been detected, matching Curiosity rover data. Whether the results reflect soil chemistry alone or could include biology remains disputed.

soil-hist-139.title: Bringing pieces of Mars back to Earth
soil-hist-139.text: Of over 79,000 known meteorites, 356 had been identified as Martian by August 2023. A proposed sample-return mission would add a second source: rock and dust collected on Mars and brought to Earth. Returned samples would allow far more extensive analysis than onboard sensors, focused on whether Mars once hosted life. Future instruments could reanalyze them. The Perseverance rover, landed in Jezero crater in February 2021, is caching rock, regolith and atmosphere samples for return. Some have raised the risk of Martian organisms contaminating Earth, but the scientific consensus is that large-scale effects are unlikely.

soil-hist-140.title: Growing plants in space, and on the Moon
soil-hist-140.text: The first plant grown on the Moon survived 2 days. It was cotton, sprouted in January 2019 in a sealed biosphere on the Chang'e 4 lander. Most space plants grow instead in pressurized, weightless space gardens in low Earth orbit. Weightlessness is the first challenge, because gravity matters for root development, soil integration and watering. For long-term growth, nutrient supply to roots, biogeochemical cycles and microbial life in soil-based substrates are particularly complex. University of Florida tests showed Arabidopsis thaliana can germinate and grow in lunar soil, but slowly and with signs of stress.

soil-hist-138.title: The labeled release test and its disputed signal
soil-hist-138.text: The labeled release experiment dosed Martian soil with a dilute nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon-14, then watched the air above for labeled gas. On both landers the first injection gave a steady stream of radioactive gas, from a sunlit surface sample and from one beneath a rock. Samples heated 3 hours at 160 °C released no gas, and at 50 °C much less. But second and third doses released no more gas Living terrestrial soil would have. Superoxides formed by ultraviolet light, or hypochlorite from irradiated perchlorate, may explain the result chemically. Its designer, Gilbert Levin, and Straat maintain the results indicate life. Most astrobiologists judge them inconclusive or negative, the work of oxidizing soil chemistry.

soil-hist-040.title: World Congress of Soil Science, every four years
soil-hist-040.text: Every four years, soil scientists from around the world meet in one city. The World Congress of Soil Science is the conference of the {{ref:soil-hist-047}}, and it has kept that rhythm apart from a break for World War II. Only members may attend. The 1st congress met in Washington, DC, in 1927 and the 2nd in Leningrad in 1930. Since the 15th, in Acapulco, Mexico, about 2000 members have come each time. Editions of the World Reference Base were launched at congresses: the first at Montpellier in 1998, the fourth at Glasgow in 2022. The 23rd met in Nanjing, China, in 2026, and the 24th is planned for Toronto in 2030.

soil-hist-027.title: From a nutrient ledger to a science of soil
soil-hist-027.text: Soil was once treated like a bank account. Early agricultural chemists held a balance-sheet theory: soil was a more or less static store of plant nutrients that crops drew down and farmers could replace. Their concepts built on the chemistry of {{ref:soil-hist-004}}, refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots. These workers rarely looked at soil below the depth of normal tillage. Early geologists accepted the balance sheet too. To them, soil was disintegrated rock, such as granite, sandstone or glacial till, modified by weathering and shaped into landforms. Many early soil surveyors were geologists, because only they had the field methods the work needed. So they saw soils mainly as weathering products of geologic formations. Surveys published before 1910 were strongly geological, and those of 1910 to 1920 added refinements without changing that foundation. The balance sheet ruled the laboratory and geology ruled the field. Many classrooms taught both until the late 1920s. Broader concepts came from {{ref:soil-hist-007}} and George Nelson Coffey in the United States and from Russian soil scientists. Yet the data behind them came from soil survey field work. The old balance sheet keeps some value today. Understanding soils, though, goes well beyond removing nutrients in crops and returning them as manure, lime and fertilizer.

soil-hist-035.title: Darwin's last book: the earthworm as a force of nature
soil-hist-035.text: Charles Darwin ended his scientific career with earthworms. His last scientific book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms, came out in October 1881, shortly before his death. It studied their habits and their part in forming and moving the soil. It carried his recurring theme: gradual changes over long periods can have large and sometimes surprising consequences. Darwin calculated that there were 53,767 earthworms per acre. He concluded that worms matter because they help decompose rock, slowly denude the land, preserve archaeological remains and improve soil for plant growth. He watched them drag leaves into their burrows by the most efficient end. Despite rudimentary sense organs, they showed complex, flexible behavior. The book was the first significant work on bioturbation, the mixing of soil by living things, though that word entered the soil literature only a hundred years later. It sold thousands of copies in its first few weeks.

soil-hist-038.title: 2015, the year the world was asked to notice soil
soil-hist-038.text: On 20 December 2013, the United Nations General Assembly declared 2015 the International Year of Soils. Its aim was to show how much soils matter for food security, agriculture, climate change mitigation, poverty alleviation and sustainable development. The FAO ran it within the Global Soil Partnership, which planned a website, a logo and activities, while organizations worldwide held local events. In the United States the USDA held a kick-off event, and the {{ref:soil-hist-050}} marked the year with monthly themes. It closed at FAO headquarters on 4 December 2015. The {{ref:soil-hist-047}} then proclaimed 2015–2024 the International Decade of Soils to continue the work.

soil-hist-077.title: Agricultural chemistry, the science behind the fertilizer bag
soil-hist-077.text: Most of the mass of dry soil is mineral matter. Agricultural chemistry is the chemistry of agriculture, especially its organic chemistry and biochemistry. When it analyzes soil, it looks at that mineral matter and at the organic matter too, including humic and fulvic acids. Its usual goal is to preserve or raise soil fertility, so that crops keep or improve their yield and quality. Time-honored organic fertilizers have largely given way to chemicals from mined phosphate rock and the Haber-Bosch process, which greatly raised crop production. Its pesticides raise yields as well, but they can contaminate ground and water and harm species they were never aimed at.

soil-hist-043.title: Soil Science Australia and its seven branches
soil-hist-043.text: Australia's soil scientists have had a professional home since 1955. The Australian Society of Soil Science Incorporated is a not-for-profit association for them and for others concerned with managing the country's soils. It was founded to advance soil science in professional, academic and technical fields, and in 2011 it adopted the public name Soil Science Australia. An elected Federal Council governs its seven branches. Members can gain accreditation as Certified Professional Soil Scientists. Its national conference meets every two years, jointly with the New Zealand Society of Soil Sciences every fourth year. In 2010 it co-hosted the 19th World Congress of Soil Science in Brisbane.

soil-hist-041.title: The World Soil Museum, a gallery of soil profiles
soil-hist-041.text: In Wageningen, in the Netherlands, the world's major soil types stand side by side. The World Soil Museum displays soil profile monoliths, preserved vertical slices of real soil profiles. It is managed by {{ref:soil-hist-049}}, an independent science-based foundation. It began as the International Soil Museum, at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science, to support the FAO-UNESCO map described in {{ref:soil-hist-117}}. Some 80 monoliths are on display. A much larger collection of some 1000, from over 70 countries, waits in its repository. Each comes with a horizon-by-horizon description and data. Visitors see examples of the 32 WRB Reference Soil Groups, a section on Dutch soils and soils much changed by long human use.

soil-hist-044.title: The Soil and Water Conservation Society
soil-hist-044.text: At a Chicago meeting on 11 November 1941, {{ref:soil-hist-019}} and three others proposed a new society. Its first minutes date from 16 February 1943, and it was formed that year as the Soil Conservation Society of America. In 1987 it took its present name. The Soil and Water Conservation Society is a professional and scientific membership society that fosters the science and art of managing natural resources sustainably. It publishes the bimonthly, peer-reviewed {{ref:soil-found-113}}. One source gives 1945 as the year it was formed.

soil-hist-031.title: From word pictures to measurements: building Soil Taxonomy
soil-hist-031.text: A soil class is only useful if two scientists would put the same soil in it. That was the weakness of the system of {{ref:soil-hist-009}} and of the 1938 USDA system. Their classes were described qualitatively, not in terms that different scientists could apply consistently. Neither linked its higher classes, defined by how soils form, to the soil series used in US soil mapping. A 1949 modification fixed some flaws. It also showed that the system's concepts and principles needed reappraisal. More than 15 years of work under {{ref:soil-hist-024}} produced a new, quantitative system. It was made official for the {{ref:soil-hist-051}} in 1965 and published in 1975 as Soil Taxonomy. The United States adopted it, and many other nations used it for their own classification.

soil-hist-028.title: When Russian scientists made soil a natural body
soil-hist-028.text: For a long time, soil counted as dead ground. It was seen as a product of physical and chemical changes in rock, a substrate from which plants take mineral nutrients. From 1870 a Russian school led by {{ref:soil-hist-001}} and N. M. Sibirtsev saw it differently. Soils, they held, are independent natural bodies with properties of their own. Each soil's unique properties come from a unique combination of climate, living matter, parent material, relief and time. Instead of inferring those properties from rocks or climate, they read the combined effect in the soil's own morphology, its visible form and layers. Considering all properties together, as one natural body, made a science of soil possible. The ideas are called revolutionary. Americans learned of them through a 1914 textbook in German by {{ref:soil-hist-008}}, and especially through its English translation of 1927 by {{ref:soil-hist-009}}. Some enthusiasts thought soil study could now ignore geology and agricultural chemistry. In fact the new concept made those sciences more useful. Morphology gave a firm basis for turning observations, experiments and experience into principles that predict how soils behave.

soil-hist-029.title: Putting the soil profile first, in America
soil-hist-029.text: In the United States, the Russian idea was rebuilt around the soil profile. Led by {{ref:soil-hist-009}}, the American version put the individual profile ahead of external soil features and surface geology. Classification, he insisted, must rest on morphology, not on theories of soil genesis, which he saw as ephemeral and dynamic. His 1935 classification relied on a "normal soil", formed in equilibrium on a landscape where downward erosion keeps pace with soil formation. The focus had costs. Early soil scientists overlooked how much soils vary even within a small area, which seriously reduced the value of their maps. Material without a genetic profile, such as recent alluvium, seemed not to be soil at all. After 1930, studies moved from single pits to trenches or series of pits. Soils were described by ranges of properties around a central concept, not by one typical profile. Yet through the 1930s, soil formation was still explained by loosely conceived regional processes such as podzolization, laterization and calcification.

soil-hist-045.title: Germany's soil society, founded in Berlin in 1926
soil-hist-045.text: In Berlin in 1926, German soil scientists formed a section of the International Soil Science Society. After the Second World War the group was re-formed in Wiesbaden. Today the Deutsche Bodenkundliche Gesellschaft, or DBG, is a non-profit society of soil science experts and others interested in the field. It has around 2000 members, with headquarters in Göttingen since 2012. Its meeting every two years is the main forum in German-speaking countries for new findings in soil science. With the German Society of Plant Nutrition, it publishes the Journal of Plant Nutrition and Soil Science.

soil-hist-039.title: World Soil Day, every 5 December
soil-hist-039.text: Each year, 5 December is set aside for the ground underfoot. World Soil Day celebrates the importance of soil in people's lives. The {{ref:soil-hist-047}} proposed the date in 2002. The UN General Assembly designated it in December 2013, when it also declared 2015 the International Year of Soils. The {{ref:soil-hist-048}} and the American Society of Agronomy invite the public to keep celebrating it every year. The FAO runs the #WorldSoilDay hashtag and campaigns such as "Stop soil erosion, Save our future", with activities for students, farmers, teachers and others.

soil-hist-042.title: The world's first soil museum, in Saint Petersburg
soil-hist-042.text: The world's first museum of soil science opened in Saint Petersburg in 1904, a year after its founder died. Its founder was {{ref:soil-hist-001}}, commonly called the father of soil science and leader of the Russian school. He set it up in 1902. He had begun his large collection of soil samples in 1880. The V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil now holds about 330 soil monoliths, from the Arctic to New Zealand. Expeditions bring new ones every year.

soil-hist-046.title: Park Grass, a hay field watched since 1856
soil-hist-046.text: One hay field in Hertfordshire has been monitored since 1856. The Park Grass Experiment, at {{ref:soil-hist-053}}, was set up to test how fertilizers and manures affect hay yields. It is one of the longest-running experiments in modern science. Its treatments changed the plant make-up and ecology of the 28,000 m² field. That made it a resource for studying natural selection and biodiversity. It showed how plant species richness, biomass and pH are related. It also showed that ordinary field trials probably underestimate long-term threats such as soil acidification. Its archive of soil and hay samples has even been used to track atmospheric pollution, including nuclear fallout.

soil-hist-037.title: How earthworms slowly bury stones and ruins
soil-hist-037.text: In December 1842, Charles Darwin spread broken chalk over a pasture near Down House. It ended up buried 18 centimeters deep, a rate of 6 millimeters per year. Earthworms bring up earth from below and leave it on the surface as castings, so objects on top slowly sink. Darwin estimated how much earth they raise from such burial rates and by weighing the castings produced over set times. He found the outer stones of Stonehenge partly buried. Worms, dust and soil wash, he concluded, had buried Roman ruins such as Abinger and Silchester. Rain and wind move castings downslope. Meanwhile the worms' humic acids and the stones they swallow help break down rock.

soil-hist-036.title: Darwin's first worm paper, read in 1837
soil-hist-036.text: At Maer Hall, Josiah Wedgwood showed his nephew Charles Darwin some curious ground. Lime and cinders spread there years before now lay beneath a layer of loam, and Wedgwood suggested earthworms were the cause. On 1 November 1837, Darwin read a paper to the Geological Society of London on the role of earthworms in forming soil. William Buckland backed its publication as "a new Geological Power". He rejected, though, Darwin's idea that chalkland formed the same way. The paper appeared in the society's Proceedings in 1838 and, with a woodcut, in its Transactions in 1840.

soil-hist-033.title: Bioturbation: a word from 1952 for an idea from Darwin
soil-hist-033.text: Darwin was first to see how much burrowing creatures matter for soil processes and landforms, and he devoted his last scientific book to it. In 1891 the geologist Nathaniel Shaler extended the idea to soil disturbed by ants and trees. The name came later. Rudolf Richter coined bioturbation in 1952 for sediment structures made by living organisms. Since the 1980s soil geomorphologists, who study soils and landforms together, have used it widely. There is now ample evidence for Darwin's conclusions. In many areas, burrowing animals and plants are major agents of soil formation.

soil-hist-030.title: Soil formation becomes a measurable science
soil-hist-030.text: From about 1940, soil formation stopped being one vague process. It became many interrelated physical, chemical and biological processes, open to quantitative study. A 1941 book by {{ref:soil-hist-010}}, Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology, summarized many basic principles of modern soil science up to that date. Since then time has gained much more weight among the soil-forming factors. Geomorphology is used to find how long material has undergone soil formation. Advances in soil chemistry, physics, mineralogy and biology added new tools. Attention moved from gross traits of the whole soil to the co-varying detail of its parts, down to grain-to-grain relationships.

soil-hist-034.title: Rethinking what soil organic matter is
soil-hist-034.text: Historically, stability was blamed on humic substances, formed from inputs and extracted with strong base and acid, then interpreted as large stable macromolecules. From the late 1990s high-resolution chemistry showed that {{ref:soil-found-045}} is recognizable plant and animal biomolecules at varying degradation stages, which can associate like larger molecules. Flaws in the old view showed in 1999, when soil models could not account for the large charcoal component of Chernozems. A newer paradigm holds that molecular structure alone does not explain persistence. Microbial carbon-use efficiency matters, and labile molecules taken up by microbes may form most stable organic matter. The debate is live. The {{ref:soil-chem-063}} still appears in textbooks while some researchers argue it is wrong. Compare {{ref:soil-bio-090}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-092}}.

soil-hist-032.title: Soil surveys move beyond the farm
soil-hist-032.text: Soil surveys were once made almost entirely for farmers, ranchers and foresters. That held until about 1950. Yet some states saw their value for highway planning by the late 1920s, and in the 1930s and 1940s they put soil interpretations into highway engineers' manuals. Then nonfarm uses of soil grew rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s. That created a great need for information on how soils affect those uses. The impact on soil survey was immense, especially during the 1960s.

soil-hist-001.title: Vasily Dokuchaev, who saw soil as a natural body
soil-hist-001.text: Chernozem, podsol, gley and solonets are Russian words, and they entered the world's soil vocabulary through one man's research. Vasily Dokuchaev (1846–1903) was a Russian geologist and geographer credited with laying the foundations of soil science. He is commonly called its father. He was perhaps the first to investigate different soil types across broad geographic areas. After extensive field studies of Russian soils in 1883 he reached his theory, and his most famous work, {{ref:soil-hist-002}}, appeared that same year. Soil, he argued, is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it. Climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age turn that bedrock into soil. Parent material alone could not explain why soil types vary from place to place. Climate, topography and the length of soil formation mattered too. On these ideas he built the very first soil classification, which described five factors of soil formation. His output was vast: from 1869 to 1901 he published 285 works, including 61 books and 4 maps. Many soil scientists took up his ideas, {{ref:soil-hist-010}} among them. The IUSS's Dokuchaev Award, likened to a Nobel Prize for soil science, honors him.

soil-hist-004.title: Justus von Liebig brings chemistry to the farm
soil-hist-004.text: In 1840 a German chemist argued that chemistry could revolutionize farming. Justus von Liebig (1803–1873) was a principal founder of organic chemistry and made major contributions to agricultural and biological chemistry. His book Organic Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology was widely translated, fiercely criticized and highly influential. Critics pointed to his inexperience in practice. Even so, his writings spurred agricultural experiment and debate in Germany, England and France. He stressed nitrogen and minerals as essential plant nutrients and popularized the law of the minimum, earning the name "father of the fertilizer industry." Around 1840 he suggested dissolving animal bones in sulfuric acid to make fertilizer, a process first used in Britain in 1841. The early idea of soil as a store of plant nutrients rested on his thinking. Seeing both synthesis and decay in living systems, he also became an early advocate of conservation, including recycling sewage.

soil-hist-010.title: Hans Jenny gives soil formation its variables
soil-hist-010.text: Hans Jenny (1899–1992) made the study of soil formation quantitative. The Swiss-born soil scientist was an expert in pedology, above all in the processes that form soils. He took a doctorate at ETH Zurich in 1927 on ion exchange reactions and joined the University of California, Berkeley, in 1936. International recognition followed his 1941 book Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology. It combined field studies with the formalism of physical chemistry. Soil properties were tied to climate, biota, relief, parent material and time, with room for further variables, the idea behind {{ref:soil-form-049}}. In 1980 he recast the factors as state variables and extended their effects to whole ecosystems. His factors underlie the CLORPT model of soil-landscape modelling and the scorpan approach of digital soil mapping. He studied the Mendocino pygmy forest, whose stunted plants grow on a 500,000-year-old marine terrace; a reserve there bears his name. In his 1980 article "Alcohol or Humus" he argued against turning crop residues and forest humus into fuel. That would curtail carbon and nitrogen cycles and speed the oxidation of humus. In 1949 he was President of the {{ref:soil-hist-048}}.

soil-hist-013.title: Sergei Winogradsky takes microbes out of the clinic
soil-hist-013.text: Sergei Winogradsky (1856–1953) was among the first to study microbes outside medicine, which makes him an early student of microbial ecology. The Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist, ecologist and soil scientist pioneered the cycle-of-life concept. He discovered several biogeochemical cycles and parts of them. In 1887 he found that Beggiatoa oxidizes hydrogen sulfide as an energy source, the first known form of lithotrophy. From 1888 in Zürich he identified the bacteria behind nitrification. Nitrosomonas and Nitrosococcus oxidize ammonium to nitrite; Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate. He described this two-step process in 1890. He also identified Clostridium pasteurianum, a free-living anaerobe that fixes atmospheric nitrogen without living in legume root nodules. From 1922 he led the Pasteur Institute's agricultural bacteriology division, studying iron and nitrifying bacteria, Azotobacter, cellulose decomposers and ways to culture soil microbes. His student Vasily Omelianski spread his concepts and methods in the Soviet Union in the following decades.

soil-hist-003.title: Friedrich Fallou, the tax assessor who named pedology
soil-hist-003.text: A land tax assessor gave soil science one of its names. Friedrich Albert Fallou (1794–1877) was a German lawyer who spent most of his career evaluating forest and farmland for Saxony. The work worried him. Soil quality was declining, and he began relating soil profiles to how they formed. His First Principles of Soil Science (1857) and Pedology or General and Special Soil Science (1862) turned his field observations into a system. The 1862 book proposed a way to describe soil profiles, discussed soils' physical and chemical properties and classified soils by their minerals. That year he argued that soil was separate in nature from geology. He introduced the term pedology to found soil study as an independent science. Pedology described soil regardless of plants or use; agrology studied soil in relation to plants and farming. Dokuchaev proved more influential. Still, {{ref:soil-hist-008}} regarded Fallou as the founder of modern soil science, and Yarilov's 1904 article called him "Founder of Soil Science".

soil-hist-016.title: Martinus Beijerinck, from root nodules to viruses
soil-hist-016.text: In 1898 filtration experiments led Martinus Beijerinck to a striking conclusion: tobacco mosaic disease is caused by an agent smaller than a bacterium. He named it a virus. The Dutch microbiologist and botanist (1851–1931) is counted among the founders of virology and of environmental microbiology. In soil, his work centered on nitrogen fixation. He revealed the symbiosis between legumes and the nodule bacteria that fix nitrogen, a reaction vital to soil fertility and agriculture. He fully described the process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth, and in 1901 showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen. He also discovered bacterial sulfate reduction. In it, bacteria use sulfate instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, the final receiver of electrons in their energy-yielding chemistry. He isolated the first known sulfate-reducing bacterium, now called Desulfovibrio desulfuricans. He invented {{ref:soil-hist-017}} and founded the Delft School of Microbiology. The maxim "everything is everywhere, but the environment selects" is often credited to him, but it was Lourens Baas Becking's.

soil-hist-008.title: Konstantin Glinka carries Russian soil science west
soil-hist-008.text: For years a language barrier kept Russian soil science from Western Europe. Konstantin Glinka (1867–1927) broke through it. A student of Dokuchaev, he did geological and soil research under him from 1889, including work in Poltava and on the Forest Department expedition. His 1908 soil science textbook included the first schematic soil map of the world. His German publication of 1914 finally carried the Russian team's work west, and {{ref:soil-hist-009}} translated a version from German into English. Glinka became the first director of the Dokuchaev Soil Science Institute and wrote over 150 works on soil, geography, mineralogy and geology. By the 1920s he had found Russian soils that did not fit present climates; they were seen as relics of warmer past climates. In 1927 he became the first soil scientist elected to the USSR Academy of Sciences. That year he also led the Soviet delegation to the First International Congress of Soil Scientists in Washington.

soil-hist-007.title: Eugene Hilgard puts climate into American soil science
soil-hist-007.text: In 1860, in Mississippi, Eugene W. Hilgard studied how rock material, climate and vegetation relate to the type of soil that develops. The German-American expert on pedology (1833–1916) is considered the father of modern soil science in the United States. He was an authority on climate as a soil-forming factor, on soil chemistry and on the reclamation of alkali soils. From 1875 to 1904 he was professor of agricultural chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley, and directed the state agricultural experiment station. For the Northern Transcontinental Survey of 1881–1883 he studied soils of the southwestern states and the Pacific slope. He related them to geology, composition, native flora and farming. His 1892 Relations of Climate to Soils won the Liebig medal in 1894. With his 1906 book Soils, it established climate as a soil-forming factor in American thinking. He and {{ref:soil-hist-022}} greatly influenced {{ref:soil-hist-009}}, turning him from geology toward soil science as a distinct field.

soil-hist-009.title: Curtis Marbut builds the first US soil classification
soil-hist-009.text: Curtis F. Marbut began as a geologist who saw soils as surface reflections of the rock beneath. He ended by giving the United States its first formal soil classification. The American soil scientist (1863–1935) directed the Soil Survey Division of the US Department of Agriculture from 1913 until his death. Hilgard and {{ref:soil-hist-022}} helped turn him toward soil science as a field distinct from geology. He began the classification work in 1920. In 1927 he translated Glinka's The Great Soil Groups of the World and their Development into English, and he applied the Russian ideas to a national scheme. It became the 1935 system, modified and published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture as the 1938 USDA soil taxonomy. At its highest level it split soils in two. Pedocals were carbonate-rich soils of drier climates; pedalfers were rich in aluminum and iron. "Alfer" became the root of alfisol. He died of pneumonia in 1935, on his way to advise the Chinese Geological Survey on organizing a soil survey.

soil-hist-023.title: Lorenzo Richards measures the water in soil
soil-hist-023.text: Lorenzo A. Richards (1904–1993) helped move the study of soil water from description to measurement and mathematics. The American was one of the most influential figures in 20th-century soil physics. His 1931 Cornell thesis on capillary conduction through porous media made the first decisive advance beyond Buckingham in extending Darcy's law to unsaturated soils. In it he set out the partial differential equation now called the {{ref:soil-water-238}}, though Lewis Richardson had published it in 1922. Richards described the principles, construction and operation of the tensiometer. He proposed the tension plate apparatus for measuring capillary potential in soil. In 1941 he described the pressure-membrane apparatus, mainly for extracting soil solution for salinity analysis. At the USDA Salinity Laboratory he and colleagues fixed the accepted limits for plant growth. Field capacity sits at −1/3 bar (−33 J/kg) and the permanent wilting point at −15 bar (−1500 J/kg). Yet he remarked that the concept of available water is oversimplified.

soil-hist-005.title: Minerals, not humus: how plants really feed
soil-hist-005.text: For a long time, many believed plants ate decayed plant matter. That humus theory held that humus was plants' main carbon source and that fertilizers worked by breaking it down. The mineral theory of plant nutrition said otherwise. Plants draw essential nutrients as inorganic minerals from the soil, and carbon and hydrogen from air and water. De Saussure's experiments of 1804 had suggested that plants took carbon from the air and that their mineral content reflected the soil they grew in. By the late 1830s {{ref:soil-hist-072}} had used Liebig's combustion analysis to show that manures owed their value to their minerals. Liebig synthesized and promoted the theory. With more precise measurements, he showed that a soil's humus could not supply enough carbon for the plants growing on it. He named nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as essential to plant growth. Inorganic materials, he held, could feed plants as well as organic ones. He also popularized the law of the minimum that Sprengel had stated: growth is limited by the scarcest essential resource, not by the total available.

soil-hist-024.title: Guy Smith and the making of Soil Taxonomy
soil-hist-024.text: More than 15 years of Guy D. Smith's work led to a soil classification that came to be used worldwide. The American soil scientist (1907–1981) originally developed the USDA system called Soil Taxonomy. After wartime service he joined the USDA. From 1946 he worked as a soil correlator for the Soil Conservation Service, and from 1952 as Director of Soil Survey Investigations. Tasked with developing a way to classify soils, he produced the first of seven iterations of the system. He developed it in collaboration with European soil scientists. It was made official in 1965 and published in 1975. After retiring in 1973 he advised international partners on applying Soil Taxonomy. He died in 1981 in Ghent, where he taught.

soil-hist-026.title: Rattan Lal and the carbon in farm soils
soil-hist-026.text: In Nigeria, between 1970 and 1987, Rattan Lal found that organic carbon and nutrients disappeared from soils after deforestation. He studied mulching, cover crops and no-till farming to restore them. The Indian-American soil scientist, born in 1944, is a pioneer of soil-centered farm management for food security and climate-resilient agriculture. His work departed from the 1970s reliance on commercial fertilizer. It showed how no-till, cover crops, residues, mulching and agroforestry rebuild degraded soils and sequester carbon. His most cited paper, in Science in 2004, was the first report that restoring soil organic matter both improves soil health and lowers atmospheric carbon dioxide. His models suggest that restoring soil health could by 2100 double global grain yield, cut the land used for grain by 30% and reduce fertilizer use. He founded the Rattan Lal Center for Carbon Management and Sequestration at Ohio State and launched the C-FARM carbon farming project in 2021. He was IUSS president in 2017–2018, won the Japan Prize in 2019 and the World Food Prize in 2020.

soil-hist-019.title: Hugh Hammond Bennett, crusader against erosion
soil-hist-019.text: Many of Hugh Hammond Bennett's colleagues held that soil was a resource that could never be exhausted. He spent his career arguing otherwise. Bennett (1881–1960) pioneered soil conservation in the United States and headed the federal erosion agency now called the {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. Working as a soil surveyor from 1903, he first linked soil quality and erosion in a 1905 Virginia survey. He came to see soil erosion as a serious problem for the planet. In 1928 he co-wrote the USDA's Soil Erosion: A National Menace, his most influential work. Congressman James P. Buchanan then secured funds in 1929 for erosion studies, and a 1930 amendment created soil erosion experiment stations whose sites Bennett chose. From September 1933 he directed the Soil Erosion Service. His Dust Bowl advocacy helped pass the act of 27 April 1935 creating the Soil Conservation Service, which he led until 1951. By May 1936, nearly 40,000 farmers in the hardest-hit Dust Bowl region had put 5.5 million acres under terraced and contour-listed cultivation. The Coon Creek Watershed Project in Wisconsin was the first of many watershed projects set up to show farmers how to conserve soil. The new service marked the US government's acceptance of interpreting soils for soil and water conservation. Bennett also helped form the Soil Conservation Society of America, now the Soil and Water Conservation Society.

soil-hist-074.title: John Bennet Lawes and the first artificial fertilizer
soil-hist-074.text: The world's oldest agricultural research facility began with manures tested on plants in pots. John Bennet Lawes started those trials at Rothamsted before leaving Oxford in 1832, and soon extended them to field crops. The English entrepreneur and agricultural scientist (1814–1900) founded the experimental farm that became {{ref:soil-hist-053}}. In 1842 he patented a manure made by treating phosphates with sulfuric acid. That superphosphate began the artificial fertilizer industry. From the following year he worked with Joseph Henry Gilbert for more than half a century on crop and animal-feeding experiments. The two jointly received the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1867. In 1889 Lawes endowed the Lawes Agricultural Trust to keep the experimental farm going.

soil-hist-020.title: Franklin Hiram King, father of American soil physics
soil-hist-020.text: Franklin Hiram King (1848–1911) has been called the father of soil physics in the United States. As professor of agricultural physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison from 1888 to 1902, he applied physics to agriculture, with his greatest impact on soil science. He studied water-holding capacity, plants' moisture needs, aeration, the movement of soil water and groundwater, and the draft of plows. At the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 he found that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yields. That undermined the views of bureau chief Milton Whitney, and King was forced to resign. He is best remembered for {{ref:soil-hist-021}}.

soil-hist-073.title: Jean-Baptiste Boussingault and the first experiment station
soil-hist-073.text: In 1836 a French chemist set up the first agricultural experiment station on his wife's estate at Pechelbronn in Alsace. That was some seven years before Rothamsted. Jean-Baptiste Boussingault (1801–1887) worked mainly on agricultural chemistry and plant and animal physiology from that year on. He revived the quantitative methods first used by de Saussure and is called the father of field plot technique. He made the first analysis of crops grown in a rotation and showed that soil nitrogen rises after legume crops. Plant growth, he found, is proportional to the available nitrogen, so applying phosphorus and nitrogen together gives greater growth. Can plants take up free nitrogen from the air? He answered no, laying a basis for what became the nitrogen cycle. In 1839 he was given the chair of agricultural and analytical chemistry at the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers in Paris. Liebig hailed him as a pioneer of soil and plant chemistry, and his nitrogen work prepared the way for nitrogen fertilizers.

soil-hist-006.title: Liebig's long argument over nitrogen
soil-hist-006.text: Even Liebig changed his mind about nitrogen. He claimed that plants feed on nitrogen compounds from the air, and the claim was contested for many years. In the end it held for legumes but not for other plants. The 1840 and 1842 editions of his book said the air held too little nitrogen and that nitrogen fertilizer, perhaps as ammonia, was needed. He later decided that ammonia in rain supplied enough, and argued for years against nitrogen fertilizer. His own nitrogen-poor fertilizer had no appreciable effect in a field test. By the seventh German edition he admitted mistakes and again called nitrogen fertilizer beneficial or even necessary. In 1863 he came to appreciate biological nitrogen fixation.

soil-hist-018.title: Selman Waksman finds medicine in soil microbes
soil-hist-018.text: The first antibiotic used to cure tuberculosis came out of soil research. Selman Waksman (1888–1973) was a Russian-born American biochemist and microbiologist who studied decomposition by soil organisms. He wrote Principles of Soil Microbiology (1927) and Humus (1936). His 1932 lignin theory is one of three main historical theories of how humic substances form. His Rutgers team found actinomycin, streptomycin and neomycin, and he gave the word antibiotic its modern sense. His student Albert Schatz isolated streptomycin from Streptomyces griseus. Credit for the discovery was disputed: Schatz went to court in 1950 and was recognized as co-discoverer. Waksman won the 1952 Nobel Prize for the soil studies that led to streptomycin.

soil-hist-072.title: Carl Sprengel, who stated the law of the minimum first
soil-hist-072.text: The law that bears Liebig's name was first stated by someone else. Carl Sprengel (1787–1859) was a German botanist and agricultural scientist. He trained under Albrecht Thaer and then with Heinrich Einhof at Möglin from 1804 to 1808. From 1821 to 1828 he studied natural sciences at Göttingen, where he became a professor. He was the first to state the 'theory of minimum' in agricultural chemistry: plant growth is limited by the essential nutrient present at the lowest concentration. The rule is often credited to Justus von Liebig as {{ref:soil-fert-182}}, but Liebig only popularized it later. Sprengel's books include an 1839 study of manures and their action and the 1844 Die Bodenkunde, with a full guide to the chemical analysis of field soils. He founded the Academy of Agriculture at Regenwalde (Resko), where he taught and researched until his death in 1859.

soil-hist-012.title: Peter Erasmus Müller reads the forest floor
soil-hist-012.text: Peter Erasmus Müller (1840–1926), a Danish forester and naturalist, described mor humus for the first time. He called it beech peat, by analogy with sphagnum peat. His Studies on Forest Soil ran as a series in 1878–84 in a journal he had founded in 1875, the first independent Danish forestry journal. It was translated into German and French. The studies showed how plant communities and their animals shape the ground surface, as in heathland formation. His last major work, in 1924, concluded that the Danish heaths continue the tundra that arose after the ice age and were never forested like nearby land.

soil-hist-014.title: Life powered by rock: the discovery of chemosynthesis
soil-hist-014.text: Until Winogradsky's work, autotrophs, organisms that build their own organic matter from carbon dioxide, were believed to get their energy only from light. He found organisms that draw energy from inorganic compounds instead. This is chemoautotrophy, popularly called chemosynthesis. His 1887 Beggiatoa work gave the first example of lithotrophy, though not of autotrophy. His nitrifying bacteria gave the first chemoautotrophy, fixing carbon dioxide into organic compounds. Organisms that oxidize hydrogen sulfide or ammonium for energy split autotrophs into photoautotrophs and chemoautotrophs. This form of metabolism is believed to occur only in prokaryotes.

soil-hist-011.title: Albert Atterberg sets the size of clay
soil-hist-011.text: Albert Atterberg (1846–1916) did his best-remembered work late, turning to soil classification and plasticity around the age of fifty-four. The Swedish chemist and agricultural scientist proposed the first texture classification, the international system, in 1905. He was apparently the first to set 0.002 mm as the upper size of clay particles. Finding plasticity characteristic of clay, he devised in 1911 the consistency limits named after him. Terzaghi brought them into geotechnics, and Casagrande standardized the tests in 1932. The International Society of Soil Science formally recognized his classification work at Berlin in 1913. Sweden still uses his grain size scale.

soil-hist-076.title: Albert Bernhard Frank names the fungus-root
soil-hist-076.text: A failed royal commission to develop truffle cultivation led Albert Bernhard Frank to work out the nature and development of mycorrhizae. The German botanist, plant pathologist and mycologist (1839–1900) named the mycorrhiza in an 1885 paper. It described how certain trees are nourished through a root symbiosis with underground fungi. In 1877 he had coined the term symbiosis to describe lichens. The bacterial genus Frankia is named after him.

soil-hist-022.title: Cyril Hopkins and the soils of Illinois
soil-hist-022.text: Cyril G. Hopkins (1866–1919) was an American agricultural chemist noted for his research and writing on Illinois soils. From 1894 until his death he was chemist at the University of Illinois Agriculture Experiment Station, latterly heading its Department of Agronomy. In 1896 he began the Illinois long-term selection experiment. With Hilgard, he greatly influenced Marbut's change from seeing soils as reflections of geology to recognizing soil science as distinct from geology.

soil-hist-025.title: Roy Simonson, soil surveyor and historian
soil-hist-025.text: During World War II, Roy W. Simonson mapped soils on Western Pacific islands for the Military Geology Unit. The American soil scientist (1908–2008) had trained under Charles E. Kellogg and Emil Truog. He taught at Iowa State College before joining the USDA soil survey programs. From 1953 to 1971 he was the survey's Director for Soil Classification and Correlation. In 1967 he became editor-in-chief of the journal described in {{ref:soil-hist-136}}. He also wrote a history of US soil survey and classification from 1899 to 1970.

soil-hist-075.title: Lorenz Hiltner names the rhizosphere
soil-hist-075.text: In an April 1904 lecture, Lorenz Hiltner introduced the term rhizosphere for the soil directly affected by root secretions and their microorganisms. The German agronomist and microbiologist (1862–1923) helped found microbial ecology. At the Tharandt research station he studied the symbiosis of legumes with root-nodule bacteria, work that produced the first cultures of rhizobium bacteria. He also showed the importance of root nodules for the nitrogen nutrition of black alder. In 1893 he and F. Nobbe published a work titled 'Inoculate the Soil'.

soil-hist-017.title: Enrichment culture: coaxing microbes into the lab
soil-hist-017.text: Enrichment culture is a fundamental method of culturing microbes taken from the environment so that they can be studied. Martinus Beijerinck invented it. With his discovery of viruses, it counts as one of his two major contributions to microbiology. Early nitrification researchers, among them Warington, Winogradsky and the Franklands, could at first only enrich cultures of nitrifiers rather than isolate them pure. The method still matters: seven of the ten described anammox species are available in laboratory enrichment cultures.

soil-hist-021.title: Farmers of Forty Centuries, King's lessons from Asia
soil-hist-021.text: In 1909 Franklin Hiram King spent nine months touring Asia, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture. His book on the long-sustained traditional farming of China, Korea and Japan recounts that tour. It discussed the advantages of sustainable agriculture and warned that such practices would be vital to farming in the future. King died before it was done. His wife Carrie Baker King finished the last chapter and published the book in 1911. Lord Northbourne called it a "classic" that no student of farming or social science can afford to ignore.

soil-hist-002.title: Russian Chernozem, the book that named soils by color
soil-hist-002.text: Studying the steppe soils of the Poltava region, Vasily Dokuchaev noticed that peasants named all soils by their color. He began to use such names himself. Russian Chernozem, his most famous work, appeared in 1883 as a complete study of the chernozem soils of European Russia. It came out of his extensive field studies of Russian soils that year, from which he arrived at his theory of soil formation. An English translation by N. Kaner was published in Jerusalem in 1967 for the USDA and NSF.

soil-hist-015.title: The Winogradsky column: a jar of sediment as an ecosystem
soil-hist-015.text: A jar of mud can teach a whole course in microbial metabolism. A Winogradsky column is a simple stratified microbial ecosystem built from sediment in a container. Columns are set up as a control and with added carbon (cellulose), sulfur (egg yolk calcium sulfate) or both, then form oxygen and sulfide gradients, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-121}}. Purple and green sulfur bacteria use sulfide to support photosynthesis, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple. Winogradsky developed it, and discovered chemosynthesis, in his early efforts to understand microbes outside the medical context. It remains an important demonstration of chemoautotrophy and microbial ecology in microbiology lectures around the world, and a window into {{ref:soil-bio-011}}.

soil-hist-048.title: The Soil Science Society of America and its grand challenges
soil-hist-048.text: In 1936 two American groups decided they were stronger as one. The Soils Section of the American Society of Agronomy merged with the American Soil Survey Association. The result was the Soil Science Society of America, now the largest soil-specific scientific society in the United States. In 1934 that Soils Section had become the official Americas section of {{ref:soil-hist-047}}, a role the society still fills. From Madison, Wisconsin, it publishes journals, magazines and books, led by {{ref:soil-hist-078}}. Its voluntary certifications set standards for Certified Professional Soil Scientists and Certified Professional Soil Classifiers. In 2011 it named the field's grand challenges: climate change, food and energy security, waste treatment and water quality, and human and ecosystem health.
