In 2017 it stretched its definition of soil to loose material at or near any planetary surface. Past presidents include William Albrecht in 1939, Hans Jenny in 1949 and Rattan Lal in 2007. Its outreach runs from the 'Secrets of Soil' exhibition at the Smithsonian to the school websites Soils4Teachers and soils4kids.

soil-hist-050.title: From Dust Bowl emergency to a national conservation agency
soil-hist-050.text: The agency was born in a crisis. On September 13, 1933, the Department of the Interior formed the Soil Erosion Service, with {{ref:soil-hist-019}} as chief. Bennett knew the soil erosion behind the 1930s Dust Bowl, and he stayed in charge until he retired in 1952. On March 23, 1935, the service moved to the Department of Agriculture and soon merged with other units as the Soil Conservation Service. Between 1933 and 1942 it ran 500 Civilian Conservation Corps camps, mainly for erosion control, and promoted contour plowing. In 1994 it became the Natural Resources Conservation Service, a USDA agency that gives technical help to farmers and other private landowners. Its money for farmers and ranchers comes through the Farm Bill, renewed every five years. It leads {{ref:soil-hist-051}}, with products such as the Web Soil Survey and the SSURGO database. Since 2015 it has also pushed soil health, with less tillage and more cover crops.

soil-hist-053.title: Rothamsted, where wheat has grown in one field since 1843
soil-hist-053.text: One field in Harpenden, England, has been sown with winter wheat every year since 1843. That is the Broadbalk Experiment at Rothamsted, one of the world's oldest agricultural research institutions. John Bennet Lawes, who had founded an early artificial fertilizer factory, set it up on his estate to test how fertilizers affect crop yields. With Joseph Henry Gilbert, trained under Liebig, he ran field trials for 57 years. They laid the foundations of scientific agriculture and crop nutrition. Thomas Way and Lawes discovered cation exchange there, and in 1878 Robert Warington confirmed soil nitrification. The mountain of data had a further payoff. Ronald Fisher, hired in 1919 to analyse it, stayed to create the theory of experimental design. Merged into the Institute of Arable Crops Research in 1987, the station now runs as Rothamsted Research.

soil-hist-047.title: How the world's soil scientists organized in 1924
soil-hist-047.text: Soil scientists from many nations met in Rome in 1924 and founded the International Society of Soil Science. Today it is the International Union of Soil Sciences, the field's international scientific union and a member of the International Science Council. Its aim is to promote every branch of {{ref:soil-found-090}}, link soil scientists and spur research and its use. It has 86 national and regional member societies with about 60,000 scientists, plus individual members in 57 countries. Every four years it holds the World Congress of Soil Science; the first met in Washington, D.C., in 1927. Its commissions, grown from six in 1924, cover soil morphology, fertility, degradation control, education and the field's own history. It endorses the World Reference Base as the international standard for soil classification. Since 2014 its Council has elected the President for a two-year term. Since January 2023 Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics has run its secretariat.

soil-hist-051.title: The National Cooperative Soil Survey maps a nation's soils
soil-hist-051.text: The first American soil surveys cost about 3/10ths of a cent per acre; by 1999 a survey cost about $3 an acre. Behind that work stands the National Cooperative Soil Survey. It is a nationwide partnership that investigates, inventories, classifies and interprets US soils and publishes the results. The {{ref:soil-hist-050}} leads it, joining federal land agencies, state agricultural experiment stations, counties and conservation districts. Land-grant universities have been partners from the start, and Cooperative Extension joins them today. Federal authority comes from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896. The work passed from an 1894 Division of Agricultural Soil to the Bureau of Soils in 1901, and to the Soil Conservation Service in 1952. Its maps judge land capability and conservation needs. More than 90% of private lands have been mapped, and in FY2001 maps were made or updated for 21,900,000 acres. The soil series it establishes form one level of {{ref:soil-class-006}}.

soil-hist-049.title: ISRIC, the world's data center for soils
soil-hist-049.text: ISRIC began in 1966 on the advice of the International Society of Soil Science, now the IUSS, and UNESCO. It is an independent, science-based foundation that supplies quality-assessed soil information for global environmental and social challenges. It writes soil information standards, builds harmonised global soil products and strengthens national and regional {{ref:soil-agri-085}}. Since 1989 it has been the accredited World Data Centre for Soils. Its flagship products are WoSIS and SoilGrids. It also houses the World Soil Museum and the World Soil Reference Collection, and its Otto Spaargaren helped draft the World Reference Base.

soil-found-104.title: Pochvovedenie, the Russian journal of soil science
soil-found-104.text: Pochvovedenie is a Russian journal of soil science, read abroad in English translation as Eurasian Soil Science. Its pages carried an early argument about the field's own origins. In a 1904 article there, its editor Arseny Yarilov, the bibliographer of Russian soil science, hailed Fallou as the founder of soil science.

soil-hist-057.title: The Soil Science Society of Poland
soil-hist-057.text: In 1937 Feliks Terlikowski, Jan Włodek and Tadeusz Mieczyński founded the society of Polish soil scientists, the Polskie Towarzystwo Gleboznawcze. It promotes soil science, pedology, agricultural chemistry and agricultural microbiology in Poland. In 2017 it had about 450 members in 14 regional and 4 thematic divisions. A member of the IUSS, it publishes Soil Science Annual, founded in 1950 as Roczniki Gleboznawcze. It also produces {{ref:soil-class-034}}, whose 5th edition appeared in 2011 and 6th in 2019.

soil-hist-052.title: How the United States began mapping its soils
soil-hist-052.text: American soil survey began with $16,000. Milton Whitney started field work on May 3, 1899, mapping about 720,000 acres that year in tobacco lands and alkali areas. The first surveyors, geologists or chemists, split soils mainly by texture and grouped soil types into series. {{ref:soil-hist-009}}, in charge from 1913, drew on Glinka's Russian school. He came to treat soil science as separate from geology and to describe soils by horizons. After years of clashes over methods, all USDA survey work was consolidated under the Soil Conservation Service in 1952.

soil-hist-055.title: The International Humic Substances Society and its reference samples
soil-hist-055.text: Coal, soil and water scientists share an interest in the same dark organic matter. On September 11, 1981, in Denver, Colorado, they founded the International Humic Substances Society to study it. The society researches natural organic matter in soil and water, the {{ref:soil-chem-058}} at its core. It keeps standard samples of humic and fulvic acids from leonardite, river water, a mineral soil and peat. Scientists in about 40 countries use them. It also backs standard lab methods and holds biennial conferences. As of 2023 it had about 450 members in 24 chapters.

soil-hist-078.title: The Soil Science Society of America Journal
soil-hist-078.text: The Soil Science Society of America Journal is the bimonthly, peer-reviewed flagship of {{ref:soil-hist-048}}, covering every aspect of soil science. It began in 1937 as Soil Science Society of America Proceedings, with J. D. Luckett as founding editor. It took its present title in 1973. Since 2013 it has appeared only online, and its articles undergo double-blind review, so neither authors nor reviewers know each other's names.

soil-found-113.title: The Journal of Soil and Water Conservation
soil-found-113.text: Conservation is a science, a practice and a policy, and one journal covers all three. The Journal of Soil and Water Conservation is a bimonthly, peer-reviewed journal on {{ref:soil-agri-059}} and the protection of water. The Soil and Water Conservation Society publishes it.

soil-hist-056.title: ICOMANTH and the soils that people make
soil-hist-056.text: From 1995 to 2013 a committee worked on a question older systems had skirted: how to classify soils made by human activity. It was the International Committee on Anthropogenic Soils, or ICOMANTH. Ray Bryant chaired it at its founding, and John Galbraith succeeded him in 2004. According to the NRCS, its main contribution was better standards for describing these soils and defining the taxa to classify them. The NRCS judged its task complete. In 2014 several of its proposals entered {{ref:soil-class-006}}.

soil-hist-054.title: The European Soil Bureau Network
soil-hist-054.text: Europe's soil problems cross borders, from agrochemical leaching and heavy metals to waste disposal, erosion and lost soil structure. In 1996 the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in Ispra created the European Soil Bureau Network to meet them. It links national soil science institutions as 'Centres of Excellence' that collect and harmonise soil information for Europe. Staff of the JRC's Land Management Unit run it and host its secretariat. They give the Commission a central source of soil information, feeding {{ref:soil-found-069}}.

soil-hist-059.title: Lunar regolith, the gunpowder-scented ground of the Moon
soil-hist-059.text: The Moon's finest dust reportedly tastes and smells of spent gunpowder. It belongs to the lunar regolith, the loose, unconsolidated material that covers the Moon's surface. Lunar soil usually means grains 1 cm across or less, and lunar dust the still finer fraction, under one millimeter. Earth's soils form through oxygen, water and life. The Moon's form by mechanical weathering instead, as impacts and charged particles from the Sun and interstellar space grind basaltic and anorthositic rock ever finer. By mass, half the soil is finer than 60–80 μm. Its density is about 1.5 g/cm³ and rises with depth. Seven elements make up 98–99% of it, led by oxygen at 41–45%. Its makeup follows the local bedrock, so it divides into highland and mare regolith. Plagioclase, olivine, pyroxenes and impact-melt glass dominate, with ice in permanently shaded craters. The fine grains are sharp, very sticky and electrically charged. Yet this hostile powder could become building material, such as {{ref:soil-hist-082}}, or a medium for growing plants.

soil-hist-067.title: Martian regolith, studied from afar under a rusty sky
soil-hist-067.text: No one has yet carried a scoop of Mars back to Earth. Everything known about its regolith, the fine blanket of loose, varied deposits covering the planet, comes from rovers and orbiters. Mars is covered with sand and dust and littered with rocks. Planet-wide storms lift fine dust that stays aloft and tints the sky reddish, the color of rusted iron minerals. Olivine, which weathers easily, is still present, so physical rather than chemical weathering seems to dominate now. Water and carbon dioxide ices are thought to lie frozen in the ground, and the Mars Odyssey orbiter measured water up to 5% by weight. In June 2008 the Phoenix lander found the soil basic, at pH 8.3, with nutrients such as magnesium, sodium, potassium and chloride. On October 17, 2012, Curiosity's first X-ray diffraction found feldspar, pyroxenes and olivine. The mix resembles the weathered basaltic soils of Hawaiian volcanoes. Researchers on Earth rely on stand-in materials such as Exolith Lab's MGS-1, and sample-return missions beginning with Mars 2020 should make them more accurate.

soil-hist-071.title: Fake moon soil, and the surprise it failed to predict
soil-hist-071.text: Before Apollo, crushed Earth rocks stood in for lunar soil. Some differed greatly from the real thing, and the Moon's pervasive sharp, fine dust came as a surprise. A lunar regolith simulant is an Earth material made to copy the Moon's regolith in its chemistry, mechanics, engineering behavior, minerals or particle sizes. Real samples are scarce, small and tainted by Earth's air, so researchers test digging and handling on simulants. Later simulants such as MLS-1 and JSC-1 came in highland and mare types., crushed and sieved from anorthosite or basalt to match Apollo and Luna samples. NASA and the Johnson Space Center developed JSC-1 in 1994 from a glass-rich basaltic ash. A version called JSC-1A, mixed into an alkaline solution, sets into a rock-like material as strong as conventional cements. The lunar scientist Larry Taylor criticized many simulants for poor quality control and money wasted on features with no documented purpose. Newer ones include Exolith Lab's LHS-1 and LMS-1, and LSS-ISAC1 from the Indian Space Research Organisation for its Chandrayaan program.

soil-hist-058.title: Astropedology, soil science for deep time and other worlds
soil-hist-058.text: Soil science has started looking up. Astropedology is the branch of pedology that studies very ancient paleosols, meteorites relevant to the origin of life, and soil systems on other planets. Its aim is to understand Earth's place in the universe. If soil is a planetary surface altered in place by biological, chemical or physical processes, a sharp question follows for Martian soils and old paleosols: were they alive? Work on other worlds has already changed the basics at home. Better understanding of soil formation elsewhere had an effect. In 2017 it helped lead the Soil Science Society of America to define soil as loose material altered at or near a planetary surface. The study of ancient soils underpins both this field, now reaching into exoplanet research, and the reconstruction of Earth's ancient ecosystems. Astropedology symposia are a new focus of soil science meetings.

soil-hist-079.title: Space weathering, the slow aging of airless worlds
soil-hist-079.text: With no air to shield them, the Moon, Mercury and the asteroids take the full force of space. Space weathering is the weathering of any object exposed to that harsh environment. Cosmic rays strike these airless bodies. The solar wind irradiates their surfaces, implants particles in them and sputters atoms away. Meteorites and micrometeorites bombard them. Much of what is known comes from lunar soils returned by Apollo. There, impacts and particles comminute, or crush, the soil, and also melt, sputter and vaporize it. Micrometeorite melt welds glass and mineral fragments into agglutinates, clumps that make up as much as 60 to 70% of mature lunar soils. Iron-bearing minerals such as olivine and pyroxene vaporize, then redeposit tiny blebs of metallic nanophase iron in agglutinates and in thin rims on grains. The effect shows from afar. As lunar soil matures it grows darker and redder, and its absorption bands grow shallower, so the bright rays of young craters fade with time. Reading remotely sensed data from planetary surfaces therefore requires understanding this process. On asteroids it works more slowly, yet grains that Hayabusa returned from Itokawa show definite alteration. Mercury should take a far harder beating. Impacts there are expected to make 13.5 times the melt and 19.5 times the vapor per unit area as on the Moon.

soil-hist-061.title: Moon dust, a hazard to machines and lungs
soil-hist-061.text: Apollo crews came in from moonwalks with coughs, throat irritation, watery eyes and blurred vision, though the symptoms cleared within 24 hours. Fine lunar dust is easily disturbed, and it can harm both equipment and crews. It darkens surfaces so they absorb more heat, abrades materials by friction, and degrades seals, lenses, solar panels, windows and wiring. In the lungs, reactive particles may cause respiratory disease, and long exposure possibly a disease similar to silicosis. A 2005 NASA study ranked dust the top challenge to study before a human Mars expedition, and its concerns apply equally to the Moon.

soil-hist-062.title: Bringing the Moon home, a few kilograms at a time
soil-hist-062.text: Apollo astronauts brought back some 360 kg of lunar rocks from six landing sites. Every returned sample carries a flaw. Earth's air and humidity contaminated the dust, which rusted and lost its chemical reactivity, so it no longer matches conditions on the Moon. After 1972 no new samples arrived until 16 December 2020. That day China's Chang'e 5 returned about 2 kg of lunar rock and soil, making China the third country to do so. In 2024 Chang'e 6 went further, returning samples from the far side of the Moon.

soil-hist-060.title: How the Moon makes soil without water or life
soil-hist-060.text: Lunar soil forms at a crawl. Crater production rates suggest it takes about 81 thousand years to overturn just the top 2 cm. This making and remaking is a case of {{ref:soil-hist-079}}. Each soil begins as a coarse, poorly sorted blanket of debris thrown out by impacts. Micrometeoroids then grind it finer, weld fragments into agglutinates with impact-melt glass, and add metallic iron, darkening it over time. Solar wind sputtering and cosmic ray spallation, which knocks fragments off atoms, keep altering the grains. Lava fire fountains also left glass beads, such as the orange soil Apollo 17 found at Shorty Crater and Apollo 15's green glass.

soil-hist-069.title: Perchlorates, the salts that make Martian soil toxic
soil-hist-069.text: The soil of Mars is laced with poison. In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander first found perchlorates there, chlorine-bearing salts such as calcium perchlorate. Later landers and the Mars Odyssey orbiter showed they are spread across the planet. Levels of around 0.5% in the regolith are considered toxic to humans, and even trace amounts interfere with the thyroid. One source puts the level on Mars at 0.05% by weight. In a 2013 study, 0.5 g per liter of perchlorate cut leaf chlorophyll, root oxidizing power and plant size, and the salts built up in the leaves. The water hyacinth Eichhornia crassipes tolerated them and could help remove them. With no ozone layer, ultraviolet light reaches the ground and makes perchlorates more lethal to bacteria, while soil iron oxides and hydrogen peroxide add to their toxicity. Yet some bacteria adapt to perchlorate or even live off it. A NASA-funded project from 2022 is studying Dehalococcoides mccartyi to break the salts into chlorides and oxygen. Perchlorates may also make the organic molecules linked to life harder to detect.

soil-hist-083.title: Living off the land on the Moon and Mars
soil-hist-083.text: Future crews could lighten what they launch from Earth by living off the land. In situ resource utilization means collecting, processing and using materials found on the Moon, Mars or other bodies, in place of materials brought from home. It could supply life support, propellants, construction materials and energy. Anyone settling a planet or moon will need local building materials such as regolith. Water bound in regolith, ice or permafrost can be recovered by heating, though ice and permafrost may be harder than rock to mine. Heating lunar regolith above 900 °C in hydrogen gas pulls oxygen out of its iron oxide.

soil-hist-068.title: Is there soil on the Moon? It depends on the definition
soil-hist-068.text: Whether the Moon has soil depends on who is asked. Earth's usual definition includes organic content, which may not fit other worlds, and sources still disagree on what should replace it. Planetary scientists use a functional rule. Fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles on the Wentworth scale, are rocks, and all other, typically loose material is soil. Planetary scientists also often adopt "medium for plant growth". A fuller definition calls soil any altered surface material that records its environmental history, with no life needed. Under Earth systems, many such soils would be Entisols in Soil Taxonomy or Regosols in the WRB, but applying those systems to such different settings is debatable. An alternative would put all non-Earth soils in a new group, tentatively called Astrosols.

soil-hist-070.title: Martian dust, lifted again and again
soil-hist-070.text: On Mars, dust that settles rarely stays put. Martian dust is the finest fraction of the regolith, under 30 micrometers across, and much of it rides in the atmosphere as particles about 3 μm across. On Earth, soil moisture and oceans gather settled dust into larger particles. Neither works on Mars, so deposited dust is free to rise again. Dust from the 2001 global storms stayed aloft only 0.6 years, against about two years for Mount Pinatubo's. Plagioclase feldspar and zeolite dominate it, which suggests it is ground mechanically from basaltic rock with little chemical alteration. One study found that it reacts with water to form highly reactive molecules, like those that cause lung disease in quartz miners.

soil-hist-082.title: Lunarcrete, concrete made from the Moon itself
soil-hist-082.text: Lunarcrete is a proposed concrete-like material made from lunar regolith to cut the cost of construction there. Like concrete it would use aggregate, water and cement, with regolith as the aggregate and cement from calcium-rich lunar rock. In 1986 Lin and colleagues made lunarcrete from 40 g of Apollo 16 regolith, and it withstood 75 MPa of compression. A waterless version binds regolith simulant with sulfur. A mix of 65% JSC-1 simulant and 35% sulfur averaged 33.8 MPa. A stranger recipe, AstroCrete, proposed for the Moon or Mars, binds regolith with human serum albumin, a protein from blood.

soil-hist-081.title: Making Mars soil on Earth
soil-hist-081.text: The first stand-in for Mars soil came from Hawaii. JSC Mars-1, made at NASA's Johnson Space Center in 1998, was palagonitic tephra: volcanic ash altered at low temperature. A Martian regolith simulant mimics the chemistry and mechanics of Martian regolith for research and prototype testing. Mojave Mars Simulant, from 2007, was crushed basalt with minimal weathering, so unlike the clay-like JSC Mars-1 it did not attract water. From 2018, MGS-1 became the first mineralogically accurate simulant, a mix of pure minerals matched to the Rocknest soil analyzed by Curiosity in Gale crater. No simulant includes the perchlorates Phoenix found in 2008, though users can add the salts. Their fine particles and crystalline silica pose some health risk.

soil-hist-080.title: Impact gardening, how meteorites till the Moon
soil-hist-080.text: The Moon's soil is tilled, but by meteorites rather than plows. Airless moons and similar bodies have almost no erosion, so impact debris builds up at the surface as a rough soil, the regolith. Later impacts, especially by micrometeorites, stir and mix it. This is impact gardening, called lunar gardening on the Moon. The top centimeter of the Moon was long thought to overturn every 10 million years. A 2016 LRO study of impact ejecta put it closer to 80,000 years.

soil-hist-065.title: Archean paleosols and early Earth's hints of soil life
soil-hist-065.text: Soils formed 3.42 to 3.46 billion years ago may carry faint signs of life. Archean paleosols are soils preserved from early Earth's Archean eon, and they give circumstantial evidence of life in soils at that time. Profiles from the Pilbara region of northwestern Australia show distinct depletion of phosphorus. Sulfates may hold another clue. Sulfur bacteria commonly oxidize sulfur to sulfates such as gypsum and barite, minerals of today's acid sulfate soils. Their work is a possible reason for sulfate build-up in Archean paleosols.

soil-hist-064.title: Can a garden grow in moon dust?
soil-hist-064.text: Lunar and Martian soils appear to hold every essential plant mineral in sufficient amounts, with one possible exception. Reactive nitrogen may be short, since Mars Pathfinder could not detect it. Nitrogen-fixing species could make up the shortfall, but fixation needs nitrogen from the air, absent on the Moon and only a trace on Mars. In a large controlled experiment, plants germinated and grew for 50 days on Mars and Moon soil simulants without added nutrients., doing much better on the Mars simulant. Plants struggle in real lunar soil, so long missions may need imported Earth soil, chemically treated regolith or plants bred for it.

soil-hist-063.title: Ancient soils on Mars, and the open question of life
soil-hist-063.text: In Gale Crater, the Curiosity rover found features much like Earth's soil horizons and structures. They included blocky angular peds, sand wedges, a shallow gypsic horizon and vesicular structure. These are Martian paleosols, ancient soils recognized by rovers and orbiters. The Yellowknife Bay paleosols, about 3.7 billion years old, show olivine weathering to smectite. They record a shift from possibly warm and wet to extremely cold and arid. Orbiters have detected phyllosilicate clays at thousands of sites dated to 4.0–3.7 billion years ago. Either hydrothermal activity or surface weathering and soil formation could explain them. Vesicular structures like those made by microbial gas in Earth's desert soils occur on Mars, but definitive evidence of life there is still lacking.

soil-hist-066.title: Was life born in the soil?
soil-hist-066.text: Life may have begun in the ground. On this idea, water held between clay grains forms countless microscopic reaction chambers where life evolved. These chambers may also promote the making of organic compounds by mechanisms shown in the Miller–Urey experiment. Soil would have kept the process going. Clayey and organic soils resist erosion, so they keep producing clay and organic matter, and early single-celled life would also have bound the soil. The idea extends {{ref:soil-chem-083}}. And the weathering cycle still supplies the ingredients that life requires.

soil-meth-029.title: Gas chromatography, sorting compounds as vapor
soil-meth-029.text: Some chemicals can be turned into vapor without breaking apart, and that is all gas chromatography needs. It is a way of separating a mixture, here made of compounds that vaporize without decomposing, and then analysing each part. Among the {{ref:soil-chem-078}}, it measures chemicals in soil, air or water, including the gases held in soil. It also works inside other instruments. The Dumas nitrogen method, described in {{ref:soil-meth-021}}, ends with a gas chromatography column that pulls nitrogen apart from carbon dioxide and water.

soil-meth-021.title: Burning soil to learn what it is made of
soil-meth-021.text: One quick way to learn what a soil contains is to set it on fire. Elemental analysis measures the elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition of a material such as soil. Its commonest form, CHNS analysis, for carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and sulfur, works by combustion: the sample burns and the oxidized products are measured. CHN analyzers borrow the flash combustion of the Dumas method. A sample burns at 800–900 °C in oxygen, {{ref:soil-meth-029}} separates the released nitrogen, and a thermal conductivity or infrared detector reads it. Each Dumas measurement takes a few minutes and uses no toxic chemicals or catalysts. The older {{ref:soil-meth-020}} takes an hour or more.

soil-meth-024.title: Reading a soil's elements in the glow of a plasma
soil-meth-024.text: Inside the instrument burns a plasma of argon at 6000 to 10,000 K. Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy, shortened to ICP-AES or ICP-OES, uses that heat to excite atoms and ions until they emit light. Each element shines at its own wavelengths, and the intensity there is proportional to its concentration. A pump feeds the sample to a nebulizer, which sprays it as a mist directly into the plasma. Detector arrays read all the wavelengths at once, so every element the unit can sense is analysed together, and quickly. Comparing line intensities with calibration curves of known standards gives the concentrations. The method has largely replaced older ones such as gravimetric analysis for routine trace work on many elements. It is fast becoming the method of choice for nutrient levels in farm soils. In a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}, those levels set the fertilizer a crop needs for yield and quality. Its skill with trace elements even helps forensic scientists trace the origin of soil found at crime scenes.

soil-meth-023.title: Atomic absorption: metals caught by the light they absorb
soil-meth-023.text: Each metal absorbs light only at its own wavelengths. Atomic absorption spectroscopy uses this to measure the concentration of metals in a sample. The metals are vaporized in a flame, and the radiation each absorbs is proportional to the density of its atoms. Alan Walsh's team at CSIRO in Melbourne developed the modern form in the 1950s, and it now serves fields from agriculture to medicine. Soil extracts from batch equilibration are commonly analysed this way. The flame version works in the mg/L range; the graphite-furnace version is 2–3 orders of magnitude more sensitive.

soil-meth-019.title: Loss on ignition: weighing what the furnace takes away
soil-meth-019.text: A furnace and a balance are all this test needs. In a loss-on-ignition test, a soil or mineral sample is heated strongly at a set temperature until its mass stops changing. The weight lost measures the volatile components driven off. A few grams go into a crucible weighed empty and already fired. They are weighed, heated in a temperature-controlled furnace for a set time, cooled in a dry, CO2-free atmosphere and weighed again. Left overnight in a drying oven at 100 °C, a sample loses all its water, which gives its dry weight and so its original water content. The test typically estimates water, carbon, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and volatile compounds. Samples burned down a profile show the organic content at each depth. A sudden rise down the profile, with other clues, is strong evidence of a buried soil surface invisible to the eye. Weighing continuously as the temperature changes is a variant called thermogravimetry.

soil-meth-020.title: The Kjeldahl method: nitrogen from a flask of boiling acid
soil-meth-020.text: Measuring nitrogen the slow way starts with a flask of hot acid. The Kjeldahl method is a wet-chemistry test, done with liquid reagents, that measures the organic nitrogen plus the ammonia and ammonium in a sample. The sample is digested in concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C. The acid oxidizes the organic matter and holds the reduced nitrogen as ammonium sulfate. Catalysts such as selenium, Hg2SO4 or CuSO4 speed the digestion, and Na2SO4 or K2SO4 raises the acid's boiling point. Sodium hydroxide then turns the ammonium into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration. The result, total Kjeldahl nitrogen or TKN, is reported in analyses of soil, water and waste water. Besides foods, the method assays soils, waste waters and fertilizers. Without modification it misses other inorganic nitrogen such as nitrate. Its hot concentrated acid and an hour or more per test compare poorly with the faster Dumas method in {{ref:soil-meth-021}}.

soil-meth-025.title: ICP-MS, counting ions down to parts per quadrillion
soil-meth-025.text: Its range starts at 1 part per quadrillion and runs up to 100 ppm. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, or ICP-MS, ionizes a sample in the same kind of plasma as {{ref:soil-meth-024}}, then counts the resulting ions. That lets it detect metals and some non-metals at very low concentrations. It covers atomic masses 7 to 250, lithium to uranium, and tells isotopes apart. It is faster, more precise and more sensitive than {{ref:soil-meth-023}}, and it scans all elements at once. Its uses run from water testing to soil analysis. Measuring Fe2+ and Fe3+ in ancient rocks even reveals the redox potential of ancient soils.

soil-meth-026.title: Ion chromatography, sorting ions by their grip
soil-meth-026.text: This separation method traces back to clay. Thompson and Way treated clays with fertilizer salts and found ammonia retained and calcium released, the swap now called {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. Ion chromatography turns that swap into a tool. It separates ions and ionizable molecules by their affinity for an ion exchanger. Anion-exchange columns carry a positive stationary phase, the fixed material inside, that holds negative ions. Cation-exchange columns carry a negative one that holds positive ions. It is a popular method for anions and complexes in environmental problems, and one of the methods used to analyse soil extracts.

soil-meth-018.title: Fine earth: the part of soil 2 mm and smaller
soil-meth-018.text: Soil scientists draw a line at 2 mm. The particles that size or smaller make up the fine earth fraction; coarser pieces such as {{ref:soil-phys-044}} fall outside it. In the {{ref:soil-class-016}}, the whole soil is the fine earth plus coarse fragments, artefacts, cemented parts and dead plant residues of any size. Many of its horizon criteria are percentages by volume related to the fine earth, such as the share of rock structure in an A or B horizon. On granite in cool climates, feldspars weather slowly and sand comes to dominate it. Its makeup also shapes {{ref:soil-found-051}}: a loam can lose its desirable qualities when clay is dispersed throughout its fine earth.

soil-meth-027.title: Ion-selective electrodes turn one ion into a voltage
soil-meth-027.text: A thin membrane can turn chemistry into electricity. An ion-selective electrode is a membrane sensor that converts the activity of one specific ion in solution into an electrical potential. The pH glass electrode is a very common type. The voltage is read against a reference electrode, and it depends on the logarithm of the ion's activity, following the Nernst equation. These electrodes are among the methods used to analyse soil extracts, and they serve environmental science and agriculture. They have one weakness. Readings drift with temperature and time, so they need frequent recalibration against standards, ideally before and after each sample.

soil-meth-022.title: Ammonium acetate, the cation that evicts the others
soil-meth-022.text: To count the cations a soil holds, chemists first push them off. Ammonium acetate extraction does that job. The ammonium ion acts as a replacement cation, taking over exchange sites and displacing potassium and the other bound cations. The extract serves to measure {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and available potassium. Ammonium is one of the cations used most often for this in {{ref:soil-chem-051}}. The chemistry hides a catch. A pure ammonium acetate solution has a pH of about 7, yet it buffers only around pH 4.75 and 9.25, not at pH 7.

soil-meth-028.title: Phosphorus turns blue: the molybdenum test
soil-meth-028.text: Phosphate can be made to turn a solution blue, and the depth of blue tells how much is there. In the molybdenum blue test, phosphate is mixed with an acid molybdate solution, and the complex is reduced to its blue form, for example by ascorbic acid. The color's depth is proportional to the phosphorus concentration. However phosphorus leaves the soil for solution, it is usually detected this way. Labs use a colorimeter; field workers use detector sticks and a color chart. Comparable amounts of arsenate spoil the test, since arsenate behaves much like phosphate. Mapped on archaeological plans, soil phosphate shows former activity areas and helps prospect for sites.

soil-meth-030.title: The soil thin section, a slice thin enough for light
soil-meth-030.text: Ground down to about 30 μm, a slice of soil lets light straight through. A soil thin section is such a slice of rock, mineral or soil, mounted on glass for study under a polarizing microscope. Soil micromorphology describes far more in it than a 10x hand lens can show. Between crossed polarizing filters, the optical properties of minerals alter the color and intensity of the light, so most rock-forming minerals can be identified. Quartz usually serves as the gauge of thickness, checked against the Michel-Lévy interference color chart. Thin sections reveal how a material's components relate to one another, features often invisible in a hand specimen. Micromorphologists have used them to characterize humus-form horizons. They also help identify paleosols: at least 60% recognizable pyroclastic fragments marks an Andisol paleosol.

soil-meth-031.title: Soil biofabric, the pellets left by ants and worms
soil-meth-031.text: Ants, worms and termites leave their signature in the soil's fabric. Soil biofabric is fabric made by organisms, typically small, often pelleted micro- and mesobiofabric, visible with a hand lens or in a {{ref:soil-meth-030}}. It is the mark of {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. As originally defined, a {{ref:soil-form-055}} must show at least 50% biofabric. Burrowing vertebrates and uprooted trees make something coarser: megabiofabric, cloddy surface spoil heaps for which the 50% criterion is moot.

soil-meth-032.title: Minerals that turn cloudy as they weather
soil-meth-032.text: Under the microscope, weathering shows itself in each grain. Mineral alteration is the change natural processes make to a mineral's chemical composition or crystal structure, as seen in a {{ref:soil-meth-030}}. Some minerals, such as feldspar, decompose readily and turn turbid. Quartz stays fresh and clear. Others yield characteristic secondary products. Thermodynamics governs the alteration under the prevailing conditions, and water is its most common and influential catalyst.

soil-meth-008.title: Geomorphometry, measuring the shape of the land
soil-meth-008.text: Water flows downhill, so the shape of the land can predict where streams will run. Geomorphometry is the science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes. It works from digital elevation models, grids of ground heights, and extracts parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms. The most basic are slope, how steep the surface is, and aspect, the direction the slope faces. Slope is computed by discrete derivatives; the Horn method uses a cell and its eight neighbors. Thanks largely to the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and lidar, elevation models now cover almost all of Earth at 100 m resolution or better. The ideas go back to Brisson in 1808 and Gauss in 1827. The field grew mainly with GIS, geographic information systems, and elevation data sets from the 1970s. Its parameters improve the mapping and modeling of soils, serving {{ref:soil-agri-089}}, precision agriculture and soil-landscape modeling.

soil-meth-014.title: Ground-penetrating radar, echoes from buried layers
soil-meth-014.text: Radar can see into the ground, but how far depends on the soil. Ground-penetrating radar sends radio waves, usually between 10 MHz and 2.6 GHz, and records their reflections from buried boundaries, such as the edge of a {{ref:soil-found-001}}. Reflections occur where materials of different permittivity, an electrical property, meet. In dry sandy soils it reaches up to 15 m; in moist or clay-rich soils, only a few centimeters. Clay soils and salt-contaminated soils limit it most, and rocky soils scatter the signal. Higher frequencies trade penetration for resolution. It is used to study soils and bedrock, and cross-borehole radar assesses the presence and amount of soil water.

soil-meth-015.title: Electrical resistivity tomography, imaging soil with current
soil-meth-015.text: A line of four electrodes can look underground. In electrical resistivity tomography, current passes between the two outer electrodes and voltage is read between the inner two. A geometric factor converts the result to apparent resistivity. As {{ref:soil-phys-042}} showed, wetter soil is less resistive, and dry and saturated soil can differ by orders of magnitude. Clays conduct through their charged particle surfaces as well as their pore water. Electrode spacings of 0.75 to 12.0 m serve shallow surveys under 10 m, and depth is usually less than the widest spacing. It maps soil moisture for precision agriculture, images root zones and tracks contaminants in soil and groundwater.

soil-meth-011.title: Multispectral imaging: a few bands beyond sight
soil-meth-011.text: A single image can show water depth, vegetation cover and soil moisture at once. Multispectral imaging captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light. Mid-infrared bands at 1550–1750 nm image vegetation and soil moisture. Far-infrared bands at 2080–2350 nm image soil, silicates and clays. Surface and subsurface soil differ spectrally. Disturbed soil emits more at 8.5 to 9.5 micrometers, which helps detect buried land mines. {{ref:soil-meth-012}} goes further, often with hundreds of contiguous bands.

soil-meth-012.title: Hyperspectral imaging, a full spectrum in every pixel
soil-meth-012.text: Every material leaves a characteristic spectral signature, and that signature can identify it. Where {{ref:soil-meth-011}} records a handful of bands, hyperspectral imaging records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel. Sensors on aircraft, satellites or drones use it to investigate plants and soils remotely, assessing ground cover and soil chemistry. In farming it is being used to detect the nutrient and water status of wheat and heavy-metal stress in plants. It is often treated as a surface technique, yet it can probe beneath the surface, to a depth set by the spectral range and the sample.

soil-meth-010.title: NDVI: reading plant health in red and near-infrared light
soil-meth-010.text: Healthy leaves absorb visible light and throw back near-infrared. Chlorophyll strongly absorbs light from 400 to 700 nm, while leaf cell structure strongly reflects near-infrared from 700 to 1100 nm. The normalized difference vegetation index, or NDVI, turns that contrast in red and near-infrared bands of {{ref:soil-meth-011}} into a measure of vegetation health and density. Values run from -1 to 1. Near zero means little or no vegetation, negative means water, and high means dense healthy vegetation. Bare soils give about 0.1 to 0.2. Because wet soil darkens, a change in soil moisture can shift the index with no change in vegetation. The soil-adjusted and enhanced vegetation indices correct for such soil background effects.

soil-meth-005.title: Why no two spots in a field are alike
soil-meth-005.text: A field known down to the last grain would still vary from spot to spot. Spatial variability is the way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place. It is not the same as uncertainty. Uncertainty depends on how the field was sampled as well as on how much it varies. Spatial descriptive statistics such as the range can describe variability. Those descriptions carry uncertainty of their own, since interpolation methods differ. {{ref:soil-meth-001}} has been used to study how the sorption and degradation of a {{ref:soil-env-237}} vary across a field. Precision agriculture studies variability within fields, such as how terrain and soil properties affect crop growth and water distribution. Urban landscapes and golf courses show high variability in soil composition, unlike uniform farm fields.

soil-meth-001.title: Geostatistics, from ore mines to farm fields
soil-meth-001.text: This branch of statistics began underground, as a way to predict the distribution of ore grades in mines. Geostatistics deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data, and it now serves soil science and agriculture, especially precision farming. Simpler interpolators such as {{ref:soil-meth-007}} came first. Geostatistics goes further by treating values at unsampled places as correlated random variables. A model of spatial continuity, often a parametric form of the {{ref:soil-meth-002}}, describes how strongly nearby values constrain the value at an unsampled point. Using one model across a whole area assumes stationarity, the same statistical properties everywhere; several methods relax that assumption. The work serves two goals. One is estimating the most likely value at each place. The other is simulating many alternative maps, called realizations, that together give probabilistic forecasts. Bayesian inference plays a growing part, implementing {{ref:soil-meth-003}} through a Gaussian process updated with Bayes' theorem.

soil-meth-002.title: The variogram: how difference grows with distance
soil-meth-002.text: Soil samples taken far apart vary more than samples taken close together. The variogram puts a number on that pattern, and it is the key tool of {{ref:soil-meth-001}}. It is a graph or function of how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them. Matheron defined the semivariogram in 1963 as half the average squared difference between values a distance h apart, such as the iron content of soil. Since nobody can sample everywhere, an empirical variogram is built from the squared differences between every pair of sample points. It is not guaranteed to be valid, so a model is fitted to it, most often linear, spherical, Gaussian or exponential. Three features summarize it. The nugget is a jump at the origin, and the sill is its limit at large distances. The range is where it nears the sill, often taken as 95% of it. The fitted model sets the weights used in {{ref:soil-meth-003}}. Usage is muddled: some authors call the semivariogram a variogram, and the word semivariance can mislead.

soil-meth-006.title: Filling the gaps between sample points
soil-meth-006.text: No survey can measure every point, so the gaps are filled by estimate. Spatial interpolation estimates the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points. Geostatistics uses it to build digital elevation models from spot heights or survey depths. For scattered points the methods include nearest-neighbor and natural-neighbor schemes, {{ref:soil-meth-007}}, variants of {{ref:soil-meth-003}}, and thin-plate or other splines. Gridding converts irregularly spaced data into a regular grid. GIS software produces interpolated surfaces with methods like these, and with trend surfaces.

soil-meth-003.title: Kriging, the best guess between boreholes
soil-meth-003.text: It started with a few boreholes in South Africa's Witwatersrand. Danie Krige's thesis estimated gold grades from them, and Georges Matheron built on it to set out the theory of kriging in 1960. Kriging predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance. The weights come from the fitted {{ref:soil-meth-002}}. Under suitable assumptions it gives the best linear unbiased prediction, or BLUP. Ordinary kriging picks weights that minimize the mean squared error, and they sum to 1 so the estimate is unbiased. Its estimation variance grows as samples lie farther from the target point. That variance depends on the sampling layout, not on the sample values. Only one realization of the random function is ever observed, so kriging must assume some degree of stationarity. Variants include simple, ordinary, universal and indicator kriging, and co-kriging of related variables. The basic form is computationally heavy, but approximations scale it to larger problems.

soil-meth-004.title: Regression-kriging: letting terrain and satellites guide the map
soil-meth-004.text: Part of a soil property's pattern follows the landscape, and part behaves like chance. Regression-kriging models the two separately, as Matheron's 1969 {{ref:soil-agri-093}} proposed. It first regresses the target variable on auxiliary layers, such as terrain from {{ref:soil-meth-008}} and remote-sensing images, fitting the trend by ordinary or generalized least squares. The leftover residuals are interpolated by {{ref:soil-meth-003}} and added back. The method is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift. With no spatial autocorrelation it reduces to multiple regression; with no useful covariates, to ordinary kriging. Odeh and colleagues named it in 1995, and Minasny and McBratney call it the empirical BLUP. It maps soil properties wherever covariate layers correlate significantly with the property. Those layers keep multiplying, from near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission to MODIS images at 250 m. Yet Minasny and McBratney found that more, better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.

soil-meth-007.title: Inverse distance weighting, a freshman's fix
soil-meth-007.text: In 1968 Donald Shepard, a Harvard freshman, was overhauling the interpolation in the SYMAP mapping program. The method he published, inverse distance weighting, estimates an unknown value as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance. Nearer points count for more, and no random model is involved. Shepard tested exponents of distance and settled near -2, close to the gravity model. It was among the simpler interpolators known before geostatistics. In Slovenia's Idrija area, it was used in GIS to turn soil samples into a raster map of mercury concentration.

soil-meth-009.title: The topographic wetness index: where hillslopes stay wet
soil-meth-009.text: Where a hillside gets soggy can be read from two quantities. The topographic wetness index combines the upslope area draining through a point, per unit contour length, with the local slope in radians, a basic product of {{ref:soil-meth-008}}. This steady-state index quantifies how topography controls hydrological processes. Areas with similar values become saturated under similar moisture conditions. Beven and Kirkby developed it within the TOPMODEL runoff model. It correlates highly with soil attributes such as horizon depth, silt percentage, organic matter content and phosphorus. It was designed for a hillslope {{ref:soil-form-054}}, and it is not meaningful on flat ground.

soil-meth-017.title: SoilGrids, a soil map of the whole world
soil-meth-017.text: The world's soil properties are now mapped in cells of 250 m. ISRIC produces those maps with SoilGrids, a system for automated global soil mapping. Machine learning fits models to the WoSIS database of soil profiles and to more than 400 global environmental covariates, and the maps come with quantified uncertainty. Like {{ref:soil-meth-004}}, it predicts soil properties from environmental layers. SoilGrids and the WoSIS database are ISRIC's flagship soil information products.

soil-meth-016.title: Mapping the soils of the Moon and Mars from orbit
soil-meth-016.text: Cosmic rays make the soils of the Moon and Mars shine in gamma rays. The rays strike nuclei in the soil, releasing neutrons and exciting nuclei that then emit gamma rays of characteristic energy. Orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers read those emissions. The energy of each line identifies an element, and its intensity gives the concentration; about 20 elements can be measured. Neutron detectors sense hydrogen in the upper meter, revealing water ice. Mars Odyssey carried one with two neutron detectors. The method fails for bodies with thick atmospheres, such as Earth and Venus.

soil-meth-013.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy, a quick scan for soil tests
soil-meth-013.text: Near-infrared light travels deep into a sample before it is absorbed. Near-infrared spectroscopy uses the part of the spectrum from 780 nm to 2500 nm, where absorption comes from weak overtone and combination vibrations. Because the light penetrates far, bulk material can be probed with little preparation. The bands are broad and overlap, so readings need multivariate calibration, such as principal components or partial least squares, built on carefully chosen calibration samples. Karl Norris at the USDA pioneered it for agricultural products in the 1980s. It is valued as accurate, rapid, non-destructive and inexpensive, and soil-testing laboratories may use near-infrared scanning in a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-phys-040.title: Why texture outranks color in the life of a crop
soil-phys-040.text: A farmer sizing up a field should care more about its grains than its color. The physical properties of soil are its measurable physical traits, and for crops they rank in a clear order. Texture comes first, then structure, {{ref:soil-phys-060}}, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. They change with depth through the soil's layers, and most govern aeration and how water enters and stays. Texture is the blend of coarse, medium and fine mineral grains. Coatings of oxides of iron ({{ref:soil-chem-163}}), carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind those grains into larger units, described in {{ref:soil-phys-003}}. Density with pores included, measured at a standard moisture, estimates compaction. Sandy soils drain fast, stay airy and warm quickly in spring, but hold little water and few nutrients. Clay soils store water and nutrients and resist pH change, yet drain very slowly and compact easily. Silty soils sit in between, and wind and rain carry them off easily.

soil-phys-015.title: One yardstick from clay specks to giant boulders
soil-phys-015.text: The finest clay and the largest boulder sit on a single scale. Engineers following ISO 14688-1 run it from clay at 0.002 mm or less to large boulders over 630 mm. That quantity is grain size: the diameter of individual grains of sediment. It also covers the particles cemented into clastic rocks, which are built from fragments of older rock. A grain is not the same as a crystal. Crystallite size is the size of a single crystal, and one grain can contain several. Above the tiny colloidal particles and clay, ever-coarser classes climb toward cobbles and boulders. The first of them is {{ref:soil-phys-013}}. The Udden-Wentworth scale, used in the United States, sets its named classes by size ranges. With texture and the spread of pore sizes, grain-size data help estimate {{ref:soil-water-193}}, the ease with which water flows through soil. One such rule of thumb is Allen Hazen's, covered in {{ref:soil-water-194}}.

soil-phys-014.title: Sand, the gritty grain that records its own journey
soil-phys-014.text: Every grain of sand carries a travel record. Sand is a granular material of finely divided mineral particles, defined mainly by grain size. Geologists set its grains between 0.0625 mm, or 1/16 mm, and 2 mm across. Freshly weathered quartz sand is angular. Grains carried far by water or wind become rounded, so their shape records origin and travel. Quartz, hard and chemically inert, is the commonest sand mineral inland and on non-tropical coasts. Calcium carbonate, such as aragonite made by coral and shellfish, comes second. US sand has five grades, from very fine at 1/16 to 1/8 mm to very coarse at 1 to 2 mm, based on {{ref:soil-phys-016}}. As a soil texture class, sand means more than 85 percent sand-sized particles by mass. Rubbed between the fingers, it feels gritty. Sandy soils drain very well and suit watermelons, peaches and peanuts. Angular sharp sand is even used to loosen clay soils.

soil-phys-013.title: Silt, the grain at the edge of eyesight
soil-phys-013.text: The unaided eye can just see a grain about 63 microns across. That marks the top of silt, a granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, mostly broken quartz. Geologists place it at about 4 to 63 microns; the USDA uses 0.05 to 0.002 mm. Near 2 to 4 microns, quartz fragments give way to {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. Dry silt feels floury, and wet silt will not hold a molded shape. Between the teeth it feels gritty, where clay feels smooth. Silt is made by grinding quartz, in dust storms of very hot climates and by glaciers in very cold ones. Wind-laid silt forms loess, some of the most fertile farmland on Earth. Its quartz adds no nutrients but helps soil build excellent structure. Silt erodes easily, has poor mechanical properties and can liquefy in earthquakes. Settling in still water, 60-micron grains fall a meter in five minutes; 2-micron grains take several days.

soil-phys-044.title: Gravel, the coarse rubble that water races through
soil-phys-044.text: Water can race through natural gravel at more than 1 cm/s. Gravel is a loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand. Its limits vary: many geologists say over 2 mm, the USDA says 2 to 80 mm, and the Udden-Wentworth scale 2 to 64 mm. Most gravel comes from weathering bedrock, and rivers round it quickly. Gravel deposits make aquifers, underground stores of water, but gravelly soils hold little moisture or nutrients. Texture tests remove fragments over 2.0 mm, yet the word "gravelly" stays in the soil's name.

soil-phys-047.title: Three bins for every grain: sand, silt and clay
soil-phys-047.text: Soil texture ignores anything wider than two millimeters. Everything finer is sorted into soil separates: set ranges of particle size called sand, silt and clay. The USDA draws the lines at fixed sizes. Clay particles are under 0.002 mm, silt runs from 0.002 to 0.05 mm, and sand is anything larger than 0.05 mm. Each bin splits further. USDA sand has five grades, from very fine sand at 0.05 to 0.10 mm up to very coarse sand at 1.00 to 2.00 mm. Silt divides into coarse and fine at 0.02 mm. Clay divides at 0.0002 mm, with fine clay at that size or less. Not every system agrees. The WRB system, for instance, puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm instead of 0.05 mm. Shape matters too. Clay particles are flat plates rather than spheres, which gives them far more surface for their mass, an idea explored in {{ref:soil-phys-043}}. The three separates behave very differently. Sand, with the least surface, is the least active; silt comes next, and clay is the most active. Water follows the same order. Sand holds little water and drains fast. Silt holds a medium to high amount and drains slowly to moderately. Clay holds a great deal and drains very slowly.

soil-phys-048.title: Albert Atterberg draws soil's first size lines
soil-phys-048.text: Soil's size classes began with studies in southern Sweden. In 1905 the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-011}} proposed the first particle-size classification, the international soil texture system. He capped silt at 20 μm for four reasons. Finer particles are invisible and clump together with salts. They also wick water upward fastest over 24 hours and leave pores too small for root hairs. Commission One of the International Society of Soil Science recommended it in 1927. Australia adopted it; its equal logarithmic size steps are seen as worth keeping. The USDA went its own way in 1938.

soil-phys-045.title: Twelve names for every blend of sand, silt and clay
soil-phys-045.text: Any soil's texture can be summed up in one name from a list of twelve. The USDA soil texture classes are those twelve named categories, assigned by a soil's percentages of sand, silt and clay. The names follow a simple logic. A class takes the name of its main particle size, or of a mix of the most abundant sizes. Sand, silt and clay each name a class of their own. Two more pair a couple of sizes, as in sandy clay and silty clay. The other seven use a fourth word for a soil with roughly equal properties of sand, silt and clay. That word stands alone or joins the others in compound names, as explained in {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Other systems count differently. The WRB also uses 12 textural classes, while the UK-ADAS system uses 11. The names earn their keep in the field. A texture class helps judge which crops suit a soil. It also predicts how the soil will respond to drought and how much lime, a source of calcium, it needs. Turning three percentages into one class takes a chart, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-046}}.

soil-phys-046.title: A triangle that turns three percentages into one name
soil-phys-046.text: Three numbers go in, and one name comes out. The soil texture triangle is a triangular chart whose three sides give percent sand, silt and clay. One side carries sand, another clay and the third silt. Once a sample's three percentages are known, the triangle assigns its texture class. The reading works starting from any side. On the USDA triangle, only one class has no dominant size among sand, silt and clay. That balanced class is the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. A soil with 70 percent sand and 10 percent clay, for example, plots in its sandy variant. The chart also runs backward, turning a class judged by hand into a rough estimate of the three percentages. That hand method is the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-049}}.

soil-phys-012.title: Loam, the balanced blend that farmers and gardeners prize
soil-phys-012.text: Farmers and gardeners prize one soil because it keeps water and nutrients yet lets the excess drain away. Loam is soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay. A typical loam is about 40 percent sand, 40 percent silt and 20 percent clay by weight. It is the only class on the USDA triangle not dominated by one size. Loams hold more nutrients, water and humus than sandy soils. They drain and aerate better than silty or clayey soils and till more easily than clays. Its subtypes, such as sandy loam, silt loam and clay loam, drain somewhat differently. Texture is not destiny. A soil dominated by one or two sizes can act like loam if organic matter gives it strong granular structure. A textural loam loses its virtues when compacted or stripped of organic matter. Most dictionaries, and many gardeners, simply call any soil containing humus loam.

soil-phys-049.title: Reading a soil's texture with thumb and forefinger
soil-phys-049.text: With practice, a hand can judge a soil's makeup with little or no equipment. Texture by feel is a qualitative field method that judges a soil's texture by moistening and working a small sample by hand. One test makes a ribbon. A moist ball of soil is pushed between thumb and forefinger into a ribbon that extends over the finger until it breaks. The unbroken length helps indicate how much clay the sample holds. A second test reads the sand. Rubbed wet in the palm, sandy soils feel gritty, silty soils smooth and clayey soils sticky. It gives no exact percentages, yet a trained person following its flowchart can judge relative proportions accurately. It takes practice, and the WRB offers an alternative flowchart of its own. Quick, frequent checks reveal how soil varies within and between fields. They also show where one soil map unit gives way to the next.

soil-phys-054.title: Two meanings of clay: a size and a mineral
soil-phys-054.text: The word clay hides two different ideas. One is a class of very fine particle sizes; the other is material made of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. The two overlap but differ. The size boundary with silt depends on the discipline: 2 μm for soil scientists, 4–5 μm for many sedimentologists, 1 μm for chemists who study {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size, using {{ref:soil-phys-021}}. A clay-sized grain may be very fine quartz, sharing clay's surface-area traits but not its {{ref:soil-chem-047}}, the holding of nutrients.

soil-phys-053.title: Why wet clay keeps any shape pressed into it
soil-phys-053.text: Press wet clay into a shape, and it stays put. That is plasticity, clay's defining mechanical property: the capacity, when wet, to be molded into a shape it then keeps. It comes from {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, whose thin plates are tough but flexible and cling together when moist. In {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, a film of water molecules holds the plates together through hydrogen bonds. The bond is weak enough to let plates slip during molding, yet strong enough to hold the new shape. Drying removes most of the water, so the plates bond directly and the clay turns rigid but fragile. Wet it again, and it turns plastic. Clay stays plastic only from just moist enough to mold to just dry enough to hold a shape. For this clay, those thresholds sit near 36% to 40% and 58% to 72% water. The dry threshold has its own entry, {{ref:soil-phys-023}}. So does the wet one, {{ref:soil-phys-022}}.

soil-phys-055.title: Heavy, wet and surprisingly fertile: farming on clay
soil-phys-055.text: Clay has a poor reputation on the farm, yet good soil needs some of it. A high clay content trades poor drainage against greater fertility. Clay soils hold water and drain poorly, so they often need artificial drainage and tillage before crops thrive. In return, their higher {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, the power to hold nutrients, makes them more fertile. That keeps more land in production rather than lying fallow. Their tightly bonded particles also resist wind and water erosion better than silty and sandy soils.

soil-phys-043.title: Specific surface area: why tiny grains do the most work
soil-phys-043.text: Surface is where soil does its chemistry. Specific surface area is the surface area of soil particles relative to their amount, defined as area per unit mass. Surface area per unit weight rises as average particle size falls, so sand has the least and is least active, silt is intermediate and clay is the most active. Clay minerals form thin plates and typically have 10 to 1,000 square metres of surface per gram. In one table, very coarse sand (2.00-1.00 mm) has 90 particles per gram and 11 cm2/g, fine sand (0.25-0.10 mm) 46,000 and 91 cm2/g, and silt 5,776,000 and 454 cm2/g. That large surface, with many negative charges, gives clay its high capacity to retain water and nutrients, and the water held at field capacity depends on it. Particles of one textural class share properties tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as cation exchange capacity. One source instead describes it as the surface-area-to-volume ratio of particles.

soil-phys-028.title: Clays that heave houses and pull roots apart
soil-phys-028.text: Damage from shrinking and swelling clay soils is estimated at $7 billion a year. Shrink–swell capacity is the degree to which certain {{ref:soil-chem-079}} in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry. The culprits include {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, {{ref:soil-chem-095}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, and more of them means more severe movement. A soil with at least 5 percent of them by weight may shrink and swell. It is measured as the coefficient of linear extensibility, or COLE. A COLE of 0.06 means 100 inches of soil swell by 6 inches, and anything above 0.06 can damage structures. Swelling heaves buildings, and shrinking lets foundations settle unevenly. Damage peaks where wet and dry seasons are sharp. These soils belong to the order covered in {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Drying opens deep cracks that let water reach lower layers, so the cycle repeats. Shrinking can pull crop roots apart, yet the cracks help the soil recover fast from compaction.

soil-phys-029.title: Expansive clay and the builders who outwit it
soil-phys-029.text: Builders sometimes leave empty space under a slab on purpose. The reason is expansive clay, a clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes. Its minerals have an expanding 2:1 layered lattice, though not every 2:1 clay expands. Lab tests look for high plasticity, a free swell test comparing water and kerosene, or {{ref:soil-chem-093}} under X-rays. Field signs include mounds and hollows, deep cracks, and moist soil that rolls into a 3 mm thread without crumbling. Builders also use piles, lime stabilizers and steady moisture.

soil-phys-030.title: Gilgai: the self-made hills and pools of cracking clay
soil-phys-030.text: In some clay landscapes the ground ripples into mounds and hollows, and the hollows fill with small seasonal pools. This microrelief is gilgai. It forms in expanding clay soils, notably the {{ref:soil-class-106}}, through repeated swelling when wet and shrinkage when dry, a churning called {{ref:soil-form-123}} that heaves underlying material to the surface. The soil cracks when dry, and loose material fills the cracks. On re-wetting the soil is forced sideways, raising a mound between cracks and a depression at each crack. The pattern feeds itself. Depressions hold water, swell more and crack more, and the cracks channel water deep, exaggerating the pattern each cycle. Pools are commonly a few metres across and under 30 cm deep, though some are several metres deep and up to 100 m across. Gilgais occur worldwide on cracking clays with marked wet and dry seasons. Crayfish and ants magnify the forms by bioturbation. Frost polygons of cold regions look similar but form by freeze-thaw. The movement is costly. It damages foundations, roads and railways, and the undulations hamper harvesting. Field surveys treat gilgai, along with deep shrinkage cracks, as a visible sign of the {{ref:soil-phys-029}} behind {{ref:soil-phys-028}}. One source differs on the word: USDA soil taxonomy's soil-order list calls the deep cracks that form in drying Vertisols gilgai.

soil-phys-018.title: A census of a soil's grains, size by size
soil-phys-018.text: Every soil hides a recipe: so much of this grain size, so much of that. A particle-size distribution spells it out. It is a list of values, or a mathematical function, giving the relative amount of particles of each size, usually by mass. For a soil, this distribution is its texture. It governs how water moves and is held, though mineralogy can strongly modify that. It also shapes the strength and load-bearing capacity of soils and rocks. Breaking soil into separate particles takes significant energy, and real particles are irregular. So a distribution is usually defined by its measuring method. The simplest method reports amounts in set ranges between sieve sizes, as described in {{ref:soil-phys-019}}. Sedimentation methods time how fast particles settle in a liquid and suit sizes below 10 μm. Laser diffraction reads size from the angle of scattered light, works best between 0.1 and 3,000 μm, and now dominates industrial measurement.

soil-phys-019.title: Shaking soil through a tower of ever-finer sieves
soil-phys-019.text: The simplest way to size grains, and probably the most common, is to shake them through holes. Sieve analysis measures particle-size distribution by passing a material through a stack of ever-finer sieves and weighing each sieve's catch. A mechanical shaker drives a weighed sample down through finer and finer sieves to a pan called the receiver. Each catch is weighed and divided by the total mass to give its percent retained. Dry sieving stays accurate down to #100 mesh, or 150 μm, but finer grains cling together. Wet sieving rinses the stack with water until it runs clear, handling fine powders mostly under 45 μm. Flat or elongated grains give unreliable results, since the method assumes near-spherical particles. Soil silt and clay below 60 μm need a second method, usually the pipette or the settling test in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. Engineers use the results to judge whether ground can carry a planned structure.

soil-phys-020.title: One curve that captures a soil's whole spread of sizes
soil-phys-020.text: A stack of sieve weighings collapses into one line. The grain-size distribution curve plots the cumulative percentage of a sample passing each sieve against sieve size, on a logarithmic scale. Adding each sieve's share of the mass to the shares above it gives the cumulative percent retained. Subtracting that from 100% gives the percent passing. The curve's shape shows the gradation, or spread of sizes. A dense gradation gives an even curve, a uniform one a steep curve, and a gap gradation a flat stretch in the medium sizes.

soil-phys-050.title: Timing how fast soil grains sink in a cylinder
soil-phys-050.text: Within 40 seconds, the sand in a stirred soil sample has sunk, yet the clay is still suspended hours later. The hydrometer method, a laboratory sedimentation test, turns that difference into a soil's percent sand, silt and clay. It rests on Stokes' law, which links settling speed to size. First the soil is shaken overnight with sodium hexametaphosphate, a dispersing agent that breaks up clumps. Water then fills a one-liter cylinder. Sand over 50 microns settles first, then silt; clay of 2 microns or finer stays above. A hydrometer, a floating gauge, reads grams per liter: at 40 seconds for silt plus clay, giving the sand, and after 6–8 hours for the clay. Silt is 100 minus the clay and sand percentages. Introduced in 1927, it is still widely used, though flaws mean its original procedure and cylinder should not be used. Flat clay plates also sink broadside, so they are sized too small.

soil-phys-052.title: Watching grains settle with a beam of X-rays
soil-phys-052.text: Settling soil can be tracked with X-rays as well as with a floating gauge. X-ray sedimentation is a hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption. Stokes' law turns each particle's terminal settling velocity, its steady sinking speed, into a size, as in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. The X-rays supply the amounts. Their absorption, read through the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, gives the relative mass concentration in each size class. It is one of several further quantitative texture methods, alongside the pipette, {{ref:soil-bio-118}} and rapid methods.

soil-phys-051.title: Sizing soil grains by the way they bend light
soil-phys-051.text: A pinch of soil from a crime scene can be sized with a beam of light. Laser diffraction particle sizing measures particle-size distribution from the way dispersed particles bend light. The angle depends on size, so the pattern records the whole mix, analyzed with Mie or Fraunhofer theory. It is fast and cost-effective, and one well-dispersed run covers the whole size range, silt and clay included. Both theories assume spheres, though. Flat clay plates are sized by their broad face and usually read larger than by sedimentation.

soil-phys-016.title: Krumbein's phi scale, where each step halves the grain
soil-phys-016.text: A 2 mm grain and a 62.5 μm grain sit five steps apart on the phi scale. W. C. Krumbein built it from the Wentworth scale in 1934. It expresses grain size as minus the base-2 logarithm of the diameter in millimeters. Each whole step halves the diameter, and higher numbers mean finer grains. Sand spans phi -1 to 4, silt 4 to 8 and clay 8 to 10. The US sand grades divide at whole phi numbers. A reference diameter of 1 mm keeps the equation dimensionally consistent.

soil-phys-017.title: How wind and rivers sift sediment by size
soil-phys-017.text: Wind is a superb sieve, very effective at separating sand from silt and clay. Sediment sorting is the removal of a range of particle sizes from a deposit by an agent such as a river or the wind. The result shows in the deposit's grain size distribution. Sorting is measured by the Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation, calculated in phi units from percentiles such as the 84th. Below 0.35 means very well sorted. Above 4.00 means extremely poorly sorted, with well, moderately, poorly and very poorly sorted in between.

soil-phys-056.title: Well graded or poorly graded: why the size mix matters
soil-phys-056.text: Poorly graded ground drains better than well-graded ground but liquefies more easily. Soil gradation is an engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil by the range of particle sizes it contains. Gravels and sands with a good spread of sizes, from the No. 4 to the No. 200 sieve, are well graded. The rest are poorly graded, either uniformly graded or gap-graded. Their extra voids explain the drainage, while well-graded soils compact further. Gradation is read from the grain-size curve covered in {{ref:soil-phys-020}}, using the AASHTO system or {{ref:soil-phys-036}}. Fine-grained silts and clays are classed instead by {{ref:soil-phys-021}}.

soil-phys-057.title: Two numbers that grade a gravel or a sand
soil-phys-057.text: Two numbers sort coarse soils into well graded and poorly graded. The coefficients of uniformity and curvature, Cu and Cc, come from grain diameters on a size-distribution curve. D60 and D10 are the diameters at which 60% and 10% of a sample passes. Cu, a crude shape parameter, uses D60 and D10; Cc adds D30 to the pair. A gravel with Cu above 4 and Cc between 1 and 3 is well graded, GW; otherwise it is GP. A sand needs Cu of 6 or more, with the same Cc band, to be SW; otherwise it is SP. The cutoffs belong to {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

soil-phys-188.title: Stokes's law: why big grains sink and fine ones linger
soil-phys-188.text: A grain's sinking speed rises with the square of its radius. That rule comes from Stokes's law. It gives the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers, that is, in slow, smooth flow. George Gabriel Stokes derived it in 1851 from the Navier–Stokes equations. A settling particle stops speeding up when drag plus buoyancy balance its weight. Its terminal velocity is then v = (2/9)(ρp − ρf)gR²/μ. The excess weight grows with R³ but the drag only with R, so speed varies greatly with particle size. The law assumes laminar flow, no inertia, and smooth, uniform spheres that do not interfere with each other. To stay within 10% error, the Reynolds number must stay below 1. It explains how small particles settle out of water, and why cloud droplets stay aloft until they grow to a critical size. Soil laboratories rely on it. Hydrometer analysis calculates a grain's diameter from how far it falls in a known time, and {{ref:soil-phys-190}} uses the same settling to measure silt.

soil-phys-187.title: Friability: soil that crumbles at a touch
soil-phys-187.text: Good soil breaks apart easily in the hand. Friability is that tendency of a solid to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing. Its opposite is indurate, and geologists use the pair to describe how well the fragments of soft rocks hold together. A good {{ref:soil-phys-039}} balances friability against the tensile strength of aggregates: high strength gives large cemented lumps that barely crumble. Soil descriptions record it. The Cecil soil's surface horizon is a very friable sandy loam. In Waikato, Māori dug sand and gravel into clay topsoils to drain better and crumble more easily for growing kūmara and taro.

soil-phys-189.title: Sizing soil grains without measuring them
soil-phys-189.text: Most ways of sizing soil particles never measure a diameter directly. Particle size analysis is the collective name for laboratory techniques that find the size range or mean size of particles in a sample. They use light, ultrasound, electric fields, gravity or centrifugation, and most infer size from another measurement. Irregular grains are treated as equivalent spheres: sieving gives a volume-based diameter, optical methods an area-based one. Different methods are therefore not expected to agree, so the method should match the use the data will serve. Sieving has long been the choice for soil texture. Laser diffraction is gaining ground because it is faster and highly reproducible.

soil-phys-186.title: Agrophysics: physics brought to the farm
soil-phys-186.text: Physics has a branch devoted to fields, crops and harvests. Agrophysics sits on the border of agronomy and physics and studies farm ecosystems with the methods of the physical sciences.
