It is close to biophysics but restricted to the plants, animals, soil and atmosphere involved in farming. It grew out of {{ref:soil-phys-059}}. It first studied relations within the soil, then widened to crop properties and the quality and safety of food and raw farm produce. Research centres include the Institute of Agrophysics of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Lublin and the Agrophysical Research Institute in St. Petersburg. Soil science lists it among its related disciplines.

soil-phys-191.title: Clods, the lumps that machines make
soil-phys-191.text: Nature builds peds; people make clods. A clod is a mass of soil formed by mechanical disturbance such as cultivation, unlike the naturally formed ped. Plowing, excavation and heavy machinery on wet soil all produce them, and compaction gives hard clods where soft peds would be. Tilling wetter or drier than the best moisture raises large clods, and hardsetting soils turn cloddy when tilled. Harrowing breaks clods up into a tilth fit for sowing. Clods of 2 to 100 mm form the second of the four classes of {{ref:soil-water-141}}.

soil-phys-190.title: The pipette method: sampling silt as it settles
soil-phys-190.text: Grains finer than 60 μm slip through the bottom sieve of a sieve analysis. The pipette method takes over from there. It is a laboratory settling method that measures the proportions of coarse and fine silt in a sample, using settling rates given by Stokes's law. Like the hydrometer, it is widely used in soil engineering and geology to classify sediments. It now has a rival. Compared with the traditional sieve-pipette method, laser diffraction analysis gave better precision.

soil-phys-167.title: From the Leaning Tower to Terzaghi: engineering with earth
soil-phys-167.text: Until the 18th century, builders designed in soil by experience alone. Problems such as the Leaning Tower of Pisa pushed them toward science. The result is geotechnical engineering, the branch of civil engineering concerned with how earth materials behave. It applies soil mechanics and rock mechanics and draws on geology, {{ref:soil-phys-207}} and geophysics. It overlaps engineering geology, but that field is a specialty of geology rather than civil engineering. In 1773 Charles Coulomb applied mechanics to earth pressure on ramparts. He took shear strength on a slip plane as cohesion plus friction. The nineteenth century added {{ref:soil-water-201}} for flow through soil, Atterberg's clay consistency indices and Reynolds's 1885 finding that shearing makes dense granular material dilate. Modern geotechnics dates from Karl von Terzaghi's Erdbaumechanik of 1925. He showed that effective stress controls shear strength and framed theories of {{ref:soil-phys-123}} and consolidation. In 1958 Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth linked volume change and shearing in {{ref:soil-phys-105}}, the basis of many advanced soil models. In foundation design, the main concerns remain how much load the ground can carry, settlement and ground movement.

soil-phys-170.title: The oedometer: squeezing soil to read its past
soil-phys-170.text: A small disc of clay can remember a glacier. The oedometer test measures a soil's consolidation properties by loading a sample and recording how it deforms. It reproduces the one-dimensional squeezing soils undergo in the field, predicting how they deform when effective stress changes. The disc sits in a rigid ring that stops sideways movement, between porous stones that let water drain. Saturated samples settle over minutes or hours, and thickness against time gives the coefficient of consolidation and the soil's {{ref:soil-water-191}}. In the common incremental test, each load stays until primary consolidation ends, tracing void ratio against effective stress. The test yields the preconsolidation pressure, the effective stress dividing stiff from soft response, usually a mark of past loading by glaciers or eroded layers. It also gives {{ref:soil-phys-111}}, Cc = Δe/Δlogσ'v above that pressure, a matching index for reloading below it, and the index of secondary compression, Cα = Δe/Δlog t. Frontard ran the first consolidation experiments in 1910. Terzaghi published his theory in 1923.

soil-phys-172.title: Porous media: solids laced with empty space
soil-phys-172.text: A sponge and a field soil share one basic design. Each is a porous medium: a solid skeleton, called the matrix, holding pores usually filled with a liquid or gas. Often both the matrix and the pore network are continuous, as in a sponge. Rocks and soils are porous media, water-bearing {{ref:soil-phys-201}} among them, and the idea is used in soil mechanics and the science of underground water. Porosity is the main descriptor. {{ref:soil-water-191}}, strength and conductivity can sometimes be derived from the constituents and pore layout, but not simply. Effective porosity is the pore space open to flow. {{ref:soil-water-201}} describes flow through fine-porous media; Forchheimer's law covers coarse ones.

soil-phys-169.title: Mohr–Coulomb: the straight line where soil gives way
soil-phys-169.text: On paper, soil fails along a straight line. Mohr–Coulomb theory models how materials fail under combined shear and normal stress, and it defines the shear strength of soils and rocks at different effective stresses. Its failure envelope is τ = σ tan(ϕ) + c, where c is the cohesion and ϕ the angle of internal friction. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb wrote a 1776 essay on it. Christian Otto Mohr generalized it near the end of the 19th century. Coulomb's friction hypothesis gives the stresses that cause failure; Mohr's circle gives the principal stresses and the angle of the failure plane. Typical friction angles are 30° to 45° for sand, 35° for gravel and 26° to 35° for silt, while clay cohesion runs from 10 to 200 kPa. With ϕ = 0 it reduces to the Tresca criterion. It has flaws. Cohesion is not a fundamental soil property and cannot be determined precisely. The theory also omits the dilation many geomaterials show under triaxial stress, so plasticity models pair it with a smooth non-associated flow potential.

soil-phys-168.title: Reading the ground before building on it
soil-phys-168.text: Before a foundation goes in, someone must find out what lies beneath. Geotechnical investigation gathers the physical properties of the soil and rock under and beside a site, to design earthworks and foundations. It combines surface and subsurface exploration, sampling and laboratory testing, sometimes with seismic, resistivity or radar surveys. Underground work usually includes in-situ tests such as the standard and cone penetration tests, and may use test pits and trenches. The standard test's split-spoon sampler collects disturbed samples; thin-walled piston samplers collect less disturbed ones. Centrifuge models reach prototype-scale stresses in small models. That matters because a soil's resistance and stiffness depend on confining pressure.

soil-phys-175.title: Trampling: what feet and hooves do to soil
soil-phys-175.text: Feet reshape the ground they cross. Trampling, repeated walking by humans or animals, destroys the above-ground parts of many plants and compacts the soil, creating a distinct microenvironment. Recreational trampling in alpine areas raises bulk density and lowers porosity. That alters the soil's moisture and temperature and increases runoff and erosion. Plots trampled in the Belianske Tatras in 2008 and retested in 2022 showed that apparent recovery can hide species losses, so damage may appear late. Hooves are not always harmful. Grazing animals can aerate soil, and planned herd trampling is credited with helping water soak in and soil store carbon.

soil-phys-173.title: How big a sample must be to tell the truth
soil-phys-173.text: Measure a tiny porous sample and the readings jump around. As the sample grows they settle. The size at which they become consistent is the representative elementary volume, or REV: the smallest volume that represents the whole material. Readings stay stable in larger samples until other hydrostratigraphic layers creep in, a size called the maximum elementary volume. An REV assumes a mixed, heterogeneous material can be replaced by an equivalent uniform one. Its size varies with the property studied. Even {{ref:soil-phys-209}} has to be defined in an REV.

soil-phys-176.title: Soil strength: what a root must push against
soil-phys-176.text: Soil strength is the resistance a soil offers to deformation, measured in the field as its resistance to a penetrometer. Most of it comes from friction between particles, which is proportional to normal stress. Pore water pressure lowers that normal stress, so it weakens soil, just as effective stress predicts. A small amount of water bridging the gaps between grains does the opposite, raising strength through attraction to mineral surfaces. Drying soils can grow too strong for life. In hardsetting soils, high strength restricts seedlings and roots, and it is one of the limits that define {{ref:soil-phys-220}}.

soil-phys-171.title: Pore structure: bodies, throats and winding channels
soil-phys-171.text: The empty space in soil has an architecture. Pore structure describes it: porosity, pore sizes, the pore-size distribution, and the shapes, roughness and winding paths of the pores in a porous medium. It controls how permeable the medium is, {{ref:soil-water-191}}, and affects {{ref:soil-water-193}} and the capacity to retain fluids. A useful picture is a network of channels, with wide pore bodies joined by narrow pore throats or necks. Pore size, usually the effective radius of a body or neck, arguably has the broadest effect. A soil's pore-size distribution, f(r), gives the relative abundance of each radius and has textural and structural parts. Pore size does not simply follow particle size: clays promote aggregation and so large pores between aggregates. Subdividing the distribution can express complex behavior, such as hysteresis in how soil holds water. Mercury intrusion porosimetry and measurements of gas taken up on pore walls gauge it; mercury needs 140 MPa to enter pores smaller than 10 nm. Pore morphology covers the shape, surface roughness and {{ref:soil-phys-174}} of the channels that hold liquid and gas.

soil-phys-174.title: Tortuosity: the long way through the pores
soil-phys-174.text: A straight line scores exactly 1. The simplest measure of tortuosity is that arc-chord ratio: a path's actual length divided by the straight-line distance between its ends. Winding pore channels score higher. The concept has many definitions. Hydraulic, electrical, diffusional and thermal tortuosities describe different transport processes, while geometrical tortuosity describes pore shape. In the study of underground water it is the ratio of diffusivity in free space to diffusivity in the porous medium. Strictly, effective diffusivity varies with the inverse square of geometrical tortuosity. In soils, flow-path tortuosity controls diffusion during leaching, and the tortuosity of large pores indicates their resistance to water flow.

soil-phys-213.title: Transpiration: how plants lift soil water into the air
soil-phys-213.text: An acre of corn gives off about 3,000–4,000 U.S. gallons (11,000–15,000 liters) of water a day. That flow is transpiration: water moving through a plant and evaporating from its leaves, stems and flowers. It is passive and costs the plant no energy. It also cools the plant and drives the mass flow of mineral nutrients. Very little of the water roots take up goes into growth; 97–99.5% is lost by transpiration and guttation. Two stretches set the pace. From soil to root, flow depends on the soil's hydraulic conductivity and the pressure gradient through the soil. Up the plant, water moves mainly down differences in water potential. When roots take up less than leaves lose, stomata close. That slows nutrient uptake and limits photosynthesis and growth. The soil's temperature and moisture influence how far stomata open, and roots struggle in dry, very fertile or salty soils. Isotope measurements show transpiration is the larger part of evapotranspiration. They also show transpired water differs from {{ref:soil-phys-203}} and streams, so soil water is less well mixed than assumed. It is measured with potometers, {{ref:soil-water-248}}, porometers, photosynthesis systems and sap flow sensors.

soil-phys-207.title: Hydrology: following water across and under the land
soil-phys-207.text: Every raindrop's path is a question for hydrology. It is the scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on Earth, including the water cycle and water resources. It divides into surface water hydrology, the hydrology of underground water, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-208}}, and marine hydrology. One of its themes is infiltration, the process by which water enters the soil, part of which percolates down to the water table. Soil moisture is measured by capacitance probe, time domain reflectometer or {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Solute sampling and geophysical methods also serve. {{ref:soil-water-240}}, one of its branches, studies how living things and the water cycle interact.

soil-phys-226.title: Ditches, pipes and wells: how farms shed water
soil-phys-226.text: Agricultural drainage systems remove water on or in the soil to improve crop production. They combine control of storm runoff, erosion and the water table. The two main types are surface drainage and subsurface drainage. Within either, field systems control the water table, while main systems collect the water, carry it off and dispose of it through an outlet. Surface systems reshape the land and drain by gravity: bedded systems on flat land, graded systems on slopes. They suit flat land with soils that take in water slowly, or places with intense rain. Subsurface systems suit shallow water tables. Their field drains can be open ditches, filled trenches, pipe, tile or mole drains, or wells, which count as vertical drainage. Modern pipe drains are perforated PE or PVC wrapped in a filter envelope that keeps soil out. That matters most in fine sandy and silty soils. Checked or controlled systems use gates or pumping to drain only when needed, saving irrigation water. In northwestern India this did not cause undue salinization. Where saline {{ref:soil-phys-203}} lies deep, shallow, closely spaced drains work better, because deeper systems yield saltier effluent.

soil-phys-227.title: Tile drainage: buried pipes that dry the root zone
soil-phys-227.text: In 1843 short earthenware pipes were first laid under English fields. Older land drains were stone-lined tunnels in clay soils and {{ref:soil-class-070}}, set deep enough to escape the plow. Tile drainage is a system of buried pipes that removes excess subsurface water from fields, leaving air space in the soil and firm ground for machinery. The name comes from the original fired-clay tiles. HDPE and PVC tubing are now common, though concrete and ceramic tiles are still used. Water enters through gaps between sections or perforations in plastic tile and usually ends up in lower streams, rivers or lakes. Lowering the water table keeps oxygen in the pores, so roots grow deeper and use water and nutrients better. Sandy soils need little tiling; clay soils hold water tightly and need lines closer together. Perforations clog with silt. Gravel and {{ref:soil-water-254}} surrounds slow this, but all land drains eventually fail. Tree roots invade the lines, so some farmers clear them every year. Flashboard risers in outlets can hold water in the root zone, storing it for the crop.

soil-phys-210.title: The water budget: every drop accounted for
soil-phys-210.text: A basin, a field or a city can keep a water budget. A water balance states that the inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval. The system can be a soil column, a drainage basin, an irrigation area or a city. For a basin, P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus the change in storage in soil or {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. The balance rests on conservation of mass and assumes a closed system, so water leaving for another basin must be accounted for. Comparing budgets across areas shows how geology, soils, vegetation and land use affect the water cycle. The balance guides irrigation, runoff assessment, flood and pollution control, and the design of subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains, ditches or wells. Monthly water balance models have been studied since the 1940s.

soil-phys-214.title: Wilting: when a plant's cells lose their pressure
soil-phys-214.text: A drooping leaf is a plant losing water faster than it can absorb it. Wilting is the loss of rigidity in a plant's non-woody parts when turgor pressure, the water pressure that keeps cells firm, falls toward zero. Soil can cause it in three ways: drought, high salinity drawing water from cells, and saturated soil that starves roots of oxygen so they cannot move water. Plants may recover overnight as stomata close and evaporation falls. Permanent wilting kills the plant. Drooping exposes less leaf area and so saves water, but it also curbs transpiration, reproduction and growth.

soil-phys-215.title: Penman–Monteith: estimating evaporation from the weather
soil-phys-215.text: Evapotranspiration can be estimated without measuring it directly. The Penman–Monteith equation does it from meteorological data. Penman published it in 1948 and Monteith revised it in 1965. Its inputs include net irradiance, ground heat flux, vapor pressure deficit, air density and heat capacity, and atmospheric and stomatal conductance. Stomatal conductance captures leaf area index, water stress and CO2, so the result is sensitive to vegetation. The FAO recommends the equation, though errors against direct measurement can range from -9 to 40%. In 1998 the FAO simplified it as FAO 56, which computes {{ref:soil-phys-217}} in mm per day from radiation, temperature, wind at 2 m and vapor pressure deficit. Stress coefficients cut the estimate for waterlogged soil starving roots of oxygen, dry soil causing wilt, and salinity. GIS-linked hydrologic models such as SWAT use it.

soil-phys-221.title: Bound water: a film a few molecules thick
soil-phys-221.text: Some soil water barely moves at all. Bound water is an extremely thin layer, a few molecules thick, held on mineral surfaces. Water molecules are strongly polar, so they bond to each other and to charged surfaces such as soil minerals. Clay is especially able to bond them. Bound water is much less mobile than the rest of soil water. It strongly affects the soil's dielectric permittivity, its response to an electric field, and how it freezes and thaws.

soil-phys-223.title: Pressure head: pressure written as a height
soil-phys-223.text: Pressure can be measured as a height. Pressure head is the height of a liquid column corresponding to the pressure the liquid exerts at its base. For a given fluid it is proportional to pressure, which is why columns of water or mercury are used to measure pressure. Combined with elevation head, it makes up hydraulic head. Below the water table, pressure head exceeds atmospheric pressure; the water table is where the two are equal. Above it, pressure head is negative, and water partly filling the pores is under suction.

soil-phys-222.title: Wetting or drying: why soil water has a memory
soil-phys-222.text: The same soil at the same suction can hold very different amounts of water. At a matric potential of 5 kPa, a fine sandy soil could hold anywhere between 8% and 25% water by volume. The cause is water retention hysteresis: water content at a given matric potential depends on whether the soil is wetting or drying, that is, on its saturation history. The matric potential–water content relationship is the basis of the water retention curve, so one curve tells only part of the story. Some matric potential sensors show hysteresis themselves, yet as of 2002 calibrations usually measured only the drying curve.

soil-phys-224.title: Kozeny–Carman: permeability from grains and gaps
soil-phys-224.text: The Kozeny–Carman equation links how easily fluid passes through a packed bed of solids to the size of its grains and the space between them. It gives the pressure drop of the flowing fluid, and from it the bed's permeability. Kozeny derived it in 1927, and Carman modified it in 1937 and 1956. They modeled the bed as curving tubes carrying Poiseuille flow, smooth flow through a narrow pipe. Permeability rises with particle diameter squared and with the cube of porosity, and falls with (1 − porosity) squared. A special case of Darcy's law, it holds only for creeping flow, with particle Reynolds numbers up to about 1.0.

soil-phys-219.title: Eddy covariance: catching vapor in the wind
soil-phys-219.text: Swirling eddies of air carry water vapor, heat and gases up from a field. Eddy covariance measures those vertical turbulent fluxes from fast readings of wind and gas concentration. The flux is the covariance, a measure of how two quantities rise and fall together, between vertical wind speed and gas concentration, times mean air density. Instruments sample at 5 to 40 Hz. Over natural ecosystems and farm fields, the method measures water loss and evapotranspiration, and carbon dioxide and methane exchange. Its source area, the flux footprint, shifts with wind direction, stability and measurement height. It assumes flat, uniform terrain and fully turbulent flow.

soil-phys-216.title: Priestley–Taylor: evaporation from radiation alone
soil-phys-216.text: One number, 1.26, carries much of the Priestley–Taylor equation. The equation is a simplified substitute for the Penman–Monteith equation that needs only radiation observations. It drops the aerodynamic terms and multiplies {{ref:soil-phys-217}} by an empirical constant, α. Over well-watered vegetation, observed evaporation was 1.26 times the reference rate. The equation assumes plants with abundant water. Arid regions with high moisture stress are estimated to have a higher α.

soil-phys-217.title: ET0: the water use of an imaginary lawn
soil-phys-217.text: Crop water use is measured against an imaginary patch of grass. Reference evapotranspiration, written ET0, is the water a standard, well-watered grass surface would lose under the current temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation. FAO 56 defines that grass precisely as a hypothetical crop 0.12 m tall, actively growing and adequately watered. It has a surface resistance of 70 s m-1 and a reflectivity of 0.23, the quantity treated in {{ref:soil-phys-177}}. The FAO derived its Penman–Monteith equation to model it. Multiplying ET0 by {{ref:soil-phys-218}} gives the evapotranspiration of unstressed plants, ET = Kc × ET0. A stress coefficient then gives actual crop use. Weather-based irrigation controllers calculate it.

soil-phys-218.title: Crop coefficients: from reference grass to real crop
soil-phys-218.text: Watering plans, the subject of {{ref:soil-water-234}}, turn a weather figure into a crop's thirst with one multiplier. The crop coefficient, Kc, is most simply the ratio of a crop's evapotranspiration to that of a reference crop. Multiplying ET0 by Kc gives the crop's actual water requirement, ETc. Kc changes through the season with growth stage, often following a trapezoidal or leaf area index curve. It can exceed 1 when the crop uses more water than the reference. Stress coefficients between 0 and 1, most often for water stress (Kw), are multiplied in to reduce the estimate.

soil-phys-203.title: Groundwater: the water held in the pores of the Earth
soil-phys-203.text: About 30 percent of the world's readily available fresh water is groundwater. It is water held beneath the Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures. In the technical sense it includes soil moisture, the frozen ground of {{ref:soil-env-129}} and immobile water in tight bedrock, not only water flowing in shallow {{ref:soil-phys-201}}. It enters naturally as infiltration that percolates down to the water table, and leaves through springs and seepage to the oceans. It is a long-term store of the water cycle, with residence times from days to millennia. In the Great Artesian Basin it travels about 1 meter per year and can be more than 1 million years old. About 70% of extracted groundwater is used in agriculture, and that use carries risks. Where salty water evapotranspires, salts are left behind. Poor drainage in irrigation districts can raise water tables to the surface, causing soil salinity and waterlogging. Pollution, often from improper waste disposal on land, spreads in plumes and is harder to clean up than surface water pollution.

soil-phys-201.title: Aquifers: not underground lakes but soaked rock
soil-phys-201.text: Despite the popular image, most aquifers are not underground rivers or lakes. They are porous rock saturated with water. An aquifer is an underground layer of permeable, porous or fractured rock, or of loose gravel, sand or silt, that holds and yields water. Recharge, water moving down from the surface, is the main way water enters. In porous aquifers it seeps slowly between sand grains; 0.3 m a day counts as a high rate. Porosity alone does not make a good aquifer: the Deccan Traps basalts are highly porous but poorly permeable. Aquifers occur from near the surface to deeper than 9,000 m. Shallower ones are more often tapped for supply and irrigation and more readily refilled by local rain. Aquitards, low-permeability beds of clay or non-porous rock, restrict flow between aquifers; a completely impermeable one is an aquiclude or aquifuge. Karst aquifers form where carbonic acid widens fissures in limestone. Their fast flow makes them far more sensitive to contamination. Pumping brings overdrafting, land subsidence, salinization and pollution.

soil-phys-208.title: Hydrogeology: the geology of water underground
soil-phys-208.text: In 1856 Henry Darcy derived the law that still anchors the study of groundwater. Hydrogeology is the branch of geology dealing with the distribution and movement of groundwater in soil and rock, mainly in aquifers. Groundwater hydrology and geohydrology are near-synonyms. It covers the laws of subsurface water movement, the water's interaction with the porous solid, and the transport of energy, chemicals and particles by flow. The type of aquifer decides what controls flow: storativity in one kind, specific yield in the other, as {{ref:soil-phys-202}} explains. Darcy's law remains its basic equation for groundwater discharge.

soil-phys-202.title: Capped or open: confined and unconfined aquifers
soil-phys-202.text: Aquifers are divided by what lies directly above them. A confined aquifer sits beneath an impermeable layer, usually clay, which may give some protection from surface contamination. An unconfined aquifer's upper boundary is the water table. Unconfined aquifers release water by draining their pores, with specific yields above 0.01, or 1% of bulk volume. Confined aquifers store water through expansion of the solid matrix and the compressibility of water, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5. A perched aquifer is a small body of groundwater held above the regional aquifer on a low-permeability layer such as clay.

soil-phys-209.title: The groundwater flow equation: diffusion underground
soil-phys-209.text: Mathematicians know it as the diffusion equation. The groundwater flow equation describes how groundwater moves through a porous medium. It is usually derived by combining Darcy's law with conservation of mass in a small control volume. The compressibility of both fluid and matrix enters it: clay's is 10−6 to 10−8 Pa−1, against 10−7 to 10−9 for sand. Its solutions do practical work. The Theis and Thiem equations, its transient and steady-state solutions for flow to a well, are used in pumping tests. The Hooghoudt equation applies it to drainage by pipes, tile drains or ditches.

soil-phys-206.title: Subsurface flow: the slow road back to the surface
soil-phys-206.text: Rain that soaks in has not left the water cycle. Subsurface flow is the movement of water beneath the Earth's surface. Infiltrated water wets the unsaturated zone above the water table and recharges aquifers, and the excess moves on as subsurface runoff. Its path is set mainly by the water gradient, the type of substrate and barriers to flow. Flow in the soil can be unsaturated, but faster subsurface flow goes with local saturation. The water returns to the surface at lower elevations through springs, seeps, wells or streams, sometimes after thousands of years in an aquifer.

soil-phys-228.title: The hidden costs of draining farmland
soil-phys-228.text: Draining wetlands caused population declines in hundreds of thousands of wetland species. Widespread tile drainage changes rivers too. By moving water off the land faster, it delivers higher volumes downstream, causing bank erosion and heavy sediment loads. Its effect on water quality cuts both ways. Soil filters water before it reaches streams, so tiling can reduce erosion and phosphorus runoff. But its outflow tends to be very high in nitrogen. On tile-drained land, controlled drainage or built wetlands ({{ref:soil-water-260}}) may work better than surface conservation practices.

soil-phys-220.title: The non-limiting water range
soil-phys-220.text: Plants do not simply need water; they need water that is not locked behind hardness or drowned in poor air. The optimum water range for plant growth is the least-limiting water range. In a well-structured soil it runs from field capacity on the wet end to the wilting point on the dry end, the limits of {{ref:soil-water-229}}. In severely compacted soil the range is much narrower. At field capacity it is still too wet because it lacks large pores, and good aeration needs at least 20% of pore space air filled. On the dry end, growth in compacted soil is commonly limited by hardness rather than lack of available water. John Letey introduced the idea in 1985 to refine available water capacity. Da Silva, Kay and Perfect refined it in 1994 as the least limiting water range (LLWR).

soil-phys-211.title: Agricultural hydrology: water budgets for farmland
soil-phys-211.text: A farm's soil can be treated as a stack of reservoirs. Agricultural hydrology studies the water balance components that matter for managing farm water, especially irrigation and drainage. It divides the soil profile into the surface, the unsaturated root zone with mainly vertical flow, a transition zone, and the aquifer with mainly horizontal flow. For the root zone, infiltration plus capillary rise equals actual evapotranspiration plus percolation plus the change in storage. Bordering zones can be combined. Over months or years storage terms are often negligible, giving steady-state balances. These water balances also underpin the salt balances of irrigated land and models such as SaltMod and the one in {{ref:soil-chem-040}}.

soil-phys-204.title: The phreatic zone, where every pore is full
soil-phys-204.text: Below the water table, the ground holds no air in its pores. The phreatic zone is that saturated zone, in which all pores and fractures are filled with water. It is the counterpart of the unsaturated vadose zone above the water table. Its size and depth fluctuate with the seasons and with wet and dry periods. Depending on particle packing and porosity, its boundary can be stable or form unstable fingering patterns known as Saffman–Taylor instability. Deep-rooted phreatophytes draw much of their water from in or near it.

soil-phys-205.title: Interflow: water that slips sideways through the soil
soil-phys-205.text: Not all water that soaks in heads straight down. Interflow is the lateral movement of water through the unsaturated zone that returns to the surface or enters a stream. It happens when infiltrated water meets hydraulic conductivity that decreases with depth and turns downslope. Throughflow is the part of interflow that returns to the surface as overland flow before reaching a stream or groundwater. If the subsurface saturates, interflow may exfiltrate as return flow and join the overland flow. Interflow and the underground tunneling of {{ref:soil-water-289}} can erode gullies, just as surface runoff does.

soil-phys-212.title: How much to irrigate, how much to drain
soil-phys-212.text: In the Netherlands, 720 mm of precipitation against 540 mm of evaporation gives a winter drainage requirement of 180 mm. Water balances tell how much water a field needs from irrigation and must lose through drains or wells. With surface evaporation neglected and actual evapotranspiration set to potential, the topsoil balance gives Irr = Epo + Osu + Per − Rai − Cap. Dividing Epo by Irr gives the fraction of irrigation water the crop consumes, the measure covered in {{ref:soil-agri-014}}. Drain and well discharges in the balances give the drainage requirements central to designing drainage systems. In the Dutch case, shallow-rooted pastures need summer irrigation; deep-rooted wheat practically does not.

soil-phys-225.title: Unsaturated conductivity: flow that depends on wetness
soil-phys-225.text: In a soil that is not saturated, the ease of water flow is not a fixed number. Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity depends on water content, and that dependence is a main complication in studying the vadose zone. It enters the Richards equation as K(h) and the soil moisture velocity equation as K(θ). Relations such as Brooks and Corey, Clapp and Hornberger, and van Genuchten–Mualem describe it, with parameters taken from the water retention curve. In the field, the Guelph permeameter measures it, using a Mariotte bottle to keep a constant head.

soil-phys-193.title: Advection, the river that carries what it holds
soil-phys-193.text: Dump ink into a river and it travels downstream as a pulse. The river's own current carries it, and that carrying has a name: advection, the transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid. It needs currents, so it cannot happen in rigid solids. It also excludes the slow drift of molecules on their own, called diffusion. The ink does both at once, riding the current while it spreads, and the sum of the two is convection. Underground the same thing happens in {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. There advection carries contaminants along the main direction of flow at the seepage velocity, the speed at which water actually moves through the pores. Physicists write it as the advection equation, a first-order hyperbolic partial differential equation. It comes from a conservation law: whatever is transported is neither created nor lost along the way.

soil-phys-192.title: How pollution travels with moving groundwater
soil-phys-192.text: A spill on the surface can turn up years later in a distant well. Contaminant transport in groundwater is the movement of dissolved contaminants with the water flowing underground, and contaminant hydrogeology is the field that studies it, a branch of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Some contaminants are man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides. Others are natural, such as arsenic or salinity. Three main mechanisms move them. {{ref:soil-phys-193}} carries them at seepage velocity. Diffusion spreads them from high to low concentration. Dispersion, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-194}}, spreads them further still. Diffusion and dispersion only spread a contaminant, though. Sticking to the soil, the process of {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, does something different: it slows the contaminant's average velocity. Precipitation and decay also change what arrives. So the properties of the {{ref:soil-phys-201}}, beyond the flow itself, shape where pollution goes. Polluted groundwater forms a plume, and its advancing edge can reach wells and springs. Hydrologists track it with transport and groundwater models.

soil-phys-194.title: Why a contaminant plume spreads as it travels
soil-phys-194.text: Water cannot flow straight through soil. At every grain it must go left, right, up or down, so dissolved substances fan out around their average path. Hydrodynamic dispersion is this spreading of dissolved contaminants away from the mean path of the groundwater carrying them. It comes from small-scale unevenness in the porous medium and uneven water speeds through its {{ref:soil-phys-063}}. Over long distances a second effect takes over. Zones of higher and lower permeability offer preferential paths, like the {{ref:soil-water-157}} met earlier, and spread contaminants irregularly. Hydrologists measure the strength of dispersion with empirical numbers called dispersivities. Longitudinal dispersivity, αL, covers solute running ahead of or behind the mean flow. Transverse dispersivity, αT, covers solute drifting to the sides. These numbers hide a surprise. They stand in for details a large-scale model averages away, such as thin gravel or clay beds in sand. Dispersivity is partly a measure of missing information. That is why it is often said to depend on scale: dispersivity through 1 m3 of aquifer differs from that through 1 cm3 of the same material. Salinity models still need it as a soil input, alongside water retention and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity.

soil-phys-196.title: Retardation: why contaminants lag behind the water
soil-phys-196.text: A contaminant does not always travel at the speed of the water that carries it. Retardation by adsorption is the slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it adsorbs to the soil, measured by a retardation factor. Adsorption holds the contaminant back until the amount set by the adsorption equilibrium has been adsorbed. The factor depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer, and it is analogous to the retardation factor of chromatography. Less soluble contaminants can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water, so only the more soluble species travel far. This differs from the spreading described in {{ref:soil-phys-192}} and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. Unlike diffusion and dispersion, which merely spread a contaminant, retardation changes its global average velocity, so it can be much slower than the water. Chromatography gives the clearest definition. There the retardation factor R is the fraction of the substance in the mobile phase at equilibrium: the quantity in the mobile phase divided by the total quantity in the system. In planar chromatography, RF is the substance's travel distance over the solvent front's. It always lies between 0 and 1, because nothing outruns the solvent. A spot that travels 2.5 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm gives 0.50.

soil-phys-195.title: Molecular diffusion, fast over millimeters, slow over meters
soil-phys-195.text: Double the distance and diffusion takes four times as long. Molecular diffusion is the random thermal movement of molecules that carries solutes from high to low concentration in the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Over small distances it matters, but it spreads solutes slowly over large ones. Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater barely moves, as in clay aquitards. Diffusion is a real physical process. Dispersion is an empirical factor that merely shares its mathematical form.

soil-phys-197.title: One equation for drifting and spreading
soil-phys-197.text: Most soil models describe salt on the move with one equation. The convection–diffusion equation, also called the advection–diffusion or scalar transport equation, tracks a quantity moved by both diffusion and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. It is a parabolic partial differential equation built on the continuity equation, which keeps account of what enters and leaves. Diffusive flux comes from {{ref:soil-phys-181}} as −D∇c; advective flux is vc. A source or sink term R adds or removes the quantity, as when a chemical reaction creates or destroys a species. In porous media, v is the superficial velocity. SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus all couple the {{ref:soil-water-238}} with it, moving salts by advection and dispersion.

soil-phys-200.title: Dye tracing, following water with color
soil-phys-200.text: Dye traces showed karst groundwater moving 0.8 to 11.3 km a day. Dye tracing tracks a flow by adding dye to the water. It can be qualitative, proving a connection exists, or quantitative, with fluorometers measuring how much dye arrives. Fluorescein, developed in 1871, and its sodium salt uranine remain among the best tracers, alongside rhodamine, pyranine and sulforhodamine B. Organic matter, other chemicals, sunlight and acidic water weaken them. The traces also proved that models assuming uniform porosity do not fit karst aquifers.

soil-phys-199.title: Vadose zone models: solute transport on a computer
soil-phys-199.text: Hydrus, SWAP, DrainMod-S and UnSatChem all solve the same pair of equations. These vadose zone transport models simulate water flow and solute transport in unsaturated soil by solving the {{ref:soil-water-238}} numerically. Most join it to the {{ref:soil-phys-197}} to move salts. Hydrus needs soil hydraulic parameters for the water retention and unsaturated conductivity functions, plus starting and boundary conditions. Its one-dimensional version, HYDRUS1D, is available online and is used to estimate groundwater recharge.

soil-phys-198.title: Colloids, the hitchhikers that carry pollutants far
soil-phys-198.text: Plutonium at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site may have traveled far on tiny passengers. In transport facilitated by {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, these particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater. Radionuclides, heavy metals and organic pollutants sorb easily onto them while they are suspended. These may be inorganic, such as clays and iron oxy-hydroxides, or organic, such as humic and fulvic substances. How far they move depends on soil structure, compaction and particle size. Compacted {{ref:soil-chem-100}} and deep clay ultrafilter them. The process drew real attention only in the 1980s.

soil-phys-177.title: Albedo, how much sunlight a surface sends back
soil-phys-177.text: Fresh snow reflects 0.80 of the sunlight that strikes it; bare soil reflects 0.17. That fraction is albedo, measured from 0 for a surface that absorbs everything to 1 for one that reflects everything. Desert sand scores 0.40, deciduous forest 0.15 to 0.18. Dark, low-albedo surfaces absorb most radiation. When snow melts off grass or soil, the darker ground warms the area and speeds further melting, a positive feedback that touches {{ref:soil-phys-137}}. Farming, deforestation and urbanization change the albedo of large areas.

soil-phys-180.title: Microclimate, the weather of a few meters
soil-phys-180.text: A valley bottom can frost sooner than the slope above it, because cold air sinks. A microclimate is a set of local conditions near the surface that differs persistently from its surroundings. It covers the air just above and the shallow soil and water below. It spans a few meters to at most a few kilometers. Moist soils damp temperature swings, while soils that dry easily swing more each day, and clay-rich soils keep heat and moisture near the ground. Farmers shape microclimate with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation.

soil-phys-181.title: Fick's laws: diffusion in two lines
soil-phys-181.text: In 1855 Adolf Fick put diffusion into two laws. The first, J = −D dφ/dx, says the diffusive flux J is proportional to the concentration gradient. D, the diffusion coefficient, has units of area per time. The second, ∂φ/∂t = D ∂²φ/∂x², says how concentration changes with time; it has the same form as the {{ref:soil-phys-183}}. Fick's law parallels Darcy's law for water and {{ref:soil-phys-182}}, and models transport in porous soils. Where porous media break these laws, diffusion is called non-Fickian.

soil-phys-179.title: Ice segregation, the real force behind frost heave
soil-phys-179.text: Freezing water expands, yet that is not what lifts most frozen ground. Most frost heaving and bedrock fracture in cold regions comes from ice segregation. In this process moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone and grows into {{ref:soil-phys-154}}s that wedge the material apart. It needs permeable soil or porous rock, temperatures at which ice and premelted water coexist, and a temperature gradient. With plenty of water one lens thickens until the heat released by freezing slows it. With little, new lenses form below. High overburden pressure or warm surfaces prevent it entirely.

soil-phys-185.title: Seasonal frost, ground that freezes and thaws each year
soil-phys-185.text: Each winter some ground freezes and each spring it thaws. This seasonal frost is one of three kinds of frozen ground classed by how long they stay frozen, beside permafrost and the frost of {{ref:soil-env-149}}. Its repeated freezing and thawing pushes larger stones toward the surface, building patterned ground such as polygons. Cryogenic earth hummocks, formed by granular convection, appear here as well as in permafrost. Builders take note: rigid retaining-wall footings must sit below the seasonal frost depth, the reach of the {{ref:soil-phys-158}}.

soil-phys-184.title: Thermal effusivity, a material's resistance to temperature swings
soil-phys-184.text: Air scores 0.006 kJ/(m2·K·s½); water scores 1.6. Those numbers measure thermal effusivity, a material's ability to exchange heat with its surroundings. It equals the square root of thermal conductivity times volumetric heat capacity. Soil ranges from 0.5 to 2.6, dry sand 0.63. Effusivity measures thermal inertia. A low value means large daily temperature swings. A high one means much smaller swings. {{ref:soil-phys-164}} sets how fast a body reaches equilibrium; effusivity sets how well it resists periodic change. In remote sensing, a surface's thermal inertia reveals particle size, rock abundance, bedrock outcrop and induration.

soil-phys-182.title: Fourier's law: heat runs downhill in temperature
soil-phys-182.text: Heat always flows from warmer to cooler. Fourier's law, the law of heat conduction, puts a number on it. Heat flow through a material is proportional to the negative temperature gradient and to the area crossed. In one dimension, q = −k dT/dx, where k is the {{ref:soil-phys-141}}. Heat flux is in W/m2, k in W/(m·K), the gradient in K/m. The conductivity can change with temperature, with direction in anisotropic materials and with place in non-uniform ones. {{ref:soil-phys-181}} are its chemical analogue; Ohm's law is its electrical one.

soil-phys-183.title: The heat equation, temperature changing through time
soil-phys-183.text: In 1822 Joseph Fourier wrote an equation for how temperature in a body changes as heat spreads. The heat equation says a point heats or cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter or cooler its surroundings are. In three dimensions it reads ∂u/∂t = α(∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y² + ∂²u/∂z²). Here α is the {{ref:soil-phys-164}}, combining thermal conductivity, specific heat and density. Where a medium is not homogeneous and isotropic, α varies with position and the equation changes slightly.

soil-phys-178.title: Ground source heat pumps, tapping the steady earth
soil-phys-178.text: A few meters down, the seasons blur. A ground source heat pump heats and cools buildings by moving heat to or from the ground, whose temperature stays nearly constant through the year. Down to about 8–20 m, surface swings fade exponentially and lag about 6 months behind, an example of {{ref:soil-phys-142}}. Annual cycles reach 18.0 m in wet clay but only 4.5 m in dry sand. Loops in wet ground work better, because water conducts and stores heat well. Horizontal loops lie below the frost line, and efficiency typically reaches a coefficient of performance of 3–6.

soil-phys-001.title: How grains and gaps build a living soil
soil-phys-001.text: A farmer cannot change the mineral grains in a field, but can wreck or rebuild the way they fit together. That arrangement is soil structure: how a soil's solid particles sit, and the pore spaces left between them. Texture is innate, fixed by the mineral particles themselves, the separates described in {{ref:soil-phys-047}}. Structure is not. It depends on how particles clump, bind and gather into aggregates, small crumbs of particles stuck together. Those clumps in turn set the pattern of pores. Through that pattern, structure shapes how water and air move, how heat travels, and how roots and seedlings push through. It also governs biological activity and how well the soil resists erosion. Structure never sits still. Tillage, wheel traffic, roots, microbes and soil animals reshape it, and so do rain, wind, wetting and drying, and freezing and thawing. Most cultivation does harm. Mechanical mixing compacts and shears aggregates, fills pores and exposes organic matter to faster decay. Continued cultivation and traffic can press compacted, impermeable layers called hardpans into the soil profile. Irrigation brings its own damage, as aggregates break apart and clay disperses on rapid wetting. {{ref:soil-chem-009}} suffer most, because sodium makes wet particles push one another apart. Yet the choice and timing of farming practices can improve structure as well as destroy it. Read with care, structure is also a record. It holds clues to a soil's texture, organic matter, biology, history and human use, and to the chemistry under which it formed.

soil-phys-003.title: Peds: the natural building blocks of soil
soil-phys-003.text: A lump of earth gets a different name depending on who made it. When soil-forming processes build it, it is a ped: a natural aggregate of soil particles, set apart from its neighbors by pores or voids. When cultivation makes it, it is merely a clod. The word, a contraction of pedolith, is used mostly for visible units larger than 1 mm seen in the field. Peds form as sand, silt and clay clump into aggregates, and aggregates clump into larger units. Coatings of carbonates, clay, silica, humus and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} glue them into fairly stable secondary structures. Some soils are structureless, while others have simple units or compound units built of smaller ones. The gaps between peds are one way large pores, or {{ref:soil-water-189}}, form, alongside roots, cracks and soil animals. Peds are best described when soil is dry or slightly moist, because wet peds blur together.

soil-phys-002.title: Plates, prisms, blocks and crumbs: the shapes of structure
soil-phys-002.text: Dig a pit and the soil's architecture shows itself as plates, prisms, columns, blocks and crumbs. These are the five major soil structure types, a grouping of structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds. Platy units are flat plates, usually lying horizontally. They form mainly in subsoil packed down by trampling or machinery, and they hinder water and roots heading downward. Prismatic units stand tall, with flat to rounded vertical faces and flat tops. They typify B horizons enriched with clay washed down from above, split apart by freezing and thawing and by wetting and drying. Columnar units resemble prisms with distinct, rounded tops. Common in subsoils rich in sodium or swelling clay, they are so dense that roots struggle to enter. Blocky units are many-sided and roughly equal in every direction, common in subsoils and clay-rich topsoils. They are angular when faces meet at sharp angles and subangular when corners are mostly rounded. Granular or crumb units are nearly round, with irregular faces that do not mold to their neighbors. They dominate organic-rich grassland and garden topsoils and give good porosity. Some soils also hold wedges, interlocking elliptical lenses often bounded by slickensides, polished surfaces where soil slid past soil. Lenticular units are overlapping lenses parallel to the surface, typical of moist, silty soils prone to frost action. Size classes shift with shape. Very coarse means over 10 mm for platy and granular peds, over 50 mm for blocky ones and over 100 mm for prisms.

soil-phys-006.title: Flocculation: how clay particles join and drift apart
soil-phys-006.text: Muddy water that clears in a few hours has usually flocculated. In colloid chemistry, flocculation is when colloidal particles leave suspension as floc or flake. Unlike precipitation, the particles were first merely suspended in a stable dispersion. The IUPAC definition is contact and adhesion that makes larger clusters. This agglomeration is reversible, so the particles can be dispersed again. In dispersed clay slurries, flocs form once agitation stops, because negative face charges attract positive edge charges. Clay plates flocculate when their slightly positive edges stick to the negative faces of other plates. Sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this and deflocculates the clay. The forces involved include van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonding. Flocculation is the opposite of dispersion, in which particles are held apart. The balance between them is set mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content. It also matters for freshwater: highly dispersible colloids make water turbid and adsorb nutrients that drive eutrophication. Floccules become lasting aggregates only once cementing agents stabilize them. The particles involved are the finest of the {{ref:soil-phys-047}}, chiefly {{ref:soil-found-040}} and {{ref:soil-chem-079}}.

soil-phys-005.title: Soil aggregation: turning loose grains into lasting crumbs
soil-phys-005.text: Earthworms, fungi, frost and chemistry all work on the same project: turning loose grains into crumbs. Soil aggregation is the joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation. Flocculated clumps become true aggregates only once something cements them. Carbonates, gypsum, clay particles, organic matter and sesquioxides, the oxides of iron and aluminum, all serve as cement. {{ref:soil-bio-050}} and fungal hyphae strengthen the bonds. So do multivalent cations bridging negatively charged particles, and hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds between organic compounds. Calcium bridges clay and organic matter. It can also replace sodium on particle surfaces, curbing the dispersion, crusting and bursting of crumbs that plague {{ref:soil-chem-009}}. The best glue depends on the clay. Organic matter is the main binder with swelling 2:1 clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, met in {{ref:soil-phys-029}}. With oxides and 1:1 clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, electrostatic bonds join in, and aggregation is weaker. Sesquioxides cement aggregates larger than 100 μm, especially in soils with more than 10% sesquioxides. Weather shuffles the pieces. Wetting and drying, and shrinking and swelling, rearrange particles and can either strengthen or weaken aggregates. Freezing wet soil breaks aggregates into smaller ones. Some shrink-swell soils even mulch themselves, building a granular surface through repeated shrinking and swelling. Life builds aggregates too, through earthworm casts, the fecal pellets of mites and collembola, roots and fungal hyphae. These biological agents matter most where swelling 2:1 clays are lacking.

soil-phys-007.title: Crumbs within crumbs: the aggregate hierarchy
soil-phys-007.text: A soil crumb is usually built of smaller crumbs, which are built of smaller ones still. The aggregate hierarchy is the idea that aggregates form in levels, larger and looser ones made from smaller, denser ones. Particles join into microaggregates below 250 μm, and these into macroaggregates above 250 μm. Fungal hyphae and roots, the temporary binders, hold macroaggregates together. Transient polysaccharides and persistent compounds hold microaggregates. Yet organic matter's role is hard to pin down, and in some soils it is not the main binder.

soil-phys-004.title: Aggregate stability: will the crumbs hold together?
soil-phys-004.text: A soil can look healthy and still fall apart in the first hard rain. Soil aggregate stability measures how well aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage. It describes {{ref:soil-phys-001}}, responds to management and serves as a soil-quality indicator because it combines physical, chemical and biological properties. It directly controls pore-size distribution, and through it water retention, water movement and air movement. Well-aggregated soil holds a mix of pore sizes: micropores retain and store water, while meso- and macropores let water and air move in. Such soil usually takes in water faster and is not prone to ponding. In compacted soil with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water and nutrients. Clay, adsorbed calcium and magnesium, and iron oxides act as cementing agents, while exchangeable sodium lowers stability by promoting dispersion. Tillage, machinery traffic and livestock traffic are the main disruptors. Reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs improve aggregation, whereas heavy or irregular rainfall, and warmer temperatures that speed decomposition and carbon loss, can lower it. See also {{ref:soil-phys-005}}.

soil-phys-008.title: Sieving and soaking: testing how tough crumbs are
soil-phys-008.text: Soil crumbs are tested the way nature attacks them, with water or with wind. Aggregate stability measurement covers tests of how well aggregates survive such stresses, or those of machinery. Wet methods usually matter more, because they mimic water erosion. Wet sieving turns slowly wetted 2-4 mm aggregates in a sieve nest at 30 rotations per minute for about 10 minutes. It reports a mean weight diameter. Arid regions, where wind erosion dominates, use a dry method that sieves 0.92-1.68 mm aggregates and reports the share above 0.42 mm.

soil-phys-009.title: Slaking: when trapped air bursts soil crumbs
soil-phys-009.text: Drop a dry crumb of soil into water, and the air trapped inside can blow it apart. That is slaking, the break-up of aggregates when entering water displaces air from pores and bursts aggregates holding trapped air. It is purely mechanical, one of the direct ways water destroys soil structure. In the field, slaking follows raindrop impact, so ground cover protects against both. Stable aggregates resist it, along with crusting and erosion. In {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, calcium that replaces sodium on particle surfaces eases slaking, dispersion and crusting alike.

soil-phys-033.title: Soil dispersion: how sodium makes clay wash away
soil-phys-033.text: A dispersive soil can look perfectly sound until digging lets running water reach it. Soil dispersion is the breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away. It is the opposite of flocculation, and soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content control both. Sodium drives the damage. At high levels, sodium ions break clay platelets apart, so wet particles repel one another and aggregates fall to pieces. Calcium and magnesium do the reverse, promoting flocculation. The key gauge is the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}, sodium's share of all the cations a soil holds. Above 5%, dispersion becomes possible, and above 15% it is highly likely. Dispersive layers usually hide in the subsoil, where clay and sodium concentrate. They feel soapy and often have prismatic or columnar structure. Such soils are commoner in old landscapes, and sodium collects low in the landscape. Once exposed, dispersed soil feeds gully and tunnel erosion, degrades structure and turns water turbid. Where the particles settle, they clog and seal the surface. Irrigation can bring the same collapse, as aggregates break down and clay disperses on rapid wetting. Management is mostly restraint: avoid disturbance, keep vegetation cover and control salt. Where the soil has already been disturbed, gypsum is added.

soil-phys-011.title: Hardsetting soil: soft when wet, hard as it dries
soil-phys-011.text: Some soils go soft in the rain, then dry too hard to push a forefinger into. A hardsetting soil loses its structure when wet and sets into a hard, structureless mass as it dries. Cracks are few, usually more than 0.1 m apart. It is not permanently cemented: after flood irrigation or one intense rain, it softens and then sets hard again. Such soil can be tilled only in a narrow moisture range, and it sheds rain as runoff. It runs deeper than a crust, often as thick as the cultivated layer.

soil-phys-031.title: Soil crust: the hard surface that turns rain away
soil-phys-031.text: When rain will not soak into bare ground, the culprit is usually the surface itself. A soil crust is a surface layer, often hardened and platy, that differs from the soil beneath it. Physical crusts form under the impact of raindrops or trampling. Salts and silica collect in them, so they are often harder than uncrusted soil. They cut infiltration, the soaking of water into soil, hinder plants trying to establish and erode quickly once broken. In arid and semi-arid regions, intense rain soon outpaces a sealed surface, and the excess runs off overland. Better soil structure means less crusting and better seedling emergence. Coarse organic matter left on the surface helps prevent crusts, and on {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, so does calcium swapped for sodium. Other crusts are alive, formed by communities of surface microorganisms, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-032}}.

soil-phys-032.title: Biological soil crust: a living skin on bare ground
soil-phys-032.text: Across about 12% of the earth's landmass, the ground between plants is covered by a living skin. A biological soil crust is a community of fungi, lichens, cyanobacteria, bryophytes and algae in the open spaces between vascular plants. Only cyanobacteria and cyanolichens fix nitrogen, so what a crust contributes depends on its makeup. Its carbon cycling happens only when it is wet. Crusts darken the surface, which lowers albedo, and their roughness traps dust. The easiest way to keep them is to remove stressors such as grazing, or to protect them from disturbance.

soil-phys-010.title: Rebuilding the crumb: how farmers repair soil structure
soil-phys-010.text: Each extra millimeter of rain that good structure lets soak in can add 10 kg/ha to a wheat yield. Improving soil structure means practices that push soil toward a granular, crumb structure. They raise porosity, organic matter and the activity of microbes and soil animals. The rewards are less erosion, more water soaking in, easier rooting and fewer crusts blocking seedlings. Mulch, manure and compost, practiced since people first settled to farm, build stable bridges between mineral particles. Where warm, moist climates break down organic matter too fast, charcoal served instead, as in pre-Columbian {{ref:soil-class-053}}. {{ref:soil-fert-050}} is the modern version. Lime helps because divalent calcium bridges negatively charged clay and organic molecules. Advisers urge pasture phases in rotations, less tillage and ground cover against raindrops. On irrigated {{ref:soil-chem-009}}, gypsum lets calcium displace sodium. Less tillage is no cure-all, though: in irrigated horticulture, no-till usually loses productivity as structure degrades.

soil-phys-039.title: Tilth: what makes soil fit for a crop
soil-phys-039.text: By one 2021 estimate, tillage turns 1840 km3 of soil a year worldwide, against 960 km3 moved by plant roots and earthworms. All that plowing chases tilth, the physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop. Soil in good tilth is spongy, with large pores for air and water and a reasonable store of water and nutrients. Its aggregates are strong enough to hold together yet friable, crumbling readily under shallow tilling. Too much strength yields large cemented clods. Tilth depends on stable aggregates, moisture, air and soil life, and it can change quickly. Tillage improves it only briefly, and long-term plowing tends to compact the soil. The most stable tilth comes from life: substances released by roots feed bacteria that secrete polysaccharides, and fungi whose hyphae bind particles. Grass and legume sods, deep-rooted perennials such as alfalfa, and cover crops help rebuild compacted soil.

soil-phys-041.title: Soil consistency: how soil feels between the fingers
soil-phys-041.text: Squeeze a moist lump between thumb and finger, and its resistance says a good deal about the soil. Soil consistency is the ability of soil to stick to itself or to other objects and to resist deformation and rupture. It is judged air-dry, moist and wet, and in each state it depends on clay content. Dry soil is rubbed to see how it crumbles, moist soil is pressed, and wet soil is checked for stickiness and plasticity. Standard terms run from loose to extremely hard when dry, and from nonsticky to very sticky when wet. Cemented soils barely change with moisture, and the most cemented, called indurated, need hammer blows to break. Because these judgments rest on feel, they are close to subjective. Still, consistency roughly predicts trouble with cultivation and with supporting buildings and roads.

soil-phys-021.title: Atterberg limits: the water contents where soil changes state
soil-phys-021.text: Add water to a dry fine-grained soil, and it passes from solid to semi-solid to plastic to liquid. The Atterberg limits are the critical water contents that mark where it crosses from one of these states to the next. A Swedish chemist and agronomist, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-011}}, devised them in 1911. He also proposed the first soil particle-size classification, described in {{ref:soil-phys-048}}. Arthur Casagrande, a pioneer of soil mechanics, later refined them. Because the changes are gradual, standard tests fix each boundary by convention. The first of those tests appears in {{ref:soil-phys-022}}. The tests suit clayey and silty soils, which shrink, swell and change strength as their moisture varies. Fine-grained soils are classified mainly by these limits rather than by grain size. The limits are simple to measure and closely tied to compressibility, permeability and strength, so they offer quick estimates of all three.

soil-phys-022.title: Liquid limit: where clay starts to flow
soil-phys-022.text: Twenty-five drops of a cup can hint at whether a clay will swell. The liquid limit is the water content at which a clayey soil stops behaving as a plastic solid and starts behaving as a liquid. In Casagrande's cup test, it is the moisture content at which 25 drops close a groove cut in the soil over 12.7 mm. Europe prefers the fall cone test, which measures how far a steel cone sinks. Values over 50 suggest significant swelling. The same value of 50 divides high- from low-plasticity fine soils in {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

soil-phys-023.title: Plastic limit: the thread that breaks at 3.2 mm
soil-phys-023.text: A standard soil test needs little more than a rolled thread of soil. The plastic limit is the water content below which a soil turns brittle and can no longer be rolled into a thin thread. Rolled on a flat, non-porous surface, the thread breaks at larger diameters as it dries. The limit is the moisture content, by weight, at which it breaks apart at 3.2 mm, about 1/8 inch. A soil that never reaches 3.2 mm at any moisture is non-plastic. Remolded soil here is quite stiff, near 200 kPa of {{ref:soil-phys-103}}.

soil-phys-024.title: Shrinkage limit: the point where drying clay stops shrinking
soil-phys-024.text: A drying clay shrinks, but only up to a point. The shrinkage limit is the water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink. It is used much less often than the liquid and plastic limits. Its value depends on the kind of clay. Reported shrinkage limits run 8.5–15% for {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, 15–17% for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 25–29% for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. So the last of these clays stops shrinking while it still holds far more water than the first does.

soil-phys-025.title: Plasticity index: the span where soil stays moldable
soil-phys-025.text: One subtraction turns two lab tests into a telling measure of a clay. The plasticity index is the span of water contents over which a soil behaves plastically: the liquid limit minus the plastic limit. A score of 0 means non-plastic, below 7 slightly plastic, 7–17 medium plastic, and above 17 highly plastic. The index tracks permeability, compressibility and shear strength. Above 35, it signals high expansion potential. Silts and clays are sorted by plotting this index against the liquid limit, the method of {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

soil-phys-026.title: Liquidity index: where a soil's water sits between limits
soil-phys-026.text: Where a soil's natural water content, W, falls between its limits says much about how strong it is once remolded. The liquidity index places W on the scale from plastic to liquid limit: LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL). At 0 the soil sits at its plastic limit, near 200 kPa of {{ref:soil-phys-103}}. At 1 it sits at its liquid limit, with only about 2 kPa. A companion consistency index, (LL − W)/(LL − PL), runs the other way, and the two always add up to 1.

soil-phys-027.title: Clay activity: same clay content, different behavior
soil-phys-027.text: Two soils with the same amount of clay can behave very differently, because {{ref:soil-chem-079}} differ. Clay activity is the ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is. Below 0.75 the clay is inactive, above 1.25 active, and in between normal. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} has liquid limits of 100–900%, against 60–120% for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 30–110% for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. The ratio links clay as a size to clay as a mineral, the split explained in {{ref:soil-phys-054}}.

soil-phys-036.title: The Unified Soil Classification System: soil in two letters
soil-phys-036.text: Engineers across North America describe a soil with just two letters. Those letters come from the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS, which classes soils by texture and grain size. It is the most common engineering classification in North America and works for most unconsolidated materials. The first letter names the main material: G for gravel, S for sand, M for silt, C for clay and O for organic soil. Peat gets PT. The second letter gives grading, W for well graded or P for poorly graded, or {{ref:soil-phys-022}}, H for high and L for low. Soils fall into three major groups: coarse-grained sands and gravels, fine-grained silts and clays, and highly organic soils, or peat. Sieves draw the first line. A soil is coarse-grained if more than 50% stays on the No. 200 sieve, whose openings are 0.075 mm. The No. 4 sieve, with 4.75 mm openings, separates sand from gravel. Under the USCS, silt particles measure 0.002–0.075 mm and sand particles 0.075–4.75 mm. Sands and gravels are then divided by grain size and grading. Silts and clays are divided by their Atterberg limits into high- and low-plasticity soils. With 5–12% fines, the silt and clay particles, both grading and plasticity count. A dual symbol may then appear, such as GW-GM for well-graded gravel with silt. Europe's standard, {{ref:soil-class-152}}, is very similar but adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays.

soil-phys-037.title: Gravels and sands: the USCS coarse-grained groups
soil-phys-037.text: In the USCS, a soil is coarse when more than half its weight stays on the No. 200 sieve. It is gravel (G) if more than 50% of its coarse fraction stays on the No. 4 sieve, and sand (S) otherwise. Clean gravels and sands, under 5% fines, are well graded (GW, SW) or poorly graded (GP, SP). GW needs Cu ≥ 4 and SW Cu ≥ 6, both with 1 ≤ Cc ≤ 3. Above 12% fines they become silty (GM, SM) or clayey (GC, SC), and in between they take dual symbols such as SW-SC.

soil-phys-038.title: Silts and clays: the USCS fine-grained groups
soil-phys-038.text: Once at least half a soil passes the No. 200 sieve, grain size stops deciding its name. Such soils are classed as silts (M) or clays (C) by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit. The A-line splits clays from silts, and a liquid limit of 50% splits high (H) from low (L) plasticity. The inorganic groups are lean clay (CL), silt (ML), fat clay (CH) and elastic silt (MH). CL needs a plasticity index above 7, and ML one below 4. Organic silts and clays (OL, OH) are told apart by changes on oven drying.

soil-phys-034.title: Hydrophobic soil: ground that sheds water
soil-phys-034.text: Fire can leave behind soil that sheds water instead of soaking it up. A hydrophobic soil is one whose particles repel water. It most often forms when fire or hot air drives waxy compounds out of surface litter to coat sandy particles below. Sand is most prone because its large grains have little surface area and are easily coated. Repellency slows infiltration, so runoff and erosion rise, and Australia has seen production losses of up to 80%. Adding clay helps: calcium-bentonite raised one barley yield from 1.7 to 3.4 t/ha.

soil-phys-035.title: Timing a water drop: measuring how much soil repels water
soil-phys-035.text: The simplest measure of a stubborn soil is how long one drop of water takes to soak in. Soil water repellency tests rate how strongly a soil repels water, usually starting with that drop. Under 5 seconds means not repellent, up to 1 minute slightly repellent, 1–10 minutes repellent, and longer severely repellent. The molarity of ethanol droplet test tries ethanol solutions of falling surface tension until one soaks in within 10 seconds. An index of 1 or less means non-repellent, and 2.2 or more severely repellent.

soil-phys-042.title: Soil resistivity: how soil resists electric current
soil-phys-042.text: Soil carries electric current, and how easily it does so affects how fast buried metal and concrete corrode. Soil resistivity is a measure of how strongly a soil resists the flow of that current. Wetter soil, or soil with a higher electrolyte concentration, has lower resistivity. Current then flows more easily, and corrosion speeds up. Values typically range from about 1 to 100,000 Ω·m. Saline soils sit at the low end, and dry soils over crystalline rocks at the high end.

soil-phys-063.title: Porosity: how much of a soil is empty space
soil-phys-063.text: Solid granite is almost all rock, with less than 0.005 of its volume left empty. Peat and clay can be more than half empty space. That share is porosity: the fraction of a material's total volume taken up by voids, given from 0 to 1 or as a percentage. Geologists, hydrologists and soil scientists use it for any of the materials described in {{ref:soil-phys-172}}, such as rock or sediment, whose voids may hold air or water. It is written ϕ or n. Porosity can be worked out from two densities. When the voids hold air, it equals one minus a ratio of two densities. On top is the density of the whole soil, in {{ref:soil-phys-060}}; below is that of its solid grains alone, in {{ref:soil-phys-062}}. Sorting matters as much as grain size. A well-sorted material is more porous than a poorly sorted one of similar size, because in the mixed one small particles fill the gaps between larger ones. A few fine grains lodged in the pores can sharply cut porosity, and the ease of water flow, while making up only a small share of the volume. In rock and sedimentary layers, porosity governs how much water or hydrocarbon they may hold. It also falls with depth. As buried sediment compacts, its porosity drops exponentially, a pattern described by the Athy (1930) equation.

soil-phys-059.title: Soil physics: the science of grains, water and air
soil-phys-059.text: How fast water sinks into a field, how air reaches a root, how warm the ground gets: these are questions for soil physics. It studies the physical properties and processes of soil across its solid, liquid and gas phases. The field borrows from physics, physical chemistry, engineering and meteorology, and turns them on practical problems in agriculture, ecology and engineering. Its results guide management and prediction in natural and managed ecosystems alike. F. H. King ({{ref:soil-hist-020}}), called the father of soil physics in the United States, studied how soils hold water, take in air and move water. Edgar Buckingham (1867–1940) worked out the theory of how gases diffuse through soil and how water flows in the unsaturated ground above the groundwater. Willard Gardner first measured capillary potential with porous cups and manometers. L. A. Richards ({{ref:soil-hist-023}}) described flow in unsaturated soil and measured how tightly soil holds its water with the instrument described in {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Later, John R. Philip found an analytical solution for soil water transport, and Martinus van Genuchten built functions for how soil holds and conducts water.

soil-phys-092.title: Soil mechanics: how a mix of grains, water and air behaves
soil-phys-092.text: A dam, a pipeline and a house foundation all rest on the same question: how will the soil behave? Soil mechanics is the branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that answers it. Unlike fluid or solid mechanics, it deals with a mixture: fluids, usually air and water, among particles of clay, silt, sand and gravel, plus organic solids. With rock mechanics it underpins engineering geology and the field traced in {{ref:soil-phys-167}}. It analyses how structures built on, made of or buried in soil deform, and how fluids flow inside them, from foundations and retaining walls to dams and pipelines. Agricultural, coastal and geophysical engineering and hydrology use its principles too. One idea runs through it. A load pressing down on soil is shared between the pore fluid and the particles. Neither gas nor liquid resists shear, though, so resistance to sliding comes from friction and interlocking of the grains. Standard classification tests miss part of the story. They use dried, sieved and remoulded samples, so the soil's structure and its pattern of pore sizes and fluids are lost.

soil-phys-060.title: Bulk density: weighing soil with its holes included
soil-phys-060.text: Quartz has a density of about 2.65 g/cm3, yet the dry bulk density of a mineral soil is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3. Bulk density is the mass of a soil divided by the whole volume it occupies, counting the spaces between and within its particles. That last clause separates it from {{ref:soil-phys-062}}, which leaves the voids out. Because it counts the gaps, bulk density depends on packing and changes with handling: a disturbed powder settles to a higher value. In soil it depends mainly on the mineral make-up and on how compacted the soil is. Organic soils sit at the light end. Soils rich in organic carbon and some crumbly clays fall below 1.0 g/cm3, and peat soils range from 0.02 to 0.98 g/cm3. Dark, well-decomposed organic matter lowers it too. The rule is simple: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its dry bulk density. A high value points either to compaction or to a mix of textures in which small particles fill the voids between coarse ones. Measured at a standard moisture content, bulk density estimates compaction. A European Union study of the top 0-20 cm found croplands almost 1.5 times denser than woodlands. Simple formulas also combine bulk density with particle size to estimate properties such as how readily water flows through soil.

soil-phys-120.title: The soil matrix, the solid frame around the pores
