soil-phys-120.text: The soil matrix is the solid phase of a soil: the mineral particles and organic matter that make it up. Around it lie the pore space, holding the soil atmosphere, and the soil solution, holding water and dissolved substances. Matrix particles are classed by size and by mineral make-up. Texture largely sets how water moves and is held, but mineralogy can strongly modify both. Gravel, sand and silt usually inherit their minerals from the parent material, most often weathering-resistant quartz. Clay is the most active part, with a high specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges, so its mineralogy matters most. Its minerals are secondary, precipitates that keep forming as long as the soil exists. The organic part of the matrix, weight for weight, holds many times more exchangeable positive ions than clay. Nutrients held this way, such as K, Ca, Mg, P and Zn, form a ready reservoir for plants.

soil-phys-069.title: Pore space, where soil keeps its water and air
soil-phys-069.text: Roots, burrowing animals and microbes all live in the gaps. Pore space is the part of a soil's volume not filled by solid mineral and organic particles, and it holds the soil's water and air. Total porosity is the pore volume divided by the total volume, often given in percent; in unsaturated soil, air and water share it. A sandy soil is more porous than a silty sand, because silt fills the gaps between sand grains. When water soaks in, the largest cracks and pores fill first, mostly by gravity. Smaller pores fill slowly by capillary forces and can trap air. Large pores and cracks largely control how fast water enters and moves. They also strongly affect gas exchange and the breathing of soil life. The ease of water movement through pores, {{ref:soil-water-193}}, depends on compaction and on how full the pores are. Roots and burrowing animals carve networks of connected pores. Microbial cells and their slime can also block pores, a process described in {{ref:soil-water-241}}.

soil-phys-082.title: Soil compaction: squeezing the air out of the ground
soil-phys-082.text: In one cotton field, the tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space. Between the rows, where wheels ran, it reached 1.67 g/cm3, and pore space fell to 37%. That is soil compaction: the densification of soil under applied stress as air is pushed out of the pores between its grains. When water rather than air is squeezed out, the process is consolidation, described in {{ref:soil-phys-110}}. In soil science and agronomy the word compaction usually covers both, and suction as water evaporates can drive it too. Heavy machinery is the usual cause, though the passage of animal feet can also compact soil. The damage follows from the lost pores. Pressed-together grains leave little room for the air and water roots need, and burrowing animals struggle to penetrate the denser soil. Compacted soil absorbs less rainfall, so runoff and erosion increase and less water recharges the groundwater. Recovery depends on climate, mineralogy and the animals living in the soil. Soils that shrink and swell strongly, such as those in {{ref:soil-class-106}}, recover quickly where dry spells shrink and crack them. Clays built of a mineral that does not crack as it dries, described in {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, cannot recover unaided. They need earthworms or other ground-dwelling animals living in them, as in the Cecil soils.

soil-phys-086.title: The hidden damage under farm fields
soil-phys-086.text: Erosion is easy to see. Compaction mostly is not. Unlike salt build-up or erosion, compaction of farmland is mainly a hidden problem below the surface, and finding it takes special methods. Soil compaction in agriculture is the rise in bulk density, or fall in porosity, of farmland soil under loads from outside or within. It is also called soil structure degradation. It can harm nearly all the physical, chemical and biological properties and functions of soil. Together with erosion it has been called the costliest and most serious environmental problem of conventional agriculture. Heavy machinery and poor management can press the subsoil into impermeable layers that hold back the movement of water and nutrients. On the farm, compaction cuts crop growth, yield and quality. Beyond it, compaction adds runoff, erosion, greenhouse gas emissions, nutrients fouling lakes and rivers, less water reaching the groundwater, and loss of biodiversity. The problem is old. Hard layers below the plough, described in {{ref:soil-agri-101}}, were linked to compaction before farming was mechanized, and modern techniques have raised the risk. In 1991 compaction was estimated at 4% of human-caused damage to soils worldwide, some 68.3 million hectares. In 2013 it was a major cause of damage in Europe (about 33 million ha), Africa (18 million ha), Asia (10 million ha) and Australia (4 million ha). In Europe about 32% of subsoils are highly vulnerable to it and 18% moderately so.

soil-phys-098.title: Pore water pressure, the push of water between grains
soil-phys-098.text: Water held between soil grains pushes back. Pore water pressure is the pressure of the groundwater in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock. Deep in saturated ground it is measured with piezometers. Where the water is not flowing it is close to hydrostatic, rising steadily with depth. The surface where it equals atmospheric pressure is the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Above that level, capillarity sets the pressure, and it is called tension, suction or matric pressure. Instruments with a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil measure it there, by methods set out in ISO 11276:1995. The pressure has several parts: the weight of overlying material, osmotic pressure from uneven ion concentrations, and pressure from water films, held by {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, that draw grains together. It matters because the load carried by the grains, {{ref:soil-phys-100}}, is the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Too much of it can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer, as in {{ref:soil-phys-160}}.

soil-phys-073.title: Void ratio: comparing the gaps with the grains
soil-phys-073.text: Porosity divides empty space by the whole volume. Void ratio divides it by the solids alone. It is the ratio of the volume of voids, filled with gas or liquid, to the volume of solids, a dimensionless number closely tied to porosity. Geotechnical engineers treat it, as the symbol e, as a state variable of soils. Because they use ϕ for the angle of shearing resistance, they write porosity as η. Void ratio predicts behaviour under load. A loose soil with a high void ratio tends to shrink as voids close and grain contacts multiply. A dense soil with a low void ratio tends to swell when unloaded. Loose soils conduct water readily, and dense ones less so. Fine particles pass through the large voids of loose soil but clog the small pores of dense soil. For a given soil, the ease with which water passes rises with the void ratio. The simple relation assumes a rigid skeleton that keeps its volume on wetting and drying. Swelling clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, with water bound between their layers, fall outside it.

soil-phys-100.title: Effective stress: the load the grains really carry
soil-phys-100.text: Soil grains do not carry the whole weight above them. Effective stress is the part of the total stress in a soil carried by its solid skeleton rather than by the pore water. Karl von Terzaghi first proposed, in 1925, that it equals the total normal stress minus the pore water pressure. It governs both the strength and the volume change of porous media, from sand to concrete. The strength of a soil, described in {{ref:soil-phys-176}}, comes mainly from friction between particles, which is proportional to the stress pressing them together. So when pore water pressure rises, strength falls. Pore water is nearly incompressible, so saturated soil can pack closer only if water is squeezed out. Water injected between grains pushes them apart and lowers effective stress; withdrawing it forces them together. {{ref:soil-phys-118}} and the sandcastle effect mark the two extremes. Effective stress is central to the stability of slopes and to land sinking from groundwater pumping. Yet in 1962 Jennings and Burland showed that partly saturated soils do not follow effective stress alone.

soil-phys-125.title: Seepage: water on the move through soil
soil-phys-125.text: Still water in soil does little harm. Moving water can bring down a levee. Seepage is the movement of water through soil. Below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}, where pore water pressure rises evenly with depth, conditions are hydrostatic and nothing flows. A sloping or perched water surface sets water seeping. The rate follows {{ref:soil-water-201}}. Flow is proportional to how fast excess pressure changes with distance, scaled by how freely the soil passes water and by the fluid's viscosity. The ease of flow varies enormously, from about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels. In steady seepage, velocities do not change with time; that does not hold while water levels are changing or the soil is consolidating. Upward seepage lowers effective stress. At the critical {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, it reaches zero, the soil loses nearly all strength, and less permeable layers may heave. This state, also called a boiling condition, is the one behind {{ref:soil-phys-116}} and {{ref:soil-phys-118}}. Strength lost to upward seepage often helps cause levee failures. Fast seepage also drags particles away from where it comes out. The erosion works back upslope as {{ref:soil-water-289}}, which can fail a structure and open sinkholes. To stop seepage below dams, engineers build impermeable curtains of {{ref:soil-chem-100}}, a clay almost fully saturated with sodium.

soil-phys-101.title: Shear strength: how hard soil can be pushed before it fails
soil-phys-101.text: Whether a slope stands or a bridge settles too far comes down to one property. Shear strength is the largest shear stress a soil can sustain before it fails. Resistance comes from friction and interlocking of particles, and sometimes from cement or bonds where they touch. Friction dominates, so resistance on a plane is roughly proportional to the effective normal stress. That makes the angle of internal friction close to the steepest slope at which loose grains will pile. Strength also depends on drainage, how densely particles pack, and the rate and direction of strain. Interlocked grains make soil expand or contract as it shears. If it expands, density and strength drop, so a peak may be followed by falling shear stress. Eventually shear stress and density hold constant while strain continues, a condition called the critical state, steady state or residual strength. If water cannot flow in or out, shearing is undrained: density cannot change, but pore pressure and effective stress do. Real soils are partly drained.

soil-phys-116.title: Liquefaction: when shaking turns solid ground to liquid
soil-phys-116.text: In the 2018 Palu earthquake, the ground itself flowed. It buried the suburb of Balaroa and Petobo village 3 metres deep in mud. Soil liquefaction is the sudden loss of strength and stiffness in a wet soil of loose, unbound grains. Under stress such as earthquake shaking, the solid behaves like a liquid. Loose sand tends to compress under load. If it is saturated, pore water pressure rises until it exceeds the contact forces between grains, and effective stress falls to essentially zero. Dense sands dilate instead. So the soils most at risk are loose, saturated, poorly drained sands and non-plastic silts; gravels and clays rarely liquefy. Young Holocene beds of well-sorted sand and silt, saturated and metres thick, along stream beds, beaches, dunes and loess areas, are the most susceptible. Allen Hazen first called soil 'liquefied' after the 1918 failure of the Calaveras Dam in California. Engineers paid closer attention after the 1964 Alaska and Niigata earthquakes. Shaking can force water and liquefied sand to the surface, and ground can slide sideways on slopes of only 1 or 2 degrees, called lateral spreading. Liquefaction damages buildings, bridges, buried services and levees. Over geological time it may also leave a dense parent material in which a fragipan can develop. Engineers fight it by densifying soil with vibro or dynamic compaction or stabilising it with grout, and cementing sand with calcite made by microbes has been proposed.

soil-phys-118.title: Quicksand, solid until it is disturbed
soil-phys-118.text: At about 2 grams per cubic centimetre, quicksand is roughly twice as dense as the human body, so a person cannot sink beyond about waist height. It is a suspension of fine sand, silt or clay in water, a kind of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, that forms when saturated loose sand is agitated and loses its strength. Upward flow, as from an artesian spring, holds the grains suspended. Undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly makes it runny. Pulling a foot out at 1 cm/s takes as much force as lifting a car. Slow movements and floating on the back allow escape.

soil-phys-107.title: Cohesion: the strength that is not friction
soil-phys-107.text: Friction explains most of a soil's strength, but not all of it. Cohesion is the part of a soil's or rock's shear strength that does not depend on friction between particles. In soils it comes from electrostatic forces in stiff clays that once bore heavier loads, from cementing by Fe2O3, CaCO3 or NaCl, and from negative capillary pressure. The pore pressure response when water cannot drain adds some, and so do plant roots. Several sources are temporary. Weathering can remove electrostatic bonds, wetting removes capillary suction, time dissipates pore pressure, and logging or fire removes root strength. The theory in {{ref:soil-phys-169}} usually measures cohesion as the shear strength at zero normal pressure on the failure surface. Values run from 0 to 48 kPa for very soft clay, through 192 to 384 kPa for stiff clay, to 384 to 766 kPa for very stiff clay. When soil loses cohesion it can slough off banks and slopes.

soil-phys-110.title: Consolidation: the slow squeeze that sinks buildings
soil-phys-110.text: Picture a spring inside a water-filled container with a hole in its lid. Press the lid and at first the water resists. Then it drains out through the hole, and the spring shortens and takes over the load. The spring is the soil skeleton. The process is soil consolidation. It is the gradual change in a soil's volume under a change in pressure, as water is slowly squeezed out of or drawn into its pores. When saturated soil is loaded, the water, far stiffer in volume than the skeleton, first carries the load as excess pore water pressure. As it seeps away, the grains take the load and the soil shrinks. Saturated clays consolidate very slowly, because water passes through them with extreme difficulty. Coarse soils drain readily and settle at once instead. Clays settle under external loads, under their own weight or that of overlying soil, and when groundwater pumping raises the effective stress on them. The effects show most where a building sits on soft, poorly permeable soil such as marine clay, which can settle a great deal over many years. In the narrow sense the term means this delayed, drainage-driven response. In the broad sense it covers any pressure-driven volume change, including compaction, sinking land, heave and swelling. Karl von Terzaghi, the 'father of soil mechanics', defined it as any loss of water from a saturated soil without air taking its place. Engineers measure it with the test in {{ref:soil-phys-170}}, loading a thin disc of soil in steps and recording its thickness over time.

soil-phys-109.title: Angle of repose: the steepest slope a pile can hold
soil-phys-109.text: Wind-blown sand piles up to about 34 degrees before it slides. That limit is the angle of repose, the steepest angle from the horizontal at which a granular material can be piled without slumping. Rough grains pile more steeply than rounded ones. A little water bridging the gaps raises the angle, but saturation lubricates the grains and can set slopes moving. Typical values are 15° for wet excavated clay, 15–30° for water-filled sand and 25–30° for natural gravel with sand. Henri Gautier recognized this 'natural slope' of soils in 1717.

soil-phys-095.title: How water climbs above the groundwater
soil-phys-095.text: Water in soil does not stop at the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. It climbs into the small pores above, held there by surface tension under negative pressure. This is capillary action in soil. For some distance above that level the soil can be fully saturated; higher up it is still wet, but holds less water with every step of height. Pore size sets the climb, from about a centimetre in coarse sand to tens of metres in silt or clay. Water held at negative pressure pulls particles together, so effective stress can stay positive even at a free surface. That is why a wet sand castle stands, held by friction where grains touch, and collapses once it is submerged. Negative pore pressures are much stronger in clay than in sand. They explain why clay soils shrink as they dry and swell when wetted, which can damage light structures and roads.

soil-phys-115.title: Overburden pressure, the weight of everything above
soil-phys-115.text: Overburden pressure is the pressure at a given depth caused by the weight of the overlying material, also called lithostatic pressure or vertical stress. It increases with depth in proportion to the density of the overlying material and gravity; in the Earth's crust the average gradient is about 270 bar/km. It squeezes pores smaller, shrinking volume without distorting the material, so it matters as sediment hardens into rock and as rock is transformed. Hard-to-measure sideways stresses are expressed relative to it through a coefficient, k. Together with excess pore water pressure, overburden can force blocks out near the base of a river bank, a popout failure.

soil-phys-127.title: Sand boils, where buried water breaks the surface
soil-phys-127.text: In a flood, water pushed through a levee can well up on the dry side as if it were boiling: a sand boil. Turbulent flow at the seep starts the underground erosion of {{ref:soil-water-289}}, which can quickly fail the embankment, so crews stack rings of sandbags to slow it. Earthquakes that liquefy saturated sediment make sand boils too, sometimes building a cone called a sand blow. The 1811–1812 New Madrid earthquakes left the largest known, 'The Beach' near Hayti, Missouri, 2.3 kilometres long. Geologists map sand blows as strong evidence of past earthquakes.

soil-phys-070.title: Five sizes of soil pore, from cracks to cryptopores
soil-phys-070.text: A pore's size decides what water it holds and what can live in it. A widely used grouping, after Brewer (1964), sorts soil pores by diameter. The largest class, {{ref:soil-water-189}}, are over 75 μm, too large for significant capillary force. Unless closed off, they drain and are usually full of air at the wetness described in {{ref:soil-water-177}}. They form where soil cracks, where peds and aggregates separate, and along roots and burrows. Mesopores, 30–75 μm, are the largest pores still full of water at that point. Called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use, so soil scientists study them closely for agriculture and irrigation. Micropores, 5–30 μm, hold water that is practically immobile yet still available to plants, so dissolved substances move through them mainly by diffusion. Ultramicropores, 0.1–5 μm, shelter microbes inside aggregates from predators such as amoebae and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, and their volume tracks bacterial biomass. Texture and organic matter set them, and compaction barely touches them. Cryptopores, under 0.1 μm, are too small for most microbes. Organic matter inside them is protected from decay, and their water is barely available to plants.

soil-phys-094.title: Relative density: how close sand is to fully packed
soil-phys-094.text: Relative density measures how densely packed a sand or gravel is. It compares the soil's void ratio in the ground with its maximum and minimum void ratios, which match its very loose and very dense states. A value of 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil. It is used for soils whose grains do not stick together, and ASTM D4254-00(2016) sets out how to calculate it.

soil-phys-128.title: Specific storage: water released as pressure falls
soil-phys-128.text: Lower the water pressure in a saturated aquifer and it gives up some of its water. Specific storage is the volume released from a unit volume of aquifer when the water's pressure level falls by one unit. It reflects how compressible both the aquifer and the water are. Storativity, or the storage coefficient, is the same release per unit area of aquifer. For a confined aquifer it is specific storage summed over the thickness. In an unconfined aquifer storativity roughly equals the {{ref:soil-phys-129}}, because release from specific storage is orders of magnitude smaller.

soil-phys-083.title: Compacting soil on purpose to carry a building
soil-phys-083.text: Not all compaction is damage. Builders densify soil on purpose with heavy equipment so it can carry foundations, roads, walkways and retaining structures. Good fill is strong, relatively incompressible, durable, suitably permeable, and stable in volume as its moisture varies. It goes down in layers called lifts. Sands and gravels are usually compacted with vibrating equipment. Silts and clays are often worked with a sheepsfoot roller, whose intense local shearing drives out air. Afterwards, ground to be landscaped must be loosened again so that plants can grow.

soil-phys-089.title: What compaction does to roots, microbes and rivers
soil-phys-089.text: Grassland soil without traffic takes in water five times faster than severely trafficked soil. Compaction chiefly cuts how readily air and water enter the ground. Denser soil with smaller pores restricts roots, partly through build-up of the hormone ethylene, and limits their access to nutrients. Shallow roots can leave the topsoil extremely dry and cracked. Oxygen diffuses poorly, so soil can turn airless. With wetter conditions this boosts {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, raising N2O emissions and leaving less nitrogen for crops. Waterlogged compacted soils also release methane through increased bacterial activity. Severe compaction can shrink {{ref:soil-bio-269}} and, by removing large pores, shift where earthworms live. Wheel tracks often start runoff and erosion, carrying sediment, nutrients and pesticides off the field to over-enrich lakes and rivers. Less water reaches the groundwater, a serious risk in dry regions. Over large areas, the yield losses may threaten food security.

soil-phys-091.title: Preventing compaction, since cures take decades
soil-phys-091.text: Partly restoring a compacted soil takes several decades, so prevention matters most. Controlled traffic keeps wheel tracks apart from rooting areas, and low tyre pressure spreads a machine's load over a larger surface. Models of field vulnerability help farmers avoid driving on susceptible soil. Where damage is done, deep ripping can loosen compacted layers. Biology helps too. Deep-rooting crops break impermeable layers, add organic matter and drive wetting and drying cycles that crack the soil. Growing crops and trees on the same site, as {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, regenerates compacted soil over the long run. The planting pits described in {{ref:soil-agri-057}}, 20–40 cm across and 10–20 cm deep, are filled with organic matter, capture water and gradually rehabilitate the soil beneath. Adding lime raises pH to suit microbes and earthworms, whose activity loosens the soil. The EU's Seventh Environment Action Programme, in force from 2014, addresses compaction, and a German federal soil law obliges farmers to guard against it.

soil-phys-087.title: How pressure turns loose soil into a dense mass
soil-phys-087.text: Press on soil and it answers by bringing its particles closer. In well-structured soil, particles bond into aggregates, and their stability grows with the number of particle interactions. Applied pressure is met with more particle contacts. The voids shrink, water and air are pushed out, bulk density rises, and water and air pass through less easily. Some soils give way more readily than others. Water films around particles can shield their interactions and weaken structure. So wet soils compact more easily than dry ones, and fine-textured, clay-rich soils more easily than coarse ones. Other traits raise resistance. Angular, mixed structure helps, as does a high starting bulk density. So does organic matter, which binds minerals and water together. Soil pH matters too, because it affects the net charges of molecules.

soil-phys-119.title: Thixotropy: clays that turn liquid when shaken
soil-phys-119.text: Some clays hold firm until disturbed, then flow. Thixotropy is that time-dependent property: a material thick at rest flows more easily when shaken or stressed, then takes time to thicken again. Its particles need time to organise, so many gels and the fine suspended particles of {{ref:soil-chem-154}} are stable at rest but turn fluid when agitated. Most suspensions of {{ref:soil-chem-100}} behave this way. {{ref:soil-water-071}} switches from stiff solid to liquid mass when disturbed, as slope failures such as the Aberfan disaster show. Herbert Freundlich coined the word, from the Greek for 'touch' and 'turn'.

soil-phys-131.title: Specific weight: density with gravity added
soil-phys-131.text: Water at 4 °C weighs 9.807 kilonewtons per cubic metre. That is its specific weight, or unit weight: weight per unit volume, equal to density multiplied by gravitational acceleration. Unlike density, it is not a fixed property, because gravity varies from place to place. Soil mechanics uses it for earthworks, distinguishing moist, dry and saturated unit weight by whether the pores hold water and air, air only, or water only. Each is calculated from the specific gravity of the solids, the void ratio and the unit weight of water, plus the moisture for moist soil.

soil-phys-067.title: The chemists' pore sizes, measured in nanometres
soil-phys-067.text: To a chemist, a micropore is under 2 nm across. The IUPAC set this standard in 1985: micropores under 2 nm, mesopores of 2 to 50 nm, and a largest class over 50 nm. The limits come from how gases adsorb on rigid solids. Micropores fill cooperatively, mesopores show capillary condensation, and in the largest pores the effects of confinement vanish. The scheme grew out of earlier work by M. M. Dubinin and D. H. Everett. Outside chemistry the limits are often ignored and the prefixes only mark relative sizes, which causes confusion between disciplines.

soil-phys-068.title: Finding the empty space in a sample
soil-phys-068.text: Computed tomography can render the voids inside a sample in three dimensions. Simpler methods also find porosity. Direct methods subtract the volume of the solid skeleton from the bulk volume, and optical ones compare pore and solid areas under a microscope. Water methods weigh a sample soaked and dry, and the difference gives the pore volume. In the gas expansion method, gas passes from the sample's container into an evacuated one, and the ideal gas law gives the answer. It detects only pores open to the surroundings. Mercury intrusion and thermoporosimetry reveal pore sizes.

soil-phys-065.title: Why the most porous soils can drain the slowest
soil-phys-065.text: Clay is full of pores yet gives up water grudgingly. It has very high porosity but very low {{ref:soil-water-193}}: it stores much water per volume but releases it slowly through narrow pore throats. Porosity and ease of flow are only loosely linked. Of two similar sandy aquifers, the more porous one usually conducts water faster, but that rule is inferred rather than direct. Flow tracks the radius of pore throats closely. As grain size or sorting decreases, the tie between throat radius and porosity breaks down, and with it the tie to flow.

soil-phys-064.title: Why heavy clay soils are full of holes
soil-phys-064.text: Sandy soil, typically 1.5 to 1.7 g/cm3 in bulk density, has a porosity between 0.43 and 0.36. Clay soil at 1.1 to 1.3 g/cm3 has between 0.58 and 0.51. Surface porosity falls as particles get coarser, because fine soils build aggregates. Calling clay soils heavy seems to imply few pores; the word reflects their moisture weight and the force needed to pull tools through them. Deeper down, gravity compacts soil, and 0.20 is normal for unsorted gravel-sized material below the biomantle. Traditional models give only approximate results, so fractal, cracking, packed-sphere and other models have been proposed.

soil-phys-066.title: Open, closed, primary and secondary porosity
soil-phys-066.text: Not every pore lets fluid through. Effective, or open, porosity is the fraction where fluid actually flows, excluding closed pores, and it matters for groundwater flow and the movement of dissolved substances. Ineffective, or closed, porosity holds fluids or gases that cannot flow. Pores also differ by origin. Primary porosity is the original pore system of a rock or alluvial deposit. Secondary porosity forms later, as minerals leach out or the rock fractures. Dual porosity treats a medium as two overlapping, interacting reservoirs, such as a rock mass and its fractures.

soil-phys-132.title: Dilatancy: why wet sand dries around a footstep
soil-phys-132.text: On a wet beach, the sand around a walker's foot seems to dry. The foot expands the sand, and water moves into the new space between grains. That is dilatancy, the change in volume of a granular material when it is sheared. In a dense packing, grains interlock and cannot slip past one another, so shearing levers them apart. A very loose material compacts instead. Osborne Reynolds first described it in 1885/1886, and Peter Walter Rowe brought it into geotechnical engineering. The denser the soil, the more it expands, and its friction angle peaks then drops abruptly.

soil-phys-133.title: Pumped dry: how wells make the land sink
soil-phys-133.text: In the United States, the land has sunk 1 m for every 13 m of lost groundwater level. Groundwater-related sinking of land comes from unsustainable pumping. Aquifers often hold compressible silt or clay layers. Pumping changes the effective stress on them, and they consolidate, often irreversibly, lowering the surface. One estimate ties 80% of serious U.S. land sinking to excessive groundwater extraction. The whole San Joaquin Valley has sunk after generations of pumping for crops. Permanent compaction can destroy much of an aquifer's storage, and in Arizona the land kept sinking for decades after water levels recovered by 100 ft.

soil-phys-077.title: Unsaturated soil, where air and water share the pores
soil-phys-077.text: In a saturated aquifer every pore is full of water, so the volume of water equals the porosity. An unsaturated soil holds less water than its porosity, so its pores hold air as well. A moist band just above the saturated zone, where water has climbed by capillarity, divides the two conditions. A whole branch of the geology of underground water ({{ref:soil-phys-208}}) studies the unsaturated ground. As a soil dries, its connected wet pathways shrink, so its ability to conduct water falls in a strongly non-linear way. Water moving into dry soil often advances in fingers, because the boundary between wet and dry zones is unstable.

soil-phys-099.title: Matric suction, the pull that holds damp soil together
soil-phys-099.text: Above the groundwater, soil water is under tension rather than pressure. Matric suction is that negative pore water pressure in unsaturated soil, caused by surface tension in the pores and defined as pore air pressure minus pore water pressure. Because the water pressure is negative, effective stress there is slightly greater than total stress. Capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore diameter, so sandy soils have much shallower capillary zones than clays and silts. Heavy rain soaking in lowers the suction, cutting the soil's shear strength and the stability of slopes. It is measured with the instrument described in {{ref:soil-water-221}}.

soil-phys-061.title: Measuring bulk density with a metal core and an oven
soil-phys-061.text: A metal corer is driven into the soil at a chosen depth and horizon, cutting out a sample of known volume. Weighed moist, the core gives the wet, or total, bulk density. Then it goes into an oven, often at 105 °C until its weight stops changing, leaving the mass of solids. The weight lost on drying is mostly water. Dry bulk density is the oven-dry mass divided by the total volume; wet bulk density counts the liquids too.

soil-phys-105.title: Critical state theory and its critics
soil-phys-105.text: Critical state theory, developed by Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth (1958), holds that a shearing soil reaches a distinct strength at which it keeps shearing at constant volume. It separates peak, critical state and residual strengths. Loose soil contracts as it shears and may show no peak above it. Dense soil must dilate once its grains interlock, so it peaks and then softens. Both head toward a critical void ratio. Residual strength, lower still, appears when plate-like clay particles align into slickensides. The concept drew much criticism for failing to match test data, chiefly because it ignores particle structure.

soil-phys-104.title: Drained shear strength and the trouble with c′
soil-phys-104.text: When pore pressures can escape as a soil shears, or the soil is dry, its strength is the drained shear strength. It is usually approximated by the Mohr–Coulomb equation, which Terzaghi combined with effective stress in 1942: strength equals c′ plus effective normal stress times tan ϕ′. Here ϕ′ is the angle of internal friction. The cohesion intercept c′ often comes from forcing a straight line through data that actually curve. So it depends on the stress range and is not a fundamental soil property. The curve arises because dilatancy depends on confining pressure.

soil-phys-102.title: Four things that set a soil's strength
soil-phys-102.text: A soil's strength rests on four things: what it is made of, its starting state, its structure and how it is loaded. Composition covers mineralogy, grain sizes, particle shape, the pore fluid, and the ions on grains and in that fluid. The initial state is set by void ratio, effective normal stress and stress history: loose or dense, contractive or dilative. Structure includes layers, fissures, slickensides and cements, such as recrystallized calcium carbonate, that bond grains where they touch. Loading means drained or undrained paths and the size, rate and history of loading, static or cyclic.

soil-phys-106.title: Steady state soil mechanics, a rival school
soil-phys-106.text: Steve J. Poulos formally defined the steady state, building on a hypothesis of Arthur Casagrande; the approach is informally called Harvard soil mechanics. In it, soil deforms continuously at constant volume, effective stress, shear stress and velocity, with a statistically steady grain structure. Elongated grains align in the direction of shear. It applies to drained and undrained shearing and to any granular material, including sands. Its proponents insist the steady state is not the critical state and list common misconceptions, so the two schools plainly disagree.

soil-phys-103.title: Undrained shear strength: when water has no time to escape
soil-phys-103.text: A pore that dilates as soil shears draws water in under negative pressure; one that contracts pushes water out. When shearing outpaces that flow, the soil is undrained, and its strength is the undrained shear strength. Rapid loading of sand in an earthquake, a clay slope failing in heavy rain and most failures during construction are all undrained. Undrained strength may be lower or higher than drained strength, depending on whether the soil contracts or dilates. It is usually defined by Tresca theory as Su.

soil-phys-072.title: Seeing soil pores in glowing resin
soil-phys-072.text: To see the cracks inside a soil, researchers fill them with glowing resin. A representative undisturbed core is soaked in low-viscosity synthetic resin mixed with a fluorescent dye such as fluorescein. The core is then ground back about 1 mm at a time. Each new face is lit with ultraviolet or blue light and photographed with a digital camera. Computer image analysis measures the depth, continuity, surface area and other properties of the resin-filled cracks.

soil-phys-071.title: Mapping and modelling the cracks in soil
soil-phys-071.text: Cracks shape how water enters soil, how gases move and how compaction plays out. Early field workers traced crack patterns by hand, or counted cracks under a wire semicircle moved along a string line and estimated their spread with Buffon's needle. Horgan and Young (2000) built a two-dimensional computer model of crack growth, in which cracks attract one another once they come close. It could not predict where cracking starts; soil often cracks along lines of weakness rather than at random. Because air has infinite resistivity, electrical resistivity imaging can map air-filled cracks.

soil-phys-123.title: Bearing capacity: how much load the ground can take
soil-phys-123.text: Well-graded gravels can carry about 8,000 pounds per square foot (39,000 kg/m2) and drain excellently. That figure is their bearing capacity, the capacity of soil to support loads such as a foundation without failing in shear. Ultimate bearing capacity is the theoretical maximum before failure. The allowable value divides it by a factor of safety or, on soft soils, is set by how much settlement can be tolerated. It depends on the soil's shear strength and on the foundation's shape, size, depth and type.

soil-phys-088.title: Wheels, hooves and tillage: what compacts farmland
soil-phys-088.text: Farmland can compact on its own, through drying and wetting, or under external pressure. Heavy machinery compacts the subsoil as well as the topsoil, and subsoil compaction is harder to reverse. Axle load, speed, number of passes and tyre pressure all set how severe it is. Working the soil can itself compact it, though over the long term it may leave less topsoil compaction than leaving the soil unworked. Heavy trampling by livestock, set by how intensively they graze, is another major cause.

soil-phys-108.title: Apparent cohesion: strength without glue
soil-phys-108.text: Soft clay can act cohesive without any chemical bonds between its particles. Its apparent cohesion comes instead from pore water suction and friction. Clay particles and chemicals in soft soil mainly create a measurable pore water suction. Remoulded, the soil flows as a ductile plastic material with constant apparent cohesion. During critical state flow, its undrained cohesion results from effective stress and friction, not from bonds. So the critical state approach treats the bearing capacity of soft clay as that of a perfectly plastic material.

soil-phys-111.title: Compression index: how much a clay gives under load
soil-phys-111.text: Clays differ widely in how much they squeeze. Most theories assume void ratio falls with the logarithm of effective stress. Plotted from oedometer test data, the slope of that line is the compression index. It ranges from 0.19 to 0.28 for {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, 0.50 to 1.10 for {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and 1.0 to 2.6 for {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, depending on the ions the clay holds. Unloaded, a consolidated soil rebounds and regains some lost volume. Reloaded, it follows a recompression curve set by the recompression index.

soil-phys-114.title: Terzaghi, Fillunger and a bitter quarrel over consolidation
soil-phys-114.text: The first modern theories of soil consolidation appeared in the 1920s, along two very different lines. Karl Terzaghi's simplified model, built on the diffusion equation, became engineering practice. Paul Fillunger's rigorous mixture-theory model was too abstract to apply to real cases. Their bitter dispute ended tragically in 1937 with Fillunger's suicide, and his results were forgotten for decades. Maurice Biot later developed the full three-dimensional theory. Terzaghi's one-dimensional model is still the most used, because it is simple and rests on cheap, reliable oedometer tests.

soil-phys-112.title: Overconsolidation: soils that remember heavier loads
soil-phys-112.text: Soils once covered by glaciers now bear less weight than they used to. They are overconsolidated: their load has been removed, so they carry less than the highest stress they have ever borne. Sinking land can produce the same state. That highest past stress is the preconsolidation stress, and the overconsolidation ratio (OCR) divides it by the current stress. A soil now under its highest stress is normally consolidated, with an OCR of one. Just after a new load, before excess pore water pressure dissipates, it is underconsolidated.

soil-phys-113.title: Creep: the settling that goes on after the water leaves
soil-phys-113.text: Peat keeps settling after the water has stopped draining. That slow change in volume at constant effective stress is secondary consolidation, also called creep or secondary compression. It differs from primary consolidation, the volume change as excess pore water pressure dissipates. Creep comes from the viscous behaviour of the clay–water system and the compression of organic matter. Most sands and low-organic clays show little of it, but peat creeps markedly, which makes it an unstable foundation for roads and buildings.

soil-phys-135.title: Terzaghi's principle: water shares the load
soil-phys-135.text: Karl von Terzaghi worked out his principle in the 1920s, studying how buildings consolidated the soil beneath them. A load on a porous material such as soil is opposed partly by the fluid pressure in its pores. The pore fluid bears part of the load, so effective stress is total stress minus pore pressure, and measurable responses follow it. It suits soil because silica grains are effectively incompressible. Maurice Biot generalised it to compressible solids in the 1940s. Experiments contradict some of its assumptions: for example, {{ref:soil-water-201}} fails at high gradients.

soil-phys-129.title: Specific yield: the water that drains out by gravity
soil-phys-129.text: Drain a block of coarse sand and 27% of its volume runs out as water; clay gives up only 2%. Specific yield, or drainable porosity, is that fraction of a material's bulk volume that drains under gravity. Average values are 8% for silt and 21% for fine sand. Dune sand yields about 38% and loess about 18%, while till that is mostly silt yields only about 6%. It is used mainly for unconfined aquifers.

soil-phys-136.title: The penetrometer, a probe that tests the ground
soil-phys-136.text: The same kind of probe has tested farm fields, cricket pitches and the surface of Titan. A penetrometer tests the strength of a material such as soil by measuring how far a probe sinks into it. Soil penetrometers, usually round or cone-shaped, are dropped on or pressed into the ground. The depth of the hole shows, for example, whether it can carry a road. On farmland they measure how much compaction raises the resistance described in {{ref:soil-phys-176}}. Since 2009 they have also tested British racecourses.

soil-phys-090.title: Finding compaction in the field, the lab and from space
soil-phys-090.text: No single method reveals compacted soil, so several are combined. Field signs include standing water, visibly fewer pores, and changed structure, moisture and colour; poorly aired soil can turn blue-grey and smell of hydrogen sulphide. A penetrometer measures the rise in strength, and crop growth patterns, pale leaves and root growth reveal it too, best judged against nearby uncompacted soil. In the laboratory, bulk density and pore-size distribution show its degree. Remote sensing can map susceptibility but cannot detect compaction directly, which often varies within a few square metres.

soil-phys-062.title: Particle density: the weight of the grains alone
soil-phys-062.text: Leave out the pores and soil grains come to a density of typically 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm3. That is particle density: the density of the solid particles alone, not counting the voids between them. It usually stays the same for a given soil. It is lower in soils rich in organic matter and higher in soils rich in the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}. Because {{ref:soil-phys-060}} includes the pores, it is always less than particle density, and it varies widely with biological activity and management while particle density does not. Together the two give {{ref:soil-phys-063}}. A mean particle density of about 2.65 g/cm3 is used for silica sediments and 2.70 g/cm3 for carbonate ones.

soil-phys-093.title: Air, water and solids: the arithmetic of soil
soil-phys-093.text: Soil holds air, water and solids, and engineers describe their proportions by volume and by mass. These are the soil mass–volume relations. The notation separates the volume, mass and weight of each phase, giving equations for how the three interact. The specific gravity of the solids, Gs, is their density divided by that of pure water, 1 g/cm3. Wet, or bulk, density is total mass over total volume, taking the mass of air as zero; dry density counts only the solids. Buoyant density, the mixture's density minus that of water, is used for soil under water. The ratio w, explained in {{ref:soil-water-164}}, is the mass of water over the mass of solids, found by weighing before and after oven drying. Void ratio e and porosity n convert freely: n equals e/(1 + e), and e equals n/(1 − n). The share of the voids filled with water, S, is described in {{ref:soil-water-166}}. Combining the definitions expresses bulk density through Gs, S, e or w and the density of water.

soil-water-180.title: How rain soaks into the ground, and when it stops
soil-water-180.text: Sand and well-aggregated soils can take in 2.5 cm of rain an hour, while high-clay soils accept as little as 0.25 cm. That intake is infiltration, the process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil. Gravity drives it, helped by capillary forces, absorption and osmosis. Infiltration capacity is the maximum rate, usually given in meters per day. It lasts only while there is room at the surface, which depends on porosity and on how fast earlier water moves down through the {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. As a storm goes on, that room shrinks. Infiltrated water fills storage and weakens capillary pull. Wetted clays swell and narrow their pores. Raindrops striking bare ground wash fine particles into surface pores. Robert E. Horton suggested that capacity drops quickly early in a storm, then settles to a near-constant value after a couple of hours. When rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in, the surplus usually runs off, unless a physical barrier holds it in place. Rates are measured in the field with devices such as {{ref:soil-water-187}}, permeameters and {{ref:soil-water-256}}.

soil-water-191.title: Permeability: how freely fluids slip through porous ground
soil-water-191.text: Well-sorted gravel is among the most pervious natural materials; unweathered clay and fresh granite are among the least. Permeability, usually written k, measures how readily a fluid, gas or liquid, flows through a porous material such as rock or soil. It depends on {{ref:soil-phys-063}}, but also on the shapes of the pores, how well they connect and the pressure inside the material. Its SI unit is the square meter. The practical unit, {{ref:soil-water-203}}, is about 10−12 m² and honors the engineer Henry Darcy. Most materials range from a fraction of a millidarcy to several thousand; unconsolidated sands may exceed 5000. Intrinsic permeability belongs to the solid skeleton alone, whatever the fluid, and forms one part of {{ref:soil-water-193}}. Keeping the two apart lets engineers allow for temperature effects on viscosity and for fluids such as brines or petroleum. Permeability matters for groundwater, oil and gas reservoirs, filtration and judging ground for construction.

soil-water-164.title: Water content, from bone dry to every pore full
soil-water-164.text: A soil's water content runs on a scale from 0, when it is completely dry, up to its {{ref:soil-phys-063}}, when every pore is full. Water content is the quantity of water a material holds; in soil it is called {{ref:soil-water-155}}. It can be given by volume, as volumetric water content, written θ, or by mass, as gravimetric water content. Soil science, like geotechnics, gives the gravimetric figure relative to the sample's dry weight. Multiplying it by the bulk specific gravity converts it to volume. Most soils hold less water than their porosity allows, which is what unsaturated means. Water content also changes what soil is: solid, semi-solid, plastic or liquid. The water contents at which it changes state are the Atterberg limits. How much moisture varies from spot to spot depends on climate. It rises with overall wetness in semiarid regions, falls with it in humid ones and peaks at intermediate wetness in temperate ones.

soil-water-155.title: Soil moisture, the quarter of a loam that keeps plants alive
soil-water-155.text: Half of a loam's volume is solid. Gas fills a quarter and water the other quarter, and only about half of that water is available to most plants. The water held in a soil, measured by volume or by weight, is soil moisture. It shapes soil formation, structure, stability and erosion, but its main importance is for plant growth. Water makes up 80–95% of a plant's protoplasm. It carries nutrients as a solvent and keeps plants upright through turgor, the pressure of water inside their cells. Water leaves a field in four ways: as runoff across the surface, as water draining through the soil, by evaporation from the surface and by transpiration from plants. Inside the soil it moves under gravity, osmosis and capillarity. Entering water drives air out of the largest pores and can burst air-filled aggregates, a process called slaking. Roots empty the largest pores first. Water in the smallest pores clings so tightly to particles that roots cannot take it, so availability depends strongly on texture. Moving water also dissolves solutes and {{ref:soil-chem-154}} and redeposits them lower in the profile, a process called leaching. Probes such as {{ref:soil-water-225}} and {{ref:soil-water-170}} measure soil moisture in place, and remote sensing estimates it from afar.

soil-water-214.title: Drainage, from Mohenjo-daro's houses to French drains
soil-water-214.text: Every house in the major Indus Valley cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had water and drainage. Drainage is the natural or artificial removal of surface and subsurface water from an area that has too much of it. The internal drainage of most farm soils keeps them from staying severely soaked. Many still need artificial drainage to raise production or manage water supplies. The invention of hollow-pipe drainage is credited to Sir Hugh Dalrymple, who died in 1753. Simple open drains, pipes and berms remain common, alongside larger earthworks and newer technologies. Surface drains carry runoff from paved ground. Subsurface drains remove water seeping into the soil, and the commonest type is the French drain, a gravel-filled trench with a perforated pipe. Drainage protects structures too. Behind an impermeable retaining wall, undrained groundwater builds hydrostatic pressure. That pressure can crack the wall and wash out soil, leaving voids and sinkholes. Most jurisdictions have a body of drainage law limiting how far a landowner may alter the drainage from a parcel.

soil-water-193.title: Hydraulic conductivity, the measure of how fast water moves
soil-water-193.text: A well sunk into sand and gravel draws water far more easily than one in clay or unfractured granite. The difference is hydraulic conductivity, written K: how easily water moves through a material's pores or fractures, in meters per second. K depends on the material's intrinsic {{ref:soil-water-191}}, on how saturated it is, and on the density and viscosity of the fluid. Formally, it is the ratio of volume flux to {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, the flow per unit area divided by the slope that drives it. Saturated hydraulic conductivity, Ksat, describes flow through saturated material. Natural values span many orders of magnitude, often in a lognormal pattern, and vary greatly from place to place. Direction matters: vertical K can be orders of magnitude below horizontal K. So does scale, since testing a cubic meter of an aquifer, a water-bearing layer, generally gives a different answer from a cubic centimeter sample. In unsaturated soil, K depends non-linearly on {{ref:soil-water-164}}. One material's unsaturated K spans a wider range than saturated K does across all materials. K is estimated from grain-size and pore-size distributions and texture, or measured in laboratory and field tests interpreted with {{ref:soil-water-201}}.

soil-water-172.title: Water potential: why water flows from soil to sky
soil-water-172.text: Water climbs from soil into roots, up a stem, out through the leaves and into the air without any pump. Each step has a more negative water potential than the one before, so the water flows passively. Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure water under reference conditions. In soils the reference is usually pure water at the soil surface. Written with the Greek letter ψ, it expresses water's tendency to move because of osmosis, gravity, mechanical pressure and matrix effects such as capillary action. Unrestricted water moves from higher to lower potential. Dissolved solutes lower the potential; added pressure raises it. In soil, total potential sums three parts: {{ref:soil-water-173}} from capillary action, an osmotic part in saline soil and a gravitational part that drives downward flow. A saturated soil sits at 0 kPa. After free drainage, at {{ref:soil-water-177}}, it is −33 kPa, and at the {{ref:soil-water-178}} −1500 kPa. Dry air is typically about −100 MPa. No single instrument covers the whole range. Electrical resistance blocks read from −90 to −1500 kPa, while {{ref:soil-water-223}} reaches −10,000 kPa.

soil-water-153.title: Soil water retention: holding water against gravity
soil-water-153.text: In temperate Victoria, Australia, water stored in wet winters carries most perennial plants through dry summers. That reserve depends on soil water retention, a soil's ability to take in water and hold much of it against the pull of gravity. Soils keep absorbing until they are full, or until their pores cannot pass water on fast enough. Some water drains by gravity to streams, but much stays, and plants and other organisms use much of what stays. Particle size sets the pattern. Water clings more tightly to fine clay particles than to coarse sand grains, so clays hold more water and sands let it pass. Clay type, organic content and {{ref:soil-phys-001}} also matter. An agricultural topsoil is roughly 25% water, 25% air, 45% mineral and 5% other, though its water ranges from about 1% to 90%. Water neither held nor used can sink to {{ref:soil-water-247}} as recharge. Saturated soils can even fail by mass movement, so soil water concerns geotechnicians and soil conservationists alike.

soil-water-201.title: Darcy's law, born in the sand filters of Dijon
soil-water-201.text: From the 1830s the engineer Henry Darcy studied water flowing through sand filters, hoping to improve the water supply of Dijon, France. In 1856 he published the result in a construction report. Darcy's law is an equation describing the flow of a fluid through a porous medium, and it became the basis of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Like Ohm's law for electricity, it makes flow rate proportional to a difference, here in {{ref:soil-phys-165}}. Hydraulic conductivity plays the part of electrical conductivity. Flow rises with the medium's permeability, its cross-section and the pressure drop. It falls with the fluid's viscosity and the length of the path. Without a pressure gradient nothing flows. The Darcy flux is a flow per unit area, not the speed of water in the pores; porosity links the two. The law holds only for slow, smooth, laminar flow, as in most groundwater, at Reynolds numbers below one, and up to 10 in tests. Very coarse sediments may flow turbulently and escape it.

soil-water-175.title: The water retention curve, a soil's moisture signature
soil-water-175.text: In 1907 Edgar Buckingham filled soil columns 48 inches tall with six soils, from sand to clay, and drew the first water retention curve. The curve links a soil's water content to its {{ref:soil-water-172}}. Also called the soil moisture characteristic, it differs between soil types and predicts water storage, plant water supply and aggregate stability. Near zero potential the soil is almost saturated and holds water mainly by capillarity. As it dries, the remaining water is bound ever more strongly, in the smallest pores, at grain contacts and as adsorbed films. Sandy soils release most of their water at higher potentials. Clayey soils, which also bind water by adhesion and osmosis, release it only at lower ones. At any given potential, peaty soils usually hold far more water than clayey soils, and clayey soils more than sandy ones. Even one soil has two curves. Pores fill and drain differently, so hysteresis, a lag between wetting and drying, gives separate wetting and drying curves.

soil-water-247.title: The water table, where saturated ground begins
soil-water-247.text: In the Nile Delta, wheat tolerates a water table 45 cm below the surface, while cotton needs 90 cm. The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation. Below it, pores and fractures are full of groundwater; above it lies the unsaturated zone. It sits where water pressure equals atmospheric pressure. In soils with strong capillarity, water is drawn up above it in a damp band. The level rises and falls with rain and with water lost by evaporation and plants. In Britain or California it is lower in summer, and the band between levels is the zone of intermittent saturation. It is rarely flat. Its slope, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, depends on recharge, withdrawal and permeability. Where it meets the surface, springs, rivers and lakes appear, and groundwater inflow sustains their base flow. A perched water table sits above the regional one, on an impermeable or slowly permeable layer. A well in a confined aquifer shows a potentiometric surface instead.

soil-water-189.title: Macropores, the soil's fast lanes for water and air
soil-water-189.text: An earthworm burrow is a fast lane for water. In soil, a macropore is any cavity larger than 75 μm. Macropores lie between peds, the natural clumps of soil, and between large sand or gravel grains. Wet–dry and freeze–thaw cycles crack soil into them. Those made by roots and organisms such as earthworms are called biopores. Water moves freely under gravity in macropores but is held by capillarity in micropores. So macropores raise hydraulic conductivity and carry fast flow along preferred paths, and water infiltrates and drains quickly. They aid recharge and gas exchange with the air, but they can also wash nitrate from fertilizers into groundwater. Their formation generally decreases with depth, as the processes behind it weaken. {{ref:soil-agri-095}} and compaction easily alter them. Compacted forest landings have little macroporosity, and added {{ref:soil-bio-114}} can improve it. Chemists use the word differently, for cavities larger than 50 nm in porous solids.

soil-found-094.title: Hollows that hold back the flood
soil-found-094.text: Every pit and hollow in a field is a small reservoir. Depression storage capacity is the ability of land to hold water in its pits and depressions so that it does not flow away. Together with infiltration capacity, it governs Horton overland flow. Once both are exceeded, water flows across the land, possibly causing flooding and erosion. Its study matters in geology and ecology, and above all in hydrology.

soil-water-187.title: Infiltrometers: rings driven into the ground
soil-water-187.text: The simplest infiltrometer is a metal ring driven into the soil and filled with water. The device measures the rate at which water infiltrates soil or another porous medium. Common types include single-ring and {{ref:soil-water-188}} designs, {{ref:soil-water-204}} instruments and falling-head infiltrometers. A single ring can be fed at constant head, a steady depth of water, often from {{ref:soil-water-244}}. Or the level is left to fall while the operator records how much water enters. Holding the head constant makes the supply rate equal the infiltration capacity, and the rate of entry relates to the soil's hydraulic conductivity. Rings have flaws. Driving one in deforms the soil, and a single ring lets water spread sideways. Rings cannot reliably represent furrow, sprinkler or rain infiltration. They measure only ponded, saturated flow, which macropores dominate wherever they are distinct.

soil-water-181.title: Why litter, cracks and roots speed water into soil
soil-water-181.text: On sandy loam, infiltration under leaf litter can be nine times that of bare ground. Bare soil forms a crust or surface seal that keeps it low. Rainfall, soil and surface conditions together control how fast water enters a soil. Rain infiltrates faster than snow or sleet. Entry is rapid early in a storm, while the soil is unsaturated, and slows as it saturates. Dry soils have the highest capacity, partly saturated soils a moderate one, and saturated soils no room for more. Fine-pored clays take water more slowly than coarse sands, except dry clays, which crack and take it quickly. Compaction lowers porosity and so capacity. After wildfires, water-repellent soils can cut infiltration sharply or stop it. Roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed it. With no vegetation, rates can be very low, causing excess runoff and erosion. Pavement prevents infiltration, and steeper slopes shed water faster. {{ref:soil-chem-019}} have poor structure, so rainwater ponds and evaporates before crops can use it.

soil-water-182.title: Calculating infiltration, from simple sums to supercomputing
soil-water-182.text: Infiltration is one term in the hydrologic budget, so if every other term is known, simple algebra gives it. Infiltration equations are methods for estimating the volume and rate of water entering a soil. The rigorous standard is a numerical solution of {{ref:soil-water-238}}, coupling groundwater and surface water through non-uniform soil. That solution is computationally expensive, not guaranteed to converge, and sometimes struggles to conserve mass. A newer approach, {{ref:soil-water-239}}, replaces it with three ordinary differential equations that always converge and conserve mass. It assumes vertical flow and uniform layers. For deep, well-drained soil that starts evenly moist, good approximate methods give the infiltration for a single rain event. At the simple end, a stripped-down use of Darcy's law assumes the gradient acts over an arbitrary length and ignores cumulative depth. Many argue it is too simple to use.

soil-water-205.title: Pedotransfer functions: turning cheap data into costly answers
soil-water-205.text: In 1989 Johan Bouma coined a name for "translating data we have into what we need". A pedotransfer function, or PTF, is a predictive function that estimates soil properties from {{ref:soil-agri-082}} data. The idea is older than the name. In 1907 Briggs and McLane gave the wilting coefficient as 0.01 sand + 0.12 silt + 0.57 clay. In the 1960s Salter and Williams linked texture classes and particle-size distribution to the water a soil can hold for plants. PTFs turn readily available data, such as field morphology, texture, structure and pH, into estimates of properties that are laborious and costly to measure. Most work has targeted the water retention curve and hydraulic conductivity, which have large databases. PTFs are empirical, built with regression and data mining. The USDA's ROSETTA program applies them with neural networks.

soil-water-160.title: A rye plant's 10,620 kilometers of root hairs
soil-water-160.text: A single winter rye plant, grown four months in 0.0283 cubic meters of loam, formed 620 km of roots and 10,620 km of root hairs. Yet it touched only 1.2% of the soil volume. Roots grow into new soil every day, so the volume they explore, and the water they take up, grows greatly over a season. Plant water uptake is how plants draw soil water into their roots. Most of it is passive. As water transpires from the leaves, it pulls the whole column of sap in the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue, up from the roots. The cohesion-tension theory describes this pull. Osmosis adds a push: salts concentrated in roots draw water in. That matters most when transpiration is low, at night or in high humidity. The root endodermis and leaf stomata regulate the upward flow, and cavitation in the xylem can break it. Root architecture, the layout of the root system, helps plants adapt to the soil's water and nutrient supply. Some roots even re-wet dry soil. Shortage costs yield: grain sorghum held at 1300 kPa soil suction from seed-head emergence to seed set lost 34% of its production.

soil-water-178.title: The permanent wilting point, past which plants cannot recover
soil-water-178.text: Keep a wilted plant in a saturated atmosphere for 12 hours. If it still cannot regain turgor, its soil has reached the permanent wilting point. That is the lowest soil water content a plant needs in order not to wilt. By convention, following {{ref:soil-hist-023}}, it is the water content at −1,500 kPa, or −15 bar, of suction. It roughly marks the boundary between available and unavailable water. There seeds will not germinate, and plants wilt and die unless adapted to recover. Closing stomata can slow transpiration and delay wilting, especially in drought-adapted plants. In 1912 Briggs and Shantz proposed the wilting coefficient, the water content at which plants first wilt beyond recovery without added water. Veihmeyer and Hendrickson of UC Davis found it to be a constant of the soil, whatever the conditions. Experiments by Richards and colleagues fixed today's limits for plant growth: −1/3 bar at {{ref:soil-water-177}} and −15 bar at the wilting point.

soil-water-161.title: Evapotranspiration, the soil's great return to the sky
soil-water-161.text: Of all the water a plant uses, only 0.1% to 1% stays inside it; transpiration carries off the rest. Evapotranspiration is the combined movement of water into the atmosphere from the Earth's surface, open water, ice, bare soil and plants. Evaporation moves water straight to the air from soil and water bodies. Transpiration carries it from the roots through the plant and out of the stomata as vapor. Together they return, on average, three-fifths to three-quarters of the precipitation that falls on land. Three things mainly control the flow: water available in soil and water bodies, the energy in air and soil, and the atmosphere's capacity to take up moisture. Drier soil means less evapotranspiration and a warmer soil surface. Where {{ref:soil-water-246}} exceeds rainfall, soil dries out unless irrigated. The flow is counted in millimeters of water over a set time. It is measured directly with a weighing {{ref:soil-water-248}}, or estimated from a catchment water balance, an energy balance or weather data. With infiltration, deep leakage beyond the roots and runoff, it is one of four main parts of the water balance at a point. It can also concentrate the salts in irrigation water to toxic levels.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated and unsaturated flow: pushed by gravity, pulled by suction
soil-water-156.text: Water in soil moves in two quite different ways, and the line between them sits at field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}). Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. That is saturated flow. At higher suctions the push gives way to a pull. Water's adhesion to soil solids sets up a suction gradient, which draws water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores. That is unsaturated flow. The lab manual states the same split in other units: saturated flow at tensions of 0 to -0.3 bar, driven by hydrostatic head, and unsaturated flow at 0.3 to 31 bars, driven by a tension gradient. ({{ref:soil-water-172}} explains these suctions.) Unsaturated flow is slow, at most about 2.5 cm a day, so roots keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. It slows because the connected wet pathways shrink as soil dries. {{ref:soil-water-193}} therefore depends on water content, and it falls in a very non-linear way as soil dries. Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, organic matter, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present, and soil temperature. Warm soils take in water faster, while frozen soils such as permafrost may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. The Richards equation gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-water-231.title: Impervious surfaces: when the city seals the soil
soil-water-231.text: In dense city centers, over 90 percent of the ground is sealed. Impervious surfaces are ground covered by water-resistant materials such as asphalt, concrete, brick or stone, mainly pavements and rooftops. Soils compacted by urban development are highly impervious too. Cover climbs with urbanization, from one or two percent in rural areas and about 10 percent in low-density suburbs to over 70 percent in industrial areas. Paving ends rainwater infiltration and natural recharge, which can cause urban flooding, and starves tree roots of air. Porous pavements, green roofs and infiltration basins make cities behave more like pervious soil.

soil-water-168.title: Measuring soil moisture without digging it up
soil-water-168.text: Soil moisture can now be gauged by a probe in one field or by satellite imagery combined with hydrological models. Soil moisture measurement means estimating water content in place, instead of drying samples. Several geophysical methods do it, among them {{ref:soil-water-223}}, {{ref:soil-water-170}}, {{ref:soil-water-226}} and {{ref:soil-water-225}}. Others include amplitude domain reflectometry, {{ref:soil-meth-015}} and {{ref:soil-meth-014}}. Geophysical sensors often monitor soil moisture continuously for agriculture and research. Each method has strengths and weaknesses, so combining techniques can reduce the drawbacks of any one. Some farmers now schedule irrigation from these readings, a practice called smart irrigation.

soil-water-223.title: Timing an electrical echo to read soil water
soil-water-223.text: The same technique that locates a fault in a kilometer-long cable, to within centimeters and without digging, can measure the water in soil. Time-domain reflectometry sends an electrical pulse along a line and reads its reflections. Wherever the impedance along a conductor changes, part of the signal reflects back, and the return time gives the distance to that change. In soil, the pulse's speed depends mainly on the permittivity of the surrounding material, its response to an electric field. Permittivity varies greatly with moisture and temperature. Hoekstra and Delaney (1974) and Topp et al. (1980) showed that it is closely tied to water content. The probe is two or more parallel metal rods, typically 10 to 30 cm long, linked to the instrument by coaxial cable. Probes at several depths record when wetting arrives after rain starts, giving the speed of infiltration.

soil-water-218.title: Waterlogging: when soil drowns the roots it feeds
soil-water-218.text: Badly run irrigation has waterlogged over 2 million hectares of Pakistan's Indus Plains and 2.19 million ha of Indian canal commands. Waterlogging is the saturation of soil with water, so that its air is restricted and anaerobic, oxygen-free, conditions prevail much of the time. All plants need oxygen to respire, and waterlogging usually blocks air from reaching the roots. Apart from rice, most crops, such as maize and potato, are highly intolerant of it. Prolonged waterlogging harms the roots of mesophytes, plants of moderately moist ground. The reducing subsoil drives {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, methane production and the reduction of iron and manganese oxides. Roots can survive by forming aerenchyma, air channels in their tissue, by switching to anaerobic metabolism and by changing their architecture. In irrigated land, salinity often follows, because waterlogged soils stop the salts brought by irrigation water from being leached out.

soil-water-228.title: Holding the water table at the right depth
soil-water-228.text: Wheat in the Nile Delta tolerates a water table 45 cm down; cotton there is sensitive and needs 90 cm. Watertable control holds the water table at a chosen height by means of drainage. On farms it raises crop yields. In cities it protects building foundations, underground transit and buried utilities. Subsurface drainage keeps once-waterlogged land at a depth that suits its use. A shallower permitted depth makes a system cheaper, but lowering the water table has side effects whose costs must be counted. Shallow open ditches gave way around 1900 to buried clay tiles about 30 cm long, and from 1960 to corrugated plastic pipes laid by trenching machines. Pumped wells give vertical drainage and can be spaced over 1000 m apart, against 100 m or less for pipes and ditches. Many large projects were over-designed and ignored environmental side effects, which gave land drainage a poor reputation. Drainage also helps control salinity, and hydraulic conductivity weighs heavily in its design.

soil-water-215.title: Draining farmland, from Dutch steam pumps to Florida citrus
soil-water-215.text: In the Netherlands, 15th-century windpumps could drain only marginal land. The Haarlemmermeer had to wait for large steam pumps, which drained it between 1849 and 1852. Agricultural land drainage removes excess water from farmland, from wetland soils to fields waterlogged for short spells, so that crops are not damaged. Clay-rich soils pass water down very slowly, and hardpans or shallow rock block it. When excess water shuts out air, roots suffocate. Even excellent soils waterlogged for a week of the year can lose their fruit trees. Ditches turned glacial marshes in the northern United States and Europe into mucklands for vegetables and other high-value crops. Florida's flatwoods citrus groves are pumped after heavy rain. Rice needs complete water control, since fields are flooded or drained at different stages. Evapotranspiration concentrates the salts in irrigation water, so irrigated land may need periodic over-irrigation and drainage. {{ref:soil-chem-030}} are an exception: subsurface drainage is normally not advisable, though surface drainage in rainy periods can help reclaim them.

soil-water-222.title: Soil moisture sensors and the sprinkler that knows better
soil-water-222.text: Wired to an irrigation clock, a soil moisture sensor makes a smart controller that skips watering when the soil is already wet. The sensor estimates the volumetric water content of soil, usually indirectly. Instead of drying and weighing a sample, it reads a proxy such as electrical resistance, dielectric constant or interaction with neutrons. The link between proxy and moisture must be calibrated, and it can shift with the kind of soil, its temperature and electrical conductivity. Technologies include frequency domain reflectometry, capacitance sensors, time domain reflectometry and transmission, neutron gauges, soil resistivity and galvanic cells. Capacitance sensors resemble the sensors covered in {{ref:soil-water-226}}. But where those work at several hundred MHz, capacitance sensors run below 1 MHz and pick up more noise. A separate class of sensors, such as {{ref:soil-water-221}} and gypsum blocks, measures water potential instead of content. Farmers use sensors to irrigate with less water, raising yield and quality through better moisture control at critical growth stages.

soil-water-225.title: The capacitance probe, a capacitor with soil inside
soil-water-225.text: Water has a dielectric constant of 80, against 4 for mineral soil and {{ref:soil-bio-114}} and 1 for air. A capacitance probe exploits that gap. It measures the dielectric permittivity of the surrounding soil, and from it the water content. Two metal rings form the plates of a capacitor, with the soil as the material between them. When soil permittivity changes, so does the frequency of the oscillator circuit. Like a {{ref:soil-water-170}}, it sits in a PVC access tube in the soil, or comes as comb-like probes wired to a logger. Oscillating at over 100 MHz in free air, the sensors are widely used to time irrigation.

soil-water-216.title: Fabric filters that keep drains from clogging
soil-water-216.text: Drain filters of the kind covered in {{ref:soil-water-254}} are synthetic fabrics that hold back fine soil particles but let water through, so a drain does not clog. In a typical drain the fabric lines a trench filled with gravel, shells or stone. It is folded over the top and covered with soil, and groundwater seeps through it to an outfall. Where groundwater is high, a perforated PVC or PE pipe along the base increases the volume carried. Prefabricated HDPE drains with such fabric, coco fiber or rag filters avoid hauling stone aggregate, which is always more expensive.

soil-water-217.title: Seattle's streets that soak up their own rain
soil-water-217.text: Seattle Public Utilities reported a 99 percent reduction in storm water leaving its Street Edge Alternatives Project. The project uses roadside ditches, plantings and uncurbed sidewalks so that runoff flows onto permeable ground. That is sustainable urban drainage, designed to imitate the natural flow of water more closely than traditional piped systems. Since 2010, UK local and neighborhood planning has been required by law to factor such systems into development projects.

soil-water-173.title: Matric potential: the grip of grains on water
soil-water-173.text: Water held in an unsaturated soil always has less energy than pure water, because the soil's solids hold on to it. That hold is matric potential, the part of water potential that comes from water's attraction to solid particles and the curved menisci it forms between them. Adhesion to solids, with cohesion among water molecules, creates surface tension, and force is needed to break it, as {{ref:soil-phys-095}} showed. Its size depends on the spacing between particles, which sets meniscus width, and on the chemistry of the solids. Matric potential is always negative and occurs only in unsaturated soil above the water table. Near zero, nearly all pores are full.
