Water draining into less moist soil of similar porosity is generally at −10 to −30 kPa. It is often large compared with the other components, and though the flow it drives may be slow, it is vital for supplying water to roots.

soil-water-184.title: Horton's equation: a fast start, then a steady soak
soil-water-184.text: Robert E. Horton saw infiltration capacity fall quickly early in a storm, then settle toward a near-constant value. His empirical equation captures that shape. Infiltration starts at an initial rate and declines exponentially with time. Once the soil is wet enough, the rate levels off at a constant equilibrium value, fc, the minimum infiltration rate. Integrated over time, the equation gives the total volume infiltrated.

soil-water-185.title: The Kostiakov equation and its missing final rate
soil-water-185.text: Taken at its word, the Kostiakov equation says a soil will eventually stop taking in water altogether. It is an empirical infiltration equation in which the intake rate declines over time as a power function. That implied final rate of zero is its main limitation, since infiltration usually approaches a finite steady value. The Kostiakov–Lewis, or modified Kostiakov, equation fixes this by adding a steady intake term.

soil-water-204.title: The disc permeameter, which ignores the biggest pores
soil-water-204.text: In 1988 Perroux and White of CSIRO developed a field instrument that deliberately leaves a soil's largest pores out of the measurement. The disc permeameter, called the tension infiltrometer in the US, measures infiltration under tension. It is used mainly to estimate hydraulic conductivity near saturation, in place. Ring infiltrometers measure only ponded flow, which macropores dominate. A slightly negative potential keeps those pores empty, so flow through the soil matrix alone can be measured. A nylon mesh membrane, a water reservoir and a bubbling tower supply potentials from −200 mm to 0 mm, excluding pores wider than 0.075 mm.

soil-water-163.title: Soil suction and pF: a scale for how hard water clings
soil-water-163.text: Oven-dry soil grips its last water with a suction of 1,000,000 kPa. Soil suction is the negative of soil water potential, the force needed to pull water out of soil. Water stays where its adhesion to soil particles beats the cohesion between water molecules, and that hold sets its availability to plants. The pF scale is the common logarithm of suction in centimeters of water, so pF 3 equals 1000 cm, 98 kPa or 0.98 bar. As roots thin a water film, suction rises to 1500 kPa (pF 4.2), the wilting point. Air-dry soil sits at 100,000 kPa (pF 6), oven-dry soil at pF 7.

soil-water-183.title: The Green–Ampt method, an equation that contains its own answer
soil-water-183.text: The Green–Ampt method estimates infiltration from four quantities: soil suction head, porosity, hydraulic conductivity and time. Named after Green and Ampt, it accounts for more variables than approaches such as the simplified Darcy's law method. It gives the cumulative infiltration depth F(t) through F(t) = Kt + ψΔθ ln[1 + F(t)/ψΔθ]. Because F appears on both sides, the equation is solved iteratively. It assumes the depth of water ponded on the surface is negligible.

soil-water-162.title: 500 kilograms of water for a kilogram of alfalfa
soil-water-162.text: Growing one kilogram of dry alfalfa may take 500 kilograms of water. That figure is alfalfa's transpiration ratio, a measure of water use efficiency: the water a plant transpires divided by the dry weight of the harvested plant. For crops, transpiration ratios range from 300 to 700.

soil-water-237.title: SaltMod, a salinity model built for the field
soil-water-237.text: Most salinity models, such as Swatre and DrainMod, solve {{ref:soil-water-238}} with hard-to-measure soil relations and daily data. SaltMod, from the Institute for Land Reclamation and Improvement (ILRI), was built simpler, for field technicians and planners. For irrigated farmland, it predicts the salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water, plus water table depth and drain flow. Working from seasonal water balances, it predicts long-term trends rather than exact future states. It tracks four reservoirs: the surface, the root zone, a transition zone holding any horizontal drains, and the aquifer. Users can test drain depths, reuse of drainage water and farmers' responses, which slow salinization toward an equilibrium.

soil-water-240.title: Ecohydrology, where water meets living systems
soil-water-240.text: In a rainforest, where water is ample, plant growth depends more on nutrients. In a semi-arid savanna, vegetation follows the water plants can draw from the soil. Ecohydrology is the interdisciplinary study of how water and ecological systems interact. It covers water bodies and land ecosystems such as forests and deserts. Its research covers plant water use, how organisms adapt to water, how vegetation affects streams, and feedbacks between ecology, {{ref:soil-env-119}} and {{ref:soil-water-079}}. A basic tool is the water balance at a point: water entering the soil equals water leaving plus the change in storage.

soil-phys-130.title: Moisture stress and the root's chemical alarm
soil-phys-130.text: When roots sense dry soil, they make the hormone ABA. It closes the stomata, cutting transpiration and photosynthesis, and loosens root cell walls so roots can grow in search of water. Moisture stress is the strain a plant suffers when water in its tissues falls below optimal levels, because transpiration outpaces uptake by the roots. Mildly stressed plants recover in 1–2 days; severely stressed ones regain only 40-60% of maximum photosynthesis the day after rewatering. Well-timed irrigation avoids it by replacing soil water before stress sets in. In strongly acidic soils, aluminum toxicity can cause it even when the soil is fairly moist.

soil-water-195.title: The constant-head test: steady water through a sample
soil-water-195.text: Few laboratory measurements of hydraulic conductivity are as simple and inexpensive as the constant-head test. Water flows through a soil specimen under a steady head, the height of water driving it, and the test is typically used on granular soil. The head defines an excess mass of water whose weight sets the pressure difference across the sample, ρgh. The volume passing in a set time is measured. Rearranging Darcy's law with the specimen's length, cross-section and head then gives K.

soil-water-196.title: The falling-head test, for fine soils as well as coarse
soil-water-196.text: Unlike the {{ref:soil-water-195}}, the falling-head test works on both fine-grained and coarse-grained soils. In this laboratory test of hydraulic conductivity, a saturated sample drains with no water added, so the head of water above it declines over time. K is calculated from how far the head drops in a given time.

soil-water-197.title: Testing permeability where the soil lies
soil-water-197.text: Digging up a sample disturbs it, and disturbance undermines laboratory results. Field permeability tests avoid that by measuring hydraulic conductivity in place, giving the most reliable values with the least disturbance. Small-scale tests watch water levels in cavities: infiltration tests above the water table and slug tests below it. Large-scale tests include pumping tests in wells and observing how existing horizontal drainage systems perform. The pumping test, in pumping-in and pumping-out forms, is called the most reliable way to find a soil's coefficient of permeability.

soil-water-198.title: The augerhole method: bail a hole, time the refill
soil-water-198.text: Auger a hole to below the water table, bail out the water, and record how fast the level rises again. That is the augerhole method, a slug test that measures hydraulic conductivity below a shallow water table. It gives the horizontal saturated hydraulic conductivity in meters per day. Hooghoudt developed it in the Netherlands in 1934, and Van Bavel and Kirkham introduced it to the US in 1948. Results vary widely: measurements across 100 ha differed by a factor of 25, with a lognormal distribution.

soil-water-194.title: Hazen's formula: flow estimated from grain size
soil-water-194.text: Allen Hazen found that a soil's coefficient of permeability is proportional to the square of particle size. His empirical formula uses that link to approximate hydraulic conductivity from a grain-size analysis, as summed up in a {{ref:soil-phys-018}}. It uses D10, the diameter at the 10th percentile of grain size, and an empirical coefficient C. Depending on the source, C lies between 0.0 and 1.5, averaging 1.0. Laboratory pumping tests have been used to check such formulas for sandy soils. Some studies found a modified Hazen formula approximates laboratory measurements reasonably well.

soil-water-200.title: Hydraulic anisotropy: when water prefers one direction
soil-water-200.text: In a layered aquifer, water runs sideways through the layers of high horizontal permeability and passes vertically through the tight ones. A soil layer or aquifer whose horizontal and vertical hydraulic conductivity differ considerably shows hydraulic anisotropy. Where an aquitard, a poorly conducting layer, overlies a highly conducting one, the aquifer is semi-confined. Flow is then mainly vertical in the first and horizontal in the second. Designs for drains or wells that control the water table must allow for anisotropy, or the result may be wrong. Mathematically, permeability becomes a symmetric, positive-definite 3 by 3 tensor whose eigenvectors give the principal flow directions.

soil-water-199.title: Transmissivity: how much water a layer can deliver
soil-water-199.text: Transmissivity measures how much water a soil layer or aquifer can transmit horizontally, as toward a pumping well. It is proportional to the layer's horizontal hydraulic conductivity and its saturated thickness; with those in m/day and m, it comes out in m²/day. An aquifer's total transmissivity is the sum of its layers', and pumping tests can find it. Layers above the water table are unsaturated and add nothing. So transmissivity changes as the water table moves, and drawdown in an unconfined aquifer reduces the flow to a well.

soil-water-171.title: Agricultural drought, which can strike without a dry year
soil-water-171.text: A farm can suffer drought without any fall in rainfall. Agricultural drought is a condition in which soil is too dry to sustain reliable plant growth. It can arise when soil conditions and erosion from poorly planned farming leave crops short of water. As soil dries, transpiration falls, because suction holds the water ever more tightly. Below the permanent wilting point plants wilt and stop transpiring. Common in arid and semi-arid environments, it is a particular focus of irrigation management. Agricultural or ecological droughts harm crop production or ecosystems generally.

soil-water-166.title: How full the pores are: degree of saturation
soil-water-166.text: Fill every pore of a soil with water and its degree of saturation is 1. Empty them all and it is 0. Degree of saturation, a measure used in soil mechanics and petroleum engineering, tells how fully a material's pore space is filled with water. Yet no real material ever reaches either end, so both values are idealizations for engineering. Soil physicists often use effective saturation instead, a dimensionless value defined by van Genuchten and also called normalized water content. It runs between two practical limits. Residual water content is where water content stops changing as suction head rises. Saturated water content equals the {{ref:soil-phys-063}}.

soil-water-192.title: Why coarse sand passes water a million times faster than clay
soil-water-192.text: Coarse sand may let water through over a million times more readily than clay. Allen Hazen found why: a soil's coefficient of permeability rises with the square of its particle size. The permeability of soils is a soil's capacity to let water pass, and grain size is only the start. Permeability also rises with {{ref:soil-phys-073}}. Plot void ratio against the logarithm of k, and every soil gives a straight line. Fine impurities in the water progressively clog the pores. Fine-grained soils carry a strongly attached film of adsorbed water that gravity cannot move, and it obstructs flow. Air pockets in partly saturated soil block water too, so permeability falls well below its saturated value and Darcy's law no longer strictly applies. Entrapped air and organic material both cut permeability considerably, which is why test samples must be fully saturated. In the field, compaction lowers permeability and raises runoff, while vegetative cover raises it.

soil-water-167.title: Weighing a soil's water by baking it out
soil-water-167.text: The most direct way to measure a soil's water is to bake it out. In the oven-dry method, a sample goes into a special oven or kiln and is weighed at regular intervals until drying is complete. The mass lost is the water. Dividing it by the wet or the dry mass, depending on the discipline, gives gravimetric water content. Volumetric water content also needs the sample's total volume, fixed by filling a container of known volume, such as a tin can, when sampling. Because it needs a sample removed, dried and weighed, soil moisture sensors estimate water indirectly instead, from electrical resistance, dielectric constant or neutron interaction.

soil-water-169.title: Reading soil moisture from orbit with microwaves
soil-water-169.text: Clouds that hide the ground from a camera do not stop a microwave. Satellites estimate surface soil moisture with microwaves, using the large contrast in dielectric properties between wet and dry soil. Microwaves are insensitive to atmospheric conditions, pass through clouds and partly penetrate vegetation to read the ground surface. Satellites used this way include WindSat, AMSR-E, RADARSAT, ERS-1-2, Metop/ASCAT and SMAP. They take {{ref:soil-water-168}} off the ground and into orbit.

soil-water-241.title: Bioclogging: when microbes seal the soil's pores
soil-water-241.text: Under water that is never drained away, soil can seal itself. Bioclogging is the blocking of soil pores by microbial cells and their byproducts, such as the slime described in {{ref:soil-bio-080}}. The biomass forms an impermeable layer that sharply cuts {{ref:soil-water-180}}. It typically appears under continuous ponding, in recharge ponds, irrigation channels, sewers and riverbeds. In submerged soil, permeability falls, rises as trapped air dissolves, then falls for 2 to 4 weeks as microbes clog the pores. Methane bubbles from microbes clog pores too. Regular drying and cleaner water reduce it. Sometimes the seal is welcome. It lines dairy wastewater ponds, cuts seepage from irrigation channels inoculated with algae and bacteria, and aids compacted clay landfill liners.

soil-water-154.title: How wet soil steadies the weather
soil-water-154.text: Soil moisture shapes more than a harvest. Water has roughly double the heat capacity of soil, so wetter soil warms and cools more slowly under the same heating. Through the soil's temperature, moisture then affects biological triggers such as seed germination, flowering and the activity of soil fauna. The effect reaches the sky. Climate modelling by Timbal and colleagues in 2002 linked soil moisture to the persistence and variability of surface temperature and rainfall in Australia. Soil water now matters for climate modelling and weather prediction, and the Global Climate Observing System lists it among its 50 Essential Climate Variables.

soil-water-174.title: Salty soil water that roots cannot drink
soil-water-174.text: A soil can be wet and still leave a seedling thirsty. Osmotic potential is the part of {{ref:soil-water-172}} lowered by dissolved solutes. Pure water is set at zero, so it can never be positive. The soil solution carries inorganic and organic solutes, and the more it holds, the lower its osmotic potential. Zones of soil are rarely separated by a semipermeable membrane, so this potential has little effect on how water moves through soil. Plants are another matter. In soils high in soluble salts, the low osmotic potential severely restricts water uptake by roots. It can fall so low that the cells of young seedlings collapse by plasmolysis.

soil-water-202.title: When water rushes too fast for Darcy's law
soil-water-202.text: {{ref:soil-water-201}} assumes that flow keeps step with pressure. Push a fluid fast enough and that breaks down. The Reynolds number compares a flow's inertia with its viscosity, and above values of about 1 to 10, inertial effects become significant. The Forchheimer equation extends Darcy's law with an inertial term, using an inertial permeability measured in metres. The cause lies at the pore scale, where recirculation zones change the shape of the flow streamlines. Flow within a sandstone reservoir is usually too slow to need it. Gas flowing into a production well, or through rough fractures, may justify it.

soil-water-186.title: Sorptivity: how readily a dry material drinks
soil-water-186.text: Soil, brick, stone and concrete all soak up water by capillarity, and sorptivity measures how readily. John Philip introduced the term in 1957 for a porous medium's capacity to absorb or release liquid by {{ref:soil-phys-095}}. In 1969 he showed how to find it from horizontal infiltration, which is mostly capillary absorption. Its SI unit is m·s−1/2. For vertical infiltration, Philip's solution adds a second parameter, giving equations valid for short times. Clapp and Hornberger derived average sorptivity values for different texture classes.

soil-water-227.title: SMAP, NASA's watch on the planet's soil moisture
soil-water-227.text: Every 2 to 3 days, one satellite takes a global snapshot of soil moisture. Soil Moisture Active Passive, or SMAP, is a NASA mission that measures soil moisture and its freeze-thaw state across the planet. It launched on 31 January 2015 with a passive L-band radiometer and an active radar. An amplifier failure ended the radar that same year, and the mission carries on with the radiometer alone. It senses the top 5 cm of soil through moderate vegetation, and hydrologic models extend the readings down to the root zone. That is often enough to catch single storms. The data improve drought monitoring, flood and landslide forecasts, weather prediction and famine early warning.

soil-found-105.title: Throughflow: water slipping sideways under a slope
soil-found-105.text: Not all water that soaks in sinks straight down. Infiltrated water still moves under gravity toward the water table, but where permeability varies sideways it can travel downslope instead. Throughflow is this lateral, unsaturated flow through the soil, typically in a permeable layer lying over a less permeable one. It usually runs during peak events such as heavy rain, at rates set by the {{ref:soil-water-193}} of the medium. The water returns to the surface as return flow before or on entering a stream or groundwater. It carries things with it: bases in the B horizon of a {{ref:soil-class-138}} may be lost this way.

soil-water-242.title: Plinthite, the red clay that sets like stone
soil-water-242.text: In highly weathered soils, a soft red clay can turn to rock in the sun. Plinthite is an iron-rich, humus-poor mixture of clay with quartz and other minerals. It forms in soil horizons saturated with water for part of the year, usually as dark red concretions in platy, polygonal or reticulate patterns. Moist, it cuts with a spade; drier, near {{ref:soil-water-177}}, it is firm. Repeated wetting and drying, especially with heat from the sun, turns it irreversibly into ironstone hardpan or irregular aggregates. A single cycle does not. Hard plinthite looks like a mineral, but it is a product of soil formation.

soil-water-176.title: The van Genuchten model: a soil's water curve in a few numbers
soil-water-176.text: A whole {{ref:soil-water-175}} can be summed up in a few fitted numbers. The van Genuchten model is an equation that describes the shape of that curve. Its parameter α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, the suction at which air starts to enter the pores. The parameter n, always greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution. Both come from field or laboratory tests, such as the instantaneous profile method, fitted by non-linear least squares. The parameterization led to a model predicting how a soil's conductivity when not saturated ({{ref:soil-phys-225}}) varies with saturation and pressure. Alternatives include the Brooks–Corey, Broadbridge–White and Rogers–Stallybrass–Clements models.

soil-water-203.title: The darcy, a unit for how easily fluids pass
soil-water-203.text: Gravel can reach 100,000 darcys, while granite falls below 0.01 microdarcys. Sand sits near 1 darcy. The darcy is a unit of {{ref:soil-water-191}}, named after Henry Darcy, with the millidarcy as its thousandth. A medium of 1 darcy lets 1 cm³/s of a fluid with viscosity 1 cP pass through 1 cm² under a pressure gradient of 1 atm/cm. That equals 9.869233×10−13 m², usually approximated as 1 μm². It is not an SI unit, yet petroleum engineers and geologists use it widely. In hydrology, 1 darcy corresponds to a water flux of 0.831 m/day under hydrostatic pressure at 20 °C.

soil-found-071.title: The perc test: timing a hole as it drains
soil-found-071.text: Before a {{ref:soil-env-195}} or infiltration basin goes in, someone digs holes and times them. The percolation test is a field test of how fast soil absorbs water. The holes are presoaked for several hours, then filled with water to a set level, and the fall in water level is timed as it soaks away. Results in minutes per inch are matched to local health codes to size the leach field. Sandy soil generally absorbs more water than clay-rich soil or soil with a shallow water table. Not everyone trusts the test. Some jurisdictions use soil texture analysis with long-term acceptance rates instead of it or alongside it.

soil-water-244.title: Mariotte's bottle, a steady flow from a falling tank
soil-water-244.text: Mariotte's bottle delivers a constant rate of flow from a closed bottle or tank. The trick is an air inlet. It keeps the pressure at its base atmospheric, so a siphon at that depth delivers water at a constant head however far the reservoir level falls. The device is named after Edme Mariotte (1620–1684), but McCarthy first reported the design in 1934. Constant head simplifies measuring water movement in soil. The Guelph permeameter uses the principle, as do single-ring infiltrometers and the double-ring type in {{ref:soil-water-188}}. The bottle is sensitive to leaks at the air inlet and cannot be refilled while running. Electronic devices now give accurate control.

soil-water-219.title: How far apart to lay the drains
soil-water-219.text: A water table held too shallow cuts yields; one dropped too deep brings drought. A drainage equation relates the depth and spacing of parallel subsurface drains to the depth of the water table and to the depth and {{ref:soil-water-193}} of the soil. The best-known steady-state form is Hooghoudt's drain spacing equation, derived from {{ref:soil-water-201}} and introduced in the USA by van Schilfgaarde. In steady state the water table stays level and drain discharge equals the recharge rate. Given discharge, a permissible water-table depth and measured soil data, it yields the drain spacing. In one example, a seasonal average water table shallower than 70 cm depressed yield.

soil-water-220.title: Drainage research: searching for the best drain design
soil-water-220.text: Draining a field has agricultural, environmental, hydrological, engineering, economic, social and political sides, and all of them are open to research. Drainage research studies agricultural drainage systems and their effects, aiming at the design that gives optimal farm production. Water-table depth is a key factor. Drainage design controls it through {{ref:soil-water-219}}, and its link to yields is optimized to set a drainage criterion. Crop response rests on linked physical, chemical and hydrological processes. Irrigated land may need subsurface drainage to leach out salts brought in with irrigation water. Leaching models such as SaltMod help set that drainage requirement.

soil-water-190.title: The maze of large pores that steers water
soil-water-190.text: A soil's macropores do not sit alone. They link into a network, irregular in shape, size and roughness, whose geometry shapes water movement, aeration and root growth. Higher connectivity usually means higher permeability, and links to the surface and to groundwater aid infiltration and recharge. Connected is not the same as continuous. Dead-end pores block or slow water and air, while continuous pores improve aeration and give roots room. Tortuosity measures the winding: the ratio of a path's actual length to the straight distance between its two ends. The more sinuous the path, the higher the tortuosity and the resistance to flow.

soil-water-208.title: One unbroken path from soil to sky
soil-water-208.text: Water can travel from soil into a root, up a stem and out of a leaf along one connected pathway. That pathway is the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. Water potential is very low in the air and higher inside leaves, so water diffuses out through the stomata, the pores of the leaf, as vapor. Water lost from leaf cells is replaced from the xylem, the plant's water-carrying tissue, where cohesion and tension pull more up from the roots. Soil physics, physiology and meteorology each describe their own segment in different terms. The continuum treats soil, plants, animals and air as one dynamic system, giving water in each part a {{ref:soil-water-172}}. That shared measure is the basis for modelling transport between them.

soil-water-209.title: Hydropedology, where soil science meets hydrology
soil-water-209.text: Hydrology likes to pair with the Earth's other spheres, as hydroclimatology, ecohydrology and the field in {{ref:soil-phys-208}} show. Hydropedology is the emerging field that joins soil science and hydrology. It studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere, the planet's water. Soil hydrology and hydropedology are both listed among the areas of practice of soil science. The biomantle shows what the field studies. Loosened by {{ref:soil-bio-047}}, it speeds downward drainage through biopores and carries throughflow downslope above dense subsoil horizons.

soil-water-246.title: Potential evapotranspiration: how much water the air demands
soil-water-246.text: Summer, clear skies, wind and nearness to the equator all raise the air's demand for water. Potential evapotranspiration is the water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if water were not limited. It reflects the energy and wind available to move water vapor, the demand side of {{ref:soil-water-161}}. Actual evapotranspiration equals it when water is ample and can never exceed it. The reference rate, ET0, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-217}}, is calculated for a short-grass surface, most widely with the FAO-recommended equation in {{ref:soil-phys-215}}. A crop factor, described in {{ref:soil-phys-218}}, and a stress coefficient then convert it into a crop's actual evapotranspiration.

soil-water-243.title: A knowledge base that infers what was never measured
soil-water-243.text: Measure a soil's basic properties, the premise goes, and all its other physical and chemical properties follow. A soil inference system, proposed by McBratney and colleagues in 2002, builds on that premise to fill digital soil databases. It infers unknown properties with minimal uncertainty through logically linked pedotransfer functions. It computes new properties from inferred values as well as from inputs. It depends on reliable inputs, on links between basic soil data, and on quantified uncertainty. A working prototype was completed in 2007–2009 at the University of Sydney with a US partner.

soil-water-232.title: Ground that sheds rain though it counts as pervious
soil-water-232.text: Not every source of runoff is paved. Natural impervious area is land usually classed as pervious that can still yield substantial surface runoff in small and large storms. It includes open water, wetlands, rock outcrops, barren ground and compacted soils. Depending on conditions, it yields stormflow by water running over the surface, as in {{ref:soil-water-020}}, or by rain falling directly on it. Development adds more by compacting soils. Felton and Lull found in 1963 that it could cut infiltration by 80 percent. Taylor found in 1982 that construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent. Its effect on runoff matters most where {{ref:soil-water-233}} is low.

soil-water-233.title: Measuring how much of a landscape is sealed
soil-water-233.text: About 76 percent of the conterminous United States has less than 1 percent impervious cover. Total impervious area is the share of an area covered by impervious surfaces, given as a fraction from zero to one or as a percentage. It is estimated with mapping software, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-165}}, from land-cover data, land-use categories, percent developed area or population density. The US NLCD maps it in 30-metre pixels, from 0 to 100 percent. Percentage imperviousness, or PIMP, matters in drainage and can be estimated as 6.4 times the square root of the number of dwellings per hectare. PIMP is about 10% for woodland and 100% for dense commercial areas.

soil-water-188.title: Two rings to keep the flow straight down
soil-water-188.text: One ring of water guards another. A double-ring infiltrometer sets a larger outer ring around an inner one, and the outer ring keeps the flow from the inner ring one-dimensional. Water is supplied at constant or falling head. The operator records how much enters the soil from the inner ring over a set time. With steady one-dimensional flow and a unit gradient below, the infiltration rate approximately equals the saturated hydraulic conductivity. The ASTM standard method uses inner and outer rings of 30 and 60 cm diameter.

soil-water-170.title: Counting slowed neutrons to find hidden water
soil-water-170.text: Hydrogen gives water away. In a neutron probe, a pellet of americium-241 and beryllium produces fast neutrons when alpha particles from the americium strike the beryllium nuclei. They slow down when they hit hydrogen nuclei in the soil. Counting the slow neutrons that return estimates the hydrogen present, and so the water. Read through an access tube installed in the soil, the probe gives farmers highly accurate deep-soil readings. Neutron probes can gauge soil water potential over a range of 0 to −1500 kPa.

soil-water-207.title: The root zone, the soil that plants can reach
soil-water-207.text: Water that sinks below the roots is water a plant will never use. The soil moisture zone, often called the root zone, is the depth of soil from which plant roots draw water. Water that moves below it after heavy rain or irrigation is lost to plants, and it can take fertilizers and nutrients with it. Good {{ref:soil-water-234}} therefore aims to wet the whole root zone while keeping overwatering to a minimum. Salts that build up in the root zone can be carried deeper, or into groundwater, by {{ref:soil-water-210}}.

soil-water-226.title: Sensing soil moisture through a circuit's frequency
soil-water-226.text: Wet soil changes the rhythm of an electronic circuit. A frequency domain sensor measures soil moisture with an oscillating circuit whose operating frequency depends on the dielectric constant of the soil around it. Its two types are capacitance probes and electrical impedance sensors. Impedance sensors commonly feed a 100 MHz oscillator signal along a coaxial line into buried probe wires, then measure the part reflected where impedance changes. These sensors are cheaper to build and respond faster than TDR. But the complex field around the probe means calibrating for each kind of soil, unless a high frequency is used.

soil-water-157.title: Shortcuts: how water races down root and worm channels
soil-water-157.text: Tree roots, living or dead, can raise infiltration rates up to 27 times. They do it by opening channels for rainwater. Preferential flow is the rapid drainage of water under gravity along connected macropores, crevices, and root and worm channels. Instead of soaking evenly through the soil, the water takes the express route. Macropores and fractures strongly influence infiltration rates, flow patterns and hydraulic conductivity in many soils. Soil mixing by organisms and other disturbances opens paths for gas in the soil as well as water. Even strongly water-repellent patches play a part, because water that cannot enter them finds pathways deeper into the profile. The shortcuts have costs. They speed drainage, but they also carry dissolved nutrients away quickly and leave water and chemicals unevenly spread. Extreme forms in depressions speed contaminants toward groundwater. They also distort measurement. In soils with distinct macropores, preferential flow dominates readings from single- or double-ring infiltrometers under ponding. Soil physics models often add it as dual-porosity or dual-permeability options. These are generally bolted onto solutions of the {{ref:soil-water-238}} without rigorous physical grounding.

soil-water-210.title: Groundwater recharge: how rain refills aquifers
soil-water-210.text: Most of the water in an aquifer arrived from above. Groundwater recharge, also called deep drainage, is the downward movement of water from the surface to groundwater, and it is the main way water enters an aquifer. Rain and snowmelt feed it mainly, rivers and lakes less. It usually takes place in unsaturated ground below plant roots and is often expressed as a flux to the water table. Diffuse recharge is rain soaking through soil over large areas. Focused recharge leaks from rivers, lakes, wetlands or depressions, and it grows more dominant as climates get drier. People push the balance both ways. Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, reduce infiltration, increase runoff and so cut recharge. Yet urban recharge can be up to ten times higher than rural, because leaking water-supply and sewage networks add water that rural areas lack. Recharge can also flush salts that accumulate in the root zone into deeper layers or into groundwater. For sustainable use, long-term pumping from an aquifer should not exceed its recharge. Climate change may cut both ways too. Fewer but more intense storms may raise recharge in many places, while harsher droughts may dry and compact soils and reduce infiltration.

soil-water-212.title: Refilling aquifers on purpose
soil-water-212.text: In Orange County, California, one facility cleans and injects 100 million gallons of water a day, or 90 billion gallons a year. That is artificial groundwater recharge: recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface. Managed aquifer recharge methods include modifying streambed channels, bank filtration, water spreading and recharge wells. In India, farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater. In 2007 the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts of seven states. Cities face a related task. Stormwater pollution collects in {{ref:soil-water-090}}, and high water tables affect how detention ponds, retention ponds and the planted basins of {{ref:soil-env-308}} should be designed.

soil-water-177.title: Field capacity: the water a soil keeps after draining
soil-water-177.text: Two to three days after rain, a well-drained soil settles down. Field capacity is the water a soil still holds after excess water has drained away and downward movement has slowed. By convention it is the water content held at −33 kPa of suction, or −10 kPa for sandy soils, after work by Richards and Weaver. At this point the smallest pores hold water and the largest hold air, the best condition for plant growth and microbial activity. The water held depends on the particles' specific surface area, so clay-rich and organic soils have higher field capacities. It is measured by wetting a profile, covering it against evaporation and tracking water content. The term came from Israelsen and West and from Veihmeyer and Hendrickson, improving on Lyman Briggs's {{ref:soil-water-245}}. Veihmeyer and Hendrickson admitted it is not strictly a constant, but a practical measure of water-holding capacity. When more water reaches a soil than its field capacity, groundwater recharge is most likely.

soil-water-229.title: Available water: the share of soil water plants can use
soil-water-229.text: Not all the water in a soil is water a plant can use. Available water capacity is the amount a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops. It is also called available water content (AWC), profile available water (PAW) or total available water (TAW). Frank Veihmeyer and Arthur Hendrickson defined readily available water as the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point. This water sits in pores of 0.1–75 μm. Smaller cryptopores hold water too tightly for roots, and macropores are generally air-filled at field capacity. The definition is disputed. Daniel Hillel argued that its two limits were never clearly defined and lack a physical basis. Water, he said, is never equally available across the range. Richards, profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-023}}, called it oversimplified, since availability also depends on how readily soil water moves in to replace what roots take. Strongly alkaline, sodium-rich soils hold little, as do thin soils of the kind in {{ref:soil-class-050}}, while the fibrous clay of {{ref:soil-chem-167}} can raise plant-available water in sandy soils.

soil-water-234.title: Deciding when to water, and for how long
soil-water-234.text: Up to 50% of landscape water is wasted by inefficient methods, the EPA WaterSense program estimates. Irrigation scheduling is how managers decide how often and for how long to water. The aim is to wet the whole root zone while minimizing overwatering and keeping water use efficiency high. Refilling depleted water before stress sets in avoids moisture stress. Methods range from watching plants for wilting and judging soil by feel, through sensors in the root zone, to {{ref:soil-water-235}}. Root-zone sensors include capacitance sensors, neutron probes for accurate deep readings, and the {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Scheduling has moved from calendar timers to smart controllers that respond to weather-based evapotranspiration or to measured soil moisture. Soil-based controllers either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold. Good scheduling prevents root rot and drought stress, and daily soil moisture estimates cut the risk of runoff and erosion.

soil-water-165.title: Four benchmarks from soaked to bone-dry
soil-water-165.text: Soil scientists routinely measure four reference water contents, each tied to a suction. Saturated water content, θs, sits at 0 kPa and is typically 0.2–0.5 by volume, equivalent to effective porosity. Field capacity, θfc, sits at −33 kPa and is typically 0.1–0.35, the moisture 2–3 days after rain or irrigation. Permanent wilting point, θpwp, sits at −1500 kPa and is typically 0.01–0.25, the lowest moisture at which a plant wilts. Residual water content, θr, is the water left at very high tension, typically 0.001–0.1. Available water content is field capacity minus wilting point. It ranges from 0.1 in gravel to 0.3 in {{ref:soil-class-070}}. Texture moves every benchmark. Average values put sand's wilting point at 3.3% and its field capacity at 9.1% by volume, against 27.2% and 39.6% for clay. Clay holds far more water, but much of it stays out of reach. Available water peaks in silt loam at 19.7% by volume, against 5.8% in sand and 12.4% in clay.

soil-water-211.title: Why low spots feed the water table
soil-water-211.text: The same rain can refill an aquifer or not, depending on where it pools. Spread evenly within a soil's field capacity, rain barely drains down. Gathered in low spots, the same volume can exceed field capacity and drain to groundwater. In depression-focused recharge, rain falls fairly evenly over an area but reaches groundwater mainly beneath depressions where runoff gathers. Water tables rise beneath them, and the process can matter greatly in arid regions. Deeper ponding forces water in faster and drives adsorbed contaminants down to the water table. In karst, focused flow can dissolve tunnels down to aquifers, an extreme form of preferential flow that speeds contaminant transport.

soil-water-245.title: Spinning soil to gauge its water
soil-water-245.text: In 1910 soil scientists put field capacity in a centrifuge. The moisture equivalent is the percentage of water a soil retains against a force 1000 times gravity, proposed as a measure of field capacity for fine-textured soils. A saturated sample 1 cm thick is spun at 1000 times gravity for 30 min. Its gravimetric water content afterwards is the moisture equivalent. Briggs and Shantz related it to texture in 1912: moisture equivalent = 0.02 sand + 0.22 silt + 1.05 clay. Soil physics no longer uses the concept, and field capacity has replaced it.

soil-water-236.title: How far to let soil dry before watering
soil-water-236.text: A vegetable crop can spare less of its water than an established tree. Management allowed depletion is the percentage of available soil water that can be used up before plants become stressed. It is often set at 50% for standard crops and 30% for sensitive crops such as vegetables. Stress-tolerant plants such as established trees get 60–70%. Soil moisture sensors can then act as a thermostat, triggering irrigation only when moisture drops below the threshold.

soil-water-235.title: Keeping a checkbook for the water in soil
soil-water-235.text: Some irrigators run their soil like a bank account. The soil water balance method, also called the checkbook method, schedules irrigation by tracking deposits and withdrawals. Rain and irrigation are the deposits. Evapotranspiration, the soil's evaporation plus the plants' transpiration, is the withdrawal. Each day's depletion equals the previous depletion plus crop evapotranspiration, minus rain and irrigation. Crop evapotranspiration is reference evapotranspiration, the loss from a standard grass surface, adjusted by a crop coefficient set out in FAO Paper 56. Coefficients above 1 mark high water users such as corn, and below 1 drought-tolerant plants such as cactus. The method relies on accurate weather data.

soil-water-159.title: Percolation: the slow trickle below the roots
soil-water-159.text: After soil drinks in the rain, gravity keeps pulling. Percolation is the downward drainage of water through a soil after the soil has absorbed it. Water draining through macropores under gravity during rain is called gravitational water. Drainage stops at field capacity, when adhesion and cohesion hold the rest. Once a soil is fully wetted, extra water percolates below the roots. It carries clay, nutrients and contaminants that may pollute groundwater, along with the dark organic material of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Magnesium, sulfur and potassium leach most readily, and phosphorus very little. Deep percolation that reaches groundwater is groundwater recharge, and groundwater in turn feeds soil moisture through percolation.

soil-water-248.title: Lysimeters: soil in a can, sometimes on a scale
soil-water-248.text: Edward Lewis Sturtevant built the first lysimeter in the United States in 1875. A lysimeter is a soil-filled container, usually a cylinder, used to study how water and dissolved substances move through soil. It can hold an undisturbed soil monolith or rebuilt layers, carry probes at several depths, and collect the water that drains out through an opening at the bottom. Weighing lysimeters sit on scales, so weight changes give evaporation, transpiration and drainage, and hence actual evapotranspiration. Suction lysimeters draw soil water through a buried porous cup under vacuum. Drainage lysimeters collect water passing through the profile to study leaching.

soil-water-230.title: The vadose zone, between the surface and the water table
soil-water-230.text: Between the land surface and the water table lies ground where air and water share the pores. This is the vadose zone, the unsaturated zone, where water in the pores is below atmospheric pressure. Adhesion and capillary action hold its water, and where the zone lies in soil, that water is soil moisture. It excludes the still-saturated {{ref:soil-water-179}} just above the water table. The zone is absent under lakes and marshes but can be hundreds of metres thick in arid regions. It often controls water's path from the surface to aquifers. So it governs recharge, and whether, where and how fast contaminants reach groundwater. Unlike the aquifers below, it is not a ready source of drinking water. Yet it supplies water and nutrients to the biosphere and is heavily used for crops, building and waste disposal. Flow through it is often described by the {{ref:soil-water-238}}, which rests partly on Darcy's law. Its study spans soil physics and hydrology.

soil-water-179.title: The capillary fringe: groundwater climbing into the soil
soil-water-179.text: Groundwater does not stop at the water table. It climbs. The capillary fringe is the layer just above a water table into which groundwater rises by capillary action to fill the pores. Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches. Because pore sizes are mixed, this tension-saturated base is shorter than the total capillary rise. Above it, water content falls with height. Definitions differ. Solute-transport workers count only the saturated base, while salinity and vapor-phase workers, and those in {{ref:soil-env-023}}, include the unsaturated part too. The fringe has consequences. Land whose surface lies within the capillary fringe of saline groundwater salinizes rapidly. Where the water table meets soil, it forms a boundary between oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions, and oxygen there feeds microbes that break down dissolved organic compounds.

soil-water-221.title: The tensiometer, a gauge of how hard soil holds its water
soil-water-221.text: A tube, a porous cup and a vacuum gauge can tell a farmer when to water. A tensiometer measures the matric potential, or moisture tension, of water in unsaturated soil. It is a water-filled glass or plastic tube with a porous ceramic cup, topped by a vacuum gauge or by a rubber cap read with a needle instrument. Buried and pumped to a partial vacuum, its water comes to balance with soil water through the cup. As plants and evaporation dry the soil, the vacuum grows; when the soil is rewetted, it falls. The gauge then reads the soil's matric potential. Irrigation managers use it to decide when to water. With a water retention curve, it also tells them how much. {{ref:soil-hist-023}} described its principles, construction and operation early in his career and kept improving the design. ISO 11276:1995 sets out tensiometer methods for pore water pressure in unsaturated and saturated soil.

soil-water-238.title: The Richards equation, a famously hard sum for moving water
soil-water-238.text: {{ref:soil-hist-023}} gave his name to an equation he did not write first. The Richards equation, published by Richards in 1931, describes water movement in unsaturated soils. Lewis Fry Richardson had introduced it nine years earlier, in 1922. It joins conservation of mass with the Darcy–Buckingham law for flow in variably saturated porous media, plus a sink term that is usually root water uptake. Its mixed form has two unknowns, water content and pressure head, linked through the water retention curve. It needs the soil's hydraulic properties, usually five van Genuchten retention parameters plus the saturated hydraulic conductivity. It is a quasilinear partial differential equation, solvable analytically only for particular conditions. Alt and Luckhaus proved that solutions exist and are unique only in 1983. Solving it numerically is among the hardest problems in earth science. Solvers may fail to converge, and rain soaking into dry soil needs grid spacing under one cm near the surface. It is still used widely, because it describes flow in the vadose zone between the atmosphere and the aquifer.

soil-water-206.title: Tracking a wetting front as it sinks
soil-water-206.text: The soil moisture velocity equation gives the speed at which water moves down through unsaturated soil under the combined pull of gravity and capillarity. It reworks Richards' equation so that its unknown is the depth of a wetting front of a given water content as it moves with time. An advection-like term carries flow driven by gravity and capillarity, and a diffusion-like term reflects the front's shape. Dropping the second term still gave over 99% accuracy in cumulative infiltration, checked against exact solutions for idealized soils. Solved by the method of lines, the advection-like term becomes three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.

soil-water-239.title: A sturdier way to simulate unsaturated flow
soil-water-239.text: Where Richards solvers can fail, this method is guaranteed to converge. The finite water-content vadose zone flow method is a one-dimensional alternative to solving Richards' equation numerically. It solves the advection-like term of the {{ref:soil-water-206}} as three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater. Being explicit, it is cheap to solve and mass-conserving, and it handles the sharp wetting fronts that Richards solvers struggle with. It assumes soil homogeneous in layers and omits soil water diffusion, which barely affects flux accuracy. It works with any monotonic retention and conductivity relations, such as Brooks and Corey or van Genuchten–Mualem.

soil-water-213.title: Estimating the recharge no one can measure
soil-water-213.text: No widely applicable method can measure groundwater recharge directly and accurately, so hydrologists estimate it. The difficulty is closing the balance. Evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated. Common methods include chloride mass balance, soil physics methods, environmental and isotopic tracers, groundwater-level fluctuations, water balances and river baseflow. Direct physical methods measure the water passing below the root zone, while indirect ones infer recharge from soil physical parameters. Numerical codes such as HYDRUS1D, UNSAT-H and SHAW use climate and soil data and some form of the Richards equation to model flow in the vadose zone.

soil-water-158.title: Fingered flow: water falling in narrow fingers
soil-water-158.text: Water does not always sink through dry soil as an even front. In fingered flow it moves down through unsaturated soil unevenly, in narrow 'gravity fingers'. Soil moisture sources attribute the fingers to surface tension between water particles. The fingering is described as a Saffman–Taylor instability. It arises mostly during drainage and leaves an unstable boundary between saturated and unsaturated soil.

soil-phys-146.title: The hidden atmosphere between soil grains
soil-phys-146.text: After a long drought, the first rain releases a familiar scent. That smell is the soil's own atmosphere, flushed out of the ground as the rain soaks in. Soil gas is the mix of gases filling the air spaces between soil particles, the pores described in {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. Its main components are nitrogen, carbon dioxide and oxygen. Nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, methane and ammonia also occur naturally. Oxygen matters most to life below ground, because plant roots and soil organisms need it to respire. As they breathe, microbes and roots use up oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Soil air therefore holds less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than the air above. Gas and water share the same pore space. Gas moves in as water drains, evaporates or is taken up by roots, so the two are often inversely related. Soil air also carries messages. Soil organisms release volatile compounds as by-products of their metabolism, as chemicals that act on their neighbors and as signals. The result is a network of chemical cues. The soil's gas budget matters for climate too. Well-ventilated soil is a net sink of methane, yet oxygen-starved soil at higher temperatures produces it. Overall, soil is a net emitter of greenhouse gases, especially where {{ref:soil-env-129}} thaws and releases its gas as the climate warms.

soil-phys-137.title: How warm the ground runs, and why it matters
soil-phys-137.text: Across the world's biomes, mean annual soil temperature runs from −10 to 26 °C. Soil temperature is how warm or cold a soil is, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses. It is one of the traits covered in {{ref:soil-phys-040}}, and a great deal of life depends on it. It regulates seed germination, the breaking of seed dormancy, plant and root growth and the availability of nutrients. Soil temperature varies by season, month and day, but the swings shrink with depth. Upper layers follow the air, while deeper layers fluctuate less. Water content, color, relief, plant cover and air temperature all shift it. Pale soils, which reflect more sunlight, stay cooler than dark ones. Water has a large effect. Wet surface soil is typically 3 to 6 °C colder than dry surface soil, because water takes more energy to heat and to evaporate. Covering the ground changes the picture as well. Clear plastic sheeting, or drying the soil, raises its temperature. A layer of plant material on the surface slows warming and damps surface swings. Farmers work around soil temperature. They time their planting, apply anhydrous ammonia below 10 °C (50 °F) and protect shallow-rooted crops from {{ref:soil-phys-153}}. Soil temperatures are now rising worldwide with climate warming. The main threats are the thaw of {{ref:soil-env-129}}, carbon loss and ecosystem collapse. How warming soils will affect carbon capture, storage and climate feedbacks is still disputed, and sources hold opposing views.

soil-phys-148.title: How oxygen finds its way into the ground
soil-phys-148.text: Soil air is never still. Its gas molecules move constantly, colliding and bouncing in a random walk. Gas diffusion is the net movement of those molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration. It is the main way {{ref:soil-phys-146}} trades with the atmosphere, and Fick's law describes it in numbers. Oxygen diffuses in from the air above and is consumed below. Excess carbon dioxide, other gases and water vapor diffuse out. The rate depends on total porosity, how well the pores connect, water content, air turbulence and temperature. Pore size itself matters less. Compaction lowers the diffusion coefficient, the measure of how readily gas spreads, and a platy structure also blocks the flow. Water is the great obstacle. In saturated soil no open air passages remain, and diffusion slows some 10,000 times. Short of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria, which live without free oxygen, reduce nitrate to N2, N2O and NO gases. This drains nitrogen from the soil. Daily and seasonal swings in temperature and moisture change the soil gas, and with it the pace of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}. When frozen soils thaw or dry soils are rewetted, microbes surge into activity. Sudden bursts of carbon dioxide and methane follow.

soil-phys-150.title: Letting the soil breathe
soil-phys-150.text: Compaction is one of the commonest reasons a soil runs short of air. Soil aeration is the exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, along with the ways of improving it. Below ground, microbial activity and root respiration use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide. A lack of oxygen can then hold back plant growth. Good aeration also lets water drain and roots grow. The pore network ventilates the soil, and wind, atmospheric pressure, convection and diffusion all drive the exchange. Soil structure strongly shapes the larger pores that control aeration, infiltration and drainage. Those pores fail in two common ways: water fills them, or compaction crushes them. Either way, nutrient uptake can fall, and bacteria short of free oxygen take it from nitrate instead. Remedies range from chemistry to animals. Liquid aeration applies solutions, commonly of ammonium lauryl sulfate, that break down dense particles and loosen compacted soil. Adding lime improves soil structure and so aeration. Digging megafauna, large burrowing animals, help too by disturbing the soil's layers.

soil-phys-147.title: Soil air: like the sky's, but rich in carbon dioxide
soil-phys-147.text: The air in soil pores can hold 10 to 100 times the atmosphere's 0.04% carbon dioxide. Soil air composition is the make-up of the soil atmosphere: similar to the air above, but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapor. One typical comparison gives soil air 79.2% nitrogen, 20.6% oxygen and 0.25% carbon dioxide, against 78.0%, 20.9% and 0.04% in the atmosphere. High carbon dioxide may inhibit root respiration, and at extreme levels it is toxic. It increases with depth, where dead plant material decomposes and roots are abundant. Soils rich in carbonates buffer it, while in acid soils the carbon dioxide that roots and microbes breathe out accumulates in the pores. Unlike the more uniform atmosphere, soil air shifts daily and seasonally. Temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind and rainfall all steer it. Methane and nitrous oxide are minor parts, but they matter for greenhouse gas flux and for human impacts on soils.

soil-phys-158.title: How deep the winter reaches
soil-phys-158.text: Across the contiguous United States, the deepest winter freezing ranges from 0 to 8 feet (2.4 m) below ground. The frost line, also called frost depth or freezing depth, is the depth to which groundwater in the soil is expected to freeze. It deepens toward the poles. It also depends on climate, on how well the soil and nearby materials transfer heat, and on nearby heat sources. Snow cover and asphalt insulate the ground, while homes warm it. During seasonal freezing and thawing, the shifting position of the frost line is called the frost front. In Arctic and Antarctic places freezing reaches year-round {{ref:soil-env-129}}, and a different term, {{ref:soil-env-147}}, is used instead. In the tropics the term can mean something else: the elevation below which frost does not occur. Building codes place foundations below frost depth, because {{ref:soil-phys-153}} can move them. Water and sewer pipes are buried below it too. Where shallow bedrock or utilities prevent deep trenches, pipes are insulated or warmed with heat tape instead.

soil-phys-153.title: Why frozen ground rises: Stephen Taber's answer
soil-phys-153.text: Water expands only about 9% when it freezes, too little to explain how far frozen ground can rise. Frost heaving is the upward swelling of soil in freezing weather as ice grows toward the surface from the freezing front. It needs three things. The soil's fine pores must pull water upward ({{ref:soil-phys-155}}). Water must be supplied from below, as by a water table. And freezing temperatures must reach into the soil. Water climbs to the freezing front by capillary action. There it feeds growing layers of ice, described in {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, that can lift soil 1 foot (0.30 m) or more. By 1930 Stephen Taber had shown the real cause: water migrates to the freeze line. He also found that benzene, which contracts as it freezes, heaves too. That ruled out volume change as the main mechanism. The damage is familiar. Uneven heave cracks road surfaces, helping form springtime potholes, and it damages building foundations. Even cold stores and ice rinks can freeze and lift the ground beneath them. Fill that does not heave, insulation or heating prevents it. At the very start of the freezing season, before the freezing front has gone deep, the same process appears as {{ref:soil-phys-159}}.

soil-phys-159.title: Needle ice: frost columns that heave seedlings from the ground
soil-phys-159.text: On a cold night, columns of ice can grow straight up out of bare soil. Needle ice is needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface. It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C: water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column. Needles are typically a few centimeters long. Ten centimeters is the recorded maximum, though specimens of 15-20 cm have been seen at Gerðuberg. It needs ice segregation, in which supercooled water freezes onto existing ice in a porous medium, and it favors soils high in silt and organic matter. It is {{ref:soil-phys-153}} at the start of the freezing season, before there is any soil overburden to lift. Taber found that pore size controls the amount of frost heave, and that a gradient of soil moisture tension drives water up toward the freezing front near the surface. Growing needles lift soil particles and crusts, which settle unevenly on melting. They disturb streambanks, aid soil creep and shape patterned ground. They also heave seedlings out of the ground, and the seedlings often die because they do not resettle or their roots dry out. Swedish pipkrake, coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman, is one of several names. Others are frost pillars, Kammeis and shimobashira. See {{ref:soil-phys-137}} for the soil temperatures involved.

soil-phys-140.title: The properties that steer heat through soil
soil-phys-140.text: Heat enters and leaves soil in three ways: radiation, conduction and convection. Soil thermal properties govern how that energy moves. They form a branch of soil physics used in engineering, climatology and agriculture. The two main ones measure how much heat a volume of soil stores, in J·m−3·K−1, and how well it passes heat along, in W·m−1·K−1. Each has its own entry later: {{ref:soil-phys-139}} and {{ref:soil-phys-141}}. Together they decide how energy is shared out through the soil profile. Basic composition matters, but water content and the volume fractions of solids and air matter strongly. Moisture and thermal properties are so closely linked that they are often measured and reported together. Both change constantly with daily and seasonal cycles, which makes general statements about any one site hard. Surface temperature swings reach deeper layers more slowly and with a delay, an effect explored in {{ref:soil-phys-142}}. The uses are broad. Engineers weigh frost effects on construction and on buried pipes and cables, and farmers time their planting. Others study greenhouse gases, store radioactive waste or search for buried land mines.

soil-env-129.title: Permafrost, ground frozen for ages
soil-env-129.text: The oldest permafrost has stayed frozen for around 700,000 years. Permafrost is soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more. In practice it occurs where the mean annual temperature is 0 °C or below. It underlies about 11% of the global land surface, around 18 million km2. That includes much of Alaska, Canada, Greenland and Siberia, and high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau. Its thickness ranges from less than a meter to more than 1,500 m. On land it usually lies beneath soil that freezes and thaws with the seasons, the {{ref:soil-env-146}}. Over millennia, dead plant and animal remains have built up in it without fully breaking down. That makes tundra soil a store of carbon. Warming now threatens that store. As the frozen ground thaws, the remains begin to break down again, releasing carbon dioxide or methane, which feeds back into climate change. Thaw also weakens the ground itself. Ice-rich soil can suddenly exceed hydraulic saturation and shift or collapse, endangering the buildings and infrastructure on it.

soil-phys-154.title: Ice lenses, the hidden engine of frost heave
soil-phys-154.text: Most of the lift in frost heave comes from ice growing in hidden layers underground. An ice lens is a body of ice that forms where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface. Ice first gathers in small pores or cracks. It keeps collecting there, wedging the soil or rock apart. Lenses grow several centimeters to several decimeters deep, and their growth is the dominant cause of soil displacement in frost heaving. They draw water from groundwater below the freezing line, through fine soils with capillary pores. The water can travel because water in fine pores stays liquid below the normal freezing point, the Gibbs–Thomson effect. The same process, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-179}}, splits rock more effectively than the freeze-thaw expansion proposed by older texts. Arctic tundra favors deep lenses, because permafrost keeps the ground frozen at depth and stops meltwater draining away.

soil-phys-149.title: Reading soil gas for oil and earthquakes
soil-phys-149.text: Gas seeping from the ground can hint at oil beneath it. Soil gas surveys put soil gases to work in research. Microseepage, the small release of hydrocarbons at the surface, is used to search for petroleum, on the assumption that hydrocarbons migrate vertically. The migration of soil gases, especially radon, is studied as a possible warning of earthquakes. Landfill waste, mining and petroleum contamination also produce gases, including volatile organic compounds, that diffuse through soil. Exchange between soil gas and the air can be analyzed by distance from the soil surface.

soil-phys-157.title: Mounds, pingos and polygons raised by frost
soil-phys-157.text: Frost heaving builds whole landscapes of mounds, on Earth and on Mars. Frost-heave landforms are raised-ground features arranged in circles, polygons and stripes. In organic soils such as {{ref:soil-class-070}} they are called {{ref:soil-water-266}}; in mineral soils, {{ref:soil-phys-161}}. They appear in alpine regions even near the equator, as such peat mounds on Mount Kenya show. {{ref:soil-env-170}} grow up to 60 meters high over hundreds of years in Arctic permafrost, fed by upwelling groundwater rather than capillary action. Small earth hummocks in seasonally frozen ground go by thúfur in Iceland and pounus in Fennoscandia. In May 2008 the Phoenix lander touched down on polygonal frost-heave ground on Mars and found ice a few centimeters down.

soil-phys-155.title: Which soils heave, and which do not
soil-phys-155.text: Frost-susceptible soil has pore sizes and particle surface area that promote capillary flow, so it can feed ice lenses and heave when it freezes. Silty and loamy soils, which contain fine particles, are the typical examples. Many agencies call a material frost susceptible if 10 percent or more passes a 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve. Passing 3 percent or more through a 0.02 mm (No. 635) sieve also counts. Dense clays pass water too slowly. Clean sands and gravels have pores too open for capillary flow. For pavements, standard tests compare a soil's heave rate and thawed bearing ratio with an established classification.

soil-phys-156.title: How soil grains travel through solid ice
soil-phys-156.text: A grain of soil can move through solid ice. The key is premelting: thin films of liquid water persist on ice below freezing. Faraday reported this unfrozen layer in 1860 and called the particle migration thermal regelation. The film is thinner on a particle's cold side. Water keeps flowing from the warm side to the cold side and refreezing, so the particle moves toward warmer soil. A 10-nanometer film around a micrometer-sized particle can move it 10 micrometers a day, in a thermal gradient as low as 1 °C m−1. The process purifies growing ice lenses by pushing fine particles away.

soil-phys-163.title: Patterned ground: circles and stripes drawn by frost
soil-phys-163.text: Stones sorted into neat circles and stripes can form with no human hand involved. Patterned ground is the distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed when ground material deforms in periglacial regions, cold lands shaped by frost. It occurs wherever soil freezing and thawing alternate, from the Arctic and Antarctica to the Australian Outback, the Atacama Desert and Mars. Computer models of the past 20 years tie its formation to frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils. Repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up. Sideways forces pile them into clusters and stripes that smooth into polygons, circles and stripes. Circles range from a few centimeters to several meters across, and stripes form on slopes of 2° to 7°. Steps occur too, and each form is either sorted or unsorted. Polygons form either in permafrost, as ice wedges, or in areas where the ground freezes and thaws each year ({{ref:soil-phys-185}}). Most of it forms in the seasonally thawing layer above permafrost, where the churning described in {{ref:soil-form-034}} also works.

soil-phys-161.title: Lithalsas, stony mounds lifted by ice
soil-phys-161.text: On the Svalbard archipelago, stony mounds have been heaved up out of the ground. They are lithalsas: frost-raised mounds in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens, one that lasts year after year, has grown within the soil. A lithalsa is the mineral-soil counterpart of {{ref:soil-water-266}} among the frost-heave landforms. The term is sometimes also used for those peat mounds and for {{ref:soil-env-170}}.

soil-phys-151.title: Spikes and cores: punching air into turf
soil-phys-151.text: Some lawn aerators are nothing more than spiked shoes. Core and spike aeration improves gas exchange mechanically. It either punctures the soil with spikes or removes cores about 1 in × 2 in (25 mm × 51 mm). Spike aerators use spikes up to a foot or more long and are sometimes used for drainage problems in turf. Core aeration on turf reduces compaction and {{ref:soil-bio-084}}, lets water and nutrients infiltrate better and encourages deeper roots. Machines range from walk-behind and ride-on models to tractor-pulled rigs.

soil-phys-139.title: Why wet soil is slow to warm
soil-phys-139.text: A gram of pure water needs about 1 calorie to warm by 1 °C; a gram of dry soil needs about 0.2. That quantity, the energy needed to raise a material's temperature by 1 °C, is its specific heat. For soil it is called soil heat capacity. Wet soil lies between 0.2 and 1, or 0.8 to 4.2 kJ per kilogram, and its specific heat rises with water content. Evaporating water also absorbs about 584 cal/g (2442 kJ/kg at 25 °C). So wet soil warms more slowly than dry soil. Volumetric heat capacity, in J·m−3·K−1, is one of the main soil thermal properties.

soil-phys-160.title: Frost boils, mud circles that churn for centuries
soil-phys-160.text: In Svalbard, the centers of frost boils heaved about 9.5 mm per day, against about 1.6 mm per day at their margins. A frost boil, or mud circle, is a small circular mound of fresh soil. Frost action and the churning in {{ref:soil-form-034}} form it. Typically 1 to 3 meters across, frost boils occur in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost. They are among the commonest features of patterned ground. Each is a nonsorted circle: a barren mineral-soil center among vegetated, peaty ground. The wetter silty or loamy centers grow more ice lenses and heave more than their surroundings. Over years, soil is carried upward, in a cycle that can take centuries.

soil-phys-152.title: Linear aeration: grooves that feed the soil
soil-phys-152.text: One pass of a machine can spread organic amendments, cut grooves and close them again. That is linear aeration, which cuts grooves into soil or turf so that water and amendments penetrate and are retained in the right amounts. Because the grooves close in the same pass, soil structure is barely disturbed. The method can add {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, topsoil, {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, sand or clay as soil softeners where needed. On lawns it relieves excess water and compaction in heavily used areas, with less surface disruption than coring.

soil-phys-144.title: Seeing soil heat from the sky
soil-phys-144.text: Reflected light reveals only the topmost few molecular layers of a soil. Thermal remote sensing of soil looks deeper. Thermal infrared sensors on satellites and aircraft detect variations in soil thermal properties at shallow depths below the surface. They pick up heat moving into and out of near-surface layers by conduction, convection and radiation. Satellite microwave sensing helps too. Unlike thermal infrared, it is not affected by cloud cover.

soil-phys-141.title: Quartz, water and air: how well soil conducts heat
soil-phys-141.text: Quartz conducts heat at 8.8 W·m−1·K−1; dry soil manages only 0.2–0.4. Soil thermal conductivity is the ability of soil to conduct heat. In the same units, typical values are 0.57 for water, 0.25 for {{ref:soil-bio-114}} and 1–3 for wet soil. Air conducts heat poorly and weakens conduction through the solid and liquid parts. The solid phase conducts best, yet the varying moisture of a soil largely decides its conductivity. Designing a shallow-loop heat pump that draws on the ground, as in {{ref:soil-phys-178}}, needs an accurate on-site reading, which a thermal heat probe can provide.

soil-phys-138.title: Measuring the flow of heat into the ground
soil-phys-138.text: When the surface is warmer than the soil below, heat is conducted down into the soil. Soil heat flux is the rate at which heat moves through soil in response to a temperature difference between two points. Its density, in W·m−2, is the energy flowing through a unit area per unit time, with both a size and a direction. It is calculated from the rule in {{ref:soil-phys-182}}, using the soil's thermal conductivity and the temperature gradient between two depths. Heat flows against that gradient, from the warmer point to the cooler one.

soil-phys-164.title: Thermal diffusivity: how fast heat spreads
soil-phys-164.text: Air at 300 K has a thermal diffusivity of 19 mm2/s; water at 25 °C has just 0.143. Thermal diffusivity measures how fast heat spreads through a material, in m2/s. It equals thermal conductivity divided by density and specific heat capacity: α = k/(ρcp). The product ρcp is the volumetric heat capacity, in J/(m3·K). A material of high diffusivity conducts heat quickly relative to how much energy it stores, so heat moves through it rapidly. Sandstone sits at 1.15 mm2/s and ice at 0 °C at 1.02. In the field, the dual-probe heat-pulse sensor measures diffusivity together with volumetric heat capacity.

soil-phys-143.title: Needle probes that read soil heat in place
soil-phys-143.text: Two needles in the ground can yield all of a soil's main thermal properties. The heat probe method measures soil thermal properties in place, with needle probes that heat the soil and record its temperature response. A single probe heats continuously and senses how fast heat is conducted away, so it measures thermal conductivity only. IEEE 442-1981 and ASTM D 5334-08 cover it. The dual-probe heat-pulse method sets a heater and a sensor needle a fixed distance apart and records the sensor's response to a heat pulse over time. It measures thermal diffusivity and volumetric heat capacity, and conductivity follows from them. Its drawbacks are a small measured volume and sensitivity to probe-to-soil contact and heater-to-sensor spacing.

soil-phys-142.title: Thermal lag: deep soil warms late and gently
soil-phys-142.text: About 50% of the Sun's heat is absorbed at the surface, where temperature swings with day and night, weather and season. Thermal lag is this damping and delay with depth: deeper soil reaches its highs and lows later and less sharply. As a result the ground below the surface is warmer than the air in winter and cooler in summer. Deep enough down, temperature stays constant year round, at about the mean of summer and winter temperatures. Sources differ on that depth. Reported values include 5–6 m, 6 m and 15 m, and 4.25 m for dry soil against 6.7 m for wet soil.

soil-phys-145.title: Banking summer sun in the ground for winter
soil-phys-145.text: The ground can carry summer's solar energy into winter. Ground heat storage uses the earth as a long-term store of heat for ground source heat pumps. The thermal effusivity of soil, its ability to exchange heat with its surroundings, lets the ground serve as underground thermal energy storage. Design criteria for shallow-loop heat pumps require an accurate on-site reading of thermal conductivity. Earth-sheltered buildings draw on the same effect. The thermal mass and thermal lag of the surrounding earth keep their need for extra heating and cooling minimal.

soil-phys-165.title: Hydraulic head, the height that tells groundwater where to go
soil-phys-165.text: What moves groundwater is not height alone, but height plus pressure. Hydraulic head is a liquid's pressure, divided by its {{ref:soil-phys-131}}, plus its elevation above a datum, expressed as a length. It is read as the height of the water surface in a piezometer, a narrow standpipe, against a common datum. Total head adds elevation head to the head described in {{ref:soil-phys-223}}, h = ψ + z, a simplified form of the Bernoulli principle. Take a piezometer 400 m deep at 1000 m elevation, with water 100 m down: z = 600 m, ψ = 300 m and h = 900 m. Each extra meter of fresh water adds about 9.8 kPa of pressure. Where head is constant, nothing flows. A head difference drives water from higher to lower head. Since density varies with temperature and salinity, heads are first converted to fresh water head. In 1907 USDA soil physicist Edgar Buckingham showed that rising atmospheric pressure lowers well water levels.

soil-phys-166.title: Hydraulic gradient, the slope that drives groundwater
soil-phys-166.text: Water needs a difference in head to move. The hydraulic gradient is the change in {{ref:soil-phys-165}} between measurement points along a flow path. Its magnitude, i = dh/dl, is the head difference between two piezometers divided by the flow path length between them. The result is a dimensionless ratio. Groundwater specialists also call it the Darcy slope, because it sets the size of the Darcy flux. As a vector, it gives both the size and the direction of flow, which runs down the gradient from high to low head. Combined with Darcy's law and a hydraulic conductivity tensor, it yields the flux of water in three dimensions.

soil-water-288.title: SWAT, a free model of whole watersheds
soil-water-288.text: Universities and government agencies around the world reach for the same free program when they model a landscape's water. The Soil and Water Assessment Tool, known as SWAT, is an open-source hydrology model and map-based simulation sponsored by the USDA. SWAT is a geographic version of {{ref:soil-water-107}}, and it works alongside commercial mapping software such as ArcGIS.

soil-water-281.title: Mineral dust, the soil that travels by sky
soil-water-281.text: Every year the world's winds lift somewhere between 1000 and 5000 million tons of soil into the air.
