That cloud is mineral dust, an atmospheric aerosol of suspended soil minerals. It is mostly crustal oxides such as SiO2, Al2O3, FeO, Fe2O3 and CaO, plus the carbonates CaCO3 and MgCO3. Most comes from deserts, but about a quarter may come from land-use change and human-made {{ref:soil-env-072}}. The Sahara is the largest source, at 60 to 200 million tons a year. Its dust feeds the Amazon rainforest and to phytoplankton in the Mediterranean. Spring dust from the Gobi, called Asian dust, harms visibility and health, yet is thought to enrich soils with trace minerals. Farming pressure and spreading desert worsened it after 1950. Soil moisture, vegetation cover, wind speed and soil type control emissions. North American dustfall rose 60% in the 1800s as land disturbance accelerated. Drought is harder to pin down: modern observations link it to more dust, but lake-sediment records of ancient megadroughts disagree.

soil-water-291.title: RUSLE, the soil loss equation revised
soil-water-291.text: An equation first built for farm fields is still among North America's busiest erosion tools. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation, or RUSLE, is an updated form of {{ref:soil-water-041}}. With the WEPP model, it is one of the two most widely used erosion models on the continent. Various techniques now compute its five factors. The support practice factor, P, is often estimated from land use and slope gradient, and a lower value means better erosion control. Much research on eroding mined land focuses on fitting or improving its parameters.

soil-water-287.title: Predicting how much a field loses to wind
soil-water-287.text: Wind moves soil in bursts. Grains sit still until the wind passes a critical speed. Then the erosion rate climbs with the cube of the friction velocity, a measure of the wind's drag on the ground. The wind erosion equation estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind as E = f(I, K, C, L, V). The five inputs are soil erodibility, ridge roughness, a climatic factor, the unsheltered distance across the field and the equivalent vegetative cover. Friction velocity is calculated from measured wind speed using the von Kármán constant, about 0.4. Most wind records come from airports and military bases, often only since the Second World War.

soil-water-274.title: Where moving sediment finally comes to rest
soil-water-274.text: Everything that erosion carries away must eventually land somewhere. Deposition is the geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass. Wind, ice, water and gravity all carry weathered material, and they drop it in layers when the flow loses enough kinetic energy. The tipping point has a name, the null point hypothesis: deposition begins when the forces moving sediment can no longer overcome gravity and friction. Grain size shapes how this plays out. Large grains come to rest when the water's drag on the bed and its turbulence fall too low. Grains held up in the water may still drift some way as they sink. Fine silt and clay particles settle one by one, following {{ref:soil-phys-188}}. In seawater, though, they flocculate, bonding electrically into clumps called flocs that sink together. Deposition is not only about broken rock. It can build sediment from organic or chemical matter too. Chalk forms from the skeletons of plankton, and coal from plant material laid down without oxygen.

soil-water-272.title: Denudation, the slow lowering of the land
soil-water-272.text: Mountains are pushed up faster than they wear down. Average mountain-building can run eight times faster than the maximum average denudation. Denudation is the sum of the processes by which moving water, ice, wind and waves wear down Earth's surface and lower its elevation and relief. Denudation is broader than {{ref:soil-water-002}}. Erosion moves soil and rock from place to place, while denudation adds up everything that lowers the surface. It combines mechanical, biological and chemical {{ref:soil-found-052}}, erosion and {{ref:soil-water-053}}, and it carries away both solid particles and dissolved material. Its pace depends on human activity, living organisms, climate, rock type, topography and tectonic activity. Tectonics works on both sides of the ledger. Uplift, volcanoes and earthquakes expose fresh crust to weathering and erosion. As denudation strips weight from the crust, the crust can rise further. The idea has a long history. It goes back to 1785 and to Hutton and Playfair, who argued that landscapes are worn down to near sea level. That view inspired planation theories such as William Morris Davis's peneplanation cycle, which faded after 1964.

soil-water-275.title: Sedimentation: when falling grains finally stop
soil-water-275.text: Settling is the fall of particles through a liquid; sedimentation is where that fall ends, with the particles at rest against a barrier. How they fall depends on the particle. Sand grains, called type 1, settle singly at constant velocity. Type 2 particles flocculate, so their settling speed changes as they clump. Above 1000 mg/L, type 3 particles settle together as a zone. Deep-sea sediment builds up at under 3 millimetres per thousand years; parts of major deltas gain several metres. Restoring the exchange of water and sediment between rivers and delta plains helps sinking deltas keep their height.

soil-water-284.title: Siltation, when eroded soil chokes the water
soil-water-284.text: A layer of mud just 1 mm thick can kill coral polyps. That sensitivity makes siltation one of erosion's costliest side effects. Siltation is water pollution by fine {{ref:soil-phys-013}} and clay particles, both as extra sediment suspended in the water and as unwanted fine deposits on the bottom. It usually starts with {{ref:soil-water-001}}, or with sediment spilled during dredging and dumping. In the countryside the source is typically soil degraded by intensive or poor farming, especially fine-grained soils such as {{ref:soil-form-106}}. In towns it is construction sites stripped of vegetation. Erosion at the source may amount to a fraction of a millimetre a year, too little to measure there. So sediment is measured in transport instead, as concentration times discharge: 50 mg/L flowing at 30 m3/s carries 1.5 kg/s. Suspended sediment disrupts filter-feeding animals, and deposits bury them. Hard-bottom communities and mussel and oyster banks suffer more than sand and mud bottoms. The first defense is keeping land covered so it does not erode. The second is trapping sediment before it reaches streams, and construction sites use short exposure times and silt screens. Silt also fills shipping channels and channels that carry water to crops, where dredging is often the only cure once it settles.

soil-water-277.title: How rivers carve, carry and build with sediment
soil-water-277.text: Each year the Yellow River is estimated to deliver 796 million tons of sediment to the sea. The Mississippi carries 406 million tons and the Po 67 million. Fluvial sediment processes are the movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms they create. Flowing water drags on its bed and lowers it where the bed is weak or loose. The sediment it carries scrapes the bed, while the fragments themselves grind smaller and rounder, a wearing called attrition. Sediment travels in three ways: rolling along the bed as bed load, held up in the flow as {{ref:soil-water-286}}, or dissolved. A single ratio, the Rouse number, sorts the grains. It compares a grain's settling velocity with the water's upward velocity. Above 2.5 a grain moves as bed load, between 0.8 and 2.5 held up in the flow, and below 0.8 as wash load, the finest fraction. Water moves bigger grains than air does because it is denser and more viscous, and floods can roll cobbles and boulders. Where flow is fast, the river picks up more than it drops. Where it is slow, dropped particles build {{ref:soil-water-264}} of {{ref:soil-form-112}}. The moving bed shapes ripples, dunes and antidunes, which preserved in rock record the direction and strength of ancient flows.

soil-water-286.title: Suspended load: sediment carried by turbulence
soil-water-286.text: Muddy river water owes its color to grains that never touch the bottom. Suspended load is the part of a flow's sediment lifted off the bed and held up by turbulence. It is mostly fine sand, silt and clay, though strong flows carry coarser sand low in the water. It forms the middle layer of transport, between bed load below and the finest wash load above, described in {{ref:soil-water-249}}. Grains are fully suspended at Rouse numbers of 0.8 to 1.2 and half suspended at 1.2 to 2.5. When the flow slows, the load drops out.

soil-water-285.title: Stream power, the energy a river spends
soil-water-285.text: A river is a machine that spends energy on its own bed and banks. In the 1960s R. A. Bagnold put a number on that energy, now called stream power. It is the product of water density, gravitational acceleration, discharge and slope, Ω = ρgQS, in watts per unit length of channel. Dividing by channel width gives unit stream power. That lets rivers of different widths be compared and better estimates how much sediment a river can carry. Critical unit stream power is the power needed to move a grain of a given size, and it sets a river's competence, the largest grain it can shift. Several studies found a threshold at 30 to 35 W m−2, where rivers switch from stable to actively reshaping themselves. Engineers use stream power to design bridges and culverts that will not start erosion, and modelers use it to simulate how rivers cut down and landscapes evolve.

soil-water-270.title: Bank erosion: how rivers eat their sides
soil-water-270.text: Rivers wear away their banks as well as their beds, and bank erosion works in two linked steps. Flowing water removes particles directly, an action called fluvial erosion. Undercutting then sets up mass failure, when a bank's weight exceeds the soil's strength and it gives way. Groundwater seeping out of a bank can also erode it, a process called piping when concentrated. Roots usually slow bank erosion, though heavy trees can overload the bank top. Erosion pins, repeated surveys and aerial or satellite images track the rates.

soil-water-278.title: Headward erosion, a stream cutting uphill
soil-water-278.text: Some streams grow backward. Headward erosion cuts away the head of a channel, moving its origin upslope and lengthening the stream, valley or gully. Water gathering in channels gains speed and erosive power, and the steep gradient at the head speeds the cutting further. Given time, a stream can break into a neighboring watershed and capture its drainage, as the Shenandoah River did to Potomac tributaries. The rock decides the pattern: branching on uniform bedrock, trellis-like on alternating weak and strong rock, and rectangular on jointed rock.

soil-water-268.title: Aggradation, when rivers raise the land
soil-water-268.text: Give a river more sediment than it can carry and it starts building the ground up. Aggradation, also called alluviation, is that rise in land elevation as sediment is deposited. The Exner equation describes the balance between sediment in transport and sediment in the bed. Lowland rivers, deltas and {{ref:soil-water-293}} are typical settings, and their slow sinking often offsets the rise. A drier climate can trigger it: sparse plants bind less soil, so more sediment enters rivers just as their flow drops. A 2009 report found reduced aggradation raising flood risk in many deltas.

soil-water-276.title: Entrainment, the moment a grain lifts off
soil-water-276.text: Every grain on a riverbed waits for a certain speed. Entrainment is the incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, and it starts erosion. Each grain size has its own entrainment velocity, the flow speed at which those grains begin to move. Once moving, grains keep traveling even below that speed, because friction with the bed drops. They settle only when the flow slows further, as {{ref:soil-water-250}} shows.

soil-water-282.title: Shear velocity, drag measured as speed
soil-water-282.text: Engineers often express the drag of a flow on its boundary as a speed. Shear velocity, also called friction velocity, is shear stress rewritten in units of velocity. It describes how particles and contaminants spread, how flow speed changes near a boundary, and how channels move sediment. It scales well with bedload transport, and in most rivers it is 5% to 10% of the mean flow velocity. Over land, the log wind profile gives it from wind speeds at two heights. Among trees or buildings, wind falls to zero at about 2/3 to 3/4 of obstacle height.

soil-water-269.title: Badlands, where clay and rare storms carve bare ground
soil-water-269.text: Some landscapes hold up to 464 kilometres of channel in a single square kilometre. These are badlands: dry terrain where soft sedimentary rocks and clay-rich soils are eroded into steep, bare ground with almost no loose cover. They form where an impermeable but easily eroded surface, sparse plants and rare heavy rains meet. Runoff cannot soak into the clay, so it cuts dense webs of gullies. Badlands National Park erodes at roughly 25 millimetres a year, helped by erodible bentonite clay. Too much grazing or poor farming can create them too, as at Ontario's Cheltenham Badlands.

soil-water-273.title: Clocking how fast a landscape wears down
soil-water-273.text: A landscape's lowering is slow enough to be quoted in centimetres per 1000 years. The commonest method starts at a river gauging station. Its suspended, bed and dissolved loads are converted to a volume and divided by the watershed area upstream. Stream load can vary fivefold between successive years, and the method assumes uniform erosion. Cosmogenic isotopes, mostly 10Be and 26Al, offer a check: their concentration in sediment leaving a basin falls as erosion speeds up. The stream power law, E = KA^m S^n, ties erosion rate to erodibility, drainage area and channel gradient.

soil-water-283.title: The Shields parameter: when a grain starts to move
soil-water-283.text: Albert F. Shields gave engineers a single number for the moment a sediment bed starts to move. The Shields parameter is a dimensionless shear stress, θ = τ / ((ρs − ρ) g D). Here τ is the shear stress, ρs and ρ the densities of sediment and fluid, and D the grain diameter. In effect it compares the fluid's push on a particle with the particle's weight. Motion starts at the critical Shields number. Shear stress belongs to the current, critical shear stress to the sediment. The Shields diagram is considered more precise than {{ref:soil-water-250}} for estimating suspended load.

soil-water-271.title: Corrasion, rock scoured by what water carries
soil-water-271.text: Running water alone barely scratches rock; the grit it carries does the cutting. Corrasion is mechanical erosion of the land by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement. On a river or sea bed, moving particles strike and grind the rock, and the wear they leave is called abrasion. Corrosion is different: the chemical, dissolving action of water on soluble rock. Lateral corrasion widens a river by cutting sideways, while vertical corrasion deepens its valley.

soil-water-279.title: Causes and triggers: why slopes fail when they do
soil-water-279.text: A landslide can have many causes but only one trigger. Causes are the conditions that make a slope vulnerable; the trigger is the single event that finally sets it moving. The trigger is easy to spot afterward but hard to predict. Causes may be geological, such as weathered or jointed material, or morphological, such as slope angle, erosion and vegetation change. Others are physical or human, such as forest clearing, excavation and mining. Following Terzaghi, internal causes weaken a material's resistance to shear stress, while external causes raise the stress. Earthquakes trigger slides by shaking and by raising pore water pressure, and the shaking is strongest at slope crests.

soil-water-280.title: Rain, the trigger behind most landslides
soil-water-280.text: Of 210 damaging landslides worldwide in the year to September 2003, over 90% followed heavy rain. Rain raises {{ref:soil-phys-098}}, which buoys slope material and weakens its grip, while groundwater flow can push downslope. Water also turns old debris into debris flows, removes suction in silty soils, undercuts a slope's toe and opens soil pipes. In 1980 Caine proposed a worldwide threshold, I = 14.82 D^-0.39, with rain intensity in mm per hour and duration in hours. It applies from 10 minutes to 10 days.

soil-water-292.title: Sediment yield, a river's report on its watershed
soil-water-292.text: A river's muddy load is a running report on the land upstream. Sediment yield is the amount of sediment per unit area of a watershed that a river removes over a period of time. It shows ecologists the health of river ecosystems, the pace of erosion and the effects of people. When late 19th-century Polish farmers switched from grains to potatoes, yields rose so much that meandering rivers became braided. Dams, reservoirs and detention basins upstream reduce it. Watershed runs of {{ref:soil-water-111}} predict it for whole catchments.

soil-water-289.title: Soil piping, erosion that tunnels underground
soil-water-289.text: Some erosion happens out of sight. Soil piping is the gradual internal erosion of soil by seeping water, which carves underground pipes that drain water downstream. Badlands sometimes hold whole systems of pipes, joints and caverns. Concentrated seepage out of a stream bank hollows out a pipe, and collapsing pipes in dispersive soils help form gullies. During rain, piping can loosen earth on slopes. In an earthen dam, a small leak can grow into a channel that leads to failure.

soil-water-290.title: Filter strips, grass that catches runoff
soil-water-290.text: A band of grass at a field's edge can catch what rain washes off the field. Such a band, described in {{ref:soil-agri-160}}, is a strip of grass or other permanent plants that shields streamside land from runoff carrying sediment, pest-killing chemicals, pathogens and nutrients. Strips work best when other conservation practices steer water toward them. Once mainly agricultural, they are now common in towns. They are not the same as a {{ref:soil-water-109}}. The mapping tool AgBufferBuilder designs them by mapping where uneven runoff flows.

soil-water-295.title: Geomorphology, the science of how landforms evolve
soil-water-295.text: Every hill, valley and beach is the running total of what has been added and what has been taken away. Geomorphology studies the origin and evolution of landforms shaped by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near Earth's surface. Water, wind, ice, fire and life all act on the land, along with the chemical reactions that form soils. Landforms change through the balance of additive processes, uplift and deposition, against subtractive ones, subsidence and erosion. The work falls into three stages: producing regolith by weathering and erosion, transporting it and depositing it. Soil scientists usually study weathering, but geomorphologists need it because it supplies the material that moves. Soil, regolith and rock travel downslope by creep, slides, flows, topples and falls, while burrowing animals and falling trees set some hillslope rates. Soil geomorphologists read soil profiles and chemistry to learn a landscape's history. The field pays its way in landslide prediction, river control, stream restoration and coastal protection.

soil-water-293.title: Alluvial fans, cones of sediment at canyon mouths
soil-water-293.text: Los Angeles and Salt Lake City sit on alluvial fans. An alluvial fan is, a cone-shaped spread of sediment that fans out from a concentrated source, such as a narrow canyon opening onto a plain. Flow leaving a confined channel spreads out and drops its load. They range from less than 1 square kilometre to almost 20,000, with slopes of 1.5 to 25 degrees that are steepest near the apex, the fan's tip. Their sediments are coarse and poorly sorted, coarsest at the apex and finer toward the edge. Debris flows, stream flow or hyperconcentrated flows carrying 20% to 45% sediment feed them. Blocked channels periodically jump to new courses, so only part of a fan is active. Bypassed lobes undergo soil formation or erosion, and over 1,000 to 10,000 years may gain desert varnish or a soil profile from windblown dust. Neighboring fans can merge into a continuous apron called a bajada. Their coarse beds are major aquifers in many regions. A channel shift on the Kosi River fan caused catastrophic flooding in 2008.

soil-water-294.title: Slope aspect: which way a hillside faces
soil-water-294.text: Two sides of the same hill can grow different soils. Slope aspect, also called exposure, is the compass direction a land surface faces. With slope grade, it describes the surface gradient, and its effects on a slope's physical and living features are called the slope effect. In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes are often shaded. South-facing slopes receive more solar radiation per unit area, so they are generally warmer and drier, with more evapotranspiration. Soil follows. A steep equator-facing slope holds about as much organic matter as level ground lower down, while a pole-facing slope resembles level soils higher up. Outside the tropics, slopes facing the early-afternoon sun usually have the least soil moisture and organic matter in a locale. Wind matters too. Windward soils tend to be shallower with more developed subsoils, while leeward soils collect more windblown particles. Aspect is one way topography shapes soil, as {{ref:soil-form-045}} describes.

soil-form-128.title: How hillslopes change shape over time
soil-form-128.text: For much of the 20th century, the shape of a slope was the central question of geomorphology. Hillslope evolution is the change over time in the erosion rates, erosion styles and shape of hill and mountain slopes. Three models competed until the 1950s. In William Morris Davis's slope decline, slope angles fall gradually as stream incision slows and slopes fill with fine regolith from weathering. In Walther Penck's slope replacement, tied to slowing denudation, the lowest part of the slope flattens first and the flattening spreads upward and backward. Flattening always runs from the bottom up. The third model, parallel slope retreat, needs constant rock strength and steady removal of debris such as talus from the slope's base. That is rare, except where a hard cap rock such as basalt overlies softer rock. Lester King championed parallel scarp retreat as globally dominant and saw slope decline as a special case in very weak rocks. He tied smooth convex-concave slopes to grass carpets that slowed surface wash, so creep did relatively more of the work. Colin Crick coined the term unequal activity: slopes in one area do not all develop at once, and with little river erosion they may be effectively stagnant. Modern work holds that slopes evolve in far more complex ways than any of the classical models imply.

soil-water-297.title: Hydrosere: how a pond becomes a wood
soil-water-297.text: Given centuries or millennia, a pond can turn into woodland. That plant succession, from open fresh water to land, is called a hydrosere. At first, sand and clay washed in from the catchment drive the change. Dead plankton decay into humus, which mixes with inwashed silt and clay into soil, and the pond grows shallower. Reed rhizomes knit the mud, and their tough litter builds reed peat. Sedge peat eventually rises above the water, so the soil is no longer waterlogged. Researchers still debate whether dry woodland is always the final stage or whether a bog can be a stable end point.

soil-water-296.title: Pedotope: all the soils of a place together
soil-water-296.text: A pedotope is the total soil part of the non-living matrix of an ecotope, the living and non-living whole of one location. It is not one kind of soil, nor even the dominant kind. It is all the soils of every variety present at that location, taken together. It is a term from {{ref:soil-found-095}}, the science of soils in their natural setting.

soil-form-129.title: Modeling the soil that slides down a slope
soil-form-129.text: W.E.H. Culling borrowed Fourier's heat equation to describe soil creeping downhill. Hillslope sediment flux models describe how much sediment moves on a slope at a given time, rather than how its shape changes. Culling wrote the flux as q = −K∇z, with K a rate constant and ∇z the slope gradient. This linear law works on gentle slopes but fails on steep ones. A nonlinear version adds a critical gradient, Sc. As the gradient nears it, erosion soars, perhaps representing landslides. Steep slope angles barely change even when erosion rises greatly, so steep topography cannot reveal erosion rates.

soil-form-130.title: Rounded soil-covered hills and the balance they hold
soil-form-130.text: Smooth, rounded hills draped in soil were long read as landscapes in balance. The idea goes back to William Morris Davis in 1892 and Grove Karl Gilbert in 1909. Such convex hills were taken to reflect a steady state between soil production and erosion. Yet soil depth on them can vary considerably, because bedrock weathers into soil at random. Formation rates may differ greatly even across a landscape in equilibrium. Models suggest broad, gentle hilltops in periglacial settings take millions of years to form. Tors often crown such hills, hinting that the original landscape was steeper.

soil-water-079.title: The water cycle, a sun-driven loop through the soil
soil-water-079.text: Each year about 505,000 cubic kilometers of water fall from the sky, and 398,000 of them land on the oceans. The rest meets the ground. The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between reservoirs on, above and below the Earth's surface, changing form as it goes. Its fluxes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, sublimation, infiltration, and flow over and beneath the surface. Energy from the sun powers every one of them. Rain reaching land has two paths. It flows over the ground as {{ref:soil-water-019}}, or it soaks in by {{ref:soil-water-180}} and becomes soil moisture or groundwater. Shallow water may seep back to streams or be drawn up and transpired by plants. Deeper water recharges aquifers, where it can stay for thousands of years. Evapotranspiration is the sum of water transpired by plants and water evaporated from the soil. Not all soil water is alike. A global study of stable water isotopes found that some soil moisture is less available for recharging groundwater or feeding plants. Moving water also remakes the land through weathering, erosion and deposition. Runoff carries almost all the eroded sediment and phosphorus that travel from land to water bodies.

soil-water-019.title: Surface runoff: rain that cannot soak in
soil-water-019.text: A roof sheds every drop that hits it, and so does a parking lot. Surface runoff is the unconfined flow of water over the ground, as opposed to flow in stream channels. It is also called overland flow. It forms when rain, stormwater or meltwater cannot soak in fast enough. Either the soil is saturated, or rain arrives faster than the soil can absorb it. Both are limits on {{ref:soil-water-180}}. Impervious areas such as roofs and pavement are a common cause, since water cannot enter the ground there at all. Soil storage absorbs light showers. On ancient Australian and southern African soils, dense networks of proteoid roots can prevent runoff even in heavy rain. Runoff is a major part of {{ref:soil-water-079}} and the main agent that wears soil away by water. It carries soil particles about 0.001 to 1.0 mm across. The larger ones settle quickly, while the small ones stay suspended over long distances. The land whose runoff drains to a common point is a drainage basin. Runoff also picks up petroleum, pesticides and fertilizers, making it a nonpoint source of pollution, one with no single outlet. Farm runoff drives {{ref:soil-env-019}} downstream, along with {{ref:soil-env-020}}. In towns it is a main cause of urban flooding, from streets under water to damp and mold in basements.

soil-water-081.title: Stormwater and the dirty first flush
soil-water-081.text: In a forest, much of a storm soaks into the soil. In a city, much of it races to the nearest stream. Stormwater is water from precipitation, including heavy rain and meltwater from hail and snow. It may infiltrate and become groundwater, pond in hollows, evaporate or run off as {{ref:soil-water-019}}. Forest plants help the soil absorb it: they improve infiltration, intercept rain and take up water through their roots. Impervious surfaces and compacted soil do the opposite. More water runs off, streams swell, and erosion and flooding follow. Because storms flush the water away, little is left to recharge groundwater or feed streams in dry weather. Most runoff reaches streams untreated, carrying trash, sediment, nutrients, bacteria, pesticides, metals and petroleum byproducts. The first flush of a storm is usually the most concentrated. Phosphorus from fertilizers, or bound to sediment from building sites and farms, feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes. Treatment facilities usually rely on Stokes' law to settle particles larger than 40 microns, and they hold water back against downstream flooding.

soil-water-084.title: Subsidence: when the ground itself sinks
soil-water-084.text: In many places, pumping water or oil out of the ground has lowered the surface by as much as 9 meters. Subsidence is the downward movement of the Earth's surface, caused by natural processes or by human activity. It involves little or no sideways motion, which sets it apart from slope movements. Its causes are varied. Groundwater can dissolve carbonate rock. Sediments compact gradually, much as in {{ref:soil-phys-110}}. Mines hollow out the ground, wells draw groundwater or petroleum from it, and tectonic forces warp the crust. The pumping alone has cost hundreds of millions of US dollars. In karst, ground of soluble rock hollowed out by caves, a weakened cave roof can collapse and drop rock and earth into the void. The sinkholes left behind may be many hundreds of meters deep. Even buildings play a part. The weight of high towers can press down the soil beneath them, a problem already felt in New York City, the San Francisco Bay Area and Lagos. Lowered ground raises flood risk, especially on river flood plains and deltas. Where it settles unevenly, buildings tilt or crack.

soil-water-086.title: Runoff, from hillslope to river channel
soil-water-086.text: Water moving across the land changes its name along the way. Runoff is the flow of water across the land, a major part of the water cycle. Before it reaches a watercourse it is surface runoff, or overland flow; once inside one it is streamflow, or channel runoff. Channel flow is fed by hillslope runoff, groundwater flowing out of the ground and discharges from pipes. Hydrologists measure it with stream gauges or estimate it with the Manning equation. A record of flow over time is a hydrograph. When the volume of water exceeds what a channel can hold, the result is a flood.

soil-water-089.title: Straw, the half of the harvest left behind
soil-water-089.text: About half the weight of a cereal crop is not grain at all. Straw is the dry stalks of cereals such as barley, oats, rice, rye and wheat, left after the grain and chaff are removed. It has a second life protecting soil. It makes an excellent mulch, covers the ground after wildfires and is built into small dams across streams. Straw bales are sometimes set out to control sediment on construction sites, but they often protect water quality poorly and need much upkeep. The US EPA prefers {{ref:soil-water-093}}, {{ref:soil-water-098}} or {{ref:soil-water-254}}. Mixed with clay-rich subsoil and water, straw also binds cob and adobe, two earth building materials.

soil-water-090.title: Retention basins, ponds that hold back the storm
soil-water-090.text: City pavement rushes rain into the drains; a retention basin slows it down. It is an artificial pond with a permanent pool of water and plants around its edge, built to manage {{ref:soil-water-081}}. The pond contains the surge and releases it slowly, reducing flooding downstream. It also traps suspended sediment, often abundant in runoff from construction and road sanding, while its plants take up dissolved nutrients. It can stand in for the absorption of a forest lost to development. A detention basin, or dry pond, holds water only for a while. An infiltration basin sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

soil-water-091.title: Land development and the soil it seals away
soil-water-091.text: Soil under a road or a building is, in effect, used up. Land development is the alteration of a landscape, such as turning natural land over to farming or housing, or dividing it into building lots. Construction brings roads, scraped topsoil, compaction, chemical change from stabilizing the soil, impervious surfaces and polluted runoff. It seals the soil off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, leaving it infertile. New farmland usually comes from forest, savanna or grassland cleared by assarting, the grubbing up of woodland, or by slash-and-burn. Reclaiming wasteland or sealed ground is rarer, for lack of fertile soil. Profitable improvement can still degrade land, through salt buildup from saline irrigation water or erosion after drainage.

soil-water-092.title: Bioswales, planted channels that clean runoff
soil-water-092.text: A bioswale is a channel that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution from it. It is planted, mulched or xeriscaped, meaning landscaped with dry-climate plants, and has gently sloping sides of less than 6%. It is built on soil with no more than 5% clay. The design keeps water in the swale as long as is safe. Plants catch pollutants and let them settle, and they then decompose or are broken down by soil bacteria. A bioswale slows runoff, recharges groundwater and reduces flooding and erosion. It suits places with much impervious surface that must handle a storm's first flush. In {{ref:soil-env-218}}, swales harvest water.

soil-water-020.title: Horton overland flow: rain faster than the ground can drink
soil-water-020.text: When rain arrives faster than the ground can take it in, the surplus runs off. Horton overland flow is water flowing across the land surface when rainfall exceeds both the soil's capacity to absorb it ({{ref:soil-water-180}}) and its depression storage capacity. It is named for Robert E. Horton, the engineer who first studied it in detail, and is also called Hortonian or unsaturated overland flow. The flow is shallow, sheetlike and fast, so it can erode soil extensively, especially on steep terrain and loose, flat farmland. Impermeable paved surfaces reach it rapidly, and it is common on construction sites and unpaved roads where vegetation has been stripped.

soil-water-024.title: Four ways to limit the damage runoff does
soil-water-024.text: Runoff mitigation covers the measures that limit the harm done by surface runoff. They fall into four groups. Land-use codes encourage narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, so that as much water as possible soaks into town ground. Controls on erosion and sediment have been required of builders by some governments since the 1960s, among them straw bales, {{ref:soil-water-093}} and limits on bare graded ground. Flood control uses holding ponds, or detention basins, to buffer peak flows, and energy dissipators to slow water in channels. Chemical controls include double containment of underground tanks, fewer approved pesticides and stricter rules for fertilizers and weedkillers.

soil-water-021.title: When the soil is already full: Dunne runoff
soil-water-021.text: Soil that is already soaked cannot take in more rain. Saturation-excess overland flow is runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on saturated soil whose surface hollows are full. It is also called saturated overland flow or Dunne runoff. Its timing depends on the {{ref:soil-water-155}} left from earlier rain, known as antecedent soil moisture. The wetter the soil starts, the sooner runoff begins. Because saturated soil absorbs less rain, the same volume of rainfall produces more runoff and more erosion.

soil-water-022.title: Throughflow, water that slips back out of the hillside
soil-water-022.text: Not all runoff travels on the surface. Subsurface return flow, also called throughflow, is water that soaks into a hillside upslope, moves sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel. Along the way the flow shrinks. Some water returns to the air by evapotranspiration, some is held in small surface hollows and some infiltrates. Whatever remains ends up in a river, lake, estuary or ocean.

soil-water-023.title: Urban runoff, from rooftops to storm drains
soil-water-023.text: In a city, rain lands mostly on surfaces that shed it. Urban runoff is surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing, created by urbanization. Roads, parking lots, sidewalks and roofs send polluted stormwater to storm drains instead of letting it percolate through soil. Less water reaches the ground below, so the water table falls and droughts grow worse. More water stays on the surface, so flooding grows worse too. Most municipal storm sewers discharge the water untreated into streams, rivers and bays. There, erosion and siltation can become major problems.

soil-water-080.title: How clearing and building rewire the local water cycle
soil-water-080.text: Change the land cover and the water moves differently. Land use and the water cycle names the local and regional changes to the water cycle that follow changes in land use and land cover. Urbanization, farm expansion and deforestation can increase {{ref:soil-phys-082}} and impervious cover. Both lower the soil's infiltration capacity and raise surface runoff. Locally, clearing forest reduces soil moisture, evaporation, rainfall and snowfall. City pipes cut both ways. Stormwater drains lower runoff rates and raise groundwater recharge, while leaking sewers add recharge but can contaminate groundwater.

soil-water-082.title: Managing stormwater for quantity and quality
soil-water-082.text: A street sweeper and a planted swale belong to the same toolkit. Stormwater management is the control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater. Its best management practices range from engineered devices, such as {{ref:soil-water-090}}, to routine chores such as street sweeping. Its technical aims include controlling flooding and erosion. Engineers build retention basins, filter vaults and vortex separators that remove coarse solids. Nature-based options, such as ponds, swales and {{ref:soil-water-260}}, work alongside pipes and concrete channels and can also give wildlife habitat. Passive treatment lets gravity carry water through ditches and pipes, with gel flocculants, jute fiber filters and silt retention mats to settle the sediment.

soil-water-083.title: How city stormwater opens sinkholes in karst
soil-water-083.text: Undisturbed karst keeps a quiet balance with the rain. Soil and rock fragments choke the openings in the rock and limit their growth, and the drainage keeps pace with most storms. Cities upset that balance. Urban karst areas lack surface streams, so extra runoff from roofs and streets moves down through the ground. Once the flow can carry soil and rock, the openings grow fast. The result is a stormwater sinkhole, a collapse caused when urban stormwater drains through karst and carries soil and rock fragments away, a sudden form of {{ref:soil-water-084}}. Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses. Planners are advised to avoid karst for new development.

soil-water-087.title: Turning a rainstorm into a predicted flood curve
soil-water-087.text: Hydrologists need to know how much water a storm will send downstream, and when. A rainfall-runoff model describes how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into {{ref:soil-water-086}}. It takes a rainfall event, entered as a hyetograph, a record of rainfall over time, and turns it into a surface runoff hydrograph. Every such model must be calibrated before use. The linear reservoir model is well known but of limited use. A non-linear reservoir applies more widely, but only where rain falls roughly evenly over the catchment. Large study areas are split into sub-catchments, whose hydrographs are combined by flood routing.

soil-water-085.title: Ground that sinks and rises with the seasons
soil-water-085.text: A felled tree can make the ground rise for up to 25 years. Seasonal subsidence and heave is the sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet. Clay's very small particles make such soils sensitive to changes in moisture, the behavior described in {{ref:soil-phys-028}}. Foundations above the depth reached by seasonal drying move with the soil, which can crack buildings with tapering cracks. Growing trees dry the soil cumulatively. When a tree declines or is felled, that deficit reverses, and the soil heaves, rising and spreading.

soil-water-107.title: Models that follow water and everything it carries
soil-water-107.text: Hydrological transport models came into use in the 1960s and 1970s, when environmental laws demanded water-quality forecasts and computing power became widely available. Such a model simulates the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater or drainage fronts and calculates water quality. Physically based versions represent surface runoff, subsurface flow, evapotranspiration and channel flow. Stochastic versions link inputs such as rainfall to outputs such as runoff statistically. Their surface runoff element lets them assess sediment, fertilizer, pesticides and other chemical contaminants. The groundwork came from Robert E. Horton's work on surface runoff, joined to quantitative treatment of erosion.

soil-water-073.title: The ion cloud that decides whether clay holds together
soil-water-073.text: Salt can decide whether a clay stands firm. Clay platelets carry permanent and pH-dependent negative charges, as {{ref:soil-chem-079}} describes, balanced by cations such as Na+ on their surfaces, in interlayers or in the pore water. The electrical double layer is that cloud of balancing cations around each platelet, and its thickness depends on the water's salinity. In salty water the layer is compressed, so the platelets flocculate into stable aggregates. When rain leaches salt out of uplifted marine clay, the layer expands. Stronger repulsion then disperses the platelets, called peptization, and the clay is destabilized. Adding salt back compresses the layer again, and {{ref:soil-water-071}} rapidly regains its strength.

soil-water-255.title: Four letters that rank soils by runoff
soil-water-255.text: The NRCS sorts soils into four hydrologic soil groups, A to D, by how readily they take in water. The group is used to choose a {{ref:soil-water-088}}. Group A, mostly deep, well-drained sands and gravels, has a final infiltration rate above 7.6 mm (0.30 in) per hour and low runoff potential. Group B takes in 3.8 to 7.6 mm per hour. Group C, often with an impeding layer or fine texture, manages 1.3 to 3.8 mm. Group D has high runoff potential. It covers swelling clays, soils with a permanent high water table or a claypan near the surface, and shallow soils over impervious material. The group is picked from measured infiltration rates, a survey such as the NRCS online one described in {{ref:soil-agri-170}}, or a soil professional's judgment.

soil-water-088.title: The curve number, one figure for a storm's runoff
soil-water-088.text: A single number between 30 and 100 can estimate how much of a storm will run off the land. That number is the runoff curve number, CN, an empirical value used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess. The US Department of Agriculture developed it, through the agency now called the {{ref:soil-hist-050}}, from runoff measured on small catchments and hillslope plots. A curve number depends on the area's {{ref:soil-water-255}}, land use, treatment and hydrologic condition. Lower numbers mean more permeable soil and low runoff potential; higher numbers mean more runoff. No runoff starts until the initial abstraction, such as infiltration and interception, is met. That threshold was long taken as 0.2 S, but 0.05 S may suit urban watersheds better. Curve numbers are adjusted for antecedent moisture: dry (AMC I), average (AMC II) and moist (AMC III). The method works storm by storm and should not be applied to a single annual rainfall total. Even so, it is widely used as an efficient way to estimate approximate direct runoff.

soil-water-001.title: Soil erosion and the 75 billion tons lost each year
soil-water-001.text: About 75 billion tons of soil are eroded from the land each year. Soil erosion is the wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of {{ref:soil-env-058}}. It is driven by erosive agents: water, ice, snow, wind, plants such as uprooted trees, and animals, including humans. Each agent names a type. There is erosion by water, by ice (glacial), by snow and by wind (aeolian), erosion by animals (zoogenic), and human-caused erosion such as {{ref:soil-water-038}}. Erosion can go on slowly and almost unnoticed, or fast enough to cause a serious loss of topsoil. People have sped it up. Human activities have raised the rate worldwide to about 28 times the natural rate, though other estimates in the sources run from 10 to 40 times. On site, accelerated erosion lowers farm productivity. By stripping the nutrient-rich upper layers it can collapse whole ecosystems, sometimes ending in {{ref:soil-env-072}}. Off site, it silts waterways, feeds {{ref:soil-env-020}} of lakes and rivers, and damages roads and houses with sediment. Erosion by water and wind together accounts for about 84% of the world's degraded land. One global model puts the yearly loss to water alone at almost 36 billion tons.

soil-water-003.title: How rain and runoff carry soil away
soil-water-003.text: Almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year, according to a global model. Water erosion is the removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces, a form of {{ref:soil-water-001}}. It begins with the rain itself. Raindrops bombard aggregates and detach small particles that are easily transported, by splash or by water running downhill, to a low area where they are deposited. Runoff, the flow described in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate (see {{ref:soil-water-180}}). Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment. Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion. Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills. If runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies, a gully being a rill too deep for tillage equipment to smooth. Sheet and rill erosion cause most soil erosion. The damage is not evenly spread, either. Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.

soil-water-011.title: Rainfall erosivity, the striking power of rain
soil-water-011.text: Not all rain is equally destructive. Rainfall erosivity is the power of rainfall to cause erosion, set mainly by how much rain falls and how intensely. It is the main climatic control on water erosion, especially where the soil surface lacks plant cover. Larger, faster raindrops carry more kinetic energy and throw soil particles further than small, slow ones. In places such as the Midwestern United States and the Amazon, intensity matters most. Western Europe is different. There, erosion follows gentle, low-intensity stratiform rain, the steady rain of layered clouds, falling on soil that is already saturated. Total rainfall counts for more than intensity. Erosivity is the R factor of the {{ref:soil-water-041}}. The Global Rainfall Erosivity Database, GloREDa, covers 3,625 stations in 63 countries and was used to map erosivity worldwide at about 1 km resolution.

soil-water-010.title: Wind erosion and the bouncing grain
soil-water-010.text: In a drought year on the Great Plains, wind erosion losses can be up to 6100 times greater than in a wet year. Wind erosion is erosion by wind, and it works in two ways. {{ref:soil-water-030}} lifts and carries away loose particles. Abrasion wears down surfaces with windborne grains. It is a major force shaping landscapes, especially in arid and semi-arid regions. That lifting moves particles in three ways. Surface creep rolls or slides them. {{ref:soil-water-251}} sends them in short, bouncing hops. Suspension lifts fine particles and carries them far. The hopping does most of the work, 50 to 70%, followed by suspension at 30 to 40% and surface creep at 5 to 25%. Silty soils such as loess suffer most, because silt particles detach and travel easily. Wind erosion needs strong winds and is worst in drought. It is worsened by {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, which dries and breaks up the soil, and clearing trees from fields gives the wind long, open runs. Where deforestation, urbanization and farming have raised it above natural rates, it drives the decline of land, the spread of desert, harmful airborne dust and crop damage. Plants shelter the soil. Rows of trees and shrubs along field edges significantly reduce wind erosion, as {{ref:soil-agri-061}} explains.

soil-water-050.title: Erosion control, from terraces to riprap
soil-water-050.text: One of the best defenses against erosion is thousands of years old: {{ref:soil-agri-073}}, practiced around the world and still extremely effective. Erosion control is the practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction. Good controls manage surface runoff and help prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and property damage. Many are physical barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water. On farms, the methods include {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}}, {{ref:soil-agri-123}} and {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, along with hydroseeding, streamside buffers, alternating crop strips and rows of sheltering trees. Crop leftovers on the surface soften raindrop impact, and the fibrous roots of forage crops anchor the topsoil. Mixing crops with trees works well, especially in rainy tropical climates and on severely degraded land. On construction sites, erosion controls are paired with controls on sediment such as {{ref:soil-water-099}} and {{ref:soil-water-093}}. In towns, they are part of stormwater programs. Bank erosion is natural, but where people want to hold a river in place, they line its banks with riprap or gabions.

soil-water-012.title: Why plant cover is the best shield against erosion
soil-water-012.text: Raindrops regain terminal velocity within about 8 meters, so drops falling from a tall canopy can still strike the ground at full speed. The leaves alone do not save a forest's soil. The forest floor does. Its litter and humus absorb the impact of the drops and let water percolate slowly. More than the canopy, the floor prevents surface erosion. Vegetation cover and erosion names this protection that living plants and their litter give the soil against wind and water. Plants make the soil more permeable to rain, which reduces runoff, and they shelter it from the wind. Their roots bind the soil and interweave into a solid mass that resists both water and wind erosion. Remove the vegetation and surface erosion speeds up. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent both wind and water erosion.

soil-water-014.title: How farming speeds erosion beyond repair
soil-water-014.text: Over a third of the U.S. Corn Belt has lost its topsoil entirely. Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far beyond what soil formation can replace. Agriculture and soil erosion names this speeding up. The culprits are practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil. {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, which breaks soil into finer particles, is a primary cause. Mechanized deep plowing makes far more soil available for water to carry off. Growing one crop year after year, farming steep slopes, row crops and irrigation that runs water over the surface all add to the loss. So do pesticides and fertilizers that kill soil-binding organisms. Heavy grazing strips plant cover and severely compacts the soil. At farm sites in the Appalachian Mountains, intensive practices have driven erosion up to 100 times the natural regional rate. Potatoes carry a higher erosion risk than cereals or oilseed crops. Erosion is also selective by size: the finer eroded fraction loses more total phosphorus than the soil as a whole. Switching U.S. fields to {{ref:soil-agri-117}} would cut their erosion by more than 70 percent.

soil-water-035.title: Dust, the soil that travels on the wind
soil-water-035.text: Each year about 132 million tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic, reaching the Caribbean and the Amazon basin. Dust is fine particles of solid matter. On Earth it is mostly airborne particles from soil lifted by wind, from volcanic eruptions and from pollution. Dust that stays suspended in the atmosphere for a long time counts as an aerosol. Windborne dust comes mainly from grains bouncing along the ground in dry regions, as {{ref:soil-water-010}} describes. Strong winds there strip mostly silt-sized material up to 1/16 mm across. Grazing, plowing, vehicles and other human activity loosen these source areas further. Dust-producing surfaces cover about one-third of the global land area, roughly 13 billion hectares. The dust can affect temperatures and rainfall, and dust from erosion suppresses rain. Since the 1970s, dust events have been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida. Soil dust is a major source of air pollution and often carries toxic chemicals such as pesticides or petroleum fuels. It poses a health risk to children, older people and people with respiratory diseases.

soil-water-045.title: Erodibility, or why some soils give way more easily
soil-water-045.text: Give two soils the same storm and one may lose far more than the other. Erodibility is the inherent lack of resistance of a soil or rock to erosion. A highly erodible material loses more for the same amount of work done by erosive processes. For soil, it is a lumped value for how a profile responds each year to detachment and transport by raindrops and surface flow. In the {{ref:soil-water-041}} it is the K factor, estimated from silt and very fine sand content, clay content, organic matter, structure and permeability. Clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones because clay binds particles together. Organic matter helps by coagulating colloids into a stronger, more stable structure. Long cultivation depletes it and raises erodibility. Wet or compacted soils absorb less rain, so more water runs off and erodes. Stone cover protects against erosion, which matters greatly in Mediterranean countries. For channels and dams, erodibility can be measured with a {{ref:soil-water-094}} or a {{ref:soil-water-095}}.

soil-water-017.title: Warmer climate, heavier rain, faster soil loss
soil-water-017.text: Warmer temperatures are expected to intensify the water cycle, bringing more extreme rainfall and so more erosion unless measures are taken. Climate change and soil erosion names this expected rise. Studies by Pruski and Nearing suggest about a 1.7% change in soil erosion for each 1% change in total precipitation. Early 21st-century studies predicted rainfall erosivity rising by 17% in the United States, 18% in Europe and 30 to 66% globally. Other routes run through shifts in plant canopy and litter, loss of soil organic matter, winter snow turning to erosive rain, and thawing permafrost.

soil-water-015.title: What happens to forest soil when the trees go
soil-water-015.text: Deforestation and soil erosion names the rise in erosion that follows removal of forest cover and its protective floor. Clearing strips away litter and humus, removes the binding roots, and lets logging machinery compact the soil. After fire or logging, erosion stays low as long as the forest floor remains intact. Severe fires followed by heavy rain cause much more. Slash-and-burn clearing of tropical forest is one of the largest contributors to erosive soil loss worldwide. In Brazilian studies, runoff and soil loss fell to forest-like levels after 4 to 5 years of regrowth. Fifteen years of rest from farming restored the original soil. Researchers still debate which does more lasting harm to tropical soils: slash-and-burn with forest regrowth, or permanent pasture and cash crops after logging.

soil-water-013.title: Steeper and longer slopes, faster soil loss
soil-water-013.text: The shape of the land sets the speed of the water. Slope and erosion names the influence of a slope's steepness and length on how fast runoff flows and how much soil it erodes. That speed sets how erosive the runoff is. Longer, steeper slopes, especially poorly vegetated ones, erode much faster in heavy rain than short, gentle ones. Steep terrain is also more prone to mudslides and other gravity-driven erosion, including {{ref:soil-water-057}}. The {{ref:soil-water-041}} represents slope length and steepness with its L and S factors.

soil-water-004.title: Splash erosion, the first blow of the raindrop
soil-water-004.text: A single raindrop can fling soil particles up to 1.5 meters. Splash erosion is the erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose. Each drop makes a small crater and throws soil out of it. The loosened particles then move off with surface runoff. On level ground without wind, they can travel up to 0.6 meters vertically and 1.5 meters horizontally. Larger, faster drops carry more kinetic energy and throw particles further. Plant cover and crop leftovers soften the impact. Splash is usually seen as the first and least severe stage of water erosion, followed by {{ref:soil-water-005}}, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}.

soil-water-016.title: Building cities, speeding erosion
soil-water-016.text: A construction site strips vegetation, alters the drainage and compacts the soil. Asphalt and concrete then increase both surface runoff and surface wind speeds. Urbanization and erosion names this increase in erosion and polluted runoff caused by construction, roads and paved urban land. Sediment in runoff from urban areas, especially roads, is often heavily contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals. The extra runoff changes how much water flows through nearby watersheds and how fast. It fills them with polluted sediment and greatly increases erosion of their banks.

soil-water-025.title: Rills, the first scratches of an erosion problem
soil-water-025.text: The first sign that a field is losing soil is often a set of tiny channels. Rills are shallow channels, no more than a few centimeters deep, cut into soil by flowing surface water, and rill erosion is the erosion that happens in them. Smaller incised channels are microrills. Larger ones are the subject of {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Hillslope runoff cuts rills into unprotected soil, as on farmland left bare, after deforestation or during construction. Rills are easy to see when first cut, so they often give the first warning of an erosion problem. Tractors help start them. They compact the soil so that water runs over it, and their wheel tracks channel the water into rills. Flow in a rill is typically a few centimeters deep or less, so its hydraulics differ greatly from flow in streams and rivers. It is still strong. Rill flow may carry nearly ten times as much as the interrill areas between rills. In moderate rain it can move rock fragments up to 9 cm across. Without conservation measures, rills can grow into those larger channels or, in semi-arid regions, into the bare, carved ground of {{ref:soil-water-269}}. Under good management, contour tilling repairs them.

soil-water-027.title: Gullies, the scars a neglected rill can become
soil-water-027.text: On Madagascar's high central plateau, gully furrows commonly exceed 50 meters deep and 1 kilometer wide. Gully erosion cuts gullies: steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or on low ground that rivers flood. Most are meters to tens of meters deep and wide. Each has a distinct headscarp, the steep wall at its head, and lengthens by uphill cutting ({{ref:soil-water-278}}) at a knickpoint, a sudden step in its bed. Gullies carry water only intermittently, after intense or long rain or snowmelt. Many begin where a rill was neglected and kept growing. Hillslope cultivation, clearing, heavy grazing and tracks worn by livestock or vehicles start or speed up gullying. Inside a gully, flowing water cuts down and erodes the banks, walls collapse and groundwater seeps out. In dispersive soils, buried soil pipes collapse as well. Gullies cut farm productivity and supply sediment that chokes downstream waters. Losses are greatest in unstable, dispersive soils. They can supply 10 to 80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land, yet the {{ref:soil-water-041}} cannot simulate them.

soil-water-041.title: The Universal Soil Loss Equation, six factors multiplied
soil-water-041.text: Six factors, multiplied together, give a field's long-term soil loss. The Universal Soil Loss Equation, or USLE, is a widely used empirical model that estimates long-term average annual soil loss from water erosion. It multiplies rainfall erosivity (R), soil erodibility (K), slope length and steepness (L and S), cover and management (C) and support practices (P). It was built in the U.S. from erosion plot and {{ref:soil-water-256}} experiments, using data the USDA collected from the 1930s. Its standard unit plot has LS = 1, a 9% slope 22.1 m long, kept bare, tilled up and down the slope, with no conservation practice. K can be read from a nomograph using particle size, organic matter, structure and permeability, and LS from a slope chart. C and P must come from plot data. It is the most commonly used soil loss model and the main one used by U.S. agencies. It helped implement the multibillion-dollar U.S. conservation program. Though plot-based, it is often applied to watersheds, continents and the globe, and it cannot simulate gully erosion. Revised (RUSLE) and Modified (MUSLE) versions remain in use, and newer models such as G2 still build on it.

soil-water-043.title: Predicting erosion, and why the forecasts often miss
soil-water-043.text: Predicted and observed erosion rates often differ widely. Erosion prediction uses data and models to forecast where, and how fast, erosion may happen. There are dozens of models. Some treat long-term natural erosion as part of landscape evolution, while many quantify erosion sped up by people. Most predict average annual soil loss from a plot, field or catchment under different land management. Most consider only water erosion. Few predict wind erosion, and models of {{ref:soil-water-038}} or gully erosion are rare. Process-based models solve equations for detachment, transport and deposition. Empirical models relate soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors. No model is fully process-based yet. Research favors process-based models, but the empirical USLE remains the standard for conservation planning. Two widely used North American models are the revised version of the USLE, {{ref:soil-water-291}}, and the Water Erosion Prediction Project model, {{ref:soil-water-111}}. Unless calibrated locally, models remain better research tools than regulatory instruments. They are also non-linear, which makes it hard or impossible to scale predictions from small plots up to large areas.

soil-water-254.title: Geotextiles, fabrics that hold the soil in place
soil-water-254.text: In the 1950s, R.J. Barrett laid fabric behind seawalls and under erosion control blocks and riprap. A geotextile is a permeable fabric laid with soil to separate, filter, reinforce, protect or drain it. Geotextiles were first meant to replace granular soil filters. Most are polypropylene or polyester, either woven or felt-like nonwoven, and they belong to the wider family of geosynthetics. They go into {{ref:soil-water-093}} and bank protection. As matting, they steady flow in channels and swales and let plants grow on steep slopes. Geotextiles of coconut fiber, {{ref:soil-agri-139}}, are popular for erosion control and for steadying slopes. They last about 3 to 5 years and then break down into humus.

soil-water-105.title: Soil loss tolerance: how much erosion is too much
soil-water-105.text: How fast can a soil lose its top layer and still farm well forever? Soil loss tolerance, the T value, answers in tons per acre per year: the maximum average yearly loss that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely. T values range from 1 to 5. Devised by the US Soil Conservation Service, the idea rests on the minimum rate of loss that would deplete organic matter and harm crop productivity. It is calculated with the formula T=υQρC+R(1−C). In 1961-1962 US soil groups were given T values of 2 to 6, later adjusted to 1 to 5, and conservation management adopted it from the mid-1960s. In depth terms, a soil deeper than 5 feet has a T of 5 tons per acre per year (11 metric tons per hectare), about 0.03 inch of depth a year, or 1 inch in 33 years. T is lower for shallow soils: with rooting depth under 10 inches it equals 0.006 inch a year, or 1 inch in 167 years. By 2007, 99 million acres, 28% of US cropland, were eroding faster than T, down from 169 million acres, 40% of cropland, in 1982. The value's validity is questioned. Critics note that T values vary across space, may not hold where soluble carbonates abound, as in karst, and should be weighed against actual soil loss. {{ref:soil-water-001}} is the loss it measures.

soil-water-102.title: Riparian buffers, green strips that guard a stream
soil-water-102.text: A nine-year University of Georgia study found that streamside buffers removed at least 60% of the nitrogen and at least 65% of the phosphorus from fertilizer in runoff. A riparian buffer is a vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from neighboring land use. It intercepts sediment, nutrients, pesticides and other materials in surface runoff, and reduces pollutants in shallow subsurface flow. It also stabilizes the stream bank, so eroding banks take less farmland out of production and less silt reaches lakes and reservoirs downstream. A typical buffer is 15 meters (50 feet) wide on each side, in three zones. Native grasses first slow the runoff, shrubs come next, and fast-growing trees shade the water and hold the bank.

soil-water-095.title: The jet erosion test, scouring soil to measure it
soil-water-095.text: One way to measure a soil's toughness is to aim a jet of water at it and watch the hole grow. The jet erosion test, done in the field or the laboratory, works exactly this way. A turbulent jet strikes the soil at constant hydraulic head. Where its shear stress exceeds the soil's critical value, it scours a hole, whose depth is measured over time. Fitting the erosion rate gives the soil's erodibility and critical shear stress. Engineers use them to design vegetated channels, road embankments, dams, levees and spillways. Its index typically ranges from 0 to 0.03. The method is disputed. Critics question its underlying assumptions, and other erosion tests can give inconsistent erodibility values. As of 2017 no method for soil erodibility was universally accepted. Depending on the fitting method, erodibility for a given critical stress can vary up to 100 times.

soil-water-038.title: Tillage erosion, when the plow moves the hill
soil-water-038.text: The pale, eroded hilltops of many farm fields are often blamed on rain. They are actually caused by the plow. Tillage erosion is soil erosion in cultivated fields caused by the movement of soil during {{ref:soil-agri-095}}. Growing evidence shows that it is a major erosion process on farmland, surpassing water and wind erosion in many fields, especially on sloping and hilly land. It strips organic-rich topsoil from convex spots. Its rate depends on two things. The erosivity of the operation is set by the implement's design, speed and depth. The erodibility of the landscape is set by slope shape and soil properties. The erosion comes from changes, across a field, in translocation, the amount of soil each pass moves. Translocation grows with slope gradient and curvature. Soil is lost from hilltops and from the downslope edges of fields. It piles up in hollows and against field boundaries, building banks of soil. As topsoil thins, plowing mixes poorer subsoil into the plow layer and spreads it across the field, cutting crop productivity for a long time. Soil degraded this way likely becomes more erodible by water and wind. The remedies are lighter cultivation, with fewer, slower and shallower passes and smaller implements, along with contour working, plowing furrows upslope and moving soil back to eroded hilltops.

soil-water-036.title: Dust control, from water trucks to paved lots
soil-water-036.text: Among sites that break dust rules, new urban housing developments are the most frequent violators. Environmental agencies such as the US EPA require facilities that generate fugitive dust to minimize it. Dust control is the suppression of airborne solid particles smaller than 500 micrometers. Construction and demolition sites are sprayed with water, and dust is kept from being tracked onto nearby roads. Unpaved lots and dirt roads are paved or graveled, or stabilized with water, vegetable oil, calcium chloride or other suppressants. The payoff is fewer allergic reactions, cases of pneumonia and asthma attacks, along with better visibility and road safety.

soil-water-110.title: Revegetation, putting plants back on bare ground
soil-water-110.text: Land stripped by wildfire, mining or floods needs plants back before its soil washes away. Revegetation is the replanting and rebuilding of the soil of disturbed land. It may happen naturally, as plants colonize and succession unfolds, or people may carry it out to repair the damage. Preventing erosion is usually the main reason. Plants hold the soil, help it absorb water in heavy rain and sharply reduce turbidity, or cloudiness, in nearby waters. Early practice simply applied seed and fertilizer, usually grasses or clover, whose fibrous roots give short-term erosion control on slopes. Restoring mined land may need soil to be amended, replaced or created. Mycorrhizal fungi are important to success, since most woody plants need them.

soil-water-113.title: Bringing back the tallgrass prairie
soil-water-113.text: By 1849, settlers had plowed up so much tallgrass prairie that most of its grass species had given way to crops. The soil lost the grasses' extensive fibrous roots. Prairie restoration is the work of returning prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state. It helps conserve topsoil, which is exposed to wind and rain erosion once prairie is plowed under. Prairie grasses also take carbon from the air by photosynthesis and store it in the soil, which makes prairie soil useful for locking carbon away. In Europe, former cropland is restored by spontaneous succession, sowing seed mixtures, transferring plant material, and removing and transferring topsoil.

soil-water-109.title: Grassed waterways, green lines down the valley floor
soil-water-109.text: Storm runoff from cropland gathers along the lowest line of a valley. There it can cut rills and gullies that speed the water on and worsen the damage downstream. A grassed waterway guards that line against erosion. It is a strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the floor of a cultivated dry valley. The grass raises soil cohesion and roughness, prevents rills and gullies, slows runoff and lets it soak back in during long winter rains. It cannot reabsorb runoff from heavy spring and summer storms, so earthen dams across it may be added to hold the flow back for a while. The grass strips of {{ref:soil-water-290}} are different. They are narrower, only a few meters wide, and placed along rivers or along or within fields.

soil-water-111.title: WEPP, the physics-based heir to the USLE
soil-water-111.text: An interagency team built WEPP to replace the Universal Soil Loss Equation. Released publicly in 1995, it is now widely used in the United States and elsewhere. WEPP, the Water Erosion Prediction Project model, is a physically based erosion simulation built on hydrology, plant science, hydraulics and erosion mechanics. It takes climate, topography, soil and management inputs. It returns the water balance, soil detachment and deposition along the slope, sediment delivery and vegetation growth. It runs for single storms or continuously, on hillslopes, roads and small parcels, or on whole watersheds of linked hillslopes, channels and impoundments. Its sediment output falls into five size classes: primary clay, silt and sand, and small and large aggregates. That lets it calculate the selective transport and enrichment of fine particles.

soil-water-026.title: The tipping point where a rill is born
soil-water-026.text: A rill starts at a tipping point. Rill initiation is the moment when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and water begins to tear particles loose. Sandy and loamy soils are especially prone to rills, while dense clays resist them. Slope steepness mainly controls whether rills form and how deep they cut. Slope length and soil permeability set how many form. Each soil has a threshold slope below which rills cannot form. On many non-cohesive slopes it is about 2 degrees, at a drag speed of 3 to 3.5 cm/s, the measure explained in {{ref:soil-water-282}}. Once rills exist, their walls add to the loss. Up to 37% of erosion in rilled areas may come from collapsing sidewalls undercut and weakened by water.

soil-water-005.title: Sheet erosion, the thin film that strips a field
soil-water-005.text: One rainstorm can remove up to a hundred tons of fine particles per acre from a freshly plowed field, without cutting a single channel. Sheet erosion is the even erosion of soil or other material across a wide area by a thin, unchanneled layer of flowing water. It works in two steps. Rainsplash loosens small particles, as in {{ref:soil-water-004}}, and then a thin, uniform sheet flow carries them a short distance. Each event moves material only a short way, but frequent repetition makes up for the small change per episode. It is common on freshly plowed fields and on bare, unconsolidated ground. On an uneven hillslope it may give way to erosion in rills, which can merge into gullies.

soil-water-042.title: The P factor, credit for conservation practices
soil-water-042.text: Stone walls and hedgerows held soil in place long before anyone wrote an equation for erosion. The support practice factor is the P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion. It is hard to determine because regional maps of conservation practices are usually lacking, so it is often estimated from land use and slope. Field boundaries such as stone walls, hedgerows, earth banks and {{ref:soil-agri-081}} effectively prevented or reduced erosion in pre-industrial farming. A European P-factor model was built from a survey that recorded stone walls and grass margins, and landscape archaeology mapping can fill gaps in the data.

soil-water-256.title: Rainfall simulators, storms on demand
soil-water-256.text: Natural rain cannot be summoned for an experiment, so researchers make their own. A rainfall simulator is a device used in soil science and hydrology to study how soil reacts to rainfall. Simulated rain speeds the study of erosion, surface runoff and leaching. The first, in the 1930s, were sprinkling cans or pipes with holes. In the 1960s, nozzles matched raindrop size, impact speed and evenness, and in the 1980s valves let the intensity vary. In the early 1990s, simulators were used in the US Water Erosion Prediction Project to update the Universal Soil Loss Equation. On bare soil, drop size and terminal velocity must be simulated accurately, because they control splash erosion.

soil-water-258.title: Steadying burned slopes before the rains come
soil-water-258.text: In 2018, after the Thomas Fire in California, floods and flows of mud and debris killed 20 people and destroyed 300 houses. Fire burns canopy, litter, fine roots and soil organic compounds, leaving the soil less protected, less stable and more water-repellent, like the {{ref:soil-phys-034}} described earlier. Post-fire hillslope stabilization covers treatments that offset this damage, to cut the risk of damaging runoff and erosion downhill. Seeding and mulching cover the soil. Surfactants and flocculants counter water repellency and lost aggregation. Contour barriers of logs or straw shorten the slope length. Risk peaks in the first year, so the work must be quick. In the USA, seeding fell from 75% of treated burned areas in the 1970s and 1980s to 30% in the 2000s.

soil-water-039.title: Measuring how far the plow drags a field
soil-water-039.text: A few buried tracers can reveal how far cultivation drags a field downhill. Tillage erosion measurement covers two approaches: tracking the soil that cultivation moves, or measuring where soil is lost and gained. To track movement, researchers mix point or bulk tracers into plots and compare their positions before and after the pass. Losses and gains show up as changes in surface elevation. These are compared against an uneroded fence line or hedgerow, or surveyed with RTK GPS or photogrammetry. Changes in soil organic matter can also signal loss, but so many other factors affect it that the method is unreliable. Since the 1980s, radioisotopes such as Cs-137 and Pb-210 have given much more accurate erosion estimates.

soil-water-040.title: Computer models of soil on the move
soil-water-040.text: Tillage erosion models are computer models that simulate how cultivation moves soil along a hillslope or across a field. The simplest are one-dimensional hillslope models such as TEP and TillERI. They use slope length, gradient and the erosivity of the operation to give erosion rates and risk. WaTEM calculates both water and tillage erosion on a grid of ground heights, as in {{ref:soil-agri-164}}. It treats the soil shifted by each pass as diffusion in the steepest-slope direction.
