Field-scale models such as SORET and TillEM add the direction of cultivation, moving soil both parallel and perpendicular to it.

soil-water-044.title: The erosion index and highly erodible land
soil-water-044.text: The erosion index, also called the erodibility index, compares how fast a soil could erode with how fast it can afford to. It is potential erosion from all sources except gullies, divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer. It is used for U.S. conservation compliance and for the Conservation Reserve Program, which requires land to have an index above 8. In the United States, farmers cultivating highly erodible land often must follow a conservation plan to qualify for agricultural assistance.

soil-water-046.title: Sediment, loose grains on their way somewhere
soil-water-046.text: A beach, a dune and a glacier's moraine are all made of the same kind of thing. Sediment is solid material made of loose particles that is carried to a new place and deposited there. It is produced by {{ref:soil-found-052}} and erosion and moved by wind, water, ice or gravity. Water moves it most often, through what geologists call fluvial processes. Beach sands and river deposits are fluvial; dunes and loess are windblown; moraines and till are carried by ice. Once buried, sand and silt can be lithified, hardened into sedimentary rocks such as sandstone and siltstone. Sediment is classified by grain size, shape and composition. Size is measured on the phi scale, a log base 2 scale running from colloid to boulder. The word clay is ambiguous here, because it names both a size range and a group of minerals. Seas and lakes accumulate terrigenous sediment, washed from land mostly by rivers, along with sediment formed in the water, often by organisms. Lake bed sediments that have not yet hardened into rock hold a record of past climates.

soil-water-002.title: Erosion, the great mover of the Earth's surface
soil-water-002.text: Eroded material may travel only a few millimeters, or for thousands of kilometers. Erosion is the removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface, by processes such as flowing water or wind. The material is carried to another place and deposited there. Movement is what sets it apart from weathering, which moves nothing. Removing material as clastic sediment, made of broken fragments, is physical or mechanical erosion. Removing it by dissolution is {{ref:soil-water-008}}. The agents are many: rainfall, river flow, waves, glaciers, flooding, wind, groundwater, and mass movements such as {{ref:soil-water-057}} and {{ref:soil-water-252}}. Physical erosion is usually fastest on steep slopes. Its rate also responds to rainfall, storminess, wind speed, wave fetch and temperature. The journey ends in deposition, when the material arrives and settles at a new location. For soil, the balance matters. Where erosion outpaces soil formation, it destroys the soil. Slower erosion can still prevent soil features that need time to develop. Inceptisols form on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have developed into Alfisols.

soil-water-029.title: Aeolian processes: how wind moves the land
soil-water-029.text: Wind carries minerals from the Sahara all the way to the Amazon basin, and Saharan dust has built red clay soils in southern Europe. That long haul is the work of aeolian processes: the erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface. The name comes from Aeolus, the Greek god who kept the winds. Worldwide, water erodes more than wind does. Yet wind matters greatly in arid and semi-arid regions such as deserts. It works best where plants are sparse, the soil is dry and loose {{ref:soil-water-046}} lies ready. Wind is also a sorter. It separates sand from silt and clay, heaping sand into sandy deposits called ergs and laying silty loess farther from the source. Grains colliding in the air chip at one another, a process called attrition. It rounds and frosts sand grains and is a major source of dust 2–5 microns across. Wind deposits are not confined to dry lands. They also form along shorelines and on glacial outwash, and much of North America and Europe rests on windblown sand and loess from the Pleistocene.

soil-water-051.title: Sediment control: keeping a building site's soil at home
soil-water-051.text: In 1965 Montgomery County, Maryland, began the first local government program to keep construction soil out of its waters. Maryland followed with a statewide program in 1970. Sediment control is any practice or device that holds eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters. It usually works alongside {{ref:soil-water-050}}, which stops soil moving in the first place and so lightens the load on sediment controls. The common tools include fabric fences, settling ponds and traps, rolls of fiber, straw bale and sand bag barriers, storm drain inlet protection and turbidity curtains. Most are temporary, though some also serve for stormwater management. Every U.S. state requires these controls on construction sites above a set size, and federal rules apply from 1 acre (0.40 ha). They must go in before clearing and grading begin and stay maintained until the disturbance ends.

soil-water-018.title: When eroded soil becomes the river's pollutant
soil-water-018.text: Each year the Yellow River carries over 1.6 billion tons of sediment to the ocean, most of it washed off the Loess Plateau by water erosion. Soil erosion, especially from farmland, is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution. Sediment harms waters in its own right. Silt fills the gaps between gravel where fish spawn, cuts their food supply and clogs their gills, and the variety of plants, algae and invertebrates declines. Eroded soil also carries attached pesticides and heavy metals, plus fertilizers that overfeed rivers with nutrients. On Madagascar's central plateau, gullies called lavakas may supply 84% of river sediment, turning rivers dark red-brown and killing fish. Near coral reefs, sediment from watershed development smothers and scrapes the corals and feeds algal blooms. Removing an estimated 135 million m3 of eroded sediment likely costs the EU and UK over 2.3 billion euros a year.

soil-water-053.title: Mass wasting: when gravity alone moves the ground
soil-water-053.text: Some soil leaves a hillside with no river, wind or ice to carry it. Mass wasting, also called mass movement, is the movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity. Unlike other erosion, the moving debris travels in no medium at all. Water usually aids it without being the carrier. With more water, a sliding mass grows ever more fluid, grading through flows of debris and mud and finally into sheetfloods. The forms range from slow creep of the soil to sudden rockfalls, acting over seconds to hundreds of years. Broadly, movements are either creeps or slides, described in {{ref:soil-water-055}} and {{ref:soil-water-057}}, and subsidence is sometimes counted as well. In mountains it is often the first stage in moving weathered material, carrying it down to where streams and glaciers can pick it up. Weak, unconsolidated material, steep slopes, freeze-thaw, heavy rain and undercutting by digging or erosion all promote it. Speed decides the damage. Slow creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, while rapid slides can be deadly. Walls, catchment dams for rockfall and debris, tree planting, better drainage of source areas and {{ref:soil-water-065}} all reduce the threat.

soil-water-064.title: Slope stability: the balance between strength and stress
soil-water-064.text: Whether a hillside stands or slides comes down to a single ratio. Slope stability is the ability of a soil or rock slope to withstand movement; its opposite is slope instability, or slope failure. Engineers express it as a safety factor: the available {{ref:soil-phys-101}} divided by the shear stress acting along a possible sliding surface. A slope is stable overall if that factor exceeds 1 on every possible surface from top to toe, and the smallest value speaks for the whole slope. Values between about 1 and 1.3 mark slopes that need watching or strengthening. Intense rain, snowmelt, earthquakes, toe erosion, building loads, road cuts and {{ref:soil-water-100}} can all trigger failure. After heavy rain, pore water pressure on the slip surface lowers the {{ref:soil-phys-100}} and the friction, while the added groundwater makes the soil heavier. A little moisture can steady a slope, but saturation acts as a lubricant. Pure clay often fails along a near-circular surface, while slab-shaped slips strip a layer of soil off the bedrock.

soil-water-057.title: Landslides: when a slope's strength gives way
soil-water-057.text: A landslide can strike a mountain, a coastal cliff, a gentle slope or the seafloor. The word covers several forms of {{ref:soil-water-053}} with relatively rapid ground movement, including rockfalls, slope failures and fast flows of mud and debris. Gravity drives them all. A slope fails when the shear strength of its material falls, the shear stress on it rises, or both, the balance set out in {{ref:soil-water-064}}. Many slides follow a specific event such as heavy rain, an earthquake or a road cut, though the trigger is not always identifiable. Natural causes include wetting and rising pore water pressure, undercutting by rivers or waves, weathering and earthquake shaking. Wildfire adds another, by destroying vegetation and soil structure. People aggravate slides through deforestation, cultivation, construction and earthworks. Removing deep-rooted plants that bind loose slope debris to bedrock does the same. Degraded land loosens the grip of plants on soil, and with extreme rainfall it makes erosion and landslides more frequent. Saturated material can turn into a flowing mass that carries off trees, houses and cars and blocks rivers. Landslides under water or into water can generate tsunamis.

soil-water-055.title: Soil creep: the slope that moves while no one watches
soil-water-055.text: In old churchyards, headstones lean and sit metres from where they were set. The ground beneath them has been moving. Downhill creep, or soil creep, is the slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope. It looks continuous but is the sum of many tiny, separate movements driven by gravity, and the steeper the slope, the faster it goes. Friction holds slope material in place. As a slope steepens, less of gravity's pull presses into it, so friction falls. Water cuts both ways. A little gives soil cohesion, like damp sand in a sandcastle, but saturation fills the pores and creates a slip plane. Clay that swells when wet pushes soil downhill and settles at its new position as it dries. Freeze-thaw and heating-cooling cycles ratchet soil down the same way. Trees grow curved and fences tilt as the soil carries them along. Plant roots bind loose material and draw off excess water, though they add weight, so bare slopes are more likely to move. Creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, so engineers drive pilings deep enough to keep it from undermining foundations. Modelled as a slow diffusion of {{ref:soil-form-097}}, creep rounds off ridges over long timescales.

soil-water-047.title: Reading a sand grain's travels from its shape
soil-water-047.text: A frosted sand grain is a strong hint that the wind once carried it. Sediment grain shape describes particles by three parameters: overall form, or sphericity, the roundness of corners, and surface texture. Form is spherical, platy or rodlike, worked out from the lengths of a grain's long, intermediate and short axes with formulas such as Krumbein's or Sneed and Folk's. Roundness runs from very angular to very rounded and is usually judged against comparison charts. Pits, fractures and scratches on the surface, studied mostly on quartz grains under an electron microscope, reveal how a grain traveled.

soil-water-008.title: Chemical erosion: landscapes carried off in solution
soil-water-008.text: A sinkhole is erosion with no solid debris to show for it. Chemical erosion is the loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes. Physical erosion, by contrast, removes rock or soil as solid particles of sediment. Because the material leaves in solution, chemical erosion is usually calculated from the dissolved load that streams carry. Sinkholes and other karst features are its extreme example. Anders Rapp pioneered its study in work on Kärkevagge, published in 1960.

soil-water-007.title: Coastal erosion: waves against the shore
soil-water-007.text: A wave's most effective weapon is the sediment it carries. Coastal erosion is the wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part. Waves work by hydraulic action, pounding, corrosion of rock such as limestone by carbonic acid, and attrition of their own load. Abrasion, also covered in {{ref:soil-water-271}}, in which waves hurl sediment at cliffs, is the fastest and most effective. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast, and erosion occurs where less arrives from upcurrent than is carried away. Sea-level rise caused by climate change has greatly increased coastal erosion rates.

soil-water-009.title: Glacial erosion: ice that sandpapers whole valleys
soil-water-009.text: A U-shaped valley takes an estimated 100,000 years to carve. Glacial erosion is the work of moving glacier ice, mainly through abrasion, plucking and ice thrusting. In abrasion, debris frozen into the base of the ice scrapes, polishes and gouges the bed like sandpaper on wood. In plucking, the glacier breaks off pieces of bedrock. In ice thrusting, a glacier frozen to its bed carries large sheets of frozen sediment forward as it surges. Ice and meltwater leave moraines, drumlins, ground moraine, kames and glacial erratics behind.

soil-water-006.title: How rivers cut their valleys down and out
soil-water-006.text: Most of a river's erosion happens during floods. River and stream erosion is the work of water flowing continuously along a channel, deepening valleys and wearing away banks. It cuts downward and also headward into the hillside, leaving head cuts and steep banks. Early on it works mostly downward, carving V-shaped valleys. Once the stream reaches a base level, erosion turns sideways and widens the valley floor. Pebbles and boulders dragged along the bed abrade it, a process called traction. Bank erosion, distinct from scour of the bed, rises sharply with heavier runoff from built-up land.

soil-water-048.title: Sediment transport: how water, wind and ice move the pieces
soil-water-048.text: Every grain on a riverbed, from clay to boulder, waits for a flow strong enough to move it. Sediment transport is the movement of solid particles by gravity together with the water, air or ice that carries them. Its study mostly serves prediction: whether erosion or deposition will happen, how much, and over what time and distance. The physics is a contest. Stronger flows raise the lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out. Water moves bigger grains than air because it is denser and more viscous. Rivers usually carry sand and gravel, and big floods shift cobbles and boulders. Moving water shapes ripples, river patterns and the flat ground beside channels by eroding and depositing on its bed. Wind moves fine sediment and builds soils from airborne dust, while glaciers carry a wide range of sizes and drop them in moraines. Changes in flow power decide where material is lost or gained. Locally that happens behind boulders and inside meanders, and regionally after a dam is built or removed. On hillslopes, soil creep, falling trees, burrowing animals and landslides move {{ref:soil-form-097}} downslope, and erosion rates climb steeply as slopes near the angle of repose. When human activity loads a river with enough fine material to fill its channels, the problem is called siltation.

soil-water-049.title: How much eroded soil actually reaches the river
soil-water-049.text: In Europe, only about 15% of eroded soil is expected to reach a river outlet. That share is the sediment delivery ratio: the fraction of gross erosion on a catchment, counting interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion, that arrives at the outlet. The rest is deposited along the way. Sediment distribution models such as WaTEM/SEDEM simulate where material is moved and where it settles, and the European figure comes from them. The share that does arrive still brings management and siltation costs to river basins.

soil-water-056.title: Solifluction: soil that creeps over frozen ground
soil-water-056.text: In 1906 Johan Gunnar Andersson coined the word solifluction for water-saturated debris moving in periglacial regions. Such slow movements were later tied to freezing and thawing instead. Solifluction now means gradual downslope mass movement of soil linked to that cycle. It is typical of arctic and alpine climates, where soil thawed and saturated in summer creeps down moderate, sparsely vegetated slopes over {{ref:soil-env-129}}. It is slow but widespread, building tongue-shaped lobes and sheets of poorly layered debris. Because it needs cold, humid conditions, it is used to infer past climates.

soil-water-071.title: Quick clay: solid ground that turns to liquid
soil-water-071.text: Some clay stands as firm ground until a shock turns it into a watery fluid. Quick clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, is a highly sensitive glaciomarine clay. It consists of very fine silt and clay-sized particles ground up by glaciers and first laid down in the sea. Its particle structure is highly unstable, so once remolded it keeps far less strength than it had on first loading. It is found only in lands near the North Pole glaciated in the Pleistocene: Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Alaska. In Canada it lies mainly in the Ottawa Valley, the St. Lawrence Valley and the Saguenay River region. Earthquake vibrations or massive rainfall can liquefy it suddenly and set off landslides. In Canada alone, quick clay it is linked to more than 250 mapped landslides. Liquefaction, described in {{ref:soil-phys-116}}, usually affects sandy or non-plastic silty soils, so quick clay is one of the rare cases in clay. Known deposits are now commonly tested before any major development.

soil-water-100.title: Internal erosion: the hidden threat inside dams
soil-water-100.text: About half of all embankment dam failures come from water quietly carrying soil away from the inside. Internal erosion is the formation of voids inside a soil as seeping water removes material. It happens when seepage through the pores and cracks of a dam or its foundation exerts enough hydraulic force to detach particles and carry them out. It is also the second most common cause of levee failure. The danger lies in how little shows. Often the only sign is a sand boil, which may be hidden under water, and a dam can breach within hours of the evidence becoming obvious. Piping is its progressive growth, eroding back from the downstream exit until a continuous pipe discharges water. Four types are recognised: a concentrated leak through a crack, backward erosion from the exit point, suffusion and contact erosion. In suffusion, fines wash through the pores between coarse grains that carry most of the {{ref:soil-phys-100}}. Widely or gap-graded cohesionless soils prone to it are called internally unstable. Contact erosion works along an interface between fine and coarse soil. Filters are the defense: layers coarser and more permeable than the soil, which pass seepage but trap eroded particles. They must be internally stable, non-cohesive, free-draining and strong. The critical shear stress that starts a concentrated leak can be estimated with the jet erosion test or the {{ref:soil-water-094}}.

soil-water-252.title: Debris flows: rivers of rock and mud
soil-water-252.text: In 1985 debris flows killed more than 20,000 people at Armero, Colombia. In 1999 they killed tens of thousands in Vargas State, Venezuela. A debris flow is a water-laden mass of soil and broken rock that rushes down mountainsides, funnels into channels and leaves thick muddy deposits on valley floors. Its bulk density is about 2000 kilograms per cubic meter, like other landslides. Yet high {{ref:soil-phys-098}} liquefies the sediment, so it flows almost like water. Sediment fills more than about 40 to 50% of its volume. Floods with about 10 to 40% solids are hyperconcentrated floods instead, and a true {{ref:soil-water-060}} is mostly finer than sand. Three things set one up: slopes steeper than about 25 degrees, plenty of loose sediment, soil or weathered rock, and enough water to almost fully saturate it. Intense rain or snowmelt, dam-break or glacial outburst floods and landslides can trigger them, and they become more frequent after forest and brush fires. In steep channels they often exceed 10 m/s (36 km/h), and flows of up to about 100,000 cubic meters are common in mountains. A boulder-rich head leads a liquefied body of finer sediment. The deposits are poorly sorted lobes edged with boulder levees. Debris basins can catch them, but they are a costly last resort that needs yearly maintenance.

soil-water-032.title: Three ways the wind moves grains
soil-water-032.text: Wind moves sediment in three ways: suspension, short skipping hops described in {{ref:soil-water-251}}, and creep, a rolling or sliding along the ground. Grains start moving at the fluid threshold wind speed, and impacts keep them moving until the wind drops below a lower threshold, a lag called hysteresis. Turbulence lets wind carry grains under 0.05 mm far from coarser ones. Hops matter most for grains up to 2 mm, and landing grains shove heavier ones along as creep, up to 25% of grain movement in deserts. A plant cover of just 15% stops most sand movement.

soil-water-030.title: Deflation: wind that scoops out the desert
soil-water-030.text: Some hollows scoured by wind in Mongolia are 8 km across and 60 to 100 m deep. Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind. It works through surface creep, suspension and grains bouncing along in short hops, and the hops likely account for 50–70% of it. The hollows it digs, called blowouts, range from dimples 0.3 m deep to those Mongolian giants. Once the fines are gone, a sheet of rock fragments is left behind, the {{ref:soil-water-253}} that floors most deflation zones and shields the material below.

soil-water-033.title: Sand dunes: hills the wind builds
soil-water-033.text: Ralph Bagnold gave the barchan and the linear seif dune their names. A sand dune is a mound or ridge of sediment heaped up by the wind, independent of any obstacle. Its windward slope is gentle, and its downwind side is a steep avalanche slope called the slipface. Under one prevailing wind, transverse dunes form, such as crescent-shaped barchans. Linear dunes run for tens of kilometres, and star dunes have more than two slipfaces. Where plant patches meet active sand such as blowouts, vegetated parabolic dunes form, crescents whose ends point upwind. John Tilton Hack added these in 1941.

soil-water-031.title: Wind abrasion: sandblasting that mattered less than thought
soil-water-031.text: Desert mushroom rocks were once blamed on blowing sand. Wind abrasion, also covered in {{ref:soil-water-271}}, is the wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains. It was long thought a major cause of desert erosion, but by the mid-20th century it was judged much less important. Mushroom rocks are now credited to other processes. Wind rarely lifts sand far: most stays within 50 cm of the surface, and practically none rises above 2 m. Yardangs, rock ridges up to tens of metres high streamlined by desert winds, are widely attributed to abrasion. Polished or faceted stones called ventifacts are rare, needing abundant sand, strong winds and no vegetation.

soil-water-093.title: Silt fences: cheap, simple and often failing
soil-water-093.text: One of the cheapest sediment barriers on a building site also has a poor field record. A silt fence is a temporary fabric fence that keeps sediment in stormwater runoff out of nearby waters. Geotextile fabric is stretched between stakes along a contour, its lower edge buried in the soil, so runoff pools behind it and sediment settles out. Low cost and simple design make it popular. Field tests show generally poor results, often from bad placement, installation or maintenance. Fine particles soon clog the fabric, and no sediment-retention device filters stormwater for long. Since 1998, static slicing has proved the most effective way to install it.

soil-water-063.title: A warming climate can raise or lower landslide risk
soil-water-063.text: Climate change does not push landslides in one direction. Shifts in temperature, rainfall and {{ref:soil-water-161}} change where, how often and how strongly slides occur. The effects vary so much between areas that they must be studied regionally. Warming can reduce landslides where faster evaporation dries soils and plant growth is stimulated. It increases them through faster snowmelt, rain on snow and glacier retreat. At high elevation, thawing frozen ground loses the cohesion its interstitial ice once gave. More extreme rainfall also focuses infiltration and increases runoff events that may trigger debris flows.

soil-water-058.title: Six ways a slope can fail
soil-water-058.text: Falls, topples, slides, spreads, flows and slope deformation: these six types of movement sort landslides in rock and soil alike. Falls are blocks in free fall. Topples rotate away from a vertical face. Slides move as an intact body over planar or spoon-shaped shear surfaces, the latter called rotational. Spreads crack and extend sideways, flows move fluidised dry or wet material, and slope deformations are slow, distributed movements. David Varnes proposed a tighter scheme in 1978. Cruden and Varnes revised it in 1996, and Hungr, Leroueil and Picarelli revised it most recently in 2014.

soil-water-061.title: Mapping where the next landslide will strike
soil-water-061.text: Landslide hazard mapping rests on one assumption: future slides will happen under the same conditions as past ones. Analysts study the factors behind earlier landslides, usually grouped as {{ref:soil-water-295}}, geology, land use and land cover, and hydrogeology. Mapping software, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-165}}, handles the many layered factors. Aerial photos and satellite images taken before and after events record where slides happened and what set them off. A good hazard map shows past events and clearly marks probable future sites, so planners can reduce losses.

soil-water-062.title: Watching slopes move to warn of landslides
soil-water-062.text: Landslide monitoring tracks slope movement to judge danger, issue timely alerts and plan protective measures. From above, InSAR measures displacement precisely over large areas, joined by repeated LiDAR point clouds, optical satellite imagery and drones. On the ground, crews use GPS, surveys of marked targets and ground-based radar. Instruments in the slope itself fill in the rest. Piezometers read pore water pressure, extensometers span cracks, and borehole inclinometers and tiltmeters track the ground's deformation.

soil-water-059.title: Shallow slides and deep-seated slides
soil-water-059.text: The depth of a landslide's sliding surface sorts it into one of two families. Shallow slides run within the soil mantle or weathered bedrock, from a few decimetres to some metres deep. Debris slides and debris flows are usually shallow. They often happen where permeable soil lies over less permeable soil, which traps water, builds pressure and lets the saturated topsoil slide. Deep-seated slides lie well below tree rooting depth, in deep {{ref:soil-form-097}}, weathered rock or bedrock. They often move along faults or bedding planes, leaving concave head scarps and steep toes. Over geological time they shape landscapes and feed sediment that strongly alters stream courses.

soil-water-067.title: Trees on a slope: anchor or burden
soil-water-067.text: The same large trees can steady a slope or help bring it down, depending on where they stand. At the toe of a slope prone to rotational failure, they could raise its factor of safety by 10%. Planted at the top, they could lower it by 10%. The link between slopes and plants runs both ways, shaped by soil type, rainfall regime, plant species, the direction a slope faces and its steepness. Plants act in four main ways: wind throw, removal of water, their added mass, called surcharge, and reinforcement by roots. Wind throw topples a tree and exposes its root plate, a risk for single trees more than for sheltered stands. Mass matters only for large trees: one 30–50m tall may load a slope with roughly 100–150 kN/m2. Felling big trees at the toe removes both their drying effect and their load. In clay soils the resulting suction can then draw in water and soften the soil.

soil-water-034.title: Dust storms: when dry ground takes to the sky
soil-water-034.text: Saharan dust storms have increased about 10-fold since the 1950s, stripping topsoil from Niger, Chad, northern Nigeria and Burkina Faso. A dust storm, also called a sandstorm, is a storm in which strong wind blows loose sand and dirt off dry ground. By one definition, it carries enough dust to cut visibility below 1 kilometre. The dust is made in the act. Skipping sand grains strike the ground and break off finer dust, which then travels in suspension, as {{ref:soil-water-032}} describes. Gusts come from thunderstorm outflows or from dry cold fronts, the type common in the years of {{ref:soil-water-075}}. Drought, wind, wildfire and poor farming and grazing all cause dust storms. Heavy plowing in dryland farming and bare ground left without crops are especially risky. The losses are selective. Storms take organic matter and the light, nutrient-rich particles first, and their abrasion damages young crops. Inhaled dust can cause dust pneumonia, and prolonged exposure can cause silicosis. Yet deposited dust can also help. Rainforests of Central and South America gain mineral nutrients from the Sahara, and ancient dust deposits form fertile loess.

soil-water-075.title: The Dust Bowl: when the Great Plains blew away
soil-water-075.text: In May 1934 a two-day storm dropped 12 million pounds (5,400 tonnes) of dust on Chicago. The dust was farm soil, lifted by the wind. The Dust Bowl was a decade of severe dust storms and drought, from 1930 to 1940. It badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies. It hit hardest in western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico. Its drought and erosion affected 100 million acres (400,000 km2). Nature supplied the drought; people had laid the soil bare. Deep plowing of the virgin prairie had removed the native deep-rooted grasses that held soil and moisture through droughts and high winds. Settlers did not use the dryland farming methods that prevent wind erosion. Cotton farmers left fields bare in winter, when High Plains winds are strongest, and burned the stubble, stripping the soil of organic matter and cover. Then drought came in three waves, in 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940. It dried the {{ref:soil-form-021}} to a powder, and failed crops left plowed fields open to the wind. Black blizzards of dust reached the East Coast. By the end of the 1930s, more than 75% of the topsoil had blown away in many regions. A key legacy was a government with a far larger role in managing land and conserving soil.

soil-water-076.title: How Washington fought the Dust Bowl
soil-water-076.text: By 1938 the conservation effort had cut the amount of blowing soil by 65%. It began in August 1933 with the Soil Erosion Service under the soil scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-019}}. In 1935 it moved to the Department of Agriculture and was renamed; today it is the NRCS. The Civilian Conservation Corps planted over 200 million trees from Canada to Abilene, Texas, to break the wind and hold soil and water. Farmers learned to rotate crops, farm in strips, plow along contours and build level steps into slopes. From 1937 they were paid a dollar an acre to do so.

soil-water-077.title: The Dust Bowl's long shadow on farm values
soil-water-077.text: By 1940, relative to low-erosion counties, farmland value per acre had fallen 28% in high-erosion counties and 17% in medium-erosion ones. In highly eroded areas, less than 25% of the original agricultural losses were ever recovered. Thinner topsoil favoured a shift from wheat to livestock and hay, but farmers were slow to switch, partly because bank failures cut off credit. The economy adjusted mainly by losing people. Population fell in the more eroded counties, both in the 1930s and through the 1950s.

soil-water-096.title: River bank failure: when the bank gives way
soil-water-096.text: Every stream eats at its banks by friction, shearing and solution. River bank failure is the sudden mass wasting of a bank, when gravity on its rock and soil exceeds the cohesive and adhesive forces holding them together. Floods, the corkscrewing helicoidal flow on the outside of bends, and downcutting rills and gullies speed the attack. Extra weight near the edge, saturation from rain, watering of crops or septic systems, groundwater undermining and loss of deep-rooted plants can all set off a collapse. The toe zone, between ordinary and low water level, is most exposed. Cohesive soils fail on rotational or planar surfaces; non-cohesive ones avalanche.

soil-water-094.title: The hole erosion test: drilling a leak to measure it
soil-water-094.text: The hole erosion test measures how well a soil resists erosion, above all for {{ref:soil-water-100}} in embankment dams. A small hole, typically 6 mm, is drilled through a soil sample compacted in a mould. Water forced through erodes and widens the hole while the flow is measured. Plotting erosion rate against hydraulic shear stress gives two values. One is the critical shear stress at which a leak starts to erode. The other is the erodibility, which sets how fast erosion then proceeds. A modified version adds a pitot-static tube to measure total head. It gives much smaller critical shear stresses, closer to the jet erosion test.

soil-water-101.title: Earthflows: slow rivers of saturated clay and silt
soil-water-101.text: An earthflow is a viscous downslope flow of water-saturated, fine-grained material moving under gravity. It sits between downhill creep and the faster {{ref:soil-water-060}}, and solid material rides along on its surface. Clay, fine sand, silt and fine pyroclastic material are prone to it once saturated with enough water. More water means faster flow, so an earthflow may take minutes or years to move. It can cover a few square meters or several hectares. Slopes undercut by rivers or construction, or made of wet clay and silt, are most at risk. Draining slopes is one of the best defences.

soil-water-099.title: Sediment basins: settling ponds for building sites
soil-water-099.text: A sediment basin is a temporary pond on a construction site that captures soil washed off in rain storms. Muddy runoff settles in the pond before the water is discharged, protecting nearby waters. Basins suit sites of 5 acres (20,000 m2) or more. Smaller sites use sediment traps, small embankments along low ground or above storm drain inlets. When earthmoving ends, a basin may be cleaned out and kept as a permanent detention or retention basin for stormwater.

soil-water-098.title: Fiber rolls: straw tubes that catch a slope's soil
soil-water-098.text: A fiber roll is a temporary tube of straw, coconut fibre or similar material laid on construction slopes to control erosion and trap sediment. Crews lay the rolls along contours in shallow trenches 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) deep and stake them down. Steeper slopes get more rows, and one goes at the slope's base. The rolls slow surface runoff without channelling it. Water passes through while sediment stays uphill, and properly installed rolls trap sediment better than straw bales. They do not suit very steep land prone to slides or creep, and poorly staked rolls can be carried off by high flows.

soil-water-060.title: Mudflows: liquefied slopes on the run
soil-water-060.text: A mudflow moves at three to five metres per second. It is a fast-moving flow of debris and soil liquefied by added water, also called a mudslide. Mudflows contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized material and up to 30% water. Their clay makes them more fluid than debris flows, so they travel farther over gentler slopes. Many begin as slides triggered by heavy rain, snowmelt or groundwater and turn into flows as they take up water. Whether mud starts to flow depends on its grain size, water content and the slope.

soil-water-052.title: Clearing muddy runoff with flocculants
soil-water-052.text: Sediment treatment systems clean muddy construction runoff by adding flocculants, chemicals that make fine particles clump, then filtering or settling the water. Active systems pump the water and dose it with natural polymers, synthetic polymers or inorganic flocculants to cut total suspended solids before discharge. The choice matters. Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish, so anionic ones are best practice in open systems. Passive systems rely on gravity, with self-dosing gel flocculants, jute filters and settling ponds, and need no power and little skill. Stormwater facilities are usually designed with Stokes' law to remove particles larger than 40 microns.

soil-water-251.title: Saltation: grains that travel in hops
soil-water-251.text: Pebbles in rivers, desert sand, soil blowing off fields and drifting snow all travel in hops. In saltation, wind or water lifts loose grains from a bed and carries them in short hops back to the surface. Slow flows only roll grains along as creep. Above the fluid threshold, drag and lift raise them into roughly ballistic arcs. Landing grains splash others into motion, and in air this bombardment makes most of the dust in dust storms. Particles of about 70 micrometres or less ride the turbulence in suspension instead. Fences with holes slow saltation, piling sand on their lee side.

soil-water-028.title: Healing a gully by taming its water
soil-water-028.text: Gully stabilisation alters the water flowing through a gully so it scours less, sediment builds up and plants return. Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes carry water safely down to the gully floor. Sediment settling on flatter stretches lets vegetation re-establish, and damaged areas should be fenced off until restoration is complete. Prevention is easier. Vegetation along drainage lines, evenly spread runoff, high soil organic matter and no over-cultivation keep gullies from forming. Evidence on how well gully controls work is scattered, and terrain, climate and landscape can make them fail.

soil-water-103.title: Gelifluction: spring meltwater sets topsoil flowing
soil-water-103.text: In some periglacial regions, spring melt releases half a year's precipitation within a couple of days. Gelifluction is what that flood does to the ground: the downslope movement of waterlogged topsoil driven by seasonal freezing and thawing. It is a close relative of {{ref:soil-water-056}}, prominent where snow lies six to eight months a year. The soaked topsoil flows like a liquid, so gelifluction can occur on slopes of less than half a degree. On slopes of 10° to 20° it builds tongue-shaped lobes, with risers up to 5 metres (16 ft) and treads up to 50 metres (160 ft). Gentler slopes get terrace-like benches.

soil-water-066.title: Calculating whether a slope will hold
soil-water-066.text: Engineers design safe embankments, road cuts, open-pit mines, excavations and landfills with slope stability analysis. It covers static or dynamic, analytical or empirical methods for judging natural slopes and dams, embankments and excavations in soil and rock. It needs site data on soil and rock properties, slope geometry, groundwater and fractures, since water pressure in pores and fractures lowers strength. Limit equilibrium is the most common and simplest method. Complex failures such as progressive creep or liquefaction need numerical modelling. Simple two-dimensional circular analysis is widely used, but finding the most probable slip plane is a primary difficulty, and real failures in mixed soils are not always circular.

soil-water-065.title: Engineering slopes that stay put
soil-water-065.text: Draining water out of a slope significantly improves its stability by reducing the forces that push it toward failure. Slope stabilization is engineering work that raises a slope's stability and lessens the effect of landslides. Its methods fall into three classes. Geometric methods reshape the slope. Hydrogeological methods lower groundwater or dry the material. Chemical or mechanical methods raise shear strength or add anchors, nails and piles. Flattening, retaining walls, grouting, and consolidation by surcharging or electro-osmosis also serve. Where landslides are shallow, vegetation is a widely used bioengineering method: roots reinforce the upper soil, while interception and transpiration dry it.

soil-water-106.title: Baer–Babinet law: blaming Earth's spin for lopsided rivers
soil-water-106.text: In 1859 Jacques Babinet proposed that the Earth's rotation makes rivers erode one bank more than the other. Karl Ernst von Baer gave a fuller explanation in 1860. Their Baer–Babinet law holds that rivers wear mostly their right banks in the Northern Hemisphere and their left banks in the Southern. The proposed cause was the Coriolis force. It is best treated as a hypothesis with too weak a mechanism. The Coriolis force is orders of magnitude weaker than local flow forces in a channel, so it is unlikely to matter in any one river. Einstein explained the true causes in 1926.

soil-water-054.title: Reading the marks gravity leaves on slopes
soil-water-054.text: Most traces of mass wasting are subtle, but a few are spectacular. Soil creep shows in curved tree trunks and tilted fences and poles, and freeze-thaw creep builds small steps on hillsides. Solifluction leaves lobed or sheet-like deposits whose rock fragments point perpendicular to the deposit's contours. Rockfall piles talus slopes at the foot of cliffs, and landslides leave scarps and step-like benches. Debris flows leave long, narrow tracks of very poorly sorted material, often with levees, and build much of the upper slopes of the sediment cones described in {{ref:soil-water-293}}.

soil-water-108.title: Soil sloughing: the shallow slip that can grow
soil-water-108.text: Active pore water pressure can cut a soil's shear strength by up to 60%. Soil sloughing is the falling of soil off banks and slopes when it loses cohesion. It is shallow, involving only the uppermost layers, and it shares the causes of landslides, very wet soil above all. Rising water content weakens shear strength and so cohesion. Bare soils slough more readily than vegetated ones, because roots hold the surface. Clearing banks therefore raises the risk, and lost root strength after harvesting can lower the safety factor so far that a moderate storm brings failure. Left unchecked, sloughing can end in massive bank or slope failure.

soil-water-104.title: Rivers that melt their way through frozen banks
soil-water-104.text: On the Lena, spring floods break river ice up to 2 m thick, discharge rises about tenfold within days, and the banks retreat about 40 m per year. That is fluvio-thermal erosion: the combined mechanical and thermal erosion of ice-rich soils and sediments by an unfrozen river. Strong flow thaws the frozen bank, and the water removes the thawed material where it can cut in. Melting ice weakens the porous soil, leaving it easy to break up, and banks may collapse along ice wedges. Cold-room experiments show that water temperature, ice temperature and discharge drive the thawing, while high ice content slows it.

soil-water-224.title: A buried cable that feels a slope shift
soil-water-224.text: Engineers use {{ref:soil-water-223}} to watch for slope movement at highway cuts, rail beds and open-pit mines. A coaxial cable is set in a vertical borehole with brittle grout. When the ground moves, the cable deforms sharply, and the bend shows up as a peak in the reflection trace. The method was once insensitive to small movements and relied on people reading the traces. Farrington and Sargand (2004) improved it with a numerical-derivative method that gives earlier warning. Probes in different layers can also time infiltration, helping judge how well best management practices cut stormwater runoff.

soil-water-078.title: Fech fech: desert powder that swallows vehicles
soil-water-078.text: Part of Egypt's Qattara Depression is impassable to most vehicles because of a powder hidden underfoot. Fech fech is a very fine powder formed by the erosion of clay-limestone terrain, found mostly in deserts. It forms a surface layer of pulverised, weakly cohesive soil under a thin crust, so it is invisible from the surface. A vehicle can break through and sink into a quicksand-like mass. It derives from ancient lake muds or certain clay-rich rocks, and it is one of the desert surfaces that produce dust.

soil-water-249.title: Bed load and suspended load: two ways a river carries
soil-water-249.text: A stream's bed load, the sediment that rolls, slides and hops along the bottom, is usually thought to be only 5–10% of its total load. It moves at a small fraction of the flow speed. The suspended load, held up in the water, moves at a large fraction of the mean flow speed. Wash load, fine material from upstream, rides with the stream, spread almost evenly through the water. The Rouse number weighs a grain's settling velocity against turbulent upward velocity and decides its mode: above 7.5 it stays put, below 0.8 it travels as wash load. Small grains settle more slowly and so travel farther downstream.

soil-water-250.title: The Hjulström curve: a classic graph now retired
soil-water-250.text: In 1935 Filip Hjulström drew a graph of the flow velocity needed to erode, transport or deposit sediment of each grain size. The Hjulström curve uses logarithmic axes, and Åke Sundborg later added separate movement thresholds for several water depths. Today it has mainly historical value. It ignores water depth, and it does not show that slowing flow causes deposition and speeding flow causes erosion. For the start of sediment motion in rivers, the accepted tool is now the dimensionless Shields diagram, based on shear stress.

soil-water-253.title: Desert pavement: a stone floor of disputed origin
soil-water-253.text: Some desert ground is tiled with closely packed, interlocking pebbles and cobbles. This is desert pavement, and geologists still debate how it forms and how old it is. A common explanation is that wind and occasional rain remove sand and dust and leave the larger stones. Clay shrink–swell has also been proposed. A newer idea runs the other way: windblown dust settles between and under the stones, building soil beneath them. In 1995, helium-3 dating in the Mojave Desert found the rocks older than the soil below. Once formed, a pavement shields the ground, and older surfaces carry better-developed pavements, so it signals aridity and relative age.

soil-water-114.title: Why rock masses fail along their cracks
soil-water-114.text: Many natural and man-made slopes fail not through solid rock but along its joints. The shear strength along a discontinuity, such as a joint, is often far lower than that of the intact blocks between. It depends on how far the discontinuity extends, its roughness, infill, fluid pressure, solution and cementation, and whether it has moved before. Weak discontinuities make a mass deform plastically rather than elastically, which can bring larger, permanent settlement of foundations. Real discontinuities cannot be calculated analytically. Their strength comes from laboratory or field tests, such as the direct shear test, or from empirical characterisation.

soil-water-072.title: How the last glaciation built a clay that can liquefy
soil-water-072.text: Quick clay began about 20,000 years ago, at the height of the last glaciation. Ice pressed the land down, and the sea reached far inland to receive the ground-up rock. Silt and clay settled loosely in the seawater, giving an unusual form of {{ref:soil-phys-006}}: a strongly bonded skeleton glued by mobile sea-salt ions. Post-glacial rebound then lifted the clay above the sea. Soft rainwater and snowmelt weakened its ionic glue, leaving a loose skeleton holding much water. A normal topsoil cover absorbs ordinary stresses. A large earthquake, extra load near a slope or saturating rain can disturb the clay and start liquefaction.

soil-water-074.title: Quick clay slides that eat their way inland
soil-water-074.text: In 1893 a quick clay slide at Verdal, Norway, killed 116 people. Such slides are retrogressive: they usually start at water and work their way upslope. Most advance at slow walking speed, but deep quick clay can collapse much faster, and slides have reached kilometres inland. Topsoil hides the clay, so settlements and roads were often built on vulnerable sites that only soil testing reveals. At Rissa in 1978, about 33 hectares of farmland liquefied and flowed into a lake within a few hours. Precautions include lightweight polystyrene fill, wick drains and cutoff walls that keep groundwater out.

soil-water-257.title: Legacy sediment: the buried record of human erosion
soil-water-257.text: Human-caused soil erosion has raised river sediment transport by 2.3 (± 0.6) billion metric tons a year. Reservoirs, meanwhile, cut delivery to the coasts by 1.4 (± 0.3) billion tons a year. Legacy sediment is sediment laid down because of human activity since the Neolithic. Its sources include land clearance, logging, mining, roads, urban growth and dams. In the eastern US, upland soil eroded from the late 17th to the late 19th centuries buried valley floors and filled mill ponds. Fine sediment can carry trace metals, nutrients and pesticides, and heavy metals may stay toxic in it for decades to centuries.

soil-water-097.title: Armoring river banks with rock, wire and willow
soil-water-097.text: The cheapest way to hold a river bank is also the most laborious: willow or cottonwood cuttings staked in trenches, left to root and grip the soil. River bank protection covers the structural and vegetative measures that keep banks from eroding and failing. Riprap, rock laid to resist erosion, is expensive and can fail but covers large areas. Gabions, stone-filled wire boxes, suit steep banks where flow is too fast for riprap. Retaining walls, sheet piling, lime stabilization and soil-cement are other options. Trees add deep, dense roots, but on steep banks they may fail to hold the toe, and their weight can bring the bank down.

soil-water-069.title: How roots stitch soil to the ground below
soil-water-069.text: Root strength generally reaches only about 1 m (3.3 ft) down, yet most slope failures occur at 1.2–1.5 m (3.9–4.9 ft). Root reinforcement is the strengthening of soil by roots that grow across potential failure planes, act as piles and limit surface erosion. Roots crossing a possible slip plane bind particles and anchor unstable surface soil to deeper stable layers or bedrock. A root stretched across the plane develops a tensile force that passes to the soil through cohesion and friction. Near the surface, fine roots of shrubs and grasses hold soil against sheet wash and overland flow, like a mesh.

soil-water-070.title: How hard a root holds before it lets go
soil-water-070.text: A root resists being pulled out of the ground with a force only a little less than its laboratory tensile strength. Tests on many species and root diameters put that strength at about 5–60 MN/m2. Thicker roots resist more than thinner ones. Unbranched roots fail in tension and slip out with little resistance. Branched roots hold a high force that declines as branches fail, or they break in stepped stages, often at weak points such as branching points, nodes or damage. A root strengthens a slope only with enough embedment and adhesion, so engineers measure its contribution with in situ pull-out tests.

soil-water-068.title: Thirsty plants that help hold slopes
soil-water-068.text: The soil around trees is drier, and drier soil is stronger. Plants draw water out of the soil and transpire it, lowering pore water pressure and offsetting the strength soil loses when wet. The help fades in storms, because plants transpire little in wet weather. Even so, transpiration still makes failure after heavy rain less likely. Studies in Malaysia linked high root length density to low soil water content, higher shear strength, lower permeability and fewer slope failures. Dry weather brings a catch: plants can deepen desiccation cracks that let water reach a slip plane. Shade from their foliage limits that drying and cracking.

soil-water-124.title: Wetlands, where the soil runs out of air
soil-water-124.text: Wetlands grow on every continent except Antarctica, from the Amazon basin and the West Siberian Plain to the Pantanal and the Sundarbans. A wetland is a semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or saturated, permanently or seasonally. Its soils therefore run short of oxygen, the condition traced in {{ref:soil-water-218}}. Wetlands sit between open water and dry land, and their plants' roots are adapted to that oxygen-poor, waterlogged ground. One short definition calls a wetland a community of water-loving plants rooted in the saturated soil described in {{ref:soil-water-119}}. There are four main kinds. {{ref:soil-water-129}} carries herbaceous plants, and {{ref:soil-water-134}} carries woody ones. {{ref:soil-water-121}} and {{ref:soil-water-125}} are both peat-forming. About 60% of the world's wetlands are made of peat. Wetlands can also be sorted by where their water comes from: tides, the mixed tide and river water of estuaries, rivers overflowing their banks, or rain and meltwater. The US Cowardin system names five types: marine, estuarine, riverine, lacustrine and the inland kind in {{ref:soil-water-152}}. US regulations define wetlands as land wet often and long enough to support plants adapted to saturated soil. That kind of soil is part of the legal test. In 2005 the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found wetlands more threatened than any other ecosystem. Since 1971 {{ref:soil-water-262}} has protected those of international importance.

soil-water-136.title: Peatlands, wetlands built from their own dead plants
soil-water-136.text: Peat more than 10 m deep is common in temperate regions, and in the tropics it can pass 25 m. A peatland is a wetland whose soil consists of organic matter from decaying plants, laid down in layers of {{ref:soil-class-070}}. It arises where waterlogging cuts off oxygen, so plant litter only partly decomposes. Ecologists apply the term to any ground with peat at least 30 cm deep, even ground that has been completely drained. Precipitation and temperature mainly control where peat forms. Relief matters too, because flat ground and basins waterlog easily. Where organic matter stays waterlogged, topography, climate, parent material, living things and time together shape the result. Peat usually starts in one of three ways: forest on mineral soil slowly waterlogs, a lake fills in, or peat forms directly on bare ground left by glaciers. As it accumulates, peat lifts the ground above the original topography. Peat also has a high cation-exchange capacity. It swaps cations such as Ca²⁺ for H⁺, so water passing through loses nutrients and its pH falls. Peatlands are therefore acidic unless plenty of groundwater flows in. They cover about 3% of the globe's surface. Around a quarter of that area serves agriculture and forestry, which means ditches to lower the water table.

soil-water-115.title: Landscape ecology, reading land as a patchwork
soil-water-115.text: In 1939 the German geographer Carl Troll used aerial photographs to study how environment and vegetation interact, and coined a word for the work: Landschaftsökologie. Landscape ecology is the science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across a range of landscape scales and spatial patterns. It treats a landscape as an uneven area of interacting patches, from forests, grasslands and lakes to farmland and towns. Traditional ecology often assumes a uniform system. Landscape ecology instead builds on differences across space and time, and its hallmark is the link between pattern, process and scale. By 1980 it was an established discipline, and the International Association for Landscape Ecology was founded in 1982. Its tools are remote sensing, GIS and models. One application estimates how much carbon a region's soils hold from landform, vegetation types and rainfall data. It also draws on the study of how geological formations give a landscape its structure ({{ref:soil-water-295}}). Humans count explicitly as agents that change landscapes, and the field proposes ways to restore degraded ones.

soil-water-119.title: Hydric soil, the ground that drowns
soil-water-119.text: When rain or flooding fills every pore, gas moves through soil some 10,000 times more slowly. Most soils are aerobic. Roots, most microorganisms and animals such as earthworms need oxygen, which travels through the connected pores described in {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. Saturation closes those passages. If anaerobic conditions last long in the growing season, different biological and chemical reactions take over from those of aerobic soils. Saturation that is prolonged and repeated over many years leaves distinctive properties that can be recognized in the field. Soils with them are called hydric soils: soils permanently or seasonally saturated until they turn anaerobic, as in wetlands. They may occupy only a small part of a landscape, yet they keep important soil functions. Their plants often have aerenchyma, internal air spaces that carry oxygen down to the roots. Rich hydric soils line the waterbodies where the wetlands of {{ref:soil-water-134}} and {{ref:soil-water-129}} form. A Gleysol is one kind: a hydric soil saturated by groundwater long enough to develop a characteristic gleyic color pattern.

soil-water-129.title: Marshes, the grassy wetlands at the water's edge
soil-water-129.text: Marsh plants root in wet mud with little oxygen, so many grow aerenchyma, air channels that carry air down to their roots. A marsh is a wetland dominated by herbaceous rather than woody plants. More loosely, the word means any low-lying, seasonally waterlogged ground. In Europe and in farming literature it also covers meadows needing drainage and embanked land. Marshes often edge lakes and streams, a transition between aquatic and land ecosystems. Vegetation sets them apart: {{ref:soil-water-134}} is dominated by trees, while peat-forming wetlands have built up deposits of acidic peat. Marsh pH tends to be neutral to alkaline, unlike the acid conditions under which peat accumulates in rain-fed wetlands. The three main types differ mainly in location and salinity: {{ref:soil-fert-144}}, freshwater tidal marshes, and the inland kind in {{ref:soil-water-146}}. The salty type flourishes on sheltered, tide-washed coasts where sediment builds up faster than the land sinks. Marshes hold 0.1% of global sequestered land carbon. Most natural marshland is threatened by sea level rise and the erosion it brings.

soil-water-134.title: Swamps, where trees stand in water
soil-water-134.text: The largest swamp on Earth spreads across the ground the Amazon River floods. Other giants line the Mississippi and the Congo. A swamp is a forested wetland, with saturated soils or standing water dominated by woody plants that tolerate water. It is a transition zone shaped by both land and water, and its water may be fresh, brackish or seawater. Freshwater swamps form along large rivers or lakes, and rain and seasonal floods drive their natural swings in water level. Saltwater swamps line tropical and subtropical coasts. Slow-moving water feeds them from precipitation, groundwater, tides and freshwater floods. That hydrology controls their chemistry, including oxygen, nutrients, pH and toxicity. As water moves through, the swamp filters out nutrients, sediment and pollutants, and excess chemicals end up buried in the bottom sediment. The two main types are true swamps, or swamp forests, and the transitional kind in {{ref:soil-water-148}}. Some swamps are peatlands, such as {{ref:soil-water-267}}. Swamps have higher pH and more available nutrients than the rain-fed peat wetlands of {{ref:soil-water-121}}.

soil-fert-144.title: Salt marshes, built by plants that trap mud
soil-fert-144.text: A salt marsh begins as a bare tidal flat. Sediment settles until plants can colonize it, and the plants then trap and bind still more. The result is a tidal wetland in the upper intertidal zone, regularly flooded by seawater or brackish water and dominated by salt-tolerant halophytes. Heavy sedimentation and abundant organic matter keep its sediments reliably anoxic, an ideal home for sulfate-reducing bacteria. Bacteria and fungi drive nutrient cycling by remineralizing organic matter, and bacteria degrade up to 88% of the lignocellulose. Nitrifiers such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrosospira, and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, are common in the mud.

soil-water-264.title: Floodplains, where rivers lay down new land
soil-water-264.text: A floodplain holds far more sediment than the river that feeds it carries. It is the land beside a river, from the channel banks to the valley sides, that floods when discharge is high. Its soils are flood-laid clays, silts, sands and gravels, the {{ref:soil-form-112}} that regular floods refresh with nutrients. The Nile and Mississippi basins farm their floodplains heavily. Most floodplains grow sideways: point bars build on the insides of meanders while the outer bank erodes, a process called lateral accretion. They also grow upward. On undisturbed rivers, water spills over the banks every one to two years and leaves a thin veneer of sediment, coarsest and thickest by the channel. This is vertical accretion. Most sand drops on natural levees beside the channel, while silt and clay settle farther out as floodplain mud. Every 10–1000 years a river may abandon its channel belt and build a new one elsewhere, a process called avulsion. An abandoned floodplain may survive as a raised step beside the valley. Draining floodplains or narrowing them with levees weakens their flood control, so floods become more severe.

soil-water-145.title: Ombrotrophic, living on rain alone
soil-water-145.text: The word means 'cloud-fed', from the Greek ómbros, rain, and trophē, food. Ombrotrophic soils or vegetation get all their water and nutrients from precipitation, not from streams or springs. Such sites are cut off hydrologically from the surrounding landscape. Rain is acidic and very low in nutrients, so they host organisms that tolerate acid, nutrient-poor conditions. Climate runs the system: precipitation supplies water and nutrients, and temperature sets how fast water evaporates. The effect can override even nutrient-rich rock. In high-rainfall areas, limestone boulders may be capped by acidic peat vegetation. The rain-fed wetlands of {{ref:soil-water-121}} rely solely on precipitation and atmospheric dust, though their slowly decaying peat releases some zinc, copper and manganese. Mercury and lead stay put in their peat, so they keep a record of past mercury deposition. High nitrogen deposition in Europe has shifted their plants toward more vascular growth and less Sphagnum, the moss that holds moisture and nutrients and aids carbon storage.

soil-water-121.title: Bogs, the acid wetlands that keep their dead
soil-water-121.text: Bodies buried in bogs thousands of years ago have come out preserved, because low oxygen, high acidity and tannic acids hold back decay. A bog is a wetland that accumulates peat, a deposit of dead plant material, often sphagnum moss. It is one of the four main wetland types, and its peat is typically over 30 centimetres thick. Bogs take most of their water and nutrients from precipitation, as {{ref:soil-water-145}} explains, so they are nutrient-poor and strongly acidic. Unlike {{ref:soil-water-125}}, they get little mineral-rich ground or surface water. Rain lacks the calcium, magnesium and carbonate that would buffer the acidity of carbon dioxide from the air. Plants grow slowly, but decay is slower still in the oxygen-poor, saturated soil. So peat piles up, sometimes many metres deep. Most bogs form in cooler northern climates in poorly draining lake basins. Quaking bogs are floating sphagnum mats about half a metre thick, anchored by sedges, that move underfoot. Undisturbed bogs take up and store carbon. Once the peat is extracted, the wetland is hard to restore, because peat accumulates slowly.

soil-water-139.title: Muskeg, the northern peat that swallows machines
soil-water-139.text: Heavy equipment has sunk into muskeg when the frozen ground thawed in spring. Muskeg is a peat-forming ecosystem of northern, mostly Arctic and boreal climates, roughly the same thing as a bog or peatland. The term is standard in Canada and Alaska and comes from the Cree maskēk, 'low-lying marsh'. It forms where permafrost, clay or bedrock blocks drainage so that rain and snowmelt collect, and it needs abundant rain and cool summers. Low oxygen and cool temperatures hold back bacteria and fungi, so plant debris decays slowly and builds up as peat. Sphagnum holds fifteen to thirty times its own weight in water, so muskeg can form even on slopes, and it can exceed 30 metres deep. Wet, acidic and relatively infertile, with the water table near the surface, it cannot grow large trees. Uncleared muskeg buckles when it freezes, so people cross it on log corduroy roads or cheaper winter ice roads.

soil-water-144.title: Polders, land held dry behind dikes
soil-water-144.text: The Dutch have turned wet ground into some 3,000 polders, and as much as 20% of the Netherlands has at some time been reclaimed from the sea. A polder is a low-lying tract enclosed by dikes, an artificial hydrological unit. It may be reclaimed lake bed or seabed, a floodplain cut off by a dike, or a marsh diked and then drained. Water keeps arriving through seepage, rainfall, rivers and canals, so it must be pumped out or let out through sluices at low tide. Drained ground subsides, and peat polders sink as their peat decomposes in air. Eventually every polder lies below the surrounding water some or all of the time.

soil-water-143.title: Slumps, when a hillside slides and tips back
soil-water-143.text: After heavy rain a hillside can let go as a single block. A slump is a form of {{ref:soil-water-053}} in which a coherent mass of loosely consolidated material or rock moves a short distance down a slope. Rain both lubricates the material and adds to its weight, which is why slumps often follow storms. In a rotational slump the block slides on a concave-upward surface and rotates backward, so its original surface becomes less steep. Translational slumps move on planes such as joints or bedding, especially where a permeable layer lies over an impermeable one. A cliff-like scarp marks where the mass broke away. Back-tilted block tops can hold ponds or swampy ground, and uneven ridges form near the toe. Earthquakes, thorough wetting, freezing and thawing, undercutting and loading can all set one off. A common trigger is removing the slope's base by stream or wave erosion or by road building. Speeds range from metres per second to metres per year. Sudden slumps may stabilize within hours, but most take months or years. Added water and lost cohesion at the toe can turn slumping material into an earthflow. On steep hillsides slumps often follow fracture zones in clay, and much stream-bank erosion happens as weakened banks fail in large slumps.

soil-water-147.title: Minerotrophic, fed by water that has touched rock
soil-water-147.text: Water that has seeped through rock arrives carrying a load. Minerotrophic environments get their nutrients mainly from such groundwater, flowing through mineral-rich soil or rock, or from surface water flowing over land. Its dissolved chemicals raise nutrient levels and reduce acidity. Where they include bases such as calcium or magnesium ions, the water is called base-rich, in the sense of {{ref:soil-chem-054}}, and is neutral or alkaline. The peat wetland of {{ref:soil-water-125}} is often minerotrophic, especially in its richer forms, while bogs and its poorest forms are often ombrotrophic. Marshes and swamps may also be partly fed by groundwater. The ions a wetland's water brings set its pH, conductivity and nutrient levels. These differ between sites where groundwater discharges and sites where it recharges, and they change with seasonal groundwater levels. Geology, soil type and surface form shape a wetland too. A steady groundwater supply supports diverse plants. It also lets peat accumulate, provided the water does not flow too fast. The terms minerogenous and geogenous often serve as synonyms, though they refer mainly to hydrology, and minerotrophic to nutrients.

soil-water-125.title: Fens, the peat wetlands fed from below
soil-water-125.text: Fens tend to lie over calcium-rich rocks such as limestone, and the rock shows in their water. A fen is a peat-accumulating wetland fed by mineral-rich ground or surface water. It is one of the main wetland types alongside marshes, swamps and bogs, and fens and bogs, both peat-forming, are grouped together as {{ref:soil-water-137}}. That water input gives fens higher mineral concentrations and a more basic pH than bogs. The chemistry of the groundwater, set by the rocks it passes through, controls the pH. The water table sits at or near the surface, so fen soils stay inundated, and oxygen diffuses in so slowly that they are anaerobic. An estimated 1.1 million square kilometres of fen exist worldwide. As peat builds up it can cut off the groundwater, so a fen turns rain-fed and more acidic and may become a bog. Draining a fen dries and aerates the peat, which then decomposes or even burns. Whether fens are net sinks or net sources of greenhouse gases is still disputed, because microbes in their oxygen-free soils produce methane.

soil-water-263.title: Riparian zones, the living edge of a stream
soil-water-263.text: Thin the plants along a stream and its water grows warmer and swings more in temperature. The riparian zone is the strip of land where a river or stream meets the land around it. Its water-loving plants matter for conserving soil, for biodiversity and the health of aquatic ecosystems. The zone acts as a natural biofilter, shielding the water from excess sediment, polluted surface runoff and erosion. Meanders, plants and roots slow the water, reducing soil erosion and flood damage, and trapped sediment replenishes soils and builds banks. The zone also lowers nitrate from manure and fertilizer in runoff, largely by denitrification, and wet riparian zones remove it especially fast. Where streamside ground holds standing water or saturated soil for a season, it is normally called a wetland because of its hydric soils. Zones damaged by building, farming or forestry are usually restored through erosion control and replanting.

soil-water-146.title: Freshwater marshes and their dark, slow-rotting soils
soil-water-146.text: Black or brown, wet and rich in organic matter: that is the soil of a freshwater marsh. Such a marsh is non-forested, with shallow fresh water that floods it continuously or often. It usually lies near a river mouth, along a lake, or in poorly drained low ground such as an abandoned oxbow lake. Most of its water comes from the surface. Its soils are hydric, saturated in the growing season. Decomposition is slow, so organic matter builds up. Microbes use up the oxygen, and anaerobic processes then accumulate or deplete reduced iron and other minerals, giving the soils a distinctive morphology. Types include river, lake, tidal freshwater and depressional marshes, the last often fed by springs or seepage.

soil-water-126.title: From bog to rich fen, a gradient set by calcium
soil-water-126.text: In wetland science, 'rich' and 'poor' count species, not money. Species richness depends strongly on pH and on calcium and bicarbonate concentrations. Bogs and fens line up along a gradient: bogs at the poor end, extremely rich fens at the rich end, and poor fens between. Rich fens are strongly minerotrophic, fed by water dominated by calcium and bicarbonate, and run neutral to slightly acidic, about pH 7 to 5. Groundwater passing limestone dissolves some calcium carbonate. The bicarbonate it produces buffers the fen and keeps its pH relatively stable. In extreme rich fens, often pH 7 or above, calcium carbonate settles out as marl when plants or the atmosphere draw down dissolved carbon dioxide. Rich does not always mean productive, though: at high concentrations calcium binds phosphate. Poor fens, about pH 5.5 to 4, have thicker peat that cuts plants off from the mineral soil below and weakens groundwater buffering. They also form where groundwater flows through weakly buffering sediments such as sand. Sphagnum mosses acidify fens, and their spread can turn a rich fen into a poor one.

soil-water-127.title: How wetland soils pass nutrients between two worlds
soil-water-127.text: Most wetland soils come in two layers. A thin oxygenated layer sits over a reduced one, and microbes adapted to each oxidize and reduce nutrients as they cycle between them. Wetland nutrient cycling is the movement of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements through soils at this boundary, driven by the chemistry of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. The reduced layer hosts denitrification, the reduction of manganese, iron and sulfate, and methanogenesis. Organic carbon has three fates: it is respired to CO2, buried as peat or decomposed to methane. Peat builds up where plant production exceeds decomposition. Methanogenic archaea in anaerobic peat make methane from CO2 and hydrogen, and sedge and brown-moss fens emit more of it than sphagnum bogs. Nitrogen shuttles between the layers. Ammonium from anaerobic decay diffuses up and is nitrified in the oxidized layer. The nitrate diffuses back down and is denitrified to nitrogen gas and some nitrous oxide. Nitrogen and phosphorus limit wetland fertility, and almost all phosphorus arrives in sediment or plant litter from other ecosystems. Iron can bind phosphate to toxic levels, but peat supplies organic anions that iron binds instead. Because wetlands are hotspots and sinks for these transformations, they can be built on purpose to treat nutrient-rich water.

soil-water-122.title: Raised bogs, domes of peat that outgrow the groundwater
soil-water-122.text: European raised bogs have been growing for about 11,000 years, roughly a millimetre a year. A raised bog is an acidic, mineral-poor bog fed only by precipitation, its peat risen into a dome above the groundwater. Many begin as fens. Lack of oxygen and high acidity stop decay, peat builds up, and the bog rises above the groundwater until rain alone feeds it. Rootless peat mosses grow upward while their lower layers turn to peat. A living upper acrotelm, where new organic matter forms, lies over the saturated, less active catotelm, and light white peat lies over well-humified black peat. Growth needs precipitation that exceeds losses to discharge and evaporation and falls evenly through the year. The dome is typically a few metres high, often fringed by fen where groundwater seeps in at the edges or along streams. Peat cutting and mineral pollution from farms and industry badly threaten raised bogs. Their last great regions are in western Siberia and Canada.

soil-water-149.title: Paludification, how dry forest turns to peatland
soil-water-149.text: Most boreal peatlands did not begin in a lake. They crept over dry land. Paludification is the build-up of peat on previously drier, vegetated mineral soil, turning forest, grassland or bare land into peatland. Organic soil starts and thickens over inorganic soil with no fully aquatic phase. Peat can also start as a lake fills in, but paludification is the most common route in the boreal zone. It requires a wet water balance in the growing season, with precipitation exceeding evapotranspiration plus runoff. Climate, geomorphology, geology and soils usually control that balance, though local peat accumulation alone can also drive the process. Tree removal, forest fires, natural or human-caused, more precipitation and podzolization can all tip the balance. Flat, low-slope ground helps, as in the world's two largest peatlands, the West Siberian Plain and the Hudson/James Bay Lowlands. Heavy clay acts as an impermeable floor that lets water collect, and surface water from melting permafrost can speed things up. Once under way in boreal forest, paludification lowers soil temperature, aeration, nutrient availability and decomposition rates. It can even lead to new permafrost.

soil-water-138.title: Peatlands, the largest carbon store on land
soil-water-138.text: Peatlands cover just 3% of Earth's land, yet they hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon. That is over half the amount in the atmosphere, and it makes them the largest natural carbon store on land. Plants take in CO2 at the surface, while living plants and decaying peat respire some back out. The water table is the main control. A high one submerges peat and slows respiration. A falling one, as in drought, speeds aerobic decomposition and CO2 release. Water level also sets the size of two zones: methane-making microbes in the anoxic peat below, and methane-oxidizing ones above. In one Alaskan study, methane flux varied by as much as 300% between seasons. Natural peat-forming wetlands are a small CO2 sink but generally net emitters of methane and nitrous oxide. Over millennia they have still had a net cooling effect. Draining one lets oxygen into the peat, and a store that was taking up carbon becomes a net emitter. Northern peatlands built up mostly in the Holocene, after the Pleistocene glaciers retreated. Estimates of their carbon vary widely, from 415 Gt to 1055 Gt.

soil-water-132.title: Prairie potholes, the ponds the glaciers left
soil-water-132.text: Glaciers once covered the plains of northern North America, and they left shallow depressions behind in great numbers. Each spring those hollows fill with water. A prairie pothole is a marsh in one of them. Some hold water only for a season, while others stay wet all year. Small as they are, such wetlands can contribute significantly to recharging regional groundwater. They are also important breeding habitat for many species of waterfowl.

soil-water-131.title: Vernal pools, ponds that vanish by summer
soil-water-131.text: No fish live in a vernal pool, which is why many amphibians breed there in spring. A vernal pool is a seasonal marsh in a shallow depression that holds water in winter and spring and may be completely dry by summer and fall.
