It forms where an impermeable or very slowly permeable layer, such as a duripan, claypan or lava flow, underlies a small hollow and perches the water table. It drains only internally, cut off from perennial inflow, yet holds ponded water at least briefly in most years. In California such pools often fill the hollows between {{ref:soil-water-133}}, on old, strongly developed soils.

soil-water-130.title: Wet meadows, flooded often yet dry in summer
soil-water-130.text: Wet meadows often hold very high plant diversity and dense stores of buried seeds. A wet meadow is a freshwater marsh that floods regularly but is often dry in summer. It occupies shallow lake basins, low-lying depressions, the ground between shallow marshes and uplands, and the edges of large lakes and rivers. As it matures, decomposing vegetation thickens the soil into raised mounds above the water. Shrubs and small trees take root there, a route toward {{ref:soil-water-148}}.

soil-water-266.title: Palsas, peat mounds with frozen hearts
soil-water-266.text: A palsa can reach 150 m (490 ft) across and 12 m (39 ft) high, its steep slopes rising above the surrounding peatland. It is a peat mound with a permanently frozen core of peat and mineral soil, typical of peatlands in the zone of discontinuous permafrost. It starts where thin snow lets frost go deeper. An ice lens grows by drawing in water and lifts the surface by frost heave, which lets the cold reach deeper still. Wet or frozen peat lets cold in during winter, while dry surface peat insulates it in summer. So palsas survive where the mean annual temperature is just below freezing. Warming thaws the frozen peat and thickens the {{ref:soil-env-146}}. The peatland grows wetter, and its methane emissions rise.

soil-water-262.title: The Ramsar Convention, a treaty for wetlands
soil-water-262.text: On 2 February 1971, at Ramsar in Iran, countries signed a treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. Also called the Convention on Wetlands, it came into force on 21 December 1975 and has 172 parties. Its definition is broad: marsh, fen, peatland or water, natural or artificial, fresh, brackish or salt, including sea no deeper than six metres at low tide. In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres. The United Kingdom has the most, 175. Every 2 February is World Wetlands Day, first celebrated in 1997. National follow-through on the treaty is often half-hearted.

soil-fert-198.title: Land loss, when coasts become open water
soil-fert-198.text: The deltas of the Danube, Ganges, Mississippi, Nile and Yellow rivers have all suffered significant land loss. Land loss is the conversion of coastal land to open water by natural processes and human activities. It is broader than coastal erosion. It also covers land lost around estuaries, bays and lakes, and land that vanishes as coastal wetlands subside. Its main causes are coastal erosion, too little sediment supply, subsidence and sea level rise.

soil-water-140.title: The Börde, Germany's black-earth plains
soil-water-140.text: Some of the best soils in Germany lie on its Börden, large, flat, nearly treeless plains of fertile loess. A Börde, a 'fertile plain', is a loess-covered lowland in North Germany, particularly important for arable farming. The Börden stretch from the North German geest to the edge of the Central Uplands. Their loess, laid down mainly by east winds and up to 10 metres thick, evens out the relief. Under a (sub-)oceanic climate it has been largely decalcified and turned to loam. The northern edge of the loess marks a boundary of soil, vegetation and settlement.

soil-water-117.title: Patches, corridors and the landscape mosaic
soil-water-117.text: Seen from above, a landscape is a patchwork. A patch is a relatively uniform area that differs from its surroundings, and patches are a landscape's basic units. They change and fluctuate in a process called patch dynamics. The matrix is the well-connected background they sit in. Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides, and linked corridors form a network. Patches, corridors and matrix together make up the mosaic. Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is. Repeated clearing beyond a critical level breaks continuous cover into isolated patches, so landscapes show a connected and a disconnected phase.

soil-water-118.title: Ecotones, where one community shades into another
soil-water-118.text: A lakeshore is an ecotone, and so is the edge of a field cleared from forest. An ecotone is a transitional zone between two communities, one kind of boundary between landscape patches. Forest giving way to marshland is a classic example, and so is the riparian zone along a stream. An ecotone keeps traits of both neighboring communities and often holds species found in neither. An ecocline is different: a gradual, continuous change in environmental conditions across an ecosystem or community. An ecotope is the smallest ecologically distinct unit used to map and classify landscapes.

soil-water-116.title: Spatial heterogeneity, why unevenness matters
soil-water-116.text: One idea sets landscape ecology apart from other branches of ecology: unevenness. Spatial heterogeneity is the uneven distribution of objects across a landscape, a measure of how its parts differ. Composition is the number and relative abundance of patch types, such as the amount of forest or wetland. Structure adds how those patches are arranged and proportioned. Scale, another main concept, has two meanings: the ratio of map to ground distance, and the extent or resolution of an object or process in space or time. The landscape stability principle holds that structural heterogeneity helps a landscape resist and recover from disturbance.

soil-water-123.title: Blanket bogs, peat draped over the hills
soil-water-123.text: Where rain falls on more than about 235 days a year, peat no longer keeps to the hollows. Blanket bog is peatland that forms where high rainfall and low evapotranspiration let peat cover broad stretches of rolling ground. The rain keeps the surface waterlogged much of the time. Blanket bog is commonest on acidic substrates, but it can form on neutral or even alkaline ones where acidic rainwater outweighs groundwater. It is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere, well studied in Ireland and Scotland, and covers vast areas of North American tundra. It is less developed in the Southern Hemisphere. In parts of Europe its spread is traced to forest clearance by prehistoric peoples.

soil-water-260.title: Constructed wetlands, built to clean dirty water
soil-water-260.text: The East Kolkata Wetlands, a natural system covering 125 square kilometres, treat Kolkata's sewage, and its nutrients feed fish farms and crops. A constructed wetland does that work by design: it is an artificial wetland built to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater. Plants, soil and organisms give secondary treatment, removing suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen and phosphorus through the processes in {{ref:soil-water-127}}. Like natural wetlands, it filters out pathogens and heavy metals, and subsurface-flow designs remove more pathogens than surface ones. Such wetlands are also built to reclaim mined land or to make up for wetlands lost to development.

soil-water-128.title: The services wetlands give for nothing
soil-water-128.text: Replacing what wetlands do would take huge spending on water treatment plants, dams and levees, and many of their services cannot be replaced at all. Wetland ecosystem services are the benefits wetlands give society. Their plants take up and store nutrients from runoff and remove nitrate. They slow the water, so sediment settles out with any heavy metals it carries. Floodplains act as natural reservoirs, spreading floodwater wide to cut its depth and speed, while headwater wetlands slow runoff and snowmelt. Peat-forming wetlands lock away large quantities of carbon that would otherwise reach the atmosphere as CO2.

soil-water-261.title: Wetlands, the largest natural source of methane
soil-water-261.text: Wetlands supply about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average about 161 Tg a year, more than any other natural source. Wetland greenhouse gas emissions are the release of methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from wetland soils. In warm, wet soil, microbes use up oxygen faster than it diffuses in. That creates the anaerobic conditions that the microbes of {{ref:soil-chem-129}} need, and warmth and organic-rich soil boost methane output further. Draining peat exposes carbon stored for thousands of years to air, where it decomposes to CO2. Peatlands cover 3% of land, yet their degradation gives 7% of all CO2 emissions. Some wetlands emit nitrous oxide, with 300 times the warming potential of CO2, though wetlands can also act as greenhouse gas sinks.

soil-water-259.title: Wetland hydrology, the water that makes a wetland
soil-water-259.text: Water, more than anything else, makes a wetland. Wetland hydrology is the flow, storage and chemistry of surface and ground water in a wetland. Water arrives as precipitation, surface water and groundwater. It leaves by evapotranspiration, surface flow, tides and subsurface outflow, and the balance sets the hydroperiod. How long flooding or saturation lasts decides whether a site carries aquatic, marsh or swamp vegetation. Most wetlands are minerotrophic, but ombrotrophic bogs fed only by precipitation have water low in minerals. Fens range from acidic to alkaline and calcium-rich. Wetlands can recharge groundwater when the surrounding water table is low and discharge it when the table is high.

soil-water-135.title: Wetland loss, draining and filling the wet ground
soil-water-135.text: Since 1900 the world's wetlands have shrunk by as much as 50%, and by 90% in some parts of the world. Wetland loss is the draining, filling and conversion of wetlands for agriculture, building and other uses. Europe has likely lost nearly half of its wetlands. More than 50% of its original peat-forming wetland area, once over 300,000 km², has gone to drainage for farming and forestry and to peat harvesting. Settlements built on drained wetlands then face subsidence and rising flood risk, as in the Mississippi delta around New Orleans. Restoration often begins by plugging drainage ditches, removing levees or returning channelized rivers to their natural course so that they flood again.

soil-water-267.title: Peat swamp forests, tropical vaults of carbon
soil-water-267.text: From 1996, Indonesia's Mega Rice Project drained over 1 million hectares of peat forest on Borneo. A peat swamp forest is a tropical moist forest on waterlogged soil. Dead leaves and wood never fully decay there, so a thick layer of acidic peat builds up. It holds far more carbon than forest on mineral soil, among the largest near-surface stores of organic carbon on land. Its peat starts on river-fed deltas, floodplains or oxbow lakes. It then domes up to 4 m on coasts or 18 m inland and turns rain-fed. About 62% of tropical peatland lies in the Indomalayan realm, 80% of it in Indonesia, and 36% lies in Africa's central Congo Basin. Peat fires, drainage and clearing release the stored carbon as CO2.

soil-water-148.title: Shrub swamps, caught between marsh and forest
soil-water-148.text: A shrub swamp is too wet to become swamp forest but too dry or shallow to become marsh. It is a freshwater wetland dominated by shrubs, and some classifications require at least 50% shrub cover and less than 20% tree cover. It often follows floods, cutting, fire or windstorms in a forested swamp, or develops from drained meadows and fens. Its water comes from runoff, streams and rivers and moves in and out through the year. So it is drier than wet meadows or forested swamps, and less water-tolerant plants grow on raised mounds. It typically sits on organic soils such as muck and shallow peat.

soil-water-137.title: Mires, peatlands still at work
soil-water-137.text: A drained peatland may keep its peat, yet it is no longer a mire. A mire is a peatland that is still actively forming peat, and once new peat stops forming, the name no longer fits. There are two types. Bogs rise above their surroundings and are fed only by precipitation. Fens lie on slopes, flats or in depressions, fed by groundwater or the surrounding mineral soil. All mires begin as fens and may become bogs once the peat rises above the land around them. Some swamps are peatlands too, but marshes, whose plants root in mineral soil, generally are not.

soil-phys-162.title: Flarks, the wet hollows between bog ridges
soil-phys-162.text: Many bogs are ribbed, with parallel hollows separated by ridges called strings. Each hollow is a flark, a depression within a bog. Early theories blamed frost heaving, but flarks have since been found where frost heaving does not occur. They are now thought to form when thickening peat slides downslope under its own weight and tears away below obstructions in the terrain beneath. Another theory ties them to patches of the bog that decay faster.

soil-water-152.title: Palustrine wetlands, the inland freshwater catch-all
soil-water-152.text: Marshes, swamps, bogs and fens can all share one label in US wetland classification. A palustrine wetland is any inland, non-tidal wetland whose ocean-derived salts stay below 0.5 parts per thousand. The category takes in inland marshes and swamps as well as bogs, fens, pocosins, tundra and floodplains. It is one of five systems in the Cowardin classification of the US Fish and Wildlife Service, beside marine, estuarine, riverine and lacustrine wetlands. Its vegetation classes are aquatic bed, emergent, scrub-shrub and forested, with woody plants 20 feet tall dividing the last two. Its depressional marshes sit in isolated hollows or on hill slopes, and include vernal pools, playas and prairie potholes.

soil-water-265.title: Floodplain soils, swinging between flood and air
soil-water-265.text: A floodplain's soils change with small steps in elevation, and higher ground farther from the river holds more oxygen. These soils stay aerated between floods. If floodwater stands long enough, though, a saturated soil can run out of oxygen. Its microbes then alternate between aerobic and anaerobic activity, which affects fine-root growth. Floodplains buffer phosphorus strongly, keeping it from reaching the river, especially when they stay connected to the stream. Wet–dry cycles shift redox state, pH and minerals, so formerly flooded soils that dry out hold phosphorus more tightly.

soil-water-120.title: When hydric soil became a legal term
soil-water-120.text: In US federal law, a hydric soil is one that, undrained, is saturated, flooded or ponded long enough in the growing season to turn anaerobic. Such soil supports water-loving vegetation. The term is part of the legal definition of a wetland in the Food Security Act of 1985. The agency in {{ref:soil-hist-050}} uses it to administer that act's 'Swampbuster' provisions. The National Technical Committee for Hydric Soils defines it as soil formed under saturation, flooding or ponding long enough to turn its upper part anaerobic. The Army Corps of Engineers and the Environmental Protection Agency use that definition for Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (1972).

soil-water-142.title: Suffosion, soil that drains away into rock
soil-water-142.text: Most sinkholes do not form when a cave roof gives way. They form by suffosion, the washing of loose soil or sediment down through fissures in the rock beneath. It happens where loose soil, loess or other non-cohesive material lies over limestone with fissures and joints. Rain and surface water carry the material into caves below, leaving a depression at the surface. Suffosion sinkholes are usually linked to karst, though they can form in chalk, gypsum and basalt. Suffosion collapses soil structure, losing both mass and volume as coarse grains lose contact. Suffusion, by contrast, removes fines from between coarse grains that stay in contact, with no change in volume.

soil-water-150.title: String bogs, ribbed peatlands of the cold north
soil-water-150.text: Low ridges 2–3 m wide and under 1 m high run across a string bog at right angles to the flow of water, with wet pools between them. A string bog alternates such slightly raised ridges and islands, carrying woody plants, with flat, wet sedge mats. It lies on gently sloping ground. Its water and its peat, over 1 m thick, are very low in nutrients, because the water drains from other ombrotrophic wetlands. String bogs are a patterned form of blanket bog in periglacial climates. There the {{ref:soil-env-146}} stays frozen for long periods and thaws in spring. They are also called aapa mires, from the Finnish, or Strangmoor, from the German.

soil-water-151.title: Hummocks, small mounds with many origins
soil-water-151.text: A hummock is a small knoll or mound above the surrounding ground, usually under 15 metres high and found in groups or fields. Hummocks form in several ways. In raised bogs such as string bogs, they are low ridges of drier peat moss alternating with shallow wet hollows called flarks. Swamp hummocks usually start as moss-covered fallen trunks or branches rising above the swamp floor. Earth hummocks form in permafrost and seasonally frozen ground, usually in moist, fine-grained soils of low relief, and differential frost heave is the most widely accepted explanation. Inside, the profile is often churned and streaked with organic matter to about the hummock's own height, a form of cryoturbation.

soil-water-133.title: Mima mounds, an unsolved puzzle in the grass
soil-water-133.text: Mima mounds can stud the ground at more than 50 per hectare. They are low, flattened, circular to oval natural mounds of loose, unlayered, often gravelly sediment that form an overthickened A horizon. They span 3 m to more than 50 m across and stand 30 cm to over 2 m high. How they form is still disputed, and no one has shown that all such mounds share one cause. Proposed origins include burrowing pocket gophers, wind-blown sediment caught around plants, earthquake shaking, and shrink–swell clays as in gilgai. Tracer studies showed gophers pushing soil toward mound centres, though they may only maintain existing mounds. In California they sit on stable landforms over 100,000 years old, where a claypan or duripan perches water into vernal pools between them.

soil-water-141.title: Soil-surface roughness, from grains to hillsides
soil-water-141.text: Rain usually smooths a rough soil surface, but on a smooth one it can do the opposite. Soil-surface roughness is the vertical variation in the micro- and macro-relief of a soil surface, together with its statistical distribution. Four classes are recognized by vertical scale. Grain-to-aggregate microrelief spans 0.053–2.0 mm, clods 2–100 mm, and roughness oriented by cultivation 100–300 mm. The fourth is macro-scale topographic curvature. The first two make up microroughness, which rainfall changes over single events and {{ref:soil-agri-095}} over seasons. It is usually measured as Random Roughness, the standard deviation of surface heights about the mean, corrected for slope and for the plow's effects. On surfaces with an initial microroughness of about 0–5 mm, rainfall can raise it considerably.

soil-form-172.title: Hydrolysis: how water cracks minerals open
soil-form-172.text: Water does more than wet a mineral; it can break it. Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds. One fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide. It is the reverse of condensation, which joins molecules by removing water. The lab manual says all minerals weather this way, and that hydrolysis is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals. In one example, orthoclase and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-. This is a main route of {{ref:soil-found-058}}. Hydrolysis also drives soil chemistry. Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids: trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with a pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly. In acid sulfate soils, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as jarosite release H+ this way. In alkali soils the carbonate anion hydrolyses to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH. The enzyme urease catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea, and highly alkaline soils, pH about 8.2 or higher, increase it.

soil-form-158.title: How a soil changes as it grows old
soil-form-158.text: A soil has an age, and it shows. Parent material has no horizons. A young soil, about 10 to 1,000 years old, has a slight profile. A mature soil, 1,000 to 10,000 years, has a well-developed one, and an old soil, 10,000 to 100,000 years, an extensive one. Typical profiles run C R, then A C R, then O A Bt C R, then O A E Bs C R. The chemistry changes too. In a young soil humus accumulates and carbonates leach. In a mature soil humus peaks and clays leach, with maximum illuviation. In an old soil humus declines, carbonates are gone and the surface is very acidic. Crop productivity follows: low to moderate in young soil, maximal in mature soil and low in old soil. Once vegetation grew, nitrogen entered from rain and from lichens, algae and legumes, and organic matter built a dark A horizon as rain leached calcium and magnesium carbonates. Where soils stay highly calcareous, the lime limits clay leaching and slows development. On permeable material, clay moved from the A into the B and formed an argillic horizon. This is {{ref:soil-form-047}} at work.

soil-form-155.title: Four ways soils gain, lose, change and move material
soil-form-155.text: What makes soil different from a layer of sediment? Four groups of processes, through which the {{ref:soil-form-043}} work: additions, losses, transformations and translocations. How far they have gone helps tell soils apart. Additions include organic matter, fertilizers, dust and other mineral soil arriving. Losses are soil moved away by wind or water, or chemical compounds leached, eroded or harvested. Transformations are the chemical or physical weathering of particles or components. Weathering releases ions from minerals or turns them into secondary minerals, which may reform deeper in the soil; ions lost altogether are leached. Translocations are movements of organic or mineral components between horizons. Eluviation removes material from a horizon and illuviation deposits it; clay, and iron and aluminium organic complexes, move down with soil water. Mixing, or turbation, is also a transfer, caused by organisms or by physical agents such as clay shrink-swell and freeze-thaw.

soil-form-159.title: Reading runoff from slope and texture
soil-form-159.text: How fast will rain run off a field? Percent slope is rise over run times 100, read directly with an Abney level or clinometer held parallel to the slope. Runoff rises with slope and falls with infiltration rate. Granular, porous soils shed less water than massive, low-porosity ones, because more water infiltrates. A moister soil saturates sooner and so runs off sooner, while plant cover intercepts raindrops and reduces erosion. In the field table, slopes of 0-1% give very slow runoff for all textures, 6-12% gives rapid runoff for loams but very rapid for clays, and over 18% is very rapid for all textures.

soil-form-156.title: From summit to toeslope: positions on a hillside
soil-form-156.text: A hillside is not one soil but a sequence. The summit is the level top of an upland feature, and the shoulder is the convex, erosional edge leading to the backslope. The backslope is the steepest part, shaped mainly by mass wasting and running water. Below it, the footslope is gently inclined and concave, where colluvium and alluvium accumulate, and the toeslope is a constructional surface where alluvium collects. Beyond lies a flood plain, built of sediment deposited during floods, and a stream terrace is a level strip of an abandoned one. This is {{ref:soil-form-045}} made concrete.

soil-form-157.title: Effective precipitation: why wetter and cooler leaches more
soil-form-157.text: Rainfall alone does not decide how leached a soil is. Precipitation and temperature together set how much water moves down through it. Leaching, described in {{ref:soil-form-050}}, moves soluble salts down the profile and can carry suspended clay into the subsoil, deeper with more precipitation. It lowers pH, removes basic cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) and lowers nutrient content, so desert soils are little leached and humid forest soils extensively. Higher temperature raises evapotranspiration, so with equal rainfall the cooler region has more effective precipitation and more leached soils. In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes get less direct sun and so tend to be more weathered, deeper and more leached than warmer, drier south-facing ones. All of this is {{ref:soil-form-044}} in action.

soil-form-160.title: How people change soil
soil-form-160.text: Plow up a forest or grassland and the soil usually loses organic matter; globally about 30% of the original soil organic carbon is lost. Human use transforms soils mainly through land conversion, erosion, mining and construction. Erosion removes the organically enriched surface layer, losing the most fertile soil and sometimes exposing a growth-limiting layer such as a high-sodium one. Where the eroded soil lands, it over-thickens lower slopes and buries the original topsoil under less fertile subsoil, giving a cumulic soil. Soils heavily disrupted by people, as by mining or pipelines, are termed anthropogenic, and reconstructed soils inevitably differ from the original profile. People thus join the {{ref:soil-form-043}}.

soil-form-162.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soil-form-162.text: No other part of Canada has soils as varied as British Columbia and Yukon, thanks to a varied geologic history, rugged terrain and a wide climate range. The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system. Podzols have the largest extent in British Columbia, on acidic parent materials under cool, humid conditions, and Luvisols are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest. Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks, while Chernozems occur only in the arid Central Interior. Regosols mark landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta, and drained Gleysols in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils. Mining leaves Anthroposols; in metal mining the chief concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as pyrite weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

soil-form-166.title: Soils of Ontario
soil-form-166.text: Ontario's soils are young, laid down by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet. The ice retreated northeast, exposing southern Ontario as much as 13,000 years ago and the far north about 8,500 to 6,500 years ago. Three ecozones now dominate. The Hudson Plains (about 25% of Ontario) are cold and semi-arid, with clayey and silty glacio-marine materials over neutral to alkaline limestones. The Boreal Shield (about 66%) lies on acidic, weathering-resistant Precambrian gneiss and granite, and Dystric Brunisols dominate the west. The Mixedwood Plains (about 9%) rest on carbonate-rich limestones, so parent material matters most; they hold the province's most productive farmland and its major cities. The Guelph series, a Brunisolic Gray-Brown Luvisol formed in loam to silt loam moraine, became Ontario's provincial soil in 2015.

soil-form-167.title: Soils of Quebec
soil-form-167.text: Quebec's soils sit in bands from south to north, and there are seven soil orders in them. They formed over the last 6,000 to 10,000 years, after the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated, on parent materials that follow the Canadian Shield, the Appalachians and the sedimentary St. Lawrence valley. Podzols cover 39% of Quebec, Brunisols 17% and Organic soils 8%. Dystric Brunisols can turn into Podzols over several thousand years, as on the North Shore. After glaciation the Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay in the St. Lawrence Lowlands; leaching of the salt and river incision made it unstable, causing over 700 landslides and earthflows. Only a small area has high agricultural potential: Canada Land Inventory Classes 1 to 3 total about 0.28 ha per Quebecer, the smallest of any province, and about 80% of them are cropland, so conserving them matters.

soil-form-169.title: Soils of the Atlantic Provinces
soil-form-169.text: Seven of Canada's ten soil orders occur in Atlantic Canada, but heavy precipitation and coarse, acidic glacial till make Podzols dominant. The soils are often stony or shallow to bedrock, so the four provinces hold only about 1.5% of Canada's farmland, and only Prince Edward Island has more farmland than forest. Four ecozones divide the region. The Atlantic Maritime is warmest, about 7 degrees C with 1250 mm of rain a year, on mostly sedimentary Paleozoic rock. The Taiga Shield and Arctic Cordillera are colder, on Precambrian gneiss and granite with thin till and exposed rock. The Canada Land Inventory finds no Class 1 land here; Class 2 is about 588,000 ha, Class 3 about 2,275,000 ha and Class 4 about 2,507,000 ha, and most of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland is Class 7.

soil-form-163.title: Soils of the Prairie Provinces
soil-form-163.text: In southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, over 80% of the land is agricultural, the most heavily converted in Canada, and the kind of farming follows soil capability. True prairie covers only the southern part. About one-third of the region sits on Canadian Shield rock and two-thirds on sedimentary rock; igneous rock yields acidic sandy, gravelly parent materials, sedimentary rock neutral to alkaline loamy ones. Chernozems dominate the southern grassland, Luvisols the northern mixed forest, Brunisols the acidic Shield and Organic Cryosols the cold, saturated peats near Hudson Bay. The pattern is set by bedrock and by the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera. Crops once centred on spring wheat with summerfallow; today canola, pulses and flax are grown, with continuous cultivation and conservation tillage or no-till. Under the Canada Land Inventory, classes 1 to 4 sustain field crops and classes 5 and 6 suit only forage.

soil-form-165.title: From grassland to forest: the Parkland transition
soil-form-165.text: Walk north from the grassland and the soil changes as tree litter replaces grass as the main organic input. In the transitional Parkland the Ah horizon lightens and begins to bleach, forming an Ahe horizon; these are Dark Gray Chernozems. Further north, in continuous Mixedwood forest, an LFH litter layer sits on the mineral soil over a bleached Ae horizon and a clay-richer Bt horizon, underlain by a carbonate-bearing C horizon. These are Gray Luvisols, which also form on glacio-lacustrine deposits in north-central Manitoba.

soil-form-164.title: Prairie Chernozems and the grasses that made them
soil-form-164.text: Across the Prairies, Chernozemic great groups follow the native grasses, which follow the regional water deficit. They are separated by the color of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added. In the driest part, with an annual water deficit near 200 mm, low grasses with little biomass give Brown Chernozems; less deficit to the west and north gives Dark Brown and Black ones. Organic carbon is highest in southern Manitoba, where the deficit is only about 70 mm. All have organically enriched Ah horizons over decalcified, slightly reddened Bm horizons.

soil-phys-249.title: Soil as solid, liquid and gas
soil-phys-249.text: Soil is never just dirt; it is three things at once. It combines solid, liquid and gas phases, and their interaction determines how it behaves. The solid phase is mineral particles (rocks, gravel, sand, silt, clay) or organic matter, and ideally takes up about 50% of the volume. The liquid phase is soil water plus dissolved nutrients, chemicals and gases, together forming the soil solution; both its quantity and its chemical composition matter. The gaseous phase is soil air, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide. Ideally it is about 25% of volume, but it is highly dynamic. Mass-volume relationships among the three phases define porosity, bulk density and the shares of water and air in pore space.

soil-phys-238.title: Critical state: when soil flows like a frictional fluid
soil-phys-238.text: Critical state soil mechanics is the branch of soil mechanics that models saturated remoulded soils on the critical state concept. At the critical state, stress and strain relate constantly: the soil keeps deforming without any further rise in stress, like a frictional fluid. In practice this marks failure. The concept was published in 1958 by Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth, from Cambridge simple shear tests and Imperial College triaxial tests. The Cam-Clay models assume an isotropic, elasto-plastic soil with no creep, and the Modified Cam-Clay of John Burland uses an elliptical yield surface. It extends the ideas of {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and {{ref:soil-phys-073}}.

soil-phys-229.title: Three kinds of compaction and how to tell them apart
soil-phys-229.text: Each kind of compaction has different signs and different remedies, so diagnosis comes first. Surface seals show broken-down aggregates, poor seedling emergence and fast runoff and erosion. Sandy loams and silt loams are especially prone, because their unstable aggregates leave small particles that fill pores into dense crusts. Surface layer compaction shows as deep wheel tracks, standing water, cloddy tillage and stubby, crooked roots with few root hairs. A penetrometer, wire flag or shovel dig can confirm it. Freshly plowed soil can falsely look uncompacted because it is loose at first, while no-tilled soil is firmer but has strong structure and worm-made large pores. Subsoil compaction is found with a penetrometer in field-moist soil, which often meets much higher resistance at the base of the plow layer (typically 6 to 8 inches), and by roots that are absent below the pan or run sideways above it. Compacted soil that stays wet becomes anaerobic, causing stunted growth and denitrification losses shown by yellow leaves. Weakened crops are more prone to root diseases such as Pythium and Fusarium. For background, see {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-233.title: Cover and rotation crops that loosen packed soil
soil-phys-233.text: Roots can do work that machines cannot. Cover and rotation crops reduce compaction by creating and stabilizing large voids and feeding microbes. Grasses have shallow dense roots that ease surface compaction but not subsoil, while deep taproots such as alfalfa and forage radish penetrate compacted subsoil, so mixes of shallow and deep rooters are often best. Perennial and cool-season crops have active early-season roots that reach compacted layers while still wet and soft. Clay soils stay plastic for long because the dry upper inch cuts evaporation; a spring cereal rye cover pumps water from below and helps the soil pass from plastic to friable, instead of fall tillage. Plowing down a crop loosens trafficked soil and speeds nitrogen mineralization, whereas cutting and mulching in no-till gives weed control and better infiltration but does not loosen the soil. This answers {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-236.title: Managing field traffic to spare the soil
soil-phys-236.text: Most compaction is avoidable if the right passes are changed. Judge traffic by soil moisture at the time and by equipment weight and load distribution. Late dry planting does little damage, but wet-harvest trucks and spring plowing of wet clay loam do much. Tracks greatly reduce subsoil compaction. Multiple axles, and wide tires at low inflation pressure, spread loads, and most compaction comes from the first tire passing. Dual wheels enlarge the footprint but cut subsoil compaction less, because pressure cones merge at shallow depth, and they tempt fieldwork on wet soil. Poorly drained fields suffer worse compaction; tile drainage dries the subsoil, and surface shaping and mole drains suit heavy clay. The problem itself is in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-232.title: How organic matter helps soil resist compaction
soil-phys-232.text: Organic matter protects soil in several ways at once. It covers everything from living roots to well-decomposed material. Surface residue dissipates the compacting force of equipment, and organic matter is less dense than mineral particles. Dead residue and organisms stabilize aggregates, while roots and large organisms create channels for air and water. Roots and mycorrhizal fungi secrete sticky substances that bind small aggregates into larger ones. One caution: heavy manure spreaders on wet soil can severely compact surface and subsoil, so organic materials should be applied without worsening compaction. The risk it guards against is {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-239.title: The headland: the most trampled part of a field
soil-phys-239.text: The ends of a field take a beating. A headland is the area at each end of a planted field, used for turning implements. It gets more traffic per unit area than the rest of the field, so its soil is more compacted and yields are generally lower. Fertility is often higher there, because overlapping fertilizer applications coincide with reduced yields.

soil-phys-237.title: Dynamic compaction: dropping tonnes to densify ground
soil-phys-237.text: Weights of 8 to 36 tonnes are dropped from 1 to 30 metres, and the stress waves can reach up to 10 metres deep. Dynamic compaction is a ground improvement method that densifies soil by repeatedly dropping a heavy weight at regularly spaced points. In cohesionless soils the waves cause liquefaction followed by compaction; in cohesive soils they raise {{ref:soil-phys-098}} before compaction. Results depend on weight, drop height and spacing. Old fills and granular soils are most often treated, and soil below the water table needs care to let excess pore pressure escape. It is an engineered form of {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-230.title: Crops that compact soil and how to offset them
soil-phys-230.text: Some crops are hard on soil. Root and tuber crops, silage corn, soybeans and many vegetable crops compact it through intensive tillage, low residue return or wet-soil harvest traffic. Countermeasures include soil-improving rotation crops, extensive cover crops, controlled traffic and extra manure or compost. In an 11-year Vermont trial on clay soil under continuous corn silage, yearly dairy manure of 0, 10, 20 and 30 tons per acre gave pore space of 44%, 45%, 47% and 50% of soil volume.

soil-phys-234.title: Deep tillage: breaking up a plow pan
soil-phys-234.text: Deeper tillage shatters a plow pan or other deep compacted layer so roots can explore deeper. It must be done when the full depth is dry and friable, otherwise it smears the soil. Subsoiling below the 6 to 8 inch depth of normal tillage is costly and energy consuming, and does little for surface compaction from aggregate breakdown; narrow-shank zone building or deep strip tillage disturbs less. It works better on coarse soils, because in fine soils the whole subsoil is strong, and tilling wet subsoil can cause smearing and drainage problems. Heavy loads must stay off afterwards to prevent re-compaction, and soils prone to washed-down fines may need repeated deep tillage.

soil-phys-235.title: Loosening soil without a full plow
soil-phys-235.text: Some tools loosen compacted soil with only minor surface disturbance, helping a tilled field move toward no-till. Aerators with rotating tines give shallow relief in dense surface layers and can incorporate manure with little tillage damage. Strip tillage, 6 to 8 inches deep with narrow shanks, disturbs soil only where plant rows will be and promotes rooting; yeoman's plows act similarly with almost no surface disturbance. Patience is needed, though. Compacted soils become addicted to tillage, so switching to no-till at once may fail. No-till benefits usually take 2 to 5 years, faster with cover crops.

soil-phys-231.title: Preventing surface sealing and crusting
soil-phys-231.text: A rotary hoe can break a soil crust, but the relief lasts only a short time. Crusting is a symptom of aggregate breakdown, so lasting control means protecting the aggregates. The long-term remedies are less or no tillage, residue or mulch on the surface, cover crops and organic matter to raise aggregate stability. Residue covering even 30% of the surface greatly reduces crusting and gives water pathways in. On very unstable, sodic soils, gypsum promotes aggregation: as it dissolves it adds calcium and raises the salt concentration of soil water. For how crusts form, see {{ref:soil-phys-031}}.

soil-phys-258.title: Osmosis: why salty soil starves roots of water
soil-phys-258.text: Salty soil can leave a plant short of water even when the ground is wet. Osmosis explains why. It is the net movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration, which is the same as from high to low {{ref:soil-water-172}}. The pressure needed from outside to stop that net flow is the osmotic pressure. It is a colligative property, so it depends on the solute's molar concentration and not on its identity. Osmotic transport is a pressure-driven viscous flow of solvent, not random molecular diffusion. In a plant cell, osmotic entry of water raises turgor pressure until it equals the osmotic pressure. In a hypertonic solution water leaves and the cell shrinks; in a hypotonic one it swells turgid. Roots take in water and nutrients across cell membranes by osmosis, so excess salt in the soil lowers water uptake and can cause leaf burn.

soil-phys-259.title: The water molecule and what makes it unusual
soil-phys-259.text: Almost everything water does in soil starts with the shape of one molecule. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom in a bent, polar molecule. It can make up to four hydrogen bonds, which explains its unusual thermodynamic properties. Cohesion and adhesion give high surface tension, 71.99 mN/m at 25 degrees C, and capillary action that lifts water over 100 m in trees. Specific heat capacity is very high at 4184 J/(kg K) at 20 degrees C, with a heat of vaporization of 40.65 kJ/mol. Density peaks at 3.98 degrees C, so between 0 and 3.98 degrees C water shows an unusual negative thermal expansion. Its high dielectric constant makes water an excellent solvent for hydrophilic substances, but not hydrophobic ones. Over long periods it weathers and erodes rock into soil and sediment.

soil-phys-253.title: Adhesion: why water clings to soil
soil-phys-253.text: Water sticks to soil grains, and it takes energy to pull it off. Adhesion is the tendency of dissimilar particles or surfaces to cling to one another, whereas cohesion is that of like particles. It requires energy from chemical or physical linkages, and the physical ones are reversible when enough energy is applied. Proposed mechanisms are mechanical, chemical, dispersive, electrostatic and diffusive. In surface science it almost always means dispersive adhesion, and a low contact angle indicates higher adhesion per unit area. Strength depends on the mechanisms present and the contact area, and liquids that wet a surface make larger contact.

soil-phys-260.title: Surface tension: the skin on a liquid
soil-phys-260.text: A liquid's surface acts like a skin pulled tight. Surface tension is the energy per unit area that comes from a liquid having a surface, or equivalently a force per unit length. Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions, but surface molecules are pulled inward, so the surface contracts toward the smallest area. It is a property of the liquid's interface with another medium, not of the liquid alone. It falls as temperature rises and reaches zero at the critical temperature, so a stated value needs its temperature. A curved liquid surface can balance a pressure difference across it, which is the basis of capillary effects.

soil-phys-252.title: Capillary action: water that climbs without a pump
soil-phys-252.text: Water can climb a narrow tube against gravity with no pump at all. That is capillary action: a liquid flowing in a narrow space without help from external forces such as gravity. It arises from {{ref:soil-phys-260}}, caused by cohesion within the liquid, combined with {{ref:soil-phys-253}} between the liquid and the wall of a small enough tube or pore. In a narrow tube water forms a concave meniscus, the curved surface of the liquid. The contact length scales with the tube radius while the liquid's weight scales with its square, so narrower tubes lift a liquid higher. Jurin's law gives the rise height, which falls as the tube radius increases. For water at 20 degrees C the rise is 0.7 mm in a tube of 2 cm radius and 70 mm in a tube of 0.2 mm radius. Mercury behaves the other way. Its internal forces exceed those to glass, so it forms a convex meniscus and a reversed capillary effect. In hydrology the term describes the attraction of water to soil particles. Differences in soil matric potential drive it, moving water from wet to dry soil. Where a high water table meets strong evaporation, capillary rise brings salts to the surface, and breaking the capillary pores is used to stop it.

soil-phys-257.title: Hygroscopy: materials that draw water from the air
soil-phys-257.text: Some materials pull water out of the air and keep it. Hygroscopy is the attracting and holding of water molecules from the surroundings by absorption or adsorption. Many fertilizer chemicals and salts are hygroscopic, and the moisture they hold is usually proportional to relative humidity. Deliquescent materials absorb enough water to dissolve into a solution, at a characteristic deliquescence relative humidity that depends on temperature and crystalline hydrate form. Soil voids stay saturated with water vapor up to the point of maximal hygroscopicity, beyond which a vapor-pressure deficit develops in the pore space.

soil-phys-255.title: The continuity equation: what enters must go somewhere
soil-phys-255.text: Whatever enters a region must either leave it or pile up inside. A continuity equation describes the transport of a quantity, and is a local form of a conservation law. It relates the change of a quantity in a region to the net flux through the boundary, plus any generation (sources) or removal (sinks) inside. In fluid dynamics it says the rate at which mass enters a system equals the rate at which it leaves plus the mass accumulating within.

soil-phys-256.title: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation for flow in a pipe
soil-phys-256.text: How much pressure does it take to push a fluid through a long thin pipe? The Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the pressure drop for an incompressible Newtonian fluid in laminar flow through a long cylindrical pipe of constant cross section. It assumes a circular pipe much longer than its diameter and no acceleration, and it rests on the mass balance of {{ref:soil-phys-255}}. Above a threshold of velocity and pipe diameter the flow turns turbulent, giving larger pressure drops than the equation predicts. It also fails near the pipe entrance and for low viscosity or wide, short pipes. Poiseuille derived it experimentally in 1838, with Hagen, and Stokes justified it theoretically in 1845.

soil-phys-254.title: Capillary pressure: the smaller the pore, the greater the pull
soil-phys-254.text: The smaller the pore, the larger the pressure. Capillary pressure is the pressure difference between two immiscible fluids in a thin tube or pore, arising from forces between the fluids and the solid walls, as in {{ref:soil-phys-252}}. The Young-Laplace equation gives it as pc = 2 γ cos θ / r, with interfacial tension γ, wetting angle θ and effective radius r of the interface. The wetting phase is the fluid that preferentially spreads across the walls. In the porous plate method, a water-saturated sample sits on a saturated plate in a gas chamber; as gas pressure is raised, the water expelled gives the saturation. Beskow defined soil moisture tension as capillary pressure in his work on frost heave.

soil-phys-262.title: Capillary water: held in small pores, only partly usable
soil-phys-262.text: Capillary water is the water held in small soil pores by adhesion and cohesion, the forces behind {{ref:soil-phys-095}}. Only part of it is available to plants. Plant available water is held between field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}) and the permanent wilting point ({{ref:soil-water-178}}), in mesopores.

soil-phys-268.title: The soil water relationship: calibrating a moisture sensor
soil-phys-268.text: A moisture sensor reports a signal, not water itself. A soil water relationship is a graph of a sensor's measured value against soil water content, which acts as a calibration for one soil. Any reading from a {{ref:soil-water-222}} must be interpreted through such a relationship. Once calibrated, sensors quantify plant available water and show whether water flows by gravity, capillarity or osmotic potential. Soil type matters: at a given water potential, water content rises with clay content, because clayey soils have higher porosity and hold more water, as the curves of {{ref:soil-water-153}} show.

soil-phys-261.title: Gravitational water: the part that drains away
soil-phys-261.text: Some water in a wet soil leaves almost at once. Gravitational water is the water that moves through the large soil pores and drains away under gravity. It is the difference between the moisture content at saturation and at field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}). It drains from macropores too fast for plants to use.

soil-phys-263.title: Hygroscopic water: the film that even dry soil keeps
soil-phys-263.text: Even air-dry soil holds water. Hygroscopic water is the thin film of water held on soil particles between the hygroscopic coefficient and the oven-dry state. The coefficient is reached when the last micropore is drained and only films of water surround the particles. Air-dry soil holds water at potentials ({{ref:soil-water-172}}) of -3000 to -10,000 kPa, in equilibrium with pore air at about 98% relative humidity. Soil dried at 105 degrees C to constant weight is oven dry, the reference for expressing water in mineral soils. Unavailable water, held at the wilting point ({{ref:soil-water-178}}), is mostly hygroscopic water held too tightly in micropores for plants.

soil-phys-251.title: The Péclet number: advection against diffusion
soil-phys-251.text: Two kinds of transport compete in any moving fluid, and the Péclet number says which one wins. It is a dimensionless number giving the ratio of advective to diffusive transport rate, the two processes of {{ref:soil-phys-193}} and {{ref:soil-phys-195}}. For mass transfer, Pe = L u / D, with L a characteristic length, u flow velocity and D the diffusion coefficient; it equals the Reynolds number times the Schmidt number. It can also be written as the ratio of diffusion time to advection time. Where Pe is much greater than 1, advection predominates in mass transport because diffusion takes much longer.

soil-phys-250.title: The breakthrough curve: watching a solute emerge from a column
soil-phys-250.text: Feed a solute into one end of a column of porous material and measure what comes out of the other. The result is the breakthrough curve: the course of the solute's concentration at the outlet after a step change in inlet concentration. A fixed bed is purged with a carrier, then the adsorptive is added so that inlet concentration changes in a step, and the outlet concentration is monitored. Chromatography instead uses pulses. Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable sorption capacity. The curve's shape carries information on mass-transfer properties, which can be found by fitting simplified models to the data. It shows adsorption of the kind described in {{ref:soil-phys-196}} at work. The source page frames this in adsorption engineering; it does not describe the soil-column version.

soil-phys-246.title: Greenhouse gases: the trace gases that warm the planet
soil-phys-246.text: Without greenhouse gases, Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18 °C instead of the present 15 °C. A greenhouse gas is a gas in an atmosphere that absorbs the heat a planet radiates and so raises its surface temperature. Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb infrared. Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other trace gases, under 0.1% of the atmosphere, absorb it because their molecules are asymmetric in charge. Water vapor causes 41-67% of the greenhouse effect, but its short residence time of about nine days means human activity barely changes it globally; it amplifies warming through water vapor feedback. Concentrations follow the balance of sources and sinks. Soil, oceans and vegetation are sinks, and about 0.55 of emitted CO2 is absorbed by land and ocean sinks in the first year. Most human CO2 comes from fossil fuels. Agriculture is a major methane source, with rice paddies giving 22% of agricultural methane and 11% of nitrous oxide.

soil-phys-240.title: Diffusion: spreading over short distances
soil-phys-240.text: Diffusion does its work over tiny distances. Under normal conditions molecular diffusion dominates only over lengths from nanometers to millimeters; beyond that, convection takes over. It is the net movement of atoms, ions, molecules or energy from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. A gradient in chemical potential drives it, which sets it apart from bulk flow, where a whole body of material moves down a pressure gradient. {{ref:soil-phys-181}} puts numbers on it. The diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, with the diffusion coefficient D as the constant. In a porous medium such as soil, the porosity must be counted in both the flux and accumulation terms. As porosity goes to zero, the molar flux for a given concentration gradient goes to zero too.

soil-phys-244.title: Partial pressure: each gas in a mixture on its own
soil-phys-244.text: In a mixture of gases, each gas acts as if it were alone. Partial pressure is the pressure a single gas in a mixture would exert if it alone filled the whole volume at the same temperature. By Dalton's law, the total pressure of an ideal gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its gases. The partial pressure of a component equals its mole fraction times the total pressure, and its mole fraction equals its volume fraction. Gases dissolve, diffuse and react according to their partial pressures, not their concentrations, which links it to {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. For non-ideal gases the concept generalizes to fugacity.

soil-phys-243.title: Molecular diffusion: the restless motion that mixes gases and liquids
soil-phys-243.text: Above absolute zero, molecules never sit still. Molecular diffusion is the motion of atoms, molecules or other particles of a gas or liquid at temperatures above absolute zero, which spreads them from high to low concentration, as in {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. The rate depends on temperature, fluid viscosity and particle size and mass. The result is gradual mixing until the distribution is uniform. After that, molecules keep moving in a dynamic equilibrium. Chemical diffusion needs a gradient; self-diffusion does not. For gases, {{ref:soil-phys-181}} gives the rate as proportional to the concentration gradient, where there is no bulk motion. Molecular diffusion is one of the slower mass-transport mechanisms.

soil-phys-242.title: Heat capacity: how much heat it takes to warm something
soil-phys-242.text: How much heat does it take to warm an object? Heat capacity is the answer: the amount of heat that must be supplied to an object to raise its temperature by one unit. The SI unit is joule per kelvin. Dividing by mass gives specific heat capacity, and dividing by volume gives volumetric heat capacity. It varies with starting temperature and pressure, and changes sharply at phase transitions such as melting or vaporization. The heat capacity of a heterogeneous object can usually be found by adding the capacities of its parts.

soil-phys-245.title: Thermal conductivity: how readily a material passes heat
soil-phys-245.text: Ice conducts heat far better than liquid water: 2.18 W/(m·K) at 0 °C against 0.56. Thermal conductivity is a measure of a material's intrinsic ability to conduct heat locally, in watts per meter-kelvin. Conduction is energy transport by random molecular motion across a temperature gradient, without macroscopic flows, and heat flows from high to low temperature. Heat capacity ({{ref:soil-phys-242}}) says how much heat a material takes up; conductivity says how readily it passes heat along. Methods of measuring are steady-state, which wait for a steady temperature profile, or transient, which use the system as it approaches steady state. Without convection, air and other gases are good insulators, so insulating materials work by trapping many gas-filled pockets that block conduction. Conductivity can differ with direction: wood conducts better along the grain than across it.

soil-phys-247.title: Global warming potential: comparing gases against carbon dioxide
soil-phys-247.text: A tonne of methane leaked equals 81.2 tonnes of CO2 over 20 years. Global warming potential, or GWP, is a dimensionless measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a chosen period, as a multiple of the warming from the same mass of CO2. CO2 has a GWP of 1 by definition. For other gases it depends on how strongly the gas absorbs thermal radiation, how fast it leaves the atmosphere and the time frame. Methane's 20-year GWP is 81.2.

soil-phys-248.title: Growing regions: where climate and soil favor a crop
soil-phys-248.text: Some regions are known by a single crop. A growing region is a geographic area whose climate, soil and farming practices favor producing particular crops, plants or livestock. A region may be dominated by one crop, such as the American Corn Belt, or be diverse where soil fertility and seasonal rainfall are high, as in Queensland and New South Wales. Cultivation may be enabled by a regional climate or a unique microclimate, and regions are often aligned along a latitude because crops need consistent climate.

soil-phys-241.title: The diffusion equation: one law for spreading heat and solutes
soil-phys-241.text: One equation describes how a diffusing material spreads in space and time. The diffusion equation is a parabolic partial differential equation that describes how the density of a diffusing material changes in space and time. It follows from the continuity equation ({{ref:soil-phys-255}}), which says material is neither created nor destroyed, combined with {{ref:soil-phys-181}}. With a constant diffusion coefficient it is linear and identical to the {{ref:soil-phys-183}}; if the coefficient depends on density it is nonlinear. It is the special case of the {{ref:soil-phys-197}} in which bulk velocity is zero.

soil-chem-231.title: Anatase: the short-lived form of titanium dioxide
soil-chem-231.text: Titanium dioxide comes in several forms, and anatase is the one that does not last. Anatase is a metastable tetragonal mineral form of titanium dioxide (TiO2), one of the oxide minerals of {{ref:soil-found-035}}. Rutile is the most common and stable polymorph. Anatase is metastable at all temperatures and pressures but often forms first because of its lower surface energy. It forms at relatively low temperatures. It occurs in minor amounts in {{ref:soil-form-135}} and {{ref:soil-form-137}}, and as microscopic crystals in sandstones, clays and slates. It converts to rutile between 550 and about 1000 degrees C, depending on impurities and sample morphology. It is also less dense than rutile, about 3.9 against 4.2.

soil-chem-238.title: How clay minerals differ in charge and surface area
soil-chem-238.text: Clay minerals of one family can differ enormously in how much they hold. Phyllosilicates differ mainly in cation exchange capacity, CEC, and in reactive surface area, which depend on isomorphous substitution and on whether the interlayer admits cations. Kaolinite has little substitution and does not expand, so its CEC is 2-16 cmol(+) per kg and its surface is only external, 5-15 m2 per g. Illite and chlorite have substantial substitution, but a tightly bound K+ or hydroxide interlayer blocks expansion, so CEC is limited: 20-40 for illite and 10-40 for chlorite. Smectite admits interlayer cations, giving CEC 60-120 and an internal surface of 570-660 m2 per g, and soils rich in it swell and shrink strongly. Vermiculite has CEC of 100-150 but expands little, because its charge, concentrated near the interlayer, binds cations tightly and restricts water entry. Fe/Al oxyhydroxides have CEC near 0-3 but 200-500 m2 per g of surface, and amorphous aluminosilicates range from 5 to 350 CEC.

soil-chem-237.title: Quartz, the mineral that fills the sand
soil-chem-237.text: Quartz (alpha-SiO2) is the most common mineral in Canadian soils, and it makes up about 40-60% of the sand fraction. It is a framework silicate ({{ref:soil-found-031}}) in which every silica tetrahedron shares all four oxygens. It is essentially pure SiO2 and needs no other bonding ions. Strong Si-O covalent bonds make its solubility very low and its dissolution extremely slow, so quartz accumulates over time, for example in Ae horizons of Podzolic and Luvisolic soils. It is also a major part of the silt and a small part of the clay fraction.

soil-chem-235.title: Secondary minerals: what weathering builds from the wreckage
soil-chem-235.text: Weathering makes new minerals as well as breaking down old ones. A secondary mineral is a by-product of chemical weathering, formed by partial alteration of a primary mineral ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) or by precipitation from components dissolved from other minerals. Primary minerals form as the original molten crust cools and solidifies, while secondary minerals form from their breakdown products. In heavily weathered soils secondary minerals dominate, including iron and aluminum oxides from primary igneous silicates. Most are hydrated aluminosilicates (phyllosilicates, or clay minerals) or Fe and Al oxyhydroxides, which are stable in soils. Clay minerals are the most chemically reactive inorganic phases in soil; their amount and type influence porosity, swelling, compressibility, sorption and exchange capacity, and hydraulic conductivity. In glaciated Canada most secondary minerals formed before the last glaciation and were redeposited, so little has formed since compared with the amount inherited.

soil-chem-232.title: Reading a sample's elements from its X-rays
soil-chem-232.text: Hit a sample with a beam and it answers in X-rays. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, or EDS, reads that answer to identify the elements present. The beam ejects an inner-shell electron, and when an outer electron fills the hole it releases an X-ray whose energy is characteristic of the element. The beam may be electrons in a microscope or X-rays in an XRF spectrometer. Overlapping peaks and absorption within the sample limit accuracy, so corrections are needed. Wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy resolves finer detail, and newer silicon drift detectors need no liquid nitrogen and work faster.

soil-chem-233.title: Variscite, the green aluminium phosphate
soil-chem-233.text: Variscite is a rare green mineral, a hydrated aluminium phosphate with the formula AlPO4·2H2O. It is a secondary {{ref:soil-found-029}}: it is deposited directly from phosphate-bearing water that has reacted with aluminium-rich rock near the surface. It turns up as fine-grained masses in nodules, cavity fillings and crusts, often alongside veins of crandallite, a calcium aluminium phosphate. The green comes from small amounts of trivalent chromium.

soil-chem-239.title: Why Canadian clays came from the ice
soil-chem-239.text: Most of the layered clay minerals in Canadian soils did not form where they now sit. The continental glaciers delivered them in the parent material. Kaolinite, mica and chlorite come straight from the Canadian Shield, while others in the Interior Plains derive from degraded Cretaceous sediments. Interior Plains clay is mostly smectite, mica, chlorite and some kaolinite. The older Devonian and Silurian sediments of the St. Lawrence Lowlands give mica, chlorite, vermiculite and kaolinite. Little alteration shows across regions. The exceptions are Podzolic and some Brunisolic and Gleysolic soils, where inherited chlorite weathers to expandable {{ref:soil-found-033}}.

soil-chem-241.title: Phosphate minerals and where soil phosphorus goes
soil-chem-241.text: Phosphate forms over 300 minerals. The commonest pure primary ones are the apatites, Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH), with fluor-, chlor- and hydroxyapatite as the end members. Rock phosphate is mined for fertilizer. Soils typically hold 400-800 mg of phosphorus per kg, against a crustal average of 1050 mg per kg. Phosphate in soil, whether from rock or fertilizer, precipitates with calcium, aluminium and iron. Wet, sub-oxic soils form iron phosphates such as vivianite and strengite. Acidic soils form aluminium phosphate, as in variscite. Calcareous soils form calcium phosphates such as brushite, which commonly precipitates where fertilizer is banded at high concentration.

soil-chem-236.title: Why some minerals vanish from soil faster than others
soil-chem-236.text: A {{ref:soil-form-140}} is not chemically stable at the Earth's surface. During {{ref:soil-found-052}} it dissolves and releases its elements, but at different speeds. Minerals containing sodium and potassium dissolve faster than those with calcium and magnesium, which dissolve faster than those made of silicon, aluminium and iron. Iron depends on conditions: it is soluble as Fe2+ under reducing conditions but forms insoluble Fe3+ oxyhydroxides, like rust, under oxidizing ones. Carbonates precipitate under alkaline conditions and dissolve under acid ones. Carbonic acid from atmospheric CO2 dissolves them, and alkaline deeper groundwater favors precipitation in C horizons.

soil-chem-240.title: Calcite, dolomite and the carbonates in soil
soil-chem-240.text: Where pH falls below 6.0, calcite is not usually found. Soil carbonates are mostly calcite and dolomite inherited from sedimentary rock, with some secondary precipitates in subsurface horizons. Calcite is sparingly soluble, more so at low pH. It dissolves from the upper solum and is redeposited lower as secondary calcite nodules. Dolomite also dissolves from the upper profile, supplying calcium to that calcite while magnesium is mostly leached or taken up by roots. Aragonite is neither common nor stable. Trona, Na2CO3, is highly soluble and found mostly in Solonetzic soils at pH about 9.5. Carbonates keep base saturation, exchangeable Ca and Mg, and pH above 7 high, precipitate phosphate and metals, and stabilize clays and structure. Their entry is {{ref:soil-found-034}}.

soil-chem-242.title: Pyrite, sulfuric acid and gypsum in soil
soil-chem-242.text: Pyrite and other sulfide minerals are absent from well-drained soils. They may occur in poorly drained Gleysolic or Organic soils, tidal soils and mine wastes. Exposed to air, pyrite oxidizes to iron and sulfuric acid: 2FeS2 + 7O2 + 2H2O gives 2Fe2+ + 4H+ + 4SO4 2-. Oxidation of sulfides can push soil pH below 2.0. Mining or excavation that exposes sulfides is mainly responsible for acid rock drainage. Sulfate from sulfide oxidation or other sources forms gypsum, usually at high pH with soluble calcium present.

soil-chem-234.title: Strengite, the purple iron phosphate
soil-chem-234.text: Strengite is a rare orthorhombic iron phosphate, FePO4·2H2O. It resembles {{ref:soil-chem-233}} but is lavender, pink or purple. It is partly soluble, particularly at low pH and low oxidation-reduction potential. The name honors the German mineralogist Johann August Streng. It is another {{ref:soil-found-029}} in which iron, rather than aluminium, holds the phosphate.

soil-chem-227.title: Van der Waals force, the weak pull that adds up
soil-chem-227.text: No single van der Waals contact is strong, yet fine powders clump because of them. The force is a weak, distance-dependent attraction between atoms or molecules that is not a chemical bond. It begins with a transient shift in electron density that creates a short-lived charge, which a nearby atom is attracted to or repelled by. The force is repulsive at very short range, zero at an equilibrium distance of 0.3 to 0.5 nm for single atoms, and attractive beyond it. Past 1.0 nm it falls off roughly as the 7th power of distance. Three parts combine: London dispersion forces, Debye forces between permanent and induced dipoles, and Keesom forces between permanent dipoles. Induction and dispersion always attract, while the electrostatic part can attract or repel depending on orientation. Strength rises with polarizability. Pairwise energy is 0.06 kJ/mol between H atoms in H2, 0.44 kJ/mol between O atoms in O2, and 2.35 kJ/mol between xenon atoms. The forces are additive, cannot be saturated and have no directional character, so many weak contacts can add up to strong attraction. For very small particles, such as fine dry powders, the attraction beats gravity and drag, so the powders are cohesive. Free flow generally needs particles larger than about 250 micrometres. In soils, organic contaminants can be held in organic matter by weak van der Waals interactions, and physisorption is the weak van der Waals form of adsorption. Small particles of the kind met in a {{ref:soil-chem-154}} are where this matters most.

soil-chem-225.title: How water plants clear mud with coagulants
soil-chem-225.text: Water treatment borrows the same behavior that clay shows in soil. Coagulation destabilizes charged particles with an added coagulant, and flocculation then gathers them into settleable clusters. Alum is the most common coagulant. Gentle mixing then speeds particle collisions, so destabilized particles enmesh in larger precipitates, depending on mixing shear, intensity, time and pH. A jar test chooses the flocculant and dose by rapid mixing, slow mixing and sedimentation in beakers with paddle mixers. Drinking-water treatment typically runs grates, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, granular filtration and disinfection. Chitosan is an increasingly popular biodegradable flocculant that binds heavy metals and organic pollutants. See {{ref:soil-phys-006}} and {{ref:soil-chem-154}} for the soil side.

soil-chem-226.title: Muscovite, the common mica
soil-chem-226.text: Muscovite splits into thin, elastic sheets. Also called common mica or potash mica, it is a hydrated phyllosilicate of aluminium and potassium, KAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2. Its TOT-c structure stacks tetrahedral-octahedral-tetrahedral layers bonded by potassium cations. Strong bonds within layers and weak ones between them give perfect basal cleavage. It is the most common {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, found in granites, pegmatites, gneisses and schists, and as an alteration product of {{ref:soil-form-141}}. Biotite is almost always much darker. Chlorite is green with inelastic sheets, and pyrophyllite and talc are softer and greasy. Up to 10% of its potassium may be replaced by sodium, and phengite has more silicon than aluminium with Mg or Fe balancing charge. As a {{ref:soil-found-033}} and a {{ref:soil-found-029}}, it is a standard of the group.

soil-chem-228.title: X-ray diffraction and the crystal's hidden order
soil-chem-228.text: A regular array of atoms scatters X-rays as secondary spherical waves. They cancel in most directions but add up in a few specific ones, giving a diffraction pattern. The Bragg model explains these as reflections from evenly spaced sheets in the crystal. Scattering is set by electron density; the heavy nuclei contribute negligibly. Laboratory sources are tubes whose electrons, accelerated through about 50 kV, hit a metal plate. Copper is most common because it cools easily and gives strong K-alpha and K-beta lines, and synchrotrons are far brighter. Where single crystals are unavailable, powder diffraction gives less detailed information. Max von Laue's 1912 observation of diffraction confirmed that X-rays are electromagnetic radiation. Neutrons scatter from nuclei and reveal light atoms such as hydrogen, nearly invisible to X-rays, while electrons scatter 1000 or more times more strongly.

soil-chem-224.title: Dispersion: particles spread through another phase
soil-chem-224.text: Stir mud into water and you make a dispersion. It is a system in which particles of one material are distributed in a continuous phase of another. Dispersions are classed by particle size relative to the continuous phase, whether precipitation occurs and Brownian motion. Particles big enough to sediment make suspensions; smaller ones make colloids and solutions. Dispersing a solid in a liquid separates agglomerated particles and creates a new interface. Molecular diffusion and convection drive it, with convection dominating in turbulent flow and diffusion where there is little turbulence. Above a critical concentration, which depends on particle size and interfacial tension, some liquid dispersions turn into gels or solids.

soil-chem-223.title: Aluminosilicates, the aluminium-silicon backbone of clays
soil-chem-223.text: Aluminosilicates contain anionic Si-O-Al linkages, with cations such as sodium, potassium or hydrogen balancing the charge. They occur as minerals, coal combustion products and synthetic materials, often zeolites, and matter technically as structural materials, catalysts and reagents. {{ref:soil-found-031}} like feldspar are the commonest example: a tectosilicate with potassium, sodium and calcium cations in a negatively charged network of silicon, aluminium and oxygen. Soil alumino-silica clays are aluminosilicates with a regular crystalline or quasi-crystalline structure, including montmorillonite, illite, vermiculite, chlorite and kaolinite. Naturally occurring microporous, hydrous aluminosilicate minerals are {{ref:soil-chem-199}}, whose varying Si/Al ratio tunes their properties. Each is a {{ref:soil-found-029}}.

soil-chem-222.title: Saline, sodic and saline-sodic: three ways soil goes salty
soil-chem-222.text: Two soils can look equally ruined and need opposite cures. Salt-affected soils are classed as saline, sodic or saline-sodic by total salt (EC) and sodium content (SAR, ESP). Saline soils have EC above 4 dS/m but SAR below 13 and ESP below 15%, with pH usually under 8.5 and flocculated colloids. Sodic soils have EC below 4 dS/m but SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%, and pH usually above 8.5 from hydrolysis of Na2CO3. Saline-sodic soils have EC above 4 dS/m, SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%. Their pH is usually below 8.5 and they stay flocculated. Sodium explains the difference. Hydrated Na+ between clay particles cancels the binding electrostatic forces, and extra water layers push the particles apart. That disperses sodic soil, and high pH also disperses organic matter. Saline soils stay aggregated with high infiltration, so they leach easily. Dispersed sodic and saline-sodic soils infiltrate poorly and usually need gypsum. Calcium replacing monovalent Na+ promotes aggregation and infiltration, and the displaced sodium and salts are leached. Saline drainage may be diverted through subsurface drains. Salt-tolerant crops such as barley or sunflower, and trees, can take up salts, but prevention is better than reclamation. Natural sources include mineral weathering, atmospheric deposition, seawater intrusion, saline groundwater and natural brines. Human sources include salty irrigation water, salty fertilizers, manure, biosolids, compost and road salt.

soil-chem-221.title: Two ways to estimate a soil's CEC
soil-chem-221.text: A soil's CEC can be estimated without a full lab run. One way sums the exchangeable cations listed in a soil analysis. The other weights typical values for the clay minerals present. The manual uses 10 cmolc/kg for kaolinite, 100 for montmorillonite/smectite and 150 for vermiculite, though real colloids vary. A soil with 10% kaolinite clay contributes 10 cmolc/kg clay times 10 kg clay per 100 kg soil, or 1.0 cmolc per kg of soil. Colloids, below 0.002 mm, are called the active fraction because their charged surfaces are highly reactive. Their small size gives large surface area per unit weight, and their ionic structure gives a net charge. See {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and {{ref:soil-chem-081}}.

soil-chem-229.title: How a solid appears out of solution
soil-chem-229.text: A solid can form out of clear liquid. Precipitation is the formation of a solid, the precipitate, from a liquid solution. Compounds precipitate when their concentration exceeds solubility, that is, when the solution is supersaturated, and precipitation is faster from strongly supersaturated solutions. Supersaturation can arise from temperature change, solvent evaporation or mixing of solvents. Without enough attractive force to aggregate the particles, they stay suspended as a colloid instead of settling. Ageing a fresh precipitate in its solution gives purer, larger recrystallized particles, through Ostwald ripening. The limit is set by {{ref:soil-chem-181}}.

soil-chem-230.title: Activity: the effective concentration of an ion
soil-chem-230.text: Real solutions do not behave as their concentrations suggest. Thermodynamic activity is a measure of the effective concentration of a species in a mixture, so that its chemical potential in a real solution depends on activity as it would on concentration in an ideal one. Activity is dimensionless. Pure solids and liquids take a = 1, and it depends on temperature, pressure, composition and the chosen standard state. The activity coefficient links activity to a measured concentration; near 1, the substance behaves almost ideally. Equilibrium constants should be defined by activities but are often defined by concentrations in practice, as in {{ref:soil-chem-181}}. The activity of a single ion such as Ca2+ cannot be measured, since cations cannot be added without anions. The mean ionic coefficient is measurable and predicted by Debye-Hückel theory in dilute systems. For water as solvent, water activity is the equilibrated relative humidity.

soil-chem-215.title: Resistivity and conductivity: how well a material carries current
soil-chem-215.text: Salty soil conducts electricity, which is why conductivity can be used to gauge it. Resistivity and conductivity are two intrinsic properties of a material that measure its ability to conduct electric current, each the reciprocal of the other. Resistivity (ρ) has the SI unit ohm-metre; conductivity (σ) has the SI unit siemens per metre. In a uniform conductor, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, with resistivity as the constant of proportionality. Resistivity and conductivity are intensive properties; resistance and conductance are the matching extensive properties of a specific object.
