In electrolytes, travelling ions carry the current, so resistivity varies tremendously with concentration. Distilled water is almost an insulator and salt water a reasonable conductor. A metal has high conductivity and low resistivity; glass has the reverse. Resistivity of metals generally rises with temperature, while that of intrinsic semiconductors falls.

soil-chem-216.title: Osmotic pressure: why salty soil starves roots
soil-chem-216.text: Water follows salt. Osmosis happens when solutions of different solute concentration are separated by a selectively permeable membrane. Solvent moves toward the higher-concentration side until osmotic equilibrium. Osmotic pressure is the minimum pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop its pure solvent flowing in. Van 't Hoff related it to solute concentration, Π = i c R T, for low-concentration ideal solutions, so it is a colligative property. In a hypotonic environment a cell takes in water. In plant cells the wall resists, creating turgor pressure that holds herbaceous plants upright and regulates stomata. Reverse osmosis applies pressure above the osmotic pressure to purify water; ocean water is about 27 atm.

soil-chem-212.title: Brønsted–Lowry: acids give protons, bases take them
soil-chem-212.text: In 1923, two chemists working apart reached the same idea. Brønsted in Denmark and Lowry in England proposed that an acid is a proton donor and a base a proton acceptor. When they react, the acid becomes its conjugate base and the base its conjugate acid by exchanging a proton (H+). The theory generalises the Arrhenius theory, and unlike it an acid need not dissociate. Acetic acid donates a proton to water and becomes acetate; water accepts it and becomes the hydronium ion. An acid is only an acid relative to a base. Water is amphoteric, acting as acid or base, and aluminium hydroxide also reacts with both OH− and H+. Metal aqua cations behave as acids in these terms. Lewis theory, from the same year, defines a base as an electron-pair donor and an acid as an electron-pair acceptor, and explains the classification through electronic structure. It underlies {{ref:soil-found-014}}.

soil-chem-213.title: Buffer solutions: why pH resists change
soil-chem-213.text: A buffer is a solution whose pH changes little on dilution or when a small amount of strong acid or base is added. It works through the equilibrium between a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A−, a pair defined in {{ref:soil-chem-212}}. Added acid shifts the equilibrium toward HA (Le Chatelier's principle), so hydrogen ion concentration rises less than expected. Added alkali likewise lowers it by less than expected. The buffer region lies at pH = pKa ± 1, centred where [HA] = [A−]; once the acid is more than 95% deprotonated, pH rises rapidly. Buffer capacity measures the strong acid or base needed to change the pH of a given volume by a given amount. It is highest when a large addition produces only a small pH change. Capacity considers a macroscopic change of 1 pH unit, whereas the buffer index considers an infinitesimal change. Polyprotic acids have several pKa values. When successive values differ by less than about 3 their ranges overlap, so citric acid buffers across pH 2.5 to 7.5. A buffer can be made by mixing an acid with its conjugate base, such as acetic acid with sodium acetate, or by adding strong acid or base to a buffering agent. Cation-exchange capacity is often measured with a buffer solution at a set pH, and fens keep a stable pH through bicarbonate buffering. For the soil quantity being held steady, see {{ref:soil-found-014}}.

soil-chem-217.title: How organic matter adds to a soil's CEC
soil-chem-217.text: In some soils, humus matters more than clay. Well-humified organic matter and clay minerals together supply cation exchange capacity, and the organic share can be estimated from pH and organic matter content. A soil's total CEC, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, is the sum of the CEC due to organic matter and that due to clays. In fine soils with medium to high-CEC clays most of it is clay-based. In sandy loams with little clay, and in southeastern US and tropical soils with low-CEC clays, organic matter may supply most. CEC is expressed as milliequivalents of negative charge per 100 g of soil. As a rule of thumb, for every pH unit above 4.5, organic matter gives 1 me of CEC per 100 g of soil for each percent of organic matter; at pH 6 and 3% organic matter this is 4.5 me/100 g. The pH link reflects {{ref:soil-chem-049}}.

soil-chem-220.title: Managing salty soil where the groundwater is deep
soil-chem-220.text: Without a shallow salty water table, salinity is a problem of drying and leaching. Keeping soil continually moist, as with low-salt drip irrigation plus mulch, stops salt concentrating as the soil dries. Tolerant plants include barley, bermuda grass, oak, rosemary and willow, but only washing salt below the root zone removes it. Poorly draining subsoil may need drainage tiles, which discharge salty water that can harm downstream water. Seawater flooding after storm surges can make soils sodic, treated by gypsum, or lime where the soil is naturally acidic. See {{ref:soil-chem-008}} and {{ref:soil-chem-013}}.

soil-chem-218.title: Copper deficiency in high-pH and organic soils
soil-chem-218.text: Copper runs short in two kinds of soil: those with high pH and organic soils. It can also be deficient in organic soils with 10-20% or more organic matter. Tomatoes, lettuce, beets, onions and spinach have relatively high copper needs. Copper sulfate and copper chelates correct a deficiency. Sulfur is a separate matter. Most soil sulfur is in organic matter, so maintaining organic matter usually supplies enough. Deficiency is likelier on acidic sandy soils and cold, dry spring soils with slow mineralization. It is spreading in places as sulfur air pollution from coal falls, while Great Plains irrigation water may supply enough sulfur.

soil-chem-219.title: Reserve acidity: the acid hiding on soil solids
soil-chem-219.text: Almost all of a soil's acid sits in reserve on the solids; only an extremely small amount is active in the soil water. Reserve acidity is that stored acid, held mostly on organic matter and as aluminum. Neutralizing only the acid in the water would need a few handfuls of lime per acre, but raising pH takes tons per acre. As H+ is removed from organic matter new CEC sites appear. As soils acidify, H+ takes over CEC sites and cuts their hold on calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium. Crops differ in what they need. Alfalfa, from semiarid high-pH regions, needs pH 6.5-6.8 or higher. Most states recommend about 6.8 only for the most sensitive crops and 6.2-6.5 for many clovers. Background is in {{ref:soil-chem-001}} and {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-214.title: Efflorescence: salt crusts on the surface
soil-chem-214.text: The white crust on old brick is the same thing as the white crust on a dry field. Efflorescence is the migration of a salt to the surface of a porous material, where it forms a coating. Water dissolves a salt held inside, carries it to the surface and evaporates, leaving the coating. It occurs in natural and built environments. In primary efflorescence the water is the invader and the salt was already inside. In secondary efflorescence salt from outside is carried in solution into the material. Salt crystals can clog pores and destroy the material through internal water pressure, as in the spalling of brick.

soil-bio-271.title: Fungi: the threads that decompose and partner
soil-bio-271.text: Most fungi grow as thread-like hyphae 2 to 10 micrometres across and up to several centimetres long. They extend at their tips and branch, and their high surface-to-volume ratio suits nutrient extraction and invading substrates. Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants, though they were once classed as plants for their immobile lifestyle. Along with bacteria they are the major decomposers in most terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, so they are central to biogeochemical cycles and food webs. They also partner with other life; see {{ref:soil-bio-226}}. Over 90% of plant species form mycorrhizal relationships with fungi and depend on them for survival, a symbiosis that dates back at least 400 million years. Lichens pair a fungus with photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria, and some ants cultivate fungi for food and nest structure. Many fungi are plant parasites, such as the rice blast fungus and those causing Dutch elm disease and chestnut blight. As of 2019 nine major lineages are recognised, including Chytridiomycota, Glomeromycota, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota. The last two form the species-rich Dikarya, with all mushrooms and most plant pathogens.

soil-bio-274.title: Protozoa: single cells that eat bacteria
soil-bio-274.text: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, free-living or parasitic, that feed on organic matter such as other microorganisms or debris. The name is now used loosely for heterotrophic single-celled protists, since Protozoa as a taxon is not monophyletic. Classic examples are Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. They range from about 1 micrometre to several millimetres, and are flagellates, ciliates or amoebae according to how they move. All need a moist habitat, but many survive dry spells as resting cysts; they are common in soils and mosses. All are heterotrophs, engulfing prey by phagocytosis or taking up dissolved matter by osmotrophy, and some are mixotrophs hosting symbiotic algae. Most reproduce asexually by binary or multiple fission; sexual exchange is generally decoupled from reproduction. In the microbial food web they are the most important bacterivores and mobilise nutrients, passing bacterial and algal production on and solubilising nutrients in microbial biomass. Termite gut flagellates help their host digest wood by breaking down complex sugars. See also {{ref:soil-bio-014}} and {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-283.title: Sporosarcina pasteurii, the bacterium that turns sand to stone
soil-bio-283.text: Give one soil bacterium calcium and urea, and loose sand sets solid. Sporosarcina pasteurii is a gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium, 0.5 to 1.2 micrometres wide and 1.3 to 4.0 micrometres long. It forms endospores and thrives at pH 9 to 10, surviving up to pH 11.2. It secretes urease to hydrolyse urea, which feeds it nitrogen, carbon and energy. The carbonate ions released react with calcium to precipitate {{ref:soil-found-118}} that cements sand grains. This is {{ref:soil-bio-067}}. The organism is non-pathogenic and makes a great deal of urease, so it is a common choice for the job. It is proposed for self-healing concrete and other bio-cement uses.

soil-bio-273.title: Fungal biocontrol: fungi that fight crop disease
soil-bio-273.text: About 300 species of fungi and fungus-like organisms, in 13 classes and 113 genera, are used as biocontrol agents against plant fungal diseases. They protect crops in two ways. Some parasitise other fungi, and organisms that do so are called mycoparasitic. Others compete with pathogenic bacteria or fungi for nutrients and space, by the competitive exclusion principle. Both tactics rely on the habits of the {{ref:soil-bio-271}} itself.

soil-bio-272.title: How fungi reproduce and spread
soil-bio-272.text: Fungi reproduce asexually, sexually or both, and spread mainly by spores. Asexual reproduction uses vegetative spores, called conidia, or mycelial fragmentation, in which pieces of mycelium each grow into a separate mycelium. An estimated third of fungi use more than one method, with a sexual teleomorph stage and an asexual anamorph stage. Spores of most studied species travel by wind. Dry, hydrophobic spores are readily scattered by raindrops. Everything here builds on the basic body of the {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-276.title: Humus: the dark, stable core of soil organic matter
soil-bio-276.text: Humus is light for its bulk. Its bulk density is just 0.05 to 0.25 g per cubic centimetre, and its cation exchange capacity tops 200 cmol(+) per kilogram. It is the stable, dark, amorphous fraction of soil organic matter left after most added residues have decomposed, bound to clays and oxides that shield it from microbes. It has high porosity and water holding capacity. Its approximate composition is 50% carbon, 35% oxygen, 8% hydrogen, 5% nitrogen and 2% sulfur. It commonly supplies 20 to 30% or more of a soil's cation exchange capacity, buffers pH and binds peds into aggregates. Arable soils average 2 to 3% humus, from under 1% to over 12%. Keeping it takes work. Cultivated soils lose humus by decomposition at 1 to 2% per year. Holding the normal level needs 1000 to 5000 kg per hectare of organic material a year, since added material does not permanently raise it. Rotations with grasses and legumes, conservation tillage and residue management help sustain it.

soil-bio-275.title: From residue to humus: how microbes recycle organic matter
soil-bio-275.text: Soil with 1% organic matter holds up to 45 million kilocalories per acre-furrow-slice, equivalent to about 6 tons of coal. Microbes oxidise that energy store partly to carbon dioxide, water and energy, leaving humus, new microbial cells and inorganic plant nutrients. Fresh residues decompose rapidly at first, releasing carbon dioxide, water, energy and small amounts of inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. The microbes' most important function is recycling organic carbon to CO2, which keeps photosynthesis going. Their oxidation also turns nutrients from unavailable organic forms into plant-available inorganic ones, so organic matter acts as a slow-release fertilizer that buffers nutrient supply. The process is wasteful. Microbes use only a small share of the energy for new cells, and making one pound of soil organic matter may destroy 10 to 20 pounds of residues. Fresh residues also accelerate decomposition of humified material already in the soil. The reward is structure. Added organic matter improves tilth, raises cation exchange and water holding capacity and aeration, and reduces erosion.

soil-bio-277.title: What controls the number of microbes in soil
soil-bio-277.text: Soil organisms make up under 0.5% of dry soil mass. Their numbers depend on temperature, moisture, pH, nutrients, energy supply and oxygen. Decay organisms work best at about 20 to 40 degrees C, and most others slow outside that range. Too much water cuts numbers and kinds through poor aeration, yet at low moisture soil organisms do better than higher plants. Below pH 6.0 fungi become the dominant microorganisms. Adding organisms to a soil is usually ineffective because the community, described in {{ref:soil-bio-011}}, is already vast. Changing the crop alters populations more.

soil-bio-281.title: How healthy soil holds pests in check
soil-bio-281.text: In any given year only a small number of bacteria, fungi, insects and nematodes might harm plants, and a diverse soil reduces their impact. Diverse soil organisms keep checks and balances that stop disease organisms and parasites from becoming major problems, a payoff of {{ref:soil-bio-008}}. Some fungi kill nematodes or insects, and some produce antibiotics. Protozoa, springtails and mites eat disease-causing fungi and bacteria. Trichoderma and Pseudomonas fluorescens colonize roots and protect them, and Bacillus thuringiensis toxin is sold as a biological control agent. Suppression is thought to arise from competition for nutrients, antagonistic substances or direct parasitism. Some beneficial organisms also induce plant immune defenses.

soil-bio-280.title: Roots as soil engineers
soil-bio-280.text: Corn sends about 20 percent of its photosynthesis sugars to its roots early to mid-season. Roots influence soil as much as soil influences them, shaping aggregates and feeding soil organisms. Root pressure brings particles closer, small roots bind them, and root hairs add soil contact for water and nutrient access and help form aggregates. Roots exude compounds that feed organisms in the surrounding zone. Mucigel, a sticky layer around roots, gives close contact between microorganisms, soil minerals and the plant. Roots add organic matter that may decompose more slowly than surface residues, and in grasses the living tissue below ground can exceed that above. They do not grow well in compact, nutrient- or water-poor, high-pathogen or extreme-pH soil.

soil-bio-278.title: Free-living bacteria that fix nitrogen
soil-bio-278.text: Plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas, or nitrogen locked in organic molecules. It must be converted to ammonium and nitrate, a bacterial process called nitrogen mineralization. Some free-living soil bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form plants can use to make amino acids and proteins. Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living fixers, and Azospirillum attaches to root surfaces and makes substances that help plants tolerate stress. They add only modest nitrogen, but it matters in natural systems where nutrient cycling is efficient. Rhizobia in legume root nodules do far more, receiving sugars from the plant and supplying usable nitrogen. An alfalfa stand may fix hundreds of pounds per acre a year, peas about 30 to 50. All of these are {{ref:soil-bio-002}} working alongside {{ref:soil-bio-003}}.

soil-bio-282.title: Soil organisms span ten orders of magnitude
soil-bio-282.text: The smallest soil bacterium is about 0.5 micrometres across. Some forest fungi form mycelia of 1 km or more. Soil organisms span nearly ten orders of magnitude in size. Soil-dwelling amphibians and mammals are about 10 cm long, and roots run 0.1 to 10 m. A colony of Armillaria ostoyae in an Oregon Douglas fir forest covers several square kilometres and may be the largest organism by area. Traditional groups are microflora, macroflora (roots), microfauna, mesofauna (0.1 to 2 mm metazoans) and macrofauna (over 2 mm). The scheme confuses, since fungi are called microflora yet are macroscopic and heterotrophic. Even the basic map changed late. Archaea were widely recognized as distinct from bacteria only in the early 1990s. DNA analysis shows them as different from bacteria as from plants or animals, in Woese's three domains Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. The cast spans {{ref:soil-bio-001}}, {{ref:soil-bio-002}}, {{ref:soil-bio-003}}, {{ref:soil-bio-012}}, {{ref:soil-bio-016}} and {{ref:soil-bio-023}}, and gives a measure of {{ref:soil-bio-008}}.

soil-bio-279.title: Soil insects and arthropods
soil-bio-279.text: Soil insects such as termites, springtails, ants, fly larvae and beetles are often secondary and tertiary consumers in the {{ref:soil-bio-025}}. Springtails eat fungi and animal remains and are prey for predacious mites. Many beetles eat other soil animals, and dung beetles bury manure balls. Millipedes are primary consumers of plant residues, while centipedes eat other organisms. Mites eat fungi, other mites, insect eggs or residues, and spiders hold insect pests down. Termites eat wood and also decomposed organic residues in soil.

soil-bio-322.title: Klebsiella oxytoca, a nitrogen fixer on barley roots
soil-bio-322.text: Klebsiella oxytoca is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium, closely related to K. pneumoniae and distinguished from it by indole production. It is a diazotroph: it colonises plant hosts and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use. It has been shown to associate with the barley {{ref:soil-bio-143}} through an entire vegetative period. The bacteria adhere strongly to root hairs and less strongly to the elongation zone and root cap mucilage.

soil-bio-321.title: Epiphytes: plants that live on plants
soil-bio-321.text: Orchids never touch the ground, yet they live well. An epiphyte is a plant or plant-like organism that grows on the surface of another plant, taking moisture and nutrients from air, rain or accumulated debris. It uses the host, called the phorophyte, only for support and, unlike parasitic plants, draws no nourishment from it. It is not rooted in soil. Without soil it depends on fog, dew, rain, mist, nutrients leached or decomposed from rooted plants, and nitrogen fixation. Holo-epiphytes never touch the ground, like orchids; hemi-epiphytes such as strangler figs spend only part of life off the ground. Epiphytes hold water in the canopy, reducing water input to the soil, and cool and moisten the host canopy, which may cut its transpiration.

soil-bio-284.title: Polysaccharides: sugar chains that store and build
soil-bio-284.text: Wood, paper and cotton are all sugar chains. Polysaccharides are large polymers of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds, ranging from linear to highly branched. Storage types include starch, glycogen and galactogen. Structural ones include cellulose, hemicellulose, chitin and pectin. Plant structural parts are mostly cellulose; wood is largely cellulose and lignin, while paper and cotton are nearly pure cellulose. Many organisms digest starch to glucose, but few can metabolize cellulose. Some bacteria and protists can, and ruminants and termites use microorganisms to process it. Humans and many animals lack an enzyme for the beta-linkages, so cellulose is indigestible except where gut bacteria supply it. Chitin yields to chitinase enzymes secreted by bacteria, fungi and some plants. Microbes that detect chitin make enzymes that cleave it to simple sugars and ammonia. It is closely related to chitosan, a more water-soluble derivative. Bacteria, fungi and algae often secrete polysaccharides to adhere to surfaces and avoid drying out, and polysaccharide matrices enclose bacterial biofilms. See {{ref:soil-bio-115}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-271}}.

soil-bio-285.title: How organic matter feeds plants
soil-bio-285.text: Plants need 17 elements. Carbon and oxygen come from air and the rest mainly from soil, with availability affected directly or indirectly by organic matter, the heart of soil fertility. Decomposition converts nutrients to plant-usable forms, produces cation exchange capacity that retains calcium, potassium, magnesium and ammonium, and makes organic molecules that hold micronutrients such as zinc and iron. Siderophores make micronutrients more available, so roots grow longer and more branched. Humic substances may stimulate roots by raising micronutrient availability and changing gene expression. In one experiment humic acids in nutrient solution increased tomato and corn growth and root branching. Soil organisms fix nitrogen and dissolve phosphorus, and with too little food they are scarce and more fertilizer is needed. Physical effects matter as well. Organic matter improves structure, raising infiltration, water-holding capacity and root growth into permeable soil. Good tilth stores more water between rains and reduces erosion. Poor tilth means broken aggregates, compaction, and less aeration and water storage, and a layer can become too compact for roots. Topsoil's good qualities arise because it is rich in organic matter and life, not because of its position. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}, {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and {{ref:soil-found-014}}.

soil-bio-300.title: Living, active and passive: three kinds of organic matter
soil-bio-300.text: Soil organic matter is usefully split into living, active (dead) and passive (very dead, humus) parts, and each serves a different role. Living matter is roots and organisms in spaces between and inside larger aggregates. Active matter is fresh or partly decomposed residue in the same spaces. Passive matter is fragments of dead microbes held on clay and silt, residue inside micro-aggregates, and compounds hard for organisms to use. A soil needs active matter as well as humus. It supplies nutrients, aggregating glues and food for diverse organisms. It is also the part that suffers first. Early losses after cultivating forest or grassland were nearly all the unprotected active part, and that part rises fastest with reduced tillage, rotation, cover crops, manure and compost. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-293.title: How soil protects its organic matter
soil-bio-293.text: Organic matter persists in soil through chemical bonding to clay, physical protection in aggregates and conversion to stable humic substances. Aggregates matter most here. Large aggregates are built from smaller ones held by sticky substances from roots, bacterial colonies and fungal hyphae. Matter outside small aggregates, and free particulate matter, is available to organisms. Use also needs a favourable chemical form, location, moisture and aeration. Compaction, dense layers or low spots with poor aeration slow use. Protection is therefore partly a matter of where the matter sits, as well as what it is. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-309.title: Why some crop residues last and others vanish
soil-bio-309.text: Only about 10-20% of a residue is converted to stable humus after decomposition. How fast it goes, and what it leaves, depends on its chemistry. Residues low in hemicellulose, polyphenols and {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, such as green legume cover crops and soybean residue, decompose fast. Their effect on organic matter is shorter than that of cornstalks or wheat straw. Manure with much bedding decomposes slowly and lasts longer in soil, and ruminant manure lasts longer than that of grain-fed chickens and hogs. Easily decomposed residues, manures, cover crops and straw boost aggregation more than compost, which has already decomposed, though compost raises water-holding capacity. A variety of residues is needed to feed diverse organisms, supply nutrients and promote aggregation. Lignin-rich straw or sawdust builds organic matter but needs added nitrogen. Otherwise the microbes run short and less becomes humus. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-304.title: Filling the soil's organic matter sites
soil-bio-304.text: When practices change to favour buildup, organic matter fills protected sites first and then accumulates mainly as free particles until the soil reaches equilibrium. Free mineral surfaces bond with organic matter first. Small aggregates then form around organic particles, and larger aggregates follow, held by mycorrhizal fungi and small roots. Once all bonding sites and small-aggregate sites are filled, the soil is saturated for that management. Extra organic matter stays as lightly protected free particles that decompose fairly quickly. Depleting practices reverse the order: free particles go first, then aggregate-protected matter, leaving matter tightly held on clay and in micro-aggregates. So a depleted soil can gain much more than one already full for its texture and drainage. With clay and poor aeration, upkeep needs less residue than in well-aerated coarse sands, where raising it is hardest. Case 1 degraded soils and case 2 suboptimal soils gain most from carbon farming. Nearly full case 3 soils should protect what they have, perhaps exporting surplus manure to grain farms. The protection itself is described in {{ref:soil-bio-293}}, and the three pools in {{ref:soil-bio-300}}.

soil-bio-306.title: A simple model of equilibrium organic matter
soil-bio-306.text: A simple model sets a soil's equilibrium organic matter from two numbers: the annual residue addition and the annual decomposition rate. Add 5,000 pounds of residue yearly to a sandy loam decomposing 3% a year, and equilibrium is about 1.7%. Add 7,500 pounds yearly to a well-drained coarse soil decomposing 5% a year, and equilibrium is only about 1.5%. More residue does not help if decomposition is faster. The approach is gradual. The 5,000-pound case, starting at 1%, nets about 350 pounds per acre per year in the first decade, falling toward zero as steady state nears. A very depleted soil starting at 0.5% might gain over 600 pounds per acre per year initially because protective sites are open, so it rises faster. Annual changes are tens to hundreds of pounds against 20,000 pounds per percent, so changes take years to detect. The idea of open sites comes from {{ref:soil-bio-304}}.

soil-bio-316.title: How minerals lock organic matter away for centuries
soil-bio-316.text: Organic matter can persist for decades to centuries. It does so largely because it binds to minerals and is physically protected inside aggregates. {{ref:soil-chem-079}} bind organic matter by covalent, ionic or van der Waals interactions, making it hard for microbes to reach. Iron and aluminium oxides do this in acidic soils. In neutral and alkaline soils, calcium and magnesium bridges link organic molecules to clay. 2:1 clays with higher surface area adsorb more carbon than 1:1 clays. Inside aggregates, organic matter is spatially separated from decomposers and has less oxygen, as described in {{ref:soil-bio-293}}. One form of carbon needs no such shelter. Pyrogenic carbon from boreal fires, with condensed aromatic structures, can persist as a long-term sink, though persistence varies with formation conditions.

soil-bio-286.title: Organic matter and the nitrogen cycle
soil-bio-286.text: Each percent of organic matter in the top 6 inches holds about 1,000 pounds of nitrogen. Almost all soil nitrogen is part of organic matter, in forms plants cannot use directly. Plants take up most of theirs as nitrate and a little as ammonium, and small amounts of amino acids and small proteins can also be absorbed. Each year bacteria and fungi convert some organic nitrogen to ammonium and other bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate. A crop may draw 20-50% of its nitrogen from mineralized organic matter. Other sources are manure, nitrogen-fixing bacteria (large amounts under legumes), rain and snow deposition, and industrially fixed fertilizer, the largest addition for most grain crops. Losses follow. Nitrate leaches readily, especially from sandy and tile-drained soils, reaching groundwater or causing dead zones. Uncomposted manure or surface fertilizer may lose up to 30% by volatilization. Denitrification by bacteria in saturated soils turns nitrate into N2 and nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas estimated as agriculture's largest greenhouse contribution that also thins the ozone layer. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-294.title: The soil organic matter balance
soil-bio-294.text: The amount of organic matter in a soil is the net result of all additions and losses over the years. If additions exceed losses it rises, as in natural soil formation. If losses exceed additions it falls, as generally when soils enter crop production. If they are equal it holds steady. Residue additions raise it, while faster decomposition or erosion deplete it. Tillage, rotation and manuring all strongly affect it. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-295.title: What cropping costs a soil's organic matter
soil-bio-295.text: A Vermont clay soil lost 20% of its organic matter in five years of silage corn after decades of sod. Many Midwest soils lost 50% within 40 years of cropping. Converting grassland or forest to cropland sharply cuts soil organic matter through less residue returned, plowing-accelerated mineralization and erosion. Cash grain systems export 55-60% of organic matter even with residue retention. Loss is rapid in early years because active organic matter is plentiful, then slows as mainly stable material remains. In Canada, converting native land to cropland cost about 25% of the carbon in the top 30 cm, about 1 Pg of emissions from 19th-century grassland soils. Most of the loss came in the first twenty years. Deep tall-grass prairie soils kept their productivity long because they began with unusually high organic matter and nutrient reserves. Increased decomposition, not erosion, is typically the main culprit, as tillage breaks aggregates and exposes organic matter. The loss is mostly the light fraction of partly decomposed young residues. Residue removal, erosion, and sometimes fire used to clear land added to it. The starting point is the {{ref:soil-bio-294}}.

soil-bio-307.title: Managing the turnover of soil organic matter
soil-bio-307.text: Organic matter decomposes in all soils, so good management continually supplies new organic matter to feed organisms and replace what is lost. Minimize soil disturbance to keep aggregates and the organic matter inside them. Keep the surface covered with living plants or cover crops, or with residue mulch. Use rotations with perennials, cover crops and extensive-rooted crops, and add composts, manures or other off-field organic materials. The logic follows the {{ref:soil-bio-294}}.

soil-bio-301.title: How management shifts the living soil
soil-bio-301.text: The weight of living organisms in soil differs with vegetation and cropping system. Fungi outweigh bacteria in forest soils, roughly equal them in grasslands, and weigh less than bacteria in routinely tilled soils. Organisms are more abundant and diverse under complex rotations with diverse residues, cover crops, manures and composts, but frequent cultivation depletes their food. Compaction removes large pores first. A 1 mm pore is large and root tips are about 0.1 mm wide, so fewer earthworms, beetles, mites and springtails survive in compacted soil. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-302.title: How much organic matter is enough
soil-bio-302.text: Two percent organic matter is very good for a sandy soil but marks severe depletion in a clay soil. There are few accepted guidelines for adequate organic matter, and the right level depends strongly on texture and erosion risk. Fine mineral particles can saturate: a soil with 20% silt and clay can store at most about 3.6%, and one with 80% about 6.1%, excluding particulate organic matter. Total organic matter changes slowly, but an active-fraction test is more sensitive and gives an early sign of improvement. Sloping, erodible or already eroded soils need more organic input than level land. See {{ref:soil-found-045}} and {{ref:soil-found-051}}.

soil-bio-303.title: Why farmed soils hold less organic matter than pasture
soil-bio-303.text: In a New York study, pasture soils averaged 4.5% organic matter and conventional vegetable soils only 2.7%. The gap follows what each system returns to the ground. Cash grain farms sell 55-60% of their aboveground biomass and replace nutrients with fertilizer, but not carbon. Dairy farms return most biomass as manure, and organic vegetable farms import compost or manure. The study put annual grain at 2.9%, dairy at 3.4% and mixed vegetable at 3.9%. Aggregates followed the same order: the share of water-stable aggregates rose from 27% in conventional vegetable soils to 70% in no-till pasture. See {{ref:soil-bio-294}} for the balance behind it.

soil-bio-308.title: Five groups of soil health practices
soil-bio-308.text: Good soil management is not one trick but five families of them. Practices aimed at {{ref:soil-env-174}} should grow healthy plants, suppress pests or increase beneficial organisms, while reducing harm to the environment. They group into minimizing disturbance, keeping soil covered, maximizing biodiversity, managing water, and maintaining pH and nutrients without excessive loss. Organic matter practices come first for long-term sustainability, because each one has multiple benefits. Good physical condition and nutrient management still need additional practices.

soil-bio-313.title: What organic matter practices do for nutrients
soil-bio-313.text: A legume cover crop does several jobs at once. It adds active organic matter, cuts erosion and supplies nitrogen to the next crop. Cover and deep-rooted crops also cycle nitrate, potassium, calcium and magnesium that might otherwise leach away. Importing manure or compost adds nutrients too, but applied routinely every year it can overload the soil. Organic matter, the {{ref:soil-found-045}} the earlier entries described, does not settle everything. Testing manure, timing nutrients, liming and soil tests are separate practices that still have to be done.

soil-bio-297.title: How a crop rotation raises or drains organic matter
soil-bio-297.text: Organic matter rises and falls as a rotation moves from crop to crop. Perennial forages build it, while annual row crops under plowing deplete it. Hay and pasture crops add much root biomass and leave the soil undisturbed. Sod crops also cut erosion and residue decomposition. What a crop returns depends on the crop and the harvest: corn grain leaves more residue than soybean, wheat or silage harvest. Cover crops protect bare soil and add organic material, in amounts set by the cover type and its biomass before termination. This is the {{ref:soil-bio-294}} played out across several seasons.

soil-bio-296.title: How erosion strips organic matter and yield
soil-bio-296.text: Erosion takes the best soil first. Topsoil is rich in organic matter, so when water, wind or tillage carries it off, organic matter, water storage and yields all drop. Agricultural practice greatly speeds all three kinds of erosion, and in the United States the loss costs about $1 billion a year in available nutrients. Yields fall 5-10% under moderate erosion and 10-20% or more under severe erosion. On Corwin soil, between slight and severe erosion, organic matter fell from 3.03% to 1.86%. Available water capacity fell from 12.9% to 6.6%, roughly halving. That is the {{ref:soil-found-045}} paying for the topsoil that left.

soil-bio-298.title: Manure and other amendments from off the field
soil-bio-298.text: Bringing manure or other organic residues onto a field helps maintain or even raise its organic matter. The amounts can be large. A Vermont study found that 20-30 tons per acre of wet dairy manure were needed every year to maintain organic matter under continuous silage corn. The effects depend on manure type, on storage and handling, and on whether it is spread on the surface or incorporated. Nitrogen is a different tool. Synthetic nitrogen raises yields and residue, but it is often applied up to 50% above what the plants need.

soil-bio-310.title: Should crop residues be burned as fuel?
soil-bio-310.text: Crop residues look like free fuel, but soil also wants them. Using residues as biofuel feedstock could starve the soil of the organic inputs that maintain its quality. Most aboveground corn residue must return to the soil: an estimated 2-5 tons are needed to keep favourable properties. A long-term New York study found that modest cornstalk removal caused limited extra deterioration under no-till. Even so, routine removal calls for caution, most of all on cash grain fields with conventional tillage and no manure or compost. In 1980 Hans Jenny argued against indiscriminate conversion of biomass and organic wastes to fuels, because the humus capital deserves to be maintained. The question is still weighed case by case, and the evidence on how much removal soil can tolerate is limited.

soil-bio-312.title: Why farms with animals keep more organic matter
soil-bio-312.text: Farms with animals hold organic matter more easily, because manure recycles carbon and nutrients from feed grown on the farm. Integrating crops and livestock can start an upward spiral. Manure improves the soil, the crops then produce more residue and feed, and more animals mean more manure. Pasture, hay and haylage give perennial forages an economic use in the rotation. A farm with no animals can still obtain manure by trading hay with neighbors.

soil-bio-311.title: Which practices help water soak in
soil-bio-311.text: A field that takes in rain cuts runoff and erosion, refills the root zone and recharges groundwater. So which practices raise {{ref:soil-water-180}}? A University of Nebraska review of 89 studies found that perennial grass or legume hay and cover crops gave the greatest gains. No-till raised it only inconsistently. It worked when combined with surface residues and cover crops.

soil-bio-305.title: How much organic material it takes to gain 1 percent
soil-bio-305.text: Raising soil organic matter by 1% sounds modest, but it takes a very large addition of material. The top 6 inches of soil weigh about 2 million pounds, so 1% organic matter in that layer is 20,000 pounds. Most of what is added never stays, because decomposers consume it. If 80% is lost and 20% ends up as stable organic matter, roughly 100,000 pounds (50 tons) of dry organic material is needed for each 1% gain. That is the arithmetic behind {{ref:soil-found-045}} changing slowly.

soil-bio-291.title: Why acidic soils pile up organic matter on top
soil-bio-291.text: Organic matter breaks down more slowly in acidic soil than near neutral pH. One reason is earthworms: acidity inhibits them. Without them, organic matter accumulates at the surface instead of being mixed through the soil layers. {{ref:soil-found-014}} therefore shapes where the organic matter sits as well as how much of it there is.

soil-bio-314.title: Forests, farmland and soil carbon
soil-bio-314.text: Cutting down a forest typically lowers its soil carbon, and planting trees again may partly restore the original levels. The rate varies. Boreal reforestation gains carbon more slowly than other climates because trees grow slowly, and the previous land use and the type of disturbance control the rate. Afforested farmland gains more soil carbon than pasture or grassland, and mine-disturbed soils also gain a lot. Where they suit the site, deciduous trees raise soil carbon faster than conifers. Over time they also store more of it in the mineral soil than in the forest floor.

soil-bio-299.title: Where organic matter sits in aggregates
soil-bio-299.text: Organic matter lives both outside and inside soil crumbs. Outside aggregates it is roots, organisms and residue. Inside them it is adsorbed on clay and small silt, or trapped in small aggregates. Organic matter inside very small aggregates is out of reach of microorganisms and enzymes, and it also helps bind mineral particles. Larger aggregates are held mainly by fungal hyphae and their secretions, other microbial products, and roots. Tiny pores inside them can shelter microbes from predators. Finer soils need more of it: for over half of aggregates to be water-stable, a 50% clay soil may need twice the organic matter of a 10% clay soil.

soil-bio-320.title: When carbonates fool a carbon test
soil-bio-320.text: A soil test can report more organic carbon than the soil really holds. Carbonates decompose to CO2 during combustion-based analysis, and the instrument counts that CO2 as organic carbon. The problem arises on limestone-derived soils, including surface soils where tillage erosion has exposed carbonate-rich horizons. Three approaches separate carbonate carbon from organic carbon: heat treatment, acid treatment and wet oxidation.

soil-bio-289.title: Why wet and low places collect organic matter
soil-bio-289.text: In a Florida drained peatland, some homes now stand on posts above a surface that has sunk. Poor aeration slows decomposition, so organic matter accumulates in wet soils and low landscape positions. Lignin does not decompose at all without oxygen. Very long wetness produces peat or muck soils with over 20% organic matter. Draining those soils reverses the effect: the organic matter decomposes rapidly and the surface sinks. The landscape matters as well. Depressions and floodplains collect runoff, sediment and organic matter, so they accumulate more, while steep slopes and knolls stay low because topsoil keeps eroding. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-317.title: Measuring carbon and nitrogen by burning the soil
soil-bio-317.text: Dry combustion measures carbon by burning it. A ground soil sample is burned in oxygen, and the CO2 and nitrogen released give total carbon and nitrogen together. Samples under 250 μm are burned at about 1250°C. Copper at 600°C reduces nitrogen oxides to N2, and a gas chromatograph separates CO2 from N2 for detection. To get organic carbon alone, carbonates are removed by acid, measured by neutralization, or avoided by burning at 860°C, which decomposes only organic carbon.

soil-bio-315.title: Why some organic matter lasts and some vanishes
soil-bio-315.text: Under aerobic conditions, microbes respire organic inputs to carbon dioxide and water, using oxygen as the electron acceptor. How fast they do it depends on the chemistry of the input. Cellulose breaks into simple sugars that are readily degraded. Lignin, a network of aromatic components, is hard to break down and is mainly degraded by fungi. More complex organic matter needs more chemical energy and oxygen to degrade, which is one reason it persists longer. Fresh plant residue can fuel microbial activity that degrades stored carbon, an effect called priming, or it can add to stored carbon. The outcome depends on input quality, microbes, oxygen, water and time. Respiration is much slower without oxygen, so conversion of plant carbon takes longer in anaerobic soils. Compare {{ref:soil-bio-115}}.

soil-bio-292.title: Why roots build more soil organic matter than shoots
soil-bio-292.text: Roots are probably the most effective way to raise soil organic matter. Weight for weight, they add a larger share to persistent organic matter than aboveground residues do. They are well distributed, in close contact with soil, and often richer in slowly decomposing {{ref:soil-bio-116}} than aboveground parts. In an oat experiment one-third of surface residue remained after a year, but 42% of root organic matter did. For hairy vetch, 13% of aboveground carbon and nearly 50% of root carbon remained after five months. Root residue also contributed much more to {{ref:soil-bio-118}} than aboveground residue. Roots decompose more slowly, add more to stable organic matter, and need no incorporation to reach depth.

soil-bio-287.title: How organic matter shapes the water cycle
soil-bio-287.text: Organic matter works on water from the field scale up to the global one. Soils rich in it, with good tilth, let rainwater infiltrate quickly and store more of it. The water may serve plants or percolate down to recharge groundwater. When organic matter is depleted, the soil accepts and stores less water. Runoff and erosion rise, and plants and groundwater recharge get less.

soil-bio-319.title: Converting organic matter to carbon, and its weakness
soil-bio-319.text: Soil organic carbon and soil organic matter are different quantities. They are routinely converted by assuming that carbon is 58% of organic matter mass, a factor of 1.72. That figure comes from Waksman and Stevens (1930), who urged caution. Organic matter also holds hydrogen (about 4%) and oxygen (about 30%), and these vary with the state of decomposition. Reviews of many studies find that actual factors are usually higher than 1.72, meaning carbon is a smaller share of organic matter. The best approach is separate direct analyses. Otherwise, state what was analyzed and how values were converted.

soil-bio-288.title: Why clay soils hold more organic matter than sand
soil-bio-288.text: Organic matter is under 1% in sands, 2-3% in loams, and 4% to over 5% in clays. Fine-textured soils hold more for three reasons. Strong bonds between organic matter and clay or fine silt protect molecules from microbes and enzymes. Tiny aggregates shield organic matter inside them. Smaller pores and less oxygen in fine soils further limit decomposition. See {{ref:soil-found-051}} and {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-290.title: Why grassland soils are richer than forest soils
soil-bio-290.text: Soils formed under grassland hold more organic matter, distributed deeper, than soils formed under forest. Grassland roots are deep, extensive and turn over quickly. Slow grass fires also add biochar that resists degradation. This helps explain why former grassland soils are highly productive. Forests do it differently. Litter piles on the surface, where organic layers often exceed 50% organic matter, but the mineral layers beneath usually contain less than 2%. The root effect is strong in crops too: about 25-40% of a perennial wheatgrass root system dies back each year, adding much more organic matter than annual wheat. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-318.title: The Walkley-Black method and its biases
soil-bio-318.text: The Walkley-Black method oxidizes organic carbon with chromate, heated by added sulfuric acid, and titrates the leftover chromate to get the carbon. It was once the standard method. It oxidizes carbon incompletely, so a correction factor that varies with soil type is needed, and this biases the results. Carbon present as charcoal may be missed, which underestimates total soil carbon.

soil-bio-324.title: Isotope-ratio mass spectrometry: weighing atoms by type
soil-bio-324.text: Isotope-ratio mass spectrometry measures the relative abundance of isotopes in a sample. It serves both stable-isotope and radiogenic-isotope studies. Stable-isotope analysis measures variations from mass-dependent fractionation, while radiogenic analysis measures decay products and underpins most long-lived radiometric dating. Magnetic sector instruments are preferred over quadrupoles because they allow multiple-collector analysis and give good peak shapes. Ions are accelerated, bent by mass-to-charge ratio and counted in Faraday cups. Light elements such as H, C and O are measured as pure gases from combustion, GC or chemical trapping, against standards: carbon uses VPDB and oxygen uses V-SMOW. Thermal ionization MS suits low-ionization elements like Sr and Pb. MC-ICP-MS reaches elements such as Hf-W and Lu-Hf that TIMS cannot. Quadrupole ICP-MS precision is only about 1%.

soil-bio-325.title: Accelerator mass spectrometry for very rare isotopes
soil-bio-325.text: Some isotopes are so rare that ordinary instruments cannot count them. Accelerator mass spectrometry is an isotope-ratio technique for such extremely low levels, and it accelerates negative ions through a mega-volt potential. Charge exchange removes interfering species, and energy-loss detectors separate ions of the same mass-to-charge ratio. This allows isotope ratios above 10^12. It extended 14C dating to about 60,000 years BP and is about 10^6 times more sensitive than conventional IRMS. It builds on {{ref:soil-bio-324}}.

soil-bio-323.title: Isotope dilution: measuring by adding a known spike
soil-bio-323.text: Isotope dilution measures how much of a substance a sample holds by adding a known amount of an isotopically enriched form of it. The enriched standard dilutes the sample's isotopic composition. The method works from signal ratios, not intensities, and is an internal standardisation method, which gives it very high metrological standing. It is almost always paired with mass spectrometry. National metrology institutes use it to certify reference materials, and it helps when analyte recovery is low. The gains are measurable. In gas chromatography it can cut uncertainty from 5% to 1%, and isotope dilution mass spectrometry measures ratios to better than 0.25%. Double (reverse) dilution first calibrates the enriched spike against a natural-composition standard, because spikes come in small amounts of questionable purity. The principle is analogous to mark-and-recapture population estimates in ecology.

soil-class-165.title: Working through the Keys to Soil Taxonomy
soil-class-165.text: To classify a soil, work through the Keys to Soil Taxonomy, starting with the key to soil orders and eliminating classes whose criteria the soil fails. The first order whose criteria the soil meets is chosen, and the same process runs through suborder, great group and subgroup. Family and series use other criteria in the Keys. Suborders rest on soil moisture regimes and diagnostic features. Great groups rest on how strongly diagnostic horizons are expressed. Subgroups rest on properties transitional to other orders, suborders and great groups. The family name combines terms such as particle size class, mineralogy of the control section, soil temperature regime, CEC and depth. The levels themselves are set out in {{ref:soil-class-006}}.

soil-class-164.title: Describing a soil profile, step by step
soil-class-164.text: A profile description records each horizon's depth, color, texture, structure, consistence, roots, pH and boundary, so one soil can be told from another. The steps are: observe the landscape setting, examine morphology to separate horizons, describe each horizon in detail, assign horizon designations, then classify the soil by its morphology and horizonation. In the Harney silt loam example, the Ap horizon is 0 to 9 in, dark grayish brown (Munsell 10YR 4/2), silt loam, with moderate medium granular structure, very friable, many fine roots and slightly acid. Classification then reads the names. Formative elements give each level a connotation, and the bolded syllable of each order name appears in the names of its suborders and lower levels. In the Clarion-Nicollet-Webster-Glencoe catena, the wetter the drainage class the more the 'aqu' element appears, because Soil Taxonomy prioritizes management concerns such as a shallow water table. See {{ref:soil-form-004}} and {{ref:soil-class-165}}.

soil-class-166.title: Canadian soil classification, level by level
soil-class-166.text: In the Canadian System of Soil Classification each pedon fits only one class, assigned by comparing its horizons with diagnostic properties. Orders reflect the overall soil environment and the dominant soil-forming process. Great groups reflect differences in the strength of those processes, or a major added process. Subgroups differ by closeness to the central (Orthic) concept, transition toward another order and special features. Families group series of one subgroup with similar management and engineering response, but are seldom used in Canada. A profile is assigned its class by comparing its field horizons with a list of diagnostic properties. A related land rating covered about 2.6 million km2, about 25% of Canada's land mass, and rated each area in 7 classes by its most severe limitation, with classes 1 to 3 the prime lands. Compare {{ref:soil-class-001}}.

soil-class-167.title: Dry quicksand: sand that swallows without water
soil-class-167.text: Quicksand without water was long doubted as folklore. It was created in the laboratory in 2004, though its prevalence in nature is unclear. Dry quicksand is loose sand whose bulk density has been lowered by blowing air through it, so it gives way easily under weight or pressure. It behaves like ordinary {{ref:soil-phys-118}} but contains no water and works on a different principle. It can also result from contractive dilatancy. In Lohse's experiment, fine sand with grains about 40 micrometers, with air blown through it, settled to a packing fraction of only 41%, against 55-60% for untreated {{ref:soil-phys-014}}. A weighted table tennis ball dropped on it sank about five diameters, and a jet of sand shot upward after about 100 ms. In nature it might form when very fine blown sand settles.

soil-fert-290.title: Trace elements: needed in minute amounts, toxic in excess
soil-fert-290.text: The same element can feed a plant or poison it, and only the dose differs. A trace element is a chemical element present in minute quantity, especially a micronutrient (see {{ref:soil-fert-179}}). Essential ones are needed in tiny amounts for growth and metabolism in plants and animals, and they act as catalysts in {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reactions. Iron, copper, cobalt, iodine, manganese, chlorine, molybdenum, selenium and zinc are essential. Silver, cadmium, mercury and lead are not, and they are toxic to mammals even at low concentration. Some heavy metals in trace amounts act as essential micronutrients, yet every one becomes toxic at high concentrations.

soil-fert-289.title: Mineral nutrients: the elements beyond carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
soil-fert-289.text: In nutrition, a mineral is any chemical element other than carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen that an organism needs. A mineral counts only if it is bioavailable, meaning it can be absorbed, so it must be soluble or readily extractable. Metallic molybdenum has no nutritional benefit, while molybdates are sources. Plants and animals need similar minerals and enzymes, with differences. Legumes host molybdenum-containing nitrogenase, and animals use iron hemoglobin for oxygen but plants do not. Boron is essential to plants but not humans. Silicon is beneficial to most plants but usually not essential. Proving that an element is essential takes a biomolecule containing it with a testable function, because chemically similar elements can be taken up without being essential. Fertilizers are often tailored to the mineral deficiencies of particular soils, such as molybdenum, manganese and zinc.

soil-fert-288.title: Organic matter as the master nutrient strategy
soil-fert-288.text: If one habit could improve nutrient management overall, the facts name it: raise soil organic matter ({{ref:soil-found-045}}). This is the best overall strategy, especially for nitrogen and phosphorus. Mineralization of phosphorus and sulfur from organic matter is an important source of both, though residues with high C:N ratios can temporarily reduce nitrogen availability. Organic matter also holds K+, Ca++ and Mg++ ions. It provides natural chelates that keep zinc, copper and manganese in plant-usable forms. Better tilth and growth-promoting substances from decomposition help plants build bigger root systems, and diverse soil organisms keep plant pathogens low. Cover crop roots feed soil organisms that mobilize nutrients and reduce leaching and runoff losses. If legumes, they add nitrogen, and they maintain mycorrhizal spores for the next crop.

soil-fert-286.title: Where nutrient deficiencies tend to appear
soil-fert-286.text: Of the 17 elements all plants need, only nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are commonly deficient in soils. Sulfur deficiency is less common but not rare. Magnesium, zinc, boron and manganese can be lacking in certain regions. Geography helps predict which (see {{ref:soil-fert-169}}). Sulfur, magnesium and some micronutrient deficiencies are more common in highly weathered mineral regions, such as the southeastern United States and the tropics, or in high-rainfall regions. Sulfur deficiency is common on sandy coastal-plain soils and in low organic matter soils, as sulfur pollution from coal plants has declined. Calcareous higher-pH soils, especially in dry regions, need watching for iron, zinc, copper and manganese deficiency and for low phosphorus availability. Potassium deficiency is less common in young, little-weathered glaciated soils with moderate to low rainfall, as in the Dakotas.

soil-fert-291.title: Closing the loop on the farm
soil-fert-291.text: Better on-farm nutrient cycling aims to cut long-distance nutrient flows and return nutrients as residue or manure to the fields they came from. It extends {{ref:soil-fert-192}}. Losses fall when infiltration and root health rise through organic matter and soil physical management. Apply only the irrigation water needed to refill the root zone, since excess causes runoff and leaching. Rotations with cover crops, perennial grasses and legumes leach less nitrogen than annual row crops such as corn and soybeans. Test manures and credit their nutrients, test soils regularly, and apply most nitrogen near crop uptake. Add animals to crop farms and match their numbers to the land base. Feeding crops to animals exports far fewer nutrients than selling crops, but animals fed on purchased feed overload a farm. Local organic materials, composting to cut manure weight and volume for transport, compost exchanges and neighboring farm partnerships also help balance flows.

soil-fert-285.title: Manganese: the chlorophyll helper
soil-fert-285.text: Plants short of manganese turn yellow between the leaf veins, a pattern called chlorosis. Manganese activates some enzymes involved in chlorophyll formation, and it is one of the micronutrients in {{ref:soil-fert-179}}. Its availability depends partly on soil pH. The facts add that plants need only trace amounts of nickel, as with other micronutrients. Some plants use molybdenum for nitrogen fixation, so it may need adding to some soils before legumes are sown.

soil-fert-284.title: Copper: electron carrier and cereal limiter
soil-fert-284.text: Rice and wheat, the two most important food crops, are highly susceptible to copper shortage. Copper is an essential trace element for plants, animals and microorganisms, one of the micronutrients in {{ref:soil-fert-179}}. Its proteins carry electrons and oxygen by easily switching between Cu(I) and Cu(II). All eukaryotes need it for aerobic respiration, and in plants it is a component of some enzymes. Deficiency shows as browning of leaf tips and chlorosis. Soil copper is not uniform worldwide, and many soils are short of it. Naturally deficient soils often need copper added, usually as copper sulfate, before cereals can be grown, and nitrogen fertilizers can worsen the deficiency. Citrus, oats, spinach and carrots are also highly susceptible, while coconuts, soybeans and asparagus are not very sensitive.

soil-fert-292.title: Fertilizer or organic source: choosing what to apply
soil-fert-292.text: Commercial fertilizers such as urea, triple superphosphate and muriate of potash are convenient, easy to blend, predictable and precise in timing and rate. They have drawbacks. Common nitrogen materials are acid forming, nitrogen fertilizer takes 25%-50% of the energy in growing corn, and high solubility can cause salt or ammonia damage to seedlings and greater losses if mismanaged. Slow-release forms, such as sulfur- or polymer-coated urea, and nitrification and urease inhibitors, better match supply to crop needs. Organic sources are the nutrients in crop residues, manures and composts. Organic farmers replace synthetic fertilizers with minerals like greensand, granite dust and rock phosphate, or with bone, fish, soybean and blood meal. The cheapest source is not always best: anhydrous ammonia is hard to inject in stony soil, diammonium phosphate gives 18% N with phosphorus, and potassium magnesium sulfate suits fields needing magnesium but no lime.

soil-fert-287.title: Why nutrient balance protects plants from pests
soil-fert-287.text: Good nutrient management is critical to general plant health and the control of plant pests ({{ref:soil-fert-192}}). Too much available nitrogen early in the season lets small-seeded weeds with few reserves establish and later out-compete the crop. Nutrient-stressed plants may be stunted, or grow too much foliage and too little fruit when nitrogen is too plentiful, and they emit fewer signals that attract beneficial insects. Specific imbalances cause specific disorders. Low potassium aggravates stalk rot of corn and winter damage to bermudagrass. Excess potassium in the peanut fruiting zone goes with pod rot, and low calcium with droughty conditions causes tomato blossom-end rot. Healthy plants with large root systems depend on good tilth, no subsurface compaction, drainage, organic matter and a thriving soil biological community.

soil-fert-275.title: Phosphatase: the enzyme that frees phosphate
soil-fert-275.text: Plants cannot use phosphorus locked in organic molecules until an enzyme cuts it loose. That enzyme is phosphatase, which uses water to cleave a phosphoric acid monoester into a phosphate ion and an alcohol. Phosphatases are hydrolases, working by {{ref:soil-form-172}}: water is split, the -OH joins the phosphate ion and the H+ protonates the alcohol. The monoester is destroyed and free phosphate appears. Kinases do the opposite job, transferring phosphate from ATP. Phosphorylases are a third group, moving phosphate from hydrogen phosphate to an acceptor. Phosphatases are sorted into 104 enzyme families by substrate specificity and catalytic-domain sequence, yet all run the same general hydrolysis. In soils and ecosystems, phosphatases from roots, microbes and fungi release phosphate from organic phosphorus, which plants can then take up.

soil-fert-276.title: Nutrient flows: sources, destinations and the farm gate
soil-fert-276.text: Every bag of fertilizer and every truck of grain is a nutrient flow. A flow is the movement of carbon or nutrients from one place to another, linking a source with a destination. Flows happen on a farm, in a grassland or forest, or globally, within the idea of the {{ref:soil-fert-146}}. Buying fertilizer or feed brings nutrients onto the farm, and selling crops, meat or milk sends nutrients and carbon off it. Flows across the farm gate are managed on purpose. Others are unplanned, such as nitrate leaching to groundwater or runoff carrying nutrients with eroded topsoil. Harvested crops fed to animals and manure returned to the land together make a cycle, because nutrients and carbon come back to the fields they left. Cycling is nearly 100% efficient in forests and natural grassland, but modern specialized farming has little real cycling, with large exports, long bare periods and bigger leaching and runoff losses. Organic matter is over half carbon, so soil nutrient cycling is tied to the carbon cycle.

soil-fert-279.title: Farm nutrient balance: living off capital or building up
soil-fert-279.text: A farm that exports more than it imports is living off capital. A farm's nutrient balance compares what it imports with what it exports, using the flows in {{ref:soil-fert-276}}. Three patterns result: imports less than, greater than, or equal to exports. A negative balance draws down mineral and organic-matter nutrients until yields fall. Crop farms export a lot per acre each year: about 135 lb N, 25 lb P and 35 lb K for corn grain, and 150 lb N, 20 lb P and 130 lb K for grass hay. Integrated crop-livestock and grass-fed beef farms keep imports and exports small and near balance, because most nutrients return as manure and urine. Animal farms with too little land for their feed import more than they export. Nutrients build up and may leach or run off, with nitrogen and phosphorus the main water pollutants. The aim is to bring fertility to optimal levels and then roughly balance inflows and outflows, using soil tests to avoid building up or drawing down too far. Crop farms can balance nutrients in theory, but carbon is hard to replace. Residues do not replace the organic matter lost, which needs manure, compost, intensive cover cropping or perennial hay. Manure must also be spread well across fields, since fields near barns tend to get excess. Soil testing and manure planning can balance each field, and rotational pastures avoid the problem.

soil-fert-278.title: How modern farming broke the nutrient cycle
soil-fert-278.text: Food travels about 1,300 miles on average from field to consumer. Older farms with crops and animals together cycled carbon and nutrients well, and modern food systems have broken that cycle in successive steps (see {{ref:soil-fert-276}}). The first break came as cities grew. Nutrients and carbon traveled with farm products to distant urban populations and rarely returned to the soils they came from. City sewage and polluted waterways became sinks for these nutrients, and effluent still carries them into waterways despite new treatment plants. The second break came with farm specialization, which separated animals from the land that grows their feed. Manure accumulates, while crop farmers buy inorganic fertilizer and do not replace lost carbon. A third, larger-scale break is the shipping of crops across continents and oceans. Nutrients from crop farms travel to animal farms and are replaced by fertilizer from elsewhere, overloading the animal farms. Fertilizer nutrients also travel far, such as potassium from Saskatchewan to Ohio or phosphorus from Morocco to Germany.

soil-fert-283.title: Ion exchange membranes: an artificial root for measuring nitrogen
soil-fert-283.text: A charged plastic strip can do what a root does. Ion exchange membranes carry charged surface groups that adsorb ions such as NH4+ and NO3- from soil, giving an index of nitrogen supply. They rely on the same charge attraction as {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. They continually remove ammonium and nitrate released from organic N or desorbed from surfaces, mimicking a root, so they measure a supply rate in µg per cm2 per day. Membranes are buried in the field or used in the lab, then washed and eluted with NaCl (anion) or HCl (cation) before analysis. Plant N uptake related more closely to membrane-adsorbed N than to chemical extractions, so membranes may be a better index of N availability. They are simple, rapid and low cost, with adsorbed N rising with fertilizer rate and varying with season and crop stage.

soil-fert-277.title: Floodplain fertility: rivers that renewed the soil
soil-fert-277.text: Early agriculture centered on low-lying places where rivers converged and flooded fields with sediment. Rivers carry eroded minerals and organic matter downstream and deposit them on low-lying floodplains, renewing the fertility of those soils each year. Monsoon rains in the upper Nile basin brought annual fertile alluvium to the lower valley and delta, sustaining a large population for several millennia. Other ancient centers on alluvial deposits include the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the North China Plain, Mesopotamia and the Valley of Mexico.

soil-fert-280.title: The nitrogen balance: a simple test of sustainable use
soil-fert-280.text: One subtraction can tell whether a field's nitrogen use is sustainable. The N balance is N inputs from nutrient additions minus N outputs in the harvested crop over a season, a check on the {{ref:soil-fert-099}}. The optimum is generally between 0 and +50 pounds per acre. Below 0 the soil is being mined of nitrogen, and above 50 the excess causes environmental damage. The 50 pounds allowance reflects that N use is never fully efficient and some leaching and N2O losses are unavoidable. Most grain farms in the developed world import more N than they export, so their balance is positive. Reaching the optimum range takes careful N management with 4R practices and end-of-season cover crops, and rotations with low-leaching crops lower average losses.

soil-fert-281.title: Losing nitrogen even when the books balance
soil-fert-281.text: A farm can import and export nearly equal nitrogen and still pollute. In high-yielding corn, roughly 150-160 lb N applied matches the 160 lb in the grain, but much of the applied N is tied up in organic matter or lost by leaching or denitrification. Corn needs large amounts of nitrate daily during its two-month growth spurt. Pollution arises when fertilizer, manure and decomposing organic matter together supply far more than the crop needs. Leftover nitrate after harvest can leach into groundwater in fall, winter or early spring, at roughly 30-70 pounds per acre depending on precipitation, and some may become nitrous oxide. Losses are reduced by predicting crop needs from all N sources, timing application close to crop demand, and planting a quick-establishing cover crop.

soil-fert-282.title: Grain trade as a nutrient pipeline
soil-fert-282.text: Every shipload of grain carries soil with it, in the form of nutrients and carbon. Traded grain and oilseed crops move these between regions, leaving deficiencies in exporting soils and excesses in importing ones. The biggest transfers are corn and soybeans shipped from the Americas to East Asia, Europe and the Middle East, driven by demand for animal protein and oils. The United States, Brazil and Argentina supply almost 90% of soybean and 75% of corn exports, and South America has met demand by converting grassland, savannah and rainforest to crops. Exporting regions show less healthy breadbasket soils that have lost organic matter. Importing countries accumulate nutrients on livestock farms and see hypoxia in nearby seas. Trade can also help: importing U.S. wheat raises selenium intake in Europe.

soil-fert-253.title: Management intensive grazing: many paddocks, short stays
soil-fert-253.text: Pastures grazed continuously produce poorly. Repeated grazing of early regrowth depletes root reserves and weakens plants. Management intensive grazing rotates animals through many paddocks and does not regraze one until its plants have regrown. Cycles run from about a week or 10 days up to 6-8 weeks depending on season and weather, and dairy cows may get a fresh paddock after every milking. Harvesting and fertilizing need little equipment or labour, and electric fencing makes new paddocks quick to set up. Intensively managed pasture often lowers production cost despite the animals' foraging energy. Well-managed pasture combines perennial forage, no tillage and regular manure. New York soil health scores for organic matter, active carbon, respiration, water capacity and aggregate stability were far higher under pasture ({{ref:soil-found-045}}). Stocking can reach about 100,000 pounds of animals per acre for 8-12 hours, used to suppress or kill poor plant species and let hooves help reseed more productive ones. Where animals roam large rangeland by day and are stocked densely at night, the carbon, nutrients and seeds they gather are excreted into the small area, boosting fertility and revegetation. Grazing crop residue after grain harvest cuts feed costs and improves nutrient and carbon cycling. Cattle grazing corn residue in winter on the Great Plains raised soil health and yields. Swath grazing leaves annual crops such as barley and triticale cut in swaths for beef cattle, which improves forage access under deep snow.

soil-fert-239.title: When farms specialize, the nutrient cycle breaks
soil-fert-239.text: Specialized crop-only and animal-only farms break the nutrient cycle, causing excess on one and depletion on the other. Animal operations such as CAFOs often import feed from afar, so the supplying crop farms need large fertilizer amounts to replace the exported nutrients. Manure piling up relative to the land base can be applied beyond crop needs, polluting ground and surface water. Stored manure ({{ref:soil-fert-023}}) can contaminate surface water directly. Animals excrete most of the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in their feed, so animal-product farms export few nutrients, whereas annual grain and vegetable farms export many. Annual-only farms have little reason to grow perennial forages. Growing only one or two annuals complicates weed control, forgoes multi-year grass and legume soil health, favours pests and demands much nitrogen fertilizer. Integrating livestock can make a farm more sustainable but more complex, and done wrongly it can add environmental problems.

soil-fert-263.title: Nitrogen and phosphorus: two nutrients, opposite habits
soil-fert-263.text: Nitrogen moves; phosphorus mostly stays put. That contrast shapes how each is supplied, lost and managed. Nitrogen comes mainly from decomposing organic matter and can be added biologically by legumes ({{ref:soil-fert-099}}, {{ref:soil-fert-127}}). No biological process adds phosphorus, which also comes from soil minerals. Nitrate, the main form plants absorb, is very mobile. Phosphorus movement is very limited, and its available form is a small dissolved amount, mainly H2PO4- and HPO4 2-. Most N loss is nitrate leaching, denitrification or ammonia volatilization. Leaching dominates in sandy soils and denitrification in heavy loams and clays. Phosphorus is lost mainly in runoff and eroded sediment, but low losses have a high effect per unit on water quality because P often limits freshwater algae. P leaching matters in artificially drained fields: after years of excess manure or compost, P-saturated sandy soils leak P, and liquid manure can flow through wormholes and cracks to drain lines. Cover crops store nitrogen that would otherwise leach, and mobilize P through mycorrhizae and store it for the next crop. Excess N pollutes water with nitrate, raises nitrous oxide from denitrification, wastes energy in manufacture, speeds loss of soil organic matter and is linked to more insect damage. Making, hauling and applying N fertilizer ({{ref:soil-fert-007}}) is about 30 percent of the energy used to grow corn.

soil-fert-262.title: Composting: what it gains and when to skip it
soil-fert-262.text: Composted material is less bulky than the feedstock, so it is cheaper to transport and nicer to handle. The pile shrinks by 30-60 percent as carbon dioxide and water escape. Heat kills many weed seeds and pathogens, odors and flies decline, and compost has about half the bulk and weight of manure. Composting removes the nitrogen drawdown that follows adding sawdust or straw to soil, reduces nutrient solubility and stream pollution, and helps lower antibiotic levels in manure. Compost stores easily for application when conditions are right. It lets farms with excess manure move nutrients to fields, gardens and landscapes that need them. Direct addition of residues can be better. Fresh residues stimulate more aggregate-binding gums, supply more readily available nutrients and cost less labour and energy. Composting suits hard-to-handle, unsafe or odorous feedstocks, long hauls, pathogen concerns or good markets.

soil-fert-270.title: Managing nitrogen and phosphorus: count, test, time, place, cover
soil-fert-270.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus behave differently in soil ({{ref:soil-fert-263}}), yet they need similar management. Take all nutrient sources into account, using soil, manure and compost tests, crop residue N, and the 4R principles of right rate, time, place and source, plus conservation practices. Place fertilizer below the surface, split N applications where leaching or denitrification threaten, and apply when leaching and runoff threats are minimal. Cover crops with minimal or no tillage improve structure, cut leaching, runoff and denitrification, and store N and P in organic form between cash crops. Reduced tillage also keeps mycorrhizal networks intact for P. Sod-type forage crops in rotation reduce nitrate leaching and P runoff, and grass cover crops such as cereal rye capture leftover nitrate. Time N close to crop uptake. Holding most fertilizer until a PSNT, sensor or model shows need lets sidedress N be applied only if wanted.

soil-fert-258.title: Tending a compost pile: air, moisture and heat
soil-fert-258.text: A compost pile is a living machine that must breathe. Managing one means keeping air, moisture and heat in the range where composting microbes work well ({{ref:soil-fert-029}}). Oxygen moves into a pile while carbon dioxide, moisture and heat rise out, so it must pass air yet hold heat. Bulking agents such as chips or chopped straw keep fine material open. Settled piles are about 3-5 feet tall and 6-10 feet across at the base, wider in winter to hold warmth. Sites must be accessible yet away from watercourses, wells, flood plains and homes. Ideal moisture is about 40-60 percent, like a wrung-out sponge. At 35 percent or less ammonia escapes as gas and molds replace beneficial organisms. Temperature is the main monitor. The most efficient range is 104-140 degrees F (40-60 C), though piles reach 170 F, and overheating kills beneficial organisms too. Turning creates a new hot center, since lower sides barely compost. Farm compost may need only one or two turns, and a pile heating uniformly needs none. Too much turning dries the pile and loses nitrogen and organic matter.

soil-fert-252.title: How much manure nitrogen a crop can use
soil-fert-252.text: Manure nitrogen is the one manure nutrient that slips away. Its availability is the share of applied nitrogen a crop can use, and it is hard to predict because nitrogen is the most dynamic nutrient ({{ref:soil-fert-099}}).
