Phosphorus, potassium and most other manure nutrients stay in the soil and can be judged by soil testing, whereas manure nitrogen is easily lost with rain. University and government guidelines give nitrogen availability factors, the fertilizer-N equivalent per pound of manure N. They suit planning but are imprecise because they ignore weather. Spring applications use manure nitrogen better than fall or winter ones, since wet northeastern winters cause losses. The type of manure matters only modestly. Prompt incorporation matters a great deal, because much ammonia is lost from manure left on the surface, especially poultry and swine manure with more ammonium and urea than ruminant manure. In the Penn State table, spring poultry manure incorporated immediately has a factor of 0.75 but only 0.15 if incorporated after more than 7 days or never. A cover crop conserves fall and winter manure nitrogen by taking it up and returning it when terminated. Analysis separating ammonia-N from organic N, and credits for earlier applications, refine the estimate. Follow-up checks such as the pre-sidedress soil nitrate test, simulation models, remote imagery and crop sensors allow in-season correction.

soil-fert-266.title: Fixed versus adaptive nitrogen recommendations
soil-fert-266.text: Nitrogen advice comes in two families. Fixed approaches ignore season-to-season weather, and adaptive approaches adjust with field data, sensors or models. The most common is the mass-balance approach: N uptake for a yield goal minus credits from soil organic matter, preceding crops and amendments. In humid regions yield and optimum N rate are only weakly related, so fixed methods suit drier climates but are very imprecise in humid ones. Pre-plant nitrate and labile N tests, measured early in the season, work better in drier climates such as the Great Plains but cannot include seasonal weather. Adaptive tools fill that gap. Leaf chlorophyll meters and satellite, aerial, drone or tractor sensors assess canopy N status to guide sidedress N, and simulation models use radar rainfall and soil databases.

soil-fert-265.title: Why this year's weather changes the nitrogen a crop needs
soil-fert-265.text: Minnesota corn trials from 2015 to 2019 gained an average of 11 bushels an acre in a quarter of cases from sidedress N. Available soil nitrogen depends on recent weather, so a crop's need for supplemental N fertilizer shifts from year to year. Mineral N rises in spring but falls in a wet spring, as leaching and denitrification exceed conversion to mineral forms ({{ref:soil-fert-173}}, {{ref:soil-fert-108}}). A drier spring leaves more. Mineralization, leaching and denitrification vary with organic matter, amendments, soil temperature (warmer means more mineralization) and wetness. Saturated warm soils lose much N. Seedlings take up little N at first, then rapidly, so an unusually wet spring may need extra sidedress N. Dry years lower yields and N need, but a drought at pollination cannot be foreseen at sidedress time. Soil tests work well for P because plant-available P is strongly adsorbed, whereas N tests cannot give all answers.

soil-fert-254.title: How regular manure builds up phosphorus and potassium
soil-fert-254.text: Manure is not unbalanced; the trouble lies in nitrogen losses. Its nutrient ratios are roughly equal to crop needs, about 2:1 nitrogen to phosphorus. Buildup arises when nitrogen losses ({{ref:soil-fert-252}}) force high rates, so phosphorus and potassium accumulate in soil. Conserving nitrogen through timing, injection or incorporation lowers the manure rate needed, cutting P and K accumulation and the fertilizer N needed where P limits manure rates. After many years the soil test P and K can reach excessive levels, and all solutions need lower fertilizer P and P-containing amendments. Erosion of P-rich topsoil carries sediment and phosphorus to streams and lakes. Remedies include exporting manure and using N fertilizer or legumes, spreading manure more evenly across fields, rotating to alfalfa, which draws phosphorus down, soil conservation to trap sediment, or sending manure to a neighbor or composting facility.

soil-fert-274.title: Managing soils overloaded with phosphorus
soil-fert-274.text: A survey found the average US dairy herd was fed about 25 percent more P than the National Research Council recommends. High-P soils result from excessive P fertilizer or, more often, heavy manure use ({{ref:soil-fert-254}}), and they need managing to limit phosphorus loss to water. They are common on livestock farms with limited land and imported feed, where feed nutrients exceed those exported in animal products and where manure or compost applied to meet N adds extra P. The extra supplemental P can cost thousands of dollars for a 100-cow herd and ends up as a potential pollutant. Risk depends on context. Sites near critical water with slope, fine texture, poor structure or poor drainage need aggressive measures, while flat, grass-bordered vegetable or urban plots pose far less. First cut P in animal diets, then stop extra P by spreading manure on more land, swapping fields, or using legume covers and forages for N. Do not use a high-P source such as compost to supply N, since P builds up over the long term. Reduce runoff and erosion with reduced tillage, contour strips, cover crops, grassed waterways and buffers. Tile drainage can still carry P, especially after heavy liquid manure. Soil-test P falls slowly once imports stop, so test every two to three years. A one-time tillage can redistribute P built up at the surface of no-till soil, followed by starter P and injected manure.

soil-fert-261.title: Composts that help plants fight disease
soil-fert-261.text: Compost can act like a vaccine for roots and leaves. Research by Harry Hoitink and coworkers at Ohio State University showed that composts can suppress root and leaf diseases of plants. Plants become healthier because microorganisms produce plant hormones and chelates that make micronutrients more available, so they resist infection better. Beneficial organisms compete with pathogens for nutrients, consume them or produce antibiotics, and springtails and mites devour pathogen propagules. Composts rich in biodegradable organic matter support microbes that induce systemic resistance in plants against root and leaf diseases. The effect has a limit. Composts rich in available nitrogen can stimulate phytophthora root rot, fusarium wilt and fire blight. Applying them months ahead, leaching salts or blending with low-nitrogen compost lowers the risk.

soil-fert-241.title: Manure as an asset, not waste
soil-fert-241.text: Nutrients in the manure from a 100-cow dairy may be worth more than $20,000 a year. A 100-sow farrow-to-finish operation yields about $16,000 and a 20,000-bird broiler operation about $6,000, and soil organic matter benefits may double the value. Farm manure ({{ref:soil-fert-023}}) thus has considerable economic value as a source of nutrients and organic matter. U.S. manure from 100 million cattle, 120 million hogs and 9 billion chickens holds about 23 million tons of nitrogen. After cheap fertilizer arrived post-war, manure came to be seen as waste to dispose of. It is better spread widely than concentrated in a few places.

soil-fert-245.title: What manure contains
soil-fert-245.text: Most of what an animal eats leaves as manure. Over 70% of nitrogen, 60% of phosphorus and 80% of potassium fed may be excreted, available for recycling on cropland ({{ref:soil-fert-023}}). Manure also holds calcium, magnesium, sulfur and micronutrients, and zinc deficiency is rare on soils regularly receiving it. Analyses vary widely by feed, supplements, bedding and storage, so manure should be analysed routinely. Average liquid dairy manure holds about 25 pounds N per 1,000 gallons but may be 10 or 40. About 10 tons of dairy solid manure or 4,000 gallons liquid supply 100 pounds N, while poultry needs about 4 tons or 1,500 gallons. Poultry manure is significantly higher in nitrogen and phosphorus than other types.

soil-fert-260.title: Composting in pits and closed vessels
soil-fert-260.text: Not every compost pile sits in the open. Small farmers in developing countries, especially in dry and hot climates, dig compost pits. A layer of soil over the top keeps animals out and holds moisture in. Home composters often choose closed vessels instead. A vessel makes turning easier, gives better control of temperature and moisture, and keeps rodents away. At commercial scale, though, vessels are generally not economical.

soil-fert-240.title: Two kinds of crop-livestock farm
soil-fert-240.text: Some farms grow all or nearly all of their animal feed, and they come in two general types. One mainly sells animal products and matches animal numbers to the land's carrying capacity: grass-fed beef, pastured hogs, or a dairy growing its own grain and forage. The other is the diversified farm, which raises all its feed but sells a range of crops and animal products. Multiple products protect against seasonal failure and price swings. On both, crops feed animals and {{ref:soil-fert-023}} returns to the soil, a continuous supply of organic materials. Perennial forages cut erosion and keep or raise soil organic matter.

soil-fert-242.title: Solid, semi-solid or liquid: how dairy manure is handled
soil-fert-242.text: On a dairy farm, the barn often decides how {{ref:soil-fert-023}} is handled. Manure with bedding at around 20% dry matter or more is spread as a solid. Liquid manure from free-stall barns is 2-12% dry matter, and the 12-20% range is semi-solid, as with pasture cow manure. {{ref:soil-fert-029}} stabilizes nutrients, though considerable ammonium is lost, and leaves less, more pleasant material to spread. Separating liquid from solids lets the solids compost without added material and eases transport. Compost barns stir the bedded pack twice daily to 8-10 inches and clear it in spring or fall. Vermicomposting uses worms to turn dairy manure into castings. Industrial hog farms use slatted floors over pits and hold liquid manure in ponds for spring and fall spreading, while small hoop-house hog systems use bedding.

soil-fert-269.title: Grading a nitrogen rate after harvest
soil-fert-269.text: Was last season's nitrogen rate too low, about right or too high? Farmers can find out after harvest. One way is to plant field strips at different N rates and compare yields. Another is to sample soil nitrate after harvest, a 'report card' assessment of residual available N. The lower stalk nitrate test also shows whether corn N rates were right, too low or too high. Each answer guides rates in the following years.

soil-fert-267.title: Maximum return to nitrogen for corn
soil-fert-267.text: One way to set a corn nitrogen rate is to pick a single number: the rate with the largest average net return over many field trials. This is the maximum return to nitrogen. It draws on extensive trials, model fitting and economics, so recommendations vary with grain and fertilizer prices. The strength is also the weakness. Because it generalizes over large areas and many seasons, it ignores soil and weather effects. For an individual field, it is imprecise.

soil-fert-264.title: How much nitrogen compost really supplies
soil-fert-264.text: The richer an amendment is in nitrogen, the larger the share of that nitrogen plants can use. Compost or another organic amendment with about 2 percent N or less, a high C:N, supplies little to no available N. At about 5 percent N, roughly 40 percent is available. At 10-15 percent N, 70 percent or more is. Fertilizer should supplement what soil organic matter, manure, compost and rotation or cover crops already supply. Organic farmers try to meet all demands from these sources.

soil-fert-268.title: The pre-sidedress nitrate test
soil-fert-268.text: In late spring, a soil sample can say whether a corn field needs more nitrogen. The pre-sidedress nitrate test measures nitrate in the top 0-12 inches and guides sidedress or topdress nitrogen. It implicitly captures early-season weather and is especially good at identifying sites that need no more N fertilizer. The catch is timing. It needs special sampling in a short late-spring window and is sensitive to timing and early-spring mineralization. In the US Midwest it is called the late spring nitrate test. It was the first approach to address dynamic N processes, giving more precise recommendations and cutting unnecessary N applications.

soil-fert-257.title: Dung patches: uneven fertility on pasture
soil-fert-257.text: A grazing animal fertilizes in spots. Animals on pasture drop excrement on the surface, making small concentrated nutrient spots between which the soil is poorer. Some ammonium and urea is lost to the air as the pies dry. Dense vegetation keeps runoff low and nitrogen leaching less of a concern. Yet because the patches are unevenly spread, nitrate leaching can still occur on intensively managed, fertilized dairy pasture.

soil-fert-256.title: When a herd outgrows its land
soil-fert-256.text: Feed bought from off the farm carries nutrients with it, and they stay behind as manure. A farm whose herd exceeds its land base therefore accumulates them. Integrated crop-livestock farms that grow most of their feed keep nutrient imports and exports near balance. Farms with animal numbers beyond their land's feed output risk nutrient buildup and groundwater and surface water pollution. The options are sharing manure with neighbours, composting and selling it, or drying it to ease transport.

soil-fert-255.title: The Phosphorus Index: scoring the risk of runoff
soil-fert-255.text: Where will phosphorus leave a field and reach a stream? The Phosphorus Index is a tool for assessing that risk. It combines source factors, such as soil test P, total soil P and the rate, method and timing of P application. It also counts transport factors: sediment delivery, field position in the watershed, conservation practices, precipitation, runoff and tile drainage. A nutrient planner uses it to rate P movement risk as low, medium or high and to suggest mitigation.

soil-fert-246.title: Three forms of nitrogen in manure
soil-fert-246.text: Manure nitrogen is not one thing. It occurs as ammonium, as urea, which is soluble and quickly converted to ammonium, and as solid organic N. Ammonium and urea are readily available to crops, but they are lost as ammonia gas when left on a drying surface, with significant losses within hours (see {{ref:soil-fert-084}}). Mixes differ by animal. Some manures have half to three-quarters of N in readily available form, others 20% or less. Cattle manure is fairly balanced between available and organic N, while swine manure N is mostly ammonium or urea. Reports give ammonium and total N, the difference being mostly organic N. This is the nitrogen in {{ref:soil-fert-023}} that behaves most differently from one load to the next.

soil-fert-249.title: How much manure to spread
soil-fert-249.text: Farmers usually spread manure at a rate judged to supply the current crop's nitrogen, drawing on the forms described in {{ref:soil-fert-246}}. Common dairy rates are 10-30 tons solid or 4,000-11,000 gallons liquid per acre, supplying about 50-150 pounds available N. Small grains need 10-15 tons, corn 20-30 tons. Higher rates may build organic matter but risk nitrate buildup in leafy crops, nitrate leaching, salt damage and excess soil phosphorus. Where soil P is far above optimum, apply by crop P need and export part of the manure. Manure on legumes is discouraged, because the legume then fixes less N, though it can suit intensive animal farms with excess N. Manure P and K availability resembles fertilizer. Twenty tons of dairy manure give about 30-50 pounds phosphate and 180-200 pounds potash.

soil-fert-272.title: Why corn wastes so much nitrogen
soil-fert-272.text: Corn turns each extra pound of absorbed nitrogen into more yield than most crops. Even so, corn systems typically use fertilizer N at under 50 percent efficiency. Leaching, denitrification and runoff losses are much higher for corn than for soybeans or wheat, and especially than alfalfa and grass. The causes are growth cycle, rates, timing and rooting depth. Many farmers also add 'insurance' N for wet years, though they may need it only about one season in four.

soil-fert-271.title: Counting the nitrogen last year's crop left behind
soil-fert-271.text: Before buying nitrogen, subtract what the field already holds. Fertilizer decisions should deduct the N supplied by manure, decomposing sods and legume or cover crops. Example credits, in pounds per acre: corn 0; soybeans 0-40; 2-year clover 70; 3-year alfalfa 70 (20-60% legume) or 120 (>60%); crimson clover, winter peas and excellent hairy vetch 110. These credits are the N available to the crop, not the total in the residue. Sandy soils get less, and cover crop growth stage and amount matter strongly. High-yielding legume covers such as hairy vetch and crimson clover can supply most or all of the N for the next crop. Many labs, however, do not ask about cover crops.

soil-fert-273.title: The risk of broadcasting fertilizer on no-till
soil-fert-273.text: Broadcast fertilizer is fast: it covers 500-800 acres in eight hours, against about 200 for injection. In no-till, the speed has a cost in nitrogen and phosphorus losses. After intense storms, surface urea can wash into wormholes and deep into the subsoil, so N should not be broadcast and left on the surface. Residue urease speeds urea conversion to ammonia gas. Phosphorus builds up on no-till surfaces, and dissolved P in runoff is often higher than from tilled soil. P should therefore be applied below the surface.

soil-fert-259.title: Curing: the last stage of compost
soil-fert-259.text: Hot composting ends with a quiet phase of one to three months called curing, in which the pile cools and finishes its decomposition. It starts once temperatures drop to about 105 degrees F and no longer rebound after turning. A pile that reheats is not finished, and the Solvita test measures CO2 loss to judge maturity. Curing further breaks down resistant chemicals and large particles, brings pH toward neutral, converts ammonium to nitrate, leaches soluble salts and lets common soil organisms colonize. Moisture should stay at or below about 50 percent. The early curing processes are thought to give compost some of its disease-suppressing quality.

soil-fert-244.title: Turning manure into biogas
soil-fert-244.text: On large livestock farms, anaerobic digesters process manure to make biogas, mostly methane. The gas fuels on-farm heat and electricity or off-farm vehicles, and digesters can cut greenhouse gas emissions, odors and pathogens. They are a major capital investment, though, and may not pay without subsidies, energy, carbon credits, tipping fees and coproducts. Nor do they solve the nutrient problem. They separate liquid and solids but generally do not change total nutrient content, so excess nutrients and runoff remain. The input is still {{ref:soil-fert-023}}, only processed.

soil-fert-247.title: Why manures differ in what they add to organic matter
soil-fert-247.text: Equal amounts of different manures do not affect {{ref:soil-found-045}} equally. The difference is how much solid is returned. Dairy and beef manures hold undigested forage and bedding rich in lignin, so they influence organic matter far more than unbedded poultry or swine manure. Sand bedding and separating solids return less organic material to fields, whereas a bedded pack is high in solids. With corn silage under conventional tillage, 20 to 30 tons of solid dairy manure per acre yearly maintain organic matter; less is needed if more residue returns. The arithmetic is humbling. Twenty tons of manure holds about 5,200 pounds of solids. Mixed into the top 6 inches, it would raise organic matter about 0.3%, but if 75% decomposes the net gain is 0.065%. Still, the effect shows in the field: New York samples of 300 fields showed dairy-crop fields receiving manure averaged 0.5% higher organic matter than cash grain fields.

soil-fert-248.title: What years of manure do to a soil
soil-fert-248.text: Manure changes a soil in biological, chemical and physical ways. An 11-year Vermont experiment grew continuous corn silage, a monoculture with low residue return. Twenty tons of dairy manure yearly kept organic matter and CEC levels, and the pH stayed close to the original, offsetting that low return. Dairy and poultry manures have a liming effect and counteract acidification. The physical changes were as clear. Manured plots were better aggregated and less dense. Organic matter was 5.2% originally, 4.3% unmanured and 5.2% at 30 tons, with pore space 44% versus 47%. Liquid manure supplying the same N would not have raised organic matter, CEC and pore space nearly as much, a link back to {{ref:soil-fert-247}}.

soil-fert-243.title: What manure loses while it waits
soil-fert-243.text: Storing manure lets farmers apply it at the best time for the crop, cutting runoff, leaching and gaseous losses. But storage itself loses nutrients. In one study, dairy manure in uncovered piles lost over a year 3% of solids, 10% of nitrogen, 3% of phosphorus and 20% of potassium. Covered piles and bottom-loading liquid systems with a surface crust conserve nutrients better. Poultry manure may lose 50% of its nitrogen as ammonia unless protected. Potassium is soluble and sits mostly in the liquid portion, so a stack that lets water drain may lose much of it. All of this concerns {{ref:soil-fert-023}} kept waiting.

soil-fert-250.title: How surface manure loses its nitrogen to the air
soil-fert-250.text: Leave manure on the surface and its nitrogen starts to vanish within a day. Ammonium and urea turn to ammonia gas as the manure dries and are lost to the air. About half of dairy manure N comes from urine urea, which converts to the ammonium that is almost all of its readily available N (see {{ref:soil-fert-246}}). Surface-left dairy manure loses about 25% of its N after one day and 45% after four days, around 70% of the readily available N. Half an inch of rain soon after application leaches ammonium in. Incorporating the manure in spring helps, and fall injection of liquid manure greatly reduces loss compared with broadcasting. Surface manure also risks nutrient runoff to surface waters.

soil-fert-251.title: Timing manure to the crop
soil-fert-251.text: Manure works best when it lands near the time the crop needs nutrients. For annual crops, apply in one dose just before tillage so it is incorporated fast. Injection close to planting cuts runoff and erosion risk. Fall application in humid climates lets ammonium convert to nitrate that leaches or denitrifies. A three-year New York study found about twice the N leaching from fall as from spring liquid manure on corn silage. Grass hay is constantly N deficient. It does best with about 50-75 pounds available N in early spring and after each harvest, though wet early-spring soils risk compaction. Spreading on frozen or snow-covered ground is legal in most states but poor practice. Injection into a shallow 2-4 inch frozen layer avoids runoff. The rates themselves are the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-249}}.

soil-water-298.title: Marine clay: soft sediment from the sea floor
soil-water-298.text: Marine clays are fine-grained sedimentary deposits made mostly of {{ref:soil-found-040}} minerals that build up in coastal environments. They derive from weathered continental rocks carried to the ocean, where they settle and consolidate on the seabed. They commonly contain {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and chlorite, plus varying silt, organic matter and biogenic material. Saline deposition shapes their structure and bonding, often giving high natural water content and low permeability. Seawater's excess ions make deposited clay flocculate into a loose, open structure (see {{ref:soil-phys-006}}). Once dried by falling sea level, it admits water easily. That fragile structure makes marine clays highly sensitive: they can lose much of their strength when disturbed. One more clue is stratigraphic. Marine clay lying over peat may mark a marine flooding surface, reflecting landward coastal shift during relative sea-level rise.

soil-water-299.title: Why clay clumps where rivers meet the sea
soil-water-299.text: Fine silt and clay stay suspended longer than sand. Small, negatively charged clay particles can resist settling altogether and stay suspended, producing turbidity. Flocculation is the process by which fine particles in water clump together into flocs, as in {{ref:soil-phys-006}}. In estuaries, changing physicochemical conditions from river to sea trigger flocculation and siltation, a main cause of harbour dredging. Organic matter plays a major role by adhering to marine clay particles. The exchange cations on the particles (sodium, potassium, calcium) set their arrangement and properties.

soil-water-300.title: Building on marine clay
soil-water-300.text: Marine clay is a geotechnical challenge because the soil is open, sensitive and weak under load. It is sensitive to weathering, which affects support under loads and limits bearing capacity and service life. Pavements over it lose durability and cost more over their life. The worst case is {{ref:soil-water-071}}: very unstable, it liquefies and flows when saturated, causing mass wasting. Ground improvement techniques can handle the problems, and marine clay can be stabilized by mixing with cement and fly ash in set proportions. The same material has uses. Marine clays serve as low-permeability landfill liners and adsorb contaminants, and they have long been used for heat-resistant ceramics. The material itself is described in {{ref:soil-water-298}}.

soil-agri-193.title: What a rotation does to soil organic matter
soil-agri-193.text: Plow up virgin forest or prairie and plant row crops, and organic matter drops rapidly for five to ten years, until a low equilibrium is reached that holds if practices stay unchanged. Under a rotation (see {{ref:soil-agri-004}}), crop type, yield, root mass, harvested portion and residue management together set {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Switching to grass or grass-legume sod raises it, but more slowly than the loss under continuous tillage. Long experiments show the spread. In a 60-year Missouri experiment, continuous corn lost over 9 inches of topsoil (21 tons per acre a year) and ended with 1.2% organic matter, against 2.2% under unfertilized timothy. A six-year rotation kept about 70% of the timothy topsoil. In eastern Canada, continuous corn added about 100 pounds of organic matter per acre yearly, corn-alfalfa 500, four-year alfalfa 800; 3% organic matter is about 60,000 pounds per acre. Perennial forages slow decomposition by reducing disturbance and add organic matter from sod roots, part of which die each year. Older grass roots die even during the growing season. Gains have a ceiling: they plateau once mineral surfaces are saturated and the soil is highly aggregated, however much residue, manure or compost is added. Life in the soil follows. In semiarid Oregon, total microorganisms under a two-year wheat-fallow system were about 25% of the amount under pasture. Moldboard plow tillage decreases earthworm and other soil organism populations, and including perennial forages enhances the diversity effect.

soil-agri-180.title: Choosing a cover crop for the job
soil-agri-180.text: Different cover crops are grown for different primary purposes. Grasses such as cereal rye and oats catch and cycle nutrients. Legumes such as hairy vetch and red clover fix nitrogen with Rhizobium as green manures (see {{ref:soil-fert-026}}). Fast-growing competitive species such as buckwheat and sorghum-sudangrass smother weeds. Brassicas such as mustards and radishes biofumigate pests with glucosinolates and isothiocyanates. Strong-rooted crops such as cereal rye, radishes, hairy vetch and alfalfa loosen compacted soil, while sorghum-sudangrass, cereal rye and sunn hemp build biomass and organic matter. Ecologists separate canopy functions (aboveground biomass) from root functions (belowground biomass), and choice can follow the traits wanted. Grass cover crops are more likely than legumes to increase {{ref:soil-found-045}}, and some grow as much or more biomass underground as above. Hairy vetch or crimson clover may yield 1.5 to over 4 tons dry weight per acre, mature cereal rye 3-5 tons, and early-terminated crops as little as half a ton. The gains are measurable. A five-year California clover experiment raised organic matter in the top 2 inches from 1.3% to 2.6%. Pooled experiments found cover crops raised organic matter 8.5% over original levels and soil nitrogen 12.8%.

soil-agri-179.title: Mineral wool as a growing medium
soil-agri-179.text: Mineral wool is a fibrous material spun or drawn from molten rock or slag. Among other uses, it is a hydroponic growth medium, a relative of the {{ref:soil-agri-031}}. Stone wool is made by blowing air or steam through molten rock at about 1600 C, giving fine intertwined fibres 2 to 6 micrometres across. Products can be engineered to hold large amounts of water and air for root growth and nutrient uptake, and the fibres give mechanical support. Its naturally high pH makes it unsuitable at first, so it needs conditioning, for example pre-soaking in nutrient solution at pH 5.5 until it stops bubbling.

soil-agri-186.title: When cover crops feed the next crop, or starve it
soil-agri-186.text: A cover crop can feed the next crop or deliberately lower available nitrogen at season end to cut losses. A productive legume grown to bud stage can make 70 to well over 100 pounds of nitrogen per acre available. Hairy vetch and crimson clover are frequent choices. How much arrives depends on growth stage, biomass and nitrogen content. Small deep-green plants contain over 3 percent N but little total N. Grasses go the other way. Cereal rye N falls below 1 percent with a C:N ratio of 80 or more at maturity. At about 1.5-2 percent N, soil organisms use all the nitrogen and little reaches the next crop.

soil-agri-182.title: Grass cover crops and what they scavenge
soil-agri-182.text: Grass cover crops include annual cereals (rye, wheat, triticale, barley, oats), forage grasses such as ryegrass, and warm-season grasses such as sorghum-sudangrass. Their fibrous root systems scavenge leftover nutrients, especially nitrogen, and some establish rapidly to greatly reduce erosion. They produce large amounts of residue and roots that add organic matter, and the residue helps suppress weed germination. Cereal rye grows in late fall and early spring as a catch crop and soil conditioner in cool regions. In Maryland it is widely used to cut nutrient loading into the Chesapeake Bay.

soil-agri-181.title: Legume cover crops, from cowpeas to clovers
soil-agri-181.text: A cover crop that feeds the next crop is hard to beat, which is why legumes, the nitrogen-fixing family in {{ref:soil-bio-182}}, are so often chosen. They sort into three groups. Summer annuals include soybeans, cowpeas and sunn hemp. Winter annuals include winter field peas, crimson clover and hairy vetch. Perennials include red clover, white clover and alfalfa. Sweet yellow clover is a biennial. Austrian winter and Canadian field peas can leave 2.5 tons or more of dry matter and fix 100-150 or more pounds of nitrogen per acre. Each species has limits. Crimson clover matures quickly but is marginal in hardiness zone 5 and on poorly drained or calcareous soils. Cowpeas thrive in heat and drought, yet even mild frost kills them. Sweet clover needs near-neutral pH and does poorly in wet clayey soils, though its roots penetrate compacted subsoil. Red clover starts slowly, so it is interseeded into small grains in early spring.

soil-agri-199.title: Old rotations and the corn-soybean rotation
soil-agri-199.text: A five- to seven-year rotation once kept northern Midwest and Northeast mixed farms in balance. Nitrogen-hungry corn followed pasture, grain grew only two years in five to seven, and oats served as a nurse crop when hay was seeded. It roughly maintained organic matter. Cheap pesticides and fertilizer, feedlots, export markets and price-support programs then narrowed production to corn and soybeans. That pair beats monoculture, but it brings erosion, nitrate and herbicide pollution, organic matter loss and sometimes more insects. Soybeans leave minimal residue. Each farm's soil, climate and economics differ, so these are examples to learn from, not recipes.

soil-agri-192.title: Crop diversification in time and space
soil-agri-192.text: Diversity can be added to a farm in time, in space, or both. Cover crops and rotations diversify over time; different crops in different fields or strips diversify across the landscape. A staggered rotation gives both. Perennials add diversity with less frequent rotations, as when dairy farmers grow alfalfa three to four years before corn. Agroforestry and integrated livestock add further dimensions. Behind all of this sits an ecological principle: diversity contributes to stability and productivity.

soil-agri-198.title: Designing a crop rotation: the main rules
soil-agri-198.text: A new rotation starts from a few guidelines. Follow a legume forage with a high-nitrogen crop such as corn, and grow oats, barley and wheat less in the second or third year after the sod. Grow the same annual crop only one year, and avoid closely related species in sequence, since they share pests and diseases. Western corn rootworm populations have lately emerged that survive corn-soybean alternation. Before carrots or lettuce, plant grains that root-knot nematodes cannot feed on for a few years. Use each crop for what it does. Small grains suppress weeds, row crops allow cultivation, and mowed or grazed sods control annual weeds. Use longer perennial periods on sloping, erosive land. Deep-rooted crops such as alfalfa, safflower or sunflower scavenge subsoil nutrients and water, and their root channels aid infiltration. Where rain is limited, water use is critical. Hay and sunflowers may leave too little moisture, and under 25% of rain during the 14-month fallow in the Central High Plains reaches the next wheat crop.

soil-agri-194.title: Active rooting period: how long roots live in a rotation
soil-agri-194.text: Some rotations keep living roots in the soil for under a third of the time. The active rooting period is the percent of a rotation during which living roots are present. It runs from 32% for corn-soybeans to 57% for soybean-wheat and 76% for a three-year soybean-wheat-corn rotation. Adding winter wheat to a corn-soybean alternation greatly lengthens it, because winter annuals, perennials and cover crops extend the growing period beyond summer annuals. Dry beans-winter wheat with a cover crop reached 92% with three species. Longer living cover decreases erosion, nitrate loss and groundwater contamination.

soil-agri-196.title: What diversified rotations cost and save in labor
soil-agri-196.text: A varied rotation makes the farm calendar easier to live with. Forage hay and early-harvested crops spread labor over the season, which eases management by family labor and gives steadier income. The costs are real, though: more equipment, and labor conflicts such as cultivating corn at the same time as harvesting hay. Integrated livestock with multi-species grazing need less specialized equipment, harvest and spread manure themselves, and diversify income.

soil-agri-195.title: How rotations protect water and cut nitrous oxide
soil-agri-195.text: In South Dakota, a four-year rotation of corn, field pea, winter wheat and soybean beat corn-soybean. It gave higher soybean yield, more soil organic matter and less nitrous oxide lost. Water quality is a big part of the reason. Spring-planted annuals leave soil without roots for much of the year, so nitrate can leach ({{ref:soil-agri-022}}), a problem accentuated by tile drainage in the Midwest and Northeast. Bare wetter soil also runs off and erodes more. Perennial forages and winter grains protect water. Cover crops help similarly but do not substitute for a good rotation, and the combination gives the greatest improvement.

soil-agri-190.title: When cover crops cause trouble
soil-agri-190.text: A cover crop is not free. It can deplete soil moisture, become a weed, compete with an intercropped cash crop for water, light and nutrients, and cost money for seed and establishment. In dry areas and on sands, late killing of a winter cover may cause moisture deficiency. In warm humid no-till climates, longer growth means less wet soil at planting and more residue. The benefits are real too: cover crops raise infiltration through macropores and water-holding capacity through organic matter, and residue slows runoff. Careful management decides which side wins.

soil-agri-185.title: Cover crop mixtures: pairing a grass with a legume
soil-agri-185.text: Mixing species gives a cover crop more than one job, and the most common pairing is a grass with a legume. Mixed stands usually suppress weeds better than a single species, and legumes with small grains offset the nitrogen decline when grains mature. In the mid-Atlantic, a rye-hairy vetch mix manages nitrogen on its own. Rye is stimulated when much nitrate remains, reducing leaching, while vetch competes better and fixes more when little is available. Erect rye also supports vetch, and vetch held up by rye is killed more easily by close mowing, which may replace herbicide in no-till.

soil-agri-187.title: When to plant a cover crop
soil-agri-187.text: A cover crop can fill a whole growing season, follow the cash crop harvest, or be interseeded into a growing cash crop. A full-season high-biomass mix builds the most organic matter and suits infertile or eroded soils and organic transition, but no income crop grows that year. Most farmers instead sow after harvest, avoiding competition with the main crop. Seed can be no-till drilled for better stands, and tillage before seeding should be avoided. The right choice depends on the goal, the cash crops, the season length and the climate.

soil-agri-189.title: Ending a cover crop: termination methods
soil-agri-189.text: Every cover crop has to stop before the cash crop can thrive. Termination kills or drastically weakens it before or during soil preparation. Methods include mowing after flowering, herbicide with no-till, plowing in, mow-roll-crimp with no-till planting in one pass, and winter injury. Waiting a week or two lets residue decompose, which eases nitrogen immobilization, allelopathy, damping-off, cutworm and wireworm problems, and gives a better seedbed. A sudex cover crop is especially allelopathic, so tomatoes, broccoli and lettuce should wait six to eight weeks.

soil-agri-191.title: Choosing cover crops to limit nematodes
soil-agri-191.text: Whether a cover crop helps or harms depends on how well nematodes can feed on it. Grain crops are nonhosts of the root-knot nematode (M. hapla), so growing grains reduces numbers, though very bad infestations may need two full grain seasons. The root-lesion nematode (P. penetrans) infects most crops. A legume such as hairy vetch will stimulate it, while sudangrass, sorghum-sudan, ryegrass and pearl millet reportedly cut numbers. Suppression comes from poor host status, stimulated microbial antagonists and toxic products released on decomposition. Brassicas and pearl millet also biofumigate. For the pests themselves, see {{ref:soil-bio-194}}.

soil-agri-188.title: Planting green into a living cover crop
soil-agri-188.text: Planting green means seeding a cash crop directly into a still-living cover crop and terminating the cover soon after. Older advice left a week or two between killing the cover and planting, which remains best in a dry spring. Now the cover is usually sprayed shortly after planting, or suppressed mechanically with a rolling stalk chopper or a cereal-rye roller-crimper ahead of a no-till planter. It has worked for soybeans, corn and cotton but is not recommended for most direct-seeded vegetables.

soil-agri-183.title: Buckwheat, the fast frost-sensitive cover
soil-agri-183.text: Buckwheat finishes quickly. It takes about six weeks from planting in warm soil to early flowering, and it can exceed 2 feet in a month. This frost-sensitive summer annual grows better than many cover crops on low-fertility soils but tolerates compaction poorly. It competes well with weeds and has been reported to suppress root pathogens including Thielaviopsis and Rhizoctonia. Its seeds do not persist for years, yet it can reseed as a volunteer weed, so mow, roll or till it before seeds develop.

soil-agri-184.title: Groundcovers in orchards and vineyards
soil-agri-184.text: Between the rows of an orchard or vineyard, a perennial groundcover can improve soil health and crop quality. The ideal cover does not overly compete with the main crop and persists with little maintenance. It gives erosion and weed control and tolerates shade, traffic and drought. Acting as a living mulch ({{ref:soil-fert-069}}), Dutch white clover gives modest nitrogen, and low-growing fescues with dense fine roots need minimal mowing. In vineyards covers are sometimes kept away from the vines but used to compete with them and curb excess vegetative growth.

soil-agri-197.title: Rotation as a tool against plant disease
soil-agri-197.text: Some diseases need only a one-year break from their host; others need several years of nonhost crops to cut inoculum. That is why careful rotations, especially alternating grains and broadleaf plants, help control plant diseases and nematodes (see {{ref:soil-agri-004}}). Pulse crops seem to stimulate beneficial organisms and reduce cereal root disease, and a multiyear broadleaf break lowers common root rot of wheat and barley. Rotation has limits. It is hard for wide-host-range pathogens, seed-borne disease and windborne wheat leaf rust, which need other tactics.

soil-agri-202.title: Faidherbia albida, the dry-season shade tree
soil-agri-202.text: Faidherbia albida is a tropical legume tree of seasonally dry climates, used in silvopasture and alley cropping. Its feathery leaves give a light canopy for corn or pasture, and it has a deep taproot. It carries foliage in the dry season when forage is scarce, blooms for bees at the dry season's end, and gives pods for livestock and wood for fuel.

soil-agri-201.title: Forest farming under the canopy
soil-agri-201.text: Forest farming grows crops in the understory of an established natural or timber forest, with no separate growing zones. Here shade is wanted, not avoided. Examples are ginseng, mushrooms, elderberries, rhododendrons and moss, many quite profitable.

soil-agri-200.title: Silvopasture: trees and grazing together
soil-agri-200.text: Silvopasture integrates trees and grazing livestock on the same land. It gives forest products and forage, so both short- and long-term income. Partial shade helps cool-season grasses in heat in temperate climates, and keeps animals cool in hot ones. It still needs agronomic care such as forage selection, fertilization and rotational grazing, and it can stabilize landslide-prone slopes.

soil-agri-203.title: Agroforestry systems that change as trees grow
soil-agri-203.text: Trees change the field as they grow, and transitional systems make use of that shading and microclimate change. A landowner may start with alley cropping between young trees ({{ref:soil-agri-134}}), then move to silvopasture, forest farming or an orchard. The other path is to trim the trees and keep alley cropping.

soil-agri-224.title: Working out residue cover after tillage passes
soil-agri-224.text: Every tillage pass buries some residue, so the surface cover shrinks, and passes in sequence are estimated by multiplication. Multiply the fraction each tool leaves. For example, 80% cover after corn, then chisel (70%), tandem disk (45%), field cultivator and planter (75%) leaves about 19%. Dropping the disk leaves 42%. After corn or cereals a moldboard plough leaves 0-10% residue, twisted-point chisel 50-70%, tandem finishing disk 30-60%, field cultivator 60-90% and a row-crop planter 85-95%. Speed, depth and soil moisture affect the amounts, and cover also depends on surface roughness and soil loosening. This arithmetic shows whether a system meets the 30% threshold of {{ref:soil-agri-099}}.

soil-agri-223.title: A short history of tillage
soil-agri-223.text: Tillage began with small-grain farmers of the Fertile Crescent, Europe and North Africa, who wanted a fine, clean seedbed. It also gave the crop a head start on weeds and stimulated mineralization of nutrients. Centuries of this system caused excessive erosion, organic matter loss and nutrient depletion, especially around the Mediterranean. Jethro Tull's 1731 book promoted row seeding with a seed drill and intensive tillage. He believed pulverized soil particles fed plants, and he grew wheat 13 years without manure by mining soil nutrients. Pre-Columbian American farmers did differently: no full-field tillage, but direct seeding with planting sticks or hoeing small hills, with corn, beans and squash intercropped. For the practice itself, see {{ref:soil-agri-095}}.

soil-agri-225.title: Frost tillage: working soil as it freezes
soil-agri-225.text: Frost tillage means tilling soil after frost has entered it but before it has penetrated more than about 2 inches (5 cm). Water moves up to the freezing front and the soil beneath dries, and the frozen layer supports equipment, so compaction is reduced. The rough surface favours water infiltration and prevents runoff, and livestock farms can use it to incorporate or inject manure in winter. Recent research in Nebraska and Australia indicates occasional tillage does not harm soil health. Purposes include weed or insect control, incorporating immobile amendments and compaction relief. Even so, it should be rare, once every 5-10 years, with tools that leave residue, because any tillage can destroy structure built by years of {{ref:soil-agri-117}}.

soil-agri-217.title: Biological pest control with living enemies
soil-agri-217.text: Sometimes the cheapest pest control is a field border. Nectar-producing plants on rice field borders cut pest densities 10- or even 100-fold, so farmers sprayed 70% less insecticide and yields rose 5%. Biological control uses other organisms to control animal pests, weeds or plant and animal pathogens. It relies on predation, parasitism and herbivory with active human management, and can be a component of {{ref:soil-agri-054}}. Three strategies exist: importing a pest's natural enemy to a new place, augmenting by releasing more of the enemies already there, and conserving existing natural enemies. Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil-dwelling bacterium, is the most widely applied bacterial control agent, used against moth, butterfly, beetle and fly pests. It infects through the gut, so it works poorly on sucking insects. There are risks. Some early introductions became serious pests themselves, and controls can attack native non-target species.

soil-agri-207.title: Structures or soil building: two ways to control erosion
soil-agri-207.text: Erosion control splits into two families. Structural measures are engineered works such as terraces, diversion ditches and drop structures, which need an up-front investment. Agronomic practices change soil and crop management: reduced tillage, cover cropping and vegetating critical areas. The difference lies in timing. Structures mainly contain runoff and sediment after erosion has started, while agronomic measures prevent erosion by lowering runoff potential. Structures cost more to build and maintain and tend to be less effective, so soil-building agronomic practices are the first choice and structures mostly complement them. Agronomic measures also improve soil health and productivity, and advances in conservation tillage machinery have shifted practice away from structures. Both families, in the end, do one of two things. They reduce the shear forces of water and wind, or they keep soil in a condition where it cannot easily erode. See {{ref:soil-water-050}} for the wider picture.

soil-agri-204.title: Erosion's damage beyond the farm
soil-agri-204.text: Sediment is the number one contaminant of most waters worldwide, and it often carries nutrients, pesticides and other chemicals. Soil carried off fields fills streams, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries, and blowing dust reaches towns. Off-site costs to fisheries, recreation and industry can exceed the lost farm productivity. So soil loss below T may be tolerable for yields but not for water and air quality. Clay-rich soils are especially troublesome. Their particles stay suspended as colloids in runoff, do not settle in ponds or filter strips, and travel far with nutrients and pesticides. Clay and silt suspended in the air also travel long distances and can cause respiratory problems. This is the downstream side of {{ref:soil-water-001}}.

soil-agri-208.title: Principles of erosion control
soil-agri-208.text: Four ideas guide most erosion control. Keep soil covered: water and wind erosion occur almost exclusively on exposed soil, and live plants protect best and stimulate soil health. Use practices that increase aggregation and infiltration, and do not disturb soil unless it is well covered, since loosening cuts runoff only briefly before the soil settles. Focus control on high-risk spots where runoff concentrates, using inexpensive biological measures such as grass in waterways and filter strips. Also target critical periods such as after winter fallow or after the dry season. Finally, erodible fields that are not profitable may be better taken out of production under conservation reserve or set-aside payments. These build on {{ref:soil-water-050}}.

soil-agri-209.title: Reduced tillage as the top erosion fix
soil-agri-209.text: Moving to tillage that leaves more surface cover and less disturbance is described as the single most effective way to reduce erosion. It generally pays better than conventional tillage. A rougher surface without secondary passes and packers prevents aggregate dispersion and surface sealing, cutting runoff and erosion. In an Ohio four-year test, conventional-till corn runoff averaged about 7 inches of water a year against under 0.1 inch for no-till. Less tillage also reduces tillage erosion, which moves soil downhill and exposes subsoil on upslopes. If tillage is needed to ease compaction, use low-disturbance tools such as zone builders or strip tillers. See {{ref:soil-agri-095}} for tillage itself.

soil-agri-206.title: How farming speeds up natural erosion
soil-agri-206.text: Erosion never stops. Sahara dust carried about 3,000 miles to South America is thought to be a major phosphorus source for the Amazon basin. It is a natural geological process, but farming greatly accelerates it, especially where soil is bare. Erosion is worst when soil has no living plants, roots or residue mulch, and tillage that breaks aggregates lowers infiltration and worsens runoff. Intense or prolonged rain drives water erosion and landslides, while drought and strong winds drive wind erosion. Soils with poor aggregation, especially silts, are more susceptible, as soil erodibility ratings reflect. See {{ref:soil-water-001}}.

soil-agri-214.title: Diversion ditches: sending runoff aside
soil-agri-214.text: A diversion ditch is a channel or swale built across a slope to carry water to a waterway or pond. Its purpose is to channel water away from upslope areas, so {{ref:soil-water-019}} does not accumulate and concentrate downslope, scouring and forming gullies. A narrow filter strip on the upslope edge removes sediment.

soil-agri-216.title: Controlling landslides on farmed slopes
soil-agri-216.text: Landslides ({{ref:soil-water-057}}) are hard to control, so unstable steep slopes are best left in forest. Where steep slopes are farmed, wide-spaced trees let roots stabilize soil while leaving light for pasture or crops, as in a New Zealand poplar experiment. Horizontal drains can dewater critical zones and prevent supersaturation in long rains, but they are costly and mainly used in urban areas and along roads.

soil-agri-215.title: Wind erosion control on farmland
soil-agri-215.text: Most water-erosion controls also curb {{ref:soil-water-010}}: reduced tillage or no-till, cover crops and perennial rotation crops. A rougher surface increases turbulence near the ground and lowers wind shear, so tilled fields without cover are best left rough-tilled. Tree shelterbelts planted perpendicular to the prevailing wind reduce evaporative demand and also serve as ecological corridors that raise biodiversity.

soil-agri-211.title: Cover crops as a shield against winter erosion
soil-agri-211.text: Winter and early spring leave many fields bare just when rain and wind erode them. Cover crops fill that gap. Their roots bind the soil, their residues maintain aggregation, and their leaves absorb raindrop energy, so less crusting occurs. They protect best when cut and mulched, or rolled and crimped, near maturity rather than worked in. At that stage they are somewhat lignified and their C:N ratios are not high enough to immobilize nutrients. Combined with mulching and no-till, they form conservation agriculture, which virtually eliminates runoff and erosion and has spread rapidly in temperate South America.

soil-agri-213.title: How organic materials hold soil in place
soil-agri-213.text: Organic matter works as a quiet erosion control. More soil organic matter gives better aggregation and less surface sealing, so more water infiltrates instead of running off and carrying soil away. Regular compost or manure additions stimulate earthworm activity and give larger, more stable aggregates. Where a farm uses zone-till or no-till, injecting manure limits disturbance, runoff and odor.

soil-agri-212.title: Sod in the rotation: perennial crops against erosion
soil-agri-212.text: A sod crop in the rotation can cut erosion to a fraction. Washington research found winter wheat losing near 4 tons per acre a year with a sod crop in the rotation, versus about 15 tons without. Grass and legume forages keep a cover on most of the soil all year, and their roots hold it. Rotated with row crops, they keep erosion and runoff lower during the row-crop phase. In strip cropping, strips of sod and row crop lie across the slope, so the sod filters erosion from the row crop. Each crop is grown two to five years on a strip, then rotated. Permanent sod as hay or pasture suits easily eroded steep soils, though slumping and landslides may concern on extremely steep slopes.

soil-agri-210.title: Surface residue cover and erosion
soil-agri-210.text: Cover on the surface decides how much soil leaves a field. Residues intercept raindrops and slow runoff. A moldboard plow may leave under 5% cover, chisel or disk systems over 30%, and continuous no-till 90% or more. Full cover virtually eliminates runoff and erosion on most agricultural land, and even 30% cover cuts erosion by 70%. Removing large amounts of residue permanently for fuel or building material harms soil health and resistance to erosion, especially when no manure is returned.

soil-agri-205.title: Why rare storms do most of the erosion damage
soil-agri-205.text: One storm can undo thirty years of care. About one-third of the water erosion damage in a field over 30 years commonly comes from a single extreme rainfall event. Wind works the same way: the 1930s Dust Bowl wind erosion followed a decade of extremely dry years. Because such events are rare, the risk is easy to underestimate, yet most erosion damage comes from them. This is a hard fact for {{ref:soil-water-001}}, which is often judged by ordinary years.

soil-agri-221.title: Land use: what people do with a parcel
soil-agri-221.text: Every parcel of land has a job. Land use describes what people do on it, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied. The FAO defines it as the products and benefits obtained from land together with the management actions people carry out to obtain them. The IPCC defines it as the total of arrangements, activities and inputs applied to a parcel, and groups it into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands. The choices matter for {{ref:soil-found-077}}, water, {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, plants and animals. Poor choices contribute to soil erosion, soil degradation, land degradation and desertification. Arable land was about 10.7% of the land surface in 2015, with 1.3% permanent cropland. Early-1990s figures were 13% arable, 26% pasture and 32% forest and woodland. Governments plan and regulate land use through zoning and other ordinances to avoid land-use conflicts. An urban growth boundary is one such tool.

soil-agri-222.title: Land use change and its carbon cost
soil-agri-222.text: Land use change is the shift from one {{ref:soil-agri-221}} category to another, mostly driven by human activity. With fossil fuel use, it is a major human source of carbon dioxide, a dominant {{ref:soil-phys-246}}. Deforestation, the permanent conversion of forest to other uses, has historically been a primary driver, and global forest cover has fallen by 35% since agriculture began. Urban areas cover just 3% of the Earth's surface, yet their growth shifts demand onto rural land and can take over adjacent cropland. Scientists track change with satellite and aircraft imagery, field observations and modelling, and use land change models to simulate futures for planning.

soil-agri-220.title: Soil phases: dividing a series by how it is used
soil-agri-220.text: A single soil series can behave very differently from one hillside to the next. Series vary so much in slope, erosion, stones or similar features that management advice could not be given if each were shown as one unit. So a {{ref:soil-class-037}} is divided into soil phases. The phase name gives the surface feature that most affects management. Vina loam 0 to 2 percent slopes and Vina gravelly loam 2 to 9 percent slopes are two of four phases of the Vina series. On a soil map, the area inside each continuous line is the delineation of a map unit, and a map unit includes the soil phase and all inclusions.

soil-agri-218.title: Reconnaissance surveys for poor land
soil-agri-218.text: Not every acre justifies a detailed survey. Large expanses with little direct agricultural or forest value are often too poor to repay the cost, so they are mapped at small scale. This is a reconnaissance soil survey. It shows regions dominated by soil associations rather than delineating individual soils, in contrast to the detailed map, where specific soils are outlined.

soil-meth-058.title: Soil test calibration: what a number really means
soil-meth-058.text: A soil test number means nothing until someone matches it to a harvest. That multi-year matching is soil test calibration. Researchers apply different nutrient levels, always including zero, to plots on many fields over several years, and compare yields. A new test cannot be called useful until it has been correlated with plant response on varied soils and weather, and small-plot results must be validated on commercial farms. Calibration matters because a {{ref:soil-fert-187}} estimates a few nutrients from a small sample meant to represent many acres, so it is not 100% accurate. A low test may fail to raise yield if it is poorly calibrated for that soil, or if drainage or compaction harms the crop. Extra nutrients on a high-testing soil occasionally help when weather reduces availability.

soil-meth-057.title: Taking a soil sample that represents the field
soil-meth-057.text: A lab can only be as right as the sample it receives. Soil sampling for fertility testing collects a representative composite of cores from a field. Samples are usually taken in fall or spring before the season and analysed for pH, lime requirement, P, K, Ca and Mg. Repeat at the same season and with the same lab so that years are comparable. Take cores from at least 15-20 random spots per field or zone, whatever its size. One sample should represent no more than 10-20 acres, or 1-5 acres for precision zone or grid management. Sample between rows, avoid old fence rows and dead furrows, and sample problem areas separately, since nutrient levels vary with crop history and topography. Depth depends on the field. Sample cultivated fields to plow depth and permanent pasture to 3 or 4 inches. Sample no-till fields twice: 6 inches for lime and fertilizer advice and 2 inches to monitor surface acidity. Mix the cores in a clean container, remove roots and stones and air dry. Sample fields at least every three years. The result feeds a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-meth-059.title: Which phosphorus test? It depends on the region
soil-meth-059.text: No single test measures plant-available phosphorus everywhere. The extractant varies by region: Olsen and AB-DTPA in arid and semiarid western areas, Mehlich 3 or Bray 1 in the humid Midwest and East, Mehlich 1 in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, and Morgan in the Northeast. In Washington and Oregon, Bray 1 is used for acidic soils and Olsen for alkaline soils. These are regional chemical extractions, each with its own numeric range. Optimum ranges in ppm P are Olsen 11-16, Bray 1 25-45, Mehlich 1 20-40 and Mehlich 3 30-50. In calcareous soil the Olsen optimum is higher, with over 25 ppm for zero P fertilizer. A soil high in P by one test is generally high by another, though the numbers differ. Low and medium levels mean likely yield gain from P, while high levels raise the potential for P pollution in runoff. Tests capture P from recent manure and from soil minerals, but active organic matter from residues or manure may supply more than the test shows. All of this builds on the {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-meth-056.title: Sample preparation before the instrument
soil-meth-056.text: Instruments rarely measure soil as it comes from the field. Sample preparation is the treatment a sample receives so it is in a form the instrument can measure. It matters because techniques are often unresponsive to the analyte in its in-situ form, or results are distorted by interfering species. Steps can include crushing and dissolution, acid or alkali digestion, extraction, clean-up and pre-concentration. They may also involve pulverizing, filtering, dilution, masking, sub-sampling or treatment with a chelating agent such as EDTA.

soil-meth-055.title: Certified reference materials: a lab's yardstick
soil-meth-055.text: Most analytical instruments are comparative: they only say how a sample differs from something known. So labs need controls or standards of known composition, used to check quality and traceability, validate methods and calibrate instruments. A certified reference material differs from a laboratory reagent in its certificate, which gives the value, its uncertainty and a statement of metrological traceability. Accreditation under ISO/IEC 17025 requires traceability to such materials where possible, and prefers them where available. ILAC lists five types: pure substances, standard solutions and gas mixtures, matrix materials, physico-chemical materials, and reference objects. Natural matrix materials are made by homogenizing a natural sample to a fine powder, since natural materials are rarely homogeneous at the gram scale, then measuring each analyte. Producers test homogeneity on 10-30 randomly chosen units with two or three subsamples each, and test stability by real-time or accelerated storage studies.

soil-meth-062.title: From test value to advice: the interpretation categories
soil-meth-062.text: A lab report turns a number into a verdict. Labs sort each value into categories, tied to the probability that adding the nutrient will raise yield, as set by {{ref:soil-meth-058}}. The categories run very low, low, optimum, high and excessive, with probability of response falling from very high to very low. For the pre-sidedress nitrate test on corn 6-12 inches tall sampled to 1 foot, nitrate-N of 11-22 ppm is low, 23-28 optimum and over 35 excessive. Ranges depend on the extractant: for Mehlich 3 in North Carolina, P is optimum at 26-50 ppm. Reports adapt advice using the manure and previous crop information supplied, but legume cover crop N is usually not credited, and manure decided on later is missed.

soil-meth-061.title: Reading odd soil test results
soil-meth-061.text: Strange numbers usually have a history behind them. Very high phosphorus comes from years of heavy poultry or other manure. Very high pH with high calcium relative to K and Mg points to lime-stabilized sewage sludge. High salt in humid regions can come from large poultry manure doses in high tunnels, where rain cannot leach salts, or from deicing salt beside a road. The other cause is the wrong extractant. Acid extractants (Morgan, Mehlich 1 or 3) dissolve free limestone and give too much calcium. On alkaline calcareous soils (pH above 7) they extract little P because the soil neutralizes the acid. Many labs also report the CEC the soil would have at pH 7 or higher, whereas the textbook estimates current CEC by summing the exchangeable bases.

soil-meth-060.title: Sensing a crop's nitrogen from the field to orbit
soil-meth-060.text: Crop nitrogen sensing assesses a crop's nitrogen status in season, to guide fertilizer rates, and extends the {{ref:soil-fert-195}}. Chlorophyll meters estimate leaf chlorophyll as an N indicator. They need field visits and adequate leaf sampling and are mainly used for final cereal applications. Canopy reflectance sensors read near-infrared and red or red-edge light. Mounted on equipment, they adjust N on the go, usually with a high-N reference strip for calibration. Satellite, aircraft or drone imagery uses the same bands at 10-30 m resolution. Satellites are limited by cloud cover, and aircraft and drones are more expensive. Computer models simulate field N dynamics daily and are cheap and scalable, but involve no direct field observation.

soil-meth-063.title: Testing the soil in a high tunnel
soil-meth-063.text: A tomato crop in a high tunnel eats far more than a field crop. Tunnel tomatoes reaching the equivalent of 60-80 tons per acre need roughly 200-300 lb N, 300-400 lb P2O5 and 700-900 lb K2O per acre. Rain does not leach salts there, so they build up. Recommendations from routine field soil tests must be adjusted upward. A saturated media extract measures water-soluble nutrients, including nitrate-N and ammonium-N, plus total salinity.

soil-meth-066.title: Digital image analysis: teaching computers to read pictures
soil-meth-066.text: Image analysis extracts meaningful information from images, mainly digital ones, by digital image processing. Computers are indispensable for large data and quantitative extraction, but human vision still cannot be replaced in many applications. Object-based analysis groups pixels into homogeneous objects by segmentation and then classifies them. Over-segmentation is often preferred when classifying high-resolution images. The method is applied in metallography, for instance to determine the mineral content of a rock sample.

soil-meth-064.title: Polarized light microscopy and birefringent minerals
soil-meth-064.text: Some samples shine under polarized light. Polarized light microscopy covers optical techniques that illuminate a sample with it, and works best on birefringent samples. A polarizing plate converts natural light into polarized light, and birefringent samples interact strongly with it, giving contrast against the background. The method is used extensively in optical mineralogy, the basis of identifying minerals in the {{ref:soil-meth-030}}. More complex variants include differential interference contrast and interference reflection microscopy.

soil-meth-065.title: X-ray microtomography: a 3D look without cutting
soil-meth-065.text: X-ray microtomography, or micro-CT, makes cross-sections of an object at micrometre pixel size and rebuilds a 3D model without destroying the sample. It is computed tomography in which the sample rotates while source and detector stay still, or the source and detector rotate around the specimen. Cone-beam systems use a 2D detector to record projection images, from which cross-sections are reconstructed. Stacking slices builds a volume of voxels that can be viewed in any plane, and segmentation separates structures that have similar density. In geology it is used to analyze micropores in reservoir rocks.

soil-meth-045.title: Spatial analysis: studying things by where they are
soil-meth-045.text: Spatial analysis is any of the formal techniques that study entities using their topological, geometric or geographic properties. It spans many methods, especially spatial statistics, and covers spatial interpolation, spatial regression and spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's I and Geary's C. Geographic information systems capture, store, manipulate and analyse spatial data, with map overlay a basic vector operation. Two errors recur. The ecological fallacy draws conclusions about individuals from aggregate data. The locational fallacy is a poor spatial characterisation of the elements. Spatial sampling picks limited locations to measure phenomena that show dependency and heterogeneity; basic schemes are random, clustered and systematic.

soil-meth-039.title: Landsat: fifty years of Earth from orbit
soil-meth-039.text: No other program has watched Earth from space for as long. Landsat is the longest-running enterprise that has acquired satellite imagery of Earth. The first satellite launched on 23 July 1972 as the Earth Resources Technology Satellite and was renamed Landsat 1 in 1975. Landsat 9 launched on 27 September 2021. Landsat 7 data has eight spectral bands with spatial resolutions from 15 to 60 m and a temporal resolution of 16 days, and a scene is about 185 km by 185 km. Instruments progressed from the Multispectral Scanner (Landsat 1-5) to the Thematic Mapper, the Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (Landsat 7) and, on Landsat 8, the Operational Land Imager plus a Thermal Infrared Sensor. The result is one of the longest uninterrupted remote-sensing time series, from 1972 to the present, widely used for land-cover determination.

soil-meth-037.title: Electromagnetic induction: a field from a changing field
soil-meth-037.text: A changing magnetic field drives a current. Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across a conductor in such a field. Faraday published its discovery in 1831, and Joseph Henry found it independently in 1832. Maxwell later described it mathematically. Faraday's law says the induced emf in a closed circuit equals the rate of change of enclosed magnetic flux, and Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that produced it. A changing current in one wire induces an emf in a second wire within reach of its magnetic field, which is the principle of the transformer. Conductors in changing magnetic fields also develop circular eddy currents in planes perpendicular to the field.

soil-meth-050.title: Conventional soil mapping and its limits
soil-meth-050.text: Conventional soil mapping is the surveyor-led production of soil maps from field inspections, building on Jenny's soil-forming factors and national taxonomic systems. The steps are objectives, background compilation and initial legend, then soil inspections, field mapping and correlation, and finally map production and a report. Soils are represented as a profile, a 1-3 m wide pedon, a polypedon of connected similar pedons, or a map unit, the polygon mapped by surveyors. The method has limits. Choropleth maps assume each map unit is homogeneous, yet units contain inclusions of minor soils too small to map, and real soil change is often a fuzzy gradation rather than a sharp boundary. Raising map-unit purity raises cost exponentially. Maps made for different objectives leave mismatched boundaries and inconsistent series names across counties and provinces. Still, legacy maps hold decades of surveyor knowledge and serve as training data for digital soil maps.

soil-meth-053.title: Judging a digital soil map: accuracy assessment
soil-meth-053.text: A digital soil map is only as good as its test against reality. Accuracy assessment measures how far predicted values differ from observed ones, using an independent validation dataset, for maps from {{ref:soil-agri-089}}. Categorical predictions use overall accuracy, the share correctly predicted, and Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance agreement. Both range from 0 to 1. Continuous predictions use mean square error, root mean square error (in the soil variable's units), R2 and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient. Lower MSE or RMSE means a more accurate model. R2 is not accuracy, because it ignores bias from systematic over- or underprediction. The concordance coefficient, which measures fit to the 45-degree line, is more appropriate.

soil-meth-054.title: Where digital soil map uncertainty comes from
soil-meth-054.text: Every predicted soil map carries error, and it should be estimated as carefully as it is validated. Uncertainty in a map from {{ref:soil-agri-089}} comes from three sources: the measured soil property, the environmental predictors, and the predictive model. Property errors arise from laboratory methods, pedotransfer functions and GPS location accuracy. Predictor errors come from DEM vertical error, sensor error, and polygon boundaries and scale. Model structure matters because linear, non-linear and hybrid models, such as model trees, capture different soil-environment relationships. International standards such as GlobalSoilMap require a 90% prediction interval map with 5% and 95% limits. A wider interval means higher uncertainty, and this applies only to continuous variables.

soil-meth-047.title: Spatial scale: how big is the space?
soil-meth-047.text: Spatial scale describes or categorises the size of a space, or the extent at which a phenomenon or process occurs. A common geography and meteorology scheme runs from micro (1 m to 1 km, local) through meso (1 to 100 km, regional) and macro (100 to 10,000 km, continental) to mega (global) and giga (superglobal). These divisions are somewhat arbitrary and shift by context, so meso and macro must be adjusted accordingly.

soil-meth-041.title: The modifiable areal unit problem
soil-meth-041.text: Change the boundaries and the answer changes. The modifiable areal unit problem, or MAUP, is a source of statistical bias that arises when point-based measures are aggregated into areal units. Summary values depend on both the shape and the scale of the aggregation unit, so results differ between, say, state and county boundaries. The scale effect changes results between aggregation levels, and correlation generally rises as unit size rises. The zoning effect changes them when data are regrouped at the same scale. Gehlke and Biehl first recognised the problem in 1934, and Openshaw described it in detail in 1984. It is closely related to ecological fallacy, a pitfall of {{ref:soil-meth-045}}. Aggregation can hide a strong correlation or create a spurious one, so sensitivity analysis with several areal units is recommended to estimate the uncertainty of coefficients.

soil-meth-043.title: Random forest: many trees voting
soil-meth-043.text: Random forest is an ensemble learning method for classification and regression that builds many decision trees during training. Classification returns the class chosen by most trees. Regression returns the average of the trees' predictions, which corrects decision trees' habit of overfitting. Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement, called bagging, and each split considers only a random subset of features. This decorrelates the trees when a few features are very strong predictors. Tin Kam Ho created the first algorithm in 1995, and Breiman and Cutler extended it. Variable importance can be ranked by permutation: permute a feature in the out-of-bag samples and see how much the error rises, or use mean decrease in impurity. The cost of higher accuracy than a single tree is lost interpretability.

soil-meth-046.title: Why nearby soil samples are not independent
soil-meth-046.text: Two soil samples taken a meter apart usually tell you more about each other than two taken kilometers apart. That is spatial autocorrelation: properties at nearby places vary together, positively or negatively, a core idea in {{ref:soil-meth-045}}. It creates a problem, because standard statistics assume independent observations, and nearby samples are not. Dependence also helps, since one location can predict another and you need not sample both. Heterogeneity limits that help: if the relation changes across space, a dependence cannot be trusted beyond a possibly small region. Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G are the classic statistics for measuring it.

soil-meth-048.title: Stratified sampling: sampling each group on its own
soil-meth-048.text: A field with a sandy ridge and a clay hollow is really two populations. Stratified sampling treats them that way. It partitions a population into subpopulations, called strata, and samples each stratum independently, for example by simple random sampling. The strata must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so every element falls in exactly one. Done well, it reduces sampling error and improves precision. The estimation error is smaller when the standard deviation within strata is lower than the overall one, and the method ensures enough samples from strata of interest. Proportionate allocation samples each stratum in proportion to its size. Optimum allocation takes larger samples where variability is greatest, and Neyman allocation is one such strategy. One trap remains: combining sub-strata to reach adequate numbers can cause Simpson's paradox, in which trends disappear or reverse.

soil-meth-035.title: Compositional data: when only the ratios matter
soil-meth-035.text: A soil analysis that reports sand, silt and clay as percentages describes parts of a whole, and that changes the statistics. Compositional data are quantitative descriptions of the parts of some whole, conveying relative information. Proportions, percentages and ppm all count, and so do molar concentrations in chemistry and the mineral fractions of a rock in geology. John Aitchison defined them in 1982 as proportions of some whole. Mathematically they are points on a simplex. Closure divides each part by the total, so only the ratios between components carry information, and scaling by any positive constant changes nothing. A three-part composition is plotted on a ternary (barycentric) triangle, where its position shows the ratios of the three variables.

soil-meth-036.title: Log-ratio transformations for compositional data
soil-meth-036.text: Ordinary statistics break down on compositions, so analysts translate them first. Log-ratio transformations map compositions from the simplex into real space, where standard methods apply. These transformations build on {{ref:soil-meth-035}}. The additive log ratio takes logs of ratios to one arbitrarily chosen component. It is common in chemistry (pH) and in multinomial logistic regression, but it is not an isometry. The centred log ratio is an isomorphism and an isometry, though it forces a linear dependency, so the covariance matrix is singular.
