The isometric log ratio gives orthonormal coordinates in D-1 dimensions, built by Gram-Schmidt, singular-value decomposition or a bifurcating tree. A caution applies: the article argues that noise distorts compositions asymmetrically, so the isometric version can create artifacts in real data.

soil-meth-051.title: Soil survey intensity levels
soil-meth-051.text: How hard a surveyor looks decides how much a soil map can be trusted. Survey intensity levels grade how densely a conventional soil survey, described in {{ref:soil-meth-050}}, is checked in the field. Level 1, very detailed, needs one inspection per polygon, with foot traverses under 0.5 km apart, and is published at 1:5,000 at series level. Level 2, detailed, inspects over 90% of polygons with traverses 2 km apart, at 1:20,000. Level 3, reconnaissance, inspects 60-80% with traverses 4 km apart, at 1:50,000. Each step down in intensity trades checking for coverage.

soil-meth-044.title: Sampling design: the odds behind every sample
soil-meth-044.text: A sample is only as good as the rule that produced it. A sampling design specifies, for every possible sample, its probability of being drawn. It is written as a function P(S) giving the probability of drawing sample S, and Bernoulli sampling is one example. Designing a sample means defining the population, the sampling frame and the sampling unit. It also means choosing the margin of error to achieve and deciding how to balance sampling and non-sampling error.

soil-meth-052.title: Choosing where to sample for a digital soil map
soil-meth-052.text: A digital soil map is only as good as the sites that train it. The aim of sampling design here is to select sites representative of the geographic area and of the soil-forming factors, the covariates, being modelled. Two families of design exist, building on {{ref:soil-meth-044}}. Geometric designs work on the map. They include grid, simple random, stratified random, transect, cluster and nested sampling. Grid sampling places points at the centre of evenly spaced cells, and stratified random applies random sampling within strata, as in {{ref:soil-meth-048}}. Cluster sampling groups sites closely to cope with rough terrain, and nested sampling quantifies variability at different distances. Feature-space designs work on the covariate values instead. Fuzzy k-means sampling minimises distance in covariate space. Conditioned Latin hypercube sampling (Minasny and McBratney, 2006) samples all covariates with one sample per stratum. An optimal design covers both geographic and feature space.

soil-meth-038.title: Fuzzy clustering: points that belong to several groups
soil-meth-038.text: Soils rarely fall neatly into one class, and fuzzy clustering admits it. Also called soft clustering, it lets each data point belong to more than one cluster. In hard clustering each point belongs to exactly one cluster. Fuzzy clustering instead gives each point a membership grade for every cluster, and points at a cluster's edge have lower grades. Fuzzy c-means, developed by Dunn in 1973 and improved by Bezdek in 1981, alternates computing membership-weighted centroids with updating each point's coefficients until they converge. A parameter m controls fuzziness: larger m gives fuzzier clusters, m near 1 reduces to k-means, and m is commonly set to 2 without other knowledge. Like k-means, it finds only a local minimum that depends on the initial weights.

soil-meth-040.title: Latin hypercube sampling: one point per slice
soil-meth-040.text: Picture a chess board with rooks placed so that none can attack another. Latin hypercube sampling works the same way. It is a statistical method for generating a near-random sample of parameter values from a multidimensional distribution. The range of each variable is split into M equally probable intervals, and M points are placed so that each interval of every variable holds exactly one point. It needs no more samples for more variables, and samples can be taken in sequence while remembering which cells were already used. Unlike plain random sampling, the number of points must be chosen beforehand. In return, every subspace is sampled with equal density.

soil-meth-049.title: Uncertainty quantification: how sure is the model?
soil-meth-049.text: A prediction without an error bar is half an answer. Uncertainty quantification is the science of quantitatively characterising and estimating uncertainties in computational and real-world applications. It tries to determine how likely outcomes are when some aspects of a system are not exactly known. Forward propagation pushes input uncertainty through a model to get the output's mean and variance, its reliability or its full distribution. Forward methods include Monte Carlo simulation, surrogate models, local and functional expansions and first/second-order reliability methods. Inverse quantification estimates the discrepancy between model and experiment, and unknown parameters. Inverse problems are harder. They face dimensionality and identifiability issues, since different parameter and discrepancy combinations can give the same prediction.

soil-meth-033.title: Chemometrics: mining chemical measurements for answers
soil-meth-033.text: Svante Wold coined the word chemometrics in a 1971 grant application, and the field emerged in the 1970s as computers came into scientific use. It is the science of extracting information from chemical systems by data-driven means. It draws on multivariate statistics, applied mathematics and computer science to solve problems in chemistry, biology, medicine and engineering. Its natural material is spectra such as those from {{ref:soil-meth-013}}. Infrared and UV/visible spectra contain thousands of measurements per sample, but strong low-rank structure lets principal components analysis and partial least squares model them compactly. Models are usually judged by root mean squared error of prediction, and model selection relies on resampling such as bootstrap, permutation and cross-validation.

soil-meth-042.title: Partial least squares regression
soil-meth-042.text: When a spectrum has more wavelengths than a lab has samples, ordinary regression fails. Partial least squares (PLS) regression is built for exactly that case. It is a reduced-rank method that projects both predictors and responses into new spaces to find the relation between them. It looks for the direction in predictor space that explains maximum variance in response space, modelling the covariance structure of two matrices with latent variables. It suits data with more variables than observations, or with multicollinearity among predictors, where standard regression fails unless regularised. Components are extracted iteratively by finding directions of maximal covariance and regressing on the scores. PLS1 handles a single response vector and PLS-DA a categorical one. Herman Wold introduced it, with his son Svante Wold, first in the social sciences, and it is now most widely used in the field described in {{ref:soil-meth-033}}.

soil-meth-034.title: Multivariate calibration: turning spectra into soil properties
soil-meth-034.text: A near-infrared scan takes seconds, while a lab analysis can take days. Multivariate calibration closes the gap by building models that predict a property of interest from measured responses such as spectra. It draws on {{ref:soil-meth-033}} and is often applied to {{ref:soil-meth-013}}. A training set pairs reference values, for example analyte concentration, with the measured spectra. Partial least squares or principal component regression then relates response to property. Methods are classed as classical, which optimally describe the measured responses, or inverse, which need less physical knowledge and usually predict better in mean-squared-error terms. The payoff is that fast, cheap, non-destructive measurements can estimate properties that would otherwise need slow or costly analysis, even under heavy interference from other analytes. Broad, non-selective spectra can still predict properties when paired with careful calibration, because selectivity comes partly from the mathematics.

soil-env-322.title: Climate tipping points
soil-env-322.text: A small push can sometimes cause a very large change. A climate tipping point is a critical threshold that, when crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the climate system. Self-reinforcing feedbacks, as in {{ref:soil-env-213}}, can make the change irreversible on a human timescale. Thawing permafrost releasing methane and melting ice sheets lowering albedo are examples, and crossing one threshold can trigger another in cascading tipping points. Three types are recognized: bifurcation-induced, noise-induced and rate-induced tipping. Only bifurcation-induced tipping shows early warning signals such as critical slowing down and rising autocorrelation and variance. Early IPCC assessments held tipping points likely only at about 4 degC or more of warming above preindustrial.

soil-env-324.title: Compost bomb instability in peatlands
soil-env-324.text: A peatland can sit quietly for years and then release its carbon all at once. This is rate-induced tipping, which occurs when an environmental change is faster than the force restoring the system to its stable state. In peatlands, after years of relative stability, it can produce an explosive release of soil carbon to the atmosphere. The phenomenon is sometimes called compost bomb instability. Peatland carbon is the subject of {{ref:soil-water-138}}.

soil-env-323.title: Permafrost thaw and its tipping dynamics
soil-env-323.text: Permafrost holds nearly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. When it thaws, microbes decompose the newly unfrozen organic matter and release CO2 and methane, a self-reinforcing feedback. Most thaw is gradual over centuries, and the process is not expected to cause a global tipping point. Ice-rich permafrost is the exception. It can thaw abruptly, slumping or forming thermokarst lakes over years to decades, and these self-sustaining local dynamics could raise greenhouse gas emissions by around 40%. The frozen ground itself is described in {{ref:soil-env-129}}.

soil-env-325.title: The Cuvette Centrale peatland in the Congo Basin
soil-env-325.text:
Found in 2017, the Cuvette Centrale in the Congo Basin is the most vulnerable store of tropical peat carbon in the world, a kind of soil described in {{ref:soil-class-081}}.

Its size is striking. It holds about 30 petagrams of carbon, 28% of all tropical peat carbon. That equals all the trees in the other 96% of the Congo Basin, even though the peatland covers only 4%. Burning all of it would release the equivalent of three years of all anthropogenic CO2 emissions.

Protection is thin. Only 8% of this peat carbon lies within existing protected areas, while 26% is open to logging, mining or palm oil.

The climate adds to the risk. It is already drier than that of other tropical peatlands, and conditions 7,500 to 2,000 years ago were dry enough to release substantial peat. For that reason the Cuvette Centrale could become a climate tipping point, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-env-322}}.

soil-env-321.title: How compaction stunts roots
soil-env-321.text: Compaction removes large pores and raises penetration resistance, restricting roots and the organisms that live in soil. The large pores between aggregates go first. That hurts fine and medium soils most, because they depend on those pores for infiltration, percolation and air exchange, while coarse soils suffer less. Compacted soil also hardens as it dries, since many small pores hold water under high suction. A good soil keeps penetration resistance below the 300 psi (2 MPa) level at which root growth ceases, but compacted soil quickly exceeds it. Growing roots need pores wider than about 0.1 mm, the size of most root tips. Without them roots stay short and thick, with few fine roots or root hairs, and take up water and nutrients poorly. Roots meeting a mechanical barrier also send a hormonal signal that slows shoot growth, an effect hard to separate from drought. Subsoil compaction limits deep rooting and raises drought losses in rain-fed farming. Earthworms, insects and aerobic microbes need large pores and air exchange, so compacted soils hold fewer of them, though they return quickly once better practices are adopted. The process itself is described in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-env-319.title: Shallow compaction of the plow layer
soil-env-319.text: Shiny, cloddy furrows and deep ruts are the signs of shallow compaction, the compaction of the surface or plow layer found to some degree in all intensively worked agricultural soils. It results from lost aggregation, typically caused by erosion, low organic matter and the weight of field equipment. The first two cut the supply of sticky binding materials, and loosely bound soil is easier to press together, as in {{ref:soil-phys-001}}. Moisture decides the damage. Soil wetter than its plastic limit is smeared into a dense mass by tillage or traffic, while friable soil below that limit crumbles and resists compaction. Sandy soils turn from plastic to friable quickly as they drain, whereas loams and clays need longer drying, and frozen soil is also resistant. The plastic limit belongs to {{ref:soil-phys-041}}. Rain adds a second route. On unprotected soil it disperses wet aggregates into a thin dense layer that seals the surface and hardens into a crust. That cuts infiltration and can block seedling emergence, though residue cover and strong aggregation reduce it. Finally, a compacted soil tills up cloddy and needs extra secondary tillage and packing, which breaks aggregates and burns organic matter. Compaction therefore recurs in a vicious cycle.

soil-env-320.title: Subsoil compaction and the plow pan
soil-env-320.text: Subsoil compaction is invisible unless you dig or push a rod into the soil. It is compaction deeper in the soil, often called a plow pan, though it has causes beyond plowing. It builds on the surface problem in {{ref:soil-env-319}}. Subsoil compacts easily because it is usually wetter, denser, higher in clay, lower in organic matter and less aggregated than topsoil, and regular tillage does not loosen it. A surface load spreads through the soil in a cone, so pressure falls with depth. Light loads do little at depth, but heavy manure spreaders or combines compact deeply, and wet soil carries the force deeper. Plows and disks press down on the layer below, and tractor wheels in an open furrow press directly on the soil under the plow layer. Such pans may persist for many years after a field goes no-till. Some soils are especially prone. Those with roughly equal sand, silt and clay and non-swelling 1:1 clays form dense subsoils when aggregates weaken from organic matter loss and silt and clay wash down into subsoil pores. Tropical oxisols with strongly aggregated clay can disperse when limed, because the raised pH lets clay particles wash into lower pores. A ball test helps with timing. A handful from the lower plow layer that molds and sticks is too wet to work, while one that crumbles is dry enough for tillage or heavy traffic.

soil-env-374.title: Assessing an urban site before sampling
soil-env-374.text: The first step in assessing urban soil happens at a desk, not in the field: research the site's past use. Land-use history comes from owners, old aerial photos, maps, permits and tax records, plus a visit to look for sources such as peeling lead paint or a nearby highway. Green-space or residential histories usually mean fewer problems than industrial ones. There are no federal contaminant limits in the US for gardens. The EPA recommends testing for pH, organic matter, nutrients, micronutrients and metals including lead. Samples may be needed per contaminant and at different depths, with metals near the surface and solvents deeper. Because distribution is unpredictable, many locations are needed, and suspect spots near old buildings, bare patches or drains need separate sampling. Lead rarely harms plants, but copper, zinc and nickel can be phytotoxic at high concentrations. A full assessment also considers slope, drainage and buried utility lines.

soil-env-373.title: Urban soil contamination and who it harms
soil-env-373.text: Contamination is much more prevalent in urban soils than agricultural ones, and lead is the most common contaminant. Lead is widespread because of its long use in gasoline, banned in the US since 1989, and in paint, banned for residential use since 1978. Other contaminants include petroleum products and legacy pesticides such as lead arsenate and copper sulfate. Of special concern are former industrial sites, roadsides, recent construction sites, waste disposal sites and junkyards, and contaminants can also arrive by atmospheric deposition. People are exposed by ingesting soil, breathing dust and volatiles, eating crops, and through skin. Risk is greatest on bare soil and for children. Plants absorb little lead, especially at neutral pH, so dirty hands, dust and unwashed produce are the larger exposure. Lead can accumulate in roots, so root crops should be avoided. Other contaminants behave differently. Solvents such as trichloroethylene move readily to groundwater, some pesticides persist for years, and petroleum products tend to stay near the surface, where they can be scraped off. Road salt (sodium chloride) causes sodic conditions, aggregate breakdown and compaction.

soil-env-375.title: Reconditioning degraded urban soil
soil-env-375.text: Reconditioning improves degraded {{ref:soil-env-306}} with physical, chemical and biological practices, generally applied in that order. Physical work comes first. Removing contaminated soil by excavation is expensive and regulated. If contamination is modest or shallow, scraping the surface and replacing it with good topsoil is more feasible. Tillage or subsoiling can dilute a thin contaminated layer into deeper soil and relieve compaction, and where compaction is the main problem, amelioration in place is better than removal. Chemical fixes follow. Phosphorus binds lead and makes it less dangerous over time, and lime or dolomite can stabilize pH. Biological and surface measures come last. Compost and other organic amendments raise organic matter, improve structure and biology, dilute toxic compounds and bind some contaminants, though the compost itself must be free of contaminants. Mulch suppresses weeds, reduces erosion and splash, and acts as a barrier to contact with contaminated soil.

soil-env-379.title: Protecting topsoil on a construction site
soil-env-379.text: Digging for pipes or drains mixes fertile topsoil with subsoil and leaves poor soil at the surface. Good construction practice limits traffic and protects topsoil to avoid lasting compaction and mixing of soil layers. Compaction, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}, matters little under pavement but is a long-term problem where land is revegetated. Controlled traffic lanes, metal plates or geotextile under gravel, and avoiding work on wet soil limit it. The sequence is simple: strip and stockpile topsoil separately, refill subsoil first and loosen it with rippers, then replace topsoil without further compaction.

soil-env-377.title: Soil mixes for containers and green roofs
soil-env-377.text: A rooftop garden has a weight limit that a field never faces. Pots, planters and green roofs need clean, light soil mixes with excellent drainage and high water- and nutrient-holding capacity, quite unlike the natural textures of {{ref:soil-found-051}}. Rooftop mixes must be light enough not to overload the roof, yet heavy enough to anchor plants against wind and water. Mixes combine heat-treated vermiculite and perlite with organic materials such as peat moss, compost or biochar. They are low in density but cost more than ordinary soil.

soil-env-378.title: Gap-graded soil: pavement that lets roots breathe
soil-env-378.text: Street trees face a dilemma. Pavement needs a compacted substrate to bear loads, while roots need a healthy rooting environment, and trees often die early from constricted roots, salt, heat and moisture stress. Gap-graded soil answers it by containing only certain particle sizes, with some sizes left out deliberately to guarantee pore space. Large uniform stones form a load-bearing skeleton, while the large pores, partly filled with high-quality soil, let roots grow under the pavement. The pores are what compaction destroys in ordinary soil, as {{ref:soil-phys-082}} explains, and the mix departs from ordinary {{ref:soil-found-051}}. Golf greens use similar gap-graded sand to support foot traffic while keeping turf healthy.

soil-env-376.title: Remediating soil in urban green spaces
soil-env-376.text: Green spaces need soil with good drainage, high water-holding capacity and good rooting at low maintenance cost. Except in extreme contamination, poor soil can be buried under trucked-in topsoil or improved with amendments, as in {{ref:soil-env-375}}. Burying in place often suffices for built sites with debris. Raised beds or berms address poor soil and drainage, and landscape fabric under imported soil limits roots reaching the original soil. Two tools handle compaction. The scoop-and-dump method mixes compost into compacted soil with excavators, and an air spader blows compacted soil from around the roots of trees to be saved.

soil-env-372.title: The Food and Agriculture Organization
soil-env-372.text: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is a specialized agency that leads international efforts to defeat hunger and improve nutrition and food security. It was founded on 16 October 1945 in Quebec City and is headquartered in Rome. It has 194 members: 193 countries and the European Union. It helps coordinate improvements in agriculture, forestry, fisheries and land and water resources, giving technical assistance and collecting agricultural data. With the World Health Organization it created the Codex Alimentarius Commission in 1961 to develop food standards.

soil-env-326.title: Holistic management and the grazing debate
soil-env-326.text: Holistic management is a systems-thinking approach to managing resources, first developed by Allan Savory for grazing management and now applied to other complex social, ecological and economic systems. It links to the whole-system thinking of {{ref:soil-env-218}}. Its decision framework tells managers to define the whole being managed, set goals, watch the earliest signs of ecosystem health such as bare ground, use any of eight tools, and test every decision. The tools include grazing, animal impact, fire and rest. Savory's principles hold that nature works as a community, that removing keystone species such as large herds has wide effects, that livestock can substitute for lost herds, and that timing is the key factor in land use. The evidence is disputed, and peer-reviewed studies disagree on whether planned grazing outperforms continuous grazing or sequesters carbon at the rates its founder claimed. A 1972-2016 meta-analysis and a 2022 review of 22 farm-scale studies found no productivity gain, while defenders say trials miss its goal setting and monitoring, and some studies show soil gains. A 2016 Swedish study put the real carbon sequestration rate of improved grazing management at seven times lower than Savory's claims. One 2011 study found multi-paddock grazing stored slightly less soil carbon than excluding livestock.

soil-env-332.title: What a healthy soil looks like
soil-env-332.text: Farmers say soil health and scientists say soil quality, and both mean how well a soil functions for the use being considered, as in {{ref:soil-env-179}}. Soil health stresses the human influence of years of intensive management, as distinct from inherent differences from parent material and climate, much as a person's health depends on how the body is treated. Farmers recognize good soil by its dark, crumbly look, higher yields for less effort, less runoff and erosion, and the lower power needed to run machinery than on compacted soil. A healthy soil has enough nutrients all season, good {{ref:soil-phys-039}}, stable structure that aids infiltration and water storage ({{ref:soil-phys-004}}), and enough depth before a compact layer or bedrock. It drains well enough for timely field work and lets oxygen in and carbon dioxide out of the root zone, with exceptions such as flooded soils for cranberries and paddy rice. It has low disease, parasite and weed pressure, many beneficial organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi, and no harmful chemicals, whether natural, like soluble aluminum or excess salts, or human-made, like fuel oil or toxic sludge. A high-quality soil also resists degradation and is resilient, recovering quickly after unfavorable changes such as compaction.

soil-env-335.title: How soil keeps cycling nutrients and organic matter
soil-env-335.text: The nutrients in soil particles start out locked in crystals. Soil water carrying carbon dioxide slowly dissolves them, a process called {{ref:soil-found-058}}, and releases them into the soil solution, the water held among the particles. Plants then take over. They capture carbon by photosynthesis, absorb water and nutrients, and store both in biomass. When plants die or are eaten, organisms decompose the residues and manure, and the nutrients become available again. This loop is the {{ref:soil-fert-146}}. Soil also keeps a reserve. Clays bond with organic molecules, and aggregates shield particles from decomposers. The result is a store of nutrients and energy, richest in the deep-rooted soils of prairie and steppe. Plowing broke the loop. It sped decomposition, so more {{ref:soil-found-045}} was lost than returned, and nutrients left with the crop. Fertilizers later replaced the nutrients, but replacing the lost carbon was mostly ignored. That matters because organic matter forms aggregates that give water storage and gas exchange. Mineral particles and pores give a soil its structure, yet organic matter mostly makes it fertile.

soil-env-349.title: What a soil health assessment can tell a farmer
soil-env-349.text: A soil health assessment answers a practical question: what is wrong with this soil, and is it getting better? It can target problems such as phosphorus deficiency or surface compaction. Over several years it can show whether cover crops, a new rotation or reduced tillage are improving the soil. It also bears on value. Well-managed healthy soil should be worth more when sold or rented, since it produces more with fewer purchased inputs. That gives owners a reason to invest in it. Assessment works at three levels of detail: general field observations, field assessments using qualitative indicators, and quantitative soil health tests. All of them build on {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-350.title: Reading soil health in the field
soil-env-350.text: A spade, a few minutes and a careful eye can reveal a lot about a field. Field indicators are observations of cover, crusting, ponding, aggregates, hardness, color, roots and organisms, and they point to a soil's key limitations. The NRCS Cropland In-Field Soil Health Assessment Worksheet rates soil cover, residue breakdown, surface crusts, ponding, penetration resistance, water-stable aggregates, structure, color, roots, biological diversity and biopores. It is one way to carry out a {{ref:soil-env-349}}. Timing matters. Soil health is best measured in early spring and late fall, when the soil is moist. Measurements vary with moisture and season: a hard soil after a dry spring may be soft after a wet one, and earthworms go deeper in dry spells. So sample at least 10 spots and avoid headlands. Problems such as runoff or drought stress show better in wet or dry periods. Absence of a sign proves little. Crusting, ponding, slaked patches downslope and rills or gullies signal poor aggregate stability, runoff and erosion, but they appear only after hard rain. Color reflects mineralogy, oxidation and organic matter. Within one soil type darker generally means better, though adding organic matter may take years to change color.

soil-env-333.title: Building a degraded soil back into a healthy one
soil-env-333.text: Some soil problems take an afternoon to fix. Liming an acid soil is one. Others are close to permanent: a shallow soil can hardly be deepened, and a clay subsoil that causes poor drainage needs tile drainage at significant economic and environmental cost. Building soil means turning a degraded or low-quality soil into a high-quality one through understanding and sustained action that mirrors how plants and organic matter build soil in nature. {{ref:soil-found-045}} benefits almost all healthy-soil characteristics, even pest management. Managing it is therefore the foundation, along with limiting compaction and managing nutrients. General approaches are to minimize {{ref:soil-agri-095}} and other disturbance, add diverse organic materials, and keep live roots in the ground through rotations and a {{ref:soil-agri-066}} with varied root systems. Further steps are to keep the soil covered with cover crops or residue against rain and temperature extremes, manage traffic to protect structure, and manage pH and nutrients without polluting water. In arid regions the sodium or salt in the soil should also be reduced.

soil-env-336.title: How farming wears soil out in a downward spiral
soil-env-336.text: Cultivated soil rarely fails all at once. {{ref:soil-agri-095}} breaks aggregates, and organic matter is lost faster. Soils with lower organic matter and weaker aggregation erode faster, and {{ref:soil-water-001}} removes the organic-rich topsoil. That starts a downward spiral of compaction, poor infiltration and root growth, and nutrient decline. In arid regions, irrigation adds another path: it can make soils saline, so salts in the water must be leached beneath the root zone. The speed depends on the soil. Tropical rainforest soils can degrade within two or three years of conversion to cropland, which is why slash-and-burn developed. Great Plains soils took many decades to show degradation. The scale is large. Degradation has cut yields on about 20% of the world's cropland and 19-27% of grasslands and rangelands, and most agricultural soils are in fair, poor or very poor condition. Some 30-40 billion tons of topsoil are eroded from the world's croplands each year. History shows the cost. Rapid soil degradation in the temperate forests of the eastern United States pushed agriculture westward. Elsewhere the lost productivity led either to colonial ventures to feed the citizenry, like the Romans invading the Egyptian breadbasket, or to the decline of the civilization. Fertility lasted for centuries only in convergence zones such as valleys and deltas, where nutrients and sediments flow together.

soil-env-337.title: From soil to plant to person: the health chain
soil-env-337.text: Soil reaches people by more than one route. It affects them directly: dust storms from bare soils can cause respiratory problems and lung damage, while frequent early contact with soil and farm animals is linked to fewer allergies and a stronger immune system. The longer route runs through plants. Crops remove nutrients that natural systems recycle. Synthetic fertilizers mostly replace nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and calcium but not trace minerals, especially where farmers apply standard blends without soil analysis. Some soils are naturally low in elements such as selenium, which affects animals and humans more than plants. Others become toxic through pollution, cadmium-rich fertilizers or Bangladesh tube-well irrigation that put arsenic into rice. The largest effect of degradation is lost capacity to produce enough nutritious food, especially for rural families in developing countries who eat from their own farms. Mineral deficiency is rare in developed societies because diets come from many regions. Proving soil-health effects on human health is hard, because of dietary complexity and ethical limits on trials. The chain starts with {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-365.title: Keeping living roots in the ground all year
soil-env-365.text: Natural forests and prairies are never bare. They keep a continuous plant cover and a litter layer, whereas annual crops leave periods with no living plants, and prairie fallow was shown early on to lower soil organic matter. The practice of continuous living plants tries to close those gaps, mainly by perennializing cropping systems, and it protects soil, diversifies systems and builds soil carbon. The root system explains much of the gain. Plants allocate roughly 40% of net photosynthetic carbon to roots, and perennials give more carbon input than annuals because of larger root systems and a longer photosynthesis period. Roots and their microbial communities improve aggregation and hydraulic conductivity. In dry regions they raise porosity and the water retained at field capacity. Longer growth and transpiration from deep in the profile also help reduce salinity, because cover and roots limit evaporation and upward salt movement. Annual systems can approximate it with winter annuals such as winter wheat or fall rye, fall and spring cover crops, relay cropping or intercropping, perennial forages and agroforestry. A {{ref:soil-agri-066}} is the simplest step.

soil-env-352.title: Laboratory tests that measure how alive a soil is
soil-env-352.text: For years the standard soil test was chemical, and that gave a chemical bias that favored quick-fix fertilizer use. Laboratory soil health tests add biological and physical indicators to the chemical ones, to assess the soil processes that support ecosystem services. As of 2020 no single standard soil health test exists, though all agree it needs biological, physical and chemical indicators and interpretation by climate and texture. This is the quantitative end of {{ref:soil-env-177}}. Aggregate stability reflects infiltration, crusting and tilth and responds fast to reduced tillage, cover crops or manure. Available water capacity depends more on texture than on management. Soil organic matter is often the single most important indicator but changes too slowly. Active carbon, oxidized by potassium permanganate, responds quickly, and soil protein does too, especially with more legumes. Soil respiration integrates microbial abundance and activity and tracks nitrogen mineralization potential. The bean root rot bioassay gauges root health and disease pressure from nematodes and fungi such as Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia. Context adds tests. Salts and sodium should be tested in arid regions and greenhouses, and heavy metals, radioactive materials, solvents and petroleum products in urban or industrial soils.

soil-env-364.title: The six Cs: practices that build soil health
soil-env-364.text: The six practices all start with C, to stress the role of carbon in soil health. They are compaction reduction, conservation tillage, continuous living plants, cover crops, crop and animal diversity, and composts and amendments. Together they protect the soil against threats, diversify or perennialize annual cropping, and build soil carbon. The threats they address are erosion, compaction, organic matter decline, nutrient depletion or excess, biodiversity loss, salinization, desertification and contamination. The practices can be used singly or combined, and in combination they interact in varying ways. At a long-term Ontario site, soil health scores rose as more of them were adopted. Each rests on {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-340.title: What undisturbed ecosystems teach about farming
soil-env-340.text: A prairie or forest left alone recovers from fire, wind or excess rain. Undisturbed natural systems are stable and rebound quickly, and their traits give a model for farming. They use energy efficiently through food webs, capture and use rainfall, and cycle nutrients, which keeps the ecosystem from running down and protects water quality. Rain enters porous soil instead of running off, recharging groundwater and releasing water slowly to streams. High aboveground and soil biodiversity, in the sense of {{ref:soil-bio-008}}, supplies nutrients and checks disease. Competition and antagonisms such as antibiotics keep soilborne pathogens from causing disease in natural grassland or forest. Efficiency and diversity make these systems nearly self-sufficient, needing only sunlight and rain. Crop production disturbs them to favor one or a few species.

soil-env-341.title: Growing healthy crops by preventing problems
soil-env-341.text: Spraying and fumigating react to trouble after it starts. Ecological management is proactive and preventive: it grows healthy plants with strong defenses, suppresses pests and enhances beneficial organisms by improving habitat both aboveground and in the soil. Routine soil fumigation or broad-spectrum herbicides create dependency on purchased inputs, weaken resilience and promote resistance. The model is the {{ref:soil-env-340}}. Aboveground practices include resistant varieties, suitable planting density, variety blends, perimeter trap crops and flowering strips for beneficial insects. In the soil, the aim is to minimize disturbance and compaction, keep soil covered with residue, perennial forages and cover crops, maximize biodiversity, manage water, and keep pH and nutrients in range by routine testing. A vigorous winter legume cover crop, such as crimson clover in the southern US or hairy vetch in the north, can supply all the nitrogen for the next crop. Complex rotations with different plant families, and sod crops left undisturbed for years, are central. Tillage buries residue and breaks aggregates, leaving soil prone to erosion.

soil-env-330.title: A quick field test for soil nitrate
soil-env-330.text: A color strip can estimate nitrate in minutes. Shake a soil subsample 1:1 by volume with distilled water, filter it, put drops on a strip and read the color change after 60 seconds. The result estimates nitrate-N in ppm, the product of {{ref:soil-fert-112}}. Nitrite rarely occurs in measurable amounts in soil, so the nitrite pad reading is not recorded. The strip reads at most 50 ppm. A sample at the limit is diluted with equal drops of water and the reading multiplied by 2, or by 4 if diluted again. Pounds of nitrate-N per acre follow from ppm, sampling depth and {{ref:soil-phys-060}}, which can be assumed to be 1.1 g/cm3 for garden topsoil and 1.5 g/cm3 for subsoil.

soil-env-355.title: Why soil health practices work best together
soil-env-355.text: Each soil health practice affects the others, so they work best combined and matched to the needs and opportunities of the farm. Practices that improve soil health generally also improve farm economics through higher, steadier yields and lower inputs. The return may take a few years, though, and may need equipment such as new tillage tools and planters. Big changes suit strategic moments, such as a new planter or good prices. Before planting an orchard, vineyard or landscape, or switching to no-till, add organic matter, relieve subsoil compaction and correct nutrient deficiencies. Managing {{ref:soil-env-174}} is a long-term commitment with no silver bullets, and it needs integration of physical, biological and chemical processes.

soil-env-358.title: Preventing soil problems before they appear
soil-env-358.text: Holistic soil health management aims to prevent problems, as preventive medicine does, and diagnoses them by observation and testing. What suits an operation depends on soils, climate, enterprise, region, markets and goals. Tests from {{ref:soil-env-177}} guide the targeting of constraints but rarely give a simple recipe. The advice is to test each field every two to three years, preferably with comprehensive soil health analyses, and to add amendments only when needed. Keeping test records lets changes be followed over the years and practices fine-tuned.

soil-env-344.title: How attacked plants call for help
soil-env-344.text: A plant under attack is not silent. Damaged plants produce extra-floral nectar that feeds beneficials, and airborne volatiles that guide small wasps to a caterpillar host, in which the wasp lays eggs that kill it. The signal can run underground, through the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. Roots of some corn varieties attacked by western corn rootworm release a chemical that attracts a nematode killing the larvae. Breeding lost this trait in US corn, but wild relatives and European varieties retain it. Neighboring plants can even sense chemicals from wounded leaves and start making defenses before being attacked.

soil-env-357.title: Protecting soil organic matter with less tillage
soil-env-357.text: Leaving residue on the surface makes it easier to hold on to organic matter. Less disturbance keeps biological activity and decomposition near the surface, and keeps a structure that lets rain infiltrate quickly. Surface residue or mulch encourages earthworms, keeps soil moist and moderates temperature extremes. Minimum tillage greatly reduces erosion compared with conventional tillage, and contour tillage, contour strip cropping and terracing also help keep organic matter. There is a catch: heavy surface residue can harbor insects and disease organisms, so rotation matters even more. Problems can be worse in {{ref:soil-agri-117}} monoculture.

soil-env-356.title: Keeping a balance sheet for soil health
soil-env-356.text: Think of soil health as a bank account. Practices that build it are credits, and practices that degrade it are debits. Credits include manure additions, reduced tillage and cover crops. Debits include compaction from field traffic and intensive tillage. Farming systems differ in their balance sheet: daily harvesting forces traffic on wet soil, and small-seeded crops need intensive tillage in the row. An unavoidable bad practice should be balanced with a good one, or its impact reduced, for example by confining traffic to certain lanes. The account is kept in terms of {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-359.title: Quick fixes and lasting fixes for soil constraints
soil-env-359.text: Management guidelines for soil constraints come in two kinds. Short-term or intermittent responses give quick results and may need repeating. Long-term approaches give no quick fix but address the concern more sustainably. The same practices are often recommended for different constraints because they address several concerns at once. For low aggregate stability the short-term fix is fresh organic materials and the long-term fix is reduced tillage, surface mulch and sod rotation. For low available water capacity it is stable organic materials such as compost, lignin-rich residues and biochar. Recommendations for physical and biological constraints are less precise than for nutrients, because those systems are more complex and the research base is weaker. The constraints themselves come from {{ref:soil-env-177}}.

soil-env-362.title: Soil care for orchards, vineyards and landscapes
soil-env-362.text: A tree stays put for decades, so its soil must be right before planting. For tree and vine crops, evaluation should look at deeper layers for hardpans, subsoil acidity and shallow water tables, since fruit quality is strongly influenced by deep roots. One-time investments such as drainage, in-row deep ripping and deep lime and compost incorporation are difficult after planting. After establishment, the emphasis shifts to the surface layer: avoiding {{ref:soil-phys-082}} and keeping good surface mulches.

soil-env-360.title: Soil health on grain farms
soil-env-360.text: Grain farms export many nutrients and usually lose organic matter. Their wide choice of equipment, though, makes it easy to adopt reduced-tillage systems. Well-drained coarse soils suit {{ref:soil-agri-117}}, and finer-textured soils do well with strip-till or zone-till. Travel should happen only when soil is dry enough to resist compaction. No-till on easily compacted soils is hard because few options relieve compaction. Controlled-traffic farming is promising but may need new equipment and GPS guidance. Even with minimum tillage, {{ref:soil-agri-004}} with perennial grass or legume forages, or small grains in a corn-soybean system, improves soil health and opens space for cover crops.

soil-env-361.title: Soil health on vegetable farms
soil-env-361.text: Vegetable farms face the hardest case. Crops are compaction-sensitive, pests are demanding and the land has long been worked hard. Most vegetable farms lack livestock, so fresh organic matter must be brought in as manure, compost, leaves, grass clippings or food waste compost, checked for contaminants. The shorter main cropping season leaves time for pre-, mid- or post-season cover crops, and mulch from them keeps fresh-market produce off the ground, reducing rot. Choice of {{ref:soil-agri-066}} or rotation crop is critical: bean root rot is suppressed by rapeseed, crown vetch, wheat and rye but enhanced by white clover.

soil-env-363.title: Terroir: why the best wine soils are not rich
soil-env-363.text: Winemakers prize a soil that is not too generous. Terroir is the complex interaction of soil, climate and vine that shapes wine. The best wines tend to come from soils that are not overly fertile and that permit some water stress, since high organic matter and nitrogen cause excess vegetative growth and reduce fruit set. Mild water stress and reduced root growth between bloom and ripening increase anthocyanin pigments, which add to wine taste and color. Many top wine soils are deep, calcareous, sandy or gravelly and low in organic matter, while poor drainage and aeration harm quality.

soil-env-331.title: Reading a fertilizer label and doing the math
soil-env-331.text: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are its grade: the percentage by weight of nitrogen, phosphorus as P2O5 and potassium as K2O. A 15-10-10 fertilizer holds 15% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O by weight, so the nutrient in a bag is its weight times the percentage. See {{ref:soil-fert-001}} and {{ref:soil-fert-003}} for the nutrients themselves. Elemental amounts convert from oxide forms by factors: P = P2O5 x 0.44, P2O5 = P x 2.29, K = K2O x 0.83 and K2O = K x 1.21. To work out how much to apply, one needs the nutrient rate per unit area, the grade and the area. For manure, one also needs the N available in the season, with a rule of thumb of 60%. In a worked example, to supply 2 lb N per 1,000 sq ft with a 30-0-0 fertilizer, divide the rate by 0.30 to get fertilizer per 1,000 sq ft. Then multiply by 150 for 150,000 sq ft.

soil-env-366.title: Biodrilling: letting roots break up compacted soil
soil-env-366.text: Roots can do the work of a subsoiler. Biodrilling, or biological tillage, uses plant roots to create channels through compacted layers. If tillage leaves them undisturbed, the bio-pores left after roots die and decompose let later crops reach soil below the {{ref:soil-phys-082}} layer. Three factors make it work: roots must grow when soil is moist, species differ in root pressure, and macropores must be left intact by avoiding tillage. Tap-rooted forage radish had about twice as many roots as fibrous-rooted cereal rye at 15 to 50 cm depth under compaction.

soil-env-327.title: Inherent versus dynamic soil quality
soil-env-327.text: Some of a soil's character is fixed, and some is up to the manager. Inherent soil quality is a soil's natural ability to function, while dynamic soil quality is how the soil changes with the way it is managed. Inherent properties change little: a sandy soil drains faster than a clayey one, and a deep soil gives roots more room than a soil with bedrock near the surface. Management can change dynamic properties such as organic matter, soil structure, and water and nutrient holding capacity. Soils respond differently to the same management because of their inherent properties, so how those properties vary across the landscape should be considered. Both belong to {{ref:soil-env-179}}.

soil-env-371.title: Adding carbon to soil with compost and other amendments
soil-env-371.text: An organic amendment is any carbon-based material added to soil. Compost is one that has been partially decomposed before application, as covered in {{ref:soil-fert-028}}. Added carbon improves infiltration, water holding capacity, microbial activity, cation exchange capacity and nutrient availability, and carbon applied over time relates positively to soil organic carbon. Composting is aerobic microbial decomposition needing managed oxygen, moisture, temperature and C:N ratio. It cuts volume by about 50% and, at high temperature, reduces pathogens. Composted manure releases more nutrients in years 2 and 3 than in the year applied, so timing relative to crop uptake matters. Degraded soils gain most, so amendments can be targeted to sandy knolls or compacted areas. Effects can last decades and offset erosion damage. The main constraints by source are pathogens in manure and biosolids, salts in food waste, and N and P immobilization from wood waste.

soil-env-370.title: What soils do for us: functions and services
soil-env-370.text: Soils work, and what they do for people are called ecosystem services. Soil functions are bundles of attributes and processes, and its capacity to function powers those services. Soil health or quality is commonly defined as the capacity of a soil to sustain biological productivity, environmental quality, and plant, animal and human health, the idea behind {{ref:soil-env-174}}. No single measurement quantifies it; it must be inferred from many attributes, processes and contexts. Example indicators are aggregate stability and organic matter for erosion control, infiltration rate and available water capacity for water supply, and respiration and organic carbon for climate regulation.

soil-env-369.title: Turning soil tests into a health score
soil-env-369.text: A soil health score converts each test result into a relative score using a curve, then averages the scores, with higher meaning healthier. Indicators should be interpreted against reference values taken from an undisturbed soil, a highly productive soil, or the distribution of samples from comparable land uses or regions. The inputs come from {{ref:soil-env-177}}. Scoring curves have three shapes: more is better (soil organic matter), optimum is best (nutrients, pH) and less is better (salinity). Curve shapes come from expert opinion or literature. With regional datasets such as Cornell CASH, scores of 0 to 100 show rank within that region. A criticism is that a soil can score high yet not support plant growth, so it would not by definition be healthy.

soil-env-368.title: Judging soil health by eye with a spade
soil-env-368.text: A spade, water and under an hour can tell you a good deal. Visual soil assessment judges soil health indicators in the field by eye and simple tools, giving quick results mainly on surface soil and physical attributes. Examining a sample coarsely shows texture, aggregation, structure, compaction and infiltration. With simple tools it can also address pH, respiration and earthworm counts, and score cards with visual keys guide non-experts. Its limit is that visual assessments alone cannot judge how well ecosystem services perform, so they work best with analytical tests. CAT scans can measure porosity, connectivity and crusting.

soil-env-367.title: Why compaction keeps coming back
soil-env-367.text: Farmers know compaction is harmful, yet it persists, because field work is often forced onto wet soil and farm equipment keeps getting heavier. Larger farms must cover more ground, so seeding, spraying or harvesting may happen when conditions are too wet. Monitoring axle loads and tire inflation, and avoiding wet-soil field work, help avoid {{ref:soil-phys-082}}. The cure is costly. Subsoiling with a chisel plow takes fuel and time, must be done when soil is dry enough to fracture the plow pan, and needs repeating after a few years if the causes are unchanged.

soil-env-339.title: Why soil problems rarely come alone
soil-env-339.text: Physical, chemical and biological properties of soil are linked, so a problem in one often causes problems in others. Soil must be managed as a whole. {{ref:soil-phys-082}} removes large pores, so large organisms such as earthworms cannot move or survive, and waterlogging can denitrify nitrate to N2 and the greenhouse gas N2O. Sodium-rich soils, common in arid climates, have aggregates that break apart, leaving few pores for air exchange and drainage. And low organic matter and poor structure limit plant growth even when nutrient supply is optimal.

soil-env-354.title: When adding beneficial microbes pays off
soil-env-354.text: In soil with high biological diversity and activity, inoculating seeds or transplants with beneficial organisms usually brings little advantage. The exception is legume seed, which should still get its rhizobia. Interest is growing in microbes that make growth hormones, help plants resist disease and pests, reach water and nutrients or cope with drought and wet stress, but no general recommendations exist. See {{ref:soil-bio-070}}. Inoculants may help in stressful settings: low organic matter, dry or moderately to highly saline soil, and newly farmed fields, especially urban soils. Dipping transplants in mycorrhizae may pay off if no cover crop was grown that year, particularly after a brassica, which forms no mycorrhizal association.

soil-env-351.title: Testing aggregate stability in a jar
soil-env-351.text: Two jars of water tell a lot about a soil. Gently drop aggregates from the top 3 to 4 inches into the water and see whether they hold or slake; a soil that seals readily has unstable aggregates, a concern covered in {{ref:soil-phys-004}}. If broken-up aggregates also stay dispersed in suspension, high sodium may be a problem, usually in arid and semiarid regions. A spade test checks structure. A good plow layer is fluffy with granules of about a quarter inch, and subsoil clumps should come apart easily into aggregates of several inches.

soil-env-334.title: Scorecards that rate a field's soil health
soil-env-334.text: You can judge a soil without a laboratory, using a shovel and some patience. A scorecard rates {{ref:soil-env-174}} on scales, drawing on what you see in the soil and in the crop growing on it. In the field, check earthworms, erosion, ease of tillage, structure and color, compaction, water infiltration and drainage. Then rate the crop's appearance, growth rate, root health, drought resistance and yield. Farmers are advised to fill out a scorecard for each major field or soil type every few years, or to send soil to a laboratory that offers soil health analyses.

soil-env-343.title: Push-pull: repelling pests while trapping them
soil-env-343.text: Some pest control works by giving insects somewhere else to go. A perimeter trap crop intercepts a pest before it reaches the main crop. Blue Hubbard squash around summer squash, for example, intercepts striped cucumber beetles. East African push-pull goes further, building on {{ref:soil-agri-217}}. Desmodium, a legume, grows within the corn rows and repels stem borers: that is the push. Grasses planted around the edge attract adult moths: that is the pull. The legume also supplies nitrogen and suppresses weeds.

soil-env-348.title: Why surface residue need not mean more disease
soil-env-348.text: Farmers are often told to bury crop residue because it can harbour pathogens. Yet the same advice promotes leaving {{ref:soil-agri-129}} on the surface and tilling less. Both claims hold, because the system differs. With rotations, conservation tillage, cover crops and organic additions, soil biological diversity and beneficial organisms increase. Crop stress falls, and disease pressure falls with it. In traditional systems a single pathogen more easily comes to dominate.

soil-env-347.title: Symphylans: the pest that likes rich soil
soil-env-347.text: Most soil pests thrive in poor, degraded ground. Symphylans do the opposite. These white, centipede-like arthropods feed on root hairs and rootlets and damage many crops. They prefer soils rich in organic matter, because good structure and old root channels let them move easily. In some fields they appear in spotty, circular patches. Biological activity is not thought to be an adequate defense. Potatoes and beans are damaged less, transplanted tomatoes do better than direct seeded ones, and denser squash planting helps maintain yield. Organic amendments should be imported with care so the pest is not introduced by accident.

soil-env-338.title: Does organic food make people healthier?
soil-env-338.text: The belief that organic food is better for you is widespread, but the evidence is thin. Plants take up nutrients almost entirely as inorganic forms, so nutrients from organic sources are not known to affect human health differently than synthetic ones. Some studies find higher antioxidant levels in organic food. Yet organic eaters usually have better diets, lifestyles and incomes, and no study has tied the antioxidants to better health outcomes. Whether better soil management and organic production improve human health is still debated. The studies cannot separate these confounding factors. See {{ref:soil-env-337}} for the wider link.

soil-env-345.title: How plants arm themselves against disease
soil-env-345.text: A plant attacked in one leaf can raise its defenses in all of them. Plants form hormones and defence proteins in response to signals from microorganisms, making the whole plant resistant to pathogens even far from the infection site. Systemic acquired resistance follows exposure to a pathogen, or even a non-pathogenic organism, and involves salicylic acid and defense proteins that protect against many pathogens. Induced systemic resistance follows root exposure to plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, and involves the hormones jasmonate and ethylene. The roots meet these bacteria in the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. Some organic amendments induce resistance, but no reliable, cost-effective indicator yet shows whether a soil or amendment is strengthening plant defense. Defenses come in depth: rhizosphere bacteria that compete with or antagonize pathogens, endophytes inside roots that produce antifungal chemicals, and the plant's own chemicals.

soil-env-346.title: Healthy plants resist pests better
soil-env-346.text: Pests are drawn to weakness. Healthy, thriving plants defend themselves better, while drought, nutrient limits or compaction stress them and make them signal weakness to pests. That makes {{ref:soil-env-174}} the foundation of crop pest management. Developing optimal soil health is the basis of it, and it should underpin integrated pest management programs.

soil-env-342.title: Soil practices that hold pests in check
soil-env-342.text: Many pest problems can be eased through the soil itself. Rotation reduces disease, insect, nematode and weed pressure. Avoiding excess inorganic nitrogen limits insect damage, and adequate calcium or potassium lowers some crop diseases. Less compaction lowers insect and root-disease damage. Composts low in available nitrogen but with active organic matter reduce root rot and leaf disease severity. A {{ref:soil-agri-066}} adds more. Cover crops, especially in reduced tillage, keep mycorrhizal spore counts high, and selected ones suppress parasitic fungi and nematodes. Cereal rye residue reduces weed seed germination. Reduced tillage and surface residue also keep weed seeds on the surface, where ground beetles, rodents, ants and crickets eat them. Biologically active soils reduce weed seed numbers.

soil-env-286.title: Active carbon: an early sign of soil health
soil-env-286.text: Most of a soil's carbon changes too slowly to watch. Active carbon is the exception: the most readily usable portion of the total organic carbon, as in {{ref:soil-env-108}}. It contributes greatly to the functioning of the soil food web. It is a newer measure that joins established ones such as microbial biomass and activity, enzymes, soil organic matter, total nitrogen, available nutrients, porosity, aggregate stability and compaction. It is the fraction oxidized by potassium permanganate, measured with an inexpensive spectrophotometer. Because it responds quickly to management, it is an early indicator of gains in soil health, as in {{ref:soil-env-177}}.

soil-env-315.title: Organic and inorganic soil contaminants
soil-env-315.text: Soil contaminants fall into two families. Organic contaminants include pesticides, solvents and industrial products. Inorganic ones include metals, salts, nutrients and radionuclides. At Canadian contaminated sites the most common organic contaminants are petroleum hydrocarbons: crude oil, fuels and lubricating oils. Dioxins, furans and PAHs are also organic. Inorganics include heavy and trace metals, metalloids, acids and bases, excess nutrients and salts, and radionuclides, from mine wastes, firing ranges, fly ash and battery disposal. Some help soil ecosystems at background levels. Copper, molybdenum, cobalt and zinc are plant micronutrients but contaminants at high concentrations. Chloride from de-icing or spills can build up and raise electrical conductivity. Excess nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur from misplaced livestock waste can also be contaminants.

soil-env-316.title: Matching the cleanup method to the contaminant
soil-env-316.text: No single cleanup suits every site. The choice depends on the contaminant, the site and the soil properties. Petroleum hydrocarbons differ in molecular weight, solubility, volatility and density. Larger compounds are less volatile and less soluble, and gasoline is lighter and more volatile than lubricating oil. Large insoluble hydrocarbons sorb strongly to soil organic matter and are hard to degrade or remove, especially in fine-textured soils, where aggregates trap them and air and water move poorly. Metals are spread among soil components depending on texture, mineralogy, pH, exchange capacity, organic matter and aeration, so remediation must consider each chemical form. Treatments are biological, chemical or physical, often combined. They are applied ex situ, meaning excavated and treated on or off site, or in situ, meaning treated in place.

soil-env-318.title: Vitrification: melting soil into glass
soil-env-318.text: At 1400 to 2000 °C, soil stops being soil. Vitrification heats it until its silica melts into stable glass and crystalline solids. The heat may come from electrodes and electrical resistance, or from plasma arc technology. Organic contaminants are volatilized, trapped and treated or destroyed. Inorganic contaminants, including radionuclides, are encased. Ex situ incineration is milder, heating soil to 870 to 1370 °C to destroy organic contaminants.

soil-env-317.title: Soil washing and flushing
soil-env-317.text: Contaminants tend to cling to the smallest particles. Soil washing, an ex situ treatment, may separate the silt and clay fines from the coarse material. Because the contaminants cling to the fines, removing them reduces the total mass and volume that needs treatment. In situ soil flushing works differently. It treats the contaminated zone with a solution of water, acid, base, chelating agent, co-solvent or surfactant. It then brings the mobilized contaminants to the surface for disposal, treatment or recirculation.

soil-env-314.title: Amendments that make reclaimed soil fit for use
soil-env-314.text: A rebuilt soil rarely matches what its new land use demands. Amendments are the materials added to correct chemical, physical or biological properties, as part of {{ref:soil-found-082}}. Lack of organic matter is common and is fixed with animal manure, straw, or forest floor (LFH) material from a cleared area. Lack of nutrients is fixed with commercial nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilizer blended for the site. Waste materials are widely used, which also keeps them out of landfills. Raw sewage supplies nutrients and organic matter but may carry salts, metals and disease organisms. Biosolids, sewage sludges treated to lower pathogen risk, are widely used. Others include calcium sources, paper mill waste, industrial sludge, biochar and wood ash. Each has properties that suit a soil need and usually a drawback to balance, and many jurisdictions regulate waste use. Micro-topography such as mounds, furrows, depressions, rocks and mulches gives micro sites for plants and microbes and reduces erosion.

soil-hist-147.title: Photosynthesis: how light becomes the food that feeds soil
soil-hist-147.text: Every sugar in a plant, and so nearly every scrap of organic matter in soil, began as light. Photosynthesis is the biological process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds. Usually the term means oxygenic photosynthesis, which splits water and releases oxygen. The stored carbohydrates are later used in cellular respiration, a reaction type that {{ref:soil-chem-113}} describes. In plants, chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs red and blue light. The light reactions make NADPH and ATP, and the Calvin cycle then builds sugars from atmospheric CO2. The scale is planetary. Photosynthesis maintains atmospheric oxygen and supplies most biological energy. Globally it captures about 130 terawatts and fixes 100-115 billion tons of carbon into biomass yearly. Individual plants are less impressive. They convert light with an efficiency usually of 3-6%, ranging from 0.1% to 8% with light, temperature and CO2. The process was long misunderstood. In 1779 Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

soil-hist-153.title: When photosynthesis began, and how it changed the air
soil-hist-153.text: Photosynthesis is older than oxygen in the air. It began early in Earth's history, probably as anoxygenic forms using hydrogen or sulfur rather than water. Possible filamentous photosynthetic fossils are 3.4 billion years old, and thylakoid membranes are preserved in 1.75-billion-year-old cherts. Using water as the electron source, the step that defines {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and depends on {{ref:soil-chem-113}}, evolved once, in a common ancestor of living cyanobacteria at least 2450-2320 million years ago. Their oxygen oxygenated Earth, an event sometimes called the oxygen catastrophe.

soil-hist-152.title: What limits how fast plants photosynthesize
soil-hist-152.text: Photosynthesis has a speed limit, and many things can set it. It is limited by light, by leaf area for capturing light, by CO2 supply to chloroplasts, by water and by temperature. Shading by other plants is a major limitation. Sugar production rises with CO2 concentration until another factor limits it. This is the pace of {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, and the electron transfers behind it are {{ref:soil-chem-113}}.

soil-hist-148.title: Light reactions: capturing sunlight as ATP and NADPH
soil-hist-148.text: The first stage of {{ref:soil-hist-147}} happens in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. Chlorophyll absorbs light, and an electron passes through pheophytin and an electron transport chain to reduce NADP to NADPH. A proton gradient meanwhile drives ATP synthase. This is a chain of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Chlorophyll regains its lost electron when water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen. Not all wavelengths work. In green plants the action spectrum peaks in violet-blue and red light, while red algae use blue-green light to grow deeper.

soil-hist-149.title: The Calvin cycle: building sugar from air
soil-hist-149.text: The second stage of {{ref:soil-hist-147}} needs no light directly, only the products of {{ref:soil-hist-148}}. RuBisCO captures CO2 and, using NADPH, makes three-carbon sugars. Those intermediates are combined into sucrose and starch. The sugars then feed cellulose, lipid and amino acid synthesis, or respiration. Reducing CO2 this way is {{ref:soil-chem-113}} at work.

soil-hist-150.title: Photorespiration: when RuBisCO grabs the wrong molecule
soil-hist-150.text: RuBisCO sometimes makes a costly mistake. When CO2 is low, it binds oxygen instead, in a wasteful process that uses energy and makes no sugar. The oxygen reaction yields phosphoglycolate, which the {{ref:soil-hist-149}} cannot use, and glycolate, which is toxic at high concentration and inhibits photosynthesis. Salvaging glycolate is energetically expensive: only 75% of its carbon returns to the cycle, and ammonia is lost, so nitrogen leaves the plant. Hot, dry conditions make it worse. Closed stomata drop CO2 and raise oxygen, increasing photorespiration. The oxygen involved is part of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}.

soil-hist-151.title: C4 and CAM: two ways to dodge photorespiration
soil-hist-151.text: Some plants have fixed the problem of {{ref:soil-hist-150}} by raising CO2 concentration at RuBisCO using PEP carboxylase. C4 plants separate the steps in space; CAM plants separate them in time. C4 plants fix CO2 in mesophyll cells into oxaloacetate, then release it in bundle sheath cells. There RuBisCO sits away from the oxygen-producing light reactions, which cuts photorespiration. They outproduce C3 plants in high light and temperature and include maize, sorghum, sugarcane and millet. Over 90% of plants are C3 and about 3% C4, yet C4 evolved in over sixty lineages. CAM plants such as cacti and succulents fix CO2 at night with open stomata, store it as malic acid and release it by day. About 16,000 species use it. All of this rests on {{ref:soil-chem-113}}.

soil-hist-146.title: Marine isotope stages: numbering ice ages
soil-hist-146.text: Deep-sea mud keeps a record of ice ages. Marine isotope stages are the alternating warm and cool periods of Earth's climate deduced from oxygen isotope data in cores, as in {{ref:soil-found-117}}. Counting back from the present (MIS 1), even-numbered stages have high oxygen-18 and are cold glacials, while odd-numbered stages are warm interglacials. The scale grew from Emiliani's 1950s work on Urey's prediction that the oxygen-18 ratio in {{ref:soil-found-118}} varies with water temperature. Shackleton showed in 1967 that ice-sheet volume was the main cause. The record matches Milankovitch orbital cycles, which helped that theory win acceptance, and it is the standard for correlating Quaternary climate records. Over 100 stages are identified. MIS 5e (about 123 kya) is the Last Interglacial, MIS 5d to 2 is the Last Glacial Period, and the list reaches MIS 104 at 2.614 million years ago.

soil-hist-145.title: Clumped isotopes: a thermometer inside carbonate
soil-hist-145.text: Some rocks carry their own thermometer. Clumped isotopes are heavy isotopes bonded to other heavy isotopes within a molecule such as carbonate, and their abundance depends on temperature. The carbonate thermometer uses the temperature dependence of 13C-18O bonding in the lattice, with more clumping as temperature falls, reported as Δ47. Unlike conventional δ18O analysis it does not need the water's δ18O, so it gives temperature and lets source-water δ18O be reconstructed. Carbonate is reacted with phosphoric acid to release CO2, which is purified and analyzed by mass spectrometry at precision near 10^-5. Uses include past lake and seawater temperatures, paleoaltimetry such as Andes uplift, and extinct animal body temperatures. The catch is that the signal is subtle (-0.0005%/°C) and the key isotopologue is about 60 ppm. Analyses take 2-3 hours and need large, uncontaminated samples.

soil-hist-144.title: OPAL Soil Centre and its earthworm survey
soil-hist-144.text: In March 2009, members of the public across England began digging up soil and counting worms. The OPAL Soil Centre ran that OPAL Soil and Earthworm Survey. It is one of five centres of expertise of the Open Air Laboratories Network, based at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London. Volunteers collected habitat and soil information and identified earthworms. Results were analysed to study soil and earthworm distribution across England and the effects humans have on soils. Its aims include community-level information on soil quality and biodiversity, and research on pollution sources and pathways in soil.

soil-hist-143.title: Central Soil Salinity Research Institute
soil-hist-143.text: The institute is an autonomous Indian body under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, devoted to salt-affected soils. It began at Hisar in 1969 after an Indo-American team's water management recommendations, and moved to Karnal that year. Four divisions cover soil and crop management, irrigation and drainage engineering, crop improvement and social science. The engineers work on groundwater recharge and subsurface drainage of waterlogged saline soils. Crop improvement breeds saline- and alkali-tolerant rice, wheat and mustard. The institute also coordinates the national project on managing salt-affected soils and using saline water.

soil-hist-142.title: Indian Institute of Soil Science
soil-hist-142.text: Founded in 1988 at Bhopal, this autonomous institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research was set up for advanced research in {{ref:soil-found-090}}. It covers coordinated projects on soil test crop response (17 centres), micronutrients and biofertilizers (11 centres each). Six divisions include soil physics, soil chemistry and fertility, soil biology and environmental soil science. It trains in soil testing, nutrient and water efficiency, carbon sequestration and soil quality assessment. Its mandate covers research on soil physical, chemical and biological processes and environment-friendly management technologies. A long-term fertilizer experiments project studies fertilizer effects on productivity and soil quality.

soil-hist-141.title: Heath: shrubland on poor, acid ground
soil-hist-141.text: Heath is what grows where soil gives little. It is a shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining, infertile, acidic soils, with open, low-growing woody vegetation. Heathland is favoured by hard, dry climates, especially in summer, and by acidic, low-fertility, often sandy soils. A small mire may form where drainage is poor. Heaths are dominated by low shrubs 20 cm to 2 m tall. They range from very species-rich in Australia and South African fynbos to depauperate in Europe, where heather, heath and gorse dominate. Many heaths are anthropogenic, made by centuries of clearing woodland by grazing and burning. They are kept by grazing and periodic burning (swailing) or rarely mowing, or they are recolonised by woodland. Heaths are widespread but rapidly disappearing and rare in Europe. Tree incursion after traditional management stopped, and urban sprawl, threaten them.

soil-hist-154.title: National Society of Consulting Soil Scientists
soil-hist-154.text: This North American professional society of soil scientists, mainly environmental consultants, merged into the Soil Science Society of America (SSSA) in August 2011. Its members worked on topics such as {{ref:soil-fert-192}}, {{ref:soil-agri-169}}, {{ref:soil-water-124}}, {{ref:soil-water-002}} and {{ref:soil-env-062}}. It awarded the Registered Professional Soil Scientist (RPSS) designation in the United States and stressed professional ethics in certification. It became an SSSA chapter in 1996, a cooperator of the National Cooperative Soil Survey in 1997, and was a member of the International Union of Soil Sciences. In 2011 the SSSA board created Division S12 for Consulting Soil Scientists, and 95% of NSCSS members voted to integrate. SSSA's corporate umbrella and Science Policy Office were cited as advantages.

openers.agri: Every field is a soil someone has decided to manage. This part of the course turns to agricultural soil science, the branch that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre. It begins with the big choices a farmer makes: whether to bring water in, which crops to grow and in what order, and whether to rely on natural inputs such as compost and manure. Each choice leaves a mark. Water poured onto a field carries soluble nutrients away, and a single crop grown year after year wears the land in ways a sequence of crops does not.
openers.farming-systems-and-growing-media: Water is where farming systems start. People apply controlled amounts of it to land to grow crops, landscape plants and lawns, spreading it over the surface by gravity or spraying it overhead from high-pressure sprinklers. Yet only part of that water is ever used by the crop, and what drains away can take soluble plant nutrients with it. This chapter also follows the crops themselves, from a single crop grown year after year to a series of different ones, and the farms that rely on compost, manure and green manure. It ends with the land and the media plants grow in: new land won from seas and lake beds, and the potting mixes that hold plants in containers.
openers.tillage-and-cultivation: Digging, stirring, overturning: farmers agitate soil mechanically to ready it for crops, and that work is tillage. The prize is land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops. Tilling loosens and aerates the topsoil for planting, yet it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil. This chapter follows that trade-off from deep primary work to shallow secondary passes, to ploughing across slopes along their contour lines, and to the stalks and stubble a harvest leaves in the field. It also visits forest sites readied for planting, and buried ancient remains such as long barrows that tilling has damaged.
openers.soil-conservation: Topsoil can be lost in two ways: carried off by erosion, or stripped of its fertility by overuse, acidification, salinization or chemical contamination. This chapter is about preventing both. Its tools range from the humble to the monumental: a crop sown only to cover the ground, rows of trees planted against the wind, long narrow strips of alternating crops, and flat steps cut into a mountainside like a staircase. Some approaches join many practices into whole farming systems that barely disturb the soil, keep it covered and mix plant species. Engineers have their own version, altering a natural soil until it can serve an engineering purpose such as carrying a road.
openers.soil-survey-and-land-evaluation: Knowing a soil is only half the work; someone must also record where it lies. This chapter starts with the soil survey, which classifies an area's soils and records them geographically, and with the soil map it produces. It then turns to judging land: predicting what soils can and cannot do for crops, building or gardens, and rating them, as the US Department of Agriculture does with {{ref:soil-agri-088}} and Germany does on a scale from 0 to 100. The last stretch moves to computers, from {{ref:soil-agri-089}} and national soil databases to the mathematics of soil variation.
openers.bio: Beneath every field and forest lives a crowd of microbes and animals, and this part of the course is about them. Soil biology studies their activity and ecology, while soil microbiology narrows the lens to the microorganisms and how they change soil properties. About 30% of arthropods live in soil, alongside earthworms and the detritivores that eat decomposing plant and animal parts and feces. Soil ecology traces how these organisms interact, and the soil food web maps the feeding links that pass energy among them. All that life breathes, too: soil respiration is the carbon dioxide given off by roots, microbes and soil animals below ground.
