openers.life-in-the-soil: Some organisms scrape by where nutrients are barely present; others harden their own tissues with minerals. This chapter meets them both, starting with the sciences that study soil life and the variety of that life. Its cast runs from microbes to earthworms, the largest members of the Oligochaeta, and to the detritivores that eat decaying plant and animal parts. A simple lab measure, total organic carbon, shows how much organic carbon a sample holds. Feeding links, mineral-making and the carbon dioxide that soil life breathes out show what all these organisms do together.
openers.roots-and-the-rhizosphere: Half of a plant lives in the dark. Its roots anchor it, take in water and dissolved nutrients, and spread through the soil as one thick central root or a dense mat of thin ones, steered by gravity, light, barriers and soil conditions. Fine outgrowths of single cells do much of the collecting, and roots can even move water from moist soil into dry. Roots also release sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA into the soil around them. This chapter follows those compounds into the narrow zone they shape, crowded with microbes, and into the legume family, about 19,000 species including soybean, pea and alfalfa.
openers.organic-matter-humus-and-decomposition: Every year a forest drops a fresh cover of leaves, bark, needles and twigs onto its soil. This chapter follows that dead material as it rots. Decomposition breaks it into carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts, and releases its nutrients in forms that roots can take up again. Part of it escapes that fate and turns into a dark, stable substance that improves soil structure and holds nutrients until plants need them. Some of it breaks down within about ten years, while the most stable part resists decay for a century or more.
openers.soil-biochemistry: Most of the work of decay happens outside the cells that do it. Microbes secrete enzymes into the soil to break large molecules down, and in leaf litter and soil most of these come from fungi. Some, such as peroxidases armed with hydrogen peroxide, attack lignin; others free phosphate or release glucose. This chapter follows those enzymes, the simple model of how fast they work, and the living microbes that make up a few percent of soil organic matter. It also shows how researchers read soil communities from copied DNA, and how the balance of elements shapes what those communities can do.
openers.chem: Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil, and much of it plays out on surfaces too small to see. Its first actors are the clay minerals: hydrous aluminium silicates built in sheets that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations. Around them sit iron and aluminium oxides and hydroxides left by weathering, including the minerals of the world's main source of aluminium. The same chemistry also decides what becomes of contaminants once they are released into soil.
openers.clay-minerals-and-colloids: Every clay mineral is built from just two kinds of sheet. One is made of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra; the other holds small cations such as aluminium or magnesium, each surrounded by six oxygens. How those sheets stack sorts the clays into two families, 1:1 and 2:1, and much follows from that choice. This chapter meets the common clays in turn, from a 1:1 clay also called kaolin to a 2:1 clay that expands greatly when heated. It then turns to the iron and aluminium minerals that weathering leaves beside them, and to a soft rock of fossil silica that crumbles into a fine white powder.
openers.charge-and-nutrient-holding: Most soil organic matter is dark, decay-resistant material left after biomass has been broken down and transformed over long periods. That material and the edges of clay carry electrical charge that changes with the soil's pH, and at one particular pH a surface's net charge falls to zero. Charged surfaces let one substance attach to another, and some molecules grip metal atoms at two or more points, like a claw. Living things make such molecules, and fertilizer makers use them to deliver manganese, iron, zinc and copper. This chapter follows those charges from the chemistry of humic material to the nutrients a soil can hold for plants.
openers.redox-and-soil-chemistry: Rust on iron and breath in the lungs share one chemistry: redox, short for reduction–oxidation, in which electrons pass from one substance to another. A donor gives electrons, an acceptor takes them, and each half of that trade has a voltage that can be measured. In soil, these transfers underlie many processes and properties, from the respiration of microbes to the gray and rust-colored patterns left by iron and manganese. This chapter follows them from single reactions to the electrical tendency of a whole soil and the ordered series of reactions it supports. It ends with the ways people use oxidation and microbes to clean polluted ground and water.
openers.acidity-alkalinity-and-salinity: A soil can turn sour, salty or sodic, and each change reshapes what will grow in it. Acidification is the build-up of hydrogen cations that lowers a soil's pH, and rain made acid by air pollutants or ammonium-based fertilizers can drive it fast. Salinity, a soil's salt content, climbs in irrigated fields because nearly all water carries dissolved salts that stay behind in the root zone, and it climbs in unirrigated landscapes too, as across much of Australia. Where sodium predominates among the cations, a different trouble begins, and an index built from sodium, calcium and magnesium helps manage it. Along the way come hard crusts of precipitated minerals and waterlogged soils that hide iron sulfide minerals.
openers.soil-mineralogy: Every soil starts with minerals, and their history shapes almost everything that follows. The study of them, {{ref:soil-chem-184}}, is one of the branches, alongside soil physics, chemistry and biology, through which soil processes are measured. This chapter begins in a cooling basaltic magma, where silicate minerals crystallize in a fixed order, and follows them to the surface, where minerals formed hot and deep weather fastest. Along the way come odd characters: glass with no crystals at all, a green mineral that crumbles at a touch, and crusts born where iron sulfides oxidize. It ends with the beams of X-rays that tell one mineral from another.
openers.soil-solution-chemistry-and-sorption: Soil water is never pure. It carries crowds of ions that shield and jostle one another, and it bathes mineral surfaces that grab some of those ions and let others pass. This chapter follows that traffic: how chemists weigh a solution's charged load, correct for ions that do not behave ideally, and describe how substances bind to surfaces or get swept into a forming solid. It ends with the tools that tie the picture together: X-ray spectra that show an atom's immediate surroundings, and computer models that calculate every species in a solution and the reactions among them.
openers.class: Every soil map, every land-use plan and every trench on a building site depends on putting soils into named groups. That systematic grouping, by distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how soils are used, is the subject of this part. Natural systems group soils by intrinsic properties, behavior or genesis; technical systems group them by fitness for a use, from foundations to trench safety. The United States sorts its soils into six levels from order to series, Canada and Australia keep national systems of their own, and an international system edited by a working group of the International Union of Soil Sciences names soils for maps worldwide. First come the systems themselves, then the soils they name.
openers.classification-systems: An engineer, a farmer and a mapmaker can look at the same soil and file it in three different places. Engineers group soils by how they behave under foundations, a U.S. safety scheme sorts them by strength so that trenches do not collapse, and natural systems group them by their properties and genesis. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's system runs through six levels from order to series, while its predecessor had just three orders, keyed to the dominant soil-forming factors. Canada, Australia and the FAO built systems of their own, and smaller classes describe a soil's own climate, such as how wet it stays through the year.
openers.usda-soil-orders: Twelve orders sort soils at the top level of USDA soil taxonomy, and this chapter meets them one by one. Their criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed. Some are young, with no development beyond an A horizon and little change from their parent material. Others are strongly weathered, from acid red clays to oxide-rich soils of the tropical rainforest. Between them lie deep, dark grassland soils, clays that crack when dry and swell when wet, soils of volcanic ash, soils made of organic materials, desert soils and soils over permafrost.
openers.world-reference-base-soil-groups: Travel from the northern forests to the tropics and the soil underfoot changes as much as the trees. Under boreal and coniferous forests lies an acid soil with a bleached, ash-grey layer below its organic topsoil. On the steppes a black earth holds 4% to 16% humus. Dry lands carry pale, salty soils, groundwater stains others grey or blue, and long human use, from irrigation to paddy fields, has remade some entirely. This chapter takes the reference soil groups of the World Reference Base one at a time, from very shallow soils over rock to strongly weathered tropical soils ruled by aluminum.
openers.other-soil-types: Not every soil fits neatly into the great classification systems, and this chapter gathers the ones worth knowing anyway. It begins with peat, partly decayed vegetation that piles up in bogs, moors and other waterlogged ground where acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions stop plants from rotting fully. Layer by layer, peat keeps a record of past vegetation and people, yet it can be drained for farming, cut and dried as fuel, worn into overhanging banks, or set smouldering underground by fires that light rain cannot put out. Then come soils named for their rock, climate or makers: an uncommon soil weathered from serpentine-bearing ultramafic rock, the fertile {{ref:soil-class-048}} of humid temperate lands, the shallow, humus-rich {{ref:soil-class-050}} on carbonate rock, and {{ref:soil-class-053}}, a dark Amazonian soil that people built with the help of {{ref:soil-class-083}}.
openers.env: Carbon never sits still. It moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere, and soil is one of its great holding places. That stored carbon takes two forms: organic matter from plants, animals and microbes, and carbonate minerals. This part of the course follows soil into the wider environment, beginning with the two-way link between soil carbon and climate. A changing climate alters soils and their carbon, and every loss or gain of that carbon alters the climate in turn, with consequences that reach from the frozen Arctic to the world's food supply.
openers.soil-carbon-and-climate: Soil organic matter is about 50% carbon by dry weight, and more carbon sits in soil as carbonate minerals. This chapter asks what happens to that store as the climate changes. Processes that pull carbon from the air and lock it away can slow warming, and so can land and farm practices that stop soils losing carbon and help them build it up. Losses run the other way and feed warming. The chapter ends in the Arctic, where carbon passes from frozen soils to plants, microbes and air, and where the top layer of ground thaws every summer and refreezes every autumn.
openers.degradation-and-desertification: Soil can go backward. Left alone, a soil and its plants evolve together toward a steady balance, the highest development their environment can produce. Destroy the vegetation, and erosion can strip the upper horizons and push the soil back toward its pioneer beginnings. This chapter follows that decline from soil degradation to land degradation, with its many human and natural drivers and its costs in lost harvests, polluted water, vanishing species and money. It covers soil sealed under housing and roads, the drylands described in {{ref:soil-env-077}}, and the practices that prevent damage, reverse it and rebuild degraded soil.
openers.soil-health-and-protection: Soil can be worn out, and it can be rebuilt. Poor management degrades it in four general ways: erosion, and physical, chemical and biological decline. To know how far a soil has slipped, scientists judge its health and quality with physical, chemical and biological measurements, sometimes against native land nearby. Repair comes through regenerative farming methods, many drawn from conservation agriculture. It also comes through the policies and decisions that nation states and local governments apply to soil.
openers.contamination-and-remediation: A field can look healthy and still hold lead, pesticides or spilled fuel. Soil contamination is the presence of human-made chemicals or other changes to the natural soil, a form of land degradation, and it arrives through mining, heavy industry, spills, leaking underground tanks, farm chemicals and waste disposal. Some contaminants, such as lead, mercury, zinc and cadmium, resist breakdown, while too much nitrogen and phosphorus washing off the land pollutes lakes and rivers. People meet these contaminants by swallowing soil or dust, eating food grown in it, touching it and breathing its vapors, and the damage to ecosystems starts with the soil's own chemistry and organisms. This chapter follows those harms, then the cleanup, from digging and walling in to bacteria, fungi and plants put to work.
openers.urban-and-human-made-soils: Cities remake their soil as thoroughly as their streets. In towns, soil is often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity. Mining and large excavations leave piles of waste earth, while building sites dig out topsoil and keep it for later use. Some soils are even defined by the objects people made and left in them. This chapter follows that human-made ground and the ways people work with it, from designed planted sites that let runoff from roofs and roads soak in and be cleaned to the care of city trees.
openers.soils-and-human-health: Soil feeds people, and sometimes it poisons, infects or starves them. In Toyama Prefecture, Japan, a mass cadmium poisoning from about 1912 was named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused. Elsewhere people inhale fungal spores, catch bacteria and roundworms from contaminated ground, or sicken because their food grows without enough iodine or selenium. Some animals and people even eat earth on purpose. This chapter follows those links between the ground and health, and ends with an approach that tries to balance the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together.
openers.fert: A plant cannot live on sunlight and water alone. It needs nutrients, the substances an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce, and sixteen chemical elements are usually listed as essential for its growth and reproduction. This part of the course follows how soil supplies them, and what happens when it stops. History offers hard lessons, from the burned and overgrazed fields of colonial New England to the worn-out land of Southern slave plantations. It also shows how laboratory analysis and careful planning try to match each field's supply to each crop's needs.
openers.nutrients-and-plant-nutrition: Growth is set not by the total resources a plant has but by the scarcest one. That simple principle runs through this chapter. It begins with the substances an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce, and with the sixteen elements a plant must have to complete its life cycle. It then asks what lets a soil sustain steady, high-quality yields, how that ability declines when what a soil gives is never replaced, and how a laboratory analysis of a soil sample can show what a field lacks.
openers.nutrient-cycles: Nitrogen gas fills the air, yet most living things cannot touch it. This chapter follows elements on the move, as they pass between living things, the atmosphere, water and Earth's crust, with the soil in the middle. Nitrogen tells the richest story: an abundant but unreactive gas turned into ammonia and nitrate, released from dead organisms as ammonium by bacteria and fungi, then oxidized to nitrate by way of nitrite. Phosphorus, sulfur and calcium travel their own routes through rocks, water and life. Along the way, microbes and plants can lock nutrients into their own bodies, out of reach of crops, before recycling feeds them back into new growth.
openers.fertilizers-manures-and-amendments: Farmers have fed their fields for thousands of years, first with animal dung and minerals and, from the 19th century, with the products of a synthetic fertilizer industry. This chapter is about what people add to soil, and why. Most additions supply nutrients, chiefly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and much of the nitrogen comes from ammonia made by the Haber–Bosch process. Other additions work on the soil itself: decomposed organic waste, a protective layer over the surface, charcoal made for burial, and materials that loosen and improve the ground. The chapter also weighs the harm fertilizers do to water, soil, air and ecosystems, and how matching their timing and amount to a crop's needs can limit it.
openers.soil-geography: Soils are not scattered at random across the land. Soil geography, a branch of physical geography, maps how they are distributed across the terrain and asks why. This short chapter tests that question in three places. In the humid tropics, most soils are strongly leached and poor in nutrients, though some are fertile. In Australia, many soils are extremely ancient and naturally short of phosphorus, while a third approach compares soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials.
openers.form: Beneath every field lies solid rock, and over it lies a blanket of loose material that soil grows in. That blanket can be rock rotted in place by long chemical weathering, or debris moved by water, wind, ice or gravity. Rivers spread clay, silt, sand and gravel across floodplains. Wind piles up silt-sized dust, and rainwash and creep gather loose sediment at the foot of hillslopes. This part of the course follows soil from those raw materials to the layered bodies they become, and it begins with the rock and loose cover themselves.
openers.weathering-and-parent-material: Soil does not start from nothing. It forms in an underlying geological material, generally bedrock or a loose surface deposit, that it inherits much from. Some of that material is rock weathered in place, so deeply that geologists call it rotten rock. Much more was carried in and is classified by how it last traveled. This chapter sorts those materials, from silt-sized wind-blown dust to the loose cover of asteroids and the icy ground of Saturn's moon Titan.
openers.horizons-and-the-soil-profile: Dig a pit almost anywhere and its walls show bands, each one a layer with its own story. The upper layer is richest in organic matter and microorganisms, and most of the soil's biological activity happens there. Beneath it lies a mix of sand, silt and clay with far less organic matter. Water percolating down strips material from the upper layers and deposits it lower down, so each band gains or loses its own ingredients. This chapter names those bands, from a surface layer of plant residues to the barely altered material above bedrock, and shows how soil scientists describe them and use them to classify soils.
openers.how-soils-form: Every soil has a history, written by place, environment and time. This chapter follows that history, the development called soil formation. Five intertwined influences steer it: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time. Vasily Dokuchaev in 1898 and Hans Jenny in 1941 each tried to capture them in a single equation. Along the way come water carrying dissolved material down through the profile, chains of different soils strung down a single slope, and ancient soils that formed in the past under conditions long gone.
openers.found: Most of what people grow and build rests on soil, a natural mixture of minerals, the remains of living things, gases, water and organisms. All of it together forms the pedosphere, the outermost layer of Earth's crust, where soil forms and wears away. Soil science studies this layer as a natural resource, from how it forms to how it should be used and managed. A turning point came when Dokuchaev argued that soil is a natural body with its own history, distinct from the solid rock beneath it. This first part lays the foundations on which the rest of the course builds.
openers.what-soil-is: Soil is a mixture of solid particles and pore space, with water and air sharing the pores. This chapter starts from that mixture and widens out to the layer of Earth's crust that soil makes up. It meets the science that studies soil and the two branches that grew from it, one asking how soils form and the other how they affect living things. It then turns to the many ways people rely on soil, and to how anyone can judge whether a soil is doing its jobs well.
openers.what-soil-is-made-of: Soil is built from two very different materials. One is mineral: naturally occurring solids, each with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. Weathering supplies them, breaking rock apart by force or remaking it through chemistry, as when iron in a mineral changes from Fe2+ to Fe3+. The other is soil organic matter: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, soil microbes and the substances they make. Climate decides how much of it builds up, and together it forms a large carbon store that can take carbon in or give it back.
openers.reading-a-soil: Dig a pit, and a soil starts to explain itself. Its layers lie roughly parallel to the surface, each different from the ones above and below, and the main ones carry capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R. Its color is often the first thing anyone notices. Beneath the visible lies a chemical reading, how acidic or alkaline the soil is, set first by the minerals it formed from and the weathering they have undergone. That one measure governs which nutrients plants can reach, whether dissolved aluminum harms their roots, and which plants and soil organisms thrive there.
openers.paleopedology-and-soil-dating: A grain of quartz can record the last time it saw daylight. Buried soils, sediments and rocks hold many such clocks, and this chapter is about reading them. Some count the carbon-14 left in organic matter. Others read the radiation dose stored in mineral grains, or the rare isotopes cosmic rays make in rock at the surface. Layers of volcanic ash, microscopic pollen and spores, and carbon isotope ratios add markers of their own, and every clock has its quirks, from shifting atmospheric carbon-14 to young humic acid that contaminates old soil and peat.
openers.forensic-and-archaeological-soil-science: Soil remembers what people did on it and what they buried in it. A ploughed-out ditch leaves a change of color, an old rubbish dump keeps its bones and shells, and medieval ploughing left ridges and troughs across Europe's fields. This chapter reads soil as a record: how remains decay or are preserved, how layers stack with the oldest at the bottom, and how DNA lingers in soil and sediment. The same reading serves the law, where a soil sample or a few pollen grains can link a person to a place.
openers.hist: Soil science is a young science with a long backstory. Its ideas first grew from the chemistry of {{ref:soil-hist-004}}, tested in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots. From 1870 a Russian school led by {{ref:soil-hist-001}} recast soils as independent natural bodies, and {{ref:soil-hist-009}} adapted that idea for America. Meanwhile Charles Darwin, in his 1881 book, showed earthworms forming and moving the soil. This part follows those people and their classifications, and the societies, museums and congresses that carry the work today, from a soil museum in Wageningen to a United Nations year for soils in 2015.
openers.history-of-soil-science: How did soil become a subject of its own? Its first concepts were built on the chemistry of {{ref:soil-hist-004}} and refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots. From 1870 the Russian school treated soils as independent natural bodies, and an American adaptation put the individual soil profile first. Later the qualitative classifications of {{ref:soil-hist-009}} and of 1938 gave way to a quantitative system built under {{ref:soil-hist-024}}. Along the way, Darwin's earthworms, museums, congresses, societies and a whole year for soils each left their mark.
openers.founders-and-pioneers: Soil science has founders, and many of them came to it from somewhere else. A German lawyer and land tax assessor born in 1794 is considered one of them; a Russian geologist and geographer born in 1846 is credited with laying the field's foundations. Chemists and microbiologists followed: a German who helped found organic chemistry, a Dutch botanist who helped found virology, a Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist who pioneered the cycle-of-life concept. Americans carried the work into the 20th century, from the man who ran the national soil survey from 1913 until his death to a leading soil physicist and the scientist who first built the USDA's Soil Taxonomy. This chapter meets them one by one, starting with {{ref:soil-hist-001}}.
openers.societies-institutes-and-journals: Science needs places to meet, publish and keep records, and soil science built many. Rothamsted, founded in 1843 at Harpenden, England, is one of the oldest agricultural research institutions in the world. In 1924 soil scientists founded an international society, and in 1936 Americans formed the Soil Science Society of America. Survey agencies, data centers and specialist societies followed, along with peer-reviewed journals in several languages. This chapter tours the institutions that keep the field running.
openers.soils-beyond-earth: The Moon and Mars have ground underfoot too, and this last chapter asks what it is. The Moon wears a blanket of loose material, made and constantly altered by impacts and space radiation. Mars has a fine layer of loose, varied deposits, laced with chlorine-bearing salts toxic enough to matter. Space missions, beginning with Apollo, have carried lunar rock and regolith back to Earth, and Earth materials are made to stand in for the rest. Beneath it all runs an unsettled question: whether Earth's definition of soil, with its organic content, fits other worlds at all.
openers.meth: A soil sample that reaches the laboratory can be heated, burned, sprayed into a plasma and colored until it gives up its composition. Strong heating at a set temperature drives off volatile components, and the weight lost measures them. In an argon plasma, atoms and ions emit light that identifies each element, while a related instrument counts the ions themselves to catch metals at very low concentrations. Simpler tests work by color and voltage: phosphate forms a blue complex whose depth tracks its concentration, and a membrane sensor turns the activity of one ion into an electrical potential. This part begins with those laboratory methods.
openers.soil-analysis-and-laboratory-methods: Most soil analysis works on the part of a soil made of particles 2 mm across or smaller. Some tests first pull something out of it: an ammonium acetate solution displaces exchangeable cations, for measuring cation-exchange capacity and available potassium. Others separate what has been extracted, sorting ions by their affinity for an ion exchanger or vaporized compounds as gases. Then come the measurements, from wet chemistry that tracks organic nitrogen and ammonium to instruments that read the light atoms absorb or emit.
openers.soil-micromorphology: Many soil features are too small to see with the unaided eye. Soil micromorphology describes, measures and interprets them. Its central tool is a slice of soil ground to about 30 μm and mounted on glass for a polarizing microscope. In such slices the pelleted fabric left by ants, worms and termites shows up, along with the changes natural processes make to a mineral's composition and crystal structure.
openers.pedometrics-and-digital-soil-mapping: A quantity measured across a field takes different values from place to place, and a soil map has to capture that. Radar pulses and electrodes image what lies below the surface. Images taken in a few wavelength bands, or in many continuous ones, read soil and vegetation from above. A branch of statistics built for spatial data then describes how much pairs of observations differ with the distance between them. From that, unsampled points are predicted as weighted averages of their neighbors, and terrain and remote-sensing layers can sharpen the predictions further.
openers.phys: A soil can be measured like any other material: by its grains, its pores and the way it holds together. Those measurable physical traits rank, in falling order of importance for crops, as texture, structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. This part of the course starts at the top of that list. Texture rests on one humble measurement, the diameter of individual grains, and on the classes built from it.
openers.soil-texture-and-structure: A soil's mineral grains span a vast range of sizes, from rock fragments coarser than sand down to clay. Sorting them into set size ranges began with Albert Atterberg in 1905, from his studies in southern Sweden. Today the USDA groups soils into twelve named classes by their percentages of sand, silt and clay. A class can be read off a triangular chart or judged in the field by working a moist sample by hand. Even the word clay turns out to carry two meanings, one about size and one about minerals.
openers.solute-transport-in-soil: Whatever dissolves in soil water can travel, and groundwater carries it wherever it flows. Some of the trip is simple carrying by the moving fluid. Some is spreading, as molecules drift from high to low concentration and water threads unevenly around the grains. Soil can also hold a substance back by adsorbing it, or tiny colloidal particles can carry it farther than it would go alone. This chapter follows those processes from first principles to the equation that combines them. It ends with the tools used to watch and predict them: colored dyes added as tracers and computer models of unsaturated soil.
openers.density-pores-and-compaction: A handful of soil is partly nothing at all: empty spaces that hold its water and air. This chapter measures that emptiness and asks what happens when weight squeezes it out. Soil physics studies the solid, liquid and gas phases of soil, and soil mechanics describes how a mix of particles, water and air behaves under load. Porosity, bulk density and the ratio of voids to solids track how tightly the solid particles pack. When machines or loads press them closer, air and water are driven out, and the balance between the push of water in the pores and the stress on the grains decides whether the ground stands firm or flows.
openers.water-in-soil: Water decides much of what a soil can do, and this chapter follows it from the surface downward. It begins with infiltration, the process by which water on the ground enters the soil, and with the quantity a soil then holds. Some soils take in water and hold much of it against the pull of gravity; others let it pass quickly through their pores and cracks. One equation, first written for beds of sand, describes how easily water flows through them; another measure describes how hard the soil pulls on the water that stays. Where there is too much, drainage removes it, and deeper down lies a surface below which the ground is fully saturated.
openers.soil-temperature-and-air: Between the grains of every soil lies a second atmosphere. Soil gas fills the air spaces between particles, much like the air above but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapor, and it trades with the open air mainly as molecules drift through the pores from higher to lower concentration. Soil also has a temperature, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses, and heat moves through it by radiation, conduction and convection. This chapter follows both, from the air that roots breathe to the depth where groundwater freezes. It ends in the cold: ice that swells the ground upward, needle-shaped columns that rise on frosty nights, and ground that stays below 0 °C for two years or more.
openers.water: Water never stays put. It circles endlessly between sky, land and sea, changing form as it goes, and on its way across the land it reshapes the ground. This part of the course follows that water as it flows over the surface, gathers into channels and carries soil away with it. It also looks at ground that sinks beneath people's feet, and at the ponds, channels and plantings people build to keep runoff from doing harm.
openers.erosion-and-sediment: Rain that cannot soak in has to go somewhere. Sometimes it falls faster than the ground can take it; sometimes the soil is already full and every hollow brimming. Either way it spreads across the surface as overland flow, and in towns, roofs and roads speed it on. This chapter starts with that flow and the ways land development changes it. It then turns to the tools people use to tame it, from ponds that hold a storm back to planted channels that clean the water, and even a humble bale of cereal straw.
openers.soils-in-the-landscape: Soil changes character where water lingers. Ground flooded or saturated, permanently or for a season, runs short of oxygen, and its soils turn anaerobic. Some of these wetlands are grassy, some forested, and some are washed by the tides. Others pile dead plants into layers of peat, fed by rain alone or by streams and springs, and in the cold north those peat-forming lands stretch across Arctic and boreal climates. This chapter follows soil through such places, from river land that floods at high water to ground enclosed by dikes, and uses a science of landscape patterns to see how they fit together.

reviews.farming-systems-and-growing-media: Irrigation lifts yields, but every method, from basins and furrows to sprinklers and drip lines, has to balance water against loss. Too much water leaches nitrate and phosphorus or raises salty water tables, and too little lets salts build up at the surface, which is why salt tolerance and efficiency matter so much. Crop choices pull the same way: rotations, fallows, intercropping and mixed farming spread crops through time and space, countering the depleted nutrients and adapted pests of monocropping. Organic and regenerative farming lean on compost, manure and legumes, though how much they help soil and climate is still disputed. Even the media and treatments, from coir and potting mixes to steaming and solarization, serve the field's long aim of keeping soils productive.
reviews.tillage-and-cultivation: Tillage loosens and aerates the topsoil and kills weeds, but it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil, sometimes into a plough pan. Its tools grew from the hoe and the ard to the heavy mouldboard plough, which turned the soil over, reshaped fields into long strips and made farming communal. In 1731 Jethro Tull argued that land could never be tilled too much, but scientific observation, and the Dust Bowl, showed the cost. The answer has been to till less and leave more crop residue on the surface: residue cover defines intensive, reduced and conservation tillage, and no-till never tills at all. Each step trades one problem for another, from slower spring warming to more herbicide, and researchers still disagree over how much carbon no-till really stores.
reviews.soil-conservation: Soil conservation fights two losses, topsoil to erosion and fertility to overuse, and every tool in this chapter targets one or both. Some work by covering the ground: cover crops shield the surface and open pores, green manures and catch crops hold nitrogen, and conservation agriculture keeps mulch on fields that are barely disturbed. Others reshape the land or tame the wind, from ancient terraces and lynchets to contour trenches, check dams, crop strips and the 220 million trees of the Great Plains Shelterbelt. Governments joined in after the Dust Bowl, paying farmers to conserve soil, while engineers strengthened soils for roads with binders, geocells and dust-binding salts. The same choices reach the climate, since soil management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon or store carbon in the soil.
reviews.soil-survey-and-land-evaluation: A soil survey classifies an area's soils and records where they lie, and its usual product is a soil map. Interpretation turns that map into predictions of what land can do, while ratings such as prime farmland, the German soil value and the Storie index rank it for crops, taxes or valuation. Paper county books have given way to databases such as SSURGO and the European Soil Database, held within soil information systems. Digital soil mapping, pedometrics and pedometric mapping now predict soil from data, using Matheron's model and the scorpan relationships. Their maps are reproducible and can carry an estimate of their own uncertainty, which hand-drawn boundaries are hard to test for.
reviews.life-in-the-soil: Soil is home to circa 59% of the world's biodiversity, from viruses and bacteria to moles and gophers. Its members form a food web in which bacteria and fungi break dead material into simple nutrients, and the bacterial and fungal channels carry most of the flow. Their combined work leaves the soil as soil respiration, about half from roots, and temperature, moisture and nitrogen speed or slow it. Earthworms and other ecosystem engineers remake the soil itself, leaving casts and burrow linings richer in nutrients than the soil around them. Most soil microbes have never been cultured, so DNA read straight from the soil is only now revealing how this living world is organized.
reviews.roots-and-the-rhizosphere: A root anchors its plant and takes in water and nutrients, whether as a single taproot or a fibrous mat, and most roots stay near the surface where nutrients and air are richest. Roots rarely work alone. They release perhaps 20–40% of their fixed carbon as sugars and organic acids, feeding a rhizosphere where up to 10 billion bacterial cells crowd each gram and cycle the nutrients plants need. Mycorrhizal fungi trade water, phosphorus and nitrogen for that carbon, while rhizobia in legume nodules turn nitrogen gas into ammonia. Signals such as flavonoids and strigolactones decide who gets in, and high nutrient levels can turn the same partners from mutualists into parasites.
reviews.organic-matter-humus-and-decomposition: This chapter followed fallen litter from the forest floor to the oldest humus. Fungi and bacteria digest it outside their bodies, while earthworms, millipedes and other animals fragment and churn it. Most of it is mineralized into carbon dioxide and nutrients such as ammonium and phosphate that roots take up again. Part is humified instead, into humus that holds water and nutrients and may last for centuries. Litter quality and soil animals decide which humus form a site develops, from earthworm-mixed mull through moder to mor, where fungi slowly work through acid litter that piles up.
reviews.soil-biochemistry: Soil microbes feed by secreting exoenzymes, and fungi supply most of them, taking apart cellulose first and lignin later with lignin and manganese peroxidases. Enzymes such as β-glucosidase and acid phosphatase release glucose and phosphate, and assays and the Michaelis–Menten model measure how fast they work, with Q10 adding temperature. The microbes doing this work form a small but active biomass with a C:N:P ratio of 60:7:1, and ecological stoichiometry explains why such ratios matter. How efficiently they use carbon, and how the microbial carbon pump turns it into stable forms, decides how much carbon the soil keeps. Amplicons, metabarcoding and stable-isotope probing reveal who these microbes are, down to the antibiotic resistance genes of the resistome.
reviews.clay-minerals-and-colloids: Clay minerals form wherever water weathers rock, and their two kinds of sheet decide much of what follows. Stacked 1:1, as in kaolinite, the layers carry almost no charge and hold few cations. Stacked 2:1, they gain a negative charge from isomorphous substitution, and the cations between the layers set their behavior: potassium locks illite shut, while magnesium and sodium let vermiculite and smectite swell. As weathering and leaching deepen, the dominant clays shift from montmorillonite through kaolinite to sesquioxide clays such as hematite, goethite and gibbsite. Together with organic colloids, these clays hold ions on their charged surfaces and trade them with the soil water.
reviews.charge-and-nutrient-holding: A soil holds nutrients because its surfaces carry charge. Some of that charge is permanent, built into clay crystals by substitution, while variable charge on clay edges and organic matter grows as pH rises and vanishes at a surface's point of zero charge. Humic substances supply 50 to 90% of a soil's cation-exchange capacity and also grip metals by chelation, as do the chelators made by microbes and by fertilizer makers. Cation exchange lets the stored calcium, potassium and ammonium trade places with the soil water, and base saturation shows how much of that capacity holds nutrients rather than acid. Yet the humic substances at the center of the story remain contested, since they may be partly products of the alkaline extraction used to find them.
reviews.redox-and-soil-chemistry: Redox comes down to a trade: a reducing agent gives electrons, an oxidizing agent takes them, and each half of the trade has a voltage. Measured in soil as Eh, that tendency sorts reactions into gradients and a ladder, with oxygen at the top and methane-making at the bottom. When water fills the pores, microbes burn through oxygen, then nitrate, iron and sulfate, until a wetland or paddy field releases methane. The iron left behind, as a gray matrix or yellow-brown mottles, records those swings in the soil's own color. People turn the same chemistry to use, with biofilters that let microbes break down pollutants and strong oxidizers injected to destroy contaminants underground.
reviews.acidity-alkalinity-and-salinity: Acid, salt and sodium are three different troubles, and this chapter has followed each from cause to cure. Acidification comes from acid rain, ammonium fertilizers, roots and oxidizing pyrite, and lime is the main remedy. Salinity rises wherever evaporation leaves dissolved salts behind, whether irrigation water brings them or cleared land lets groundwater lift them, and leaching water, drains and deep roots carry them back out. Sodium works differently: it disperses clay and blocks infiltration, so indices such as SAR and ESP track it, and gypsum's calcium undoes it. In dry climates the same chemistry builds rock, as calcium carbonate and gypsum harden into caliche and gypcrust.
reviews.soil-mineralogy: A mineral's birth sets how long it lasts in soil. Bowen's reaction series orders silicates as they crystallize from magma, and the Goldich series turns that order into a weathering ranking, from fast apatite to enduring quartz. Fragile materials such as volcanic glass and glauconite break down into new minerals, while jarosite and schwertmannite record iron sulfides oxidizing in acid settings. Because most plant nutrients come from mineral breakdown, identifying minerals matters. Diffraction, X-ray fluorescence, the electron probe, infrared spectra, selective extractions and magnetism each read a different trait.
reviews.soil-solution-chemistry-and-sorption: Ionic strength weighs a solution's ions by their charge, and the activity coefficient corrects for how those ions crowd one another. Debye–Hückel theory explains the gap with clouds of opposite charge and links the two through a square-root law. At mineral surfaces, ions in inner sphere complexes bind directly, while Langmuir's model fills identical sites one molecule each and the Freundlich equation fits uneven surfaces whose strong sites fill first. Partition coefficients and coprecipitation trace other routes out of solution, into a second liquid or a growing solid. X-ray absorption fine structure shows how adsorbed atoms sit, and speciation calculations and geochemical models join it all, solving for every species and mineral at once.
reviews.classification-systems: Every system in this chapter answers one question differently: which traits should decide a soil's name? Engineering schemes sort soils by behavior and strength, natural systems by properties and genesis, and U.S. soil mapping runs both side by side. The 1938 U.S. system keyed soils to climate, vegetation and local factors; its replacement, USDA soil taxonomy, uses measurable properties across six levels, down to more than 14,000 series. Canada, Australia, Poland and France built national systems with orders that fit their own land, from Cryosolic soils over about 40% of Canada to Australia's acid Kurosols. Above them all, the FAO legend gave way in 1998 to the WRB, whose 32 Reference Soil Groups and their qualifiers let a soil carry the same name everywhere.
reviews.usda-soil-orders: The twelve orders run from barely changed Entisols to deeply weathered Oxisols, and diagnostic horizons do much of the sorting. A mollic epipedon marks Mollisols, a spodic horizon Spodosols, and 35% base saturation divides fertile Alfisols from more leached Ultisols. Climate and parent material shape the rest: Aridisols where water is short, Gelisols over permafrost, Andisols on volcanic ash, Histosols wherever organic matter outpaces decay. Suborders refine each order by moisture, temperature and, in Vertisols, how long the cracks stay open. Most fossil soils fit the same orders, so the record traces land plants from early forest Alfisols to Mollisols that spread with Miocene grasslands.
reviews.world-reference-base-soil-groups: The soil groups of this chapter read like a record of the forces that make soil. Water sorts many of them: rising groundwater makes Gleysols, stagnant surface water makes Stagnosols and Planosols, and water washing clay downward builds the argic subsoils of Luvisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Retisols. Dry climates leave salts, lime, gypsum or silica behind, in Solonchaks, Calcisols, Gypsisols and Durisols. Dark, humus-rich topsoils mark Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems, though how the Chernozem's black layer formed is still debated, while Fluvisols, Leptosols, Regosols and Cambisols show soil formation barely begun. People leave their mark too, from the plaggen fields of north-west Europe to the landfills and mine spoil of Technosols.
reviews.other-soil-types: Peat runs through much of this chapter: partly decayed plants that pile up where waterlogging stalls decay, storing up to 550 Gt of carbon on just 3% of the land, then releasing it when drained, burned or thawed. Rewetting, by blocking drainage channels, lets damaged bogs begin to rebuild that store. Other soils here are named for their rock, from metal-laden serpentine soils and the sliding blue goo to rendzinas and terra rossa on limestone. People made some of them, from Amazonian terra preta, rich in charcoal that lasts thousands of years, to the dark earth of old towns and the fill that raised Kansai's airport island. Still others are defined by climate or water, from the brown earths of temperate Europe and the red soils that make up about 13% of Earth's soil to subaqueous soils beneath shallow estuaries.
reviews.soil-carbon-and-climate: Soils hold about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere, and about 60 GtC a year flows into them and back out again. Warming tilts that balance, because warmer soils respire and decompose faster, while tillage and land clearing have already stripped much soil organic carbon. The largest frozen store, northern permafrost, holds about twice the carbon of the atmosphere, and as the active layer deepens, gradual and abrupt thaw let microbes release it as carbon dioxide and methane. Not every feedback runs toward warming. Plants, mycorrhizal fungi, peatlands and slow rock weathering draw carbon down, and practices from carbon farming to wetland restoration and enhanced weathering aim to strengthen them.
reviews.degradation-and-desertification: Soil can slide backward, from a stable climax toward bare rock, and land degradation spreads that loss across a quarter or more of the world's land and billions of people. Most of the drivers are human, from tillage, overgrazing and monocultures to sealing and land consumption, and a warming climate makes them worse while it enlarges the drylands. In those drylands the end point is desertification, with its dust storms, hunger, poverty and migration, though how much people rather than climate drive it is still disputed. Grasslands show the same pattern, losing grass to overgrazing, burrowing mammals and encroaching shrubs. Against all this stand sustainable land management, tree belts, farmer-managed regeneration and the UNCCD's goal of land degradation neutrality, with results that are real but often contested.
reviews.soil-health-and-protection: Soil health proved to be a matter of perspective as well as measurement. Users weigh soil functions differently, so tests, indicators and native-land benchmarks all chase a moving target. The threats are clearer: erosion, compaction, pollution and fertilizer that suppresses soil microbes, which have cost soils an estimated 133 billion tonnes of carbon since farming began. Regeneration answers with less tillage, cover crops, amendments and living plants on unstable slopes, while drain fields show soil cleaning wastewater every day. Because soil forms over thousands of years and human change is fast, governance matters, from World Soil Day to India's soil health cards and Europe's unfinished soil law.
reviews.contamination-and-remediation: Soil contamination starts at mines, factories, spills, farm fields and waste dumps, and it ends in people's food, water and dust. Some pollutants never break down: heavy metals cannot be degraded, while persistent organic pollutants such as DDT and PFAS travel to the poles and concentrate up food chains. Other harm is diffuse, as nitrogen and phosphorus leaving fields drive eutrophication and dead zones far downstream. Cleanup ranges from digging soil out and walling it in to drawing off vapors, heating the ground or passing electric current through it. Bacteria, fungi and plants offer cheaper, gentler cleanup, but they are slow, rarely used at scale, and can only lock up or harvest the metals they cannot destroy.
reviews.urban-and-human-made-soils: Every soil in this chapter carries a human signature. Urban soil, stripped of topsoil, compacted and laden with lead, copper and nickel, limits roots and tree health, so urban forestry picks species that tolerate compacted soil and low soil volume. Rain gardens turn the same city surfaces to use, sending runoff through an engineered bioretention soil mix that filters out suspended solids, heavy metals and nutrients. Construction and mining move soil in bulk: stockpiles save topsoil for later restoration, while spoil tips can trap heat, erode, leach chemicals and, at Aberfan, collapse with deadly force. Artefacts record that history in the soil itself, and enough of them make a soil a Technosol.
reviews.soils-and-human-health: Soil reaches human health along several paths at once. It can poison, as cadmium did through the rice paddies of the Jinzū River, or starve, as iodine-poor and selenium-poor soils do from inland mountains to a belt across China. It harbors fungi, bacteria, roundworms and clay-bound prions, often stirred up by rain, drought, dust or bare feet. Yet animals and people also eat earth on purpose, and clay and soil microbes may protect the stomach or tune the immune system. Medical geology and One Health share one lesson: as Paracelsus put it, the dose makes the poison, and health depends on balance.
reviews.nutrients-and-plant-nutrition: Every thread in this chapter leads back to sixteen elements and the soil that holds them. A fertile soil supplies them in adequate amounts and proportions, and the scarcest one limits growth, a rule later refined to allow for interactions between nutrients. Mass flow, diffusion and root interception carry dissolved ions to roots, and each nutrient's mobility inside the plant decides where a shortage shows. When harvests remove more than is replaced, as in colonial New England and on Southern plantations, soils are depleted. Soil tests, tissue analysis and nutrient management plans aim to put the right source at the right rate, time and place, while losing as little as possible to air and water.
reviews.nutrient-cycles: Matter in this chapter went round while energy passed through once, and microbes drove nearly every turn. Nitrogen showed the full loop: lightning, diazotrophs and the Haber–Bosch process fix it, ammonification and nitrification turn dead matter into ammonium and then nitrate, and denitrification returns it to the air. Phosphorus, with almost no gas phase, creeps from weathered apatite into soils that bind it tightly, while sulfur, iron and calcium shift between oxidized and reduced or dissolved and solid forms. Immobilization showed that microbes can compete with crops for the same nitrogen, and enzymes and solubilizing bacteria showed how locked nutrients are freed. People now push these cycles hard: fertilizer and fuel burning have more than doubled the flow of usable nitrogen, and phosphate mining has risen 72-fold since 1900.
reviews.fertilizers-manures-and-amendments: This chapter followed what people add to soil, from crushed battlefield bones and marl pits to factory ammonia and acid-treated phosphate rock. Some materials feed plants directly, like urea, UAN and superphosphate; others, like compost, mulch, lime and biochar, change the soil itself, its pH, structure, water and carbon. Each gain carries a cost to manage: nitrogen lost to the air as ammonia, phosphate feeding algae in rivers and lakes, cadmium and uranium in phosphate rock, pathogens and drug residues in manure. Coatings, inhibitors, careful timing and the multiple barrier approach all aim to keep nutrients in the soil and hazards out of the food chain. And as the best phosphate ore declines, urine, struvite, biosolids and digestate offer a way to close the loop between what people waste and what crops need.
reviews.soil-geography: Soil geography explains where soils lie by the factors that formed them: topography, climate, soil life and minerals. The tropics show climate at work, as heat and heavy rain leach soils until their fertility rests almost wholly on organic matter. Australia shows the weight of time, with ancient soils so short of phosphorus that only specialists such as cluster-rooted plants thrive. Lithosequences hold climate steady and change only the rock, giving the clearest view of what parent material does. Phosphorus runs through the chapter: it cannot be replenished from the air, so intense leaching and weathering leave old soils short of it.
reviews.weathering-and-parent-material: Soil begins where bedrock gives way to regolith, the loose blanket that covers rock on Earth and on other worlds. Part of that blanket is rock weathered in place: saprolite keeps its bedrock's structure, residuum has lost it, and deep weathering builds such profiles over millions of years in stable, warm, humid lands. Most soils, though, grow in material that wind, water, ice or gravity carried in. Each carrier leaves a signature: well-sorted alluvium, poorly sorted colluvium, unsorted till, silty loess and fine lake clays. Whatever its origin, the parent material passes on much of a soil's structure and minerals, so shale gives clay-rich soils and sandstone gives sandy ones.
reviews.horizons-and-the-soil-profile: A soil profile reads from the top down as a stack of horizons, from the leaf litter of the O horizon to the hard rock of the R layer. Water drives much of the pattern: eluviation strips the E horizon, and illuviation fills the B horizon below, leaving cutans on the surfaces it passes. Where silica, carbonates or iron oxides cement the subsoil, or plows and traffic compact it, hardpans form that stop roots and water. Describers record each layer in horizon designations and suffixes, and classifiers check every horizon of a pedon against the criteria for diagnostic horizons. Above it all lies topsoil, which takes 500 to 1,000 years to build one inch (2.5 cm) and is now lost faster than it forms.
reviews.how-soils-form: Soil formation begins with weathering of parent material and answers to five intertwined factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Dokuchaev and then Jenny wrote those factors as equations, and slopes arrange their effects into catenas while chronosequences isolate time. Water moving down the profile does much of the building, by leaching dissolved material, washing clay down in lessivage, and stripping sesquioxides in podzolisation or leaving them behind in red laterites. Burrowing life pushes the other way, churning the biomantle, sinking stones into stonelayers and blurring the horizons that water builds. Soils formed long ago survive as paleosols, polygenetic records of past climates and atmospheres that later development can overprint.
reviews.what-soil-is: Soil is a three-state system of solids, water and gas, and about half of a typical soil is pore space. Since Dokuchaev it has been studied as a natural body with its own history, formed in the pedosphere where rock, air, water and life meet. Pedology reads that history, while edaphology asks what soil does for plants and people, from producing 98.8% of human food to filtering groundwater. Climate steers the outcome: forest soils leach into contrasting layers, dry soils pile up calcium, and tropical soils weather to rusty red. Soil health and soil quality measure how well a soil keeps doing its jobs, and even where soil ends is still debated.
reviews.what-soil-is-made-of: Soil's solid matter arrives from two directions. From below, rock formed hot and under pressure meets the cool, wet surface, and physical, chemical and biological weathering take it apart. Feldspars and other silicates turn into clay minerals and iron oxides, while tough quartz survives as sand and silt. From above, plant debris decays into soil organic matter, and climate decides how much of it builds up. The two meet on clay and oxide surfaces, which bind organic molecules for centuries.
reviews.reading-a-soil: This chapter read a soil in two ways. By eye, its horizons follow a shared code of capital letters, though Australia and the international WRB scheme spell it differently, and its colors are recorded on Munsell charts: red for oxidized iron, black for organic matter, gray for the waterlogging that drives gleying. By chemistry, pH acts as a master variable that controls nutrient availability, sets the danger from dissolved aluminum and decides whether calcifuges or calcicoles take hold. Rain, roots, fertilizers and parent minerals push pH up or down, while buffering capacity resists them and decides how much lime a correction takes. Soil life both answers to pH and changes it, from acid-excreting fungi to earthworms whose mucus buffers it.
reviews.paleopedology-and-soil-dating: Every clock in this chapter reads a signature locked inside the material itself. Carbon-14 dates organic matter back about 50,000 years, once calibrated against past atmospheric levels and cleaned of the younger humic acid that troubles soil and peat. Mineral grains count the radiation dose since sunlight or heat last emptied them, cosmogenic nuclides record how long rock and soil have lain exposed, and lead-210 and the bomb pulse time the last century. Volcanic ash layers, pollen diagrams and the δ13C of soil carbonates add markers and past climates. Together they reach back to the roots that first broke rock into soil between 428 and 359 million years ago.
reviews.forensic-and-archaeological-soil-science: Everything in this chapter rests on one idea: every contact leaves a trace. Buried walls, ditches and graves change the soil above them, showing up as soil marks, cropmarks, magnetic and electrical anomalies, or patches rich in phosphate. Layers stack with the oldest at the bottom, so contexts sealed between dated layers fix the order of a site's past, while middens, Celtic fields, ridge and furrow and raised fields record how people lived and farmed. The courts use the same evidence: soil color, particle size and pollen tie suspects to scenes, and the looser, darker soil of a grave guides the search for a body.
reviews.history-of-soil-science: Soil science began with two narrow views: a chemist's balance sheet of nutrients and a geologist's picture of weathered rock. The Russian school recast soils as natural bodies, an American adaptation put the profile first, and the quantitative Soil Taxonomy replaced word-picture classes in 1965. Darwin, from his 1837 paper to his 1881 book, showed that earthworms bury objects and remake the ground, an idea later named bioturbation. Park Grass, two soil museums, congresses and societies keep long records and bring scientists together. Even now the science revises itself, as the old textbook theory of soil organic matter comes under challenge.
reviews.founders-and-pioneers: Soil science grew from several roots at once. Fallou argued that soil was separate in nature from geology, and Dokuchaev saw it as a natural body shaped by climate, vegetation, parent material, relief and age; Glinka and Marbut then carried those ideas into English and into a national US classification, which Guy Smith later developed into Soil Taxonomy. Chemists such as Sprengel, Liebig, Boussingault and Lawes asked what plants take from soil, from the law of the minimum to superphosphate and the long argument over nitrogen. Microbiologists such as Winogradsky, Beijerinck, Hiltner and Waksman showed that much of soil's chemistry is the work of living things. Jenny, Richards, Bennett and Lal turned the field toward equations, measurement and the conservation and restoration of soil itself.
reviews.societies-institutes-and-journals: Soil science runs on institutions as well as ideas. Rothamsted's long-term field trials, begun in 1843, gave the field data, cation exchange and modern experimental design. American survey work grew from Whitney's first mapping in 1899 into the National Cooperative Soil Survey, led by the agency Bennett founded during the Dust Bowl. Worldwide, the IUSS links national societies from America to Poland, and ISRIC, which it helped create, keeps the world's soil data. Journals from Pochvovedenie to the Soil Science Society of America Journal, and committees like ICOMANTH, carry the results into classification and practice.
reviews.soils-beyond-earth: The Moon and Mars both wear regolith, but neither made it the way Earth makes soil. On the Moon, impacts and charged particles grind rock finer and weld it into agglutinates, while impact gardening stirs the result over tens of thousands of years. Mars adds wind-lifted dust and perchlorates, and rovers, simulants and returned lunar samples show what settlers would face, from dust in the lungs to lunarcrete and gardens grown in simulant. Paleosols on Mars and in Earth's Archean rocks raise astropedology's central question: were these soils ever alive? That work has fed back home, helping redefine soil in 2017 as loose material altered at or near a planetary surface, though sources still disagree on what soil means off Earth.
reviews.soil-analysis-and-laboratory-methods: The chapter's methods form a chain from sample to number. Laboratories work on the fine earth, displace exchangeable cations with ammonium acetate, and separate extracts by ion chromatography. Nitrogen comes from the Kjeldahl method's hot acid in an hour or more, or from Dumas combustion and gas chromatography in a few minutes. Metals are read from the light their atoms absorb or emit, or counted as ions by ICP-MS down to 1 part per quadrillion. Simpler tools still earn their place: a furnace and balance give organic content down a profile, a blue color gives phosphorus, and an electrode gives one ion's voltage.
reviews.soil-micromorphology: Under the microscope, a soil becomes a record of its own history. A thin section shows how its components relate to one another, features often invisible in a hand specimen. Ants, worms and termites leave pelleted biofabric, and a biomantle as originally defined must be at least 50% biofabric. The minerals record weathering, as feldspar turns turbid while quartz stays fresh and clear. Together these clues help identify paleosols, such as an Andisol paleosol marked by at least 60% recognizable pyroclastic fragments.
reviews.pedometrics-and-digital-soil-mapping: Mapping soil starts from a plain observation: samples far apart differ more than samples close together. The variogram measures that change, and kriging uses it to weight nearby samples when predicting unsampled points. Regression-kriging adds covariates, from terrain derived by geomorphometry to satellite images, while SoilGrids fits machine learning models to profiles and over 400 covariates to map the whole world. Ground-penetrating radar and resistivity image what lies beneath, and multispectral and hyperspectral sensors read the surface from above. Even so, more and better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.
reviews.solute-transport-in-soil: Every contaminant in groundwater is moved by the same few processes. Advection carries it along at the seepage velocity, while diffusion and dispersion spread it around that path without changing its average speed. Adsorption alone slows the plume, so less soluble substances can lag hundreds or thousands of times behind the water. Colloids work the other way, letting radionuclides and metals travel farther. The convection–diffusion equation joins these processes, and models such as Hydrus couple it to the Richards equation, while dye traces test the predictions in the field.
reviews.soil-texture-and-structure: Texture, the mix of sand, silt and clay, is fixed by the mineral particles, but structure is how those particles clump into peds and aggregates. Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind the crumbs, and their pattern of pores steers water, air and roots. Unlike texture, structure is dynamic: tillage, traffic, sodium and rapid wetting tear it down, while roots, fungi, earthworms, lime and gypsum rebuild it. Water also sets a fine-grained soil's behavior, and the Atterberg limits mark where it shifts from solid to plastic to liquid. The USDA groups textures into twelve classes, farmers judge tilth, and engineers reach for sieves, those limits and two-letter USCS symbols.
reviews.density-pores-and-compaction: Soil is part grain and part gap, and this chapter has measured both. Bulk density, particle density, porosity and void ratio describe how tightly the particles pack, and the pore size classes show which gaps hold water, air or microbes. Press on soil and its particles crowd closer: on farmland that is compaction, which slows water soaking in, starves roots of air and can take several decades to undo. In saturated soil the water first shares the load, so effective stress, total stress minus pore water pressure, governs strength, consolidation and settlement. When pore pressure climbs far enough, through upward seepage or earthquake shaking, effective stress falls to zero and solid ground turns to quicksand or liquefies.
reviews.water-in-soil: Water that enters a field leaves it as surface runoff, as drainage through the soil, or by evaporation and transpiration, and this chapter has followed each route. Infiltration lets water in only while there is room at the surface, hydraulic conductivity and Darcy's law set how fast it moves, and water potential sets the direction, always from higher to lower. What stays is held against gravity, more tightly by fine clay than by coarse sand, and field capacity and the permanent wilting point bracket the share plants can use. Below the roots, percolation and recharge carry water through the vadose zone to the water table, flow the Richards equation describes and solvers struggle with. Drainage design, irrigation scheduling and tools from the drying oven to SMAP turn that physics into decisions about when to drain and when to water.
reviews.soil-temperature-and-air: Water ties this chapter together, because it competes with air for the same pores and slows the soil's warming. Roots and microbes use up oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so soil air depends on diffusion, which slows some 10,000 times once water fills the pores. Wet soil also stores more heat and conducts it better than dry soil, while temperature swings at the surface fade and lag with depth. When freezing reaches below the surface, water drawn up through silty soils feeds ice lenses that heave roads, uproot seedlings and sort stones into patterned ground. Where the ground stays frozen as permafrost, thaw threatens to release carbon dioxide and methane from dead remains stored there for millennia.
reviews.erosion-and-sediment: Rain, runoff and wind loosen soil and carry it away, cutting sheets, rills and gullies on slopes and lifting dust from dry, bare ground, as the Dust Bowl showed on a ruinous scale. Gravity works alone in mass wasting, from slow creep to sudden landslides and debris flows, and a slope holds only while its shear strength exceeds the stress on it, a balance that water, roots and quick clay can tip. Whatever moves, grain size and flow speed decide how far it travels, and only part of it reaches rivers, where it smothers spawning beds and carries pesticides and fertilizers. Farmers and engineers answer with plant cover, erosion models such as the Universal Soil Loss Equation, silt fences, sediment basins and slope stabilization.
reviews.soils-in-the-landscape: Water ties this chapter together. Where saturation lasts, soils turn anaerobic and hydric, decay slows, and peat builds up in bogs and fens until peatlands hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon. Whether a wetland is fed by rain or by groundwater that has passed through rock sets its pH and nutrients, from acidic bogs to rich fens over limestone. Beside rivers, floods lay down fertile floodplain soils, while riparian strips and marshes trap sediment and strip nitrate from runoff. Drainage undoes this work: drained peat decomposes to CO2, polders sink, and wetlands have shrunk by as much as 50% since 1900.

soil-found-077.q: What are the two main historical branches of soil science, and how do they differ?
soil-found-077.a: Pedology studies soil in its natural setting, while edaphology studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it.

soil-found-097.q: In a typical soil, how is the volume shared between solids and pores?
soil-found-097.a: About half is solids (45% mineral and 5% organic matter) and half is pores, split equally between water and gas.

soil-found-091.q: Before Fallou and Dokuchaev, how was soil generally seen?
soil-found-091.a: As a product of chemical transformations of rocks: a dead substrate from which plants draw nutrients.

soil-found-096.q: Why do classifications not rest on soil genesis alone?
soil-found-096.a: Soil-forming processes are seldom observed and change over time, so genesis aids classification but cannot be its only basis.

soil-found-089.q: Why do tropical soils turn rusty red instead of showing podzolized layers?
soil-found-089.a: Fast decomposition leaves little fulvic acid to leach metals, so mobile magnesium, iron and aluminium precipitate as oxide minerals.

soil-found-098.q: What did van Helmont conclude from his willow experiment?
soil-found-098.a: Seeing the tree gain more weight than the soil lost, he concluded the willow was made of water, which was only partly correct.

soil-found-052.a: Weathering happens in place, while erosion carries rock and mineral material away by water, ice, wind, waves or gravity.

soil-found-063.q: True or false: rainwater can dissolve quartz.
soil-found-063.a: True: given enough time even quartz dissolves, going into solution as silicic acid.

soil-found-048.q: Which three elements make up most of the dry weight of plant debris, and how much of it?
soil-found-048.a: Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen, which together make up about 92% of the dry weight.

soil-found-056.q: How does pressure release make rock break into sheets?
soil-found-056.a: When erosion strips the rock above, the outer parts of deep-formed rock expand, opening fractures parallel to the surface along which sheets break away.

soil-found-037.q: Why does a quartz-rich rock count as mature?
soil-found-037.a: Quartz is the primary mineral that survives heavy weathering, so its abundance shows long weathering.

soil-found-051.q: Unlike soil structure, can farming change a soil's texture?
soil-found-051.a: No: texture is fixed by the soil's mineral component and does not change with farming.

soil-found-043.q: Why do igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed?
soil-found-043.a: Acid hydrolysis breaks the weakest cation–oxygen bonds first, following Bowen's reaction series.

soil-found-038.q: Why is a pH of 3.5 so much more acidic than a pH of 9.5?
soil-found-038.a: The pH scale is logarithmic, so a solution at pH 3.5 has one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5.

soil-found-024.q: Why does a clay- and humus-rich soil need more lime to change its pH?
soil-found-024.a: Its colloids buffer strongly, and lime must also neutralise the exchangeable acidity they hold, or the stored cations restore the original pH.

soil-found-016.q: What does litmus paper show when dipped in a soil–water mix?
soil-found-016.a: It turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if it is basic.

soil-found-022.q: Why can roots in strongly acidic soil suffer moisture stress even when the soil is fairly moist?
soil-found-022.a: Aluminium toxicity limits root growth so much that the plant cannot take up enough water.

soil-found-026.q: In the Munsell notation 10R 4/8, what do the three parts stand for?
soil-found-026.a: 10R is the hue, 4 the value and 8 the chroma, written as hue, then value/chroma.

soil-form-100.q: How does saprolite differ from saprock?
soil-form-100.a: Saprolite is weathered rock, oxidised in its upper part and partly weathered below, while saprock is fractured bedrock weathered only along its fractures.

soil-form-087.q: Which plant nutrients does rock not supply to soil?
soil-form-087.a: Nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon; rock is the source of every other plant nutrient.

soil-form-113.q: What is the soil of the Loess Plateau known for?
soil-form-113.a: It has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth.

soil-form-108.q: How does residuum differ from saprolite?
soil-form-108.a: Saprolite keeps its bedrock's structural features, while residuum has lost them, being transformed further and shrunk in volume.

soil-form-095.q: Why do soils formed in lake deposits tend to have low permeability?
soil-form-095.a: Lacustrine material has a high clay content.

soil-form-092.q: How do inflowing rivers sort sediment in a lake?
soil-form-092.a: They drop larger rocks and stones near the lake edge, while suspended sediment settles across the whole lake bed.

soil-form-021.q: How is the depth of topsoil measured, and what horizons does it correspond to?
soil-form-021.a: From the surface to the first densely packed layer, the subsoil; classification systems call it the O or A horizon.

soil-form-017.q: How do hardpans made by people differ in origin from natural ones?
soil-form-017.a: Natural pans form when deposits such as silica, iron oxides or calcium carbonate bind soil particles; man-made ones are compacted by repeated ploughing, heavy traffic or pollution.

soil-form-034.a: Illuviation moves material basically vertically within the soil, while alluviation is the horizontal transfer by running water.

soil-form-024.q: In a horizon label such as 2Bt2, what do the leading and trailing numbers mean?
soil-form-024.a: The prefix 2 marks a lithologic discontinuity, a change in parent material; the suffix 2 marks a subdivision of one horizon.

soil-form-014.q: What does a sequence like O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21 reveal about a soil's history?
soil-form-014.a: A fully formed profile was buried by sediments that later formed a new profile; the buried one starts at 2A2.

soil-form-028.q: How can a fragipan be told apart from a duripan?
soil-form-028.a: Air-dry fragipan fragments slake in water, unlike duripans and petrocalcic horizons.

soil-form-020.q: Why do micromorphologists use thin sections rather than a hand lens?
soil-form-020.a: A petrographic polarizing microscope shows far more in thin sections, including the relation of components to one another, often invisible in a hand specimen.

soil-form-030.q: What do the old terms pedocal and pedalfer distinguish?
soil-form-030.a: Marbut split soils into pedocals, with calcite building up as caliche in the B horizon, and pedalfers, rich in aluminium and iron.

soil-form-031.q: What does a cambic horizon become as a soil develops into an Alfisol?
soil-form-031.a: An argillic (Bt) horizon, which holds more clay than the cambic horizon.

soil-form-042.q: Which soil-forming factor is regarded as dominant?
soil-form-042.a: Climate: soils show the distinctive characteristics of the climate zones in which they form.

soil-form-044.q: How do animals that mix soil affect the horizons?
soil-form-044.a: Their mixing, sometimes called pedoturbation, tends to undo the processes that create distinct horizons.

soil-form-049.q: Why are crest soils on a catena drier than toeslope soils?
soil-form-049.a: Crests drain freely, while toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter.

soil-form-055.q: What key assumption does a chronosequence make, and why is it debated?
soil-form-055.a: It assumes nothing but age differs between sites, which often cannot be tested.

soil-form-061.q: In Erhart's theory, what happens to soils during rhexistasy?
soil-form-061.a: A drier climate thins vegetation, physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt.

soil-form-064.q: Why is the mean soil taxonomic distance a better measure of pedodiversity than conventional indices?
soil-form-064.a: Conventional indices ignore how similar soil classes are, while the mean soil taxonomic distance accounts for it.

soil-form-073.q: Why can laterite be cut from the ground yet serve as durable building stone?
soil-form-073.a: It is mined below the water table while wet and soft; as it dries, iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather.

soil-form-067.q: How is ferrallitisation the reverse of podsolisation?
