soil-form-067.a: In ferrallitisation silica is leached away and iron and aluminium sesquioxides remain; in podsolisation silica remains and iron and aluminium are removed.

soil-form-052.q: In biosorting, why do large stones end up at the base of the biomantle?
soil-form-052.a: Burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer.

soil-form-062.q: How does soil memory in soils differ from memory in layered sediments?
soil-form-062.a: Soils store records palimpsest-wise, with features overprinting each other, while sediments store them book-wise, in datable order.

soil-phys-014.q: Why do geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size?
soil-phys-014.a: Size does not fix mineral makeup, so engineers use plasticity measured with the Atterberg limits instead.

soil-phys-053.q: What makes loam the only distinctive class in the USDA texture triangle?
soil-phys-053.a: It is the only class not dominated by sand, silt or clay.

soil-phys-046.q: In the ribbon test, what does the length of the unbroken ribbon indicate?
soil-phys-046.a: How much clay the sample holds.

soil-phys-003.q: What is the difference between a ped and a clod?
soil-phys-003.a: A ped forms naturally as particles clump into aggregates, while a clod is a mass of soil made artificially, for example by cultivation.

soil-phys-019.q: Why can sieving alone not complete a soil's particle-size analysis?
soil-phys-019.a: Silt and clay below 60 μm need a second method, usually the hydrometer or pipette, on the material from the bottom sieve.

soil-phys-051.q: Why does laser diffraction usually size platy clay larger than sedimentation analysis does?
soil-phys-051.a: Its theories assume spherical particles, so a clay plate is sized by its cross-section.

soil-phys-021.q: In the USCS symbol CH, what do the two letters mean?
soil-phys-021.a: C names the main material, clay, and H means a high liquid limit.

soil-phys-017.q: How is cumulative percent passing found from cumulative percent retained?
soil-phys-017.a: It equals 100% minus the cumulative percent retained.

soil-phys-026.q: What do the liquidity and consistency indices always add up to?

soil-phys-024.q: Why does sodium make clay deflocculate?
soil-phys-024.a: Clay flocculates when the slightly positive edges of plates stick to the negative faces of others, and sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this.

soil-phys-039.q: Above what exchangeable sodium percentage does dispersion become highly likely?

soil-phys-011.q: Is every crusting soil also hardsetting?
soil-phys-011.a: No: a hardsetting horizon is thicker than a crust, often as thick as the cultivated layer or more.

soil-phys-057.q: When is a sand classed as well graded (SW) under the USCS?
soil-phys-057.a: When Cu ≥ 6 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (SP).

soil-phys-063.q: How do bulk density and porosity relate in a dry soil?
soil-phys-063.a: Inversely: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.

soil-phys-069.q: Why is compaction harder to manage than salinization or erosion?
soil-phys-069.a: It is mainly a hidden, sub-surface problem, so special methods are needed to locate it.

soil-phys-073.q: Why does higher pore water pressure make soil weaker?
soil-phys-073.a: Strength comes mainly from friction proportional to normal stress, and effective stress is total stress minus pore water pressure.

soil-phys-116.q: Why does a saturated clay settle so much more slowly than a sand under load?
soil-phys-116.a: Clay's extremely low hydraulic conductivity lets water drain only slowly, while coarse soils drain readily and settle at once.

soil-phys-109.q: Why does a wet sandcastle stand but collapse when submerged?
soil-phys-109.a: Water above the water table is at negative pressure, pulling grains together so friction holds them; submerged, that pull is lost.

soil-phys-094.q: What do relative densities of 100% and 0% mean?
soil-phys-094.a: 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil.

soil-phys-091.q: Why are fine-textured, wet soils most easily compacted?
soil-phys-091.a: Water films shield the contacts between particles, and clay-rich soils are more susceptible than coarse ones.

soil-phys-068.q: Why can clay be highly porous yet conduct water poorly?
soil-phys-068.a: It stores much water per volume but releases it slowly through narrow pore throats.

soil-phys-133.q: Why does pumping groundwater make the land surface sink?
soil-phys-133.a: Pumping changes the effective stress on compressible silt or clay layers, which consolidate, often irreversibly, and lose volume.

soil-phys-104.q: Why is the cohesion intercept c′ not treated as a fundamental soil property?
soil-phys-104.a: It often comes from forcing a straight line through data that actually curve, so its value depends on the stress range.

soil-phys-072.q: How are a soil core's cracks made visible for image analysis?
soil-phys-072.a: The core is impregnated with resin carrying a fluorescent dye, ground back step by step, and each face is lit with ultraviolet or blue light and photographed.

soil-phys-111.q: Which clay mineral has the highest compression index: kaolinite, illite or montmorillonite?
soil-phys-111.a: Montmorillonite, at 1.0 to 2.6, against 0.50 to 1.10 for illite and 0.19 to 0.28 for kaolinite.

soil-phys-129.q: True or false: clay has a higher specific yield than coarse sand.
soil-phys-129.a: False: clay averages about 2%, while coarse sand averages about 27%.

soil-water-180.q: What usually happens when rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in?
soil-water-180.a: Runoff usually follows, unless a physical barrier holds the water.

soil-water-214.q: Who is credited with inventing hollow-pipe drainage?
soil-water-214.a: Sir Hugh Dalrymple, who died in 1753.

soil-water-201.q: Darcy's law is often compared with which law from electricity, and why?
soil-water-201.a: Ohm's law: both relate flow linearly to a potential difference, with hydraulic conductivity playing the part of electrical conductivity.

soil-water-187.q: Why does a single-ring infiltrometer tend to give misleading readings?
soil-water-187.a: Driving the ring in deforms the soil, and with only one ring the water can spread sideways.

soil-water-178.q: At what suction is the permanent wilting point set by convention?
soil-water-178.a: At −1,500 kPa (−15 bar), as Lorenzo A. Richards proposed.

soil-water-231.q: How does paving over soil contribute to urban flooding?
soil-water-231.a: It seals the surface, ending rainwater infiltration and natural recharge.

soil-water-228.q: In the Nile Delta, which tolerates a shallower water table, wheat or cotton?
soil-water-228.a: Wheat, at 45 cm, is very tolerant; cotton is sensitive and needs 90 cm.

soil-water-217.q: How does Seattle's Street Edge Alternatives Project handle runoff?
soil-water-217.a: Roadside ditches, plantings and uncurbed sidewalks let runoff flow onto permeable ground.

soil-water-183.q: Why must the Green–Ampt equation for cumulative infiltration be solved iteratively?
soil-water-183.a: Because F(t) appears on both sides of the equation.

soil-water-237.q: What four reservoirs does SaltMod track?
soil-water-237.a: The surface, the root zone, a transition zone that holds any horizontal drains, and the aquifer.

soil-water-197.q: Why are field methods preferred over laboratory samples for measuring hydraulic conductivity?
soil-water-197.a: They give the most reliable values with the least disturbance, whereas disturbing laboratory samples undermines their results.

soil-water-199.q: Why does an unconfined aquifer's transmissivity change as the water table moves?
soil-water-199.a: Layers above the water table are unsaturated and add nothing, so the saturated thickness changes.

soil-water-192.q: According to Allen Hazen, how does permeability depend on particle size?
soil-water-192.a: It is proportional to the square of particle size, so coarse sand may be over a million times more permeable than clay.

soil-found-071.q: What is a percolation test's result used for?
soil-found-071.a: Its result, in minutes per inch, is matched to local health codes to size a leach field.

soil-found-105.a: During peak events such as heavy rain, at rates set by the hydraulic conductivity of the medium.

soil-water-220.q: Why might irrigated land need subsurface drainage?
soil-water-220.a: To leach salts brought in with irrigation water; models such as SaltMod help set the drainage requirement.

soil-water-209.q: How does the biomantle show soil hydrology at work?
soil-water-209.a: Loosened by bioturbation, it speeds percolation through biopores and carries throughflow downslope above dense subsoil horizons.

soil-water-188.q: Under what conditions does a double-ring infiltrometer's rate approximate saturated hydraulic conductivity?
soil-water-188.a: When flow is steady and one-dimensional with a unit gradient below.

soil-water-226.q: What advantages do capacitance and impedance sensors have over TDR, and what is their drawback?
soil-water-226.a: They are cheaper and respond faster, but usually need calibrating for each soil type.

soil-water-229.q: How did Veihmeyer and Hendrickson define readily available water?
soil-water-229.a: As the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point.

soil-water-236.q: How can soil moisture sensors act like a thermostat for irrigation?
soil-water-236.a: They trigger irrigation only when soil moisture drops below a set depletion threshold.

soil-water-179.q: Why can the capillary fringe stay saturated much higher in some soils than others?
soil-water-179.a: Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches.

soil-water-213.q: Why is groundwater recharge hard to quantify?
soil-water-213.a: Evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated to close the water balance.

soil-phys-137.q: Why does a pale soil stay cooler than a dark one?
soil-phys-137.a: Paler soils have a higher albedo, so they stay cooler than dark soils.

soil-phys-140.q: Why are soil moisture and soil thermal properties often measured together?
soil-phys-140.a: Thermal properties depend strongly on volumetric water content, so the two are closely linked.

soil-phys-159.q: What temperature conditions produce needle ice?
soil-phys-159.a: Soil above 0 °C under surface air below 0 °C, so water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column.

soil-phys-155.q: Why are clean sands and gravels not frost susceptible?
soil-phys-155.a: Their pores are too open for capillary flow.

soil-phys-139.q: Why does wet soil warm more slowly than dry soil?
soil-phys-139.a: Water raises its specific heat, and evaporating water takes up a great deal of energy.

soil-phys-138.q: On a day when the surface is warmer than the soil below, which way does heat flow?
soil-phys-138.a: Into the soil, since heat flows against the temperature gradient.

soil-chem-076.q: Who is considered the father of soil chemistry?
soil-chem-076.a: J. Thomas Way, who ran many experiments on ion exchange in soils in the early 1870s.

soil-chem-104.q: What chemical change in iron accompanies the formation of goethite?
soil-chem-104.a: Ferrous iron, iron(II), is oxidized to ferric iron, iron(III).

soil-chem-088.a: Tight hydrogen bonding between its layers keeps water from entering.

soil-chem-077.q: Why does it matter to know the reactions a chemical undergoes once it reaches soil?
soil-chem-077.a: They can raise or lower its toxicity, so knowing them helps predict a contaminant's fate and design cost-effective clean-up.

soil-chem-083.q: Why do clay minerals feature in theories of the origin of life?
soil-chem-083.a: Montmorillonite has been shown to catalyse joining nucleotides into RNA and forming lipid membranes.

soil-chem-098.q: In what kind of soil is imogolite found?
soil-chem-098.a: In soils formed from volcanic ash.

soil-chem-110.q: How does palygorskite's structure differ from that of layered smectites?
soil-chem-110.a: It has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains with long water channels inside, and it does not swell.

soil-chem-091.a: Its layers are not rigidly joined, so water and hydrated cations can enter the interlayer reversibly.

soil-chem-092.q: What happens to smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater?
soil-chem-092.a: Potassium replaces sodium and collapses the interlayer, turning it into non-swelling illite.

soil-chem-058.q: What three fractions make up humic substances, and how do they differ?
soil-chem-058.a: Humic acid, fulvic acid and humin, which differ in solubility.

soil-chem-073.q: How can leonardite help on metal-contaminated ground?
soil-chem-073.a: Added to the soil, especially with compost, it reduces the uptake of metals by plants.

soil-chem-072.q: Why do micronutrient fertilizers need a chelating agent such as EDTA?
soil-chem-072.a: Without one, the phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn the metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants.

soil-chem-066.q: Besides serving as a soil amendment, what geological role may humate deposits play?
soil-chem-066.a: They may play an important role in forming uranium ore bodies.

soil-chem-074.q: Which source gives the best potassium humate, and why?
soil-chem-074.a: Well-oxidised lignite (leonardite), since the less oxidised the coal, the less potassium humate it yields.

soil-chem-053.q: In what kind of soil can anion exchange capacity exceed cation exchange capacity?
soil-chem-053.a: In highly weathered soils such as ferralsols (oxisols).

soil-chem-050.q: Why does adding salt destabilise a clay suspension?
soil-chem-050.a: Higher electrolyte concentration thins the double layer around the particles, destabilising the colloid.

soil-chem-118.q: Which variable, alongside pH, is called a master variable of soil reactions?
soil-chem-118.a: Redox potential, expressed as Eh or pe.

soil-chem-116.q: In a redox reaction, is the reducing agent oxidized or reduced?
soil-chem-116.a: Oxidized: it passes electrons to the oxidant, which is reduced.

soil-chem-131.q: How are oxidants delivered underground where permeability is low?
soil-chem-131.a: By soil mixing or hydraulic fracturing, rather than only direct-push rods or injection wells.

soil-chem-129.q: In sediments, where do methanogens dominate over sulfate reducers?
soil-chem-129.a: In the lower layers, where sulfate has been depleted.

soil-chem-126.q: Where do organic pollutants break down fastest, and why?
soil-chem-126.a: At the oxic–anoxic interface, such as the groundwater capillary fringe, where electron donors and acceptors abound.

soil-chem-002.q: How does acid rain harm trees such as sugar maple through the soil?
soil-chem-002.a: Its hydrogen ions displace calcium and magnesium from clay, leaching these base cations and mobilizing aluminium.

soil-chem-039.q: What is the dominant mineral in a calcrete, and in a silcrete?
soil-chem-039.a: Calcium carbonate in calcrete, and silica in silcrete.

soil-chem-012.q: Above what ECe is a soil classed as saline?
soil-chem-012.a: Above 4; it is severely saline above 16.

soil-chem-007.q: What is the trade-off between deep liming and surface liming?
soil-chem-007.a: Deep liming works better but is costlier and harder.

soil-chem-038.q: Why is gypcrete found mostly in very dry regions?
soil-chem-038.a: Gypsum is moderately soluble and leaches away under higher rainfall.

soil-chem-015.q: In the sacrificial-strip method, why do the dry strips become salty?
soil-chem-015.a: Groundwater rises in them by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts behind.

soil-chem-026.q: Why can a soil that enters winter dry reduce recharge to groundwater?
soil-chem-026.a: The drier it starts, the more water it can store instead of leaking to groundwater.

soil-chem-034.q: What happened when potentially acid sulfate soils were aggressively drained?
soil-chem-034.a: The results were disastrous: barren land and clear, lifeless water.

soil-chem-020.q: How does fly ash from coal-fired boilers raise alkalinity downstream?
soil-chem-020.a: Its calcium oxide dissolves to slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, which runoff carries into rivers and irrigation systems.

soil-bio-001.q: What counts as soil life, or edaphon?
soil-bio-001.a: Every organism that spends a significant part of its life cycle in the soil profile or at the soil-litter interface.

soil-bio-078.q: Since analysers measure only total carbon, how is organic carbon found?
soil-bio-078.a: The inorganic carbon is subtracted, or first driven off with acid.

soil-bio-040.q: How do earthworms breathe, given that they have no special respiratory organs?

soil-bio-041.q: Which ecological group of earthworms builds deep vertical burrows and pulls leaves down into mineral soil?
soil-bio-041.a: Anecic worms, such as Lumbricus terrestris, which come up from permanent vertical burrows to gather leaves.

soil-bio-075.q: Which two groups of microbes produce geosmin?
soil-bio-075.a: Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, and actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces.

soil-bio-043.q: What can invading earthworms do to the banded profile of a podzol?
soil-bio-043.a: They can erase it, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.

soil-bio-070.q: Which bacterium is the most commonly applied microbial inoculant, and what does it do?
soil-bio-070.a: Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules.

soil-bio-009.q: Why do soil microbes respire less as salinity rises?
soil-bio-009.a: Because they have less available water.

soil-bio-085.q: If springtails do not decompose organic matter directly, how do they speed decomposition?
soil-bio-085.a: By fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbial communities.

soil-bio-016.q: How does a lysogenic phage differ from a lytic one?
soil-bio-016.a: A lytic phage kills its host to release virions; a lysogenic phage joins the host genome.

soil-bio-081.q: What largely sets the stature of tropical montane elfin forests?

soil-bio-036.q: What is the difference between basal and substrate-induced respiration?
soil-bio-036.a: Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars.

soil-bio-066.q: How far below the sea floor have mineral-forming microorganisms been found?

soil-bio-010.q: Why is the diversity of soil life hard to measure?
soil-bio-010.a: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed.

soil-bio-032.q: Why can isopods die if kept from eating their own faeces?
soil-bio-032.a: On nutrient-poor litter, the microbes colonising their pellets enrich the food.

soil-bio-027.q: Which energy channels carry the largest flow in soil flow webs?
soil-bio-027.a: The bacterial and fungal channels; the root-herbivory channel carries much less.

soil-bio-062.q: On the sandplains of southern Western Australia, what do most plants rely on to get phosphorus and sulfur?

soil-bio-193.q: True or false: nematodes decompose organic matter.
soil-bio-193.a: False: they feed on living material, regulating bacterial numbers and community composition.

soil-bio-088.q: Why do copiotrophs lose out to oligotrophs once nutrients run out?
soil-bio-088.a: They live a feast-and-famine life, using nutrients fast but surviving poorly when supplies run out.

soil-bio-068.q: Why is biocementation unsuited to soils rich in fines?
soil-bio-068.a: Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm.

soil-bio-080.q: How can extracellular polymeric substances lower a soil's hydraulic conductivity?
soil-bio-080.a: Together with microbial cells they block soil pores, a process called bioclogging.

soil-bio-139.q: Name a crop whose taproot serves as a storage organ.
soil-bio-139.a: Carrot, radish or turnip: many taproots are storage organs.

soil-bio-135.q: Why do most roots of most plants lie fairly close to the surface?
soil-bio-135.a: Nutrients are more available and aeration is better there.

soil-bio-198.q: What happens to a root's growth if its cap is removed?
soil-bio-198.a: It grows at random, because statoliths in the cap's statocytes drive gravitropism.

soil-bio-149.q: Compared with the rhizosphere, are microbes in bulk soil more varied or more abundant?
soil-bio-149.a: More varied; they are more abundant in the rhizosphere.

soil-bio-173.q: What does an ectomycorrhizal fungus supply its host in return for food?
soil-bio-173.a: Nitrogen: it gets about 15% of the host's food and supplies up to 86% of its nitrogen needs.

soil-bio-202.q: When can a non-systemic endophyte turn pathogenic?

soil-bio-168.q: How does tillage reduce a crop's phosphorus supply from arbuscular fungi?
soil-bio-168.a: It breaks up soil macrostructure and the hyphal network, leaving the network non-infective.

soil-bio-192.q: When do microbes switch on siderophore production?

soil-bio-145.q: Why can strigolactones released by roots backfire on a plant?
soil-bio-145.a: The parasitic plant Striga germinates when it detects them.

soil-bio-185.q: What is traded across the Hartig net?
soil-bio-185.a: Nutrients from the fungus's outer mycelium pass into the root's apoplast, and plant sugars pass back to feed the fungus.

soil-bio-169.q: For restoring desertified land, which worked best: a native fungal mixture, a single exotic species or no inoculum?
soil-bio-169.a: The mixture of native arbuscular fungi, which improved soil quality more over the long term.

soil-bio-200.q: Which enzyme lets Frankia turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia?

soil-bio-189.q: What can happen to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi under high nitrogen?

soil-bio-190.q: Which two symbioses use the common symbiosis signalling pathway?
soil-bio-190.a: Arbuscular mycorrhiza, its ancestral user, and the younger root-nodule symbiosis with rhizobia.

soil-bio-106.q: What separates the L, F and H litter layers?
soil-bio-106.a: How decomposed they are: L is little decomposed, F partly and H fully.

soil-bio-112.q: On land, where does detritus occur?
soil-bio-112.a: As plant litter and as organic matter mixed into the soil, such as the humic soil beneath fallen leaves.

soil-bio-094.q: How does humus help a soil withstand drought?
soil-bio-094.a: It can hold the equivalent of 80–90% of its weight in moisture.

soil-bio-095.q: Why do humus profiles change faster than whole soil profiles?
soil-bio-095.a: Soil organisms drive them, so they change over a few years, while pedons take decades to centuries.

soil-bio-110.q: Give one way a plant has adapted to life in the leaf litter layer.
soil-bio-110.a: Bluebell shoots pierce the layer in spring, and rhizomatous wood sorrel thrives there.

soil-bio-117.q: What is the difference between positive and negative priming?
soil-bio-117.a: Positive priming speeds mineralization; negative priming causes immobilization, leaving nitrogen unavailable.

soil-bio-121.q: What evidence suggests that glomalin-related soil protein comes from fungi?
soil-bio-121.a: It declines when arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are removed from soil or fungicides are applied.

soil-bio-128.q: Which dissolved organic molecules stay on soil minerals longer, hydrophobic or hydrophilic ones?

soil-bio-197.q: How does coarse woody debris on slopes help the soil?
soil-bio-197.a: It slows the downslope movement of organic matter and mineral soil, traps leaves, improves infiltration and slows evaporation.

soil-bio-122.q: Why may the soil-glue effect credited to glomalin not come from glomalin?
soil-bio-122.a: The heated citrate extraction also co-extracts humic substances.

soil-bio-092.q: What do supporters of the Soil Continuum Model say the evidence does not support?
soil-bio-092.a: The formation of large, persistent humic molecules in soils.

soil-class-016.q: What are the two levels of the World Reference Base?
soil-class-016.a: Reference Soil Groups, each refined by adding qualifiers.

soil-class-023.q: Which category does the Canadian system drop from the U.S.-style hierarchy?
soil-class-023.a: The suborder: its levels are order, great group, subgroup, family and series.

soil-class-012.q: In the 1938 U.S. system, how did intrazonal soils differ from zonal soils?
soil-class-012.a: Zonal soils reflected climate and vegetation; intrazonal soils reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them.

soil-class-007.q: At which level of USDA soil taxonomy do soil moisture regime names act as modifiers?

soil-class-038.q: Which soil is the state soil of North Carolina?
soil-class-038.a: The Cecil soil, which runs from Virginia to Alabama.

soil-class-019.q: In a WRB map unit, how much area must a dominant soil cover?

soil-class-034.q: In the Polish system, what three things describe each soil?
soil-class-034.a: Its type, from genesis and diagnostic horizons; its kind, the bedrock's geological origin; and its texture class.

soil-class-025.q: What property separates the great groups of Canada's Organic soils?
soil-class-025.a: Their degree of decomposition, measured by fibre content.

soil-class-031.q: What splits Canada's Luvisolic soils into two great groups?
soil-class-031.a: Soil temperature: Gray Brown Luvisols are at 8 °C or more, unlike Gray Luvisols.

soil-class-026.q: What tells the two great groups of Canada's Vertisolic order apart?
soil-class-026.a: The darkness of the A horizon, which separates Vertisols from Humic Vertisols.

soil-class-046.q: What has superseded the Handbook of Australian Soils?

soil-class-101.q: What base saturation must a Mollisol have?

soil-class-098.q: Why does organic matter build up to form a Histosol?
soil-class-098.a: It accumulates faster than it is destroyed, usually because poor drainage prevents aerobic decay.

soil-class-100.q: What horizon usually lies beneath the epipedon of an Inceptisol?

soil-class-095.q: Why are most skeletal soils so shallow on steep mountain slopes?
soil-class-095.a: Erosion strips material too fast for deep soil to form.

soil-class-107.q: Which Vertisol suborder is the most extensive worldwide?
soil-class-107.a: Usterts, whose cracks stay open at least 90 cumulative days a year.

soil-class-114.q: Why is a baseline needed to judge how far a soil has formed?
soil-class-114.a: Soils start much like their parent material and lose its features over time.

soil-class-138.q: What does the name podzol mean, and why?
soil-class-138.a: 'Under-ash' in Russian, after peasants who ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash.

soil-class-148.q: What mainly decides where arid areas lie?
soil-class-148.a: The general circulation of the atmosphere, which shifts with climate change.

soil-class-122.q: Why are Cambisols widespread in lands glaciated in the Pleistocene?
soil-class-122.a: There the parent material is young and soil formation is slow.

soil-class-118.q: Why can Alisols poison intolerant plants?
soil-class-118.a: At their low pH, aluminium and manganese dissolve.

soil-class-130.q: Where does the name Kastanozem come from?
soil-class-130.a: From the Russian and Latin words for chestnut, after the colour of the chestnut's husk.

soil-class-140.q: Why are most Retisols left under forest or pasture?
soil-class-140.a: Water drains through their clay-poor tongues while the dense clay parts are often too dry and hard to root, and earthworms avoid them.

soil-class-124.q: What does the high magnetic susceptibility of chernozem suggest about how it formed?
soil-class-124.a: Heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, so it points to fire, likely set by early humans.

soil-class-074.q: Why does draining a peatland release carbon dioxide?
soil-class-074.a: Drainage exposes organic carbon, built up underwater over thousands of years, to the air, where it decomposes to CO2.

soil-class-053.q: Why does terra preta resist leaching when the soils around it do not?
soil-class-053.a: Its charcoal stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients.

soil-class-078.q: Which kind of peat is the least decomposed: fibric, hemic or sapric?
soil-class-078.a: Fibric peat, which consists of intact fibre; sapric peat is the most decomposed.

soil-class-051.q: Why is terra rossa popular for growing wine?
soil-class-051.a: The karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage, surprisingly good for a clay-rich soil.

soil-class-081.q: How does tropical peat differ in origin from the temperate kind?
soil-class-081.a: It forms mostly from dead trees rather than the sphagnum typical of temperate peat.

soil-class-049.q: Why do brown podzolic soils lack the continuous E horizon of a true podzol?
soil-class-049.a: Soil creeping downslope keeps supplying iron and aluminium oxides, which build up as an orange-brown B horizon.

soil-class-067.a: A shallow depression of heavy clay floods after seasonal rains, and as the water evaporates a dried, fissured crust forms on the surface.

soil-class-052.q: Why does a latosol lose its fertility once the rainforest above it is felled?
soil-class-052.a: Its fertility lies in a thin humus layer fed by the forest; once that is no longer replaced, the nutrients leach away quickly.

soil-fert-181.a: An organism needs it for normal function but cannot make it itself, at all or in sufficient amounts.

soil-fert-169.q: Which plant nutrients do not come originally from the soil's mineral fraction?
soil-fert-169.a: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, supplied by carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen, supplied by nitrogen fixation.

soil-fert-153.q: What did Albert Howard call the basis of the public health system of the future?
soil-fert-153.a: Soil fertility; he wrote that all future studies of disease must begin with the soil.

soil-fert-150.q: Why do inorganic fertilizers act at once?
soil-fert-150.a: Plants take up nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in inorganic forms, which these fertilizers supply directly.

soil-fert-197.q: Why do legumes short of molybdenum fix less nitrogen?
soil-fert-197.a: Molybdenum is needed for nitrogenase, the enzyme of nitrogen fixation.

soil-fert-157.q: How do root hairs free cations held on soil particles?
soil-fert-157.a: They pump hydrogen ions into the soil, which displace cations held on negatively charged particles.

soil-fert-188.q: What does liming a garden soil to pH 6.5 do about lead?

soil-fert-159.q: Is iron part of the chlorophyll molecule?
soil-fert-159.a: No, but it is essential for making chlorophyll.

soil-fert-161.q: How can heavy phosphate applications cause zinc deficiency?

soil-fert-180.q: Why can cobalt matter to legumes though it seems inessential for most plants?
soil-fert-180.a: It is essential for nitrogen fixation by bacteria associated with legumes.

soil-fert-194.q: Why is nitrogen usually the hardest nutrient to manage?
soil-fert-194.a: Plant-available nitrogen changes quickly with soil water.

soil-fert-191.q: What does a soil nitrate test reading above the optimal range tell a corn grower?
soil-fert-191.a: Adding more nitrogen will not increase yield.

soil-fert-099.q: If nitrogen gas is the largest nitrogen store, why is usable nitrogen scarce in many ecosystems?
soil-fert-099.a: Little of the atmosphere's nitrogen gas is available to living things.

soil-fert-121.q: Why can ploughing in straw leave a crop short of nitrogen?
soil-fert-121.a: High-carbon straw stimulates microbes, which raise their nitrogen demand and out-compete the crop for ammonium and nitrate.

soil-fert-113.q: Which two groups of nitrifying bacteria work together, and what does each make?
soil-fert-113.a: Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria make nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn it into nitrate.

soil-fert-143.q: Why is iron a limiting nutrient in most regions despite being abundant in the crust?
soil-fert-143.a: Where oxygen is present iron takes the stable ferric form, which dissolves poorly.

soil-fert-123.q: How does a build-up of ammonium in farm soil make it more acid?
soil-fert-123.a: Nitrification of the ammonium releases hydrogen ions that acidify the soil.

soil-fert-141.q: What separates a reservoir from an exchange pool in an element cycle?
soil-fert-141.a: A reservoir, generally abiotic, holds a chemical for a long time, while an exchange pool, generally biotic, holds it only briefly.

soil-fert-115.q: Why might ammonia-oxidizing archaea contribute more to ammonia oxidation in soils than bacteria do?
soil-fert-115.a: They outnumber ammonia-oxidizing bacteria in soils.

soil-fert-148.q: What gives salt marshes and mud flats their rotten-egg smell?
soil-fert-148.a: Hydrogen sulfide expelled by sulfate-reducing microorganisms.

soil-fert-130.q: What can soil phosphatase activity indicate?
soil-fert-130.a: The soil's potential for phosphorus mineralization and its phosphorus availability.

soil-fert-126.q: Why does the final microbial step to nitrogen gas matter for reactive nitrogen?
soil-fert-126.a: The atmosphere is the ultimate sink for reactive nitrogen, and denitrification returns it there as nitrogen gas.

soil-fert-110.q: What is unusual about the comammox Nitrospira found in 2015?
soil-fert-110.a: A single organism carries out complete nitrification, where two groups were long thought necessary.

soil-fert-001.q: Why do legumes generally need no nitrogen fertilizer?

soil-fert-050.q: What lets biochar serve for carbon removal?
soil-fert-050.a: Its refractory stability lets it persist in soils for thousands of years.

soil-fert-004.q: How does a compound NPK fertilizer differ from an NPK blend?
soil-fert-004.a: A compound binds the three nutrients chemically, while a blend is a physical mixture of single-nutrient fertilizers.

soil-fert-023.q: What did the once-common term artificial manure mean?
soil-fert-023.a: What are now called artificial fertilizers.

soil-fert-055.q: Where does the acidity of most acid soils generally come from?
soil-fert-055.a: From aluminium hydrolysis, since most acid soils are saturated with aluminium rather than hydrogen ions.

soil-fert-029.a: Aerobic bacteria need oxygen above 5%, so turning keeps up oxygen and the right moisture.

soil-fert-071.q: Why is ammonium nitrate a greater security risk than urea?
soil-fert-071.a: It forms explosive mixtures with fuels, while urea is not an oxidizer.

soil-fert-048.q: Can biofertilizers replace synthetic fertilizers today?
soil-fert-048.a: Not yet; they can reduce the use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides but cannot yet replace them.

soil-fert-039.q: Why do nutrients in vermicompost wash away less readily?
soil-fert-039.a: The worm mucus coating the castings slows nutrient release and keeps nutrients from washing away.

soil-fert-084.q: Why does rain soon after spreading urea reduce nitrogen loss?
soil-fert-084.a: It moves urea into the soil, where the ammonia it forms can react with water to become ammonium instead of escaping.

soil-fert-032.q: What is the trade-off of cold composting in a small home heap?
soil-fert-032.a: It needs no turning, but it can take up to a year and parts may go anaerobic.

soil-fert-088.q: Why might a new hügelkultur bed be less fertile at first?
soil-fert-088.a: Wood has one of the highest carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, so its decay may tie up soil nitrogen for perhaps one to two years.

soil-fert-069.q: How does a living mulch differ from a cover crop?
soil-fert-069.a: A living mulch keeps growing with the crop, whereas a cover crop is worked into the soil or killed.

soil-fert-087.q: Why can soils farmed by slash-and-char keep cropping when slash-and-burn soils are abandoned?
soil-fert-087.a: Slash-and-char keeps much of the organic carbon as stable char, and such biochar-enriched soils can sustain cropping indefinitely, while slash-and-burn soils soon lose their nutrients.

soil-fert-204.q: How does Azolla fertilize a rice paddy?
soil-fert-204.a: Its partner cyanobacterium fixes atmospheric nitrogen, which Azolla releases to the rice as it dies.

soil-fert-091.q: Why does lime have to neutralize more than the acid in the soil water?
soil-fert-091.a: Acid-forming ions held on soil colloids will otherwise restore the original pH.

soil-fert-027.q: What goes wrong if green manure is worked in too short a time before planting?
soil-fert-027.a: Nitrogen immobilization can leave too little nitrogen for the next crop.

soil-fert-060.q: Why must agricultural lime be finely ground?
soil-fert-060.a: Soil acids are weak, so only fine particles react well: those finer than 60 mesh are fully effective, while those over 8 mesh are of little value.

soil-fert-037.q: Why does adding urine help a humanure compost heap?
soil-fert-037.a: It raises the heap's temperature, helping destroy pathogens and seeds.

soil-fert-044.q: Which part of human excreta carries most of its nitrogen?
soil-fert-044.a: Urine, which can hold up to 90% of the nitrogen in human excreta.

soil-fert-202.q: What is the main advantage of coated urea?
soil-fert-202.a: It releases urea gradually, lowering the risk of fertilizer burn and allowing less frequent applications.

soil-fert-017.q: Why does fluoride from phosphate fertilizers concern livestock more than crops?
soil-fert-017.a: Plants take up little fluoride, so the risk lies with livestock that eat contaminated soil.

soil-fert-046.q: Name an alternative to mined phosphate ore.
soil-fert-046.a: Phosphorus recovered from excreta, for example as struvite from urine.

soil-water-019.q: What are the two reasons rain can fail to soak in and become surface runoff?
soil-water-019.a: The soil is already saturated, or rain arrives faster than the soil can absorb it.

soil-water-089.q: Why does the US EPA prefer silt fences to straw bales for construction sediment control?
soil-water-089.a: Straw bales often protect water quality poorly and need much upkeep.

soil-water-020.q: Why can Horton overland flow erode soil extensively?
soil-water-020.a: The flow is shallow, sheetlike and fast, especially on steep terrain and loose, flat farmland.

soil-water-023.q: Why can paving a town both worsen droughts and cause floods?
soil-water-023.a: Less water reaches groundwater, so the water table falls, while more water left on the surface causes flooding.

soil-water-085.q: Why can felling a tree on clay soil damage a nearby building?
soil-water-085.a: The soil the tree had dried heaves as the deficit reverses, rising and spreading for years, and shallow foundations move with it.

soil-water-088.q: What does a low curve number say about an area?
soil-water-088.a: Its soil is more permeable and its runoff potential low.

soil-water-050.q: How do many erosion controls work physically?
soil-water-050.a: They are barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water.

soil-water-045.q: Why does long cultivation make a soil more erodible?
soil-water-045.a: It depletes organic matter, which coagulates colloids into a stronger, more stable structure.

soil-water-004.q: Why do crop residues and plant cover reduce splash erosion?
soil-water-004.a: They soften the impact of raindrops, whose kinetic energy is what throws soil particles out of the crater each drop makes.

soil-water-043.q: How does a process-based erosion model differ from an empirical one?
soil-water-043.a: A process-based model solves equations for detachment, transport and deposition, while an empirical model relates soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors.

soil-water-095.q: Why are the pale, eroded hilltops in many fields wrongly blamed on water erosion?
soil-water-095.a: They are actually made by tillage erosion, which strips organic-rich topsoil from convex spots.

soil-water-113.q: What left prairie soil open to erosion once settlers plowed it?
soil-water-113.a: Plowing replaced the prairie grasses and their extensive fibrous roots with crops, exposing the topsoil to wind and rain.

soil-water-005.q: What are the two steps of sheet erosion?
soil-water-005.a: Rainsplash first loosens small particles, then a thin, uniform sheet flow carries them a short distance.

soil-water-039.q: Why is a change in soil organic matter an unreliable sign of tillage erosion?
soil-water-039.a: Many other factors also affect organic matter, so a change does not necessarily mean soil was lost.

soil-water-029.q: Why does wind build separate sandy and silty deposits?
soil-water-029.a: Wind sorts sand from silt and clay, laying sand down as ergs and carrying silt further from the source to form loess.

soil-water-064.q: How does heavy rain make a slope more likely to fail?
soil-water-064.a: Pore water pressure on the slip surface lowers effective normal stress and friction, while the added groundwater makes the soil heavier.

soil-water-008.q: How does chemical erosion differ from physical erosion?
soil-water-008.a: Physical erosion removes rock or soil as solid sediment particles, whereas chemical erosion is usually measured from the dissolved load streams carry.

soil-water-049.q: What share of eroded sediment reaches rivers in Europe, according to WaTEM/SEDEM estimates?
soil-water-049.a: About 15%: that is the estimated sediment delivery ratio.

soil-water-252.q: A debris flow is as dense as other landslides; why does it flow almost like water?
soil-water-252.a: High pore-fluid pressure liquefies the sediment.

soil-water-031.q: Why do silt fences often give poor results in the field?
soil-water-031.a: Fine particles soon clog the fabric, and fences are often badly placed, installed or maintained.

soil-water-062.q: Why do shallow landslides often occur where permeable soil lies over less permeable soil?
soil-water-062.a: The lower layer traps water, pressure builds, and the saturated topsoil slides off.

soil-water-076.q: Which agency did the Soil Erosion Service become, and who led it?
soil-water-076.a: Hugh Hammond Bennett led it; it became the Soil Conservation Service, now the NRCS.

soil-water-101.q: What is one of the best defences against earthflows?
soil-water-101.a: Draining slopes, since saturated clay, fine sand and silt begin to flow and more water means faster flow.

soil-water-052.q: Why are anionic rather than cationic flocculants best practice in open systems?
soil-water-052.a: Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish.

soil-water-066.q: How does vegetation help stabilize a slope with shallow landslides?
soil-water-066.a: Roots reinforce the upper soil, and interception and transpiration dry it.

soil-water-108.q: Why does harvesting trees on a slope raise the risk of sloughing and slope failure?
soil-water-108.a: Roots hold the surface, and losing their strength can lower the safety factor so far that a moderate storm brings failure.

soil-water-250.q: Why is a desert pavement taken as a sign of a surface's relative age?

soil-water-257.q: When might gabions be chosen over riprap to protect a bank?
soil-water-257.a: On steep banks where the flow is too fast for riprap.

soil-water-124.q: What separates a marsh from a swamp?
soil-water-124.a: A marsh has herbaceous plants, while a swamp has woody plants.

soil-water-129.q: How do marsh plants cope with wet mud low in oxygen?
soil-water-129.a: Many have aerenchyma that carry air down to their roots.

soil-water-121.q: Why does peat accumulate in bogs even though plant growth there is slow?
soil-water-121.a: Decay is slower still in the oxygen-poor, saturated bog soil.

soil-water-147.q: What makes minerotrophic water neutral or alkaline?
soil-water-147.a: Dissolved bases such as calcium or magnesium ions make it base-rich.

soil-water-126.q: What keeps the pH of a rich fen relatively stable?
soil-water-126.a: Bicarbonate from calcium carbonate that groundwater dissolves as it passes limestone buffers the pH.

soil-water-138.q: What is the main control on whether a peatland releases carbon dioxide?
soil-water-138.a: The water table: a high one submerges the peat and slows respiration, while a falling one speeds aerobic decomposition and CO2 release.

soil-water-266.q: How does a palsa begin to grow?
soil-water-266.a: Where thin snow lets frost go deeper, an ice lens draws in water and lifts the surface by frost heave, a positive feedback.

soil-water-118.q: What sets landscape ecology apart from other branches of ecology?

soil-water-261.q: Why does draining peat add to carbon dioxide emissions?
soil-water-261.a: It exposes carbon stored for thousands of years to air, where it decomposes to CO2.

soil-water-137.q: Why is a drained peatland that still has a peat layer no longer a mire?
soil-water-137.a: Because new peat no longer forms there.

soil-water-142.q: How does suffosion differ from suffusion?
soil-water-142.a: Suffosion collapses the soil structure, losing mass and volume, while suffusion removes fines from between coarse grains that stay in contact, with no change in volume.

soil-agri-013.q: Besides growing crops, name two other uses of irrigation.
soil-agri-013.a: It revegetates disturbed soils in dry areas, protects crops from frost, suppresses weeds in grain fields and prevents soil consolidation.

soil-agri-046.q: How can farmers slow the evolution of herbicide-resistant weeds?
soil-agri-046.a: By using herbicides with different modes of action.

soil-agri-049.q: In surface irrigation, what decides the depth of water applied at any point?
soil-agri-049.a: The opportunity time, how long water stands on the surface there.

soil-agri-017.q: How do self-watering containers and wicking beds supply water to plants?
soil-agri-017.a: They draw water up from a reservoir by capillary action.

soil-agri-007.q: In a crop rotation, what should precede a nitrogen-depleting crop?

soil-agri-022.q: How do catch crops reduce nitrate leaching?
soil-agri-022.a: They take up the nitrogen left over from fertilizing the previous crop, so it is not leached.

soil-agri-010.q: How does following GPS guidance lines help the soil?

soil-agri-023.q: Why does newly added phosphorus leach from soils with 'legacy phosphorus'?
soil-agri-023.a: Decades of surplus phosphorus have filled their sorption sites, so the new phosphorus cannot adsorb.

soil-agri-032.q: Why is field soil steaming only a partial disinfection?
soil-agri-032.a: Heat-resistant spore-forming bacteria survive it; true sterilization needs laboratory autoclaving.

soil-agri-036.q: Which geological raw material is used against copper deficiency, and which to conserve nitrogen?
soil-agri-036.a: Malachite against copper deficiency, and zeolite to conserve nitrogen.

soil-agri-051.q: How does surge irrigation speed the advance of water down a furrow?
soil-agri-051.a: Pulsing the flow on and off wets and dries the surface, sealing it and reducing infiltration.

soil-agri-134.q: Why are Inga trees suited to alley cropping on acid tropical soils?
soil-agri-134.a: They fix nitrogen, grow on acid tropical soils and drop a thick mulch that protects the soil and shades out weeds.

soil-agri-056.q: What compounds make brassicas useful for biofumigation?
soil-agri-056.a: Isothiocyanates released from their glucosinolates, which are toxic to soil bacteria, fungi and nematodes.

soil-agri-025.q: What unit is soil salinity most often expressed in?
soil-agri-025.a: As ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.

soil-agri-106.q: Why does ploughing turn over the uppermost soil?
soil-agri-106.a: To bring fresh nutrients to the surface and bury weeds and crop remains to decay.

soil-agri-114.q: How does the soil disturbance of a harrow differ from that of a cultivator?
soil-agri-114.a: A harrow disturbs the whole surface, while a cultivator disturbs only narrow tracks between rows.

soil-agri-104.q: What might explain copper and iron deficiencies in white spruce on burned clearcuts?
soil-agri-104.a: Burning raises soil pH, and the higher pH may cause them.

soil-agri-117.q: Why may no-till delay spring planting?
soil-agri-117.a: Light-coloured residue absorbs less solar energy than bare soil, so the soil warms and dries more slowly.

soil-agri-109.q: How do a mouldboard plough's coulter and share work together?
soil-agri-109.a: The coulter cuts down into the soil and the share cuts horizontally, freeing a strip of sod that rolls over upside down.

soil-agri-107.q: Why did fields worked with an ard tend to become squarish?
soil-agri-107.a: The ard left undisturbed strips between furrows, so fields were cross-ploughed both ways.

soil-agri-115.q: How do the teeth of a toothed cultivator differ in purpose from chisel plough shanks?
soil-agri-115.a: The teeth work near the surface against weeds, while chisel shanks work deep to break hardened layers.

soil-agri-120.q: What does strip tillage combine from conventional tillage and from no-till?
soil-agri-120.a: The soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till.

soil-agri-059.q: How does irrigation leave soils saline?
soil-agri-059.a: Salt is left behind when irrigation water evaporates or rises from shallow saline water tables.

soil-agri-140.q: How do trees in agroforestry help water enter the soil?
soil-agri-140.a: They slow runoff and evaporation, so more water infiltrates.

soil-agri-065.q: How has the view of tillage changed in conservation agriculture?
soil-agri-065.a: Once thought to raise fertility through mineralization, it is now seen to destroy organic matter and cause erosion and crusting.

soil-agri-064.q: What three things raise soil carbon sequestration?
soil-agri-064.a: More biomass inputs, smaller losses of soil organic carbon and a longer mean residence time of that carbon.

soil-agri-075.q: How does a contour trench help crops in the drier growing season?
soil-agri-075.a: It catches downhill runoff so it soaks into the soil, and crops between trenches draw on that subsoil reserve.

soil-agri-141.q: If a check dam is not mainly a sediment trap, how does it reduce erosion?
soil-agri-141.a: It flattens the channel gradient and slows the flow, which induces infiltration.

soil-agri-082.q: Where are US soil surveys published now, and how does that differ from before?
soil-agri-082.a: On the NRCS Web Soil Survey, where changes go live in moments, rather than as county books that could take years to publish.

soil-agri-089.q: How does digital soil mapping differ from traditional soil mapping?
soil-agri-089.a: Traditional mapping has field soil scientists draw boundaries by hand, while digital mapping links observations to environmental data by quantitative relationships.

soil-agri-091.q: What does pedometric mapping produce instead of polygon maps of soil types?
soil-agri-091.a: Continuous grids of measured soil properties, with maps of prediction error.

soil-env-102.q: What is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the atmosphere for living things?
soil-env-102.a: Photosynthesis, which moves it into land and ocean life.

soil-env-212.q: How is carbon sequestration different from carbon capture and storage?
soil-env-212.a: Carbon capture and storage separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed, whereas biological sequestration captures CO2 through living processes such as photosynthesis.

soil-env-111.q: Why have peatlands such as those in East Anglia and the California Delta subsided?
soil-env-111.a: Tillage and drainage exposed their organic matter to oxygen.

soil-env-168.q: Why can biochar lock away carbon for so long?
soil-env-168.a: It retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years.

soil-env-112.q: How does a healthy soil with good water holding capacity protect waterways?
soil-env-112.a: It cuts overland flow, and nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways.

soil-env-114.q: What is the main reason warming soils release more carbon?
soil-env-114.a: Faster soil respiration: warming speeds up decomposition of soil organic matter.

soil-env-213.q: Does a positive climate feedback mean a good one?
soil-env-213.a: No. Positive or negative says nothing about good or bad; methane from wetlands, for example, is a positive feedback that adds to warming.

soil-env-152.q: Why does thawing yedoma matter for the climate?
soil-env-152.a: It may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, and as it thaws it becomes a significant methane source.

soil-env-136.q: How do palsas and pingos push the ground up?
soil-env-136.a: Meltwater trapped over deep permafrost freezes into ice lenses that lift the ground into mounds.

soil-env-132.q: Why is subsea permafrost slowly shrinking?
soil-env-132.a: It formed on land during the last Ice Age when sea levels were low, and has declined since being submerged under warmer, saltier conditions.

soil-env-140.q: Will permafrost thaw cause runaway warming?
soil-env-140.a: No. There is widespread agreement that its emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small for runaway warming.

soil-env-163.q: How does warmer soil lose its ability to hold water and nutrients?
soil-env-163.a: Warmth speeds the decomposition of organic matter, lowering soil organic carbon and with it the soil's capacity to hold nutrients and water.

soil-env-119.q: What shrinks the soil carbon sponge, and what builds it?
soil-env-119.a: Bare soils, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation shrink it; afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build it.

soil-env-215.q: Why does permafrost thaw at waterlogged sites produce methane?
soil-env-215.a: Methanogenesis needs fully anaerobic conditions, so thaw that exposes organic material without oxygen lets methanogens make methane.

soil-env-160.q: Why did climate models long overlook abrupt permafrost thaw?
soil-env-160.a: Abrupt thaw is hard to model, so models focused on gradual thaw.

soil-env-125.q: How does enhanced weathering store carbon dioxide?
soil-env-125.a: Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 from the air and stores it permanently in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity.

soil-env-124.q: How do ectomycorrhizal fungi increase soil carbon storage?
soil-env-124.a: They reduce decomposer activity, for example by taking organic nitrogen and leaving decomposers nutrient-limited.

soil-env-065.q: Do densely populated areas always suffer land degradation?
soil-env-065.a: No. High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

soil-env-101.q: Why is land take also called land loss?
soil-env-101.a: The activities that consume land, such as building on it, are virtually irreversible.

soil-env-072.q: What is the immediate cause of desertification?
soil-env-072.a: The loss of most vegetation, which leaves dry topsoil unprotected to blow away or wash off.

soil-env-086.q: What is the best-known approach to halting desertification?
soil-env-086.a: Large tree-planting belts, such as China's Green Wall and the African Union's Great Green Wall along the Sahara.

soil-env-073.q: Does desertification mean that deserts are physically expanding?
soil-env-073.a: No. That original idea has been rejected; the UNCCD defines it as land degradation in drylands caused by climatic variations and human activities.

soil-env-082.q: How has cashmere demand worsened desertification in Mongolia?
soil-env-082.a: Herders shifted from sheep to goats, which eat roots and flowers and so degrade grazing land.

soil-env-064.q: Name two types of soil degradation that emerged only in the last 50 years.
soil-env-064.a: Any two of pollution, loss of arable land to construction, artificial radioactivity, and land-use limits from armed conflict.

soil-env-074.q: How does overcultivation turn soil to desert?
soil-env-074.a: It drains nutrients, so the soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks.

soil-env-207.q: How do bush encroachers differ from invasive species?
soil-env-207.a: Encroachers are native to the ecosystem; they count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species.

soil-env-098.a: Severely degraded grassland, also called black beach: bare, unusable black soil.

soil-env-208.q: According to the two-layer theory, why does overgrazing favour woody plants?
soil-env-208.a: Grasses use topsoil moisture and woody plants subsoil moisture, so removing grass lets more water reach the subsoil for woody plants.

soil-env-185.q: What carbon to nitrogen ratio must be kept for optimal plant growth?

soil-env-178.q: What did soil quality mean before soil health replaced it?
soil-env-178.a: Fitness for a use, such as quality of soil for maize production or for roadbed preparation.

soil-env-188.a: Each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients, so carbon and nutrients run down.

soil-env-187.q: Which holds more carbon: the top two meters of soil, or the atmosphere and vegetation together?
soil-env-187.a: The soil, with an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes against 879 billion in the atmosphere and 600 billion in vegetation.

soil-env-216.q: Why does a septic tank need pumping out from time to time?
soil-env-216.a: Sludge builds up faster than it decomposes, so it is pumped out by vacuum truck.

soil-env-190.q: What body did the partnership's First Plenary Assembly establish?
soil-env-190.a: The Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils, whose experts advise the partnership on science.

soil-env-019.q: Why does phosphorus reach water mostly through erosion, while nitrate travels in water?
soil-env-019.a: Many forms of phosphorus adsorb onto soil particles, whereas nitrate moves in water flowing through the soil, such as tile drainage.

soil-env-033.q: Why can fungi break down pollutants that bacteria degrade poorly?
soil-env-033.a: Their non-specific enzymes attack substances such as pharmaceuticals and fragrances.

soil-env-020.q: Why does excess phosphorus drive eutrophication in lakes but nitrogen in the sea?
soil-env-020.a: Phosphorus usually limits plant growth in fresh water and nitrogen in the sea.

soil-env-026.q: Why can the same amount of a contaminant be toxic in one soil and harmless in another?
soil-env-026.a: Soil pH, organic matter and texture change how mobile, bioavailable and toxic a pollutant is, so risk assessment must be soil-specific.

soil-env-010.q: How does biomagnification differ from bioaccumulation?
soil-env-010.a: Bioaccumulation is build-up within one organism from its food and surroundings; biomagnification is the increase across food-chain levels.

soil-env-055.q: What is the main advantage of biostimulation?
soil-env-055.a: Native microbes, already suited to the subsurface and spread through it, do the work.

soil-env-025.q: How does biosparging differ from bioventing?
soil-env-025.a: Bioventing aerates the unsaturated zone, while biosparging targets the saturated zone below the water table.

soil-env-053.q: Why is landfarming unsuitable for metal-polluted soil?
soil-env-053.a: Inorganic contaminants are not degraded by it.

soil-env-041.q: How do plant roots help microbes clean contaminated soil?
soil-env-041.a: Roots release carbohydrates and acids that stimulate microbes, which then biodegrade the contaminants.

soil-env-204.q: Why can a factory outfall be modelled as a mathematical point?
soil-env-204.a: A point source has negligible extent, unlike nonpoint and area sources.

soil-env-036.q: How do mycorrhizal fungi lower the bioavailability of heavy metals?
soil-env-036.a: They produce proteins that bind the metals.

soil-env-051.q: Why has phytomining had limited commercial success?
soil-env-051.a: A review judged it slow and inefficient; by mid-2024 one nickel project had extracted less than a kilo of usable nickel.

soil-hist-040.q: Which classification system has had its editions launched at World Congresses of Soil Science?
soil-hist-040.a: The World Reference Base, first at Montpellier in 1998 and in its fourth edition at Glasgow in 2022.

soil-hist-043.q: What accreditation can members of the Australian Society of Soil Science gain?
soil-hist-043.a: They can become Certified Professional Soil Scientists.

soil-hist-029.q: Why did Marbut base classification on morphology rather than genesis?
soil-hist-029.a: He saw theories of soil genesis as ephemeral and dynamic.

soil-hist-046.q: What did the Park Grass Experiment reveal about ordinary field trials?
soil-hist-046.a: They probably underestimate long-term threats such as soil acidification.

soil-hist-030.q: Which soil-forming factor gained much more weight after 1940?
soil-hist-030.a: Time, with geomorphology used to find how long material has undergone soil formation.

soil-hist-004.q: Why is Liebig called the father of the fertilizer industry?
soil-hist-004.a: He stressed nitrogen and minerals as essential plant nutrients and popularized the law of the minimum.

soil-hist-008.q: What did Glinka's 1908 soil science textbook contain for the first time?
soil-hist-008.a: The first schematic soil map of the world.

soil-hist-024.q: When did Guy Smith's soil classification become official?
soil-hist-024.a: In 1965, after more than 15 years of work; it was published in 1975 as Soil Taxonomy.

soil-hist-073.q: What did Boussingault show about legumes in a crop rotation?
soil-hist-073.a: Soil nitrogen rises after legume crops.

soil-hist-014.q: What did chemoautotrophy overturn about how autotrophs get energy?
soil-hist-014.a: Autotrophs were thought to get energy only from light; some instead oxidize hydrogen sulfide or ammonium.

soil-hist-075.q: What did Hiltner mean by the rhizosphere?
soil-hist-075.a: The soil directly affected by root secretions and their microorganisms.

soil-hist-048.q: Which two bodies merged to form the Soil Science Society of America?
soil-hist-048.a: The Soils Section of the American Society of Agronomy and the American Soil Survey Association.

soil-hist-049.a: The World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) and SoilGrids.

soil-hist-055.q: Why does the society keep standard samples of humic and fulvic acids?
soil-hist-055.a: So scientists in many countries can work from the same reference materials, drawn from leonardite, river water, a mineral soil and peat.

soil-hist-059.q: How does lunar soil form differently from Earth's soil?
soil-hist-059.a: Mainly by mechanical weathering, as impacts and charged particles grind rock finer, not by oxygen, water and life.

soil-hist-079.q: Why do young crater rays on the Moon fade over time?
soil-hist-079.a: Space weathering makes lunar soil darker and redder as it matures.

soil-hist-083.q: How can oxygen be extracted from lunar regolith?
soil-hist-083.a: By heating its iron oxide above 900 °C in hydrogen gas.

soil-hist-080.q: Why does impact debris build up as regolith on airless bodies?
soil-hist-080.a: Lacking an atmosphere, they have almost no erosion to remove it.

soil-found-115.q: Where does the critical zone end at depth?
soil-found-115.a: At some depth in bedrock, where life and water cease to change the chemistry significantly.

soil-found-047.q: How long does mineral-associated organic matter typically persist, compared with particulate organic matter?
soil-found-047.a: Typically for centuries, whereas particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

soil-form-097.q: Which part of the regolith is conventionally called soil?
soil-form-097.a: Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter.

soil-form-146.q: What silica content and enrichments mark mafic rocks?
soil-form-146.a: They have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium.

soil-form-105.q: What features typically mark a meandering river?
soil-form-105.a: Point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

soil-form-023.q: Why does the subsoil get most of its colour from iron oxides?
soil-form-023.a: Because it holds little organic matter.

soil-form-019.q: What is the defining feature of Mollisols?
soil-form-019.a: A fertile mollic epipedon, built by long additions of root-derived organic matter.

soil-form-070.q: How much phosphorus did laterite remove from solution in laboratory tests and at pilot scale?
soil-form-070.a: 99% in laboratory tests and 96% in a pilot-scale facility.

soil-form-127.q: Why is phosphorus often the most deficient nutrient in tropical soils?
soil-form-127.a: Intense leaching and weathering deplete the mineral pool, and unlike nitrogen it cannot be replenished from the air.

soil-phys-189.q: How much surface per gram do clay minerals typically have?
soil-phys-189.a: Typically 10 to 1,000 square metres per gram, as they form thin plates.

soil-phys-125.q: Over what range does hydraulic conductivity vary from clays to gravels?
soil-phys-125.a: From about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels.

soil-phys-064.q: Why are clay soils called heavy, despite their high porosity?
soil-phys-064.a: The word reflects their moisture weight and the extra force needed to pull tillage tools through them.

soil-phys-114.q: How is the overconsolidation ratio (OCR) defined?
soil-phys-114.a: It divides the preconsolidation stress, the highest stress a soil has carried, by the current stress.

soil-water-182.q: Why is Richards' equation hard to use for infiltration?
soil-water-182.a: It is computationally expensive, not guaranteed to converge, and sometimes struggles to conserve mass.

soil-phys-210.q: What is the general basin form of the water balance?
soil-phys-210.a: P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus change in storage.

soil-water-174.q: Why does a high salt content restrict water uptake by roots?
soil-water-174.a: Solutes lower the osmotic potential of the soil solution, which severely restricts uptake by roots.

soil-phys-221.q: What is the pressure head at the water table?
soil-phys-221.a: There it equals atmospheric pressure; below it pressure head exceeds atmospheric pressure, and above it is negative.

soil-phys-201.q: Why are karst aquifers more sensitive to contamination than porous aquifers?
soil-phys-201.a: Their fast flow, through limestone fissures widened by carbonic acid, makes them far more sensitive.

soil-phys-194.q: Why do less soluble contaminants travel only short distances?
soil-phys-194.a: Adsorption holds them back, so they can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water.

soil-phys-180.q: What does Fick's first law state?
soil-phys-180.a: J = −D dφ/dx: diffusive flux equals the diffusion coefficient times the concentration gradient, with a minus sign.

soil-phys-145.q: How deep do annual temperature cycles penetrate in wet and dry clay?
soil-phys-145.a: About 18.0 m in wet clay but only 6.5 m in dry clay.

soil-chem-107.q: What size are the particles of the colloidal fraction of soil?
soil-chem-107.a: Tiny clay and humus particles under 1 μm across, whose charges vary with soil pH.

soil-chem-097.q: What does allophane alter to when silica is added, and when it is removed?
soil-chem-097.a: To halloysite where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed.

soil-chem-085.q: Why is the cation exchange capacity of kaolinite low?
soil-chem-085.a: Kaolinite has undergone almost no isomorphous substitution.

soil-chem-071.q: How many milliequivalents are 1 mmol of Na+ and 1 mmol of Ca2+?
soil-chem-071.a: 1 milliequivalent for Na+ but 2 for Ca2+, since equivalents are moles multiplied by valence.

soil-chem-130.q: When and where was biofiltration first introduced?
soil-chem-130.a: In England in 1893, as a trickling filter for wastewater.

soil-chem-180.q: Between which two lines is water stable on a Pourbaix diagram?
soil-chem-180.a: Between EH = −0.05916 pH and EH = 1.229 V − 0.05916 pH; outside them it is reduced to hydrogen or oxidized to oxygen.

soil-chem-142.q: How does alkalinity differ from basicity?
soil-chem-142.a: Basicity is an absolute position on the pH scale, while alkalinity is measured by titrating with an acid to an endpoint.

soil-chem-021.q: How does gypsum reclaim an alkali soil?
soil-chem-021.a: It supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex and turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulphate.

soil-bio-212.a: They are primarily detritivores, eating dead plants at any stage of decay.

soil-bio-071.q: What did a 2007 study find to be the main global determinant of bacterial diversity?

soil-bio-225.q: Which compound gives soil its earthy odour?
soil-bio-225.a: Geosmin, a volatile compound released by soil bacteria that mostly also produce spores.

soil-bio-054.q: How fast do bacteria turn over in the rhizosphere?
soil-bio-054.a: In just 12–19 hours, shorter on younger roots, because root exudates make the rhizosphere a special case.

soil-bio-178.q: What do rhizobia and legumes exchange in their mutualism?
soil-bio-178.a: The bacteria supply ammonia or amino acids and receive organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source.

soil-bio-240.a: Hyphae aggregated into durable, water-repellent transport structures that work like xylem.

soil-bio-248.a: Secreted by mycorrhizal hyphae, it builds stable aggregates that resist erosion and accounts for about 5% of global organic carbon and nitrogen storage.

soil-bio-196.q: Why do autumn leaves decompose more slowly than most compost ingredients?
soil-bio-196.a: They are low in nitrogen and made largely of cellulose and lignin, which resist decay.

soil-bio-258.q: What does the Michaelis constant Km represent?
soil-bio-258.a: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of the limiting rate V.

soil-class-021.q: What system replaced the FAO soil classification, and when?
soil-class-021.a: The World Reference Base replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-155.q: Where does the ustic moisture regime sit relative to the aridic and udic?
soil-class-155.a: It is wetter than the aridic and drier than the udic.

soil-class-116.q: Which soil order covers the largest share of U.S. land?
soil-class-116.a: Mollisols, at an estimated 21.5%, followed by Alfisols at 14%.

soil-class-139.q: Which soils are excluded from the Regosols?
soil-class-139.a: Weakly developed soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols; Regosols are a leftover group for soils that fit no other.

soil-class-065.q: Why must fill be as free of organic matter as possible?
soil-class-065.a: Decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures built on it.

soil-fert-165.q: At what concentration in soil water is boron toxic to most plants?

soil-fert-195.q: What do preplant and late-spring soil nitrogen tests show?
soil-fert-195.a: Preplant tests show the soil's nitrogen-supplying power, and late-spring or pre-side-dress tests decide whether more is needed.

soil-fert-119.q: What do denitrifying bacteria use in place of oxygen?
soil-fert-119.a: Nitrate and nitrite, as the final electron acceptor.

soil-fert-138.q: What share of soil potassium is in the soil solution, the form plants absorb most readily?
soil-fert-138.a: Only 0.1–0.2% of the total; fixed potassium makes up 96–99%.

soil-fert-082.q: Why does excess salt around roots make a plant respond as in drought?
soil-fert-082.a: When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots.

soil-fert-067.q: Why can straw or sawdust mulch briefly slow plant growth?
soil-fert-067.a: Their wide carbon-to-nitrogen ratio lets decomposing microbes draw nitrogen from the soil.

soil-fert-013.q: What do the numbers of a fertilizer grade such as 10-10-10 give?
soil-fert-013.a: The percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O.

soil-water-079.q: What two fates await rain that reaches land?
soil-water-079.a: It either flows over the ground as surface runoff or soaks in by infiltration, becoming soil moisture or groundwater.

soil-water-083.q: Why are planners advised to avoid karst for new development?
soil-water-083.a: Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses.

soil-water-042.q: Why must drop size and terminal velocity be simulated accurately on bare soil?

soil-water-006.q: How do earth and debris differ in landslide classification?
soil-water-006.a: Earth has less than 20% by weight of particles over 2 mm; debris has more.

soil-water-098.q: Why are anionic flocculants best practice in open systems?
soil-water-098.a: Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish.

soil-water-253.q: What does a well-developed desert pavement indicate?
soil-water-253.a: Aridity and an older surface, since older surfaces carry better-developed pavements.

soil-water-280.q: What share of damaging landslides in the year to September 2003 were triggered by heavy rainfall?

soil-water-267.q: How does tropical peatland forest compare with forest on mineral soil as a carbon store?
soil-water-267.a: It holds far more carbon as soil organic matter, among the largest near-surface stores of land organic carbon.

soil-water-297.q: How do dead plankton help fill in a pond?
soil-water-297.a: They decay into humus that mixes with inwashed silt and clay to form soil, making the pond shallower.

soil-agri-030.q: What is the difference between monoculture and monocropping?
soil-agri-030.a: Monoculture describes crop diversity in space, whereas monocropping describes diversity over time.

soil-agri-011.q: In what units is soil salinity most often expressed?
soil-agri-011.a: As ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.

soil-agri-110.q: Why did the heavy carruca plough make farming communal?
soil-agri-110.a: Pulling it took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had.

soil-agri-067.a: The ability of cover crops, such as nitrogen-fixing legumes, to stand in for chemical nitrogen fertilizer.

soil-agri-159.q: How wide do filter strips need to be?
soil-agri-159.a: At least 15 feet (4.6 m), and they can often serve as a cheap substitute for terraces.

soil-agri-167.q: What do the two Not Suitable land classes, N1 and N2, mean?
soil-agri-167.a: N1 has limitations that might be overcome in time but not at acceptable cost now; N2 has limitations ruling out any sustained use.

soil-meth-007.q: Which exponent of distance did Shepard settle on for inverse distance weighting?
soil-meth-007.a: Near -2, close to the gravity model.

soil-env-283.q: How can lowering a wetland's water table affect its methane balance?
soil-env-283.a: It increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs and can turn the wetland into a methane sink.

soil-env-085.q: How does contour trenching prevent erosion?
soil-env-085.a: Trenches 150 m long and 1 m deep are dug along the contour and edged with stone walls, so water cannot flow.

soil-env-090.q: How much agricultural land had unsustainable farming degraded by 2025?
soil-env-090.a: 996 Mha, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation.

soil-env-217.q: In what order are materials replaced when an open-cut mine is reclaimed?
soil-env-217.a: Rock backfills the pit, stored pre-mining soil goes on top, then topsoil, and finally vegetation is restored.

soil-env-038.a: Adding a chelator to make heavy metals, often too immobile for plants to absorb, more soluble.

soil-env-034.q: Why can ligninolytic fungi degrade many organic pollutants?
soil-env-034.a: Lignin and cellulose are long-chain carbon compounds much like many organic pollutants.

soil-env-252.q: Which nanoparticle has been used in most field applications of nanoremediation?

soil-env-229.q: Why does electrical resistance heating (ERH) work in any soil type?
soil-env-229.a: Current travels mainly through the thin water film on grains, which is also why it cannot dry the ground out.

soil-env-296.q: How does Finland raise soil selenium?
soil-env-296.a: It adds selenium salts to chemical fertilizers.

soil-hist-127.q: What is the half-life of beryllium-10, and what does it date?
soil-hist-127.a: 1,387,000 years; it dates exposure of rocks, soils and ice cores.

soil-hist-096.q: Who first proposed the law of superposition, and when?

soil-hist-042.q: What did Darwin's chalk experiment near Down House show?
soil-hist-042.a: Chalk spread in December 1842 ended up buried 18 centimetres deep, a rate of 6 millimetres per year.

soil-hist-016.q: Which bacterium was shown in 1901 to fix atmospheric nitrogen?
soil-hist-016.a: Azotobacter chroococcum, in work that fully described the fixation process found by Hellriegel and Wilfarth.

soil-hist-107.q: Which soil did the Wisconsin legislature name the official state soil in 1983?

soil-hist-068.q: How do planetary scientists functionally separate rock from soil?
soil-hist-068.a: Rocks are fragments of about 10 cm or more, larger than cobbles; soil is all other, typically loose material.

soil-found-017.q: How does plant species diversity tend to change across the soil pH range, and why?
soil-found-017.a: It tends to increase from pH 3.5 toward pH 9, because there are more calcicole species, which prefer lime-rich soils, than calcifuge species, which prefer acid ones.

soil-form-147.q: Why does limestone erode into karst landscapes?
soil-form-147.a: It is partly soluble, especially in acid: water and organic acid from the soil slowly widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the calcium carbonate into pavements, caves and gorges.

soil-form-103.q: What materials make up superficial deposits, and how do they usually lie onshore?
soil-form-103.a: Mostly gravel, sand, silt and clay, forming relatively thin, often discontinuous patches.

soil-form-107.q: How did periglacial loess come to be deposited?
soil-form-107.a: As meltwater dwindled each autumn and winter, bare floodplains dried and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, depositing it downwind.

soil-form-008.q: What is bioturbation in the A horizon?
soil-form-008.a: The mixing of organic matter into the mineral matter by burrowing animals.

soil-form-118.q: Besides a mollic epipedon, what must a Mollisol have, and where are Mollisols common?
soil-form-118.a: A base saturation above 50%; they are common in grasslands.

soil-form-125.q: How does primary succession differ from secondary succession?
soil-form-125.a: Primary succession colonizes new surfaces with no life, such as bare rock, lava flows or freshly exposed till; secondary succession follows a disturbance.

soil-phys-001.a: How individual particles clump, bind and aggregate, which in turn sets the pattern of pores between them.

soil-phys-030.q: How does gilgai form in Vertisols?
soil-phys-030.a: Repeated shrinking and swelling churns the soil and heaves underlying material to the surface.

soil-phys-118.q: What kind of fluid is quicksand, and how does it respond to stress?
soil-phys-118.a: A shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluid: undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly lowers its viscosity.

soil-phys-099.q: How does heavy rain affect slope stability through matric suction?
soil-phys-099.a: Raising infiltration lowers matric suction along the soil water characteristic curve, cutting the soil's shear strength and slope stability.

soil-phys-175.q: How does recreational trampling change alpine soils?
soil-phys-175.a: It raises bulk density and lowers porosity, altering soil moisture and temperature and increasing runoff and erosion.

soil-water-156.q: Over what suction range does saturated flow occur, and what drives it?
soil-water-156.a: Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, with gravity and differences in water pressure pushing water away from where it was applied.

soil-water-195.q: How is hydraulic conductivity found in a constant-head test?
soil-water-195.a: The volume of water passing in a set time is measured, and K follows by rearranging Darcy's law with the specimen's length, cross-section and head.

soil-water-176.q: What do the parameters α and n describe in the van Genuchten model?
