soil-water-176.a: α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, and n, greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution.

soil-water-157.q: By how much can tree roots raise infiltration rates through preferential flow?
soil-water-157.a: Up to 27 times, because living or dead roots open preferential channels for rainwater.

soil-phys-202.q: How do confined aquifers store water, and how large are their storativities?
soil-phys-202.a: By matrix expansion and water compressibility, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5.

soil-phys-200.q: When was fluorescein first developed, and what is its sodium salt called?
soil-phys-200.a: In 1871; its sodium salt is uranine, and both remain among the best dye tracers.

soil-phys-160.q: How large are frost boils, and where do they occur?
soil-phys-160.a: Typically 1 to 3 metres across, in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost.

soil-chem-187.q: Who derived the Goldich dissolution series, and when?
soil-chem-187.a: S. S. Goldich, in 1938, after studying soil profiles and their parent rocks.

soil-chem-095.q: How does vermiculite form from biotite or phlogopite?
soil-chem-095.a: By weathering or hydrothermal alteration: the micas lose the potassium between their sheets, which is replaced by magnesium and iron.

soil-chem-158.q: What are the two fates of growing agglomerates during particle aggregation?
soil-chem-158.a: They settle out as sediment, or in concentrated suspensions link into a colloidal gel.

soil-chem-102.q: Which minerals are products sold as fuller's earth usually made of?

soil-chem-051.q: Which exchanger cations are frequently used to measure cation-exchange capacity?

soil-chem-177.q: Name some substances in soil that can act as electron donors.
soil-chem-177.a: Soil organic matter, petroleum hydrocarbons, less chlorinated solvents such as vinyl chloride, and reduced inorganic compounds.

soil-chem-005.q: Which nitrogen fertilizers do not acidify the soil?
soil-chem-005.a: Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate.

soil-chem-033.q: How is net acidity calculated in acid base accounting?
soil-chem-033.a: Potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralising capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil.

soil-bio-044.q: Which earthworms are usually used in vermicomposting?
soil-bio-044.a: The brandling worm Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil.

soil-bio-013.q: How do soil algae survive below the surface, out of the light?
soil-bio-013.a: Given steady temperature and moisture, they feed heterotrophically on easy carbon sources such as glucose.

soil-bio-229.q: Why do many northern forests of North America have a deep detritus layer that invasive earthworms can disrupt?
soil-bio-229.a: Most northern forests lost their native earthworms to the Wisconsin glaciation, so a deep detritus layer is typical and many native plants rely on it.

soil-bio-214.q: How much soil do small burrowers such as ants, termites and earthworms move worldwide?
soil-bio-214.a: So much that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift.

soil-bio-187.q: Which way do roots move water during drought in hydraulic redistribution?
soil-bio-187.a: Groundwater is drawn up the taproot and released from the lateral roots into the dry surface soil; under flooding, roots move water the other way.

soil-bio-176.q: Where do ericoid mycorrhizal fungi trade nutrients with the plant, and how long do these sites last?
soil-bio-176.a: In coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars; the coils work for only a few weeks before degrading.

soil-bio-246.q: Which genera of mycorrhiza helper bacteria are most commonly reported?
soil-bio-246.a: Pseudomonas and Streptomyces; Bacillus is another.

soil-bio-093.q: Why has much humus persisted for more than 100 years?
soil-bio-093.a: It is hidden inside small soil aggregates or tightly sorbed or complexed to clays, out of reach of microbes and enzymes.

soil-bio-098.q: On what substrates do tangel and mor humus each develop in cold, humid mountains?
soil-bio-098.a: Tangel develops on alkaline substrates and mor on acidic ones.

soil-bio-256.q: What reaction does acid phosphatase catalyse, and at what pH does it work best?
soil-bio-256.a: It hydrolyses a phosphate monoester with water to give an alcohol and phosphate, at an optimum pH below 7.

soil-class-003.q: Why are natural soil classes useful?
soil-class-003.a: Experience shows that natural classes, based on morphology, behaviour or genesis, can be interpreted for many different uses.

soil-class-014.q: Why do soils on river flood plains stay azonal, or immature?
soil-class-014.a: New alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile.

soil-class-112.q: How does soil climate differ between well-drained and waterlogged soils?
soil-class-112.a: In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate; in waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere.

soil-class-135.q: On what materials and under what vegetation do Phaeozems form?
soil-class-135.a: On loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe.

soil-class-156.q: Why do conditions in the acrotelm swing between aerobic and anaerobic?
soil-class-156.a: Its lower boundary usually coincides with the lowest level of the water table, which fluctuates within it.

soil-fert-185.q: What carbon-to-nitrogen ratio do composting microbes prefer in their feedstock?

soil-fert-232.q: At what pH range is the least soil phosphorus bound up?

soil-fert-218.q: Which paper is counted a milestone of biogeochemistry?
soil-fert-218.a: An 1844 paper by Dumas and Boussingault.

soil-fert-012.q: What share of fertilizers is applied as solids, and which are most common?
soil-fert-012.a: About 90%, most commonly urea, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride.

soil-fert-092.q: How fast did Tukey and Wittwer find leaf-sprayed nutrients moving through the plant?
soil-fert-092.a: About one foot per hour, tracing radioactive phosphorus and potassium sprayed on leaves in the 1950s at Michigan State.

soil-fert-045.q: What proportion of biosolids is organic matter?

soil-fert-210.q: How did Peru treat guano from 1840, and what did that mean for its finances?
soil-fert-210.a: Peru made guano an exclusive state resource, and its royalties became the country's largest source of revenue.

soil-water-086.q: What three conditions cause surface runoff to form?
soil-water-086.a: Water cannot infiltrate fast enough because the soil is saturated, rain arrives faster than it can be absorbed, or surfaces are impervious.

soil-water-011.q: What is the main climatic control on water erosion?
soil-water-011.a: The amount and intensity of precipitation, especially when the soil surface lacks plant cover.

soil-water-044.q: What erosion index does the Conservation Reserve Program require land to have?

soil-water-071.q: Why does quick clay lose so much strength once remolded?
soil-water-071.a: Its clay particle structure is highly unstable, so it keeps far less strength than it had on first loading.

soil-water-028.q: Which structures carry water safely down to a gully floor?
soil-water-028.a: Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes.

soil-water-097.q: When are gabions chosen over riprap for river bank protection?
soil-water-097.a: On steep banks where flow is too fast for riprap; gabions are stone-filled wire boxes.

soil-water-263.q: How does a riparian zone protect water?
soil-water-263.a: It acts as a natural biofilter, shielding water from excess sediment, polluted surface runoff and erosion.

soil-water-259.q: What decides whether a wetland carries aquatic, marsh or swamp vegetation?
soil-water-259.a: How long flooding or groundwater saturation lasts.

soil-agri-016.q: What is Low Energy Precision Application (LEPA) in centre pivot irrigation?
soil-agri-016.a: Hanging drop heads just above the crop, or dragging hoses that wet the ground directly, to limit evaporation.

soil-fert-208.q: What forms of nitrogen are most commonly supplied by fertigation?
soil-fert-208.a: Anhydrous ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea; nitrogen is the most common nutrient supplied.

soil-agri-003.q: Whose 1974 concept is considered the foundation of modern agroecology?
soil-agri-003.a: Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s.

soil-agri-125.q: For several soils, how does the optimum water content for tillage relate to the plastic limit?
soil-agri-125.a: The optimum equals 0.9 times the lower plastic limit.

soil-agri-081.q: According to the traditional theory, how do lynchets form?
soil-agri-081.a: Long ploughing makes soil slip downslope, building a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops.

soil-agri-088.a: It has the soil quality, growing season and moisture supply to give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management.

soil-meth-029.q: What role does gas chromatography play in the Dumas nitrogen method?
soil-meth-029.a: The method ends with a gas chromatography column that separates nitrogen from carbon dioxide and water.

soil-meth-008.q: What does geomorphometry extract from digital elevation models?
soil-meth-008.a: Surface parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms.

soil-env-161.q: What did preliminary 2011 analyses estimate permafrost emissions to be, and what could they not account for?
soil-env-161.a: Around 15% of human emissions, but they could not account for abrupt thaw.

soil-env-269.q: What share of Earth's land do forests now cover, and how does that compare with before agriculture spread?
soil-env-269.a: About 31%, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half that loss in the last century.

soil-env-075.q: What is Sahel drought now thought to stem from mainly?
soil-env-075.a: Rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures, which are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases.

soil-env-313.q: Why did rangeland management develop in the United States?
soil-env-313.a: In response to rangeland deterioration from overgrazing and misuse of arid lands, shown by the Dust Bowl.

soil-env-037.q: What are the main mechanisms of phytoremediation?
soil-env-037.a: Phytoextraction, phytostabilization, phytovolatilization and phytofiltration, along with breakdown of pollutants by plants and by root-zone microbes.

soil-env-047.q: Which two migrations drive electrokinetic remediation, and which dominates?
soil-env-047.a: Electromigration (electrophoresis) of charged particles, the dominant one, and electro-osmotic flow of pore fluid running the opposite way.

soil-env-241.q: What limit does the WHO recommend for arsenic in drinking water, and why is it often unattainable?
soil-env-241.a: 10 μg/L; it is often unattainable in problem areas because arsenic is hard to remove.

soil-env-243.q: Above what fluoride concentration can groundwater cause dental fluorosis?

soil-env-263.q: How does the Raymond process circulate groundwater?
soil-env-263.a: Groundwater is pumped up downstream, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream in a loop.

soil-env-297.q: What caused Keshan disease across its belt of China, and when did it peak?
soil-env-297.a: Selenium-deficient soil; it peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands.

soil-hist-126.q: How is an age calculated in thermoluminescence dating?
soil-hist-126.a: The dose measured by heating is divided by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays.

soil-hist-100.q: How did non-reversible ploughs build ridge and furrow?
soil-hist-100.a: They turned soil toward the centre of the same strip each year, gradually building a ridge with a furrow between strips.

soil-hist-033.q: Who extended Darwin's idea of bioturbation to ants and trees, and when?

soil-hist-009.q: When did Curtis F. Marbut begin developing the first formal soil classification scheme for the United States?

soil-hist-021.q: What journey does Farmers of Forty Centuries recount?
soil-hist-021.a: A nine-month tour of Asia in 1909, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture.

soil-hist-066.q: Why would clayey and organic soils have kept producing clay and organic matter on the early Earth?
soil-hist-066.a: They resist erosion, and early unicellular life would also have bound the soil.

soil-found-060.q: In what order do igneous minerals weather, and why?
soil-found-060.a: Roughly in the order they formed, Bowen's reaction series, because the weakest cation–oxygen bonds go first.

soil-found-011.q: How is a soil colour written in Munsell notation?
soil-found-011.a: As hue, then value/chroma, as in a Cecil soil horizon recorded as red (10R 4/8) clay.

soil-form-137.q: At weathering rates of 20 m per million years, how long do deep regoliths take to form?
soil-form-137.a: Several million years, and longer still in cooler climates.

soil-form-112.q: How does alluvium differ from colluvium in sorting, and why?
soil-form-112.a: Running water lays down alluvium, so it is generally fine-grained and well sorted; colluvium moves without running water and is poorly sorted.

soil-form-096.q: How much richer in manganese is black rock varnish than the Earth's crust?
soil-form-096.a: It holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%.

soil-form-027.q: Which test separates a duripan from petrocalcic horizons and fragipans?
soil-form-027.a: A duripan slakes in KOH but not in HCl.

soil-form-076.q: Why does modern soil classification fit paleosols poorly?
soil-form-076.a: Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago; an alfisol, a forest soil, could not exist before trees.

soil-form-124.q: In biosorting, why do large stones end up at the base of the biomantle?
soil-form-124.a: Burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer there.

soil-phys-052.q: What law is used to calculate particle size from terminal settling velocities?

soil-phys-092.q: How does the dry bulk density of a mineral soil compare with the density of quartz?
soil-phys-092.a: Quartz is about 2.65 g/cm3, but a mineral soil's dry bulk density is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3, because the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.

soil-phys-115.q: What do relative densities of 100% and 0% mean?
soil-phys-115.a: 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil.

soil-phys-123.q: Why is a soil's bulk density always less than its particle density?
soil-phys-123.a: Bulk density includes the pores; particle density, typically 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm3, does not.

soil-water-153.q: Why do clay soils hold more water than sandy soils?
soil-water-153.a: Water clings more tightly to fine clay particles than to coarse sand grains, so clays hold more water while sands let it pass more easily.

soil-water-223.q: Why does a capacitance probe's reading depend mostly on soil water?
soil-water-223.a: Water's dielectric constant (80) is far above that of mineral soil (4), organic matter (4) and air (1).

soil-water-200.q: How quickly do plants recover from water stress after rewatering?
soil-water-200.a: Mildly stressed plants recover in 1–2 days, but after severe stress they regain only 40-60% of maximum photosynthesis the day after rewatering.

soil-water-208.q: How much can development cut infiltration?
soil-water-208.a: Felton and Lull (1963) found a potential 80 percent cut, and Taylor (1982) found construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent.

soil-phys-218.q: At what suction is field capacity conventionally defined?
soil-phys-218.a: At −33 kPa (−0.33 bar), or −10 kPa for sandy soils.

soil-phys-206.q: Where does subsurface water return to the surface?
soil-phys-206.a: At lower elevations through springs, seeps, wells or streams, sometimes after thousands of years in an aquifer.

soil-phys-158.q: Why can't the expansion of freezing water explain frost heave?
soil-phys-158.a: Water expands only about 9%, too little; by 1930 Stephen Taber had shown that water migrates to the freeze line, and that benzene, which contracts on freezing, also heaves.

soil-phys-185.q: How does wetting change a soil's thermal conductivity?
soil-phys-185.a: It raises it: dry soil conducts about 0.2–0.4 W·m−1·K−1 and wet soil 1–3, and varying moisture largely determines a soil's conductivity because air conducts heat poorly.

soil-chem-198.q: How do soil minerals retain phosphorus in acid and in calcareous soils?
soil-chem-198.a: In acid soils by adsorption onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides; in neutral to calcareous soils by precipitation onto calcite.

soil-chem-108.q: What conditions does bauxite formation need?
soil-chem-108.a: Intense weathering and very good drainage, which dissolve kaolinite and precipitate gibbsite.

soil-chem-161.q: Which iron(III) oxyhydroxides matter most in soils?
soil-chem-161.a: Goethite and lepidocrocite, the commonest forms and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils.

soil-chem-103.q: Rank AlCl3, CaCl2 and NaCl by how well they flocculate colloids.
soil-chem-103.a: AlCl3 > CaCl2 > NaCl, because multivalent cations flocculate colloids more efficiently than monovalent ones.

soil-chem-203.q: What does the Langmuir isotherm predict at low and high pressure?
soil-chem-203.a: θ = Kp/(1 + Kp), the fraction of sites occupied, is about Kp at low pressure and approaches 1 at high pressure.

soil-chem-174.q: Below what redox potential do methanogens grow, and to which domain do they belong?
soil-chem-174.a: Below −0.3 V; all known methanogens belong to the domain Archaea.

soil-chem-028.q: Why did land clearing bring salt to the surface in Australia?
soil-chem-028.a: Deep-rooted native vegetation had used groundwater year-round; once crops and pasture replaced it, rising groundwater brought stored salt up, and evaporation left it in the soil.

soil-chem-025.q: How do seeps differ from scalds?
soil-chem-025.a: Both are saline discharge areas: seeps are where groundwater meets the soil surface, scalds where water is lost by evaporation only.

soil-bio-067.q: What do Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter each oxidize?
soil-bio-067.a: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate.

soil-bio-065.q: Why are earthworm casts taken as a sign of healthy soil?
soil-bio-065.a: Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the surrounding soil and build stable soil aggregates, marking biologically active soil.

soil-bio-030.q: Which energy channels did soil flow webs reveal?
soil-bio-030.a: The bacterial and fungal channels, which carry the largest flow, and the root-herbivory channel, which carries much less.

soil-bio-208.q: Why do the pines of the pygmy forest stay so small?
soil-bio-208.a: Their podzol, the Blacklock series, is very acid, nutrient-poor and high in exchangeable aluminium, and its iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage.

soil-bio-151.q: How do mycorrhizal hyphae reach soil that roots cannot?
soil-bio-151.a: Most are far finer than the smallest root or root hair, so they explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface.

soil-bio-163.q: Why do orchid seedlings depend on a fungus?
soil-bio-163.a: Orchid seeds, 0.35–1.50 mm long, carry virtually no energy reserve, so seedlings get their carbon from the fungus.

soil-bio-153.q: How much nitrogen do grain legumes fix each year?
soil-bio-153.a: Grown on about 1.5 million km2 a year, they fix about 44–66 million tons, almost half of the nitrogen used in agriculture.

soil-bio-111.q: How do detritivores and microbes break detritus down together?
soil-bio-111.a: Detritivores digest mainly the protein-rich microbes and excrete the detritus barely changed; microbes regrow on that dung and it is eaten again, until the detritus is fragmented and its complex carbohydrates disappear.

soil-bio-101.q: How much of the carbon in soil can microbial necromass make up?
soil-bio-101.a: 30 to 80%, because microbes cycle soil carbon so extensively.

soil-bio-270.q: What does a Q10 of 2 to 3 mean for a biological rate?
soil-bio-270.a: The rate doubles or triples with every 10 °C, as in most biological systems.

soil-class-017.q: What organic carbon content separates mineral from organic material?
soil-class-017.a: Mineral material has less than 20% soil organic carbon; organic material has 20% or more.

soil-class-106.q: What base saturation separates Alfisols from Ultisols?
soil-class-106.a: Alfisols have at least 35% base saturation; the more leached Ultisols fall below 35%.

soil-class-120.q: In the WRB, what decides whether redox features make a Gleysol or a Stagnosol?
soil-class-120.a: Features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol; those from stagnant surface water make a Stagnosol or Planosol.

soil-class-146.a: Repeated wetting and drying: plinthite, a red clay-rich material sometimes over 80% iron oxides, then hardens irreversibly.

soil-fert-184.q: Why does residue with a C:N above 30:1 lower the nitrogen available to plants?
soil-fert-184.a: Microbes are left short of nitrogen, so they take up soil ammonium and nitrate and immobilize them; below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants.

soil-fert-231.q: Why do older leaves yellow first when nitrogen runs short?
soil-fert-231.a: The plant moves nitrogen out of them to younger tissue.

soil-fert-227.q: Why does calcium deficiency show first in new, fast-growing parts?
soil-fert-227.a: Calcium does not move in the phloem, so low-transpiring tissues and new, fast-growing parts suffer first.

soil-fert-137.q: Why does potassium leach from plants faster than nitrogen or phosphorus?
soil-fert-137.a: It exists only as the small soluble K+ ion.

soil-fert-079.q: Why may marled crops show magnesium deficiency?
soil-fert-079.a: Marl's carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, so magnesium must be supplied as well.

soil-fert-026.q: How much nitrogen does a green manure release?
soil-fert-026.a: Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre), and usually 40-60% of the crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.

soil-fert-057.q: Why must agricultural lime be finely ground?
soil-fert-057.a: Soil acids are weak: particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and finer than 60 mesh fully effective.

soil-fert-207.q: How much phosphogypsum does making phosphoric acid leave behind?
soil-fert-207.a: Five tons for each ton of phosphoric acid, an impure radioactive waste; 100 to 280 million tons are produced yearly.

soil-water-091.q: What happens to soil under buildings and roads?
soil-water-091.a: It is sealed off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, so it is in effect consumed and made infertile.

soil-water-014.q: Why do clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones?

soil-water-055.q: What safety factor makes a slope stable, and which values call for monitoring?
soil-water-055.a: A slope is globally stable if the safety factor exceeds 1 along every potential sliding surface; values between about 1 and 1.3 mark marginally stable slopes that need monitoring or stabilization.

soil-water-030.q: How high does wind usually lift sand?
soil-water-030.a: Most stays within 50 cm of the surface, and practically none rises above 2 m.

soil-water-106.q: How much can active pore water pressure cut a soil's shear strength?
soil-water-106.a: By up to 60%, because rising water content weakens shear strength and so cohesion.

soil-water-269.q: What does the Shields number compare?
soil-water-269.a: It is proportional to the ratio of the fluid force on a particle to the particle's weight.

soil-water-146.q: Why does a rich fen keep a fairly stable pH?
soil-water-146.a: Groundwater passing limestone dissolves some calcium carbonate, and the bicarbonate produced buffers the fen's pH.

soil-phys-162.q: In Penck's slope replacement, where does flattening begin?
soil-phys-162.a: At the lowest slope, spreading upward and backward: flattening always occurs from the bottom up.

soil-agri-006.q: Why is crop rotation not a form of intercropping?
soil-agri-006.a: Its crops grow in separate seasons.

soil-agri-057.q: Why does filling planting pits with manure and compost raise yields so much?
soil-agri-057.a: The organic matter attracts termites whose tunnels break up the soil; yields of trees, sorghum and millet can rise by up to 500 percent.

soil-agri-098.q: How much can no-till cut nitrous oxide emissions?
soil-agri-098.a: By 40–70% depending on rotation, which matters because nitrous oxide is 300 times stronger than CO2 and lasts 120 years.

soil-agri-112.q: How deep does a subsoiler work compared with most tillage tools?
soil-agri-112.a: Most tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in); a subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more.

soil-agri-158.q: How do buffer strips protect surface waters?
soil-agri-158.a: By slowing surface runoff, they trap sediment and filter out nutrients and pesticides before these reach the water.

soil-agri-083.q: How does a digital terrain model differ from a digital surface model?
soil-agri-083.a: A digital terrain model shows the bare ground surface, while a digital surface model may include tree canopy and buildings.

soil-meth-019.q: How does the Kjeldahl method measure nitrogen?
soil-meth-019.a: Concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C digests the sample and holds its nitrogen as ammonium sulfate; sodium hydroxide turns this into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration.

soil-meth-012.q: Why can soil moisture shift the NDVI without any change in vegetation?
soil-meth-012.a: Wet soil darkens, and bare soils themselves give small positive values of about 0.1 to 0.2.

soil-env-273.q: How much CO2 does silicate weathering sequester per mole of calcium or magnesium released?
soil-env-273.a: In theory 1 mol of CO2 for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure.

soil-env-070.q: How much land do drylands cover, and how many people live there?
soil-env-070.a: 41.3% of Earth's land surface, home to more than 2 billion people.

soil-env-091.q: Why did soils improve under agrivoltaic systems in the Kubuqi Desert?
soil-env-091.a: Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation, and the panels acted as windbreaks that stopped sand burying plants, creating a better microclimate with the vegetation.

soil-env-097.q: What removal rates do bioretention systems typically achieve?
soil-env-097.a: About 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals; a 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%.

soil-env-002.q: How long does DDT persist in soil?
soil-env-002.a: Its half-life in soil is 2–15 years, so residues are still found in people, though at levels 5 to 10 times lower than in the 1970s.

soil-env-031.q: Why can heavy metal pollutants never biodegrade?
soil-env-031.a: Almost all compounds biodegrade given time, but elements do not.

soil-env-013.q: Which fuels does air sparging suit, and which does it not?
soil-env-013.a: It suits light gasoline constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene, but not heavier fuels such as kerosene and diesel.

soil-env-221.q: Why are LNAPLs easier to locate and remove than DNAPLs?
soil-env-221.a: An LNAPL is buoyant, so it stops at the water table and floats on it.

soil-env-266.q: How much caesium did mustard greens remove in the Chernobyl zone?
soil-env-266.a: Up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season.

soil-env-299.q: What most likely drives parrots on the Manu River to eat soil?
soil-env-299.a: Sodium: consumed soils are consistently higher in it, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean.

soil-hist-129.q: How does lead-210 reveal soil erosion?
soil-hist-129.a: Excess lead-210 from fallout builds up in surface soils, and its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century, giving erosion and deposition rates.

soil-hist-091.q: How do a buried wall and a buried ditch show up as cropmarks?
soil-hist-091.a: A buried wall diverts water and displaces fertile soil, stunting crops, while an organic-rich ditch fill holds water and boosts growth.

soil-hist-115.q: Why did grain output on the Kazakh steppe fall after early success?
soil-hist-115.a: Only 200 to 350 mm of rain fell a year, the soils were salty, winds caused erosion in spring, and grain monoculture, on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted nutrients.

soil-hist-108.q: Where did Lawes and Gilbert find that cereals get their nitrogen?
soil-hist-108.a: From the soil, contrary to Liebig's view that it came only from the air.

soil-hist-078.q: Since when has the Soil Science Society of America's flagship journal appeared only online?
soil-hist-078.a: Since 2013, with double-blind review of its articles.

soil-found-118.q: How can a drop of acid help identify calcite?
soil-found-118.a: Acid dissolves calcite and releases carbon dioxide, giving a characteristic fizz.

soil-found-028.q: Why do gleyed soils show yellow-brown or orange mottles on a gray background?
soil-found-028.a: Under saturation microbes reduce iron to its soluble ferrous form, which can be removed and leaves gray silicate minerals; when the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidises locally into the coloured mottles.

soil-form-141.q: Why are clays such abundant weathering products in soils?
soil-form-141.a: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust, and hydrolysis turns them into clay minerals such as illite, smectite and kaolinite.

soil-form-109.q: What happens to the fertility of Iowa's Loess Hills once their topsoil erodes?
soil-form-109.a: Their fertility comes from 10,000 years of prairie humus, so the loess left beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

soil-form-150.q: How does a terminal moraine differ from a recessional moraine?
soil-form-150.a: A terminal moraine forms at the glacier's foot and marks its furthest advance; a recessional moraine is a small ridge left where a retreating glacier paused.

soil-found-072.q: What does the name paralithic mean?
soil-found-072.a: Akin to stony: from the Greek para, "akin to", and lithic, "stony".

soil-form-057.q: Which pedogenic process appears to be the most active in many soils?
soil-form-057.a: Bioturbation, which dominates the upper part of most soils, except possibly vertisols and cryosols.

soil-phys-009.q: How does fast wetting destroy soil structure by slaking?
soil-phys-009.a: Water entering aggregates displaces air from their pores and aggregates with trapped air burst; the faster the wetting, the more slaking occurs.

soil-phys-082.q: How did wheel traffic change the soil in one cotton field?
soil-phys-082.a: Tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space, while wheel-trafficked inter-rows had 1.67 g/cm3 and 37%.

soil-phys-070.q: Which pores are the largest still water-filled at field capacity, and why do they matter?
soil-phys-070.a: Mesopores, 30–75 μm; called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use.

soil-phys-093.q: How is a soil's water content w measured?
soil-phys-093.a: As the mass of water over the mass of solids, found by weighing a sample before and after oven drying.

soil-found-094.q: How does depression storage capacity help govern Horton overland flow?
soil-found-094.a: Together with infiltration capacity: once both are exceeded, water flows across the land, possibly causing flooding and soil erosion.

soil-water-185.q: What is the main limitation of the Kostiakov equation, and how is it fixed?
soil-water-185.a: It implies a final intake rate of zero, whereas infiltration usually approaches a finite steady value; the Kostiakov–Lewis equation adds a steady intake term.

soil-water-202.q: When does Darcy's law stop holding?
soil-water-202.a: Above Reynolds numbers of about 1 to 10, when inertial effects become significant.

soil-water-243.q: What is the premise of a soil inference system?
soil-water-243.a: That a soil's basic properties are enough to infer all its other physical and chemical properties, through logically linked pedotransfer functions.

soil-water-234.q: How do soil-based irrigation controllers decide when to water?
soil-water-234.a: They either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold.

soil-phys-212.q: In the Netherlands, how large is the winter drainage requirement, and where does it come from?
soil-phys-212.a: About 180 mm: 720 mm of precipitation against 540 mm of evaporation.

soil-env-129.q: Why can thawing permafrost add to climate change?
soil-env-129.a: Dead biomass has built up in it over millennia without fully decomposing; as warming thaws it, decomposition restarts and releases carbon dioxide or methane.

soil-phys-184.q: Which changes temperature more over a day: a material of low or high thermal effusivity?
soil-phys-184.a: One of low effusivity; a material of high effusivity changes much less.

soil-chem-191.q: What can electron probe microanalysis reveal inside a mineral grain?
soil-chem-191.a: Chemical zoning from core to rim, which records the grain's history.

soil-chem-111.q: Why can ferrihydrite hold so much arsenic, lead or phosphate?
soil-chem-111.a: Its nanoporous particles give several hundred square metres of surface per gram, which adsorb these substances.

soil-chem-164.a: When iron-bearing substances rust underwater, and commonly where primary iron minerals weather.

soil-chem-146.q: What does the Langmuir isotherm assume about a surface?
soil-chem-146.a: Equivalent sites holding one molecule each, an energetically uniform surface and at most a monolayer, assumptions seldom all true.

soil-chem-205.q: How does surface heterogeneity explain the Freundlich equation?
soil-chem-205.a: High-energy sites fill first, then low-energy ones, so the heat of adsorption weakens with coverage.

soil-chem-124.a: With a platinum electrode, read relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.

soil-chem-014.q: How does controlled drainage save irrigation water?
soil-chem-014.a: Where wet and dry seasons are marked, drains run only in the wet season.

soil-chem-043.q: In the Maas–Hoffman model, what is the breakpoint?
soil-chem-043.a: The salinity up to which yield is unaffected; beyond it, yield falls.

soil-bio-217.a: In two stages: its hyphae secrete enzymes that break polymers into small units such as monomers, which are then absorbed.

soil-bio-059.q: How do bacteria such as Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans cause acid mine drainage?
soil-bio-059.a: They use iron sulfide to generate sulfuric acid, which drains from the mine with runoff and can drive the pH of groundwater and streams down to 2–3.

soil-bio-205.q: How does a chemoautotroph differ from a chemoheterotroph?
soil-bio-205.a: A chemoautotroph builds all its organic compounds from carbon dioxide; a chemoheterotroph, like most animals and fungi, cannot fix carbon into its own organic compounds.

soil-bio-209.q: Why can microarthropod communities be used as bioindicators?
soil-bio-209.a: They are very sensitive to changes in ecosystems.

soil-bio-166.q: How widespread is arbuscular mycorrhiza among plants?
soil-bio-166.a: It is the most widespread plant symbiosis known, found in about 80% of plant species, on every continent except Antarctica.

soil-bio-181.q: What do endophytic fungi give a plant in exchange for carbohydrates?
soil-bio-181.a: They can increase its water or nutrient uptake and protect it from insects, birds or mammals.

soil-bio-252.q: How does a rhizotron let researchers watch roots?
soil-bio-252.a: A central corridor usually has viewing windows into the soil profiles on either side.

soil-bio-131.q: Which kind of kerogen yields oil, which yields gas, and which yields none?
soil-bio-131.a: Labile kerogen yields mainly oil, refractory kerogen mainly gas, and inert kerogen no hydrocarbons but graphite.

soil-bio-253.q: Why do bacteria and fungi release exoenzymes into their surroundings?
soil-bio-253.a: Breaking macromolecules into small pieces lets their constituents pass through the cell membrane and be used inside the cell.

soil-class-001.q: What traits do soil classification systems group soils by?
soil-class-001.a: Measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed.

soil-class-044.q: Why were human-made soils long left out of classification systems?
soil-class-044.a: Criteria built for natural soils often do not apply to them.

soil-class-093.q: What is the defining trait of an Aridisol?
soil-class-093.a: Water deficiency: an aridic moisture regime, with fewer than 90 consecutive moist days in the growing season, and no leaching.

soil-class-131.q: Which Leptosols are the most extensive on Earth?
soil-class-131.a: Lithic Leptosols, less than 10 cm deep, in mountain regions.

soil-class-058.q: What gives red soils their colour?
soil-class-058.a: High iron content, which gives colours from reddish brown to reddish yellow.

soil-fert-175.q: How does potassium help a plant tolerate drought?
soil-fert-175.a: It opens and closes stomata through an ion pump, so it controls water loss from leaves.

soil-fert-171.q: How much of a plant's dry mass is carbon?

soil-fert-146.q: How does a nutrient cycle differ from the flow of energy through an ecosystem?
soil-fert-146.a: Energy flows one way through ecosystems, but mineral nutrients cycle.

soil-fert-125.q: What did a 15-year nitrogen-addition study at Harvard Forest find?
soil-fert-125.a: More leaching, higher pine mortality and an end to biomass accumulation.

soil-fert-030.q: Which compost organisms are the most abundant and important?
soil-fert-030.a: Bacteria, which excrete plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium; mesophilic or thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase.

soil-fert-209.q: Why did demand for guano fall rapidly after 1910?

soil-fert-215.q: What does wood ash supply as a fertilizer?
soil-fert-215.a: Potassium, and calcium carbonate, which acts as a liming agent to neutralise acid soils.

soil-fert-040.q: How does phosphate rich organic manure free the phosphorus locked in rock phosphate?
soil-fert-040.a: Microbial organic acids slowly dissolve its insoluble tricalcium phosphate, and the organic matter stops other ions locking the phosphorus into insoluble forms.

soil-water-021.q: Why does saturation-excess overland flow start sooner after earlier rain?
soil-water-021.a: Antecedent soil moisture sets how soon soil saturates: the wetter it starts, the sooner runoff begins.

soil-water-036.q: How are unpaved lots and dirt roads kept from raising dust?
soil-water-036.a: They are paved or gravelled, or stabilized with water, vegetable oil, calcium chloride or other suppressants.

soil-water-284.q: How can as little as 1 mm of silt harm coral?
soil-water-284.a: Suspended sediment disrupts filter-feeding organisms and deposits bury them; 1 mm of accumulation may kill coral polyps.

soil-water-249.q: How does bed load move along a stream?
soil-water-249.a: It rolls, slides and hops along the bed at a small fraction of the flow speed.

soil-water-069.q: How do roots crossing a potential failure plane stabilize a slope?
soil-water-069.a: They raise shear strength by binding particles and anchor unstable surface soil to deeper stable layers or bedrock.

soil-water-293.q: Why does an alluvial fan form where a channel opens out?
soil-water-293.a: Flow leaving a confined channel spreads out and loses the capacity to carry its sediment.

soil-water-120.q: How does the National Technical Committee for Hydric Soils define a hydric soil?
soil-water-120.a: As soil formed under saturation, flooding or ponding long enough to turn its upper part anaerobic.

soil-agri-150.q: Why does burning the slash raise soil fertility for a time?
soil-agri-150.a: It leaves a nutrient-rich ash layer and temporarily removes weeds and pests.

soil-agri-145.q: How does expanded clay aggregate help a heavy soil?
soil-agri-145.a: Mixed in, its pellets improve aeration and drainage.

soil-agri-124.q: Why does keyline cultivation give water more time to infiltrate?
soil-agri-124.a: Cultivating parallel to the keyline drifts runoff away from the valley centre, delaying runoff concentration.

soil-agri-063.q: How do reduced-tillage and no-till systems protect soil?
soil-agri-063.a: They keep residues on the surface for erosion protection and water retention.

soil-agri-068.q: What does a catch crop do with nitrogen left from the previous crop?
soil-agri-068.a: It takes up the surplus, keeping it from loss by leaching, denitrification or volatilization, and returns it to the soil when worked in as green manure or decomposed.

soil-agri-094.q: Why can a single poor rating make a Storie index zero?
soil-agri-094.a: The index multiplies its ratings, so a zero in any one makes the whole result zero.

soil-meth-018.q: In the WRB, what does the whole soil include besides the fine earth?
soil-meth-018.a: Coarse fragments, artefacts, cemented parts and dead plant residues of any size.

soil-meth-002.q: What are the nugget, sill and range of a variogram?
soil-meth-002.a: The nugget is a jump at the origin, the sill its limit at large distances, and the range the distance where it nears the sill.

soil-env-275.q: What mainly decides the net methane flux from a wetland?
soil-env-275.a: How much methane made by methanogens reaches the surface before methanotrophs oxidize it.

soil-env-100.q: What sets the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification apart from other agreements on land?
soil-env-100.a: It is the only internationally legally binding framework on desertification, and the only convention stemming directly from the Rio Conference's Agenda 21.

soil-env-080.q: What happens to people when desertified rural land can no longer support them?
soil-env-080.a: They migrate to cities, particularly in Africa, creating unemployment and slums.

soil-env-311.q: What caused the spoil tip at Aberfan, Wales, to collapse in 1966?
soil-env-311.a: It was built over a spring and saturated by heavy rain; it collapsed onto a school, killing 144 people.

soil-env-200.q: How does PFAS in soil reach people?
soil-env-200.a: Crops take it up: soil contamination raises PFAS in foods such as white rice, coffee and animals reared on the land.

soil-env-017.q: Why are coliform bacteria in runoff measured if they do not cause disease?
soil-env-017.a: They are a common indicator of water pollution.

soil-env-050.q: What makes a plant a hyperaccumulator?
soil-env-050.a: It concentrates metals to levels toxic to related species not adapted to metalliferous soils, for example over 1000 mg/kg of dry weight for nickel, copper, cobalt, chromium or lead.

soil-env-247.q: How does bioslurping recover oil from above the water table?
soil-env-247.a: A slurp tube reaching into the free-product layer draws up liquid and soil gas together, lifting oil off the water table and capillary fringe.

soil-env-298.q: How did cadmium from upstream mines reach the people who developed itai-itai disease?
soil-env-298.a: Residents irrigated rice with the Jinzū River water, so the highly soluble cadmium contaminated paddies and rice and raised body burdens.

soil-hist-119.q: How do absolute and relative ages differ in the methods that produce them?
soil-hist-119.a: Absolute ages come from radioactive isotopes, while relative ages come from tools such as paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios.

soil-hist-088.q: Into which two stages does taphonomy divide its processes?
soil-hist-088.a: Biostratinomy, between death and burial, and diagenesis, after burial.

soil-hist-077.q: What does agricultural chemistry often aim to do for soil?
soil-hist-077.a: Preserve or raise soil fertility so as to keep or improve crop yields and crop quality.

soil-hist-001.q: Besides parent material, what did Dokuchaev show explains how soil types vary from place to place?
soil-hist-001.a: Climate, topography and the length of soil formation.

soil-hist-076.q: What did a failed royal commission on truffle cultivation lead Albert Bernhard Frank to discover?
soil-hist-076.a: The nature and development of mycorrhizae, which he named in an 1885 paper.

soil-hist-069.q: What level of perchlorate in Martian regolith is considered toxic to humans?
soil-hist-069.a: Around 0.5%, and even trace amounts interfere with human thyroid function.

soil-env-174.q: Under what conditions need inorganic fertilizers not harm soil health?
soil-env-174.a: When they are not used in excess and they boost plant growth that returns more carbon-containing residues.

soil-found-092.q: What is the familiar vernacular distinction between soils, and what makes light soils easier to cultivate?
soil-found-092.a: Heavy (clayey) versus light (sandy) soils. Light soils are easier to cultivate and resist compaction by trampling cattle, but they erode more easily.

soil-found-088.q: Why do tropical soils turn rusty red and lack marked layer contrasts?
soil-found-088.a: Fast decomposition leaves little fulvic acid to leach metals, so mobile magnesium, iron and aluminium precipitate as oxide minerals that colour the soil rusty red.

soil-found-079.q: Why is soil water more accurately called the soil solution?
soil-found-079.a: Because it is never pure: it carries hundreds of dissolved organic and mineral substances.

soil-found-042.q: How are clay minerals most easily identified?
soil-found-042.a: By X-ray diffraction rather than by chemical or physical tests.

soil-form-136.q: What is the minimum share of silt- and clay-sized particles in a mudrock?

soil-form-111.q: How do luminescence methods date loess?
soil-form-111.a: They date when the grains were last exposed to daylight.

soil-form-152.q: What happens when volcanic ash is washed into the soil, and when is heavy ashfall harmful?
soil-form-152.a: Its minerals form a nutrient-rich andisol layer that is very good for farming. Heavy ashfalls can bury pasture and sterilize the soil by oxygen deprivation.

soil-form-154.q: What is rock varnish made of, and how does its clay arrive?
soil-form-154.a: It is made mainly of clay with iron and manganese oxides, and the clay can only arrive by wind.

soil-form-022.q: Does the United States have a legal definition of topsoil sold in commerce?
soil-form-022.a: No, it has no federal legal definition.

soil-form-026.q: Why can a perched water table form on top of a claypan?
soil-form-026.a: Its dense structure restricts roots and water infiltration.

soil-form-040.q: Why does caliche form in the B horizon under a thin A horizon?
soil-form-040.a: Calcite and other soluble minerals that water would normally remove build up there as a cemented layer.

soil-form-035.q: Why are tepetates a problem for farming at the surface?
soil-form-035.a: They are hard, poorly drained and infertile.

soil-form-123.q: What kind of soils show this wetting-drying mixing, and what does it require?
soil-form-123.a: It is specific to vertisolic soils, driven by wetting-drying cycles, and needs at least 30% clay.

soil-form-158.q: How does humus change as a soil ages from young to old?
soil-form-158.a: In a young soil humus accumulates; in a mature soil it peaks; in an old soil it declines.

soil-form-156.q: Which part of a hillslope is steepest, and what shapes it?
soil-form-156.a: The backslope, shaped mainly by mass wasting and running water.

soil-form-167.q: What made the St. Lawrence Lowlands clays unstable after glaciation?
soil-form-167.a: The Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay there, and leaching of the salt plus river incision made it unstable, causing landslides and earthflows.

soil-form-164.q: What separates the great groups of the Chernozemic order?
soil-form-164.a: The colour of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added.

soil-phys-186.q: How did agrophysics develop from soil physics?
soil-phys-186.a: It first studied relations within the soil, then widened to crop properties and the quality and safety of food and raw farm produce.

soil-phys-167.q: What did Coulomb contribute to soil design in 1773?
soil-phys-167.a: He applied mechanics to earth pressures on ramparts, taking shear strength on a slip plane as cohesion plus friction.

soil-phys-067.q: How do IUPAC pore size limits relate to how gases adsorb on rigid solids?
soil-phys-067.a: Micropores fill cooperatively, mesopores show capillary condensation, and in macropores confinement effects vanish.

soil-phys-066.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary porosity?
soil-phys-066.a: Primary porosity is the original pore system of a rock or alluvial deposit; secondary porosity forms later, through leaching of minerals or fracturing.

soil-phys-087.q: Why are wet, clay-rich soils more susceptible to compaction?
soil-phys-087.a: Water films shield particle contacts, and fine-textured clay-rich soils are more susceptible than coarse ones, wet more than dry.

soil-phys-229.q: Why can freshly plowed soil falsely look uncompacted?

soil-phys-232.q: Why does a field headland usually yield less?
soil-phys-232.a: It gets more traffic per unit area than the rest of the field, so its soil is more compacted.

soil-phys-235.q: Why may switching compacted soil to no-till at once fail?
soil-phys-235.a: Compacted soils become addicted to tillage, and no-till benefits usually take 2 to 5 years, faster with cover crops.

soil-water-198.q: How is horizontal saturated hydraulic conductivity measured with the auger hole method?
soil-water-198.a: A hole is augered to below the water table, water is bailed out, and the rate at which the level rises again is recorded.

soil-phys-130.q: What does a root do when it senses dry soil?
soil-phys-130.a: It makes the hormone ABA, which closes stomata, cutting transpiration and photosynthesis, and loosens root cell walls so roots grow in search of water.

soil-water-167.q: How is gravimetric water content found by oven drying?
soil-water-167.a: The sample is dried and weighed until drying is complete; the mass lost is the water, divided by the wet or the dry mass.

soil-water-242.q: What turns plinthite irreversibly into ironstone hardpan?
soil-water-242.a: Repeated wetting and drying, especially with heat from the sun; a single cycle does not.

soil-water-190.a: The ratio of actual path length to the straight distance between two points; the more sinuous the path, the higher it is.

soil-phys-255.q: What is the premise of pedotransfer functions?
soil-phys-255.a: That a soil's basic properties are enough to infer all its other physical and chemical properties.

soil-phys-262.q: Between which two points is plant available water held?
soil-phys-262.a: Between field capacity and the permanent wilting point, in mesopores.

soil-water-211.q: Why does ponded water reach groundwater more readily than evenly spread rain?
soil-water-211.a: Rain spread evenly within field capacity barely percolates, but pooled in low spots the same volume can exceed field capacity and drain down to groundwater.

soil-phys-208.q: Which equation is the basic constitutive law for groundwater discharge, and who derived it?
soil-phys-208.a: Darcy's law, derived by Henry Darcy in 1856.

soil-water-158.q: How is fingering in the unsaturated zone described?
soil-water-158.a: As a Saffman-Taylor instability, arising mostly during drainage and leaving an unstable boundary between saturated and unsaturated soil.

soil-water-165.q: At what suction is field capacity defined, and what moisture does it represent?
soil-water-165.a: At -33 kPa; it is the moisture 2-3 days after rain or irrigation.

soil-water-162.q: What does a general basin water balance say?
soil-water-162.a: P = Q + ET + change in storage: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus change in storage in soil or groundwater.

soil-phys-211.q: What reservoirs does this water balance model divide the soil profile into?
soil-phys-211.a: The surface, the unsaturated root zone with mainly vertical flow, a transition zone, and the aquifer with mainly horizontal flow.

soil-phys-219.q: What does the eddy covariance flux measure, and what is it the covariance of?
soil-phys-219.a: It is the covariance between fluctuations of vertical wind speed and of gas concentration, times mean air density.

soil-phys-213.q: How much of the water roots take up is lost by transpiration and guttation?
soil-phys-213.a: 97-99.5%; only a small part is used for growth.

soil-phys-146.q: Why does soil air hold less oxygen and more CO2 than the air above?
soil-phys-146.a: Microbes and roots consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

soil-phys-150.q: What commonly causes poor soil aeration?
soil-phys-150.a: Soil compaction, and a pore network blocked when water fills the pores.

soil-phys-163.q: What drives the formation of patterned ground?
soil-phys-163.a: Frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils: repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up, and lateral forces pile them into clusters and stripes.

soil-phys-161.q: What do low-albedo and high-albedo surfaces do with radiation?
soil-phys-161.a: Low-albedo surfaces look dark and absorb most radiation; high-albedo surfaces such as snow look bright and reflect most of it.

soil-phys-244.q: What does Dalton's law say about a gas mixture?
soil-phys-244.a: The total pressure of an ideal gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its gases.

soil-phys-245.a: Without convection, gases are good insulators, so they trap many gas-filled pockets that block conduction.

soil-phys-179.q: What conditions does ice segregation need?
soil-phys-179.a: A permeable soil or porous rock, temperatures at which ice and premelted water coexist, and a temperature gradient across the zone.

soil-phys-164.q: What is the formula for thermal diffusivity, and what does high diffusivity mean?
soil-phys-164.a: alpha = k/(rho cp). Heat moves rapidly through a material of high diffusivity because it conducts heat quickly relative to how much energy it stores.

soil-phys-183.q: What does the heat equation say about how a point heats or cools?
soil-phys-183.a: A point heats or cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter or cooler its surroundings are.

soil-chem-231.q: Why does anatase often form first even though rutile is more stable?
soil-chem-231.a: Anatase has a lower surface energy, though rutile is the most common and stable TiO2 polymorph.

soil-chem-232.q: Why does each element give its own X-ray emission peaks?
soil-chem-232.a: An incident beam ejects an inner-shell electron, and the X-ray released when an outer electron fills the hole has an energy characteristic of the element.

soil-chem-188.q: What does Bragg's law link together?
soil-chem-188.a: The wavelength, the lattice spacing and the glancing angle.

soil-chem-233.q: What gives this phosphate mineral its green colour?

soil-chem-242.q: What happens when pyrite is exposed to air?
soil-chem-242.a: It oxidizes to iron and sulfuric acid, and oxidation of sulfides can push soil pH below 2.0.

soil-chem-227.q: How does the van der Waals force change with distance?
soil-chem-227.a: It is repulsive at very short range, zero at an equilibrium distance, and attractive beyond it.

soil-chem-109.q: Where does green rust occur as a mineral?
soil-chem-109.a: As the mineral fougerite in Gleysols.

soil-chem-089.q: What alternating conditions helped kaolinite form on basalt in Kivu?
soil-chem-089.a: Alternating wet and dry seasons; it did not form in perennially swampy ground.

soil-chem-148.q: How many milliequivalents is 1 mmol of Ca2+?
soil-chem-148.a: 2, because the equivalents of an ion equal its moles multiplied by its valence (1 mmol of Na+ is 1).

soil-chem-054.q: Does base-richness predict nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium availability?
soil-chem-054.a: No: base-richness shows no correlation with their availability.

soil-chem-115.q: What is the main source of electrons in soil?

soil-chem-229.q: Why do particles sometimes stay suspended as a colloid instead of settling?
soil-chem-229.a: There is not enough attractive force to aggregate them.

soil-chem-173.q: What role does manganese play in plants?
soil-chem-173.a: It is a key micronutrient, acting as a catalyst in the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II.

soil-chem-041.q: Why can both over-irrigation and under-irrigation cause salinity?
soil-chem-041.a: Over-irrigation raises water tables; under-irrigation fails to flush out salts.

soil-chem-040.q: Which equation does this model numerically solve to compute groundwater levels and flows between polygons?

soil-chem-042.q: How does framboidal pyrite form in acid sulfate soils?
soil-chem-042.a: Bacteria such as Desulfovibrio desulfuricans reduce sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, which reacts with ferrous iron.

soil-chem-220.q: What is the only way to remove salt from soil, rather than just tolerate it?
soil-chem-220.a: Washing salt below the root zone.

soil-bio-008.q: What is the primary role of soil biota?
soil-bio-008.a: To recycle organic matter that comes from the above-ground, plant-based food web.

soil-bio-271.q: Why does the hyphal form suit fungi?
soil-bio-271.a: Its high surface-to-volume ratio suits nutrient extraction and invading substrates.

soil-bio-056.q: What do lithotrophs get their name from?
soil-bio-056.a: The Greek lithos (rock) and troph (consumer): they are 'eaters of rock'.

soil-bio-017.q: Why are slime molds not found far below the surface?
soil-bio-017.a: They need light, so they are spread wherever sunlight and moderate moisture reach.

soil-bio-274.q: How are protozoa classified by how they move?

soil-bio-083.q: How do entomopathogenic nematodes kill an insect?
soil-bio-083.a: An infective juvenile enters it and releases gut bacteria, Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus, that kill it within 24-48 hours.

soil-bio-064.q: What distinguishes biologically controlled mineralization from induced mineralization?
soil-bio-064.a: In controlled mineralization the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location; in induced mineralization microbial metabolism merely creates conditions that favour mineral growth.

soil-bio-211.q: Why are millipedes called soil ecosystem engineers?
soil-bio-211.a: Their burrowing mixes organic with mineral matter, especially where earthworms are absent or scarce.

soil-bio-006.q: What are root tips hotspots of?

soil-bio-031.q: How does a Baermann funnel collect nematodes?
soil-bio-031.a: Nematodes sink into the collecting vial because they cannot swim.

soil-bio-221.q: How does metagenomics differ from amplicon sequencing?
soil-bio-221.a: Amplicon sequencing of marker genes such as 16S rRNA shows which taxa are present; metagenomics sequences all DNA and also recovers enzymes and pathways.

soil-bio-273.a: Organisms that parasitise fungi are called mycoparasitic.

soil-bio-276.q: What share of humus do arable soils typically hold?
soil-bio-276.a: On average 2 to 3%, within a range from under 1% to over 12%.

soil-bio-210.q: After a disturbance such as agriculture, how quickly do soil mites recolonise?
soil-bio-210.a: Most recolonise within a few months, but Oribatida take several years.

soil-hist-015.q: In a Winogradsky column, which bacteria use sulfide for photosynthesis, and which tolerate more of it?
soil-hist-015.a: Purple and green sulfur bacteria use it, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple.

soil-bio-223.q: Which fatty acid indicates fungi in a PLFA analysis?

soil-bio-162.q: What happens to plants in sterile soils unless mycorrhizal spores or hyphae are added?
soil-bio-162.a: They often do poorly, because there are no fungi to colonise their roots.

soil-bio-239.q: Who first isolated a microbe from legume nodules, and when?
soil-bio-239.a: Martinus Beijerinck, in 1888, naming it Bacillus radicicola; it is now placed in Rhizobium.

soil-bio-321.q: Do epiphytes draw nourishment from their host?
soil-bio-321.a: No. They use the host only for support and draw no nourishment from it, and they are not rooted in soil.

soil-bio-089.q: What carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is typical of humus?
soil-bio-089.a: Commonly between 8:1 and 15:1, with a median of about 12:1.

soil-bio-090.q: Which organic materials decompose first and quickly, and which persist longest?
soil-bio-090.a: Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids go first and quickly; fats, waxes and resins persist longest.

soil-bio-126.q: Which layers does the term mean in Canada, and what do specialists disagree about?
soil-bio-126.a: In Canada it means the L, F and H horizons; specialists disagree on whether it equals the O horizon or leaves out the litter.

soil-bio-284.q: Why is cellulose hard for most organisms to use, and who manages it?
soil-bio-284.a: Few organisms can metabolize it; some bacteria and protists can, and ruminants and termites use microorganisms to process it.

soil-bio-300.q: What are living and active organic matter?
soil-bio-300.a: Living matter is roots and organisms in the spaces between and inside aggregates; active matter is fresh or partly decomposed residue in the same spaces.

soil-bio-304.q: What happens to extra organic matter once a soil is saturated for its management?
soil-bio-304.a: It stays as lightly protected free particles.

soil-bio-127.q: Why does mor litter decompose slowly?
soil-bio-127.a: Low pH, low nutrients and high lignin, tannin or terpene contents make needle and heath litter slow to decompose.

soil-bio-295.q: How does the rate of organic matter loss change after cropping begins?
soil-bio-295.a: It is rapid in early years, while active organic matter is plentiful, then slows as mainly stable material remains.

soil-bio-303.q: How did water-stable aggregates vary with organic matter and tillage in the New York study?
soil-bio-303.a: The share rose with organic matter and no tillage, from 27% in conventional vegetable soils to 70% in no-till pasture.

soil-bio-298.q: How much wet dairy manure did a Vermont study say was needed yearly under continuous silage corn?

soil-bio-291.q: Why does organic matter pile up at the surface of acid soils?
soil-bio-291.a: Acidity inhibits earthworms, so organic matter is not mixed through the soil layers.

soil-bio-317.q: Which is harder to break down, cellulose or lignin, and why?
soil-bio-317.a: Lignin: it is a network of aromatic components, mainly degraded by fungi, while cellulose breaks into simple sugars that are readily degraded.

soil-bio-288.q: How does organic matter content vary with soil texture?
soil-bio-288.a: Under 1% in sands, 2-3% in loams and 4% to over 5% in clays.

soil-bio-263.q: Which isotope is used most often in stable isotope probing, and why is 15N weaker?
soil-bio-263.a: 13C; 15N gives a weaker DNA density shift because DNA holds fewer nitrogen atoms.

soil-class-011.q: At which level do moisture regime names modify USDA soil names, and what defines aquic soils?
soil-class-011.a: At the suborder level; aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling.

soil-class-020.q: Which soil groups open the WRB key?
soil-class-020.a: Histosols, with thick organic layers, then soils under strong human influence: Anthrosols and Technosols.

soil-class-008.q: How do typic, intergrade and extragrade subgroups differ?
soil-class-008.a: Typic carries the basic concept of its great group; intergrade grades toward another class without being strong enough to place there; extragrade has aberrant properties that keep it out of any other class.

soil-found-101.q: What defines udic soils in USDA soil taxonomy?
soil-found-101.a: They are moist enough year-round in most years to meet plant needs.

soil-class-045.q: How does clay accumulate in an argillic horizon?
soil-class-045.a: Mainly by illuviation, the downward washing of existing clay, with some clay formed in place.

soil-class-042.q: Is the term pedalfer still used in U.S. soil classification?
soil-class-042.a: No, but it survives in college geology texts, and its 'alf' lives on in the name Alfisol.

soil-class-028.q: What happens when flooding comes with soil warmer than about 5 °C?
soil-class-028.a: Microbes use up the oxygen within days and nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced.

soil-class-047.q: How many FAO groups were there originally, and how many in 1988, for Greyzems?
soil-class-047.a: One of the original 26 FAO groups, it remained among the 28 of the 1988 revision.

soil-class-084.q: Why should fill be as free of organic matter as possible?
soil-class-084.a: Decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures on it.

soil-class-157.q: Why are constructed soils preferred to imported topsoil?
soil-class-157.a: Harvesting topsoil degrades a second site and usually costs more.

soil-class-167.q: When was this quicksand without water first created in the laboratory?
soil-class-167.a: In 2004, after long being doubted as folklore.

soil-fert-190.q: Who should avoid soil with estimated total lead above 300 ppm?

soil-fert-164.q: At what concentration in soil water is boron toxic to most plants?

soil-fert-186.q: What carbon-to-nitrogen ratios point to marine sources, and what to land plants?
soil-fert-186.a: Ratios of 4-10:1 usually mean marine sources, while land vascular plants tend to exceed 20.

soil-fert-229.q: How does manganese deficiency show on leaves, and which leaves first?
soil-fert-229.a: Leaves yellow between the veins in a chequered pattern; young leaves show it first because manganese is immobile.

soil-fert-291.q: Which rotations leach less nitrogen than annual row crops?
soil-fert-291.a: Rotations with cover crops, perennial grasses and legumes.

soil-fert-284.q: How does copper deficiency show in plants?
soil-fert-284.a: As browning of leaf tips and chlorosis.

soil-fert-292.q: What do slow-release nitrogen forms and inhibitors do?
soil-fert-292.a: They better match nitrogen supply to crop needs.

soil-found-066.q: In which three oxidation states does mercury occur?

soil-fert-128.q: What limits how much phosphorus an ecosystem has?
soil-fert-128.a: The rate at which weathering releases phosphorus; apatite dissolution is a key control on productivity.

soil-fert-117.q: Who first suggested, and when, that oxidizing ammonia to nitrate is biological?

soil-fert-224.q: How does urea hydrolysis change the pH around it?
soil-fert-224.a: It raises it, because the basic ammonia released is produced in two stages through carbamic acid.

soil-fert-221.q: What view did Nitrospira inopinata overturn?
soil-fert-221.a: That the two steps of nitrification need two organisms; it carries out complete nitrification (comammox).

soil-fert-279.q: What is a farm with a negative nutrient balance doing?
soil-fert-279.a: Living off capital, drawing down mineral and organic-matter nutrients until yields fall.

soil-fert-225.q: Which organisms can turn N2O into N2?
soil-fert-225.a: Only denitrifying prokaryotes, though some denitrifiers lack the step and stop at N2O.

soil-fert-277.q: What is the optimum nitrogen balance, and what do values below 0 and above 50 mean?
soil-fert-277.a: Generally between 0 and +50 pounds per acre; below 0 the soil is being mined of nitrogen, and above 50 the excess causes environmental damage.

soil-fert-035.q: How is compost tea usually made?
soil-fert-035.a: By adding compost to water at 1:4-1:10 and stirring occasionally to release microbes, with or without aeration.

soil-fert-033.q: Why does stabilized compost pose very little risk?
soil-fert-033.a: It has reached 50-70 °C, which kills pathogens and makes even oocysts unviable.

soil-fert-081.q: Which seaweeds are used most, and in what forms?
soil-fert-081.a: Brown seaweeds; laid as mulch, composted, dried and powdered, or made into liquid extracts.

soil-fert-077.q: What did a 2013 study find about a single compost application on grassland?
soil-fert-077.a: It significantly and durably raised carbon storage by 25-70%.

soil-fert-083.q: Which has the highest salt index: potassium chloride, urea or diammonium phosphate?
soil-fert-083.a: Potassium chloride, at 116.2, against 74.4 for urea and 29.2 for diammonium phosphate.

soil-fert-262.q: By how much does a compost pile shrink?
soil-fert-262.a: By 30-60 percent as carbon dioxide and water escape.

soil-fert-205.q: As of 2016, did any country have a specific regulatory framework for biostimulants?
soil-fert-205.a: No; with no agreed definition, some treat them under fertilizer law.

soil-fert-274.q: What should be cut first when phosphorus surpluses build up on livestock farms?
soil-fert-274.a: P in animal diets; a survey found US dairy herds fed about 25% more P than NRC advice.

soil-fert-216.q: What factor converts P2O5 to elemental phosphorus, and K2O to potassium?
soil-fert-216.a: P2O5 is 43.6% phosphorus, so multiply by 0.436; K2O is 83% potassium, so multiply by 0.83.

soil-fert-240.q: What are the two types of integrated crop-livestock farm?
soil-fert-240.a: One mainly sells animal products and matches animal numbers to carrying capacity; the other is a diversified farm that raises all its feed but sells a range of crops and animal products.

soil-fert-268.q: What is the late-spring nitrate test especially good at identifying?
soil-fert-268.a: Sites that need no more N fertilizer, since it implicitly captures early-season weather.

soil-fert-249.q: What should be done where soil P is far above optimum?
soil-fert-249.a: Apply manure by crop P need and export part of it.

soil-fert-244.q: Why do dairy and beef manures influence organic matter more than poultry or swine manure?
soil-fert-244.a: They hold undigested forage and bedding rich in lignin.

soil-fert-251.q: What happens to fall-applied manure in humid climates?
soil-fert-251.a: Ammonium converts to nitrate that leaches or denitrifies; a New York study found about twice the N leaching from fall as from spring application.

soil-water-022.q: What does impervious surface do to groundwater and flooding?
soil-water-022.a: Less water reaches groundwater, so the water table falls and droughts worsen, while more water left on the surface causes flooding.

soil-water-103.q: Why can gelifluction occur on slopes of less than half a degree?
soil-water-103.a: The waterlogged topsoil flows like a liquid.

soil-water-251.q: Which particles are held up by turbulence and travel in suspension?
soil-water-251.a: Particles of about 70 micrometres or less in air.

soil-water-067.q: In which four main ways do plants act on slopes?
soil-water-067.a: Wind throw, removal of water, the added mass of the vegetation (surcharge) and mechanical reinforcement by roots.

soil-water-300.q: What happens to quick clays when saturated?
soil-water-300.a: They liquefy and flow, causing mass wasting.

soil-agri-001.q: Before pedology arose in the 19th century, what was the only branch of soil science?

soil-agri-044.q: What does fallowing do for land and for pests?
soil-agri-044.a: It lets land recover and store organic matter while keeping moisture, and breaks pest and soil-borne pathogen cycles by removing their hosts.

soil-agri-042.q: What did a 2020 review of 229 articles find about the definition of regenerative agriculture?
soil-agri-042.a: No legal or widely accepted definition: some stress practices, others outcomes.

soil-agri-133.q: Why is crop rotation not intercropping?
soil-agri-133.a: Its crops grow in separate seasons.

soil-agri-034.q: What temperature must soil reach in solarization, and to what depth do pathogens die?
soil-agri-034.a: 35-60 °C, which kills pathogens in the top 30 cm.

soil-agri-138.q: Who is called the father of the Green Revolution, and what prize did he receive?
soil-agri-138.a: Norman Borlaug, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.

soil-agri-139.q: How much does 1 kg of dry coco peat expand to when moist?
soil-agri-139.a: 15 litres, with a pH of 5.5 to 6.5.

soil-agri-012.q: What do permanent indicators and point indicators describe?
soil-agri-012.a: Permanent indicators, chiefly soil properties, describe a field's main constants; point indicators track crop status such as disease, water stress or nitrogen stress.

soil-agri-039.q: How long can rock powder supply nutrients?
soil-agri-039.a: Up to 5 years: plants take what they need and the rest stays crystallized.

soil-agri-045.q: What should susceptible crops such as corn follow, rather than a fallow?
soil-agri-045.a: A cover crop that hosts the fungi, such as oats or another small grain.

soil-agri-148.a: No tillage, no fertilizer, no pesticides or herbicides, no weeding and no pruning.

soil-agri-179.a: By blowing air or steam through molten rock at about 1600 C, giving fine intertwined fibres 2 to 6 micrometres across.

soil-agri-182.q: Why do grass cover crops scavenge nitrogen and reduce erosion?
soil-agri-182.a: Their fibrous root systems scavenge leftover nutrients, especially nitrogen, and some establish rapidly.

soil-agri-198.q: What should follow a legume forage in rotation?
soil-agri-198.a: A high-nitrogen crop such as corn.

soil-agri-190.q: How do cover crops raise infiltration and water-holding capacity?
soil-agri-190.a: Infiltration through macropores, and water-holding capacity through organic matter; residue also slows runoff.

soil-agri-191.q: Are grain crops hosts of root-knot nematode?
soil-agri-191.a: No, they are nonhosts, so growing grains reduces numbers; very bad infestations may need two full grain seasons.

soil-agri-197.q: How long a break do diseases need from their host crops?
soil-agri-197.a: Some need only a one-year break; others need several years of nonhost crops to cut inoculum.

soil-agri-203.q: What is considered the foundation of modern agroecology?

soil-agri-223.q: What did centuries of tillage cause, especially around the Mediterranean?
soil-agri-223.a: Excessive erosion, organic matter loss and nutrient depletion.

soil-agri-061.q: What is the difference between shelterbelts and woodlots?
soil-agri-061.a: Shelterbelts are rows of trees set perpendicular to the prevailing wind, while woodlots are more extensive areas of woodland.

soil-agri-070.q: What is the smother effect of a flattened cover crop?
soil-agri-070.a: It forms a nearly impenetrable mat that blocks light, cutting weed germination.

soil-agri-079.q: What did the act passed after the Supreme Court struck down the Agricultural Adjustment Act do?
soil-agri-079.a: It amended and renamed the Soil Conservation Act of 1935 to preserve soil fertility and reduce exploitation and unprofitable use of national soil resources.

soil-agri-078.q: In what climate does this road dust suppressant work best, and what is its chief benefit?
soil-agri-078.a: It works better in humid than in arid climates, and its chief benefit is lower maintenance costs for gravel roads.

soil-agri-208.q: Why does keeping soil covered reduce erosion?
soil-agri-208.a: Water and wind erosion occur almost exclusively on exposed soil, and live plants protect it best.

soil-agri-206.q: When is erosion worst, and what does tillage do to runoff?
soil-agri-206.a: It is worst when soil has no living plants, roots or residue mulch; tillage that breaks aggregates lowers infiltration and worsens runoff.

soil-agri-213.q: How does more soil organic matter reduce runoff?
soil-agri-213.a: It gives better aggregation and less surface sealing, so more water infiltrates instead of running off and carrying soil away.

soil-agri-163.q: When is a remote sensor called active, and when passive?
soil-agri-163.a: It is active when it emits a signal and detects its reflection, and passive when it detects reflected sunlight.

soil-agri-166.q: Into which four categories of decreasing generality is this land suitability classification divided?
soil-agri-166.a: Orders (kinds of suitability), classes (degrees), subclasses (kinds of limitation) and units (minor management differences).

soil-agri-218.q: Why are large expanses of poor land mapped by reconnaissance survey?
soil-agri-218.a: They have little agricultural or forest value and are often too poor to justify a detailed survey, so they are mapped at small scale, showing soil associations.

soil-meth-023.q: How does atomic absorption measure a metal?
soil-meth-023.a: The metal is vaporized in a flame and absorbs at its own wavelengths; the absorbed radiation is proportional to the density of its atoms.

soil-meth-059.q: Which extractants suit acidic and alkaline soils in Washington and Oregon?
soil-meth-059.a: Bray 1 is used for acidic soils and Olsen for alkaline soils.

soil-meth-061.q: What can very high phosphorus in a soil test point to?
soil-meth-061.a: Years of heavy poultry or other manure.

soil-meth-027.q: What does the voltage of an ion-selective electrode depend on?
soil-meth-027.a: It depends on the logarithm of the ion's activity, following the Nernst equation, and is read against a reference electrode.

soil-meth-066.q: Why is human vision still needed in image analysis despite computers?
soil-meth-066.a: Computers are indispensable for large data and quantitative extraction, but human vision cannot be replaced in many applications.

soil-meth-045.q: Name two spatial autocorrelation statistics covered by spatial analysis.

soil-agri-090.q: What two factors does the scorpan model add to the classical five?
soil-agri-090.a: s, intrinsic soil properties captured by remote and proximal sensors, and n, spatial coordinates or position.

soil-meth-053.q: What does Cohen's kappa add to overall accuracy?
soil-meth-053.a: It corrects for chance agreement; both measures range from 0 to 1.

soil-meth-001.q: What was geostatistics first developed to predict?
soil-meth-001.a: The distribution of ore grades in mines.

soil-meth-004.q: What does regression kriging model separately?
soil-meth-004.a: The deterministic and stochastic parts of variation, following Matheron's 1969 universal model.

soil-meth-048.q: What must stratified sampling strata satisfy?
soil-meth-048.a: They must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so every element falls in exactly one.

soil-meth-052.q: What does conditioned Latin hypercube sampling do?
soil-meth-052.a: It samples all covariates with one sample per stratum.

soil-meth-016.q: How does gamma-ray spectroscopy of soil identify elements?
soil-meth-016.a: Cosmic rays make nuclei emit gamma rays; each emission line's energy identifies an element and its intensity gives the concentration.

soil-meth-033.q: Who coined the term chemometrics, and when?
soil-meth-033.a: Svante Wold, in a 1971 grant application.

soil-env-106.q: How much carbon do soils hold compared with the atmosphere?
soil-env-106.a: About 2,700 Gt, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere.

soil-env-110.q: What does plant uptake do to carbon in soil?
soil-env-110.a: It fixes carbon dioxide in soil, building a pool of around 1500 Pg in the first few metres, 20-40% of it lasting more than 100 years.

soil-env-103.q: What does the fast carbon cycle include?
soil-env-103.a: It runs through living things, with annual cycles driven by photosynthesis and decadal cycles of vegetation growth and decomposition.

soil-env-105.q: Why does replacing forest with cropland leave more carbon in the atmosphere?
soil-env-105.a: Cropland and urban land store comparatively little carbon.

soil-env-141.q: What visible sign shows permafrost thaw weakening soil structure?
